interpretation: This verse refutes a claim of special, unconditional favor with God made by certain Jewish and Christian communities of the time, who considered themselves exempt from divine accountability due to a presumed familial or especially beloved status. The Qur'an's rebuttal is sharp and logical: if they were truly God's favored children, immune to His justice, why does worldly and otherworldly punishment still befall them for wrongdoing? This rhetorical question dismantles the notion of inherited or claimed spiritual privilege. The verse reorients the understanding of the human-divine relationship away from tribal or communal favoritism toward a universal principle—moral accountability based on one's deeds, not on bloodline, heritage, or self-proclaimed closeness to God. All humans, regardless of their religious community, are described as 'bashar' (ordinary human beings) from among God's creation, subject to the same divine law of reward and punishment. The statement that God 'forgives whom He wills and punishes whom He wills' underscores His absolute sovereignty and the fact that mercy and justice are dispensed according to divine wisdom and the true conduct of individuals, not according to self-ascribed status. The verse closes by affirming God's complete ownership and control over all creation—the heavens, the earth, and everything between them—reminding humanity that ultimate judgment and return are to Him alone. Thus, the verse serves as a broader theological corrective against religious exceptionalism, emphasizing humility, personal responsibility, and the universality of divine justice over any claim of being inherently exempt from accountability due to presumed special status.

translation: O People of the Scripture, Our Messenger has come to you, making things clear to you after a gap in the succession of messengers, lest you say, 'There came not to us any bringer of good tidings nor a warner.' So there has come to you a bringer of good tidings and a warner. And Allah is over all things competent.
interpretation: This verse addresses the Jews and Christians, explaining that after a long interval without a prophet, God sent Muhammad to remove any excuse they might offer for not accepting divine guidance. Since both glad tidings (of reward) and warnings (of punishment) have now reached them through a clear messenger, they cannot claim ignorance or lack of guidance. The closing affirmation of God's power over all things underscores that His will to send revelation, interrupt or resume prophetic succession, and hold people accountable is beyond human control or objection.

translation: And [mention] when Moses said to his people, 'O my people, remember the favor of Allah upon you when He appointed prophets among you and made you kings and gave you that which He had not given anyone among the worlds.'
interpretation: This verse is part of Moses's address to the Children of Israel, reminding them of the unique blessings Allah bestowed upon them as a nation: the raising of numerous prophets from among them, the establishment of sovereignty and self-governance (kingship), and other distinguishing favors not granted to other peoples of that era. The purpose of this reminder is pedagogical and rhetorical—Moses invokes these blessings to call his people to gratitude and obedience, setting up the subsequent command to enter the Holy Land. It underscores a recurring Quranic theme that divine favor carries with it the responsibility of faithfulness; the mention of these blessings serves as a prelude to testing the people's willingness to act upon Allah's command, which they ultimately fail by refusing to enter the land out of fear, demonstrating that recounting past favors is meant to strengthen resolve and trust in Allah, not merely to recall historical pride.

translation: O my people, enter the Holy Land which Allah has decreed for you, and do not turn back on your heels, for then you will become losers.
interpretation: This verse records Moses's exhortation to the Israelites to enter the Promised Land that God had designated for them. It represents a pivotal moment of testing faith and courage: the people are called to move forward in obedience and trust despite fear of the land's inhabitants. The warning against turning back 'on your heels' symbolizes regression into cowardice, disobedience, and lack of trust in divine promise. Turning away would not be a neutral retreat but would actively transform their status from a chosen, favored people into losers—forfeiting the blessings and inheritance promised to them. This illustrates a broader Quranic theme: divine blessings and promises are conditional upon human effort, courage, and willingness to act upon faith rather than remain passive or regress out of fear. The subsequent refusal of the Israelites (in later verses) to heed this call, leading to their forty years of wandering, underscores the severe consequences of spiritual cowardice and the rejection of divine guidance when faced with worldly challenges.

translation: They said, 'O Moses, indeed in it is a people of tyrannical strength, and indeed, we will never enter it until they leave it; but if they leave it, then we will enter.'
interpretation: This verse reflects the cowardice and lack of faith shown by the Israelites when Moses commanded them to enter the Holy Land. Rather than trusting in God's promise of victory and support, they focused on the physical might of the land's inhabitants, described as 'jabbareen' (giants or tyrants of great strength), and used this as an excuse for disobedience. Their conditional statement—that they would only enter if the inhabitants left first—reveals a fundamental breakdown of trust in divine guidance and in their prophet's leadership. This moment becomes a pivotal example in the Qur'an of a people who, despite witnessing numerous miracles and receiving divine favor, succumbed to fear and defiance when faced with a direct command requiring courage and faith. Their refusal leads to the well-known punishment of wandering in the wilderness for forty years, serving as a broader lesson about the consequences of disobedience to God's commands and the importance of trusting in divine support even when faced with seemingly insurmountable human obstacles.

translation: Two men from among those who feared [Allah], upon whom Allah had bestowed favor, said, 'Enter upon them through the gate, for when you enter it, you will surely be victorious. And upon Allah put your trust, if you should be believers.'
interpretation: This verse recounts the episode within the story of Moses and the Children of Israel when they were commanded to enter the Holy Land but recoiled in fear upon hearing of its powerful inhabitants. Among the twelve scouts sent to survey the land, two men—identified in tradition as Joshua (Yusha') and Caleb (Kalib)—stood apart from the fearful majority. The phrase 'those who feared' refers to their fear of Allah rather than fear of the enemy, and it was this God-consciousness, combined with Allah's favor upon them (understood as knowledge, faith, or prophetic insight), that gave them courage and clarity where others faltered. Their counsel to enter through the main gate boldly, rather than through fear or hesitation, reflects a strategic and spiritual confidence: boldness itself, grounded in trust in Allah, would secure victory. Their declaration that victory was assured was not based on their own might but on reliance upon Allah (tawakkul), which they explicitly invoke in the final clause. The verse thus illustrates a contrast between the majority who allowed fear of worldly powers to override faith, and the minority whose fear of Allah produced courage, resolve, and right action. It serves as a broader lesson on the nature of true faith: that reliance on Allah must be paired with decisive action, and that the righteous few who trust in Allah can summon a strength that the fearful majority lack, regardless of apparent odds.

translation: They said, 'O Moses, indeed we will never enter it so long as they remain within it. So go, you and your Lord, and fight; we will stay right here.'
interpretation: This verse captures a pivotal moment of defiance from the Israelites after Moses urged them to enter the Promised Land, which God had decreed for them. Having heard reports of powerful, giant-like inhabitants, their fear overrides their faith in divine support, and they refuse outright, despite witnessing numerous miracles under Moses's leadership. Their response is strikingly insolent—not only do they refuse to fight, but they flippantly tell Moses to let 'him and his Lord' go do the fighting, revealing a shocking lack of reverence and a transactional, almost mocking attitude toward their covenant with God. This episode illustrates a recurring theme in the Qur'an: the consequences of weak faith and moral cowardice when confronted with trials, and it foreshadows the punishment of wandering the wilderness for forty years as a consequence of this rebellion. The verse serves as a warning against abandoning trust in God's promises when faced with hardship, and against disrespect toward divinely appointed leadership.

translation: He said, 'My Lord, indeed I have power over no one but myself and my brother, so separate us from the defiantly disobedient people.'
interpretation: This verse records the anguished prayer of Moses (Musa) after the Israelites refused to enter the Holy Land and defied his command, preferring to wait while he and God fought on their behalf. Realizing he could not compel his own people to obedience despite being their prophet and leader, Moses turns to God in humility, acknowledging the limits of his authority—he has control only over himself and his brother Aaron (Harun). His plea for separation from 'the defiantly disobedient people' (al-qawm al-fasiqin) is not a request for their destruction but a disavowal of responsibility for their rebellion, distancing himself and Aaron from the consequences of their people's transgression. This moment illustrates a profound theological point: even prophets, who carry divine guidance, cannot force true faith or obedience upon others, as guidance and submission remain matters of individual will and divine decree. It also demonstrates a model of turning to God in moments of communal crisis and interpersonal failure, placing judgment and justice in God's hands rather than attempting to impose control beyond one's actual capacity. The verse underscores themes of accountability, the boundaries of human agency, and the appropriate response of a sincere believer when faced with the obstinate rejection of truth by those around him—seeking divine arbitration rather than human vengeance.

translation: He [God] said, 'Then indeed, it is forbidden to them for forty years, [during which] they will wander lost in the land. So do not grieve over the defiantly disobedient people.'
interpretation: This verse addresses the consequence of the Israelites' refusal to enter the Holy Land out of fear, despite the encouragement of Moses and the two righteous men who urged them to trust in God. As punishment for their cowardice, disobedience, and lack of faith, God decreed that they would wander in the wilderness (often identified with the Sinai desert) for forty years, during which that entire disbelieving generation would pass away, and a new generation would arise to eventually enter the Promised Land. The verse closes with God consoling Moses, instructing him not to grieve over the fate of those who transgressed and rejected His command. This teaches a broader lesson about the consequences of disobedience to God, the testing of faith through trials, and the idea that leaders of faith should not despair over those who willfully reject guidance, as each soul bears responsibility for its own choices. It also illustrates the theme found throughout the Qur'an that defiance against divine guidance leads to loss and hardship, while patience and trust in God's plan lead to eventual relief and progress.

translation: And recite to them the story of the two sons of Adam, in truth, when they both offered a sacrifice, and it was accepted from one of them while it was not accepted from the other. He said, 'I will surely kill you.' The other said, 'Allah only accepts from the righteous (those who are mindful of Him).'
interpretation: This verse recounts the story of Habil (Abel) and Qabil (Cain) to establish a foundational moral principle: that outward acts of worship or devotion hold no value before God unless they stem from sincere faith, piety, and righteousness of heart. The rejection of Qabil's offering was not arbitrary but a reflection of the state of his heart—his lack of taqwa (God-consciousness). Rather than responding with self-reflection or increased devotion, Qabil reacted with envy and threatened violence, revealing that his spiritual failure was rooted in an inner corruption of jealousy and anger rather than any injustice from God. Habil's calm response—attributing the matter entirely to divine standards of righteousness rather than engaging in a dispute over fairness—models the ideal believer's reaction to envy and provocation: trust in God's just judgment rather than retaliation. The verse thus serves as an early Qur'anic lesson on the destructive nature of envy, the true measure of acceptable worship, and the contrast between righteous patience and violent reaction to one's own spiritual shortcomings, foreshadowing the first murder in human history as a direct consequence of unchecked jealousy.

translation: If you stretch out your hand against me to kill me, I shall not stretch out my hand against you to kill you. Indeed, I fear Allah, the Lord of the worlds.
interpretation: This verse records the response of one of the sons of Adam (traditionally identified as Abel/Habil) to his brother's murderous intent, forming part of the Quranic narrative of the first murder in human history. It establishes a foundational ethical principle: that righteousness and fear of God preclude responding to aggression with aggression, particularly when it comes to the sanctity of human life. The speaker's refusal to retaliate, even in self-defense through violence, stems not from weakness but from a conscious theological conviction—his fear of Allah as 'Lord of the worlds' takes precedence over the instinct for self-preservation through killing. This establishes a model of piety wherein submission to divine will and moral restraint triumph over the human impulse toward vengeance or violent self-defense, foreshadowing broader Quranic teachings about the sanctity of life (as elaborated in the following verses of this surah, which state that killing one soul unjustly is akin to killing all of humanity). The narrative also sets up a moral contrast between the two brothers: one motivated by jealousy and willing to commit murder, the other guided by taqwa (God-consciousness) and willing to accept victimhood rather than become a perpetrator of injustice.

translation: Indeed I wish that you should bear my sin and your sin, and so become one of the companions of the Fire; and that is the recompense of the wrongdoers.
interpretation: These are the words of Abel to his brother Cain when Cain threatened to kill him. Rather than retaliate or defend himself through violence, Abel chooses restraint, declaring that he would rather let his brother bear the full weight of sin—both the sin of the impending murder and his own prior sin—than stain his own hands with wrongdoing. This verse illustrates the principle that responding to evil with righteousness and patience is preferable to responding with violence, and it places moral responsibility for aggression squarely upon the aggressor. It also establishes an early Qur'anic teaching on the sanctity of human life and the severe consequence awaiting those who commit injustice, foreshadowing the broader prohibition against killing an innocent soul found later in the same passage (5:32).

translation: Then his soul permitted him the murder of his brother, so he killed him, and he became among the losers.
interpretation: This verse recounts the story of the first murder in human history, that of Qabil (Cain) killing his brother Habil (Abel), as narrated earlier in Surah Al-Ma'idah. The phrase 'his soul permitted him' (tawwa'at lahu nafsuhu) indicates an internal psychological process whereby Qabil's ego, driven by jealousy and wounded pride after his sacrifice was not accepted while his brother's was, gradually made the unthinkable act of fratricide seem acceptable to him. This reflects the Qur'anic understanding of how the nafs (self/ego) can rationalize and embellish sin, making it appear easy or justified to the one contemplating it, until the person is emotionally and mentally prepared to commit it. The verse emphasizes the gradual nature of moral corruption and self-deception that precedes grave sin. The outcome—'he became among the losers'—signifies not merely worldly loss but profound spiritual and existential loss. Qabil lost his brother, his own moral integrity, and his standing before God, setting a precedent of loss that he initiated for himself and, symbolically, for humanity, as this act introduced murder into human experience. The verse serves as a timeless lesson on the dangers of envy, the manipulative nature of the ego, and the irreversible consequences of yielding to destructive impulses rather than restraining them through God-consciousness (taqwa), as his brother had done when he chose not to retaliate despite being threatened.

translation: Then Allah sent forth a crow which scratched in the ground to show him how to conceal the corpse of his brother. He said: 'Woe unto me! Am I unable to be like this crow and conceal the corpse of my brother?' And he became of those who regret.
interpretation: This verse completes the narrative of Cain's murder of his brother Abel, highlighting humanity's moral struggle and the role of divine guidance even in nature. The crow serves as an instrument of Allah's teaching, demonstrating that even the natural world can convey moral and practical lessons to humans. Cain's shame and ignorance—he did not even know how to bury his brother—underscore his lack of wisdom and the chaos that resulted from his unchecked jealousy and anger. His exclamation of regret, calling himself inferior to an animal in terms of knowledge or response, symbolizes the depth of his guilt and the recognition of his own moral failure. The verse emphasizes that remorse (nadam) came only after the irreversible act, illustrating a broader Qur'anic theme: sin often blinds a person to consequences until it is too late, and only then does true awareness of wrongdoing emerge. This story is used in the Qur'an to warn against envy and violence between kin, situating the first murder in human history as a lesson in humility, the sanctity of life, and the inevitability of moral accountability before God.

translation: On account of that, We decreed upon the Children of Israel that whoever kills a soul for other than a soul or for corruption [done] in the land - it is as if he had slain mankind entirely. And whoever saves one - it is as if he had saved mankind entirely. And our messengers had certainly come to them with clear proofs. Then indeed many of them, after that, throughout the land, were transgressors.
interpretation: This verse establishes the supreme sanctity of human life as a universal moral principle, using the particular case of the Children of Israel to teach a timeless and universal ethic applicable to all humanity. By stating that killing one innocent person is equivalent to killing all of mankind, the verse elevates each individual human life to a status representing the whole of humanity - emphasizing that no single life is of lesser value or significance than the collective. Conversely, saving a life is equated with saving all of humanity, underscoring the profound moral weight assigned to preserving life. The verse carefully carves out exceptions for legitimate justice (retribution for a life) and necessary societal protection (preventing corruption/mischief in the land), acknowledging that there are circumstances under which taking a life may be lawfully sanctioned, such as capital punishment for murder or combating active threats to societal order. The mention that messengers came to the Children of Israel with clear proofs, yet many continued to transgress afterward, serves as a sobering commentary on human nature - that even with clear divine guidance and moral instruction, many people will still choose to exceed proper limits and commit excesses. This serves both as a historical critique of the Israelites' transgressions despite receiving prophetic guidance, and as a broader warning to all who receive this message that knowledge of moral law does not guarantee ethical behavior; human beings retain the capacity for excess and corruption even after being shown the right path.

translation: Indeed, the recompense of those who wage war against Allah and His Messenger and strive upon earth [to cause] corruption is none but that they be killed or crucified or that their hands and feet be cut off from opposite sides, or that they be exiled from the land. That is for them a disgrace in this world, and for them in the Hereafter is a great punishment.
interpretation: This verse addresses the establishment of a legal framework for dealing with those who commit acts of violent rebellion, banditry, and disorder against the social fabric of the Muslim community—framed here as warring against God and His Messenger. The phrase 'strive upon earth to cause corruption' broadens the scope beyond mere armed insurrection to encompass acts that threaten the security, stability, and moral order of society, such as highway robbery, terrorism, and wanton destruction. The listed punishments—execution, crucifixion, amputation of limbs from opposite sides, or exile—are presented as a graduated scale of response, traditionally understood by jurists to correspond to the severity of the crime committed (e.g., murder combined with theft warranting the harshest penalty, while lesser disruption warrants exile). The verse emphasizes that such punishments serve a dual purpose: they function as a deterrent and source of humiliation in the temporal world, underscoring the gravity with which the Quran treats threats to communal security, while also affirming that ultimate and more severe accountability awaits in the Hereafter. This reflects a broader Quranic principle that worldly justice, however severe, is incomplete without the eschatological dimension of divine judgment, reinforcing that true justice transcends mere earthly retribution and finds its completion in God's final reckoning.

translation: Except for those who repent before you gain power over them. And know that Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation: This verse follows the severe punishments prescribed for those who wage war against Allah and His Messenger and spread corruption in the land (hirabah). It establishes a crucial principle of mercy within the framework of justice: repentance has transformative power, but only if it occurs before the authorities apprehend the wrongdoer. The timing is significant—it must be a genuine, voluntary turning back to righteousness before capture, not a convenient claim made under duress or to escape punishment once caught. This distinguishes sincere repentance from mere expediency. The verse reflects a broader Qur'anic theme that divine law is not merely punitive but redemptive, offering a path back to the community for those who abandon their criminal ways on their own accord. The closing affirmation that Allah is Forgiving and Merciful reminds believers that even in matters of strict criminal justice, the door to forgiveness remains open, and that human legal systems should incorporate mechanisms for redemption rather than operating on pure retribution alone. This also serves as a deterrent-reducing mechanism, encouraging wrongdoers to abandon their criminal associations and return to righteousness rather than persisting in corruption out of hopelessness.

translation: O you who have believed, fear Allah and seek the means [of nearness] to Him and strive in His cause that you may succeed.
interpretation: This verse establishes a three-part framework for a believer's relationship with God: taqwa (God-consciousness/fear of Allah as a protective awareness), al-wasilah (actively seeking means of closeness to Him through righteous deeds, worship, and devotion), and jihad fi sabilillah (striving/struggling in His path, encompassing both inner spiritual struggle and outward effort in good works). The term 'wasilah' implies that nearness to God is not automatic but must be actively pursued through legitimate, sanctioned means—acts of obedience, good deeds, and sincere worship—rather than through innovated practices or intermediaries not sanctioned by revelation. The verse frames success (falah) not as a guaranteed outcome but as something contingent upon genuine effort, humility before God, and sustained striving, reflecting the Qur'anic theme that faith must be accompanied by active, continuous effort rather than passive belief alone.

translation: Indeed, those who disbelieve - if they had all that is in the earth and the like of it with it, that they might ransom themselves thereby from the punishment of the Day of Resurrection, it would not be accepted from them, and for them is a painful punishment.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes that on the Day of Judgment, no amount of worldly wealth—however vast, even doubled—can serve as a ransom to escape divine punishment for disbelief. It underscores that salvation cannot be purchased through material means; faith and righteous deeds are the only currency that matters before God. The verse serves as a stark warning against relying on wealth, status, or possessions as a means of escaping accountability, highlighting the ultimate powerlessness of materialism in the face of divine justice. It reflects a broader Quranic theme that true value lies in one's spiritual state and actions, not in earthly riches, and that the consequences of disbelief are inescapable regardless of one's material resources.

translation: They will wish to come out of the Fire, but they will not come out of it, and for them is an enduring punishment.
interpretation: This verse describes the state of the disbelievers in the Hereafter, emphasizing the finality and permanence of their punishment. Their desire to escape the Fire represents the natural human instinct to flee from suffering, yet this desire will be utterly futile, underscoring that the consequences of rejecting faith and guidance in this life are irreversible once the Day of Judgment has come. The phrase 'enduring punishment' (عذاب مقيم) reinforces that this is not a temporary trial from which one might eventually be freed, but a lasting state resulting from their choices in worldly life. Theologically, this serves as a stern warning to believers to take heed in the present life, as the opportunity for repentance and correction exists only before death, not after. It also reflects the Qur'anic theme of divine justice, where the eternal nature of the punishment corresponds to the willful and persistent rejection of truth, rather than being an arbitrary or disproportionate decree.

translation: As for the thief, male and female, cut off their hands as a recompense for what they have earned, an exemplary punishment from Allah. And Allah is Exalted in Might, Wise.
interpretation: This verse establishes a legal prescription within the Qur'anic penal code (hudud) for the crime of theft, but it is not meant to be applied mechanically or without context. Classical and modern jurists have emphasized that the apparently severe punishment is bounded by strict conditions that make its actual application quite narrow: the theft must involve property of a certain minimum value (nisab) taken from secure custody, without ambiguity of ownership, without coercion or necessity (such as theft to avoid starvation, as famously suspended by Caliph Umar during a famine), and the accused must be a sane adult who acted with clear intent. The Arabic word 'nakalan' (an exemplary deterrent) signals that the primary purpose is not vengeance but the protection of the social fabric—private property, trust, and economic order—through a punishment severe enough to discourage the act before it is committed. The phrasing treats the male and female thief with precise grammatical symmetry, underscoring equality before the law regardless of gender. The verse closes with God's attributes of being 'Exalted in Might' (Aziz) and 'Wise' (Hakim), reminding the reader that this law, however stern, emerges from both divine power and perfect wisdom—implying that it is not arbitrary cruelty but a calculated measure meant to secure justice and communal stability, to be implemented by a just and functioning legal authority with mercy and discernment, not by individuals acting on personal judgment.

translation: But whoever repents after his wrongdoing and reforms, indeed, Allah will accept his repentance. Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation: This verse, which follows the Qur'anic prescription for theft, establishes a fundamental principle of divine justice and mercy that pervades Islamic theology: repentance is always available to those who have wronged, whether themselves or others, provided it is sincere and accompanied by genuine reform (islah) in conduct, not merely verbal regret. The pairing of 'tawbah' (repentance) with 'islah' (making right, amendment) indicates that true repentance is not simply an internal emotional state but must manifest in changed behavior and, where possible, rectification of harm done. The verse closes the door on despair, affirming that even after serious transgression, Allah's mercy remains accessible, reflecting the broader Qur'anic theme that divine punishment is never the final word for those who turn back sincerely. The names Ghafur (Forgiving) and Rahim (Merciful) reinforce that Allah's character is fundamentally oriented toward mercy and restoration rather than mere retribution, offering hope to the sinner while still upholding the seriousness of the original transgression and the necessity of genuine moral correction.

translation: Do you not know that to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth? He punishes whom He wills and forgives whom He wills, and Allah is over all things competent.
interpretation: This verse affirms God's absolute sovereignty over all creation, establishing that His authority over the heavens and earth is total and uncontested. The rhetorical question 'Do you not know' serves to remind the listener of a truth they should already recognize, emphasizing that divine justice and mercy both stem from this comprehensive power rather than operating independently of it. The pairing of punishment and forgiveness as both proceeding from divine will underscores that God's judgments are not arbitrary but flow from perfect knowledge and wisdom that humans cannot fully grasp or predict. This is not an endorsement of moral relativism but a call to humility—human beings cannot presume to know who deserves punishment or forgiveness, as this prerogative belongs to God alone. The verse concludes by grounding both attributes (punishing and forgiving) in God's omnipotence, suggesting that His capacity to exercise either mercy or justice at will is itself a manifestation of His unlimited power, and that no force in creation can compel Him toward one outcome or another.

translation: O Messenger, let them not grieve you - those who hasten into disbelief among those who say, 'We believe' with their mouths while their hearts believe not, and among the Jews - [they are] avid listeners to falsehood, listeners to other people who have not come to you. They distort words from their [proper] places, saying, 'If you are given this, take it; but if you are not given it, then beware.' And he for whom Allah intends fitnah (trial/misguidance) - never will you possess for him [power to do] anything against Allah. Those are the ones for whom Allah does not intend to purify their hearts. For them in this world is disgrace, and for them in the Hereafter is a great punishment.
interpretation: This verse addresses the Prophet directly, consoling him amid the betrayals and hostility of hypocrites and some among the Jewish community of Medina who outwardly professed neutrality or alliance but inwardly worked against him. It identifies a particular moral corruption: deliberately listening to falsehood and lies, and worse, distorting revealed words from their original context and meaning for political or personal advantage. The reference to 'other people who have not come to you' points to intermediaries manipulating information, coaching others on what to accept or reject from the Prophet's judgments for self-serving reasons, as in the context of legal rulings they sought to manipulate. The verse teaches that such calculated deception reflects a deeper spiritual disease - hearts that Allah has not willed to purify, not because purification was impossible, but because they persistently chose falsehood over truth. The Prophet is told not to carry the emotional burden of their rejection, since guidance and misguidance ultimately rest with Allah's will, not human effort alone. This serves as both comfort to the Prophet and a warning that intellectual dishonesty and the manipulation of sacred texts for worldly gain lead to disgrace in this life and severe punishment in the next.

translation: [They are] avid listeners to falsehood, devourers of unlawful gain. So if they come to you, [O Muhammad], judge between them or turn away from them. And if you turn away from them, they will not harm you at all. And if you judge, judge between them with justice. Indeed, Allah loves those who act justly.
interpretation: This verse describes a segment of the People of the Book (particularly some Jewish leaders in Medina) who are characterized by two moral failings: they eagerly absorb and spread falsehoods, and they consume ill-gotten gains such as bribes, usury, or illicit profits. Despite their corrupt character, when such people bring their disputes to the Prophet for arbitration, he is given a choice—he may either judge between them or decline to do so, since he is under no obligation to adjudicate for those outside the Muslim community who do not accept his authority as binding. Crucially, the verse reassures him that refusing to engage does not diminish his authority or harm him, emphasizing that a leader's legitimacy does not depend on satisfying every petitioner, especially those acting in bad faith. However, if he chooses to judge, the standard is unwavering: justice must be upheld irrespective of the disputants' faith, character, or relationship to the judge. This establishes a universal principle in Islamic governance that impartiality and fairness are divine values transcending communal boundaries—even those who habitually lie or profit through corruption are entitled to a just ruling if judged at all. The closing affirmation that God loves the just underscores that justice is not merely a legal technicality but a moral and spiritual virtue intrinsic to righteousness, applicable even toward one's critics or adversaries.

translation: But how is it that they come to you for judgment while they have the Torah, in which is the judgment of Allah? Yet they turn away after that; and those are not [truly] believers.
interpretation: This verse rebukes the hypocrisy of those (specifically referring to some among the Jews of Medina) who, despite possessing their own revealed scripture containing divine law, approach the Prophet Muhammad for arbitration only when they expect a ruling favorable to them, while rejecting his judgment and even the clear rulings of their own Torah when these do not suit their desires. The verse exposes a pattern of selective faith—accepting revelation only when convenient and turning away when it demands accountability or unwelcome rulings. This inconsistency is presented as proof that such behavior is incompatible with genuine faith (iman), since true belief requires submission to divine law in its entirety, not selective application based on self-interest. The verse underscores a broader Qur'anic theme: that authentic faith is demonstrated through consistent submission to God's judgment, not through opportunistic appeals to religious authority.

translation: Indeed, We sent down the Torah, in which was guidance and light. The prophets who submitted [to Allah] judged by it for the Jews, as did the rabbis and scholars, by that with which they were entrusted of the Scripture of Allah, and they were witnesses thereto. So do not fear the people but fear Me, and do not exchange My verses for a small price. And whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed - then it is those who are the disbelievers.
interpretation: This verse establishes a principle of continuous prophetic authority and accountability in religious leadership. It emphasizes that divine guidance given through scripture (here, the Torah) was meant to be implemented faithfully by those entrusted with it—prophets, rabbis, and scholars alike—without alteration or compromise for worldly gain. The warning against fearing people rather than God underscores the temptation that religious authorities face to distort or soften divine rulings to please congregations, political powers, or for personal benefit. The phrase about not exchanging verses for a 'small price' is a direct condemnation of corruption among religious scholars who manipulate scripture for material or social advantage. The concluding statement, equating failure to judge by Allah's revelation with disbelief, serves as a severe admonition to religious leaders across traditions that fidelity to divine law is not optional but constitutes the very essence of faith; deviation for expedience or self-interest is tantamount to rejecting God's authority itself.

translation: And We ordained for them therein: a life for a life, an eye for an eye, a nose for a nose, an ear for an ear, a tooth for a tooth, and for wounds, retaliation in kind. But whoever forgoes it (as charity), it will be an expiation for him. And whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed, then it is they who are the wrongdoers.
interpretation: This verse, addressed in the context of the law given to the Children of Israel in the Torah, establishes the principle of proportional retribution (lex talionis / qisas) as a foundation of justice: punishment must be strictly equivalent to the harm inflicted, preventing excessive revenge or disproportionate punishment. Yet the verse immediately tempers strict justice with mercy by praising and rewarding forgiveness—if the victim or their family forgoes the right to retaliate, this act of charity serves as spiritual expiation for their own sins, elevating mercy above the letter of the law. The closing statement, warning that those who fail to judge by what God has revealed are wrongdoers, serves both as a rebuke to the Israelites of the past who distorted or abandoned these laws, and as a broader principle applicable to all who hold authority to judge: true justice requires adherence to divine law rather than human whim, bias, or corruption. Thus the verse weaves together three themes—the necessity of equitable retribution to maintain social order, the superiority of forgiveness and mercy when freely chosen, and the moral imperative that governance and judgment must be grounded in divine guidance rather than human caprice.

translation: And We sent, following in their footsteps, Jesus son of Mary, confirming what was before him of the Torah; and We gave him the Gospel, in which there is guidance and light, confirming what was before it of the Torah, and a guidance and admonition for the God-fearing.
interpretation: This verse situates Jesus within the continuous chain of prophetic revelation sent to the Children of Israel, emphasizing continuity rather than rupture between the Torah and the Gospel. By describing Jesus as 'confirming what was before him,' the verse establishes that his message did not abrogate the Torah's core truths but affirmed and built upon them. The Gospel itself is characterized as containing 'guidance and light,' paralleling the earlier description of the Torah, suggesting that divine revelation progressively illuminates the same essential moral and spiritual truths. The repetition of the confirming function underscores a theological point central to the Qur'an's self-understanding: that all scriptures originate from a single divine source and share a unified purpose. The closing phrase, 'a guidance and admonition for the God-fearing,' indicates that the efficacy of revelation is contingent upon the receptiveness of the believer—scripture illuminates only for those whose hearts are oriented toward piety and moral consciousness. This verse thus serves a dual function: validating the Gospel's divine origin while simultaneously setting up the Qur'an's own claim, in subsequent verses, to be the final confirming and preserving revelation in this same prophetic lineage.

translation: And let the People of the Gospel judge by what Allah has revealed therein. And whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed - then it is those who are the defiantly disobedient.
interpretation: This verse addresses the followers of the Gospel (Christians), commanding them to govern their affairs according to the divine revelation given to them, just as the preceding verses commanded the Jews to judge by the Torah. It establishes a universal principle that runs throughout this portion of Surah Al-Ma'idah: each community of believers is obligated to adhere to and implement the law that Allah revealed to them, rather than following human desires, political expediency, or selective interpretation. The warning that follows - that those who fail to judge by Allah's revelation are 'fasiqun' (transgressors/defiantly disobedient) - underscores the seriousness of abandoning divine guidance in favor of other authorities. This establishes a broader theological point about the continuity of prophetic revelation: Allah sent guidance to various communities through their respective scriptures, and faithfulness to that guidance is a marker of true submission to Allah, while deviation from it constitutes a form of moral and spiritual corruption. The verse also sets up a rhetorical parallel with the subsequent verse about the Qur'an being revealed to confirm and serve as a criterion over previous scriptures, suggesting a progression of revelation while still holding each community accountable to what it received.

translation: And We have revealed to you (O Muhammad) the Book (the Qur'an) in truth, confirming whatever remains of the Scripture before it and a guardian over it. So judge between them by what Allah has revealed, and do not follow their desires away from the truth that has come to you. To each of you We have prescribed a law and a method. Had Allah willed, He would have made you one nation, but [He intended] to test you in what He has given you; so race to [all that is] good. To Allah is your return all together, and He will inform you concerning that over which you used to differ.
interpretation: This verse establishes the Qur'an's role as the final, authoritative revelation that both confirms the truth found in earlier scriptures (Torah and Gospel) and acts as a criterion to judge what in them is authentic versus altered. It commands the Prophet to govern strictly by divine revelation rather than human desires or the varying inclinations of the People of the Book. The verse acknowledges that God deliberately gave different communities different laws and paths of practice throughout history—not because truth is relative, but as a trial to test obedience and sincerity. Had God willed absolute uniformity, He could have created one single religious community with no variation at all; instead, diversity in law serves a divine pedagogical purpose. The proper response to this diversity is not sectarian dispute but competition in righteousness—racing toward good deeds rather than quarreling over differences. The verse closes with the eschatological reminder that all humanity will return to God, who alone will resolve the disputes and differences that divided them in worldly life, shifting the burden of final judgment away from human contention and toward divine reckoning.

translation: And [We commanded you]: Judge between them by what Allah has revealed, and do not follow their desires, and beware of them lest they tempt you away from some of what Allah has revealed to you. And if they turn away, then know that Allah only intends to afflict them for some of their sins. And indeed, many among the people are defiantly disobedient.
interpretation: This verse, addressed to the Prophet Muhammad, establishes the principle that judgment and governance among people must be grounded strictly in divine revelation rather than personal inclination or the pressures of vested interests. The warning to 'beware of them' acknowledges that those accustomed to worldly power or corrupt practices would attempt to manipulate the Prophet into compromising even partial aspects of revealed law for their own benefit. The verse teaches that such people's rejection of divine judgment is not a failure of the message or the messenger but a manifestation of their own moral corruption, and their worldly misfortunes are framed as consequences of their sins rather than as evidence against the truth being conveyed. The closing statement about 'many among the people' being 'defiantly disobedient' serves as a broader theological reflection: the resistance to divine law is a recurring human trait, not limited to the specific community addressed, and righteous leadership requires resilience against the temptation to dilute truth for the sake of appeasing those who reject it.

translation: Is it then the judgment of [the time of] ignorance that they seek? But who is better than Allah in judgment for a people who are certain [in faith]?
interpretation: This verse was revealed in the context of the Prophet's dealings with the Jewish tribes of Medina, particularly the Banu Qurayza and Banu Nadir, who sometimes sought to apply their own customary or pre-Islamic tribal judgments rather than submitting to the revealed law of Allah or the arbitration of the Prophet. The verse rebukes this tendency by contrasting 'the judgment of Jahiliyyah' (the pre-Islamic age of ignorance, characterized by tribalism, bias, and self-interest rather than objective justice) with the perfect, just, and impartial judgment of Allah. It establishes a principle that applies beyond its immediate historical context: any law or system of judgment not grounded in divine guidance is, by definition, a form of jahiliyyah—ignorance—regardless of how sophisticated or ancient it may appear. The rhetorical question 'who is better than Allah in judgment' asserts the absolute superiority of divine law over human-made systems driven by tribal loyalty, self-interest, or cultural custom. The concluding phrase 'for a people who are certain [in faith]' indicates that recognizing the superiority of Allah's judgment requires yaqin—firm, unshakeable conviction. Those with weak or wavering faith may be swayed by other systems of judgment, but those with true certainty recognize that divine law is inherently superior because it emanates from complete knowledge, justice, and wisdom, free from the biases and limitations that characterize human judgment.

translation: O you who believe! Do not take the Jews and the Christians as allies; they are allies of one another. And whoever among you takes them as allies, then indeed he is one of them. Indeed, Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people.
interpretation: This verse was revealed in the context of specific political circumstances facing the early Muslim community in Medina, where certain Jewish and Christian tribes had entered into treaties with the Muslims but were suspected of conspiring with external enemies against them. The term 'awliya' (allies/protectors/patrons) here refers specifically to political and military alliance in a context of active hostility and betrayal, not to ordinary social relations, friendship, or kindness toward non-Muslims, which the Qur'an elsewhere explicitly permits and even encourages (e.g., Qur'an 60:8). Classical commentators such as al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir contextualize this verse within the Battle of Uhud and related events, when some believers sought protection from Jewish or Christian tribes against the Muslim community itself, effectively siding with those working against the nascent Muslim polity. The warning 'whoever among you takes them as allies is one of them' addresses the specific danger of dissolving communal and political loyalty at a time when the Muslim community's survival depended on internal cohesion against active threats. The verse should not be read as a timeless prohibition on friendship or cooperation with Jews and Christians in general, but as a situational directive about not forming alliances that would compromise the integrity and security of the believing community when faced with active betrayal or conspiracy. The closing statement that God does not guide 'the wrongdoing people' reinforces that the concern is with injustice and betrayal—those who abandon their community in times of need—rather than with religious identity per se.

translation: So you see those in whose hearts is disease hastening into [association with] them, saying, 'We fear that a misfortune may strike us.' But perhaps Allah will bring victory or a decision from Himself, and they will become, over what they concealed within themselves, regretful.
interpretation: This verse addresses the hypocrites within the Muslim community who, out of fear and lack of true faith, sought alliances with disbelievers and other external powers as a hedge against potential setbacks for the Muslims. Their professed justification—fear of a turn of fortune against the believers—masked a deeper spiritual weakness: a lack of trust in God's promise and support. The verse warns that such calculated self-protection through compromising loyalty will prove futile and shameful. When God grants victory or issues a decisive judgment in favor of the believers, as He ultimately does, these waverers will be exposed and will feel profound regret for the doubt and divided loyalty they harbored secretly. The passage underscores a broader Quranic theme: that true security comes not from hedging bets with worldly powers but from steadfast faith in divine providence, and that those who compromise their principles out of fear will eventually face the consequences of their lack of conviction.

translation: And those who believe will say, 'Are these the ones who swore by Allah their most solemn oaths that they were indeed with you?' Their deeds have become worthless, and they have become losers.
interpretation: This verse addresses the hypocrites who outwardly professed strong allegiance to the believers, swearing emphatic oaths of loyalty and solidarity, yet secretly harbored doubt, disbelief, or allegiance to the enemies of the believers. The verse depicts a moment of exposure—likely on the Day of Judgment or at a moment when hypocrisy is unveiled in this world—where true believers express astonishment at discovering the falseness of those who had sworn such strong oaths. The rhetorical question 'Are these the ones...' conveys shock and disbelief at the gap between the hypocrites' loud protestations of faith and loyalty and the reality of their inner disbelief or betrayal. The verse teaches that oaths and outward declarations of faith are meaningless without sincerity and consistent righteous action; because their faith was false, all their deeds—even acts that might have appeared virtuous—are nullified ('their deeds have become worthless'). This nullification is not merely a loss of reward but a comprehensive spiritual bankruptcy, rendering them 'losers' in both worldly and eternal terms. The verse serves as a warning against hypocrisy (nifaq) and emphasizes that Allah knows the true state of hearts regardless of outward oaths, reinforcing the Quranic theme that sincerity (ikhlas) is the foundation upon which all deeds are judged and accepted.

translation: O you who have believed, whoever among you should revert from his religion - Allah will bring forth [in place of them] a people He will love and who will love Him, humble toward the believers, mighty toward the disbelievers, striving in the cause of Allah and not fearing the blame of a critic. That is the favor of Allah; He bestows it upon whom He wills. And Allah is all-Encompassing and Knowing.
interpretation: This verse establishes that the faith community's strength does not depend on any individual member's steadfastness, for Allah's cause is not contingent upon human loyalty. Should any believer abandon the faith, Allah has the power to replace them with others who embody true devotion—characterized by a mutual love between themselves and their Creator. The qualities described outline the ideal believer: humility and gentleness toward fellow believers, yet firmness and strength when confronting disbelief and falsehood, without this firmness crossing into arrogance. Such believers actively strive in Allah's cause, undeterred by social pressure, ridicule, or the criticism of others—they are not swayed by the opinions of those who would mock or discourage their commitment. This fearlessness in the face of blame signifies a spiritual maturity where one's relationship with the divine takes precedence over social approval. The verse concludes by framing these qualities as a divine gift bestowed according to Allah's will, not something earned purely through human effort, while affirming Allah's limitless knowledge and capacity to sustain His religion through whomever He chooses across generations.

translation: Your guardian and protector is only Allah, His Messenger, and those who believe - those who establish prayer and give zakah while they are bowing down [in humility].
interpretation: This verse establishes the principle of wilayah (guardianship, authority, and allegiance) within the Muslim community, defining it as belonging exclusively to Allah, His Messenger, and true believers characterized by specific qualities of devotion. Many classical and Shia commentators hold that this verse was revealed in connection with a specific incident involving Ali ibn Abi Talib, who, according to this interpretation, gave his ring in charity to a beggar while bowing in prayer (ruku'). The phrase 'while they are bowing' is seen as pointing to this singular act of charity performed during worship, elevating the spiritual significance of combining ritual devotion with social responsibility. Sunni commentators generally read the verse more broadly, understanding it as describing the general quality of true believers who are devoted to prayer and charity, with 'bowing' serving as a synecdoche for the state of humility and submission to God that characterizes the believer's entire life and worship, rather than referring to a single historical event. The verse as a whole underscores that true authority and loyalty in matters of faith and community derive from righteous character and sincere devotion to God, not merely from worldly power or lineage.

translation: And whoever takes Allah, His Messenger, and those who believe as allies - indeed, the party of Allah is the victorious.
interpretation: This verse establishes that true allegiance (wilayah) belongs exclusively to Allah, His Messenger, and the believing community, in contrast to the preceding verses which warn against taking Jews, Christians, or hypocrites as allies in matters of religious loyalty and protection. The term 'Hizbullah' (the party/faction of Allah) refers to those whose primary loyalty, love, and support are directed toward Allah and the community of true believers, rather than toward external powers based on worldly considerations. The promise of ultimate victory ('al-ghalibun') is not necessarily about immediate worldly triumph in every instance, but speaks to the ultimate and enduring success - whether spiritual, moral, or eventual worldly success - of those who align themselves with divine guidance rather than compromising their faith commitments for temporary alliances. This verse reinforces the Quranic theme that true strength and security come from unity with Allah and the believing community, not from alliances formed out of fear or worldly expediency that might compromise core religious principles.

translation: O you who have believed, do not take as allies those who have taken your religion in ridicule and amusement among those who were given the Scripture before you nor the disbelievers. And fear Allah, if you should be believers.
interpretation: This verse establishes a principle for the believing community regarding the boundaries of loyalty and alliance. It distinguishes not between all People of the Book or all disbelievers broadly, but specifically targets those who mock and trivialize the faith of the believers. The warning is against forming close bonds of allegiance (wilayah) with those who treat the believers' religion as a joke or a game, as such alliances could compromise the integrity of faith and invite ridicule upon sacred matters. The verse ties this prohibition directly to one's faith commitment—taqwa (God-consciousness) and true belief (iman) require discernment in choosing allies, especially when the religion itself is the object of derision. This is not a blanket condemnation of all non-Muslims, but a specific caution against aligning with those whose stance toward Islam is one of mockery and hostility, as such alliances could undermine the believers' dignity, resolve, and spiritual integrity.

translation: And when you call to prayer, they take it in mockery and as a jest. That is because they are a people who do not reason.
interpretation: This verse addresses the mocking attitude of certain disbelievers and hypocrites toward the Islamic call to prayer (adhan). Rather than responding with reverence to this sacred summons to worship, they ridiculed it as a joke. The Qur'an attributes this behavior not merely to stubbornness or hostility, but to a deeper deficiency: a failure to use reason ('la ya'qiloon'). The implication is that proper use of the intellect would lead one to recognize the seriousness and beauty of the call to worship God. Mockery of sacred rituals is thus framed as a symptom of intellectual and spiritual failure rather than a sign of sophistication or critical thinking. This verse also serves to console believers who may have faced ridicule for their religious practices, reassuring them that such mockery stems from the mockers' own deficiency rather than any flaw in the practice itself.

translation: Say: 'O People of the Scripture, do you resent us for any reason other than that we believe in Allah and in what has been revealed to us and what was revealed before, and that most of you are defiantly disobedient?'
interpretation: This verse addresses the criticism and hostility that the People of the Book (Jews and Christians) directed at the Muslims. It poses a rhetorical question, highlighting the irrationality of their resentment: the only 'fault' they can find in the believers is their faith in Allah and in the entirety of revealed scripture, including the Torah, the Gospel, and the Qur'an. This should not be a cause for resentment but rather common ground, since the People of the Book also claim to believe in divine revelation. The verse suggests that the true source of hostility is not genuine theological disagreement but rather the moral and spiritual corruption ('fisq') of many among them, meaning their deviation from the covenant and guidance of their own scriptures. It implies that their opposition stems from stubbornness, envy, or rejection of truth rather than legitimate reasoning, since belief in prior revelation should unite rather than divide them from the Muslims.

translation: Say: 'Shall I inform you of something worse than that in terms of recompense from Allah? It is he whom Allah has cursed, and with whom He is angry, and some of whom He has turned into apes and swine, and he who worships false gods (Taghut). Such people are in a worse position, and further astray from the right path.'
interpretation: This verse is understood as a rebuke to certain People of the Book who, through their disbelief, disobedience, and transgression against divine commandments, incurred Allah's curse and wrath. The transformation into apes and swine is interpreted literally by many classical exegetes as referring to a specific group among the Israelites who violated the Sabbath by fishing, and were consequently transformed as a punishment—serving as a visible sign of divine retribution. Others interpret this transformation metaphorically, as a description of moral degeneration—where human reason and dignity are lost, reducing a person to bestial or base behavior characterized by greed, lust, or blind imitation. The mention of worshipping Taghut (false deities, tyrannical powers, or anything worshipped besides Allah) extends the condemnation to all forms of idolatry and submission to illegitimate authority. The verse concludes with a comparative judgment: those who follow such paths of disbelief and corruption are spiritually and morally in a worse position than even the Jews and Christians whom the earlier part of the surah criticizes, since they have strayed further from the straight path through willful associating of others with Allah in worship and authority.

translation: And when they come to you, they say, 'We believe,' but they entered with disbelief and left with it, and Allah is most knowing of what they were concealing.
interpretation: This verse addresses a group of hypocrites—or disbelievers feigning faith—who outwardly profess belief when they come before the Prophet and the believers, yet their hearts remain unchanged, entering and departing in the same state of rejection. Their declaration of faith is merely a verbal performance meant to deceive or to gain social and political advantage, not a genuine transformation of belief. The verse exposes the futility of such deception by emphasizing that God's knowledge penetrates beyond outward speech and action to the concealed intentions of the heart. It serves as both a warning to the hypocrites that their duplicity is fully known to God despite their attempts at concealment, and a reassurance to the believers that no false profession of faith can ultimately escape divine scrutiny. The verse underscores a recurring Qur'anic theme: true faith (iman) must be sincere and consistent, not merely a tactical utterance, and God is the ultimate judge of what lies hidden within the human heart.

translation: And you see many of them hastening into sin and transgression and consuming unlawful gain. Evil indeed is what they used to do.
interpretation: This verse is part of a passage in Surah al-Ma'idah criticizing certain scholars and leaders among the People of the Book for their moral failure: rather than restraining their communities from wrongdoing, many raced eagerly toward sin ('ithm), aggression against others ('udwan), and the consumption of 'suht' — ill-gotten gain such as bribes, usury, or unlawfully acquired property. The verse frames this behavior as a collective societal corruption, where the pursuit of unlawful wealth and transgression against others becomes normalized and even competitive ('yusari'un' implies rushing eagerly, not reluctantly). The closing rebuke, 'evil indeed is what they used to do,' underscores a moral indictment of communities whose economic and ethical practices diverge from righteousness, serving as a broader warning against the corrosive effects of greed and injustice when left unchecked by religious or communal authority.

translation: Why do not the rabbis and the scholars forbid them from their saying of sin and their consuming of the forbidden? Evil indeed is what they have been doing.
interpretation: This verse rebukes the religious leaders and scholars among the Children of Israel for their failure to fulfill their duty of moral and social accountability. Possessing knowledge and spiritual authority, they had both the capacity and the responsibility to forbid wrongdoing—specifically the sinful speech and the consumption of unlawfully acquired wealth (such as bribery or usury) occurring among their people. Their silence and inaction in the face of corruption amounted to complicity, since failing to prevent evil when one has the power and position to do so is itself condemned. The verse establishes a broader principle in Islamic ethics: that those entrusted with religious knowledge and communal leadership bear a special obligation to actively enjoin good and forbid evil, not merely to abstain from wrongdoing themselves. Their negligence in exercising this duty is portrayed as a grave failing, deserving of divine censure, because the corruption of a community is often enabled by the silence of its moral guardians rather than solely by the actions of wrongdoers themselves.

translation: And the Jews say, 'The hand of Allah is chained.' Chained are their hands, and cursed are they for what they say. Rather, both His hands are extended wide; He spends as He wills. And that which has been sent down to you from your Lord will surely increase many of them in transgression and disbelief. And We have cast among them enmity and hatred until the Day of Resurrection. Every time they kindle a fire for war, Allah extinguishes it. And they strive throughout the land spreading corruption, and Allah does not love the corrupters.
interpretation: This verse responds to a blasphemous claim attributed to some among the Jews that God's hand is 'chained,' meaning miserly or withholding—an accusation implying that God is stingy toward His creation, perhaps stemming from resentment over hardships they faced. The Qur'an reverses this charge: it is their own hands that are figuratively bound through their avarice and moral failings, and they are condemned for uttering such a blasphemy against God. In contrast, God's generosity is described as boundless—'His hands are extended wide'—meaning His bounty, provision, and mercy flow without restriction, and He dispenses according to His infinite wisdom and will, not subject to human calculation or limitation. The verse then explains a sociological and spiritual law: when divine revelation comes to a people whose hearts are already inclined toward rejection, it does not soften them but rather deepens their defiance and disbelief, exposing underlying arrogance. The mention of perpetual enmity and hatred sown among them refers to the internal divisions and factionalism that would persist among the Jewish communities (and by extension, a warning applicable to any community that turns from guidance), preventing lasting unity even when they conspire together. The image of kindling 'a fire for war' that God repeatedly extinguishes suggests that their schemes to wage war against the believers or to achieve dominance will be continually thwarted by divine intervention, not through their own righteousness but as a check on their corruption. The closing statement about striving to spread corruption 'in the land' broadens the critique to describe a pattern of behavior—exploitation, treachery, and moral decay—that God explicitly condemns, affirming that divine love and support are withheld from those who sow corruption rather than justice and peace.

translation: And if only the People of the Book had believed and been righteous, We would have removed from them their misdeeds and We would have admitted them into Gardens of Bliss.
interpretation: This verse establishes that faith and righteousness are the universal criteria for divine favor, not ethnic or religious lineage alone. Addressed to the People of the Book (Jews and Christians), it affirms that had they truly believed in what was revealed to their prophets and remained faithful to God's guidance—including recognizing subsequent revelation—God's mercy would have been extended to them fully, erasing their sins and granting them Paradise. The verse underscores a conditional promise rooted in sincere faith (iman) coupled with taqwa (God-consciousness and righteous conduct), rather than mere claims of religious identity or inherited status. It implicitly critiques those among the People of the Book who rejected truth despite possessing scripture, while simultaneously affirming that the path to salvation remains open to them through genuine faith and piety. This reflects the Qur'anic theme that God's covenant and mercy are not exclusive to any one community but are accessible to all who meet the conditions of belief and righteous living.

translation: And if only they had upheld the Torah and the Gospel and what was revealed to them from their Lord, they would have eaten from above them and from beneath their feet. Among them is a moderate community, but many of them - evil is what they do.
interpretation: This verse addresses the People of the Book, particularly Jews and Christians, emphasizing that true adherence to their own revealed scriptures would have led to divine blessings and abundance, symbolized by provision from above (rain) and below (earth's produce). The 'eating from above and below' represents comprehensive material and spiritual prosperity that follows genuine faith and righteous practice. The verse acknowledges that not all People of the Book are the same - it recognizes a 'moderate' or 'balanced' community (ummatun muqtasidah) among them who maintain integrity and follow a middle path in faith and conduct. However, it criticizes the majority who have strayed from the authentic teachings of their scriptures, engaging in corruption, distortion, or disobedience. The verse illustrates a broader Quranic theme that blessings and hardship are often tied to one's faithfulness to divine guidance, and that failing to implement revealed law - whether Torah, Gospel, or Quran - results in loss of both spiritual and worldly good. It also serves as an implicit call to the Muslim community to uphold the Quran fully, lest they fall into the same pattern of neglect as previous communities.

translation: O Messenger! Proclaim that which has been sent down to you from your Lord, and if you do not do so, then you will not have conveyed His message. And Allah will protect you from the people. Indeed, Allah does not guide the disbelieving people.
interpretation: This verse addresses Prophet Muhammad directly, commanding him to deliver the entirety of the divine revelation without omission, hesitation, or fear of the reaction of those who might oppose it. The phrase 'if you do not do so, then you will not have conveyed His message' underscores the gravity of complete and faithful transmission—partial delivery would be tantamount to failure in the prophetic mission itself. The assurance that Allah will protect him from the people addresses the Prophet's human concerns about physical danger or social backlash, particularly relevant given the opposition and threats he faced from various groups, including hostile tribes and those resistant to the message. This divine guarantee of protection removes any valid excuse for withholding or softening the message out of fear. The verse concludes by noting that Allah does not guide those who deliberately reject faith, implying that the Prophet's responsibility is limited to clear and complete proclamation; the matter of whether people accept guidance rests with Allah's will and their own choices, not with the Prophet's capacity to persuade. This distinction relieves the Prophet of the burden of forcing belief while placing full weight on the duty of transmission.

translation: Say, "O People of the Scripture, you are not upon anything until you uphold the Torah, the Gospel, and what has been revealed to you from your Lord." And that which has been revealed to you from your Lord will surely increase many of them in transgression and disbelief. So do not grieve over the disbelieving people.
interpretation: This verse addresses the People of the Book—Jews and Christians—asserting that genuine faith and standing before God require actual adherence to the core teachings of their own revealed scriptures, the Torah and the Gospel, including the recognition of subsequent revelation sent to them, namely the Qur'an. Mere affiliation or heritage is insufficient without practicing these teachings' true guidance. The verse further acknowledges a painful reality: rather than drawing many of them closer to truth, the revelation given to the Prophet Muhammad provokes greater defiance and denial among those who reject it, deepening their transgression. This phenomenon reflects a broader Qur'anic theme that guidance does not automatically soften every heart—some respond to clear signs with increased resistance due to pride, vested interests, or stubbornness. The closing command, telling the Prophet not to grieve over the disbelievers, serves as both consolation and a reminder that his responsibility is to convey the message faithfully, not to guarantee its acceptance. It underscores the principle that human free will determines response to guidance, and the Prophet's emotional burden over others' rejection should not overwhelm him, as ultimate judgment and accountability rest with God.

translation: Indeed, those who believed, and those who were Jews, and the Sabians, and the Christians - whoever believed in Allah and the Last Day and did righteousness - no fear shall come upon them, nor shall they grieve.
interpretation: This verse establishes a principle that salvation and divine reward are not restricted to a particular group by name or label, but are contingent upon genuine faith in God and the Last Day coupled with righteous action. By listing various religious communities of the time - Muslims, Jews, Sabians, and Christians - the verse emphasizes that sincere belief and virtuous conduct are the true criteria for salvation, transcending communal or sectarian identity. This has been understood by many commentators as affirming that God judges individuals based on the sincerity of their faith and the quality of their deeds, rather than mere formal affiliation with a religious community. It underscores a universal moral and spiritual standard: those who truly believe in the One God, anticipate accountability in the afterlife, and act righteously will be free from fear and sorrow, highlighting God's mercy as extending to the sincere faithful across different traditions, provided they meet these essential criteria of belief and righteous action.

translation: Indeed, We took the covenant of the Children of Israel and sent to them messengers. Every time a messenger came to them with what their souls did not desire, a party [of them] they denied, and another party they killed.
interpretation: This verse highlights a recurring pattern of rejection and hostility toward divine guidance among the Children of Israel. Despite God's solemn covenant with them and the continuous sending of prophets to guide them, their response was often shaped by self-interest and desire rather than truth. When a messenger brought teachings that conflicted with their personal inclinations, social norms, or vested interests, their reaction was severe: some prophets were simply disbelieved and rejected, while others faced the ultimate violence of being killed. This illustrates a broader human tendency—not limited to one people—where truth that challenges comfort, power, or desire is met with resistance, and the depth of that resistance can escalate from denial to violent suppression. The verse serves as a warning about the dangers of prioritizing personal or communal desires over accepting guidance that calls for moral and spiritual accountability.

translation: And they thought there would be no trial, so they became blind and deaf. Then Allah turned to them in forgiveness, yet again many of them became blind and deaf. And Allah is Seeing of what they do.
interpretation: This verse addresses a recurring pattern of spiritual heedlessness among certain people who presumed that their wrongdoing would carry no consequence, no test, no accountability. Their 'blindness' and 'deafness' are metaphorical, referring not to physical impairment but to a willful refusal to perceive truth and heed guidance—they closed themselves off from recognizing signs and warnings. Despite this, God extended mercy and forgiveness to them, offering a renewed opportunity for insight and reform. Yet rather than seizing this chance for lasting change, a great many of them relapsed into the same spiritual blindness and deafness, repeating their pattern of denial and heedlessness. The verse underscores a theme found throughout the Qur'an: divine mercy is real and repeatedly offered, but human beings often squander it through stubbornness and complacency. The closing statement that God is 'Seeing of what they do' serves as both reassurance and warning—nothing escapes divine awareness, and ultimately people will be held accountable for their choices, including their persistent refusal to learn from forgiveness already granted.

translation: They have certainly disbelieved who say, 'Allah is the Messiah, son of Mary,' while the Messiah [himself] said, 'O Children of Israel, worship Allah, my Lord and your Lord.' Indeed, whoever associates partners with Allah - Allah has forbidden him Paradise, and his refuge is the Fire. And there are no helpers for the wrongdoers.
interpretation: This verse directly confronts and refutes the Christian doctrine that identifies Jesus (the Messiah) with God Himself. The Qur'an presents Jesus as a mortal prophet who explicitly rejected any claim to divinity, instead calling his own people to worship the one true God, whom he refers to as both his Lord and theirs - establishing shared servitude rather than divine equivalence. By quoting Jesus's own words, the verse uses Jesus as a witness against the very doctrine attributed to him, suggesting that deifying him constitutes a distortion of his actual teaching rather than a faithful representation of it. The verse then universalizes the principle: shirk (associating partners with God) in any form - whether applied to Jesus or anyone else - is the gravest theological error, warranting exclusion from Paradise and consignment to the Fire. The closing reference to 'wrongdoers' having no helpers underscores the finality and severity of this judgment, reinforcing the Qur'an's uncompromising monotheism (tawhid) as the central theological axis distinguishing Islam from the trinitarian or incarnational claims of Christianity as the Qur'an understood them.

translation: Certainly they have disbelieved who say, 'God is the third of three.' But there is no god except One God. And if they do not desist from what they say, there will surely afflict those who disbelieve among them a painful punishment.
