The verse illustrates that salvation is tied to faith and righteous conduct rather than mere family or marital ties—kinship with a prophet does not guarantee deliverance if one does not share his faith and obedience to God. It also serves as a warning that betrayal of truth, even from within one's own household, leads to the same fate as those who openly reject it.

translation: And We rained down upon them a rain [of stones]. So see how was the end of the criminals.
interpretation: This verse refers to the destruction of the people of Lot, who were punished for their persistent sin and rejection of divine guidance through a devastating rain of stones upon their city. The verse serves as a didactic conclusion to a narrative of divine justice, inviting the listener to reflect ('so see') on the ultimate consequences faced by those who persist in corruption and defiance against God's messengers. It functions as a warning to the Prophet Muhammad's contemporaries and all future audiences that divine retribution, though sometimes delayed, is certain for those who transgress moral and spiritual boundaries. The phrase 'how was the end' emphasizes the Qur'an's recurring theme that history itself testifies to the pattern of destruction that befalls unjust communities, reinforcing the moral order underlying the universe.

translation: And to Madyan [We sent] their brother Shu'ayb. He said, 'O my people, worship Allah; you have no deity other than Him. There has come to you clear evidence from your Lord. So give full measure and weight and do not deprive people of their due, and do not cause corruption on the earth after its reform. That is better for you, if you should be believers.'
interpretation: This verse establishes a direct link between faith in God and ethical conduct in commerce and social life. Shu'ayb's message to the people of Madyan ties monotheism to economic justice—honest measurement and fair dealing—suggesting that spiritual belief must manifest in tangible, everyday integrity. The reference to 'corruption after its reform' implies that society had once been set right, perhaps through earlier prophetic guidance or natural moral order, and that greed, fraud, and exploitation represent a regression from that state. The verse frames righteousness not as an abstract piety but as the maintenance of trust and fairness in human transactions, positioning economic honesty as a form of worship itself. Shu'ayb's appeal to self-interest ('that is better for you') reflects a pragmatic approach to moral exhortation, indicating that ethical behavior ultimately serves the practitioner's own well-being, both spiritually and socially, reinforcing the Qur'anic theme that divine law and human welfare are inherently aligned.

translation: And do not sit in wait on every path, threatening and turning away from the path of Allah those who believe in Him, seeking to make it crooked. And remember when you were few and He multiplied you, and look how was the end of the corrupters.
interpretation: This verse is part of the address of the Prophet Shu'ayb to his people, Madyan, who used to sit along the roads and marketplaces threatening and intimidating travelers and believers, obstructing them from the path of Allah by casting doubts, spreading falsehood, and distorting the straight way to make it appear crooked and undesirable. The verse warns against using positions of social or economic power to obstruct others from faith and truth, and against actively working to twist and corrupt sound guidance so that people are led astray. It then calls on the people to remember Allah's favor upon them, how He increased their numbers and strength from a state of weakness, as a reminder that all blessings come from Him and should not be used to oppress others. Finally, it directs them to reflect upon history and the fate of those before them who spread corruption on earth, their ultimate destruction and humiliation, as a warning that obstructing the truth and transgressing against others always leads to ruin.

translation: And if there is a group among you who has believed in that with which I have been sent and a group who has not believed, then be patient until Allah judges between us. And He is the best of judges.
interpretation: This verse records the words of Prophet Shu'ayb to his people, who had split into believers and disbelievers in response to his message. Rather than calling for immediate confrontation or forcing unity through coercion, Shu'ayb counsels patience and defers ultimate judgment to God alone. This reflects a broader Quranic principle regarding religious division within a community: the prophet's role is to convey the message clearly, not to compel belief or adjudicate the fates of those who accept or reject it. The phrase 'He is the best of judges' reassures the believers that divine justice, which accounts for all hidden intentions and truths, surpasses any human attempt at judgment, and that patience in the face of communal division is itself an act of faith and trust in God's ultimate wisdom and timing.

translation: The chiefs who were arrogant among his people said, 'We will surely drive you out, O Shu'ayb, and those who have believed with you, from our city, unless you return to our religion.' He said, 'Even if we were unwilling?'
interpretation: This verse illustrates the tactic of powerful elites who, unable to counter the Prophet Shu'ayb's arguments with reason, resort to threats of expulsion and coercion to suppress dissent and maintain their religious and social dominance. Shu'ayb's response—'Even if we were unwilling?'—exposes the absurdity and tyranny of forcing belief through compulsion, highlighting that true faith cannot be coerced and that submission to falsehood under threat is not a genuine choice. It underscores a recurring Qur'anic theme: that rejecting truth is often rooted not in rational disagreement but in the powerful's desire to preserve their status, wealth, and control over others, and that the righteous must be prepared to face persecution and exile rather than compromise their convictions.

translation: We would have invented a lie against Allah if we returned to your religion after Allah has saved us from it. And it is not for us to return to it, except if Allah, our Lord, should will. Our Lord has encompassed all things in knowledge. Upon Allah we have relied. Our Lord, decide between us and our people in truth, and You are the best of those who decide.
interpretation: This verse records the steadfast declaration of Prophet Shu'ayb and the believers who followed him, made in response to the threats of their disbelieving people, who demanded that they return to their former religion or be expelled from their city. The believers' response establishes several theological principles. First, they affirm that returning to disbelief after having tasted the clarity and truth of monotheism would constitute a deliberate fabrication against Allah, a conscious betrayal of the truth they had come to recognize. Second, by stating that they could not return "except if Allah wills," they acknowledge Allah's absolute sovereignty over all matters, including matters of the heart and belief, while simultaneously expressing their own firm resolve never to actually will such a return themselves. This is not a hedging of their conviction but rather a humble recognition that all things, even their own steadfastness, remain within Allah's power and knowledge. Third, their declaration that Allah's knowledge "encompasses all things" serves as a statement of trust that Allah is fully aware of their sincerity, their predicament, and the injustice of their people's demands. Finally, their prayer for Allah to "decide between us and our people in truth" reflects the believers' recourse to divine judgment when human persuasion and argument have been exhausted, and their recognition that Allah alone renders perfect, just verdicts between truth and falsehood. This verse exemplifies the posture of reliance (tawakkul) upon Allah that believers are called to maintain when facing persecution for their faith, combining firm resolve with humble submission to divine will and judgment.

translation: And the chiefs of those who disbelieved among his people said, 'If you follow Shu'ayb, indeed, you would then be losers.'
interpretation: This verse depicts the response of the arrogant ruling elite of Prophet Shu'ayb's people (the people of Madyan) to his call for monotheism and ethical dealings in trade. The 'mala' (chiefs/nobles) represent entrenched power structures that felt threatened by Shu'ayb's message, which challenged their corrupt economic practices—particularly fraud in weights and measures—and their idolatrous beliefs. Their warning that following Shu'ayb would lead to 'loss' is deeply ironic, as it inverts the true spiritual reality: those who reject the prophet and persist in corruption are the actual losers, both in this world (as the subsequent verses reveal their destruction) and in the Hereafter. This rhetorical strategy of the disbelieving elite—framing righteousness and faith as a path to loss or disadvantage—is a recurring pattern in Quranic narratives of prophets facing resistance from powerful social classes who have vested interests in maintaining the status quo. Their fear was fundamentally about losing their social, political, and economic dominance if the community embraced the egalitarian and ethical message of the prophet, revealing how worldly power often positions itself against prophetic truth by manipulating the language of loss and gain to maintain control over the masses.

translation: So the earthquake seized them, and they lay lifeless, fallen prone (face down) in their homes.
interpretation: This verse describes the sudden and total destruction visited upon a disbelieving people who rejected their prophet's warnings despite clear signs. The 'rajfah' (violent tremor or earthquake) represents divine retribution that struck without further delay after the people persisted in arrogance, mockery, and rejection of truth. The imagery of bodies lying motionless and face-down in their own homes emphasizes the completeness of their downfall—struck down in the very place of their comfort and security, with no chance to flee or defend themselves. This serves as a stark admonition about the consequences of persistent disbelief and moral corruption, illustrating that worldly power and settled life offer no protection against divine justice when a community willfully turns away from guidance after it has been made clear to them. The verse functions within a recurring Quranic pattern of destruction narratives meant to warn later generations through the fate of earlier ones.

translation: Those who denied Shu'ayb - it was as though they had never dwelt therein. Those who denied Shu'ayb - it was they who were the losers.
interpretation: This verse, repeating the structure of similar passages about other destroyed nations (such as the people of Thamud), emphasizes the completeness of the destruction that befell the people of Madyan who rejected the prophet Shu'ayb. The repetition of the phrase 'those who denied Shu'ayb' underscores that their specific sin was disbelief and rejection of the prophetic message, not merely their social or economic transgressions (such as fraud in trade and corruption) which Shu'ayb had also warned them against. The statement 'as though they had never dwelt therein' conveys the totality of their erasure - their homes, their civilization, and their very presence vanished so completely that it was as if they had never existed. The closing declaration that they were 'the losers' serves as a direct rebuttal to their earlier mockery of Shu'ayb, when they had taunted him and suggested that he and his followers were the ones who would suffer loss. The irony is that those who believed they were secure in their wealth and power, and who dismissed the prophet's warnings, were ultimately the true losers in both this world and the hereafter, while Shu'ayb and the believers were saved. This serves as a broader Quranic theme: worldly power and scorn for prophetic guidance do not protect against divine recompense, and those who deny truth, however confident they may be, are the ones who truly lose.

translation: So he turned away from them and said, 'O my people, I have certainly conveyed to you the messages of my Lord and have advised you, but how could I grieve for a disbelieving people?'
interpretation: This verse refers to Prophet Shu'ayb (or similarly situated prophets in the Qur'anic narrative) after his people rejected his message and were subsequently destroyed for their persistent disbelief and wrongdoing. His turning away symbolizes the completion of his prophetic duty—he had fulfilled his obligation to deliver God's message faithfully and sincerely counsel his people, leaving no excuse for them. His rhetorical question, 'how could I grieve for a disbelieving people,' reflects his acceptance of divine justice: since they consciously chose rejection despite clear guidance and sincere warning, their fate was a consequence of their own willful disbelief, not a cause for the prophet's lasting sorrow. This illustrates a broader Qur'anic theme that the responsibility of prophets is only to convey the truth clearly, not to force belief, and that people are held accountable for their own choices once truth has been made evident to them.

translation: And We did not send to any town a prophet except that We seized its people with adversity and hardship that they might humble themselves.
interpretation: This verse establishes a divine pattern in which communities receiving prophetic guidance are tested through suffering and hardship. The purpose of such trials, as stated explicitly in the verse, is to break human arrogance and self-sufficiency, driving people toward humility and dependence on God (tadarru'). Affliction serves as a spiritual mechanism designed to soften hardened hearts, strip away false confidence in worldly power or wealth, and awaken awareness of one's vulnerability and need for the divine. This reflects a broader Qur'anic theology of suffering as pedagogical rather than merely punitive—hardship is sent not simply to punish disbelief but to create conditions conducive to repentance and return to God. The verse also implies a consistent historical pattern across all prophetic missions, suggesting that resistance to divine guidance is a recurring human trait that necessitates such corrective measures, and that the testing of nations through calamity is part of a just and purposeful divine governance of human affairs.

translation: Then We changed the bad condition into good, until they increased and prospered and said, 'Our forefathers, too, were touched by hardship and ease.' So We seized them suddenly, while they did not perceive.
interpretation: This verse describes a recurring pattern in the moral history of nations as presented in the Qur'an: God tests communities first with adversity to prompt humility and reflection, and when they fail to respond, He grants them ease and prosperity as a further test. Rather than recognizing this shifting fortune as a sign of divine mercy and a call to gratitude and righteousness, the people grow complacent, attributing the natural ebb and flow of hardship and comfort to mere historical cycle or fate—'our forefathers also experienced both'—thus naturalizing and dismissing it as random rather than purposeful. This complacency, which breeds moral heedlessness and arrogance, becomes the very condition that invites sudden divine punishment, striking when they least expect it. The verse serves as a warning against interpreting worldly ease as entitlement rather than trial, and against spiritual numbness that develops when people forget that calamity and comfort alike serve as reminders meant to awaken consciousness of accountability before God.

translation: And if the people of the towns had believed and feared Allah, We would have opened upon them blessings from the heaven and the earth; but they denied, so We seized them for what they used to earn.
interpretation: This verse establishes a divine principle linking faith and righteousness to material and spiritual prosperity. It teaches that communities which embrace belief and taqwa (God-consciousness, piety) create the conditions for divine blessings to flow abundantly into their lives—both in natural abundance (rain, harvest, resources) and in spiritual wellbeing. The 'opening of blessings from heaven and earth' suggests a holistic prosperity encompassing both the physical and metaphysical dimensions of life. Conversely, the verse warns that denial and rejection of truth lead to a withdrawal of this potential prosperity and ultimately to divine punishment or consequence. Importantly, the retribution mentioned is explicitly tied to 'what they used to earn'—emphasizing that the suffering of nations and communities is not arbitrary but a direct consequence of their own collective choices and actions. This verse thus serves as both a promise and a warning, illustrating a moral causality in which societies bear responsibility for their spiritual and ethical orientations, and face natural consequences—whether blessing or calamity—based on those choices.

translation: Do the people of the towns feel secure that Our punishment will not come to them by night while they are sleeping?
interpretation: This verse is part of a series of rhetorical questions in Surah Al-A'raf that warn against spiritual complacency and false security. It highlights human tendency to feel immune from divine reckoning, especially when life seems stable and comfortable. The imagery of punishment arriving at night during sleep emphasizes vulnerability and the suddenness with which consequences can befall a heedless community. The verse serves as a broader admonition that worldly ease should not be mistaken for divine approval, and that moral and spiritual accountability can manifest unexpectedly, urging continuous vigilance, humility, and awareness of one's actions rather than complacent assurance of safety.

translation: Do the people of the towns then feel secure that Our punishment will not come to them in the morning while they are at play?
interpretation: This verse continues the Qur'an's warning to communities that grow complacent in their worldly engagements, highlighting the suddenness and unpredictability of divine retribution. The imagery of 'morning' and 'play' emphasizes that punishment can arrive during moments of ordinary life, routine, or leisure, when people are least prepared and most absorbed in mundane or frivolous pursuits. The rhetorical question underscores human heedlessness: a false sense of security bred by prosperity and daily distractions can blind people to moral and spiritual accountability. It serves as a broader admonition that no amount of normalcy or comfort guarantees immunity from consequences for a community's collective wrongdoing or rejection of divine guidance, urging constant mindfulness rather than complacency.

translation: Do they then feel secure from the plan (makr) of Allah? None feels secure from the plan of Allah except the losing people.
interpretation: This verse warns against complacency and false security in matters of faith. The term 'makr' (plan, scheme, or subtle strategy) of Allah refers to His perfect and just response to the deeds of human beings—especially to those who disbelieve, transgress, or deceive others while assuming they are safe from divine accountability. Those who enjoy worldly prosperity, power, or apparent success may mistakenly believe that their favorable circumstances are permanent proof of Allah's approval or that they are beyond the reach of His judgment. The verse teaches that true believers remain ever mindful of Allah's justice, balancing hope in His mercy with fear of His requital, since no one can be certain of their ultimate fate except through sincere faith and righteous action. Only those destined for loss—the heedless, arrogant, or spiritually blind—allow themselves to feel immune from Allah's subtle and inevitable reckoning, failing to recognize that ease or delay in punishment is not the same as exemption from it.

translation: Is it not evident to those who inherit the earth after its former people that, had We willed, We could have struck them for their sins? And We seal up their hearts so that they do not hear.
interpretation: This verse addresses the generations that come after past nations who were destroyed for their wrongdoing, asking rhetorically whether they have learned nothing from this history. It warns that the same fate—divine punishment for sin—could befall them as well, since God's justice is not limited to any one people or era but applies universally to all who persist in corruption and disbelief. The 'inheritance of the earth' refers to the succession of generations and civilizations, each replacing the one before, and the verse calls on them to reflect on the lessons of those who perished before them due to their own transgressions. The sealing of hearts represents the spiritual consequence of persistent heedlessness and arrogance: when people willfully ignore warnings and signs repeatedly, their capacity to perceive truth becomes diminished, not as an arbitrary punishment but as a natural result of their own choices to turn away from guidance. This serves as both a historical reminder and a moral caution to every generation that succeeds another upon the earth.

translation: Those are the cities (towns) whose tidings We relate to you. Indeed, their messengers came to them with clear proofs, but they were not [then] to believe in that which they had denied before. Thus does Allah seal over the hearts of the disbelievers.
interpretation: This verse reflects on the fate of past nations—such as the peoples of Noah, Hud, Salih, and Lot—whose stories are recounted in the preceding verses of Surah Al-A'raf as moral lessons. It emphasizes that despite receiving clear signs and proofs from their messengers, these communities persisted in their disbelief because their prior rejection had hardened into an entrenched pattern. The phrase 'they were not to believe' points to a spiritual consequence rather than a predetermined fate imposed arbitrarily: their repeated, willful denial of truth led to a psychological and spiritual condition where belief became practically impossible for them, as their hearts grew closed off through their own choices. The 'sealing' of hearts mentioned at the end is thus presented as both a natural consequence of persistent disbelief and a divine law describing how continuous rejection of truth results in spiritual blindness. This serves as a warning to the listeners of the Qur'an (and by extension, all people) that stubborn denial of clear truth, when repeated, can calcify into a state where guidance no longer penetrates, underscoring the importance of responding to signs of truth with openness rather than habitual rejection.

translation: And We did not find most of them true to any covenant; but We found most of them indeed defiantly disobedient.
interpretation: This verse reflects on the recurring pattern throughout human history whereby people, when bound by covenants—whether with God, with prophets, or with one another—fail to uphold their commitments. The verse speaks to a broader theme in the Qur'an regarding human nature's tendency toward unfaithfulness and moral failure when tested. It is not a blanket condemnation of all humanity, but rather an observation about the general trend among those who were given opportunities to honor sacred trusts and obligations, particularly in the context of previous nations and peoples who received divine guidance yet broke their promises, whether explicit covenants with God or implicit covenants of moral and social responsibility. The verse underscores the Qur'anic concern with fidelity, trustworthiness, and the fulfillment of promises as central markers of righteousness, while highlighting transgression (fisq) as a departure from the natural and intended path of obedience to divine command.

translation: Then We sent, after them, Moses with Our signs to Pharaoh and his chiefs, but they wrongfully rejected them. So see how was the end of the corrupters.
interpretation: This verse continues the Qur'anic pattern of recounting the stories of earlier prophets and nations to draw lessons for the present community. Moses is presented as a successor in the prophetic lineage, sent with clear divine signs (miracles such as the staff and the hand) to Pharaoh and his ruling elite, who represent entrenched worldly power. Their 'wrongdoing' (zulm) with respect to the signs refers to their conscious rejection and denial of truth despite clear evidence, an act rooted in arrogance and the desire to preserve their own authority rather than genuine disbelief from ignorance. The verse ends with a rhetorical invitation to reflect on history: 'so see how was the end of the corrupters,' pointing to the destruction of Pharaoh and his people as a historical fact and moral lesson. This serves as a warning to the Quraysh and to all who reject prophetic guidance - that worldly power and arrogance in the face of divine truth inevitably lead to downfall, reinforcing the Qur'an's recurring theme that corruption (fasad) on earth, especially moral and spiritual corruption through rejecting truth, brings about inevitable consequences as part of God's moral order governing history.

translation: And Moses said, 'O Pharaoh, indeed I am a messenger from the Lord of the worlds.'
interpretation: This verse marks the beginning of Moses' direct confrontation with Pharaoh, establishing the fundamental theme of prophetic mission versus worldly tyranny. By addressing Pharaoh—who claimed divinity and absolute authority over Egypt—with the declaration that he is sent by 'the Lord of the worlds' (Rabb al-'Alamin), Moses immediately challenges the very foundation of Pharaoh's claimed power. The phrase 'Lord of the worlds' is significant because it asserts a universal sovereignty that transcends and supersedes any earthly ruler's claimed dominion, including Pharaoh's self-proclaimed godhood over Egypt. This moment represents the archetypal pattern found throughout the Quran of prophets confronting worldly power with divine truth, emphasizing that true authority belongs to God alone, not to kings or rulers no matter how absolute their earthly control may seem. Moses' courage in making this declaration despite the obvious power imbalance—a former fugitive addressing the most powerful ruler of his time—illustrates the Quranic theme that reliance on divine backing gives believers strength to speak truth to power regardless of worldly consequences.

translation: Bound [by duty] to say nothing about Allah except the truth. I have come to you with clear evidence from your Lord, so send with me the Children of Israel.
interpretation: This verse is part of Moses' declaration to Pharaoh, establishing the ethical foundation of his prophetic mission. By affirming that he is duty-bound to speak only truth regarding Allah, Moses distinguishes his message from mere personal ambition or political maneuvering, grounding his authority in divine integrity rather than worldly power. The mention of 'clear evidence' (bayyinah) refers to the miraculous signs given to him, intended to validate his claim to prophethood before a skeptical and tyrannical ruler. His demand to release the Children of Israel is not merely a political request but a divine command to liberate an oppressed people from bondage, framing the confrontation with Pharaoh as a moral and spiritual struggle between truth and tyranny, with truthful speech serving as the weapon of the oppressed against the falsehood of unjust power.

translation: He [Pharaoh] said, 'If you have come with a sign, then produce it, if you are among the truthful.'
interpretation: This verse captures Pharaoh's challenge to Moses after Moses declared himself a messenger sent by the Lord of the worlds. Pharaoh's demand reflects both skepticism and a rhetorical trap—by framing the request conditionally ('if you have come with a sign'), he positions himself as the arbiter of truth, demanding empirical proof while implicitly doubting Moses' claim. This moment establishes the pattern seen throughout the Qur'an where prophets are asked for miraculous validation by those in power who resist their message. Pharaoh's response also reveals the nature of worldly authority confronting divine revelation: rather than engaging with the moral or spiritual content of Moses' call, Pharaoh reduces the test of truth to a demand for a spectacle, setting the stage for the subsequent miracles (the staff becoming a serpent, the hand turning white) that follow in the narrative. It underscores a recurring Qur'anic theme that tyrants and disbelievers often demand tangible proofs not out of genuine seeking of truth, but as a means to maintain control and dismiss the message, setting up their eventual downfall when the signs are indeed shown and they persist in rejection.

translation: So he threw down his staff, and behold, it was a serpent, manifest (for all to see).
interpretation: This verse recounts the moment Moses, before Pharaoh's court, cast down his staff as proof of his prophethood, and it transformed into a real, unmistakable serpent. The word 'mubin' (manifest/clear) emphasizes that this was not an illusion or trick but an undeniable, visible miracle meant to confront Pharaoh's claims of divinity and to validate Moses as a true messenger of God. This moment represents a direct divine intervention that overturns the natural order to demonstrate God's power exceeding human and even magical capabilities, setting the stage for the subsequent confrontation with Pharaoh's magicians. The miracle serves as a sign of truth that even skilled sorcerers would later recognize as beyond their own craft, reinforcing the theme that divine signs surpass human artifice and that ultimate authority belongs to God alone, not earthly rulers.

translation: And he drew out his hand, and behold, it was white [radiant] to the observers.
interpretation: This verse describes one of the two primary miraculous signs given to Prophet Musa (Moses) by Allah to demonstrate his prophethood to Pharaoh and his court. When Musa withdrew his hand from his garment (or from under his arm), it shone with a brilliant white light, unrelated to any disease like leprosy, but as a pure divine sign. This miracle, alongside the staff turning into a serpent, served as tangible proof of divine support for Musa's mission, overwhelming the sorcerers and officials of Pharaoh's court who were accustomed to evaluating feats of magic and illusion. The radiant hand symbolizes the purity and truth of prophetic revelation cutting through worldly power and deception, showing that Allah's signs transcend human trickery and cannot be replicated by ordinary means.

translation: The chiefs/nobles of Pharaoh's people said, 'Indeed, this is a learned magician.'
interpretation: This verse describes the reaction of Pharaoh's ruling elite upon witnessing the miraculous sign shown by Prophet Musa (Moses) when his staff turned into a serpent. Rather than acknowledging the possibility of divine truth, the nobles immediately sought to dismiss and rationalize the miracle by categorizing it as sorcery, something familiar and explainable within their own frame of reference, since magic was highly esteemed and practiced in Pharaonic Egypt. By calling Musa 'a learned magician' ('alim), they simultaneously acknowledged his extraordinary skill while denying any prophetic or divine significance to his actions. This reflects a recurring Quranic theme of how those in positions of power and privilege often react to divine truth with denial and deflection when it threatens their authority and established order, preferring familiar explanations over confronting uncomfortable spiritual realities that would require them to change their status quo.

translation: He wants to drive you out of your land, so what do you advise?
interpretation: This verse depicts the words of Pharaoh's chiefs and advisers to him regarding Moses (peace be upon him), warning that Moses' growing influence and his call to the truth posed a threat to their authority and homeland. They frame Moses' mission not as a matter of truth versus falsehood, but as a political and territorial threat, urging Pharaoh to consult his council on how to respond. This reflects a common tactic of oppressive rulers throughout history: deflecting from the substance of a prophet's message by recasting it as a danger to power, land, and social order, thereby rallying support through fear rather than engaging with the truth itself. It also shows the collective decision-making of tyrannical regimes, where the ruler consults his inner circle to maintain control and suppress dissent.

translation: They said, 'Put him off, and his brother, and send among the cities gatherers,'
interpretation: This verse depicts the response of Pharaoh's council of nobles after witnessing the miraculous sign Moses presented (his staff transforming into a serpent). Rather than acknowledging the sign's divine origin, they counseled Pharaoh to delay confronting Moses and his brother Aaron directly. Instead, they advised mobilizing messengers to summon skilled magicians from across the cities of Egypt to challenge Moses, believing that his miracle could be matched or discredited through sorcery. This reveals the strategic thinking of worldly power when confronted with divine truth: rather than submit or reflect, those invested in maintaining the status quo seek to neutralize the threat through competition and spectacle, reducing a sign of God to a mere contest of tricks. It also shows how Pharaoh's court, despite being alarmed by Moses's sign, remained committed to opposing him through calculated political and social maneuvering, setting the stage for the dramatic confrontation between the magicians and Moses that would ultimately vindicate the truth of his message.

translation: They will bring to you every skilled sorcerer.
interpretation: This verse occurs within the narrative of Moses and Pharaoh, spoken by Pharaoh's counselors advising him on how to confront Moses after witnessing the miraculous signs of his staff and hand. Rather than acknowledging the possibility of divine truth, Pharaoh's court resorts to worldly strategy, suggesting that Moses' miracles could be countered by assembling the most expert magicians in the land. This reflects a broader theme in the Qur'an about the arrogance of worldly power confronting divine truth—Pharaoh and his advisors assume that Moses' sign is merely a clever trick of sorcery, something that can be matched or outdone by human skill. The irony embedded in this response is profound: by gathering the greatest sorcerers to compete with Moses, Pharaoh inadvertently sets the stage for an even greater demonstration of God's power, as the very magicians he employs will later recognize the truth of Moses' message and submit to it. This moment in the story underscores the Qur'anic motif that human cunning and worldly expertise are ultimately powerless against divine will, and that those most skilled in deception can become among the first to recognize and embrace truth when confronted with it directly.

translation: And the magicians came to Pharaoh. They said, 'Indeed, for us is a reward if we are the predominant [winners]?'
interpretation: This verse highlights the transactional and worldly mindset of the magicians whom Pharaoh had summoned to confront Prophet Moses. Before committing to the contest, their primary concern was material compensation and status, revealing that their motivation was rooted in worldly gain and ambition rather than any true conviction or interest in truth. This sets up a dramatic contrast with their later transformation: after witnessing the undeniable truth of Moses's miracle, these same magicians would abandon their mercenary stance entirely, submitting to faith in the Lord of Moses and Aaron even at the cost of their lives under Pharaoh's threatened punishment. The verse thus serves as a narrative pivot, illustrating how sincere encounter with divine truth can transform people who initially approached matters of faith and falsehood merely as a means to earthly reward and recognition.

translation: He said, "Yes, and indeed you will be among those brought near [to me]."
interpretation: This verse occurs in the story of Pharaoh and the magicians in Surat al-A'raf/ash-Shu'ara. The magicians, before confronting Moses, asked Pharaoh whether they would receive a reward if they prevailed. Pharaoh answered 'Yes' and promised them not merely payment but elevated status—being counted among those close to him, his inner circle of trusted courtiers. This reveals Pharaoh's strategy of using worldly incentives—wealth, status, and proximity to power—to secure loyalty and motivate the magicians to perform their utmost against Moses. It highlights the contrast between the fleeting, worldly rewards offered by tyrannical power and the eternal truth represented by Moses' miracle, foreshadowing the magicians' sudden conversion once they recognized that truth, at which point they abandoned Pharaoh's promised nearness for the far greater prize of nearness to God through faith.

translation: They said, 'O Moses, either you throw [your staff], or we will be the ones to throw.'
interpretation: This verse captures a pivotal moment of confrontation between Prophet Moses and Pharaoh's sorcerers. The magicians, confident in their skills and numbers, extend an offer of politeness or challenge to Moses, giving him the choice of who goes first. This seemingly courteous gesture actually reveals their arrogance and certainty in their own abilities, as they believed their tricks and illusions would overwhelm Moses before an audience. The moment sets the stage for a divine demonstration of truth over falsehood, as Moses, through God's command, would ultimately show that his staff's transformation into a real serpent was genuine prophetic miracle, not mere sorcery, thereby exposing the limits of human trickery against divine power. This episode underscores a broader Quranic theme: worldly power and skill, no matter how impressive, cannot stand against divine truth when God wills to manifest it.

translation: He [Moses] said, 'Throw [what you will throw].' And when they threw, they bewitched the eyes of the people and struck fear into them, and they produced a great [feat of] magic.
interpretation: This verse depicts the pivotal moment in the contest between Prophet Moses and Pharaoh's magicians. Moses, instructed by God, invites the magicians to demonstrate their skills first, displaying confidence and divine backing rather than fear. When the magicians cast down their ropes and staffs, the illusion was so convincing that it appeared the objects had transformed into moving serpents, deceiving the onlookers' perception and instilling awe and terror in the crowd. The phrase 'they bewitched the eyes of the people' indicates that the magic affected perception and psychology rather than actual physical reality—it was sophisticated illusion and sleight of hand rather than genuine transformation of matter, which Islamic theology maintains only God can truly perform. This sets the stage for the subsequent miracle of Moses's staff, which, by God's command, swallows up their illusions, demonstrating the superiority of divine truth over human trickery and showing that what appears overwhelming and 'great' in human terms is powerless before God's authority.

translation: And We inspired Moses: 'Throw your staff.' And at once it swallowed up what they were falsifying.
interpretation: This verse recounts the climactic moment in the contest between Moses and Pharaoh's sorcerers. After the magicians had cast down their ropes and staffs, creating an illusion of moving serpents through sorcery that captivated and deceived the onlookers, God commanded Moses to throw his own staff. The staff miraculously transformed into a real serpent and consumed all the illusory creations of the magicians. The word 'ya'fikun' (what they were falsifying/fabricating) emphasizes that the magic was mere deception and trickery, not genuine transformation, contrasting sharply with the divine miracle given to Moses. This instant and decisive act demonstrated the superiority of divine truth over human deception and magic, and it served as the turning point that led the sorcerers themselves to recognize the authenticity of Moses's miracle, ultimately causing them to believe in the God of Moses and Aaron despite Pharaoh's threats. The verse illustrates a recurring Quranic theme: that falsehood, no matter how skillfully presented, is ultimately powerless against truth when God wills to make truth manifest.

translation: So the truth was established, and what they were doing was nullified.
interpretation: This verse refers to the moment when Moses cast down his staff before Pharaoh's sorcerers, and it miraculously swallowed up their illusions. The 'truth' here signifies the manifest sign of God's power through Moses, which immediately exposed and invalidated the false magic performed by Pharaoh's magicians. This moment represents the triumph of divine truth over deception and falsehood—no matter how elaborate or convincing human trickery may appear, it collapses instantly in the face of genuine divine reality. The verse illustrates a broader principle in the Qur'an: falsehood (batil) is inherently fragile and temporary, destined to be nullified when confronted with truth (haqq), regardless of how much effort or skill was invested in constructing it.

translation: So they [Pharaoh and his sorcerers] were defeated there, and they turned back humiliated.
interpretation: This verse concludes the dramatic confrontation between Prophet Musa (Moses) and Pharaoh's magicians. After the magicians cast down their ropes and staffs, which appeared through sorcery to be moving serpents, Musa threw down his staff which became a real serpent and swallowed their illusions. This verse declares the outcome: the magicians and Pharaoh's cause were decisively defeated, and they returned in disgrace and humiliation. The defeat carries deep symbolic significance - it represents the triumph of divine truth over human trickery and falsehood, showing that no amount of worldly power, skill, or deception can prevail against God's truth. Notably, this public humiliation of Pharaoh's power before his own court led the magicians themselves to recognize the truth and fall into prostration, believing in the Lord of Musa and Harun, despite Pharaoh's threats of brutal punishment. The verse thus marks a turning point where apparent worldly authority is shown to be powerless against divine signs, and where sincere seekers of truth (the magicians) recognize reality even when it means abandoning their former positions and facing mortal danger.

translation: And the magicians were cast down, prostrating themselves.
interpretation: This verse depicts the dramatic turning point in the confrontation between Moses and Pharaoh's magicians. After witnessing Moses' staff miraculously overcome their illusions, the magicians—who were experts in their craft and would have recognized true divine power versus mere trickery—immediately recognized that what they witnessed was beyond human sorcery. Their sudden, involuntary prostration ('ulqiya' implying they were 'cast down' almost against their will, overwhelmed by the truth) signifies the overpowering nature of divine truth when it is directly witnessed. This moment illustrates that true faith can strike even hardened hearts instantaneously when confronted with undeniable truth, regardless of one's prior position or profession. The magicians, who had just moments before been competing against Moses for Pharaoh's favor, instantly abandoned worldly allegiance and status for recognition of the one true God, demonstrating that sincere recognition of truth transcends pride, fear of authority, and self-interest.

translation: They said, 'We believe in the Lord of the worlds.'
interpretation: This verse captures the pivotal moment when Pharaoh's magicians, having witnessed the miraculous power of Moses' staff overcoming their sorcery, immediately recognized divine truth and submitted to it. Their declaration represents an instantaneous and complete transformation of heart—they had been summoned by Pharaoh to defeat Moses and uphold his authority, yet upon seeing undeniable truth, they abandoned worldly loyalty, status, and the fear of Pharaoh's wrath without hesitation. This moment illustrates the Qur'anic theme that true faith is recognized by the heart when confronted with clear signs (ayat) of God, transcending social position, self-interest, or prior allegiance. Their swift conversion, despite knowing it would provoke Pharaoh's brutal punishment (as follow-up verses describe), exemplifies sincere faith that prioritizes truth over safety and worldly consequence, serving as a powerful model of courage and conviction in acknowledging the Lord of all creation once truth becomes manifest.

translation: The Lord of Moses and Aaron.
interpretation: This phrase is spoken by the magicians of Pharaoh's court after they witnessed Moses' staff miraculously overcome their sorcery. Falling down in prostration, they declared their belief in 'the Lord of the worlds, the Lord of Moses and Aaron.' By specifying 'the Lord of Moses and Aaron,' they clarified that their faith was not in some vague or Pharaoh's claimed divinity, but specifically in the one true God who sent Moses and Aaron as His messengers. This declaration represents a dramatic reversal: those who were assembled to support Pharaoh against Moses instantly recognized divine truth when confronted with genuine miraculous power versus their own magical tricks. Their immediate and unwavering conversion, despite Pharaoh's subsequent threats of severe punishment (cutting off hands and feet, crucifixion), demonstrates the overwhelming nature of truth when directly witnessed, and foreshadows how worldly power structures crumble before divine truth. The specificity of naming Moses and Aaron also affirms the legitimacy of their prophethood against Pharaoh's claims to supreme authority.

translation: Pharaoh said, 'Have you believed in him before I gave you permission? Indeed, this is a plot you have devised in the city to drive out its people therefrom. But you are going to know.'
interpretation: This verse captures Pharaoh's furious reaction to the sudden conversion of his magicians, who, upon witnessing the miraculous truth of Moses' staff, immediately believed in the Lord of Moses and Aaron. Pharaoh's response reveals several dimensions of tyrannical power confronted by truth. First, he asserts his presumed authority over even matters of belief, demanding that faith itself require his permission—exposing the totalitarian nature of his rule, where he claims dominion not just over bodies but over souls and convictions. Second, unable to accept that genuine, spontaneous conviction could arise from witnessing divine truth, he resorts to conspiracy theory, accusing the magicians and Moses of staging an elaborate plot. This is a common psychological and political tactic of oppressive rulers: when truth undermines their authority, they reframe it as treachery or foreign collusion rather than confronting the possibility that they themselves are wrong. Pharaoh's claim that this was all a scheme 'to drive out its people' from the city reveals his paranoia about losing control over Egypt and its population, projecting his own fear of losing power onto his opponents. Finally, his closing threat—'you are going to know'—foreshadows the brutal punishment he intends to inflict (cutting off hands and feet, crucifixion, as described in parallel verses), demonstrating that tyrants, when their authority is challenged by truth, resort to violence and intimidation rather than reason. The verse illustrates the futility of worldly power against sincere faith, as the magicians, despite knowing the horrific consequences, remain steadfast, setting up a dramatic contrast between Pharaoh's hollow threats and the magicians' newfound unshakeable conviction.

translation: I will surely cut off your hands and your feet on opposite sides, then I will surely crucify you all.
interpretation: This verse records the furious threat of Pharaoh against the sorcerers who, after witnessing the miracle of Moses's staff overcoming their magic, immediately fell down in prostration and declared their faith in the Lord of Moses and Aaron. Enraged at this sudden and public defection from his authority, Pharaoh accused them of having conspired with Moses beforehand and vowed the most brutal punishment—amputating their limbs from opposite sides (right hand with left foot, or vice versa) and then crucifying them all. The episode illustrates the theme of tyrannical power confronted by sincere faith: the sorcerers, who moments before had served Pharaoh's court, now fear God more than they fear the king's threats of mutilation and death. Their response (recorded in the following verses) that they do not mind, since they will return to their Lord, exemplifies the Qur'anic motif that true conviction transforms fear of worldly punishment into steadfastness, showing that genuine faith can overturn the apparent order of power—where the ruler who claims divinity is powerless to shake the conviction of those who have truly submitted to God.

translation: They said: 'Indeed, to our Lord we will return.'
interpretation: This verse is part of the story of the magicians who, after witnessing the truth of Moses' message, believed in the One God despite Pharaoh's threats of brutal punishment including crucifixion and amputation of limbs. Their response reflects a profound spiritual transformation and fearlessness in the face of worldly power. By declaring that they will ultimately return to their Lord, they express their acceptance of death as merely a transition back to God, not an end to be feared. This statement embodies the Islamic theological principle that earthly life is temporary and that true believers find their ultimate security and identity in their relationship with the Divine rather than in physical safety or worldly status. Their courage stemmed from a reordering of priorities—having tasted spiritual truth, they no longer feared Pharaoh's threats, since they understood that their essential journey was toward God regardless of what happened to their bodies in this world. This verse illustrates how genuine faith can transform fear of death into acceptance, since death becomes reframed not as annihilation but as a homecoming to one's Creator.

translation: And you do not resent us except that we believed in the signs of our Lord when they came to us. Our Lord, pour upon us patience and let us die as Muslims (those submitting to You).
interpretation: This verse records the declaration of the magicians of Pharaoh after they witnessed the truth of Moses' miracle and immediately believed, despite Pharaoh's threats of torture and death. Their statement reveals the nature of true faith: it is not contingent on worldly safety or benefit, but is a response to recognizing divine truth once it becomes manifest. They acknowledge that their only 'crime' in Pharaoh's eyes is belief itself—there is no other wrongdoing being punished, only conviction being persecuted. Their prayer that follows shows the proper response of a believer facing persecution: not a plea for rescue from suffering, but a request for the inner strength (patience/steadfastness) to endure it without wavering, and ultimately for a death that seals their submission to God. This encapsulates a core Qur'anic theme that sudden, sincere faith—even arising late in life and even among those previously serving tyranny—can transform a person completely, making them willing to face death rather than renounce truth. Their example also serves as a rebuke to Pharaoh's claim of absolute authority, demonstrating that genuine conviction cannot be coerced by power, and that the human soul's recognition of truth transcends fear of worldly punishment.

translation: And the chiefs of Pharaoh's people said, 'Will you leave Moses and his people to spread corruption in the land and abandon you and your gods?' He said, 'We will slaughter their sons and spare their women, and indeed, we are dominant over them.'
interpretation: This verse depicts the escalation of tyranny and fear among Pharaoh's ruling elite as Moses' message began to threaten their political and religious authority. The chiefs' concern was not merely about Moses personally, but about the broader social and ideological 'corruption' (fasad) his monotheistic message represented to their established order of idol worship and absolute rule. Pharaoh's response—renewing the policy of killing male infants while keeping females alive—reveals a strategy of domination rooted in fear and insecurity rather than genuine strength. The repetition of this infanticide policy (previously used against the Israelites before Moses' birth) shows how oppressive power structures resort to extreme violence when their authority feels threatened by liberating ideas. Pharaoh's closing assertion 'we are dominant over them' reflects the hubris of tyrannical power, asserting control through fear and bloodshed rather than legitimate authority. The verse ultimately illustrates how entrenched systems of oppression perceive truth and justice as existential threats, and how they mobilize violence against the vulnerable to maintain their grip on power, setting the stage for the divine intervention that would later liberate the Israelites from this persecution.

translation: Moses said to his people, 'Seek help in Allah and be patient. Indeed, the earth belongs to Allah; He gives it as a heritage to whom He wills of His servants. And the final outcome is for the righteous.'
interpretation: This verse captures Moses' response to the Israelites when they grew fearful and despondent under the oppression of Pharaoh, complaining that they had been persecuted both before and after Moses' arrival. Rather than offering a simple reassurance, Moses redirects their focus toward two spiritual disciplines: seeking divine help and cultivating patience (sabr). These are presented not as passive resignation but as active postures of faith during trial. The verse then grounds this counsel in a theological truth—that sovereignty over the earth belongs to God alone, not to Pharaoh or any worldly power, however entrenched it may seem. Dominion and inheritance of the land are gifts God bestows according to His own wisdom and will, not according to human might or apparent permanence of power structures. This serves as a direct refutation of Pharaoh's claim to supreme authority and a reminder that tyranny, however powerful, is temporary and subject to divine will. The closing phrase, 'the final outcome is for the righteous (muttaqin),' introduces a moral and eschatological principle that runs throughout the Qur'an: history bends toward justice for those who maintain piety and God-consciousness, even when present circumstances suggest otherwise. This teaches that true security lies not in immediate victory or worldly comfort but in steadfast faith and ethical integrity, trusting that ultimate vindication belongs to those who remain devoted to God regardless of present suffering.

translation: They said, 'We were harmed before you came to us and after you came to us.' He said, 'It may be that your Lord will destroy your enemy and make you successors in the land, so that He may observe how you act.'
interpretation: This verse recounts the exchange between Moses and the Israelites, who had suffered under Pharaoh's oppression both before and after Moses's arrival with his message. Their complaint reflects the natural human tendency to measure the success of a mission by immediate relief from suffering, and their disappointment when persecution persisted or even intensified following the call to faith. Moses's response reframes their perspective: deliverance and justice are in God's hands and unfold according to His timing and wisdom, not according to human expectation of instant results. The phrase 'it may be' (asa) indicates hope grounded in trust in divine providence rather than a guaranteed timeline. Crucially, Moses links the promise of future power—becoming successors (khulafa) in the land—not to an end in itself, but to a test: 'so that He may observe how you act.' This establishes a recurring Qur'anic principle that worldly authority and inheritance of the land are trusts given by God, contingent upon moral conduct, gratitude, and justice, not rewards for passive suffering. The verse thus teaches patience in adversity, trust in divine justice despite delayed outcomes, and the understanding that power, when granted, carries with it accountability rather than mere entitlement.

translation: And indeed, We seized the people of Pharaoh with years of drought and a shortage of fruits, so that they might take heed.
interpretation: This verse describes how God tested Pharaoh and his people with hardship—prolonged famine and scarcity of produce—as a form of warning and admonition before the more severe plagues that would follow. The purpose of such trials, as stated in the verse, was not merely punitive but pedagogical: 'so that they might take heed' (la'allahum yadhakkarun). It reflects a recurring Qur'anic theme that God afflicts nations with hardship, scarcity, and economic distress as signs meant to prompt reflection, humility, and turning back to Him, rather than as purely retributive acts. The tragedy of Pharaoh's people is that, despite experiencing these tangible signs of divine power and warning through their suffering, they failed to draw the appropriate lesson, persisting instead in arrogance and denial, which set the stage for their eventual destruction.

translation: But when good came to them, they said, 'This is for us (we deserve it).' And if evil befell them, they attributed it to the ill omen of Moses and those with him. Unquestionably, their fate (omen) is with Allah, but most of them do not know.
interpretation: This verse addresses the psychological pattern of Pharaoh's people, who attributed prosperity to their own merit while blaming Moses and his followers for any misfortune, treating them as a bad omen. The Qur'an corrects this superstitious and self-serving worldview by asserting that all outcomes—good and bad—originate from Allah's decree, not from the presence of a righteous person or group. This reflects a broader critique of human tendency to deny personal or collective responsibility, instead scapegoating others for calamities while claiming credit for blessings. The verse highlights the ignorance ('la ya'lamun') of those who fail to recognize divine causation behind all events, revealing their flawed theology that mixes superstition with selective acknowledgment of divine will only when convenient for their egos.

translation: And they said, 'Whatever sign you bring us with to bewitch us with it, we will not be believers in you.'
interpretation: This verse depicts the obstinate response of Pharaoh's people to Moses, illustrating a pattern of willful disbelief that persists regardless of the evidence presented. By declaring in advance that any miracle would be dismissed as mere sorcery, they reveal that their rejection was not based on a rational evaluation of proof but on an entrenched refusal to submit to truth that threatened their power and way of life. This reflects a broader Qur'anic theme: that disbelief is often rooted not in a lack of evidence but in pride, vested interest, and a hardened heart that predetermines its conclusions before encountering any sign. The verse serves as a warning about the nature of denial—when a people commit to rejecting truth regardless of what proof is shown, no amount of miracles or signs will penetrate their resistance, placing the moral responsibility for their disbelief squarely upon their own choice rather than any deficiency in the message or the messenger.

translation: So We sent upon them the flood, the locusts, the lice, the frogs, and the blood as distinct signs, but they were arrogant and were a criminal people.
interpretation: This verse refers to the plagues sent upon Pharaoh and his people as recounted in the story of Moses. Each affliction—flood, locusts, lice, frogs, and blood—was a clear, distinguishable sign meant to demonstrate God's power and to prompt repentance and belief. The term 'mufassalat' (distinct/detailed) emphasizes that these were not random calamities but deliberate, separated signs, each serving as a warning and an opportunity for reflection. Despite the clarity of these signs, Pharaoh's people responded with arrogance (istikbar), refusing to acknowledge the truth or change their ways. The verse concludes by characterizing them as a 'criminal people' (qawman mujrimin), indicating that their rejection of clear divine signs, compounded by their pride, constituted a moral and spiritual transgression. This illustrates a recurring Quranic theme: that the rejection of manifest truth, especially when compounded by arrogance, leads to a state of sin and estrangement from God's guidance, ultimately resulting in divine punishment.

translation: And when the punishment fell upon them, they said, 'O Moses, call upon your Lord for us by whatever covenant He has made with you. If you remove this punishment from us, we will surely believe you, and we will surely send with you the Children of Israel.'
interpretation: This verse reveals the psychology of Pharaoh and his people when confronted with divine punishment (one of the plagues sent upon Egypt). Their appeal to Moses demonstrates a pattern of behavior common to those who reject faith only to turn to God in moments of desperation and crisis, making promises of belief and obedience that are contingent on relief from suffering rather than genuine conviction. The phrase 'by whatever covenant He has made with you' acknowledges Moses's special relationship with God even while they continue to resist true submission. This sets up the recurring theme in the Exodus narrative of broken promises—for as subsequent verses show, once the punishment was lifted, Pharaoh and his people reverted to their disbelief and oppression. The verse serves as a timeless illustration of insincere faith born of fear rather than sincere acknowledgment of truth, a faith that dissolves once the immediate danger passes, contrasting with the steadfast faith that Islam calls believers to maintain in both hardship and ease.

translation: But when We removed the plague from them until a term which they were to reach, behold, they broke their word.
interpretation: This verse refers to Pharaoh and his people, who, when struck by various plagues as signs from God through Moses, would promise to believe and release the Israelites if the punishment were lifted. Yet each time God mercifully removed the affliction, they reverted to their arrogance and reneged on their promises. The verse illustrates a recurring pattern of human behavior wherein hardship prompts temporary sincerity or repentance, but ease and relief lead back to denial and treachery. It serves as a moral lesson about the fragility of faith that is motivated by fear of punishment rather than genuine conviction, and highlights the theme of broken covenants as a characteristic of those who resist divine guidance despite witnessing clear signs.

translation: So We took retribution upon them and drowned them in the sea because they denied Our signs and were heedless of them.
interpretation: This verse refers to the fate of Pharaoh and his people, who were destroyed by drowning as a consequence of their persistent rejection of the signs and miracles sent by God through Moses. The verse emphasizes two intertwined causes for their punishment: their active denial (takdhib) of divine signs despite witnessing them, and their heedlessness (ghafla), a deeper spiritual negligence that prevented them from reflecting on and internalizing the truth those signs pointed to. This pairing suggests that destruction came not merely from intellectual disbelief but from a willful inattentiveness to divine guidance, a moral failing of the heart as much as the mind. The sea, which had earlier served as a path of deliverance for Moses and the believers, becomes here an instrument of divine justice, illustrating the Qur'anic theme that the same signs and elements of creation can serve as mercy for the faithful and retribution for the heedless rejecters. The verse thus serves as a warning to all who witness divine signs yet fail to engage with them seriously, suggesting that such heedlessness carries grave consequences.

translation: And We caused the people who had been oppressed to inherit the eastern parts of the land and the western parts thereof, which We had blessed. And the good word of your Lord was fulfilled for the Children of Israel because of what they had endured. And We destroyed what Pharaoh and his people had made and what they had erected.
interpretation: This verse speaks to a divine principle of justice that transcends a single historical moment: the ultimate vindication of the oppressed through steadfast patience (sabr). The Israelites, who endured generations of persecution under Pharaoh, are granted inheritance of the land in its entirety—east and west—symbolizing a complete and total reversal of their former powerlessness. The phrase 'the good word of your Lord' refers to God's prior promise of deliverance and establishment, now fulfilled precisely because the people persevered through hardship rather than despairing or abandoning faith. This links endurance directly to divine reward, suggesting that suffering under tyranny, when met with patience and trust in God, becomes the very condition for eventual empowerment. Simultaneously, the destruction of Pharaoh's constructions and achievements—the material monuments of his power and arrogance—demonstrates that worldly dominance built on oppression is inherently impermanent before divine will. The verse thus establishes a paradigm repeated throughout the Quran: tyrannical power structures, however seemingly invincible, are temporary, while the patient endurance of the oppressed aligns with a cosmic justice that ultimately restores balance, making the last first and granting inheritance of blessed lands to those who were once powerless.

translation: And We brought the Children of Israel across the sea, and they came upon a people devoted to idols they had. They said, 'O Moses, make for us a god just as they have gods.' He said, 'Indeed, you are a people behaving in ignorance.'
interpretation: This verse captures a striking moment of spiritual regression immediately following a monumental act of divine deliverance. Having just witnessed the miraculous parting of the sea and their salvation from Pharaoh's tyranny—an event that should have cemented their faith in the One God who saved them—the Israelites encounter an idolatrous community and immediately request that Moses fashion for them a similar object of worship. This reveals the deep psychological pull of visible, tangible religion over abstract monotheism; despite having experienced God's power directly, they still crave an idol they can see and touch, mistaking outward religious practices of other nations for genuine spiritual superiority. Moses's sharp response—labeling them as 'a people behaving in ignorance'—is not merely a rebuke of foolishness but a condemnation of a deeper spiritual blindness: the inability to recognize that true divinity cannot be reduced to a crafted object, and that imitating the customs of others without understanding their meaning represents a regression into pre-rational, instinctive behavior rather than the elevated consciousness that monotheism demands. This episode serves as a timeless commentary on human nature's tendency to conflate faith with ritualistic mimicry, and how quickly liberation from physical bondage can be followed by a relapse into spiritual bondage if the deeper lessons of divine encounter are not internalized.

translation: Indeed, these [people] - destroyed is that in which they are engaged, and worthless is that which they have been doing.
interpretation: This verse comes from the story of Prophet Musa (Moses) and his people, who, after witnessing great miracles, encountered a community devoted to idol worship. When the Israelites asked Musa to make them an idol like the one worshipped by this community, he rebuked them and pointed to this truth: that the religious practices and beliefs of the idolaters were utterly futile and doomed to ruin. The verse establishes a foundational theological principle in the Qur'an - that worship directed at anything other than God is inherently without substance or lasting value, regardless of how elaborate or sincere such devotion might appear. The destruction mentioned is not necessarily immediate physical destruction but refers to the ultimate spiritual and existential emptiness of such practices - they yield no true benefit, no salvation, no lasting reality, because they are directed at powerless objects or false conceptions rather than at the one true source of existence and sustenance. This serves as a warning against following the practices of others merely because they appear established or widespread, urging believers instead to critically evaluate the object and validity of worship itself.

translation: He [Moses] said, "Is it other than Allah I should seek for you as a god, while He has favored you above all the worlds?"
interpretation: This verse records Moses' rebuke to the Children of Israel after they witnessed a people devoted to idol worship and asked Moses to make for them a god like it, shortly after their deliverance from Pharaoh and crossing the sea. Moses' response expresses astonishment and reproach, reminding them of the favor Allah had shown them—rescuing them from oppression, granting them signs and blessings above other nations of their time. The rhetorical question underscores the absurdity and ingratitude of seeking another object of worship besides the very God who had elevated and distinguished them. It serves as a broader lesson on the human tendency toward spiritual forgetfulness even after experiencing manifest divine favor, and establishes the principle that true gratitude for blessings is inseparable from exclusive devotion to the One who bestows them.

translation: And [recall] when We saved you from the people of Pharaoh, who afflicted you with the worst torment, slaughtering your sons and sparing your women. And in that was a great trial from your Lord.
interpretation: This verse recalls the historical suffering of the Children of Israel under Pharaoh's oppression as a reminder of God's favor in delivering them, while also framing their persecution as a divine test. The 'trial' (bala') is双-edged: it was a hardship for the oppressed, but also a test of their faith and gratitude once liberated. By invoking this memory, the verse calls on the Israelites (and by extension all believers) to recognize God's power to save the afflicted and to respond with gratitude and faithfulness, rather than the disobedience and forgetfulness that the subsequent verses in this surah go on to describe.

translation: And We appointed for Moses thirty nights and completed them with ten, so the appointed time of his Lord was completed as forty nights. And Moses said to his brother Aaron: 'Take my place among my people, act righteously, and do not follow the way of those who cause corruption.'
interpretation: This verse recounts the period during which Moses was called to Mount Sinai to receive divine revelation and commune with God, a span extended from an initial thirty nights to forty, symbolizing a complete and sacred cycle of spiritual preparation and purification before receiving the Torah. In entrusting leadership to his brother Aaron during his absence, Moses demonstrates the Islamic principle of ensuring continuity of righteous governance and communal order even when a leader is temporarily absent. His instruction to Aaron—to act rightly and avoid the path of corrupters—underscores the perpetual struggle between righteousness (islah) and corruption (ifsad) that exists within every community, and the responsibility of leaders to actively resist moral and social decay rather than passively allow it to spread. This moment also sets the stage for the subsequent narrative of the Israelites' worship of the golden calf, highlighting how quickly a community can fall into corruption without vigilant and righteous leadership, even when warned and prepared in advance.

translation: And when Moses came at Our appointed time and his Lord spoke to him, he said, "My Lord, show me [Yourself] that I may look at You." [Allah] said, "You will not see Me, but look at the mountain; if it remains in its place, then you will see Me." But when his Lord appeared to the mountain, He made it collapse into dust, and Moses fell unconscious. And when he awoke, he said, "Exalted are You! I repent to You, and I am the first of the believers."
interpretation: This verse conveys the profound truth that direct, unmediated vision of the Divine Essence is beyond the capacity of created beings in this worldly life, even for a prophet as exalted as Moses. Moses's request stemmed from intense longing and love for closeness to God, not doubt or arrogance. God's response—directing him to the mountain—serves as a teaching device: the mountain, a massive and seemingly permanent fixture of creation, crumbles instantly upon the mere manifestation (tajalli) of divine glory, demonstrating the infinite gulf between Creator and creation. Moses's fainting represents the overwhelming of human faculties when confronted with even an indirect manifestation of divine power, let alone the Essence itself. His recovery and immediate declaration of God's transcendence (subhanak) and repentance signifies his acknowledgment of having asked for something beyond human capacity, and his humility in accepting the limits placed upon creation. His proclamation of being "the first of believers" affirms his renewed faith and submission, having directly experienced the reality of divine majesty and the impossibility of perceiving God as one perceives created things. The verse ultimately teaches believers about the nature of divine transcendence (tanzih), the appropriate etiquette in seeking nearness to God, and that true vision of God, if granted at all, belongs to the Hereafter, not to this finite world.

translation: He [Allah] said: 'O Moses, I have chosen you above the people with My messages and with My speech, so take what I have given you and be among the grateful.'
interpretation: This verse marks the moment on Mount Sinai (Tur) when Allah honors Moses with a unique distinction among prophets: direct, unmediated speech from Allah, in addition to the messages and revelations given to him. The phrase 'I have chosen you above the people' signifies a special election for prophethood and for this singular honor of divine conversation, setting Moses apart even among other messengers who typically received revelation through an angel. The command to 'take what I have given you' refers to accepting the responsibility of prophethood, the Torah, and the mission to guide his people, while 'be among the grateful' establishes gratitude as the proper response to divine favor and honor. This teaches that such immense blessings carry with them an obligation of thankfulness, not merely in words but in fulfilling the duty entrusted. The verse also underscores a broader theological principle recognized in Islamic theology: that Allah's speech to Moses was a real, direct communication, which becomes foundational for understanding the nature of prophecy and revelation, and Moses is given the honorific title 'Kalim Allah' (the one who spoke with Allah) based on this verse.

translation: And We wrote for him upon the tablets [something] of all things - instruction and explanation for all things, [and said], 'Take hold of them with determination and order your people to take the best of it. I will show you the home of the defiantly disobedient.'
interpretation: This verse signifies the comprehensive nature of the revelation given to Moses, encompassing moral guidance, legal rulings, and wisdom for all aspects of life. The command to grasp the tablets 'with strength' implies steadfast commitment, seriousness, and earnest effort in upholding divine law, not merely passive acceptance. The instruction to Moses's people to adopt 'the best of it' suggests a principle of seeking the most excellent and beneficial interpretation or application of the teachings, encouraging believers to strive for moral excellence rather than settling for the minimum. The closing warning—that God will show them the fate of the defiantly disobedient—serves as a reminder that those who reject or distort divine guidance, favoring ease over righteousness, will witness the consequences of corruption and transgression, reinforcing the link between moral choice and ultimate outcome in both this world and the hereafter.

translation: I will turn away from My signs those who are arrogant upon the earth without right; and if they see every sign, they will not believe in it. And if they see the way of right conduct, they will not adopt it as a way; but if they see the way of error, they will adopt it as a way. That is because they denied Our signs and were heedless of them.
interpretation: This verse addresses the spiritual consequence of persistent arrogance and pride (takabbur) when it is unjustified—that is, pride not rooted in truth but in self-exaltation and rejection of divine guidance. God describes a kind of divine law of consequence: when people consistently reject truth out of haughtiness, He allows their hearts and perception to become veiled from recognizing further signs, not as an arbitrary punishment but as a natural result of their own choices. Their arrogance blinds them to reality—they see miracles, proofs, and signs of truth, yet their pride prevents belief; they see the path of guidance (rushd) but refuse it because it demands humility and submission, while they willingly follow the path of misguidance (ghayy) because it flatters their self-will. The verse closes by identifying the root cause: their denial of God's signs stemmed from heedlessness (ghaflah)—a willful inattentiveness to truth rather than an honest inability to perceive it. Thus, the verse teaches that spiritual blindness is often self-inflicted, born from ego and heedlessness, and that God's 'turning away' from such people is a mirror of their own turning away from Him.

translation: And those who deny Our signs and the meeting of the Hereafter - their deeds are rendered worthless. Will they be recompensed except for what they used to do?
interpretation: This verse establishes a moral principle about the relationship between belief and the efficacy of deeds.
