translation: He said, "O Noah, indeed he is not of your family; indeed, he is [one whose] work was other than righteous, so ask Me not for that about which you have no knowledge. Indeed, I advise you, lest you be among the ignorant."
interpretation: This verse addresses Noah's plea to save his son from the flood, with God clarifying that familial bonds of blood are not the ultimate criterion for belonging to the faithful community. True kinship in the sight of God is defined by righteousness and faith, not biological descent. The son's rejection of faith and his corrupt deeds severed him from being considered part of Noah's true 'family' in the spiritual and covenantal sense, despite the biological relationship. God's rebuke to Noah—though gentle, calling him by name with affection—serves as a lesson that prophets, despite their exalted station, must submit entirely to divine wisdom and refrain from questioning matters beyond their knowledge, even when driven by natural parental love and concern. This teaches the broader principle that submission to God's will must supersede personal attachments and incomplete human understanding, and that even the righteous must be humble enough to recognize the limits of their knowledge before God's omniscience.

translation: He said: 'My Lord, I seek refuge in You from asking You that of which I have no knowledge. And unless You forgive me and have mercy on me, I will be among the losers.'
interpretation: This verse depicts Prophet Nuh (Noah) after he pleaded with God on behalf of his son who drowned in the flood, not realizing his son's disbelief had severed the familial bond that would have warranted his salvation. Upon being corrected by God, Nuh immediately recognizes his error in questioning divine wisdom and judgment without full knowledge of the matter. His response models the proper posture of a believer before God: swift acknowledgment of human limitation, humility in the face of divine decree, and urgent seeking of forgiveness rather than self-justification. The verse teaches that even prophets can err in judgment when emotion (paternal love) clouds perception, but true righteousness lies in immediate repentance and submission to God's greater knowledge rather than persisting in one's own understanding. It also establishes a theological principle that one should not question or demand explanations for God's decisions in matters beyond human comprehension, and that salvation ultimately depends on divine mercy and forgiveness rather than one's own righteousness or lineage alone.

translation: It was said, 'O Noah, disembark in peace from Us, and blessings upon you and upon nations [descended] from those who are with you. But [there will be other] nations to whom We will grant enjoyment [for a time]; then a painful punishment from Us will touch them.'
interpretation: This verse marks the resolution of the story of Noah's flood, signifying divine mercy and the renewal of human civilization after the destruction of the disbelievers. The command to 'descend in peace' from God symbolizes a new covenant and a fresh start for humanity, with blessings extended not only to Noah but to future generations born from those who survived with him on the Ark. However, the verse also contains a sobering warning: among these future nations, some will be granted worldly prosperity and enjoyment as a temporary test, but this ease is not a sign of divine approval—rather, it is a deferred trial, and those who misuse this blessing by turning to arrogance, corruption, or disbelief will eventually face a painful punishment. This reflects a recurring Quranic theme that worldly comfort is not synonymous with righteousness, and that the patterns of destruction and mercy seen in Noah's time will echo through subsequent generations who similarly choose disbelief despite being given respite and provision.

translation: These are accounts of the unseen which We reveal to you [O Muhammad]; neither you nor your people knew them before this. So be patient; indeed, the [best] outcome is for the righteous.
interpretation: This verse comes at the conclusion of the story of Prophet Yusuf (Joseph) and serves as a direct address to Prophet Muhammad, affirming the divine source of his knowledge. Since he had no access to scripture, prior revelation, or historical learning about the detailed narrative of Yusuf and his brothers, the fact that he could recount it accurately is presented as evidence of genuine revelation (wahy) rather than human invention or borrowing from existing traditions. The verse also carries a pastoral and consoling function: by linking this proof of prophethood to a command for patience (fasbir), it draws a parallel between Yusuf's trials—betrayal by his brothers, enslavement, false accusation, imprisonment—and the hardships Muhammad faced from his own people in Mecca. The underlying message is that just as Yusuf's patience and steadfastness in the face of injustice ultimately led to vindication, honor, and reunion with his family, so too will Muhammad's patience in conveying the message be rewarded with eventual triumph. The closing phrase about the righteous (al-muttaqin) inheriting the good outcome (al-'aqibah) encapsulates a broader Quranic theme: history is not random but moves toward a moral resolution.wherein steadfast faith and God-consciousness are vindicated against arrogance and persecution.

translation: And to [the tribe of] 'Aad [We sent] their brother Hud. He said, 'O my people, worship Allah; you have no deity other than Him. You are not but inventors [of falsehood].'
interpretation: This verse recounts the mission of the prophet Hud to his own tribe, the 'Aad, emphasizing the pattern seen throughout the Qur'an of prophets being sent from within their own communities to call their people back to the worship of the one true God. Hud's declaration that 'you have no deity other than Him' establishes the core message of tawhid (the oneness of God) as the foundation of his prophetic mission. His accusation that the 'Aad are 'but inventors' refers to their fabrication of idols and false gods, implying that their polytheistic beliefs are human inventions rather than divinely sanctioned truths. This confrontation sets up the broader narrative of the 'Aad's subsequent rejection of Hud's message and the divine punishment that follows, serving as a cautionary tale about the consequences of arrogance and disbelief in the face of clear prophetic guidance. The verse also reinforces the Qur'anic theme that monotheism is the natural and original religion of humanity, with polytheism being a later corruption or invention by misguided peoples.

translation: O my people, I ask not of you for it any reward. My reward is only from the One who created me. Then will you not use reason?
interpretation: This verse reflects a recurring Qur'anic motif in which prophets assert the sincerity and selflessness of their mission. By declaring that he seeks no material compensation from his people, the prophet (here, Hud) removes any suspicion that his call to monotheism is motivated by personal gain, power, or wealth. This strengthens the credibility of his message, since a true messenger of God is driven by divine purpose rather than worldly interest. The phrase 'my reward is only upon the One who created me' emphasizes complete reliance on God alone, underscoring the relationship between creature and Creator as the ultimate source of guidance, sustenance, and justice. The closing rhetorical question, 'Will you not then reason?', is a challenge to the audience's intellect, implying that rejecting such a selfless and rational message is itself a failure of reason. It invites reflection on the authenticity of prophethood and situates true wisdom in recognizing sincerity, humility, and dependence on the Creator rather than in the pursuit of worldly incentives.

translation: And O my people, ask forgiveness of your Lord and then repent to Him; He will send [rain from] the sky upon you in showers and increase you in strength added to your strength. And do not turn away as criminals.
interpretation: This verse records the preaching of Prophet Hud to his people, the tribe of 'Ad, calling them to seek forgiveness and turn back to God in repentance. The promise of abundant rain and increased strength illustrates a key Quranic principle: that spiritual reform and material prosperity are interconnected, and that a community's righteousness directly affects the blessings bestowed upon it, such as sustenance and power. The call to not 'turn away as criminals' emphasizes that rejecting this message is not a neutral act but an act of active wrongdoing (ijram) against oneself and one's community, setting the stage for the consequences that befall those who persist in heedless rejection of divine guidance despite clear warning and the offer of mercy.

translation: They said, 'O Hud, you have not brought us any clear proof, and we will not abandon our gods on account of your word, nor will we believe in you.'
interpretation: This verse records the defiant response of the people of 'Ad to their prophet Hud, who called them away from idolatry to the worship of the one God. Their reply exemplifies the typical pattern of denial found throughout the Qur'an's prophetic narratives: a rejection of the messenger's credentials ('you have not brought us any clear proof'), an entrenched attachment to inherited ancestral customs and idols ('we will not abandon our gods'), and an outright refusal to believe regardless of argument or evidence. The demand for a 'clear proof' (bayyinah) reveals their unwillingness to accept the moral and rational force of Hud's preaching itself as sufficient evidence, insisting instead on some miraculous or tangible sign. Their stubborn loyalty to ancestral gods over reasoned appeal illustrates the Qur'an's broader critique of blind traditionalism (taqlid) that resists truth simply because it challenges inherited customs and social identity. The verse thus serves as a paradigm for human resistance to prophetic guidance, showing how pride, social conformity, and attachment to tradition can harden hearts against even sincere and reasonable calls to monotheism, foreshadowing the destruction that befalls 'Ad for their persistent rejection.

translation: They said: "We say nothing but that some of our gods have struck you with some evil (madness)." He said: "Indeed, I call Allah to witness, and bear witness yourselves, that I am free from whatever you associate [with Allah]."
interpretation: This verse captures a pivotal moment in the confrontation between the Prophet Hud and his people, the tribe of 'Aad. Faced with his unwavering call to abandon idol worship and return to the worship of the One God, his people resort to superstition and slander rather than rational engagement with his message—accusing him of being afflicted with madness by their own false deities. This reflects a common pattern in prophetic narratives throughout the Qur'an, where communities faced with uncomfortable truths dismiss the messenger through personal attacks rather than addressing the substance of the message. Hud's response is significant: he does not argue on their terms by debating the power of their idols, but instead makes a formal, solemn declaration calling Allah as witness and inviting his people themselves to witness his complete disassociation from their polytheistic practices. This is a legal and spiritual act of bara'ah (disavowal), establishing a clear boundary between monotheistic truth and the shirk (associating partners with God) of his people. The verse demonstrates the steadfastness required of those who call to truth in the face of ridicule and threats, showing that the proper response to baseless accusations is not to engage with their irrationality but to firmly and publicly affirm one's own position and innocence before God, leaving the judgment of such claims to a higher authority.

translation: ...besides Him. So plot against me, all of you together, and then give me no respite.
interpretation: This phrase is part of the Prophet Hud's declaration to his disbelieving people in Surah Hud. Having renounced their idols and declared his trust solely in God, Hud challenges his people and their false gods to do their worst against him without delay. This expresses the supreme confidence and fearlessness that comes from true reliance on God (tawakkul). By inviting all his opponents—human and the powerless idols they worship—to conspire against him immediately, Hud demonstrates that genuine faith eliminates fear of worldly powers, since ultimate control belongs to God alone, who grasps every creature by its forelock (a symbol of complete dominance). The verse underscores the Qur'anic theme that those who place their trust entirely in God need not fear the schemes of disbelievers, no matter how numerous or seemingly powerful, because divine protection renders human and false divine plots ultimately powerless.

translation: Indeed, I have put my trust in Allah, my Lord and your Lord. There is no creature but that He holds it by its forelock. Indeed, my Lord is on a straight path.
interpretation: This verse, spoken by the Prophet Hud to his people, expresses absolute reliance on God in the face of rejection and threats from his community. The declaration that Allah is 'my Lord and your Lord' emphasizes the shared sovereignty of God over believer and disbeliever alike, undermining any claim to power the idolaters might assert against him. The imagery of God holding every creature 'by its forelock' is a powerful metaphor for complete control and dominion—the forelock symbolizing a position of command, as one who seizes another by the forelock has full mastery over them. This conveys that no being, regardless of its strength or defiance, can act outside of God's will or escape His grasp. The concluding assertion that God is 'on a straight path' affirms that divine governance is characterized by perfect justice, wisdom, and moral rectitude—God's control over creation is not arbitrary or tyrannical but aligned with truth and righteousness. Together, these statements serve as a declaration of fearlessness rooted in tawakkul (trust in God): since all power ultimately belongs to a just and all-controlling Lord, the believer need not fear the threats or schemes of those who oppose the truth.

translation: But if you turn away, then I have already conveyed to you that with which I was sent to you. And my Lord will replace you with another people, and you will not harm Him at all. Indeed, my Lord is Guardian over all things.
interpretation: This verse concludes the account of Prophet Hud's address to his people, the 'Ad. Having fulfilled his duty of conveying the message, he makes clear that rejection of the message does not harm God in any way, nor does it ultimately harm the messenger who has discharged his responsibility. Rather, rejection harms only those who reject, for God is self-sufficient and capable of raising up other peoples to replace the disobedient. This establishes a recurring Quranic principle: prophetic responsibility ends at clear communication (balagh), not at compelling belief, and divine sovereignty means no community is indispensable to God's plan—if one generation turns away, others will be raised in their place. The phrase 'my Lord is Guardian over all things' (hafeez) affirms God's complete oversight and preservation of creation, assuring both the prophet and the listener that nothing escapes divine knowledge and control, including the ultimate consequences of accepting or rejecting guidance.

translation: And when Our command came, We saved Hud and those who believed with him, by a mercy from Us, and We saved them from a harsh punishment.
interpretation: This verse illustrates the recurring Qur'anic principle that divine mercy, not human merit alone, is the ultimate cause of salvation for the righteous. Hud's deliverance, along with his small community of believers, from the devastating punishment that befell the disbelieving people of 'Ad serves as a paradigm for all later communities: those who heed a warner and hold fast to faith will be rescued when calamity strikes the obstinate, demonstrating that God's grace actively intervenes in history to protect the faithful even amid widespread destruction.

translation: And that was 'Aad; they rejected the signs of their Lord and disobeyed His messengers and followed the order of every obstinate tyrant.
interpretation: This verse recounts the fate of the people of 'Aad as a historical and moral lesson. Their destruction is attributed not merely to disbelief in abstract terms, but to a specific pattern of behavior: rejecting clear divine signs, disobeying the messengers sent to guide them, and—crucially—following the command of arrogant, stubborn tyrants. This highlights a recurring Qur'anic theme that the downfall of nations often stems from blind allegiance to proud and obstinate leaders who oppose truth and resist correction. The verse serves as a warning that following unjust authority against divine guidance leads to collective ruin, emphasizing the responsibility of individuals to discern truth rather than succumb to the pressures of domineering figures.

translation: And they were pursued in this worldly life by a curse, and [also] on the Day of Resurrection. Unquestionably, 'Aad denied their Lord. So away with 'Aad, the people of Hud.
interpretation: This verse seals the narrative of the 'Aad, the people to whom the prophet Hud was sent. It declares that their punishment is not limited to their destruction in this world but extends into a lasting legacy of disgrace, a 'curse' that follows them in historical memory and will be reaffirmed on the Day of Judgment. The repeated phrase 'الا' (Unquestionably/Verily) emphasizes certainty and finality in God's judgment. By naming them 'the people of Hud,' the verse underscores the tragedy of their fate: despite having been sent a clear prophet and warner from among themselves, they chose arrogance and disbelief (kufr) in rejecting their Lord. Their story thus serves as a moral lesson in the Qur'an's broader pattern of recounting the fates of nations who rejected their prophets—showing that worldly power and strength (the 'Aad were known for their might) cannot protect against divine retribution when a people persist in rejecting truth and gratitude toward their Creator.

translation: And to Thamud [We sent] their brother Salih. He said, 'O my people, worship Allah; you have no deity other than Him. He has created you from the earth and settled you in it, so seek His forgiveness and then turn to Him in repentance. Indeed, my Lord is near and responsive.'
interpretation: This verse establishes the core monotheistic message common to all prophets, delivered here by Salih to his tribe, Thamud. The phrase 'created you from the earth' refers both to the origin of Adam and humanity's material composition, while 'settled you in it' (ista'marakum) implies a divine trust - humanity as stewards or cultivators of the earth, responsible for its development and proper use. This establishes a theological link between worship of God and responsible stewardship of creation; recognizing God's sovereignty naturally entails recognizing one's role as a caretaker rather than an owner of the earth's resources. The call to seek forgiveness and repent is not merely about past sins but about returning to the natural state of submission to God. The closing assurance that God is 'near and responsive' offers comfort and immediacy - repentance is not a distant, difficult process but one met with swift divine mercy, encouraging sincere believers to turn to Him without despair over their shortcomings.

translation: They said, 'O Salih, you were indeed among us a source of hope before this. Do you forbid us to worship what our fathers worshipped? Indeed, we are in disquieting doubt about what you call us to.'
interpretation: This verse captures the moment the people of Thamud turn against their prophet Salih after he calls them to abandon idolatry and worship God alone. Their words reveal the psychological pattern common to many communities confronted with prophetic truth: before Salih delivered his message, he was respected, even seen as promising—perhaps because he embodied wisdom, integrity, or leadership qualities they admired and hoped would benefit them within their existing social and religious order. The phrase 'a source of hope' suggests they expected him to rise among them as a conventional leader, reinforcing their traditions rather than challenging them. His call to monotheism, however, disrupts this expectation, and their admiration curdles into suspicion. Their objection rests on two pillars common to resistance against prophets throughout the Quran: blind adherence to ancestral custom ('what our fathers worshipped') and a refusal to engage honestly with new truth, dismissing it instead as 'disquieting doubt.' This doubt is not presented as intellectual skepticism born of inquiry, but as a defensive posture—an unwillingness to examine their own beliefs critically. The verse thus illustrates how inherited tradition can become an idol in itself, and how communities often prefer the comfort of ancestral familiarity over the unsettling demands of truth, even when that truth comes from someone they once trusted and esteemed.

translation: He said, 'O my people, have you considered: if I am upon clear evidence from my Lord, and He has given me mercy from Himself, then who would help me against Allah if I disobeyed Him? So you do not increase me except in loss.'
interpretation: This verse is spoken by the Prophet Shu'ayb (or similarly Noah/Hud in parallel narratives) to his disbelieving people. He confronts them with a rhetorical challenge: his prophethood rests on clear proof and divine mercy, not personal whim, so rejecting Allah's command to appease them would be irrational self-destruction, since no one could shield him from Allah's reckoning. The verse illustrates the prophetic burden of standing firm on truth despite social pressure, showing that compromising divine guidance for the sake of pleasing one's community only compounds loss rather than offering any real benefit, since ultimate accountability is to God alone.

translation: And O my people, this is the she-camel of Allah, a sign for you. So leave her to eat within Allah's land and do not touch her with harm, lest a near punishment seize you.
interpretation: This verse records the words of Prophet Salih to his people, Thamud, concerning the miraculous she-camel that Allah sent forth from solid rock as a tangible, undeniable sign of his prophethood and of Allah's power. By calling her 'the she-camel of Allah,' Salih emphasizes that she belongs to the divine order and must be respected as sacred, not to be exploited, harmed, or restricted from grazing freely on Allah's earth. The warning that harming her would bring 'a near punishment' underscores a central Quranic theme: that rejecting manifest signs of Allah and transgressing the boundaries He sets leads to swift consequences. The she-camel thus functions as both a literal test of obedience and a symbol of the broader human tendency to defy clear truth out of arrogance, pride, or self-interest—qualities that ultimately led Thamud to hamstring her in defiance, triggering their destruction. The verse illustrates how divine signs are given as mercy and guidance, but free will allows humans to either honor or violate the sacred trust placed before them, with real consequences following from that choice.

translation: But they hamstrung her, so he said, 'Enjoy yourselves in your homes for three days. That is a promise not to be denied (belied).'
interpretation: This verse refers to the story of Prophet Salih and his people, the Thamud. After Allah sent them a she-camel as a miraculous sign, warning them not to harm her, the people defied this command and hamstrung her, effectively killing her. In response, Prophet Salih delivered Allah's judgment: the people were given a specific, limited reprieve of three days before divine punishment would befall them. The phrase 'a promise not to be denied' emphasizes the certainty and inevitability of divine retribution once a warning has been given and rejected. This passage illustrates a broader Quranic theme of the consequences of defying divine signs and commands, the mercy shown even in the face of defiance through a grace period, and the ultimate certainty of justice being served. The three-day countdown also serves as a narrative device building tension before the destruction of the Thamud, reinforcing the lesson that divine patience has limits, and once the appointed time of judgment arrives, it cannot be averted or falsified.

translation: So when Our command came, We saved Salih and those who believed with him, by a mercy from Us, and from the disgrace of that day. Indeed, your Lord is the Powerful, the Exalted in Might.
interpretation: This verse concludes the narrative of the Prophet Salih and the people of Thamud, who were destroyed for their arrogant rejection of him and their defiant slaughter of the she-camel sent as a divine sign. The salvation of Salih and the believers is presented not as a result of their own strength or cleverness, but purely as an act of divine mercy (rahmah). This underscores a recurring Qur'anic theme: deliverance from destruction is a grace from God, not an earned right. The phrase 'disgrace of that day' (khizy yawmi'idhin) emphasizes that the punishment of the disbelievers was not merely physical annihilation but also a profound humiliation, a public demonstration of the consequences of defying God. The closing affirmation that God is 'the Powerful, the Exalted in Might' (al-Qawiyy al-Aziz) serves as a theological seal on the narrative, reminding the listener that God's power is absolute both in destroying the defiant and in rescuing the faithful. This pairing of attributes suggests that true strength is coupled with moral authority and justice, reinforcing the idea that God's might is never arbitrary but always tied to His wisdom and mercy toward those who submit to Him.

translation: And the Blast seized those who had wronged, and they became, in their homes, fallen prone (lifeless).
interpretation: This verse describes the sudden and total destruction of a disbelieving people—understood in context as the tribe of Thamud—who rejected their prophet and persisted in wrongdoing despite clear warnings. The 'Shout' (al-sayhah) represents an instantaneous, overwhelming divine punishment, likely a thunderous blast or cry of such intensity that it extinguished all life immediately, without struggle or escape. The imagery of them being found 'jathimin'—fallen prone, motionless, face down in their own dwellings—emphasizes the suddenness and totality of their demise; they were caught in the midst of their daily lives, within the very homes they had built and felt secure in, underscoring the futility of worldly security against divine will. This serves as a broader Qur'anic motif: that persistent injustice (zulm) and arrogant rejection of truth invite swift and inescapable consequence, and that no fortification, wealth, or civilization can shield a people from accountability when they collectively choose corruption over guidance. The verse functions as both historical narrative and moral warning to later generations about the fate of nations that defy higher truth.

translation: As though they had never dwelt there in flourishing ease. Behold! Indeed, Thamud disbelieved in their Lord. So away with Thamud!
interpretation: This verse concludes the account of Thamud, the people to whom the Prophet Salih was sent and who defied God's command regarding the she-camel, ultimately slaughtering it and bringing destruction upon themselves. The phrase 'as if they had never prospered therein' emphasizes the completeness of their annihilation—their once-thriving civilization was erased so thoroughly that no trace of their former prosperity remained, serving as a stark reminder of the transience of worldly power when divorced from righteousness. The repeated exclamation 'ألا' (behold/unquestionably) functions rhetorically to draw the listener's attention emphatically to the moral lesson being conveyed—that their destruction was not arbitrary but a direct consequence of their disbelief ('kufr') in their Lord, despite having received clear signs and warnings through their prophet. The final curse 'away with Thamud' (بعدا لثمود) represents a formal consignment to divine rejection and exclusion from mercy, a pattern repeated for other disbelieving nations in the Qur'an (such as 'Ad), establishing a rhetorical and theological template: disbelief and rejection of prophets leads to total removal from divine favor and historical memory, except as a cautionary tale for later generations. This verse thus serves both as a historical closure to the narrative and as a timeless admonition for all who might repeat the same arrogance and denial.

translation: And certainly Our messengers (angels) came to Ibrahim with good tidings. They said, 'Peace!' He said, 'Peace!' And he did not delay in bringing a roasted calf.
interpretation: This verse illustrates the sacred Near Eastern tradition of hospitality that was central to Ibrahim's character and to Arab customs more broadly. Upon seeing unfamiliar guests, Ibrahim did not inquire about their identity or purpose first; he immediately extended the greeting of peace and swiftly prepared a generous meal—a roasted calf, indicating lavish and immediate hospitality to strangers. This episode establishes Ibrahim as a model of generosity and graciousness, virtues highly esteemed in Islamic ethics. The angels' appearance in human form, their exchange of greetings, and Ibrahim's prompt action set the stage for the subsequent revelation of their divine mission—to deliver glad tidings of a son (Ishaq) and to warn of the impending destruction of the people of Lot. The verse also subtly foreshadows that these are no ordinary guests, as their refusal to eat the food (mentioned in the following verses) alerts Ibrahim to their supernatural nature, prompting fear until they reveal themselves as messengers of God.

translation: But when he saw their hands not reaching towards it, he distrusted them and felt a fear of them. They said, 'Fear not, we have been sent to the people of Lot.'
interpretation: This verse recounts the episode of Prophet Ibrahim's angelic visitors who came in human form to bring him news of a son, and who later proceeded to the people of Lot to bring down punishment upon them. When Ibrahim offered them food (a roasted calf, as mentioned in surrounding verses) and observed that they did not eat, he grew suspicious and afraid, since in the customs of hospitality of that era, a guest who refused to eat was often considered to have hostile intentions, as eating together was a sign of peace and trust. The angels, sensing his fear, immediately reassured him by revealing their true identity and divine mission: they were not human enemies but angels sent by God specifically to execute judgment upon the sinful people of Lot, not to harm Ibrahim at all. This moment demonstrates several theological points: first, it shows Ibrahim's very human and natural reaction of fear and caution when faced with something inexplicable, reminding readers that even great prophets experience ordinary human emotions and uncertainties when encountering the unknown. Second, it illustrates God's mercy and care in quickly relieving His prophet's distress through clear communication, as the angels did not let Ibrahim remain in fear but promptly explained their purpose. Third, it sets up the narrative transition to the account of Lot's people and their impending destruction, linking the story of Ibrahim's hospitality and the annunciation of Isaac's birth to the broader narrative of divine justice being carried out against those who persisted in immorality and rejected the warnings of their prophet. The verse also subtly reinforces the theme found throughout the Quran that God's messengers and angels operate with specific, purposeful missions, and nothing happens without divine decree and wisdom, even when it involves the destruction of a wicked nation of the past.

translation: And his wife was standing, and she laughed. So We gave her glad tidings of Isaac, and after Isaac, of Jacob.
interpretation: This verse occurs within the story of the angelic messengers who visited Abraham, bringing news of impending judgment upon the people of Lot, and also delivering glad tidings to Abraham and his wife Sarah. Sarah's laughter here is traditionally understood as an expression of astonishment and joy at the news that she would bear a son, Isaac, despite her old age and the fact that she had long been barren—a seemingly miraculous occurrence. The additional promise of Jacob, Isaac's son, extends the glad tidings further, assuring continuity of lineage and prophecy through multiple generations. This moment underscores God's power to bring about events beyond ordinary human expectation or biological possibility, reinforcing the theme found throughout the Qur'an that divine will is not bound by natural limitations. It also affirms the special status of Abraham's household, chosen to carry forward a line of prophets, which becomes foundational to the subsequent narrative of the Israelite line through Isaac and Jacob.

translation: She said: 'Woe is me! Shall I bear a child while I am an old woman, and this, my husband, is an old man? This is indeed a strange thing!'
interpretation: This verse refers to Sarah, the wife of Prophet Ibrahim (Abraham), upon hearing the angelic messengers' glad tidings that she would bear a son (Ishaq/Isaac) despite her advanced age and that of her husband. Her reaction expresses natural human astonishment at the prospect of childbirth occurring outside the normal biological expectations of age. This moment illustrates a recurring Qur'anic theme: that Allah's power is not bound by the natural laws or limitations that govern human understanding. Sarah's exclamation of disbelief, rooted in human experience and reason, sets up the divine response that follows—affirming that nothing is impossible for Allah, who is capable of decreeing matters beyond ordinary expectation. The verse also reflects the human tendency to measure possibility through worldly experience, while faith calls for trust in divine decree that transcends such limits.

translation: They said, 'Do you wonder at the decree of Allah? The mercy of Allah and His blessings be upon you, O people of the house. Indeed, He is Praiseworthy and Glorious.'
interpretation: This verse recounts the angels' response to Sarah's astonishment upon hearing the news that she would bear a son (Isaac) despite her old age and her husband Abraham's advanced years. Her laughter and disbelief were natural human reactions to what seemed biologically impossible. The angels' reply redirects her attention from the apparent impossibility of the event to the limitless power of Allah, reminding her that divine decree operates beyond ordinary natural constraints. By addressing her and Abraham as 'Ahl al-Bayt' (people of the house), the verse elevates their household to a position of special honor, foreshadowing the prophetic lineage that would emerge through Isaac and later through Ishmael. The invocation of Allah's mercy and blessings upon them signifies that this miraculous birth is not merely a biological anomaly but a manifestation of divine favor and grace bestowed upon a righteous family chosen for a significant role in sacred history. The verse closes with two divine attributes—Hamid (Praiseworthy) and Majid (Glorious)—emphasizing that Allah's actions, however astonishing they may seem, are always rooted in wisdom deserving of praise and in a majesty that transcends human understanding. This serves as a broader lesson that believers should not measure divine possibilities by the limits of human experience or expectation, but trust in the encompassing power and benevolence of Allah's will.

translation: So when the fright had left Abraham and the glad tidings had reached him, he began to argue with Us concerning the people of Lot.
interpretation: This verse depicts the moment after the angelic messengers had delivered to Abraham the glad tidings of a son (Isaac), and his initial fear and apprehension at their unusual, non-eating guests had subsided. Once reassured, Abraham's compassionate and forbearing nature came to the fore. Knowing that the angels were now headed to the people of Lot to deliver punishment, Abraham began to plead and reason with God's messengers on their behalf, hoping that the punishment might be averted or lessened if any righteous people could be found among them. This exchange illustrates Abraham's deep sense of mercy, his concern for justice, and his role as an intercessor, foreshadowing the subsequent dialogue about the fate of the town and the eventual rescue of Lot and his believing family before the destruction fell upon the sinful people.

translation: Indeed, Abraham was most forbearing, imploring, and penitent [in turning to Allah].
interpretation: This verse describes three exalted qualities of Prophet Ibrahim (Abraham) that explain his character, particularly in the context of his pleading with Allah on behalf of the people of Lut (Lot). 'Haleem' (forbearing) indicates his patience and gentleness even when faced with the wrongdoing of others, never rushing to anger or harsh judgment. 'Awwah' (imploring/lamenting) reflects his deep, frequent supplication to Allah, a heart tender with humility and constant remembrance, often understood to mean one who sighs and groans in earnest prayer out of fear and love of Allah. 'Muneeb' (penitent/turning back) signifies his continual returning to Allah in repentance and devotion, always orienting his heart back to his Lord despite his esteemed status as a prophet. Together, these traits illustrate why Ibrahim interceded compassionately for Lut's people despite their sins—his inherent mercy, humility, and devotion compelled him to hope for their forgiveness before divine justice was finally decreed. This serves as a model for believers: that true righteousness combines patience with others, heartfelt prayerfulness, and constant repentance to Allah.

translation: O Ibrahim, turn away from this. Indeed, the command of your Lord has come, and indeed, there will come to them a punishment that cannot be repelled.
interpretation: This verse depicts the moment when the angels, after delivering glad tidings to Ibrahim of a son, inform him that they are also sent to destroy the people of Lut. When Ibrahim begins to plead and argue on behalf of these sinful people, hoping for their reprieve, he is gently but firmly told to desist from his intercession. The phrase 'turn away from this' signals that Ibrahim's compassionate pleading, while noble in spirit, cannot alter a divine decree that has already been finalized. This illustrates a broader theological principle in the Qur'an: once God's judgment is decreed in response to a people's persistent corruption and rejection of warnings, it becomes irreversible, and no amount of intercession—even from a beloved prophet—can avert it. The verse also underscores the limits of human intercession before divine justice, reminding believers that God's wisdom and timing in matters of reward and punishment are beyond negotiation once the threshold of inevitability has been crossed. It further emphasizes Ibrahim's compassionate nature, showing that his concern extended even to communities not his own, while simultaneously affirming that mercy operates within the bounds of divine justice rather than overriding it entirely.

translation: And when Our messengers came to Lot, he was distressed on their account and felt himself powerless to protect them, and he said, 'This is a hard day.'
interpretation: This verse depicts the arrival of the angelic messengers in human form to Lot, and his immediate anguish upon recognizing the danger they faced from his corrupt people, who were known for assaulting travelers and strangers. Lot's distress stems not from doubt in God's power, but from his acute awareness of his own limited ability to shield his guests from the hostility of his community, reflecting the heavy burden of responsibility and hospitality placed upon him as a host and prophet. His declaration that 'this is a hard day' encapsulates the moral and social crisis he faces, foreshadowing the impending confrontation between divine justice and human depravity, while also illustrating the loneliness and vulnerability of a righteous individual surrounded by a sinful society. The verse sets the stage for the subsequent divine intervention and destruction of Lot's people, emphasizing themes of protection of the righteous, the limits of human strength against evil, and the certainty of God's support arriving even when a believer feels overwhelmed.

translation: And his people came rushing toward him, and before that they had been committing evil deeds. He said, 'O my people, these are my daughters; they are purer for you. So fear Allah and do not disgrace me concerning my guests. Is there not among you a right-minded man?'
interpretation: This verse depicts the moral crisis facing Prophet Lut as his people, habituated to sexual immorality and same-sex acts, rush toward his house intending to violate his angelic guests (who had come in the form of handsome men). Lut's desperate offer of his daughters in marriage is understood by most commentators not as a literal transactional proposal but as an appeal to lawful, natural relations within marriage as opposed to the unlawful acts his people sought—an attempt to shame them by presenting the legitimate alternative sanctioned by God. His plea 'fear Allah' invokes their accountability to a higher moral law, while 'do not disgrace me concerning my guests' reflects the sacred duty of hospitality and protection of guests in the ancient moral order, a duty his people were about to violate in the most humiliating way. His final question, 'Is there not among you a right-minded man?' expresses his anguish at finding not a single person of sound moral reasoning (rushd) among his entire community—underscoring the totality of their corruption and foreshadowing the destruction that follows as divine judgment upon a society that had abandoned both reason and righteousness.

translation: They said, 'You certainly know that we have no right to [i.e., no desire for] your daughters, and indeed, you know what we want.'
interpretation: This verse records the response of Lot's (Lut's) people when he offered them his daughters in marriage as a lawful alternative, attempting to dissuade them from their intent toward his male guests. Their reply exposes the depth of their moral corruption and the entrenchment of their sin: they bluntly admit that lawful, natural relations hold no appeal for them, and they openly confess their deviant desire. This verse is often read as illustrating the hardening of hearts that occurs when a people persist unrepentantly in transgression—their rejection is not out of ignorance but open, acknowledged defiance of what is righteous, which sets the stage for the divine punishment that follows. It underscores the Quranic theme that moral corruption, when normalized within a society, leads people to reject even clear, decent alternatives offered to them.

translation: He said, 'If only I had power to resist you, or could take refuge in some strong support.'
interpretation: This verse depicts the anguish of Prophet Lut (Lot) when his people approached his house demanding to seize his guests (the angels who had come in the form of handsome men) in order to commit vile acts against them. Lut, distressed by his inability to protect his guests through his own strength or through the support of a powerful clan or tribe, expresses his helplessness. In the customs of that time, a person's protection often depended on the backing of a strong tribe or family network; Lut, being a stranger among his people without such tribal support, felt acutely vulnerable. This moment highlights the depth of his moral courage, as despite his personal weakness and lack of worldly power, he stood firm in trying to protect his guests from his corrupt and sinful community. It also sets the stage for divine intervention, as the angels soon reveal their true identity and reassure Lut that they have come with God's judgment against his people, relieving him from relying on his own might and instead on God's support and plan.

translation: They said, 'O Lot, indeed we are messengers of your Lord; they will never reach you. So depart with your family during a portion of the night, and let not any of you look back - except your wife; indeed, what strikes them will strike her. Indeed, their appointment is for the morning. Is not the morning near?'
interpretation: This verse depicts the angelic messengers reassuring Prophet Lot that the threat posed by his hostile townspeople has been neutralized, as divine punishment is imminent. The instruction to flee under cover of night without looking back symbolizes a complete, decisive break from a doomed community and its corruption - a forward-looking act of faith and obedience rather than lingering attachment to what is being destroyed. The exception of Lot's wife signals her complicity or sympathy with the sinful people, despite her familial bond, illustrating that righteousness is determined by one's deeds and allegiances rather than mere kinship. The rhetorical question 'Is not the morning near?' conveys the certainty and swiftness of divine justice, reassuring the faithful that even though the punishment is delayed until morning, it is not distant in any meaningful sense - God's timing is precise and deliberate, not a sign of weakness or doubt. Overall, the verse underscores themes of divine protection for the righteous, the inevitability of consequences for persistent sin, and the need for clear separation from corruption to preserve one's own safety and faith.

translation: So when Our command came, We turned it (the city) upside down, and We rained upon it stones of baked clay, layered one upon another.
interpretation: This verse describes the destruction of the people of Lut (Lot), whose city was overturned and destroyed with a rain of stones as divine punishment for their persistent sin and rejection of the Prophet's warning. The verse emphasizes the totality and precision of divine judgment—the catastrophe was not random but a deliberate act of justice, with the physical inversion of the city symbolizing the moral inversion of its inhabitants, who had turned natural human relations upside down. The 'layered' stones (mandud) suggest an organized, purposeful destruction rather than chaotic calamity, reinforcing that this was a controlled act of divine will rather than a mere natural disaster. This passage serves as a sobering lesson about the consequences of communal moral corruption and the certainty of divine retribution when warnings are persistently ignored.

translation: Marked [for destruction] from your Lord. And it is not far from the wrongdoers.
interpretation: This verse concludes the account of the destruction of the people of Lut (Lot), describing the stones of baked clay that rained down upon them as being specifically 'marked' or designated by God for this particular purpose—each stone inscribed, as it were, with the name of its intended target, signifying divine precision and intentionality rather than random catastrophe. The closing phrase broadens the lesson beyond the historical moment: though addressed to the Prophet Muhammad in the immediate context, it serves as a timeless warning that such punishment is 'not far' from wrongdoers in any era. This proximity is both literal, in that the ruins of these ancient cities lay along trade routes well known to the Quraysh and other Arabs, and metaphorical, in that moral corruption and transgression against natural law and divine command carry consequences that are never truly distant, no matter how secure the wrongdoers feel in their power or prosperity. The verse thus functions as a bridge between a specific historical judgment and a universal principle about the nature of divine justice—it is patient but not negligent, and its reach extends to all who persist in oppression, deviance, and rejection of warnings, regardless of time or place.

translation: And to Midian [We sent] their brother Shu'ayb. He said, 'O my people, worship Allah; you have no deity other than Him. And do not give short measure and weight. Indeed, I see you in prosperity, but indeed, I fear for you the punishment of an encompassing Day.'
interpretation: This verse establishes the prophetic mission of Shu'ayb to the people of Midian, linking two seemingly distinct concerns: theological monotheism and commercial honesty. The pairing is deliberate, demonstrating that true worship of God cannot be separated from ethical conduct in daily economic dealings. Shu'ayb's acknowledgment that his people currently enjoy prosperity ('I see you in khayr') makes his warning more poignant—he is not addressing a people in desperate poverty who might be tempted to cheat out of necessity, but rather a comfortable society that has normalized fraud despite having no material excuse. The phrase 'a Day that encompasses' (yawm muhit) evokes an inescapable reckoning, suggesting that divine justice will surround and overtake those who exploit others through deceptive measures, mirroring how their fraudulent practices have 'encompassed' and corrupted their entire community. This connects to a broader Quranic theme that social justice, particularly in trade and economic relationships, is inseparable from faith itself—worship of God is incomplete without just dealing with His creation.

translation: And O my people, give full measure and weight in justice, and do not deprive people of their due, and do not go about the earth spreading corruption.
interpretation: This verse, spoken by the Prophet Shu'ayb to his people (the people of Madyan), establishes economic justice and honest dealing as a core religious obligation, not merely a civil matter. By linking fair weights and measures directly to faith, the verse teaches that spirituality is inseparable from everyday conduct, particularly in commerce and trade, where exploitation and fraud were rampant among Shu'ayb's people. The command not to 'deprive people of their due' extends beyond literal measurements to encompass all forms of cheating others of their rights—whether material, social, or otherwise. The concluding phrase against 'spreading corruption in the earth' broadens the scope further, framing dishonest economic practices as a form of corruption that destabilizes society as a whole. Thus, the verse presents honest trade and fair dealing as foundational to a just social order, suggesting that moral and economic integrity are intertwined, and that exploitation of others for material gain is tantamount to corrupting the earth itself.

translation: That which remains [lawful] from Allah is best for you, if you are believers. And I am not a guardian over you.
interpretation: This verse is part of the Prophet Shu'ayb's address to the people of Madyan, who were notorious for cheating in trade through fraudulent weights and measures. Shu'ayb urges them to be content with the lawful profit that remains after honest dealing, rather than seeking illicit gain through deception, reminding them that what Allah permits and blesses is superior to any ill-gotten wealth. By conditioning this truth on their faith, he emphasizes that recognizing this wisdom requires sincere belief in Allah's oversight and justice. The closing statement, where Shu'ayb disclaims being a guardian over them, underscores the prophetic role as one of warning and guidance rather than coercion—he delivers the message but leaves accountability to Allah, affirming human free will and the personal responsibility each person bears for heeding or rejecting righteous counsel.

translation: They said, "O Shu'ayb, does your prayer command you that we should leave what our fathers worshipped or that we not do with our wealth what we please? Indeed, you are the forbearing, the right-minded!"
interpretation: This verse captures the sarcastic and mocking response of Shu'ayb's people to his call for monotheism and ethical dealing in trade. They sarcastically invoke the qualities of forbearance and sound judgment that Shu'ayb was known for, using these very virtues to mock him, implying that a man of his supposed wisdom should know better than to challenge ancestral traditions and interfere with how people choose to conduct their own financial and economic affairs. Their rhetorical question reveals the deep resistance of entrenched power and wealth to any religious or moral critique, especially one that touches upon both spiritual devotion (prayer) and material practices (honest dealing in trade, weights and measures). The verse exposes a common human tendency to dismiss ethical and spiritual reform as unwarranted interference in personal or economic freedom, defending exploitative practices under the guise of tradition and autonomy, while sarcastically undermining the prophet's authority by turning his own praised qualities into instruments of ridicule.

translation: He said, 'O my people, have you considered: if I am upon clear evidence from my Lord, and He has provided me with a good provision from Himself [should I not warn you]? And I do not intend to differ from you [in conduct] by engaging in that which I forbid you from. I only intend reform as much as I am able. My success is not but through Allah. Upon Him I rely, and to Him I return.'
interpretation: This verse, spoken by the Prophet Shu'ayb to his people, encapsulates the ethical foundation of prophetic reform: the reformer must embody the very principles he calls others to uphold. Shu'ayb's declaration that he does not wish to oppose his people by doing himself what he forbids them from doing establishes integrity and consistency between word and deed as prerequisites for legitimate moral authority. His acknowledgment that his capacity for reform (islah) is limited to what he is able to achieve reflects a realistic humility about human agency, while his attribution of all success to divine enablement (tawfiq) reframes reform not as a purely human achievement but as a collaborative act between sincere human effort and divine grace. The verse thus presents a model of social and moral reform that is neither coercive nor self-righteous, but grounded in clear conviction, personal consistency, humble effort, and ultimate reliance upon God, with the final phrase 'to Him I return' signaling that all reformist efforts are oriented toward an ultimate accountability beyond worldly outcomes.

translation: And O my people, let not your opposition to me cause you to be struck by that which struck the people of Noah or the people of Hud or the people of Salih, and the people of Lot are not far from you.
interpretation: This verse is part of the Prophet Shu'ayb's address to his people, warning them against the consequences of rejecting his message. He invokes the fate of previous nations—the people of Noah, Hud (the 'Ad), and Salih (the Thamud)—who were destroyed for their persistent disbelief and wrongdoing, as a cautionary lesson. The mention that the people of Lot 'are not far from you' serves a dual purpose: it is a reminder both in terms of time (their destruction was relatively recent history) and in terms of place (Sodom, associated with Lot's people, was geographically near the land of Midian where Shu'ayb's people lived). This proximity—temporal and spatial—intensifies the warning, making the example more immediate and harder to dismiss. The verse illustrates a broader Qur'anic theme that disbelief and moral corruption lead to divine punishment, and that history offers repeated evidence of this pattern, which rational people should heed.

translation: And seek forgiveness of your Lord, then turn in repentance to Him. Indeed, my Lord is Merciful and Loving.
interpretation: This verse, spoken by the Prophet Shu'ayb to his people, establishes a two-part spiritual process: istighfar (seeking forgiveness) addresses specific past wrongs, while tawbah (repentance/turning back) represents a deeper, ongoing reorientation of the heart and will toward God. The sequence matters—forgiveness for sins precedes and enables genuine repentance, which is a sustained commitment to change rather than a single act. The verse concludes by grounding this call in two divine attributes: Raheem (Merciful) emphasizes God's compassionate response to human weakness, while Wadood (Loving/Affectionate) is a rarer and more intimate divine name, suggesting that God's relationship with repentant believers is not merely one of judicial pardon but of genuine warmth and tenderness. This pairing reassures the audience that turning back to God is not an act of groveling before a distant judge, but a return to a loving relationship, making repentance an act of hope rather than fear.

translation: They said, 'O Shu'ayb, we do not understand much of what you say, and indeed we see you as weak among us. Were it not for your clan, we would have stoned you, for you are not mighty against us.'
interpretation: This verse captures the arrogant response of the people of Madyan to the Prophet Shu'ayb's call to righteousness, honest trade, and worship of God alone. Their words reveal several layers of rejection rooted in worldly values rather than spiritual reasoning. First, they claim not to understand his message—not due to genuine confusion, but as a dismissive rhetorical tactic to avoid engaging with his call for justice and monotheism. Second, they judge his worth by tribal and social standards, perceiving him as 'weak' because he apparently lacked the numbers, wealth, or status they valued. Crucially, they admit that only the protection of his clan—his blood relations—prevents them from executing him through stoning, exposing that tribal loyalty and fear of retaliation, not respect for truth or moral restraint, governed their behavior. This reflects a recurring Qur'anic theme: prophets were often protected not because societies valued truth, but because of social structures like kinship. The verse also highlights the irony that worldly power structures afford more practical protection than righteousness itself in the eyes of disbelievers, while simultaneously showing the moral bankruptcy of a people who equate truth with strength in numbers and status rather than evidence and reason.

translation: He said, 'O my people, is my clan more respected by you than Allah? And you have taken Him behind your backs, disregarded. Indeed, my Lord encompasses all that you do.'
interpretation: This verse is from the story of Prophet Shu'ayb addressing his people. It highlights a profound critique of misplaced loyalties: the people feared and respected Shu'ayb's tribal clan more than they feared or respected God Himself, to the point that they threatened to harm or expel him only because of his kinship ties, not out of any genuine reverence for divine authority. Shu'ayb rebukes them for this inverted sense of priority, pointing out the absurdity that worldly tribal affiliations could command more weight than their Creator, whom they have effectively cast aside and ignored ('taken behind your backs'). The phrase conveys total disregard, as if God's commands and warnings were irrelevant to their conduct. The verse closes with a reminder of divine omniscience, that God fully encompasses and is aware of all their actions, serving as both a warning and an assurance that no deed escapes His knowledge, and that ultimately accountability rests with Him rather than with tribal power structures.

translation: And O my people, act according to your position; indeed, I am acting. You are going to know to whom will come a punishment that will disgrace him and who is a liar. So watch; indeed, I am with you a watcher.
interpretation: This verse records the words of Prophet Shu'ayb to his people after they rejected his message and mocked him. Having exhausted argument and warning, he tells them to proceed as they see fit, just as he will continue upon his own path of faith and righteousness, leaving the ultimate judgment to time and to God. The phrase 'act according to your position' is not a concession to their wrongdoing but a declaration that each party will be held accountable for the path it chooses. The verse emphasizes the certainty of divine justice: disgraceful punishment awaits those who persist in falsehood and arrogance, and the truth of the liar will be exposed. Shu'ayb's call to 'watch' and his own vow to watch alongside them reflects a posture of patient confidence in God's decree, teaching believers that when confronted with rejection and mockery, one need not despair but can trust in the eventual unveiling of truth and consequence by God, who is Himself the ultimate Watcher over all deeds.

translation: And when Our command came, We saved Shu'ayb and those who believed with him, by a mercy from Us; and the Cry seized those who had done wrong, so they became, in their homes, fallen prone (lifeless).
interpretation: This verse recounts the fate of the people of Madyan who rejected the Prophet Shu'ayb's call to honest dealing, justice in trade, and the worship of God alone. The salvation of Shu'ayb and the believers is explicitly attributed to 'a mercy from Us,' emphasizing that deliverance from divine punishment is not earned by human merit alone but is a grace bestowed by God upon those who maintain faith and righteousness in the face of a corrupt and hostile society. The sudden, overwhelming 'Cry' (as-sayhah) that destroys the wrongdoers represents divine punishment that requires no elaborate mechanism—it is instantaneous and total, striking them down in the very homes where they felt secure in their wealth and power. The imagery of being left 'jathimeen' (fallen prone, crouched lifeless) in their own dwellings underscores the completeness of their destruction and the irony that the very communities and economic systems they built on exploitation became their tombs. This pattern—recounted similarly for other destroyed nations in the Qur'an—serves as a warning that moral corruption, particularly in economic and social dealings, invites divine retribution, while steadfast faith amid persecution secures divine mercy and protection.

translation: As though they had never prospered therein. Ah, away with Madyan, even as Thamud was done away with!
interpretation: This verse serves as a solemn closing refrain to the account of the people of Madyan (Midian), who were destroyed for their corruption, fraudulent dealings, and rejection of the Prophet Shu'ayb. The phrase 'as though they had never prospered therein' emphasizes the completeness of their annihilation—their homes, wealth, and civilization vanished so thoroughly that it was as if they had never existed, erasing all trace of their former flourishing. The curse 'away with Madyan' echoes the earlier destruction of Thamud, deliberately linking the two peoples to underscore a recurring divine pattern: nations that persist in arrogance, injustice, and disbelief despite the warnings of their prophets meet the same fate regardless of era or location. By pairing Madyan with Thamud, the verse reinforces the Qur'anic theme that the laws of divine retribution are consistent throughout history, and that worldly prosperity offers no protection against accountability when a people choose corruption over righteousness and reject clear guidance sent to them.

translation: And We certainly sent Moses with Our signs and a clear authority.
interpretation: This verse affirms the prophetic mission of Moses, emphasizing that he was not sent merely with a claim but was supported by tangible divine 'ayat' (signs/miracles) and a 'sultan mubin' (manifest authority or proof) that validated his message before Pharaoh and his people. The 'clear authority' refers to the undeniable, self-evident nature of the miracles given to him—such as the staff and his radiant hand—which left no room for doubt or ambiguity. This sets a pattern repeated throughout the Qur'an: that prophets are sent with evidence sufficient to establish the truth of their message, placing the responsibility of belief or rejection squarely on those who witness it, particularly tyrannical figures like Pharaoh who possess power but lack true authority or legitimacy before God.

translation: To Pharaoh and his chiefs, but they followed the command of Pharaoh, and the command of Pharaoh was not rightly guided.
interpretation: This verse, from the account of Moses sent to Pharaoh and his elite, highlights a recurring Qur'anic theme: the danger of blind obedience to worldly authority instead of divine guidance. Pharaoh's court, despite witnessing the signs brought by Moses, chose to follow their king's directives rather than truth. The phrase 'the command of Pharaoh was not rightly guided' is a decisive moral judgment, signaling that political power or social dominance does not equate to righteousness or wisdom. It serves as a warning to all believers across time that following leaders uncritically, especially when their guidance contradicts justice and truth, leads to misguidance and ultimately destruction, as seen in Pharaoh's eventual downfall. The verse underscores the Qur'anic principle that legitimacy of leadership must be measured by its alignment with moral and divine truth, not by its authority or might.

translation: He will precede his people on the Day of Resurrection and lead them into the Fire; and wretched is the watering place to which they are led.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 11:98) refers to Pharaoh and the fate awaiting him and his people on the Day of Judgment. The imagery is deliberately ironic: in life, Pharaoh led his people as their sovereign, promising them glory and security, and they followed him in disbelief and oppression of the Israelites. In the Hereafter, he continues in that same leading role, but now it is toward damnation. The word 'ورد' (ward) normally refers to a watering place—a destination associated with relief, nourishment, and life-giving water in the desert context so familiar to the verse's original audience. By applying this word to the Fire, the verse creates a jarring inversion: what should be a source of relief becomes a site of eternal torment. This rhetorical choice underscores the utter reversal of expectations for those who followed corrupt leadership—seeking satisfaction and security in worldly power, they instead arrive at ruin. The verse also carries a broader moral lesson about the shared responsibility of leaders and followers: Pharaoh is condemned for his tyranny and false guidance, but his people are not absolved either, for they chose to follow him despite having the capacity for independent judgment. It stands as a warning against blind allegiance to unjust authority, emphasizing that ultimate accountability before God cannot be deflected by claiming one was 'only following' a leader's command.

translation: And they were followed in this [world] by a curse, and on the Day of Resurrection. Wretched is the gift which is given.
interpretation: This verse concludes the account of Pharaoh and his people in Surah Hud, describing the ultimate fate of those who followed a tyrannical leader into disbelief and oppression. The 'curse' (la'nah) represents being cut off from God's mercy—manifesting in this world through historical condemnation, destruction, and being remembered with infamy, and in the Hereafter through eternal punishment. The phrase 'wretched is the gift which is given' uses the image of a 'rifd' (a gift, reward, or provision bestowed upon someone, often used in the context of hospitality or support given to a leader by followers). Here it is used ironically: whereas followers might expect support or reward from aligning with a powerful leader like Pharaoh, what they actually receive is the opposite—condemnation and curse, both temporally and eternally. This underscores a Qur'anic theme that worldly power and tyranny, when opposed to divine guidance, lead not to the rewards one might expect from loyalty, but to a doubled punishment: disgrace in historical memory and torment in the afterlife. It serves as a warning against blind allegiance to oppressive authority at the expense of truth and righteousness.

translation: That is from the accounts of the cities which We relate to you; some of them are still standing, and some are mown down (harvested/destroyed).
interpretation: This verse comes at the conclusion of the narratives about previous peoples and their prophets—Noah, Hud, Salih, Lot, and Shu'ayb—recounted in Surah Hud. God affirms that these are true historical accounts being revealed to the Prophet Muhammad, not mere legends. The imagery of cities being 'standing' (qa'im) versus 'mown down' (hasid) uses an agricultural metaphor: some ruins remained visible as structures still standing, like stalks left in a field, while others were completely leveled, like crops cut down at harvest. This serves as a physical testament and warning—travelers could still see the remnants of these destroyed civilizations, providing tangible evidence of divine judgment upon nations that rejected their prophets and persisted in wrongdoing. The verse emphasizes that these are not abstract moral lessons but accounts rooted in real, observable history, meant to serve as a sobering reminder for those who reflect on the consequences of denying truth and persisting in oppression or disbelief.

translation: And We did not wrong them, but it was they who wronged themselves. So their gods that they invoked besides Allah availed them not at all when the command of your Lord came; and they added nothing for them but ruin.
interpretation: This verse, concluding the accounts of destroyed nations such as the peoples of Noah, Hud, Salih, and Lot, establishes a core theological principle: divine justice is never arbitrary or oppressive. The destruction that befell these peoples was not an act of injustice from God but the direct consequence of their own choices—their persistent rejection of truth, their idolatry, and their moral corruption. The phrase 'they wronged themselves' shifts moral responsibility entirely onto human agency, emphasizing that sin and disbelief are self-inflicted harms before they become divine punishments. The verse then exposes the futility of idolatry: the false gods these nations worshipped and relied upon for protection and intercession proved utterly powerless when God's decree of punishment arrived. Far from helping, these false objects of worship only deepened the worshippers' ruin—perhaps by fostering false security, misplaced trust, and spiritual deception that left them unprepared for the reality of divine judgment. This serves as a broader warning to all who place their trust in anything other than God, suggesting that reliance on false powers not only fails to protect but actively compounds one's destruction when truth finally confronts falsehood.

translation: And thus is the seizure of your Lord when He seizes the cities while they are committing wrong. Indeed, His seizure is painful and severe.
interpretation: This verse establishes a divine law of history: communities and civilizations that persist in wrongdoing—injustice, oppression, and rejection of truth—will eventually face a reckoning. The phrase 'and thus' connects this statement to the preceding narratives of destroyed peoples (such as those of Pharaoh, 'Ad, and Thamud), presenting their fate not as isolated incidents but as a consistent pattern of divine justice. The seizure described is not arbitrary or hasty; it comes after warnings, after opportunities for repentance, and only when a society's injustice becomes entrenched ('while they are wrongdoing' indicates an ongoing, persistent state rather than a momentary lapse). The emphasis on the seizure being 'painful and severe' underscores the gravity of divine justice when it finally manifests—it is not a gentle correction but a decisive consequence proportional to sustained moral corruption. This serves as both a warning to the Prophet's contemporaries who were rejecting his message and a timeless principle for any community: worldly power, wealth, or apparent stability do not exempt a people from accountability if they persist in systemic injustice and transgression against divine guidance.

translation: Indeed, in that is a sign for whoever fears the punishment of the Hereafter. That is a Day for which mankind will be gathered, and that is a Day [that will be] witnessed.
interpretation: This verse comes at the close of the account of Pharaoh's tyranny and destruction, presenting it as a 'sign' (ayah) - a lesson embedded in history for those whose hearts are receptive through fear of accountability. The verse then pivots from the historical to the eschatological, describing the Day of Judgment with two key characteristics: it is 'majmu' lahu an-nas' (a day for which all humanity is gathered) and 'mashhud' (witnessed). The gathering signifies the universal and inescapable nature of this reckoning - no soul, from any era or nation, is exempt. The term 'witnessed' carries multiple layers of meaning: it is a day witnessed by all creation (angels, jinn, and humans across all generations), a day when every soul witnesses the consequences of its own deeds, and a day that itself serves as testimony to divine justice. The connection between Pharaoh's fate and the Day of Judgment is deliberate - just as Pharaoh's worldly punishment served as a visible sign of divine justice, the ultimate gathering represents the complete and final manifestation of that same justice, where no tyranny goes unaddressed and no truth remains hidden. This serves as both warning and consolation: warning to those who, like Pharaoh, exalt themselves beyond their station, and consolation to believers that temporal injustices will find their ultimate resolution.

translation: And We delay it not except for a specified, appointed term.
interpretation: This verse refers to the Day of Judgment and the punishment awaiting the wrongdoers mentioned in the preceding verses. It emphasizes that God's postponement of this reckoning is not due to negligence, inability, or forgetfulness, but is a deliberate act within His complete control, bound to a precise and predetermined time known only to Him. This underscores the divine attributes of omniscience and omnipotence—nothing happens outside of God's will and timing. For believers, it serves as both a warning and a reassurance: a warning to the unjust that their respite is temporary and purposeful, not an escape from accountability, and a reassurance to the faithful that divine justice, though it may seem delayed, is certain and precisely ordained. The verse reflects a broader Quranic theme that all events unfold according to a fixed decree, reinforcing trust in God's wisdom even when human beings cannot perceive the reasons behind delays in justice or reward.

translation: The Day it comes, no soul will speak except by His permission; then among them will be the wretched and the blessed.
interpretation: This verse describes the Day of Judgment, emphasizing God's absolute sovereignty over that momentous event. The imagery of souls being unable to speak except by divine permission underscores the complete powerlessness of created beings before their Creator on that day—contrasting sharply with worldly life where people argue, make excuses, and assert themselves. The division of humanity into 'wretched' (shaqiyy) and 'blessed' (sa'eed) reflects the Qur'anic theme of ultimate accountability, where the outcomes of each soul's earthly choices and deeds become manifest and irreversible. This verse reinforces the broader Qur'anic message that worldly life is a trial period during which moral and spiritual choices determine one's eternal destiny, and that on the Day of Judgment, the illusion of human autonomy gives way to the stark reality of divine judgment and permission governing every action, including speech itself.

translation: As for those who are wretched, they will be in the Fire; for them therein is sighing and wailing (groaning and gasping).
interpretation: This verse describes the fate of the damned on the Day of Judgment, contrasting them with the blessed mentioned in the surrounding verses. The 'zafir' and 'shahiq' refer to the sounds of extreme distress—deep groaning on exhaling and a rasping, gasping intake of breath—likened to the braying of a donkey, symbolizing unbearable anguish and suffering. This imagery conveys that the punishment of Hellfire is not merely physical pain but a state of perpetual torment that manifests even in the involuntary sounds of breathing, emphasizing the totality and inescapability of the suffering experienced by those who rejected faith and righteousness. The verse serves as a stark warning, urging believers to reflect on the consequences of their choices in worldly life and to seek the mercy and guidance that lead to salvation rather than this described wretchedness.

translation: Abiding therein for as long as the heavens and the earth endure, save what your Lord wills. Indeed, your Lord is the accomplisher of whatsoever He intends.
interpretation: This verse, part of the passage describing the fate of the damned in Hellfire (following verse 106), has long occupied Islamic theologians because of its seemingly open-ended qualification: 'khalidina fiha' (abiding therein) is immediately modified by 'ma damat as-samawatu wal-ardu illa ma sha'a rabbuka' (as long as the heavens and earth endure, except what your Lord wills). Rather than asserting an absolute, unconditional eternity of punishment, the verse ties the duration of chastisement to the continuance of the heavens and earth—themselves created, finite things destined to pass away at the Hour—and then adds a further exception clause tied explicitly to divine will. This grammatical and theological structure has been read by some exegetes (including certain early scholars and later thinkers like Ibn Taymiyyah and Ibn al-Qayyim) as leaving open the possibility that God's mercy may ultimately encompass even the people of the Fire, since His will is not bound by human expectation of permanence. Others insist the 'heavens and earth' here refers to those of the Hereafter, which are indeed everlasting, thus preserving the doctrine of eternal damnation for disbelievers while still honoring the exception clause as a reminder of God's absolute sovereignty. The closing statement, 'inna rabbaka fa''alun lima yurid' (indeed your Lord is the accomplisher of what He intends), underscores that no rule, including the fate of the damned, operates independently of God's will; He is not constrained by His own decrees but acts entirely according to His unconstrained power and purpose.
