The verse thus functions less as a precise doctrinal pronouncement on the eternality of Hell and more as a profound assertion of divine omnipotence and the mystery of God's will, which transcends human categories of permanence and exception, leaving the ultimate disposition of souls to His inscrutable wisdom and mercy.

translation: And as for those who are blessed [with happiness], they will be in Paradise, abiding therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure, except as your Lord wills - a gift uninterrupted.
interpretation: This verse describes the eternal reward of the righteous in Paradise, using the duration of the heavens and earth as a metaphor for perpetuity, since these were considered the most enduring things known to the original audience. The phrase 'except as your Lord wills' affirms God's absolute sovereignty and power even over the nature of eternal reward itself, reminding believers that all blessings, including eternal ones, exist entirely at His discretion and are not owed by necessity. The concluding phrase 'a gift uninterrupted' emphasizes that this heavenly reward, unlike worldly gifts, will never be cut off, diminished, or withdrawn, representing a state of perfect and lasting divine grace and favor that stands in contrast to the fleeting and limited nature of earthly existence.

translation: So be not in doubt concerning what these [people] worship. They worship not except as their fathers worshipped before. And indeed, We will give them their share undiminished.
interpretation: This verse, addressed to the Prophet Muhammad, offers reassurance regarding the futility and irrationality of the idolatry practiced by his people. It clarifies that their worship of false deities is not based on reasoned conviction but merely on blind imitation of their ancestors, a tradition inherited without critical reflection. The verse warns against being troubled or uncertain about the fate of such idolaters, affirming a principle of divine justice: those who persist in error, like their forefathers, will receive the full consequence of their deeds—whether reward for any good or punishment for wrongdoing—without any reduction. This underscores the Quranic theme that God's justice is precise and complete, applying consistently across generations to those who choose misguidance over truth, while also serving as a subtle critique of following tradition blindly rather than through independent reasoning and faith.

translation: And We certainly gave Moses the Scripture, but it was disputed over. And had it not been for a word that preceded from your Lord, the matter would have been decided between them. And indeed, they are, concerning it, in disquieting doubt.
interpretation: This verse draws a parallel between the disputes that arose among the followers of Moses over the Torah and the disputes among the Prophet Muhammad's contemporaries over the Qur'an, offering him consolation. It establishes a pattern: whenever divine revelation is sent, disagreement and division inevitably follow among those who receive it, not because of any flaw in the message but because of human inclination toward dispute, bias, and skepticism. The 'word that preceded from your Lord' refers to God's prior decree to delay final judgment and punishment until the appointed Day of Resurrection, granting humanity respite and the opportunity for faith, repentance, or further misguidance in the interim, rather than settling disputes immediately through worldly destruction as happened with some earlier disbelieving nations. This divine patience, however, is not indifference; it coexists with the reality that many remain in deep, troubling doubt about revelation, a doubt rooted not in honest inquiry but in stubbornness and spiritual unease that gives rise to skepticism, highlighting that deferred judgment serves a wise purpose.

translation: And indeed, to each of them your Lord will surely pay in full [the recompense of] their deeds. Indeed, He is Acquainted with what they do.
interpretation: This verse affirms the principle of divine justice and absolute accountability. Coming after a series of narratives about previous nations and their disputes over faith, it serves as a conclusion emphasizing that despite the different paths people take—belief or disbelief, righteousness or corruption—none will escape the ultimate reckoning. The repetition of emphatic particles (inna, lamma, la) in the Arabic underscores the certainty of this recompense; it is not a mere possibility but an inevitable outcome. The verse also highlights that God's judgment is not based on superficial appearances or human assumptions about who is righteous, but on complete and intimate knowledge (khabeer) of every action, intention, and circumstance. This serves both as a warning to those who do wrong, that nothing escapes divine awareness, and as a consolation to believers who may suffer injustice in this world, assuring them that ultimate justice will prevail in the Hereafter.

translation: So remain steadfast as you have been commanded, and those who have repented with you, and do not transgress. Indeed, He is Seeing of what you do.
interpretation: This verse commands the Prophet Muhammad and his followers to remain firm and committed to the straight path of faith exactly as divinely instructed, without deviation, excess, or innovation. The inclusion of 'those who have repented with you' extends this responsibility to the entire community of believers, not just the Prophet alone, emphasizing collective moral accountability. The prohibition against 'transgressing' (tatghaw) warns against exceeding proper limits—whether through extremism in religious practice, arrogance, injustice toward others, or any form of excess that violates divine boundaries. The verse concludes with a reminder of God's constant awareness of human actions, serving as both a comfort to the sincere and a warning to those who might stray. This balance between steadfastness and moderation reflects the Quranic ideal of the 'middle way'—unwavering commitment to faith without falling into either negligence or fanatical excess. Classical commentators note that this verse was considered so weighty that the Prophet reportedly said it had 'aged' him, due to the immense responsibility of maintaining unwavering righteousness.

translation: And do not incline toward those who do wrong, lest the Fire touch you, and you have no protectors besides Allah, nor would you then be helped.
interpretation: This verse warns believers against leaning toward, relying upon, or aligning themselves with wrongdoers—whether through political alliance, moral compromise, or dependence on their favor for worldly gain. The 'inclining' (rukun) implies a subtle drift of the heart and loyalty toward injustice, even without active participation in it, and this is enough to bring consequence. The warning of the Fire signifies that moral compromise with oppression carries spiritual and possibly eschatological danger, not merely political risk. The verse emphasizes that true protection and support come only from Allah; seeking refuge or alliance in the structures of the unjust is ultimately futile, since no human power can shield one from divine accountability. It calls for integrity, independence of conscience, and trust in divine providence over expedient worldly alliances.

translation: And establish prayer at the two ends of the day and in the hours nearest the night. Indeed, good deeds do away with evil deeds. That is a reminder for those who remember.
interpretation: This verse establishes the regular rhythm of prayer as a means of spiritual purification woven into the natural structure of the day. By anchoring worship to the two ends of the day and the approach of night—times corresponding to the dawn, the sunset or evening periods—the verse ties remembrance of God to the recurring cycle of light and darkness, making devotion a constant, renewable practice rather than an occasional act. The assurance that good deeds erase evil ones speaks to the redemptive power of consistent righteous action: sincere worship and virtuous conduct can counteract and dissolve the effects of past wrongdoing, offering hope rather than despair to the sinner who turns back toward good. This is not a mechanical cancellation but reflects the transformative effect that sustained mindfulness of God and ethical striving have on the soul, gradually displacing bad habits and moral failures with righteousness. The closing phrase, calling this 'a reminder for those who remember,' underscores that this truth is accessible and meaningful specifically to those whose hearts are inclined toward reflection and God-consciousness (dhikr)—it is not a universal automatic law but a lesson grasped through active spiritual attentiveness. Thus the verse links ritual discipline, moral psychology, and divine mercy: regular prayer cultivates the remembrance that makes a person receptive to the erasing power of good deeds over sin.

translation: And be patient, for indeed, Allah does not allow the reward of the doers of good to be lost.
interpretation: This verse offers a divine assurance that serves as both comfort and motivation to believers facing hardship, persecution, or the slow pace of righteous outcomes in a world often dominated by injustice. The command to 'be patient' (isbir) is not passive resignation but an active, sustained endurance in righteousness despite trials. The reasoning clause that follows—'Allah does not allow the reward of the doers of good to be lost'—grounds this patience in a theological guarantee: moral effort and good deeds (ihsan) are never wasted in God's accounting, even if they go unrecognized or unrewarded in worldly terms. This connects patience (sabr) with ihsan (excellence in action and intention), suggesting that true righteousness requires sustained commitment over time, often without immediate visible reward. The verse implicitly critiques a transactional view of morality where one expects instant recompense, instead pointing toward a cosmic justice that operates beyond human timeframes and perceptions. It was revealed in a context where early Muslims faced significant adversity, and its placement affirms that steadfastness in the face of difficulty is itself part of the muhsin's (doer of good) character, not a separate virtue. The verse thus binds together patience and excellence as complementary components of a life oriented toward God, reassuring believers that their struggles and good deeds exist within a moral economy that Allah alone fully perceives and will ultimately honor.

translation: So why were there not, among the generations before you, people of lasting virtue who forbade corruption in the land - except a few of those We saved among them? But those who did wrong pursued the luxury they were given, and they were criminals.
interpretation: This verse reflects on the pattern of moral decline in past nations and poses a rhetorical question lamenting the scarcity of righteous reformers within them. It suggests that the destruction of previous civilizations was not merely due to their wrongdoing, but also due to the failure of a critical mass of conscientious people to stand up against corruption and injustice when it mattered. Only a small remnant possessed the moral fortitude and foresight to oppose societal decay, and it was this remnant whom God spared from the punishment that befell the rest. The majority, however, became absorbed in the pursuit of material luxury and comfort - the very prosperity that corrupted their values - which in turn led them into transgression and criminality. This establishes a broader Quranic principle: the fate of nations is often tied not just to the sins of individuals, but to the collective failure of a society to cultivate and heed voices calling for justice and restraint against moral and social corruption. The verse implicitly calls on the Prophet's community to learn from this history, emphasizing the vital role of those who actively resist corruption as a safeguard against divine punishment, and warning against the seductive dangers of worldly luxury that can lead entire communities toward wrongdoing.

translation: And your Lord would never destroy the towns unjustly while their people were reformers (righteous doers of good).
interpretation: This verse establishes a fundamental principle of divine justice: God's destruction of communities in history was never arbitrary or capricious, but always a direct consequence of pervasive corruption, wrongdoing, and moral decay among their inhabitants. The phrase 'bi-zulm' (unjustly) clarifies that divine punishment is never inflicted without cause—it is not God who commits injustice, but rather the communities who bring destruction upon themselves through their own injustice (zulm), whether against themselves, each other, or in disbelief toward their Creator. The qualifier 'wa ahluha muslihun' (while their people were reformers/doers of good) indicates that as long as a sufficient core of righteousness, reform, and ethical conduct exists within a society, divine mercy holds back punishment. This reflects a broader Quranic theme found in stories like that of Lot's people, where the presence or absence of righteous individuals determined the fate of entire communities. The verse serves as a theological reassurance that the moral order of the universe is coherent and just—nations and civilizations are not destroyed capriciously but as a natural consequence of their own collective moral failure, while those who maintain righteousness and work to correct wrongs are protected. This places responsibility on human communities themselves: continuous self-reform, justice, and ethical conduct serve as a shield against calamity, while sustained corruption, oppression, and moral decay invite the natural consequences of divine law operating in history.

translation: And if your Lord had willed, He could have made mankind one single community, but they continue to differ (remaining in constant disagreement) —
interpretation: This verse addresses the reality of human diversity and disagreement, particularly in matters of religion and belief. It establishes that God possesses the absolute power to have created all of humanity as a single, uniform community with one creed and one path, leaving no room for dissent. However, He chose not to exercise this power in that manner. Instead, He endowed human beings with free will and the capacity for independent reasoning and choice, which inevitably results in diversity of thought, belief, and interpretation. This difference among people is thus not an accident or a flaw in creation, but a deliberate feature of the divine plan tied to the gift of free will. The verse suggests that the very purpose of human testing and moral responsibility depends on this capacity to choose differently, since without the possibility of disagreement, there would be no meaningful faith, no genuine choice between guidance and misguidance, and no basis for accountability. This sets up the broader Quranic theme that people will be held responsible for how they exercise this freedom, and that ultimate judgment will resolve the differences that human free will has produced in this world.

translation: Except those on whom your Lord has mercy; and for that He created them. And the word of your Lord has been fulfilled: 'I will surely fill Hell with jinn and men all together.'
interpretation: This verse comes at the conclusion of a passage (11:118-119) discussing human disagreement and diversity of belief. It teaches that while people will inevitably differ and diverge in matters of faith, those who receive God's mercy are exempted from the negative consequences of this discord. The phrase 'for that He created them' has been interpreted in various ways by scholars: some understand it as referring to God creating humanity for the purpose of receiving mercy and living in harmony with divine guidance, while others connect it to the broader context of creating people with the capacity for both guidance and error, diversity of belief and practice. The verse then affirms the certainty of divine decree regarding the ultimate sorting of creation—that Hell will be filled with those among jinn and humans who reject guidance and persist in wrongdoing, fulfilling a word/decree that was established as part of God's foreknowledge and justice. This serves as both a warning about accountability and a reminder of divine mercy as the saving exception to humanity's capacity for division and error.

translation: And each [story] We relate to you from the news of the messengers is that by which We make firm your heart. And there has come to you, in this, the truth and an admonition and a reminder for the believers.
interpretation: This verse, from Surah Hud, articulates the divine purpose behind the Qur'an's narrative accounts of earlier prophets and their communities. It addresses the Prophet Muhammad directly, explaining that these stories of past messengers—their struggles, the rejection they faced, and their eventual vindication—are not mere historical recounting but serve a specific psychological and spiritual function: to strengthen and steady his heart amid the hardships of prophethood. By seeing that previous prophets endured similar patterns of denial, mockery, and persecution from their own peoples, and that they persevered through divine support, the Prophet is reassured that his own trials are part of a recurring divine pattern rather than a sign of failure or abandonment. The verse then broadens its scope beyond this consolation function, declaring that these narratives also constitute 'the truth,' meaning they are accurate and purposeful revelations rather than mere literature or legend. Furthermore, they serve as a 'moezah' (admonition or exhortation), warning against the consequences of rejecting divine guidance, and as a 'dhikra' (reminder) specifically for believers, who are meant to draw lessons, strengthen their faith, and find patterns of hope and warning in these accounts. The verse thus encapsulates a threefold function of prophetic storytelling in the Qur'an: emotional and spiritual fortification for the Prophet himself, affirmation of revelatory truth, and moral-spiritual instruction for the community of believers who look to these stories as a mirror for their own circumstances of faith and trial.

translation: And say to those who do not believe: 'Act according to your position (or capability); indeed, we are acting (as well).'
interpretation: This verse is a declaration of resolute steadfastness addressed to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) to convey to the disbelievers. It is not a command granting permission to persist in disbelief, but rather a form of stern warning and ultimatum, similar in tone to 'do as you will.' It conveys that the believers will continue on their path of faith and righteous action regardless of the opposition and rejection they face, while the disbelievers are free to continue on their own path. The phrase carries an implicit threat, as it is often followed in the Quran by statements indicating that the outcome and ultimate triumph will be made clear in time, and that each party will eventually see the consequences of their choices. It underscores themes of free will, moral responsibility, and the certainty of divine justice, affirming that both parties will witness who achieves a good end and who faces disgrace, as the matter is left to unfold according to God's will and judgment.

translation: "And wait; indeed, we [too] are waiting."
interpretation: This verse is part of a recurring Qur'anic motif in which prophets, after delivering their message and facing rejection or mockery from disbelieving peoples, declare that both sides should simply wait to see the outcome. It is a statement of confident resignation to divine justice: the believers wait for God's promised help, vindication, or the fulfillment of His warning to the wrongdoers, while the disbelievers wait, often mockingly, to see if the threatened punishment will actually materialize. The phrase underscores the theme of patience (sabr) and trust in God's timing, affirming that ultimate judgment and truth will be revealed in due course, regardless of human impatience or skepticism. It also carries a subtle warning tone—suggesting that the waiting of the disbelievers will end in regret, while the waiting of the believers will end in reward and vindication.

translation: To Allah belongs the unseen of the heavens and the earth, and to Him the whole matter will be returned. So worship Him and put your trust in Him. And your Lord is not unaware of what you do.
interpretation: This verse affirms Allah's exclusive knowledge of all that is hidden in the heavens and earth, and establishes that all affairs ultimately return to His judgment and authority. From this foundation of divine omniscience and sovereignty, the verse draws a practical conclusion: since Allah alone possesses complete knowledge and control, the appropriate human response is twofold—worship (ibadah) as acknowledgment of His supreme authority, and tawakkul (trust/reliance) as acknowledgment of one's own limitations in controlling outcomes. The closing assurance that Allah is not heedless of human actions serves as both comfort to the believer, who knows their efforts are not unseen, and as a subtle warning against moral complacency, since nothing escapes divine awareness. The verse thus links metaphysical claims about Allah's nature to ethical and spiritual practice, suggesting that correct theology naturally gives rise to correct worship and correct disposition toward one's own agency and limitations.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Alif, Lam, Ra. These are the verses of the clear Book.
interpretation: The verse opens with disjointed letters (muqatta'at) whose precise meaning is known only to Allah, serving to draw attention to the miraculous nature of the Qur'an, which is composed of the same letters Arabs used daily yet remains inimitable. The declaration that these are verses of 'the clear Book' emphasizes that the Qur'an is manifest in its guidance, clear in its language, and unambiguous in conveying truth, distinguishing right from wrong, and clarifying matters of faith. This clarity serves as a proof of its divine origin, as it illuminates the path for those who seek understanding and removes doubt for sincere seekers of truth.

translation: Indeed, We have sent it down as an Arabic Qur'an so that you might understand.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes that the divine revelation was deliberately revealed in Arabic, the language of its first recipients, so that they could directly comprehend, reflect upon, and apply its guidance without the barrier of translation or foreign idiom. The choice of Arabic is not presented as a statement of linguistic superiority but as a matter of communicative wisdom—revelation must come in a language intelligible to the community it first addresses. The phrase 'so that you might understand' (la'allakum ta'qilun) links the act of revelation directly to the faculty of reason ('aql), suggesting that the Qur'an is meant to engage the intellect, not merely to be recited or believed blindly. It implies that full comprehension of the message requires active rational engagement, reflection, and contemplation, not passive reception. This also underscores the broader Qur'anic theme that guidance and belief are meant to be grounded in understanding, making the human intellect a partner in the process of receiving divine truth.

translation: We relate to you [O Prophet] the best of stories in what We have revealed to you of this Qur'an, although before it you were among those unaware.
interpretation: This verse opens the narrative of Surah Yusuf (Joseph) by establishing the divine source and unique quality of the story about to be told. By calling it 'the best of stories,' God signals that the account of Yusuf is not merely entertainment or folklore but a masterfully crafted narrative containing profound lessons on patience, trust in divine providence, forgiveness, and the fulfillment of destiny despite betrayal and hardship. The verse also serves an apologetic and evidentiary function: it emphasizes that Muhammad, being unlettered and having no prior access to the detailed historical and scriptural traditions of the Israelites, could not have fabricated or learned this intricate story through ordinary means. His previous 'unawareness' underscores that the knowledge came through revelation alone, reinforcing the authenticity of his prophethood and the divine origin of the Qur'an. Thus, the verse functions both as an introduction to a didactic story and as a proof of revelation, inviting the listener to trust what follows as truth communicated directly by God rather than human invention or inherited folklore and to attend closely to the moral and spiritual lessons the narrative that follows is designed to impart to its audience.

translation: When Joseph said to his father, 'O my father, indeed I have seen [in a dream] eleven stars and the sun and the moon; I saw them prostrating to me.'
interpretation: This verse opens the narrative of Prophet Joseph (Yusuf) with a divinely inspired dream that foreshadows his future elevation and prophetic destiny. The eleven stars symbolize his eleven brothers, while the sun and moon represent his parents, indicating that one day his entire family would show him honor and deference. The dream is not merely a personal vision but a form of divine revelation, hinting at the trials Joseph would endure—including betrayal by his brothers and separation from his father—before ultimately rising to a position of power and reunion with his family in Egypt. Joseph's innocent and trusting disclosure of this dream to his father, whom he addresses with the tender term 'my father,' reflects the close, loving bond between them, and sets the stage for the father's protective wisdom, as he will later caution Joseph not to reveal the dream to his brothers, fearing their jealousy. This verse thus introduces the broader themes of the surah: divine providence, the trials of patience and faith, and the eventual triumph of righteousness and family reconciliation despite human treachery and envy, even using natural celestial sybols of cosmic order that hint at Joseph's divinely guided fate.

translation: He said, 'O my son, do not relate your vision to your brothers, or they will devise a plot against you. Indeed, Satan is a clear enemy to mankind.'
interpretation: This verse reveals Jacob's prophetic wisdom and foresight. Upon hearing Joseph's dream of eleven stars, the sun, and the moon prostrating to him—a clear sign of future greatness and prophethood—Jacob immediately recognizes the danger this knowledge poses if revealed to Joseph's brothers. His warning demonstrates deep psychological insight into human jealousy: he understands that his evident favoritism toward Joseph, combined with this dream signifying Joseph's exalted status, could ignite devastating envy among the brothers. Jacob's invocation of Satan as 'a clear enemy to mankind' frames sibling rivalry and envy not merely as a family dynamic but as part of the cosmic struggle between divine guidance and satanic temptation. This teaches that Satan often exploits natural human emotions—especially envy among kin—to sow discord and incite people toward harm. Jacob's counsel also illustrates a broader principle in Islamic thought: that wisdom involves not just knowing the truth but knowing when and to whom it should be disclosed, as premature or imprudent revelation of blessings can invite harm from those susceptible to jealousy.

translation: And thus will your Lord choose you and teach you the interpretation of events (or dreams/sayings) and complete His favor upon you and upon the family of Jacob, as He completed it upon your two forefathers before, Abraham and Isaac. Indeed, your Lord is Knowing and Wise.
interpretation: This verse is part of the Quranic narrative of Prophet Joseph (Yusuf), spoken by his father Jacob after hearing Joseph's dream of eleven stars, the sun, and the moon prostrating to him. Jacob recognizes that this dream signifies divine selection, foretelling that Joseph will be chosen by God for a special purpose—both prophethood and a position of worldly authority. The 'interpretation of events' (ta'wil al-ahadith) refers to the ability to interpret dreams and understand the hidden meanings behind occurrences, a gift that becomes central to Joseph's later role in Egypt, particularly in interpreting the Pharaoh's dream and his own brothers' earlier plot against him. By linking Joseph's selection to that of his forefathers Abraham and Isaac, the verse establishes a continuous lineage of prophetic favor and divine wisdom within this family, reinforcing the theme that God's blessings are bestowed through a chosen prophetic line based on His infinite knowledge and wisdom. This also serves as a subtle foreshadowing that despite the hardships Joseph will face—including betrayal by his brothers—his ultimate destiny of honor and favor from God is already secured and will unfold according to divine plan.

translation: Indeed, in [the story of] Joseph and his brothers were signs for those who ask.
interpretation: This verse opens the Surah of Yusuf by announcing that the narrative to follow contains profound lessons and signs ('ayat) for those genuinely seeking understanding. The phrase 'for those who ask' suggests the story addresses real questions that arise from human experience: about jealousy and its destructive power, about betrayal within families, about the patience required to endure injustice, and ultimately about divine providence working through seemingly tragic circumstances. The mention of Joseph's brothers alongside him emphasizes that this is not merely a personal story but a story of relationships, family dynamics, and the moral struggles that occur within the closest of bonds. The signs referred to include demonstrations of God's wisdom in orchestrating events—turning what appeared to be calamity (being thrown into a well, sold into slavery, imprisoned unjustly) into the means by which Joseph rose to a position of authority and was eventually reunited with his family. This verse serves as an invitation to the listener to pay close attention to the subsequent narrative as a source of spiritual and practical wisdom, applicable beyond the specific historical context to universal human experiences of trial, patience, forgiveness, and trust in divine plan.

translation: When they said: 'Surely Joseph and his brother are dearer to our father than we are, though we are a strong group. Indeed, our father is in manifest error.'
interpretation: This verse reveals the inner jealousy and resentment harbored by Joseph's brothers, exposing the psychological roots of the conspiracy that follows. Their complaint reflects a flawed understanding of fatherly love and divine favor, as they measure worth in terms of numbers and strength ('we are a strong group') rather than character or spiritual merit. By accusing their father Jacob of being in 'manifest error,' they attempt to rationalize their planned betrayal, projecting their own moral failing onto him. This moment illustrates how envy distorts perception and judgment, leading individuals to justify unethical actions through self-serving narratives. It also sets up a broader Quranic theme: that human jealousy, especially among kin, can become a catalyst for trials that ultimately serve a greater divine purpose, as Joseph's story will later demonstrate through his eventual rise and reconciliation with his brothers.

translation: Kill Joseph or cast him out to [another] land; your father's attention will [then] be only for you, and after that you will be righteous people.
interpretation: This verse records the internal deliberation of Joseph's brothers as they plot against him out of jealousy, since their father Jacob showed him particular love and favor. Their proposal reveals a rationalized self-deception common to human wrongdoing: they frame a grave sin—killing or abandoning their own brother—as a path to restoring familial harmony and even becoming 'righteous' afterward. This illustrates how envy and desire for a parent's exclusive attention can corrupt moral judgment, leading people to justify cruelty through false reasoning that promises repentance or virtue as an outcome of sin. The verse sets up the broader Quranic theme of how Allah's plan unfolds despite human schemes, as Joseph's eventual rise to power in Egypt emerges precisely through the very hardship his brothers inflict upon him.

translation: A speaker among them said, 'Do not kill Joseph, but throw him into the bottom of the well; some travelers will pick him up—if you are going to do [anything].'
interpretation: This verse records the intervention of one of Joseph's brothers (traditionally identified as either Judah or Reuben) who, while still complicit in the plot against Joseph, proposes a less violent alternative to murder. His suggestion reveals a moral compromise rather than genuine righteousness: he seeks to avoid bloodguilt while still removing Joseph from the family through abandonment, calculating that passing caravans would likely rescue the child, thus easing his own conscience while still achieving the brothers' shared goal of being rid of Joseph. This episode illustrates how envy can corrupt family bonds, and how even partial restraint from evil can still serve as a step within a broader sinful scheme. It also sets the stage for divine providence to work through human treachery, as this seemingly cruel act of casting Joseph into the well becomes the very means by which God's plan for Joseph's eventual rise to power in Egypt unfolds.

translation: They said, 'O our father, why do you not trust us with Joseph, while indeed, we are to him sincere advisors?'
interpretation: This verse marks the beginning of the narrative of Joseph's brothers' deception. Their words reveal a striking irony and foreshadowing: they publicly profess sincerity and trustworthiness toward Joseph while secretly harboring jealousy and plotting to harm him. The rhetorical question posed to their father Jacob is manipulative, designed to make his natural caution and protective instinct seem unreasonable or unjustified. This illustrates a broader Qur'anic theme about the gap between outward speech and inward intention, and how envy can corrupt family bonds, leading people to mask malice with claims of good will. Jacob's hesitance, rooted in a father's intuition, is set against his sons' persuasive but false reassurance, setting the stage for the test of patience and trust in divine wisdom that unfolds throughout the surah.

translation: Send him with us tomorrow that he may enjoy himself and play, and indeed, we will be his guardians.
interpretation: This verse records the deceptive plea of Yusuf's (Joseph's) brothers to their father Ya'qub (Jacob), asking permission to take young Yusuf out with them. Their words are laced with dramatic irony, as the reader/listener already senses or will soon learn of their jealousy and ill intentions toward him. The phrase 'that he may enjoy himself and play' appeals to a father's natural desire to see his child experience carefree joy with companions his own age, while 'we will be his guardians' is a solemn assurance meant to dispel any paternal worry. The verse illustrates how deceit often cloaks itself in reasonable-sounding, even affectionate language, exploiting trust and familial bonds for a hidden, harmful purpose. It sets the stage for the ensuing betrayal, highlighting themes of sibling envy, the vulnerability of innocence, and the human capacity to mask malice behind words of care.

translation: He [Jacob] said, 'Indeed, it saddens me that you should take him away, and I fear that the wolf would eat him while you are unaware of him.'
interpretation: This verse captures Jacob's (Ya'qub) deep paternal love and anxiety regarding his son Joseph (Yusuf). When Joseph's brothers requested to take him out to play, Jacob expressed his emotional distress at being separated from Joseph, revealing the special bond and affection he held for him. His stated fear of the wolf serves as the surface reason for his reluctance, but it also foreshadows the deception his sons would later construct, as they would indeed claim a wolf devoured Joseph to cover up their act of throwing him into a well. Jacob's intuition and fatherly instinct sensed potential danger, though he could not have known the actual betrayal that awaited. This moment illustrates the theme of a parent's protective love clashing with the hidden jealousy and malice within his own family, setting the stage for the trials that follow in the story of Joseph, which ultimately demonstrate Allah's wisdom in orchestrating events despite human scheming.

translation: They said, 'If a wolf should eat him while we are a group [of so many], then indeed, we would be losers.'
interpretation: This verse captures the deceptive reassurance Joseph's brothers gave to their father Jacob when they asked to take Joseph out with them, after Jacob expressed fear that a wolf might devour him. Their statement is laden with dramatic irony, as the audience of the Quran knows that the brothers themselves intend harm to Joseph, and later use the very excuse of a wolf to cover up their plot. Their confident assertion that their collective strength ('we are a group') would prevent such a fate serves to lull their father's suspicions, while foreshadowing their own treachery. The use of 'losers' (khasirun) is particularly poignant, as it is the brothers who ultimately become spiritually and morally diminished through their betrayal, not through any wolf's attack. This verse exemplifies how the Quran often reveals human capacity for calculated deception, masking malicious intent behind seemingly logical and reassuring words, while also setting up the narrative tension that drives the rest of the Joseph story forward.

translation: So when they went with him and agreed to put him into the bottom of the well, We inspired him: 'You will surely inform them of this deed of theirs when they do not perceive [who you are].'
interpretation: This verse marks a divine intervention at the very moment of Yusuf's greatest vulnerability and betrayal by his own brothers. As they cast him into the darkness of the well, God does not abandon him but communicates directly with him, granting him both comfort and a prophetic promise. The revelation assures Yusuf that the very crime being committed against him will one day be exposed by his own testimony, delivered to the perpetrators themselves, at a time when they will not even recognize him. This foreshadows the later scene in Egypt where Yusuf, now a powerful figure, reveals his identity to his unsuspecting brothers. The verse teaches that divine providence operates even in moments of apparent helplessness and injustice, planting seeds of future vindication and reversal of fortune. It also establishes a theme central to the entire surah: that human schemes and betrayals, however severe, are ultimately encompassed within a greater divine plan that will unfold in due time, often through means the perpetrators cannot anticipate.

translation: And they came to their father in the evening, weeping.
interpretation: This verse describes the brothers of Yusuf (Joseph) returning to their father Ya'qub (Jacob) after having thrown Yusuf into the well, pretending grief to mask their deception. Their choice of evening time and their feigned weeping were calculated to make their fabricated story more believable, exploiting a parent's vulnerability and trust. This moment illustrates the depth of their jealousy-driven betrayal and foreshadows the layers of deception that run throughout the story of Yusuf. It also sets up the dramatic irony central to the narrative, as the audience knows the truth while Ya'qub is being manipulated by his own sons, highlighting themes of trust, betrayal, and the eventual triumph of truth and divine justice that unfold later in the surah.

translation: They said, 'O our father, indeed we went racing each other and left Joseph with our belongings, and the wolf ate him. But you will not believe us, even if we are truthful.'
interpretation: This verse captures the moment when Joseph's brothers return to their father Jacob with their fabricated story after having thrown Joseph into a well. Their statement is psychologically revealing: by preemptively declaring that Jacob won't believe them 'even if we were truthful,' they attempt to shield themselves from suspicion through a clever rhetorical strategy, acknowledging his likely doubt before he can even express it. This anticipatory defense actually betrays their guilt, as truthful people rarely need to argue for their own credibility in such a manner. The verse illustrates the nature of deception and guilt, showing how liars often overcompensate in their speech, inadvertently revealing the falsehood they attempt to conceal. Jacob's deep intuition and paternal love, which the brothers anticipate correctly, foreshadows his continued grief and refusal to fully accept their account, setting the stage for his famous patience ('beautiful patience') in enduring the loss of his beloved son while harboring suspicion about the true fate of Joseph.

translation: And they brought upon his shirt false blood. He [Jacob] said, 'Rather, your souls have made an affair seem fair to you. So patience is most fitting. And Allah is the one sought for help against that which you describe.'
interpretation: This verse recounts the moment when Joseph's brothers returned to their father Jacob with his shirt stained with false blood, falsely claiming that a wolf had devoured him, when in fact they had thrown him into a well out of jealousy. Jacob, through his spiritual insight and deep understanding of his sons' characters, immediately perceived the deception, recognizing that their fabricated story concealed a scheme devised by their own desires and envy rather than an actual tragedy caused by a wild animal. His response demonstrates profound faith and emotional discipline: rather than succumbing to accusations, despair, or visible anguish, he resolves to practice 'beautiful patience' (sabrun jameel), a patience characterized by dignity, trust in God, and the absence of complaint to other human beings. This concept of sabrun jameel becomes a model in Islamic spirituality for enduring hardship and betrayal, particularly from those closest to us, without losing faith or resorting to despair. Jacob's declaration that 'Allah is the one sought for help' underscores the Quranic theme that ultimate recourse in the face of injustice and grief lies in reliance upon God alone, who possesses full knowledge of hidden truths and will ultimately bring justice and resolution, as the subsequent narrative of Joseph's story reveals. This moment also illustrates the painful reality of family betrayal and the strength required to maintain faith and composure when confronted with lies from those who should be trustworthy.

translation: And there came a caravan, and they sent their water-drawer, and he let down his bucket. He said, 'Good news! Here is a boy.' And they concealed him, [treating him] as merchandise. And Allah is Knowing of what they do.
interpretation: This verse marks the turning point in Yusuf's trial, where divine providence intervenes through seemingly ordinary human activity. The caravan's water-drawer, performing a mundane task, becomes the unwitting instrument of Allah's plan to rescue Yusuf from the well where his brothers had left him to die. The water-drawer's exclamation of joy reveals human nature's immediate reaction to a fortunate discovery, yet it is tinged with self-interest, as he and his companions see Yusuf not as a vulnerable child to be returned to his family, but as 'bidā'ah' (merchandise) - valuable property to be exploited for profit. Their decision to conceal him and treat him as a commodity rather than seeking his true identity or family reveals the moral compromise and exploitation of the vulnerable that existed in that society, where a human being could be reduced to an object of commerce. The closing phrase, 'Allah is Knowing of what they do,' serves as a subtle but powerful reminder that even as these men act out of greed and deception, their actions remain within the full knowledge and ultimately the orchestration of Allah's greater plan. This divine knowledge is not merely passive observation but active oversight, suggesting that the very schemes meant to exploit Yusuf become the means by which Allah elevates him to a position of honor and authority. This illustrates a recurring Quranic theme: that human schemes, whether born of jealousy, greed, or malice, cannot thwart the divine decree, and that Allah often works through imperfect human intentions and actions to bring about His perfect and merciful outcomes.

translation: And they sold him for a paltry price - a few dirhams - and they were, in regard to him, indifferent (having little interest or desire for him).
interpretation: This verse refers to the moment when the brothers of Prophet Yusuf (Joseph), after drawing him out of the well, sold him to a passing caravan for a trivial sum of money. The phrase 'thaman bakhs' (a reduced/paltry price) and 'darahim ma'dudah' (a few counted dirhams) emphasizes how little value was placed on him despite his immense worth and future prophethood - highlighting the injustice and blindness of those who undervalued him. The closing phrase indicates that his own brothers, who sold him, had little attachment or desire to keep him, showing their eagerness to be rid of him due to their jealousy, rather than any genuine interest in profiting from the transaction. This underscores a broader Quranic theme: that worldly transactions and human judgments of worth are often starkly disconnected from true, divinely-recognized value - Yusuf's true station would later be revealed through his rise to power in Egypt, demonstrating that what is sold cheaply by men may be exalted by God.

translation: And he who bought him, from Egypt, said to his wife, 'Make his stay comfortable; perhaps he will benefit us, or we may take him as a son.' And thus We established Joseph in the land, that We might teach him the interpretation of events. And Allah is predominant over His affair, but most people do not know.
interpretation: This verse marks the turning point in Joseph's trial, where the humiliation of being sold as a slave is transformed by divine providence into the very means of his elevation. The Egyptian official's kindness—born of worldly motives of profit or adoption—is shown to be an instrument of a far greater, unseen plan. The phrase 'We established Joseph in the land' signals that God was already orchestrating events toward Joseph's eventual position of authority, using even his enslavement as a stage in that process. The reference to teaching him 'the interpretation of events' (or dreams) foreshadows the skill that will later save him and an entire nation from famine. The closing statement—that God is dominant over His affair while most people remain unaware—captures a central theme of the Surah: human beings act according to their limited perceptions and immediate desires, not realizing they are instruments within a comprehensive divine design that unfolds gradually and purposefully, often through what appears to be misfortune or coincidence.

translation: And when he reached his full strength, We gave him judgment and knowledge. Thus do We reward the doers of good.
interpretation: This verse refers to the Prophet Yusuf (Joseph), describing how, upon reaching physical and intellectual maturity, God bestowed upon him wisdom (hukm) and knowledge ('ilm). This divine gift was not merely a natural consequence of growing older but a special favor granted by God as a reward for Yusuf's righteous character and moral excellence (ihsan) throughout his trials, including his resistance to temptation and his patience in adversity. The verse establishes a broader principle beyond the specific narrative: God consistently rewards those who do good (al-muhsinin) with wisdom, sound judgment, and deeper understanding. This reflects a recurring Qur'anic theme that spiritual and intellectual gifts are often earned through moral conduct and steadfastness rather than simply bestowed arbitrarily. The pairing of 'hukm' (wisdom/authority to judge rightly) and 'ilm' (knowledge) suggests that true wisdom involves both the acquisition of knowledge and the practical capacity to apply it justly—qualities that would later enable Yusuf to interpret dreams, administer justice, and govern wisely in Egypt.

translation: And she, in whose house he was, sought to seduce him from his self, and she closed the doors firmly and said, "Come, you." He said, "I seek refuge in God! Indeed, he (your husband) is my master, who has made good my residence. Indeed, wrongdoers do not prosper."
interpretation: This verse recounts the trial of Prophet Joseph (Yusuf) when the wife of al-Aziz, the Egyptian official in whose household he served, attempted to seduce him. The verse highlights several key themes: her deliberate and determined action (locking all the doors to ensure privacy), her direct invitation to him, and his immediate, resolute refusal rooted in piety and gratitude. Joseph's response demonstrates moral integrity on multiple levels—he invokes God's protection, acknowledges the trust placed in him by her husband who had treated him kindly, and recognizes that succumbing would constitute a grave betrayal and injustice (zulm). His declaration that "wrongdoers do not prosper" serves as both a personal conviction and a broader theological principle, affirming that ultimate success and prosperity, in this life and the hereafter, belong to those who maintain righteousness even under intense temptation and pressure. This episode establishes Joseph as an exemplar of chastity and steadfastness in the face of seduction, particularly significant given his youth, vulnerability as a servant, and the power differential between him and his mistress.

translation: And she certainly determined [to seduce] him, and he would have inclined to her had he not seen the proof of his Lord. Thus [it was] that We might avert from him evil and immorality. Indeed, he was of Our chosen servants.
interpretation: This verse addresses the moment of extreme temptation faced by Prophet Yusuf (Joseph) when the wife of al-Aziz attempted to seduce him. The verse acknowledges the natural human inclination he may have felt, yet emphasizes that divine intervention—'the proof of his Lord' (burhan rabbihi)—protected him from succumbing to sin. This 'proof' is often understood by commentators as a moment of spiritual clarity, a vision, or an innate God-given insight that reminded Yusuf of his faith, his moral obligations, and the consequences of betraying the trust placed in him by al-Aziz. The verse illustrates a central Qur'anic theme: that true righteousness is not the absence of temptation, but the capacity to resist it through reliance on God's guidance. By describing Yusuf as one of God's 'chosen' or 'sincere' servants (al-mukhlasin), the verse underscores that his purity was not merely a personal virtue but a mark of divine selection and protection, affirming that God safeguards His chosen prophets from falling into moral corruption even in the face of intense human desire.

translation: And they both raced to the door, and she tore his shirt from behind, and they found her husband at the door. She said, 'What is the recompense of one who intended evil for your wife except that he be imprisoned or suffer a painful punishment?'
interpretation: This verse depicts the pivotal moment in the story of Yusuf (Joseph) when he flees from the advances of the wife of al-Aziz, who tears his shirt from behind as he runs toward the door—a detail of forensic significance, since a tear from behind would later prove his innocence and her guilt. Upon finding her husband unexpectedly at the door, she quickly fabricates an accusation against Yusuf, reversing the truth of the situation to protect her own reputation and honor, demonstrating both her cunning and her moral corruption. This moment underscores a recurring Qur'anic theme: the vindication of the righteous through subtle physical evidence (the torn shirt from behind rather than the front), illustrating divine justice operating through natural, circumstantial means. It also highlights the vulnerability of the innocent when facing false accusations from those in positions of power, while simultaneously planting the seeds for the eventual unveiling of truth, as the household witness (mentioned in the subsequent verses) reasons through the physical evidence to determine true culpability.

translation: He [Joseph] said, 'She sought to seduce me.' And a witness from her household testified: 'If his shirt is torn from the front, then she has told the truth, and he is of the liars.'
interpretation: This verse recounts the moment when Joseph, falsely accused by the wife of al-'Aziz, is defended through a clever piece of circumstantial evidence proposed by a member of her own household. The witness's logic—examining whether Joseph's shirt was torn from the front or the back—serves as an early example of forensic reasoning within the Qur'anic narrative, demonstrating that truth can be established through careful observation of physical evidence rather than relying solely on testimony. The fact that the witness comes from 'her household' (some commentators suggest this was a wise relative or infant child, per differing interpretations) underscores that justice and truth are values that transcend family loyalty or social position—even someone connected to the accuser is compelled to point toward an impartial method of discerning the truth. This episode highlights broader Qur'anic themes of divine protection for the sincere and righteous: Joseph, despite being in a vulnerable position as a slave in the house of a powerful man, is vindicated through means beyond his own power, illustrating that Allah safeguards those who maintain integrity even when human social structures seem stacked against them.

translation: But if his shirt was torn from behind, then she has lied, and he is of the truthful.
interpretation: This verse is part of the testimony given by a witness from the household during the incident involving Yusuf (Joseph) and the wife of al-Aziz. The witness proposes a logical test: if Yusuf's shirt was torn from the front, it would indicate he was pursuing her and she tore it while resisting him, making her truthful. But if it was torn from behind, it would mean she was pursuing him as he fled, and he tore it while escaping, making her the liar and him truthful. This demonstrates the Quranic emphasis on rational evidence and fair investigation before passing judgment, even in sensitive matters involving accusations of immorality. The physical evidence of the torn shirt becomes the deciding factor that exonerates Yusuf, showing that truth can be established through careful observation of circumstantial evidence rather than relying solely on testimony or social status. This moment also highlights Yusuf's innocence and moral integrity despite being in a vulnerable position as a servant in the house.

translation: So when he (the master) saw his shirt torn from behind, he said, 'Indeed, this is from your (women's) guile. Surely your guile is great.'
interpretation: This verse occurs in the story of Yusuf (Joseph) and the wife of al-Aziz. The torn shirt serves as physical evidence that determines the truth of the matter: because it was torn from behind, it proves Yusuf was fleeing from her, not pursuing her, thus establishing his innocence. The husband's declaration about the 'guile of women' reflects the social and psychological context of the narrative, acknowledging the scheming and manipulation the wife employed in attempting to seduce Yusuf and then falsely accuse him. This moment demonstrates how Allah protects His righteous servants through seemingly small, providential details—the physical evidence of the torn garment becomes the means by which Yusuf's integrity is vindicated despite his lower social standing as a servant. The verse also illustrates a broader Quranic theme about how truth can be uncovered through careful attention to evidence and reasoning, even in matters of private accusation where witnesses are absent.

translation: Joseph, turn away from this. And [to the woman], ask forgiveness for your sin; indeed, you were of the sinful.
interpretation: This verse occurs in the story of Joseph (Yusuf) after his innocence became evident to the husband of the woman who had attempted to seduce him and falsely accused him. The husband, recognizing the truth of the matter from the evidence (the torn shirt), addresses Joseph, telling him to disregard the incident and not dwell on it or publicize it further, protecting both his dignity and the matter from becoming a greater scandal. He then turns to his wife, commanding her to seek forgiveness for her sin, explicitly acknowledging her guilt and placing her among the sinners. This moment demonstrates the Quranic theme of truth prevailing despite false accusations, and it shows a measured, dignified response to wrongdoing - the husband does not seek public humiliation or excessive punishment, but rather calls for private repentance and moving forward. It also exemplifies Joseph's exemplary character, as he is counseled to let go of the matter rather than seek retribution, reflecting values of restraint, forgiveness, and maintaining social harmony even after being wronged.

translation: And women in the city said, 'The wife of al-'Azeez is seeking to seduce her young man; he has impassioned her with love. Indeed, we see her in clear error.'
interpretation: This verse depicts the social consequences of Zulaykha's infatuation with Yusuf becoming public knowledge. The women of the city, likely motivated by gossip and perhaps envy of the wife of a powerful official, openly criticize her behavior, judging her as having fallen into manifest error or misguidance. Their comment reveals the human tendency to judge others' private struggles with desire without understanding the full context, and sets up the narrative for Zulaykha's subsequent response—inviting these very women to a banquet where she dramatically demonstrates Yusuf's extraordinary beauty to justify her own overwhelming attraction, showing that even those who judge may themselves succumb to the same temptation when confronted with it directly.

translation: So when she heard of their scheming, she sent for them and prepared for them a banquet [with cushions to recline upon], and she gave each one of them a knife, and she said [to Joseph], 'Come out before them.' Then when they saw him, they greatly admired him and cut their hands, and they said, 'Perfect is Allah! This is not a man; this is none but a noble angel.'
interpretation: This verse captures the moment when Zulaikha, the wife of the Egyptian official, seeks to vindicate herself before the women of the city who had been gossiping about her infatuation with her slave Yusuf (Joseph). Rather than arguing verbally, she stages a dramatic demonstration: she invites the women to a banquet, gives each a knife ostensibly for cutting fruit, and then calls Yusuf to appear before them. The overwhelming beauty of his presence so stuns the women that they unconsciously cut their own hands instead of the fruit, not even feeling the pain due to their astonishment. Their exclamation 'This is not a man; this is none but a noble angel' serves a dual narrative purpose: it validates Zulaikha's own susceptibility to Yusuf's extraordinary beauty, showing that her attraction was not simply a moral failing unique to her but a natural human response to an almost supernatural comeliness, and it elevates Yusuf's character by associating his physical beauty with spiritual nobility and angelic purity. The episode also functions as a test and trial for Yusuf himself, foreshadowing the temptation he will face, while illustrating the theme that outward beauty can be a divine gift carrying both blessing and trial. The women's loss of self-control symbolizes how overwhelming beauty or truth can disarm human senses, and the incident sets the stage for the subsequent imprisonment of Yusuf, as Zulaikha, now publicly vindicated in the eyes of the women yet still consumed by desire, proceeds to pressure him further, leading him to choose prison over sin.

translation: She said, 'That is the one about whom you blamed me. And I did indeed seek to seduce him, but he resisted firmly. And if he does not do what I order him, he will surely be imprisoned and will be among the humiliated.'
interpretation: This verse captures the moment when the wife of al-Aziz, having orchestrated a scene to vindicate herself before the women who had criticized her, openly admits her attempted seduction of Yusuf in front of witnesses rather than hiding it, revealing both her desperation and a kind of brazen confidence once his beauty has silenced her critics. Her open confession paradoxically serves her reputation among the women, since his extraordinary beauty now explains, even excuses, her infatuation in their eyes. Yet the verse also exposes the raw abuse of power she wields over Yusuf, a slave in her household: she threatens him with prison and degradation if he will not submit to her will. This juxtaposition highlights Yusuf's moral integrity and self-restraint against the coercive power of his mistress, setting up the stark contrast between worldly authority and spiritual steadfastness that runs throughout his story. His refusal, despite the threat of punishment, shows that righteousness for him takes precedence over worldly comfort or safety, reinforcing the Qur'anic theme that true honor lies in resisting temptation and injustice even when the powerful demand compliance.

translation: He said: 'My Lord, prison is dearer to me than that to which they invite me. And if You do not turn away their plot from me, I will incline toward them and be of the ignorant.'
interpretation: This verse captures the prayer of Prophet Yusuf (Joseph) when faced with the temptation of the wife of al-Aziz and the other women of the city who had also been captivated by his beauty. Rather than yielding to seduction and worldly comfort, Yusuf prefers imprisonment, demonstrating that steadfast faith and moral integrity take precedence over physical ease or pleasure. His plea acknowledges human vulnerability—he recognizes that without divine protection, he could succumb to temptation despite his piety. This reflects the Islamic theological principle that resistance to sin requires God's grace, not merely human willpower alone. The term 'al-jahileen' (the ignorant) here refers not to lack of knowledge but to moral and spiritual ignorance—succumbing to desire would align him with those who act without wisdom or restraint. The verse thus illustrates true prophetic humility: strength lies not in self-reliance but in total dependence on God to safeguard one's virtue, and righteousness is shown to require active struggle and supplication, not passive assumption of one's own immunity to temptation.

translation: So his Lord responded to him and turned away from him their scheming. Indeed, He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.
interpretation: This verse refers to the story of Prophet Yusuf (Joseph) and his response to the temptation presented by the wife of al-Aziz and the other women of the city. Having prayed to God, saying he would rather be imprisoned than yield to their scheming, Yusuf's sincere supplication was answered: God shielded him from succumbing to temptation and from the trap being set for him. The verse emphasizes several theological points: first, that true protection from sin and moral corruption comes from reliance on God rather than one's own strength or cleverness; second, that God's attributes of being 'All-Hearing' and 'All-Knowing' assure believers that sincere prayers are heard and that God is fully aware of both the plots of those who scheme and the struggles of those who resist temptation. The verse also illustrates a broader Qur'anic theme of divine intervention in the lives of the righteous, protecting them from harm not through miraculous physical rescue alone, but through strengthening their resolve and steering circumstances away from sin, affirming that steadfastness in faith invites God's safeguarding grace.

translation: Then it occurred to them, after they had seen the signs [of his innocence], that they should surely imprison him for a time.
interpretation: This verse refers to the story of Prophet Yusuf (Joseph) and the aftermath of the incident with the wife of al-Aziz. Despite the clear evidence (the signs) pointing to Yusuf's innocence—such as the torn shirt from behind, the testimony of witnesses, and the women's reaction upon seeing him—the ruling household nonetheless decided to imprison him temporarily. This decision was likely made to silence the scandal and protect the reputation of al-Aziz's wife, rather than being based on justice. It illustrates how worldly authorities may act against clear truth for the sake of social expediency, reputation, or political convenience. Yusuf's wrongful imprisonment, despite his innocence being evident, sets the stage for his eventual rise to a position of trust and power, demonstrating the Qur'anic theme that Allah's plan unfolds justly even through seemingly unjust human actions, and that patience in adversity leads to eventual vindication and elevation.

translation: And there entered the prison with him two young men. One of them said, 'Indeed, I see myself pressing wine.' The other said, 'Indeed, I see myself carrying bread upon my head, from which the birds are eating. Inform us of its interpretation; indeed, we see you to be of those who do good.'
interpretation: This verse introduces Prophet Yusuf's encounter with two fellow prisoners in Egypt, marking the beginning of a pivotal episode in his story. Their request reveals that Yusuf's reputation for righteousness and wisdom had already become known within the prison, as they specifically address him as one 'of those who do good' (al-muhsinin). This recognition of his character, despite his status as an imprisoned slave, foreshadows the trust and authority he would eventually be granted. The dreams themselves symbolize the fates of the two men—one destined for restoration to a position of service (wine-pressing being associated with the king's cupbearer) and the other facing execution (the birds eating from his head symbolizing death by crucifixion, as later explained). The episode demonstrates how Allah orchestrates circumstances—even imprisonment—to position His chosen servants where their gifts of interpretation and wisdom can be recognized, setting the stage for Yusuf's eventual rise to power in Egypt.

translation: He said, "No food will come to you both, as your provision, but that I will inform you of its interpretation before it comes to you. That is from what my Lord has taught me. Indeed, I have left the religion of a people who do not believe in Allah, and who, in the Hereafter, are disbelievers."
interpretation: In this verse, spoken while imprisoned alongside two fellow inmates who had just related their dreams to him, Yusuf (Joseph) first establishes the divine source of his ability to interpret dreams—framing it not as guesswork or magic but as a gift bestowed by God—before he actually delivers the interpretation they are waiting for. This rhetorical delay serves a strategic purpose: it allows him to pivot the conversation toward a declaration of faith. By announcing that his knowledge comes from his Lord, and then explicitly renouncing the polytheism of the surrounding Egyptian culture, Yusuf uses what could have been a simple transactional exchange (dream interpretation for favor) as an opportunity for da'wah, planting the seeds for his subsequent call to monotheism in the following verses. The verse thus illustrates how Yusuf's prophetic role and personal piety are inseparable from the everyday circumstances of his trials, turning even imprisonment into a platform for guiding others toward belief in one God and warning against disbelief in the Hereafter.

translation: And I have followed the religion of my fathers, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. It was not for us to associate anything with Allah. That is from the favor of Allah upon us and upon mankind, but most of mankind are not grateful.
interpretation: This verse is spoken by Prophet Yusuf (Joseph) as part of his testimony to his two fellow prisoners, affirming his lineage from the great monotheistic patriarchs—Ibrahim, Ishaq, and Ya'qub—who exemplified pure, uncompromising monotheism (tawhid). By declaring that associating partners with Allah was never an option for him or his forefathers, Yusuf establishes his religious authority and the legitimacy of the message he is about to deliver regarding the oneness of God. The verse frames monotheism not merely as a personal choice but as divine favor and guidance bestowed upon the prophetic family and, through them, extended as a mercy to all humanity. The closing observation—that most people fail to be grateful—serves as a broader commentary on human nature's tendency toward heedlessness despite being recipients of clear guidance and blessings. This sets the stage for Yusuf's subsequent call to his prison companions to abandon polytheism in favor of worshipping Allah alone, using his own family heritage as proof of the truth and consistency of monotheistic revelation across generations of prophets.

translation: O my two companions of the prison, are separate lords better, or Allah, the One, the Irresistible?
interpretation: This verse captures Prophet Joseph's rhetorical appeal to his fellow prisoners, using his position of trust (having just interpreted their dreams) to pivot toward the central message of his mission: the call to pure monotheism (tawhid). By posing the question as a stark contrast—scattered, competing deities versus the singular, all-powerful God—Joseph exposes the logical incoherence of polytheism. Multiple lords would imply division of authority, conflicting wills, and inherent limitation, whereas 'al-Wahid al-Qahhar' (the One, the Subjugator) signifies total sovereignty and supremacy over all creation. The term 'Qahhar' also implies that this God's oneness is not passive but assertive, overpowering any rival claims to divinity. Joseph's approach here is pedagogical: rather than simply asserting doctrine, he invites his companions to reason for themselves, suggesting that true faith arises from reflection, not coercion. Contextually, this moment reveals Joseph's prophetic identity emerging through unjust circumstances—imprisoned despite his innocence, he nonetheless seizes the opportunity to call others to truth, embodying the Quranic theme that hardship can become a platform for guidance. The verse also sets up the subsequent lines where he explains that the idols his companions worship are mere names inherited from ancestors, devoid of divine sanction, reinforcing that true authority (hukm) belongs to Allah alone.

translation: You worship not besides Him except [mere] names you have named them, you and your forefathers, for which Allah has sent down no authority. Judgment belongs only to Allah. He has commanded that you worship none but Him. That is the right religion, but most of the people do not know.
interpretation: This verse, spoken by Prophet Yusuf to his prison companions, strikes at the heart of idolatry by exposing it as a fabrication without substance. The gods worshipped besides Allah are described as mere 'names' - human inventions lacking any real divine authority or power, passed down through generations as inherited custom rather than truth. The verse establishes that ultimate authority (al-hukm) belongs exclusively to Allah, encompassing legislative, judicial, and cosmic sovereignty. This exclusivity of divine command naturally leads to the exclusivity of worship - since Allah alone governs reality, He alone deserves worship. The phrase 'that is the right religion' (al-deen al-qayyim) presents monotheism not as one option among many but as the inherently correct, straight path that aligns with the true nature of reality. The closing observation that 'most people do not know' serves as both explanation and lament - ignorance, not malice, often drives people away from this self-evident truth, as they become trapped in inherited traditions without examining their rational and spiritual foundations.

translation: O my two companions of the prison! As for one of you, he will give his master wine to drink; but as for the other, he will be crucified, and the birds will eat from his head. The matter has been decreed concerning that about which you both inquired.
interpretation: This verse records Prophet Yusuf's interpretation of the dreams of his two fellow prisoners, delivered with directness and compassion despite the harshness of one man's fate. It illustrates Yusuf's prophetic gift of dream interpretation as a form of divine knowledge granted to him, and underscores the Quranic theme that the future is already written and decided by God—human inquiry into fate through dreams merely uncovers what has already been predetermined rather than changes it. The episode also serves a narrative function, setting up Yusuf's eventual release from prison through the surviving companion who later remembers him before the king, showing how God orchestrates seemingly minor events and relationships to bring about His greater plan for Yusuf's rise to power in Egypt.

translation: And he said to the one whom he knew would be saved among the two, 'Mention me to your master.' But Satan caused him to forget to mention [it] to his master, so he [Joseph] remained in prison several years.
interpretation: This verse recounts how Prophet Yusuf (Joseph), while imprisoned, interpreted the dreams of two fellow inmates, one of whom he predicted would be released and restored to the king's service. Yusuf asked this man to mention his case to the king, hoping this would lead to his release from unjust imprisonment. However, Satan caused the man to forget this request, resulting in Yusuf remaining in prison for several additional years. This episode illustrates the theme of relying on worldly means while ultimately trusting in divine timing and wisdom. Yusuf's placement of hope in a human intermediary, rather than solely in God, is often seen as a subtle lesson about the nature of tawakkul (trust in God) versus taking practical action. The delay he endured was not a punishment but part of a divinely orchestrated plan that would later elevate his status profoundly, teaching that human forgetfulness and setbacks can still serve a greater, hidden purpose within God's design. It also underscores Satan's role in causing forgetfulness in small but consequential matters, extending the trials of the righteous even when relief seems near.

translation: And the king said, 'Indeed, I have seen [in a dream] seven fat cows being eaten by seven lean ones, and seven green ears of corn and others [that were] dry. O eminent ones, explain to me my vision, if you can interpret visions.'
interpretation: This verse marks the beginning of the episode that will lead to Yusuf's release from prison and his eventual rise to a position of authority in Egypt. The king's dream, though puzzling to his courtiers, is divinely orchestrated to create the circumstance through which Yusuf's gift of interpretation—granted to him by God—becomes known to the ruling authority. The juxtaposition of fat and lean cows, and green and dry ears of corn, symbolizes cycles of abundance and scarcity, foreshadowing the seven years of plenty followed by seven years of famine that will affect Egypt and the surrounding region. The king's request to his courtiers, who prove unable to interpret the dream, sets up a contrast between worldly wisdom and the God-given insight possessed by Yusuf, demonstrating that true understanding and knowledge come from divine guidance rather than human status or position. This moment also serves a narrative function: it is through this dream that Yusuf is remembered by the cupbearer who had been imprisoned with him, creating the link that brings Yusuf out of prison and into a position where he can ultimately be reunited with his family, fulfilling the prophecy of his own dream from his youth and illustrating God's perfect orchestration of events toward a just and merciful resolution.

translation: They said, 'Confused dreams, and we are not learned in the interpretation of dreams.'
interpretation: This verse depicts the response of the king's courtiers and advisors when he recounted his perplexing dream of seven fat cows being devoured by seven lean ones, and seven green ears of corn alongside seven dry ones. Rather than admitting their own limitations honestly, they dismiss the dream as mere 'confused dreams' (adghath ahlam), a phrase used to describe meaningless, jumbled visions unworthy of serious interpretation. This serves a narrative purpose in the story of Yusuf: it highlights the intellectual bankruptcy of the king's court, who possessed worldly status but lacked true wisdom and spiritual insight. Their admission of ignorance ultimately creates the opening for Yusuf's re-entry into the narrative, as the cupbearer who had been imprisoned with Yusuf suddenly remembers his gift for dream interpretation. The verse thus functions as a pivotal turning point, demonstrating how divine wisdom, embodied in Yusuf despite his lowly prisoner status, surpasses the supposed sophistication of royal advisors, and sets the stage for Yusuf's vindication and rise to power.

translation: And the one of the two who had been released, remembering [Joseph] after a long time, said, 'I will inform you of its interpretation, so send me forth.'
interpretation: This verse marks a pivotal turning point in the story of Yusuf (Joseph). The 'one who was freed' refers to the king's cupbearer, who had been imprisoned alongside Yusuf and for whom Yusuf had earlier interpreted a dream predicting his release and restoration to the king's service. The phrase 'after a time' (ba'da ummah) indicates that a significant period had passed—traditionally understood as several years—during which the cupbearer had forgotten his promise to mention Yusuf to the king, despite Yusuf's request that he do so. This forgetfulness itself is a subtle commentary on human nature and the fickleness of worldly gratitude, contrasted with Yusuf's enduring patience and trust in God during his unjust imprisonment. The cupbearer's sudden recollection occurs precisely when the king has a troubling dream that none of his courtiers can interpret, creating the necessary circumstance for Yusuf's wisdom to become useful to the court.
