The cupbearer's eagerness—'send me forth'—shows his belated recognition of Yusuf's extraordinary gift and sets in motion the chain of events that will lead to Yusuf's vindication, release from prison, and eventual rise to a position of authority in Egypt. Theologically, this illustrates the Quranic theme that God's plan unfolds in its appointed time despite human delay or forgetfulness, and that those who maintain patience and righteousness during trials (as Yusuf did in prison) will ultimately be elevated, often through unexpected means and the very people who initially failed them.

translation: "Joseph, O man of truth, explain to us about seven fat cows being devoured by seven lean ones, and seven green ears of corn and others withered, that I may return to the people so they may know."
interpretation: This verse recounts the request made by the king's messenger to Prophet Joseph (Yusuf) in prison, asking him to interpret the king's dream. The address 'O man of truth' (al-Siddiq) reflects Joseph's established reputation for truthfulness and wisdom, even after years of imprisonment on a false charge, showing that his integrity had not been forgotten despite his circumstances. The dream itself—seven fat cows eaten by seven lean ones, and seven green ears of corn alongside seven dried ones—serves as a symbolic representation of future events in Egypt. The phrase 'that I may return to the people so they may know' indicates the messenger's awareness that Joseph possessed special knowledge in dream interpretation, and his desire to bring back a credible answer to satisfy the king and his court. This moment marks a turning point in Joseph's story, as his God-given gift of interpretation becomes the means by which he is eventually freed from prison and elevated to a position of authority, demonstrating how divine wisdom can transform adversity into opportunity and how patience in the face of injustice can lead to vindication and purpose.

translation: He [Joseph] said, 'You will sow for seven years consecutively, and what you harvest leave in its ears, except a little from which you eat.'
interpretation: This verse records Joseph's practical guidance to the king after interpreting his dream of seven fat cows and seven lean ones. Beyond mere dream interpretation, Joseph demonstrates divinely-inspired wisdom in statecraft and resource management. His advice to leave harvested grain in its husks reflects sound agricultural knowledge, as grain stored in its ears resists spoilage, pests, and decay far better than threshed grain, allowing provisions to last through the seven years of abundance and into the seven years of famine that would follow. This moment marks Joseph's transition from a falsely imprisoned man to a trusted advisor, showing how Allah grants him not only the gift of interpreting visions but also practical knowledge necessary to save an entire nation from catastrophe. It illustrates a recurring Quranic theme: that true wisdom combines spiritual insight with practical competence, and that those who are patient through trials are eventually elevated to positions where they can benefit others on a large scale.

translation: Then there will come after that seven hard (years) which will consume what you have laid up in advance for them, except a little of what you have preserved.
interpretation: This verse is part of Prophet Joseph's (Yusuf) interpretation of the King of Egypt's dream, in which seven fat cows were eaten by seven lean ones, and seven green ears of grain were followed by seven dry ones. Joseph explains that after seven years of agricultural abundance, Egypt would face seven years of severe drought and famine that would consume nearly all the surplus grain stored during the prosperous years. The verse demonstrates Joseph's God-given wisdom in dream interpretation and practical foresight in economic planning, as he advises storing grain in its husks to preserve it longer, thereby showing how divine revelation combines with practical wisdom to save a nation from catastrophe. This episode also illustrates a broader Quranic theme of cycles between abundance and hardship, and the importance of prudent provision during times of plenty to prepare for times of scarcity.

translation: Then there will come after that a year in which the people will be given relief (rain), and in which they will press (olives, grapes, etc.).
interpretation: This verse concludes Prophet Yusuf's interpretation of the king's dream, foretelling that after seven years of abundance followed by seven years of severe famine, a year of relief would follow. The mention of rain and pressing (of olives, grapes, or other produce) signifies the end of the drought and the return of agricultural prosperity. This verse carries a broader message of hope and divine mercy: that hardship, no matter how prolonged, is followed by relief and ease. It reflects the Quranic theme that difficulty is never permanent, and that Allah's wisdom encompasses both trial and subsequent restoration, encouraging patience and trust in divine planning even during the darkest periods of hardship.

translation: And the king said, 'Bring him to me.' But when the messenger came to him, [Joseph] said, 'Return to your master and ask him, what is the case of the women who cut their hands? Indeed, my Lord is Knowing of their plan.'
interpretation: This verse reveals Joseph's wisdom, patience, and insistence on clearing his name before accepting release from prison. Rather than rushing to freedom, he demands a formal investigation into the matter of the women, particularly the wife of al-Aziz, who had falsely accused him and caused his imprisonment. This reflects Joseph's integrity and his desire for public vindication rather than merely a pardon granted by the king. By invoking that 'my Lord is Knowing of their plan,' Joseph affirms his trust in God's knowledge of the truth, even when human testimony was initially corrupted by deceit. The verse underscores a broader Quranic theme: that worldly exoneration should follow from truth and justice, not expedience, and that the innocent should seek proper acknowledgment of their innocence rather than silently accept release. It also sets up the dramatic unfolding where the women publicly testify to Joseph's innocence and his moral superiority, reinforcing his status as a righteous and patient servant of God.

translation: He [the king] said, 'What was your affair when you sought to seduce Joseph?' They said, 'Perfect is Allah! We know of no evil concerning him.' The wife of al-'Azeez said, 'Now the truth has come to light. It was I who sought to seduce him, and indeed, he is of the truthful.'
interpretation: This verse marks the moment of public vindication for Joseph after years of false accusation and imprisonment. The king, troubled by the women's testimony during the banquet scene, summons them to clarify what truly happened. Their unanimous declaration of Joseph's innocence—invoking Allah's perfection as a testament to their certainty—sets the stage for the wife of al-'Azeez's own confession. Her admission is significant not merely as an acknowledgment of her past wrongdoing, but as a moral turning point: she takes full responsibility for her actions without deflecting blame, stating plainly 'ana rawadtuhu' (it was I who sought to seduce him). This open confession, coming from someone of high social standing, underscores a Qur'anic theme that worldly status does not exempt one from the necessity of truth and repentance. Her acknowledgment that Joseph is 'of the truthful' (la-mina as-sadiqin) serves to restore his honor completely in the eyes of society, aligning the external truth with what Allah already knew of his innocence throughout his trials. The verse also illustrates how patience and integrity in the face of injustice are eventually rewarded with vindication, a message that resonates with the broader narrative arc of Surah Yusuf regarding divine justice unfolding through human affairs.

translation: That is so that he [al-‘Azīz] may know that I did not betray him in [his] absence, and that Allah does not guide the scheming of the betrayers.
interpretation: This verse is understood to be spoken by Prophet Yusuf (Joseph) after the truth of his innocence was revealed through the women's testimony and the torn shirt. He explains his motive for wanting the truth to come out: not simply for his own vindication, but so that his master (al-‘Azīz) would know that Yusuf had remained loyal and had not betrayed his trust even when the opportunity for wrongdoing presented itself in private, away from any witness. The phrase 'in [his] absence' (bi’l-ghayb) emphasizes that true integrity is tested not when one is watched, but when one could act wrongly without anyone knowing. Yusuf's affirmation that 'Allah does not guide the scheme of betrayers' serves as a theological statement: treachery and deceit, however cleverly planned, cannot ultimately succeed or be blessed by divine guidance, for Allah's support and guidance are reserved for the truthful and sincere, not for schemers. The verse thus underscores themes of personal integrity, divine justice, and the ultimate triumph of truth over deceit, which is a central motif in the story of Yusuf throughout the surah.

translation: And I do not absolve myself. Indeed, the soul is a persistent enjoiner of evil, except whom my Lord has mercy upon. Indeed, my Lord is Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation: This verse is part of the speech attributed to the wife of al-'Aziz (or, in some interpretations, to Yusuf) in the story of Prophet Yusuf, offered as a confession following the revelation of her attempted seduction and false accusation. It expresses a profound theological and psychological insight: human nature (al-nafs) has an inherent inclination toward wrongdoing and self-indulgence unless restrained by divine grace. The statement serves as a humbling acknowledgment that moral failure is a natural human tendency rather than an exception, and that righteousness is not a matter of self-congratulation but of God's mercy acting upon the soul. This verse is often cited in Islamic ethical and spiritual discourse as a caution against self-righteousness and moral complacency, encouraging believers to continually seek divine guidance and forgiveness rather than relying on their own perceived virtue. It also underscores the balance between human responsibility for sin and the necessity of divine mercy for spiritual purification, reflecting the broader Quranic theme that no soul is inherently pure without God's intervention and that God's forgiveness and mercy are the ultimate recourse for human moral weakness.

translation: And the king said, "Bring him to me that I may appoint him exclusively to myself." So when he spoke with him, he said, "Indeed, today you are with us established [in position] and trusted."
interpretation: This verse marks the turning point in Yusuf's story where his long trial of patience, integrity, and wisdom finally yields open recognition. The king's summons, after hearing of Yusuf's correct interpretation of the dream and his wise counsel on managing the coming famine, reflects how truth and competence eventually surface despite years of injustice—false imprisonment, betrayal, and slander. The king's direct encounter with Yusuf, and his immediate perception of Yusuf's trustworthiness and capability through conversation, underscores the Qur'anic theme that sincerity and wisdom reveal themselves through speech and conduct, not merely status or background. The description of Yusuf as 'mighty and trusted' signals his transition from prisoner to statesman, illustrating divine favor working through human affairs: those who maintain patience, moral integrity, and reliance on God during adversity are eventually elevated to positions where their righteousness can benefit others. It also reflects a model of ideal governance—the king seeking out capable and trustworthy individuals regardless of their past circumstances, valuing demonstrated wisdom and character over social origin.

translation: He [Joseph] said, 'Appoint me over the storehouses of the land. Indeed, I am a knowledgeable guardian.'
interpretation: This verse depicts Prophet Joseph (Yusuf) requesting a position of authority over Egypt's treasuries and resources after he had correctly interpreted the king's dream and demonstrated his wisdom. His request is notable because it shows that seeking a position of responsibility is permissible, even praiseworthy, when one possesses the necessary qualifications and intends to use that position for the benefit of others—in this case, to manage resources wisely during the coming years of famine. Joseph explicitly justifies his request by citing his own qualifications: he describes himself as 'hafiz' (a trustworthy guardian/protector) and 'alim' (knowledgeable/skilled). This reflects an important principle in Islamic thought regarding leadership and public office: that competence and integrity are the legitimate grounds for seeking or accepting positions of power, rather than personal ambition or desire for status. Joseph's self-description combines both moral character (trustworthiness in safeguarding resources) and technical competence (knowledge of how to manage and plan), suggesting that effective governance requires both ethical integrity and practical expertise. This moment also marks a turning point in the narrative, as Joseph—previously imprisoned unjustly—is now positioned to rise to a place of significant influence, demonstrating how patience through adversity can lead to eventual vindication and the opportunity to serve a greater good.

translation: And thus We established Joseph in the land, settling therein wherever he willed. We bestow Our mercy upon whom We will, and We do not allow the reward of the doers of good to be lost.
interpretation: This verse affirms that the elevation of Joseph from imprisonment to a position of authority in Egypt was a direct manifestation of divine providence rather than mere circumstance. The phrase 'We established him in the land' signals that worldly power and security, when granted, flow from God's mercy and are placed in service of a greater plan rather than being ends in themselves. The verse ties this empowerment explicitly to divine will ('whom We will'), underscoring that such favor is not earned through human effort alone but granted according to God's wisdom. Yet the closing clause—'We do not allow the reward of the doers of good to be lost'—connects this mercy to Joseph's patient endurance of trials, his integrity in the face of temptation, and his forgiveness of those who wronged him. The verse thus establishes a moral principle extending beyond Joseph's individual story: righteous conduct, steadfastness, and good deeds performed in adversity are never ultimately wasted, even if their reward is delayed. It offers reassurance to believers that suffering endured with patience and virtue will be met with divine recompense, reframing worldly hardship as a passage toward eventual vindication rather than a sign of abandonment.

translation: And the reward of the Hereafter is better for those who believe and are ever mindful of God.
interpretation: This verse, from the story of Prophet Yusuf (Joseph), comes after his rise to a position of authority in Egypt despite the hardships and injustices he endured—being thrown into a well by his brothers, sold into slavery, falsely accused, and imprisoned. The verse establishes a contrast between worldly gain and the eternal reward of the Hereafter, teaching that whatever status, power, or success one achieves in this life is secondary to the true and lasting reward that awaits the believers who maintain faith and taqwa (God-consciousness) through trials. It suggests that Yusuf's worldly elevation, though significant, is not the ultimate measure of his success—rather, his patience, integrity, and unwavering faith throughout his tribulations are what secure him the greater reward in the Hereafter. This serves as a broader lesson to all believers: that steadfastness in faith and righteous conduct during adversity holds value beyond immediate worldly outcomes, and that the Hereafter represents the true and superior recompense for those who remain patient and God-conscious regardless of their earthly circumstances.

translation: And the brothers of Joseph came and entered upon him, and he recognized them, but they recognized him not.
interpretation: This verse marks the dramatic turning point in the story of Joseph, when, years after being betrayed and sold into slavery by his own brothers, he encounters them again in Egypt, now in a position of power and authority as a trusted minister. The asymmetry of recognition is profound and deliberate: Joseph, who had been a young boy when they wronged him, immediately recognizes his brothers despite the passage of time, while they fail to recognize him at all, since the Joseph they knew was a powerless youth cast into a well, not the dignified Egyptian official before them. This moment underscores several key themes in the Quranic narrative. First, it demonstrates divine justice and providence—God had preserved Joseph through hardship, elevated him to a position where his former oppressors would need to seek his help, yet without revealing his identity to them prematurely. Second, it reveals Joseph's remarkable character: despite now holding power over those who betrayed him, he does not immediately expose or punish them, showing restraint, wisdom, and a a plan guided by patience rather than vengeance. Third, the brothers' failure to recognize him symbolizes their spiritual blindness and the irony of fate—they had sought to erase Joseph from their lives, yet now stand before him dependent on his mercy without even knowing it. This sets the stage for the eventual reconciliation, where Joseph's forgiveness becomes a testament to prophetic virtue and the triumph of righteousness over the schemes of those who sought to destroy him.

translation: And when he had equipped them with their provisions, he said, 'Bring me a brother of yours from your father. Do you not see that I give full measure, and that I am the best of hosts?'
interpretation: This verse depicts Yusuf (Joseph), now a powerful figure in Egypt, as he deals with his brothers who do not recognize him. His request for Benjamin, their younger brother from the same father, is a strategic move to reunite with his full brother while testing his other brothers. Yusuf's mention of giving full measure and being a generous host serves a dual purpose: it establishes his credibility and fairness as a ruler, making his request seem like a natural extension of hospitality rather than suspicious, while also subtly incentivizing their compliance by reminding them of the benefits of maintaining good relations with him. This moment reveals Yusuf's wisdom and patience in orchestrating circumstances toward the eventual reunion with his beloved brother and ultimately his father, all while maintaining his concealed identity and demonstrating ethical governance through fair dealing.

translation: But if you do not bring him to me, then there shall be no measure [of grain] for you from me, nor shall you come near me.
interpretation: This verse records Prophet Joseph's (Yusuf) words to his brothers when they came to Egypt seeking provisions during the famine. Without revealing his true identity, Joseph had treated them generously and now instructed them to bring their youngest brother (Benjamin) on their next visit, using the withholding of grain as leverage. This was part of Joseph's divine plan to eventually reunite with his full brother and ultimately his father, Jacob, after years of separation caused by his other brothers' jealousy and betrayal. The verse illustrates Joseph's wisdom and strategic thinking, as he orchestrates circumstances to bring about a reunion while still testing his brothers' characters and intentions, particularly regarding how they now treat the remaining son of Jacob's beloved wife Rachel. It also reflects the broader Quranic theme of divine providence working through human affairs, where Joseph's earlier suffering becomes the means by which he gains the position to eventually save his family and demonstrate Allah's mercy and justice.

translation: They said, 'We will endeavor to persuade his father to let him come with us, and we will surely do so.'
interpretation: This verse occurs in the narrative of Prophet Yusuf (Joseph) in Egypt, after he, then serving as a trusted official, recognized his brothers when they came seeking grain during the famine. Yusuf requested that they bring their youngest brother (Benjamin, his full brother) on their next visit, using this as a pretext to reunite with him. The brothers respond here, promising to use persuasive efforts (muraw'adah) on their father Ya'qub (Jacob) to permit Benjamin to travel with them. The use of the word 'muraw'adah' is significant—the same root used earlier in the surah for the attempted seduction of Yusuf by the wife of al-Aziz—suggesting a careful, calculated effort to overcome resistance through persistent appeal rather than force. This reflects their awareness of their father's deep attachment to Benjamin, especially after the loss of Yusuf, and foreshadows the emotional tension to come when they must convince Ya'qub, who already suffers profound grief, to risk losing another beloved son. Their confident declaration 'we will surely do so' reveals their determination to fulfill this task, driven by their own need to secure further provisions from Egypt, setting the stage for the test of faith and patience that Ya'qub must endure once again.

translation: And he said to his young men (servants), 'Put their merchandise back into their saddlebags, so that they may recognize it when they have returned to their family, so that perhaps they will come back.'
interpretation: This verse depicts Prophet Yusuf (Joseph), now a powerful figure in Egypt though unrecognized by his brothers, secretly ordering his servants to return the payment his brothers had given for the grain they purchased. His motive is twofold and deeply strategic: first, by discovering the returned money upon reaching home, his brothers would realize the extraordinary generosity and honor of the Egyptian official they had dealt with, which would encourage their trust and ease any hesitation about returning. Second, and more subtly, Yusuf's underlying hope was to compel them to come back to Egypt, since honorable men would feel obligated to return the money or at least feel drawn back by the inexplicable kindness shown to them. This act demonstrates Yusuf's wisdom, foresight, and the retention of familial love and longing despite the wrongs done to him by his brothers. It also sets the stage for the eventual reunion with his full brother Benjamin and the broader plan of reconciliation with his family, showing how divine wisdom often works through careful human planning and seemingly small, generous acts that carry far-reaching consequences.

translation: So when they returned to their father, they said, 'O our father, grain has been denied to us [unless we bring our brother], so send our brother with us that we may obtain measure [of provisions]. And indeed, we will be his guardians.'
interpretation: This verse captures the moment Jacob's sons return from Egypt and relay the condition set by the Egyptian official (unbeknownst to them, their brother Joseph) that they must bring their youngest brother, Benjamin, if they wish to receive further grain rations. Their plea to their father reveals both the practical urgency of securing food during the famine and their awareness of Jacob's deep anxiety about letting Benjamin go, given the earlier loss of Joseph. Their promise 'we will be his guardians' is an attempt to reassure their father, yet it echoes painfully with their earlier assurance regarding Joseph before his disappearance, which Jacob has not forgotten. This repetition of language creates dramatic tension, as the reader is aware that the brothers' past claims of protection did not prevent Joseph's loss, foreshadowing the father's reluctance and the emotional weight of trust, memory, and family responsibility that pervades the surah. The verse underscores themes of necessity overriding caution, as survival needs compel the family to confront unresolved grief and renewed risk.

translation: He said, "Should I entrust you with him except as I entrusted you with his brother before? But Allah is the best guardian, and He is the most merciful of the merciful."
interpretation: This verse captures the deep anguish and cautious wisdom of Prophet Jacob (Ya'qub) when his sons sought to take Benjamin with them to Egypt. Having already suffered the loss of Joseph—entrusted to the same brothers who had betrayed him—Jacob's rhetorical question exposes his lingering distrust and the weight of past grief. Yet rather than succumbing entirely to despair or refusing outright, Jacob pivots to an expression of profound faith: he surrenders the matter to Allah, acknowledging that ultimate protection lies beyond human guarantees. This reflects a central theme of the Joseph narrative—that human caution and love, however justified by prior wounds, must ultimately yield to trust in divine mercy and providence. Jacob's declaration that Allah is the "best guardian" and "most merciful of the merciful" signals his acceptance that he cannot control outcomes through his own vigilance alone; true security rests in surrendering to God's care. This moment also foreshadows the eventual resolution of the story, where Allah's mercy indeed proves greater than human fear, reuniting Jacob with both sons in due time.

translation: And when they opened their baggage, they found their merchandise returned to them. They said, 'O our father, what [more] could we desire? This is our merchandise returned to us. And we will obtain supplies for our family and protect our brother and add a measure of a camel's load. That, [coming from the king], is an easy measurement.'
interpretation: This verse captures a pivotal moment of persuasion in the story of Yusuf, where the brothers use the unexpected return of their trade goods as evidence of the Egyptian ruler's honesty and generosity, in order to convince their reluctant father Ya'qub to allow Benjamin to accompany them on their next journey. Their argument operates on multiple levels: practically, the returned merchandise represents additional capital they can use to purchase more grain for their starving family, addressing the material need of the household. The phrase 'what more could we desire' suggests they frame this discovery as providential favor, implicitly arguing that a ruler who deals with such unexpected fairness and generosity is unlikely to harm or mistreat Benjamin. They layer their persuasion by promising multiple benefits—provisioning the family, personally guarding their brother, and gaining an extra camel-load of grain—addressing Ya'qub's economic concerns, his emotional anxiety about losing another son after Yusuf, and practical abundance for the family. The closing phrase, calling this additional measure 'easy' or 'simple' for the ruler to grant, subtly indicates the ruler's generosity and power, reinforcing their argument that engaging with this authority poses minimal risk while offering substantial reward. The verse also reflects the brothers' evolving characters; having already shown signs of remorse and responsibility regarding Yusuf's fate, they now actively work to secure trust and demonstrate reliability, setting the stage for the eventual reunion and reconciliation within the family, orchestrated through Allah's unseen plan that uses even mundane trade transactions as instruments of a far greater design.

translation: He [Jacob] said, 'I will not send him with you until you give me a solemn pledge before Allah that you will surely bring him back to me, unless you are totally overpowered.' And when they had given him their solemn pledge, he said, 'Allah is Witness over what we say.'
interpretation: This verse captures Jacob's deep anguish and caution after having already lost Yusuf, making him extremely protective of Benjamin. His demand for a solemn oath 'before Allah' reflects his understanding that human promises alone are insufficient guarantees against fate or betrayal; only a pledge invoking the Divine carries true weight and accountability. The exception clause—'unless you are totally overpowered'—shows Jacob's realism and wisdom, acknowledging that no oath can bind people against overwhelming, uncontrollable circumstances; he is not asking for the impossible, but for sincere intention and effort. By concluding with 'Allah is Witness over what we say,' Jacob elevates the covenant beyond a mere family agreement into a matter of divine accountability, reminding his sons that ultimately it is Allah who oversees human intentions and actions, not just outward words. This moment also reflects a turning point in Jacob's character: despite his sorrow and mistrust born from past experience, he still acts within the bounds of Tawakkul (trust in Allah) combined with prudent caution, a balance the Qur'an consistently commends among the prophets.

translation: And he said, 'O my sons, do not enter from one gate but enter from different gates; and I cannot avail you against Allah at all. The decision is for none but Allah. Upon Him I have relied, and upon Him let those who would rely, rely.'
interpretation: This verse recounts the advice of Prophet Ya'qub (Jacob) to his sons as they prepared to travel to Egypt. His instruction to enter the city through separate gates reflects worldly wisdom and prudence—a precaution against drawing undue attention from onlookers, warding off envy, or protecting the group from potential harm, given their number and prominence as the sons of a single notable family. Yet Ya'qub immediately qualifies this practical counsel with a profound theological statement: no human precaution, however wise, can shield anyone from the decree of Allah. This juxtaposition teaches that taking sensible measures is not in contradiction with faith in divine providence; rather, believers are enjoined to combine reasonable effort with complete trust in Allah's ultimate control over outcomes. The verse underscores the principle of tawakkul (reliance on Allah), showing that human agency and planning operate within, not against, the sovereignty of divine decree. Ya'qub's declaration that 'the decision is for none but Allah' affirms that ultimate authority and judgment belong solely to Him, and his personal avowal of trust models for believers the proper disposition of combining effort with surrender to Allah's will.

translation: And when they entered from where their father had commanded them, it did not avail them against Allah in anything, except it was a need in the soul of Jacob which he satisfied. And indeed, he was a possessor of knowledge because of what We had taught him, but most of the people do not know.
interpretation: This verse refers to Jacob's instruction to his sons to enter the city of Egypt through separate, different gates rather than all together through one gate. His motivation stemmed from paternal concern—likely fear of the evil eye befalling his sons due to their notable number and appearance, or fear of drawing suspicion or envy from onlookers given their striking collective presence. The verse clarifies an important theological point: this precaution, though born of wisdom and insight granted to Jacob by God, could not alter or avert Allah's decree in any way. Human foresight, however divinely inspired, operates within the bounds of means (asbab) and does not supersede divine will (qadar). Jacob's knowledge, described here as something Allah specifically taught him, represents prophetic insight into human nature and subtle dangers, yet even such knowledge is limited to practical precaution rather than control over destiny. The closing statement—that most people do not know—underscores the deeper lesson that true knowledge lies in recognizing both the value of prudent action and the ultimate submission to God's overriding decree, a nuanced understanding many fail to grasp.

translation: And when they entered upon Joseph, he drew his brother to himself and said, 'Indeed, I am your brother, so do not despair over what they used to do.'
interpretation: This verse marks the private revelation of Joseph's identity to Benjamin, his full brother, before Joseph's identity is revealed to the rest of his brothers. Joseph, now a powerful figure in Egypt, finally has the chance to reconnect intimately with the one sibling who shared his mother and who, like him, suffered at the hands of their other brothers. By embracing Benjamin and revealing himself privately, Joseph demonstrates compassion, wisdom, and strategic patience—he does not yet expose himself to the other brothers, perhaps to set up the subsequent test with the drinking cup that will allow him to keep Benjamin with him. His words of comfort, telling Benjamin not to grieve over the past mistreatment by their brothers, show forgiveness and an attempt to console him, signaling that the pain of the past will soon be resolved through divine will and reconciliation. This moment also foreshadows the larger reunion and forgiveness that will extend to all the brothers, illustrating the Qur'anic themes of patience, divine planning, and the eventual triumph of righteousness over the plots of those who wronged the righteous.

translation: So when he had furnished them with their provisions, he placed the drinking-cup in his brother's saddlebag. Then a caller called out: 'O caravan, indeed you are thieves!'
interpretation: This verse occurs in the story of Yusuf (Joseph), describing the stratagem he devised to keep his brother Benjamin with him in Egypt. After providing his brothers with their supplies, Yusuf secretly placed his drinking-cup (used to measure grain) in Benjamin's bag without his brothers' knowledge. This was a planned ruse, inspired by divine guidance, so that Yusuf would have a legitimate pretext to detain Benjamin without revealing his true identity to his brothers. The subsequent accusation of theft, announced publicly by a caller, sets up the dramatic confrontation that follows, in which the brothers are searched and the cup is found, leading to Benjamin's detention. This episode demonstrates Yusuf's wisdom and the unfolding of Allah's plan to eventually reunite him with his family and brother, showing how apparent deception serves a higher, benevolent purpose within the divine narrative of reconciliation and justice.

translation: They said, turning towards them, 'What is it that you are missing?'
interpretation: This verse occurs in the story of Prophet Yusuf (Joseph), when his brothers came to Egypt to buy grain and were accused of theft after a royal drinking cup was found missing. The officials of Yusuf's entourage called out to the brothers, who turned back to face them and asked what had gone missing. This moment marks the beginning of the test that Yusuf devised to keep his full brother Benjamin with him, as part of the divine plan to eventually reunite the family and fulfill the earlier dream of Yusuf. The verse illustrates the unfolding of a carefully orchestrated scheme, showing how Allah's plan works through seemingly ordinary human interactions and accusations to bring about a greater purpose of reunion, justice, and revelation of truth.

translation: They said, "We are missing the measure of the king, and for whoever brings it is [the reward of] a camel's load, and I guarantee it."
interpretation: This verse occurs in the story of Yusuf (Joseph), at the point when his brothers are about to be searched after a drinking cup (or measuring vessel) belonging to the king is found missing. The officials announce the loss and offer a reward—a camel's load of grain—to whoever returns it, with one of them personally guaranteeing the reward. This moment is part of Yusuf's carefully orchestrated plan to detain his full brother Benjamin, after he had secretly placed the cup in Benjamin's bag. The verse illustrates the dramatic tension of the narrative, highlighting themes of hidden wisdom, divine planning, and the testing of the brothers' character, as their earlier sin against Yusuf is echoed in this accusation of theft, setting the stage for the eventual revelation of Yusuf's identity and the resolution of the family's reconciliation.

translation: They said, 'By Allah, you have certainly known that we did not come to cause corruption in the land, and we are not thieves.'
interpretation: This verse occurs in the story of Yusuf (Joseph), at the moment when his brothers are accused of theft after the royal drinking cup is discovered in their youngest brother's belongings—a scheme Yusuf devised to keep his brother with him. The brothers' indignant denial reveals their self-perception and the reputation they had built during their time in Egypt: men of integrity who had conducted themselves honorably, unlike their earlier, morally compromised actions against Yusuf himself years before. Their oath 'by Allah' underscores the gravity of the accusation in their eyes and their confidence in their established trustworthiness among the Egyptians. Yet the verse carries deep irony for the reader who knows the full story: these same brothers, who vehemently proclaim their innocence of theft and corruption, had once plotted against their own brother, deceived their father, and effectively 'stolen' Yusuf from his family through betrayal. This irony highlights a recurring Qur'anic theme—human beings often present themselves as righteous while being unaware of or conveniently forgetting their own past transgressions, and divine justice (here orchestrated by Yusuf) has a way of bringing hidden truths to light and creating situations that mirror or expose earlier sins, setting the stage for eventual repentance and reconciliation within the family.

translation: They said, 'Then what will be its recompense if you are liars?'
interpretation: This verse occurs in the story of Prophet Yusuf (Joseph), during the episode in which his brothers come to Egypt and a drinking cup belonging to the king is found in the saddlebag of their youngest brother (Benjamin), after Yusuf's officials secretly placed it there. When the brothers are accused of theft, they deny it and are asked what the penalty should be if their denial proves false. This question tests their sense of justice and sets the stage for them to pronounce a judgment that will lead to Yusuf's plan unfolding—namely, that the one who stole should himself become a bondsman to the one from whom he stole, a legal practice they recognized from their own tradition. The verse thus functions as a narrative device within Yusuf's wider strategy, inherited from divine wisdom, to reunite with his brother Benjamin and ultimately with his entire family, demonstrating the unfolding of God's plan through Yusuf's cleverness and patience despite the earlier wrong done to him.

translation: They said, 'His recompense is that he in whose bag it is found - he himself shall be his recompense (i.e., he shall be enslaved). Thus do we recompense the wrongdoers.'
interpretation: This verse recounts the response of Joseph's brothers when the royal cup was found missing and they were asked what the punishment should be for theft, according to their own tradition and law. Unaware that the trap had been set by Joseph himself to retain his brother Benjamin, they confidently proposed a penalty from their own Canaanite custom: that the thief himself would become the bondsman of the one from whom he stole. This moment reveals divine orchestration within human affairs - the brothers, in their self-assurance and ignorance of Joseph's identity and plan, pronounce the very judgment that serves God's greater purpose of reuniting Joseph with his full brother Benjamin. The phrase 'thus do we recompense the wrongdoers' operates on multiple levels: it is the brothers affirming their own law, yet within the broader narrative it echoes the pattern of divine justice, for these same brothers had once wronged Joseph by casting him into a well, and now circumstances conspire, through their own words, toward a resolution engineered by providence. The verse illustrates how God's plan unfolds through the very words and judgments of those unaware they are instruments of a larger design.

translation: So he began with their bags before the bag of his brother, then he extracted it from the bag of his brother. Thus did We plan for Yusuf; he could not have taken his brother within the religion (law) of the king, except that Allah willed it so. We raise in degrees whom We will, but above every possessor of knowledge is one more knowing.
interpretation: This verse illustrates how divine providence operates through human schemes and legal technicalities. Yusuf could not have lawfully detained his brother Benjamin under Egyptian law, which did not prescribe enslavement for theft, so God inspired the stratagem of the hidden cup to be found in Benjamin's bag, invoking instead the law of Yusuf's own people (Canaanite custom), which did permit such a penalty. The passage emphasizes that human intelligence and planning, however clever, operate within and are ultimately subordinate to God's will and knowledge. The closing statement that 'above every possessor of knowledge is one more knowing' establishes a hierarchy culminating in God's omniscience, reminding the reader that even the wisest schemes of men like Yusuf are instruments of a greater divine plan, and that true elevation in rank and understanding comes only through God's will, not human cunning alone.

translation: They said, 'If he steals, a brother of his stole before.' But Joseph kept it secret within himself and did not reveal it to them. He said, 'You are in a worse position, and Allah is most knowing of what you describe.'
interpretation: This verse occurs during the episode in which Benjamin is found with the king's measuring cup, and his brothers—seeking to distance themselves from suspicion and perhaps still harboring old resentment—accuse him of being like a brother who stole before, an indirect reference to Joseph himself, unaware they were speaking to him. Joseph, now in a position of power and recognizing the slander and the depth of his brothers' enduring envy and moral failings, chooses restraint: he conceals his pain and anger rather than exposing their lie or revealing his identity prematurely. His response—'You are in a worse position'—is a quiet but pointed rebuke, asserting moral superiority without resorting to open confrontation, while reminding them that Allah alone truly knows the truth behind their accusations and their own hidden faults. The verse illustrates themes of patience, forbearance, and the contrast between surface appearances and divine knowledge, as well as Joseph's continued exercise of restraint and wisdom even when unjustly maligned.

translation: They said, 'O Aziz, indeed he has a father, old and advanced in age, so take one of us in his place. Indeed, we see you as one of the doers of good.'
interpretation: This verse occurs during the dramatic climax of the story of Yusuf (Joseph), when his brothers—unaware that the powerful Egyptian official (al-Aziz) they are pleading with is in fact their long-lost brother Yusuf—plead with him not to detain their youngest brother Benjamin, who had been found with the king's drinking cup through Yusuf's own design. Their appeal invokes their elderly father's emotional attachment to this son, referencing Jacob's (Ya'qub's) deep grief over losing Yusuf earlier and his fear of losing Benjamin too. They offer themselves as substitutes, hoping to spare their father further sorrow, and appeal to the Aziz's reputation for generosity and good character, addressing him with high respect and flattery. This moment reveals the brothers' growth in compassion and responsibility toward their father, in contrast to their earlier jealousy and cruelty toward Yusuf. It also builds dramatic tension before Yusuf reveals his true identity, highlighting themes of family bonds, repentance, and the unfolding of divine providence despite human scheming.

translation: He [Joseph] said, 'God forbid that we should take except him with whom we found our property; indeed, we would then be wrongdoers.'
interpretation: This verse captures a pivotal moment in the story of Yusuf (Joseph), where he responds to his brothers' plea to take one of them in place of Benjamin, in whose bag the king's measuring cup had been planted. Joseph's refusal, framed as seeking refuge in God from such injustice, demonstrates his unwavering commitment to justice and righteousness even when he could have shown leniency toward his brothers who had once wronged him. The phrase 'God forbid' (ma'adha Allah) signals the gravity of the ethical principle at stake—that one should not punish the innocent for the guilt of another, nor accept a substitute for true justice. This reflects a broader Qur'anic principle of individual accountability, where no soul bears the burden of another's wrongdoing. Joseph's insistence on taking only the one who possessed the stolen item, rather than succumbing to his brothers' request out of convenience or mercy, underscores his integrity and adherence to divine law over personal or familial pressures, even as he orchestrates a plan that will ultimately lead to reconciliation with his family.

translation: So when they despaired of him, they withdrew privately, conferring together. The eldest of them said: 'Do you not know that your father has taken from you a solemn pledge before God, and before that how you failed in your duty concerning Joseph? I will not leave this land until my father permits me, or God decides for me, and He is the best of judges.'
interpretation: This verse occurs in the story of Joseph (Yusuf), when his brothers, having failed to secure the release of Benjamin from Egypt (he had been found with the king's cup and was to be kept as a slave under the law they themselves proposed), retreat to consult among themselves away from Joseph's presence. The eldest brother reminds them of two binding obligations: the solemn oath they swore to their father Jacob to bring Benjamin back safely, and their prior guilt in their treachery against Joseph, which still weighs upon them and makes them reluctant to return empty-handed and face their father's grief and distrust again. His declaration that he will not leave Egypt until his father permits him or until God judges in his favor reflects both a sense of personal honor and piety—placing trust ultimately in divine judgment rather than merely human reasoning or family politics. This moment underscores themes central to the surah: the burden of past sin and guilt, the importance of keeping one's word, and submission to God's judgment as superior to any human verdict. It also sets the stage for the eventual unfolding of divine providence, as the brothers' separation and individual responses pave the way for the reconciliation and revelation of Joseph's identity, affirming that God's plan, though hidden, is always just and wise.

translation: Return to your father and say, 'O our father, indeed your son has stolen, and we did not testify except to what we knew, and we were not guardians of the unseen.'
interpretation: This verse occurs in the story of Prophet Yusuf (Joseph), spoken by his brothers after Benjamin was found with the king's drinking cup and accused of theft. The brothers, having already lost credibility with their father Ya'qub (Jacob) due to their earlier deception regarding Yusuf, now instruct one another on how to report this new incident honestly, at least in their own telling. Their statement reveals an attempt to distance themselves from blame by emphasizing that they only testified to what they directly witnessed—the cup being found in Benjamin's bag—and could not have known or prevented anything beyond their immediate knowledge, since they are not privy to unseen matters or hidden truths. This reflects a human tendency to protect oneself from accusation by appealing to the limits of one's knowledge, while also subtly acknowledging the family's repeated pattern of returning to their father with grievous news about his beloved sons. The phrase 'we were not guardians of the unseen' underscores a broader Quranic theme: only Allah possesses complete knowledge of the unseen (al-ghayb), and human beings are limited to acting upon what is apparent and knowable to them, bearing responsibility only for what falls within their perception and control.

translation: Ask the town in which we were, and the caravan with which we returned; indeed, we are truthful.
interpretation: This verse is part of the brothers' plea to their father Ya'qub (Jacob) after Benjamin was detained in Egypt on the pretext of theft. Having returned without their younger brother, they anticipated their father's doubt and distress, so they urged him to verify their account through independent, external testimony—the people of the town where the events occurred and the fellow travelers of the caravan who accompanied them. This appeal to objective, corroborating witnesses rather than relying solely on their own word reflects an attempt to reinforce credibility, especially significant given their earlier history of deception regarding Yusuf (Joseph). It subtly acknowledges their father's justified wariness due to past events while asserting their innocence in this particular matter through verifiable means, illustrating a human tendency to seek validation through external sources when trust has been previously broken by one's own actions.

translation: He [Jacob] said, 'Nay, but your souls have enticed you to something [else]. So patience is most fitting. Perhaps Allah will bring them to me all together. Indeed, it is He who is the Knowing, the Wise.'
interpretation: This verse depicts Prophet Jacob's response upon hearing his sons' fabricated story—this time about Benjamin being detained in Egypt as a thief, echoing their earlier deception regarding Joseph. Jacob's immediate recognition that his sons have again concocted a scheme reveals his deep insight and unwavering discernment, undiminished by grief or old age. Rather than succumbing to despair, he chooses 'beautiful patience' (sabr jameel)—a patience devoid of complaint, rooted in complete trust in Allah's wisdom and timing. His hope that Allah will restore all his sons to him together signals his unbroken faith that Allah's mercy and power can reverse even the most hopeless circumstances. The verse closes with an affirmation of Allah's omniscience and wisdom, reminding the reader that behind every trial and apparent loss lies a divine plan beyond human comprehension. Jacob's steadfastness here serves as a model of righteous endurance, showing that true patience is not passive resignation but active, hopeful trust in God's ultimate justice and mercy, even when the full picture remains hidden from human eyes.

translation: And he turned away from them and said, 'O my grief over Joseph!' And his eyes became white from sorrow, for he was a suppressor of grief.
interpretation: This verse depicts the depth of Prophet Ya'qub's (Jacob's) sorrow over the loss of his beloved son Yusuf (Joseph), years after Yusuf's brothers had deceived him. Despite the passage of time, Ya'qub's grief remained so intense that it physically manifested in the whitening of his eyes, traditionally understood as blindness caused by excessive weeping. The phrase 'fahuwa kazeem' reveals a crucial aspect of his character: he suppressed his sorrow internally, bearing his pain with patience and dignity rather than voicing complaints against God's decree. This illustrates the Islamic concept of sabr (patience) in the face of profound loss—Ya'qub's grief was genuine and overwhelming, yet he maintained his faith and trust in Allah, never losing hope that he might be reunited with Yusuf. His turning away from his other sons symbolizes his withdrawal into private sorrow, choosing to grieve in solitude rather than burden others or display his pain publicly, while still harboring unwavering certainty in divine wisdom and the eventual fulfillment of the vision Yusuf had seen in his youth.

translation: They said, 'By Allah, you will not cease remembering Yusuf until you become weak and wasted away, or until you become of those who perish.'
interpretation: This verse captures the exasperation of Prophet Yaqub's (Jacob's) remaining sons toward their father's unrelenting grief over the loss of Yusuf. Years after Yusuf's disappearance, and now also mourning the detention of his brother Binyamin in Egypt, Yaqub's sorrow has become so profound and persistent that his sons fear it is destroying his health. Their words, sworn 'by Allah,' reveal both their concern and their frustration—they cannot comprehend why their father continues to grieve so intensely for one son when they too have suffered loss. This moment underscores the depth of a parent's love and grief, which rational argument or the passage of time cannot diminish. It also subtly foreshadows the sons' partial awareness of their own guilt in the matter, as their impatience with Yaqub's mourning may stem from an unspoken discomfort with their role in Yusuf's fate. Yaqub's response, in the following verse, where he states he complains only to Allah, demonstrates the proper recourse for grief: patience (sabr) combined with trust in God, rather than either suppressing emotion or succumbing to despair.

translation: He said, 'I only complain of my suffering and my grief to Allah, and I know from Allah that which you do not know.'
interpretation: This verse records the response of Prophet Ya'qub (Jacob) to his sons when they suggested he would ruin his health grieving over Yusuf (Joseph). It demonstrates the proper etiquette of a believer facing immense and prolonged hardship: rather than complaining to other created beings, which would be seen as a lack of trust in Allah's wisdom, Ya'qub directs his sorrow exclusively to Allah. This is not a denial of his very real human pain and grief, but rather an affirmation that the only appropriate recipient of one's deepest anguish is the Divine, who alone has the power to relieve it. His statement 'I know from Allah what you do not know' reflects his unwavering certainty and hope, rooted in divine knowledge and prophetic insight, that his son Yusuf was still alive and that reunion was possible, even though all apparent circumstances suggested otherwise. This verse teaches the balance between expressing genuine human emotion and maintaining steadfast faith (sabr) and trust (tawakkul) in Allah's plan, showing that patience in Islam is not the suppression of feeling but the channeling of one's deepest emotional expression toward Allah alone, coupled with unshaken hope in His wisdom and mercy even amid profound loss.

translation: O my sons, go and inquire about Joseph and his brother, and do not despair of the mercy (relief) of Allah. Indeed, no one despairs of the mercy of Allah except the disbelieving people.
interpretation: These are the words of Prophet Jacob (Ya'qub) to his sons, spoken after the loss of two of his sons—Joseph, lost years earlier, and Benjamin, detained in Egypt. Despite his prolonged grief and blindness from weeping, Jacob's faith remains unshaken, and he instructs his sons to actively search for answers rather than succumb to hopelessness. The verse establishes a profound theological principle: despair of God's mercy is characteristic of disbelief (kufr), while hope and perseverance are hallmarks of true faith (iman). Jacob's unwavering trust in divine mercy, even after decades of apparent loss, models the proper relationship between a believer and their Lord—one must continue striving and maintain hope regardless of how dire circumstances appear, because God's mercy and ability to resolve seemingly impossible situations transcends human understanding or expectation. This teaches that true faith requires active effort (going and searching) combined with internal trust in divine providence, rejecting both passive fatalism and despairing resignation.

translation: So when they entered upon him, they said, 'O Governor, adversity has touched us and our family, and we have come with goods of little value, so give us full measure and be charitable to us. Indeed, Allah rewards the charitable.'
interpretation: This verse depicts the moment when Joseph's brothers, driven by famine and desperation, return to Egypt and appeal to the powerful 'Aziz—unaware that he is their own brother Joseph. Their humble plea reveals a dramatic reversal of fortune: those who once held power over Joseph, casting him into a well and selling him into slavery, now stand before him in need, offering meager goods and begging for mercy. Their appeal to charity reflects both genuine distress and perhaps an unconscious irony, given their past betrayal of family ties. The verse underscores themes of divine justice and the cyclical nature of fate, where the humbled become supplicants and the once-wronged holds the position of authority and generosity. It also emphasizes the Quranic value of charity (sadaqah) as a trait beloved by Allah, setting the stage for Joseph's eventual act of mercy and forgiveness toward those who wronged him, reflecting the broader Quranic message of compassion overcoming vengeance.

translation: He said, 'Do you know what you did to Joseph and his brother when you were ignorant?'
interpretation: This verse marks the dramatic turning point of the Joseph narrative, the moment of anagnorisis when Joseph reveals his identity to his brothers who have come to Egypt seeking grain, unaware that the powerful official before them is the very brother they wronged decades earlier. Joseph's question is not merely rhetorical but deeply pedagogical and merciful. By asking if they remember what they did 'when you were ignorant' (idh antum jahilun), he frames their past cruelty—casting him into a well and deceiving their father—as a product of youthful jahiliyyah, a state of moral and spiritual ignorance rather than irredeemable evil. This framing opens the door to forgiveness rather than vengeance, suggesting that human beings can act destructively out of ignorance, envy, or immaturity, yet are capable of growth and repentance. Joseph's gentle confrontation, devoid of bitterness after years of suffering through slavery and imprisonment, demonstrates prophetic magnanimity and models the Quranic ideal of responding to wrongdoing with wisdom and eventual reconciliation rather than retribution. The verse also underscores the theme of divine providence throughout the surah: what seemed like pure misfortune and betrayal was part of a larger design that ultimately elevated Joseph and preserved his family, revealing that human ignorance and malice can be woven into a greater pattern of mercy and restoration that only becomes clear in retrospect.

translation: They said, "Is it really you who is Joseph?" He said, "I am Joseph, and this is my brother. Allah has indeed been gracious to us. Truly, whoever is mindful of Allah and remains patient - then surely Allah does not let the reward of the doers of good be lost."
interpretation: This moment of revelation marks the climax of the Surah's narrative arc, where decades of separation, betrayal, and suffering culminate in recognition and reunion. Joseph's brothers, who once cast him into a well out of jealousy, now stand before the powerful Egyptian vizier unable to believe their eyes. Joseph's response is remarkable for its humility and theological framing: rather than dwelling on vengeance or even on his own extraordinary journey from slave to ruler, he immediately attributes everything to Allah's favor (minnah). His declaration that 'Allah does not allow the reward of those who do good to be lost' serves as the moral thesis of his entire story - it retroactively explains why he maintained righteousness through enslavement, false accusation, and imprisonment. The verse links two essential virtues, taqwa (God-consciousness) and sabr (patience), presenting them as the formula through which hardship transforms into honor. Joseph's identification of the man beside him as 'my brother' (referring to Benjamin, his only full brother, not the ones who betrayed him) subtly distinguishes between the sibling who remained loyal and those who did not, without yet delivering judgment on the latter - judgment that he withholds moments later when he declares no blame upon them. This restraint itself exemplifies ihsan (excellence in conduct), demonstrating that true forgiveness flows from one who has internalized trust in divine justice rather than seeking it through human retribution.

translation: They said, 'By Allah, certainly has Allah preferred you over us, and indeed, we have been sinners.'
interpretation: This verse captures the climactic moment of confession and remorse in the story of Joseph (Yusuf). After years of deception, jealousy, and the grave sin of abandoning their brother in a well, Joseph's brothers finally recognize him when he reveals his identity in Egypt. Their admission is total and unreserved—they swear by God Himself, acknowledging both Joseph's elevated status through divine favor and their own culpability as wrongdoers (khāti'īn). The verse illustrates the Quranic theme that truth and justice eventually surface despite human attempts at concealment, and that divine wisdom often elevates those who endure injustice with patience. The brothers' confession, free of excuses or rationalization, exemplifies the sincere repentance (tawbah) that the Quran considers necessary for forgiveness, setting the stage for Joseph's magnanimous response in the following verses where he forgives them completely, reflecting the prophetic virtue of mercy over vengeance even when one has the power to retaliate.

translation: He said, 'No blame will there be upon you today. May Allah forgive you; and He is the most merciful of the merciful.'
interpretation: This verse captures the moment when Yusuf (Joseph) reveals his identity to his brothers who had wronged him years earlier by throwing him into a well and selling him into slavery. Despite having the power and position to seek revenge, Yusuf immediately absolves them of guilt, demonstrating profound forgiveness and nobility of character. His statement models the highest form of human mercy - releasing others from blame even when one has been deeply wronged - while simultaneously pointing beyond himself to divine mercy as the ultimate source and standard. By invoking Allah's forgiveness rather than claiming credit for his own magnanimity, Yusuf teaches that true forgiveness mirrors and seeks alignment with God's own boundless compassion. This moment serves as a powerful lesson on letting go of past grievances, the transformative power of forgiveness in healing family and relationships, and the recognition that human mercy, however great, remains but a reflection of the infinite mercy of the Divine.

translation: Take this shirt of mine and cast it over the face of my father; he will regain his sight. And bring to me your entire family.
interpretation: This verse captures the climactic moment of reconciliation and restoration in the story of Yusuf (Joseph). After revealing his true identity to his brothers who had once betrayed him, Yusuf demonstrates profound forgiveness and generosity rather than seeking revenge. The shirt serves as a powerful symbol of his survival and transformation—just as a shirt had once been used deceitfully to convince their father Ya'qub (Jacob) of Yusuf's death (stained with false blood), now a shirt becomes the instrument of truth and healing. Yusuf's request that the shirt be placed on his father's face so he may see again represents a miracle rooted in faith and divine mercy, restoring not just physical sight but also restoring hope and emotional wholeness to a father who grieved for years. The command to bring the entire family together signifies complete reconciliation and the reunification of the family unit, symbolizing how Allah's plan, though it unfolded through trials, betrayal, and separation, ultimately leads to restoration and blessing for those who remain patient and faithful. This moment also reflects Yusuf's elevated moral character—despite his position of power in Egypt, he seeks to heal rather than punish, embodying the Quranic values of forgiveness, family loyalty, and trust in divine wisdom even through hardship.

translation: And when the caravan departed [from Egypt], their father said, 'Indeed, I find the smell of Joseph [and would say that he was alive] if you did not think me weakened in mind.'
interpretation: This verse illustrates the extraordinary spiritual sensitivity and intuition of Prophet Jacob (Ya'qub), whose love and longing for his lost son Joseph had never diminished despite decades of separation and grief. Even at a great physical distance, before any messenger had arrived with news, Jacob perceived a sign—the scent of Joseph—that confirmed what his heart had long sensed: that Joseph was alive. His qualifying statement, acknowledging that others might accuse him of senility or confused thinking due to his old age and prolonged sorrow, reveals his awareness of how his certainty appeared to those around him, particularly his other sons who had long dismissed his hope as the irrational attachment of an aging father. Yet this moment affirms a central theme of the surah: that Jacob's unwavering faith and perceptiveness, rooted in his trust in God's wisdom and the fulfillment of the dream revealed to Joseph in his youth, were ultimately vindicated. The verse underscores that deep faith can grant insight beyond ordinary sensory or rational limits, and that patience and trust in divine providence are eventually rewarded, even when such trust seems implausible or excessive to others.

translation: They said, 'By Allah, indeed you are in your old error.'
interpretation: This verse occurs in Surah Yusuf, spoken by the sons of Prophet Ya'qub (Jacob) in response to their father's declaration that he could sense the scent of Yusuf (Joseph), even though Yusuf had been separated from the family for many years and was presumed by others to be lost or dead. Ya'qub had maintained unwavering faith and hope that Yusuf was alive, despite the passage of time and the skepticism of those around him. His sons, not sharing his conviction and perhaps still carrying guilt or disbelief regarding Yusuf's fate, dismiss his perception as a continuation of an old, persistent delusion—implying that his grief and longing had clouded his judgment for years. This moment highlights the contrast between Ya'qub's deep spiritual insight and patient faith (sabr) in Allah's plan versus the limited, worldly perspective of his sons. Shortly after this statement, the truth of Ya'qub's perception is validated when Yusuf's shirt is brought to him and his sight is restored, demonstrating that what others dismissed as delusion was in fact a form of spiritual certainty granted to a righteous, patient believer. The verse underscores the theme that those with strong faith may perceive truths that are inaccessible to others, and that steadfastness in belief, even when mocked or doubted, can ultimately be vindicated by divine will.

translation: Then when the bearer of good news arrived, he cast it [the shirt of Joseph] over his [Jacob's] face, and he returned [to] seeing clearly. He said, 'Did I not tell you that I know from Allah what you do not know?'
interpretation: This verse depicts the miraculous restoration of Prophet Jacob's eyesight, which he had lost due to prolonged grief over the loss of his son Joseph. When Joseph's shirt was brought from Egypt and placed upon Jacob's face, his sight was immediately restored, fulfilling what Jacob had sensed through divine inspiration earlier in the story when he told his sons that he could perceive Joseph's presence even though they doubted him. Jacob's closing statement is a vindication of his unwavering faith and patience (sabr), affirming that his certainty was not mere wishful thinking but a form of knowledge granted to him by Allah—a knowledge rooted in prophetic insight and trust in divine wisdom that transcends ordinary human understanding. The verse underscores the theme that true believers may possess insight or certainty about Allah's plans that others, lacking such faith, cannot perceive, and that patience in adversity is ultimately rewarded with relief and vindication from God.

translation: They said, 'O our father, ask forgiveness for us of our sins; indeed, we have been sinners.'
interpretation: This verse depicts the moment when Joseph's brothers, confronted by the enormity of their past wrongdoing against him, turn to their father Jacob and openly confess their guilt, asking him to intercede with God on their behalf. It reflects a profound act of repentance and humility, acknowledging that their actions—driven by jealousy and resentment—were sinful. By asking their father to seek forgiveness for them rather than approaching God directly, they recognize Jacob's righteousness and closeness to God, seeking his intercession as a means of spiritual restoration. This moment underscores broader Qur'anic themes of family reconciliation, the possibility of redemption through sincere repentance, and the importance of acknowledging one's faults rather than remaining in denial or pride.

translation: He said, 'I will ask forgiveness for you from my Lord. Indeed, He is the Forgiving, the Merciful.'
interpretation: This verse records the response of Prophet Jacob (Ya'qub) to his sons after they confessed their wrongdoing regarding Joseph and sought his forgiveness. Rather than granting immediate absolution himself, Jacob defers the matter to God, promising to intercede through supplication. The phrase 'sawfa' (I will, in the future) suggests a deliberate delay—some commentators suggest Jacob chose a propitious time, such as the last part of the night, to make this plea, reflecting the Islamic tradition that certain times are more conducive to having prayers answered. This demonstrates several key themes: the primacy of seeking divine forgiveness over human forgiveness alone, a father's enduring compassion and willingness to intercede for his children despite their grave sin against him and their brother, and trust in God's attributes as al-Ghafur (the Forgiving) and al-Rahim (the Merciful). It models the proper response to repentance—not harsh judgment but a path toward reconciliation through turning to God. It also foreshadows the eventual reunion and resolution of the family's suffering, reinforcing the Quranic theme that patience and trust in God's mercy can transform even the deepest family betrayals into eventual restoration and peace.

translation: And when they entered upon Joseph, he took his parents to himself and said, 'Enter Egypt, if Allah wills, in security.'
interpretation: This verse marks the emotional culmination of the story of Joseph, depicting the long-awaited reunion between Joseph and his parents after years of separation and hardship. The act of Joseph embracing his parents and drawing them close symbolizes the restoration of family bonds broken by jealousy and deception earlier in the narrative, as well as the fulfillment of Joseph's childhood dream of honor and reunion. His invitation for them to enter Egypt in safety, qualified by 'if Allah wills,' demonstrates his humility and piety even at the height of his power and success, as he attributes all outcomes to divine will rather than his own doing. This phrase also reflects Islamic etiquette in acknowledging that security and blessings are ultimately granted by God, not guaranteed by human effort alone. The verse thus encapsulates themes of divine providence, the triumph of patience and faith over trial, and the proper comportment of a believer who recognizes God's hand in all affairs, even in moments of personal triumph and joy.

translation: And he raised his parents upon the throne, and they fell down before him in prostration. And he said, 'O my father, this is the interpretation of my vision from before. My Lord has made it reality. And He was certainly good to me when He took me out of prison and brought you from the bedouin life after Satan had induced [estrangement] between me and my brothers. Indeed, my Lord is subtle in what He wills. Indeed, it is He who is the Knowing, the Wise.'
interpretation: This verse marks the triumphant resolution of Yusuf's lifelong trial, fulfilling the dream he had as a boy that his parents and brothers would one day bow before him. His parents' prostration is not an act of worship but a customary gesture of honor and respect in that era, acknowledging Yusuf's elevated status as ruler of Egypt. Yusuf's speech reveals his humility and piety rather than pride in his achievement; he immediately attributes his success to God's will, framing the entire narrative of his suffering and triumph as divine orchestration. He explicitly names the stages of his trial, imprisonment and the estrangement caused by his brothers, not as random misfortunes but as part of a providential plan subtly guided by God, whom he describes as 'Latif' (subtle, gracious) in executing His will in ways beyond human perception. This verse encapsulates the surah's central theme: that God's wisdom operates through hidden, gradual means, turning adversity into eventual honor for those who remain patient and trust in divine justice. It also underscores reconciliation and forgiveness, as Yusuf does not dwell on blame against his brothers but recognizes Satan's role in sowing discord, thus absolving human relationships from eternal enmity and emphasizing restoration of family bonds under God's grace.

translation: My Lord, You have given me [something] of sovereignty and taught me of the interpretation of events (dreams). Originator of the heavens and the earth, You are my protector in this world and the Hereafter. Cause me to die as a Muslim [one submitting to You] and join me with the righteous.
interpretation: This verse is the culmination of the story of Prophet Yusuf (Joseph), spoken after he has been reunited with his family and risen to a position of authority in Egypt. Having endured betrayal by his brothers, enslavement, false accusation, and imprisonment, Yusuf now reflects on the totality of his journey with profound gratitude and humility. Rather than reveling in his newfound power and status, he immediately attributes all of it—sovereignty and the gift of interpreting dreams—to God's grace, acknowledging that worldly success is a divine trust rather than a personal achievement. His prayer then pivots dramatically: instead of asking for continued prosperity or a long life to enjoy his hard-won position, he asks for a righteous death and companionship with the righteous in the afterlife. This represents a spiritual pinnacle in the narrative—Yusuf, having achieved everything one could want in worldly terms (power, vindication, family reunion), demonstrates that his ultimate concern is not this world at all but his standing before God. The invocation of God as 'Originator of the heavens and the earth' and 'protector in this world and the Hereafter' frames his entire life's trials as part of a divine plan, and his request to die 'as a Muslim' (one submitting to God) and be joined with the righteous (likely referring to his forefathers Ibrahim, Ishaq, and Ya'qub) shows that true success in the Quranic worldview is measured by one's relationship with God and ultimate fate in the afterlife, not by temporal achievements. This verse thus serves as a model of prophetic humility and a reorientation of values away from worldly attainment toward eternal salvation.

translation: That is from the news of the unseen which We reveal to you [O Muhammad]. You were not with them when they put together their plan while they were scheming.
interpretation: This verse, from the story of Prophet Yusuf (Joseph), serves as a direct proof of Muhammad's prophethood. By affirming that he was not physically present when Yusuf's brothers conspired against him, the verse emphasizes that such detailed knowledge of past, unwitnessed events could only come through divine revelation (wahy). It establishes that the Qur'an is not a product of human historical research, legend, or hearsay, but authentic information from God about the unseen (al-ghayb), thereby validating the truth of the message and the messenger to the skeptics among his audience who were familiar with earlier scriptural traditions.

translation: And most of the people, even if you desire it eagerly, will not be believers.
interpretation: This verse addresses Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) directly, consoling him regarding his deep concern and eagerness for people to accept faith. It conveys a profound truth about human nature and free will: that despite the Prophet's sincere desire and relentless efforts to guide people toward belief, the majority of humanity would not embrace faith. This is not a reflection of any shortcoming in the message or the messenger, but rather an acknowledgment that faith is a matter of the heart that cannot be forced or guaranteed through human effort alone, no matter how earnest. The verse serves to comfort the Prophet by removing the burden of responsibility for others' disbelief from his shoulders, reminding him that guidance ultimately comes from God, and that his role is to convey the message, not to ensure universal acceptance of it. This principle extends beyond the immediate context to speak to the nature of faith itself—it is a personal choice and divine gift that cannot be imposed, and throughout history, true believers have often constituted a minority even when confronted with clear signs and sincere calls to belief.

translation: And you ask them not for it any reward. It is not except a reminder to the worlds (all mankind).
interpretation: This verse underscores the sincerity and universality of the Prophet Muhammad's mission. By emphasizing that he sought no material compensation for delivering the message, it establishes his credibility and removes any suspicion that his preaching was motivated by worldly gain, power, or wealth. This selflessness serves as evidence of the divine origin of his message rather than a personal agenda. Furthermore, by describing the Qur'an as 'a reminder to the worlds,' the verse affirms the universal scope of its guidance—it is not limited to a particular tribe, nation, or era, but is meant for all of humanity across time. The term 'reminder' (dhikr) also suggests that the truths conveyed are not entirely new revelations alien to human nature, but rather a reawakening of innate knowledge of God and moral truth that already resides within the human soul, which people have forgotten or neglected. This reflects the Qur'anic view that monotheism and moral consciousness are part of human nature (fitrah), and the role of prophets is to remind people of what they already intuitively know deep within.

translation: And how many a sign in the heavens and the earth do they pass by, while they are turning away from it.
