This teaches that scarcity or abundance in the world is not due to any lack in God's capacity, but rather reflects a deliberate, wise apportionment. It instills trust in God's providence, encouraging believers to understand that what reaches them is neither more nor less than what divine wisdom has ordained, and that behind every apparent limitation in the material world lies an unlimited source controlled by perfect knowledge and purpose.

translation: And We send the winds as fertilizers (pollinators), and We send down water from the sky, and We give it to you to drink, and you are not the ones who store it up.
interpretation: This verse highlights Allah's providence and sovereignty over the natural processes that sustain life. The winds are described as 'lawaqih' (fertilizing/pollinating), referring to their role in carrying pollen for plant fertilization and in gathering moisture to form rain clouds—a phenomenon of atmospheric science referenced long before it was scientifically understood. The rain that falls from the sky is a direct gift from Allah, not something humanity creates or controls. The final phrase emphasizes human dependency: despite building reservoirs, wells, and storage systems, humans do not truly control or own the source of water—they are merely recipients and temporary custodians of a resource whose origin and sustained supply rest entirely with the Creator. This serves as a reminder of human limitation and the necessity of gratitude, countering any illusion of self-sufficiency or mastery over nature's life-giving forces.

translation: And indeed, it is We who give life and cause death, and We are the Inheritor.
interpretation: This verse establishes God's absolute sovereignty over existence itself, affirming that life and death are entirely within His power and occur by His will alone, not by chance or the agency of any other being. The declaration 'We are the Inheritor' conveys the theological truth that all creation, all wealth, all dominion ultimately returns to God alone—everything that exists is temporary and borrowed, while God's existence and ownership are eternal and permanent. When all created beings perish and all temporal possessions and kingdoms pass away, God remains as the sole and everlasting inheritor of all that was. This serves as a profound reminder of human mortality and the transient nature of worldly life, encouraging believers to recognize that true and lasting ownership belongs to God alone, and that attachment to worldly possessions and power is ultimately futile since everything will revert to its true Owner. The verse also reinforces the theme of resurrection and accountability—since God who gives life and takes it away is also the One to whom all things return, He alone has the right to judge and determine the fate of His creation in the Hereafter.

translation: And We have certainly known those of you who hastened forth (went before), and We have certainly known those who lag behind (come later).
interpretation: This verse affirms God's comprehensive and eternal knowledge encompassing all generations of humanity—those who lived in the past and those yet to come, as well as those who were foremost in faith and good deeds versus those who lagged behind. Nothing escapes divine awareness; every soul's place in the sequence of creation, its deeds, and its spiritual standing are fully known to God. This serves as both a reminder of accountability—since no one can claim ignorance shields them from judgment—and a consolation, affirming that God's knowledge and justice span all of human history without exception.

translation: And indeed, your Lord - He will gather them. Indeed, He is Wise, Knowing.
interpretation: This verse affirms that on the Day of Resurrection, God Himself will gather all created beings together for judgment and recompense. The emphasis on 'He' (huwa) underscores that this gathering is solely God's affair, not dependent on any intermediary, highlighting His absolute sovereignty over creation and the certainty of the final reckoning. The verse concludes with two divine attributes - Wise (Hakim) and Knowing (Alim) - which together assure that this gathering and subsequent judgment will be conducted with perfect wisdom and complete knowledge of every being's deeds, intentions, and circumstances. Nothing escapes God's awareness, and His decisions in judgment are rooted in infinite wisdom rather than arbitrary will. This pairing of attributes often appears in the Qur'an to reassure believers that divine justice is neither capricious nor uninformed, but grounded in both comprehensive knowledge of all things and the wisdom to act rightly upon that knowledge.

translation: And indeed, We created man from dried clay of black mud altered [in shape and smell].
interpretation: This verse describes the origin of humanity's physical creation, emphasizing that Adam was formed from a specific type of earthly material—clay that had been left to dry and transform in color and odor before being shaped into human form. The detailed description of the clay's state (dried, derived from altered black mud) underscores the humble, earthly origins of mankind, serving as a reminder of human mortality and dependence on the Creator. This contrasts later in the surah with the creation of Iblis from fire, highlighting a thematic distinction between the two creations and foreshadowing Iblis's arrogance in refusing to bow to a being he considered inferior in substance, despite the divine honor bestowed upon humanity through the breathing of God's spirit into this humble clay.

translation: And the jinn We created before, from the fire of scorching wind (samum).
interpretation: This verse establishes the origin of the jinn as a distinct category of creation, made before humankind from a piercing, scorching fire (samum), as opposed to Adam who was created from clay/dust. The mention of 'before' situates the jinn's creation temporally prior to humanity, affirming that spiritual, unseen beings existed before the physical creation of man. The nature of their origin—fire that penetrates and scorches—also hints at the jinn's qualities: their subtlety, their ability to move swiftly and unseen, and their fiery, volatile temperament, which contrasts with the more stable, earthly composition of humans. This distinction is foundational for understanding the different natures, responsibilities, and capacities given to jinn versus humans within the Qur'anic worldview, while also affirming divine power in creating diverse forms of life from different elements.

translation: And [mention] when your Lord said to the angels, 'Indeed, I am going to create a human being out of clay from altered black mud.'
interpretation: This verse marks the beginning of the divine announcement to the angels about the creation of Adam, the first human. The description of the material—dry clay (salsal) derived from black mud that has been transformed (hama masnun)—emphasizes the humble, earthly origin of humankind in contrast to the angels, who were created from light, and Iblis, who was created from fire. This sets up the theological framework for understanding human nature as a synthesis of base physical matter and, as later verses reveal, the breath of God's spirit. The verse also establishes God's sovereign will and foreknowledge in creation, as He declares His intention before the act itself, highlighting that human creation was a deliberate, purposeful divine act rather than a random occurrence. This moment is pivotal because it sets the stage for the subsequent command for angels to prostrate before Adam, Iblis's refusal, and the entire cosmic drama of obedience, free will, and the distinct status granted to humanity despite—or perhaps because of—its lowly physical origins.

translation: So when I have fashioned him in due proportion and breathed into him of My spirit, then fall down before him in prostration.
interpretation: This verse depicts God's declaration to the angels regarding the creation of Adam, establishing humanity's unique status among creation. The 'breathing of His spirit' signifies the endowment of a soul, intellect, and consciousness that elevates humankind above mere physical matter, granting the capacity for moral reasoning, spiritual connection, and free will. The command for the angels to prostrate is not worship of Adam himself, but an act of honoring God's creative act and acknowledging the dignity bestowed upon the human being by divine will. This moment establishes humanity as a trustee (khalifa) on earth, carrying within it a spark of the divine breath, which grounds human dignity, moral responsibility, and the potential for spiritual elevation—while also setting the stage for Iblis's refusal and fall, illustrating the themes of arrogance, obedience, and the testing of free will that permeate the broader Quranic narrative of creation.

translation: So the angels prostrated themselves, all of them together.
interpretation: This verse describes the complete and unanimous obedience of the angels to God's command to prostrate before Adam after his creation. The emphasis on 'all of them together' (kulluhum ajma'un) underscores the totality of this obedience—no angel abstained or hesitated, highlighting the angels' nature as beings who do not disobey God's commands. This collective prostration sets up a crucial contrast with Iblis (Satan), who alone refuses to comply in the verses that follow, marking him as an exception to the angels and revealing his pride and disobedience. The verse thus establishes the theme of obedience versus arrogance, and foreshadows the cosmic drama of temptation and human vulnerability that results from Iblis's refusal. It also affirms the special honor given to Adam as the father of humanity, whom even the angels were commanded to honor through this act of prostration—not as worship of Adam himself, but as a sign of respect for God's creation and a symbol of humanity's potential spiritual rank when guided by divine knowledge.

translation: Except Iblis; he refused to be among those who prostrated.
interpretation: This verse recounts the pivotal moment when Allah commanded the angels to prostrate before Adam, and all complied except Iblis (Satan). His refusal stemmed from arrogance and a sense of superiority—he believed himself better than Adam because he was created from fire while Adam was created from clay. This single act of disobedience marks the origin of Iblis's fall from grace and his transformation into the eternal adversary of humankind. The verse illustrates a central theme in the Qur'an: that pride and the refusal to submit to divine command, even when one possesses knowledge or a seemingly superior nature, leads to spiritual ruin. Iblis's defiance was not born of ignorance but of conscious rebellion against a direct divine order, making his sin particularly grave. This moment establishes the theological foundation for the ongoing struggle between guidance and temptation, as Iblis subsequently vows to mislead humanity as a consequence of his own fall, having blamed Adam for his disgrace rather than accepting responsibility for his own choice to disobey.

translation: He [Allah] said, 'O Iblis, what is [the matter] with you that you are not with those who prostrate?'
interpretation: This verse records Allah's direct questioning of Iblis after the angels prostrated to Adam in obedience to the divine command, while Iblis alone refused. The question is rhetorical and carries a tone of reproach rather than genuine inquiry, as Allah already knows the reason for Iblis's refusal. It highlights the moment of Iblis's defiance, rooted in pride and his refusal to acknowledge Adam's honored status, which marks the origin of his fall from grace and his transformation into the eternal adversary of humankind. The verse underscores the theme of free will and accountability—Iblis had the choice to obey like the other angels but chose arrogance instead, setting the precedent for his subsequent justification based on feeling superior to Adam due to his creation from fire versus clay.

translation: He [Iblis] said, 'I would not prostrate myself to a human whom You created from clay, from an altered black mud.'
interpretation: This verse captures Iblis's defiant refusal to obey God's command to bow before Adam, revealing the root of his rebellion: arrogance rooted in a false sense of superiority based on physical origin. Iblis reasons that since Adam was fashioned from mere clay and mud, a seemingly base and inferior substance, he is unworthy of such reverence. This moment represents the primordial sin of pride (kibr), where Iblis prioritizes his own judgment over divine command, refusing to see the dignity God bestowed upon Adam despite his humble material origin. The verse serves as a warning about the dangers of arrogance, envy, and judging worth by superficial measures rather than recognizing the honor God can confer upon any of His creation. It establishes Iblis as the archetype of prideful disobedience, setting the stage for the eternal enmity between Iblis and humankind.

translation: He [Allah] said: "Then get out of it (Paradise), for verily you are accursed/expelled."
interpretation: This verse marks the divine verdict against Iblis (Satan) following his act of disobedience in refusing to prostrate before Adam. The command 'get out of it' signifies Iblis's expulsion from the elevated spiritual station and the company of the angels, stripping him of the honor he once held. The term 'rajim' (accursed/expelled, from the root meaning 'to stone' or 'to cast away') conveys both a curse and a sense of being violently cast out, as one would drive away something unwanted and undeserving of proximity. This moment establishes a paradigm in the Qur'an of pride (kibr) as the root sin that leads to spiritual downfall—Iblis's arrogance in considering himself superior to Adam due to his creation from fire versus clay becomes the archetype of rebellion against divine command through self-exaltation. The verse also inaugurates the cosmic enmity between Iblis and humanity, as his expulsion leads him to vow to misguide Adam's progeny, setting the stage for human free will and moral struggle. Theologically, this passage underscores that status and honor in the divine order are contingent upon obedience, not upon one's origin or nature, and that rejection of God's command—regardless of one's prior standing—results in spiritual exile and disgrace.

translation: And indeed, upon you is the curse until the Day of Recompense.
interpretation: This verse is part of God's address to Iblis (Satan) after his refusal to prostrate before Adam, found in Surah Al-Hijr and similarly in Surah Sad. It signifies the divine decree of banishment and condemnation placed upon Iblis as a consequence of his arrogance and disobedience. The curse is not a temporary punishment but one that extends until the Day of Judgment, marking the entirety of worldly existence as the period during which Iblis is spiritually exiled from God's mercy. This establishes the cosmic narrative of Iblis as the eternal adversary of humanity, granted temporary reprieve to tempt mankind, yet already condemned in his ultimate spiritual standing. The verse underscores the seriousness of pride and disobedience before God, and sets the stage for the ongoing struggle between guidance and temptation that characterizes human moral life until the final reckoning.

translation: He said, 'My Lord, then reprieve me until the Day they are resurrected.'
interpretation: This verse recounts Iblis's (Satan's) plea to God after he was cursed and expelled for refusing to prostrate to Adam. Rather than seeking forgiveness or redemption, Iblis asks only for a delay—a reprieve from death until the Day of Resurrection—so that he may use the intervening time to mislead humankind. This request reveals the nature of his defiance: it is not born of ignorance but of conscious, prideful rebellion. His choice to seek time rather than mercy underscores the theme found throughout the Qur'an that Satan's enmity toward humanity is deliberate and purposeful, rooted in jealousy and arrogance over his refusal to honor Adam. God's granting of this request (stated in the following verses) also illustrates a broader theological point: that even the respite given to evil is bounded by divine will and serves as a test for humanity, allowing people to exercise free will in choosing to follow or resist temptation until the appointed Day of Judgment.

translation: He [Allah] said, "Indeed, you are of those given respite."
interpretation: This verse records Allah's response to Iblis (Satan) after he refused to prostrate before Adam and was cast out, then requested a delay until the Day of Judgment to lead humanity astray. Allah's granting of this respite is not a sign of weakness or indulgence toward Iblis, but rather demonstrates the principle of free will and divine wisdom in testing humanity. By allowing Iblis to exist and tempt until the appointed time, Allah establishes the arena for moral choice—human beings are given the capacity to resist temptation and earn their spiritual standing through genuine struggle against evil, rather than being protected from it entirely. This reflects a broader Quranic theme that life itself is a trial, and the presence of temptation (symbolized by Iblis) is necessary for human beings to demonstrate faith, patience, and moral integrity through their own choices rather than through compulsion or the absence of evil.

translation: Until the Day of the appointed time.
interpretation: This phrase is part of God's response to Iblis (Satan) after he refused to prostrate before Adam and was cast out, yet requested a reprieve until the Day of Resurrection. God granted him respite, but specified it would last only 'until the Day of the known time' — meaning the precise, predetermined moment of the Day of Judgment, a time known only to God Himself. This establishes that even Iblis's ability to tempt and mislead humanity operates within divinely set limits and a fixed duration; his reprieve is not open-ended or eternal, but bounded by God's complete knowledge and control over all time and destiny. It underscores the theological principle that no creature, however defiant, operates outside the sovereign decree of God, and that the ultimate reckoning is fixed and certain, even if hidden from human knowledge.

translation: He [Satan] said: 'My Lord, because You have sent me astray, I will surely make [disobedience] attractive to them on earth, and I will mislead them all together.'
interpretation: This verse records Iblis's defiant response after his expulsion from Allah's mercy for refusing to prostrate before Adam. Rather than accepting responsibility for his own arrogance and disobedience, he attributes his fall to Allah's decree ('bima aghwaytani' - 'because You have sent me astray'), revealing his rebellious and unrepentant nature. He then vows to dedicate himself to corrupting humanity by making sin, disobedience, and worldly temptations appear beautiful and desirable ('la-uzayyinanna lahum fi'l-ard'), thereby leading people away from the straight path. This declaration establishes the cosmic drama of temptation that runs throughout human history - Satan's strategy is not to make evil appear as evil, but to disguise it as something attractive, worthwhile, or even virtuous. The verse underscores the nature of spiritual trial in worldly life: humans are tested through allurements that mask harmful or sinful choices as appealing. It also highlights the theological point that while Allah's decree encompasses all things, moral responsibility remains with the one who chooses to act upon temptation - Iblis's blame-shifting is portrayed as characteristic of his corrupted character, setting a pattern for how humans might similarly deflect responsibility for their own sins.

translation: "Except, among them, Your sincere servants."
interpretation: This phrase is part of Iblis's (Satan's) declaration before God after his expulsion, found in Surah Al-Hijr (15:40) and similarly in Surah Sad (38:83). Having vowed to mislead humankind by tempting them through every possible avenue, Iblis makes this crucial exception, acknowledging that he will have no power over God's 'mukhlaseen'—those servants who are sincerely devoted, purified in faith, and chosen by divine grace. The term 'mukhlaseen' implies a special category of believers whose sincerity and devotion are so complete that they are protected from Satan's deceptions, not merely by their own effort but through God's grace in purifying them. This verse establishes a theological distinction between ordinary believers, who may be vulnerable to temptation, and these sincere servants, whose hearts have been cleansed of worldly attachments and ego-driven desires, making them immune to Satan's whispers and schemes. It underscores the Qur'anic theme that true protection from evil comes through sincere devotion to God and that this sincerity itself is a divine gift bestowed upon those who seek Him wholeheartedly.

translation: He [Allah] said: 'This is a path, straight, incumbent upon Me.'
interpretation: This verse comes in the context of Allah's response to Iblis (Satan) after Iblis vowed to mislead humanity and lead them astray, except for Allah's sincere servants. Allah's declaration here affirms that the straight path—the path of true guidance, sincere devotion, and righteousness—is a path that Allah Himself guarantees and takes responsibility for protecting. The phrase 'upon Me' (عليّ) signifies that maintaining and safeguarding this path of guidance is something Allah has undertaken as a matter of His own will and grace, particularly for those who sincerely devote themselves to Him. It serves as a divine assurance that despite Satan's efforts to corrupt and mislead, those who are sincere in their servitude to Allah will be protected and guided, for the true path leading to Him remains secure under His direct care and will not be overcome by the whisperings or temptations of Iblis. This sets up the contrast explored in the following verses, where Iblis is told he will have no authority over Allah's sincere servants, only over those who choose to follow him astray.

translation: Indeed, over My servants you (Satan) have no authority, except those who follow you among the deviators.
interpretation: This verse, part of Allah's response to Iblis after his rejection to bow before Adam, establishes a fundamental principle regarding the nature of spiritual authority and free will. It declares that Satan possesses no inherent power or compulsive control over Allah's sincere, devoted servants (al-'ibad al-mukhlisin). His influence is limited to whisperings, temptations, and suggestions—he cannot force anyone into sin or disbelief. The only people who fall under his sway are those who willingly choose to follow him, the ghawin (those who stray or are led astray), meaning that their own misguidance and poor choices open the door to his influence. This verse thus places ultimate responsibility on human beings themselves: Satan can tempt, but he cannot compel. The protection from his influence is tied to one's sincerity and devotion to Allah, while vulnerability to his schemes is tied to one's own inclination toward deviation. It underscores the Quranic theme that human beings are accountable for their choices, and that true faith and sincerity serve as a shield against satanic influence, whereas straying from righteousness creates an opening for it.

translation: And indeed, Hell is the promised meeting-place for them all.
interpretation: This verse refers to those who follow Satan and his offspring in misguidance, as mentioned in the preceding verses about Iblis and his followers. It establishes Hell as the destined gathering place for all who choose to follow Satan's path rather than divine guidance. The verse serves as a stern warning that despite the apparent success or power that those who are misguided may enjoy in worldly life, their ultimate destination is unified and certain - Hell awaits them collectively. This emphasizes both the certainty of divine justice and the solidarity of consequence that unites all who reject truth, regardless of their differences in this world. The verse underscores the Quranic theme that this worldly life is temporary and that true accountability occurs in the Hereafter, where the deceptive promises of Satan will be shown for what they truly are - a path leading to eternal consequence rather than the false hopes he offers his followers.

translation: It has seven gates; for each gate is an assigned portion of them.
interpretation: This verse describes Hell (Jahannam) as having seven gates, each designated for a specific group or portion of those who are condemned to it, as mentioned in the preceding verses addressing Iblis and his followers who lead people astray. The division into seven gates with assigned portions reflects a structured allocation based on the nature and degree of misguidance or sin of those who enter. This imagery conveys the comprehensive and organized nature of divine justice, where every soul's destination is precisely determined according to their deeds and the extent to which they followed Satan's temptations rather than divine guidance. The number seven also carries symbolic weight in Islamic tradition, often representing completeness or totality, suggesting that every category of wrongdoing has its corresponding consequence.

translation: Indeed, the righteous (those who are mindful of God) will be amid gardens and springs.
interpretation: This verse opens a passage (continuing in Surah Al-Hijr) describing the ultimate reward awaiting the muttaqin—those who maintain taqwa, a conscious awareness of and reverence for God that shapes their moral conduct. The imagery of gardens and flowing springs evokes a paradise of lush abundance, tranquility, and refreshment, standing in deliberate contrast to the barren, arid landscape familiar to the verse's original desert audience. Water and greenery symbolize life, purity, and divine favor, representing not merely physical comfort but a state of spiritual fulfillment and peace that comes from closeness to God. The verse functions as a promise of requital: the trials, restraint, and moral discipline that taqwa demands in earthly life are met with eternal ease and beauty. It also serves a rhetorical purpose within the surah, reassuring believers who remain steadfast amid disbelief and mockery from others that their patience and devotion will be vindicated in the Hereafter, where the transient hardships of this world give way to everlasting delight.

translation: Enter it in peace, secure.
interpretation: This verse is addressed to the righteous believers as they are welcomed into Paradise, following the preceding verses that describe the gardens and springs prepared for the pious. The command 'enter it in peace, secure' signifies the complete removal of fear, anxiety, and hardship that characterized worldly life. 'Peace' (salām) reflects the greeting and the state of tranquility that pervades Paradise, free from conflict, envy, or malice among its inhabitants, as the following verse clarifies that God removes any rancor from their hearts. 'Secure' (āminīn) indicates permanent safety from death, expulsion, illness, or any form of loss—an eternal, unshakeable security that contrasts with the uncertainties and trials of earthly existence. Together, these two words encapsulate the ultimate reward: a state of perfect contentment, safety, and harmony granted by God to those who maintained piety and patience in their worldly lives.

translation: And We shall remove whatever rancor is in their breasts, [so they will be] brothers, on couches facing one another.
interpretation: This verse describes the state of the believers in Paradise, where Allah purifies their hearts of any residual envy, grudges, or ill feelings that may have existed among them in worldly life. The removal of 'ghill' (rancor/malice) signifies a complete spiritual purification that accompanies entry into the eternal abode, ensuring that Paradise is a realm of perfect harmony and brotherhood. The image of reclining on thrones facing one another emphasizes equality, intimacy, and mutual joy among the believers—there is no hierarchy of resentment or awkwardness, only companionship and shared bliss. This also reflects a broader Quranic theme that true felicity requires not just external rewards (gardens, rivers, thrones) but inner peace and reconciliation of the heart, suggesting that the ultimate human fulfillment includes restored relationships and the dissolution of worldly conflicts and jealousies that often mar human bonds.

translation: No fatigue will touch them therein, nor will they ever be expelled from it.
interpretation: This verse describes the eternal state of the righteous in Paradise, emphasizing two complementary aspects of perfected bliss: freedom from toil and permanence of residence. In worldly life, pleasure is almost always tempered by exhaustion, effort, or the fear of loss—joy is fleeting and existence itself is laborious. Here, the Qur'an negates both limitations that mar earthly happiness. The absence of 'nasab' (fatigue, weariness, or exertion) signifies that the blessings of Paradise are not earned through continued struggle once attained; they are a state of effortless rest and contentment, contrasting with the toil of worldly life and even the hardships of worship and trial that preceded this reward. The second clause, that they will not be expelled, addresses the anxiety of impermanence—unlike worldly gardens, kingdoms, or joys which are always subject to loss, decay, or expulsion (as Adam was expelled from the first Garden), the dwellers of Paradise are granted security and permanence. Together, these two assurances complete the picture of ultimate felicity: an existence free from both the inner burden of weariness and the outer threat of loss, representing the fulfillment of human longing for lasting, unearned peace.

translation: Inform My servants that I am indeed the Forgiving, the Merciful.
interpretation: This verse comes immediately after the account of Ibrahim's guests and before the story of Lut's people, situating divine mercy and forgiveness as a central theme between narratives of judgment. God instructs His Prophet to proclaim directly to His servants—all of humanity, not just believers—that His essential nature is forgiveness and mercy. This placement is significant: it balances the stern warnings about punishment found elsewhere in the surah with an assurance that God's primary disposition toward His creation is compassion. The use of 'My servants' (ibadi) rather than a more restrictive term emphasizes the universality of this divine attribute, offering hope to all who might fear their sins are too great to be forgiven, provided they turn to Him sincerely.

translation: And that My punishment is the painful punishment.
interpretation: This verse comes as the counterpart to the preceding declaration that God's forgiveness and mercy are boundless. Together, the two verses establish a balance between divine hope and divine fear (raja' and khawf) that is central to Islamic theology. By affirming that His punishment is indeed 'the painful punishment,' God warns against complacency or presumption—one should not take His mercy for granted to the point of abandoning righteous conduct. This pairing teaches that true faith requires holding both attributes of God in mind simultaneously: His infinite mercy should inspire hope and repentance, while the certainty of His justice and the reality of painful consequences for wrongdoing should inspire caution, humility, and sincere moral effort. The verse serves as a sobering reminder that divine justice is real and severe, particularly for those who reject guidance after it has been made clear to them, ensuring that mercy is not misunderstood as license for heedlessness.

translation: And inform them about the guests of Abraham.
interpretation: This verse introduces the narrative of the angelic visitors who came to Prophet Abraham in human form, setting the stage for the subsequent account of their announcement of a son to him and their mission to the people of Lot. God instructs the Prophet Muhammad to relate this story to his people, the Quraysh, as a reminder of divine power and the fate that befell nations who rejected truth and righteousness. The mention of 'guests' (dayf) emphasizes the theme of hospitality central to Abraham's character, while also foreshadowing the serious and weighty purpose of their visit—one that carries both glad tidings and warning. This serves as a pedagogical device within the Qur'an, using the story to draw lessons about faith, divine mercy, and justice for those who listen.

translation: When they entered upon him and said, 'Peace!' He said, 'Indeed, we are fearful of you.'
interpretation: This verse refers to the angelic visitors who came to Prophet Ibrahim (Abraham) in human form. Upon their greeting of peace, Ibrahim's response reveals his initial apprehension as a gracious host, since the strangers did not partake of the food he offered them (as mentioned in other verses), which in the customs of hospitality of that time signaled potential hostile intent. This moment captures the human instinct of caution toward the unknown, even amid courteous exchange, and sets the stage for the angels to reveal their true identity and purpose—delivering glad tidings of a son to Ibrahim and announcing the impending judgment upon the people of Lot. The verse illustrates the Qur'anic theme that divine messengers often appear in ways that test and engage human perception before their true nature and mission are disclosed.

translation: They said, 'Do not be afraid; indeed, we bring you good tidings of a knowledgeable boy.'
interpretation: This verse depicts the angels addressing Prophet Ibrahim (Abraham), reassuring him not to fear their presence—since he had initially been apprehensive when they did not eat the food he offered them, suspecting they might intend harm. The angels then deliver divine glad tidings of a son, Ishaq (Isaac), who is described as 'alim (knowledgeable or possessing great knowledge), foretelling that this son would grow to be a man of wisdom and prophethood. This moment illustrates a recurring Qur'anic theme: that divine messengers often bring news that defies natural expectation, as Ibrahim and his wife were elderly and had given up hope of having children. The reassurance 'do not be afraid' highlights the compassion embedded in divine communication, while the promise of a learned son underscores that true blessings from God include not just progeny, but progeny endowed with knowledge and righteousness, linking lineage to spiritual and intellectual legacy rather than mere biological continuation.

translation: He said, "Do you give me good tidings although old age has come upon me? Then how is it you give me this good tidings?"
interpretation: This verse recounts the reaction of Abraham when angels/messengers announced to him the glad tidings of a son, despite his advanced age. His response reflects a natural human astonishment at receiving news that seems to defy the ordinary course of nature, given his old age. Rather than outright disbelief, it demonstrates Abraham's wonder and his seeking of clarification and reassurance, prompting a response that affirms the certainty of God's promise despite apparent natural limitations. It underscores the theme that divine power transcends human expectations and biological norms, offering a lesson in faith that God's will and ability to bring about the seemingly impossible should not be doubted, even when circumstances suggest otherwise.

translation: They said, 'We have given you glad tidings in truth, so do not be among the despairing.'
interpretation: This verse occurs in the story of Prophet Ibrahim (Abraham) when angels came to him with the news that he would have a son (Isaac) despite his and his wife's old age. When Ibrahim expressed astonishment and questioned how this could be, the angels affirmed that their message was true and certain, coming from Allah, and they gently rebuked him for any hint of doubt by telling him not to be among those who despair of Allah's mercy. The verse carries a broader theological lesson central to Islamic theology: that despair of God's mercy and power is inappropriate for believers, since Allah's ability to fulfill His promises is not bound by ordinary human limitations such as old age or apparent impossibility. The angels' words serve as a reminder that divine promises, once given, are certain truths (al-haqq) that should inspire hope and trust rather than skepticism, reinforcing the Quranic theme that despairing of Allah's mercy is considered a serious spiritual failing, associated elsewhere in the Quran with disbelief itself.

translation: He said: 'And who despairs of the mercy of his Lord except those who are astray?'
interpretation: This verse is spoken by the Prophet Ibrahim (Abraham) in response to his own momentary astonishment upon receiving news from the angelic visitors that he would be granted a son despite his old age. When the angels reassured him and told him not to be of those who despair, Ibrahim affirmed that only those who have strayed from true faith and understanding of God's nature would ever give up hope in divine mercy. The verse establishes a foundational theological principle: despair of God's mercy is characterized as a form of spiritual misguidance (dalal), equivalent to a failure to properly comprehend God's limitless capacity for compassion and power to do what seems impossible. This teaching extends beyond the immediate narrative context to serve as a broader admonition to believers that no matter how dire one's circumstances appear, maintaining hope in divine mercy is a marker of true faith, while despair reflects a deficient understanding of God's attributes. The rhetorical question format emphasizes the near-impossibility of a true believer falling into such despair, since recognizing God's omnipotence and boundless mercy naturally produces hope even in the face of seemingly insurmountable circumstances.

translation: He [Abraham] said, 'Then what is your business, O messengers?'
interpretation: This verse depicts Prophet Ibrahim (Abraham) addressing the angelic visitors who had come to him in human form, after they had delivered the glad tidings of a son. Having already received their news of a child, Ibrahim perceives that these are not ordinary guests but messengers with a further, weightier mission. His question reflects both hospitality and perceptiveness—he recognizes that beings of such nature would not visit without a significant purpose. This sets up the dramatic revelation that follows: the angels are on their way to destroy the people of Lot for their transgressions. The verse illustrates the prophetic insight of Ibrahim, who discerns the deeper reality behind appearances, and introduces the narrative of divine justice meted out to a sinful nation, serving as a lesson about God's response to persistent wrongdoing and His protection of the righteous amid judgment upon others.

translation: They said, 'Indeed, we have been sent to a criminal people,'
interpretation: This verse depicts the angels responding to Abraham, explaining the purpose of their mission after they had delivered glad tidings of a son to him. They clarify that beyond this announcement, their primary mission is one of divine judgment—they have been dispatched to destroy the people of Lot, described as 'mujrimin' (criminals or sinners), referring to their persistence in immorality, particularly their infamous practice of same-sex acts and their rejection of Lot's warnings. This moment illustrates a recurring Qur'anic theme: that divine messengers serve dual roles of mercy (glad tidings) and justice (punishment), and that societies which persist in corruption and reject guidance ultimately face consequences. The term 'mujrimin' is significant throughout the Qur'an, denoting those who have crossed moral boundaries through willful wrongdoing, emphasizing that the destruction to come upon them is a direct result of their own actions rather than arbitrary divine wrath.

translation: Except the family of Lot; indeed, We will save them all,
interpretation: This verse occurs within the narrative of the angelic messengers who visited Prophet Lot (Lut) before the destruction of his people for their grave sins. The angels, who had earlier given glad tidings to Abraham, informed him that they were sent to destroy a sinful nation. Here, they specify an exception: the household of Lot would be spared from the impending punishment, with the sole exception of his wife, who is excluded in subsequent verses because she sided with the disbelievers and betrayed Lot's mission. This verse highlights the Qur'anic theme that divine punishment is precise and just, sparing the righteous even amid wholesale destruction, while also showing that familial relation alone does not guarantee salvation—one's own faith and conduct determine one's fate, as exemplified by the differing destinies within Lot's own household.

translation: Except his wife; We have decreed that she is indeed among those who remain behind [to be destroyed].
interpretation: This verse refers to the wife of Prophet Lot (Lut), who, despite being married to a prophet, remained inwardly aligned with the disbelieving and sinful people of her town rather than with her husband's message. While the angels sent to Lot instructed him to depart with his family under cover of night to escape the impending destruction, his wife was excluded from this divine mercy because of her complicity with the wrongdoers—she is said to have supported or sympathized with them, possibly by signaling to the townspeople about the guests. The phrase 'We have decreed' (qaddarna) emphasizes that her fate was not incidental but a matter of divine decree, underscoring the Qur'anic theme that kinship or marital ties to a righteous person do not themselves guarantee salvation; what matters is one's own faith and conduct. She is described as being 'among those who remain behind' (al-ghabirin), meaning she stayed in the city and perished with its people when the divine punishment fell, illustrating the principle that each soul bears responsibility for its own choices irrespective of its proximity to righteousness.

translation: And when the messengers came to the family of Lot,
interpretation: This verse introduces the narrative of the angelic messengers arriving at the household of the Prophet Lot (Lut). These are the same angels who had earlier visited Abraham with glad tidings, and now they proceed to Lot's town to carry out the divine judgment against his people, who were engaged in grave moral corruption and sinful practices. The verse sets the stage for the dramatic events that follow, including Lot's distress at hosting these guests given the depravity of his townspeople, and the eventual destruction of the wicked city as a warning and lesson for all generations about the consequences of persisting in sin and rejecting moral guidance.

translation: He said, 'Indeed, you are a people unknown [to me].'
interpretation: This verse refers to Prophet Lot (Lut) addressing the angelic visitors who came to him in human form. Unaware of their true identity as angels sent by God, Lot expressed caution and unfamiliarity toward these strangers, reflecting the customary wariness of hosts toward unknown guests in that cultural context, especially given the hostile and corrupt environment of his people in Sodom. This statement sets the stage for the unfolding narrative in which the angels reveal their purpose: to warn of impending divine punishment upon Lot's wicked people and to ensure the safety of Lot and his righteous family before the destruction occurs. The phrase underscores themes of hospitality, the testing of faith, and divine intervention in human affairs.

translation: They said, 'Rather, we have come to you with that about which they were in doubt.'
interpretation: This verse occurs in the narrative of Prophet Lot (Lut) when angels, appearing as human guests, visited him. Lot was distressed and fearful for their safety because he knew his people's wicked intentions toward strangers. The angels respond by revealing their true purpose: they have come bearing the divine punishment that Lot's people had persistently doubted and disputed when warned about it. The phrase 'what they were in doubt about' refers to the threatened destruction that the people of Sodom dismissed and mocked despite Lot's repeated warnings about their immorality. This moment marks the transition from warning to execution of divine judgment, demonstrating that the consequences the disbelievers scoffed at and considered impossible were, in fact, imminent and real. The verse underscores a recurring Quranic theme: that divine retribution, though delayed, is certain for those who persist in corruption and reject prophetic guidance, and that mockery or disbelief in warnings does not negate their eventual fulfillment.

translation: And we have come to you with the truth, and indeed, we are truthful.
interpretation: This verse occurs within the narrative of the angelic messengers who visited Prophet Lut (Lot) to inform him of the impending destruction of his wrongdoing people and to instruct him to depart with his family by night. Facing Lut's distress and disbelief at their arrival, the angels affirm the certainty and truthfulness of their message, emphasizing that their warning is not mere rumor or deception but a divine decree that will certainly come to pass. The repetition of truth claims ('with the truth' and 'we are truthful') underscores the gravity and inevitability of divine judgment against the people of Lut, who had persisted in immorality despite warnings. This exchange illustrates a broader Quranic theme: that divine messages delivered through angels or prophets carry absolute certainty, and human doubt or fear does not alter the reality of God's decree. It also reflects the compassion embedded in divine justice, as the angels' purpose included rescuing the righteous (Lut and his believing family) before executing punishment upon the transgressors.

translation: So travel with your family during a portion of the night, and follow behind them, and let not any among you look back, and proceed to where you are commanded.
interpretation: This verse, addressed to Prophet Lot (Lut) by the angels sent to destroy the wicked city, instructs him to lead his believing family away under cover of darkness before the impending divine punishment falls upon his disobedient people. The command to travel at night symbolizes urgency, secrecy, and the need for swift separation from a doomed community. Lot's instruction to walk behind his family signifies his role as protector, ensuring none fall behind or are left vulnerable, while also allowing him to watch for any who might falter or turn back out of weakness or attachment. The prohibition against looking back carries deep symbolic weight beyond mere physical caution—it represents a complete psychological and spiritual break from a corrupt past, a refusal to feel nostalgia, doubt, or longing for a place and life about to be utterly destroyed for its sins. This connects thematically to his wife's fate, who, according to the broader narrative, disobeys this command (or is complicit with the people left behind) and is destroyed along with the city, illustrating that physical proximity to a prophet does not guarantee salvation without obedience and inner conviction. The final phrase, 'proceed to where you are commanded,' underscores the theme of total submission to divine guidance without question or hesitation, even when the destination or full plan is not entirely known to the one obeying. It reflects a broader Quranic principle that true faith requires decisive action and trust in God's command, moving forward into the unknown while leaving behind corruption without a backward glance.

translation: And We decreed to him that matter: that the last remnant of those [people] would be cut off by the morning.
interpretation: This verse refers to the divine revelation given to Prophet Lut (Lot) informing him of the impending destruction of his people due to their persistent immorality and rejection of his message. The phrase "We decreed" emphasizes that this was a settled matter of divine will, communicated directly to Lut so that he could prepare himself and his believing family members to leave before the punishment fell. The term "cut off" signifies total and complete destruction, leaving no trace or remnant of the wrongdoers, while "by the morning" specifies the timing of this judgment, indicating that the punishment would come swiftly and decisively at dawn, catching the disbelievers unaware in their complacency. This illustrates the Quranic theme that divine justice, though sometimes delayed, is certain and that those who persist in corruption despite clear warnings will ultimately face consequences determined by God's will, while the righteous are granted mercy and guidance to escape the fate of the wrongdoers.

translation: And the people of the city came rejoicing.
interpretation: This verse refers to the people of the city of Sodom, who came to the house of Prophet Lut (Lot) upon learning that handsome male guests had arrived—these guests were in fact angels sent in human form. Their 'rejoicing' was not innocent joy but eager anticipation of committing the sin of approaching the male guests for immoral purposes, a practice that had become rampant and shameless among them. This moment in the narrative highlights the depth of their moral corruption, as they openly and without shame rushed toward transgression, despite Lut's attempts to protect his guests and call his people to righteousness. The verse sets the stage for the divine punishment that follows, illustrating how unchecked immorality and public shamelessness in sin lead a community toward destruction. It serves as a warning about societies that normalize and celebrate sin rather than conceal or repent from it.

translation: He said, 'Indeed, these are my guests, so do not disgrace me.'
interpretation: This verse depicts Prophet Lot pleading with his wayward people, who had come intending to molest the angelic visitors (appearing as handsome young men) who were guests in his home. Lot's appeal invokes the sacred Arab tradition of hospitality and protection of guests, emphasizing that violating a guest's safety brings shame upon the host. This moment highlights Lot's moral integrity and desperation as he tries to shield his guests from his people's depraved intentions, setting up the narrative of divine judgment that follows when his people refuse to heed this appeal and persist in their transgression.

translation: And fear Allah, and do not disgrace me.
interpretation: This verse is part of Prophet Lot's (Lut) plea to his people, who had come to his house intending to commit indecency with his guests (who were actually angels in human form). Lot appeals to his people's consciousness of God, urging them to be mindful of Allah's watchfulness over their actions, and personally implores them not to humiliate him in front of his guests by carrying out their shameful intentions. This reflects the broader Quranic theme of taqwa (God-consciousness) as the foundation for righteous behavior, and highlights the social dimension of sin—how immoral acts bring disgrace not only upon the perpetrators but also upon those connected to them, such as a host responsible for his guests' safety and honor. The verse underscores the gravity of violating the sanctity of hospitality and guest-protection, a deeply valued virtue in the Arab and Quranic ethical tradition, while also condemning the specific sexual transgression that the people of Lot were infamous for.

translation: They said, "Did we not forbid you from [sheltering] the people [i.e., strangers]?"
interpretation: This verse occurs within the narrative of Prophet Lut (Lot) and his people in Surah Al-Hijr. The wicked people of his town had previously warned and forbidden Lut from hosting or offering protection to strangers and travelers, since their intent was to commit indecent acts against male visitors. When angels came to Lut in the form of handsome young men, his people arrived at his door demanding access to them, and here they reproach him, reminding him of their earlier prohibition. This exchange highlights the moral corruption of Lut's people, who had institutionalized hostility toward outsiders and guests to facilitate their sinful practices, in stark contrast to the Arab and prophetic tradition of honoring and protecting guests. Lut's isolation and vulnerability before his own community—who had normalized such depravity that they resented his hospitality—underscores the depth of their transgression and sets the stage for the divine punishment that follows.

translation: He said, 'These are my daughters, if you must be doing [so].'
interpretation: This verse is spoken by Prophet Lut (Lot) to his people when they came seeking to violate his angelic guests, who had taken the form of handsome young men. In desperation to protect his guests from the shameful and sinful intentions of his people, Lut offered his daughters (meaning the women of his community, as 'daughters' here refers to the women of his nation in a broader sense) as a lawful alternative through marriage, if they were intent on satisfying their desires. This reflects Lut's anguish and his attempt to appeal to decency and the natural, lawful relationship between men and women as opposed to the people's persistence in same-sex acts and violation of guests, which was considered a grave transgression against both moral law and the sacred duty of hospitality. The verse illustrates the depth of moral corruption of Lut's people and the Prophet's helplessness in the face of their defiance, setting the stage for the divine punishment that would soon befall them as recounted in subsequent verses.

translation: By your life, [O Muhammad], indeed they were, in their intoxication [of error], wandering blindly.
interpretation: This verse is part of the narrative concerning the people of Lot (Lut). God swears by the life of the Prophet Muhammad—a rare and significant oath emphasizing the gravity of what follows—to describe the moral and spiritual state of Lot's people. The 'intoxication' referred to is not literal drunkenness but a metaphor for being utterly consumed and blinded by their transgressions, arrogance, and indulgence in sin, particularly their persistence in immorality despite warnings. Their 'wandering blindly' (ya'mahoon) conveys a state of confusion and heedlessness, where they could not perceive the truth or recognize the impending consequences of their actions, even as divine messengers stood before them. This verse underscores a broader Quranic theme: that sin and arrogance can so thoroughly cloud human judgment that people become unable to see reality clearly, rushing toward their own destruction while remaining oblivious to the signs around them.

translation: So the Blast seized them at sunrise.
interpretation: This verse refers to the destruction of the people of Lot, who were seized by a devastating cry or blast from the heavens at the time of sunrise, just after the angels had warned Lot to leave with his family before dawn. The timing—daybreak, a moment typically associated with renewal and the start of a new day—underscores the suddenness and totality of divine punishment, striking when the people least expected it despite having received clear warnings. This serves as a reminder that God's judgment can arrive swiftly and decisively upon those who persist in wrongdoing and reject guidance, regardless of how secure or complacent they feel at any given moment.

translation: So We turned it [the city] upside down and rained down upon them stones of baked clay.
interpretation: This verse describes the divine punishment that befell the people of Lot (Sodom) for their persistence in sexual immorality and rejection of the Prophet Lot's warnings. The complete inversion of the cities—turning the highest parts to the lowest—symbolizes the total overturning of the natural moral order that these people had themselves inverted through their transgressions. The stones of baked clay (sijjil) represent a supernatural, targeted form of destruction distinct from ordinary natural disasters, emphasizing that this was a deliberate divine judgment rather than a random calamity. The verse serves as a sobering reminder throughout the Qur'an of the consequences of persistent moral corruption and the rejection of prophetic guidance, while also demonstrating God's power to execute justice in decisive and unmistakable ways. This narrative is repeated at several points in the Qur'an as a lesson for later generations about accountability and the real consequences of defying established moral and social boundaries.

translation: Indeed, in that are signs for those who perceive and discern closely.
interpretation: This verse comes in the context of the account of the people of Lot, after their cities were overturned and destroyed as punishment for their transgression. The 'signs' refer to the visible remnants and ruins of these destroyed towns, which travelers of later generations could still see along their trade routes. The phrase 'al-mutawassimin' describes those who possess insight, who look beyond the surface of things to discern underlying truths, lessons, and divine patterns in creation and history. The verse suggests that such physical evidence of past punishment is not merely a historical curiosity but a meaningful sign for those with the spiritual and intellectual capacity to reflect deeply—implying that true understanding of divine signs requires a perceptive, contemplative mind rather than casual observation. This underscores a broader Qur'anic theme that the natural and historical world is filled with lessons accessible only to those who actively seek wisdom and moral insight from what they witness.

translation: And indeed it is on a road that remains [i.e., still exists today].
interpretation: This verse refers to the ruins of the people of Lot, mentioned in the preceding verses, which lay destroyed along a well-traveled, still-existing road—likely the trade route between the Hijaz and Syria (Sham). By noting that the destroyed cities' remains still stand visibly on a road that travelers continue to use, the Qur'an is presenting physical, verifiable evidence for its audience: the Meccan Arabs who regularly journeyed along this path to Syria for trade would literally pass by these ruins and could see for themselves the tangible proof of the fate that befell a people who rejected their prophet and persisted in grave sin. This serves as both a historical confirmation of the Qur'anic narrative and a warning, inviting reflection on divine justice through evidence available in the immediate, everyday experience of the listeners rather than through abstract or distant claims.

translation: Indeed, in that is a sign for the believers.
interpretation: This recurring refrain appears throughout the Qur'an following accounts of natural phenomena, historical events, or the fates of earlier peoples. It emphasizes that while the physical universe and human history are full of signs pointing to God's existence, power, and wisdom, only those with faith—or an openness to faith—truly perceive and internalize these signs as meaningful lessons. The verse suggests that evidence of the divine is abundant and accessible, but spiritual perception, humility, and a receptive heart are required to recognize it as such. Mere intellectual observation of the world is insufficient; it is the believer's faith that transforms ordinary phenomena into profound signs (ayat) that strengthen conviction and guide conduct. This also implies a distinction between those who see such signs and disregard them versus those whose hearts are attuned to discern divine purpose behind the workings of creation and history.

translation: And the companions of the Wood (Aykah) were indeed wrongdoers.
interpretation: This verse refers to the people of Prophet Shu'ayb (often identified with the people of Madyan or a nearby community known as the 'companions of the thicket/wood'), who were condemned for their persistent idolatry, dishonest commercial practices such as cheating in weights and measures, and rejection of their prophet's message. By grouping them among the ranks of earlier destroyed nations—following mentions of the people of Lot and others in this surah—the verse serves as part of a recurring Qur'anic pattern: citing a sequence of past communities that disbelieved and were punished, to warn the Prophet Muhammad's contemporaries that persistence in disbelief and injustice (zulm) invites the same fate. The term 'zalimeen' (wrongdoers) emphasizes that their punishment was a direct consequence of their own injustice—both toward God through disbelief and toward other people through corrupt dealings—reinforcing the Qur'anic theme that divine justice responds proportionately to human moral conduct.

translation: So We took retribution upon them, and indeed, the two of them are on a clear, well-known highway.
interpretation: This verse follows the Qur'an's recounting of the destruction of the people of Lot and the people of the Thicket (Ashab al-Aykah, often linked to the people of Shu'ayb), two communities punished for their transgressions and disbelief. The phrase 'the two of them are on a clear highway' refers to the physical ruins of these ancient towns, which lay along a well-traveled trade route known to the Arabs of the Prophet's time. By pointing to tangible, visible remains that travelers could still see with their own eyes, the verse transforms a historical narrative into an empirical, undeniable witness: the fate of these peoples is not merely a story but a physical sign embedded in the landscape, meant to provoke reflection whenever people pass by. It underscores a recurring Qur'anic theme that divine retribution leaves lasting evidence in the world as a warning to later generations who have the capacity to see, travel, and learn from history, inviting the reader to draw moral and spiritual lessons from the visible remnants of the past rather than dismissing accounts of allegedly destroyed civilizations as myth.

translation: And indeed, the companions of al-Hijr (the rocky tract) denied the messengers.
interpretation: This verse refers to the people of Thamud, who dwelt in the rocky region known as al-Hijr (located in the northern Arabian Peninsula). Though only one messenger, Salih, was specifically sent to them, the Qur'an states that they 'denied the messengers' (plural) because rejecting one prophet's message is equivalent to rejecting the entire prophetic tradition, since all messengers call to the same fundamental truth of monotheism and righteousness. This establishes a broader theological principle: disbelief in any single messenger constitutes disbelief in the unified message of all messengers, as their core teachings are consistent across time. The mention of Thamud serves as a historical warning and admonition to the people of Mecca and to all later generations, illustrating the recurring pattern of communities who received divine guidance, rejected it out of arrogance or stubbornness, and consequently faced destruction. It reinforces the Qur'anic theme that history offers tangible lessons (ayat) for those who reflect, showing that defiance against God's messengers leads to worldly ruin as well as spiritual loss.

translation: And We gave them Our signs, but they turned away from them.
interpretation: This verse speaks to a recurring pattern in the Qur'anic narrative concerning nations who received divine signs—whether through scripture, prophets, or miraculous evidence—yet chose willful disregard rather than reflection or acceptance. The emphasis on 'turning away' (i'rad) suggests not mere ignorance but a deliberate act of aversion, implying that the signs were clear and accessible, but the recipients exercised their free will to reject them. This reflects the Qur'an's broader theme of human accountability: divine guidance is made evident, but acceptance requires an openness of heart that cannot be forced. The verse serves as both a historical reference to past communities and a timeless warning to any audience that might encounter truth yet choose complacency or denial over engagement and gratitude.

translation: And they used to carve out houses from the mountains, feeling secure.
interpretation: This verse refers to the people of Thamud, who possessed great skill and strength, carving their dwellings into mountains for protection and permanence. Their sense of security, however, was misplaced—it was a false confidence rooted in material achievement and worldly power rather than in faith or righteousness. The verse serves as a warning that physical security, engineering prowess, and worldly stability cannot shield a people from divine judgment if they persist in arrogance, rejection of truth, and disobedience to God. Their eventual destruction, described in the verses that follow, demonstrates that true safety lies not in fortified structures but in submission to God and heeding the warnings of His messengers.

translation: So the Blast seized them at early morning.
interpretation: This verse refers to the destruction of the people of Thamud, the nation of Prophet Salih, who were struck by a devastating cry or blast (al-sayhah) sent by Allah as punishment for their persistent rejection of the prophet and their defiant slaughter of the she-camel that served as a divine sign to them. The timing 'at early morning' emphasizes the suddenness and totality of the catastrophe—it came upon them while they were in the vulnerable, unsuspecting state of dawn, when people typically feel secure after a night's rest, underscoring that divine retribution can arrive instantaneously and without warning despite prior warnings given to the community. This serves as a cautionary narrative within the Qur'an's broader pattern of recounting the fates of previous nations who rejected their prophets, reminding listeners of the consequences of arrogance and disbelief, and reinforcing the theme that worldly security offers no true protection against divine justice when a people persist in transgression after clear warnings have been delivered to them.

translation: So that which they used to earn availed them not.
interpretation: This verse serves as a sobering conclusion to narratives about communities or individuals who accumulated wealth, power, status, or worldly achievements, only to face divine judgment or destruction. The Arabic word 'kasaba' (to earn/acquire) encompasses all forms of worldly gain—material wealth, social standing, and the fruits of human effort. The verse establishes a stark theological principle: worldly accomplishments, no matter how substantial, hold no power to shield a person from the consequences of disbelief, arrogance, or transgression against divine law when the reckoning comes. This is not a condemnation of effort or earning itself, but rather a corrective to the human tendency to place ultimate trust and security in material accumulation rather than in righteousness and submission to God. The verse functions rhetorically as a moment of reckoning within the broader narrative, often following descriptions of peoples who scoffed at warnings, trusted in their own resources, and believed their status made them immune to accountability. Their earnings—whether wealth, offspring, or achievements—could not negotiate, bargain, or shield them from the truth they had rejected. It underscores the Quranic theme that true security lies not in what one accumulates but in one's relationship with the Creator and adherence to moral and spiritual obligations.

translation: And We did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them except in truth (for a just purpose). And indeed, the Hour is coming; so overlook [their faults] with gracious forgiveness.
interpretation: This verse establishes that the entire cosmos was created with purpose and justice, not in vain or by chance—implying that ultimate accountability (the Hour) is a certainty woven into the very fabric of creation. Because the universe operates on divine truth and justice, human wrongs will eventually be judged; there is no need for the Prophet (or believers) to seek immediate revenge or retaliation against those who mock or oppose them. Instead, they are commanded to practice 'al-safh al-jameel'—a beautiful, gracious forgiveness that is free of resentment, bitterness, or desire for reproach. This is a higher form of forbearance than mere patience; it involves actively releasing grievance and trusting that divine justice, tied to the certainty of the Hour, will ultimately prevail. The verse thus links cosmic order and purpose to ethical conduct, teaching that confidence in God's ultimate justice should inspire magnanimity and restraint in dealing with adversaries in the present life.

translation: Indeed, your Lord is the All-Knowing Creator.
interpretation: This verse affirms two interconnected divine attributes: God as al-Khallaq (the supreme, ceaseless Creator) and al-'Alim (the All-Knowing). The pairing is significant because it links creation with knowledge—God does not create randomly or without purpose, but with complete and perfect knowledge of what He creates, why He creates it, and its ultimate destiny. In the context of Surah Al-Hijr, this verse follows discussions of human creation from clay and jinn from fire, as well as the story of Iblis's refusal to bow to Adam. The verse serves as a reassurance to the Prophet Muhammad (the 'you' addressed) and by extension to believers, that despite the rebellion of Iblis, the mockery of disbelievers, and the apparent chaos of human affairs, everything unfolds within God's complete knowledge and creative wisdom. Nothing escapes His awareness, and every created thing—including human choices, trials, and the unfolding of history—fits into a purposeful design. This serves as a source of comfort during times of adversity or opposition, reminding the believer that the Creator who fashioned the heavens, earth, and all beings also possesses perfect knowledge of their circumstances and needs, and that His creation is never arbitrary but imbued with wisdom and purpose.

translation: And We have certainly given you seven of the oft-repeated [verses] and the Great Qur'an.
interpretation: This verse refers to Surah Al-Fatihah, known as 'the seven oft-repeated verses' (sab'an min al-mathani), which consists of seven verses recited repeatedly in every unit of prayer. The term 'mathani' derives from the root meaning 'to repeat,' signifying both its constant recitation in daily prayers and its foundational, comprehensive nature encapsulating the core themes of the Qur'an—praise of God, acknowledgment of His sovereignty, and supplication for guidance. By pairing this surah with 'the Great Qur'an,' the verse honors the Prophet Muhammad with a unique gift: a concise yet complete summary of divine guidance (Al-Fatihah) alongside the entirety of the revealed scripture. This juxtaposition emphasizes that the opening chapter, though brief, holds a status and significance equal in spiritual weight to the whole of the Qur'an, serving as its essence and key.  The verse also serves as a consolation to the Prophet during a period of hardship, reminding him of the immense blessing and honor bestowed upon him through revelation, encouraging him to find solace and strength in what he has been given rather than focusing on the wealth or worldly pleasures granted to others.

translation: Do not extend your eyes toward what We have given pairs of them [disbelievers] to enjoy, and do not grieve over them, and lower your wing to the believers.
interpretation: This verse addresses the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him), instructing him not to be dazzled or envious of the worldly wealth, pleasures, and comforts that disbelievers have been granted as a temporary trial in this life. It reminds him that such material enjoyment is fleeting and insignificant compared to the eternal reward of the Hereafter, and that he should not feel sorrow or distress over the disbelievers' rejection of his message or their apparent prosperity. Instead, he is commanded to show humility, gentleness, and compassion toward the believers—the phrase 'lower your wing' being a metaphor drawn from a bird lowering its wing protectively and tenderly over its young, symbolizing care, patience, and kindness toward the community of faith regardless of their social status or material means. The verse thus establishes a spiritual principle for all believers: true value lies not in worldly possessions but in faith and mutual compassion within the community of believers, and leaders or those with influence should treat their followers with humility rather than being swayed by the apparent success of those who reject truth.

translation: And say, 'Indeed, I am the clear warner.'
interpretation: This verse instructs the Prophet Muhammad to openly declare his role and mission to the people. The term 'clear warner' (an-nadhir al-mubin) emphasizes two key aspects of prophethood: first, that his purpose is to warn humanity of the consequences of disbelief and wrongdoing, specifically regarding accountability in the afterlife; and second, that this warning is delivered with clarity and transparency, leaving no ambiguity about its message or source. By commanding him to explicitly state 'I am,' the verse underscores the directness and personal responsibility inherent in prophetic communication—it is not a vague or indirect caution but an unambiguous proclamation. This directive also serves to distinguish true prophetic warning from false claims, as the clarity (mubin) suggests both linguistic clarity in the Quran's Arabic revelation and moral clarity in distinguishing right from wrong, truth from falsehood. The verse situates itself within a broader Quranic theme where prophets are repeatedly described as warners rather than compellers of faith, highlighting that their duty is to convey the message plainly, while the response to that warning remains a matter of individual choice and accountability.

translation: Just as We sent down [punishment] upon those who divided [the Scripture],
interpretation: This verse refers to the people of earlier scriptures—commonly understood as the Jews and Christians, or more specifically certain groups among them—who took their revealed Book and split it into fragments, believing in some parts while rejecting others according to their own desires and interests. Some commentators also apply this to the Quraysh, who divided the Qur'an by labeling different portions of it as poetry, sorcery, or the tales of the ancients, so as to dissuade people from taking it as a unified, coherent revelation. The verse serves as a warning: just as earlier communities who treated divine revelation selectively or dismissively brought punishment upon themselves, a similar fate awaits anyone who approaches the Qur'an with the same fragmenting, dismissive attitude rather than accepting it as a whole and integrated guidance from God.

translation: Those who have divided the Qur'an into fragments [picking and choosing from it].
interpretation: This verse refers to those—traditionally understood as the disbelievers among the Quraysh—who dealt with the Qur'an in a fragmentary, inconsistent manner: accepting parts of it while rejecting others, or labeling different portions variously as poetry, sorcery, soothsaying, or legend depending on what suited their argument at the time. Rather than engaging with the Qur'an as a coherent, unified revelation, they tore it apart selectively to dismiss or ridicule it, reflecting a deeper unwillingness to accept its message as a whole. The verse serves as a warning against such selective, insincere engagement with revealed scripture, implying that true acceptance requires embracing its totality rather than cherry-picking convenient fragments while discarding the rest.

translation: So by your Lord, We will surely question them all,
interpretation: This verse is a solemn divine oath affirming the certainty of universal accountability on the Day of Judgment. By swearing upon Himself as the Lord of the Prophet (peace be upon him), God emphasizes the absolute certainty of this reckoning—no human being will be exempt from being questioned about their deeds, beliefs, and choices in worldly life. In its immediate context, this verse follows mention of those who fragmented the scripture, accepting parts of it while rejecting others for their own convenience, as well as the disbelievers who mocked the Prophet. The verse serves as a warning that despite any denial, mockery, or selective engagement with divine guidance in this life, every soul will ultimately stand before God to answer for their choices. This reinforces the Quranic theme that this worldly life is a temporary testing ground, and ultimate justice will be served when all accounts are settled, leaving no one—whether believer or disbeliever, whether they took faith seriously or treated it with levity—beyond the scope of divine questioning and judgment.

translation: For [recompense of] what they used to do.
interpretation: This phrase typically appears at the end of verses discussing reward and punishment, serving as the concluding clause that ties divine recompense directly to human conduct. It emphasizes the principle of divine justice in Islamic theology: that God's treatment of individuals—whether reward in Paradise or punishment in Hell—is not arbitrary but is a direct consequence of the deeds people freely chose to perform in their worldly lives. The phrase underscores accountability, suggesting that nothing is hidden from God's knowledge and that every action, whether good or evil, carries consequences in the ultimate reckoning. It reinforces the broader Quranic theme that life is a test, and the hereafter is the arena where the results of this test are manifested based on one's actions, intentions, and choices made with free will.

translation: So proclaim openly that which you are commanded, and turn away from the polytheists.
interpretation: This verse, from Surah Al-Hijr (15:94), marks a pivotal command to Prophet Muhammad ﷺ to move from a phase of private, cautious preaching to open, public proclamation of Islam's message despite anticipated opposition. The word 'اصدع' carries connotations of splitting or cleaving openly, suggesting a bold, unambiguous declaration that would divide truth from falsehood and believers from disbelievers in the public sphere of Mecca. The instruction to 'turn away from the polytheists' does not mean to abandon the mission of calling them to faith, but rather to not be deterred, intimidated, or emotionally burdened by their mockery, rejection, and hostility.
