translation: When the youths took refuge in the cave, they said, 'Our Lord, grant us mercy from Yourself, and provide for us right guidance in our affair.'
interpretation: This verse marks the beginning of the story of the People of the Cave (Ashab al-Kahf), young believers who fled persecution for their faith in the One God, seeking refuge from a tyrannical society. Their prayer embodies a model of true reliance on God (tawakkul): rather than relying solely on their own strategy of physical withdrawal into the cave, they turn to God for two essential things—divine mercy (rahma) and rightly-guided direction (rushd) in their affair. This reflects the Islamic principle that outward action must be paired with inward submission and supplication to God, acknowledging that ultimate guidance and protection come from Him alone. The youths' flight represents a willingness to sacrifice worldly security for the preservation of faith, and their prayer demonstrates the proper etiquette of asking God not just for safety, but for wisdom to navigate their uncertain circumstances. This sets the stage for the miraculous protection God provides them, as the chapter goes on to describe their long sleep and eventual awakening, symbolizing God's power over time, death, and resurrection, and serving as a reminder to believers facing trials of faith that God shelters and guides those who turn to Him sincerely.

translation: So We cast [a cover of sleep] over their ears within the cave for a number of years.
interpretation: This verse refers to the young believers known as the Companions of the Cave (Ashab al-Kahf), who fled religious persecution and took refuge in a cave to preserve their faith. The phrase 'We cast upon their ears' is an idiom indicating that Allah caused them to fall into a deep, sustained sleep, effectively sealing their hearing from the outside world so nothing could disturb them. This miraculous, extended sleep—lasting many years—demonstrates divine power over time, life, and the senses, and serves as a sign of God's ability to protect and preserve those who seek refuge in Him for the sake of their faith. It also sets up the broader lesson of the surah about trusting in God's timing and the illusory nature of worldly time compared to divine power and planning.

translation: Then We raised them up [from their sleep] that We might know which of the two parties was most precise in calculating the time they had remained.
interpretation: This verse refers to the Companions of the Cave (Ahl al-Kahf) after their long sleep. The phrase 'that We might know' does not imply that God lacked knowledge beforehand—since His knowledge is absolute and eternal—but rather expresses the purpose of making the knowledge manifest and testable in the empirical, observable sense, for the people involved and for those who would hear the story. The 'two parties' refers to the differing views among the sleepers themselves (or among the people who later debated about them) regarding how long they had stayed in the cave. This highlights a broader Qur'anic theme: human estimation of time, especially under extraordinary or miraculous circumstances, is inherently uncertain, while God's knowledge and control over time and duration is absolute. The verse also serves as a literary device to transition the narrative toward the dialogue of the youths upon waking, setting up the dramatic irony that they debate a duration whose reality is already known to God, underscoring human limitation against divine omniscience.

translation: We relate to you their story in truth. Indeed, they were young men who believed in their Lord, and We increased them in guidance.
interpretation: This verse introduces the story of the Companions of the Cave (Ashab al-Kahf) and establishes several key points. First, Allah emphasizes that this account is 'bil-haqq' (in truth/with truth), affirming its historical and spiritual authenticity despite its seemingly miraculous nature. Second, the verse highlights that these were 'fityah' (young men), a term that in Arabic carries connotations of youthful strength, idealism, and moral courage. This is significant because it suggests that steadfast faith and the courage to stand against societal pressure often come from the young, who have not yet been fully compromised by worldly attachments. Third, their defining characteristic is that they 'believed in their Lord' - a declaration of pure monotheistic faith that set them apart from and in opposition to their idolatrous society. Finally, Allah's response to their faith was to 'increase them in guidance' - illustrating the Quranic principle that faith is not static but grows and deepens when nurtured through sincere belief and righteous action. This increase in guidance would manifest in the supernatural protection and extended sleep that forms the central miracle of their story, demonstrating that those who sacrifice worldly security for the sake of their faith receive divine support and guidance beyond ordinary human experience.

translation: And We strengthened their hearts when they stood up and said: 'Our Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth; never shall we call upon any deity besides Him, for then we would have said an outrageous transgression.'
interpretation: This verse describes the youths of the Cave (Ashab al-Kahf) as they took their courageous stand against the polytheistic society around them. God Himself fortified their hearts, granting them steadfastness and inner strength to publicly declare their monotheistic faith despite the danger this posed to their lives in a society that persecuted believers in one God. Their declaration demonstrates a clear, rational theological position: they affirm that the Lord of the heavens and the earth—the Creator and Sustainer of the entire cosmos—cannot logically share His divinity with lesser beings or idols. To call upon any other god beside Him would constitute 'shatatan,' an enormity, an extreme deviation from truth and justice. This word choice emphasizes that polytheism is not a minor error but a profound violation of reason and cosmic order. The verse illustrates a recurring Qur'anic theme: that true faith often requires divine assistance to sustain human resolve against overwhelming social pressure, and that the youths' firmness came not merely from their own courage but from God's direct intervention in 'binding their hearts,' making them exemplars of steadfast belief for future generations facing similar trials of faith against conformist or oppressive societies.

translation: These, our people, have taken besides Him [other] deities. Why do they not bring for [worshiping] them a clear authority? And who is more unjust than one who invents a lie against Allah?
interpretation: This verse is spoken by the youths of the Cave (Ashab al-Kahf) as they privately affirm their faith and distance themselves from the polytheism of their community. Their statement serves as a rational challenge to idolatry: true belief should rest upon clear, demonstrable proof (sultan mubin), not blind inherited custom. By pointing out the absence of any such proof for the deities their people worship, they expose the irrationality and injustice of shirk (associating partners with God). The closing rhetorical question—'who is more unjust than one who invents a lie against Allah?'—frames idolatry not merely as error but as a moral transgression, a fabrication against the truth of God's oneness. This reflects a broader Qur'anic theme in which true faith is portrayed as reasoned conviction rather than social conformity, and where the youths' willingness to abandon their society's beliefs, even at great personal risk, exemplifies steadfast monotheism (tawhid) in the face of collective error.

translation: And when you withdraw from them and what they worship, except Allah, then retreat to the cave; your Lord will spread over you some of His mercy and will prepare for you ease in your affair.
interpretation: This verse refers to the Companions of the Cave (Ahl al-Kahf), young believers who fled their idolatrous society to preserve their faith in the One God. It illustrates the principle of hijrah—physical or spiritual withdrawal from an environment of disbelief and corruption when one cannot openly practice or safeguard one's faith. The cave symbolizes a place of refuge where divine mercy and providence operate even in isolation and apparent helplessness. The promise that God will 'spread His mercy' and 'prepare ease' teaches that sincere sacrifice for the sake of faith is met with divine care, and that withdrawal from falsehood, rather than being a loss, becomes a means through which God provides unexpected solutions and protection.

translation: And you would have seen the sun, when it rose, inclining away from their cave to the right, and when it set, passing them by on the left, while they lay in the open space within it. That is from the signs of Allah. Whoever Allah guides is rightly guided, and whoever He sends astray - never will you find for him a protecting guide.
interpretation: This verse describes the miraculous protection of the Companions of the Cave (Ahl al-Kahf), young believers who fled persecution for their faith and took refuge in a cave, where Allah caused them to sleep for centuries. The sun's movement avoiding direct contact with them - inclining right at sunrise and left at sunset - while they rested in an open space within the cave, ensured they received ventilation and indirect light without the harmful effects of direct sunlight, preserving their bodies during their extraordinarily long sleep. This natural phenomenon is presented as a divine sign (ayah), demonstrating Allah's power to orchestrate even the movements of celestial bodies to protect and sustain the faithful. The verse then transitions to a broader theological principle: guidance and misguidance are ultimately in Allah's hands. Just as Allah controlled the physical elements to protect the sleepers, He controls the spiritual guidance of hearts. This teaches that true guidance is a divine gift, and no human effort can guide a soul whom Allah has allowed to go astray, nor can anyone misguide one whom Allah guides. The story thus serves both as a testament to Allah's omnipotence over nature and as a reminder of His sovereignty over faith and guidance.

translation: And you would think them awake, while they were asleep. And We turned them to the right and to the left, while their dog stretched his forelegs at the threshold. If you had looked upon them, you would have turned from them in flight and been filled with terror of them.
interpretation: This verse describes the Companions of the Cave (Ashab al-Kahf) in their miraculous sleep, which lasted for centuries, yet their bodies and eyes gave the appearance of wakefulness, demonstrating God's power to preserve life in a dormant state. The turning of their bodies from side to side was a divine mercy to prevent physical harm to the earth-contact points of their bodies over such a long period, showing that even in a miraculous suspension of normal life, natural care for the body continues. The presence of their guard dog, stationed loyally at the cave's entrance with paws outstretched, adds a vivid, almost tender detail that humanizes the scene and shows how even an animal shared in this sacred protection. The final statement, that any onlooker would flee in terror, emphasizes the awe-inspiring, supernatural nature of the scene: a group of seemingly living yet motionless, open-eyed bodies lying still for centuries would appear eerie and overwhelming to an ordinary observer. This serves to highlight that true understanding of the sleepers' condition and divine protection belongs to God alone, inaccessible to ordinary human perception, and underscores the theme of God's sovereign power over life, death, and time itself.

translation: And similarly, We awakened them that they might question one another. A speaker among them said, 'How long have you remained [here]?' They said, 'We have remained a day or part of a day.' They said, 'Your Lord is most knowing of how long you remained. So send one of you with this silver coin of yours to the city and let him look to which is the best of food and bring you provision from it and let him be cautious and not make known about you to anyone.'
interpretation: This verse captures the moment the Companions of the Cave awaken after their long, miraculous sleep, unaware of how much time has actually passed. Their confusion about the duration—guessing a day or part of a day—underscores the theme of divine power over time and human perception, reminding believers that true knowledge of such matters belongs to God alone. The practical instructions that follow, about discreetly obtaining food, reflect the tension between the miraculous nature of their preservation and the mundane necessities of life, as well as their continued need for caution against a hostile society that had once persecuted them for their faith. This blend of the miraculous and the practical emphasizes trust in God while still exercising wisdom and discretion in a dangerous world.

translation: Indeed, if they come to know of you, they will stone you or return you to their religion; and then you will never succeed, ever.
interpretation: This verse is part of the narrative of the Companions of the Cave (Ashab al-Kahf) in Surah Al-Kahf. It reflects the internal dialogue among the youths who fled their idolatrous society to preserve their monotheistic faith. Their concern expressed here reveals the severity of the persecution faced by early believers who diverged from the dominant religious order of their community—death by stoning or forced reversion to disbelief. The phrase 'never would you succeed, then, ever' underscores a theological principle central to the Qur'an: that worldly or spiritual success (falah) is inseparable from steadfastness in faith, and that apostasy under compulsion, even to save one's life, represents an irrecoverable loss in the eyes of the Divine. The verse also illustrates the lengths to which believers were willing to go—self-imposed exile and isolation—to safeguard their faith from corruption or coercion, highlighting the Qur'anic theme of trial (fitna) as a test of sincerity and the preservation of one's religious identity against communal pressure.

translation: And thus We caused them to be discovered so that they [the people] would know that the promise of Allah is true and that the Hour, there is no doubt about it. [That was] when they disputed among themselves about their affair and [then] said, 'Build over them a structure. Their Lord knows best about them.' Said those who prevailed in the matter, 'We will surely take over them a place of worship.'
interpretation: This verse conveys a profound lesson about divine power and resurrection through the miraculous awakening of the sleepers of the cave after centuries. By causing their discovery, God provided tangible proof to the surrounding community that His promises—including the resurrection and the Day of Judgment—are certain truths, not matters of doubt. The subsequent dispute among the people about how to honor the sleepers reveals human tendencies toward both reverence and the risk of excessive veneration. Those who had authority decided to build a place of worship over the site, which can be read as a cautionary note about how sacred sites and the memory of righteous figures can become objects of ritual devotion that may verge on exceeding proper bounds, a theme consistent with the Quran's broader concern about avoiding shirk (associating partners with God) even through well-intentioned acts of commemoration. The verse thus balances the affirmation of God's miraculous signs with an implicit critique of how communities memorialize the sacred.

translation: Some will say: 'They were three, their dog being the fourth,' and others will say: 'Five, their dog being the sixth,' guessing at the unseen; and yet others will say: 'Seven, and their dog was the eighth.' Say: 'My Lord knows best their number; none knows them except a few.' So do not argue about them except with an outward argument, and do not ask anyone concerning them.
interpretation: This verse addresses the believers' tendency to become absorbed in idle speculation about details of sacred narratives that carry no spiritual benefit. The precise number of the Companions of the Cave is deliberately left ambiguous by God, a matter known fully only to Him, to teach that faith should not hinge on satisfying curiosity about unseen particulars. The phrase 'guessing at the unseen' (rajman bi'l-ghayb) criticizes those who speak confidently about matters beyond human knowledge without any real basis, essentially engaging in baseless conjecture. By instructing the Prophet not to argue about this issue except in a superficial manner and not to consult anyone about it, the verse redirects attention away from trivial numerical disputes toward the moral and spiritual lessons of the story itself—namely, the themes of faith, withdrawal from corruption, trust in divine protection, and the limits of human knowledge before the mystery of God's power. It serves as a broader caution against the human impulse to fixate on peripheral details of revelation while neglecting its deeper guidance, and it models intellectual humility: acknowledging that some knowledge belongs to God alone.

translation: And do not say about anything, 'Indeed, I will do that tomorrow,'
interpretation: This verse teaches the principle of acknowledging human limitation and divine sovereignty over the future. It instructs believers never to assert certainty about future actions without recognizing that all events are ultimately subject to God's will, which is completed in the following verse's command to add 'if God wills' (in sha' Allah). The lesson addresses human arrogance in presuming control over outcomes that have not yet occurred, emphasizing humility, dependence on God, and awareness that human knowledge and power are finite. It cultivates a mindset of continuous remembrance of God in planning and speech, guarding against overconfidence and encouraging trust in divine providence for all future intentions and commitments.

translation: Except [by adding], 'If Allah wills.' And remember your Lord when you forget [to do so] and say, 'Perhaps my Lord will guide me to [something] nearer than this to right conduct.'
interpretation: This verse follows the Qur'an's instruction (18:23-24) not to make definitive statements about future actions without acknowledging God's will. It establishes the principle of saying 'in sha' Allah' (if God wills) when speaking of future plans, recognizing human limitation and divine sovereignty over all outcomes. The verse addresses human forgetfulness with compassion rather than condemnation—acknowledging that people will inevitably forget this practice, and instructing them to simply remember and invoke God's name when they do recall, rather than feeling paralyzed by guilt over the lapse. The phrase 'perhaps my Lord will guide me to something closer than this to right conduct' carries a deeper humility: even when one believes they have found the right path or correct answer, they should remain open to the possibility that God may guide them to something even better or more precise. This teaches intellectual and spiritual humility, countering arrogance or overconfidence in one's own knowledge or plans, and placing ultimate trust in divine guidance over human certainty.

translation: And they remained in their cave for three hundred years, and increased by nine [more].
interpretation: This verse specifies the duration of the sleep of the Companions of the Cave, addressing the debate among the People of the Book about how long they had slept. By stating three hundred solar years, which equals three hundred and nine lunar years, the Qur'an reconciles different calendrical traditions and affirms the precision of divine knowledge over human speculation. The miracle of their prolonged sleep serves as a sign of God's power over life, death, and time itself, demonstrating that resurrection after death is no more difficult for God than preserving these youths for over three centuries in a dormant state resembling death. The specific mention of the extra nine years also subtly corrects any who might calculate using solar years alone, as was common among Christians, by clarifying the exact span according to the lunar calendar used by Arabs, thus ensuring clarity and removing grounds for dispute among those who would later argue about the story's details.

translation: Say: Allah knows best how long they remained. To Him belongs the unseen of the heavens and the earth. How well He sees and how well He hears! They have no protector besides Him, and He associates no one in His judgment.
interpretation: This verse, following the account of the People of the Cave, redirects attention away from speculative debates about the exact duration of their sleep toward the absolute and exclusive knowledge of Allah. It emphasizes divine omniscience over hidden matters that exceed human capacity, particularly regarding the unseen realms of the heavens and earth. The rhetorical exclamation about Allah's perfect sight and hearing underscores His complete awareness of all things, visible and invisible, leaving no room for human speculation to rival divine knowledge. The verse concludes with a declaration of Allah's absolute sovereignty: no being can serve as a guardian or ally independent of Him, and His authority in judgment is undivided, shared with none. This serves as a broader theological statement affirming monotheism (tawhid), teaching believers to relinquish anxiety over unknowable details and to trust fully in Allah's unique and uncontested knowledge and authority over all creation.

translation: And recite what has been revealed to you from the Book of your Lord. There is no changer of His words, and you will never find besides Him a refuge.
interpretation: This verse commands the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) to continue conveying and reciting the Qur'anic revelation without alteration, affirming that God's words are immutable and protected from distortion. It also establishes that there is no other source of protection, guidance, or refuge for humanity apart from God, emphasizing both the authenticity and permanence of divine revelation and the absolute sovereignty of God over all matters of guidance and security. This serves as reassurance to the Prophet amid opposition and pressure from disbelievers who sought to have him alter or compromise the message, reminding him that his duty is simply to transmit the revelation faithfully, trusting in God's protection rather than seeking alliances or refuge elsewhere.

translation: And keep yourself patient [by being] with those who call upon their Lord in the morning and the evening, seeking His face. And let not your eyes pass beyond them, desiring the adornment of worldly life. And do not obey one whose heart We have made heedless of Our remembrance, and who follows his own desire and whose affair is ever [in] neglect.
interpretation: This verse was revealed to counsel the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) to maintain close companionship with the poor and sincere believers who devoted themselves to worship, rather than being swayed by pressure from wealthy Meccan leaders who wanted him to distance himself from lowly followers in exchange for social status. It establishes a principle that true value lies in sincerity of devotion to God rather than worldly rank or wealth, and warns against prioritizing the company of the privileged over the righteous poor. It further admonishes against following those whose hearts have become heedless of God due to their own choices, who pursue only their desires and whose conduct is characterized by excess and disregard for moral limits. The verse thus draws a contrast between two types of people: those who turn to God in devotion seeking only His pleasure, and those consumed by worldly desire and negligence of spiritual remembrance.

translation: And say: 'The truth is from your Lord. So whoever wills, let him believe, and whoever wills, let him disbelieve.' Indeed, We have prepared for the wrongdoers a Fire whose walls will surround them. And if they call for relief, they will be relieved with water like molten brass, which scalds the faces. Wretched is the drink, and evil is the resting place.
interpretation: This verse establishes a foundational Quranic principle of free will and moral agency: faith cannot be coerced, and each soul bears responsibility for its own choice to believe or reject truth. The declaration 'the truth is from your Lord' affirms that guidance has been clearly delivered, removing any excuse of ignorance; what remains is the individual's free response. The stark offer—'let him believe, let him disbelieve'—is not divine indifference but a statement of the seriousness of human accountability, since choice carries consequence. The ensuing depiction of the Fire, with its encircling walls symbolizing inescapable confinement, and the grotesque inversion of relief—where water, which should quench thirst and comfort, instead burns the face like molten metal—serves as a vivid warning of the self-entrapment of wrongdoing (zulm). The imagery suggests that in rejecting truth, the wrongdoers not only face punishment but experience the inversion of everything that should have brought them ease, reflecting the spiritual logic that persistent injustice and denial corrupt what could otherwise nourish the soul. The verse thus binds free will to its ultimate moral consequence, framing disbelief not as a neutral option but as a path toward self-inflicted suffering mirrored in the horrifying imagery of false relief.

translation: Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds - indeed, We will not allow the reward of those who do good deeds to be lost.
interpretation: This verse establishes a fundamental principle of divine justice: sincere faith coupled with righteous action is never wasted in God's sight. The emphasis using 'إنا' (indeed We) underscores divine assurance and certainty, reinforcing that God personally guarantees the preservation and reward of good deeds, regardless of whether human beings recognize or acknowledge them. The phrase 'من أحسن عملا' (those who do good deeds) suggests not merely performing righteous acts, but doing them with excellence and sincerity (ihsan), implying that quality and intention matter as much as the deed itself. This verse often follows narratives of worldly trials and the transient nature of material wealth and status, serving as a comforting reminder that spiritual and moral investments yield eternal returns, unlike worldly pursuits that may perish or prove illusory. It encourages believers to maintain hope and steadfastness in righteousness, trusting that no act of goodness, however small or unnoticed by others, escapes divine recognition and recompense.

translation: Those will have Gardens of Eden beneath which rivers flow; they will be adorned therein with bracelets of gold and will wear green garments of fine silk and heavy brocade, reclining therein on raised couches. Excellent is the reward, and good is the resting place.
interpretation: This verse depicts the ultimate reward for the righteous believers—those who held fast to faith and good deeds—by describing Paradise in sensory, tangible terms that would resonate deeply with its original audience. The imagery of flowing rivers, gold adornments, luxurious silk garments, and comfortable reclining couches represents eternal ease, dignity, honor, and beauty, standing in stark contrast to the toil, scarcity, and hardship of earthly life. The mention of gold bracelets and fine garments evokes royal or noble status, suggesting that believers will be elevated to a position of honor and glory in the Hereafter. Reclining on couches signifies rest, leisure, and freedom from labor or worry, symbolizing the end of struggle and the beginning of eternal contentment. The closing phrase emphasizing the excellence of this reward and resting place serves as a divine affirmation of the surpassing value of Paradise compared to anything the worldly life can offer, encouraging believers to remain steadfast in faith despite temporal difficulties, since the ultimate compensation is both spiritually and physically fulfilling beyond comparison.

translation: And strike for them a parable of two men: We made for one of them two gardens of grapevines, and We surrounded them with palm trees, and We placed between them cultivated fields.
interpretation: This verse opens the parable of the two men found in Surah al-Kahf, contrasting a wealthy, worldly man with a poor but faithful companion. The lush description of the garden—grapevines, palm trees, and fertile crops between them—paints an image of abundant prosperity and material success. This sets the stage for a broader lesson about the nature of worldly wealth: it is a test from God, and its beauty and abundance can either lead one to gratitude and humility or to arrogance and heedlessness of the divine source of all blessings. The elaborate detail given to the garden's richness foreshadows the owner's coming pride and the fragility of relying on material possessions rather than faith in God, a theme that unfolds as the parable continues.

translation: Each of the two gardens brought forth its produce and did not fall short therein in anything, and We caused a river to gush forth in their midst.
interpretation: This verse is part of the parable of the two men in Surah Al-Kahf, one granted abundant wealth and lush gardens, the other poor but faithful. The description of the gardens' flawless productivity and the flowing river running through them emphasizes the completeness of the material blessing given to the arrogant owner. This abundance becomes the very source of his spiritual downfall, as material prosperity breeds pride, self-sufficiency, and forgetfulness of God, leading him to boast to his companion that his wealth would never perish. The verse thus sets up a broader lesson about the illusory permanence of worldly blessings and the danger of attributing one's success solely to one's own effort rather than to divine providence. The vivid imagery of overflowing orchards and gushing rivers serves as a metaphor for how worldly abundance, however complete and perfect it may appear, carries within it the seed of moral and spiritual corruption when it is not tempered with gratitude and humility before God.

translation: And he had fruit [wealth], so he said to his companion while conversing with him, 'I am greater than you in wealth and mightier in [number of] men.'
interpretation: This verse introduces the parable of the two men found in Surah Al-Kahf, illustrating the arrogance that can arise from material prosperity. The man with abundant gardens and wealth boasts to his companion, measuring his worth by the size of his fortune and the number of his dependents or followers. This represents a common human failing: equating material success with personal superiority or security. The Qur'an sets up this scene as a prelude to a cautionary tale, showing how such boastfulness, when it leads to forgetting God and denying the reality of resurrection, ultimately results in loss and regret, as the narrative continues to show the destruction of his gardens as a consequence of his arrogance and ingratitude.

translation: And he entered his garden while he was wronging himself. He said, 'I do not think that this will ever perish.'
interpretation: This verse depicts the owner of the prosperous garden—mentioned in the parable in Surah Al-Kahf—entering his property filled with arrogance and a false sense of permanence. His 'wronging himself' refers to his spiritual corruption through disbelief, ingratitude, and pride, as he attributes his wealth entirely to his own merit while forgetting God's role as the true provider. His declaration that the garden would never perish reveals a deep heedlessness about the transient nature of worldly possessions and a failure to acknowledge divine power over all creation. This moment sets up the dramatic reversal that follows in the narrative, where the garden is indeed destroyed, teaching that arrogant self-sufficiency and forgetfulness of God inevitably lead to loss and regret, regardless of how secure one's blessings may seem.

translation: And I do not think the Hour will come to pass. And even if I am brought back to my Lord, I will surely find better than this as a return.
interpretation: This verse is part of the parable of the two men in Surah al-Kahf (18:36), where the wealthy owner of the gardens, arrogant due to his riches and possessions, boasts to his companion. His statement reveals a dual error: first, a denial or doubt about the reality of the Resurrection and the Day of Judgment, and second, an assumption that even if there were an afterlife, his worldly success is proof of his favored status with God, entitling him to even greater rewards hereafter. This reflects a common human delusion where material prosperity is mistaken for divine approval, leading to spiritual heedlessness, arrogance, and a false sense of security that ignores accountability and the transient nature of worldly blessings.

translation: His companion said to him, while arguing with him, 'Have you disbelieved in Him who created you from dust, then from a sperm-drop, then fashioned you into a man?'
interpretation: This verse is part of the parable of the two men in Surah Al-Kahf, one arrogant and boastful of his wealth, the other a believer who tries to correct him. The believing companion's rebuke highlights a core Qur'anic argument for faith in God and the resurrection: reflection on one's own origin. The stages of creation—from inert dust, to a humble fluid, to a fully formed human being—are presented as undeniable evidence of a Creator's power and purposeful design. The rhetorical question 'Have you disbelieved...' is meant to shame the arrogant man by reminding him that his own existence, which he takes for granted, is proof of the very power that he denies, particularly the power to resurrect and to make one accountable for their deeds. It serves as a lesson that pride in worldly possessions should not lead one to forget their humble origins and their ultimate dependence on their Creator.

translation: But as for me, He is Allah, my Lord, and I do not associate anyone with my Lord.
interpretation: This verse is spoken by the believing companion in the parable of the two men (one wealthy and arrogant, the other poor but faithful) as a response to his companion's boastfulness about his wealth and his doubt about the Resurrection. In contrast to his companion's arrogance and implicit shirk (attributing his prosperity to his own efforts without acknowledging God), this believer declares his pure monotheism (tawhid). The phrase 'لكنا' (but as for me) sets up a sharp contrast between the two men's worldviews—one rooted in materialism and self-sufficiency, the other in humble submission to God alone. This declaration serves as a model of faith: true recognition that all blessings come from Allah, and that no partner, intermediary, or false pride should be placed alongside one's devotion to the one true Lord. It is a statement of unwavering monotheistic conviction in the face of worldly temptation and the seduction of wealth.

translation: And why did you not say, when you entered your garden, 'What Allah has willed; there is no power except in Allah'? Though you see me as less than you in wealth and children,
interpretation: This verse is part of the parable of the two men, one arrogant with his wealth and gardens, the other poor but faithful, found in Surah al-Kahf. The believing companion rebukes the wealthy man for failing to acknowledge that his prosperity is entirely a gift from God, not a result of his own merit or power. The phrase 'Ma sha' Allah, la quwwata illa billah' is presented as the proper response of gratitude and humility one should express upon witnessing or possessing blessings, recognizing that all strength and provision ultimately belong to God alone. The poor man's rhetorical question—asking why his wealthy companion did not utter this phrase—highlights the spiritual failure of pride and self-sufficiency that stems from forgetting God's sovereignty over all things. It also sets up the contrast between material wealth, which is temporary and can vanish, and true security, which comes only through faith and reliance upon the Divine. The reference to being 'less in wealth and children' establishes that worldly abundance is not a sign of one's true worth or favor with God; rather, it is a test, and the proper attitude toward it is humble acknowledgment of divine will rather than boastful self-congratulation.

translation: Then it may be that my Lord will give me something better than your garden, and will send upon it a reckoning (a calamity/thunderbolt) from the sky, so that it becomes a slippery barren ground.
interpretation: This verse is spoken by the believing companion in the parable of the two men (Surah Al-Kahf), responding to his arrogant friend who boasted of his wealth, fertile garden, and worldly power while denying the Day of Judgment and attributing his success to his own merit. Rather than responding with envy or despair, the believer places his trust entirely in God's power and justice, expressing hope that God may grant him something superior to his companion's garden in the Hereafter, and warning that God has the power to utterly destroy the garden's lush abundance, turning it into barren, slippery wasteland—a stark image of total devastation where nothing can even take root or stand firm. This reflects the Qur'anic theme that worldly wealth and achievement are transient and contingent entirely upon divine will, not human effort or entitlement, and that arrogance in the face of blessings invites potential ruin. The verse teaches humility, reliance on God (tawakkul) rather than one's possessions, and serves as a reminder that material prosperity can vanish instantly by divine decree, underscoring the folly of forgetting God while enjoying worldly bounty.

translation: Or that its water will sink into the earth, so you would never be able to seek it out.
interpretation: This verse is part of the parable of the two men in Surah Al-Kahf, where the believing companion warns his arrogant, wealthy counterpart—who boasts of his lush garden and denies the Day of Judgment—that all worldly possessions are utterly contingent upon divine will. The sinking of the water represents the ultimate form of loss: not merely destruction that one might see and mourn, but a vanishing so complete that the source of life and sustenance disappears beyond human reach or recovery. This serves as a sobering reminder that material wealth, however abundant and seemingly secure, can be stripped away instantly by forces entirely outside human control, exposing the folly of arrogance, self-sufficiency, and forgetfulness of God in the face of worldly prosperity.

translation: And his fruits were encompassed [by ruin], so he began to turn his hands about [in distress] over what he had spent on it, while it had collapsed upon its trellises, and he said, 'Oh, I wish I had not associated anyone with my Lord!'
interpretation: This verse depicts the dramatic downfall of the wealthy, arrogant man from the parable of the two gardens who had boasted of his riches and doubted the Resurrection, even claiming his prosperity proved his superiority over his believing companion. When God destroys his garden as a consequence of his arrogance and ingratitude, he is left in anguish, wringing his hands over the ruin of everything he had invested in and taken pride in. His belated cry of regret—wishing he had never set up partners with his Lord—reveals that his wealth and self-sufficiency had led him into a subtle form of shirk: trusting in his own power and possessions rather than attributing his blessings to God. The verse serves as a powerful warning about the transient nature of worldly wealth and the spiritual danger of pride and self-reliance, illustrating that true loss is not merely material ruin but the realization, often too late, of one's error in forgetting God's sovereignty over all things. The imagery of the collapsed trellises symbolizes how quickly and completely worldly achievements can be reduced to nothing when they are not grounded in gratitude and faith.

translation: And he had no group to help him besides Allah, nor could he defend himself.
interpretation: This verse concludes the parable of the arrogant owner of the two gardens who boasted of his wealth and denied the Hereafter, believing his prosperity would last forever and that even if resurrected, he would find something better. When Allah destroyed his gardens as a consequence of his arrogance and disbelief, he was left utterly helpless. This verse emphasizes that all the wealth, status, and apparent power he once had could not save him when Allah's decree came upon him—he had no allies, no supporters, and no ability to rescue himself. The lesson underscores the Qur'anic theme that true power and security rest with Allah alone, and that reliance on worldly possessions, social standing, or human alliances is ultimately futile when divine justice is enacted. It serves as a warning against arrogance, ingratitude, and forgetting the true source of one's blessings, reminding believers that no one has independent power to save themselves or others except through Allah's will.

translation: There, all authority/protection belongs to Allah, the True. He is best in reward and best in outcome.
interpretation: This verse concludes the parable of the two garden owners, one arrogant and boastful of his wealth, the other humble and trusting in God. When the arrogant man's garden was destroyed and his wealth proved powerless to save him, the verse declares that true wilayah—sovereignty, guardianship, and protective authority—belongs exclusively to Allah, 'al-Haqq' (the True, the Ultimate Reality). The word 'hunalika' (there/at that point) signals a moment of reckoning when illusions of self-sufficiency collapse, revealing that no wealth, status, or human alliance can substitute for reliance on God. The verse reorients the believer's sense of security away from worldly possessions and toward divine protection, affirming that genuine reward (thawab) and the best ultimate outcome ('uqba, often linked to the Hereafter) are found only in submission to and trust in Allah, not in accumulated riches or false pride in one's own achievements.

translation: And present to them the example of the life of this world: it is like water which We send down from the sky, and the vegetation of the earth mingles with it and absorbs it, but then it becomes dry stubble which the winds scatter. And Allah is, over all things, Perfectly Capable.
interpretation: This verse uses the metaphor of rainwater-fed vegetation to illustrate the fleeting and transient nature of worldly life. Just as rain brings forth lush plant growth that flourishes briefly before withering into dry debris scattered by the wind, so too are the pleasures, achievements, and attachments of earthly existence—vibrant and seemingly substantial for a time, yet ultimately temporary and destined to fade away. The verse closes by affirming God's absolute power over all things, reminding the listener that the One who gives life and causes decay controls the entire cycle, and that true permanence lies not in worldly life but in what endures with Him. This serves as a call to recognize the illusory permanence of material pursuits and to orient one's values toward what is lasting rather than what is transient.”

translation: Wealth and children are the adornment of the worldly life, but the enduring good deeds are better with your Lord in reward and better in hope.
interpretation: This verse draws a contrast between the transient allurements of worldly life—material wealth and offspring—and righteous deeds that endure beyond this life. Wealth and children, while valued and often sources of pride and comfort, are temporary and belong strictly to the life of this world; they can vanish, be lost, or fail to accompany a person into the afterlife. In contrast, 'the enduring good deeds' (al-baqiyat al-salihat), understood by commentators to include righteous actions, acts of worship, charity, and good words, persist in value before God and yield lasting reward. The verse teaches believers to reorient their priorities and sense of security away from fleeting worldly possessions and status toward actions that have eternal consequence. It also addresses human psychology: just as people place their hopes and aspirations in wealth and children as sources of future security and legacy, true and lasting hope should be placed in righteous deeds, which alone offer real and lasting benefit both in this life and the Hereafter. This verse is often read in connection with the preceding narrative in Surah Al-Kahf about the two men with gardens, one who boasted of his wealth and lineage, illustrating through contrast the folly of pride in worldly possessions versus the wisdom of valuing enduring righteousness.

translation: And [mention] the Day when We will set the mountains in motion, and you will see the earth laid bare, and We will gather them all together, leaving not one of them behind.
interpretation: This verse is a depiction of the Day of Judgment, emphasizing the complete dissolution of the familiar physical world as a prelude to divine reckoning. The mountains, which in human experience symbolize permanence, stability, and immovability, are set into motion—suggesting that even the most seemingly eternal features of creation are subject to God's command and will be utterly transformed. The earth being 'laid bare' indicates the removal of all that conceals or obstructs—vegetation, structures, geographical features—so that nothing is hidden; everything becomes exposed and visible, symbolizing that on this day, no secret or deed can remain concealed, paralleling the exposure of human souls' true nature before God. The gathering of 'all of them' without exception underscores the universality and inescapability of resurrection and judgment: every soul, every race, every generation throughout history will be assembled, with God's power ensuring total accountability and leaving no one exempt. This verse serves as both a warning and an assurance: a warning against complacency and heedlessness regarding the certainty of this reckoning, and an assurance that divine justice is comprehensive and nothing will be overlooked. It also theologically reinforces the omnipotence of God, who can reshape and move the very foundations of the physical world as easily as He gathers every created being, reminding humanity of their utter dependence and the transient nature of worldly permanence compared to the eternal reality of the Hereafter.

translation: And they will be presented before your Lord in rows, [and it will be said]: 'You have certainly come to Us as We created you the first time. But you claimed that We would never make for you an appointed time [of resurrection].'
interpretation: This verse depicts the Day of Judgment when all of humanity will be lined up before God, stripped bare of worldly status, wealth, and pretense—just as they were created initially, with nothing to distinguish them except their deeds. The rebuke that follows exposes the folly of those who denied the resurrection, highlighting the contrast between human arrogance and denial in worldly life versus the undeniable reality they face in the afterlife. It serves as a powerful reminder of accountability, emphasizing that disbelief in the appointed meeting with God does not negate its eventual occurrence. The verse underscores the theme of divine justice and the ultimate exposure of truth, warning against complacency regarding one's ultimate fate and the certainty of being held accountable for one's beliefs and actions.

translation: And the Book will be placed [open], and you will see the criminals fearful of what is in it, and they will say, 'Oh, woe to us! What is this book that leaves nothing small or great except that it has enumerated it?' And they will find what they did present [before them], and your Lord does injustice to no one.
interpretation: This verse depicts the moment of final judgment when every soul's record of deeds is unveiled in complete and exacting detail. The imagery of 'the Book' being 'placed' evokes a formal legal proceeding where evidence is laid bare, leaving no room for denial or negotiation. The criminals' terror stems not from vague accusation but from the shocking comprehensiveness of the record—every minor sin and major transgression has been preserved, countering human assumptions that small wrongs go unnoticed or forgotten. Their exclamation 'ya waylatana' (oh, woe to us) captures the existential horror of confronting an unerasable, perfect account of one's own moral history, stripped of the self-deception and rationalization available in worldly life. The phrase 'found what they did present' suggests not merely reading about past deeds but experiencing their reality immediately before them, as if time collapses and the consequences of choices become tangible and inescapable. The verse closes with a theological affirmation of divine justice: God's judgment is not arbitrary or exaggerated, but precisely reflects what was done—neither adding false charges nor diminishing just due. This serves as a sobering reminder that ultimate accountability is rooted in truth and fairness, and human beings should not underestimate the weight of seemingly minor sins or overestimate their ability to escape consequence, for divine record-keeping is both total and just.

translation: And [mention] when We said to the angels, 'Prostrate to Adam,' and they prostrated, except for Iblis. He was of the jinn and departed from the command of his Lord. Then will you take him and his descendants as allies other than Me while they are enemies to you? Wretched it is for the wrongdoers as a substitute.
interpretation: This verse recalls the primordial command given to the angels to prostrate before Adam, a gesture signifying honor to humanity and acknowledgment of Adam's special status as God's vicegerent. Iblis's refusal, rooted in arrogance and his origin from fire-born jinn rather than angelic nature, marks the first act of disobedience and establishes him as the archetype of rebellion against divine command. The verse then shifts to a pointed rhetorical question directed at humanity: given this known history of enmity, why would people choose Iblis and his offspring—the forces of temptation and deception—as protectors, guides, or allies instead of God? This highlights the irrationality and spiritual danger of aligning oneself with forces that are openly hostile to human well-being. The closing statement condemns this choice as a terrible exchange, emphasizing that wrongdoers who substitute true divine guidance and protection with satanic allegiance have made the worst possible bargain, trading eternal well-being for transient and ultimately harmful companionship. The verse serves as both a historical account and a moral warning about the nature of true loyalty and the consequences of misplaced trust.

translation: I did not make them witness the creation of the heavens and the earth, nor the creation of themselves, and I would not take the misleaders as helpers.
interpretation: This verse addresses those who took false deities or misleading forces as partners with God, refuting the basis of such claims by establishing that these so-called helpers or partners had no role whatsoever in the act of creation—neither in the cosmic creation of the heavens and earth nor even in their own coming into being. The rhetorical force of the verse undermines any claim to divine partnership, since true creative power belongs exclusively to God, who required no assistance or witness in bringing existence into being. Furthermore, the verse makes clear that God does not rely upon those who lead others astray (al-mudillin) as aides or supporters in His governance of creation. This serves as a broader theological statement against shirk (associating partners with God), emphasizing divine self-sufficiency and sole sovereignty over creation, and it implicitly warns against following those who mislead, since they themselves are powerless and were never party to the originating acts of existence.

translation: And [warn them of] the Day when He will say, "Call My 'partners' whom you claimed," and they will call upon them, but they will not respond to them. And We will put between them a barrier of destruction.
interpretation: This verse depicts a dramatic scene from the Day of Judgment in which the polytheists are commanded to summon the false deities and intermediaries they worshipped and relied upon in worldly life. The scene exposes the utter powerlessness of these false partners—when called upon in this moment of ultimate need, they remain silent and unresponsive, revealing that the associations and loyalties people formed with them were baseless illusions. The word 'mawbiqan' suggests a place or barrier of destruction and perdition, symbolizing the complete and irrevocable severance between the worshippers and the objects of their false worship. This separation represents not merely physical distance but a theological unveiling: all the imagined power, intercession, and support attributed to these partners dissolves in the face of divine reality. The verse functions as a stark warning against shirk (associating partners with Allah), demonstrating that whatever one depends upon besides Allah will ultimately prove impotent and abandon its worshippers precisely when they are most desperate, leaving them isolated in their consequences.

translation: And the criminals will see the Fire and will know with certainty that they are about to fall into it, and they will find no way to escape from it.
interpretation: This verse depicts a pivotal moment on the Day of Judgment when the wrongdoers finally confront the ultimate consequence of their choices. The certainty described—'they will be certain they are to fall into it'—conveys a stark psychological shift from denial or doubt in worldly life to absolute, undeniable knowledge in the Hereafter. There is no more room for rationalization, bargaining, or hope of reprieve; the inevitability of their fate is total. The phrase 'they will find no way to escape' underscores the absence of any intercessor, excuse, or alternative path at that moment, in contrast to the many opportunities for repentance and guidance they were offered during their lives. The verse serves as a sobering reminder of accountability, emphasizing that the deferred nature of divine justice does not diminish its certainty, and that the moment of reckoning, once it arrives, leaves no room for negotiation or retreat.

translation: And We have certainly diversified in this Qur'an for the people every [kind of] example, but man is, more than anything, disputatious.
interpretation: This verse reflects on the comprehensive nature of the Qur'anic message, emphasizing that God has presented truths in multiple forms—parables, arguments, stories, and warnings—so that people of different dispositions and intellects might find a path to understanding and guidance. Despite this diversity of approach designed to reach every type of person, the verse notes a persistent trait of human nature: a tendency toward argumentation and disputation, often arising from stubbornness, pride, or a resistance to accepting truth even when presented clearly. This highlights a tension between divine effort to communicate and human inclination to resist, debate, or rationalize away what challenges one's assumptions, desires, or sense of control. The verse serves as both a reminder of the thoroughness of divine communication and a critique of humanity's argumentative nature, which can obstruct genuine reflection and acceptance of guidance.

translation: And nothing prevented the people from believing when guidance came to them, and from asking forgiveness of their Lord, except that they wished for the precedent (fate) of the former peoples to come upon them, or that the punishment should come upon them face to face.
interpretation: This verse addresses the stubborn disbelief of Quraysh and other deniers despite clear guidance (the Qur'an and Prophet Muhammad) reaching them. It highlights a psychological and spiritual pattern: rather than responding to guidance with faith and repentance, the disbelievers demanded tangible proof in the form of destruction similar to what befell earlier disbelieving nations (such as the peoples of Noah, 'Ad, or Thamud), or they demanded that punishment confront them directly and visibly. This reflects their arrogance and insistence on empirical, immediate proof rather than accepting spiritual truth through reason and revelation. The verse implicitly warns that such demands are dangerous, for when punishment does come in that direct manner, it leaves no further opportunity for repentance - unlike the grace period granted through patient exposure to guidance. It underscores a broader Qur'anic theme: divine mercy delays punishment to allow genuine reflection and belief, yet human arrogance often squanders this mercy by demanding immediate, catastrophic signs instead of embracing faith through contemplation of existing guidance.

translation: And We send not the messengers except as bringers of good tidings and warners. But those who disbelieve dispute by means of falsehood to refute thereby the truth, and they take My verses and that whereof they are warned in mockery.
interpretation: This verse establishes that the sole purpose of prophetic messengers is to deliver glad tidings of mercy and reward for believers and warnings of consequence for wrongdoers—not to perform miracles on demand or force belief through coercion. It then contrasts this noble purpose with the behavior of disbelievers, who resort to baseless argumentation (al-batil) specifically designed to destabilize and extinguish the truth (al-haqq), rather than engaging in sincere inquiry. Their rejection is not rooted in intellectual doubt but in willful dismissal, as shown by their choice to mock both the divine signs and the warnings given to them. This mockery reveals a deeper spiritual arrogance: rather than reflecting on the revelation's content, they treat sacred truth as a subject of ridicule, demonstrating that their disbelief stems from stubbornness and pride rather than a genuine lack of evidence.

translation: And who is more unjust than one who is reminded of the verses of his Lord but turns away from them and forgets what his hands have sent forth? Indeed, We have placed over their hearts coverings, lest they understand it, and in their ears deafness. And if you invite them to guidance, they will never be guided, then, at all.
interpretation: This verse addresses the willful rejection of divine guidance by those who, having been clearly reminded of God's signs, deliberately turn away and forget the consequences of their own past deeds. The imagery of coverings over the heart and deafness in the ears is not presented as an arbitrary punishment imposed without cause, but as the natural spiritual consequence of persistent denial and heedlessness—when a person repeatedly rejects truth, their capacity to perceive and accept it becomes progressively diminished, almost as if sealed. This reflects a broader Qur'anic theme that human choices shape spiritual receptivity: continual avoidance of truth hardens the heart until guidance can no longer penetrate it, not because God denies them the chance, but because they have forfeited their own ability to respond through repeated refusal. It serves as a warning about the self-inflicted nature of spiritual blindness that results from arrogance, denial, and forgetting one's accountability for past actions.

translation: And your Lord is the Forgiving, Possessor of mercy. If He were to seize them for what they have earned, He would have hastened the punishment for them. But for them is an appointed time, from which they will find no refuge besides it.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes God's attribute of mercy and forbearance, explaining why wrongdoers are not immediately punished for their sins despite deserving it. Divine justice operates on a deferred timeline rather than instant retribution, giving people opportunity for repentance and reflection during their worldly life. However, this delay should not be mistaken for divine indifference or weakness—it is a manifestation of mercy coupled with wisdom. The 'appointed time' refers to a fixed moment of reckoning, whether death or the Day of Judgment, which is inescapable and from which no alternative sanctuary or escape exists. The verse thus balances two divine attributes: mercy, which grants respite, and justice, which ensures accountability is never ultimately avoided, teaching believers that God's patience with sinners is purposeful rather than permanent, and that true security lies only in turning to Him before that appointed moment arrives.

translation: And those towns—We destroyed them when they did wrong, and We appointed for their destruction a fixed time.
interpretation: This verse, from Surah Al-Kahf, follows the narrative of Moses and reflects on the fate of ancient communities whose ruins stood as visible lessons for later generations. It establishes a theological principle central to the Qur'an: that divine punishment is not arbitrary or immediate but follows a decreed timeline (mawʿid), and it is triggered by persistent wrongdoing (zulm) rather than mere disbelief alone. The mention of 'appointing a time' underscores God's sovereignty over history—He grants communities respite and opportunity to repent before justice is enacted, demonstrating both divine patience and ultimate accountability. The verse serves as a warning to the Prophet's contemporaries, using the physical remains of destroyed civilizations as tangible evidence that moral corruption and oppression inevitably lead to downfall, regardless of a society's apparent power or permanence.

translation: And [mention] when Moses said to his young servant, 'I will not stop until I reach the junction of the two seas, even if I must travel for a long period (years).'
interpretation: This verse opens the narrative of Moses' journey to meet al-Khidr, a figure of divine wisdom. It reflects Moses' determination and resolve in pursuit of knowledge, illustrating that seeking sacred or hidden knowledge requires perseverance, patience, and willingness to endure hardship over an extended period. His address to his young companion (traditionally identified as Joshua, son of Nun) shows the value of companionship and support in a spiritual or intellectual quest. The 'junction of the two seas' symbolizes a meeting point between two forms of knowledge—the apparent law that Moses possesses as a prophet, and the esoteric wisdom embodied by al-Khidr, which operates beyond conventional religious law. Moses' resolve to continue 'for a long time' underscores the Quranic theme that true knowledge is not easily attained but requires sustained effort, humility, and the acknowledgment that even a prophet like Moses still has more to learn.

translation: So when they reached the junction between the two [seas], they forgot their fish, and it took its way into the sea, slipping away.
interpretation: This verse marks the pivotal turning point in the story of Musa (Moses) and his unnamed servant/companion as they journey in search of al-Khidr. The forgetting of the fish was not a mere accident but had been established earlier as the divinely appointed sign for the exact location where Musa would meet his destined teacher. The fish miraculously coming back to life and swimming away into the sea symbolizes a break from the natural order, signaling that this place is touched by divine power and mystery. Musa's forgetfulness here is significant: it shows that even a great prophet can be subject to ordinary human lapses of memory, demonstrating that knowledge of the unseen and control over signs ultimately belongs to God alone, not even to His chosen messengers. The episode also sets up the deeper theme of the narrative—that beneath the surface of ordinary events (like forgetting a fish) lie hidden divine purposes, foreshadowing the entire encounter with al-Khidr, where apparently strange or troubling actions will later be revealed to conceal wisdom beyond Musa's immediate understanding. Thus, the sign of the fish escaping into the sea becomes a metaphor for the limits of human knowledge and the vast, unseen workings of divine wisdom that guide events in ways people cannot always perceive at the time.

translation: So when they had passed beyond it, he [Moses] said to his young companion, 'Bring us our morning meal. We have certainly suffered much fatigue from this, our journey.'
interpretation: This verse marks a pivotal moment in the story of Moses' quest for knowledge beyond his own, found in Surah Al-Kahf. Moses and his young companion (traditionally identified as Joshua, son of Nun) had been traveling toward the junction of the two seas, following a divine sign involving a fish that would come back to life and slip into the water, indicating the location where Moses would meet the mysterious servant of God, Khidr. In their fatigue and preoccupation with the journey, they unknowingly passed beyond the very spot where the miraculous sign occurred—forgetting about the fish entirely. Moses, feeling the physical exhaustion of travel, asks for food, unaware that the purpose of the journey's marker had already been fulfilled and left behind. This moment illustrates human forgetfulness even amid a divinely guided mission, and sets up the subsequent realization and backtracking that leads to the actual encounter with Khidr. It subtly teaches that even prophets experience ordinary human needs and lapses in attention, and that divine signs can pass unnoticed until one reflects and retraces one's steps with humility.

translation: He said, 'Did you see, when we took refuge at the rock, that I indeed forgot the fish—and nothing made me forget it except Satan, so that I would not remember it—and it took its way into the sea in a wondrous manner.'
interpretation: This verse recounts a pivotal moment in the story of Moses and his young companion during their journey to meet al-Khidr, the righteous servant of God endowed with special divine knowledge. The forgetting of the fish was not a mere lapse but the very sign Moses had been told to watch for, marking the location where he would find his destined teacher. The companion's admission that Satan caused him to forget reveals a theological point about human fallibility and the subtle ways distraction and forgetfulness are attributed to spiritual adversity, even in matters that ultimately serve a divine purpose. The miraculous detail of the fish coming back to life and swimming away 'in a wondrous manner' signals that this entire episode is governed by extraordinary, divine causation rather than ordinary natural law. This moment teaches that God sometimes conceals His signs within seemingly mundane human errors like forgetfulness, and that what appears as a failure or shortcoming can actually be the precise mechanism through which divine guidance unfolds. It also illustrates the necessity of returning and retracing one's steps when one realizes a sign has been missed, as Moses does immediately after this revelation, demonstrating humility in the pursuit of knowledge and willingness to acknowledge human limitation even for a prophet.

translation: He said, 'That is what we were seeking.' So they returned, retracing their footsteps.
interpretation: This verse marks the turning point in the story of Moses (Musa) and his young companion during their journey in search of Khidr. They had been traveling in pursuit of the meeting place of the two seas, and the sign for finding it was the disappearance of their fish. When Moses's companion recalls that the fish had indeed slipped away miraculously at the rock where they had rested, Moses recognizes this as the very sign they had been told to look for. His exclamation 'That is what we were seeking' reflects a moment of recognition that what seemed like a lapse or forgetfulness (losing track of the fish) was in fact the divinely ordained marker guiding them to their destination. Their retracing of steps symbolizes humility and attentiveness to signs that may appear as small or incidental but carry profound purpose. This moment sets the stage for their encounter with Khidr, a figure of hidden divine knowledge, teaching Moses—and by extension, the reader—that true guidance often requires patience, retracing one's steps, and recognizing that what seems like an error or oversight may actually be part of a larger divine plan.

translation: Then they found a servant from among Our servants to whom We had given mercy from Us and had taught him knowledge from Our own presence.
interpretation: This verse introduces al-Khidr, the mysterious figure whom Moses seeks out after being told that there is one who possesses knowledge beyond his own. The description emphasizes two distinct gifts: 'rahmah' (mercy) and 'ilm' (knowledge) that come directly 'min ladunna' (from Our own presence) rather than through ordinary means of acquisition like study or prophetic revelation. This signifies a special category of spiritual knowledge ('ilm ladunni) that is unmediated and experiential, granted directly by God to those He chooses, distinct from the revealed law (shari'ah) that Moses represents as a prophet. The encounter that follows between Moses and this servant illustrates the tension and complementarity between exoteric knowledge (based on outward law and apparent justice) and esoteric knowledge (based on hidden wisdom and understanding of divine decree), teaching that even a great prophet like Moses must humble himself to learn that there are dimensions of divine wisdom that operate beyond apparent moral logic, requiring patience and trust in a higher, often concealed, purpose.

translation: Moses said to him, 'May I follow you on the condition that you teach me from that which you have been taught, [something of] right guidance?'
interpretation: This verse captures the moment Moses, despite being a great prophet with profound knowledge, humbly approaches al-Khidr to request to learn from him. It illustrates the Islamic principle that true knowledge requires humility, and that even the most learned individuals should seek to learn from others who possess different forms of wisdom. Moses's respectful request, phrased as a conditional question rather than a demand, demonstrates proper adab (etiquette) in seeking knowledge—acknowledging the teacher's authority over what they know and asking permission to become a student. This encounter sets up the broader lesson of the narrative: that divine wisdom (represented by al-Khidr's actions) often transcends apparent human logic and righteousness (rushd), and that patience and trust are required to understand matters beyond one's immediate comprehension.

translation: He said, "Indeed, you will not be able to have patience with me."
interpretation: This verse is spoken by al-Khidr to Musa (Moses) at the beginning of their famous encounter in Surah al-Kahf. Al-Khidr possesses a form of divine knowledge granted directly from God that operates beyond conventional religious law and apparent reasoning—knowledge of hidden wisdom behind seemingly troubling events. His warning to Musa is prophetic foresight: he knows that the actions he is about to undertake (damaging a boat, killing a youth, rebuilding a wall without payment) will appear unjust or incomprehensible on the surface, and that Musa, bound by his prophetic duty to uphold visible justice and law, will be unable to withhold objection when witnessing them. This encounter teaches a profound epistemological lesson about the limits of human judgment: that beneath the apparent surface of events—especially those that seem cruel, wasteful, or inexplicable—there may lie a deeper divine wisdom inaccessible to ordinary perception. Al-Khidr's statement is not a boast but a realistic assessment of human psychology: patience with incomprehensible hardship, especially when one has the knowledge or position to object, is extraordinarily difficult. The verse sets up the entire narrative's purpose: to illustrate that true wisdom sometimes requires withholding judgment and trusting a process whose ultimate purpose remains hidden, a lesson applicable to how believers should approach the trials and seemingly inexplicable aspects of divine decree in their own lives.

translation: And how can you have patience for that which you cannot encompass in knowledge?
interpretation: This verse is spoken by al-Khidr to Prophet Musa (Moses) in Surah Al-Kahf, when Musa requests to accompany him and learn from him. Al-Khidr poses this rhetorical question to highlight the fundamental challenge Musa will face: he will witness actions that appear to violate the sacred law and conventional morality—killing an innocent youth, damaging a boat belonging to poor fishermen, and repairing a wall for an ungrateful town without payment—without being given the underlying wisdom or divine knowledge that justifies these acts. The verse speaks to a profound epistemological and spiritual truth: patience with the unknown requires a particular kind of faith and humility that differs from patience with hardships we can rationally understand. Musa, despite being a great prophet with access to revealed law (shari'ah), lacks the special, experiential knowledge ('ilm laduni) granted to al-Khidr directly from God. This encounter illustrates the limits of human judgment when evaluating divine wisdom through apparent outcomes alone, and teaches that true patience (sabr) is hardest when we cannot see the reasons behind events—when we must trust in a wisdom beyond our comprehension rather than our own immediate perception of justice or benefit.

translation: He [Moses] said, "You will find me, if Allah wills, patient, and I will not disobey you in any order."
interpretation: This verse captures Moses' humble response to Khidr's warning that Moses would not be able to bear witness to his actions without questioning them. Moses, eager to learn, commits to patience and obedience, but importantly qualifies his promise with 'if Allah wills' (in sha Allah), acknowledging that human resolve alone is insufficient without divine support. This reflects the Islamic principle of recognizing one's limitations and dependence on God's will even when making sincere commitments. The verse also foreshadows the narrative tension to come, as Moses will indeed struggle to maintain this patience when confronted with Khidr's seemingly inexplicable and troubling actions, ultimately breaking his promise multiple times. This teaches a broader lesson about the difficulty of withholding judgment when witnessing actions that defy apparent logic or morality, and the importance of trusting a process or wisdom that may not be immediately comprehensible.

translation: He said, 'Then if you follow me, do not ask me about anything until I mention to you about it.'
interpretation: This verse is part of the narrative of Musa (Moses) and Khidr in Surah Al-Kahf. Khidr sets a condition for Musa before allowing him to accompany him on their journey: Musa must refrain from questioning Khidr's actions until Khidr himself chooses to explain them. This encapsulates a profound lesson about patience, trust, and the limits of human knowledge. Khidr represents a form of knowledge granted directly by God that operates beyond apparent outward reasoning or conventional religious law (sharia), while Musa represents knowledge based on revealed law and rational judgment. The condition highlights that true understanding sometimes requires withholding judgment and questioning until the full context or divine wisdom behind seemingly incomprehensible or troubling actions is revealed. It teaches the broader spiritual lesson that human beings often lack the full picture behind events that may appear unjust or confusing, and that patience and trust in a higher wisdom—whether in the context of this story, divine wisdom—is essential for spiritual growth and understanding of God's plan, which unfolds according to its own timing and logic, not immediate human comprehension.

translation: So they both set out until, when they had embarked on the ship, he [al-Khidr] made a hole in it. [Moses] said: 'Have you made a hole in it to drown its people? You have certainly done a grave thing.'
interpretation: This verse is part of the narrative of Moses and al-Khidr, a story illustrating the limits of human knowledge and the wisdom behind divine decree that may appear, on the surface, to be harmful or unjust. Moses, bound by the apparent and the visible, reacts with alarm at what seems to be a destructive and senseless act—damaging a vessel that carries passengers, endangering their lives. His protest represents the natural human response to judge actions solely by their immediate, observable consequences. Al-Khidr's action, however, is guided by a deeper knowledge granted to him by God, one that perceives hidden outcomes and ultimate purposes beyond human comprehension. The episode as a whole teaches that what appears evil or harmful from a limited human perspective may, in reality, serve a greater good or prevent a greater harm, as is later revealed when al-Khidr explains that the boat belonged to poor men and he damaged it to prevent a tyrant king from seizing it forcibly. Thus, the verse sets up a central theme of the story: the tension between zahir (apparent reality) and batin (hidden reality/wisdom), and the necessity of trust and patience when confronted with divine wisdom that exceeds human understanding.

translation: He said: 'Did I not say that you would never be able to bear with me in patience?'
interpretation: This verse is part of the narrative of Musa (Moses) and al-Khidr in Surah al-Kahf, repeated after Musa breaks his promise to remain silent and patient for the second time, this time after al-Khidr kills a young boy, an act that outwardly appears to be a grave and inexplicable injustice. Al-Khidr's gentle rebuke underscores the central theme of the story: the limits of human knowledge and judgment when confronted with divine wisdom that operates beyond apparent cause and effect. Musa, a great prophet possessing revealed law and moral clarity, nonetheless cannot restrain his sense of justice when witnessing what seems to be an unprovoked killing of an innocent child. His reaction is understandable and even commendable from the standpoint of conventional morality, yet it demonstrates precisely the point al-Khidr had anticipated from the outset: that true patience in the face of actions whose ultimate wisdom is hidden from human perception requires a surrender of judgment that even a prophet finds difficult to maintain.
