This moment sets the stage for Jesus's own miraculous speech from the cradle, through which God vindicates Mary's honor and reveals the divine nature of the virgin birth, silencing the accusations rooted in human assumptions about lineage and conduct.

translation: So she pointed to him. They said, 'How can we speak to one who is in the cradle, a child?'
interpretation: This verse occurs in the story of Mary (Maryam) after she gives birth to Jesus ('Isa) and returns to her people carrying him, facing accusations of unchastity. Rather than defending herself with words, Mary silently points to the infant Jesus, trusting in God's promise that He would speak on her behalf. Her people's incredulous response—questioning how an infant in a cradle could possibly speak—sets up the miracle that follows, where Jesus speaks from the cradle to proclaim his prophethood and defend his mother's honor. This moment emphasizes several theological points central to Islamic belief: first, it demonstrates God's power to work miracles beyond natural expectation, as an infant speaking with full coherence and wisdom is itself a sign of divine intervention. Second, it reinforces the Quranic narrative that affirms Mary's piety and innocence against those who doubted her, placing the burden of proof and vindication in God's hands rather than through human testimony alone. Third, the scene foreshadows Jesus's special status as a prophet who speaks with divine authority from the very beginning of his life, countering later Christian theological claims about his divinity by portraying him explicitly as a created being and a servant of God who speaks as a prophet, not as God incarnate. The people's skepticism represents a natural human reaction to what seems impossible, and their doubt is answered immediately by the miracle itself, reinforcing the Quran's recurring theme that God's signs often defy ordinary human logic and expectation.

translation: He said, "Indeed, I am the servant of Allah. He has given me the Scripture and made me a prophet."
interpretation: This verse records the miraculous speech of the infant Jesus (Isa), speaking from the cradle to defend his mother Mary against accusations of impropriety following his birth. The declaration serves a profound theological purpose within Islamic doctrine: by having Jesus himself proclaim that he is "the servant of Allah" (abd Allah) rather than the son of God, the Qur'an establishes from the very moment of his miraculous speech the Islamic position on his nature and status. This directly counters Christian trinitarian theology by having Jesus's own first words assert his servanthood to God rather than divine sonship. The mention that Allah has already given him the Scripture and made him a prophet—despite his being a newborn—emphasizes that prophethood and divine revelation are gifts bestowed by God's will and decree, not something earned through human development or achieved through divine nature. This early, miraculous articulation of his mission also authenticates Mary's chastity and the virgin birth as a sign of God's power, since the infant's rational speech itself constitutes a miracle validating the entire narrative. The verse thus serves multiple functions: vindicating Mary, establishing Jesus's prophetic credentials from the start of his life, and firmly situating him within the Islamic framework of prophethood rather than divinity.

translation: And He has made me blessed wherever I may be, and has enjoined upon me prayer and zakah (charity) as long as I remain alive.
interpretation: This verse is part of the miraculous speech of Prophet Isa (Jesus) as an infant, spoken to defend his mother Maryam against accusations. By declaring that God made him blessed and obligated him to prayer and charity throughout his life, the verse establishes that Isa's prophethood and righteousness were decreed by God from the very beginning of his life, refuting any notion of illegitimacy and affirming his status as a servant of God rather than a divine being. It also emphasizes that worship (prayer) and social responsibility (charity) are lifelong, continuous obligations rather than occasional acts, setting a model for all believers regardless of their special status or circumstances.

translation: And [He has made me] dutiful to my mother, and He has not made me domineering, miserable.
interpretation: This verse is part of the miraculous speech of Jesus (Isa) as an infant in the cradle, recounted in Surah Maryam, where he defends his mother Mary against accusations of unchastity. By speaking of his own righteousness, Jesus affirms that God has made him kind and devoted to his mother, emphasizing filial piety as a divine blessing and a mark of righteousness. Furthermore, he states that God did not make him 'jabbaran shaqiyyan'—arrogant, tyrannical, or wretched—explicitly rejecting any notion of pride, coercion, or misery in his character. This serves a dual theological purpose: it refutes any claim to divinity or arrogance that might later be falsely attributed to Jesus by his followers, affirming his status as a humble servant and prophet of God rather than a domineering figure, and it establishes honoring one's parents as a core virtue tied to spiritual humility rather than self-exaltation. The verse thus encapsulates humility, familial duty, and submission to God as intertwined markers of righteousness, serving as a model for believers and a clarification of Jesus's true nature within Islamic theology.

translation: And peace be upon me the day I was born, the day I die, and the day I am raised alive.
interpretation: This verse is spoken by Prophet Yahya (John) in Surah Maryam, describing the divine peace and blessing bestowed upon him at the three most critical transitional moments of existence: birth, death, and resurrection. These three junctures represent the passages between non-existence and life, life and death, and death and the afterlife—moments of greatest vulnerability and uncertainty for any human being. By declaring God's peace upon him at each of these thresholds, the verse emphasizes that true security comes only from divine favor, not from worldly power or status. This same phrase is echoed later in the surah regarding Prophet Isa (Jesus), highlighting the shared humanity and prophetic dignity of both figures, countering theological claims of Jesus's divinity by showing he experienced the same mortal transitions as other prophets, all under God's care and peace.

translation: That is Jesus, son of Mary - the word of truth concerning which they are in doubt (or dispute).
interpretation: This verse serves as a decisive conclusion to the Quranic narrative of Jesus's miraculous birth and his speech from the cradle. It affirms that the preceding account—of Jesus as a created being, born miraculously to the virgin Mary, and granted prophethood—is the truthful and authoritative statement on his identity, in contrast to the various disputed claims made about him by different religious communities. The phrase 'the word of truth' asserts the Quran's own account as definitive, directly countering Christian doctrines that elevate Jesus to divinity or sonship of God, as well as any other speculative claims. The verse underscores the Islamic theological position that Jesus was a human prophet and servant of God, not divine, and that the controversies and sectarian disputes (mentioned here as 'they are in doubt') surrounding his nature stem from departures from this original, clear truth. It thus functions polemically and doctrinally, settling the matter of Jesus's true status within the Quran's monotheistic framework.

translation: It is not befitting for Allah that He should take a son; glory be to Him! When He decrees a matter, He only says to it, 'Be,' and it is.
interpretation: This verse emphatically negates the Christian doctrine of Jesus as the literal son of God, affirming instead the absolute transcendence and uniqueness of Allah, who is beyond human-like procreation or need for offspring. The declaration 'subhanahu' (glory be to Him) underscores His purity from any attributes of createdness or limitation that begetting a child would imply. The verse then pivots to explain divine creative power through the phrase 'kun fayakun' (Be, and it is), which illustrates that Allah's will is instantaneous and unmediated—He requires no biological process, no partner, and no passage of time to bring anything into existence, including the miraculous creation of Jesus himself through His word alone. This serves as a rebuttal to those who would elevate a prophet to divine sonship by showing that the very miracle of Jesus's birth (without a father) is itself proof of Allah's absolute power to create as He wills, rather than evidence of literal divine parentage. The verse thus reframes Jesus's extraordinary birth as a sign of God's omnipotence rather than a basis for theological claims about God having a son.

translation: Indeed, Allah is my Lord and your Lord, so worship Him. This is a straight path.
interpretation: This verse, spoken by Jesus (Isa) as reported in the Qur'an, serves as a decisive theological corrective to the doctrine of his divinity. By explicitly stating that Allah is both his Lord and the Lord of his listeners, Jesus places himself firmly within the category of creation and servitude, rejecting any notion of shared divine status with God. The declaration functions as a unifying call to pure monotheism (tawhid), asserting that worship belongs to God alone, not to any prophet or messenger, however exalted. The phrase 'this is a straight path' identifies this understanding—recognizing God's sole lordship and devoting worship exclusively to Him—as the correct and unambiguous way to righteousness, in contrast to the deviations introduced by those who later elevated Jesus to divine status. The verse thus underscores the continuity of the prophetic message: all messengers, including Jesus, came with the same essential teaching of submission to the one God.

translation: But the factions differed among themselves, so woe to those who disbelieved from the scene of a tremendous Day.
interpretation: This verse refers to the disputes that arose among various religious sects and groups regarding the nature of Jesus (Isa), after the clear account of his birth and mission had been given. Despite receiving the same revealed truth, different factions split into conflicting doctrines—some denying him, others deifying him, and others going to various extremes. The verse delivers a stern warning that such disbelief and distortion of truth, bred from division and dispute rather than honest reflection, will lead to severe consequences on the Day of Judgment, a 'tremendous Day' when all will be forced to witness the reality they denied or corrupted in worldly life. The warning underscores a broader Qur'anic theme: that theological division caused by following desires or dogma rather than clear guidance leads to spiritual loss, and that ultimate accountability before God awaits all who turn away from the truth.

translation: How clearly will they hear and see on the Day they come to Us! But the wrongdoers today are in manifest error.
interpretation: This verse contrasts the spiritual blindness and deafness of the wrongdoers in worldly life with the perfect clarity of perception they will have on the Day of Judgment, when denial is no longer possible. In this life, disbelievers willfully ignore truth, reject guidance, and remain heedless of signs pointing to God, choosing instead to follow desires and misconceptions—this is their 'manifest error.' Yet on the Day they meet their Lord, every veil will be lifted; their senses will be sharpened to perceive reality as it truly is, including the consequences of their choices. The verse serves as a warning: the faculties of hearing and seeing that are dulled by arrogance, heedlessness, or deliberate rejection of truth in this world will one day function with painful clarity, when such clarity can no longer benefit them or allow for repentance. It underscores the Qur'anic theme that denial of truth is a self-imposed blindness, not an absence of evidence, and that the Hereafter will expose the folly of worldly heedlessness in the starkest possible terms.

translation: And warn them [O Muhammad] of the Day of Regret, when the matter will be decided; and [yet] they are in heedlessness, and they do not believe.
interpretation: This verse refers to the Day of Judgment, called the 'Day of Regret' because on that day every soul will feel profound sorrow—the disbelievers will regret their rejection of truth and missed opportunities for faith, while even the believers may feel regret over any shortcomings in worship. The phrase 'when the matter will be decided' indicates finality—all affairs will be settled irrevocably, with destinies sealed between Paradise and Hell. The verse highlights a tragic irony: despite the certainty of this momentous reckoning, people in this worldly life remain heedless, absorbed in trivial pursuits and worldly distractions, and refuse to believe in what is coming. This serves as a powerful warning to the Prophet's audience and all people to awaken from heedlessness before it is too late, since the chance for genuine belief and righteous action exists only in this life, not after the matter has been 'decided.'

translation: Indeed, it is We who inherit the earth and whoever is upon it, and to Us they will be returned.
interpretation: This verse affirms God's ultimate and eternal ownership of all creation, emphasizing that all worldly possessions, power, and life itself are transient and will ultimately return to Him. The use of 'We' (the royal plural often used in Arabic to denote majesty) underscores divine sovereignty. The statement that God 'inherits' the earth and all upon it means that after all human life perishes and worldly structures collapse, only God remains eternal and in possession of all things—nothing of this world is truly owned by its temporary inhabitants. This serves as a reminder to believers not to become overly attached to material wealth, status, or worldly life, since everything will eventually pass away and return to its true and everlasting Owner. The verse also carries an implicit warning and comfort: a warning against arrogance or heedlessness in misusing what one has been given, and comfort for the believers that injustice and loss in this world are not final, for all will be returned to God for judgment and reckoning, where true justice will prevail.

translation: And mention in the Book, Ibrahim (Abraham). Indeed, he was a man of truth and a prophet.
interpretation: This verse opens the account of Abraham within Surah Maryam, which presents a series of prophetic figures to remind the listeners of the continuity of divine guidance. By describing Abraham as 'siddiq' (a man of truth, utterly truthful and sincere) before calling him 'nabi' (prophet), the verse emphasizes that prophethood is rooted in personal integrity and unwavering commitment to truth. The designation 'siddiq' suggests that Abraham's inner conviction and honesty in both belief and conduct preceded and qualified him for the prophetic mission. This sets the stage for the following verses, which recount Abraham's courageous confrontation with his idol-worshipping father, highlighting that true prophethood involves standing firmly for truth even against one's own family, through wisdom, compassion, and unwavering faith in the One God.

translation: [Mention] when he said to his father, 'O my father, why do you worship that which neither hears nor sees nor can avail you in anything?'
interpretation: This verse depicts the Prophet Ibrahim's gentle yet firm confrontation with his father's idolatry, using the respectful address 'O my father' (ya abati) to demonstrate that rational critique of falsehood can and should be paired with filial compassion rather than hostility. Ibrahim's argument proceeds through logical appeal rather than mere assertion of authority: he points to the idols' fundamental incapacities—they cannot hear prayers, cannot see the one who worships them, and cannot provide any benefit or protection. This threefold critique systematically dismantles the rationale for idol worship by highlighting the absence of the very qualities that would justify devotion—sensory awareness and the power to help. The verse establishes a model for da'wah (invitation to faith) that is both intellectually rigorous and emotionally respectful, showing that true monotheism rests on recognizing that only a being with actual power, awareness, and capacity to respond deserves worship, while blind adherence to ancestral custom in worshipping lifeless objects represents a failure of basic reasoning rather than genuine piety.

translation: O my father, indeed there has come to me of knowledge that which has not come to you, so follow me; I will guide you to a straight path.
interpretation: This verse is part of Prophet Ibrahim's (Abraham's) respectful yet firm address to his idol-worshipping father. Despite the cultural weight of filial deference and the father's position of authority, Ibrahim speaks with humility and love—addressing him tenderly as 'my father'—while asserting the superiority of divine revelation over inherited tradition and ancestral custom. The verse establishes a profound principle: that prophetic knowledge, as a gift from God, surpasses human experience, age, or social status, and that truth must take precedence even over filial piety when it comes to matters of faith. Ibrahim does not claim personal superiority but attributes his insight entirely to what has reached him from God, modeling how one should invite others—especially elders or loved ones—to truth with gentleness, honesty, and sincere concern for their guidance rather than arrogance or confrontation.

translation: O my father, do not worship Satan. Indeed, Satan has ever been disobedient to the Most Merciful.
interpretation: This verse is part of Prophet Ibrahim's gentle yet firm appeal to his idolatrous father, as recorded in Surah Maryam. Rather than directly condemning his father's idol worship, Ibrahim reframes the issue by identifying the true object of such worship: Satan himself, who inspires and benefits from humanity's devotion to false gods. By addressing his father with the tender term 'ya abati' (O my father), Ibrahim demonstrates the Qur'anic model of calling others to truth with compassion and respect even while delivering an uncompromising message. The verse establishes a theological principle that worship of anything other than God ultimately traces back to Satan's influence, since idol worship serves his rebellious agenda against the Most Merciful. Satan's defining characteristic here is 'disobedience' ('asiyyan) to Ar-Rahman specifically—invoking God's mercy underscores the tragedy that Satan rejects a Lord characterized by compassion rather than harshness. This sets up the father's choice as one between following a merciful God or a rebellious, ungrateful being who leads others astray out of his own defiance.

translation: O my father, indeed I fear that a punishment from the Most Merciful will touch you, and you will become a companion to Satan.
interpretation: This verse is part of Prophet Ibrahim's (Abraham's) tender yet firm appeal to his idol-worshipping father, Azar. It demonstrates the proper manner of calling others to truth: with compassion, respect, and genuine concern rather than condemnation or arrogance. Ibrahim does not say his father is already doomed, but expresses fear and worry out of love, showing that the goal of warning is protection, not humiliation. The phrase 'companion to Satan' illustrates the spiritual reality that persistent rejection of truth and continued disobedience creates an alliance with misguidance, as Satan becomes the patron and guide of those who turn away from God. This verse teaches that calling one's family to righteousness should be rooted in sincere care for their ultimate wellbeing, using soft speech even when addressing deeply held wrongful beliefs, and that the consequence of rejecting divine guidance is not just future punishment but a present spiritual kinship with the forces of misguidance.

translation: He said, 'Have you turned away from my gods, O Abraham? If you do not desist, I will surely stone you, so leave me for a long while.'
interpretation: This verse depicts the response of Abraham's father (traditionally named Azar) to his son's call to abandon idol worship and turn to the one true God. Rather than engaging with Abraham's reasoned arguments—which in the preceding verses included gentle, respectful appeals about the futility of worshipping powerless idols—the father reacts with hostility and threat rather than reflection. His response reveals several things: first, the threat of violence ('I will surely stone you') in the face of a peaceful invitation to truth illustrates how entrenched falsehood often responds to truth with aggression rather than argument. Second, his dismissal of Abraham ('leave me for a long while') shows a rejection not just of the message but of the relationship itself, prioritizing his idols over his own son. This episode serves as a powerful illustration of the cost of prophetic truth-telling—even within one's own family—and foreshadows Abraham's eventual emigration from his people. It also sets up the contrast between Abraham's continued gentleness and respect toward his father (seen in his response in subsequent verses) and his father's harshness, emphasizing the Quranic theme that truth should be delivered with patience and kindness even when met with rejection and threats.

translation: He said, 'Peace be upon you. I will ask forgiveness for you from my Lord. Indeed, He has always been gracious to me.'
interpretation: This verse depicts Prophet Ibrahim's gentle and respectful response to his father, who had just threatened to stone him and told him to leave after Ibrahim tried to guide him away from idol worship. Despite his father's hostility and rejection, Ibrahim does not respond with anger or contempt, but instead offers a peaceful farewell and promises to pray for his father's forgiveness. This demonstrates the Islamic ideal of maintaining kindness and respect toward parents even when they oppose one's faith, while still not compromising on monotheistic principles. Ibrahim's reference to God's graciousness toward him personally also reflects his humility and recognition that any guidance he has received is a mercy from God, not his own achievement, and this personal relationship with God gives him the patience to deal gently with his father's rejection rather than responding in kind.

translation: And I will withdraw from you and from that which you invoke besides Allah, and I will invoke my Lord. It may be that in invoking my Lord I will not be unblessed (unsuccessful).
interpretation: These are the words of Ibrahim (Abraham) to his idolatrous father, as recounted in Surah Maryam. Having failed to persuade his father to abandon idol worship, Ibrahim makes the decisive choice to separate himself physically and spiritually from his father's polytheism, choosing exile over compromise with falsehood. This verse illustrates a foundational principle in the Qur'an: that devotion to God may require severing ties with one's closest kin when their practices contradict monotheism. Ibrahim's humility is notable in his phrasing 'asa' (it may be, perhaps), expressing hope rather than certainty about his own righteousness before God, despite his evident faith and sacrifice. This reflects the proper posture of a believer—confident in God's mercy yet never presumptuous about one's own standing. The verse also sets up the narrative trajectory where God rewards Ibrahim's sacrifice by granting him descendants (Isaac and Jacob) who become prophets, demonstrating that what is given up for God's sake is restored manifold.

translation: So when he had withdrawn from them and from what they worshipped besides Allah, We bestowed upon him Isaac and Jacob, and each [of them] We made a prophet.
interpretation: This verse concerns Prophet Ibrahim (Abraham), who, after separating himself from his idolatrous people and family—including his own father—and forsaking their false gods, was rewarded by God with righteous offspring who would carry forward his mission of monotheism. The granting of Isaac, and then Jacob as a further generation, signifies divine compensation for the worldly ties and community Ibrahim sacrificed for the sake of his faith. It illustrates a recurring Quranic principle: that sincere devotion and willingness to abandon falsehood, even at great personal cost such as isolation from one's own kin, results in abundant blessing from God, not only in immediate reward but in lasting legacy. The bestowal of prophethood upon both Isaac and Jacob further establishes the continuity of the prophetic line through Ibrahim, affirming him as the patriarch from whom many future messengers would descend, thereby cementing his spiritual honor across generations.

translation: And We granted them of Our mercy, and We bestowed upon them a lofty and truthful tongue (a praiseworthy reputation that endures).
interpretation: This verse refers to the prophets mentioned earlier in Surah Maryam, particularly Abraham and his descendants. Beyond material blessings, God granted them 'lisan sidq aliyya'—an elevated, truthful legacy of remembrance among later generations. This means their names, teachings, and righteous example continued to be honored and invoked with praise and truth by people of all subsequent faiths and nations, not through false fame but through genuine recognition of their sincerity and devotion to God. It illustrates that true honor bestowed by God transcends time, ensuring that the righteous are remembered with truth and dignity by later generations, serving as an enduring testament to divine mercy and justice in preserving the legacy of those who are faithful.

translation: And mention in the Book, Musa (Moses). Indeed, he was devoted [exclusively to Allah], and he was a messenger and a prophet.
interpretation: This verse introduces Moses as a model of sincere devotion (ikhlas), emphasizing that his heart and actions were purified for God alone, free from hypocrisy or worldly motive. By pairing the titles 'messenger' (rasul) and 'prophet' (nabi), the verse underscores that Moses held the complete prophetic office: he received revelation (the Torah) and was commissioned to actively convey and implement a law and guide a nation, not merely receive divine communication privately. His sincerity is presented as the root quality that qualified him for this dual responsibility—suggesting that true spiritual leadership and the capacity to bear a divine message arise from an inner purity of intention before any outward mission is granted. The verse, appearing within a sequence introducing various prophets in Surah Maryam, also serves to link Moses' story to the broader Quranic theme that all prophets, despite different missions and peoples, shared this same essential sincerity toward God as the foundation of their prophethood.

translation: And We called him from the right side of the mount, and We brought him near in intimate communion (najiyyan).
interpretation: This verse refers to Prophet Musa (Moses) and his encounter with Allah at Mount Tur (Sinai). The 'right side' signifies a place of honor and blessing, not merely a geographic direction. The verse emphasizes the extraordinary closeness granted to Musa, who was drawn near to Allah for intimate, direct communication (munajat), a unique honor among prophets. This establishes Musa's special status as one who spoke directly with Allah (Kalimullah), illustrating the theme found throughout this surah (Maryam) of Allah's mercy and special favor shown to His chosen prophets, each in a manner suited to their circumstance. It demonstrates that divine nearness is not bound by physical distance but is a spiritual elevation granted by Allah's will.

translation: And We granted him, out of Our mercy, his brother Aaron as a prophet.
interpretation: This verse refers to Moses (Musa), and describes how God, as an act of mercy and in response to Moses's prayer (as recounted earlier in Surah Taha, where Moses asks God to appoint Aaron as a helper due to his own difficulty in speech), granted him his brother Aaron as a prophet and companion in his mission. This reflects the broader Quranic theme that prophethood and support in carrying out divine missions are gifts of God's mercy, not something earned solely through human effort. It also highlights the importance of companionship and support in fulfilling a difficult calling, as Aaron was given to Moses specifically to strengthen him and share the burden of confronting Pharaoh and guiding the Israelites. The verse underscores that even prophets, chosen and strengthened by God, are not meant to bear their responsibilities in isolation, and that family bonds can be instruments through which God's mercy and support are delivered to those entrusted with a mission.

translation: And mention in the Book Ishmael. Indeed, he was true to his promise, and he was a messenger and a prophet.
interpretation: This verse highlights Prophet Ishmael (Isma'il) as a model of steadfast character, particularly emphasizing his faithfulness to promises—a trait considered central to moral and spiritual integrity in Islamic teaching. By noting that he was both a 'messenger' (rasul) and a 'prophet' (nabi), the verse underscores his elevated status in the lineage of prophets sent by God. The specific mention of his truthfulness to his word is often linked to the tradition of his willingness to submit to being sacrificed by his father Ibrahim, as commanded by God, and his patience in fulfilling what he promised despite hardship. This serves as an exemplary lesson for believers on honoring commitments and trusting divine will, reinforcing the broader Qur'anic theme of righteous conduct exhibited by the prophets as moral exemplars for humanity.

translation: And he used to enjoin upon his family prayer and zakah, and he was to his Lord pleasing.
interpretation: This verse describes Prophet Isma'il (Ishmael), praising him for two complementary qualities: his active role as a spiritual leader within his own household and his personal standing before God. By commanding his family to establish prayer (salah) and give charity (zakah), he demonstrated that true piety is not confined to private devotion but extends to guiding one's family toward righteousness—fulfilling the responsibility of leadership in faith that begins at home. The verse then affirms that this outward responsibility was matched by inward sincerity, as he was 'pleasing' to his Lord, meaning his worship and conduct earned divine approval and satisfaction. Together, these two aspects illustrate the Quranic ideal of a believer who integrates personal righteousness with social and familial responsibility, showing that true faith is both practiced and transmitted to others.

translation: And mention in the Book, Idris. Indeed, he was a man of truth, a prophet.
interpretation: This verse highlights Idris (identified by many commentators with the biblical Enoch) as an exemplar of righteousness, combining two elevated qualities: being 'siddiq' (a person of utmost truthfulness and sincerity whose inner faith is matched by outer conduct) and being a prophet chosen by God to convey His message. The pairing of these attributes emphasizes that true prophethood is inseparable from personal integrity and devotion to truth. By instructing the Prophet Muhammad to 'remember' Idris in the Quran, God situates him within the continuous chain of prophets who upheld monotheism and moral uprightness across human history, reinforcing the Quran's theme that all prophets shared a unified mission despite being sent to different peoples at different times. Idris is traditionally associated with early human civilization, and some traditions credit him with being among the first to receive wisdom in writing, astronomy, or other knowledge, symbolizing the harmony between faith and the pursuit of knowledge within the prophetic tradition. His inclusion here, alongside other prophets mentioned in this chapter like Ibrahim, Musa, and Ismail, serves to remind listeners of the universality and antiquity of God's guidance to humanity.

translation: And We raised him to a high station.
interpretation: This verse refers to Prophet Idris (Enoch), mentioned earlier in the passage, and describes the honor Allah bestowed upon him by elevating his rank and status. Scholars have offered various interpretations of this 'high station' - some understand it literally as a physical elevation to the heavens, reflecting traditions that speak of Idris being raised to a celestial realm without experiencing death in the normal sense. Others interpret it more figuratively, as an elevation in spiritual rank, prophethood, and honor among Allah's creation, signifying the exalted status he achieved through his righteousness, patience, and truthfulness mentioned in the preceding verses. This elevation serves as a divine reward for his devotion and serves as an example of how Allah honors His righteous servants, placing them in positions of dignity that transcend ordinary human experience. The verse also reinforces the Quranic theme that true honor and elevation come from Allah alone, granted to those who maintain steadfast faith and righteous conduct, rather than from worldly status or power.

translation: Those are the ones whom Allah has favored from among the prophets, of the descendants of Adam, and of those We carried [in the ship] with Noah, and of the descendants of Abraham and Israel, and of those We guided and chose. When the verses of the Most Merciful were recited to them, they fell in prostration and weeping.
interpretation: This verse serves as a concluding summary to the preceding narratives of the prophets mentioned in Surah Maryam—Zechariah, John, Mary, Jesus, Abraham, Moses, Ishmael, and Idris—establishing a unified lineage of prophethood stretching from Adam through Noah, Abraham, and Israel (Jacob). The verse emphasizes that divine favor and guidance are not random but are bestowed through a continuous chain of chosen individuals across generations, linking all the prophets in a single spiritual family united by submission to God. The culminating image of falling into prostration and weeping upon hearing divine revelation illustrates the proper emotional and physical response of the truly guided heart: profound humility, awe, and overwhelming reverence in the presence of God's words. This is presented as the hallmark of authentic faith—contrasted implicitly with later generations (mentioned in the following verse) who abandon prayer and follow their desires. The prostration and tears symbolize complete submission, not merely intellectual acknowledgment of the message but a visceral, emotional surrender to the majesty of the Most Merciful.

translation: Then there succeeded them a generation who neglected prayer and followed desires; so they will meet evil consequences (or a valley in Hell called Ghayy).
interpretation: This verse warns of the spiritual decline that occurs when later generations abandon the devotional and moral discipline of their predecessors. The neglect of prayer symbolizes a broader abandonment of one's connection to God and the structured remembrance that keeps a person anchored to higher purpose, while the pursuit of desires represents the unchecked indulgence of base impulses once that anchor is lost. The verse establishes a causal chain: when ritual and spiritual obligation are discarded, moral dissolution follows naturally, as there is nothing left to restrain human appetite. The consequence—meeting 'ghayy,' often understood as ruin, error, or even a specific place of torment—is not an arbitrary punishment but the natural outcome of a life unmoored from discipline and higher accountability. The verse serves as a timeless caution about generational decay, suggesting that the loss of religious practice among descendants is frequently the first sign of broader moral and social collapse, and that the pursuit of worldly desire without spiritual restraint leads inevitably to self-destruction.

translation: Except for those who repent, believe, and do righteous deeds - it is they who will enter Paradise, and they will not be wronged in anything.
interpretation: This verse establishes a universal principle of divine mercy and justice that runs throughout the Qur'an: no matter how far one has strayed - whether through following falsehood, poetic deception, or other sins mentioned in the preceding context - the door to redemption remains open. The three conditions given (repentance, faith, and righteous action) are presented as a complete and sufficient formula for salvation, emphasizing that Islam is not merely about correcting past wrongs but requires a holistic transformation: sincere remorse (tawbah), correct belief (iman), and consistent righteous conduct (amal salih). The phrase 'will not be wronged in anything' underscores God's perfect justice - those who fulfill these conditions will receive the full reward promised to them, with nothing diminished or withheld. This reflects the Qur'anic theme that divine judgment, while strict, is never arbitrary or unfair; the scales of justice are precise, and genuine transformation is always met with corresponding mercy and reward.

translation: Gardens of Eden, which the Most Merciful has promised to His servants in the unseen. Indeed, His promise is ever coming to pass.
interpretation: This verse underscores the theological principle of belief in al-ghayb (the unseen) as a defining feature of true faith. The reward of Paradise is deliberately described as something promised 'in the unseen' (bil-ghayb), meaning the servants of God have not witnessed it with their own eyes but accept it purely through trust in divine revelation and the truthfulness of God's word. This stands in contrast to those mentioned in the preceding verses who abandoned prayer and succumbed to worldly desires, favoring the visible and immediate over the unseen and eternal. The closing affirmation—that His promise is 'ever coming to pass'—functions as a reassurance of certainty: what God has pledged is not speculative or contingent but destined to be fulfilled with the same inevitability as any observed law of creation. In this way, the verse ties eschatological hope to epistemological humility, teaching that ultimate truths about reward and the afterlife lie beyond human sensory experience, yet are no less certain for being unseen.

translation: They will not hear therein any vain talk, but only [words of] peace, and they will have therein their provision, morning and evening.
interpretation: This verse describes the serene nature of Paradise, contrasting it with the discord and idle speech of worldly life. The exclusion of 'laghw' (vain, frivolous, or harmful talk) signifies that the inhabitants of Paradise are free from the social friction, gossip, arguments, and meaningless chatter that characterize earthly existence. Instead, all communication is reduced to 'salam'—peace, both as a greeting and as a state of being, reflecting complete harmony among its inhabitants and with God. The mention of provision arriving 'morning and evening' uses familiar temporal language from worldly life to convey continuous, assured sustenance, yet paradoxically in Paradise there is no sun or night as known on earth—suggesting these are symbolic time markers denoting constancy and completeness rather than literal diurnal cycles. This reflects a divine accommodation to human understanding, describing eternal bliss using concepts of regularity and security that are meaningful to mortal experience, assuring believers that their needs are met without the toil, uncertainty, or conflict that mark worldly provision.

translation: That is the Paradise which We shall give as inheritance to those of Our servants who were righteous/God-fearing (muttaqin).
interpretation: This verse concludes a passage describing the rewards of the righteous in the afterlife, framing Paradise not as something earned through mere birthright, lineage, or external status, but as an inheritance granted by God's grace to those who cultivated taqwa—conscious God-fearing righteousness—in their earthly lives. The use of the word 'inherit' (nurith) suggests that Paradise is the true, lasting possession that passes to the faithful, in contrast to worldly inheritances which are temporary and often contested. It reframes ultimate reward as a matter of spiritual merit and devotion rather than social privilege, lineage, or wealth, emphasizing that all believers, regardless of their background, have equal access to this eternal inheritance through piety and faithfulness to God.

translation: [The angels say]: "We descend not except by the command of your Lord. To Him belongs what is before us and what is behind us and what is between that. And your Lord is never forgetful."
interpretation: This verse is spoken by the angel Gabriel (or the angels collectively) in response to the Prophet Muhammad's apparent longing for more frequent revelation, addressing a context in which revelation had paused for a time, causing him distress. The angels clarify that their descent is entirely subject to divine command, not their own will or the Prophet's wishes, affirming God's absolute sovereignty over the timing of revelation. The phrase describing God's dominion over "what is before us, what is behind us, and what is between" is a sweeping declaration of divine omniscience and control over all time and space—past, future, and present, or alternatively the various states and stations of the angels themselves. This serves to reassure the Prophet that any delay is not neglect or abandonment, countering accusations from skeptics that God had forsaken him. The closing statement that "your Lord is never forgetful" directly addresses and dispels any fear of divine abandonment, emphasizing that God's plan unfolds with perfect wisdom and timing, even when that timing is not immediately apparent to human beings. The verse thus teaches patience and trust in divine providence, affirming that apparent silence or delay from God is never due to oversight but is purposeful within a framework of knowledge that transcends human perception.

translation: Lord of the heavens and the earth and all that is between them - so worship Him and be steadfast in His worship. Do you know of anyone equal or similar to Him?
interpretation: This verse establishes the absolute uniqueness and transcendence of God as the sole sovereign of all creation, which serves as the foundation for the command to worship Him exclusively. The rhetorical question at the end - asking whether anyone knows of a being comparable to Him or worthy of sharing His name - is a decisive rejection of any form of polytheism or association of partners with God. The term 'samiyyan' (one with the same name or equal status) emphasizes that God's essence, attributes, and names are utterly singular and cannot be shared or replicated by any created being, including the angels, prophets, or idols that some communities worshipped. The command to 'persevere steadfastly' (istabir) in worship acknowledges that maintaining consistent devotion requires effort and patience, especially in the face of opposition, doubt, or the allure of competing loyalties. This verse thus combines theological assertion with practical spiritual guidance, teaching that true recognition of God's incomparable nature should translate into sustained, disciplined devotion rather than mere intellectual acknowledgment.

translation: And man says, 'When I am dead, will I surely be brought forth alive?'
interpretation: This verse captures the voice of human skepticism toward resurrection, expressed as a rhetorical question tinged with disbelief or mockery. It reflects the natural human difficulty in conceiving of life after death, especially after the body has decomposed into nothing. The Qur'an raises this question here as a prelude to answering it in the following verses, where it reminds man that he was created from nothing in the first place, making his re-creation no more difficult for God than his original creation. The verse thus serves a rhetorical and theological purpose: to confront human doubt about resurrection by appealing to the logic of first creation—if God created man from non-existence initially, bringing him back after death poses no greater difficulty. It also subtly critiques human forgetfulness, as the same being who doubts his own resurrection fails to reflect on the miracle of his original emergence into existence.

translation: Does man not remember that We created him before, when he was nothing?
interpretation: This verse comes in the context of Surah Maryam's discussion of those who deny the resurrection and mock the idea of being raised again after death. God responds by directing man's attention to his own origin: before his existence, he was utterly nothing—no matter, no life, no consciousness. The rhetorical question challenges human forgetfulness and intellectual inconsistency: if one can accept that an all-powerful Creator brought him into being from absolute non-existence, there is no rational basis to deny that the same Creator can restore him to life after death, which is logically a lesser feat than the original creation from nothing. The verse thus serves as a proof by analogy (qiyas), appealing to man's own existence as evidence against his doubt. It also carries a deeper call to humility, reminding man that his sense of self-importance and autonomy is misplaced, since his very being is a gift from God, not something he achieved or deserved. This remembrance is meant to dissolve arrogance and awaken gratitude and faith in the power of God over all things, including resurrection and judgment.

translation: So by your Lord, We will surely gather them together with the devils; then We will surely bring them to kneel around Hell.
interpretation: This verse serves as a solemn divine oath emphasizing the certainty of resurrection and judgment for those who denied it, particularly addressing the disbelievers mentioned earlier in the surah who scoffed at the idea of being raised after death. By swearing 'by your Lord,' God underscores the absolute certainty of this outcome, countering human doubt with divine assurance. The pairing of disbelievers with the devils (shayatin) who misled them in worldly life illustrates the principle of accountability extending to those who followed falsehood and those who propagated it—they will share the same fate since they were companions in misguidance. The imagery of being made to kneel (jathiyan) around Hell depicts a posture of utter humiliation and helplessness, a stark reversal of the arrogance and pride these disbelievers displayed in life when they rejected faith and mocked believers. This kneeling position suggests exhaustion, terror, and submission—qualities they refused to show toward God during their lives but will be forced into on the Day of Judgment. The verse thus reinforces the Quranic theme that rejection of truth and alliance with corrupting forces leads to inevitable consequences, and that the arrogant will ultimately be brought low in the most dramatic reversal of fortune, standing exposed and powerless at the very edge of the punishment they once denied.

translation: Then We will surely drag out from every sect those among them who were most defiant in rebellion against the Most Merciful.
interpretation: This verse comes in the context of describing the Day of Judgment, following verses that speak of the fate of the wicked and the righteous. It conveys that on that Day, Allah will single out from every community, sect, or faction the most obstinate and rebellious individuals—those who showed the greatest arrogance and defiance toward the Most Merciful (ar-Rahman) during their worldly lives. The use of the name 'ar-Rahman' here is deliberate and striking: it emphasizes that these people rebelled not against a harsh tyrant but against the Source of boundless mercy and compassion, making their defiance all the more inexcusable. The verse underscores that no group—whether based on tribe, religion, ideology, or faction—will be collectively spared or collectively condemned; rather, judgment will be individualized according to the degree of each person's rebellion. The 'ringleaders' or most hardened among the disbelievers and sinners in every faction will be identified and dealt with first, highlighting divine justice that pierces through group identity to assess individual culpability. This serves as a warning that leadership in misguidance or excessive arrogance before Allah's mercy carries a heavier reckoning.

translation: Then surely We know best those most deserving of being burned therein.
interpretation: This verse comes in the context of Surah Maryam's description of the Day of Judgment, where all people are gathered and led to kneel around Hell (verses 68-69). God affirms His complete and perfect knowledge of every soul's true inner state, merits, and sins, declaring that He knows with absolute certainty exactly who most deserves to endure the Fire's punishment. The phrase underscores divine omniscience and justice: judgment is not arbitrary or based on outward appearances, lineage, or human claims to righteousness, but on God's perfect knowledge of hearts and deeds. It serves as a warning to those who arrogantly assumed their status or wealth exempted them from accountability, reminding humanity that ultimate judgment belongs to God alone, who alone possesses complete knowledge of who truly merits punishment based on their rebellion, disbelief, and persistence in wrongdoing.

translation: And there is not one of you except that he will come to it [i.e., Hell]. This is, upon your Lord, an inevitability decreed.
interpretation: This verse refers to the universal passage over or encounter with Hell (Jahannam) that every human being, believer and disbeliever alike, will experience on the Day of Judgment. According to the predominant interpretation among classical exegetes, 'wuruduha' (coming to it) refers to crossing the Sirat, the bridge stretched over Hell that all of creation must traverse. For the righteous believers, this crossing will be swift and painless, a mere formality on their way to Paradise, while for the wicked and disbelievers, they will fall into its depths. This decree is described as 'hatman maqdiyya'—an absolute, unavoidable decree already sealed by divine will, emphasizing that no soul, regardless of status or piety, is exempt from confronting the reality of Hell in some form. The verse serves as a sobering reminder of divine justice: even the most righteous will pass near the fire as a test or a witnessing of what they were spared, reinforcing both the fear of accountability and gratitude for salvation through God's mercy rather than one's own deeds alone.

translation: Then We will save those who were righteous and leave the wrongdoers within it, fallen to their knees.
interpretation: This verse comes after a description of Hellfire and the passage of all people over or near it. It establishes a clear principle of divine justice: salvation is granted to those who maintained taqwa (God-consciousness, piety, and mindfulness of accountability to God), while those who persisted in wrongdoing (zulm) are left behind in a state of utter humiliation and helplessness, depicted as being 'jathiyyan'—kneeling or crouching on their knees. This posture symbolizes the complete reversal of the arrogance and pride wrongdoers displayed in worldly life; before the overwhelming reality of divine judgment, they are reduced to abject submission, unable to stand, unable to escape, confronted directly with the consequences of their choices. The verse underscores that the distinction between the saved and the condemned is not arbitrary but rests entirely on the moral and spiritual orientation each soul cultivated in life—whether one lived guarding against sin and injustice, or whether one persisted in transgression against God and others.

translation: And when Our clear verses are recited to them, those who disbelieve say to those who believe: 'Which of the two parties is better in position and finer in assembly?'
interpretation: This verse exposes the flawed reasoning of the disbelievers, who measure truth and divine favor by worldly standards—wealth, social status, and material comfort—rather than by faith and righteousness. Confronted with the clear signs of God, instead of reflecting on their content, the disbelievers resort to a boastful comparison, pointing to their own apparent prosperity and social standing as proof of their superiority over the believers, who may have been materially poorer or socially marginalized. The underlying assumption is that God's favor should be visibly reflected in earthly success, so if they are more prosperous, they must be on the right path, while the believers' relative hardship suggests error. This reflects a recurring human temptation to equate material success with spiritual truth, ignoring that worldly fortune can be a test or even a form of respite before judgment, not necessarily a sign of divine approval. The verse sets up a rebuttal (found in the verses that follow) that worldly position is fleeting and ultimately insignificant compared to the lasting consequences of faith and disbelief in the Hereafter.

translation: And how many a generation have We destroyed before them, who were better in possessions and appearance!
interpretation: This verse serves as a warning against being deceived by worldly wealth, material comfort, and outward beauty, as these were precisely the qualities possessed by earlier generations who were ultimately destroyed for their disbelief and arrogance. The Qur'an frequently uses the example of past civilizations—people who had greater resources, finer belongings, and more impressive appearances than the Quraysh or later audiences—to demonstrate that worldly prosperity is not a sign of divine favor or a guarantee of continued existence. The destruction of these earlier, materially superior peoples underscores the Qur'anic theme that worldly success without faith and righteousness holds no protective value, and that God's judgment operates independently of material standing. This serves as a direct rebuke to those who measure truth and favor by outward material success, reminding them that such things have failed to save previous nations from consequences of their disbelief.

translation: Say: 'Whoever is in error, let the Most Merciful prolong his respite, until, when they see what they are promised—either the punishment or the Hour—they will know who is in the worse position and weaker in forces.'
interpretation: This verse addresses the apparent worldly success and prosperity of disbelievers and those who reject the truth, which might lead some to mistakenly think that their error is validated or rewarded by their continued ease. The verse clarifies that this apparent prosperity is not a sign of divine favor but rather a form of respite (istidraj) granted by God's mercy—allowing them more time, which may lead to greater accountability rather than being a blessing. This extension of worldly fortune is temporary and deceptive. The verse then shifts to the ultimate reckoning: whether through worldly punishment or the Hour of Judgment, the disbelievers will eventually confront reality and realize that their seemingly favorable position was illusory. At that point, the true weakness of their situation—both in terms of spiritual standing ('worse in position') and actual power ('weaker in forces')—will become undeniably clear, reversing their mistaken assumption that worldly success indicated they were on the right path or had the upper hand against the believers.

translation: And Allah increases in guidance those who follow guidance. And the enduring good deeds are better in the sight of your Lord for reward and better for return.
interpretation: This verse establishes a spiritual principle of reciprocity: guidance is not a static gift but a dynamic, growing state that Allah expands for those who actively seek and follow it, suggesting that faith and righteousness compound over time through divine grace responding to sincere effort. The second part of the verse contrasts transient worldly achievements with 'al-baqiyat al-salihat' (the enduring righteous deeds)—often understood to include acts of worship, remembrance of Allah, and good deeds that leave lasting spiritual benefit. Unlike wealth, status, or worldly accomplishments that are temporary and will not follow a person beyond death, these righteous deeds persist and accumulate value in the eternal reckoning. The verse uses two measures of superiority—'thawaban' (reward) and 'maraddan' (return/outcome)—to emphasize that enduring good deeds surpass worldly gains both in immediate recompense from Allah and in their ultimate consequence in the afterlife, reinforcing the Quranic theme of prioritizing eternal spiritual investment over fleeting material pursuits.

translation: Have you seen the one who disbelieved in Our signs and said, 'I will surely be given wealth and children'?
interpretation: This verse refers to a specific disbeliever—traditionally identified as al-'As ibn Wa'il—who rejected the signs and revelations of Allah, yet arrogantly boasted that he would continue to receive wealth and offspring, implying also that he expected such blessings to continue even in a life after death, mocking the very resurrection he denied. The verse exposes the absurdity and arrogance of relying on worldly success as proof of divine favor or as a basis for denying accountability before God. It sets up a rebuke (in the verses that follow) demonstrating that such a person has no real knowledge of the unseen and that his claims are baseless presumption, not a promise from Allah. The passage ultimately warns against the error of equating material prosperity with spiritual truth or divine approval, and against the arrogance of assuming entitlement to Allah's favor while rejecting His signs.

translation: Has he looked into the unseen, or has he taken a covenant with the Most Merciful?
interpretation: This verse is a rhetorical rebuke directed at the disbeliever mentioned in the preceding verse, who arrogantly claimed that he would surely be granted wealth and children even in the Hereafter, mocking the believers' warnings about resurrection and judgment. God poses two sharp rhetorical questions exposing the baselessness of such a claim: has this person somehow gained access to the unseen realm (al-ghayb), which only God possesses knowledge of, to know with certainty what awaits him after death? Or has he secured some formal covenant or promise from the Most Merciful guaranteeing him such favor? Both questions expect a negative answer, highlighting the sheer audacity and irrationality of making definitive claims about unseen matters without any legitimate basis—neither through genuine knowledge nor through a binding divine promise. The verse underscores a broader Quranic theme: that no human possesses knowledge of the unseen except what God chooses to reveal, and that arrogant presumption about one's fate, especially when rooted in worldly success being mistaken as a sign of divine favor, is a form of self-deception. The rejection of this claim sets up the following verses where God affirms that such a person's words are being recorded and that his worldly possessions will not shield him from accountability.

translation: Nay! We shall record what he says, and We shall prolong for him the punishment at length.
interpretation: This verse responds to the arrogant disbeliever who boasts of future wealth and children, denying resurrection and divine accountability. God's firm rejection—'Kalla' (Nay!)—refutes his false claims. The verse affirms that every word spoken by such a person, including his blasphemous boasts and denial of truth, is being meticulously recorded. Rather than the increase he sought in worldly provision, he will instead receive an increase in punishment, extended and prolonged in the Hereafter. This illustrates a principle of divine justice: those who use God's blessings as a basis for arrogance and disbelief, rather than gratitude, will find that their punishment grows in proportion to their transgression. The verse also serves as a warning to all who speak carelessly against truth, reminding believers that nothing escapes divine record-keeping, and that worldly success is no guarantee of spiritual standing or ultimate salvation.

translation: And We will inherit from him what he says, and he will come to Us alone.
interpretation: This verse refers to the disbeliever who boasts of future wealth and children (mentioned in the preceding verses). God declares that whatever worldly possessions, status, or claims this person makes will ultimately be inherited by God alone—meaning all his wealth and achievements will pass away and return to God's dominion, as everything belongs to Him. The verse emphasizes the temporary nature of worldly boasting and material possessions. Furthermore, despite having accumulated wealth and perhaps surrounded himself with family, allies, and supporters in worldly life, this individual will arrive before God on the Day of Judgment utterly alone—stripped of all the possessions, companions, and status he once prided himself on. This underscores a central Quranic theme: that worldly wealth, lineage, and social connections cannot accompany a person into the afterlife or serve as a defense before God. Each soul faces judgment in solitude, bearing only its deeds, demonstrating the ultimate insignificance of material boasting in the face of divine accountability.

translation: And they have taken besides Allah [other] deities that they might be for them a source of honor/strength.
interpretation: This verse exposes the flawed reasoning of the polytheists who worshipped idols, ancestors, or other beings instead of God, believing these entities would grant them status, protection, or intercession before God. The verse highlights a deep irony: rather than seeking honor and strength through reliance on the one true source of power, they placed their trust in powerless, man-made objects or beings. The broader context in the surah reveals that these false deities will ultimately fail them, disowning their worshippers and becoming a source of disgrace rather than honor on the Day of Judgment. The verse serves as a critique of misplaced trust and the human tendency to seek validation, power, or security through false means rather than through sincere devotion to God, who alone possesses true honor ('izzah) and the ability to bestow it upon His servants.

translation: Nay! They will deny their worship, and they will become opponents against them.
interpretation: This verse follows the Qur'an's critique of those who take other deities besides God hoping they will bring them honor or intercession (19:81). It declares that on the Day of Judgment, these false objects of worship—whether idols, angels, or other beings wrongly venerated—will utterly disown the worship directed at them, denying any relationship with their worshippers. Far from interceding on their behalf, these very beings will turn into adversaries, testifying against those who worshipped them and contributing to their condemnation. The verse underscores the futility and danger of shirk (associating partners with God): the objects of misplaced devotion offer no real power or protection, and in the end will reverse roles, becoming accusers rather than saviors. This serves as a stark warning about the ultimate powerlessness of anything worshipped besides God and the self-defeating nature of such devotion.

translation: Do you not see that We have sent the devils upon the disbelievers, inciting them to commotion (provoking them to sin with vehement incitement)?
interpretation: This verse illustrates a divine law of cause and effect: when people reject faith and turn away from God's guidance, they are left spiritually unguarded and become susceptible to the whisperings and incitements of devils (shayatin). The devils do not have forced control over them, but rather they stir, agitate, and provoke the disbelievers, intensifying their rebellion, sin, and heedlessness. This can be understood as a natural consequence of disbelief - rejecting divine guidance opens one up to being driven by satanic impulses that push a person further into transgression, restlessness, and moral corruption. It serves as a warning that the absence of faith is not a neutral state but one that invites active spiritual harm and incitement toward evil.

translation: So do not be hasty against them; We are only counting out for them a count [of days].
interpretation: This verse addresses the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him), consoling him regarding the disbelievers who mocked and opposed him. God instructs him not to be impatient for their punishment, assuring him that divine justice operates on a precise and measured timeline. The phrase 'counting out for them a count' conveys that every moment of their respite, every breath they take, and every day that passes is being meticulously recorded and numbered by God. This serves as a reminder that God's delay in punishing wrongdoers is not negligence but rather a deliberate withholding of judgment until the appointed time, allowing the full measure of their deeds to be completed before reckoning. It reflects the broader Quranic theme that divine timing is perfect and that apparent delays in justice should not be mistaken for divine indifference, but rather should be approached with patience and trust in God's ultimate plan and wisdom.

translation: On the Day We will gather the righteous to the Most Merciful as a delegation of honor.
interpretation: This verse depicts the Day of Judgment not as a moment of fear for the righteous, but as a dignified arrival—like honored guests or envoys (wafd) received by a noble host. The imagery contrasts sharply with the fate of the wicked described in the following verses, who will be driven to Hell like thirsty, degraded beasts. Here, the muttaqeen (those mindful of God) are portrayed as being escorted with honor and ceremony into the presence of the Most Merciful, reflecting the Quranic theme that true nobility and reward come from piety rather than worldly status. The term 'wafd' evokes the image of a delegation of dignitaries approaching a king, suggesting that the righteous will be welcomed with hospitality and respect, reversing earthly hierarchies where believers may have been marginalized or oppressed.

translation: And We shall drive the guilty (criminals/sinners) to Hell, like a thirsty herd driven to water.
interpretation: This verse draws on the image of a herd of animals being driven toward a watering place, but inverts its ordinary comfort: here the destination is not refreshment but Hellfire. The word 'wirdan' evokes creatures who are thirsty and compelled, without will of their own, to move toward what they expect will quench their need. By applying this to the guilty on the Day of Judgment, the Qur'an conveys their utter helplessness and lack of control over their fate—they are herded, not walking by choice, toward their doom. This stands in stark contrast to the preceding description of the righteous, who are honored and welcomed into Paradise as distinguished guests. The juxtaposition underscores a central Qur'anic theme: those who lived in arrogance and rejection of truth will, in the end, be reduced to a state of degradation and compulsion, driven like beasts to their punishment, while those who lived in humility and faith will be elevated and received with honor. The imagery emphasizes that worldly power and defiance count for nothing before divine justice; ultimate control lies with God alone, who determines the fate of every soul according to its deeds.

translation: They have no power of intercession, except for those who have taken a covenant with the Most Merciful.
interpretation: This verse addresses the false beliefs of polytheists who relied on idols, angels, or other beings to intercede for them before God without any basis. It establishes that intercession on the Day of Judgment is not an automatic right possessed by any being, but a privilege granted only to those who have established a covenant with God—understood by most commentators as faith in His oneness (tawhid), righteous deeds, and sincere devotion. This 'covenant' refers to the testimony of faith and the commitment to worship God alone, as exemplified by prophets, righteous believers, and those permitted by God to intercede, such as angels or prophets who intercede only with His permission and for those who qualify through their faith. The verse underscores the theological principle that all power, including the power to intercede, belongs solely to God, and any intercession that occurs happens only through His will and for those who have earned it through genuine faith and righteousness.

translation: And they say, 'The Most Merciful has taken a son.'
interpretation: This verse addresses a grave theological claim made by various groups contemporary to the Qur'anic revelation—including certain Arab polytheists who considered angels to be daughters of God, Christians who affirmed Jesus as the son of God, and Jews who in some contexts referred to Ezra in filial terms. The verse opens a passage that sharply refutes this assertion as a fundamental misunderstanding of divine nature. The term 'ittakhadha' (took/adopted) implies a deliberate act of acquiring something that was not inherently possessed, which the Qur'an uses to highlight the absurdity of attributing a son to God—an act that would suggest need, physicality, or limitation, all of which are incompatible with the Qur'anic conception of Allah as absolutely transcendent, self-sufficient (As-Samad), and beyond the categories of begetting or being begotten. This verse sets up the subsequent verses' forceful denunciation, emphasizing tawhid (the oneness of God) and rejecting anthropomorphic or mythological conceptions of divinity that were prevalent in surrounding religious traditions.

translation: You have certainly come forth with a monstrous thing.
interpretation: This verse addresses those who claim that the Most Merciful has taken a son (a child or offspring), condemning this assertion as an enormity. The context in Surah Maryam describes the severity of such a claim—attributing a son to Allah—as so grave that it is depicted as nearly causing the heavens to be torn apart, the earth to split, and the mountains to collapse in ruin (as described in the following verses). The word 'إدًّا' (idda) conveys something monstrous, hideous, or utterly unacceptable, emphasizing the absolute transcendence of Allah above having offspring, a concept fundamentally incompatible with pure monotheism (tawhid). This verse serves as a powerful rebuke to Christians and others who ascribe a son to God, underscoring that such a claim violates the very nature of divine oneness and perfection, and represents one of the gravest theological errors a person can make in reference to the Creator.

translation: The heavens are almost torn apart thereby, and the earth is split asunder, and the mountains fall down in ruins —
interpretation: This verse depicts the cosmic magnitude of divine displeasure at the claim that God has taken a son, as mentioned in the preceding verses. The imagery of the heavens nearly rupturing, the earth splitting, and mountains collapsing is not meant literally but serves as a rhetorical device to convey the enormity and gravity of this theological error. The Qur'an employs this dramatic cosmic reaction to emphasize that attributing offspring to God contradicts His absolute transcendence and oneness (tawhid), suggesting that even inanimate creation, in its submission to divine order, would recoil from such a monstrous claim about its Creator. The passage underscores that ascribing partners or progeny to God is not a minor error but a fundamental violation of the created order's inherent recognition of divine unity, highlighting the seriousness with which the Qur'an treats shirk (associating partners with God) in its various forms, including the Christian doctrine of divine sonship and other similar claims found among pre-Islamic Arabian beliefs about angels being daughters of God.

translation: Because they attributed to the Most Merciful a son.
interpretation: This verse refers to the claim made by certain groups—whether Christians regarding Jesus, or Arab polytheists who called angels 'daughters of God'—that God has offspring. The Qur'an presents this as a grave transgression because it ascribes a human-like biological or relational attribute to God, who is utterly transcendent and self-sufficient (samad), without need of progeny or partners. The preceding and following verses describe the cosmic gravity of this claim, stating that the heavens would nearly be torn apart, the earth split asunder, and the mountains fall down in ruin at such an assertion. This dramatic imagery underscores that attributing a son to God violates the fundamental nature of divine oneness (tawhid) and is considered a cosmic affront to the very order of creation, not merely a theological error but a rupture in the metaphysical fabric that sustains existence.

translation: It is not befitting the Most Merciful that He should take a son.
interpretation: This verse asserts the absolute transcendence and uniqueness of God (Allah), rejecting the notion of divine offspring. It directly refutes theological claims—such as those found in certain Christian doctrines regarding Jesus as the 'Son of God'—by emphasizing that God is self-sufficient, eternal, and utterly unlike His creation. The concept of begetting or being begotten implies physical, temporal, or relational limitations that are incompatible with God's nature as the Most Merciful (al-Rahman), who is beyond need, division, or partnership. This verse reinforces the core Islamic principle of tawhid (the oneness of God), affirming that God's sovereignty and majesty cannot be shared or diminished by attributing to Him a son, as such an attribution would imply imperfection, dependency, or anthropomorphic qualities unbefitting the Creator of all things.

translation: There is none in the heavens and the earth but that he comes to the Most Merciful as a servant.
interpretation: This verse asserts the absolute sovereignty of God over all creation, emphasizing that every being—angels, humans, jinn, and all creatures—exists in a state of servitude and submission before the Divine. It serves as a rebuke to those who claimed God had a son or partners, as mentioned in the preceding verses of Surah Maryam, by affirming that even the highest beings in creation, far from being divine offspring or associates of God, are themselves humble servants who will stand before Him. The universality of the statement—encompassing everyone 'in the heavens and the earth'—underscores the theological principle of tawhid (the oneness of God), leaving no room for intermediaries or beings who share in God's divine status. It also carries an eschatological dimension, pointing toward the Day of Judgment when all creation will be gathered in total submission before their Creator, stripped of any worldly pretensions to power or divinity.

translation: He has certainly counted them and numbered them precisely.
interpretation: This verse refers to God's complete and exact knowledge of every created being—often understood in context as referring to all beings who will come before Him on the Day of Judgment, including those who claim offspring or partners for God (as in the preceding verses about denying that God has a son). The emphasis on 'counted' and 'numbered precisely' underscores divine omniscience: nothing escapes God's record, no soul is overlooked, and every individual—however insignificant they may seem in the vastness of creation—is known and accounted for by their Creator. This serves as a reminder that human beings cannot hide in anonymity before God, and that ultimate accountability is inescapable, reinforcing the theme of divine power and justice that runs through the surah.

translation: And each one of them will come to Him on the Day of Resurrection, alone.
interpretation: This verse concludes a passage refuting the claim that God has taken a son—whether angels, Jesus, or any other being venerated as divine offspring. It emphasizes that despite whatever status, following, or power anyone held in this worldly life, on the Day of Judgment every single being—without exception, regardless of rank—will stand before God utterly alone, stripped of titles, companions, wealth, intercessors, and worldly supports. The verse underscores radical individual accountability: no one can rely on lineage, group identity, or the intercession of those they worshipped besides God. It dismantles the notion of divine sonship by stressing that even those claimed as 'children of God' will themselves be subject to the same solitary reckoning as every other creature, proving their creaturely status rather than any shared divinity with the Creator.

translation: Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds - the Most Merciful will appoint for them affection (love).
interpretation: This verse promises that true faith accompanied by righteous action does not go unnoticed or unrewarded, even in ways that are not always materially visible. Allah, through His quality as Ar-Rahman (the Most Merciful), will place genuine love and goodwill for the believers in the hearts of others - both among people and, according to many commentators, within the celestial realm itself, including the angels. This is a divine assurance that sincerity and good deeds generate a natural, almost spiritual magnetism: people are drawn to those who embody faith and righteousness, often without any deliberate effort on the believer's part to seek popularity or approval. It also serves as a subtle rebuke to worldly methods of seeking love or influence through manipulation, wealth, or status - true and lasting affection, the verse suggests, is a gift from God that flows from internal righteousness rather than external striving. This can be understood as part of a broader Quranic theme where outward struggles, trials, or seeming obscurity for the sake of faith are eventually met with unexpected forms of honor, acceptance, or love, reinforcing trust in divine wisdom and timing.

translation: So We have only made it [the Qur'an] easy in your own tongue [O Muhammad], that you may give glad tidings thereby to the righteous (al-muttaqin), and warn thereby a people given to stubborn hostility (qawman luddan).
interpretation: This verse articulates the dual rhetorical purpose of revelation and the wisdom behind its linguistic accessibility.
