The verse concludes by affirming that righteousness was granted to all of them—Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob—establishing that prophethood and moral integrity go hand in hand, and that righteousness is itself a divine gift bestowed upon the chosen, not merely a human achievement. This reflects a broader Quranic theme of the righteous lineage of prophets, where each generation is shown to carry forward the legacy of faith and moral uprightness as a continuation of God's covenant and favor.

translation: And We made them leaders guiding by Our command, and We inspired to them the doing of good deeds, the establishment of prayer, and the giving of zakah; and they were worshippers of Us alone.
interpretation: This verse, referring to the prophets of the lineage of Abraham, establishes the principle that true spiritual leadership (imamah) is granted by divine command and is inseparably linked to righteous action rather than mere status or claim. The leaders described here are not self-appointed; they guide others only through God's authority, emphasizing that legitimate guidance in religion flows from divine sanction. The pairing of practical virtues—doing good, maintaining prayer, and giving charity—with sincere worship illustrates that faith in Islam is holistic: inward devotion to God must manifest in outward ethical and social conduct. Their worship was exclusive and sincere ('to Us alone'), underscoring that true leadership and guidance are rooted in pure monotheism (tawhid), free from the corruption of serving other than God. This verse thus sets a model for leadership in faith communities, one grounded in divine inspiration, moral integrity, and consistent devotional practice.

translation: And to Lot We gave judgment and knowledge, and We saved him from the city that was committing wicked deeds. Indeed, they were a people of evil, defiantly disobedient.
interpretation: This verse affirms that Lot was granted wisdom and sound knowledge by God, qualities that equipped him to guide his people righteously, though they rejected his counsel. His deliverance from the doomed city underscores a recurring Qur'anic principle: that God preserves the righteous even amid the destruction of corrupt societies. The people's wickedness is described not as an isolated act but as an entrenched communal practice, and their condemnation as 'fasiqin' (defiantly disobedient) emphasizes that their punishment stemmed from willful, persistent transgression rather than mere error. The passage serves as both a vindication of Lot's prophetic integrity and a warning about the fate of societies that institutionalize moral corruption.

translation: And We admitted him into Our mercy; indeed, he was among the righteous.
interpretation: This verse refers to Prophet Lut (Lot), peace be upon him, following his deliverance from the destruction that befell his sinful people. It affirms that divine mercy is granted to those who maintain righteousness and steadfastness in faith even amid moral corruption surrounding them. The phrase 'admitted him into Our mercy' signifies not merely physical rescue but a deeper spiritual embrace—God's protection, honor, and favor bestowed upon him because of his righteous character. This serves as a reassurance to believers that steadfast righteousness, even in the face of overwhelming societal wrongdoing, will ultimately be recognized and rewarded by God's encompassing mercy.

translation: And [remember] Noah, when he called out [to Us] before, so We responded to him and saved him and his family from the great calamity.
interpretation: This verse refers to Prophet Noah's supplication to God after enduring centuries of rejection and ridicule from his people, who persisted in disbelief and idolatry despite his persistent calls to righteousness. 'Before' indicates that his plea preceded those of other prophets mentioned in this chapter, marking him as an early exemplar of unwavering faith under extreme hardship. The 'great calamity' refers to the catastrophic flood sent as both punishment for his people's obstinate rejection and vindication for Noah's long-suffering patience. God's response was not immediate but came after Noah had exhausted conventional means of guidance, teaching that divine rescue arrives for those who maintain faith and perseverance through trials, even when deliverance seems delayed. The salvation of Noah 'and his family' (excluding his disbelieving son, as detailed elsewhere in the Quran) underscores that ultimate salvation is tied to faith and righteousness rather than mere blood relation, while also demonstrating God's mercy in preserving a righteous remnant to continue humanity's story after judgment fell upon the corrupt civilization.

translation: And We helped him against the people who denied Our signs. Indeed, they were a people of evil, so We drowned them, all together.
interpretation: This verse refers to Prophet Nuh (Noah) and the divine support granted to him against his disbelieving people who rejected his message and the signs of God. The description of them as 'a people of evil' signifies not merely their disbelief but their entrenched moral corruption, persistent arrogance, and refusal to heed repeated warnings over a very long period of time. The drowning of 'all together' underscores the totality of divine judgment—none of the wrongdoers were spared, emphasizing that when a community collectively persists in rejecting truth and sinks into corruption despite sustained warning and opportunity to repent, divine justice ultimately prevails comprehensively rather than selectively. The verse also serves as a broader theological statement on the nature of prophetic struggle: that God's help (nasr) for His messengers is not merely spiritual but can manifest as decisive historical intervention, vindicating the prophet and his followers while serving as a sign and warning for later generations about the consequences of collective moral failure and rejection of guidance.

translation: And [mention] David and Solomon, when they gave judgment concerning the field, when the sheep of the people strayed and grazed therein by night, and We were witnesses to their judgment.
interpretation: This verse refers to a dispute brought before Prophets David and Solomon involving a farmer whose crop had been destroyed by a neighbor's sheep that had wandered into his field at night. David ruled that the sheep should be given to the farmer as compensation for the loss of his crop, since the value of the sheep was deemed equivalent to the damage done. Solomon, however, proposed an alternative solution: that the sheep's owner should tend the ruined field until it was restored to its former state, while the farmer would benefit from the milk, wool, and offspring of the sheep in the meantime; once the field was restored, the sheep would be returned to their owner and the farmer would receive his field back fully productive. This account illustrates that both father and son were divinely guided and inspired with wisdom and knowledge, yet their judgments could differ based on the depth of insight each possessed, showing that revelation does not preclude the exercise of reasoned, practical judgment (ijtihad) in worldly affairs. Solomon's solution, which more equitably restored both parties to their original state rather than simply transferring ownership, demonstrates a more refined and comprehensive form of justice—one that considers restitution and long-term fairness rather than a strict, immediate equivalence. Importantly, God's declaration that He was a witness to their judgment affirms that even in matters of human legal reasoning, divine oversight and approval validate the pursuit of just solutions through wisdom, and it establishes a precedent for juristic reasoning (ijtihad) in Islamic law, where different qualified scholars may arrive at different, yet equally valid, judgments based on the same set of facts.

translation: So We made Solomon understand it, and to each of them We gave judgment and knowledge. And We subjected the mountains to glorify [Us] along with David, and the birds as well; and it was We who did that.
interpretation: This verse follows the account of David and Solomon adjudicating a dispute over a field damaged by sheep. While both were granted wisdom and knowledge, Solomon was given a deeper, more nuanced understanding of the specific case, showing that even among prophets endowed with divine knowledge, there are gradations of insight granted by God according to His will. The mention of the mountains and birds glorifying God alongside David highlights a miraculous sign of his prophethood—nature itself was made to join him in worship, demonstrating that all creation is inherently oriented toward glorifying its Creator and can be made to do so in extraordinary ways at God's command. The closing phrase 'We were doing this' underscores that these phenomena were not incidental but deliberate acts of divine power, reinforcing the theme that all authority, knowledge, and control over creation ultimately belong to God alone, who distributes gifts and miracles among His prophets as He wills.

translation: And We taught him the making of coats of armor [mail] for you, to protect you from your [mutual] violence. So are you grateful?
interpretation: This verse refers to Prophet David (Dawud), to whom God taught the craft of fashioning body armor from iron. The 'bas' (violence/warfare) mentioned reflects the reality of human conflict, and the armor represents a divinely-inspired technology given for protection and preservation of life amid such conflict. The verse highlights several theological points: that beneficial knowledge and craftsmanship originate from God as a form of revelation or inspiration, even practical and technical skills; that such gifts are meant to serve humanity's collective welfare, not just the individual prophet's benefit; and the rhetorical question at the end—'will you then be grateful?'—serves as a reminder that human ingenuity and technological progress are ultimately divine blessings requiring gratitude rather than achievements to be attributed solely to human effort or pride. It also subtly acknowledges the tragic persistence of human conflict (baas) even as God provides means to mitigate its harm, suggesting a relationship between divine providence and human responsibility to use given gifts wisely and thankfully.

translation: And to Solomon [We subjected] the wind, blowing forcefully, running by his command toward the land which We had blessed. And We are ever, of all things, Knowing.
interpretation: This verse highlights one of the miraculous gifts bestowed upon Prophet Solomon (Sulayman) as a sign of divine favor and prophethood: mastery over the wind itself. The 'land which We had blessed' is traditionally understood to refer to Greater Syria (the Levant), a region noted elsewhere in the Qur'an for its blessedness. The wind's obedience to Solomon's command, carrying him and his forces swiftly to this land, demonstrates God's power to subject the forces of nature to His chosen servants, illustrating that true dominion belongs to God, who merely lends portions of it to whom He wills. The closing phrase, 'We are ever, of all things, Knowing,' reinforces that such extraordinary gifts are not random but are granted through God's comprehensive knowledge and wisdom. This serves as a reminder of God's omnipotence over creation, showing that even the most elemental forces—wind, in this case—operate under divine command. It also reflects the broader Qur'anic theme of prophets being granted unique abilities not as personal achievements but as signs of God's mercy and as proofs of their prophetic missions, meant to strengthen faith and demonstrate that all power ultimately originates from God alone.

translation: And among the devils were those who dived for him and performed tasks beyond that; and We were watchful over them.
interpretation: This verse refers to the jinn and devils that God subjected to the service of Prophet Solomon (Sulayman), granting him dominion over supernatural forces as a sign of his unique prophethood and the extraordinary favor bestowed upon him. The diving mentioned refers to the jinn retrieving pearls and treasures from the sea, while the other tasks likely included construction, craftsmanship, and other labors beyond human capability, as described elsewhere in the Qur'an regarding Solomon's kingdom. The closing phrase, 'We were watchful over them,' emphasizes that despite granting Solomon this extraordinary power over these rebellious spiritual beings, God remained in ultimate control, preventing them from causing harm or escaping their assigned duties. This serves as a reminder that all power, even the miraculous command over jinn, operates within divine oversight and is never beyond God's watchful authority.

translation: And [mention] Job, when he called out to his Lord, 'Indeed, adversity has touched me, and You are the Most Merciful of the merciful.'
interpretation: This verse recounts the trial of the Prophet Job (Ayyub), who endured prolonged illness, loss, and hardship with patience. His supplication is notable for its brevity, humility, and restraint—he does not demand relief or list his sufferings in detail, but simply states his condition and appeals to God's mercy as the defining attribute of the Divine. This models the proper etiquette of supplication in times of distress: acknowledging one's affliction honestly before God while placing complete trust in His compassion rather than one's own merit or specific requests. The verse teaches that true patience (sabr) is not the suppression of feeling or the denial of pain, but the channeling of one's pain toward God in trust and hope. Job's story becomes a paradigm for believers facing illness or calamity, showing that steadfast faith combined with sincere, humble prayer leads to divine relief, as the verses that follow confirm when God answers his call and restores him.

translation: So We responded to him and removed the affliction that was upon him, and We gave him his family and the like thereof along with them, as a mercy from Us and a reminder for the worshippers.
interpretation: This verse refers to the Prophet Ayyub (Job), who endured prolonged suffering—illness, loss of family, and hardship—with patience and unwavering faith in God. When he called upon God in his distress, God answered his supplication, removed his affliction, and restored to him his family, doubling his blessings as a sign of divine mercy. The verse emphasizes several key theological points: first, that sincere supplication to God is always heard, especially from those who remain patient and steadfast during trials; second, that God's mercy can restore and even exceed what was lost, demonstrating His power over all circumstances; and third, that this story serves as a 'reminder for the worshippers'—meaning it is meant to instruct and inspire believers to maintain faith and patience during their own trials, trusting that God's mercy is ever-present and that hardship can be followed by relief and even greater blessings. The story of Ayyub is often cited as the ultimate example of patience (sabr) in the Qur'an, and this verse specifically highlights the resolution of his trial as proof of God's responsiveness to the prayers of the faithful.

translation: And [mention] Ishmael, Idris, and Dhul-Kifl; all were among the steadfast.
interpretation: This verse continues a sequence in Surah al-Anbiya in which God recalls various prophets to remind the Prophet Muhammad and the believers of a common virtue uniting them: sabr, steadfast patience and perseverance in adversity. Ishmael, Idris, and Dhul-Kifl are mentioned together, not for lengthy narratives of their individual trials as with other prophets in the surah, but simply to affirm that they, too, endured hardship with patience and trust in God. This brevity itself carries meaning: it suggests that patience is the defining quality that qualifies one to be counted among God's chosen servants, regardless of the specific nature of each prophet's trial. By grouping these three figures together under the single attribute of steadfastness, the verse teaches that the essence of prophethood and righteousness lies not in the particulars of one's hardships but in the quality of one's response to them—enduring faithfully without complaint or despair. For the listener, this serves as both comfort and instruction: whatever difficulty one faces, the path of the righteous predecessors was one of patient perseverance, and this is presented as a timeless model for all who seek to walk in their footsteps.

translation: And We admitted them into Our mercy. Indeed, they were among the righteous.
interpretation: This verse concludes a passage praising specific prophets noted for their patience and steadfastness, affirming that divine mercy is the ultimate reward for righteousness. It teaches that entry into God's mercy is not arbitrary but is earned through sustained moral and spiritual excellence—being 'of the righteous' describes a settled character, not a single act. The verse also reflects a recurring Qur'anic pattern: after recounting the trials and virtues of prophets, God affirms their honored status as a model for believers, showing that mercy and righteousness are intertwined, and that those who embody patience, humility, and devotion are drawn close to God's grace as an enduring state rather than a momentary gift.

translation: And [mention] the Man of the Fish (Dhun-Nun, i.e., Jonah/Yunus), when he departed in anger and thought that We would not restrict/straiten him. Then he cried out in the darknesses: 'There is no deity except You; exalted are You above all imperfection. Indeed, I have been among the wrongdoers.'
interpretation: This verse recounts the story of Prophet Yunus (Jonah), who left his people in anger and frustration without waiting for God's command, believing he would face no consequence for this departure. He ended up swallowed by a great fish and found himself in a triple darkness—the darkness of the sea, the darkness of the fish's belly, and the darkness of night. In this utterly helpless state, he turned to God in sincere repentance, acknowledging God's absolute oneness and his own wrongdoing. This verse illustrates that true relief and salvation come only through humble acknowledgment of one's faults and complete reliance on God's mercy, no matter how dire or hopeless the circumstances. It teaches that even prophets can err, but what distinguishes the righteous is their immediate turn to sincere repentance (tawbah) and their recognition of God's transcendence and their own human limitations.

translation: So We responded to him and saved him from the distress. And thus do We save the believers.
interpretation: This verse refers to Prophet Yunus (Jonah), who, after being swallowed by the whale as a consequence of leaving his people without divine permission, called upon God in the depths of darkness, acknowledging His glory and his own wrongdoing. God answered his sincere supplication and delivered him from that overwhelming distress. The verse then generalizes this specific act of divine mercy into a universal principle: this is how God characteristically rescues those who have true faith when they turn to Him in genuine repentance and humility during times of hardship. It underscores the themes of divine mercy, the power of sincere prayer, and the assurance that faith coupled with repentance leads to deliverance from affliction, serving as a model of hope for all believers facing their own trials.

translation: And Zachariah, when he called out to his Lord, 'My Lord, leave me not childless, though You are the best of inheritors.'
interpretation: This verse recalls the prophet Zachariah's intimate and earnest supplication to God, born from his longing for an heir who would continue his mission of guidance and worship after him. His plea 'leave me not without offspring' reflects a deeply human concern, yet it is immediately tempered by his acknowledgment that 'You are the best of inheritors'—a recognition that God's will and provision surpass any human lineage, since ultimately all things return to and are inherited by God alone. This moment teaches that even prophets express personal hopes and vulnerabilities before God, and that true faith lies in asking sincerely while submitting to divine wisdom, trusting that whatever God provides or withholds is rooted in a greater, all-encompassing care and authority. The verse also sets the stage for the miraculous granting of his son, Yahya (John), demonstrating God's power to answer prayers in ways beyond ordinary expectation, especially in old age or seemingly hopeless circumstances.

translation: So We responded to him, and We bestowed upon him Yahya, and We cured his wife [of barrenness] for him. Indeed, they used to hasten to good deeds and supplicate Us in hope and fear, and they were to Us humbly submissive.
interpretation: This verse concludes the account of the Prophet Zakariya's supplication for a righteous heir despite his old age and his wife's barrenness. God's response—granting him Yahya (John) and restoring his wife's fertility—illustrates that divine power transcends natural limitations when answering sincere prayer. The verse then generalizes beyond Zakariya to describe the character of the prophets as a class: they competed eagerly in righteous deeds, called upon God balancing hope in His mercy with fear of His justice (raghaban wa rahaban), and maintained deep humility and submission before Him. This pairing of hope and fear is presented as the ideal spiritual posture of the believer—neither so confident as to become complacent nor so fearful as to despair of God's mercy—while khushu' (humble submissiveness) is marked as the inner disposition that validates outward righteous action and prayer.

translation: And she who guarded her chastity, so We breathed into her of Our spirit, and We made her and her son a sign for all the worlds.
interpretation: This verse refers to Mary (Maryam), mother of Jesus (Isa), praising her for preserving her chastity and purity. Because of her devotion, God honored her with a miraculous conception through His command ('We breathed into her of Our spirit'), without any human father involved. The verse emphasizes that both Mary and her son Jesus were made as a sign ('ayah') for all of humanity and all peoples throughout time, demonstrating God's power to create life in extraordinary ways and serving as a testament to divine omnipotence. This miraculous birth stands as proof that God's will transcends the normal laws of nature, and it is presented as a universal sign meant to guide and inspire reflection among all nations, not just a particular community.

translation: Indeed, this [religion/community] of yours is one religion/community, and I am your Lord, so worship Me.
interpretation: This verse affirms the fundamental unity of true religion and the community of believers across time, declaring that all the prophets and their followers belonged essentially to one single faith community founded on the worship of the one God. Despite the diversity of peoples, languages, laws, and historical circumstances among the various prophetic communities (ummah), the core message delivered by every messenger was identical: the oneness of God (tawhid) and the obligation to worship Him alone. The verse thus serves as a corrective to religious sectarianism and division, reminding humanity that differences introduced later—through human interpretation, cultural accretion, or deliberate schism—are deviations from an original, unified divine guidance. It calls believers back to this essential unity, grounding communal identity not in tribal, ethnic, or historical particularity, but in shared submission to and worship of the single Lord who created and sustains them all.

translation: And they split up their affair [i.e., matter of religion] among themselves into sects; each [group] to Us will return.
interpretation: This verse addresses the fragmentation of the religious community—originally united in the worship of the One God as conveyed by all the prophets—into divided sects and factions, each following its own path and interpretation, often to the point of mutual hostility. Despite this human division and disagreement, the verse offers a powerful reminder that ultimate accountability rests with God alone: every faction and every individual will be returned to Him for judgment. This serves both as a warning against sectarianism and schism within the faith community, and as reassurance that God, not human factionalism, will be the final arbiter of truth and falsehood. It emphasizes that the unity of true religion transcends the divisions created by people, and that these divisions will be resolved and judged justly before God on the Last Day.

translation: So whoever does righteous deeds while being a believer - there will be no denial of his effort, and indeed, We are recording it for him.
interpretation: This verse establishes a foundational principle of divine justice: that faith and righteous action together guarantee recognition and reward from God, with nothing of one's good deeds ever being lost, ignored, or unjustly discounted. The pairing of belief (iman) with good works (salihat) indicates that the two are interdependent in Islamic theology—sincere faith without action is incomplete, just as action without faith lacks its proper foundation and ultimate value. The phrase 'no denial of his effort' uses the word kufran, which shares a root with kufr (disbelief), creating a subtle linguistic connection suggesting that just as disbelief rejects God's truth, God will never reject or negate the sincere efforts of the believer. The verse also emphasizes divine omniscience and the meticulous recording of human deeds, reassuring believers that no act of goodness, however small or unnoticed by others, escapes God's awareness or goes unrewarded. This serves as both a comfort to those who strive sincerely in faith and a motivation to maintain consistent righteous action, knowing that ultimate justice and recognition rest with God who keeps perfect account of all things.

translation: And it is forbidden (decreed impossible) for a city which We have destroyed that they will return.
interpretation: This verse responds to those who deny bodily resurrection by affirming its certainty through a subtle grammatical device. Many classical commentators explain that the negative particle 'la' here functions as an emphatic rather than a true negation (laa al-za'idah), so the verse's deeper meaning is the reverse of its literal surface reading: it is decreed/certain for every community that We have destroyed that they will indeed return to Us. In other words, no people annihilated by divine judgment—no matter how utterly destroyed or long vanished—are exempt from being resurrected and brought back for reckoning on the Day of Judgment. The verse thus serves as a rhetorical proof against skeptics who argue that resurrection is impossible once a body has decayed or a civilization has vanished: if even the most thoroughly destroyed nations of the past must return before God, then resurrection is an inescapable law applying to all of creation, not a far-fetched claim reserved for the living alone.

translation: Until, when Gog and Magog are let loose, and they come swiftly down from every highland.
interpretation: This verse refers to one of the major signs of the approach of the Day of Judgment: the release of Gog and Magog (Ya'juj and Ma'juj), a destructive force that had been held back behind a barrier built by Dhul-Qarnayn, as described earlier in Surah Al-Kahf. Their sudden emergence 'from every elevation' or 'from every mound' signifies their overwhelming number and the speed and chaos with which they spread across the earth, pouring forth from all directions without obstruction. Classical exegetes understand this as a literal eschatological event signaling that the barrier restraining them has been breached, either through divine decree or the natural crumbling of the barrier over time, marking the nearing of the Hour. The verse conveys an atmosphere of inevitability and impending upheaval, emphasizing that once this restraint is lifted, the resulting turmoil will be rapid and uncontainable, serving as a stark reminder to humanity that the appointed signs of the Last Day, however delayed, will surely come to pass when God wills it.

translation: And the true promise has drawn near; then behold, the eyes of those who disbelieved are staring in fright, [and they say]: 'O woe to us! We were indeed heedless of this; nay, we were wrongdoers.'
interpretation: This verse describes the imminent arrival of the Day of Judgment, 'the true promise,' which had been repeatedly warned about but dismissed by disbelievers. The sudden terror in their fixed, staring eyes conveys the shock of confronting a reality they had denied. Their cry of 'woe' and admission of heedlessness reveals a moment of too-late realization. Significantly, they correct themselves—moving from claiming mere 'heedlessness' (ghaflah), which might suggest innocent forgetfulness, to confessing they were actual 'wrongdoers' (zalimeen), acknowledging willful injustice and rejection of truth rather than simple oversight. This self-correction underscores the Qur'anic theme that disbelief is not innocent ignorance but a culpable turning away from clear signs, and that on the Day of Reckoning, such rationalizations collapse under the weight of truth.

translation: Indeed, you [disbelievers] and whatever you worship besides Allah are the firewood of Hell; you will come to it.
interpretation: This verse was revealed in response to the polytheists of Mecca who worshipped idols alongside Allah. It serves as a stern rebuke, declaring that both the idolaters and the false deities they venerate—whether carved idols, celestial bodies, or other objects of worship—will together become fuel for Hellfire. The verse dismantles the polytheists' assumption that their idols could intercede for or protect them; instead, these very objects of misplaced devotion will share in the punishment, becoming kindling for the fire. The phrase 'you will come to it' emphasizes the inevitability of this fate for those who persist in associating partners with Allah, underscoring the Quranic theme that worship directed at anything other than the one true God is ultimately futile and leads to ruin. This verse specifically excludes righteous figures like Jesus or angels who were worshipped by some without their consent, as clarified in subsequent verses, distinguishing between willing false deities and those wrongly venerated against their will.

translation: If these had been gods, they would not have come to it (Hell), but all of them will abide therein forever.
interpretation: This verse addresses the polytheists who worshipped idols and false deities alongside Allah. It presents a logical refutation of their belief: if the idols and false gods they worshipped truly possessed any divine power or status, they would not be cast into Hell alongside their worshippers. The fact that both the false objects of worship and those who worshipped them will dwell in Hell together proves the falsity of these deities. This serves as a rhetorical argument demonstrating that anything other than Allah that is worshipped is powerless to save itself, let alone intercede for its followers, and thus exposes the futility and error of associating partners with Allah (shirk). The eternal nature of this punishment underscores the gravity of this theological error in Islamic teaching.

translation: For them therein is sighing (groaning), and therein they do not hear.
interpretation: This verse describes the state of the disbelievers in Hellfire, portraying their suffering through two sensory deprivations and afflictions. The 'zafeer' (sighing or groaning) refers to a deep, anguished sound drawn from the depths of the chest, similar to the braying of a donkey, symbolizing extreme distress and torment. The phrase 'they do not hear' indicates a form of sensory isolation—despite the chaos and torment surrounding them, they are cut off from any sound that might bring comfort, explanation, or connection to others. This could suggest that their suffering is intensely personal and isolating; even amid the collective punishment, each soul experiences profound loneliness, unable to hear words of mercy, the pleas of others, or anything that might ease their anguish. It underscores the totality of their separation from divine mercy and the finality of their punishment, where communication and solace are entirely absent, deepening the sense of hopelessness and eternal suffering.

translation: Indeed, those for whom the best [reward] has preceded from Us - they will be kept far away from it (Hell).
interpretation: This verse refers to believers whose righteous deeds and faith have earned them God's prior decree of good reward - paradise. The phrase 'has preceded from Us' indicates that God's mercy and promise of goodness toward these righteous servants was established beforehand, reflecting divine foreknowledge and grace rather than mere chance. These individuals, through their sincere faith and righteous conduct, are assured protection from the Hellfire mentioned in the preceding verses about idolaters and their false deities. The verse emphasizes the distinction between those who worship false gods expecting intercession, and true believers who have earned genuine divine favor through their devotion to God alone. This serves as a comforting assurance to the faithful that their ultimate destiny is secured by God's prior promise, contrasting sharply with the fate of those who associate partners with Him.

translation: They will not hear the slightest sound of it [Hellfire], and they will abide eternally in that which their souls desire.
interpretation: This verse describes the ultimate reward for the righteous believers mentioned in the preceding verses of Surah Al-Anbya—those for whom the good has already been decreed by Allah. Such people will be kept entirely away from Hell, so far removed that they will not even perceive its faintest sound or crackling, let alone feel its heat or suffering. This emphasizes the completeness of their safety and distance from punishment, in contrast to the wrongdoers. Furthermore, they will dwell eternally in Paradise amid everything their souls could possibly desire, indicating a state of perfect, unending fulfillment and contentment. The verse underscores the totality of divine reward: not merely an absence of pain, but the presence of complete joy and the satisfaction of every wish, reflecting Allah's abundant generosity toward those who earned His pleasure through faith and righteous deeds.

translation: The greatest terror will not grieve them, and the angels will receive them, [saying], 'This is your Day which you were promised.'
interpretation: This verse describes the reward awaiting the righteous believers on the Day of Judgment, a day characterized by immense terror and fear for most of humanity. While the 'greatest terror' (al-faza' al-akbar) - referring to the horrifying events of the Resurrection, the Judgment, or the moment of being commanded to the Fire - will cause widespread distress, those who maintained faith and righteousness in their worldly lives are granted immunity from this grief through God's mercy. The angels personally welcoming them signifies the honor and dignity bestowed upon these believers, transforming what is otherwise a day of fear into a day of joyous fulfillment. The angels' greeting, declaring this to be the very day that was promised, serves as confirmation that the believers' faith and patience throughout their lives were not in vain - everything they were told about divine justice, reward, and the fulfillment of God's promises comes to fruition in this moment, validating their trust in the unseen and their steadfastness against doubt and temptation.

translation: The Day when We shall roll up the heaven like the rolling up of a written scroll for records. Just as We originated the first creation, We will repeat it - a promise binding upon Us. Indeed, We have been doing it.
interpretation: This verse affirms the certainty of resurrection and the Day of Judgment by drawing a powerful analogy: just as a scribe rolls up a completed scroll, God will fold up the entire cosmos, signaling the end of this worldly order. The image evokes both finality and precision, suggesting that creation itself is like a written record that will be closed and reviewed. The verse then grounds the doctrine of resurrection in the logic of God's original act of creation - the same power that brought the universe into being from nothing is fully capable of recreating it, making the reconstitution of life after death no more difficult than its initial formation. This argument from analogy was a common rhetorical strategy in the Quran to counter skeptics who doubted bodily resurrection, appealing to their own observation of the natural world and divine power already demonstrated. The phrase 'a promise binding upon Us' emphasizes divine self-obligation - God has committed to this outcome as a matter of justice and truthfulness, not mere possibility. The closing declaration 'We have been doing it' reinforces that this is not a hypothetical future event but consistent with God's established pattern of action throughout history, lending certainty and inevitability to the eschatological vision. The verse thus serves both as a cosmic warning and a theological proof, using the dissolution and re-creation of the heavens as evidence for divine omnipotence and the moral seriousness of the Last Day.

translation: And We have already written in the Psalms (al-Zabur), after the Reminder (al-Dhikr), that the earth shall be inherited by My righteous servants.
interpretation: This verse affirms a consistent divine promise reiterated across scriptures (here specifically the Zabur given to David, preceded by the 'Dhikr'—understood either as the Torah or the Preserved Tablet, al-Lawh al-Mahfuz) that ultimate dominion and inheritance of the earth belongs to the righteous. It establishes continuity among revealed scriptures, showing that this principle is not unique to the Qur'an but is a timeless divine law. The 'inheritance of the earth' signifies that true, lasting success—whether understood as worldly flourishing, moral authority, or eschatological reward in a renewed creation—belongs not to the powerful or arrogant, but to those who live in righteousness and submission to God. It serves as both a promise of hope to believers facing oppression and a moral criterion: the measure of who deserves lasting possession of the earth is piety and righteous conduct, not mere strength or worldly power.

translation: Indeed, in this is a [sufficient] message for a worshipping people.
interpretation: This verse concludes a passage affirming that the Qur'an, and the account of God's promise of inheritance of the earth to righteous servants, constitutes a complete and sufficient communication from God. The word 'balagh' implies both a message delivered and a sufficiency—enough guidance to fulfill one's purpose. It is addressed specifically to 'a worshipping people' ('abidin), indicating that true benefit from divine revelation is received by those whose hearts are oriented toward devotion and submission to God. The verse underscores that the Qur'an is not merely information but a complete provision for those who seek to live in service to God, implying that sincerity in worship is the condition for deriving full guidance and benefit from revelation. It also serves as a closing seal on the preceding discourse, affirming that what has been conveyed is sufficient proof and reminder for those predisposed to heed it.

translation: And We have not sent you (O Muhammad) except as a mercy to all the worlds (all of creation).
interpretation: This verse encapsulates the universal purpose of the Prophet Muhammad's mission, declaring that his role transcends any single nation, era, or religious community. Rather than being sent merely as a warner to the Arabs or as a lawgiver for a specific people, he is presented as a manifestation of divine mercy (rahmah) intended for all of creation—humanity, jinn, and indeed the entire cosmos. This mercy operates on multiple levels: through the guidance of revelation that offers a path to spiritual salvation and moral clarity; through his personal conduct, which modeled compassion, justice, and gentleness even toward enemies; and through the example he set for how mercy should govern relationships between people, communities, and even the treatment of animals and the environment. The verse suggests that the very existence of prophethood, and the message of Islam itself, is fundamentally an act of divine compassion rather than an imposition of harsh judgment—offering humanity a chance at guidance before accountability, and establishing a framework in which justice is always to be tempered with mercy. This universality also implies that the benefits of his message are not restricted to those who accept it in his lifetime, but extend across time and space, making him a mercy for 'the worlds' in the broadest sense—past, present, and future generations, believers and non-believers alike, who may benefit from the ethical, spiritual, and civilizational legacy his mission inaugurated.

translation: Say: It is only revealed to me that your God is but One God; will you then submit (become Muslims)?
interpretation: This verse encapsulates the core message of the Prophet Muhammad's mission: pure monotheism (Tawhid). He is instructed to clarify that his role is not to perform miracles or possess supernatural powers, but simply to convey the divine revelation he receives. The central content of that revelation is the absolute oneness of God, which stands in contrast to polytheistic beliefs. The rhetorical question at the end—'will you then submit?'—serves as a direct and urgent call to action, inviting the listeners to accept this fundamental truth and surrender themselves to the one God, which is the literal meaning of becoming 'Muslim.' It frames submission to God's oneness as the logical and necessary conclusion for anyone who hears and understands this simple, profound truth.

translation: So if they turn away, say, 'I have announced to you all equally, and I do not know whether what you are promised is near or far.'
interpretation: This verse addresses the Prophet Muhammad's response to those who reject or turn away from his message. It emphasizes two key principles of prophetic mission: first, that the warning and message of truth have been delivered equally and fairly to all people, without concealment or favoritism, so that no one can claim ignorance or unequal treatment; the responsibility for belief now rests with the listener. Second, it reflects the limits of human and even prophetic knowledge regarding the unseen—specifically the timing of divine judgment or the fulfillment of warnings about resurrection and accountability. The Prophet is instructed to admit humbly that he does not possess knowledge of the exact timing of these events, as such knowledge belongs to God alone. This serves to distinguish the role of a messenger, who conveys guidance, from that of a soothsayer or one who claims to predict the future, reinforcing the theme of prophetic humility and the transcendence of divine knowledge over human understanding.

translation: Indeed, He knows what is declared openly in speech, and He knows what you conceal.
interpretation: This verse affirms God's comprehensive and perfect knowledge, encompassing both the outward and the hidden dimensions of human existence. It teaches that there is no distinction before God between what is spoken aloud and what is kept secret within the heart, nor between public conduct and private intention. This establishes a theological foundation for sincerity (ikhlas) in worship and moral accountability, since human beings cannot deceive God through outward appearances while harboring contrary thoughts or intentions. The verse also serves a consoling function for believers who face persecution or who must conceal their faith out of fear, assuring them that God is fully aware of their true state regardless of what they are compelled to hide or reveal. Simultaneously, it carries a warning to those who scheme secretly against truth or against the Prophet's mission, reminding them that their concealed plots are already known to God. This reflects a broader Qur'anic theme of divine omniscience as both a comfort to the sincere and a deterrent to the deceitful, reinforcing that ultimate judgment rests not on external appearances alone but on the complete reality known only to God.

translation: And I do not know; perhaps it is a trial for you, and an enjoyment for a time.
interpretation: This verse reflects the humility of the Prophet in acknowledging the limits of his own knowledge regarding divine wisdom. He admits that he cannot be certain why Allah delays punishment or grants respite to disbelievers—it may be that this delay itself constitutes a test (fitnah) for people, to see whether they will be grateful and turn to righteousness, or whether they will take the temporary worldly enjoyment (mata' ila heen) as a sign of approval and continue in heedlessness. The verse underscores the theme that worldly pleasures and the postponement of consequences are transient and are not necessarily indicators of divine favor; rather, they may serve as a means of testing human character and faith before an appointed time of reckoning.

translation: He said, 'My Lord, judge with truth. And our Lord is the Most Merciful, the One whose help is sought against that which you describe.'
interpretation: This verse records a prophetic supplication made in the face of disbelief and false attributions made against God by the disbelievers (such as ascribing partners or false descriptions to Him). The prophet, having delivered the message, turns to God asking Him to render true judgment between himself and those who reject the truth, affirming his confidence that divine judgment is just. The phrase 'our Lord is the Most Merciful' reminds the listener that despite the conflict with disbelievers, God's essential nature is mercy and compassion, not merely vengeance. The final clause, 'the One whose help is sought against that which you describe,' turns toward the disbelievers directly, expressing reliance upon God alone to deal with the false and blasphemous things they attribute to Him—whether denying His signs, mocking the prophet, or ascribing partners to Him. The verse thus models complete trust in God's justice and mercy as the appropriate response to the slander and misrepresentation of divine truth, leaving the matter of judgment entirely in God's hands rather than resorting to human retaliation.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. O mankind, fear your Lord. Indeed, the earthquake of the Hour is a tremendous thing.
interpretation: This opening verse of Surah Al-Hajj serves as a dramatic call to awaken human consciousness to the reality of the Day of Judgment. The 'earthquake' (zalzalah) mentioned here is both literal and symbolic—it refers to the cosmic upheaval that will occur at the end of time, when the very foundations of the universe will be shaken, but it also evokes the psychological and spiritual shock that the realization of accountability before God should produce in believers. By addressing 'all mankind' rather than just believers, the verse universalizes its message, reminding every human being regardless of faith that they are subject to divine judgment. The command to 'fear your Lord' (ittaqu rabbakum) is not meant to instill paralyzing terror but rather a reverential awareness (taqwa) that should motivate righteous action and moral accountability in this life. The verse sets the tone for the rest of the surah, which goes on to describe in vivid detail the terrifying physical and emotional consequences of this cosmic event—nursing mothers forgetting their infants, pregnant women miscarrying, and people appearing drunk from sheer terror though they are not intoxicated. This serves as a profound reminder that the magnitude of the Hour should inspire believers to live with constant mindfulness of their ultimate return to God, making righteous deeds and ethical conduct a priority over worldly attachments and transient pleasures.

translation: On the Day you see it, every nursing mother will forget what she was nursing, and every pregnant woman will deliver her burden, and you will see mankind as if intoxicated, though they are not intoxicated; but the punishment of Allah is severe.
interpretation: This verse describes the terrifying magnitude of the Hour (the earthquake of the Last Day mentioned in the preceding verse) by depicting how it will overwhelm even the deepest natural instincts of humanity. The nursing mother's bond with her infant and her instinctive devotion to its care represent one of the strongest, most selfless human attachments, yet even this will be forgotten in the face of such terror. Similarly, a pregnant woman giving birth prematurely from sheer shock illustrates the physical and psychological devastation of that moment. The image of people appearing drunk, stumbling and disoriented, despite not having consumed any intoxicant, conveys that their state is not due to any substance but to the overwhelming fear and awareness of divine reckoning. The verse closes by clarifying that this apparent madness is not without cause: it stems from the severity of God's punishment, which will strip away all pretense, composure, and worldly attachments, forcing humanity to confront the ultimate reality of judgment in a state of absolute vulnerability.

translation: And among the people is he who disputes concerning Allah without knowledge and follows every rebellious devil.
interpretation: This verse addresses the phenomenon of individuals who engage in arguments about God, His nature, or religious matters without genuine knowledge, understanding, or sound evidence. Their disputes are not grounded in reflection, revelation, or reason, but are often driven by arrogance, stubbornness, or blind imitation of others. The verse links this ignorant disputation to following 'every rebellious devil' (shaytanin marid), suggesting that such baseless argumentation is not a neutral intellectual exercise but is actually satanic in origin and effect—it leads people away from truth rather than toward it. The devil referenced here represents any force of misguidance, whether an actual jinn or a human being who whispers doubt and falsehood. This verse serves as a warning against speaking about sacred and metaphysical matters casually or out of ego, pride, or inherited prejudice rather than genuine understanding. It implicitly calls believers to seek knowledge before making claims about divine matters, and to be wary of those who argue about religion merely to sow confusion, doubt, or division, as such people are described as being led by forces of corruption rather than guided by truth.

translation: It has been decreed for him that whoever takes him as a guardian/ally, he will mislead him and guide him to the punishment of the Blazing Fire (Sa'ir).
interpretation: This verse refers to Satan, continuing from the preceding verses about rebellious devils who argue about God without knowledge. It establishes a divine decree: Satan's nature and function are fixed—his destiny and role are to misguide those who follow him. The verse emphasizes a cosmic principle of cause and effect: alliance with Satan inevitably leads to spiritual ruin, not because God arbitrarily punishes such people, but because Satan's guidance by definition leads away from truth and toward the Fire. The paradoxical phrase 'guide him to the punishment' underscores the irony that Satan appears to offer guidance and direction, but this apparent guidance is actually a path toward destruction. This serves as a warning to believers about the real consequences of succumbing to satanic whispers, which manifest as doubt, misguidance, and ultimately spiritual destruction in the Hereafter. It reinforces the broader Quranic theme that humans have a choice in whom they follow—God's true guidance or Satan's false guidance—and that this choice has eternal consequences.

translation: O mankind! If you are in doubt concerning the Resurrection, then indeed, We created you from dust, then from a sperm-drop, then from a clinging clot, then from a lump of flesh, partly formed and partly unformed, that We may make clear to you. And We settle in the wombs whom We will for a specified term, then We bring you out as an infant, then that you may reach your maturity. And among you is he who dies [young], and among you is he who is brought back to the most decrepit age so that he knows, after having known, nothing. And you see the earth barren, but when We send down upon it water, it quivers and swells and produces of every lovely kind [of growth].
interpretation: This verse addresses human doubt about resurrection by drawing a direct analogy between the stages of human embryonic development and the stages of life after death. The progression from dust to sperm-drop to clot to fetus demonstrates God's power to transform matter through distinct phases, which serves as evidence that He is equally capable of restoring life after death. The mention of varied human lifespans—some dying young, others reaching senility where they lose the knowledge they once had—emphasizes that human existence is entirely governed by divine decree, not human control, countering any claim that natural processes alone explain life without a Creator's will. The closing image of dead, barren earth suddenly springing to life with vegetation after rainfall functions as a tangible, observable parallel to resurrection: just as lifeless soil can be revived and made fertile, so too can lifeless bodies be revived on the Day of Judgment. The verse thus moves from the intimate biological process within the human body to the cosmic process within nature, using both as complementary proofs that the God who initiates life through gradual, ordered stages—whether in the womb or in the soil—possesses the power to resurrect the dead, making doubt about resurrection illogical given the evidence already present in creation itself.

translation: That is because Allah is the Truth, and He gives life to the dead, and He is over all things competent (able to do all things).
interpretation: This verse establishes a causal link between the preceding affirmations of Allah's reality and power and the certainty of resurrection. The phrase 'that is because' points back to signs of divine power in creation—such as rain reviving dead earth—used as evidence for the resurrection of the dead. The verse argues that since Allah is al-Haqq (the ultimate, absolute Truth and Reality, as opposed to the falsehood of other deities), His actions and promises are necessarily true and will come to pass. His demonstrated ability to bring life from lifelessness in the natural world (such as vegetation from barren soil) serves as rational and observable proof of His capacity to resurrect human beings after death. This is reinforced by the concluding universal statement of His omnipotence, that He has power over absolutely everything, making the resurrection not a matter of doubt but a logical certainty given who Allah is. The verse thus serves as a theological conclusion, moving from observable cosmic phenomena to a confirmation of core eschatological belief in the Day of Judgment.

translation: And that the Hour is coming, there is no doubt about it, and that Allah will resurrect those who are in the graves.
interpretation: This verse affirms two foundational pillars of Islamic eschatology: the certainty of the Day of Judgment and the reality of bodily resurrection. By stating that the Hour is 'coming' with 'no doubt,' the verse emphasizes absolute certainty despite human inability to know its timing, countering skepticism about an afterlife. The mention of Allah resurrecting 'those in the graves' affirms that death is not an end but a transition, and that physical bodies will be restored to life for accountability. This serves as a theological anchor for moral responsibility—since judgment is certain, human actions in worldly life carry eternal consequence. The verse functions rhetorically to silence doubt (nafy al-rayb) by presenting resurrection and the Hour as self-evident truths rooted in God's power over life and death, reinforcing that His creative ability, as seen in the natural world, extends to recreating the dead.

translation: And among mankind is he who disputes concerning Allah without knowledge, without guidance, and without an illuminating Book.
interpretation: This verse criticizes those who argue about matters of faith and theology based on mere opinion, ignorance, or blind conjecture rather than on sound knowledge, divine guidance, or revealed scripture. It warns against arrogance in religious debate, where individuals assert claims about God's nature, will, or decrees without any legitimate epistemological foundation—neither rational proof, prophetic guidance, nor textual evidence. The verse implicitly calls believers to ground their understanding of the divine in authentic sources of knowledge rather than speculation, pride, or inherited customs devoid of substance.

translation: Turning his side (in arrogance/disdain) to lead [others] astray from the path of Allah. For him is disgrace in this world, and We will make him taste, on the Day of Resurrection, the punishment of the Burning Fire.
interpretation: This verse depicts the posture and inner state of a person who disputes about Allah without knowledge, as described in the preceding verses of this passage (Surah Al-Hajj, 22:8-9). The phrase 'turning his side' (thaniya 'itfahu) is a physical gesture conveying haughty disdain and contemptuous dismissal—literally twisting the neck or shoulder away as if too proud to listen or acknowledge truth. This arrogance is not merely a personal flaw but an active force: such a person works to divert others from Allah's path, using pride and rhetorical manipulation to mislead. The verse establishes a moral law of consequence operating on two levels of time: immediate worldly humiliation (khizy) as a corrective exposure of his false pride before others, and ultimate otherworldly torment (the Burning Fire) as the fitting recompense for one who sought to burn away others' faith through arrogant misguidance. The pairing of disgrace now and fire later suggests a thematic resonance—his arrogant 'heat' of pride in life is answered by the literal heat of punishment in the Hereafter, illustrating the Qur'anic principle that the nature of one's sin mirrors the nature of one's punishment.

translation: That is for what your hands have sent forth, and because Allah is not unjust to [His] servants.
interpretation: This verse comes as a conclusion to a description of the torment faced by the wrongdoers in the Hereafter, affirming the principle of divine justice: whatever suffering or recompense a person receives is the direct consequence of their own deeds, freely committed during their life. The phrase "what your hands have sent forth" emphasizes personal responsibility and agency—one's actions are like deposits made in advance, whose returns are collected later. By explicitly stating that Allah is never unjust to His servants ("laysa bi-zallamin lil-'abeed"), the verse forecloses any possibility of attributing suffering to arbitrary divine will or injustice. The emphatic structure (ظلام, an intensive form) rules out even the slightest injustice, not merely gross injustice. This establishes a moral universe where cause and effect are perfectly aligned with human choice, reinforcing accountability and removing excuses of fatalism or blaming God for the consequences of one's own wrongdoing.

translation: And among the people is he who worships Allah on the edge [i.e., on a verge/doubt]: if good befalls him, he is content with it; but if a trial befalls him, he turns back on his face, losing [both] this world and the Hereafter. That is the manifest loss.
interpretation: This verse describes a person whose faith is conditional and superficial rather than deeply rooted, likened to someone standing precariously on the edge of something, ready to fall either way depending on circumstance. Such a person treats worship and belief as a transaction contingent upon personal benefit: when life brings prosperity, ease, or blessings, they remain outwardly devout and feel reassured in their faith. However, the moment they encounter hardship, trial, or adversity—illness, loss, persecution, or any test of commitment—their faith collapses entirely, and they abandon their devotion, turning away completely. The imagery of turning 'on his face' suggests a complete reversal, a total abandonment rather than a partial wavering, indicating the shallowness of their original commitment. The verse emphasizes that such opportunistic faith yields a double loss: forfeiting the spiritual and worldly benefits that genuine faith provides, while also failing to secure reward in the Hereafter, since their belief was never sincere but merely transactional. This is characterized as 'manifest loss' because, unlike losses that might be hidden or ambiguous, this person loses on both fronts—worldly stability through lack of true resilience and patience, and eternal salvation through lack of authentic conviction—making their failure complete and unmistakable.

translation: He calls upon, besides Allah, that which neither harms him nor benefits him. That is the far straying.
interpretation: This verse describes the futility of idolatry and polytheism, depicting a person who directs worship and supplication toward false deities—whether idols, objects, or other created beings—that possess no real power to cause harm or bring benefit. Unlike Allah, who has true control over all things, these false objects of worship are utterly powerless and unresponsive. The verse characterizes this behavior as 'far straying' (الضلال البعيد), emphasizing not just error but a profound and extensive deviation from truth and rational understanding. The phrase suggests a misguidance so deep that the person has wandered far from the straight path, wasting devotion on something that can neither help nor hurt them, highlighting the irrationality and spiritual emptiness of seeking aid from anything other than the one true God who alone possesses actual power over benefit and harm.

translation: He invokes [as a god] one whose harm is closer than his benefit — how wretched a protector, and how wretched a companion!
interpretation: This verse continues the depiction, begun in the previous ayah, of the person whose faith is weak and conditional—serving God only at the margins, contingent on receiving worldly benefit. Having abandoned sincere devotion to God when trials come, such a person turns instead to false objects of worship: idols, intermediaries, or worldly powers that can neither truly help nor save him. The verse exposes the absurdity and self-destructiveness of this choice: what he appeals to for protection and companionship is, in truth, far more likely to harm him than to help him, since it has no real power at all. The idol or false patron cannot intercede with God, cannot avert calamity, and offers no true loyalty or support in difficulty—unlike God, who is the true Protector (Wali) and sufficient Companion for the believer. The repetition of 'how wretched' underscores by contrast the immense difference between the true, unfailing Lordship of God and the worthless, actually harmful reliance placed in false deities. It is a rebuke of spiritual confusion that mistakes powerless things for sources of real security and support.

translation: Indeed, Allah admits those who believe and do righteous deeds into gardens beneath which rivers flow. Indeed, Allah does what He wills.
interpretation: This verse affirms both the promise of divine reward and the absolute sovereignty of God. The first part establishes a clear principle of divine justice: faith alone is insufficient without being paired with righteous action, and together these two elements—belief and good deeds—are what qualify a person for entry into Paradise, depicted here through the recurring Qur'anic image of gardens with flowing rivers, symbolizing eternal abundance, peace, and life. The second part of the verse, 'Allah does what He wills,' serves as a theological anchor reminding believers that this reward is not owed to them as a transaction they can demand, but is granted by God's own will and mercy. It underscores that God's power is not bound by human expectation or logic; He is the ultimate authority who determines outcomes according to His own wisdom. This closing phrase also guards against complacency or a sense of entitlement among believers, reinforcing that salvation is ultimately a matter of divine grace intertwined with human effort, not a guaranteed mechanical result of deeds alone.

translation: Whoever thinks that Allah will not help him [i.e., the Prophet] in this world and the Hereafter - let him extend a rope to the sky, then let him cut it off, and let him see whether his effort will remove that which enrages him.
interpretation: This verse addresses those who resent or are enraged by the success and divine support given to the Prophet Muhammad, wishing for his failure. The imagery is deliberately challenging and somewhat enigmatic: the one consumed by such resentment is told, in effect, to take the most extreme and futile action imaginable - stretching a rope up to the sky and then cutting it, symbolizing an attempt to sever or escape from the reach of heaven itself, or alternatively to hang himself in his fury. Either way, the verse conveys that no amount of frustrated effort, however desperate or extreme, can alter divine decree or extinguish the support Allah has granted His messenger. The rhetorical challenge exposes the futility of human rage against a reality ordained by God, suggesting that such people should exhaust every possible means of resistance only to discover that their scheming and anger change nothing. It is ultimately a statement about the limits of human power against divine will and the impotence of malice directed at those under God's protection.

translation: And thus We have sent it down as clear signs (verses), and [it is attested] that Allah guides whom He wills.
interpretation: This verse affirms that the Qur'an was revealed as a set of unambiguous, self-evidencing signs so that its truth would be accessible to those who reflect upon it. The latter clause establishes the theological principle of divine guidance as a gift bestowed according to God's will and wisdom rather than something humans can secure purely through their own effort or merit. It underscores the relationship between clarity of revelation and the human need for divine grace: the signs are made plain, but true inner guidance—the acceptance and comprehension of faith—ultimately depends on God's will, acknowledging His sovereignty while not negating human responsibility to seek and respond to the signs presented.

translation: Indeed, those who believed, and those who were Jews, and the Sabians, and the Christians, and the Magians, and those who associated partners with Allah - indeed, Allah will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection. Indeed Allah is, over all things, Witness.
interpretation: This verse establishes that ultimate judgment regarding religious truth and the sincerity of each community's faith belongs to God alone, not to human beings. It lists multiple religious groups—believers, Jews, Sabians, Christians, Magians (Zoroastrians), and polytheists—acknowledging the plurality of religious communities existing in the world. Rather than commanding believers to pass judgment on who is right or wrong among these groups in worldly terms, the verse defers that final reckoning to the Day of Resurrection, when God will distinguish between them based on truth, sincerity, and deeds known only to Him. The closing affirmation that God is witness over all things underscores divine omniscience: God alone possesses complete knowledge of every soul's inner faith and outer conduct, making Him the only just arbiter of competing religious claims. This verse is often cited in discussions of religious pluralism, tolerance, and the limits of human judgment over others' faith, while also serving as a reminder that accountability before God is real and inescapable for every community, regardless of their professed beliefs.

translation: Have you not seen that to Allah prostrates whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth, and the sun, the moon, the stars, the mountains, the trees, the moving creatures, and many of the people? But upon many the punishment has been justified. And whoever Allah humiliates - for him there is no bestower of honor. Indeed, Allah does what He wills.
interpretation: This verse presents a cosmic vision of universal submission in which every element of creation—celestial bodies, natural phenomena, and living beings—exists in a state of prostration (sujud) to its Creator, meaning they follow the laws and purposes for which they were made, entirely obedient to divine will. Humanity, however, is singled out as the exception where division occurs: 'many of the people' prostrate willingly and consciously, while implicitly others do not, and it is upon this second group—those who reject or turn away from submission—that punishment becomes justly deserved. This highlights the unique position of human beings in creation: unlike the sun, moon, or mountains, which have no choice but to follow their created nature, humans possess free will and can choose whether to align themselves with the natural order of submission to God or to defy it. The verse then pivots to the theme of honor and humiliation, declaring that true honor (ikram) comes only from Allah, and if He decrees humiliation upon someone—due to their arrogance, rejection of truth, or moral corruption—no other being or power in existence can bestow honor upon them to counteract this divine judgment. This serves as a sobering reminder that worldly status, wealth, or human-granted titles are meaningless if one stands disgraced before God, and that ultimate dignity and disgrace are entirely within divine prerogative, not human control. The closing statement, 'Indeed, Allah does what He wills,' reinforces the theme of absolute divine sovereignty—underscoring that the entire order of creation, including the fate and standing of every soul, unfolds according to God's will and wisdom, not according to human expectation or desire. The verse ends with a call to physical prostration (indicated by the sajdah mark), inviting the reader to personally enact the very submission being described, thereby aligning oneself with the rest of creation in acknowledging Allah's sovereignty.

translation: These are two adversaries who disputed concerning their Lord. As for those who disbelieved, garments of fire will be cut out for them, and boiling water will be poured over their heads.
interpretation: This verse opens a passage (continuing in the following verses) describing the fate of two opposing groups on the Day of Judgment—believers and disbelievers—who dispute about God and His truth. The 'two adversaries' represent the fundamental division among humanity between those who accept faith and those who reject it, a conflict that will ultimately be resolved in the Hereafter. The vivid imagery of garments of fire being 'cut out' for the disbelievers, as if tailored specifically for them, emphasizes the inescapable and fitting nature of their punishment—it is measured precisely to their disbelief. The boiling water poured over their heads intensifies the torment, striking at the seat of thought and will, symbolizing the complete overwhelming of those who used their reason to deny rather than affirm truth. This graphic depiction serves as a severe warning, contrasting sharply with the rewards promised to believers in the verses that follow, and underscores the seriousness with which the Qur'an treats matters of faith and disbelief—framing them not as abstract philosophical positions but as choices with ultimate, visceral consequences.

translation: With it will be melted what is in their bellies, and their skins [as well].
interpretation: This verse is a continuation of the description of the punishment prepared for disbelievers in the Hereafter, specifically boiling water poured over their heads (as mentioned in the preceding verse, 22:19). The imagery depicts a punishment of such intense heat and severity that it melts and dissolves both the internal organs (what is in their bellies) and the external skin of the condemned. This graphic portrayal serves several purposes in the Quranic discourse: it emphasizes the totality and thoroughness of divine justice, leaving no part of the body unaffected by the consequences of disbelief and wrongdoing; it underscores the vast difference between temporal, worldly suffering and the infinitely more severe suffering of the Hereafter; and it functions as a powerful deterrent, urging listeners toward reflection and righteous action. The mention of both internal and external destruction suggests completeness - that the punishment penetrates to the very core of one's being, symbolizing that the consequences of one's choices in life are inescapable and all-encompassing in the life to come. Classical commentators note that this imagery, while severe, is meant to awaken moral consciousness and remind believers of the gravity of their choices and the justice of God, who knows and judges what lies hidden within, not merely outward appearances.

translation: And for them are maces (hooked rods/clubs) of iron.
interpretation: This verse comes from Surah Al-Hajj (22:21), within a passage describing the Fire prepared for those who reject the truth and are arrogant toward God's signs. The 'maces of iron' (maqami' min hadid) refer to instruments of punishment used by the angels of torment against the disbelievers whenever they attempt to escape the Fire due to its unbearable anguish, as the following verse (22:22) indicates they will be driven back into it. The imagery emphasizes the severity and inescapability of divine retribution for those who persisted in disbelief and oppression, serving as a stark warning about the consequences of rejecting guidance and mistreating others, particularly in the context of this surah's broader themes about those who bar people from the path of God and the sacred mosque.

translation: Every time they seek to come out of it (Hell), from anguish, they will be returned to it, and [it will be said], 'Taste the punishment of the Burning Fire!'
interpretation: This verse conveys the inescapable nature of the punishment for those who persist in disbelief and wrongdoing. It depicts the psychological and physical torment of the people of Hell, who, overwhelmed by distress and suffering, attempt to escape but are forcibly driven back into the fire. The repetition of 'every time' emphasizes the perpetual and cyclical nature of this torment, highlighting that there is no respite or permanent escape from divine punishment once it is justly decreed. The command to 'taste' the punishment underscores the direct experiential nature of the suffering, as if it is a consequence they must fully experience as a result of their choices in life. This serves as a stark warning about the consequences of rejecting truth and justice, reinforcing the Qur'anic theme of accountability and the seriousness of one's actions and beliefs in the worldly life, which determine one's fate in the hereafter.

translation: Indeed, Allah admits those who believe and do righteous deeds into gardens beneath which rivers flow. They will be adorned therein with bracelets of gold and pearls, and their garments therein will be of silk.
interpretation: This verse affirms that divine reward is contingent upon the union of faith (iman) and righteous action ('amal salih), emphasizing that belief alone, without corresponding deeds, is incomplete in the Qur'anic worldview. The imagery of Paradise described here—flowing rivers, gold bracelets, pearls, and silk garments—employs sensory luxury familiar to the verse's original audience to convey a reality beyond ordinary human comprehension. Notably, items forbidden to believers in worldly life (gold and silk for men, according to later juridical tradition) become permissible and even characteristic adornments in the afterlife, suggesting that earthly restrictions serve a temporal and disciplinary purpose rather than reflecting an inherent moral flaw in these materials themselves. The eternal garden thus represents not merely physical comfort but the removal of worldly constraints, symbolizing a state of complete fulfillment, dignity, and honor granted to the faithful as a direct consequence of divine grace responding to human moral effort.

translation: And they were guided to the good word, and they were guided to the path of the Praiseworthy One.
interpretation: This verse refers to the believers who, through God's grace, are directed toward speech and belief that is pure, truthful, and wholesome—such as the declaration of faith (there is no god but God) and words of remembrance and praise—while simultaneously being guided along the straight path that leads to God, who is described here as al-Hamid, the Praiseworthy, the one deserving of all praise. The pairing of 'good word' with 'the path of the Praiseworthy' suggests an inseparable link between righteous speech and righteous conduct: true guidance is not merely intellectual or verbal but manifests in a way of life oriented toward the One who is inherently worthy of all gratitude and commendation. This dual guidance—of tongue and of path—is often understood as a divine favor granted specifically to the righteous as a reward and distinguishing mark, contrasted with those who are led astray in both their speech and their conduct.

translation: Indeed, those who disbelieve and turn [others] away from the path of Allah and from the Sacred Mosque, which We have made [open] for all people equally - the resident therein and the visitor - and whoever intends therein any deviation [through] wrongdoing, We shall make him taste a painful punishment.
interpretation: This verse establishes a profound principle of universal access and sanctity regarding the Sacred Mosque in Mecca, declaring it a place belonging to all humanity rather than any particular tribe, lineage, or group with exclusive claims. The phrase equating 'the resident' with 'the visitor' dismantles pre-Islamic notions of tribal ownership over the Ka'ba, instead framing it as a shared spiritual inheritance for all who seek it, local inhabitant and traveling pilgrim alike.
