interpretation: This verse is part of a Qur'anic argument form in which the Prophet is instructed to pose rhetorical questions to the polytheists, compelling them to acknowledge through their own reason that God alone is the true owner and sovereign of all creation. By asking to whom the earth and all its inhabitants belong, the verse exposes the logical inconsistency in the disbelievers' position: they readily affirm that God is the Creator and Possessor of the earth, yet they still worship other deities alongside Him or deny the resurrection and accountability that logically follow from His sovereignty. The rhetorical question is designed to lead the listener step by step toward admitting that ultimate ownership, power, and authority belong to God alone, undermining the rational basis for associating partners with Him or rejecting the Day of Judgment, since the One who owns and sustains the earth and all upon it certainly has the power to resurrect and judge them.

translation: They will say, 'To Allah.' Say, 'Then will you not remember?'
interpretation: This verse is part of a rhetorical sequence in which the Qur'an poses questions to the disbelievers about the true ownership and sovereignty of the earth and all that is within it. When confronted with the question of to whom everything belongs, even the polytheists are compelled by reason and innate recognition (fitrah) to admit that it all belongs to Allah alone. The verse highlights the contradiction in their position: despite acknowledging Allah as the sole Creator and Sovereign, they still associate partners with Him in worship. The rhetorical question 'will you not remember?' serves as a call to reflection, urging them to recognize the logical inconsistency of affirming Allah's exclusive lordship while simultaneously worshipping other deities. It is an appeal to innate human reason and conscience, suggesting that the truth of monotheism is not something foreign to be imposed, but something intrinsic that people already acknowledge, if only they would pause to genuinely reflect upon it.

translation: Say, 'Who is the Lord of the seven heavens and Lord of the Mighty Throne?'
interpretation: This verse is part of a rhetorical sequence in which the Prophet is instructed to pose a series of questions to the polytheists about the true source of creation and sovereignty. The rhetorical strategy here is significant: rather than asserting a doctrine outright, the verse invites the disbelievers to acknowledge through their own reasoning what they already implicitly know. The expected answer—which the following verses confirm they would give—is 'Allah.' This exposes a fundamental inconsistency in their position: they recognize Allah as the Creator and Sovereign of the heavens and the magnificent Throne (a symbol of ultimate authority and dominion over all creation), yet they persist in associating partners with Him in worship. The verse thus functions as a logical trap, using the polytheists' own theological admissions against their practical idolatry, demonstrating that true tawhid (monotheism) is not merely an abstract belief but should logically extend to exclusive devotion and worship, since the One who controls the vast cosmic order and holds the Throne of ultimate power is the only one deserving of worship.

translation: They will say, 'To Allah.' Say, 'Then will you not be mindful of Him?'
interpretation: This verse is part of a rhetorical sequence in which the Qur'an poses a series of questions to the disbelievers about the ownership and sovereignty of the heavens, the earth, and all that exists within them. Even those who reject the message are compelled to admit that everything belongs to Allah alone, since this truth is self-evident and undeniable even to their own reason. The verse exposes a profound contradiction: they acknowledge Allah's absolute sovereignty and lordship, yet they fail to translate this acknowledgment into reverence, obedience, and righteous conduct. The rhetorical question 'will you not fear Him' or 'will you not be mindful of Him' challenges them to recognize the logical and moral inconsistency of affirming Allah's dominion while simultaneously associating partners with Him or disobeying His commands. It underscores that true faith requires not merely intellectual acknowledgment of God's existence and power, but a consistent life of taqwa (God-consciousness) that flows naturally from that recognition. The verse thus serves as a powerful indictment of those who possess correct knowledge yet fail to act upon it.

translation: Say: 'In whose hand is the dominion of all things, and He protects while none can be protected against Him, if you know?'
interpretation: This verse is part of a rhetorical sequence in which the Prophet is instructed to question the polytheists about the true source of ultimate authority and protection in the universe. By asking who holds sovereign power (malakut) over all things, and affirming that this sovereign both grants protection and cannot be shielded against, the verse exposes the logical inconsistency of worshipping intermediaries or idols while implicitly acknowledging, as the disbelievers themselves often did, that God alone is the Creator and Sustainer. The rhetorical question format is a method of argumentation meant to lead the listener to the inevitable conclusion of God's absolute oneness and supreme authority, since no one can answer the question except by affirming that God alone possesses this power. It underscores the theme of tawhid (monotheism) by showing that true refuge and protection come only from the One who governs all existence, making any reliance on other deities or protectors logically and spiritually futile.

translation: They will say, 'To Allah.' Say, 'Then how are you deluded/bewitched [away from the truth]?'
interpretation: This verse is part of a rhetorical sequence in which the Qur'an compels the disbelievers to acknowledge, through their own reasoning, that Allah is the sole creator and sovereign of all things—the heavens, the earth, and everything within them. Having secured their admission that everything belongs to Allah, the verse then poses a pointed challenge: if they already know and affirm this truth, why do they still turn to idolatry and polytheism? The word 'tusharūn' (bewitched/deluded) suggests that their persistence in disbelief despite their own admission is akin to being under a spell—an irrational state where they are led away from the obvious truth their own intellects affirm. This highlights the Qur'anic argument that disbelief is not due to lack of evidence or reason, but a kind of self-imposed blindness or deception that prevents people from acting upon what they intuitively know to be true.

translation: Nay, We have brought them the truth, and indeed, they are liars.
interpretation: This verse responds to the polytheists' false claims about God having offspring or partners, as discussed in the preceding verses. It affirms that Allah has sent clear truth—through revelation and rational proof of His oneness—to refute the baseless assertions of those who attribute partners or children to Him. The verse underscores that the disbelievers' claims are not based on evidence or knowledge but are fabrications, while the truth conveyed through the Prophet and the Qur'an stands firm against their falsehood. It reflects the Qur'anic theme that divine truth is self-evident and sufficient to expose human deception when people reject sound reasoning about God's unity (tawhid) in favor of inherited or invented beliefs.

translation: Allah has not taken any son, nor is there any god along with Him. [If there were], then each god would have taken away what it created, and some of them would have surely overpowered others. Glory be to Allah above what they describe.
interpretation: This verse presents a logical argument against polytheism, known as the argument from mutual exclusion or the 'proof of corruption' (burhan al-tamanu). It reasons that if multiple deities truly existed, each possessing independent power and will, conflict and competition between them would be inevitable, as each would seek to claim and control what it had created, leading to a struggle for dominance. Such rivalry would result in disorder and the eventual breakdown of the universe's harmonious order. Since the cosmos operates with observable consistency, balance, and order—from the precise movements of celestial bodies to the interdependent systems of nature—this coherence itself testifies to a single, unified source of command and creation. The verse thus uses rational deduction from the observed order of creation to establish divine oneness (tawhid), rejecting both the notion that Allah has offspring and the existence of any co-deity alongside Him. It concludes with an affirmation of Allah's transcendence, declaring Him utterly free from the false attributes, partners, and descriptions that polytheists ascribe to Him.

translation: [He is the] Knower of the unseen and the witnessed; exalted is He above what they associate [with Him].
interpretation: This verse emphasizes God's absolute and comprehensive knowledge, encompassing both the hidden realm (al-ghayb) - that which is beyond human perception, including the unseen world, future events, and the inner thoughts of hearts - and the witnessed realm (ash-shahada) - the observable, tangible world accessible to human senses. This totality of knowledge is presented as a defining divine attribute that distinguishes God from any created being or false deity. The verse then transitions to a declaration of God's transcendence (ta'ala) above shirk, the act of associating partners or equals with Him. The logical connection between these two ideas is significant: precisely because God alone possesses complete knowledge of all realms of existence—seen and unseen—it is irrational and theologically absurd to attribute divinity to other entities, whether idols, celestial bodies, or any created thing, since none of these possess such comprehensive knowledge or power. The verse thus serves as both an affirmation of monotheism (tawhid) and a refutation of polytheism, grounding this refutation not merely in command but in the demonstrable incomparability of God's nature to anything else that might be worshipped alongside Him.

translation: Say, 'My Lord, if You should show me that which they are promised,'
interpretation: This verse captures a moment of the Prophet Muhammad being taught how to respond to the punishment and consequences promised to disbelievers who rejected his message. It reflects a posture of humility before God even in anticipation of divine justice being manifested. The verse continues in the following ayah where the Prophet asks not to be placed among the wrongdoers when such reckoning occurs, teaching believers to seek personal righteousness and to leave judgment of others entirely to God rather than reveling in anticipated punishment of adversaries. It models a spiritual etiquette: even when vindication is promised, one's immediate concern should be one's own standing before God, not triumph over others.

translation: My Lord, then do not place me among the wrongdoing people.
interpretation: This supplication reflects the Prophet's plea to God for protection from being counted among, or implicated with, those who commit injustice and disbelief, even if divine punishment befalls them. It expresses a believer's constant awareness that righteousness is not guaranteed by status or knowledge alone, but requires continual divine safeguarding from moral corruption and the company of the unjust. The prayer also signals humility, recognizing that one's own standing before God depends on His mercy and protection rather than personal merit, and it underscores the Qur'anic theme that association with wrongdoers can lead to shared consequences, making dissociation from injustice both a spiritual and ethical imperative.

translation: And indeed, We are able to show you that which We have promised them.
interpretation: This verse reassures the Prophet Muhammad that God has complete power to carry out the punishment He has promised for the disbelievers and wrongdoers, even within the Prophet's own lifetime, were He to will it. It comes in a context where God instructs the Prophet to seek refuge from the promptings of devils and to respond to evil with good, counseling patience regarding the ultimate reckoning of the wicked. The verse affirms divine omnipotence and serves to comfort the Prophet and believers who witness the arrogance and persecution of disbelievers, assuring them that retribution is entirely within God's capability and timing, not contingent on human desire for immediate justice. It also implicitly teaches that the delay in punishment is not due to divine weakness but divine wisdom and mercy, giving wrongdoers opportunity to repent before the appointed reckoning arrives.

translation: Repel evil with that which is better (good). We are most knowing of what they describe.
interpretation: This verse instructs the Prophet Muhammad (and by extension all believers) to respond to hostility, mockery, and false accusations with patience, kindness, and good conduct rather than retaliation in kind. It establishes a moral principle that evil should not be met with evil but transformed through goodness, which can disarm hostility and demonstrate the superior character of the believer. The verse concludes by reminding the Prophet that God is fully aware of the false descriptions, insults, and slanders being leveled against him, offering reassurance that divine knowledge and justice will ultimately prevail, so there is no need for the believer to seek personal vengeance or become consumed by the negativity of detractors. This teaching reflects a broader Quranic ethic found in other verses (such as 41:34) that emphasizes transforming enmity into friendship through patient forbearance and excellence in behavior, trusting that God sees and knows all things even when human eyes and judgments are clouded by malice.

translation: And say: 'My Lord, I seek refuge in You from the incitements of the devils.'
interpretation: This verse teaches a supplication that acknowledges the subtle, persistent nature of satanic temptation—'hamazat' refers to the whispers, promptings, and provocations that devils use to incite anger, doubt, arrogance, or sin within the human heart. By instructing the Prophet to say this prayer, God is modeling for all believers an attitude of humility and vigilance: recognizing that one cannot resist these spiritual incitements through willpower alone, but must actively seek divine protection. The verse frames spiritual struggle as an ongoing reality requiring constant recourse to God rather than self-reliance. It also implies that the devils' influence operates through suggestion and instigation rather than direct force—they 'prod' or 'provoke' rather than compel—making mindfulness and refuge-seeking the appropriate defense. This phrase is often recited as part of daily supplications, reflecting its practical function in the believer's spiritual life as a shield against internal temptation and external provocation alike.

translation: And I seek refuge in You, my Lord, lest they come near me.
interpretation: This verse continues the supplication begun in the preceding verse, where the Prophet is instructed to seek Allah's protection from the whisperings and incitements of devils (shayatin). Here, the prayer intensifies into seeking refuge not merely from their evil promptings but from their very presence and proximity. It reflects a profound spiritual awareness that evil influences seek to draw near to a believer, and that true protection comes only through reliance on Allah. The verse teaches that the believer's defense against spiritual corruption is not self-reliance or willpower alone, but active, continuous supplication and seeking divine refuge, acknowledging human vulnerability to unseen malevolent forces and the necessity of maintaining a protective barrier through faith and remembrance of Allah.

translation: Until, when death comes to one of them, he says: 'My Lord, send me back,'
interpretation: This verse depicts the moment of death for a disbelieving or heedless soul, when the reality of the afterlife becomes undeniably clear. Confronted with the truth they denied or neglected during their worldly life, the dying person pleads for a second chance to return to life so they might act righteously and make amends for their failures. This plea represents a universal human response to the realization, often coming too late, of what truly matters. The verse serves as a powerful warning to the living: the opportunity for righteous action and repentance exists only in this present life, and such desperate requests at the moment of death will not be granted, as the following verses make clear. It underscores the Quranic theme of urgency in faith and good deeds before it is too late, emphasizing that the veil of heedlessness lifts completely only when it is no longer possible to change one's fate.

translation: "That I might do righteous deeds in that which I have left behind." No! It is only a word he speaks; and behind them is a barrier (barzakh) until the Day they are resurrected.
interpretation: This verse depicts the desperate plea of a disbeliever at the moment of death, begging for a return to worldly life so that he might finally perform good deeds and make amends for his neglect of faith and righteousness. The divine response—"No!"—firmly rejects this plea, exposing it as an empty, insincere utterance born of panic rather than genuine conviction; had he truly been given more time, he would have continued in his former ways, as the Qur'an elsewhere suggests about the nature of such last-minute promises. The mention of the "barzakh," an impassable barrier or intermediate state, establishes a theological concept of the soul's existence between death and resurrection, a realm from which there is no return to correct one's deeds or alter one's fate. This underscores a central Qur'anic theme: that the time for righteous action is the present life, and that death marks an irreversible threshold after which repentance and good works are no longer efficacious. The verse serves as a solemn warning against procrastination in matters of faith and morality, emphasizing that the opportunity for righteousness is bounded by mortality itself.

translation: Then, when the Trumpet is blown, there will be no kinship ties among them that Day, nor will they ask about one another.
interpretation: This verse describes the terror and magnitude of the moment when the Trumpet is blown to signal the onset of the Day of Judgment. On that Day, the social bonds and lineage ties that people relied upon in worldly life—family connections, tribal affiliations, and ancestry that conferred status, protection, or obligation—will become utterly meaningless. The verse emphasizes that each soul will be so overwhelmed by its own reckoning and fear of judgment that people will not even think to inquire about their relatives, friends, or loved ones. This stands in stark contrast to worldly life, where lineage and kinship were sources of pride, support, and social structure. The verse underscores the theme of radical individual accountability before God: wealth, status, and relationships that mattered in this life will have no bearing on that Day, as every person will be consumed by concern for their own fate. It serves as a sobering reminder that ultimate reliance should be placed not on human relationships or worldly connections, but on one's deeds and relationship with God.

translation: Then those whose scales [of good deeds] are heavy - it is they who will be the successful.
interpretation: This verse refers to the Day of Judgment, when the deeds of every soul will be weighed on a divine scale (mizan). It establishes a direct correlation between the weight of one's good deeds and ultimate success in the afterlife. The 'heaviness' symbolizes not merely the quantity of good deeds but their quality, sincerity, and value in the sight of God. Success (falah) here is not worldly prosperity but eternal salvation—entry into Paradise. This verse serves as both a warning and an encouragement: it reminds believers that life is a test where actions have lasting consequences, and it motivates them to prioritize righteous deeds, sincere faith, and moral conduct over fleeting worldly pursuits. The imagery of scales also conveys divine justice—that every soul will be judged fairly, with nothing lost or added, emphasizing accountability and the ultimate justice of God's judgment.

translation: But those whose scales are light - they are the ones who have lost their souls, abiding eternally in Hell.
interpretation: This verse addresses the outcome for those whose good deeds, when weighed on the Day of Judgment, prove insufficient or light in comparison to their sins and negligence. The 'scales' (mawazin) represent the divine system of justice by which every soul's deeds are measured with perfect fairness. A light scale signifies a life lived without sufficient faith, righteous action, or accountability to God - a life where one may have pursued worldly gains, desires, or self-interest at the expense of spiritual and moral obligations. The phrase 'lost their souls' (khasiru anfusahum) is particularly significant: it indicates that the ultimate loss is not of wealth or worldly status, but of one's own self and eternal wellbeing. This is the deepest form of bankruptcy - squandering the very purpose of one's existence. The eternal abiding in Hell underscores the severity and finality of this loss, serving as a stark warning that this life is the only opportunity to accumulate the weight of good deeds that will matter in the ultimate reckoning. The verse calls believers to constant self-examination and striving, recognizing that true success is measured not by worldly achievement but by one's standing before God.

translation: The Fire will scorch their faces, and they will grimace therein with their lips distorted (baring their teeth).
interpretation: This verse vividly depicts the physical torment of the people condemned to Hellfire, emphasizing the intensity and direct nature of their suffering. The scorching of the faces signifies that the punishment is immediate and inescapable, afflicting the most expressive and sensitive part of the human body. The description of their lips being drawn back as if grinning—though not from joy but from the searing pain and shrinking of the skin from intense heat—conveys a grotesque image meant to instill fear and serve as a deterrent. This imagery contrasts sharply with descriptions elsewhere in the Qur'an of the joy and radiance of the faces of the righteous in Paradise, reinforcing the moral lesson that actions in this worldly life have direct, visceral consequences in the Hereafter. The verse serves as a warning against disbelief and wrongdoing, urging reflection on accountability before God.

translation: Were not My verses recited to you, and you used to deny them?
interpretation: This verse depicts a scene of divine interrogation on the Day of Judgment, in which the disbelievers are confronted directly by God with the reality of their past rejection. The rhetorical question format serves to strip away any excuses or justifications they might offer, establishing that they had indeed received clear revelation ("My verses") and had the opportunity to believe, yet chose deliberate denial ("takdhib") rather than simple ignorance or lack of exposure. This moment represents the closing of the argument against them—they cannot claim they were never informed, since the verses were "recited" (tutla) to them, implying a clear, accessible, and repeated transmission of guidance. The verse underscores a central Quranic theme: that disbelief is often not a matter of insufficient evidence but of willful rejection despite evidence being presented. It also reflects the justice of divine judgment, as accountability is tied to the reception of guidance—those who heard and rejected bear responsibility distinct from those who never received the message at all.

translation: They will say: 'Our Lord, our wretchedness overcame us, and we were a people astray.'
interpretation: This verse depicts the confession of the damned on the Day of Judgment, who acknowledge before God that their own misery and misguidance overpowered them, leading them to stray from the right path. It reflects a moment of regretful self-awareness, where sinners admit that their choices and inner corruption, rather than any external compulsion, were responsible for their downfall. The admission underscores the Islamic theological principle of personal accountability: despite being given guidance and free will, they succumbed to error and moral weakness. Their words are not merely an excuse but an acknowledgment of truth before divine justice, highlighting the futility of denial in the face of God's knowledge, and serving as a warning to the living about the consequences of choosing misguidance over faith and righteousness.

translation: Our Lord, bring us out of it, and if we return [to disbelief and sin], then indeed we would be wrongdoers.
interpretation: This verse depicts the desperate plea of the damned in Hellfire, begging God for a second chance to return to worldly life. Their admission is significant: they acknowledge in advance that should they be granted release and return to their former ways, they would deserve condemnation as wrongdoers. This reflects a key Qur'anic theme about human nature—that even in the face of ultimate consequence, there is doubt about whether people, given another chance, would truly reform their behavior. The verse serves as a warning to the living that such pleas will come too late, and that genuine repentance and righteous action must occur in this life, not be postponed in the vain hope of a future opportunity that will not be granted. It underscores the finality of divine judgment and the Qur'anic insistence that deathbed or afterlife promises of reform carry no weight when the time for choice has already passed.

translation: He will say, 'Remain despised therein, and do not speak to Me.'
interpretation: This verse comes from Surah Al-Mu'minun (23:108) and depicts the final, decisive response of God to the disbelievers after they beg from the Fire to be given another chance to return to worldly life and do righteous deeds. It follows their desperate plea in the preceding verses, where they admit their wretchedness and ask for a reprieve. God's curt and harsh reply—commanding them to remain in their degraded state and forbidding them from speaking further—signifies the closing of the door to mercy and repentance once the Hereafter has fully arrived. It underscores the Quranic theme that the opportunity for faith and righteous action belongs only to worldly life; once death and judgment have occurred, pleading is futile. The harshness of the language ('اخسئوا,' an expression used for driving away a despised dog) emphasizes the depth of degradation and divine rejection that the disbelievers have brought upon themselves through their choices, and the silencing ('do not speak to Me') represents the finality of their fate and the end of any dialogue or negotiation with God.

translation: Indeed, there was a party among My servants who said, 'Our Lord, we have believed, so forgive us and have mercy upon us, and You are the best of those who show mercy.'
interpretation: This verse recalls the sincere supplication of the faithful believers who, despite facing mockery and derision from disbelievers (as described in the surrounding verses of Surah Al-Mu'minun), remained steadfast in their devotion to God. Their prayer exemplifies true humility and faith: they acknowledge their belief, seek forgiveness for their shortcomings, and appeal to God's mercy rather than relying on their own righteousness. The phrase 'You are the best of those who show mercy' reflects their complete trust in God's compassion exceeding any mercy that could be shown by created beings. This verse serves as a model for believers to maintain patience and continue in heartfelt prayer even when ridiculed by others, trusting that God will ultimately vindicate those who remain devoted to Him, as the following verses reveal that those who mocked the believers will face consequences while the believers who maintained this attitude of humble supplication will be among the successful.

translation: But you took them in mockery until they made you forget My remembrance, and you used to laugh at them.
interpretation: This verse is addressed to the disbelievers on the Day of Judgment, reminding them of how they treated believers in the worldly life. It refers to sincere servants of God who, in their devotion, called upon Him saying 'Our Lord, we have believed, so forgive us and have mercy upon us, for You are the best of the merciful' (as mentioned in the preceding verse). The disbelievers mocked these believers for their faith and devotion, ridiculing them to the point that this mockery consumed the disbelievers' attention so thoroughly that they themselves forgot to remember God. Their derision of the faithful became such an obsession that it supplanted any thought of divine remembrance or accountability. The verse illustrates a profound reversal of values: those who were scorned and laughed at for their piety are vindicated, while those who indulged in ridicule are shown to have been spiritually negligent, so consumed by their contempt for believers that they neglected their own souls and relationship with God. This serves as a warning about the spiritual danger of mockery and arrogance toward the faithful, showing how such behavior can become a barrier that blinds one to the remembrance of God entirely.

translation: Indeed, I have rewarded them this Day for their patient endurance, so that it is they who are the triumphant.
interpretation: This verse comes as the divine conclusion to the account of the believers who were mocked and scorned by disbelievers in worldly life for their faith. Allah declares that on the Day of Judgment, the patience and steadfastness these believers showed in enduring ridicule, hardship, and persecution for the sake of their faith is now being repaid. The verse establishes a direct causal link between sabr (patient perseverance) and ultimate success (al-fawz), teaching that true triumph is not measured by worldly status or the mockery of others, but by steadfastness in faith that is vindicated in the Hereafter. It reassures believers throughout history that temporary suffering and derision for upholding truth will be transformed into eternal reward and honor before Allah, while those who scorned them will face the consequences of their arrogance and rejection of truth.

translation: He will say, 'How long did you remain on earth, in number of years?'
interpretation: This verse depicts a scene from the Day of Judgment in which God questions the disbelievers about the duration of their worldly life. The question itself serves a rhetorical and didactic purpose: it is not that the answer is unknown, but that the query is meant to prompt the wrongdoers themselves to recognize how brief and insignificant their earthly sojourn truly was when measured against the eternity of the afterlife. Their forthcoming answer (in the following verse) reveals their own confusion and the diminished significance they now place on worldly life, having wasted it in heedlessness and disbelief. This exchange underscores a central Quranic theme: the deceptive brevity of worldly existence contrasted with the eternal consequences of one's deeds, and the regret that comes too late when the truth of the Hereafter is finally confronted.

translation: They said, 'We remained a day or part of a day; ask those who keep count.'
interpretation: This verse depicts the response of people—often understood to be the disbelievers or those who denied the Resurrection—when they are questioned in the Hereafter about how long they stayed in the grave or in worldly life. Their uncertain answer, estimating only 'a day or part of a day,' reveals how insignificant and fleeting their earthly existence now appears to them in light of the vastness of eternity they now face. Their deferral to 'those who keep count' (the angels, or those skilled in reckoning) reflects their own confusion and loss of a true sense of time, underscoring a central Qur'anic theme: that the life of this world, however long it seemed while being lived, will appear as a mere moment when compared to the eternal reality of the Hereafter. This serves as a warning to the listener to not be deceived by the seeming permanence of worldly life, and to recognize its true, transient nature relative to the everlasting life to come.

translation: He will say, 'You stayed not except a little, if only you had known.'
interpretation: This verse depicts a scene from the Day of Judgment in which Allah (or an angel) addresses those who are being questioned about their time spent on earth or in the grave (barzakh). When asked how long they remained, they will realize that, in comparison to the eternity of the Hereafter, their worldly life or the time between death and resurrection was but a fleeting moment. The phrase 'if only you had known' is a rebuke, highlighting that had they truly understood during their lifetime how brief and insignificant worldly existence is compared to the eternal life to come, they would have lived differently—prioritizing faith, righteousness, and preparation for the Hereafter rather than being absorbed in transient worldly pursuits. The verse serves as a powerful reminder of the illusory nature of time's perception and the importance of maintaining eternal perspective while living a temporal life.

translation: Did you then think that We created you in vain, and that to Us you would not be returned?
interpretation: This verse rebukes the assumption that human existence is purposeless and devoid of accountability. It affirms that creation is deliberate and meaningful, not a frivolous or random act, and that life is oriented toward an inevitable return to God for judgment. By posing the question rhetorically, the verse challenges a worldview that denies resurrection and moral responsibility, implying that such a denial would render God's creative act absurd. It thus serves as a foundational argument for the reality of the afterlife, grounding ethical seriousness in the belief that human actions have ultimate consequence and that life is not merely a transient, meaningless episode but part of a purposeful divine plan culminating in accountability before the Creator.

translation: So exalted is Allah, the True King; there is no deity except Him, Lord of the Noble Throne.
interpretation: This verse establishes the absolute sovereignty and transcendence of Allah as the ultimate ruler whose kingship is based on truth and reality, unlike worldly kings whose authority is temporary and often unjust. The declaration of monotheism ("there is no deity except Him") reinforces that all power, dominion, and worship belong exclusively to Him. The mention of the "Noble Throne" (al-Arsh al-Karim) symbolizes His supreme authority over all creation, emphasizing both His majesty and His generosity toward His creatures. This verse often appears as a conclusion to passages discussing human arrogance or false claims to power, serving as a corrective reminder that true, everlasting sovereignty belongs only to Allah, contrasting the impermanence of human rule with the eternal and righteous kingship of the Divine.

translation: And whoever invokes, along with Allah, another god for whom he has no proof - his reckoning is only with his Lord. Indeed, the disbelievers will not succeed.
interpretation: This verse establishes a clear theological principle: the invocation of any deity besides Allah is fundamentally unjustifiable because such worship lacks any rational or evidentiary foundation (burhan). The verse implies that true faith rests upon evidence and sound reasoning, not blind imitation of ancestral customs or baseless speculation - polytheism is condemned not merely as sinful but as intellectually unsupportable. The phrase 'his account is only with his Lord' shifts the matter from human judgment to divine judgment, indicating that ultimate consequences for this transgression are deferred to the Hereafter, where Allah alone will render the reckoning. This serves as both a warning and a point of moral and legal restraint - humans are not necessarily tasked with punishing such disbelief in this world, as final judgment belongs to God. The closing statement, 'the disbelievers will not succeed,' functions as a general declaration of the ultimate failure of kufr (disbelief) and shirk (associating partners with God), reinforcing the Quranic theme that true success (falah) is contingent upon monotheistic faith and righteous action, while rejection of this truth leads inevitably to spiritual and eschatological loss.

translation: And say, 'My Lord, forgive and have mercy, and You are the best of the merciful.'
interpretation: This closing verse of Surah Al-Mu'minun presents a concise, humble supplication that the Prophet (and by extension every believer) is instructed to make directly to God. It encapsulates the entirety of human spiritual need in two simple requests: forgiveness (maghfirah) for past shortcomings and sins, and mercy (rahmah) for ongoing sustenance and compassion in this life and the next. The verse affirms that God is 'khayr al-rahimeen' - the best of those who show mercy - surpassing any mercy humans might show one another, since divine mercy is boundless, unconditional, and free from the limitations of human compassion. Coming at the end of a surah that has discussed the nature of true believers, the stages of human creation, the fate of disbelievers, and the transience of worldly life, this prayer serves as a humble acknowledgment that despite all righteous deeds and belief, ultimate salvation depends on God's forgiveness and mercy, not merely human effort. It teaches that even the most devoted servants should approach God with humility, recognizing their constant need for divine grace rather than relying solely on their own righteousness.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. [This is] a surah which We have sent down and made obligatory, and We have sent down therein clear verses so that you might remember.
interpretation: This opening verse of Surah An-Nur establishes the authority and seriousness of the chapter that follows, which deals with laws concerning chastity, modesty, and social conduct. By emphasizing that the surah is both 'sent down' (revealed) and 'made obligatory' (its rulings are binding), Allah underscores that the injunctions to come—regarding adultery, false accusation, marriage, and the regulation of gazes and dress—are not mere suggestions but divine law requiring compliance. The phrase 'clear verses' (ayat bayyinat) indicates that the guidance given is unambiguous and leaves no room for misinterpretation, making the responsibility of the believers to follow it even greater. The purpose stated—'so that you might remember'—reveals that these laws are not arbitrary restrictions but reminders of innate moral truths that safeguard individual dignity and communal harmony, calling people back to their natural disposition (fitrah) of modesty and righteousness that may be forgotten amid worldly distractions.

translation: The woman and the man guilty of illegal sexual intercourse (zina) - flog each one of them with a hundred lashes, and let not pity for them overcome you in the religion (ordainment) of Allah, if you believe in Allah and the Last Day. And let a group of believers witness their punishment.
interpretation: This verse establishes a fixed legal penalty (hadd) for the crime of zina (illicit sexual intercourse outside marriage), applying equally to both the man and the woman involved, underscoring the Qur'an's principle of shared accountability regardless of gender. The instruction not to let 'pity' or 'compassion' interfere with carrying out this divinely ordained punishment emphasizes that personal emotion should not override the implementation of established law when justice is at stake, particularly for a matter the Qur'an treats as a serious transgression against the moral order of the community. This does not negate compassion as a value elsewhere in Islamic ethics, but asserts that in the specific context of executing a judicial ruling, sentimentality should not be allowed to obstruct the rule of law as commanded by Allah. The requirement that a group of believers witness the punishment serves multiple purposes: it ensures transparency and accountability in the execution of justice (preventing secret or arbitrary punishment), it acts as a public deterrent to discourage others from committing the same transgression, and it reinforces the communal nature of upholding moral and legal standards in the society. The verse as a whole reflects the Qur'an's broader framework of combining strict legal consequences with high evidentiary standards (established in surrounding verses requiring four witnesses) for such grave accusations, balancing deterrence with safeguards against false accusation.

translation: The fornicator does not marry except a fornicatress or an idolatress, and the fornicatress - none marries her except a fornicator or an idolater. And that has been made unlawful for the believers.
interpretation: This verse establishes a moral and social principle linking marriage partnerships to spiritual and ethical compatibility. It suggests that those who persist in sexual immorality tend to be drawn to others of similar character, while the righteous believers are forbidden from such unions. The verse serves as both a description of natural affinity between like-minded individuals and a prescriptive moral boundary, encouraging believers to seek marriage partners who share their commitment to chastity and faith, thereby protecting the integrity of the Muslim community's family structure and moral fabric.

translation: And those who accuse chaste women [of unlawful sexual intercourse] and then do not produce four witnesses - lash them with eighty lashes and do not accept their testimony ever after. And those are the defiantly disobedient.
interpretation: This verse establishes a severe legal and social safeguard within Islamic jurisprudence, addressing the grave offense of slandering chaste women with accusations of adultery (qadhf). By requiring four eyewitnesses to such an intimate act - a nearly impossible evidentiary standard - the verse effectively makes it extremely difficult to level such accusations casually or maliciously, thereby protecting individuals' honor and reputation from baseless rumor and slander. The prescribed punishment of eighty lashes for false accusers, combined with the permanent disqualification of their testimony in any future matter, reflects the Quran's serious concern with protecting the dignity and social standing of women specifically, and the broader community from the corrosive effects of unsubstantiated gossip and character assassination. The characterization of such false accusers as 'fasiqun' (defiantly disobedient/morally corrupt) elevates this from merely a legal matter to a spiritual one, indicating that baseless slander constitutes a serious moral transgression against both the accused individual and the broader social fabric that depends on trust and the presumption of innocence. This legislation effectively discourages a culture of suspicion and public shaming that could otherwise destroy reputations based on hearsay, establishing instead a high threshold of proof before such serious accusations can be entertained by the community.

translation: Except for those who repent after that and reform themselves, for indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation: This verse offers a path of redemption to those who have committed wrongdoing, such as false accusations against the chaste (as discussed in the preceding verses of Surah An-Nur regarding slander). It emphasizes that the door to Allah's mercy remains open even after serious transgressions, provided the sinner takes two essential steps: sincere repentance (tawbah) and genuine reformation of conduct (islah). The pairing of these two conditions is significant—mere verbal repentance without changed behavior is insufficient, and outward behavioral change without sincere inner repentance lacks spiritual substance. The verse concludes with two divine attributes, Ghafur (Forgiving) and Raheem (Merciful), which together convey that Allah not only pardons the sin but also extends compassionate care to the repentant sinner, restoring them to a state of grace. This reflects the broader Quranic theme that Allah's justice is always balanced with mercy, and that no sin is too great to be forgiven when approached with true contrition and a commitment to change.

translation: And those who accuse their wives [of adultery] and have no witnesses except themselves - then the testimony of one of them [shall be] four testimonies [swearing] by Allah that indeed, he is of the truthful.
interpretation: This verse introduces the legal procedure known as li'an, designed for the difficult situation where a husband accuses his wife of infidelity but cannot produce the four witnesses normally required to substantiate such a charge under Islamic law. Rather than leaving the husband without recourse or forcing him to either remain silent or face punishment for unproven slander (qadhf), the verse establishes an alternative: the husband may testify to the truth of his accusation by swearing four times by Allah that he is truthful. This mechanism substitutes the weight of witness testimony with the solemnity of repeated divine oaths, placing the matter before God rather than requiring human corroboration. The procedure reflects the gravity with which accusations of sexual impropriety are treated in Islamic jurisprudence, balancing the protection of individuals from false accusation with the practical reality that such acts often occur without witnesses. The fivefold invocation of God's name (continued in the following verse with a curse upon himself if lying) underscores that this is not a casual legal technicality but an act meant to invoke divine awareness and consequence, deterring false swearing through the fear of God's judgment rather than human proof alone.

translation: And the fifth [oath should state] that the curse of Allah be upon him if he should be among the liars.
interpretation: This verse is part of the li'an (mutual imprecation) procedure described in Surah An-Nur, which provides a legal mechanism for a husband who accuses his wife of adultery without having the required four witnesses. In this process, the husband must swear four times that he is telling the truth, and then a fifth time invoking Allah's curse upon himself if he is lying. This fifth oath intensifies the seriousness of the testimony by calling down divine curse—a severe spiritual consequence—as a deterrent against false accusation. It reflects the Qur'anic principle that serious accusations affecting a person's honor and family lineage require solemn, self-incriminating oaths when ordinary evidentiary standards (four witnesses) cannot be met, placing the matter ultimately in God's judgment rather than human courts alone. This mechanism protects the wife from being falsely accused while allowing the husband a legal recourse to dissolve the marriage without being subjected to the punishment for slander (qadhf), provided he is willing to invoke such a serious curse upon himself if false.

translation: And it shall avert the punishment from her if she bears witness four times by Allah that he is indeed of the liars.
interpretation: This verse is part of the li'an (mutual imprecation) procedure prescribed for a husband who accuses his wife of adultery without producing four witnesses. The wife can avert the legal punishment for adultery by countering her husband's accusation with her own four oaths by Allah testifying that he is lying, followed by a fifth invoking Allah's wrath upon herself if he is truthful. This mechanism reflects the Qur'anic principle that severe punishments require either overwhelming evidentiary proof or, in its absence, a solemn oath-based resolution that places the matter in God's judgment rather than human certainty. It demonstrates a balance of accountability between spouses, giving the accused wife a formal legal recourse to protect herself from punishment based solely on her husband's unsubstantiated claim, while leaving the ultimate truth and consequence to divine reckoning.

translation: And the fifth [testimony] is that the wrath of Allah be upon her if he (her husband) was among the truthful.
interpretation: This verse is part of the li'an procedure described in Surah An-Nur (24:6-9), a legal mechanism in Islamic jurisprudence for cases where a husband accuses his wife of adultery without having four witnesses to support the claim. In such cases, the husband must swear four times by Allah that he is truthful in his accusation, and a fifth time invoking Allah's curse upon himself if he is lying. This verse describes the wife's counter-testimony: she can refute the accusation by swearing four times by Allah that her husband is lying, with a fifth oath invoking Allah's wrath upon herself if he is telling the truth. This mechanism allowed both parties to resolve the matter through solemn oaths before God rather than through unsubstantiated accusations, effectively dissolving the marriage without the punishment for adultery being applied to either party, while leaving ultimate judgment to Allah. The verse reflects the Qur'anic emphasis on due process, the seriousness of accusations of sexual misconduct, and the protection of individuals from slander in the absence of proper evidence.

translation: And if not for the favor of Allah upon you and His mercy, and that Allah is Accepting of repentance and Wise... [the consequences would have been severe].
interpretation: This verse is part of a longer passage (from Surah An-Nur) addressing the aftermath of a serious accusation of slander within the Muslim community, specifically the incident known as 'Ifk' (the slander against Aisha, the wife of the Prophet Muhammad). The verse serves as a conditional clause, implying that had it not been for Allah's grace, mercy, and His nature as the Accepter of repentance and the Wise, severe punishment would have befallen those involved in spreading the false accusation. It emphasizes that divine mercy tempers justice, allowing room for forgiveness and correction rather than immediate retribution. The mention of Allah being 'Tawwab' (Accepting of repentance) and 'Hakim' (Wise) underscores that His mercy is not arbitrary but is paired with wisdom, meaning that forgiveness is granted in a manner that maintains moral and social order, teaching the believers the gravity of slander while also offering a path to redemption through sincere repentance.

translation: Indeed, those who brought forth the lie (al-ifk) are a group among you. Do not think it bad for you; rather, it is good for you. For every person among them is what he has earned of the sin, and the one among them who took on the greater portion of it will have a great punishment.
interpretation: This verse was revealed concerning the slander spread against the Prophet's wife Aisha (the incident known as 'hadith al-ifk'), when a group of hypocrites and some believers circulated a false accusation against her honor. The verse establishes several important principles: first, it identifies the slanderers as 'a group among you,' indicating they were a faction within the Muslim community rather than outsiders, which made the betrayal more painful yet also more containable. Second, it reframes the trial as ultimately beneficial ('khayr lakum') rather than purely harmful, teaching that such tests can purify the community, expose hypocrisy, strengthen the bonds of those who remain steadfast in faith and loyalty, and result in divine legislation (such as the laws of slander, li'an, and evidentiary standards) that protects honor for all future generations. Third, the verse individualizes moral and legal responsibility—each person bears only the sin they personally committed, rejecting collective guilt. Finally, it singles out the ringleader who orchestrated or amplified the slander for the greatest punishment, emphasizing that those who initiate or lead corruption bear heavier accountability than those who merely participate or are misled. This verse thus combines theodicy (finding wisdom in trials), jurisprudence (individual accountability), and moral hierarchy (graduated culpability based on one's role in wrongdoing).

translation: Why, when you heard it, did not the believing men and believing women think well of themselves and say, 'This is an obvious lie'?
interpretation: This verse refers to the incident of the slander (ifk) against the Prophet's wife Aisha. God rebukes the believers for not immediately rejecting the false rumor out of good faith and solidarity with their fellow believers. The verse establishes a principle of Islamic ethics: that believers should assume good of one another (husn al-zann) rather than readily believing or spreading slander, especially without evidence. It criticizes the community's failure to exercise this charitable judgment, implying that true faith should produce an instinctive defense of the honor of other believers and immediate skepticism toward unverified accusations, particularly ones that threaten someone's reputation and lack any supporting proof.

translation: Why did they not bring four witnesses to it? Since they did not bring the witnesses, then it is they, in the sight of Allah, who are the liars.
interpretation: This verse is part of the Qur'anic response to the slander (ifk) against Aisha, the wife of the Prophet Muhammad. It establishes a strict legal principle regarding accusations of adultery or fornication (zina): such a grave charge cannot be accepted on the basis of rumor or hearsay but requires the testimony of four eyewitnesses who directly observed the act. This is an extraordinarily high evidentiary bar, deliberately set to protect individuals' honor and reputation from baseless slander and to deter false accusations. By declaring that those who fail to produce such witnesses are themselves liars in God's sight, the verse shifts moral and legal culpability onto the accusers rather than the accused, emphasizing the severity of spreading unverified accusations that damage someone's honor. This principle became foundational in Islamic jurisprudence for handling accusations of sexual immorality, ensuring that such serious charges are not used as tools for gossip, defamation, or social persecution.

translation: And were it not for the favor of Allah upon you and His mercy in this world and the Hereafter, a great punishment would have touched you for that [slander] in which you had indulged.
interpretation: This verse was revealed in connection with the incident of ifk (the slander against Aisha, the Prophet's wife), addressing those believers who had spread or listened to and spread false rumors without verifying them. It serves as a sobering reminder that divine mercy, not human merit, shielded the community from severe consequences for their collective moral failure in spreading slander. The verse underscores the gravity of engaging in gossip and unverified accusations, especially those that harm reputations and violate trust within the community. It also illustrates a broader theological principle: that Allah's grace often spares people from the full weight of punishment their actions might otherwise warrant, serving as both a warning and a call to gratitude. The phrase 'in this world and the Hereafter' emphasizes that divine mercy operates across both temporal and eternal dimensions, protecting believers from immediate social catastrophe as well as eternal consequence, provided they turn back in repentance and learn from the lapse.

translation: When you received it with your tongues and said with your mouths that which you had no knowledge of, and you thought it was insignificant, while it was, in the sight of Allah, tremendous.
interpretation: This verse addresses the believers regarding the incident of slander (al-Ifk) when a false accusation spread through the community without verification. It highlights the grave danger of uncritically repeating rumors and gossip, emphasizing that speech itself carries moral weight even when one merely passes along what others say rather than originating it. The verse condemns the casual attitude with which people treat the spreading of unverified claims, noting the dangerous gap between human perception of triviality and divine judgment of severity. This establishes a broader ethical principle in Islam regarding the sanctity of reputation, the obligation to verify information before repeating it, and accountability for speech that may seem harmless but can cause profound harm to individuals and the social fabric of the community.

translation: And why, when you heard it, did you not say, 'It is not for us to speak of this. Glory be to You [O Allah]; this is a great slander'?
interpretation: This verse comes from the account of the slander (ifk) against the Prophet's wife Aisha. It rebukes the believers who heard the false accusation and, instead of immediately rejecting it as impossible and sinful to repeat, allowed themselves to entertain or pass along the rumor. Allah teaches that the proper response upon hearing slander about someone's honor—especially without evidence—is instant denial and recognition of its impossibility, exclaiming God's glory and condemning the falsehood outright, rather than engaging in gossip or doubt. This establishes a broader ethical principle for believers: to guard the honor of others, presume good faith, and refuse to spread unverified claims that could damage someone's reputation.

translation: Allah admonishes you never to repeat the like of it again, if you are believers.
interpretation: This verse refers to the aftermath of the incident of the slander (ifk) against Aisha, and more broadly to the grave sin of spreading false accusations and rumors that harm the honor of others. Allah is warning the believers that such behavior—hastily spreading unverified gossip and slander—is incompatible with true faith. The conditional clause 'if you are believers' is a powerful rhetorical device that ties genuine faith directly to one's conduct in protecting the reputation and dignity of others within the community. It implies that true belief necessitates self-restraint, verification before speaking, and avoidance of participating in harmful gossip, establishing a moral and social standard for the Muslim community regarding slander and the circulation of unverified claims.

translation: And Allah makes clear to you the signs; and Allah is Knowing and Wise.
interpretation: This verse affirms that the detailed rulings and guidance revealed by Allah—particularly those preceding it concerning modesty, accusations of unchastity, and social conduct—are not arbitrary but are clarified explanations rooted in divine knowledge and wisdom. By emphasizing both attributes together, the verse teaches that God's legislation is purposeful: His omniscience ('Alim) ensures that He fully understands human nature, society, and the consequences of actions, while His wisdom (Hakim) ensures that the laws He reveals are perfectly suited to establish justice, protect honor, and maintain social harmony. The clarification of 'the signs' (al-ayat) refers not only to verbal revelation but to the unfolding of moral and legal guidance that serves as a sign of divine care for human welfare. This phrase reassures believers that the sometimes difficult or intimate rulings given by God are not burdens imposed without reason, but are rooted in a comprehensive understanding of human psychology and social needs, aimed at protecting individuals and communities from corruption, slander, and moral decay.

translation: Indeed, those who love that immorality (or slander) should spread among those who believe will have a painful punishment in this world and the Hereafter. And Allah knows, while you do not know.
interpretation: This verse was revealed in the context of the slander (ifk) spread against the Prophet's household, addressing those who took pleasure in spreading false accusations and scandal within the Muslim community. It establishes a serious moral and legal principle: deliberately desiring and working to propagate indecency, slander, or scandal about believers—damaging their honor and sowing social corruption—is a grave sin deserving severe punishment, both through worldly consequences (such as the prescribed legal penalties for slander) and divine retribution in the Hereafter. The verse emphasizes intent ('those who love') showing that the sin lies not only in the act of spreading rumors but in the inner desire and satisfaction derived from seeing immorality and scandal circulate among the faithful. The closing phrase 'Allah knows, while you do not know' serves as a humbling reminder that human judgment is limited and fallible, often based on assumption, gossip, or incomplete information, whereas Allah's knowledge is complete and perfect. This encourages believers to withhold judgment, verify information, protect the reputations of fellow believers, and trust in divine wisdom and justice rather than participating in or enjoying the spread of unverified claims that harm the social fabric of the community.

translation: And were it not for the favor of Allah upon you and His mercy, and that Allah is Full of Kindness, Most Merciful...
interpretation: This verse appears as a recurring refrain in contexts dealing with human error, hasty judgments, or susceptibility to slander and false accusations, such as in the aftermath of the incident of slander (ifk) in Surah An-Nur. The sentence is deliberately left incomplete (a grammatical construction called apodosis omission), creating a dramatic pause that invites the listener to contemplate the unstated consequence: were it not for God's grace, mercy, and compassionate nature, severe punishment or ruin would have befallen those who erred. This rhetorical device emphasizes that human beings are inherently prone to misttakes, rash judgments, and sin, and that their continued well-being and the opportunity for correction depend entirely on divine mercy rather than human merit. The pairing of 'ra'uf' (full of kindness/tenderness) and 'rahim' (most merciful) underscores two dimensions of God's compassion—a gentle, caring kindness and an active, redemptive mercy—suggesting that God's forbearance is both emotionally tender and practically manifested in forgiveness and guidance. The verse serves as a humbling reminder that divine grace is the sole reason for the community's stability, protection from the full consequences of their errors, and the possibility of repentance and moral correction.

translation: O you who have believed, do not follow the footsteps of Satan. And whoever follows the footsteps of Satan - indeed, he enjoins immorality and wrongdoing. And if not for the favor of Allah upon you and His mercy, not one of you would have been purified, ever, but Allah purifies whom He wills. And Allah is Hearing and Knowing.
interpretation: This verse warns believers against being led by Satan's incremental temptations, which begin with seemingly small steps but lead toward indecency and sin. It emphasizes that human purification and moral uprightness are not achieved through one's own effort alone, but are fundamentally a gift of divine grace and mercy. This serves as a humbling reminder against self-righteousness, teaching that spiritual growth depends on God's will and favor rather than human merit alone, while also affirming that God's purification is not arbitrary but granted according to His perfect knowledge of who is receptive to guidance. The verse thus balances human responsibility to resist temptation with reliance on divine grace for true moral purity.

translation: And let not those among you who possess virtue and affluence swear not to give to relatives, the needy, and those who emigrated in the way of Allah. Let them pardon and overlook. Do you not wish that Allah should forgive you? And Allah is Forgiving, Merciful.
interpretation: This verse was revealed in connection with the incident involving Abu Bakr, who had vowed to withdraw financial support from a relative implicated in the slander against Aisha. Allah instructs that personal wealth and moral standing should not become the basis for withholding generosity or holding grudges, even against those who have erred or caused personal offense. The verse establishes a profound ethical principle: that the capacity to forgive and continue acts of charity, even toward those who have wronged us, is intrinsically linked to one's own hope for divine forgiveness. By posing the rhetorical question 'Do you not wish that Allah should forgive you?', the verse draws a direct parallel between human forgiveness and divine mercy—suggesting that those who wish to receive Allah's boundless forgiveness must themselves embody forgiveness and generosity toward others, refusing to let anger or vindictiveness override compassion and communal responsibility.

translation: Indeed, those who accuse chaste, unaware, believing women [of unchastity] are cursed in this world and the Hereafter, and they will have a great punishment.
interpretation: This verse addresses the grave sin of slandering chaste and innocent believing women by falsely accusing them of adultery or immorality, especially in contexts where they have given no cause for suspicion. It establishes that such slander is not merely a social offense but a spiritual transgression carrying divine condemnation both in this life and the next. The emphasis on the women being 'unaware' (ghafilat) highlights their innocence and lack of involvement in any wrongdoing, making the accusation particularly unjust. This verse is understood by scholars to be connected to the broader Quranic teachings on protecting personal honor and reputation, and it reinforces the severe legal and moral consequences for those who engage in baseless slander (qadhf), which requires four witnesses to substantiate accusations of adultery. The verse serves as a deterrent against spreading rumors and emphasizes the sanctity of a believer's reputation, particularly women's, within the community.

translation: On the Day when their tongues, their hands, and their feet will testify against them as to what they used to do.
interpretation: This verse describes the Day of Judgment, emphasizing the theme of absolute accountability before God. It conveys that on that Day, human attempts at denial or deception will be rendered futile, for the very parts of the body that were instruments of a person's deeds in worldly life—the tongue used for speech, lies, or slander, and the hands and feet used for actions—will be made to speak the truth against their owner. This signifies that nothing can be hidden from God, who has complete knowledge of every action, and that each person bears full responsibility for how they used their faculties. The verse underscores the idea that the body itself is a witness, highlighting the totality of divine justice and the impossibility of escaping the consequences of one's own conduct.

translation: On that Day, Allah will pay them in full their just due (recompense), and they will know that Allah is the Manifest Truth.
interpretation: This verse refers to the Day of Judgment, when every soul will be fully recompensed for its deeds with perfect justice—'their just due' (دينهم الحق) signifying that no wrong will be done to anyone, whether in reward or punishment. The phrase underscores divine justice as absolute and uncorrupted by the deception, slander, or false accusations that characterized worldly life, particularly connecting to the broader context of the surah which deals with slander and the protection of honor. The second half of the verse, declaring that people will then know Allah as 'al-Haqq al-Mubin' (the Manifest, Self-Evident Truth), suggests that on that Day, all illusions, doubts, and denials that existed in worldly life will be dispelled. Allah's truth, justice, and reality will become utterly clear and undeniable, in contrast to the ambiguity, suspicion, and falsehood that often cloud human judgment in this life. This serves as both a warning to wrongdoers and a consolation to the wronged, affirming that ultimate truth and justice are guaranteed, even if obscured in the temporal world.

translation: Evil women are for evil men, and evil men are for evil women; and good women are for good men, and good men are for good women. Those [good people] are innocent of what [the slanderers] say. For them is forgiveness and a generous provision.
interpretation: This verse was revealed in the context of the slander against 'A'isha, the wife of the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him), affirming her innocence and establishing a broader principle: there is a natural affinity between people of similar moral character—corrupt individuals gravitate toward corruption, while virtuous individuals align with virtue. The verse functions as a decisive rebuttal to the slanderers, implying that it would be inconceivable for a pure and righteous man like the Prophet to be married to an impure woman, since purity attracts purity. Beyond the immediate historical context, the verse establishes a timeless spiritual principle about the congruence between inner character and the company or relationships one attracts, while also offering comfort and vindication to those who are falsely accused, promising them divine forgiveness and generous reward for enduring slander with patience and integrity.

translation: O you who have believed, do not enter houses other than your own houses until you ascertain welcome and greet their inhabitants with peace. That is best for you, that you may be reminded (or take heed).
interpretation: This verse establishes a foundational principle of social etiquette and respect for privacy in Islamic ethics. It teaches that one's home is a sanctuary, and entering another's private space without permission violates their dignity and security. The requirement to 'seek permission' (tasta'nisu) implies more than a mere knock—it suggests a mutual process of familiarization and consent, ensuring the host is comfortable and prepared for a visitor's presence. The accompanying greeting of peace (salam) transforms the act of entry from an intrusion into a blessed social exchange, setting a tone of goodwill from the very first moment of contact. By framing this practice as 'better for you,' the verse suggests that such boundaries ultimately serve the believer's own moral and spiritual development, cultivating humility, patience, and respect for others rather than being a mere restrictive rule. The closing phrase 'that you may be reminded' ties this social command to a broader spiritual consciousness—suggesting that mindfulness in small interpersonal matters nurtures a more encompassing God-consciousness (taqwa), reinforcing that Islamic ethics extend into the most intimate aspects of daily life, including how one approaches another's home.

translation: And if you find no one therein, do not enter them until permission is given to you. And if it is said to you, 'Go back,' then go back; it is purer for you. And Allah is Knowing of what you do.
interpretation: This verse continues the Qur'anic etiquette of entering others' homes, establishing that respect for privacy takes precedence over one's own desire or perceived right to enter. If no one is found to grant permission, one must not assume access is allowed simply because the house appears empty—boundaries and consent remain in effect regardless of circumstance. Likewise, if asked to leave or turn back, compliance without resentment or insistence is required, as graciously accepting such a request reflects humility and social harmony rather than a loss of dignity. The phrase 'it is purer for you' frames this etiquette not merely as a social nicety but as a matter of moral and spiritual cleanliness—avoiding intrusion, suspicion, or offense keeps one's heart and conduct wholesome. The closing reminder that God is fully aware of all actions reinforces that these social codes are not just human conventions but are tied to divine observation and accountability, encouraging sincerity in practicing modesty and respect even when no one else is watching to enforce it.

translation: There is no blame upon you that you enter uninhabited houses in which there is convenience for you. And Allah knows what you reveal and what you conceal.
interpretation: This verse continues the etiquette of entering homes established earlier in Surah An-Nur, clarifying that the requirement to seek permission before entering applies specifically to inhabited dwellings where privacy is a concern. Uninhabited or non-residential structures—such as storerooms, shops, inns, or public facilities—that serve a practical benefit or convenience do not require the same formality of asking permission, since no one's private space or dignity is being intruded upon. The verse closes with a reminder that Allah is fully aware of both what people disclose and what they hide, underscoring that the rules of privacy and permission are not merely social formalities but are rooted in a moral consciousness of divine oversight. Even in matters where outward permission may not be strictly necessary, believers are reminded that their intentions and inner states remain known to God, encouraging sincerity and restraint from exploiting such allowances for improper purposes.

translation: Say to the believing men that they should lower their gaze and guard their private parts. That is purer for them. Indeed, Allah is Acquainted with what they do.
interpretation: This verse establishes a foundational principle of Islamic sexual ethics and social modesty directed primarily at men, though a parallel command follows for women in the next verse. The command to 'lower the gaze' addresses the first point of temptation and potential sin—the eyes—recognizing that illicit desire often begins with a look. By placing responsibility on men first, the verse counters any notion that modesty is solely a female obligation, establishing mutual responsibility between the sexes in maintaining a chaste society. The pairing of lowering the gaze with guarding one's private parts links the visual and physical dimensions of chastity, suggesting that discipline of the eyes serves as a safeguard against more serious transgressions. The phrase 'that is purer for them' frames this not merely as a legal restriction but as a matter of spiritual and moral purification (zakat), suggesting that self-restraint in this area cultivates inner cleanliness and dignity. The verse closes with a reminder that God is fully aware of what people do, reinforcing that this command is not merely a social convention but a matter of accountability before God, even in private or seemingly inconsequential glances that others may not witness.

translation: And tell the believing women to lower their gaze and guard their private parts and not expose their adornment except that which is apparent, and to draw their veils over their bosoms and not expose their adornment except to their husbands, their fathers, their husbands' fathers, their sons, their husbands' sons, their brothers, their brothers' sons, their sisters' sons, their women, what their right hands possess, male attendants having no physical desire, or children who are not yet aware of the private aspects of women. And let them not stamp their feet to make known what they conceal of their adornment. And turn to Allah in repentance, all of you believers, that you might succeed.
interpretation: This verse establishes a comprehensive code of modesty for believing women as a complement to the modesty required of believing men in the preceding verse, situating personal virtue within a broader social and spiritual framework. The instruction to lower the gaze and guard chastity addresses both outward behavior and inward discipline, suggesting that modesty is as much about self-restraint and intention as about physical covering. The specification of a close circle of male relatives before whom adornment may be shown reflects an understanding of natural, familial intimacy where temptation or impropriety is not a concern, thereby distinguishing between private domestic life and public social interaction. The inclusion of 'those who are not yet aware of the private aspects of women' acknowledges the innocence of childhood, while the mention of servants or attendants 'having no physical desire' shows a pragmatic recognition of household dynamics. The prohibition against stamping the feet to draw attention to hidden adornments reveals that modesty is concerned not only with visible exposure but also with the subtler forms of allure, emphasizing an ethic of restraint that extends to gesture and sound, not just dress. The verse closes with a call for collective repentance, reminding both men and women that the pursuit of modesty and moral integrity is a shared and ongoing struggle, requiring humility, mutual accountability, and continual turning toward God rather than self-righteous judgment of one gender over another. Overall, this verse frames female modesty not as repression but as an expression of dignity, boundary-setting, and spiritual discipline within the just and balanced social order intended by divine guidance.

translation: And marry the unmarried among you and the righteous among your male slaves and female slaves. If they are poor, Allah will enrich them from His bounty. And Allah is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing.
interpretation: This verse establishes marriage as a social institution to be facilitated for all free members of the community as well as for enslaved people deemed righteous, without allowing poverty to be used as a barrier or excuse to prevent unions. It reflects a communal responsibility to support marriage as a means of social stability and moral protection, trusting that economic hardship is not a permanent condition but something God can alleviate through His provision. The mention of slaves alongside free believers also signals an early move toward recognizing the dignity and marital rights of enslaved persons within the community, challenging purely economic or status-based objections to marriage. The closing divine attributes—vastness and knowledge—reassure believers that God's capacity to provide is boundless and that He understands the true circumstances and needs of each individual, encouraging trust in divine provision over worldly calculation when it comes to fulfilling this social and personal obligation.

translation: And let those who cannot find [the means for] marriage abstain [from sin] until Allah enriches them from His bounty.
