The specific mention of 'with the Messenger' emphasizes that true guidance was accessible and clear, making the wrongdoer's deviation a matter of choice rather than ignorance, which intensifies the bitterness of the regret.

translation: Oh, woe is me! I wish I had not taken so-and-so as a close friend!
interpretation: This verse depicts the anguished regret of a wrongdoer on the Day of Judgment, lamenting the companionship he kept in worldly life that led him astray from the path of truth and guidance. The phrase 'so-and-so' (fulanan) is deliberately unspecified, making the warning universal rather than pointing to a particular historical individual—it applies to anyone who allows a companion to divert them from righteousness. This illustrates the profound influence that close friendships and chosen companions exert on a person's beliefs, values, and ultimate spiritual trajectory. The verse serves as a stark warning about the importance of choosing one's intimate associates wisely, since on the Day of Reckoning, the wrongdoer will recognize too late that blind loyalty to a friend who encouraged disbelief or sin led to his own destruction. It underscores the Quranic theme that human relationships carry moral weight and accountability, and that one must prioritize guidance and truth over social loyalty when the two conflict, for the regret of having followed misguided companionship will be eternal and inconsolable in the Hereafter.

translation: Indeed, he led me astray from the Remembrance after it had come to me. And Satan is ever, to man, a deserter.
interpretation: This verse depicts the regret of a wrongdoer on the Day of Judgment, who confesses that a companion or false friend led him away from the Qur'an and the remembrance of God after it had reached him and he had the opportunity to follow it. The verse serves as a warning about the danger of choosing companions who distract from faith and righteous guidance. It also highlights the nature of Satan: he incites people to sin and promises support, but ultimately abandons and forsakes them when they are held accountable, offering no help or protection in their time of need. The verse underscores the theme of personal responsibility—while Satan and bad companions may tempt and mislead, the individual bears accountability for yielding to that temptation, and such alliances prove worthless in the end.

translation: And the Messenger said, "O my Lord, indeed my people have taken this Qur'an as a forsaken thing."
interpretation: This verse captures the Prophet Muhammad's lament to God concerning the response of his own people to the divine revelation entrusted to him. The word 'mahjoor' conveys the sense of being abandoned, shunned, or treated with neglect—not merely disbelieved, but actively set aside, ignored, mocked, or avoided in practice. The complaint reflects the grief of a messenger watching his community reject guidance meant for their benefit, choosing instead avoidance or ridicule rather than engagement. Beyond its historical context describing the Quraysh's rejection, the verse carries a timeless admonition: it implicitly warns future generations of believers against treating scripture as a relic to be shelved rather than a living guide to be read, understood, reflected upon, and acted upon. Abandonment of the Qur'an can take many forms—failing to recite it, failing to comprehend its meanings, or failing to implement its teachings in one's life—and the verse suggests that such neglect, even among those who nominally accept the faith, is a serious spiritual failing that grieves the Messenger and displeases God.

translation: And thus have We made for every prophet an enemy from among the criminals. But sufficient is your Lord as a guide and a helper.
interpretation: This verse establishes a divine pattern that runs throughout human history: opposition to prophets and messengers is not an anomaly but an expected, recurring reality ordained by God's wisdom. The phrase 'thus have We made' indicates that this adversarial relationship serves a purpose within the divine plan—it is through such trials and opposition that the sincerity, patience, and resolve of the prophets and their followers are tested and proven. The enemies are specifically described as being 'from among the criminals' (al-mujrimin), those steeped in wrongdoing and rebellion against truth, suggesting that resistance to prophetic guidance stems from moral corruption rather than legitimate intellectual or spiritual objection. This serves as a consolation to the Prophet Muhammad, who faced fierce opposition from the Meccan elite, by placing his struggle within a continuous chain of prophetic experience shared by Noah, Abraham, Moses, Jesus, and others before him—none of whom were exempt from hostility despite their righteousness. The verse concludes by redirecting reliance away from human allies or strategies toward God alone, affirming that His guidance (hidayah) and support (nasr) are sufficient and complete. This serves both as reassurance and as a theological statement: the ultimate victory and direction do not depend on the absence of enemies but on steadfast trust in divine providence, which alone can illuminate the right path and grant the strength to overcome adversity.

translation: And those who disbelieve say, "Why was the Qur'an not revealed to him all at once?" Thus [it is] that We may strengthen your heart thereby, and We have recited it in distinct, measured recitation.
interpretation: This verse addresses the disbelievers' objection to the gradual, piecemeal revelation of the Qur'an over approximately 23 years rather than its being sent down complete in a single instance, as earlier scriptures were believed to have been. The divine response reframes this gradualism not as a deficiency but as a deliberate pedagogical and psychological strategy. The phrase "to strengthen your heart" speaks directly to the Prophet Muhammad's emotional and spiritual fortitude—facing persistent rejection, ridicule, and hardship, he received revelation in stages that corresponded to unfolding events, questions, and crises, allowing each portion to serve as timely reassurance, guidance, and resolve. This method allowed the Prophet to internalize, memorize, and gradually implement the teachings, while allowing his followers to absorb profound theological and legal changes incrementally rather than being overwhelmed all at once. The term "tartīl" (measured, distinct recitation) further emphasizes deliberate pacing and clarity in both the mode of revelation and its oral transmission—suggesting that meaning and memorization are best served not by speed but by careful, rhythmic unfolding. Thus, the verse transforms what critics saw as evidence against the Qur'an's divine origin into proof of divine wisdom and compassionate design, tailored to human capacity, historical circumstance, and the Prophet's own need for sustained courage amid opposition.

translation: And they do not come to you with any argument [or strange example] except that We bring you the truth and the best explanation.
interpretation: This verse reassures the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) in the face of the objections, false analogies, and rhetorical challenges raised by his opponents to discredit his message. It affirms that whatever doubts, comparisons, or seemingly clever arguments the disbelievers devise to undermine the Qur'an or prophethood, God's response through revelation will always surpass them—providing not only the truth but the clearest, most complete, and most eloquent explanation. It underscores the Qur'an's self-description as a definitive and ever-sufficient source of guidance, capable of answering every objection with greater precision and insight than any human argument could offer, thereby affirming divine support for the Prophet and the intellectual superiority of revealed truth over human skepticism.

translation: Those who are gathered upon their faces unto Hell - they are the worst in position and the most astray in path.
interpretation: This verse contrasts the fate of the disbelievers with the believers mentioned in the surrounding verses. Being 'dragged on their faces' into Hell is a symbolic depiction of utter humiliation and loss of dignity, reversing the natural upright posture that symbolizes human honor and rational guidance. The face, which represents one's identity, dignity, and the direction one faces in devotion, becomes the very instrument of degradation. This serves as a powerful rhetorical device: those who used their faculties of perception and reason to reject truth and pursue misguidance in worldly life will find themselves utterly debased, with the very faces they held high in arrogance now dragging in the dust toward their ultimate destination. The verse establishes a moral logic of requital - the worst conceivable position and the most complete form of being lost - emphasizing that misguidance in this life leads to total disorientation and ignominy in the Hereafter, standing in stark contrast to those who found the right path through guidance and will be honored accordingly.

translation: And We certainly gave Moses the Scripture and appointed with him his brother Aaron as an assistant.
interpretation: This verse highlights the principle of divine support through partnership in the burden of prophethood. Moses, though chosen to deliver the message and confront Pharaoh, was not left to shoulder this immense responsibility alone; God appointed his brother Aaron as a 'wazir' - a minister, helper, and support - to assist him in conveying the message and bearing the weight of leadership. This reflects a broader Quranic theme that even the greatest of God's messengers needed companionship, counsel, and shared responsibility to fulfill their mission effectively. The verse also subtly draws a parallel to Prophet Muhammad's own situation, suggesting that just as Moses was supported by Aaron, Muhammad too had companions and supporters in his prophetic mission, reinforcing the idea that no messenger acts in isolation but within a community of support that God provides.

translation: So We said, 'Go both of you to the people who have denied Our signs.' Then We destroyed them with [complete] destruction.
interpretation: This verse refers to Moses and Aaron being sent to Pharaoh and his people, who rejected the signs of God despite clear evidence presented to them. The phrase 'destroyed them with destruction' uses an emphatic grammatical construction (the cognate accusative, tadmiran) to stress the totality and severity of their ruin—emphasizing that rejection of divine signs after being given a clear warning and messenger leads to decisive consequences. The verse underscores a recurring Qur'anic theme: that messengers are sent with proofs, and those who persist in denial despite clear signs face inevitable downfall, serving as a lesson and warning to later generations who hear the stories of these destroyed nations.

translation: And the people of Noah - when they denied the messengers, We drowned them and made them a sign for mankind. And We have prepared for the wrongdoers a painful punishment.
interpretation: This verse recounts the fate of the people of Noah as a paradigmatic example of divine justice. Though Noah was the only messenger sent to them, the verse speaks of their rejection of 'the messengers' in the plural, indicating that denying one true messenger amounts to denying the entire prophetic message and its unified call to monotheism and righteousness. Their destruction by the flood was transformed into a lasting 'sign' (ayah) - a historical and moral lesson preserved for all subsequent generations to contemplate regarding the consequences of persistent disbelief and arrogance toward divine guidance. The verse closes by generalizing this specific historical event into an eternal principle: that wrongdoers (az-zalimin) - those who transgress against truth and justice - face a prepared, painful punishment. This serves both as a warning to the Prophet Muhammad's contemporaries who rejected him, drawing a parallel between their disbelief and that of Noah's people, and as a timeless admonition that divine justice operates consistently throughout history, holding accountable those who knowingly reject truth after it has been made clear to them.

translation: And [We destroyed] 'Aad and Thamud and the companions of the Rass, and many generations between them.
interpretation: This verse continues a litany of past nations that were destroyed for their disbelief and rejection of their prophets, serving as a warning to the Quraysh and to humanity at large. 'Aad and Thamud were well-known Arabian peoples destroyed for their arrogance and rejection of the prophets Hud and Salih respectively. The 'companions of the Rass' refers to another ancient people, whose precise identity is debated among commentators but who likewise met destruction for their rejection of divine guidance, possibly associated with a well (rass) around which their community was built. The mention of 'many generations between them' emphasizes that these are not isolated incidents but part of a recurring historical pattern: whenever a people persistently reject truth and persist in corruption and arrogance, divine justice eventually intervenes. The verse functions rhetorically to situate the Prophet Muhammad's contemporaries within this same moral and historical continuum, implying that the law of consequence—destruction following sustained rejection of truth—is not an anomaly but a consistent feature of human history, meant to instill reflection and caution in the listener.

translation: And to each [of them] We set forth examples (parables/warnings), and each [of them] We destroyed utterly.
interpretation: This verse concludes a passage recounting the fates of earlier disbelieving peoples—such as the nations of Noah, 'Ad, Thamud, and the people of Lot—who rejected their prophets. God states that He gave each of these communities clear signs, parables, and warnings to guide them toward truth, yet because they persisted in denial and corruption, He brought total devastation upon them. The repetition of 'each' (kullan) emphasizes that this pattern was not arbitrary or isolated but a consistent divine law applied uniformly across history: every rejecting nation received adequate warning before being held accountable, and none escaped the consequences of their obstinate disbelief. The verse serves as an implicit warning to the Prophet Muhammad's contemporaries in Mecca, who were likewise being given signs and arguments, that persistent rejection carries the same risk of ruin that befell earlier peoples. It underscores the Qur'anic theme of divine justice tempered by prior warning—destruction only follows after the truth has been made clear through examples and arguments suited to each community's understanding.

translation: And indeed, they have passed by the town which was showered with an evil rain [of stones]. Did they not then see it? Nay, but they did not expect resurrection.
interpretation: This verse refers to the people of Lot, whose town was destroyed by a rain of stones as divine punishment for their sins. The Quraysh and other disbelievers in Mecca would pass by the ruins of this town on their trade journeys to Syria, physically witnessing the evidence of divine retribution. The rhetorical question 'Did they not then see it?' emphasizes that the disbelievers had tangible, visible proof of God's power to punish wrongdoers, yet they failed to draw the appropriate lesson from it. The verse concludes by identifying the root cause of their heedlessness: it was not a lack of evidence but a lack of faith in resurrection and the afterlife. Because they did not believe they would be held accountable after death, they saw no connection between the fate of past nations and their own eventual reckoning. This illustrates a broader Quranic theme that disbelief in resurrection leads to moral complacency, as the fear of ultimate accountability is what should motivate reflection on historical signs of divine justice and reform of one's own behavior.

translation: And when they see you, [O Muhammad], they take you not except as an object of mockery, [saying], 'Is this the one whom Allah has sent as a messenger?'
interpretation: This verse reflects the derision and disbelief faced by Prophet Muhammad from the pagans of Mecca, who mocked his claim to prophethood, finding it inconceivable that an ordinary man from among them could be chosen as Allah's messenger. Their scorn stemmed from their worldly standards of status and power, expecting a messenger to possess wealth, angels, or supernatural attributes rather than being a human being who ate food and walked in the markets. This verse serves to console the Prophet by illustrating a recurring pattern in the history of prophethood: messengers of God were frequently ridiculed and rejected by their own people, not because of any deficiency in their message, but because of human arrogance, attachment to worldly values, and resistance to spiritual truth that challenges the status quo. The mockery of disbelievers is thus portrayed as a test of patience and conviction for the Prophet, affirming that rejection by the proud does not diminish the truth of divine revelation.

translation: Indeed, he would have almost led us astray from our gods had we not remained steadfast in [worshipping] them. But they will come to know, when they see the punishment, who is most astray from the way.
interpretation: This verse depicts the words of disbelievers regarding a prophet (understood to be Muhammad, peace be upon him) who called them away from idol worship toward the worship of God alone. They acknowledge, almost admiringly, how close his message came to persuading them to abandon their ancestral deities, and they credit their own obstinate perseverance in idolatry as what kept them from being swayed. This reveals the psychological reality of stubborn disbelief: it is not that the truth lacked power to convince, but that willful attachment to tradition and pride prevented acceptance. The verse then pivots to a divine rebuttal, declaring that these same people will realize the truth only when they face the punishment, at which point they will understand with certainty who was truly misguided—not the prophet who called them to truth, but themselves, who clung to falsehood out of obstinacy. This reflects a broader Qur'anic theme that rejection of truth often stems not from lack of evidence but from pride, social pressure, and attachment to inherited customs, and that such self-deception becomes unmistakably clear only when it is too late, at the moment of reckoning.

translation: Have you seen the one who has taken his own desire as his god? Then would you be a guardian over him?
interpretation: This verse addresses the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) and, by extension, all believers, highlighting a profound form of idolatry that goes beyond worshipping physical idols: the deification of one's own whims, desires, and ego. When a person consistently follows whatever their base desires dictate—without regard for divine guidance, moral principle, or reason—they have effectively made their desire into a god, obeying it as one would obey a deity. The rhetorical question that follows, asking whether the Prophet could be a 'wakil' (guardian, trustee, or one responsible) over such a person, serves to console and relieve the Prophet of an impossible burden. It was not his duty to force guidance upon people who have surrendered their rational and moral faculties to their own caprice; his role was only to convey the message. This verse speaks to the nature of free will and misguidance: God does not compel belief, and some people choose to be guided by nothing higher than their own fleeting passions, making them, in effect, their own deity. This serves as a broader warning against moral relativism and the spiritual danger of prioritizing personal desire over objective truth and divine command.

translation: Or do you think that most of them hear or understand? They are only like cattle; nay, they are even further astray from the way.
interpretation: This verse addresses the Prophet Muhammad (and by extension all believers) regarding those who reject the truth despite having the faculties of hearing and reason. It emphasizes that mere physical capacity for hearing and intellectual capacity for reasoning are insufficient if they are not used purposefully to seek and recognize truth. The comparison to cattle is significant: animals follow instinct and immediate appetite without reflection on purpose, meaning, or moral consequence. Yet the verse goes further, declaring the heedless disbelievers worse than cattle, because animals, lacking the gift of intellect altogether, cannot be blamed for their lack of guidance, whereas humans possess reason and the capacity for spiritual insight but choose not to employ them. This constitutes a greater failure and deviation, as it represents a willful waste of a God-given faculty rather than an inherent limitation. The verse thus serves as a stern warning about the moral and spiritual responsibility that comes with human reason, and the deeper culpability of those who possess the tools for guidance yet remain heedless, following whims and desires rather than engaging in genuine reflection on existence, purpose, and divine signs.

translation: Have you not seen how your Lord extends the shadow? Had He willed, He could have made it stationary. Then We made the sun its guide.
interpretation: This verse invites reflection on a seemingly ordinary natural phenomenon—the lengthening and shifting of shadows—as a sign of God's deliberate design and power. The shadow does not exist in a fixed, static state; rather, it is extended and ever-changing, and this change is only perceptible and measurable because of the sun's movement across the sky. By noting that God could have made the shadow 'ساكنا' (stationary, motionless) but chose not to, the verse emphasizes divine will and purposeful creation rather than mere chance or necessity. The sun's role as a 'دليل' (guide or indicator) for the shadow suggests a broader metaphor: just as the sun makes the shadow's extent and movement knowable, allowing humans to track time and orient themselves, so too do God's signs in nature serve as guides to deeper truths about His power and wisdom. The passage calls on the listener to move from casual observation to genuine contemplation—'ألم تر' (have you not seen/considered)—suggesting that spiritual insight begins with attentiveness to the workings of the natural world, which are neither random nor self-sustaining but continuously governed by divine decree.

translation: Then We drew it [the shadow] in towards Ourselves with a gentle, gradual withdrawal.
interpretation: This verse continues the imagery of the preceding verses about the shadow that God spreads out and could have made stationary. Here it describes how the shadow, once the sun rises, is gradually retracted and shortened by the sun's light. This natural phenomenon serves as a sign and metaphor for God's gentle, measured control over creation—nothing happens abruptly or without divine ordering. The 'easy' or 'gentle' withdrawal reflects how God manages the cosmos with precision and gradualism rather than violent disruption, inviting reflection on the subtlety of divine power manifest even in everyday phenomena like the changing of shadows with the sun's movement, which itself points to the orderly cycle of day and the eventual return of all things to their Creator.

translation: And it is He who has made the night a garment for you, and sleep a rest, and has made the day a time for rising and dispersal (to seek livelihood).
interpretation: This verse highlights God's wise design in the natural rhythm of night and day as signs of His mercy and power. The night, likened to a garment, envelops and conceals, providing darkness and stillness that allow the body and mind to rest through sleep, itself described as a form of 'death-like' repose (sabat) that restores vitality. The day, by contrast, is depicted as a time of 'nushur'—a word that evokes resurrection and spreading out—symbolizing both the practical resumption of work, movement, and social life, and metaphorically pointing to the resurrection after death. Just as sleep is a temporary death from which one awakens refreshed, so too will humankind be revived after death, scattered forth from their graves as people scatter forth from their homes at dawn to pursue their livelihoods. This juxtaposition subtly reinforces the Qur'an's broader theme of resurrection by rooting it in the familiar, observable cycle of daily life, inviting reflection on divine order and the promise of life after death.

translation: And it is He who sends the winds as glad tidings before [the coming of] His mercy, and We send down from the sky pure, purifying water.
interpretation: This verse presents the winds and rain as signs of God's providence and mercy, illustrating a natural pattern that serves as a metaphor for divine compassion: just as the winds herald the coming of life-giving rain to revive dead land, they signal the broader mercy of God that precedes and prepares the way for blessings. The description of the water as 'tahuran' (pure and purifying) emphasizes not only its physical cleansing properties but also its symbolic function—rain in the Qur'an often represents spiritual renewal, the revival of faith, and the purification of the soul, paralleling how rain revives the earth after drought. The verse invites reflection on the interconnectedness of natural phenomena and divine mercy, suggesting that attentiveness to the signs in nature (ayat) should lead one to recognize God's care and the cyclical nature of renewal, both physical and spiritual, that He provides for His creation.

translation: That We may give life thereby to a dead land and provide drink for many of the cattle and people We have created.
interpretation: This verse, part of a passage describing the sending down of rain from the heavens, uses the imagery of reviving dead, barren land as a powerful metaphor for Allah's power to give life, both literally through sustaining the earth's ecosystems and metaphorically through spiritual revival and resurrection. The mention of providing drink for both animals and humans emphasizes the comprehensive nature of divine mercy, which extends to all of creation without distinction. This serves as a sign (ayah) for reflection on Allah's power, wisdom, and the interconnectedness of creation, pointing toward the broader theme in the Qur'an that just as Allah revives dead land with rain, He has the power to resurrect the dead on the Day of Judgment.

translation: And We have certainly diversified it [i.e., the rain] among them that they might remember, but most of the people refused [anything] except disbelief and ingratitude.
interpretation: This verse follows directly after verses describing how Allah sends down pure water from the sky to give life to dead land and to provide drink for the creatures and cattle He has created. The pronoun 'it' refers to this life-giving rain, which Allah distributes and varies across different lands and seasons—sometimes abundant, sometimes scarce, falling in one place and not another—as a deliberate sign meant to provoke reflection on divine power, mercy, and the dependence of all life on God's provision. The repeated, patterned distribution of rain is presented as a natural proof of a wise, sustaining Creator, something humans could easily reflect upon and be grateful for. Yet despite this clear and recurring sign, the verse laments that the majority of people respond not with gratitude or faith but with 'kufr'—a word carrying the double meaning of disbelief and ingratitude. This highlights a recurring Quranic theme: that human beings, when confronted with manifest blessings and signs in nature, often fail to draw the intended spiritual lesson, choosing instead heedlessness or outright denial. The verse serves as both a description of human nature's tendency toward ingratitude and an implicit call to overcome this tendency by recognizing and acknowledging divine favor in the ordinary phenomena of the natural world.

translation: And if We had willed, We could have sent into every town a warner.
interpretation: This verse affirms God's absolute power and sovereignty in choosing how and when to deliver His message to humanity. It emphasizes that the dispatch of prophets and warners is not haphazard but follows a deliberate divine plan. Rather than sending a warner to every single town or community individually, God chose a more universal approach through select messengers whose message would spread to all people. This underscores the idea that the limited number of prophets is not due to any limitation in God's power—He could have multiplied warners infinitely if He so willed—but reflects divine wisdom in how guidance is disseminated. It also serves as a reminder to those who reject the message that their rejection cannot be excused by claiming insufficient warning, since God's capacity to warn is boundless, and the warning that has been given is sufficient for those willing to heed it.

translation: So do not obey the disbelievers, and strive against them with it [the Qur'an] with great striving.
interpretation: This verse, addressed to the Prophet Muhammad, instructs him not to compromise with or yield to the demands of those who reject the message of Islam. The phrase 'strive against them with it' refers to using the Qur'an itself—its arguments, proofs, and guidance—as the primary tool of resistance and persuasion, rather than relying solely on armed conflict. This establishes that the 'great striving' (jihad kabir) commanded here is fundamentally intellectual and spiritual: engaging disbelievers through recitation, argumentation, and the moral force of revelation to counter their claims and invite them to truth. It underscores that steadfastness in conveying and upholding the Qur'anic message, with patience and unwavering commitment despite opposition, constitutes one of the most demanding forms of struggle, requiring sustained effort, courage, and resilience against hostility and rejection.

translation: And He it is Who has let loose the two seas (bodies of water), this one palatable and fresh, and that one salty and bitter, and He has set between them a barrier and an impassable, forbidding boundary.
interpretation: This verse points to the divine power manifest in the natural order, where fresh and salt waters meet yet do not mix, maintaining their distinct qualities through an unseen barrier (barzakh). Beyond its literal reference to hydrology—such as where rivers meet seas—the verse serves as a sign (ayah) of God's meticulous design and control over creation, demonstrating that even seemingly similar substances (both are vast bodies of water) are kept distinct according to divine decree. Symbolically, this separation of pure and bitter waters has been understood by commentators as an allegory for the distinction God maintains between truth and falsehood, the sacred and profane, or the believer and disbeliever, as well as a metaphor for the boundaries and limits (hudud) that God sets in the moral and spiritual order of existence. Just as the two seas do not overwhelm one another despite being adjacent, human life is governed by divine limits that preserve order, justice, and distinction between opposites, preventing chaos from merging what God has decreed to remain separate.

translation: And it is He who created from water a human being and made for him lineage and marriage kinship; and your Lord is ever All-Powerful.
interpretation: This verse highlights both the humble origin of human beings—created from a simple substance, water—and the dignity and complexity God bestowed upon them through social bonds of kinship (nasab, blood relation) and marriage (sihr, relation by marriage). It emphasizes that human social structures, family ties, and the institution of marriage are divinely ordained aspects of creation, not incidental. The closing affirmation that God is 'Qadir' (All-Powerful) underscores that the One who could create something as intricate as human beings and their intricate social relationships from mere water possesses limitless power, capable of anything, including resurrection and other matters questioned by disbelievers in the surrounding verses of this chapter.

translation: And they worship besides Allah that which can neither benefit them nor harm them, and the disbeliever is ever a helper against his Lord.
interpretation: This verse highlights the irrationality of idolatry by pointing out that the objects of worship besides Allah are powerless—they can neither bring benefit nor inflict harm, making their worship utterly futile. The latter part of the verse, describing the disbeliever as 'a helper against his Lord,' underscores the active role disbelievers play in opposing truth and supporting falsehood, whether through aiding others in disbelief, defending idols, or rallying against the message of monotheism. This portrays disbelief not merely as a passive error but as an active alignment with forces opposed to divine guidance, emphasizing personal responsibility and the deliberate choice involved in rejecting faith.

translation: And We have not sent you except as a bearer of good tidings and a warner.
interpretation: This verse defines and limits the prophetic mission of Muhammad to two essential functions: delivering glad tidings of divine mercy and reward to those who believe and act righteously, and warning of consequences for those who reject faith and persist in wrongdoing. The verse emphasizes that the Prophet's role is fundamentally one of communication and guidance rather than compulsion—he is not given power to force belief, control outcomes, or judge people's hearts, but only to convey the message clearly in both its hopeful and cautionary dimensions. This establishes a theological boundary on prophetic authority, clarifying that ultimate judgment and the granting of guidance belong to God alone, while the Prophet's responsibility is restricted to faithful transmission of revelation through encouragement and admonition. The phrase also serves to console the Prophet during moments of rejection by his people, reminding him that his duty ends with conveying the message, and that people's acceptance or rejection does not diminish the completeness of his mission.

translation: Say, 'I do not ask of you for it any payment - only that whoever wills might take a path to his Lord.'
interpretation: This verse addresses the Prophet Muhammad's sincerity and the purity of his mission, instructing him to clarify that he seeks no worldly compensation, wealth, or personal gain for conveying the message of Islam. This disassociates the message from any suspicion of self-interest, reinforcing that the call to faith is purely for the benefit of humanity. The verse emphasizes free will in matters of faith - the only 'reward' the Prophet seeks is that people voluntarily choose to follow a path toward righteousness and nearness to God. This reflects the broader Quranic principle that faith cannot be coerced; it must be a conscious choice made by the individual who recognizes truth and decides to pursue a relationship with their Creator through their own volition, free from any external pressure or the messenger's personal interest.

translation: And put your trust in the Ever-Living who does not die, and glorify Him with His praise. And sufficient is He as being All-Aware of the sins of His servants.
interpretation: This verse instructs the Prophet (and by extension all believers) to anchor their trust and reliance exclusively in Allah, emphasizing His attribute of eternal life as the only being who never dies, unlike all created things which perish. This is a call to stability and confidence in the face of worldly uncertainties, opposition, and the transient nature of human power and alliances. By pairing tawakkul (trust) with tasbih (glorification and praise), the verse links reliance on God with active worship and gratitude, suggesting that true trust is expressed not passively but through continuous remembrance and acknowledgment of God's perfection. The concluding phrase about Allah's complete awareness of the sins of His servants serves as a theological assurance that nothing escapes divine knowledge—every human failing, hidden or apparent, is fully known to Him. This serves both as a comfort (since He alone judges with full knowledge and can forgive) and a warning (since no sin is hidden from Him). Together, the verse constructs a worldview where human beings, faced with mortality, moral failure, and the fleeting nature of worldly supports, should orient their entire sense of security toward the one being who is eternal, deserving of praise, and fully cognizant of human conduct.

translation: He who created the heavens and the earth and what is between them in six days, then established Himself upon the Throne. The Most Merciful - so ask about Him one who is well informed.
interpretation: This verse affirms God's absolute power and sovereignty as the Creator of the entire universe, emphasizing the orderly and deliberate nature of creation (in six days, not instantaneously, though these 'days' are understood by many scholars as vast cosmic periods rather than literal 24-hour days). The mention of 'establishing Himself upon the Throne' (al-istiwa 'ala al-'Arsh) signifies His complete authority and governance over all creation, though the exact nature of this is left as one of the mutashabihat (ambiguous matters) that Muslims are encouraged not to over-literalize or anthropomorphize. The invocation of 'Ar-Rahman' (the Most Merciful) right after describing His creative power serves to balance divine majesty with divine compassion - the same God who has absolute power over the cosmos is also infinitely merciful. The final instruction to 'ask one who is well informed' about Him is often understood as directing people toward knowledge of God through revelation and those who possess true understanding, particularly relevant given the context of this surah's address to disbelievers who questioned the Prophet's description of Ar-Rahman. It suggests that true knowledge of God comes through proper guidance rather than speculation, and implicitly rebukes those who were unfamiliar with or rejected this divine name despite its self-evident connection to the signs of creation all around them.

translation: And when it is said to them, "Prostrate to the Most Merciful (ar-Rahman)," they say, "And what is the Most Merciful? Shall we prostrate to whatever you command us?" And it increases them in aversion.
interpretation: This verse depicts the arrogant rejection of the pagan Arabs when called to worship God under the name 'ar-Rahman' (the Most Merciful), a name they were unfamiliar with or refused to acknowledge, since they already worshipped other deities. Their question 'And what is the Most Merciful?' reveals willful ignorance and disdain rather than genuine inquiry—they are not seeking knowledge but expressing contempt for submission itself. Their refusal to bow to a command simply because it is a command demonstrates the deeper sin of pride: rejecting guidance not due to lack of evidence but due to resistance to authority and humility before the divine. The closing phrase notes that rather than softening their hearts, the call to prostration only deepened their nufoor—their flight, estrangement, and aversion from truth. This illustrates a psychological and spiritual principle found throughout the Qur'an: for hearts hardened by arrogance, even clear signs and calls to worship can provoke greater resistance rather than acceptance, as submission itself becomes repugnant to a soul that prizes its own autonomy over recognition of the Creator's sovereignty.

translation: Blessed is He who has placed great stars in the sky and has placed therein a [burning] lamp [the sun] and an illuminating moon.
interpretation: This verse extols God's majesty and creative power by directing attention to the cosmos as a sign of His sovereignty. The word 'tabaraka' (Blessed) signals transcendence and abundant goodness emanating from God. The 'buruj' (great stars or constellations) refer to the grand celestial structures that order the heavens, often understood by classical commentators as the zodiacal constellations that mark the paths of the sun and moon, demonstrating precise cosmic design. The 'siraj' (lamp) describes the sun as a source of intense light and heat, while the moon is described as 'munir' (illuminating), reflecting light rather than generating it, a distinction that early exegetes noted shows a nuanced observation of the two celestial bodies' differing natures. Together, these contrasts—between the self-luminous sun and the reflective moon—serve as a rational proof of a Deliberate Designer, reinforcing the Qur'an's recurring theme that the orderly, purposeful arrangement of the universe testifies to the existence and oneness of the Creator. This verse, appearing in a passage that critiques the disbelievers' skepticism, functions rhetorically to shift the discourse from human disputation to the incontrovertible grandeur of the natural world, inviting reflection on the Creator's power as self-evident through the structured beauty and function of the heavens.

translation: And it is He who made the night and the day in succession, for whoever desires to remember or desires gratitude.
interpretation: This verse highlights the alternation of night and day as a continuous, divinely ordained sign woven into the natural order, offering humanity repeated opportunities for spiritual reflection. Because night and day succeed each other endlessly, no one is ever permanently deprived of the chance to engage in remembrance (dhikr) of God or to express gratitude (shukr) for His blessings—if one misses an opportunity during the day, the night offers another, and vice versa. This rhythm serves as a built-in reminder system: the changing times of day prompt moments for prayer, reflection, and acknowledgment of divine favor, such as the blessings of rest during the night and productivity during the day. The verse underscores that the cosmic order itself is designed with human spiritual benefit in mind, inviting those with sincere intention—whether motivated by a desire to remember God or to be thankful—to recognize His signs in the natural cycle and to use the passage of time purposefully rather than letting it pass unnoticed.

translation: And the servants of the Most Merciful are those who walk upon the earth in humility, and when the ignorant address them, they say 'Peace.'
interpretation: This verse describes the distinguishing character traits of the true servants of God (ibad al-Rahman), marking the beginning of a longer passage in Surah al-Furqan that enumerates their qualities. Walking upon the earth 'hawna' signifies humility, gentleness, and dignity in demeanor—neither arrogant nor ostentatious, but calm and measured in bearing. This humility is not weakness but a reflection of inner spiritual contentment and trust in God, freeing one from the need to assert superiority over others. The second half of the verse addresses their response to provocation: when confronted by the ignorant (al-jahilun)—those who speak rudely, mockingly, or with hostility—these servants respond not with equal hostility or argument, but with 'salama,' a word of peace. This does not necessarily mean passive submission to insult, but rather a dignified disengagement from foolish conflict, a refusal to be drawn into lowering oneself to the level of ignorance or strife. It reflects the Qur'anic ideal of responding to evil or foolishness with wisdom and grace rather than retaliation, preserving one's own moral integrity while avoiding unnecessary conflict. Together, the verse establishes that true servanthood to God is expressed through everyday conduct and interpersonal relations—humility in movement and restraint in speech—rather than through claims of status or spiritual superiority.

translation: And those who spend the night prostrating themselves before their Lord and standing [in prayer].
interpretation: This verse describes one of the defining characteristics of 'Ibad al-Rahman' (the servants of the Most Merciful) mentioned in this passage of Surah Al-Furqan. It highlights their devotion to voluntary night prayer (tahajjud/qiyam al-layl), a practice that goes beyond the five obligatory daily prayers. The combination of 'sujud' (prostration) and 'qiyam' (standing) represents the two primary physical postures of prayer, symbolizing complete submission and devotion. By choosing to spend portions of the night in worship rather than sleep, these believers demonstrate sincere faith, self-discipline, and a deep personal relationship with God that is not merely performed for social recognition but is practiced privately in the quiet hours of night. This nocturnal devotion is presented as a mark of true piety and spiritual excellence, distinguishing these servants through their willingness to sacrifice comfort and rest for closeness to their Creator.

translation: And those who say, 'Our Lord, avert from us the punishment of Hell. Indeed, its punishment is ever adhering (inseparable torment).'
interpretation: This verse describes one of the qualities of the 'Servants of the Most Merciful' (Ibad al-Rahman), the righteous believers praised in this passage of Surah Al-Furqan. Their constant supplication reflects a deep awareness of divine accountability and humility before God, even as righteous people who strive to do good. Rather than feeling secure or complacent about their salvation, they remain fearful and continually seek refuge from Hellfire, recognizing that no one is guaranteed Paradise by their deeds alone without God's mercy. The word 'gharama' (translated as 'adhering' or 'inseparable torment') conveys the idea of a persistent, inescapable debt or affliction—emphasizing that the punishment of Hell, once incurred, becomes a relentless and clinging burden from which there is no relief or escape. This reflects the Qur'anic theme that true faith combines hope in God's mercy with a healthy fear of His justice, motivating believers to maintain righteous conduct and humble prayer throughout their lives.

translation: Indeed, it is evil as an abode and as a resting place.
interpretation: This verse, from Surah Al-Furqan, refers to Hellfire (Jahannam) as described in the preceding verses, where the wrongdoers plead for destruction upon seeing their fate. The verse emphasizes the utter wretchedness of Hell both as a permanent dwelling place (mustaqarran) and as a temporary station or stopping point (muqaaman). This dual description underscores that there is no relief in Hell whether one considers it from the perspective of eternal settlement or even momentary residence—every aspect of it is evil and miserable. The rhetorical structure serves as a severe warning to those who reject faith and follow their desires, contrasting sharply with the believers' ultimate abode of Paradise described as beautiful in both permanence and temporary rest. The verse functions as a divine commentary affirming the justice of the punishment described, confirming that such an end is a fitting consequence for arrogance and disbelief.

translation: And [the servants of the Most Merciful are] those who, when they spend, are neither extravagant nor miserly, but are between that, moderate [in a just balance].
interpretation: This verse establishes moderation (wasatiyyah) as a defining trait of the righteous servants of God, placing financial conduct within a broader ethical framework that rejects both excess and stinginess. Spending is not condemned, nor is wealth itself, but the manner of spending reveals one's character: extravagance (israf) wastes resources and often stems from vanity or lack of self-control, while miserliness (taqtir) denies oneself and others rightful benefit out of fear or greed. The ideal is 'qawama'—a steady, balanced equilibrium that is neither excessive nor deficient. This reflects a larger Qur'anic principle that virtue often lies in the middle path between two extremes, and that true piety is expressed not merely in belief but in the disciplined, just management of one's material life, treating wealth as a trust to be used wisely rather than hoarded or squandered.

translation: And those who do not invoke another god besides Allah, nor kill the soul which Allah has forbidden, except by right, nor commit unlawful sexual intercourse. And whoever does that will meet a penalty of sin.
interpretation: This verse enumerates three of the gravest sins forbidden in Islam - shirk (associating partners with God), unlawful killing, and adultery/fornication - presenting them as defining characteristics of the righteous servants of the Merciful (Ibad al-Rahman) described in this passage of Surah Al-Furqan. The structure establishes these three prohibitions as foundational pillars of moral and spiritual integrity: the first safeguards the purity of monotheistic belief (tawhid), the second protects the sanctity of human life, and the third preserves the sanctity of lineage, family structure, and sexual morality. The phrase 'except by right' acknowledges that killing is permissible only in legally sanctioned circumstances such as just retribution or lawful warfare, distinguishing murder from justice. The verse concludes with a warning that transgressing these boundaries results in meeting 'athama' - a term suggesting not merely sin but its weighty consequence or requital, emphasizing that these are not minor infractions but major sins carrying serious spiritual and possibly worldly repercussions. The grouping of these three sins together reflects their severity and interconnection in Islamic ethical teaching, as violations against God, against life, and against sexual morality are seen as fundamentally destabilizing to both individual souls and the social fabric of the community.

translation: The punishment will be doubled for him on the Day of Resurrection, and he will abide therein forever, humiliated.
interpretation: This verse continues from the preceding verses of Surah Al-Furqan, which describe the severe consequences awaiting those who commit the gravest sins—associating partners with Allah, unlawfully taking a life, and committing adultery—without repentance. The doubling of punishment signifies the compounded weight of multiple serious transgressions, while the eternal abiding in humiliation underscores that the disgrace is not merely physical suffering but a profound spiritual degradation—a reversal of whatever worldly status, pride, or power such a person may have held in life. The verse serves as a stark warning that unrepented major sins carry consequences that are both intensified and everlasting, contrasting sharply with the mercy promised to those who sincerely repent, as mentioned in the verse that follows it.

translation: Except for those who repent, believe, and do righteous deeds—for them Allah will replace their evil deeds with good deeds. And Allah is ever Forgiving, Merciful.
interpretation: This verse offers profound hope and underscores the transformative power of sincere repentance (tawbah) combined with faith and righteous action. It teaches that the door to redemption remains open to all, regardless of past wrongdoing, provided the repentance is genuine and accompanied by a change in behavior toward righteousness. The promise that Allah will transform past sins into good deeds suggests not merely forgiveness but an active spiritual transformation—where the very record of one's past failures becomes a source of reward, perhaps because the struggle to overcome past sins and the humility gained from recognizing one's weaknesses themselves become virtues. This reflects the divine attributes of Ghafur (Forgiving) and Rahim (Merciful), emphasizing that Allah's mercy is not merely reactive but transformative, capable of turning the darkest aspects of a person's history into sources of light and merit, provided one turns to Him with sincerity and follows through with consistent righteous action.

translation: And whoever repents and does righteous deeds has truly turned to Allah with sincere repentance.
interpretation: This verse establishes that repentance (tawbah) is inseparable from righteous action. True repentance is not merely verbal remorse or regret for past wrongdoing, but must be accompanied by a genuine transformation in behavior demonstrated through good deeds. The verse emphasizes Allah's mercy and the open door of forgiveness for sinners, assuring that sincere repentance combined with reformed conduct is fully accepted by Allah. This reflects a broader Qur'anic theme that Allah's mercy is vast and accessible to anyone who turns back to Him with sincerity, regardless of the magnitude of their previous transgressions, as long as that turning is substantiated by a real change in one's actions and way of life. The phrase 'turns to Allah with repentance' underscores that the acceptance of repentance is itself a form of returning to a right relationship with the Divine, completing a cycle of error, recognition, amendment, and restoration.

translation: And those who do not bear false witness, and when they pass by idle talk [vanity/frivolity], they pass by with dignity.
interpretation: This verse describes a quality of the righteous servants of God (mentioned in the broader passage of Surah Al-Furqan as 'Ibad al-Rahman'): their integrity and moral self-restraint in social conduct. Avoiding false witness (al-zur) encompasses not only perjury but also falsehood, deception, and participation in slander or baseless gossip—emphasizing truthfulness as a cornerstone of character. The second part, passing by idle talk 'with dignity' (kiraman), illustrates their refusal to engage with vain, frivolous, or morally corrupting speech and activity. Rather than stopping to indulge in gossip, mockery, or meaningless distraction, they disengage gracefully and move on without compromising their composure or descending to the level of such talk. Together, these traits reflect a believer's commitment to truth and their elevated sense of self-respect and purpose, refusing to let trivial or corrupt matters consume their time, words, or moral standing. It teaches that true piety is expressed not just in ritual worship but in everyday social ethics—honesty in speech and wise discernment in choosing what to engage with or ignore.

translation: And those who, when reminded of the signs of their Lord, do not fall upon them deaf and blind.
interpretation: This verse describes one of the qualities of the true servants of the Most Merciful (ʿibād al-Raḥmān). Unlike those who dismiss or ignore divine signs out of arrogance or heedlessness, these believers respond to reminders of Allah's verses—whether in the Qur'an or in the signs of creation—with genuine attentiveness and understanding. The phrase 'fall upon them deaf and blind' metaphorically describes a heart and mind closed off from guidance, someone who hears the words but does not truly listen, who sees the signs but does not truly perceive their meaning. By contrast, the believers engage with revelation consciously and reflectively, allowing it to move them, inform their understanding, and shape their actions. Their receptivity to divine guidance stands as evidence of sincere faith, contrasting with those who treat sacred signs with indifference or willful blindness.

translation: And those who say, 'Our Lord, grant us from among our spouses and our offspring comfort to our eyes, and make us leaders for the righteous.'
interpretation: This verse describes one of the qualities of the righteous servants of the Most Merciful (ʿIbād al-Raḥmān), as outlined in this section of Surah al-Furqan. Their supplication reveals a comprehensive vision of faith that extends beyond individual piety to encompass family and community. By asking for spouses and offspring who are a 'comfort to the eyes,' they express a desire that their loved ones be sources of righteousness, joy, and spiritual contentment rather than distraction or sin—recognizing that true happiness in family life comes through shared devotion to God. The second part of their prayer, asking to be made 'leaders for the righteous' (imams for the muttaqin), reveals an aspiration not merely for personal salvation but for a legacy of guidance—to become exemplars whose faith and conduct inspire others toward righteousness. This reflects a mature spiritual ambition: these believers do not seek status or power for its own sake, but leadership in piety itself, understanding that the highest form of influence is to be a model that draws others closer to God. The verse thus intertwines personal devotion, family values, and communal responsibility as integrated aspects of a complete faith.

translation: Those will be rewarded with the high chamber [in Paradise] for what they patiently endured, and they will be met therein with greetings and peace.
interpretation: This verse describes the reward awaiting the true servants of the Most Merciful, whose qualities were described in the preceding verses of Surah Al-Furqan—those who walk humbly, respond to ignorance with peace, spend their nights in prayer, avoid major sins, and remain steadfast in faith and righteous deeds. The 'high chamber' (al-ghurfah) refers to an elevated station in Paradise, signifying honor and nearness to divine favor, granted specifically as recompense for their patience (sabr). This patience encompasses endurance in worship, restraint from sin, and perseverance through hardship and trials in the worldly life. The verse emphasizes that spiritual elevation in the Hereafter is directly tied to steadfastness in faith during difficulty. Furthermore, the believers' reception in this exalted abode is marked by mutual greetings of peace and honor, contrasting with the suffering and hostility they may have faced in the temporal world. The repetition of peace-related imagery (tahiyyatan wa salaman) reflects the eternal security and tranquility that replaces the struggles of earthly existence, reinforcing the Quranic theme that ultimate justice and comfort are reserved for those who remain patient and faithful despite adversity.

translation: Abiding therein forever. How excellent it is as a settlement and a resting place.
interpretation: This verse concludes a description of the reward granted to the sincere servants of the Most Merciful (ʿibād al-Raḥmān), described in the preceding verses of Surah al-Furqan as those who walk humbly, spend the night in prayer, avoid excess, and remain patient and steadfast. As a result of their righteousness, they are granted the highest chamber of Paradise, where they will dwell eternally. The verse emphasizes two qualities of this abode: it is both a 'mustaqarr' (a place of permanent settlement, stability, and rest) and a 'muqam' (a place of standing, residence, and dignity). This dual description underscores that Paradise is not merely a transient waystation but a perfect and everlasting home, combining comfort with honor. The exclamation 'how excellent' underscores the surpassing bliss and satisfaction that awaits the righteous, contrasting the impermanence and hardship of worldly life with the eternal stability promised to the faithful.

translation: Say: My Lord would not care for you were it not for your prayer/supplication. But you have indeed denied [the truth], so the punishment will be inevitable.
interpretation: This verse establishes that human worth in the divine sight is intrinsically tied to one's relationship with God through prayer and supplication (du'a). It suggests that without this connection—without turning to God in need, worship, and reliance—humanity would hold no special significance to the Lord. The verse then shifts to address those who reject this call to faith: having been given the message and having denied it despite clear signs, they face an inescapable consequence. The word 'lizaman' (inevitable/inseparable attachment) conveys that the punishment for persistent denial becomes an inevitable, clinging reality—not an arbitrary external imposition but the natural and binding consequence of turning away from the very purpose for which one was valued: the capacity to call upon God. The verse thus frames prayer not merely as ritual obligation but as the essential link that gives human existence its meaning and worth before the Divine, while disbelief and rejection sever this link and bring about an unavoidable reckoning.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Ta, Seen, Meem.
interpretation: These disjointed letters (al-huruf al-muqatta'at) open several surahs of the Qur'an, including this one (Ash-Shu'ara), and their precise meaning remains among the mutashabihat (ambiguous matters) known fully only to Allah. Scholars have offered various views: that they serve to draw the attention of listeners, especially the Meccan disbelievers who prided themselves on eloquence, demonstrating that the Qur'an is composed of the same letters they used daily yet is inimitable in its eloquence and meaning; that they affirm the miraculous nature of the Qur'an's composition; or that they stand as a testimony to the divine origin of the revelation, challenging humanity to produce anything comparable. Their placement at the start of the surah also serves as a solemn oath-like opening, signaling that what follows is weighty revelation from Allah, setting the tone for the narratives of the prophets and the warnings to the disbelievers that follow in the surah.

translation: These are the verses of the clear Book.
interpretation: This opening verse, found at the beginning of several Qur'anic chapters (such as Surah Yusuf, Al-Hijr, and Ash-Shu'ara), serves as a solemn declaration affirming the divine origin and clarity of the Qur'an. The term 'al-Kitab al-Mubin' (the clear Book) emphasizes that the revelation is not ambiguous or obscure but is manifest in its guidance, clear in its message, and self-evidently distinguishing truth from falsehood. The demonstrative 'tilka' (these/those) points to the verses that follow, signaling their importance and divine authority, while also creating a sense of majesty and distance that elevates the sacred text above ordinary speech. Scholars have noted that this clarity refers not only to the linguistic eloquence of the Qur'an but also to its function as a clear criterion for faith, morality, and law—illuminating the path for those who reflect upon it. The verse thus sets the stage for the narrative or legal content that follows, framing it as part of a luminous, unambiguous divine communication meant to guide humanity.

translation: Perhaps you would kill yourself with grief that they will not become believers.
interpretation: This verse addresses Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) directly, acknowledging the intensity of his sorrow and distress over the persistent disbelief of his people despite his sincere efforts to guide them. The word 'bakhi'' conveys the sense of someone destroying or exhausting themselves through excessive grief, suggesting that the Prophet's compassion and concern for his people's salvation was so profound that it threatened his own wellbeing. This reflects the deep burden of prophethood—carrying the responsibility of delivering a divine message while witnessing its rejection by those he cared for deeply. The verse serves as both a tender acknowledgment of his emotional state and a gentle corrective, reminding him that guidance ultimately comes from God alone, not from his own exertions. It establishes a theological principle that runs throughout the Quran: human beings, even prophets, are not responsible for forcing belief upon others; their duty is to convey the message clearly, while the acceptance or rejection of that message lies within the sphere of each individual's free will and God's wisdom. This verse thus functions as a form of divine consolation, alleviating the Prophet from an impossible burden he had seemingly placed upon himself, and redirecting his profound love for humanity's salvation into patient perseverance rather than self-destructive grief.

translation: If We willed, We could send down upon them a sign from the heaven, so that their necks would remain bowed [in submission] to it.
interpretation: This verse addresses the disbelievers' persistent rejection of faith despite the clear signs already presented to them. It emphasizes that God has the power to compel belief through an overwhelming, undeniable miraculous sign—one so forceful that it would physically humble them, bending their necks in forced submission. However, the verse implicitly conveys that God does not choose to coerce faith in this manner, because true faith must come through free will, reflection, and sincere choice rather than being forced upon people through overpowering displays of divine power. This reflects the Qur'anic principle that belief achieved through compulsion lacks the spiritual value of belief chosen freely after contemplation of existing signs in creation and revelation.

translation: And there does not come to them any new reminder from the Most Merciful except that they turn away from it.
interpretation: This verse addresses the recurring pattern of disbelief among those who reject revelation. Each time a new sign, message, or reminder is sent from God, the disbelievers respond with the same dismissive attitude, regardless of the clarity or freshness of the message. The term 'muhdath' (newly revealed/renewed) emphasizes that this rejection is not due to the message being old, repetitive, or stale—it is a persistent human failing regardless of how the truth is presented. The verse illustrates a spiritual stubbornness rooted in arrogance or heedlessness rather than genuine intellectual objection, since even continually renewed guidance fails to break through their resistance. This serves as both a warning about the dangers of complacency and pride, and a form of consolation to the Prophet Muhammad, reassuring him that the rejection he faces follows a historical pattern seen with previous messengers and is not a reflection of deficiency in his message.

translation: So they have indeed denied [the truth], and there will come to them the tidings of that which they used to mock.
interpretation: This verse addresses those who reject the Prophet's message and mock it, warning that the consequences and realities of what they dismissed will inevitably confront them. The 'tidings' refer to the eventual manifestation of truth—whether through worldly events, the fulfillment of prophecy, or the reckoning in the afterlife—that will prove the seriousness of what they treated with scorn. It serves as both a warning and a consolation to the believers, affirming that mockery of divine truth does not diminish its reality, and that denial only delays an inevitable confrontation with that truth.

translation: Have they not looked at the earth, how much We have caused to grow therein of every noble kind (pair)?
interpretation: This verse invites reflection on the natural world as a sign of God's power and generosity. The reference to 'every noble kind' or 'pair' points to the diversity and abundance of plant life, each species flourishing in its own form, as evidence of a deliberate, purposeful creation rather than random occurrence. By directing attention to something as ordinary and ever-present as vegetation, the verse challenges human complacency and forgetfulness, urging people to move from passive seeing to active perception—recognizing in the earth's fertility a continuous demonstration of divine care, order, and the capacity to bring forth life, which by extension affirms God's power to resurrect and recreate.

translation: Indeed in that is a sign, but most of them were not believers.
interpretation: This verse functions as a recurring refrain throughout Surah Ash-Shu'ara, appearing after each narrative concerning a prophet and his people—Noah, Abraham, Lot, Shu'ayb, and others. The 'sign' (āyah) refers to the destruction of disbelieving nations and the salvation of the believers, serving as empirical, historical proof of divine power, justice, and the truth of prophetic warnings. By noting that 'most of them were not believers,' the verse underscores a recurring theological point: that clear signs and undeniable evidence do not guarantee faith, because belief requires an inner receptivity that many refuse to cultivate despite witnessing or hearing of manifest truths. This serves both as a consolation to the Prophet Muhammad, whose message was similarly rejected by most of his people despite clear signs, and as a warning to the Meccan audience that their refusal to believe follows the same pattern as earlier nations who faced destruction for their disbelief.

translation: And indeed, your Lord - He is the Exalted in Might, the Merciful.
interpretation: This verse, which recurs as a refrain throughout Surah Ash-Shu'ara after recounting the stories of various prophets and their peoples, serves as a theological conclusion drawn from each narrative. It pairs two seemingly contrasting divine attributes - 'Aziz (the Almighty, the Invincible) and Raheem (the Merciful, the Compassionate) - to convey a balanced understanding of God's nature. The 'Izzah (might) is demonstrated through God's power to destroy those who reject His messengers and persist in disbelief and oppression, as seen in the fates of peoples like those of Noah, Hud, Salih, Lot, and Shu'ayb. Yet this same God is also Raheem, extending mercy by sending warners and guidance before enacting judgment, giving people chances to repent, and sparing the believers among destroyed nations. The conjunction of these attributes teaches that divine justice and divine mercy are not contradictory but complementary - God's power is never arbitrary or purely punitive, and His mercy is never weak or without moral consequence. This refrain invites reflection on how each prophetic story, despite its particular tragedies and triumphs, ultimately testifies to this same unified truth about God's character, reinforcing that the patterns of history - reward, punishment, guidance, and destruction - all flow from this single source of perfect power exercised through perfect compassion.

translation: And [recall] when your Lord called to Moses: 'Go to the wrongdoing people -
interpretation: This verse opens the narrative of Moses's commissioning by God to confront Pharaoh and his people. It emphasizes divine initiative—God Himself 'calls' Moses, establishing prophethood as a selected mission rather than a self-appointed role. The phrase 'the wrongdoing people' identifies Pharaoh's nation specifically by their moral condition (zulm, oppression/wrongdoing) rather than merely their political status, framing the coming confrontation as fundamentally a moral and spiritual struggle against tyranny and injustice rather than a political rivalry. This sets up the broader Quranic theme that prophets are sent specifically to communities in moral crisis, and that the call to prophethood often involves being directed toward danger and powerful opposition, requiring complete trust in divine support against seemingly insurmountable odds.

translation: The people of Pharaoh. Will they not fear [Allah] and be righteous?
interpretation: This verse comes from the account of Moses' commissioning, where Allah instructs him to go to Pharaoh's people. The rhetorical question 'Will they not fear Allah?' underscores divine astonishment and reproach at their persistent arrogance and disbelief despite having been given reason, signs, and opportunities to recognize the truth. It frames the mission of Moses not merely as a political confrontation with tyranny but as a call to spiritual awakening—urging a people entrenched in power and heedlessness to attain taqwa, that is, conscious awareness of God and accountability. The verse also reflects a broader Qur'anic theme: that every nation, regardless of its worldly strength, is ultimately answerable to moral and divine law, and willful ignorance of this truth is the root of corruption and downfall.

translation: He said, 'My Lord, indeed I fear that they will deny me.'
interpretation: This verse captures the moment of Moses's (Musa's) human apprehension when God commands him to go to Pharaoh. Despite having received the divine call to prophethood, Moses expresses a genuine, deeply human fear of rejection and disbelief from those he is sent to guide. This fear is not a sign of weakness in faith but an honest acknowledgment of the difficulty of his mission—confronting a powerful tyrant and a people entrenched in denial. The verse illustrates that prophets, though chosen and supported by God, were not devoid of natural human emotions such as fear, anxiety, and self-doubt. It also sets up the subsequent divine reassurance and support that God provides (as seen in the following verses), demonstrating that such fears, when expressed sincerely to God, are met with guidance, strength, and solutions rather than rebuke. Moses's fear specifically about being disbelieved (as opposed to fear for his physical safety) reflects his deep concern for the success of his prophetic mission and the spiritual wellbeing of the people he is sent to warn, not merely personal distress.

translation: And my breast is straitened, and my tongue is not fluent, so send for Harun (Aaron).
interpretation: This verse captures Prophet Musa's candid expression of his human limitations when confronted with the immense responsibility of delivering Allah's message to Pharaoh, a tyrant of overwhelming power. Rather than viewing his anxiety and speech difficulty as disqualifying him from the mission, Musa models the proper response to daunting divine commands: honest acknowledgment of weakness combined with continued willingness to fulfill the task, while seeking appropriate support. His request for Harun demonstrates that seeking help is not a lack of faith or trust in Allah, but a wise recognition that Allah's plan often involves granting believers companions and helpers to strengthen them in their missions. This passage also humanizes the prophets, showing that even those chosen for the highest spiritual missions experienced real psychological burdens—fear, self-doubt, and physical limitations—yet these did not prevent them from proceeding in obedience to divine command. It teaches believers that admitting vulnerability to Allah while still moving forward in faith is itself an act of trust and sincerity, not contradiction to it.

translation: And they have a charge (crime) against me, so I fear that they will kill me.
interpretation: This verse is part of Prophet Musa's (Moses) supplication to Allah when he was commanded to go to Pharaoh. Musa is referring to the Egyptian man he had killed (unintentionally, in defense of an Israelite) before fleeing Egypt, as recounted earlier in the Quran. He acknowledges that in the eyes of Pharaoh's people, this constitutes a crime for which he could be held accountable and executed. This expression of fear reveals Musa's human vulnerability and honesty before God, showing that even the most esteemed prophets experienced genuine fear and sought divine reassurance when facing danger. It sets up Allah's response of reassurance that He would protect Musa and his brother Harun, demonstrating that sincere reliance on God in the face of legitimate fear is compatible with prophetic mission and courage. The verse also implicitly teaches that acknowledging one's past deeds and their potential consequences is part of sincerity before God, rather than denial or pretension of fearlessness.

translation: He said, 'No! Go both of you with Our signs; indeed, We are with you, listening.'
interpretation: This verse is part of the narrative of Moses in Surah Ash-Shu'ara, addressing Moses' fear expressed in the preceding verses about being rejected or harmed by Pharaoh, and his concern over his speech impediment and the charge against him from killing an Egyptian. God's response—'Kalla' (No! By no means!)—is a decisive rejection of Moses' fear and self-doubt, reassuring him that his apprehensions will not materialize as he imagines. The command 'fadh-haba' (go, both of you) refers to Moses and his brother Aaron, sent together as a demonstration of divine mercy, since Aaron would support Moses in eloquence and testimony. 'Our signs' (ayatina) refers to the miracles given to Moses, such as the staff and his hand, which serve as proofs of prophethood before Pharaoh. The closing assurance, 'indeed, We are with you, listening,' is profound theological comfort: it signifies God's direct attentiveness and protective presence, hearing every word exchanged between Moses, Aaron, and Pharaoh, and implicitly guaranteeing divine support and intervention. This encapsulates a central Quranic theme—that those sent on a divine mission, however daunting the opposition, are never alone, for God's knowledge and support accompany them intimately, countering fear with certainty of divine companionship and oversight.

translation: So go both of you to Pharaoh and say: 'Indeed, we are the messenger of the Lord of the worlds.'
interpretation: This verse is addressed to Moses and Aaron, commanding them to approach Pharaoh together despite the danger involved, as Pharaoh was a tyrant who claimed divinity. The use of 'messenger' in the singular form, despite referring to two individuals, signifies the unity of their mission and message—they spoke with one voice and purpose, representing a single divine commission rather than two separate ones. This reflects the Qur'anic theme that prophets and messengers, though many, carry one unified message from one Lord. The verse also establishes the courage required of those who carry divine truth to worldly power: they must identify themselves clearly and boldly, asserting their authority as being granted by 'the Lord of the worlds'—a phrase emphasizing God's sovereignty over all creation, including Pharaoh himself, who falsely claimed to be lord over his people. This sets up the central confrontation of the narrative: the clash between worldly tyranny and divine truth, between a man who declared 'I am your lord, most high' and the messengers who came only as humble conveyors of a message from the true, universal Lord.

translation: [Saying]: 'Send with us the Children of Israel.'
interpretation: This verse is part of the narrative in Surah Ash-Shu'ara recounting the mission of Prophets Musa (Moses) and Harun (Aaron) to Pharaoh. After being commanded by Allah to go to Pharaoh and remind him of his tyranny, Musa and Harun deliver this core demand: the liberation of the Children of Israel from generations of bondage and oppression under Pharaoh's rule. This simple yet profound request encapsulates the central conflict of the narrative—a confrontation between worldly tyrannical power and divine justice.
