The 'baraza' (brought forth/made manifest) indicates that Hell, though always existing, will be unveiled and made starkly visible to those who strayed from the path of guidance - 'al-ghawin' referring to those who deliberately chose misguidance over truth despite having the capacity to discern it. The imagery emphasizes the stark contrast often drawn in the Qur'an between the fate of the righteous and that of the misguided at the moment of ultimate reckoning. This unveiling serves multiple rhetorical purposes: it represents the final removal of worldly illusions and denials that the disbelievers maintained in life, it completes the inversion of perceived reality (where the disbelievers may have thought themselves secure or correct in their worldview), and it establishes the certainty and visibility of consequences as opposed to the unseen nature of divine threats in worldly life. The verb choice suggests a dramatic, almost theatrical revealing - as if Hell has been waiting, hidden, and is now presented as direct evidence of the truth of what prophets had warned. This moment of unveiling is characteristically paired in Qur'anic rhetoric with the opposite scene of Paradise being brought near to the righteous, creating a dualistic structure that reinforces moral accountability and the reality of unseen consequences for choices made in worldly life.

translation: And it was said to them, "Where are those you used to worship,"
interpretation: This verse depicts a moment on the Day of Judgment when disbelievers are confronted and mockingly asked about the false deities and idols they worshipped in worldly life. The rhetorical question exposes the utter powerlessness and absence of these false gods when they are needed most—they cannot intercede, help, or even appear to defend their former worshippers. This serves as a severe rebuke, highlighting the folly of associating partners with God, as these idols, who received devotion and sacrifice, are revealed to be completely impotent and irrelevant in the face of divine judgment. The verse underscores a central Quranic theme: that worship directed at anything other than God is ultimately worship of nothing, as these false objects of devotion vanish or prove useless precisely when accountability is demanded.

translation: Besides Allah? Can they help you, or can they help themselves?
interpretation: This verse comes in the context of the Day of Judgment, addressing the idols and false deities that polytheists worshipped instead of Allah. It is a rhetorical question exposing the utter powerlessness of these false gods. The verse challenges the fundamental premise of polytheism by pointing out that the very objects of worship cannot even defend or save themselves, let alone come to the aid of their worshippers. This serves as a devastating critique of idolatry, demonstrating through simple logic that anything other than Allah that is worshipped lacks true power, agency, or the capacity for intervention. The verse invites reflection on true sovereignty and strength, asserting that ultimate help and salvation can only come from Allah, who alone possesses real power over all things, while everything else—no matter how revered—is fundamentally helpless.

translation: So they will be hurled into it [Hellfire], they and the misguided ones,
interpretation: This verse depicts the scene of judgment where the false deities that were worshipped alongside Allah—along with those who strayed from the truth by worshipping them—are cast headlong into the Fire. The imagery of being 'kabkaba' (tumbled or hurled down in succession, one upon another) conveys utter humiliation and disgrace, contrasting sharply with the honor these idols were given in worldly life. The verse serves as a decisive refutation of polytheism, showing that the objects of false worship possess no power to save either themselves or their followers; both the misguided worshippers and the false gods they exalted share the same fate of degradation, underscoring the futility of placing trust and devotion in anything other than the one true God.

translation: And the soldiers (hosts) of Iblis, all of them [will be gathered together in Hell].
interpretation: This phrase, occurring in the context of describing the fate of the wrongdoers and those who reject faith, refers to the complete assembly of Iblis (Satan) and all his followers—the hosts of jinn and devils who work to misguide humanity—on the Day of Judgment. The verse emphasizes totality: not a single one of Iblis's forces will escape accountability. This underscores the Qur'anic theme that evil, though it may seem powerful and pervasive in worldly life, is ultimately finite and subject to divine justice. The grouping of Iblis's hosts together with wrongdoers (as found in the fuller context of the passage) illustrates the principle that those who follow a corrupting influence will share in its consequences, reinforcing the idea of collective responsibility and the ultimate powerlessness of satanic forces before God's authority. It serves as a warning that allegiance to misguidance, whether through active following of Satan's whispers or through heedlessness, leads to a shared destiny with the very source of that misguidance.

translation: They will say, while they dispute therein:
interpretation: This verse depicts a scene of Hell where the disbelievers and the false deities they once worshipped are cast together, and they engage in bitter mutual recrimination. The imagery conveys the complete reversal of worldly relationships in the afterlife—those who were once adored and depended upon become sources of blame and regret. This dispute underscores the Qur'anic theme that false objects of worship, whether idols, wealth, or other creatures, will offer no help or companionship on the Day of Judgment, and will instead be implicated in mutual blame, highlighting the futility and ultimate isolation that results from misplaced devotion in worldly life.

translation: By Allah, we were indeed in manifest error,
interpretation: This verse depicts the confession of the disbelievers in the Hereafter, specifically those who had worshipped false deities alongside Allah. Upon witnessing the reality of the afterlife and facing the consequences of their misguidance, they swear by Allah Himself—the very One they had denied or associated partners with—to acknowledge the depth of their error. The use of an oath ('By Allah') intensifies the admission, showing their complete and undeniable recognition of the truth they once rejected. This moment represents the ultimate regret of those who followed their forefathers or false leaders blindly, equating created beings with the Creator, only to realize in the end that such misguidance was 'manifest'—clear and unmistakable, with no excuse for having fallen into it. It serves as a warning to the living about the peril of blind imitation and the worship of anything other than Allah alone.

translation: [They will say]: 'When we equated you [idols] with the Lord of the worlds.'
interpretation: This verse depicts the confession and regret of the disbelievers in the Hereafter, as they admit to their fellow idols or false deities that they had wrongfully placed them on an equal footing with Allah, the Lord of all creation. This is an acknowledgment of the grave error of shirk (associating partners with God) and highlights the moment of realization that comes too late, after death, when the truth of Allah's absolute oneness and supremacy becomes undeniably clear. It serves as a warning to the living about the severity of equating any created being or object with the Creator, emphasizing that such equivalence is fundamentally irrational and spiritually destructive, as nothing in existence can be compared to or share in the dominion and lordship of Allah over all the worlds.

translation: And none led us astray except the criminals.
interpretation: This verse depicts a scene from the Day of Judgment, where the followers who are condemned to Hell confess and lament, blaming the ringleaders and corrupters—those who promoted falsehood and misguidance—for their own perdition. It illustrates a moment of futile regret, as these followers acknowledge that they abandoned truth and guidance in favor of following sinful leaders, mentors, or societal figures who deceived them. However, this admission comes too late to absolve them of responsibility, since the Qur'an elsewhere clarifies that each soul bears accountability for its own choice to follow misguidance rather than seeking truth independently. The verse serves as a warning against blind conformity and the abdication of personal moral responsibility, showing how those who willingly follow corrupt leaders without critical thought or independent verification of truth will ultimately share in the consequences of that misguidance, even as they attempt to shift blame in the hereafter.

translation: So now we have no intercessors,
interpretation: This verse is part of the confession made by the people of Hell as they recount their misdeeds and realize the futility of their situation (Surah Ash-Shu'ara, 26:100-101). Having rejected the warnings of the prophets in worldly life and followed their leaders and societal norms instead of divine guidance, they come to the devastating realization in the Hereafter that none of the intercessors they once relied upon—whether idols, ancestors, or powerful figures—can help them now. This reflects the Quranic theme that intercession on the Day of Judgment is only granted by Allah's permission to those He wills, and that false hopes placed in intermediaries other than sincere faith and righteous deeds will prove worthless. The verse serves as a stark warning against relying on false intercessors and emphasizes the importance of direct accountability before God.

translation: Nor will any intimate friend ask about another.
interpretation: This phrase comes from the description of the Day of Judgment in Surah Al-Ma'arij, depicting the overwhelming terror and isolation of that moment. Despite the deep bonds of friendship and loyalty that exist in worldly life—where a 'hamim' (intimate, devoted friend) would typically be the first to inquire about and support a companion in times of distress—on that Day, such bonds will dissolve entirely. Each soul will be so consumed by its own reckoning and fear of judgment that even the closest of friends will have no capacity to think of, ask about, or come to the aid of another. This underscores the absolute singularity of each person's accountability before God, stripping away all worldly supports, relationships, and intercessions that people might normally rely upon. It serves as a sobering reminder that ultimate salvation cannot be borrowed from the love or loyalty of others, but rests solely on one's own deeds and standing before the Divine.

translation: Then if only we had another chance [at life], we would be among the believers.
interpretation: This verse depicts the regretful lament of the disbelievers and those who followed false leaders, spoken in the Hereafter after they witness the reality of judgment and the consequences of their misguidance. Having seen the truth too late, they express a desperate wish to return to worldly life for a second opportunity, believing that this time they would choose faith and righteousness. This expression of futile longing serves as a powerful warning to the living: it illustrates the overwhelming regret that awaits those who reject truth and follow falsehood, while also underscoring that such wishes in the afterlife are in vain—there is no return, no second chance once the appointed time has passed. The verse functions didactically, urging believers and unbelievers alike in this world to recognize that the opportunity for faith and repentance exists only in this life, and procrastination or rejection of truth leads to irreversible consequences that cannot be undone by mere wishful thinking after death.

translation: Indeed, in that is a sign, but most of them were not believers.
interpretation: This verse is a refrain that recurs throughout Surah Ash-Shu'ara, following accounts of earlier prophets and the fate of their disbelieving peoples. It teaches that the stories of past nations—their destruction, their trials, and the miracles sent to them—contain clear signs (ayat) pointing to God's power, justice, and the truth of prophetic messages. Yet despite the clarity of these signs, the verse laments that most people throughout history failed to believe. This highlights a central Quranic theme: faith is not simply a matter of evidence but also of the heart's willingness to submit and reflect. The repetition of this refrain after each prophetic narrative in the surah serves as a rhetorical device, reinforcing that disbelief is not due to a lack of signs but to human stubbornness, pride, or heedlessness. It also serves as a warning and consolation to the Prophet Muhammad, reminding him that rejection by the majority is a historical pattern among all nations who received messengers, not a sign of the message's falsehood.

translation: And indeed, your Lord - He is the Almighty, the Most Merciful.
interpretation: This verse combines two of God's attributes that together express the balance of divine justice and mercy. 'Al-Azeez' (the Almighty/Exalted in Might) signifies God's absolute power, sovereignty, and ability to execute His will without opposition - particularly relevant in the context of this surah, where it follows accounts of prophets facing rejection from their peoples and precedes narratives of punishment befalling those who disbelieved. 'Ar-Raheem' (the Most Merciful) tempers this power with compassion, indicating that God's might is never exercised arbitrarily or cruelly, but is always accompanied by mercy toward His creation. This pairing recurs throughout Surah Ash-Shu'ara as a refrain after each prophetic narrative, reminding the listener that despite the destruction of disbelieving nations, God's essential nature includes profound mercy - He gives ample opportunity for repentance before any punishment, and His power is ultimately in service of a just and merciful order. The verse serves as a reassurance to the Prophet Muhammad (to whom 'your Lord' refers) that the same God who possesses irresistible power to vindicate truth and deal with opposition also embodies boundless mercy, offering hope and consolation amid the trials of prophethood.

translation: The people of Noah denied the messengers.
interpretation: Although Noah was but one messenger sent to his people, the verse states that they denied 'the messengers' (plural). This reflects a key Qur'anic principle: because the fundamental message of all prophets—submission to the One God—is the same, rejecting one messenger is tantamount to rejecting all of them. The unity of the prophetic message means that disbelief in any single prophet constitutes disbelief in the entire chain of revelation, since they all called to the same essential truth. This sets the pattern for the subsequent verses in the surah, which describe how other peoples ('Aad, Thamud, the people of Lot, the people of the Grove) similarly denied their respective prophets, each account being described with this same formula to emphasize that the rejection of one prophet is rejection of the shared divine message delivered through all messengers.

translation: When their brother Noah said to them, 'Will you not fear Allah?'
interpretation: This verse introduces the mission of Prophet Noah to his people, highlighting that he is described as their 'brother' not by faith but by kinship and tribal relation, emphasizing that he was one of them, familiar and trustworthy, not a stranger. This establishes a rhetorical and compassionate approach—he came from among them, understanding their ways, yet calling them to abandon idolatry and turn to piety and God-consciousness (taqwa). The question 'Will you not fear Allah?' is not merely interrogative but a profound invitation to self-reflection, urging his people to recognize the moral and spiritual consequences of their disbelief. It sets the tone for the recurring prophetic pattern in the Qur'an, where messengers are sent from within their own communities to warn and guide, reinforcing the theme that divine guidance is always accessible and relatable, delivered through voices the people know and trust.

translation: Indeed, I am to you a trustworthy messenger.
interpretation: This declaration, repeated by several prophets in Surah Ash-Shu'ara (Noah, Hud, Salih, Lot, and Shu'ayb) when addressing their respective peoples, establishes the foundational basis of prophetic authority: trustworthiness (amanah). Before calling their communities to worship God alone and abandon corruption, each prophet first affirms his personal integrity and reliability, reminding his people of his known character among them. This reflects a broader Quranic principle that the credibility of a message is inseparable from the demonstrated honesty of its messenger—since trust must be earned through consistent conduct before people can be expected to accept a call to transform their beliefs and behavior. The repetition of this exact phrase across multiple prophetic narratives in this surah also serves a literary and theological purpose, binding different messengers across time into a single continuous tradition of truthful guidance, showing that every prophet, despite being sent to different nations, shared the same essential quality of trustworthiness as the basis of his mission.

translation: So fear Allah and obey me.
interpretation: This phrase is a recurring refrain spoken by various prophets—such as Noah, Hud, Salih, Lot, and Shu'ayb—as they addressed their disbelieving peoples throughout the Qur'an. It encapsulates the core message of prophethood: a call to two inseparable duties. 'Fear Allah' (taqwa) calls for inner consciousness of God, awareness of His power, and accountability before Him, which should govern one's beliefs and actions. 'Obey me' follows logically, since the prophet's authority is not personal but derived entirely from his role as a messenger conveying divine guidance; obedience to him is, in essence, obedience to God's command delivered through him. The pairing emphasizes that true faith is not merely abstract belief but must translate into practical submission to guidance brought by a trustworthy messenger. The repetition of this phrase across different prophetic narratives in the Qur'an underscores the continuity and unity of the prophetic message throughout history—every nation was given the same fundamental call, and their rejection of their respective prophets parallels the rejection faced by Muhammad from his own people, offering him reassurance and a warning to his audience about the consequences faced by earlier nations who refused this same message.

translation: And I do not ask you for any payment for it; my reward is only from the Lord of the Worlds.
interpretation: This verse, repeated by several prophets in Surah Ash-Shu'ara (Noah, Hud, Salih, Lot, and Shu'ayb), establishes a crucial criterion for discerning true prophethood: the absence of worldly self-interest. By explicitly disavowing any demand for material compensation, wages, or worldly benefit from their people, the prophets demonstrate that their call to monotheism and righteousness is motivated purely by sincerity to God rather than personal gain. This serves multiple purposes: it removes any suspicion that the message is a scheme for wealth, status, or power; it places the entire burden of proof on the truth of the message itself rather than the messenger's potential ulterior motives; and it establishes a timeless pattern recognizable across all prophetic missions—genuine divine guidance comes without a price tag attached to the people being guided. The phrase 'Lord of the Worlds' (Rabb al-'Alamin) reinforces that true recompense comes only from God, the Sustainer of all creation, not from human transactions, thereby elevating the prophet's mission above worldly economics into the realm of pure service to the Divine will and genuine concern for humanity's spiritual welfare.

translation: So fear Allah and obey me.
interpretation: This phrase is a recurring refrain in Surah Ash-Shu'ara, uttered by several prophets—Nuh, Hud, Salih, Lut, and Shu'ayb—to their respective peoples. It encapsulates the core message of prophethood: a call to taqwa (God-consciousness, reverent fear of Allah) paired with obedience to the messenger who conveys divine guidance. The pairing is significant—fearing Allah is the internal spiritual state, while obeying the prophet is its external manifestation, since the prophet's authority derives entirely from his role as a conduit for divine revelation, not from personal status. The repetition of this exact phrase across different prophets and different eras underscores the unity of the prophetic mission throughout history: despite varying contexts, peoples, and specific laws, the essential call remains constant. It also implicitly rebukes the prophets' people for their resistance, framing obedience to the messenger not as blind submission to a man, but as a natural extension of fearing God, since the messenger speaks only what God has commanded. This phrase thus serves as a rhetorical anchor point, linking the trials of earlier nations to the Quraysh's own rejection of Muhammad, suggesting that the pattern of rejecting prophets is ancient and that the consequences of disobedience are equally enduring.

translation: They said, "Shall we believe you while the lowest [class of people] follow you?"
interpretation: This verse recounts the response of the arrogant elite among Noah's people when he called them to believe in God. They dismissed his message by pointing to his followers—the poor, the weak, and the socially marginalized—as proof that his message was unworthy of serious consideration. This reveals a recurring pattern among those who reject prophetic messages: judging truth not by its content but by the social status of those who accept it. The elite's objection reflects classist arrogance, assuming that spiritual truth and divine guidance would naturally be reserved for or recognized first by the privileged and powerful, rather than understanding that sincerity of heart and willingness to submit to truth often come more readily to those without worldly status to protect. The verse implicitly critiques this mindset, as the Quran consistently affirms that nobility before God is based on piety and faith, not social rank, wealth, or lineage.

translation: He said, 'And what knowledge do I have of what they used to do?'
interpretation: This verse is part of the narrative of Prophet Nuh (Noah) and his people, found in Surah Ash-Shu'ara. The context is that the disbelieving elite among Nuh's people objected to his message, pointing out that only the lowest and most humble members of society had believed in him, implying that he should reject them or that their following somehow discredited his prophetic mission. Nuh's response here reflects a profound principle: he refuses to judge people based on their social status, past occupations, or worldly standing. He declares that it is not his place—nor within his knowledge or authority—to inquire into or evaluate what people did before they came to faith. His role as a prophet is to accept and guide those who believe, regardless of their background, leaving judgment of their inner selves and deeds to God alone. This establishes an essential Quranic theme: faith and sincerity before God are not measured by worldly status, wealth, or lineage, and no human has the right to turn away a sincere believer based on such criteria. It also implicitly rebukes the elite's classist arrogance, showing that their objection was rooted in pride rather than genuine concern for truth.

translation: Their reckoning is only upon my Lord, if you could perceive.
interpretation: This verse is part of Prophet Nuh's (Noah's) response to his people who objected to the lowly, poor believers who followed him. They demanded he drive away these followers in order for them to accept his message, judging people by worldly status rather than faith. Nuh's reply establishes a fundamental principle: the final accounting and judgment of people's inner hearts, sincerity, and deeds belongs exclusively to God, not to any human being. He refuses to dismiss the believers based on their social class, asserting that it is not his place—or anyone's—to weigh the worth of a soul by outward circumstances. The phrase 'if you could perceive' underscores the spiritual blindness of his people, who judge by appearances and worldly status while remaining ignorant of true spiritual worth, which only God can discern and judge. This teaches that human value before God is not measured by wealth or social standing, but is a matter reserved for divine judgment alone.

translation: And I am not one to drive away the believers.
interpretation: This verse is spoken by Prophet Nuh (Noah) in response to the chieftains of his people who demanded that he expel the poor and lowly believers who had followed him, as a condition for them to accept his message. They viewed these followers with contempt, considering themselves too noble to associate with them. Nuh's response establishes a profound principle: faith and sincerity of belief are the only criteria for standing before God and within the community of believers, not social status, wealth, or worldly prestige. By refusing to expel the believers, Nuh rejects the elitist logic of his opponents and affirms that the truth of a message is not diminished by who accepts it first or who among the followers appears lowly in the eyes of society. This reflects a recurring Qur'anic theme found in the stories of multiple prophets, where the arrogant elite dismiss the message partly because it attracts the poor and marginalized, while the prophets insist that spiritual worth is measured by sincerity of faith and righteousness, not social standing. Nuh's steadfastness here also demonstrates moral courage and loyalty to those who believed in him despite pressure from the powerful to abandon them for the sake of winning over the elite.

translation: I am not but a clear warner.
interpretation: This declaration, placed on the lips of various prophets throughout the Qur'an, serves as a crucial clarification of the prophetic role and a corrective to the excessive demands and expectations placed upon messengers by their skeptical communities. When people repeatedly demanded miracles, signs, or proof beyond what was given, or attributed to the prophets powers of knowledge of the unseen, control over guidance, or divine authority in themselves, this phrase reorients the relationship between messenger and message. The prophet's function is strictly delimited: to deliver a clear, unambiguous warning of consequences—whether of disbelief, moral corruption, or rejection of truth—without being the source of that truth or the one who compels its acceptance. The word 'mubin' (clear/manifest) underscores that the warning itself is not obscure or esoteric; the message's clarity removes excuse for those who reject it, since the fault lies not in ambiguity of communication but in human refusal to accept what has been plainly conveyed. This verse also implicitly humbles the prophetic figure before God, affirming that ultimate judgment, guidance, and power to bring belief into hearts rest with the Divine alone, while the human messenger's task is limited to sincere transmission and admonition.

translation: They said, "If you do not desist, O Noah, you will surely be among those stoned (to death)."
interpretation: This verse captures the hostile response of Noah's people to his persistent call to worship God alone and abandon idolatry. Their threat of stoning—a severe and shameful form of execution—reveals both their rejection of his message and their attempt to silence him through intimidation rather than reasoned argument. This exchange illustrates a recurring Quranic theme: prophets throughout history faced not just denial but violent threats from their communities when their message challenged entrenched beliefs and social structures. The people's response demonstrates intellectual bankruptcy, as they resort to threats rather than addressing Noah's arguments. This pattern of persecution faced by messengers serves to console the Prophet Muhammad and early Muslims facing similar opposition in Mecca, showing that rejection and threats of violence against God's messengers are not a sign of the message's falsehood but rather a historical pattern of how truth is often met with hostility by those invested in maintaining the status quo.

translation: He said, 'My Lord, indeed my people have denied me.'
interpretation: This verse depicts the Prophet Nuh (Noah) turning to God in supplication after facing persistent rejection from his people despite his prolonged efforts to guide them. It illustrates the archetypal struggle of prophets who are sent with divine truth yet encounter stubborn disbelief from their communities. Nuh's complaint to God is not one of despair but of seeking divine support after exhausting human means of persuasion. This moment marks a turning point in the narrative, as it precedes God's response and the eventual decree of the flood as a consequence of the people's persistent denial. The verse underscores themes of patience in prophethood, the loneliness of conveying truth to a resistant audience, and the ultimate reliance on God when human efforts reach their limits. It also establishes a pattern seen with other prophets in the Qur'an, where rejection by one's own people becomes a trial that tests faith and commitment to the divine message, while placing the matter of judgment and justice solely in God's hands.

translation: So judge decisively between me and them, and save me and those with me of the believers.
interpretation: This verse records the supplication of Prophet Noah after his people persistently rejected his message and mocked him despite his prolonged efforts to guide them. Having exhausted all means of persuasion, Noah turns to God and asks for a definitive judgment ('fath', literally an 'opening' or decisive verdict) between himself and his disbelieving people, essentially asking God to render the final decision on who is right. The request for judgment is paired with a plea for deliverance - asking not only for his own salvation but for that of the believers who stood with him, emphasizing the communal nature of faith and the responsibility a prophet feels toward his followers. This prayer became the catalyst for the subsequent flood narrative, demonstrating a recurring Quranic theme wherein divine justice ultimately intervenes when a people reach a point of irredeemable rejection of truth, while those who maintain faith are granted deliverance. The verse illustrates the appropriate response of a believer under persecution: rather than seeking personal revenge, Noah entrusts the matter entirely to God's judgment, modeling patience and reliance on divine wisdom even after enduring centuries of rejection.

translation: So We saved him and those with him in the laden ship.
interpretation: This verse refers to the salvation of Prophet Nuh (Noah) and his believing companions from the catastrophic flood that destroyed his disbelieving people. The 'laden ship' (al-fulk al-mashhun) indicates the ark was fully loaded with pairs of creatures, provisions, and the faithful few who heeded Nuh's call after centuries of patient preaching. This event demonstrates a recurring Qur'anic theme: divine justice ensures that those who reject truth despite clear warnings face destruction, while those who maintain faith and righteousness, even as a small minority, are granted deliverance through God's mercy. The narrative serves as both a historical account and a moral lesson for the Prophet Muhammad's contemporaries who rejected his message, drawing a parallel between ancient disbelieving nations and the Quraysh, while offering hope and reassurance to the believers who remained faithful despite opposition and hardship.

translation: Then, after that, We drowned the rest.
interpretation: This verse refers to the drowning of Pharaoh and his people after the Israelites had safely crossed the sea. The phrase "the rest" signifies Pharaoh's army and followers who pursued Moses and the Israelites with intent to harm them. This event serves as a demonstration of divine justice, where those who persisted in arrogance, tyranny, and disbelief despite witnessing numerous signs were ultimately destroyed. It underscores a recurring Quranic theme: that worldly power and rejection of truth lead to downfall, while those who place their trust in God are delivered. The drowning stands as a sign and a lesson for later generations about the consequences of oppression and denial of divine guidance.

translation: Indeed, in that is a sign; but most of them were not believers.
interpretation: This recurring Qur'anic refrain follows narratives of earlier prophets and nations who faced destruction or deliverance due to their response to divine guidance. The verse asserts that the preceding story contains a genuine sign (ayah) pointing to God's power, justice, and the truth of His message—observable in the natural or historical outcome described. Yet it immediately notes that despite the clarity of this sign, most people did not believe. This juxtaposition highlights a central Qur'anic theme: divine signs are made evident and accessible to human reason and reflection, but belief is not merely a function of evidence—it requires humility, sincerity, and willingness to submit. The verse thus serves both as a consolation to the Prophet Muhammad and believers, who may be discouraged by widespread rejection of their message, and as a warning to disbelievers, situating their rejection within a historical pattern of human ingratitude and heedlessness. It implies that the fault lies not in insufficient evidence but in moral and spiritual resistance to truth.

translation: And indeed, your Lord is the Mighty, the Merciful.
interpretation: This verse, which concludes numerous narrative passages in the Qur'an (particularly in Surah Ash-Shu'ara), pairs two seemingly contrasting divine attributes to convey a complete picture of God's nature. 'Al-Aziz' (the Mighty/Exalted in Might) emphasizes God's absolute power, invincibility, and sovereignty—He is never overcome or defeated, and His will is supreme over all creation. 'Ar-Raheem' (the Merciful) emphasizes His compassion, forgiveness, and tender care for His creation. The juxtaposition is theologically significant: it teaches that divine power is never exercised arbitrarily or cruelly, but is always tempered by mercy. Conversely, God's mercy is not a sign of weakness but flows from a position of absolute strength and authority. This combination appears repeatedly after accounts of prophets and the destruction of disbelieving nations, serving as a reminder that even in meting out justice or punishment, God's essential mercy remains active—extended to the believers who were saved, and even in the respite given to wrongdoers before their reckoning. It reassures believers that the same God who possesses irresistible power toward those who reject truth is also infinitely compassionate toward those who turn to Him, encouraging both reverent awe and hopeful trust in the divine nature.

translation: The people of 'Aad denied the messengers.
interpretation: This verse highlights that the people of 'Aad rejected the message brought to them by their prophet Hud, and by extension denied all the messengers, since the message of all prophets—calling to the worship of the One God—is fundamentally the same. Denying one true messenger is tantamount to denying them all, as they share the same essential truth. This sets the stage for recounting the fate of a people who, despite their strength and achievements, met destruction due to their arrogance and rejection of divine guidance.

translation: When their brother Hud said to them, 'Will you not fear Allah (be mindful of Him and guard against His punishment)?'
interpretation: This verse introduces the prophet Hud's address to the people of 'Ad, and the phrase 'their brother' signifies that Hud was one of their own kin and tribe, not an outsider, which is meant to establish his credibility and the natural bond of trust that should have made his message easier to accept. The rhetorical question 'Will you not fear Allah?' is not a request for information but a gentle yet firm rebuke, awakening their dormant conscience and calling them to self-examination. It implies that piety (taqwa) is already within their innate capacity, and their failure to attain it is due to heedlessness rather than inability. This opening sets the tone for the entire narrative that follows, establishing the pattern common to the accounts of earlier prophets in this surah: a messenger from among the people, a call to fear God, and the people's subsequent rejection despite the reasonableness and familiarity of the call.

translation: Indeed, I am to you a trustworthy messenger.
interpretation: This declaration is made by various prophets (Noah, Hud, Salih, Lot, and Shu'ayb) in Surah Ash-Shu'ara when addressing their respective peoples who had fallen into disbelief and transgression. By emphasizing their trustworthiness (amanah), the prophets establish their credibility before delivering the call to worship God alone. This phrase underscores a key quality required of any messenger: honesty and reliability, meaning they would not distort, fabricate, or add anything to the divine message for personal gain. It reflects the broader Quranic theme that prophets are chosen individuals known for their moral integrity even before their prophethood, making their call to truth more compelling to their communities. The repetition of this exact phrase across multiple prophets' stories in this surah also serves a literary purpose, demonstrating the continuity and unity of the prophetic message throughout history—every messenger, regardless of era or nation, came with the same fundamental call to monotheism and carried the same quality of trustworthiness as a seal of authenticity for their mission.

translation: So fear Allah and obey me.
interpretation: This phrase is spoken by various prophets in the Qur'an (such as Nuh, Hud, Salih, Lut, and Shu'ayb) as they call their respective peoples to monotheism. The pairing of 'fear Allah' with 'obey me' establishes that obedience to the prophet is not independent authority but is directly tied to and derived from reverence for God—the prophet's command carries weight precisely because he conveys divine guidance. This formula emphasizes that true taqwa (God-consciousness) naturally manifests in heeding the messenger sent to guide humanity, linking inner faith with outward compliance to prophetic teaching.

translation: And I do not ask you for it any payment. My reward is only from the Lord of the worlds.
interpretation: This verse, repeated by several prophets in the Qur'an (such as Nuh, Hud, Salih, Lut, and Shu'ayb), emphasizes the sincerity and selflessness of the prophetic mission. By declaring that they seek no worldly compensation from their people for conveying the message, the prophets demonstrate that their call to faith is not motivated by personal gain, wealth, or status. Instead, their recompense lies solely with God, the Lord and Sustainer of all creation. This serves multiple purposes: it removes any suspicion that the prophet might be driven by ulterior motives, it establishes a model of selfless devotion for those who carry religious truth, and it underscores the principle that true guidance comes from divine source rather than human transaction. The statement also implicitly invites the listeners to examine the message on its own merits, free from concerns about the messenger's personal interests, since he has explicitly renounced any claim to material reward from them.

translation: Do you build on every high place a monument, amusing yourselves?
interpretation: This verse is part of Prophet Hud's rebuke to his people, the 'Ad, who were known for their great strength and architectural prowess. He questions their practice of erecting elaborate landmarks, towers, or monuments on every elevated location not out of necessity but merely for show, vanity, or idle amusement. The underlying criticism is that they squandered their God-given power and resources on frivolous displays of grandeur and worldly pride rather than using their abilities for righteous purposes or remembrance of God. This reflects a broader Quranic theme warning against hubris, wastefulness, and the construction of monuments to one's own glory, which distracts from spiritual purpose and leads to moral corruption, foreshadowing the destruction that befell the 'Ad for their arrogance and rejection of their prophet's message.

translation: And you take for yourselves fortresses (or grand structures), that you might abide forever?
interpretation: This verse is part of Prophet Hud's rebuke to his people, the 'Ad, who were renowned for their architectural prowess and construction of monumental structures. The rhetorical question exposes the folly of their worldly ambitions: they built elaborate fortresses, palaces, or reservoirs as if such constructions could grant them immortality or permanence in this world. Hud challenges their misplaced priorities, pointing out the absurdity of investing so heavily in worldly grandeur while neglecting the finite nature of human life and the inevitability of death. The verse serves as a broader admonition against the illusion that material wealth, power, or physical monuments can secure permanence or escape mortality. It calls attention to the vanity of worldly pursuits when divorced from spiritual preparation for the afterlife, suggesting that true and lasting value lies not in physical edifices but in righteous deeds and devotion to God. The underlying message resonates as a timeless critique of human tendencies toward materialism and the false sense of security that accumulated wealth and grand constructions can provide against the reality of mortality.

translation: And when you seize [in attack or punishment], you seize as tyrants.
interpretation: This verse is part of Prophet Hud's address to his people, the 'Aad, in which he catalogues their moral corruption as evidence of their need for reform and warning. After criticizing them for building monuments on high places out of vanity and for constructing strongholds as if they would live forever, he condemns their use of power: when they exercised force or authority over others—whether in punishment, conflict, or domination—they did so with excessive cruelty, arrogance, and disregard for justice, behaving as tyrants rather than with restraint or mercy. This highlights a broader Qur'anic theme that physical strength and power are moral trusts; when wielded without conscience or accountability to God, they become instruments of oppression. The verse implicitly contrasts the tyranny of worldly power with the justice that comes from submission to God's guidance, suggesting that true strength is tempered by righteousness, not expressed through brutality against the weak.

translation: So fear Allah and obey me.
interpretation: This phrase is a recurring refrain spoken by various prophets throughout the Qur'an (such as Nuh, Hud, Salih, Lut, and Shu'ayb) as they addressed their disbelieving communities. It encapsulates the core message of prophethood: a call to taqwa (God-consciousness, reverence, and fear of Allah) paired with obedience to the messenger who conveys divine guidance. The pairing is significant because it establishes that obedience to the prophet is not independent of or equal to obedience to Allah, but rather flows from and is validated by one's fear and awareness of Allah—the prophet is merely the conduit of divine command, not an autonomous authority. This phrase typically appears after the prophet has reminded their people of Allah's blessings or warned them of consequences of previous nations, serving as the logical conclusion and urgent appeal following that reminder. The brevity and directness of the imperative form underscores the urgency of the prophetic mission and the simplicity of the message being delivered, cutting through the people's rationalizations, excuses, or attachment to ancestral ways. It also reflects the prophet's role as a sincere advisor (nasih) who, out of genuine concern for his people's wellbeing in this life and the next, urges them toward the straightforward path of submission to divine will rather than continuing in heedlessness or rebellion.

translation: And be mindful of (fear) Him who has supplied you with all that you know.
interpretation: This verse is part of the Prophet Hud's admonition to the people of 'Ad, reminding them that every blessing they possess—their knowledge, skills, resources, and worldly achievements—originates from God alone. By invoking 'that which you know,' the verse appeals to their own awareness of their prosperity and achievements, urging them to trace these blessings back to their true source rather than attributing them to their own strength or ingenuity. The call to taqwa (mindfulness/fear of God) here is rooted in gratitude: recognizing divine provision should naturally lead to humility and reverence rather than arrogance. It serves as a corrective to the 'Ad's pride in their worldly power, reminding them that the Giver of gifts has the authority to withdraw them, and that true wisdom lies in acknowledging dependence on the Creator rather than being deluded by apparent self-sufficiency.

translation: He supplied you with cattle and children.
interpretation: This verse, part of a passage recalling God's favors to the people of 'Ad through the warning of their prophet Hud, reminds them of the material blessings—livestock and offspring—that God bestowed upon them. These gifts represent wealth, sustenance, and the continuation of lineage, all signs of divine generosity. The underlying message is a call to gratitude and humility: the prosperity they enjoyed was not self-generated but granted by God, and it should have led them to recognize His sovereignty and worship Him alone rather than fall into arrogance, idolatry, and denial of the prophetic message. The mention of these blessings serves as a prelude to the warning that such favors can be withdrawn if met with ingratitude and rebellion against divine guidance.

translation: And gardens and springs,
interpretation: This verse is part of a recurring Qur'anic motif describing the worldly possessions—gardens, springs, treasures, and honorable positions—that a powerful and privileged people (commonly understood to refer to Pharaoh and his court) left behind when they were destroyed for their tyranny and rejection of truth. The verse serves as a reminder of the transient nature of worldly wealth and status; no matter how lush the gardens or abundant the springs, such possessions cannot save a people from divine judgment when they persist in arrogance and oppression. It underscores the Qur'anic theme that material prosperity is not a sign of divine favor, and that those who enjoyed such blessings were ultimately made to depart from them, leaving everything behind for others to inherit.

translation: Indeed, I fear for you the punishment of a tremendous Day.
interpretation: This statement is attributed to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) as a declaration of his sincere concern for his people regarding the Day of Judgment. It reflects the Prophet's role as a warner whose mission was motivated by genuine care for humanity's ultimate fate, not by personal gain or arrogance. The phrase emphasizes the magnitude and severity of the punishment awaiting those who reject faith and righteousness, underscoring the seriousness of the Day of Judgment as 'tremendous' (azeem) - a day of overwhelming consequence that dwarfs worldly concerns. This expression of fear on behalf of others, rather than for himself, demonstrates the compassionate nature of prophetic warning, showing that the purpose of divine revelation is protective guidance rather than mere condemnation. It also serves as a rhetorical device to awaken the conscience of the listeners, prompting them to reflect on their choices and the eternal consequences that follow from this worldly life.

translation: They said, 'It is all the same to us whether you admonish us or are not of those who admonish.'
interpretation: This verse records the defiant response of the people of 'Ad to their prophet Hud, who had called them to abandon idolatry and worship God alone. Their reply reveals a heart hardened beyond the point of receptivity—they declare that admonition, no matter how sincere or repeated, will have no effect on them whatsoever. This represents a profound spiritual state of willful rejection, where the problem is not lack of evidence or clarity in the message, but a stubborn attachment to inherited customs and ancestral ways that overrides reason and conscience. It illustrates a recurring Qur'anic theme: that guidance cannot be forced upon those who have decisively closed themselves off from it, and that the rejection of prophets often stems not from the weakness of the message but from the arrogance and complacency of those who refuse to relinquish their familiar way of life, even when confronted with truth. Their statement is essentially an admission of obstinacy, exposing the moral responsibility that will fall upon them for choosing persistence in error over the possibility of change.

translation: This is nothing but the fabrication (or customary way) of the former peoples.
interpretation: This verse records the response of the disbelieving people of Prophet Hud to his call to worship God alone and abandon idolatry. They dismissed his message as nothing new or divinely inspired, claiming it was merely an old tradition or invented practice (or, in another reading, simply 'the nature of creation from ancient times,' i.e., 'we live and die as our forefathers did, and there is nothing beyond this'). Their statement reflects a stubborn attachment to inherited customs and ancestral ways over divine revelation, a recurring theme in the Qur'an where communities reject prophets by appealing to tradition rather than engaging with the truth of the message. It illustrates the human tendency to resist change and cling to the familiar, even when confronted with clear signs and warnings, underscoring the arrogance and heedlessness that led to their eventual destruction.

translation: And we are not to be punished.
interpretation: This statement is part of the defiant response given by a disbelieving people—in context, the people of Thamud addressing their prophet Salih—to the warnings delivered by their messenger. Confident in their worldly power, traditions, and the fact that their ancestors lived the same way without divine retribution, they dismiss the possibility of punishment as mere fabrication or empty threat, saying essentially, 'This is just the old ways of our forefathers, and we will not be punished for following them.' This reflects a broader Quranic theme of human arrogance and complacency, where people mistake the delay of punishment for its impossibility, and cling to tradition and present security as proof against accountability. The verse serves as a cautionary illustration of the psychological state of denial that precedes divine chastisement, highlighting the danger of dismissing warnings simply because consequences are not immediately visible.

translation: But they denied him, so We destroyed them. Indeed, in that is a sign, yet most of them were not believers.
interpretation: This verse follows the recurring narrative pattern in Surah Ash-Shu'ara, where the stories of various prophets (here referring to Nuh/Noah and his people) are recounted with an identical refrain emphasizing rejection, divine retribution, and the lesson to be drawn. The destruction of the disbelieving people serves as a concrete historical 'sign' (ayah) meant to instruct later generations about the consequences of rejecting divine messengers. The closing phrase acknowledging that 'most of them were not believers' underscores a central Quranic theme: that truth is often rejected by the majority, and faith is the exception rather than the rule among a prophet's immediate community. This serves both as a consolation to Muhammad, who faced similar rejection from his own people, and as a warning to the Meccans that persistent denial of a messenger invites the same fate as previous nations. The structural repetition across multiple prophet narratives in this surah reinforces the universality of this pattern—human communities repeatedly reject truth-tellers, and divine justice repeatedly intervenes, yet belief remains rare despite overwhelming evidence.

translation: And indeed, your Lord - He is the Exalted in Might, the Merciful.
interpretation: This verse, which recurs as a refrain throughout Surah Ash-Shu'ara after recounting the stories of various prophets and their peoples, encapsulates the dual nature of God's dealings with humanity. 'Al-Aziz' (the Exalted in Might/All-Mighty) conveys God's absolute power and ability to punish those who reject His messengers and persist in wrongdoing, as demonstrated in the destruction of nations like those of Noah, Hud, Salih, Lot, and Shu'ayb. 'Ar-Raheem' (the Merciful) simultaneously emphasizes that this power is tempered with compassion and mercy, offering forgiveness and salvation to those who believe and repent. The pairing of these two attributes after each prophetic narrative serves as a theological lesson: divine justice and divine mercy are not contradictory but complementary aspects of God's character. The verse reassures believers that God's might is never exercised without mercy, and His mercy never compromises His justice, making this a recurring moral conclusion to the historical lessons presented in the surah.

translation: Thamud denied the messengers.
interpretation: Though only one messenger, Salih, was sent to the people of Thamud, the Qur'an states that they denied 'the messengers' (plural). This reflects a recurring Qur'anic principle: rejecting a single prophet is equivalent to rejecting the entire chain of prophethood, since all messengers call to the same essential truth—the oneness of God and the call to righteousness. By denying Salih, Thamud effectively denied the whole message that every prophet before and after him carried, demonstrating that disbelief in one divine messenger constitutes disbelief in the unified mission of all messengers.

translation: When their brother Salih said to them, 'Will you not fear Allah?'
interpretation: Salih, like all prophets, is called the 'brother' of his people not by faith but by kinship and lineage, signifying that he came from among them, spoke their language, and was known to them for his integrity before his prophethood—this made his message harder to dismiss as foreign or strange. His opening question, 'Will you not fear Allah (taqwa)?', is a direct call to moral consciousness and accountability, confronting the people of Thamud with their heedlessness. This rhetorical question implies that they already possess the innate capacity to recognize truth and righteousness, and the rebuke is that they have willfully suppressed this awareness through arrogance and attachment to their worldly power and idolatrous traditions. It sets the stage for the narrative of Thamud's rejection of Salih's message despite the clear sign given to them (the she-camel), illustrating a recurring Qur'anic theme: prophets arise from within communities to call them back to a truth already latent in human nature, and rejection of that call stems from pride rather than ignorance.

translation: Indeed, I am to you a trustworthy messenger.
interpretation: This declaration is repeated by several prophets (Noah, Hud, Salih, Lot, and Shu'ayb) in Surah Ash-Shu'ara when addressing their disbelieving peoples. By emphasizing trustworthiness (amin), the prophet establishes his moral credibility before delivering the message of monotheism, implying that since he has never been known to lie or deceive them in worldly matters, his call to worship God alone should likewise be trusted. This verse underscores the Qur'anic principle that the character and integrity of a messenger are foundational to the legitimacy of divine revelation, and it draws a parallel across different prophets to show that the core message of all prophets—sincerity, honesty, and calling people to God—is consistent throughout prophetic history.

translation: So fear Allah and obey me.
interpretation: This phrase is repeated by several prophets (Noah, Hud, Salih, Lot, Shu'ayb) in Surah Ash-Shu'ara as they call their peoples to monotheism. It encapsulates the core message of prophethood: reverence for God (taqwa) coupled with obedience to His messenger, since the messenger's guidance is itself a means of fulfilling one's duty to God. The pairing suggests that true piety is not merely internal fear or belief but must manifest in practical submission to divine guidance as conveyed through the prophet. It also underscores the prophets' role as trustworthy conduits of revelation, asking not for personal allegiance but for alignment with God's will, distinguishing their call from self-serving leadership.

translation: And I do not ask you for any payment for it. My payment is only from the Lord of the worlds.
interpretation: This verse is spoken by prophets who remind their people that their call to worship God alone is sincere and free of worldly motive. By declaring that their reward rests solely with God, the Lord of the worlds, the prophets establish a crucial criterion for discerning true guidance: it is not tied to personal gain, wealth, or power over others. This disassociation from material reward serves to validate the purity of the message, inviting the audience to evaluate the call on its own merits rather than suspecting ulterior motives. It also reflects a broader theological principle—that true service to God transcends transactional relationships with people, and that ultimate recompense and accountability belong to God alone, who sustains and nurtures all of creation.

translation: Will you be left secure in that which is here?
interpretation: This verse is part of Prophet Hud's rhetorical questioning to his people, the 'Aad, who had been granted great blessings—gardens, flowing springs, crops, and tall palm trees—yet lived in heedless complacency and arrogance. The question challenges their false sense of permanence and security, implying that earthly comfort and prosperity are not guarantees of continued safety or divine favor. It serves as a warning that worldly ease can be deceptive, lulling people into forgetting their moral and spiritual obligations, and that such security is contingent upon gratitude and righteousness rather than being an unconditional, eternal state. The rhetorical nature of the question invites the listener to recognize the folly of assuming that present comfort will last indefinitely without regard to accountability before God.

translation: In gardens and springs.
interpretation: This verse is part of a Qur'anic description of the reward awaiting the righteous (al-muttaqin) in Paradise, often found in contexts like Surah Al-Hijr or Adh-Dhariyat. The mention of 'gardens and springs' evokes an image of lush, flourishing abundance and ease—a stark contrast to the arid, desert landscape familiar to the original audience. Gardens symbolize beauty, growth, shade, and permanence, while springs represent purity, life-giving sustenance, and continuous flow (unlike stagnant or seasonal water sources). Together, they signify a state of everlasting comfort, spiritual and physical satisfaction, and divine generosity granted to those who lived with piety and self-restraint in the worldly life. This imagery is meant to inspire hope and motivate believers toward righteousness by illustrating the tangible, sensory joys of the Hereafter as a reward for faith and good deeds.

translation: And crops and palm trees with tender, delicate spathes.
interpretation: This verse is part of a passage (Qur'an 26:146-149) in which Allah, through the Prophet Salih, reminds the people of Thamud of the abundant blessings they enjoyed—gardens, springs, fertile fields, and palm trees bearing soft, delicate fruit clusters. The mention of such agricultural prosperity serves a rhetorical purpose: it underscores the ingratitude of a people who, despite being settled securely and given a fertile land with comfort and ease, denied their prophet and rejected the call to worship God alone. The imagery of lush crops and tender date-palm shoots evokes a sense of security, abundance, and ease of life, which makes their subsequent arrogance and defiance (and their demand for a miraculous she-camel as proof, which they later killed) all the more striking. The verse thus functions as part of a larger argument about divine favor, human responsibility, and the consequences of rejecting guidance despite having been given means and comfort to recognize and appreciate the Creator's benevolence. The destruction that befalls Thamud in the following verses becomes a lesson in how prosperity and ease, if not met with gratitude and righteousness, lead to ruin.

translation: And you carve out of the mountains, homes, with great skill.
interpretation: This verse addresses the people of Thamud, the nation of Prophet Salih, who were renowned for their architectural prowess, carving elaborate dwellings directly into the rock faces of mountains. This was mentioned as evidence of their worldly skill, strength, and the material prosperity they had achieved. However, this skill and craftsmanship, while impressive, is cited in the broader context of the surah as an example of a people who became arrogant due to their achievements and power, believing themselves secure and self-sufficient. Despite their technical mastery and the apparent permanence of their stone-carved homes, they are being reminded that such worldly accomplishments do not grant exemption from divine accountability or protect against God's judgment when a people turn to corruption and reject the guidance sent to them. The verse serves as a reminder that human ingenuity and material success, however impressive, are insufficient substitutes for righteousness and heedfulness toward the Creator.

translation: So fear Allah and obey me.
interpretation: This phrase is a recurring refrain in Surah Ash-Shu'ara, uttered by several prophets—Nuh, Hud, Salih, Lut, and Shu'ayb—as they call their respective peoples to monotheism and righteousness. The repetition underscores a unified prophetic message across different eras and nations: true piety (taqwa) toward God must be paired with obedience to His chosen messenger, since the prophet's guidance is the practical means by which reverence for God is expressed. By linking fear of God with obedience to the prophet, the verse establishes that sincere faith is not merely an inner sentiment but must manifest in following divine guidance as conveyed through revelation. The use of this identical phrase by multiple prophets also serves a rhetorical purpose in the Qur'an, reinforcing to the Meccan audience that Muhammad's call was not novel but part of a continuous chain of prophetic missions facing similar resistance, and that rejection of any prophet's message follows the same pattern of denial and consequent destruction for earlier disbelieving nations.

translation: And do not obey the command of the transgressors (those who exceed all bounds).
interpretation: This verse is part of the Prophet Saleh's warning to his people, the Thamud, urging them to reject the authority of their arrogant leaders who were leading them toward corruption and disbelief. It establishes a broader principle in Islamic thought: obedience to authority is not absolute but conditional upon that authority being just and righteous. When those in power exceed legitimate bounds—whether through tyranny, moral corruption, or leading people away from truth—followers bear responsibility to withhold obedience rather than comply blindly. The verse thus places moral accountability on individuals, rejecting the excuse of merely following orders or societal leaders when those leaders promote transgression (israf, meaning excess or going beyond proper limits). It reflects a recurring Qur'anic theme where prophets challenge entrenched power structures that perpetuate injustice, calling instead for discernment and courage to resist harmful authority even when it holds social or political dominance.

translation: Those who spread corruption in the land and do not set things right.
interpretation: This verse, drawn from the account of the Prophet Salih's warning to his people, describes the ruling elite and transgressors whose influence leads only to corruption, injustice, and moral decay rather than reform or benefit. It serves as a caution against following those in positions of power or influence whose actions disrupt social, moral, or spiritual order without ever contributing constructively to society. The phrase underscores a key Qur'anic theme: that true leadership and righteousness are measured not merely by status or authority, but by whether one's actions result in positive reform ('islah') or destructive corruption ('fasad'). Those who only corrupt and never correct represent a moral failure condemned throughout the Qur'an, as opposed to the prophets and righteous believers who strive to reform and improve the state of the earth and human affairs.

translation: They said, "You are only one of the bewitched."
interpretation: This verse records the response of the people of Thamud to their prophet Salih when he called them to worship God alone and warned them against their idolatry. Rather than engaging with his message, they dismissed him by claiming he was merely one who had been bewitched or placed under a magical spell, implying his mind had been affected and his words carried no real authority or divine origin. This accusation reflects a common pattern in the Qur'an where prophets are mocked and their sanity questioned as a way for disbelieving communities to avoid confronting the truth of the message. It demonstrates the arrogance and willful rejection of these people, who preferred baseless accusations over honest consideration of the signs presented to them, ultimately leading to their destruction as recounted in the subsequent verses.

translation: You are but a human being like ourselves, so bring us a sign, if you are among the truthful.
interpretation: This verse records the demand of a disbelieving people to their prophet (traditionally understood as Salih's people, the Thamud), who reject his message on the grounds that he shares their human nature and therefore cannot possess any special status or divine commission. Their reasoning reflects a common pattern of prophetic rejection throughout the Qur'an: disbelievers often argue that if a messenger eats, sleeps, and walks in the markets like other men, he cannot be a genuine vehicle of revelation, expecting instead that a true messenger would be an angel or superhuman being. By demanding a miraculous sign as proof, they set a condition for belief that reveals their skepticism is less about honest inquiry and more about resistance to accountability—once such signs are given, as with the she-camel sent to Salih's people, many such communities still refuse to believe, bringing upon themselves divine punishment. The verse thus illustrates the recurring theme that outward human resemblance between prophet and people is not a valid objection to prophethood, since the message's truth lies in its content and moral demand, not in the messenger's biological nature.

translation: He said, 'This is a she-camel. She has a right to drink, and you have a right to drink, on a known day.'
interpretation: This verse records the words of the Prophet Salih to the tribe of Thamud regarding the miraculous she-camel that God brought forth from the rock as a sign to them. Salih establishes a divinely ordained arrangement of shared resources: the she-camel would have her allotted day to drink from the communal water source, and the people would have their own separate allotted day. This was a test of their obedience and patience, requiring them to respect the sign of God and not to harm the she-camel or deny her the water on her appointed day. The arrangement also symbolizes a broader principle of equitable sharing and the sanctity of divine signs—violating this order, as the Thamud later did by killing the she-camel, became the direct cause of their destruction, illustrating the severe consequences of rejecting God's commands and signs even when given clear and reasonable terms.

translation: And do not touch her with harm, lest there seize you the punishment of a terrible day.
interpretation: This verse is part of the narrative of the Prophet Salih and his people, the Thamud, concerning the she-camel that God sent as a miraculous sign to them. Salih warned his people not to harm this camel, which was granted a share of their water and pasture, as a test of their faith and obedience. The warning here emphasizes that any transgression against this divine sign—an act of defiance against God's command—would bring immediate and severe consequences, specifically a catastrophic punishment on a 'great day.' This serves as a broader lesson about the seriousness of violating divine commandments, especially those tied to visible signs of God's power and mercy. It also reflects a recurring Qur'anic theme: that communities who reject or harm the signs sent to guide them face inevitable divine retribution, underscoring the themes of accountability, the consequences of disbelief, and the mercy-turned-wrath of God when His signs are disregarded.

translation: But they hamstrung her [the she-camel], and so they became regretful.
interpretation: This verse refers to the story of Prophet Salih and the people of Thamud, who were given a she-camel as a miraculous sign from Allah. Despite being warned not to harm her, they defied the command and killed her by hamstringing her legs. Their regret came too late—after committing the transgression, they realized the gravity of their sin, but remorse without timely repentance could not avert the consequences. This illustrates a recurring Qur'anic theme: human beings often recognize their wrongdoing only after acting upon arrogance, impulsiveness, or collective pressure, by which point the opportunity for correction has passed. Shortly after this act, the Thamud were struck with a devastating punishment, demonstrating that defying divine signs and covenants leads to irreversible consequences despite subsequent feelings of regret. The verse serves as a warning about the dangers of succumbing to collective wrongdoing and the importance of restraining oneself before transgressing rather than lamenting afterward when it is already too late to change the outcome.

translation: So the punishment seized them. Indeed in that is a sign, but most of them were not believers.
interpretation: This verse is a recurring refrain found throughout Surah Ash-Shu'ara, appearing after the Qur'an narrates the stories of various prophets—including Noah, Hud, Salih, Lot, and Shu'ayb—and the destruction that befell their disbelieving peoples. The phrase serves as a structural and theological punctuation mark, closing each prophetic narrative with the same conclusion: divine punishment inevitably came upon those who rejected their messengers despite clear warnings and evidence. The declaration that 'in that is a sign' (ayah) points to these historical destructions as lessons or proofs for later generations, including the Prophet Muhammad's contemporaries, who are being implicitly warned by comparison. The final clause, 'but most of them were not believers,' delivers a sobering commentary on human nature—suggesting that even in the face of undeniable signs and the certainty of consequences, the majority of people throughout history have chosen disbelief over faith. This repetition across multiple prophetic stories reinforces the Qur'anic theme that rejection of truth is a persistent pattern in human societies, not limited to one people or one era, and that the consistency of this pattern itself constitutes evidence for those willing to reflect upon it.

translation: And indeed, your Lord - He is the Exalted in Might, the Merciful.
interpretation: This verse, repeated as a refrain throughout Surah Ash-Shu'ara after recounting the stories of various prophets and their peoples, serves as a theological anchor that balances two seemingly opposing divine attributes: power (al-'Aziz) and mercy (ar-Rahim). Each time a nation rejects its prophet and faces consequences—whether destruction or deliverance of the believers—this phrase reminds the listener that God's might is never divorced from His compassion, and His mercy is never a sign of weakness. The repetition reinforces that divine justice operates within a framework of mercy, meaning that punishment is never arbitrary or purely punitive but is tempered with purpose, giving people chances to repent before any reckoning. For the believers, this serves as reassurance that the same God who holds ultimate power over all creation is also inherently compassionate, making His might something to be trusted rather than merely feared.

translation: The people of Lot denied the messengers.
interpretation: This verse refers to the people of Lot (Sodom and Gomorrah) who rejected Prophet Lot (Lut), peace be upon him. Although only one messenger, Lot, was sent to them, the verse uses the plural 'messengers' because denying one prophet is equated with denying all prophets, since they all came with the same fundamental message of monotheism and righteous conduct. This reflects a broader Qur'anic principle that the message of all prophets is unified in essence, so rejecting any single messenger is tantamount to rejecting the entire chain of prophethood. The verse sets up the narrative of the moral corruption of Lot's people, particularly their infamous practice of same-sex relations among men, which the Qur'an presents as a transgression against natural order, and their subsequent destruction serves as a warning sign for later generations about the consequences of persistent disbelief and moral transgression despite clear warning from a messenger of God.

translation: When their brother Lot said to them, 'Will you not fear Allah (be mindful of Him)?'
interpretation: This verse introduces the prophet Lot's address to his people, referring to him as 'their brother' not in a tribal or familial sense of shared belief, but in the sense of common lineage and kinship—he was one of them, from their own community, which underscores that he came to them not as a stranger but as someone deeply familiar with them, making his warning more intimate and harder to dismiss. The rhetorical question 'Will you not fear Allah?' is a call to conscience, urging them to awaken to their moral and spiritual responsibility before engaging in the sinful practices for which they became infamous. This opening mirrors a recurring pattern in the Qur'an where various prophets (Noah, Hud, Salih, Lot, Shu'ayb) are introduced with nearly identical phrasing to their respective peoples, emphasizing that the message of monotheism and righteousness is universal and consistent across all prophetic missions, and that each community's rejection of its prophet follows a similar trajectory of disbelief despite having a credible, familiar messenger from among themselves.

translation: Indeed, I am to you a trustworthy messenger.
interpretation: This verse is part of the recurring narrative structure in Surah Ash-Shu'ara where various prophets—here Noah—address their disbelieving people. By emphasizing 'trustworthy' (amin), the prophet establishes his moral credibility before delivering his call to monotheism, reminding his people of his known reputation for honesty among them. This establishes that the message itself should be judged on its own merit, since the messenger has no history of deception, and that rejecting him cannot be justified by claiming he is untrustworthy or seeking personal gain, as he goes on to clarify he asks for no reward for his guidance.

translation: So fear Allah and obey me.
interpretation: This phrase is a recurring refrain in Surah Ash-Shu'ara, uttered by several prophets—including Nuh, Hud, Salih, Lut, and Shu'ayb—as they call their respective peoples to monotheism and righteousness. The pairing of 'fear Allah' (taqwa) with 'obey me' establishes the prophetic authority as derived directly from and in service to God's authority; obedience to the messenger is not independent of piety toward God but is its natural extension, since the messenger conveys divine guidance. The repetition across different prophets and nations underscores a central Qur'anic theme: that the core message of all prophets throughout history has been identical—consciousness of God coupled with heeding His chosen messengers—and that rejection of this message, despite its consistency, is what leads nations to destruction, as the surah goes on to illustrate through the fates of these peoples.

translation: And I do not ask you for any payment for it (the message); my reward is only from the Lord of the Worlds.
interpretation: This verse, repeated by several prophets throughout the Qur'an (including Noah, Hud, Salih, Lot, and Shu'ayb), establishes a foundational principle of prophetic sincerity: the messengers sought no worldly compensation, wealth, status, or benefit from those they called to guidance. By disclaiming any desire for payment from their people, the prophets demonstrate that their motivation is purely for the sake of God and the wellbeing of humanity, not self-interest. This serves as powerful evidence of their truthfulness, since a false claimant to prophethood would typically seek personal gain, power, or material advantage. The verse also redirects the locus of reward away from human transactions entirely to divine recompense, teaching believers that true sincerity in any righteous endeavor, especially in conveying truth or doing good, should be oriented toward seeking reward from God alone rather than from people. This principle has broader implications for how one should approach acts of guidance, teaching, and charity, emphasizing purity of intention and freedom from seeking worldly return for spiritual or moral service.

translation: Do you approach males among the worlds [i.e., among all creatures]?
interpretation: This verse is part of the narrative of Prophet Lut (Lot) addressing his people, who were engaging in sexual relations with other men instead of their wives. The rhetorical question emphasizes the unprecedented and unnatural nature of this behavior by noting that of all the creatures in existence ('the worlds'), his people were uniquely engaging in this practice, having abandoned the natural order of male-female relations established for procreation and family.
