interpretation: This verse, part of the narrative of Moses and the miracles given to him, offers a universal principle of divine mercy: that God's forgiveness is available even to one who has committed wrongdoing, provided they genuinely repent and replace their evil deeds with righteous ones. It establishes that the door to redemption remains open regardless of past transgressions, emphasizing that sincere transformation - not permanent condemnation - is the measure by which God judges human beings. The verse underscores that divine mercy surpasses divine wrath, and that change of heart and conduct can overwrite a history of sin.

translation: And insert your hand into the opening of your garment, it will come out white (radiant) without any disease or blemish - [one] among nine signs to Pharaoh and his people. Indeed, they have been a defiantly disobedient people.
interpretation: This verse refers to one of the miraculous signs given to Prophet Musa (Moses) as part of a set of nine signs sent to confront Pharaoh and his people. The hand turning radiantly white without blemish symbolizes a divine miracle meant to demonstrate God's power beyond natural explanation, serving as evidence of Musa's prophethood. The nine signs collectively represent comprehensive proof against Pharaoh's tyranny and disbelief. The verse concludes by characterizing Pharaoh's people as 'fasiqeen' (defiantly disobedient/transgressors), establishing that despite clear miraculous evidence, their moral corruption and arrogance led them to reject divine guidance. This illustrates a recurring Quranic theme where even overwhelming miraculous evidence fails to guide those whose hearts are hardened by pride and habitual wrongdoing, emphasizing that guidance ultimately depends on one's sincere disposition toward truth rather than merely witnessing miracles.

translation: But when Our signs came to them, plainly visible, they said, 'This is clear magic.'
interpretation: This verse illustrates a recurring pattern in the Qur'anic narrative wherein a people are presented with unmistakable, illuminating signs from God—miraculous proofs meant to guide them toward truth—yet instead of reflecting upon them with open hearts, they dismiss them as mere sorcery. The phrase 'mubsirah' (clear, giving insight) emphasizes that the signs were not ambiguous or open to honest doubt; their truth was self-evident. The rejection, therefore, is not attributed to a lack of clarity in the message but to the arrogance, stubbornness, and vested interests of those who received it. By labeling divine truth as 'sihr mubin' (clear magic), they attempt to discredit what they cannot rationally refute, revealing a psychological defense mechanism common to disbelief: when confronted with undeniable truth that threatens one's worldview or power structure, it is easier to attack the messenger or the sign itself than to change one's convictions. This verse thus serves as a warning about human tendency toward willful denial even in the face of overwhelming evidence, and about how pride and self-interest can blind individuals to truths that are otherwise 'mubsirah'—plain for all to see.

translation: And they denied them, while their souls were convinced thereof, out of injustice and arrogance. So see how was the end of the corrupters.
interpretation: This verse refers to Pharaoh and his people in their rejection of the signs brought by Moses. Despite the clarity of these signs—miracles that left no doubt in their hearts about their divine origin—they chose to reject them outwardly due to pride, arrogance, and a refusal to submit to truth that would require them to relinquish their power and privilege. This illustrates a profound psychological and moral phenomenon: conscious denial of truth despite inner certainty, driven by injustice (zulm) and haughtiness ('uluw). The verse highlights that disbelief is not always due to lack of evidence or genuine doubt, but can stem from willful arrogance and the refusal to accept truths that threaten one's status or worldview. The concluding rhetorical question—inviting reflection on the fate of the corrupters—serves as a warning: those who knowingly reject truth out of arrogance and work corruption in the land will ultimately face destruction, as Pharaoh and his people did when they were drowned. It underscores the Qur'anic theme that worldly power and willful denial of truth lead only to ruin, while it affirms that truth remains internally undeniable even to those who reject it outwardly.

translation: And We had certainly given knowledge to David and Solomon, and they said, 'Praise be to Allah, who has favored us over many of His believing servants.'
interpretation: This verse highlights that true knowledge is a divine gift leading to humility and gratitude rather than arrogance. Despite their elevated status as prophets and kings, David and Solomon immediately attribute their favor to Allah, acknowledging that all distinction comes from Him alone. Their response models the proper attitude toward blessings: recognizing that knowledge and power are entrusted gifts meant to be met with praise and thankfulness, not pride. The verse also subtly affirms that being favored above others does not diminish the value or faith of those others—it is simply a reflection of Allah's wisdom in distributing His gifts among His believing servants.

translation: And Solomon inherited from David, and he said, 'O people, we have been taught the speech of birds, and we have been given from everything. Indeed, this is evident bounty.'
interpretation: This verse establishes Solomon as David's successor not merely in political kingship but in prophethood and divine knowledge, emphasizing a continuity of guidance rather than mere dynastic succession. Solomon's announcement of being taught the language of birds symbolizes an extraordinary dimension of knowledge granted to him, one that transcends ordinary human understanding and extends dominion over the natural world, including creatures often seen as insignificant. His declaration that 'we have been given from everything' reflects the vast scope of resources, wisdom, and power bestowed upon him, encompassing wealth, authority, and supernatural abilities alike. Crucially, Solomon attributes all of this to divine favor rather than personal merit, framing his accomplishments and gifts as 'manifest bounty' from God. This serves as a model of gratitude and humility in the face of immense privilege, reminding believers that true achievement and knowledge originate from God's grace, and that acknowledging this bounty openly is itself an act of piety rather than boastfulness, since the praise is directed toward the Giver rather than the self.

translation: And gathered for Solomon were his hosts of jinn, men, and birds, and they were marshaled in ranks.
interpretation: This verse highlights the extraordinary dominion granted to Prophet Solomon (Sulayman), whose authority extended beyond the human realm to encompass jinn and birds, creatures of entirely different natures and realms of existence. The mention that these diverse forces were 'marshaled' or organized in disciplined ranks (yuza'un) emphasizes not merely the scope of his power but its orderly, administrative quality—suggesting that true dominion requires not just command over diverse beings but the wisdom to organize them effectively. This serves as a sign of God's favor and the special prophetic gifts bestowed upon Solomon, while also illustrating a kingdom of unparalleled scale and harmony, where different orders of creation work together under righteous leadership. It underscores the Quranic theme that worldly power, when granted by God, can serve as a platform for demonstrating divine wisdom and justice.

translation: Until, when they came upon the Valley of the Ants, an ant said: 'O ants! Enter your dwellings, lest Solomon and his hosts crush you while they perceive not.'
interpretation: This verse, part of the narrative of Prophet Solomon (Sulayman), illustrates several key themes. It demonstrates the miraculous gift granted to Solomon by God: the ability to understand the speech of animals and other creatures, a sign of his unique prophethood and the vastness of divine knowledge that extends to all of creation, even the smallest of beings like an ant. The ant's warning to its colony reveals an awareness and social order within the animal kingdom, suggesting that all creatures possess their own forms of communication, community, and instinct for self-preservation, which are part of God's grand design. Furthermore, the verse implicitly praises Solomon's justice and the way his army moved with such discipline that even a tiny ant recognized they would not intentionally cause harm, but could do so unknowingly due to their sheer scale and power. This highlights the responsibility of the powerful to be mindful of the smaller, more vulnerable beings in their path, even if unaware of their presence. It also serves as a reminder of human and animal coexistence, and the idea that every creature, no matter how small, has its own world of experience, communication, and value in the eyes of God, deserving of consideration and protection.

translation: So he [Solomon] smiled, amused at her speech, and said, 'My Lord, enable me to be grateful for Your favor which You have bestowed upon me and upon my parents, and to do righteousness of which You approve, and admit me by Your mercy among Your righteous servants.'
interpretation: This verse captures a pivotal moment of humility and spiritual awareness in Solomon's character, despite his immense worldly power—command over jinn, humans, winds, and even the ability to understand the speech of animals. Rather than reacting with pride or indifference upon overhearing the ant warning her colony about his army, Solomon smiles with genuine delight and immediately turns to God in prayer. This reaction reveals that true greatness lies not in the possession of extraordinary gifts but in one's response to them. Solomon's prayer models the proper etiquette of gratitude: he does not take credit for his abilities but acknowledges them as divine favor ('ni'mataka'), extending this gratitude to include blessings upon his parents, recognizing that his lineage and upbringing were also gifts from God. His request to 'do righteousness that You approve' shows an understanding that good deeds must align with divine will rather than human judgment of what seems righteous. Finally, his plea to be admitted 'by Your mercy' among the righteous servants—rather than by his own merit, power, or accomplishments—demonstrates profound theological insight: even a prophet-king endowed with miraculous abilities recognizes that salvation and righteousness are ultimately gifts of divine mercy, not achievements earned through status or power. The humble ant, in her wisdom and concern for her community, becomes an unlikely teacher, prompting one of the most powerful figures in human history to a moment of genuine spiritual reflection.

translation: And he [Solomon] inspected the birds and said, 'Why do I not see the hoopoe, or is he among the absent?'
interpretation: This verse illustrates Prophet Solomon's meticulous and just leadership, demonstrating that even in his vast kingdom over jinn, humans, winds, and birds, he paid careful attention to every member of his dominion, noticing the absence of even a small bird like the hoopoe. This reflects the Quranic theme that true authority and wisdom involve accountability and vigilance over those under one's care, no matter how seemingly insignificant. It also sets up the narrative that follows, where the hoopoe's absence turns out to be purposeful—he had been scouting the land and returns with important news about the Queen of Sheba, showing how Allah can bring benefit through unexpected means and that no creature's role, however small, is without divine significance in the unfolding of events.

translation: I will surely punish him with a severe punishment, or slaughter him, or he must bring me a clear authority (a valid reason/proof).
interpretation: This verse is part of the story of Prophet Sulayman (Solomon) and the hoopoe bird (Surah An-Naml, 27:21), found within the narrative of Sulayman reviewing his army of birds and discovering the hoopoe absent. The verse reflects the stern warning Sulayman issues upon noticing the hoopoe's absence from the ranks without prior permission. It illustrates the strict discipline and accountability Sulayman, as a just ruler endowed with authority over creatures including birds and jinn, demanded from those under his command. The threefold ultimatum—severe punishment, death, or a compelling justification—underscores the gravity of unauthorized absence in matters of duty and leadership, while also setting up the narrative tension that leads to the hoopoe's significant report about the Queen of Sheba (Bilqis) and her kingdom. The verse demonstrates that even in a position of power, accountability was expected, and a reasonable explanation could avert punishment, foreshadowing the hoopoe's valid and consequential excuse that follows this threat, which ultimately leads to one of the more significant episodes in Sulayman's prophetic mission—the correspondence with and eventual guidance of Bilqis toward monotheism.

translation: But he [the hoopoe] stayed not long and said, 'I have encompassed [in knowledge] that which you have not encompassed, and I have come to you from Sheba with certain news.'
interpretation: This verse recounts the moment when the hoopoe bird, having been absent from Solomon's assembly, returns and boldly addresses the prophet-king. The hoopoe's declaration is remarkable for its audacity—a small bird claiming to possess knowledge that the great prophet Solomon, who could command jinn, humans, and understand the speech of birds, did not have. This illustrates a profound Qur'anic theme: that knowledge and wisdom are not necessarily correlated with worldly power or status, and that Allah may grant insight to the humblest of creatures that even the mightiest lack. The hoopoe's confidence also stems from its special role as a scout with knowledge of hidden water sources, a skill unique to it. The phrase 'naba'in yaqeen' (certain/definite news) emphasizes that the bird is not bringing mere rumor or speculation, but verified intelligence about the kingdom of Sheba, setting up the subsequent narrative about Queen Bilqis and her people's sun-worship. This moment teaches humility—even Solomon, given extraordinary gifts, listens to and verifies the report of a bird rather than dismissing it, demonstrating the Islamic value of seeking truth from any source, regardless of how insignificant that source may appear in worldly terms.

translation: Indeed, I found a woman ruling over them, and she has been given of all things, and she has a great throne.
interpretation: This verse is spoken by the hoopoe bird to Prophet Sulaiman (Solomon) upon returning from its journey to the land of Saba' (Sheba). The hoopoe reports discovering a prosperous kingdom ruled by a woman—identified in the tradition as Bilqis, the Queen of Sheba—who possesses great wealth, resources, and authority, symbolized by her magnificent throne. The phrase 'given of all things' indicates the extent of her worldly power and the completeness of her kingdom's resources, setting up the narrative that follows regarding her eventual encounter with Sulaiman and her conversion to the worship of the one true God. The verse also subtly highlights a theme found throughout the Qur'an: that worldly power and splendor, no matter how great, are ultimately subordinate to divine guidance and truth, as the subsequent verses reveal that she and her people worship the sun instead of Allah, which becomes the central issue Sulaiman seeks to correct.

translation: I found her and her people prostrating to the sun instead of Allah, and Satan had made their deeds seem pleasing to them, and so turned them away from the path, so they are not guided.
interpretation: This verse, spoken by the hoopoe to Prophet Sulayman regarding the Queen of Sheba and her people, illustrates how misguided worship arises not merely from ignorance but from the active deception of Satan, who beautifies falsehood and sin in the eyes of people so that they perceive their wrongdoing as right and good. The verse highlights a key Quranic theme: deviation from truth is often not due to a lack of intelligence or capability (the Queen was clearly a competent ruler), but due to the psychological and spiritual manipulation that makes falsehood attractive and obscures the path to truth. This serves as a warning that people can be sincerely devoted and diligent in their practices while being entirely misguided, if the object of their devotion is not rightly placed, emphasizing the necessity of divine guidance over human custom or inherited tradition in determining the proper object of worship.

translation: [Satan prevented them from the right path] so that they would not prostrate to Allah, who brings forth what is hidden in the heavens and the earth, and who knows what you conceal and what you proclaim.
interpretation: This verse comes from the account of the hoopoe bird reporting to Prophet Sulayman about the people of Sheba, who worshipped the sun instead of Allah. The verse explains that Satan had adorned their misguided deeds, diverting them from true worship. It contrasts the limited, visible sun—an object of their worship—with Allah, who possesses absolute and hidden knowledge, bringing forth rain, vegetation, treasures, and all that is concealed within the heavens and earth. The rhetorical question underscores the irrationality of prostrating to a created, finite being like the sun while ignoring the Creator who knows both the hidden and the manifest, including the innermost secrets of human hearts and their outward actions. It serves as a call to recognize Allah's all-encompassing knowledge and power as the sole rightful object of worship, exposing the folly of idolatry and the external deception of Satan who makes such falsehoods appear appealing.

translation: Allah - there is no deity except Him, Lord of the Great Throne.
interpretation: This verse is part of the hoopoe bird's speech to Prophet Sulayman (Solomon) in Surah An-Naml, recounting what it discovered about the people of Sheba who worshipped the sun instead of Allah. The hoopoe declares this fundamental truth of tawhid (the oneness of Allah) to contrast with the misguided worship it witnessed. The verse establishes two core theological principles: first, the absolute uniqueness and exclusivity of Allah as the only true deity worthy of worship, rejecting all forms of polytheism; second, Allah's sovereignty as Lord of the 'Great Throne' ('Arsh al-'Azim), symbolizing His supreme authority and dominion over all of creation. The Throne in Islamic theology represents the pinnacle of Allah's kingdom, signifying that His power and control extend over everything that exists, including the sun that the Sabaeans mistakenly worshipped. This declaration serves as a powerful theological rebuke to sun-worship and any form of associating partners with Allah, emphasizing that true sovereignty belongs to Allah alone, who governs the entire cosmos from His magnificent Throne, far above any created object or being that might be mistakenly venerated.

translation: He [Solomon] said: 'We shall see whether you have spoken the truth or whether you are of the liars.'
interpretation: This verse captures Prophet Sulaiman's (Solomon's) measured and just response upon receiving an extraordinary report from the hoopoe bird, which had been absent and then returned with news of the Queen of Sheba and her people's sun-worship. Rather than reacting with immediate credulity or punishing the bird for its unauthorized absence, Sulaiman demonstrates the principle of verification before action—a model of prudent governance and leadership. His response reflects a broader Qur'anic value: that claims, even from seemingly reliable sources, should be tested against evidence rather than accepted or dismissed on first hearing. This moment also underscores Sulaiman's authority and composure; as a prophet-king endowed with the ability to understand the speech of birds and command vast resources, he still subjects information to scrutiny, modeling accountability at every level of his kingdom. The verse sets the stage for the dispatching of a letter to the Queen of Sheba, testing the hoopoe's claim through concrete action, which becomes the mechanism by which truth is established and the subsequent narrative of diplomacy, power, and eventual submission to the one true God unfolds.

translation: Go with this letter of mine and deliver it to them, then withdraw from them and see what response they return.
interpretation: This verse occurs in the story of Prophet Sulayman (Solomon) and the Queen of Sheba (Bilqis), recounted in Surah An-Naml. Sulayman, having learned of the Queen's people worshipping the sun instead of God through the report of the hoopoe bird, composes a letter calling her and her people to monotheism and submission to God. He instructs the hoopoe to deliver this letter and then to withdraw and observe their reaction. This episode illustrates several important themes: the use of wisdom and measured diplomacy in calling others to truth rather than immediate confrontation; the importance of allowing people the space to deliberate and respond freely to a message rather than being pressured in the moment; and the acknowledgment that true guidance requires an internal response from the hearts of those being called, not mere compliance under duress. The directive to 'withdraw and see what they return' demonstrates a method of patient observation, testing the sincerity and nature of a response before proceeding further, a principle of prudent engagement applicable broadly to how messages of truth should be conveyed and received.

translation: She said, 'O chiefs, indeed a noble letter has been delivered to me.'
interpretation: This verse refers to the Queen of Sheba (Bilqis) addressing her council of nobles after receiving a letter from Prophet Solomon (Sulayman). She describes the letter as 'karim' (noble/honorable), indicating her recognition of its significance even before revealing its contents, likely due to its respectful tone, the authority of its sender, and perhaps the manner in which it was delivered (by a hoopoe bird, as the narrative explains). This moment marks the beginning of a diplomatic exchange that ultimately leads to her acknowledgment of Solomon's God and her submission to monotheism. The verse illustrates themes of leadership, consultation (shura) with advisors before making important decisions, and the power of respectful communication in resolving conflicts between nations or rulers.

translation: Indeed, it is from Solomon, and indeed, it reads: 'In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.'
interpretation: This verse quotes the opening lines of a letter sent by the Prophet Solomon (Sulayman) to Bilqis, the Queen of Sheba, as narrated in Surah An-Naml. A hoopoe bird had informed Solomon about a kingdom ruled by a woman whose people worshipped the sun instead of God, prompting Solomon to send this letter. The verse is significant for establishing the formula 'Bismillah ir-Rahman ir-Raheem' as a proper opening for formal correspondence, a practice that Solomon employs here even as a prophet-king addressing a foreign ruler. This demonstrates that invoking God's name at the beginning of important undertakings was a practice established among earlier prophets, not unique to the Qur'an itself, and it models the proper etiquette of beginning significant communications by acknowledging divine authority and mercy before addressing worldly matters. The brevity and directness of the letter's opening also reflects Solomon's confidence and authority, as he identifies himself simply by name before invoking God, showing that true power is exercised with humility before the Divine.

translation: [Saying], 'Be not haughty with me, but come to me in submission [as Muslims].'
interpretation: This verse is part of the letter sent by Prophet Sulayman (Solomon) to the Queen of Sheba (Bilqis), as recounted in Surah An-Naml. The message combines firm authority with an invitation to peaceful submission to the truth of monotheism. Sulayman, granted immense power over jinn, birds, and the wind, does not resort to threats of violence but instead calls the Queen and her people to recognize the authority of God and to come willingly in submission rather than through arrogance or defiance. The phrase 'alla ta'lu alayya' (do not exalt yourselves above me) warns against pride and resistance to truth, while 'wa'tuni muslimeen' (come to me in submission) emphasizes that the ultimate goal is not political submission to Sulayman himself, but spiritual submission to God, with Sulayman acting as His messenger and representative of divine guidance. This reflects a broader Quranic theme that true strength and wisdom lie in humility before God, and that worldly power, when guided by prophethood, is meant to invite others toward righteousness rather than to dominate through coercion.

translation: She said, 'O chiefs, advise me in this matter of mine; I would never decide a matter until you testify [are present with me].'
interpretation: This verse refers to the Queen of Sheba (Bilqis) addressing her council of nobles after receiving a letter from Prophet Solomon. It illustrates a model of consultative leadership (shura), showing that even a powerful monarch sought counsel from her advisors before making significant decisions rather than acting unilaterally. Her statement reflects wisdom, humility, and respect for collective deliberation, demonstrating that sound governance involves seeking input from others and not committing to important matters without the knowledge and presence of one's trusted council. This sets the stage for the narrative of her eventual recognition of Solomon's prophethood and her conversion, highlighting themes of wise leadership and openness to truth.

translation: They said, 'We are possessors of strength and possessors of great military might, but the command is yours, so look into what you will command.'
interpretation: This verse depicts the response of the chiefs and nobles of Sheba to their Queen (Bilqis) when she consulted them about the letter she received from Prophet Sulayman (Solomon). While they affirm their military capability and readiness for war, they notably defer the final decision to her authority, saying 'the command is yours.' This reflects a model of consultative leadership (shura) where advisors offer their counsel and resources but ultimately respect the sovereign's decision-making authority. It also sets up the contrast with the Queen's subsequent wisdom in verse 34, where she demonstrates superior judgment by cautioning against war and its destructive consequences, choosing instead a path of diplomacy. Her wisdom in restraining the martial impulse of her advisors, despite their stated strength, foreshadows her eventual peaceful submission to Sulayman's call to worship Allah alone, highlighting themes of prudent governance, the value of diplomacy over conflict, and feminine wisdom in leadership within the Qur'anic narrative.

translation: She said, 'Indeed, when kings enter a city, they ruin it and make the honored of its people humble. And thus do they do.'
interpretation: This verse is part of the Queen of Sheba's (Bilqis) deliberation with her counselors upon receiving a letter from Prophet Sulayman (Solomon). She demonstrates political wisdom and foresight by articulating a general principle about the nature of conquering kings: that military invasion and domination inevitably bring destruction and humiliation upon the conquered people, particularly their nobility and leadership. Her statement reflects her reluctance to provoke conflict and her preference for a diplomatic approach—she subsequently sends gifts to test Sulayman's intentions rather than risk war. This verse highlights her sagacity as a ruler, setting up the narrative contrast between worldly power politics and the prophetic authority of Sulayman, who seeks submission to God rather than mere political conquest or material wealth.

translation: And indeed, I will send to them a gift and see with what [reply] the messengers return.
interpretation: This verse captures the political wisdom and strategic caution of the Queen of Sheba (Bilqis) upon receiving Solomon's letter summoning her to submit to God. Rather than responding with immediate war or outright submission, she chooses a diplomatic test: sending gifts to gauge Solomon's true nature and intentions. In the customs of ancient diplomacy, how a king responds to a gift—whether with greed, acceptance as a peace offering, or rejection—would reveal whether he sought worldly power and wealth or something greater. Her shrewdness reflects a leader who understands that Solomon's demand could stem either from a worldly king seeking tribute and dominance, or from a prophet motivated by divine mission rejecting material bribery. This moment sets up the narrative contrast between worldly kingship and prophetic kingship, as Solomon will indeed reject the gift, demonstrating that his call is rooted in faith rather than material ambition, thereby compelling Bilqis to reconsider her own position and ultimately recognize the truth of his message and submit to God alongside him.

translation: So when [the messenger] came to Solomon, he said, 'Do you provide me with wealth? But what Allah has given me is better than what He has given you. Rather, it is you who rejoice in your gift.'
interpretation: This verse occurs in the story of Solomon and the Queen of Sheba (Bilqis), after she sent gifts to him in an attempt to avert conflict or test his intentions. Solomon's rejection of the material gift demonstrates that his authority and mission were rooted in prophethood and divine favor rather than worldly wealth or political appeasement. By stating that what Allah gave him was better than what she offered, he signals that his concern was not materialistic but was about guiding her and her people toward the truth of monotheism. The verse also contrasts spiritual wealth—knowledge, prophecy, and righteous kingship—with the transient value of material riches, suggesting that those who are truly favored by God find joy in divine gifts rather than worldly possessions. This moment also sets the stage for Bilqis's eventual recognition of Solomon's God-given wisdom and power, leading to her submission to the truth.

translation: Go back to them, for we will surely come to them with soldiers that they cannot resist, and we will surely drive them out from it, humiliated and disgraced.
interpretation: This verse is part of the narrative of Prophet Sulayman (Solomon) and the Queen of Sheba. After the Queen sent him a gift intended to placate or test him, Sulayman rejected the gift, recognizing it as an attempt to buy him off with worldly wealth rather than submit to the truth he was calling to. He sends her envoy back with this stern warning, demonstrating that his mission was not about material gain or worldly power but about the sovereignty of divine truth. The threat of overwhelming military force that cannot be resisted, followed by humiliation and disgrace, is not mere political posturing but underscores a central Qur'anic theme: that worldly power and wealth, such as what the Queen's kingdom possessed, mean nothing before the authority granted by God. Sulayman's confidence stems from his God-given dominion over both the seen and unseen (jinn, birds, wind), illustrating that true strength lies in submission to God rather than in material or military might. The verse also sets up the eventual peaceful resolution of the story, where the Queen of Sheba, confronted with undeniable signs of Sulayman's God-given authority, ultimately submits to the truth and acknowledges the One God, rather than the conflict escalating into actual warfare. This reflects a broader Qur'anic pattern where displays of power serve to invite reflection and submission rather than to glorify conquest itself.

translation: He [Solomon] said: 'O chiefs, which of you will bring me her throne before they come to me in submission?'
interpretation: This verse depicts Prophet Solomon (Sulayman) addressing his court—comprised of jinn, men, and other beings under his command—regarding the throne of the Queen of Sheba (Bilqis). Solomon seeks to have her throne brought to him before she and her delegation arrive to submit to him in peace (as Muslims, i.e., those who submit to God). This moment demonstrates Solomon's extraordinary God-given authority over supernatural forces and his strategic wisdom as a ruler. By requesting the throne beforehand, Solomon intends to present Bilqis with a sign of divine power so overwhelming that it will help guide her toward recognizing the truth of monotheism and the reality of God's might, preparing the way for her conversion. The episode underscores themes of divine favor bestowed upon prophets, the testing of faith through miraculous signs, and the use of worldly power in service of a higher spiritual purpose—to invite others to submission before God rather than mere political conquest.

translation: A powerful one from among the jinn said, 'I will bring it to you before you rise from your place, and indeed, I am for this task strong and trustworthy.'
interpretation: This verse occurs within the narrative of Prophet Solomon (Sulayman) and his request for someone in his court to bring him the throne of the Queen of Sheba before she and her delegation arrived. An ifrit, a powerful and formidable being from among the jinn whom Allah had subjected to Solomon's command, volunteered for this task, boasting of his strength and trustworthiness, and estimating that he could accomplish it within the short span of time before Solomon concluded his audience and rose from his seat. The passage illustrates the extraordinary powers granted to Solomon, who commanded not only humans and birds but also jinn, demonstrating the vastness of the kingdom and abilities Allah bestowed upon him as a sign of His favor and as a test of Solomon's gratitude. The ifrit's eagerness to prove his capability also reflects the hierarchical and competitive nature among the jinn serving Solomon, each seeking to demonstrate value and loyalty, while the subsequent verse reveals that an even more capable being, one with knowledge of the Scripture, accomplished the task in an instant, highlighting that true power lies not merely in physical strength but in knowledge and divine proximity.

translation: He who had knowledge of the Scripture said, 'I will bring it to you before your glance returns to you.' And when he [Solomon] saw it placed firmly before him, he said, 'This is from the favor of my Lord to test me, whether I will be grateful or ungrateful. And whoever is grateful, his gratitude is only for [the benefit of] himself. And whoever is ungrateful, then indeed my Lord is Self-Sufficient and Generous.'
interpretation: This verse, part of the story of Solomon and the Queen of Sheba's throne, illustrates that true power and knowledge are divine gifts, not personal achievements to boast about. The man with 'knowledge of the Scripture' performs a miraculous feat instantaneously, yet the focus shifts immediately to Solomon's humble response rather than to marveling at the power displayed. Solomon recognizes the event as a trial from God testing his character, not a reward for his status. This establishes a profound theological principle: every blessing, talent, or extraordinary ability a person possesses is fundamentally a test of their moral and spiritual response. Gratitude (shukr) is framed not as something that benefits God, who is described as 'Ghani' (Self-Sufficient, needing nothing) and 'Karim' (Generous, giving without needing return), but as something that benefits the grateful person themselves—it refines the soul, deepens consciousness of dependence on the Creator, and multiplies blessing. Conversely, ingratitude harms only the ungrateful individual, severing them from the recognition of grace and fostering spiritual arrogance. The verse thus universalizes Solomon's personal moment into a template for all believers: when faced with success, power, knowledge, or miracles, the proper response is not pride in one's own capability but humble acknowledgment that such gifts originate from divine favor, and gratitude becomes the measure of one's spiritual integrity rather than an obligation God requires for His own sake.

translation: He [Solomon] said, 'Disguise for her, her throne; we shall see whether she is rightly guided or is one of those who are not guided.'
interpretation: This verse reflects Solomon's wisdom in testing the Queen of Sheba's perception and discernment. By altering her throne's appearance after it was miraculously transported to his court, Solomon sought to assess not merely her ability to recognize a physical object, but her deeper capacity for insight and truth-seeking. The test symbolizes a broader theme in the Qur'an about distinguishing genuine guidance from assumption or pride. If she recognized the throne despite its alteration, it would demonstrate her sharp intellect and honesty in acknowledging truth even when it defies expectation—a quality linked to spiritual guidance itself. Her eventual correct, nuanced answer ('It is as though it were the same') shows discernment without false certainty, foreshadowing her readiness to accept monotheism and submit to the truth Solomon represents. The verse thus uses a test of worldly perception as a metaphor for the human capacity to recognize and accept divine truth when confronted with it, even when it appears transformed or unfamiliar.

translation: So when she arrived, it was said, 'Is your throne like this?' She said, 'It is as though it were it.' [Solomon said], 'And we were given knowledge before her, and we had submitted [to Allah].'
interpretation: This verse from Surat an-Naml recounts the moment the Queen of Sheba (Bilqis) arrives at Solomon's court and is confronted with her own throne, which had been miraculously transported there and altered in appearance. Her cautious, non-committal answer—'It is as though it were it'—reveals her discernment and intelligence; she neither denies nor rashly confirms the throne is hers, recognizing something uncanny about the test without being deceived by the alteration. This moment is a turning point in her story, demonstrating both her wisdom and her growing awareness of Solomon's extraordinary, divinely granted powers. The concluding remark, attributed to Solomon or inserted as a narratorial aside, shifts attention to the deeper theme of the passage: true knowledge ('ilm) is paired with submission (islam) to God. The recognition of Solomon's miracles was meant to lead Bilqis toward recognizing the one true God, and the verse foreshadows her eventual conversion to monotheism. The phrase 'we were given knowledge before her' emphasizes that prior access to revealed knowledge naturally results in submission to God's will, framing knowledge not as mere intellectual achievement but as inherently linked to faith and surrender to the divine.

translation: And that which she used to worship besides Allah had hindered her [from true faith]; indeed, she was from a disbelieving people.
interpretation: This verse refers to the Queen of Sheba (Bilqis) before her encounter with Prophet Sulayman led her to recognize the truth of monotheism. It highlights how her prior idolatrous upbringing and the cultural practices of her people had been an obstacle preventing her from recognizing and submitting to Allah alone. The verse illustrates a broader Qur'anic theme: that inherited customs, societal conditioning, and false worship can act as barriers that blind even intelligent and capable individuals—like Bilqis, who is portrayed elsewhere as wise and politically astute—from perceiving divine truth. Her disbelief is attributed not to any inherent deficiency but to the environment and traditions she was raised in, following the religion of her people rather than independent reasoning. This sets up the narrative resolution in subsequent verses where, upon witnessing the miraculous signs of Sulayman and the transportation of her throne, she ultimately abandons her former worship and submits to Allah, demonstrating that sincere exposure to truth can overcome the hindrance of cultural conditioning and lead to guidance even for those raised among disbelievers.

translation: It was said to her, 'Enter the palace.' But when she saw it, she thought it was a pool of water, and she uncovered her legs. He said, 'Indeed, it is a palace made smooth with glass.' She said, 'My Lord, indeed I have wronged myself, and I submit with Solomon to Allah, Lord of the worlds.'
interpretation: This verse depicts the climactic moment of the Queen of Sheba's encounter with Solomon's extraordinary kingdom, serving as the final test that leads to her conversion. The glass palace, with water flowing beneath its transparent floor, represents a marvel of divine-granted technology and wisdom given to Solomon, so advanced that it deceives even a powerful and intelligent queen into mistaking solid ground for water. Her instinctive reaction—lifting her garment to wade through what she believes is a pool—is a moment of vulnerability and humility, stripping away her royal composure and worldly assumptions. This physical unveiling parallels a spiritual unveiling: confronted with the limits of her own perception and the superiority of the knowledge and power granted to Solomon by God, she recognizes the insufficiency of her prior sun-worship and the idolatrous rule of her people. Her declaration 'I have wronged myself' is an acknowledgment of her past misguidance, while her immediate submission 'with Solomon' to 'the Lord of the worlds' signifies that her conversion is not to Solomon's earthly authority but to the same God that Solomon serves—emphasizing that true submission (Islam) is to God alone, with Solomon as a fellow worshipper rather than an object of worship himself. The verse thus illustrates how divine signs, even through illusion and the senses, can lead a sincere seeker to truth and tawhid (monotheism).

translation: And We certainly sent to Thamud their brother Salih, [saying], 'Worship Allah,' and at once they became two factions quarreling.
interpretation: This verse illustrates a recurring pattern in prophetic history: when a messenger is sent with the simple, unifying call to worship God alone, the response is division rather than unity. The people of Thamud split into opposing factions—those who believed Salih and those who rejected him—despite the clarity and singularity of his message. This division foreshadows the conflict that leads to the story of the she-camel and the eventual destruction of the disbelieving faction. The verse highlights how truth, even when presented plainly, often becomes a source of contention among people due to differing inclinations, pride, attachment to ancestral customs, or vested interests, rather than being universally embraced. It underscores the theme that faith is a test requiring sincere submission, and that communities are not monolithic in their response to divine guidance.

translation: He said, 'O my people, why do you hasten the evil before the good? Why do you not seek forgiveness of Allah, that you may receive mercy?'
interpretation: This verse records the Prophet Salih's rebuke to his people, the Thamud, who demanded that the punishment (the 'evil') be brought upon them quickly rather than seeking the 'good' of divine mercy and guidance. Their impatience and mockery reflected a deeper spiritual arrogance—a refusal to take the warning seriously and a challenge to the Prophet to prove his message by invoking immediate calamity. Salih's response highlights a fundamental misunderstanding: punishment is not something to be rushed toward in defiance, but something to be avoided through repentance. The rhetorical question 'why do you not seek forgiveness' points to the open door of mercy that remains available even to those who have transgressed, provided they turn to God sincerely. This verse underscores a recurring Quranic theme that human beings often rush toward their own destruction through pride and denial, when the wiser and more natural course would be humility, repentance, and reliance on God's compassion. It also illustrates the patience of prophets who, even when faced with mockery and hostility, continue to call their people toward salvation rather than wishing destruction upon them.

translation: They said, "We see an evil omen in you and in those who are with you." He said, "Your omen is with Allah. Rather, you are a people being tested."
interpretation: This verse reflects a recurring pattern in the Qur'anic narratives of rejected prophets, here specifically attributed to the people of Thamud and their response to Prophet Salih. When faced with warnings about their wrongdoing, the disbelievers resorted to superstition, blaming the prophet and his followers for any misfortune that befell them, rather than examining their own conduct. This represents a psychological defense mechanism common among those who reject divine guidance—externalizing blame rather than engaging in self-reflection. The prophet's response redirects their superstitious reasoning back to its true source: all events, fortunate or unfortunate, originate from Allah's will and knowledge, not from the presence of righteous people. The phrase "you are a people being tested" (تفتنون) reveals the deeper spiritual reality—that the hardships and trials they experienced were not omens caused by the prophet's presence, but rather tests of their faith and moral character, exposing their true nature and the corruption already present in their hearts. This verse illustrates the broader Qur'anic theme that superstition and irrational blame-shifting are symptoms of spiritual blindness, while true believers understand that trials are divinely ordained tests meant to reveal and refine character, not punishments caused by the righteous among them.

translation: And there were in the city nine family heads (a group of nine men) who caused corruption in the land and did not do right.
interpretation: This verse refers to the story of the Prophet Salih and his people, the Thamud. It describes a faction of nine men who held positions of leadership or influence within the city and who used their power not to benefit the community but to spread corruption and mischief. Their corruption was not limited to passive wrongdoing; the verse emphasizes that they actively avoided reform, refusing to act righteously even when given the chance. These nine individuals are traditionally understood to be the ones who later plotted to kill the she-camel sent as a miracle from Allah and conspired to assassinate Salih himself, believing they could escape accountability by acting in secret and in a group. The verse highlights a recurring Qur'anic theme: that corruption often originates from entrenched elites who resist moral and social reform because such change threatens their status or interests. Their secretive planning and collective denial of truth ultimately led to their destruction, illustrating that worldly power and conspiracy cannot shield anyone from divine justice when a community chooses persistent wrongdoing over correction and righteousness.

translation: They said, 'Swear to one another by Allah that we will attack him and his family by night, then we will say to his heir [or next of kin], We did not witness the destruction of his family, and indeed, we are telling the truth.'
interpretation: This verse recounts the conspiracy of nine men among the tribe of Thamud who plotted to assassinate the Prophet Salih and his household under cover of darkness, seeking to eliminate him before he could further challenge their rejection of his message. Their plan reveals a calculated wickedness: not only did they intend to commit murder, but they also premeditated a cover-up, swearing a pact to lie to Salih's family afterward, denying any knowledge of the crime and falsely swearing their innocence by invoking God's name itself—compounding their treachery with blasphemous false oaths. This episode illustrates the depths of deception and cold premeditation that those hostile to divine guidance resorted to, believing they could outmaneuver both the Prophet and God Himself through secrecy and false testimony. Yet the Qur'an's immediate follow-up verses reveal that their scheme utterly failed, as God's plan superseded their plotting, and they themselves were destroyed along with their entire people. The verse serves as a reminder that human schemes against the righteous, no matter how secretly plotted or deceptively justified, cannot escape divine knowledge and justice, and that invoking God's name to mask falsehood only deepens the moral culpability of the wrongdoers.

translation: And they devised a plot, and We devised a plan, while they perceived it not.
interpretation: This verse refers to the nine leaders among the people of Thamud who conspired to kill the Prophet Salih and his family by night, thinking to eliminate him and deny any involvement. God's 'plan' here is not a plot in the human sense, but His sovereign response that turns their scheming back upon themselves—He foiled their conspiracy and brought about their destruction instead, while they remained completely unaware of His decree until it overtook them. The verse illustrates a recurring Qur'anic theme: that human schemes against the righteous or against divine guidance are ultimately subordinate to God's overarching plan, which operates with perfect knowledge and timing beyond human perception. It teaches that no matter how secret or cunning a plot against truth may be, divine justice encompasses and surpasses it, often using the very mechanisms of the plotters' scheme to bring about their own downfall.

translation: So look how was the end of their plotting: We destroyed them and their people, all together.
interpretation: This verse concludes the account of the nine men who conspired to kill the Prophet Salih and his family by night, believing they could carry out their plot secretly and escape divine retribution. The rhetorical command 'So look' invites the listener to reflect on the inevitable outcome of scheming against God's messengers: total and collective destruction, encompassing not only the plotters themselves but their entire people who failed to stop or disavow the wrongdoing. The verse underscores a recurring Qur'anic theme that human schemes devised against divine truth and its bearers are ultimately futile, and that complicity through silence or association with corruption brings shared consequence. It also serves as a warning and a lesson for later generations about the swift and comprehensive nature of divine justice when a community collectively turns to arrogance and conspiracy against righteousness.

translation: So those are their houses, fallen into ruin because of the wrong they did. Indeed, in that is a sign for a people who know.
interpretation: This verse refers to the people of Thamud, the nation of Prophet Salih, whose dwellings were left desolate as a consequence of their persistent injustice, arrogance, and rejection of divine guidance after they had slaughtered the she-camel sent to them as a sign. The ruins of their homes stand as a physical, visible testimony in history to the consequence of transgression (zulm) against God's commands. The verse emphasizes that such destruction is not random misfortune but a direct result of their own wrongdoing, underscoring the moral causality embedded in divine justice. The closing phrase, 'a sign for a people who know,' suggests that true understanding of these historical remnants requires reflection and knowledge—those who contemplate history, archaeology, and the fate of past nations can perceive the spiritual lesson: that societies which persist in oppression, corruption, and disbelief ultimately face downfall, while the ruins themselves serve as enduring admonitions for those who possess insight and are willing to learn from the past rather than merely observe it.​

translation: And We saved those who believed and were ever mindful of Allah (had taqwa).
interpretation: This verse, occurring in the context of the story of Lot and the destruction of his people, establishes a universal divine principle: salvation from catastrophe and punishment is granted to those who combine faith (iman) with consistent righteous conduct (taqwa). The pairing of belief with taqwa signifies that true faith is not merely intellectual assent but is proven through sustained God-consciousness and ethical action. The verse underscores that divine mercy operates through a law of moral cause and effect—those who align their inner conviction with outer piety are shielded from the destruction that befalls corrupt societies, while the community's wrongdoing, no matter how widespread, cannot engulf the righteous minority within it.

translation: And [remember] Lot, when he said to his people, 'Do you commit indecency while you can see?'
interpretation: This verse refers to Prophet Lot (Lut) condemning his people for engaging in same-sex acts between men, a practice he identifies as a transgression unprecedented among nations before them. The phrase 'while you can see' carries multiple layers of meaning: it can suggest that they commit this act openly, in plain sight of one another without shame or privacy; it can also mean that they do so despite having clear sight and reason, i.e., despite knowing full well through their own faculties of perception and judgment that this behavior is wrong; and it may further imply spiritual blindness contrasted with physical sight, that they can see with their eyes yet fail to perceive the moral and natural order they are violating. The verse establishes Lot as a prophetic figure sent to call his community back to righteousness, using rhetorical questioning to confront them with the irrationality and shamelessness of their collective conduct, a rhetorical strategy common throughout the Qur'an when prophets address the moral failings of their people.

translation: Indeed, do you approach men with desire instead of women? Nay, but you are a people behaving ignorantly.
interpretation: This verse is part of the account of Prophet Lut (Lot), addressing his people regarding their sexual practices with other men rather than women. The rhetorical question underscores the Qur'anic framing of this behavior as a transgression against the natural order established for procreation and lawful relations between spouses. The phrase 'behaving ignorantly' characterizes their conduct not merely as a moral failing but as a fundamental departure from sound reasoning and divine guidance—implying that their actions stemmed from a willful disregard for what is beneficial and permissible. The verse serves as a condemnation within the broader narrative of Lut's people, who are depicted as persisting in this and other transgressions despite his warnings, ultimately leading to their destruction. It reflects the Qur'an's broader ethical framework concerning lawful sexuality, confined to the marital relationship between men and women.

translation: But the answer of his people was nothing but that they said: 'Drive out the family of Lot from your city; indeed, they are people who keep themselves pure.'
interpretation: This verse depicts the response of the people of Lot to his call for righteousness and his condemnation of their immoral practices. Rather than reflecting on his message, they mocked his family's piety, using their purity and moral uprightness as grounds for expulsion. The statement 'they are people who keep themselves pure' was intended sarcastically, revealing how corrupted societies often invert moral values—treating virtue as a fault and decency as deviance. This illustrates a recurring pattern in the Qur'an where communities reject prophets not due to lack of evidence but because righteousness threatens their entrenched sinful norms. The episode serves as a warning about the moral blindness that overtakes people who normalize wrongdoing, to the point that they view goodness itself as alien or offensive.

translation: So We saved him and his family, except his wife; We destined her to be among those who remained behind (to be destroyed).
interpretation: This verse, referring to the Prophet Lut (Lot) and his people, emphasizes that salvation and divine mercy are granted on the basis of individual faith and righteousness, not merely through family or blood ties. Although Lut's wife was part of his household, she sided in heart and loyalty with the disbelieving, corrupt people of her city rather than with her husband's message of truth. Her exclusion from salvation, despite her close relation to a prophet, illustrates a central Qur'anic theme: that no person's proximity to righteousness — whether through kinship, marriage, or social bond — guarantees their own spiritual salvation if their own belief and actions do not align with truth. The term 'qaddarnaha' ('We destined her') also underscores the concept of divine decree (qadar), showing that her fate was determined by God according to her own choices and disposition, reinforcing the principle of personal responsibility in matters of faith and judgment aaf

translation: And We rained down upon them a rain [of stones], and evil was the rain of those who had been warned.
interpretation: This verse refers to the destruction of the people of Lot, who were destroyed by a rain of stones as divine punishment for their persistent sin and rejection of the Prophet Lot's warnings. The phrase 'rain of those who were warned' emphasizes the justice of this punishment—it did not come without prior warning. The people had been repeatedly cautioned by their prophet about the consequences of their immoral behavior, yet they persisted in disbelief and transgression. The 'evil rain' stands in stark contrast to rain as it is normally understood—a symbol of mercy, life, and blessing in the Qur'an. Here, the very element that typically brings sustenance and renewal becomes an instrument of destruction, illustrating how divine mercy can transform into divine wrath when a people reject guidance after being given clear warning. This serves as a broader lesson about accountability: those who receive warnings and reject them face consequences proportional to their persistent defiance, and the verse stands as a historical lesson for future generations about the seriousness of heeding prophetic guidance.

translation: Say: 'Praise be to Allah, and peace be upon His servants whom He has chosen. Is Allah better, or what they associate with Him?'
interpretation: This verse combines an expression of gratitude and praise to God with a rhetorical challenge to polytheism. The Prophet is instructed to begin with praise (hamd) for Allah, acknowledging His sovereignty and blessings, and to extend a greeting of peace to the chosen servants—understood by many commentators to refer to the prophets and righteous believers whom God has selected for guidance and favor. The verse then pivots to a pointed rhetorical question directed at the disbelievers who worship idols or other deities alongside God. By asking whether Allah is better than what they associate with Him, the verse exposes the absurdity of shirk (associating partners with God) through logical comparison: the false deities people worship have no power to create, sustain, or benefit anyone, whereas Allah is the source of all existence and blessing. This rhetorical device, common in this surah's style, invites reflection rather than offering a debate, since the answer is self-evident to anyone who considers the nature of true divinity versus powerless idols. The juxtaposition of praise and peace for the faithful with the challenge to idolaters also reinforces a broader Quranic theme: true security and peace come from recognizing and submitting to the one true God, while shirk leads to spiritual confusion and loss.

translation: Is He [not best] who created the heavens and the earth and sent down for you rain from the sky, causing to grow thereby gardens of joyful beauty, whose trees you could not cause to grow? Is there a deity with Allah? Nay, they are a people who equate [others with Him].
interpretation: This verse is part of a rhetorical series in Surah An-Naml in which Allah presents evidence of His unique sovereignty and power drawn from the natural world, challenging the polytheists' logic. By highlighting the creation of the vast heavens and earth, and the precise, life-giving phenomenon of rainfall that produces lush, beautiful gardens beyond human ability to replicate, the verse argues that only a singular, all-powerful Creator could be responsible for such intricate and sustaining design. The rhetorical question 'Is there a deity with Allah?' exposes the irrationality of attributing partners to God when no other being has demonstrated such creative capability. The closing statement condemns those who persist in idolatry not because of ignorance of these signs, but because of willful deviation—'equating' false gods with the true Creator despite the self-evident proofs of His oneness found throughout creation. The verse thus functions as both a theological argument and a moral indictment of heedlessness toward manifest truth.

translation: Is He [not best] who made the earth a stable abode and made rivers within it and set firm mountains for it and placed between the two seas a barrier? Is there a deity with Allah? Nay, but most of them do not know.
interpretation: This verse is part of a rhetorical series in Surah An-Naml challenging the polytheists by pointing to the signs of divine power and order in creation—the earth's stability, the flowing rivers, the firm mountains, and the separation between bodies of water—as evidence that only One Being, Allah, could be responsible for such precise and purposeful design. The rhetorical question 'Is there a deity with Allah?' underscores the absurdity of associating partners with the Creator when the very fabric of the natural world testifies to a singular, all-powerful source of order. The closing statement, that most people do not know, highlights human heedlessness in failing to reflect upon these manifest signs and draw the rational conclusion of monotheism (tawhid).

translation: Is He [not best] who responds to the distressed one when he calls upon Him and removes the evil, and makes you successors upon the earth? Is there a god besides Allah? Little do you remember.
interpretation: This verse is a rhetorical challenge establishing God's unique sovereignty through His demonstrable actions in human experience. It points to three distinct evidences: His responsiveness to the desperate prayers of the afflicted, His power to lift suffering and hardship, and His sovereign authority in appointing successive generations as stewards of the earth. The rhetorical question 'Is there a god besides Allah?' demands an obvious negative answer, since no other being can be credited with these acts. The verse concludes with a rebuke of human forgetfulness, noting that despite clear and repeated evidence of divine power and mercy in everyday life, people rarely pause to reflect on or acknowledge it. The reference to being made 'successors of the earth' also carries the theological weight of human accountability-each generation inherits the earth as a trust from God, not as autonomous owners, which reinforces the argument that gratitude and worship should be directed to Him alone.

translation: Or who is it that guides you in the darknesses of the land and sea, and who sends the winds as glad tidings before His mercy? Is there a god besides Allah? Exalted is Allah above what they associate with Him.
interpretation: This verse is part of a rhetorical series in Surah An-Naml that challenges the polytheists by pointing to phenomena of divine providence and power that even they would acknowledge only God can perform. Guidance through the darknesses of land and sea evokes both the literal peril of travelers navigating by stars and unknown terrain, and a metaphorical darkness of ignorance and uncertainty in life from which only divine guidance can rescue a person. The sending of winds as a herald of rain—'glad tidings before His mercy'—illustrates God's mercy as something that is preceded by signs, teaching that His compassion operates through discernible, patterned workings in nature that people can learn to recognize if they reflect. The rhetorical question 'Is there a god besides Allah?' is not a request for information but a logical challenge: since no idol or partner can perform such feats of guidance or control nature's mercpercies, the attribution of divinity to anything other than God is exposed as baseless. The closing declaration of God's transcendence above what is associated with Him reaffirms the Qur'an's central theme of tawhid (the oneness of God), condemning shirk (associating partners with God) as both a theological error and a practical ingratitude toward the One who alone sustains and guides creation.

translation: Is He [not best] who begins creation and then repeats it, and who provides for you from the sky and the earth? Is there a deity with Allah? Say, 'Produce your proof, if you should be truthful.'
interpretation: This verse is part of a rhetorical sequence in Surah An-Naml challenging polytheists to justify their worship of other deities alongside Allah. By pointing to the uniquely divine acts of originating creation, resurrecting the dead, and sustaining all life through provision from both heaven (rain) and earth (resources and produce), the verse establishes that these are powers no partner or idol possesses. The challenge 'produce your proof' is a decisive logical demand: since no evidence exists for any other being sharing in these creative and sustaining powers, the claim of other deities collapses under rational scrutiny. The verse thus uses the method of reasoned argument (burhan) rather than mere assertion, inviting reflection on the natural order as self-evident testimony to Allah's singular lordship, and exposing the irrationality of shirk (associating partners with Allah) when subjected to honest demand for evidence.

translation: Say, "None in the heavens and the earth knows the unseen except Allah, and they do not perceive when they will be resurrected."
interpretation: This verse addresses the polytheists who attributed knowledge of the unseen (al-ghayb) to idols, intercessors, or other beings they worshipped alongside Allah. The Prophet is commanded to declare unequivocally that absolute knowledge of the unseen—including the exact timing of the Resurrection, future events, and hidden realities—belongs to Allah alone. This is a fundamental assertion of tawhid (divine oneness), stripping away any claim that angels, jinn, saints, or idols possess independent knowledge of hidden matters. The verse specifically singles out ignorance of the timing of resurrection (ayyana yub'athun) as an example of this unseen knowledge, emphasizing that even the heavenly beings and all creation remain unaware of when the Hour will come. This serves a dual purpose: it humbles human and even angelic claims to foreknowledge, and it redirects ultimate trust and reliance back to Allah as the sole possessor of complete knowledge. The verse implicitly critiques those who sought knowledge of the future through soothsayers, astrologers, or false intermediaries, reminding believers that such knowledge is reserved exclusively for the Creator, and that even the Prophet himself, despite his elevated station, does not possess independent access to the unseen except what Allah chooses to reveal to him.

translation: Nay, their knowledge of the Hereafter has failed to attain certainty. Nay, they are in doubt about it. Nay, they are blind to it.
interpretation: This verse describes a progressive deterioration in the disbelievers' relationship to the truth of the Hereafter, using the rhetorical device of 'bal' (nay/rather) to move through escalating stages of spiritual failure. First, their knowledge is shown to be deficient and never reaches real certainty—they have not grasped it properly despite whatever partial awareness they may claim. Second, this deficiency manifests as outright doubt, an unsettled uncertainty about whether the Hereafter is even real. Third, and most severely, this doubt hardens into total blindness—a complete inability to perceive or comprehend the reality at all, not merely uncertainty but a willful or ingrained spiritual blindness that forecloses understanding. The progression from deficient knowledge to doubt to blindness illustrates how denial of the Hereafter is not a single static state but a worsening condition, reflecting the Qur'anic theme that rejection of truth, when persisted in, leads to deeper and deeper layers of heedlessness until the heart and mind become entirely sealed off from perceiving what should be self-evident through reflection on creation, resurrection, and divine justice.

translation: And those who disbelieve say, 'When we have become dust, we and our forefathers, will we indeed be brought forth [from the graves]?'
interpretation: This verse captures the recurring objection raised by disbelievers against the doctrine of bodily resurrection. Their argument rests on the apparent finality of death and physical decomposition—once a body turns to dust and merges with the earth, it seems inconceivable that it could ever be restored to life. By invoking both themselves and their ancestors, the skeptics emphasize the scale of the claim: not just one person, but countless generations reduced to dust over the ages would need to be reconstituted. This rhetorical question reflects a worldview limited to material cause and effect, unable to conceive of a Creator's power extending beyond the observable laws of decay. The Qur'an repeatedly responds to this objection elsewhere by pointing to God's original creation of humans from nothing, arguing that the One who initiated creation can surely repeat it. The verse thus serves as a foil, setting up the broader Qur'anic argument for resurrection as a demonstration of divine omnipotence that transcends human intuitions about the irreversibility of physical decomposition.

translation: Indeed, we have been promised this, we and our forefathers before; this is nothing but tales of the ancients.
interpretation: This verse reflects the recurring argument made by disbelievers across generations who dismiss warnings of resurrection and judgment as empty promises repeated without fulfillment, akin to old legends passed down through time. It highlights a pattern of skepticism rooted in generational tradition rather than reasoned reflection, where the disbelievers assume that because such promises were made to their ancestors and remained unfulfilled in their lifetimes, they must therefore be fictional myths rather than divine truth. This reveals a deeper theme in the Qur'an about the limits of human impatience and the inability to grasp matters beyond immediate worldly experience, as well as the tendency to inherit doubt from forefathers rather than engaging critically with revelation.

translation: Say: Travel through the land and observe how was the end of the criminals (those who persisted in sin and rejected the truth).
interpretation: This verse commands the Prophet to instruct people to journey through the earth and reflect upon the physical ruins and historical remnants of past nations who rejected divine guidance and persisted in wrongdoing, such as the peoples of 'Ad, Thamud, and others mentioned elsewhere in the Qur'an. The call to 'travel' is both literal and metaphorical, urging believers to study history and archaeology as a means of drawing moral and spiritual lessons. The destruction of these civilizations serves as tangible evidence of the consequences of disbelief, arrogance, and moral corruption. By witnessing the desolation left behind, people are meant to understand that worldly power, wealth, and civilization cannot protect against divine justice when a society collectively turns away from truth and righteousness. This verse thus functions as a rational and empirical appeal, encouraging observation of the world as a source of faith-strengthening evidence rather than relying solely on abstract argument, reinforcing the Qur'anic theme that history itself testifies to the moral order governing human affairs.

translation: And do not grieve over them, nor be in distress from what they plot.
interpretation: This verse offers consolation and reassurance to the Prophet Muhammad (and by extension, to all believers) in the face of rejection and hostility from disbelievers. It addresses two emotional burdens: grief over those who reject the message, and anxiety over the schemes and plots devised against the believers. The verse instructs the Prophet not to let sorrow over people's disbelief consume him, since guidance is ultimately in God's hands and not something he can force upon others. Similarly, he is told not to feel constrained or distressed by the plotting of his enemies, as God is aware of their schemes and is fully capable of protecting His messenger and ultimately bringing their plans to nothing. This reflects a broader Quranic theme of trust in divine providence (tawakkul), teaching believers to maintain inner peace and steadfastness even amid opposition, by placing full confidence in God's power and wisdom rather than being overwhelmed by the apparent strength or cunning of adversaries.

translation: And they say, 'When will this promise be, if you should be truthful?'
interpretation: This verse reflects the challenge posed by disbelievers who mock the warnings of resurrection, judgment, or divine punishment promised by the Prophet. Their demand to know the exact timing is not a genuine inquiry but a rhetorical device meant to express skepticism and ridicule, implying that since the event has not yet occurred, it never will. This rhetorical question represents a recurring pattern in the Qur'an where deniers demand empirical proof of unseen matters, revealing their flawed reasoning that delay equals falsehood. The verse implicitly critiques this mindset by setting up a contrast with the certainty of divine knowledge and timing, which operates beyond human impatience or doubt, and which will ultimately be fulfilled regardless of their disbelief or mockery.

translation: Say, 'Perhaps some of that which you seek to hasten is close upon you.'
interpretation: This verse addresses the disbelievers who mockingly demanded that the promised punishment or Day of Judgment be brought forward immediately, as a challenge to the Prophet Muhammad's warnings. The response conveys a solemn warning: rather than the punishment being distant or avoidable, it may already be imminent, 'close behind' them, following closely on their heels. The phrase 'some of that which you seek to hasten' suggests that what they mockingly demanded was not a single, distant event but could include immediate consequences, such as defeat in battle, drought, or other worldly calamities, as a prelude to the ultimate reckoning. The verse highlights the folly of demanding divine punishment out of arrogance or disbelief, when such punishment, once set in motion, cannot be stopped or delayed by human will. It also underscores a recurring Quranic theme: God's timing is not bound by human impatience, and what seems delayed may in fact be near, serving as both a warning and a reminder of divine authority over fate and judgment.

translation: And indeed, your Lord is full of bounty for mankind, but most of them do not give thanks.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the boundless generosity and mercy of God toward humanity, highlighting that His blessings—material, spiritual, and existential—are granted continuously regardless of human merit. The second half of the verse draws attention to a key moral failing: despite constant divine favor, most people fail to recognize or express gratitude for it. This serves as both a reminder of God's grace and a gentle rebuke, urging believers toward mindfulness (shukr) as a core spiritual discipline. Gratitude in this context is not merely verbal thanks but an active acknowledgment that shapes one's relationship with God, fostering humility and awareness that all sustenance, protection, and opportunity ultimately originate from divine bounty rather than human effort alone. The verse also implicitly warns against the heedlessness that accompanies comfort and ease, where blessings are taken for granted rather than seen as signs requiring reflection and thankfulness.

translation: And indeed, your Lord surely knows what their breasts conceal and what they declare.
interpretation: This verse affirms God's complete and comprehensive knowledge of the inner and outer dimensions of human existence—both the hidden thoughts, intentions, doubts, and feelings that people harbor within themselves, and the words and actions they openly display to others. It serves as a reminder and reassurance, particularly in context, to the Prophet Muhammad regarding the hostility, mockery, and disbelief he faced from his opponents, many of whom concealed enmity or schemes while outwardly presenting different attitudes. The verse underscores that no concealment from human beings can escape divine awareness, establishing a theological principle of God's omniscience that encompasses the deepest recesses of the heart as well as manifest speech and deeds. This serves both as a consolation to believers who may suffer from the secret malice of others—knowing that God is aware and will ultimately judge accordingly—and as a warning to those who harbor disbelief, arrogance, or hostility while feigning righteousness or indifference, reminding them that their inner states are fully known to God regardless of outward appearances.

translation: And there is no hidden thing in the heaven and the earth except that it is in a clear Record (Book).
interpretation: This verse affirms the all-encompassing divine knowledge of Allah, asserting that nothing—no secret, no concealed matter, however small or vast—escapes His awareness, whether in the celestial realms or on earth. The 'clear Book' (al-Kitab al-Mubin) refers to the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz), a metaphysical record in which all that was, is, and will be is inscribed. This serves theological purposes: it reassures believers that justice will ultimately prevail since every deed, however hidden, is accounted for; it underscores Allah's omniscience as a component of His absolute sovereignty; and it situates human and cosmic events within a predetermined divine order, countering any notion of randomness or escape from accountability.
