This all-encompassing knowledge is immediately followed by the attributes of mercy and forgiveness, signifying that God's omniscience is not primarily a basis for judgment or fear, but rather the foundation for compassion: because He knows the full context, weaknesses, and struggles of His creatures, He respond with forgiveness and mercy rather than harsh accounting. The verse thus reassures believers that divine knowledge of their every secret is coupled with a disposition of grace, encouraging trust in God's benevolent oversight of both the cosmos and the human soul.

translation: And those who disbelieve say, 'The Hour will not come to us.' Say, 'Yes, by my Lord, it will surely come to you - [He is] the Knower of the unseen.' Not absent from Him is an atom's weight within the heavens or within the earth, nor is there anything smaller than that or larger except that it is in a clear register.
interpretation: This verse addresses the denial of resurrection and the Day of Judgment by disbelievers, who confidently assert that it will never occur. The Prophet is commanded to respond with an oath affirming its certainty, invoking God directly as witness to the truth of this claim. The verse then expands into a profound theological statement about divine omniscience: God's knowledge encompasses every particle of existence, no matter how infinitesimally small, in both the heavens and the earth. The mention of 'atom's weight' (mithqal dharrah) emphasizes the totality and precision of God's awareness - nothing escapes His knowledge, whether smaller or larger than this smallest conceivable unit. This comprehensive knowledge is said to be recorded in a 'clear register' (kitab mubin), often understood as reference to the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz), symbolizing that all of creation's history, present, and future are already known and documented by God. The logical connection between denying the Hour and affirming God's exhaustive knowledge is significant: if God knows every atom's location and fate, then surely He has complete knowledge of when and how the Resurrection will occur, making human denial of it merely a reflection of limited human knowledge rather than any actual uncertainty in divine reality. This verse thus serves both as a rebuttal to skepticism about the afterlife and as a broader affirmation of God's absolute and perfect knowledge of all creation.

translation: That He may reward those who believe and do righteous deeds. Those will have forgiveness and a noble provision.
interpretation: This verse comes in the context of affirming the reality of the Hour and God's complete knowledge of all things, down to the smallest particle in the heavens and earth. Having established that nothing escapes divine awareness and that the reckoning is certain, the verse explains the purpose behind this precise accounting: it is so that God may justly reward those who combine faith (iman) with righteous action (amal salih). The pairing of belief and deeds is significant—faith alone is insufficient without its manifestation in righteous conduct, and righteous conduct without sincere faith lacks its proper foundation and ultimate value in the sight of God. The reward described has two dimensions: 'maghfirah' (forgiveness), addressing the believer's shortcomings and sins, and 'rizqun karim' (noble or generous provision), referring to the sustenance and blessings of Paradise that are dignified and unending, unlike worldly provision which can be mixed with hardship or shame. The use of 'karim' (noble/generous) emphasizes that this provision is not merely abundant but honorable—free from any humiliation, interruption, or deficiency. This verse thus serves as a promise and encouragement to believers, assuring them that the precise divine accounting mentioned in the preceding verses is not a cause for fear alone but ultimately serves the purpose of perfect justice, ensuring that no righteous deed goes unrewarded and no sincere believer is left without mercy.

translation: And those who strive against Our signs, seeking to invalidate [them] and escape [Our power] - for them is a punishment of painful affliction.
interpretation: This verse addresses those who actively work to discredit or undermine the divine revelations and signs of God, believing they can thwart His will or escape accountability for their opposition. The term 'mu'ajizin' implies an active, deliberate effort to render God's signs ineffective or to prove oneself beyond divine reach - a kind of intellectual and spiritual arrogance that denies both the truth of revelation and the reality of ultimate judgment. The verse serves as a counterpoint to the preceding promise of reward for believers who do good works, establishing a clear moral symmetry in the Quranic worldview: just as sincere faith and righteous action lead to honorable provision and forgiveness, deliberate rejection and opposition to truth - especially when driven by the arrogant belief that one can outmaneuver divine justice - leads to severe consequence. The 'painful punishment of wrath' (adhabun min rijzin alim) suggests a particularly harsh and humiliating torment, befitting the arrogance of those who imagined themselves capable of escaping accountability to their Creator. This serves as a warning throughout the Quran that human cleverness or power can never ultimately circumvent divine will or judgment.

translation: And those who have been given knowledge see that what has been revealed to you from your Lord is the truth, and it guides to the path of the Almighty, the Praiseworthy.
interpretation: This verse highlights the special discernment granted to people of knowledge, who recognize the divine revelation's truth through genuine understanding rather than mere acceptance. It establishes that true knowledge, when sincere and properly cultivated, leads one to recognize divine truth and its guidance toward the correct path, associated here with two of God's attributes: His might (al-'Aziz) and His praiseworthiness (al-Hamid). The pairing of these attributes suggests that the path to which revelation guides combines both power and glory with qualities deserving of praise and gratitude, indicating that submission to this path is not blind obedience to mere force, but recognition of a guidance system worthy of admiration. This verse implicitly distinguishes between those who possess knowledge in its truest sense—which naturally leads to recognition of divine truth—and those who lack such insight and thus may reject or doubt revelation despite claims to education or learning.

translation: And those who disbelieve say, 'Shall we point you to a man who will inform you that when you have been torn apart in disintegration, you will [then be brought] into a new creation?'
interpretation: This verse records the mocking skepticism of the disbelievers regarding the Prophet Muhammad's (peace be upon him) message of bodily resurrection after death. They express incredulity that a human being could claim that after the body completely decomposes and scatters into dust and particles—described as being 'torn apart in disintegration'—it could be reconstituted and brought back to life in a new creation. Their rhetorical question, phrased with sarcasm, is meant to ridicule the very concept of resurrection as absurd and to cast doubt on the Prophet's credibility for proclaiming such a belief. This reflects a common objection raised by disbelievers throughout the Qur'an against the doctrine of the afterlife, rooted in their inability to reconcile physical decay with the power of divine recreation. The verse implicitly sets up a rebuttal (found in subsequent verses) affirming that God, who created humans initially from nothing, has full power to resurrect them regardless of how thoroughly their bodies have decomposed, emphasizing His limitless power over creation and recreation.

translation: Has he invented a lie about Allah, or is there madness in him? Nay, but those who do not believe in the Hereafter are in torment and far error.
interpretation: This verse records the accusations leveled by disbelievers against the Prophet (or a messenger figure), who, confronted with his message of monotheism and warning of the Hereafter, could only dismiss him as either a fabricator of lies against God or as someone afflicted with madness—two contradictory charges that reveal the desperation of those unable to refute his message on its merits. The divine response reverses the accusation entirely: it is not the messenger who is deluded or mad, but rather those who reject belief in the Hereafter who are truly lost. Their denial places them in a state of 'torment' (al-'adhab), suggesting an inner spiritual suffering and anxiety that stems from a worldview with no ultimate accountability or meaning, and 'far error' (al-dalal al-ba'eed), indicating a deviation from truth so profound that return becomes increasingly difficult. The verse thus exposes a psychological and spiritual inversion: those who accuse others of madness or deception are themselves suffering from a far graver affliction—a denial that cuts them off from ultimate truth and leaves them wandering in error, confused about reality, purpose, and consequence.

translation: Have they not looked at what is before them and what is behind them of the heaven and the earth? If We willed, We could cause the earth to swallow them, or cause fragments from the sky to fall upon them. Indeed, in that is a sign for every servant who turns to Allah in repentance.
interpretation: This verse invites reflection on the vastness and order of the sky above and the earth below as evidence of divine power and sovereignty. The rhetorical question challenges disbelievers to recognize the proof surrounding them in creation. The mention of Allah's ability to make the earth swallow people or send falling fragments from the sky serves as a warning of divine omnipotence over life and death, underscoring that the natural world's stability is not a given but a continuous act of divine will and mercy. The verse closes by noting that such signs are meaningful specifically to the 'munib,' the servant who is spiritually attuned and inclined to turn back to God—suggesting that physical evidence of God's power only becomes a true 'sign' (ayah) for those whose hearts are receptive to guidance, while it may pass unnoticed by the heedless. This reflects a broader Qur'anic theme that knowledge and signs require an inward disposition of humility and repentance to be truly perceived and internalized.

translation: And indeed We bestowed upon David grace/favor from Us: 'O mountains, echo [Our praise] with him, and the birds as well.' And We made iron pliable for him.
interpretation: This verse highlights the special, direct favor God granted David, manifesting in both spiritual and material gifts. The command to the mountains and birds to join David in glorifying God depicts creation itself as attuned to divine praise, with David's voice (in his psalms) so powerful and sincere that it resonated throughout nature, uniting the inanimate and animate world in worship. This symbolizes the harmony between a righteous, God-conscious ruler and the natural order, suggesting that true spiritual authority brings all creation into concord. The softening of iron represents a practical, technological blessing—traditionally understood as enabling David to craft armor and tools without need for fire or hammering, symbolizing mastery over the material world granted by divine will. Together, the two gifts—mastery over sound/spirit (commanding mountains and birds) and mastery over matter (iron)—illustrate a holistic form of kingship: one that unites spiritual leadership with practical craftsmanship and strength, serving as a model of a prophet-king who integrates worship, governance, and productive work (traditionally, David is also credited with the craft of making chainmail), all under divine guidance and favor.

translation: [We said], 'Make full-length coats of mail and measure well the links [thereof], and work righteousness, [all of you], for indeed I am Seeing of what you do.'
interpretation: This verse refers to Prophet Dawud (David), to whom Allah granted the skill of working iron and crafting armor. The command to 'measure well the links' signifies the importance of precision, diligence, and excellence in one's craft and work—whatever that work may be. The verse then broadens from this specific craft to a universal principle: 'work righteousness,' linking skilled, careful labor to righteous deeds in general. This establishes that doing good work—executed with care, competence, and integrity—is itself a form of worship and righteousness. The closing reminder that Allah is Seeing of all actions underscores that both the quality of one's work and the sincerity of one's intentions are always under divine observation, encouraging believers to strive for excellence (ihsan) in all endeavors, not merely for human recognition but because God witnesses all.

translation: And to Solomon [We subjected] the wind: its morning course was a month's journey and its evening course was a month's journey. And We caused a fount of molten copper to flow for him. And among the jinn were those who worked before him by the permission of his Lord. And whoever among them deviated from Our command - We would make him taste the punishment of the blazing Fire.
interpretation: This verse illustrates the extraordinary favors God bestowed upon Solomon as signs of prophetic authority and divine power, showing that dominion over nature and unseen creatures is entirely subject to God's will rather than inherent human capability. The wind's service, covering vast distances in mere hours, and the flow of molten copper symbolize mastery over natural forces granted specifically to Solomon for the fulfillment of his mission, including monumental construction works. The jinn's labor under Solomon's command, explicitly tied to divine permission, underscores that even supernatural beings are creatures bound by God's law, not autonomous powers. The warning of punishment for those jinn who deviated from command reinforces the theme of accountability that pervades creation: that disobedience to divine order carries consequences regardless of one's nature, whether human, jinn, or otherwise. The passage ultimately emphasizes that all power, whether exercised by a prophet-king or unseen beings, flows from and remains answerable to God's sovereign will.

translation: They made for him whatever he willed of elevated chambers, statues, basins like reservoirs, and cooking pots fixed in place. [We said], "Work, O family of David, in gratitude." But few of My servants are grateful.
interpretation: This verse describes the jinn working under Solomon's command, fashioning grand structures and vessels for him, demonstrating the extraordinary power and dominion God granted to him. The command to the family of David to "work in gratitude" signifies that the proper response to divine favor is not complacency but active service and righteous deeds—gratitude is to be expressed through action, not merely words. The concluding statement that few of God's servants are truly grateful serves as a sobering reminder that despite the abundance of blessings bestowed upon humanity, genuine thankfulness—which involves recognizing the Giver and using blessings in His service—is rare. This teaches that true gratitude is demonstrated through righteous conduct and the proper use of one's gifts and circumstances, not simply through verbal acknowledgment, and that such sincere gratitude is a mark of spiritual distinction achieved by only a few.

translation: Then, when We decreed death for him [Solomon], nothing indicated his death to them except a creature of the earth which ate away at his staff. So when he fell down, the jinn realized that if they had known the unseen, they would not have remained in humiliating punishment.
interpretation: This verse reveals the truth about the jinn's claimed knowledge of the unseen (al-ghayb), which many ancient and pagan traditions attributed to supernatural beings. Solomon, according to Islamic tradition, had died while standing, leaning on his staff, and the jinn who were compelled to labor for him continued their toil for a prolonged period without realizing he had passed away. It was only when a termite (or worm) had eaten through his staff, causing his body to fall, that the truth became apparent. The verse serves as a decisive refutation of the notion that jinn possess knowledge of hidden or unseen matters—if they truly had such knowledge, they would have known immediately of Solomon's death and would not have continued laboring under what the verse calls 'humiliating punishment' for an extended time. This theological point reinforces the Quranic principle that knowledge of the unseen belongs exclusively to God, dismantling pre-Islamic and popular beliefs that attributed prophetic or supernatural insight to jinn, who were often consulted by soothsayers and believed to have access to hidden knowledge. The verse thus serves both a narrative function, concluding the story of Solomon's reign and power over the jinn, and a doctrinal function, correcting misconceptions about the limits of creaturely knowledge versus divine omniscience.

translation: Indeed, there was for Sheba a sign in their dwelling place: two gardens, on the right and on the left. [They were told], 'Eat from the provision of your Lord and be grateful to Him. A good land and a forgiving Lord.'
interpretation: This verse recalls the prosperous civilization of Sheba (Saba') in ancient Yemen, whose people were blessed with abundant agricultural wealth symbolized by the two flourishing gardens flanking their land, likely irrigated through the famous Marib Dam system. The 'sign' (ayah) refers to the clear evidence of divine favor and blessing that was visible in their fertile environment and prosperity. The command to 'eat and be grateful' establishes the proper relationship between sustenance and gratitude—that material blessings are a trust requiring acknowledgment of their divine source. The description of the land as 'good' (tayyibah) and the Lord as 'forgiving' (ghafur) sets up a theological framework where physical blessing is paired with spiritual mercy, creating an ideal state of harmony between people and their Creator. This verse serves as a preface to the subsequent narrative (in following verses) where Sheba's people turn away from gratitude, leading to the destruction of their gardens and the breaking of the dam—illustrating the Quranic theme that prosperity without gratitude leads to downfall, and that worldly blessings are tests of faith rather than mere entitlements.

translation: But they turned away [in ingratitude], so We sent upon them the flood of the dam (Sayl al-'Arim), and We replaced their two [fruitful] gardens with two gardens bearing bitter fruit, tamarisks, and a few sparse lote trees.
interpretation: This verse recounts the fate of the people of Saba (Sheba), who had been blessed with extraordinary prosperity—fertile lands, abundant harvests, and a sophisticated irrigation system sustained by a great dam. Despite living in comfort and security, they turned away from gratitude to God and rejected His signs, choosing heedlessness over thankfulness for their blessings. As a consequence, divine punishment came in the form of a catastrophic flood that destroyed their dam and irrigation system, transforming their once-flourishing gardens into barren lands producing only bitter fruit and thorny, unproductive vegetation. The verse serves as a powerful lesson on the transient nature of worldly prosperity and the principle that material blessings are contingent upon gratitude and righteousness; when a people become arrogant or complacent in their abundance and fail to acknowledge the Source of their favor, that favor can be swiftly withdrawn. It also reflects the Quranic theme that civilizations and nations rise and fall based on their moral and spiritual conduct, not merely by chance, and that the natural world itself can serve as an instrument of divine justice.

translation: That is how We recompensed them for their disbelief (ingratitude); and do We recompense thus except the ungrateful disbeliever?
interpretation: This verse concludes the account of the people of Saba' (Sheba), whose prosperous gardens were destroyed and replaced with bitter, thorny, fruitless growth after they turned away from gratitude to God despite His abundant blessings upon them. The rhetorical question at the end—'do We recompense thus except the ungrateful disbeliever?'—establishes a universal principle rather than merely describing a historical event: severe retribution of this kind is reserved specifically for those who meet blessings with kufr (disbelief/ingratitude), not for ordinary human failings or lesser sins. The verse thus functions as both a closure to the narrative and a general warning, teaching that the destruction of Saba' was not arbitrary but a direct, fitting consequence of their willful rejection of gratitude toward their Sustainer. It reinforces a recurring Qur'anic theme: that material blessing carries with it moral responsibility, and persistent, collective ingratitude invites corresponding consequence in the natural and social order.

translation: And We placed between them and the towns which We had blessed [other] towns [set up] prominently [in sight of one another], and We determined between them the stages [of journey]. Travel between them by night and day in safety.
interpretation: This verse recalls the prosperity granted to the people of Saba', whose land lay along the trade route linking Yemen to the blessed lands of Syria. God had arranged visible, closely-spaced towns along this route, making travel easy, safe, and measured in comfortable stages, so that merchants and travelers could journey night or day without fear of hunger, thirst, bandits, or getting lost. This divine favor represented an extraordinary blessing of security and ease of livelihood. Yet, as the following verses reveal, the people of Saba' responded to this abundance with ingratitude, asking God to lengthen the distances between their journeys out of arrogance and a desire to show off their wealth and self-sufficiency rather than acknowledging His provision. The verse thus sets up a contrast between divine generosity and human ingratitude, illustrating how ease and prosperity can lead people away from gratitude toward heedlessness, ultimately resulting in the destruction of their civilization as a lesson for later generations about the transient nature of worldly blessings when met with arrogance rather than thankfulness.

translation: But they said, 'Our Lord, lengthen the distance between our journeys (stages),' and they wronged themselves. So We made them narratives (legends/tales to be told), and We scattered them in complete dispersal. Indeed, in that are signs for everyone patient and grateful.
interpretation: This verse refers to the people of Saba' (Sheba), who had been blessed with a prosperous land where towns were close together, allowing travelers to journey safely from one town to another without hardship or need for provisions, as mentioned in the preceding verses. Rather than being grateful for this ease and abundance, they grew arrogant and discontented, asking God to increase the distances between their settlements—essentially rejecting the blessing of convenience and closeness in favor of challenge or distinction, revealing an ingratitude and a perverse desire for hardship over the ease granted to them. This request reflected their inner corruption: they wronged themselves through arrogance and ingratitude rather than any external oppressor wronging them. As a consequence, God turned their once-flourishing civilization into mere stories and legends told by later generations—a byword for ruin—and scattered their peoples far and wide, destroying the unity and prosperity they had taken for granted. The verse closes with a broader moral lesson: in the rise and catastrophic fall of Saba' there are signs and lessons for those who possess two essential qualities—patience (sabr) in adversity and gratitude (shukr) in prosperity. The destruction of Saba' demonstrates that material blessings are tests, and that failure to appreciate them with gratitude, replaced instead by complacency or audacious demands, invites their loss. True believers are those who remain steadfast through hardship and thankful through ease, recognizing both as opportunities for devotion to God.

translation: And Iblis certainly found true his assumption about them, so they followed him, except a party of the believers.
interpretation: This verse recalls Iblis's (Satan's) declaration before Allah that he would mislead humanity and that most of them would prove ungrateful and easily deceived. The verse confirms that his prediction was vindicated by the actual behavior of most people, who succumbed to his whispers and temptations, following desires and misguidance rather than divine guidance. The exception clause—'except a party of the believers'—serves a crucial theological function: it affirms that Satan's power is not absolute or coercive but operates through suggestion and temptation that can be resisted. Those who maintain sincere faith (iman) and God-consciousness (taqwa) are shown to possess a protective immunity against his influence, as stated elsewhere in the Quran that Satan has no authority over Allah's sincere servants. This verse thus serves as both a historical commentary on human weakness and a moral exhortation, highlighting that falling into Satan's trap is a choice reflecting the weakness of one's faith, while steadfast believers demonstrate that resistance is always possible through reliance on God.

translation: And he (Satan/Iblis) had no authority over them except that We might know who believes in the Hereafter from who is in doubt about it. And your Lord is, over all things, a Guardian.
interpretation: This verse clarifies that Iblis's power to tempt and whisper to human beings was never a form of coercive control; it was a limited permission granted by God. The purpose of this allowance was not for God's own knowledge—since God's knowledge is all-encompassing and eternal—but to manifest and distinguish, within the observable reality of human choice and history, who genuinely believes in the Hereafter and who harbors doubt about it. In other words, temptation serves as a trial that makes visible the true nature of each soul's faith, separating sincere believers from the doubtful through their actual responses to temptation. This establishes the principle of human free will and moral responsibility: Satan can suggest and entice, but he cannot force belief or disbelief upon anyone. Ultimately, the verse closes with the reassurance that God remains the ultimate Guardian and Preserver over all things, meaning that despite the apparent freedom given to Satan to tempt humanity, nothing occurs outside of God's watchful oversight and control. The trial of temptation is thus purposeful, bounded, and supervised, serving the divine wisdom of revealing true faith through real-world tests rather than abstract declarations.

translation: Say, [O Muhammad], "Call upon those you claim [as deities] besides Allah. They do not possess an atom's weight [of ability] in the heavens or on the earth, nor do they have therein any partnership [with Him], nor is there for Him among them any assistant."
interpretation: This verse is a decisive refutation of polytheism, directly challenging the Meccan disbelievers to invoke the idols and intermediaries they worship alongside God. The verse systematically dismantles any possible basis for their divinity by denying them power (they possess not even the weight of an atom in creation), denying them partnership or shared ownership in the cosmos, and denying them any role as helpers or assistants to God in His governance of the universe. The rhetorical structure—moving from a challenge to a threefold denial—serves to expose the complete powerlessness and irrelevance of these false deities, emphasizing that true divinity and sovereignty belong exclusively to Allah, who requires no partners, associates, or helpers in creating, sustaining, or ruling the heavens and earth. This establishes the logical foundation for tawhid (the oneness of God) by showing that the objects of worship besides Allah have no legitimate claim to any aspect of divine power or authority.

translation: Intercession will not avail with Him except for one whom He permits. Until, when fear is removed from their hearts, they say, 'What did your Lord say?' They say, 'The truth.' And He is the Most High, the Most Great.
interpretation: This verse addresses the nature of intercession on the Day of Judgment, clarifying that no being—angel, prophet, or otherwise—can intercede with God on behalf of another except by His explicit permission. This refutes the polytheistic belief that idols or intermediaries could intercede on behalf of worshippers without divine sanction, emphasizing that all authority belongs solely to God. The imagery of angels being overcome with fear until it is lifted from their hearts depicts the awe and terror that even the highest celestial beings experience in God's presence, awaiting His command. When the fear subsides, they ask one another what God has decreed, affirming that His word is always 'the truth,' underscoring the absolute certainty and infallibility of divine speech. The verse concludes by affirming God's transcendent attributes—His supreme highness and greatness—situating the entire discourse within a framework of radical monotheism where no power, however exalted, operates independently of God's will and permission.

translation: Say: 'Who provides for you from the heavens and the earth?' Say: 'Allah. And indeed, we or you are either upon guidance or in clear error.'
interpretation: This verse presents a rhetorical and logical challenge to the polytheists of Mecca. By first establishing through their own admission that Allah alone is the Provider from the heavens and earth, the Prophet then poses a striking rational dilemma: both parties—the believers and the disbelievers—cannot simultaneously be correct, since their positions are mutually exclusive. One side must be upon true guidance, the other in manifest error. The verse employs a tone of intellectual humility and fairness, not asserting outright which side is right (though the answer is obvious given the preceding acknowledgment), but inviting the listener to use reason to reach the inevitable conclusion themselves. This rhetorical strategy disarms stubborn resistance by appealing to logical consistency rather than simply asserting authority, demonstrating that true faith in Allah's sole power to sustain creation logically necessitates recognizing His sole right to be worshipped and obeyed, and that deviation from this truth constitutes the 'clear error' referenced in the verse.

translation: Say: 'You will not be questioned about what we have sinned, nor shall we be questioned about what you do.'
interpretation: This verse instructs the Prophet to tell the disbelievers that each soul bears responsibility only for its own deeds. It establishes the principle of individual accountability before God: no person will be held liable for another's sins, and no one will be interrogated about actions that are not their own. The statement is meant to close off debate with those who sought to blame the believers or the Prophet for their own rejection of faith, or who tried to shift responsibility onto others. It affirms a broader Qur'anic theme that every soul earns what it labors for, and that on the Day of Judgment, each person will stand accountable solely for their own choices and conduct, not for the wrongdoing of others.

translation: Say: Our Lord will bring us together, then He will open [judge] between us in truth, for He is the Opener [Judge], the All-Knowing.
interpretation: This verse instructs the Prophet to tell the disbelievers that the ultimate resolution of their dispute with him lies with God alone. Rather than engaging in endless argumentation, the matter is deferred to a final, decisive judgment on the Day of Resurrection, when God will gather all parties together and judge between them with perfect justice. The term 'al-Fattah' (the Opener/Judge) conveys the sense of opening a case to render a true verdict, resolving disputes that human beings cannot settle through debate alone. Coupled with 'al-'Alim' (the All-Knowing), the verse emphasizes that God's judgment will be based on complete knowledge of truth and falsehood, intentions and actions, leaving no room for deception or injustice. This serves as both a warning to those who reject the message and a source of reassurance to the believers that justice will ultimately prevail, even if it is not immediately apparent in worldly terms.

translation: Say: "Show me those whom you have attached to Him as partners. No indeed! Rather, He is Allah, the Exalted in Might, the Wise."
interpretation: This verse is a decisive challenge to the polytheists, demanding empirical proof for the deities they worship alongside God. The rhetorical command 'Show me' exposes the baselessness of idolatry—there is no evidence, no divine attribute, no creative power that can be pointed to in these so-called partners. The emphatic rejection 'No indeed!' (kalla) forcefully dismisses the very premise of associating partners with God before affirming the truth: He alone is Allah, possessing absolute power (al-'Aziz) and perfect wisdom (al-Hakim). The pairing of these two divine names is significant—God's might is not arbitrary or tyrannical but is guided by wisdom, and His wisdom is backed by the power to enact it. This verse thus serves as both a logical refutation of polytheism and a reaffirmation of tawhid (divine oneness), emphasizing that true divinity requires attributes of supreme power and wisdom that cannot be shared or divided among multiple beings.

translation: And We have not sent you except comprehensively to mankind as a bringer of good tidings and a warner. But most of the people do not know.
interpretation: This verse establishes the universal nature of Prophet Muhammad's mission, emphasizing that his message was not confined to a particular tribe, nation, or era, but was intended for all of humanity across time. Unlike earlier prophets who were often sent to specific peoples, Muhammad's prophethood represents a final and comprehensive message meant to reach every person. The dual role described—as a bearer of good news and a warner—reflects the balanced nature of divine guidance, offering hope for those who believe and do good, while cautioning against the consequences of disbelief and wrongdoing. The concluding phrase about most people not knowing suggests a lament over humanity's general failure to recognize or accept this universal truth, whether due to ignorance, arrogance, or attachment to inherited traditions and tribal identities that resist the idea of a message meant to transcend all human divisions.

translation: And they say, "When will this promise be fulfilled, if you should be truthful?"
interpretation: This verse captures the recurring challenge posed by disbelievers to the Prophet and believers regarding warnings of resurrection, judgment, and divine punishment. Their demand for an immediate timeline reflects skepticism and mockery rather than genuine inquiry—they use the delay in the promise's fulfillment as 'evidence' against its truth. This reflects a broader human tendency to equate the unseen or future with the unreal, and to demand empirical proof on their own terms rather than accepting matters of faith that unfold according to divine timing. The Qur'an's response elsewhere emphasizes that God's promises are certain regardless of when they manifest, and that the appointed time is known only to Him, teaching believers patience and trust in divine wisdom over human demands for immediacy.

translation: Say, "For you is the appointment of a Day you cannot postpone by an hour, nor can you advance."
interpretation: This verse addresses the disbelievers who demanded to know when the promised Day of Judgment would occur, often as a taunt or challenge to the Prophet Muhammad. The response instructs him to affirm that this appointed Day is fixed with absolute precision by God's decree, and no human effort, desire, or power can alter its timing—not even by a single hour, whether to delay or hasten it. This underscores a central theme in the Qur'an: divine sovereignty over time and destiny lies entirely beyond human control or negotiation. The verse serves as both a warning and a reassurance—a warning to those who mock or dismiss the reality of resurrection and accountability, and a reassurance to believers that God's promises, including justice and judgment, will be fulfilled exactly as ordained, regardless of how long it may seem to take from a human perspective. It also reflects the futility of trying to use the uncertainty of the exact timing as an excuse for disbelief, since the certainty of the event itself is what matters, not its precise moment of arrival.

translation: And those who disbelieved say, "We will never believe in this Qur'an nor in that which came before it." If only you could see when the wrongdoers are made to stand before their Lord, casting the blame on one another. Those who were considered weak will say to those who were arrogant, "If not for you, we would have been believers."
interpretation: This verse depicts the psychological and social dynamics of collective disbelief, revealing how rejection of divine guidance often stems from social hierarchies of power and influence rather than genuine intellectual conviction. The scene of mutual recrimination on the Day of Judgment exposes the hollow nature of the excuses offered by those who followed others into disbelief - they attempt to shift responsibility onto their leaders and those who held worldly power over them. This highlights a central Qur'anic theme: that following others blindly, whether due to social pressure, fear, or admiration of worldly status, does not absolve an individual of personal accountability for their choices of belief. The "weak" were not merely powerless but complicit in their own self-deception, having allowed social dynamics to override their capacity for independent moral and spiritual judgment. The verse serves as a warning against the abdication of personal responsibility in matters of faith, suggesting that ultimately each soul will stand alone before God, unable to deflect blame onto those who may have influenced or misled them in worldly life.

translation: Those who were arrogant will say to those who were deemed weak, 'Was it we who barred you from guidance after it had come to you? Rather, you yourselves were wrongdoers.'
interpretation: This verse depicts a scene from the Day of Judgment in which the oppressors and leaders who misled others attempt to deny responsibility for the wrongdoing of their followers. When the weak and oppressed blame their former leaders for leading them astray from faith, the arrogant leaders retort by shifting the blame back, claiming they never forced anyone to disbelieve—rather, their followers willingly chose wrongdoing and criminality themselves. This exchange illustrates a central Qur'anic theme: ultimate moral responsibility rests with the individual. While leaders and societal pressures may present temptations or obstacles, no human being can claim absolute compulsion when it comes to matters of faith and moral choice. Every person retains the capacity for independent judgment and is accountable for their own decisions, even when influenced by charismatic or powerful figures. The verse serves as a sobering reminder that on the Day of Judgment, the convenient excuse of 'I was only following others' will not be accepted, exposing the mutual blame and disownment that will occur between those who led others astray and those who followed them, as both groups attempt to escape accountability for their shared sin.

translation: And those who were weak will say to those who were arrogant, 'Rather, it was your scheming by night and day, when you commanded us to disbelieve in Allah and to set up rivals to Him.' And they will conceal their regret when they see the punishment; and We will put shackles on the necks of those who disbelieved. Will they be recompensed except for what they used to do?
interpretation: This verse depicts a scene of mutual blame on the Day of Judgment between the weak followers and their arrogant leaders who led them astray in worldly life. The followers reject the leaders' attempt to shift blame by pointing out that it was the leaders' continuous scheming, day and night, that coerced them into disbelief and idolatry. The mention of concealing regret suggests a futile, private shame felt by the wrongdoers once they witness the certainty of punishment, too late for it to matter or be expressed openly in a way that could help them. The shackles symbolize the binding consequence of disbelief, representing how sin and false choices ultimately enslave a person, foreshadowing divine justice. The rhetorical closing question emphasizes the principle of just recompense: the punishment is not arbitrary cruelty but a direct and fair consequence of one's own choices and actions, reinforcing the Qur'anic theme of personal accountability—leaders cannot excuse followers, and followers cannot wholly blame leaders, since each bears responsibility for their own complicity in wrongdoing.

translation: And We did not send a warner to any city except that its affluent ones said, 'Indeed, in that with which you have been sent, we are disbelievers.'
interpretation: This verse reveals a recurring sociological pattern throughout the history of prophetic missions: it is consistently the wealthy, privileged elite within a society—those whom affluence has made complacent and invested in the status quo—who lead the rejection of divine warnings. Their resistance stems not from intellectual doubt but from material interest; the message of reform and accountability threatens their social position, economic privileges, and the comfortable order from which they benefit. By highlighting 'mutrafuha' (its luxury-indulged ones) specifically, the verse exposes how prosperity can breed moral and spiritual corruption, making the privileged class resistant to truth when that truth demands justice, humility, or redistribution of power. This pattern serves as a warning to every generation: those most comfortable with worldly power and wealth are often the first to oppose messages calling for righteousness, equity, and submission to a higher authority, since such messages inherently challenge unearned privilege and demand accountability from those who have the most to lose from change.

translation: And they said, 'We have more wealth and children, and we are not to be punished.'
interpretation: This verse exposes a recurring human fallacy: equating worldly prosperity with divine favor and spiritual security. The speakers—wealthy disbelievers—reasoned that since God had blessed them abundantly with riches and offspring in this life, this must indicate His approval of them, and therefore they would be shielded from any future punishment or accountability. This logic reflects a deep spiritual error, mistaking material success for a sign of righteousness rather than understanding it as a test. The Qur'an consistently refutes this assumption elsewhere, clarifying that wealth and children are trials, not rewards guaranteeing salvation, and that true success is measured by faith and righteous deeds rather than worldly possessions. The verse serves as a warning against the arrogance that often accompanies affluence, where material abundance breeds a false sense of invulnerability and exemption from moral and spiritual responsibility.

translation: Say: Indeed, my Lord extends provision for whom He wills and restricts it, but most people do not know.
interpretation: This verse addresses the common misconception that material wealth is a direct indicator of one's standing or righteousness before God. The Prophet is instructed to clarify that the distribution of sustenance—wealth, resources, and provision—is entirely within God's wisdom and will, not a reward system based on merit that humans can calculate or predict. Some are given abundance as a test of gratitude and responsibility, while others are given less as a test of patience and trust. The phrase 'most people do not know' points to a widespread human error: judging divine favor by worldly success, assuming that the wealthy are blessed and the poor are overlooked. This verse corrects that assumption, teaching that true wisdom lies in understanding that provision is a matter of divine prerogative tied to unseen purposes, not a simple reflection of one's worth. It invites reflection on contentment and trust in God's plan, regardless of one's economic circumstances.

translation: And it is not your wealth or your children that bring you nearer to Us in position, but it is those who believe and do righteous deeds - for them there is a multiplied reward for what they did, and they will be in the lofty chambers, secure.
interpretation: This verse dismantles a common human measure of worth and status—material wealth and the number or prestige of one's offspring—as having no inherent value in determining one's closeness to God. In the social context of the Quraysh and many societies, wealth and progeny were seen as signs of divine favor or personal merit. The verse corrects this by redirecting the criterion for nearness to God entirely toward faith and righteous action, which are matters of personal moral choice rather than inherited or accumulated advantage. The promise of a 'multiplied reward' underscores divine generosity exceeding the proportion of the deed itself, while the image of dwelling securely in 'lofty chambers' evokes both physical elevation and spiritual safety, symbolizing the ultimate reversal of worldly hierarchies: those who were truly devoted, regardless of their material standing in this life, are elevated and granted security in the next, free from fear or loss. The verse as a whole serves as a corrective theology against materialism and nepotism, affirming that ultimate value lies in sincere faith and ethical conduct rather than external markers of success.

translation: And those who strive against Our signs, seeking to cause [them] failure - those will be brought into the punishment.
interpretation: This verse contrasts with the preceding description of believers who are honored and provided for in Paradise. Here, the focus shifts to those who actively work against the revealed signs of God, attempting to discredit, oppose, or render them powerless - believing they can escape divine accountability through their efforts. The term 'mu'ajizeen' suggests they see themselves as capable of thwarting or outrunning God's plan, perhaps through mockery, argumentation, or active opposition to the Prophet's message. The verse delivers a decisive rebuttal to this arrogance: far from escaping consequence, they will be forcibly brought forth and presented before the punishment, emphasizing the certainty and inescapability of divine justice. The word 'muhdaroon' (brought/presented) implies a lack of choice or agency - unlike their worldly attempts to assert control and resist truth, in the end they will be compelled, summoned against their will to face what they tried to deny. This creates a powerful irony: those who sought to demonstrate power over divine signs will themselves be rendered powerless, dragged to their reckoning.

translation: Say, 'Indeed, my Lord extends provision for whom He wills of His servants and restricts it for him. But whatever you spend of anything, He will compensate it; and He is the best of providers.'
interpretation: This verse addresses the believer's understanding of sustenance (rizq) as entirely within God's wise control, not merely a product of human effort or circumstance. By affirming that God both expands and restricts provision according to His will, it counters anxiety over wealth and removes grounds for arrogance in abundance or despair in scarcity, since both states are divinely ordained tests. The second part directly confronts a natural human fear—that giving charity or spending in God's cause will diminish one's wealth. The Qur'an reframes spending not as loss but as a transaction with God Himself, who promises to replace what is given, whether through material increase, blessing, protection from calamity, or reward in the afterlife. The phrase 'best of providers' reinforces trust in God's provision as surpassing any human source of sustenance, encouraging generosity rooted in faith rather than calculation. Thus the verse links theology (divine control over provision) to ethics (encouragement of charitable spending), presenting economic behavior as an expression of trust in God's sovereignty and generosity.

translation: And on the Day when He will gather them all together, He will say to the angels, 'Was it you that these people used to worship?'
interpretation: This verse depicts a scene from the Day of Judgment in which God confronts those who worshipped angels (or jinn, whom some polytheists mistook for angels or associated with them) during their earthly lives. By posing this question directly to the angels in the presence of their worshippers, God publicly exposes the futility and error of such worship. The angels, as will be shown in the following verses, disown any responsibility for being worshipped, declaring their own devotion to God alone and stating that it was not themselves but rather the jinn who deceived these people into idolatry. This serves as a decisive refutation of shirk (associating partners with God), demonstrating that even the beings elevated to the status of intermediaries or objects of worship categorically reject such status and affirm their complete servitude to God. The verse thus underscores the Quranic theme that on the Day of Judgment, the true nature of worship will be unveiled, and those who worshipped other than God—even seemingly righteous or exalted beings like angels—will find that their devotion was fundamentally misplaced, as the worshipped themselves testify to their innocence and exclusive worship of the One God.

translation: They [the angels] will say, 'Glory be to You! You are our Protector, not them. Rather, they used to worship the jinn; most of them believed in them.'
interpretation: This verse depicts a scene on the Day of Judgment where those who worshipped angels are confronted, and the angels disown any association with their worshippers, declaring their sole allegiance to God. The angels clarify that these idolaters were not truly worshipping them, but were in fact worshipping jinn (unseen spiritual entities, possibly linked to Satanic forces) who had deceived them into polytheism. This highlights the Qur'anic theme that false worship often stems from deception by unseen forces rather than genuine devotion to the intended objects of worship, and it emphasizes that on the Day of Judgment, those who were falsely worshipped will testify against their worshippers, exposing the true nature of their misguided faith and absolving themselves of responsibility for others' idolatry.

translation: So this Day none of you has the power to benefit or harm another, and We will say to those who did wrong, 'Taste the punishment of the Fire which you used to deny.'
interpretation: This verse addresses the Day of Judgment, emphasizing the complete powerlessness of created beings in that ultimate moment—false deities, idols, and even human allies or intercessors that people relied upon in worldly life will have no ability to help or harm one another. This dismantles the illusion of power and intercession that polytheists attributed to their idols or that people place in worldly connections and status. The verse then shifts to direct divine address to the wrongdoers (those who associated partners with God or persisted in disbelief and injustice), commanding them to 'taste' the punishment—a vivid, sensory term that underscores the inescapable, experiential reality of the consequence they once dismissed as impossible. The phrase 'which you used to deny' highlights the theme of accountability: the punishment is explicitly tied to their prior rejection and mockery of warnings about the Fire. This serves as a sobering reminder that disbelief and denial of divine truth, however confidently asserted in this life, will be met with an undeniable confrontation with reality in the Hereafter, where no worldly power, wealth, or relationship can intervene on one's behalf.

translation: And when Our clear verses are recited to them, they say, "This is not but a man who wishes to avert you from that which your fathers used to worship." And they say, "This is not except a lie invented." And those who disbelieved say of the truth when it has come to them, "This is not but obvious magic."
interpretation: This verse illustrates the psychological and social mechanisms by which disbelievers reject divine truth—not through reasoned refutation, but through dismissive labeling. The progression of accusations (a mere man with ulterior motives, a fabricated lie, obvious sorcery) reveals how rejection escalates when the truth cannot be rationally countered. Rather than engaging with the content of the revelation, the disbelievers attack the messenger's character and motives, suggesting he seeks to sever them from ancestral tradition—appealing to inherited custom over independent verification of truth. This reflects a recurring Qur'anic theme: that resistance to prophetic guidance often stems not from lack of evidence but from attachment to inherited social and religious structures, and that the accusation of "magic" or "fabrication" is a common defense mechanism of those unwilling to abandon familiar paradigms, even when confronted with clear signs (ayat bayyinat).

translation: And We had not given them any scriptures which they studied, nor did We send to them before you any warner.
interpretation: This verse addresses the disbelievers among the Meccans who rejected the Prophet Muhammad's message. It refutes any excuse they might offer for their rejection of the Quran by pointing out that they had received no previous scripture to study, nor had any prior warner or prophet been sent to them before Muhammad. This establishes that their disbelief cannot be attributed to confusion from competing religious texts or to the absence of divine guidance in their history, as sometimes argued by those who claimed their ancestors followed an older, perhaps more authentic tradition. The verse implicitly contrasts their situation with that of the People of the Book (Jews and Christians), who had received scriptures and prophets before. By clarifying that the Meccans had no such prior access to revelation, the verse underscores the significance of Muhammad's mission as something entirely new to this community, placing the burden of their response squarely on their own reasoning and conscience rather than on any conflicting prior guidance. It also implicitly validates the Quran as a necessary and unprecedented mercy to a people who had been without clear prophetic guidance for a very long time, countering their arrogance in rejecting this message despite having no competing prior revelation to justify their skepticism.

translation: And those before them denied [the truth], and these [people of Makkah] have not attained a tenth of what We had given to those [earlier nations]. Yet they denied My messengers, so how terrible was My reproach!
interpretation: This verse serves as a sobering historical reminder and warning to the Quraysh and all who deny the message of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ. God points out that earlier nations who rejected their prophets possessed far greater wealth, power, numbers, and civilizational achievements than the people addressed here—yet none of that worldly strength availed them when they persisted in disbelief and denial. Despite their might, these former peoples were destroyed when divine punishment came upon them. The rhetorical question 'how terrible was My reproach' emphasizes the severity and certainty of this punishment, inviting the listener to reflect on the ruins and historical accounts of these vanished civilizations as tangible proof of God's justice. The underlying message is a warning against complacency: lesser resources and power are no excuse for rejecting truth, and if mighty nations before were not spared, those with even less should take heed rather than assume immunity from accountability. The verse underscores a broader Quranic theme that worldly might is irrelevant before divine will, and that the true measure of security lies in faith and righteousness, not material or numerical superiority.

translation: Say: 'I exhort you to one thing only: that you stand up for God's sake, in pairs or singly, and then reflect. Your companion is not possessed by any madness; he is only a warner to you before a severe punishment.'
interpretation: This verse calls upon people to set aside collective pressures, biases, and preconceptions, and to engage in sincere, independent reflection—whether in small groups or alone—about the message and character of the Prophet. By urging them to 'stand for God,' it emphasizes sincerity of intention purified from self-interest or blind following of others. The rhetorical defense against the accusation of madness ('jinnah') underscores that the Prophet's warnings are not the ravings of a disturbed mind but a rational, urgent caution rooted in concern for humanity's fate. The mention of a 'severe punishment' ahead serves not merely as a threat but as a call to moral seriousness—urging the listener to weigh the stakes of denial and heedlessness through calm, unbiased contemplation rather than impulsive reaction or social conformity.

translation: Say: Whatever reward I might have asked of you, it is yours; my reward is only upon Allah, and He is a witness over all things.
interpretation: This verse instructs the Prophet Muhammad to declare his sincerity and disinterestedness in his mission of conveying the message. By stating that any reward he might have asked for belongs to the people themselves, he emphasizes that he seeks no worldly gain, wealth, or benefit from them for his prophetic duty. His true recompense rests solely with Allah, underscoring the purity of his intention and the divine origin of his message, free from ulterior motives. The closing declaration that Allah is a witness over all things reinforces accountability—both the Prophet's sincerity and the people's response to the message are known and observed by God, leaving no room for doubt about the authenticity of the call or the fairness of its presentation.

translation: Say: Indeed, my Lord casts forth the truth, [He Who is] the Knower of all unseen things.
interpretation: This verse affirms that divine truth is actively sent down by God—revelation is not a passive emanation but a forceful, decisive 'casting' of truth into the world to dispel falsehood, much as light dispels darkness. The pairing of this declaration with God's title as 'Knower of the Unseen' (Allam al-Ghuyub) underscores the source and authority of this truth: because God alone possesses complete knowledge of all hidden realities—past, present, and future, as well as the inner secrets of hearts—the truth He reveals through His prophets is absolute and unerring, not subject to human speculation or doubt. The verse serves as a rebuttal to those who doubted the Prophet Muhammad's message, affirming that his words are not his own invention but originate from the One who knows all that is concealed from human perception, including the true nature of idols, the reality of the afterlife, and the ultimate outcome of human deeds.

translation: Say: 'The truth has come, and falsehood can neither originate anything nor restore anything.'
interpretation: This verse affirms the final triumph of truth over falsehood, declaring that with the arrival of divine truth—revelation and guidance—falsehood is rendered utterly powerless. The phrase 'can neither originate anything nor restore anything' uses idiomatic Arabic expressing total incapacity: falsehood has no creative power to begin something new, nor any restorative power to bring back what has passed or been destroyed. It is a declaration that once truth manifests, falsehood collapses entirely, having no independent existence or lasting effect of its own. This reflects the Qur'anic theme that truth (haqq) is inherently real and enduring, while falsehood (batil) is inherently empty and transient, lacking any true substance despite its temporary appearances of strength or persuasion.

translation: Say: 'If I err, I err only to my own detriment, but if I am guided, it is because of what my Lord reveals to me. Indeed, He is All-Hearing, Ever-Near.'
interpretation: This verse instructs the Prophet Muhammad to respond to accusations of error or misguidance from his opponents with humility and clarity about the source of his guidance. He is to acknowledge that any potential error would be his own personal failing, bearing no reflection on the truth of the message itself, while any guidance he possesses comes directly from divine revelation rather than his own devising. This distinction protects the integrity of the revelation from being judged by the Prophet's human fallibility, while simultaneously affirming that his guidance is not self-generated but divinely sourced. The closing affirmation that God is 'All-Hearing, Ever-Near' reassures the Prophet that God is intimately aware of his sincere efforts and the accusations leveled against him, providing comfort that he is not alone in facing skepticism or hostility. This verse establishes a model for prophetic humility combined with confidence in revealed truth, separating personal fallibility from the certainty of divine guidance.

translation: If you could but see when they are seized with terror, with no escape, and they are seized from a nearby place.
interpretation: This verse depicts the terror of disbelievers when they finally witness the punishment or the reality of the Hereafter that they once denied. The phrase 'no escape' (fa-la fawt) signifies that once divine judgment arrives, there is no fleeing or avoiding it, no matter how one tries. 'Seized from a nearby place' suggests that their doom comes swiftly and from an unexpected, close proximity, underscoring that God's power encompasses them entirely and they cannot distance themselves from His reach. The verse serves as a warning about the suddenness and inevitability of divine retribution, contrasting the disbelievers' earlier heedlessness and mockery of warnings with their eventual terror and helplessness when the truth confronts them directly. It emphasizes the futility of seeking refuge once the appointed time of reckoning arrives, reinforcing the Qur'anic theme that such moments of truth come without prior notice to those who reject faith until it is too late.

translation: And they will say, 'We believe in it!' But how can they attain it from a place so far off?
interpretation: This verse describes the disbelievers' reaction on the Day of Judgment when they finally witness the reality of resurrection, punishment, and divine truth that they had denied in worldly life. Overwhelmed by the undeniable evidence before them, they suddenly proclaim their belief. However, this declaration comes far too late. The 'distant place' symbolizes the vast gulf between the moment of true opportunity—their worldly life, when faith could have been freely chosen and acted upon—and the moment of compulsion, when faced with inescapable truth in the Hereafter. Faith declared under such circumstances, when all doubt has been removed by direct confrontation with the signs of the afterlife, holds no value, since true faith requires belief in the unseen out of sincere conviction, not coerced acknowledgment after the time for choice has passed. The verse serves as a stark warning that repentance and belief must occur during one's lifetime, as there is no 'reaching back' to seize the chance once death and judgment have arrived; the moment of opportunity is irretrievably distant once the next life begins.

translation: And they had already disbelieved in it before, and they utter conjectures about the unseen from a far-off place.
interpretation: This verse describes the disbelievers' reaction when they finally confront the truth of the Hereafter or divine punishment, often understood as occurring at the moment of death or on the Day of Judgment when they suddenly declare belief. The verse points out the futility of this belated declaration by reminding that these very people had rejected faith before, when it could have benefited them. The phrase 'casting at the unseen from a far-off place' is a vivid metaphor describing how they speculate and make baseless guesses about matters of the unseen (ghayb)—such as prophecy, resurrection, and divine revelation—without any real knowledge, as if hurling a projectile blindly from a great distance with no hope of hitting the target. This illustrates the epistemological failure of those who rely on conjecture rather than guidance, highlighting the vast gap between their speculative claims and the actual truth, which remains entirely beyond their reach precisely because they have placed themselves too far from the source of true knowledge—revelation and the Prophet's teaching. Their belief, offered only when confronted with undeniable proof or imminent punishment, is rendered meaningless, as true faith requires belief in the unseen through sincere conviction, not coerced acknowledgment after the fact.

translation: And a barrier will be placed between them and what they desire, just as was done with their kind before. Indeed, they were in disquieting doubt.
interpretation: This verse describes the fate of disbelievers at the moment of death or on the Day of Judgment, when they finally recognize the truth of faith but are then prevented from attaining it—salvation, repentance, or the fulfillment of worldly desires they clung to. The barrier symbolizes the finality of divine judgment: once the appointed time has passed, there is no opportunity to change one's course. The reference to 'their kind before' situates this fate within a historical pattern, recalling previous nations who similarly rejected prophets and faced destruction despite belated recognition of truth. Their persistent 'disquieting doubt' throughout their lives—an unsettled skepticism that never resolved into either firm belief or firm disbelief—is presented as the root cause of their ultimate exclusion, suggesting that willful irresolution and hesitation in matters of faith, when sustained until it is too late, carries its own spiritual consequence.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Praise be to Allah, Originator of the heavens and the earth, who made the angels messengers with wings, two, three, and four. He increases in creation what He wills; indeed, Allah is over all things competent.
interpretation: This opening verse of Surah Fatir establishes Allah as the sole originator and creator of the heavens and the earth, emphasizing His absolute power and creative will. By describing the angels as messengers with varying numbers of wings, the verse highlights the diversity and wonder inherent in Allah's creation, showing that even beings tasked with carrying out divine commands are themselves created with distinct forms suited to their functions. The phrase 'He increases in creation what He wills' underscores that creation is not static or limited to what humans can perceive or imagine; Allah's creative capacity is boundless and continuously active, extending beyond the visible and known world. This serves as a declaration of Allah's limitless power and wisdom, inviting reflection on the vastness and intricacy of the universe as evidence of His sovereignty. The verse sets a tone of praise and awe, reminding believers that all aspects of existence, from the cosmic to the angelic, originate from and depend upon Allah alone, reinforcing the theme of tawhid (the oneness of God) that runs throughout the Qur'an.

translation: Whatever mercy Allah opens up for mankind, none can withhold it; and whatever He withholds, none can release thereafter. And He is the Almighty, the All-Wise.
interpretation: This verse establishes that all blessings, provisions, and favors—whether material or spiritual—flow entirely from Allah's will and are not subject to human control or interference. It emphasizes the absolute sovereignty and power of Allah over the distribution of mercy and sustenance, teaching believers that true reliance should be placed in Him alone rather than in worldly means or other creatures. The pairing of 'the Almighty' (al-Aziz) with 'the All-Wise' (al-Hakim) indicates that this divine control is not arbitrary but exercised with perfect wisdom and justice, even when the reasons behind withholding or granting mercy are not immediately apparent to human understanding. This serves as both a source of comfort for believers facing hardship and a reminder of humility regarding one's dependence on divine grace.

translation: O mankind, remember the favor of Allah upon you. Is there any creator other than Allah who provides for you from the sky and the earth? There is no deity except Him. So how are you deluded (turned away)?
interpretation: This verse calls upon all of humanity to reflect on the blessings bestowed by Allah and to recognize that sustenance—rain, crops, resources from the earth, and all provisions of life—comes solely from Him. By posing the rhetorical question of whether any other creator exists who could provide such sustenance, the verse emphasizes the absurdity of associating partners with Allah (shirk) when no other being has this creative and sustaining power. The closing question, asking how people can be turned away from this evident truth, serves as a rebuke to those who, despite clear evidence of Allah's sole authority over creation and provision, still turn to idols or other deities. It underscores the Qur'anic theme that gratitude and worship should be directed exclusively to the one true God who alone creates and sustains all things.

translation: And if they deny you, [O Muhammad], then messengers before you were denied as well. And to Allah all matters are returned.
interpretation: This verse offers consolation to the Prophet Muhammad amid the rejection and disbelief he faced from his people, reminding him that he is not unique in experiencing such denial—every prophet before him encountered similar rejection from their communities. This places his mission within the continuity of prophetic history, affirming that opposition to divine truth is a recurring pattern rather than a sign of failure or falsehood in the message itself. The verse then shifts to a broader theological assurance: ultimately, all affairs, including the outcome of this conflict between truth and denial, return to Allah for judgment. This serves to relieve the Prophet of the burden of forcing acceptance or feeling personal failure when faced with rejection, redirecting responsibility and final resolution to divine authority rather than human effort alone. It also implicitly warns the deniers that their rejection does not go unanswered, as all matters will ultimately be adjudicated by Allah.

translation: O mankind, indeed the promise of Allah is truth, so let not the worldly life delude you, and let not the Deceiver [Satan] delude you about Allah.
interpretation: This verse delivers a direct warning to all of humanity concerning two primary sources of spiritual danger. The first is the seductive nature of worldly life (al-hayat al-dunya) itself—its pleasures, wealth, and status can create a false sense of permanence and distract people from the certainty of the Hereafter and divine accountability, which is affirmed as 'haqq' (absolute truth). The second danger is more insidious: Satan's deception specifically regarding God's nature. This refers to the way the Deceiver exploits misconceptions about divine mercy or forgiveness, encouraging people to sin while falsely assuming that God's compassion will automatically negate consequences, or that they can delay repentance indefinitely while being lulled into complacency about their ultimate fate. The verse thus distinguishes between being deceived by the world's temporary allure and being deceived in one's very understanding of God's justice and promise, both of which lead to the same spiritual peril of forgetting the reality of resurrection and judgment.

translation: Indeed, Satan is an enemy to you, so take him as an enemy. He only calls his followers so that they may become among the companions of the Blazing Fire.
interpretation: This verse establishes a clear doctrinal stance on the nature of Satan and the necessity of human vigilance against his influence. Rather than being a passive or ambiguous force, Satan is defined as an active, declared adversary of humankind, and believers are commanded to respond with equally active opposition—not mere avoidance but conscious resistance. The verse frames Satan's enmity as purposeful and strategic: his 'invitation' refers to the whispered temptations, rationalizations, and desires he plants to lead people toward sin and away from righteousness. The phrase 'his party' (hizbahu) suggests an organized following, those who heed his call and align themselves with falsehood, whether through outright disbelief or through moral corruption. The ultimate consequence—being among the 'companions of the Blazing Fire'—reveals that Satan's goal is not merely mischief but the eternal destruction of souls. This verse functions as both warning and empowerment, reminding believers that recognizing evil's true nature is the first step toward resisting it, and that one's companionship in the Hereafter is determined by whose call one answers in this life.

translation: Those who disbelieve will have a severe punishment, while those who believe and do righteous deeds will have forgiveness and a great reward.
interpretation: This verse establishes a fundamental Quranic principle of divine justice: that outcomes in the afterlife are directly tied to one's faith and actions in this life. It presents a clear binary contrast between two paths—disbelief, which leads to severe punishment, and the combination of faith with righteous deeds, which leads to forgiveness and great reward. Notably, the verse emphasizes that belief alone is insufficient; it must be paired with righteous action ('amal al-salihat') to merit forgiveness and reward. This pairing of faith and deeds recurs throughout the Quran, underscoring that genuine faith manifests itself through ethical conduct and good works. The verse serves as both a warning and a promise, motivating believers toward righteousness while cautioning against the consequences of rejecting divine guidance.

translation: Then is he whose evil deed has been made fair-seeming to him so that he sees it as good, [like one who is rightly guided]? Indeed, Allah leaves astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills. So let not your soul perish from grief over them. Indeed, Allah is Knowing of what they do.
interpretation: This verse addresses the Prophet Muhammad directly, consoling him regarding his deep distress over those who reject his message and persist in wrongdoing. The rhetorical question at the start highlights the tragic self-deception of those whose corrupted moral sense causes them to perceive their own sinful deeds as righteous and good—a state of spiritual blindness that makes guidance nearly impossible to receive. The verse then situates this phenomenon within divine will: Allah's leaving some to stray and guiding others reflects His comprehensive knowledge of each soul's receptivity to truth, their choices, and their inner dispositions, rather than arbitrary favoritism. This theological point serves a pastoral purpose—it releases the Prophet from an impossible burden. He is told not to destroy himself with grief and anguish over the disbelief of those who reject him, because their rejection stems from a self-imposed blindness that is beyond his power to cure through sheer force of will or emotional investment. The responsibility for conveying the message is his, but the responsibility for the heart's response lies between the individual and Allah. The closing affirmation that Allah is fully aware of what they do reinforces that ultimate judgment and accounting rest with divine knowledge, not human despair, offering comfort to anyone who carries the weight of trying to guide others who refuse to see.

translation: And it is Allah who sends the winds, and they stir the clouds, and We drive them to a dead land and give life thereby to the earth after its death. Thus is the Resurrection.
interpretation: This verse employs the natural phenomenon of rainfall as an empirical, observable proof for the theological doctrine of bodily resurrection. The argument proceeds analogically: just as barren, lifeless earth is demonstrably revived through the cycle of wind, cloud formation, and rain, so too will lifeless bodies be revived on the Day of Judgment. The repeated natural cycle of death and renewal in the physical world serves as a rational and experiential basis for believing in an event (resurrection) that lies beyond direct human experience. The verse implicitly critiques those who find resurrection difficult to believe by pointing to a parallel process they witness regularly and accept without question. The phrase 'thus is the Resurrection' (كذلك النشور) draws a direct conceptual equivalence between divine power manifest in nature and divine power that will be manifest in the afterlife, suggesting that the same God who orchestrates ecological renewal possesses the capacity to restore life to the dead. This reflects a broader Quranic rhetorical strategy of using the observable order and revival patterns in nature as signs (ayat) pointing to metaphysical truths that transcend ordinary sensory experience.

translation: Whoever desires honor [power] - then to Allah belongs all honor. To Him ascends good speech, and righteous deeds raise it up. But those who plot evil deeds will have a severe punishment, and the plotting of those - it will perish.
interpretation: This verse redirects the human pursuit of honor, status, and power away from worldly means toward God as the sole source of true dignity. It establishes a spiritual economy in which sincere words of faith and remembrance ("good speech") ascend to God, while righteous deeds act as the vehicle that elevates and validates that speech—suggesting that belief without corresponding action lacks the power to truly rise. The verse then contrasts this upward spiritual trajectory with the downward fate of those who scheme and plot evil: their machinations, however cleverly devised, are ultimately futile and self-destructive ("it will perish"), while they also face severe punishment.
