interpretation: This verse addresses the disbelievers on the Day of Resurrection, confronting them with the reality they had rejected during worldly life. The 'Day of Decision' (Yawm al-Fasl) refers to the Day when God will separate truth from falsehood, believers from disbelievers, and render final judgment on every soul. The address is direct and accusatory, emphasizing the irony that what they mocked and denied as myth or impossibility has now become their undeniable present reality. This serves as a powerful warning within the Qur'anic narrative about the certainty of resurrection and divine justice, reminding listeners that denial of eschatological truths does not negate their eventual occurrence. The verse functions rhetorically to validate the prophetic warnings given to disbelievers throughout their lives, now manifesting before them with inescapable clarity.

translation: Gather those who did wrong, and their companions/mates, and what they used to worship,
interpretation: This verse depicts a scene of the Day of Judgment in which a divine command is issued to the angels to assemble the wrongdoers—those who persisted in disbelief and injustice—together with their 'spouses' or counterparts, meaning those who shared and supported them in their wrongdoing or were of like disposition, as well as the false deities, idols, and objects they worshipped besides God. The purpose of this gathering is to confront them with the futility of what they relied upon: their idols and false objects of worship will be unable to help them or respond to their pleas, demonstrating the error of their ways and the justice of their punishment. It also emphasizes the principle of being grouped with those of similar beliefs and deeds in the Hereafter, underscoring the theme of accountability and the exposure of falsehood before divine justice.

translation: [Gather] those who, besides Allah, [were worshipped] - and guide them to the path of Hellfire.
interpretation: This verse is part of a command given to the angels on the Day of Judgment regarding the wrongdoers and the false deities or objects of worship they took besides Allah. The full context (from the preceding verse) is: 'Gather those who did wrong, their companions, and what they used to worship besides Allah, and guide them to the path of Hellfire.' This illustrates the complete reversal of expectations for polytheists on the Day of Judgment - the very things and beings they worshipped and relied upon instead of Allah, hoping for intercession or benefit, will instead be gathered together with them and will lead them, ironically, not to salvation but to the path leading to Hell. The guidance mentioned here is a bitter irony: just as the disbelievers sought 'guidance' and support from their false gods in worldly life, now that guidance literally directs them to their doom, emphasizing the futility and danger of shirk (associating partners with Allah) and the absolute powerlessness of anything worshipped besides the one true God.

translation: And stop them, for indeed they are to be questioned.
interpretation: This verse refers to the Day of Judgment, when the disbelievers and wrongdoers will be halted in their tracks—unable to proceed further—so that they may be interrogated about their beliefs, deeds, and the choices they made in worldly life. The command 'stop them' signifies a moment of forced accountability, where no soul can evade questioning about what it did, said, or believed. This echoes a broader Qur'anic theme that every person will be held responsible for their actions, and that on that Day, excuses and arrogance will give way to forced confrontation with truth. It serves as a warning to the living: a reminder that all deeds are recorded and that ultimate justice is inescapable, urging reflection and accountability in this life before the questioning of the next.

translation: What is the matter with you? Will you not help one another?
interpretation: This verse depicts a scene from the Day of Judgment in which the disbelievers, who in worldly life relied upon each other, their leaders, their idols, or their wealth and allies for support, find themselves utterly abandoned in the Hereafter. It is a rhetorical, mocking question posed to them—either by angels or by each other—highlighting their helplessness and the collapse of the false solidarity they once trusted. In this life they boasted of mutual support, factions, and powerful alliances against the truth, but on that Day, every soul is concerned only with itself, and no one can intercede or come to another's aid. The verse underscores the Qur'anic theme that worldly power structures, tribal loyalty, and collective arrogance against God's message will prove utterly worthless when true accountability arrives, exposing the illusion of self-sufficiency apart from reliance on God.

translation: Nay, but this Day they are in utter submission.
interpretation: This verse describes the state of disbelievers on the Day of Judgment, when the arrogance and defiance they displayed in worldly life collapse entirely. Those who once argued, denied the truth, and refused to submit to God's authority now find themselves utterly powerless and compliant, forced to accept the reality of divine judgment with no ability to resist or argue. The verse highlights the stark contrast between the false sense of control and independence people may feel in this life and the undeniable truth they face in the Hereafter, where all pretense and rebellion against God's will become impossible. It serves as a sobering reminder that ultimate submission to God is inevitable for everyone, and it is far better to submit willingly through faith in this world than to be compelled into submission when it is too late to benefit from it.

translation: And they will turn to one another, questioning each other.
interpretation: This verse depicts a scene on the Day of Judgment, where people—particularly those who followed misguidance or those who led others astray—turn to one another in mutual recrimination and questioning. Having faced the consequences of their choices and now standing before divine reckoning, they seek to understand how they arrived at this fate, often blaming one another for their misguidance. This mutual questioning reflects the breakdown of worldly alliances, friendships, and leader-follower relationships that once seemed strong but prove utterly powerless and meaningless in the face of divine judgment. It serves as a warning that on that Day, no one will be able to shift blame successfully, and the illusions of worldly power, status, or collective wrongdoing will dissolve into individual accountability before God.

translation: They will say: 'Indeed, you used to come to us from the right side.'
interpretation: This verse depicts a scene of mutual recrimination among the people of Hell. The followers address their leaders or those who misguided them, accusing them of having approached them 'from the right' — a phrase understood by commentators to mean approaching from the position of truth, authority, or trust, the direction from which oaths, good counsel, and sincere guidance are expected. By coming 'from the right,' the misguiders cloaked falsehood in the appearance of righteousness, using persuasive and seemingly trustworthy means to lead others astray from faith. This accusation reflects the human tendency to shift blame onto others for one's own choices, yet the Qur'an elsewhere clarifies that such excuses will not absolve anyone of personal responsibility, since each soul chose to follow misguidance despite having the capacity to discern truth from falsehood.

translation: They will say, 'Nay, you yourselves were not believers.'
interpretation: This verse occurs in Surah As-Saffat within a dramatic exchange that takes place on the Day of Judgment between those who were led astray and those who led them astray—often understood as followers and the leaders or false deities they once worshipped and obeyed. The followers will attempt to shift blame onto their misguiders, claiming they were deceived or coerced into disbelief. In response, those being blamed reject this excuse, asserting that the followers were not forced into disbelief but rather lacked true faith and conviction of their own accord. This exchange underscores a central Quranic theme: ultimate responsibility for one's faith and choices rests with the individual. No one will be able to deflect blame entirely onto others on the Day of Judgment, as each soul bears the consequences of its own willful rejection of truth or submission to misguidance. The verse serves as a sobering reminder that external influences, while real, do not absolve a person of their own agency and accountability for belief and disbelief.

translation: And we had no authority over you; rather, you were a transgressing people.
interpretation: This verse is part of a dialogue that will take place in the Hereafter between those who led others astray (such as devils, idols, or corrupt leaders) and their followers, as they argue and blame one another before punishment. The misleaders deny ultimate responsibility, asserting that they possessed no real power or compulsion over their followers—no coercive authority that forced anyone into disbelief or sin. Instead, they place the blame squarely on the followers themselves, describing them as 'taghoon' (transgressors who exceeded proper bounds), implying that their followers' own arrogance, rebelliousness, and willingness to transgress against truth made them receptive to misguidance. This highlights a core Quranic theme: that while Satan and corrupt leaders may entice and invite people toward evil, they cannot force belief or disbelief—human beings retain free will and moral agency, and are therefore accountable for the choices they freely make. It serves as a warning that one cannot excuse personal wrongdoing by shifting all blame onto external influences, since the capacity to resist temptation and transgression lies within each individual's own will and conscience.

translation: So the word of our Lord has come due upon us; indeed, we are to taste [the punishment].
interpretation: This verse depicts the confession of the misguided—those who followed falsehood and led others astray—on the Day of Judgment. Having been warned repeatedly in worldly life, they now acknowledge that God's decree of punishment has rightfully been fulfilled against them because of their persistent disbelief and transgression. The phrase 'we are to taste' conveys that the punishment is not merely something they will witness or hear about, but something they will directly experience in its full reality, as a just consequence of the choices they freely made. This admission underscores the Qur'anic theme that divine justice is inescapable, and that on that Day, all pretense, denial, and arrogance will give way to plain acknowledgment of truth.

translation: So We led you astray; indeed, we were ourselves astray.
interpretation: This verse appears in Surah Ash-Shu'ara within a dramatic Day of Judgment dialogue. It represents the confession of those who misled others—whether false deities, Satan, or arrogant leaders who were blindly followed—when confronted by their former followers. Having just heard their followers swear that they had been in clear error for equating these false objects of worship with the Lord of the worlds, the misleaders now admit the truth: they possessed no real power to guide or misguide anyone; rather, they themselves were lost in error, and their followers chose to follow them into that same error. This verse exposes the utter bankruptcy of blind following and idol worship—those who are worshipped or obeyed besides God have no true guidance to offer, since they themselves lack it. It also illustrates a central Quranic theme regarding accountability: on the Day of Judgment, the chain of blame unravels, for neither the leader nor the follower can fully shift responsibility onto the other, as both were complicit in turning away from truth. The leaders' admission does not exonerate them, nor does it remove guilt from the followers who chose to abandon their own reason and innate recognition of truth to follow the deluded.

translation: Indeed, on that Day they will all share in the punishment.
interpretation: This verse refers to the shared fate of wrongdoers and disbelievers, particularly those who led others astray and those who followed them, including false deities or leaders who were worshipped or obeyed instead of God. On the Day of Judgment, all who participated in disbelief and wrongdoing—whether as instigators or followers—will jointly share in the punishment, emphasizing the principle of collective accountability for those who colluded in sin. It underscores that any supposed power or alliance formed in worldly life, such as the false hope that idols or partners would intercede or help, will prove futile; instead, those who shared in disbelief will likewise share in suffering, highlighting divine justice that leaves no injustice unaddressed and no false companionship rewarded.

translation: Indeed, thus do We deal with the criminals.
interpretation: This verse appears in Surah As-Saffat as part of a passage describing the fate of disbelievers and wrongdoers on the Day of Judgment, following an account of mutual blame between the misguided followers and those who misled them. The statement serves as a divine affirmation that the punishment and humiliation described is the consistent and just consequence for those who persist in sin, rejection of truth, and corruption. The word 'mujrimin' (criminals/sinners) refers broadly to those who transgress divine law and reject guidance despite having access to it. This declaration emphasizes the principle of divine justice as a fixed law—God's treatment of wrongdoers is not arbitrary but follows a consistent pattern across all generations, reinforcing the idea that moral accountability and consequence are built into the fabric of creation. It also serves as a warning to the listener or reader, inviting reflection on one's own choices and the ultimate outcomes of persistent wrongdoing versus righteousness.

translation: Indeed, when it was said to them, 'There is no deity except Allah,' they were arrogant.
interpretation: This verse describes the psychological and spiritual disposition of the disbelievers who rejected faith not out of ignorance or lack of evidence, but out of pride and arrogance (istikbar). The declaration 'La ilaha illallah' (There is no deity but Allah) is the simplest and most fundamental call to monotheism, requiring only humility and submission to accept. Yet these individuals, often tied to inherited status, wealth, or tribal pride, refused to submit because doing so would mean acknowledging a power greater than themselves and abandoning the false gods or self-importance they had built their identities around. Their rejection stemmed from arrogance rather than genuine doubt, illustrating a recurring Qur'anic theme that the primary barrier to faith for many is not intellectual but moral—the unwillingness to lower oneself before truth when it threatens one's pride, status, or way of life. This verse serves as a warning that arrogance blinds people to even the clearest and simplest truths.

translation: And they said, "Are we to leave our gods for a mad poet?"
interpretation: This verse reflects the scornful reaction of the Meccan disbelievers to Prophet Muhammad's (peace be upon him) call to abandon idol worship and embrace monotheism. They dismissed him with the accusations commonly leveled against him—calling him a "poet" (implying his message was mere fabricated verse rather than divine revelation) and "mad" (implying he was not in his right mind). Their rhetorical question expresses incredulity and resistance to change, prioritizing ancestral traditions and inherited beliefs over the new message being presented. This verse illustrates a common pattern in the Qur'an where the disbelievers respond to prophetic messages not with reasoned arguments but with insults and dismissive characterizations, revealing their unwillingness to seriously engage with the message's content. Their defensiveness stems from the fact that accepting the message would require abandoning their gods, their social status derived from idol worship, and their forefathers' ways—a psychological and social cost they were unwilling to bear, so they attacked the messenger's character instead of addressing the substance of his call to monotheism.

translation: Rather, he has come with the truth and confirmed the messengers.
interpretation: This verse comes as a direct rebuttal to the disbelievers' accusations against the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him), who had been labeled a poet, a madman, or a fabricator in the verses preceding this one. The verse firmly asserts the opposite: far from being false or deluded, he arrived bearing the truth itself. Moreover, his message did not contradict or replace what came before but rather validated and confirmed the teachings of the earlier messengers and prophets. This establishes a continuity of divine revelation, positioning Muhammad's prophethood as the culmination and affirmation of a long line of messengers sent with the same essential truth—monotheism and submission to God. The verse serves both as a defense of the Prophet's integrity and as a theological statement about the unity and consistency of divine guidance throughout history.

translation: Indeed, you will taste the painful punishment.
interpretation: This verse is addressed to the wrongdoers and disbelievers, often in the context of those who rejected the truth, mocked the believers, or persisted in idolatry and sin. It serves as a solemn warning that the punishment awaiting them in the Hereafter is certain and unavoidable—described as 'الأليم' (painful) to emphasize its severity. The use of 'ذائقو' (tasters) conveys that they will directly experience and feel the consequences of their deeds, not merely hear of them. This phrase underscores the Qur'anic theme of divine justice: that mockery, arrogance, and disbelief in this worldly life will be met with inevitable retribution, reinforcing the moral accountability central to Islamic theology and serving as a deterrent for believers to remain steadfast in righteousness.

translation: And you will not be recompensed except for what you used to do.
interpretation: This verse establishes the divine principle of perfect justice in recompense, affirming that reward or punishment in the Hereafter is directly and solely tied to one's own deeds in worldly life. It eliminates any notion of arbitrary punishment or reward, emphasizing personal accountability—no soul bears the burden of another, and no one receives more or less than what their actions warrant. This serves as both a warning to the wrongdoers, whose suffering is self-earned through their choices, and a consolation to the righteous, whose reward is a just and fitting consequence of their faith and good works. It underscores the coherence of divine justice, where the Hereafter is not an arbitrary judgment but a natural, fair outcome mirroring the moral quality of one's earthly conduct.

translation: Except the sincere servants of Allah.
interpretation: This phrase appears in Surah As-Saffat as an exception clause following descriptions of the punishment and misguidance that will befall most of humanity, particularly those who followed Satan or worshipped false deities. The 'sincere servants of Allah' (al-mukhlaseen) refers to those believers whose devotion to God is pure, undivided, and free from hypocrisy or ulterior motives. These are individuals whom Satan himself acknowledged he could not mislead, as mentioned elsewhere in the Quran (15:40, 38:83), because their sincerity and complete devotion to God serves as a protection against spiritual corruption and deviation. This verse establishes a crucial theological distinction between the general mass of people who may fall into error, polytheism, or disbelief, and a select group whose authentic, wholehearted submission to God exempts them from the consequences described in the surrounding verses. The concept of ikhlas (sincerity/purity of intention) is central to Islamic spirituality, representing the highest form of worship where one's devotion is entirely for God's sake alone, without seeking worldly recognition, reward, or being swayed by desires or external pressures.

translation: Those will have a known provision.
interpretation: This verse refers to the sincere, devoted servants of Allah mentioned in the preceding verses of Surah As-Saffat—those who were saved from punishment and granted Paradise. The 'known provision' (rizq ma'lum) signifies the specific, pre-ordained sustenance and blessings awaiting them in the afterlife, distinguished by its certainty and quality. Unlike the uncertain and fleeting provisions of worldly life, this provision is described as 'known' to emphasize its guaranteed nature—promised by Allah and free from any doubt, interruption, or diminishment. Classical commentators suggest this refers to the delights of Paradise that will be recognizable and familiar to its inhabitants, including fruits and sustenance that arrive at set times, in contrast to the toil and labor required to obtain provision in this worldly life. The verse serves as a reassurance to believers of the reward that awaits those who maintain sincere devotion to Allah, resist misguidance, and remain steadfast in faith despite worldly trials.

translation: Fruits [of all kinds] - and they will be honored.
interpretation: This verse describes the blessed state of the righteous believers in Paradise. It appears in a passage describing the rewards awaiting the people of faith, often identified in exegesis with the righteous servants of God. The mention of 'fruits' signifies the sensory, abundant pleasures and delights that await them - a provision requiring no labor or toil, freely given as a gift. More significantly, the phrase 'and they will be honored' (مكرمون) elevates the description beyond mere physical enjoyment. It emphasizes their dignified status - they are not merely served or rewarded, but held in honor by God Himself. This honor encompasses being welcomed with respect, served by attendants, seated in positions of nobility, and treated with the dignity befitting those who remained faithful during their worldly trials. The pairing of material delight with spiritual/social honor reflects the Qur'anic vision of Paradise as a complete reward - satisfying both physical desires and the deeper human need for recognition, respect, and honored status, contrasting sharply with the humiliation and disgrace that awaits the wrongdoers in the verses that typically surround this passage.

translation: In gardens of bliss (delight).
interpretation: This phrase describes the eternal reward awaiting the righteous in Paradise. 'Jannat al-Na'im' (Gardens of Bliss) refers specifically to the highest state of comfort, pleasure, and contentment granted to believers, free from any hardship, grief, or deficiency. It emphasizes that the joy experienced there is not merely physical but encompasses complete spiritual and emotional fulfillment—a state where every need is met and every desire for goodness is satisfied, as a direct reward from God for faith and righteous deeds performed in the worldly life.

translation: Upon couches, facing one another.
interpretation: This verse depicts the people of Paradise reclining on thrones or couches arranged so that they face each other, symbolizing the perfected social harmony of the afterlife. Unlike worldly gatherings marked by rivalry, envy, hidden resentment, or hierarchy, the believers in Paradise sit as equals in mutual love and companionship. The imagery of facing one another emphasizes intimacy, open fellowship, and the absence of all malice that God removes from their hearts (as mentioned in nearby verses). It reflects an ideal community bound by brotherhood, free from the social tensions that marked their earthly lives, enjoying eternal companionship in comfort and honor.

translation: There will be circulated among them a cup from a flowing spring.
interpretation: This verse describes a scene of paradise in which the righteous are served drink from a pure, ever-flowing spring, poured into cups that are passed around among them by attendants. The imagery emphasizes continuous abundance and effortless enjoyment—there is no need to seek or labor for refreshment, as it is brought directly to the inhabitants of paradise. The 'flowing spring' (ma'in) suggests a source that is clear, pure, and inexhaustible, unlike earthly drinks that may spoil or run out. This reflects the Qur'anic theme that the rewards of paradise are free from the imperfections and limitations of worldly pleasures—later verses clarify that this drink, unlike wine on earth, causes no headache or intoxication-induced sin, symbolizing a purified, perfected form of joy and camaraderie among the believers in the afterlife.

translation: White, delicious to those who drink it.
interpretation: This phrase is part of a description of the rivers of wine promised to the righteous in Paradise (found in Surah As-Saffat, 37:46). Unlike earthly wine, which can be murky or cause negative effects, this heavenly drink is described as pure white in color and purely pleasurable to consume. The verse emphasizes that the wine of Paradise is free from the drawbacks associated with worldly intoxicants—there is no headache, no loss of reason, and no sickness that follows, as clarified in the subsequent verses. This represents the perfected, flawless nature of all pleasures in the afterlife, where physical delights are granted without any accompanying harm or negative consequence, contrasting sharply with the imperfect nature of worldly indulgences.

translation: No headiness (or harm) is in it, nor will they be intoxicated (lose their senses) from it.
interpretation: This verse describes the wine of Paradise, contrasting it sharply with worldly wine. Unlike earthly intoxicants, which cause headaches, sickness, loss of reason, and regret, the drink offered to the believers in Paradise brings only pure pleasure without any negative physical or mental consequence. The absence of 'ghoul' (harm, headache, or corrupting effect) and the fact that the believers will not become stupefied or lose control of their senses signifies the perfected, flawless nature of divine rewards—pleasures free from the defects and dangers inherent in worldly equivalents. It reflects a broader Qur'anic theme that the delights of Paradise are purified versions of worldly pleasures, granted without sin, harm, or impairment, allowing the righteous to enjoy them in a state of full awareness, dignity, and companionship as suggested by the following verses.

translation: And with them will be maidens of modest gaze, with beautiful, wide eyes.
interpretation: This verse describes one of the rewards for the righteous believers in Paradise (Jannah). It depicts companions characterized by two key qualities: 'qasirat al-tarf' (restrained or modest of gaze), meaning they look at none but their husbands, embodying chastity, devotion, and purity of heart; and 'in' (having wide, beautiful eyes), a classical Arabic description of beauty. Beyond the physical description, classical commentators (such as Ibn Kathir and Al-Tabari) emphasize that this verse speaks to the perfection of companionship in Paradise—a relationship free from jealousy, wandering desire, or impurity, in contrast to the imperfections of worldly relationships. It symbolizes the complete contentment, loyalty, and tranquility that await the inhabitants of Paradise, where physical beauty is matched by purity of character and faithfulness.

translation: As if they were eggs well-protected (hidden from sight/touch).
interpretation: This verse is part of a Qur'anic depiction of the rewards awaiting the righteous in Paradise, describing the companions (houris) granted to the believers. The comparison to 'hidden eggs' evokes an image of pristine, delicate purity—something carefully shielded from dust, blemish, or any external contact, much like an egg protected beneath a bird's wing. The simile conveys qualities of untouched beauty, modesty, and preciousness, suggesting these companions possess a flawless, luminous complexion and a protected chastity, never having been exposed or touched before. The imagery draws on something familiar and tender from the natural world to convey an otherworldly perfection, emphasizing purity and sheltered delicacy as ideals of beauty in the Qur'anic depiction of Paradise.

translation: Then they will turn to one another, questioning each other.
interpretation: This verse depicts a scene from the Day of Judgment or the aftermath of divine reckoning, where those who had been companions, followers, or accomplices in wrongdoing on earth turn to each other in mutual recrimination and bewilderment. The act of 'questioning each other' suggests a moment of reckoning where false certainties collapse, and people seek to understand who led whom astray, who is to blame, and how they arrived at their dire situation. It captures the psychological unraveling of those who placed trust in worldly alliances, false leaders, or misguided beliefs, only to find in the Hereafter that such bonds offer no refuge or answers. The mutual questioning symbolizes the isolation of each soul in the face of judgment, despite the human tendency to seek solidarity in blame-shifting, ultimately underscoring the Quranic theme that each person bears individual responsibility for their choices and will stand accountable alone before God, regardless of the company they kept in life.

translation: A speaker among them said, 'Indeed, I had a companion [in worldly life].'
interpretation: This verse is part of a scene depicting the people of Paradise conversing with one another, reflecting on their past lives. One of them recalls having had a close companion in the worldly life who used to doubt and mock the idea of resurrection and divine judgment. This sets up the following verses where he recounts his companion's skepticism and then looks down to see that companion's fate in Hell, illustrating the vast difference in outcomes between those who believed and remained steadfast and those who denied the Hereafter. The verse highlights themes of companionship, the influence of one's associates on faith, and the ultimate accountability each soul faces based on the choices made in life, regardless of worldly relationships or social pressures to disbelieve.

translation: He says, 'Are you indeed among those who believe [in resurrection]?'
interpretation: This verse depicts a scene in Paradise where one of its righteous inhabitants recalls a companion he had in worldly life—a skeptic who used to mock him for believing in resurrection and the Day of Judgment. The words quoted here are those of that skeptical companion, who incredulously questioned the believer's faith in an afterlife, considering it an irrational or fanciful conviction. The verse serves to highlight the stark contrast between the fate of the disbeliever, who denied the truth of resurrection, and the believer, who is now enjoying the rewards of Paradise, thereby vindicating his faith. It underscores a broader Qur'anic theme: those who mocked and doubted the believers' certainty in divine justice and the afterlife will ultimately witness the truth of what they once dismissed, often from a position of eternal regret or torment, while the faithful are shown to have been vindicated and rewarded for their conviction despite worldly ridicule.

translation: [He will say], 'Is it [true] that when we die and become dust and bones, we will indeed be recompensed?'
interpretation: This verse is part of a dialogue recounted in Surah As-Saffat, where a believer in Paradise recalls the skeptical words once spoken by a companion during their earthly life. The rhetorical question captures the disbelief and incredulity that many held toward the concept of resurrection and divine judgment—viewing it as implausible that after decomposing into dust and bones, human beings could be brought back to life to face accountability for their deeds. The verse highlights the materialist mindset that denies an afterlife on the grounds that physical decay seems irreversible and final. By placing this skepticism in the past tense as something 'used to be said,' the verse implicitly contrasts this doubt with the reality the speaker now experiences in the Hereafter, underscoring the Qur'anic theme that resurrection, however difficult to imagine, is within God's power and is indeed the truth that doubters will ultimately confront.

translation: He will say, 'Will you look down [with me]?'
interpretation: This verse occurs in Surah As-Saffat within a scene depicting the people of Paradise. One of the believers, recalling a companion he had in worldly life who used to mock him for believing in the Resurrection and the Day of Judgment, invites his companions in Paradise to look down with him so he can see what became of that former companion. This moment highlights the dramatic reversal of fortunes between the believer and the disbeliever: the one who was mocked for his faith is now honored in Paradise, while the one who mocked him is shown to be suffering in Hell. The verse sets up the next verses where the believer looks down and sees his companion in the midst of the Fire, serving as a powerful illustration of divine justice and the ultimate vindication of faith over worldly skepticism and ridicule.

translation: Then he will look and see him in the midst of the Blazing Fire.
interpretation: This verse is part of a scene in Paradise where one of its righteous inhabitants recalls a companion he had in worldly life who used to mock him for his belief in the Resurrection and Judgment. The believer, now enjoying the bliss of Paradise, looks down and peers into Hell to see what became of his former companion, and finds him suffering in the depths of the Blazing Fire. This dramatic contrast illustrates the ultimate reversal of fortunes between those who believed and remained patient in faith and those who denied and mocked the truth. It serves as a vivid reminder of divine justice, showing how the deniers' arrogance and mockery in this life will be answered with eternal regret, while the believers' patience will be rewarded with the ability to witness, and perhaps even feel gratitude or relief, at having been spared the fate of the wrongdoers.

translation: He said, 'By Allah, you almost ruined me!'
interpretation: This verse is part of a narrative in Surah As-Saffat (37:56) depicting a dialogue among the people of Paradise. One of the believers recalls a companion he had in worldly life who used to mock and deny the Resurrection and the Day of Judgment. Now, from the vantage point of Paradise, the believer addresses this concept, reflecting on how close he came to being led astray by his companion's skepticism and denial of the afterlife. The phrase 'By Allah, you almost ruined me' conveys the gravity of the near-miss—had he followed his companion's doubts and disbelief, he too would have faced perdition rather than salvation. This serves as a powerful reminder of the real spiritual danger posed by companionship with those who deny faith and mock sacred truths, and it underscores the theme of accountability: that the choices of belief or disbelief, and the influences we allow into our lives, have eternal consequences. The verse also illustrates the joy and relief of the saved soul recognizing how perilously close he came to following a destructive path, now safely in Paradise while his former companion faces a different fate.

translation: And were it not for the favor of my Lord, I would have been among those brought [to punishment].
interpretation: This verse is spoken by a believer in Paradise, recounting to his companions the story of a disbelieving friend he had in worldly life who mocked and doubted the resurrection and the Day of Judgment. Looking down and seeing that former companion now in the midst of the Hellfire, the believer reflects with humility and gratitude that he himself could very easily have been swayed by his companion's doubts and arguments against faith, and consequently could have ended up condemned alongside him. He attributes his salvation not to his own merit, cleverness, or strength of argument, but entirely to Allah's grace and favor (ni'mah) upon him, which guided and preserved him in true belief. This underscores a central theological point: steadfastness in faith is itself a divine blessing, not something one can take credit for or guarantee, and even a person of faith remains constantly dependent on God's mercy to avoid the fate of those who reject truth. It serves as a counsel of humility rather than arrogance toward the believer's good outcome, whilst also implicitly highlighting the serious peril of succumbing to persistent doubt and mockery regarding core matters of faith such as resurrection and divine justice.

translation: Then, are we not to die
interpretation: This verse is part of a conversation among the believers in Paradise, who marvel at their eternal bliss after recalling their earthly life and a companion who used to doubt resurrection. Having been granted salvation, they ask each other in astonished gratitude whether death—other than the one death they already experienced in the worldly life—is truly behind them forever. This rhetorical question expresses overwhelming relief and joy at the permanence of their blessed state: no further death awaits them, and (as the following verse confirms) no punishment will touch them. It underscores the Qur'anic theme that the hereafter is the realm of eternity, where the fleeting nature of worldly existence is replaced by everlasting life for those who merited Paradise, in stark contrast to the finality of a single death they underwent in the world before being resurrected to eternal reward.

translation: Except our first death, and we are not to be punished?
interpretation: This verse captures the astonished and grateful exclamation of the people of Paradise as they reflect on their eternal state. Having been rescued from the Fire and granted everlasting bliss, they marvel at the fact that death itself is now behind them—they experienced it only once, in the worldly life, and will never taste it again. Moreover, they recognize that they are forever secure from punishment. This rhetorical questioning format underscores their disbelief at their own good fortune, turning to one another in wonder and joy, confirming among themselves that their blessed state is permanent and not fleeting. It reflects a broader Quranic theme of contrasting the finality of worldly death with the eternity of the Hereafter, reminding listeners that true life without end is reserved for those who attain Paradise, and that earthly death, once passed through, gives way to a state beyond further mortality or suffering for the righteous.

translation: Indeed, this is the great triumph.
interpretation: This verse appears at the culmination of descriptions of the rewards granted to the righteous in Paradise—safety, eternal bliss, nearness to God, and deliverance from the Fire. By declaring this state to be 'the great triumph,' the Qur'an redefines what true success means, shifting the standard away from worldly gain, status, or power toward eternal salvation and divine favor in the Hereafter. It serves as a rhetorical seal, inviting reflection on the transient nature of earthly achievements compared to the everlasting reward of righteousness. The emphatic structure of the Arabic (إن...لهو) underscores certainty and intensity, assuring believers that the ultimate measure of success lies not in this life's fleeting victories but in attaining God's pleasure and eternal felicity.

translation: For the like of this let the workers work.
interpretation: This phrase occurs at the end of the depiction of the believers' reward in Paradise in Surat as-Saffat (37:61), following the vivid description of the fruits, drink, and companionship enjoyed by the righteous in the gardens of bliss. It serves as a rhetorical call to action, urging that the ultimate goal worth striving and competing for in life is not worldly gain, status, or fleeting pleasure, but the eternal reward that God has prepared for those who are faithful and righteous. The verse functions as a motivational conclusion, inviting the listener to reflect on the described reward and then to reorient their efforts, labor, and ambitions in this worldly life toward earning that everlasting outcome. It emphasizes that true effort and competition among people should be directed toward righteous deeds that lead to salvation and divine pleasure, rather than toward transient worldly achievements.

translation: Is that [Paradise] a better accommodation, or the tree of Zaqqum?
interpretation: This verse employs a rhetorical question to draw a stark contrast between the eternal bliss of Paradise, described in the preceding verses, and the torment of Hell, symbolized by the tree of Zaqqum. The Zaqqum tree, which grows from the bottom of Hellfire, produces fruit likened to the heads of devils, and it serves as the only sustenance for the people of Hell, causing them excruciating pain rather than nourishment. By posing this comparison, the verse invites reflection on the consequences of one's choices in worldly life—emphasizing that the righteous who believe and do good deeds are rewarded with everlasting gardens of delight, while those who reject faith and persist in wrongdoing face a reality of suffering and despair. The rhetorical nature of the question underscores the absurdity of equating these two vastly different outcomes, reinforcing the Quranic theme of divine justice and the ultimate accountability of human actions.

translation: Indeed, We have made it a trial for the wrongdoers.
interpretation: This verse refers to the tree of Zaqqum, a tree that grows from the depths of Hellfire, as mentioned in the surrounding verses of Surah As-Saffat. The 'trial' or 'fitnah' refers to the fact that the disbelievers in Mecca mocked and disbelieved in the existence of this tree, finding it absurd that any tree could grow in the fire, since fire typically consumes vegetation. Their rejection of this concept became a test of their faith, highlighting their arrogance in applying worldly logic to matters of the unseen (ghayb) and divine power. The verse underscores that for the wrongdoers, even clear signs and warnings from God become occasions for increased disbelief and mockery, demonstrating how their own arrogance and denial serve as a trial that deepens their heedlessness and ultimately contributes to their punishment, as they will be forced to eat from this very tree they once ridiculed.

translation: Indeed, it is a tree that grows from the depths of Hellfire.
interpretation: This verse refers to the tree of Zaqqum, mentioned in the Qur'an as a form of torment for the inhabitants of Hell. Its description—growing from the very root of the Hellfire—emphasizes its unnatural and horrific nature, contrasting sharply with the fruit-bearing trees of Paradise that provide nourishment and pleasure to the righteous. The Zaqqum tree serves as a vivid symbol of divine justice, illustrating that the sustenance of the wrongdoers in the afterlife will be as bitter and tormenting as their deeds were in worldly life. It is part of a broader Qur'anic rhetorical strategy that uses contrasting imagery of Paradise and Hell to impress upon believers the consequences of their moral choices, reinforcing the theme of accountability and the vivid, almost sensory nature of eschatological recompense.

translation: Its emerging fruit is as if it were the heads of devils.
interpretation: This verse describes the tree of Zaqqum, which grows from the depths of Hellfire and serves as a torment for its inhabitants, who are forced to eat from it. The comparison of its fruit to the 'heads of devils' is a powerful rhetorical device rather than a literal physical description. Since no one has actually seen the heads of devils, the comparison works by evoking the hideousness, ugliness, and terror associated with devils in the human imagination. The Arabs often used such imagery to describe things of extreme repulsiveness, drawing on the psychological association between devils/Shayateen and horror, evil, and monstrosity. By invoking this image, the verse conveys the monstrous, repugnant nature of this infernal tree and its fruit in the most vivid way possible, emphasizing that nothing about Hell's sustenance offers any relief, comfort, or nourishment—quite the opposite of the delightful fruits of Paradise described elsewhere in the Qur'an. This serves as a stark contrast to reinforce the consequences of disbelief and sin, making the torment of Hell more viscerally imaginable to the listener.

translation: Then indeed, they will eat from it (the tree of Zaqqum), and fill with it their bellies.
interpretation: This verse is part of a description of the punishment awaiting the people of error and denial in Hellfire, specifically describing the tree of Zaqqum. Unlike nourishing food that sustains and satisfies, this infernal tree represents a form of torment disguised as sustenance—the damned are compelled to eat from it, filling their stomachs with something that brings no nutrition, pleasure, or relief, but instead causes burning agony and will later require them to drink scalding, festering water. The imagery emphasizes the inversion of worldly comforts: what should nourish instead torments, illustrating the complete reversal of fortune for those who rejected faith and indulged in worldly pleasures without regard for the Hereafter. The verse serves as a stark warning, contrasting the fate of the disbelievers with the delightful fruits and provisions promised to the righteous in Paradise, reinforcing the Qur'anic theme of divine justice where actions in this life directly shape one's experience in the next.

translation: Then indeed, they will have after it [i.e., after eating from the tree of Zaqqum] a mixture of scalding water.
interpretation: This verse continues the Qur'an's depiction of the torment awaiting the people of Hell, specifically those who deny the Day of Judgment and persist in disbelief and sin. After describing how the damned are forced to eat from the tree of Zaqqum—a tree growing from the depths of Hellfire whose fruit resembles the heads of devils and which fills their bellies with bitterness—this verse adds a further torment: they are then given a scalding, boiling drink mixed with their food, which only intensifies their suffering rather than offering any relief. The imagery serves as a stark warning, reversing the comforts of worldly feasting and drinking into instruments of punishment, emphasizing that the pleasures the disbelievers sought and indulged in during their earthly lives will be inverted into torment in the Hereafter. It underscores the totality and relentlessness of divine retribution for those who rejected truth and mocked the warnings of the prophets.

translation: Then indeed, their return will be to the Blazing Fire (Hellfire).
interpretation: This verse comes in the context of Surah As-Saffat's description of the fate of the wrongdoers and deniers, particularly those who followed misguided ancestors and were deceived by false leaders. After describing their indulgence in disputation while facing the tree of Zaqqum and their fate in the Hereafter, this verse emphasizes the inevitability and certainty of their punishment. The phrase 'ثم إن' (then indeed) signals a continuation of their fate after whatever temporary respite or worldly pleasure they experienced—ultimately, despite any delay, their final and definite destination remains the Hellfire. This underscores a central Quranic theme: that disbelief and following falsehood without accountability leads inevitably to divine punishment, no matter how events unfold in the interim. The verse serves as a stark warning that worldly life, however it progresses, cannot alter the ultimate reckoning awaiting those who reject truth and guidance.

translation: Indeed, they found their fathers astray.
interpretation: This verse exposes the flawed reasoning behind blind imitation of ancestral traditions. It addresses those who justify their rejection of divine guidance by appealing to the practices of their forefathers, without examining whether those practices were actually correct. The verse reveals that their fathers themselves were misguided, meaning the entire chain of inherited belief was built upon error rather than truth or sound reasoning. This highlights a recurring Qur'anic critique of unreflective traditionalism—following a path simply because it was inherited, rather than evaluating it through reason, evidence, or revelation. It underscores the principle that ancestral custom alone carries no inherent authority or legitimacy; truth must be assessed on its own merits, not merely accepted because it was 'always done this way.' The verse serves as a broader caution against intellectual complacency and the uncritical transmission of error across generations.

translation: So they rush eagerly in their footsteps (following them).
interpretation: This verse continues the Qur'an's critique of blind imitation (taqlid) of ancestors without critical examination. The preceding verses describe how previous disbelieving generations found their forefathers astray in misguidance, yet rather than pausing to question or reflect, they eagerly and hastily rushed to follow in those same footsteps. The word 'يُهْرَعُونَ' conveys a sense of being driven or hurried, almost involuntarily, suggesting a lack of independent thought—an unreflective, almost compulsive attachment to inherited tradition and ancestral ways, even when those ways lead to falsehood. This serves as a broader warning against following customs, beliefs, or practices merely because they were passed down, without examining their truth or validity. It highlights a recurring theme in the Qur'an: that mere ancestral precedent is not sufficient justification for belief or practice, and that true guidance requires conscious reflection and verification rather than hasty, unthinking conformity to what came before.

translation: And indeed, most of the former peoples went astray before them.
interpretation: This verse comes within a passage of Surah As-Saffat that addresses the recurring pattern of disbelief throughout human history. It serves as a consolation and explanation to the Prophet Muhammad regarding the obstinate rejection he faced from his own people: their refusal to accept monotheism was not a new or unique phenomenon, but rather a continuation of the same error committed by the majority of earlier nations and civilizations. The verse establishes a principle that straying from truth and following ancestral traditions blindly has historically been the condition of the majority, not the minority, while true guidance has always been embraced by only a faithful few who resist the pull of inherited falsehood. This sets the stage for the subsequent verses, which recount specific examples of earlier prophets—like Noah, Abraham, and others—who were sent as warners to their respective peoples, most of whom rejected the message, establishing a pattern that connects the plight of previous prophets with that of Muhammad, reinforcing that divine guidance has always encountered widespread resistance from the majority while preserving a righteous remnant who heed the warning.

translation: And We had certainly sent among them warners.
interpretation: This verse affirms God's consistent pattern of mercy and justice toward previous nations, particularly those destroyed for their wrongdoing, such as the people mentioned in the preceding verses (like the people of Lot or similar punished communities). Before any divine punishment was sent, God ensured that warners (prophets and messengers) were dispatched to these communities to caution them about the consequences of their disbelief and immoral conduct, and to call them back to righteousness. This establishes a key theological principle: God does not punish a people without first providing them clear guidance and warning, leaving no excuse for those who reject the message. The verse underscores divine justice—accountability only follows after the truth has been conveyed—and serves as a reminder to the Prophet Muhammad's audience that they too have received warners, making their rejection of the message inexcusable.

translation: So observe how was the end of those who were warned.
interpretation: This verse serves as a call to reflection, inviting the listener to contemplate the fate of peoples who received divine warnings through their prophets but persisted in disbelief and rejection. The phrase refers to communities such as the people of Noah, Lot, or others mentioned in the Quran's narratives, who were given clear warnings about the consequences of their wrongdoing yet chose to ignore them. Their eventual destruction serves as a historical and moral lesson for future generations, demonstrating that divine warnings are not empty threats but carry real consequences for those who reject guidance. The verse functions rhetorically as a bridge between narrative and moral instruction, using the specific fate of past nations to draw a universal principle about the relationship between warning, rejection, and consequence that applies to all people across time, including the verse's immediate audience.

translation: Except the chosen servants of Allah.
interpretation: This phrase appears as an exception clause in several places in the Qur'an, most notably in Surah As-Saffat, following descriptions of the misguided who follow Satan and face punishment, or amid condemnations of those who make false claims about Allah (such as attributing daughters to Him, as the pagan Arabs did with angels). The verse carves out an exception for 'the sincere, chosen servants of Allah'—those who have purified their devotion exclusively for Him, free from polytheism, hypocrisy, and whims of the self. These are the ones protected from Satan's deception and from the misguidance that befalls the rest of humanity. Their sincerity (ikhlas) is the very quality that secures their immunity from ruin, as Satan himself concedes in the Qur'an that he has no power over Allah's sincere servants. The phrase underscores a central Qur'anic theme: that purity of intention and devotion directed solely to Allah is the believer's true protection and the mark that distinguishes the saved from the doomed.

translation: And indeed, Noah called upon Us, and [how] excellent are We as responders [to prayer].
interpretation: This verse commemorates the moment when Prophet Noah, after enduring centuries of rejection, mockery, and disbelief from his people, finally turned to God in heartfelt supplication, asking for deliverance and divine judgment upon those who refused to heed his message. The verse emphasizes God's immediate and perfect responsiveness to the prayers of His sincere servants, especially those who have been patient through great trials. It serves as a reassurance to believers that no matter how dire the circumstances or how long the struggle, God hears and answers the call of those who remain steadfast in faith and turn to Him in their moment of need. The phrase 'best of responders' underscores not just God's willingness to respond, but the perfection and timeliness of His response, as He subsequently saved Noah, his family, and the believers through the Ark while delivering justice upon the disbelieving nation.

translation: And We saved him and his family from the great distress.
interpretation: This verse refers to Prophet Nuh (Noah) and his deliverance, along with his believing family, from the overwhelming flood that destroyed his disbelieving people. The 'great affliction' (al-karb al-'azim) signifies not only the physical calamity of the deluge but also the prolonged years of hardship, rejection, and mockery Nuh endured while calling his people to faith. His salvation represents a broader divine principle: that God rescues His sincere, patient servants from calamity when all worldly means of escape seem exhausted. The verse underscores that true deliverance comes through unwavering faith and reliance on God, especially when facing overwhelming adversity from one's own community. It also distinguishes between Nuh's household of faith and those who, despite blood ties, rejected the truth and were not included among the saved—emphasizing that spiritual kinship through belief surpasses mere familial bonds in matters of ultimate salvation.

translation: And We made his descendants the survivors (those who remained/endured).
interpretation: This verse refers to Prophet Noah (Nuh), peace be upon him, following the account of the flood. After the destruction of the disbelievers who rejected his message, Allah preserved Noah and those who believed with him in the ark, and decreed that it is specifically his descendants who would continue as humanity's lineage afterward. This establishes Noah as a second father of mankind, since all subsequent generations trace back through his surviving offspring. The verse underscores a recurring Qur'anic theme: that divine justice results in the destruction of corrupt and rejecting peoples, while the righteous and their lineage are preserved and granted continuity. It also highlights Allah's sovereignty over generational succession and history, showing that the perpetuation of human civilization after the flood was by divine decree and favor upon Noah for his faith and perseverance in conveying the message despite centuries of rejection.

translation: And We left for him [a mention of praise] among later generations.
interpretation: This verse refers to Prophet Noah (Nuh), following the account of his deliverance from the flood and the destruction of the disbelievers. God grants him an enduring legacy of honor and remembrance among all subsequent generations and nations, meaning that Noah's name, story, and righteous reputation would be preserved and praised by peoples who came after him, across different faiths and cultures. This is part of a recurring pattern in these verses of Surah As-Saffat, where several prophets (Noah, Abraham, Moses, Aaron, etc.) are described as having been granted lasting praise and remembrance in later generations, emphasizing that steadfast faith and righteousness result in an eternal positive legacy that transcends one's own lifetime, serving as a divine reward and a lesson for humanity about the enduring nature of truth and righteousness against falsehood and corruption.

translation: Peace be upon Noah among all the worlds (peoples).
interpretation: This verse is part of a recurring refrain in Surah As-Saffat where God bestows eternal peace and honorable remembrance upon His prophets who remained steadfast in faith and delivered their message despite great hardship. By declaring 'peace upon Noah among all the worlds,' God establishes that Noah's legacy would be preserved with praise and blessing across all nations and generations, not merely in his own time. This reflects a broader Quranic theme: that those who patiently endure trials in service of truth and righteousness are granted lasting honor that transcends the limitations of a single era or people. Noah's story—his centuries of patient preaching, his endurance of mockery and rejection, and his ultimate deliverance alongside the believers during the flood—serves as a model of steadfastness. The universal nature of this peace ('in all the worlds') signifies that his example and the gratitude owed to him for his perseverance is recognized by all of creation, and that divine commendation is not limited by time or geography but becomes a permanent part of how humanity remembers righteous figures who upheld God's call against immense opposition.

translation: Indeed, thus do We reward the doers of good.
interpretation: This verse affirms a divine principle of recompense: those who excel in righteousness, faith, and good deeds—exemplified in the preceding narrative (commonly understood to refer to the story of Prophet Yusuf or similar accounts of prophets tested and then rewarded)—will be granted reward, honor, and favor by God. The phrase establishes a universal law rather than a one-time event: ihsan (excellence in conduct, sincerity, and devotion) is met with divine generosity and elevation in status, both in this world and the hereafter. It serves as both a reassurance to believers that virtuous conduct is never in vain, and as a subtle exhortation to strive for ihsan, since it is the quality that merits God's special favor and reward.

translation: Indeed, he was among Our believing servants.
interpretation: This phrase is used in Surah As-Saffat as a recurring affirmation following accounts of various prophets (such as Noah, Abraham, and others), serving as Allah's seal of approval on their faith and righteousness. It establishes that true honor and distinction in the sight of Allah comes not from lineage, wealth, or worldly status, but from sincere faith (iman) and devoted servitude ('ibadah) to Him. By repeating this declaration after each prophet's story, the Qur'an creates a unifying thread showing that all prophets, despite facing different trials and opposition from their peoples, shared this fundamental characteristic of being devoted believing servants of Allah. This serves as a model for all believers, reminding them that their ultimate identity and worth is rooted in their relationship with God through faith and submission, and that perseverance through trials while maintaining this faith leads to divine commendation.

translation: Then We drowned the rest (the others).
interpretation: This verse refers to the climactic destruction of a disbelieving people who rejected a prophet's message—most commonly understood in the context of Pharaoh and his army being drowned in the sea after refusing Moses, or alternatively the disbelievers from Noah's nation who were destroyed by the flood while the believers were saved. The phrase 'the others' or 'the rest' signifies those who remained in disbelief after the righteous had been delivered, emphasizing a pattern in the Qur'an where salvation is granted to the faithful while divine punishment falls upon those who persist in rejecting truth. This serves as a sobering reminder of accountability: God's mercy extends to those who heed warnings, while those who arrogantly dismiss divine guidance face inevitable consequences. The verse functions within a broader narrative structure in the Qur'an that recounts the destruction of past nations as a lesson for the Prophet Muhammad's contemporaries and all future generations, illustrating the recurring theme that disbelief and moral corruption lead to downfall, regardless of how powerful or resistant to change a nation might seem.

translation: And indeed, among those who followed his [Noah's] way was Abraham.
interpretation: This verse establishes a spiritual lineage connecting Abraham to Noah, indicating that Abraham followed in the same tradition of monotheistic faith and submission to God that Noah had established. The word 'shi'atihi' (his party/sect/way) suggests that despite the passage of generations, Abraham inherited and continued the same fundamental message of pure monotheism (tawhid) that Noah had preached to his people. This connection emphasizes the continuity of prophetic mission throughout history - that all prophets, despite coming to different peoples at different times, were united in calling humanity to the same essential truth of worshipping one God alone. It also serves to validate Abraham's later confrontation with his idol-worshipping people and his father, showing that his monotheistic stance was not a novel innovation but part of an unbroken chain of true guidance transmitted from earlier prophets like Noah.

translation: When he came to his Lord with a sound heart.
interpretation: This verse refers to Prophet Ibrahim (Abraham) and describes the purity of his heart and faith as he turned to God. A 'sound heart' (qalb saleem) signifies a heart free from doubt, idolatry, hypocrisy, and spiritual corruption—one devoted entirely to the worship of the One God. This quality is what enabled Ibrahim to confront his father and his people's idolatry, to reject false gods, and to willingly submit to God's commands, including the test of sacrificing his son. The sound heart represents the ideal spiritual state that the Qur'an holds up as the key to salvation, as reinforced elsewhere in the Qur'an (26:88-89) where it states that on the Day of Judgment, neither wealth nor children will benefit anyone except one who comes to God with a sound heart. Thus, this verse establishes Ibrahim as an exemplar of sincere, unwavering faith and moral integrity rooted in inner purity rather than outward show.

translation: When he said to his father and his people, 'What do you worship?'
interpretation: This verse marks the beginning of Prophet Ibrahim's (Abraham's) confrontation with his father Azar and his people regarding their idolatrous practices. The question is not posed out of ignorance but is a rhetorical and pedagogical device—a Socratic opening meant to provoke reflection and expose the irrationality of idol worship. By asking 'what' rather than 'whom,' Ibrahim subtly reduces their deities to mere objects, stripping them of any presumed divine status before the dialogue even begins. This moment represents the start of Ibrahim's mission of monotheistic reasoning (hanif), where he uses logic and direct questioning to lead his community toward recognizing the futility of worshipping created, powerless objects instead of the one true Creator. It establishes Ibrahim as a model of rational inquiry in matters of faith, demonstrating that true belief should be arrived at through contemplation and reasoned conviction rather than blind adherence to ancestral customs.

translation: Is it a lie—gods other than Allah that you desire?
interpretation: This verse records the rebuke delivered by Prophet Ibrahim (Abraham) to his people, confronting them about their worship of fabricated deities instead of the one true God. The word 'ifk' (lie/falsehood) emphasizes that idol worship is not merely a mistaken choice but a deliberate fabrication—a deceit perpetrated either by those who crafted the idols or by the people's own self-deception in attributing divine power to lifeless objects. Ibrahim's question is rhetorical and confrontational, designed to expose the irrationality of his people's beliefs by forcing them to confront the absurdity of worshipping created, powerless things while turning away from the Creator. This moment in the narrative marks a pivotal point of Ibrahim's public defiance against idolatry, setting the stage for his later destruction of the idols and his people's violent response. The verse encapsulates a broader Quranic theme: that polytheism is fundamentally a falsehood, a deviation from the innate truth (fitrah) of monotheism that humanity is created to recognize.

translation: So what do you think about the Lord of the worlds?
interpretation: This verse is part of Prophet Ibrahim's (Abraham's) address to his people when he confronted them about their idol worship. After rejecting their false gods, he poses this rhetorical question, challenging them to consider what opinion they truly hold about the Lord of all creation. The question carries an implicit rebuke: how could they think so little of the Creator of the universe as to worship powerless idols instead of Him? It calls upon the listener to reflect seriously on God's majesty, power, and sole right to worship, exposing the absurdity and injustice of associating partners with Him. The verse functions as a moment of confrontation and self-examination, urging humanity to recognize the true magnitude and uniqueness of the Divine in contrast to the triviality of false worship.

translation: Then he glanced at the stars,
interpretation: This verse refers to Prophet Ibrahim (Abraham), peace be upon him, who cast a glance at the stars as a pretext to avoid accompanying his idol-worshipping people to their festival. By looking up and indicating he was contemplating the stars, he implied he was ill or troubled, giving him a reason to stay behind. This moment sets the stage for his subsequent actions, where he would go to the temple and destroy the idols in the absence of his people, demonstrating his rejection of idolatry and his resourcefulness in standing firm against his community's false beliefs. The glance at the stars is also seen as a reflection of his earlier contemplation of the heavens in his search for the true God, as described elsewhere in the Qur'an, showing his intellectual and spiritual journey toward monotheism.

translation: Then he said, "Indeed, I am sick."
interpretation: This verse refers to Prophet Ibrahim (Abraham), peace be upon him, when his people invited him to join them at their festival where they would worship their idols. Seeking a pretext to avoid participating in their idolatrous practices and to remain behind so he could carry out his plan to demonstrate the powerlessness of their idols, Ibrahim claimed he was sick. This statement is understood by scholars as a form of "ta'rid" (a indirect statement that is not an outright lie but conceals a deeper truth) - some commentators suggest he meant he was "sick at heart" over witnessing his people's idolatry, while others view it as a strategic statement allowing him the opportunity to later break the idols, as narrated in the following verses. This episode demonstrates Ibrahim's cleverness and resolve in confronting shirk (idolatry) and sets the stage for his dramatic confrontation with his people about the futility of worshipping lifeless idols.

translation: So they turned away from him, departing.
interpretation: This verse refers to the moment when Prophet Ibrahim (Abraham) confronted his people about the futility of worshipping lifeless idols, challenging them with rational arguments about the Creator of the heavens and earth. Rather than engaging with his message or offering a counter-argument, his people simply turned their backs on him and walked away, unwilling to confront the truth of his words. This turning away represents a common response throughout the Qur'an to prophetic guidance: rather than refuting the message with reason, disbelievers often resort to avoidance, dismissal, or physical withdrawal when faced with truths that challenge their inherited traditions and comfortable beliefs. Their departure signifies intellectual and spiritual cowardice—an unwillingness to engage honestly with a challenge to their idol worship, preferring instead to retreat into the safety of unexamined custom rather than risk the discomfort of genuine reflection.

translation: Then he turned secretly to their gods and said, "Do you not eat?"
interpretation: This verse describes Prophet Ibrahim (Abraham) slipping away to confront the idols worshipped by his people. His question, "Do you not eat?", is deeply sarcastic and rhetorical, mocking the food offerings that had been placed before the lifeless statues. By addressing inanimate objects as though they could respond, Ibrahim exposes the utter absurdity and futility of idol worship. This moment sets up his subsequent action of smashing the idols, demonstrating through direct confrontation that these so-called gods have no power, cannot eat, cannot speak, and cannot defend themselves—let alone grant benefit or harm to their worshippers. The verse illustrates Ibrahim's method of using reason and ridicule to awaken his people from blind ritualism toward recognizing the sole worthiness of the one true God.

translation: What is the matter with you that you do not speak?
interpretation: This verse is part of the narrative of Prophet Ibrahim (Abraham) in Surah As-Saffat, where he turns to the idols worshipped by his people after breaking them into pieces (except the largest one) and mockingly asks them this question. The rhetorical question highlights the absurdity of idol worship—these objects, fashioned by human hands, have no life, no voice, and no power to respond or defend themselves, let alone grant benefit or harm to their worshippers. Ibrahim's challenge is meant to expose the irrationality of his people's beliefs through direct confrontation with the lifeless nature of what they venerate, pushing them toward the self-evident truth that these idols are utterly powerless. The silence of the idols becomes itself the proof of their falsity as objects of worship, contrasting sharply with the living, speaking, all-powerful God who alone deserves worship.

translation: Then he turned upon them, striking with his right hand.
interpretation: This verse is part of the narrative of Prophet Ibrahim (Abraham) in Surah As-Saffat, describing the moment he secretly turned against the idols worshipped by his people and began smashing them. Having previously mocked the idols for their inability to eat the food offered to them, Ibrahim seized the opportunity when his people were away to attack the idols physically, breaking them with his right hand—a detail often understood to emphasize strength, deliberateness, and perhaps the sanctity or power associated with the right hand in Arabic cultural and religious symbolism. This act was a bold, decisive demonstration of Ibrahim's rejection of idolatry and his commitment to monotheism, setting the stage for his subsequent confrontation with his people and their false deities. The verse captures a pivotal moment of defiance against polytheism, illustrating Ibrahim's courage in directly challenging the religious practices of his society despite the personal risk involved, as he sought to expose the powerlessness of the idols his people worshipped alongside God.

translation: So they came to him, hastening.
interpretation: This verse refers to the people of Prophet Ibrahim (Abraham) rushing toward him in anger after discovering that he had destroyed their idols, leaving only the largest one intact. Having previously declared his intention to scheme against their idols, and upon finding them smashed, the people hurried to confront Ibrahim, having been told that he was the one who had spoken against the gods. The word 'يزفون' conveys a sense of swift, agitated movement, suggesting their urgency and anger as they approached him to demand an explanation. This moment sets the stage for the famous dialogue in which Ibrahim challenges them to question the very idols they worship, exposing the futility of idolatry through reason, since the idols could neither speak nor defend themselves. The scene illustrates the clash between truth and blind tradition, and the courage required to stand against a hostile crowd in defense of monotheism.

translation: He said, 'Do you worship that which you yourselves carve?'
interpretation: This verse depicts Prophet Ibrahim (Abraham) confronting his people about the irrationality of idol worship. He points out the absurdity that they worship objects they themselves have shaped and carved with their own hands from stone or wood. The rhetorical question exposes the logical contradiction at the heart of idolatry: how can something fashioned by human craftsmanship, something with no inherent power, life, or agency, be deserving of worship or have any divine authority over its makers? This moment represents Ibrahim's method of reasoning with his community, using logic and direct questioning to awaken them to the truth of monotheism (tawhid) rather than simply declaring their practices wrong. It underscores a central Quranic theme that true divinity must be self-sufficient and not dependent on human creation, contrasting starkly with man-made idols that are entirely dependent on their creators for their very existence and form.

translation: And Allah created you and what you do.
interpretation: This verse is part of the story of Prophet Ibrahim (Abraham) confronting his people about their idol worship, found in Surah As-Saffat (37:96). After Ibrahim questioned why they worshipped carved idols they themselves made with their own hands, he declares this powerful theological argument: Allah is the Creator of both the worshippers and their actions, including the very act of carving and crafting the idols they foolishly venerate. This statement dismantles the logic of idolatry by pointing out the absurdity of worshipping objects that are themselves created things, fashioned by human hands, which are in turn created by Allah. The verse establishes a foundational principle of Islamic theology: Allah's creative sovereignty extends not only to physical beings and objects but encompasses human actions and deeds themselves. This has been understood by many scholars to affirm that while humans possess agency and will be held accountable for their choices, the ultimate power to create and bring into existence—whether it be a person, an object, or an action—belongs solely to Allah. The verse thus serves both as a rebuke to those who worship created things instead of the Creator, and as a broader theological statement about the relationship between divine creation and human action, a topic that has been extensively discussed in Islamic theological discourse regarding free will and divine decree.

translation: They said, 'Build for him a structure and throw him into the blazing fire.'
interpretation: This verse refers to the people of Prophet Ibrahim (Abraham) who, after he destroyed their idols and exposed the futility of idol worship, conspired to punish him severely for his defiance. Unable to counter his rational arguments against idolatry, they resorted to violence, deciding to build a furnace and cast him into the flames. This episode illustrates a recurring pattern in the Qur'an where those who challenge entrenched falsehood with truth face persecution from those who cannot refute them intellectually but respond with power and cruelty instead. The verse sets up the dramatic demonstration of divine protection that follows, where Allah commands the fire to be cool and safe for Ibrahim, showing that ultimate power belongs to God alone, and that sincere devotion to truth will be protected even against seemingly insurmountable odds.

translation: So they intended a plot against him, but We made them the lowest.
interpretation: This verse refers to the attempt by Abraham's people to harm him after he destroyed their idols and declared his rejection of their false gods. They conspired to throw him into a blazing fire as punishment, seeking to eliminate him and his message through this scheme. Yet God intervened directly, commanding the fire to be cool and safe for Abraham, thereby thwarting their plot entirely. The phrase 'We made them the lowest' signifies a complete reversal of their intended outcome—rather than triumphing over Abraham, they were utterly humiliated and defeated, both in their immediate failure to harm him and in the broader historical and spiritual sense, as their schemes against a prophet of God came to nothing.
