This illustrates a recurring Quranic theme: those who plot against God's chosen messengers and the truth they bring will ultimately find their efforts turned against them, while those who stand firm in faith, like Abraham, are protected and vindicated by divine power.'

translation: And he said, 'Indeed, I am going to my Lord; He will guide me.'
interpretation: This verse refers to Prophet Ibrahim (Abraham) after he broke the idols of his people and was threatened with being thrown into the fire. Having renounced his people's idolatry and their false gods, he declares his intention to migrate—both physically and spiritually—in devotion to the one true God. His statement reflects complete trust in divine guidance (tawakkul), affirming that true direction in life comes only from God. This moment marks a pivotal turning point in his life as he prepares to leave his homeland and people, trusting that God will guide him to a path of righteousness and purpose. It establishes the archetype of the believer who, when faced with persecution or spiritual isolation, surrenders his journey entirely to God's guidance rather than relying on worldly plans or support.

translation: My Lord, grant me [a child] from among the righteous.
interpretation: This supplication is uttered by Prophet Ibrahim (Abraham) in Surah As-Saffat, after he had left behind idolatry and his people, migrating in devotion to God alone. Having endured trials of faith, loneliness, and separation from his community, he turns to God with a deeply personal plea—not merely for offspring, but specifically for a righteous child who would continue his legacy of monotheism and moral uprightness. This prayer reflects the human longing for continuity and legacy through progeny, but more importantly, it reveals Ibrahim's priorities: he does not ask simply for a son, but for one who embodies righteousness (salih), indicating that spiritual integrity matters more to him than lineage alone. This moment foreshadows the subsequent narrative of Ibrahim's son, understood by most commentators to be Ismail, and sets the stage for the profound test of sacrifice that follows. The verse also illustrates a broader Quranic theme: that righteousness is not inherited by blood but must be sought through prayer and divine grace, and that the righteous servants of God actively desire righteous progeny as a means of sustaining faith across generations.

translation: So We gave him good tidings of a forbearing son.
interpretation: This verse refers to Allah's glad tidings to Prophet Ibrahim (Abraham) after his prayers for righteous offspring, as mentioned earlier in Surah As-Saffat. The son announced here is understood by most commentators to be Ismail (Ishmael). The description 'halim' (forbearing, patient, mild-tempered) is significant—it foreshadows the boy's character and foreshadows the trial that follows in subsequent verses, where this same son demonstrates remarkable patience and submission when Ibrahim shares with him the vision commanding his sacrifice. The choice of this particular attribute to describe the child is a literary and theological setup: a forbearing, patient son is precisely what is needed to willingly accept such a monumental test of faith without resistance or despair. This verse thus serves as both a moment of joy and divine favor to Ibrahim after years of supplication, and a narrative pivot preparing the reader for the profound test of submission (to Allah's will) that both father and son would soon face together.

translation: And when he reached the age of working with him, he said, 'O my son, indeed I have seen in a dream that I am sacrificing you, so look, what do you think?' He said, 'O my father, do as you are commanded. You will find me, if Allah wills, among the patient.'
interpretation: This verse recounts the trial of Prophet Ibrahim (Abraham) when he was commanded in a vision to sacrifice his son, understood to be Isma'il (Ishmael). Dreams of prophets are considered a form of revelation, so Ibrahim took this vision as a divine command. Rather than acting unilaterally, he consulted his son, demonstrating a model of dialogue, respect, and shared submission to God's will even in the most difficult of circumstances. The son's response reveals extraordinary faith and maturity: he does not resist or plead for his life but affirms his willingness to submit to what he believes is God's command, asking only that his father proceed as instructed. His qualification 'if Allah wills' reflects humility and an acknowledgment that true steadfastness (sabr) is a gift from God, not something one can guarantee of oneself through sheer willpower. The verse ultimately illustrates the theme of complete submission (Islam) to God, where both father and son willingly submit to a test that challenges natural human attachment and fear, setting up the dramatic resolution of divine mercy that follows in the subsequent verses, where God provides a ransom in place of the sacrifice, transforming this trial into the foundation of the Islamic practice of Eid al-Adha.

translation: So when they had both submitted [to Allah's will], and he laid him down upon his forehead,
interpretation: This verse depicts the pivotal moment in the story of Prophet Ibrahim (Abraham) and his son Ismail (Ishmael), where both father and son achieve complete submission (islam) to God's command. The phrase 'aslama' (submitted) used for both of them signifies that this was not merely Ibrahim's test alone, but a shared act of faith and surrender - Ismail willingly consented to be sacrificed, and Ibrahim was prepared to carry out what he believed was a divine command. The act of laying him on his forehead (or temple, depending on interpretation) rather than facing him was practically so that Ibrahim would not see his son's face at the moment of the intended sacrifice, sparing him the anguish of eye contact while proceeding with what he understood to be God's will. This moment represents the ultimate test of faith, where both father and son demonstrate complete trust in God even in the face of what seems like the most unbearable sacrifice imaginable. It establishes the theological principle that true submission to God must sometimes transcend even the deepest human attachments and instincts, while also foreshadowing that God's mercy would intervene, as the following verses reveal that a ram was provided as a substitute, demonstrating that God does not desire human sacrifice but rather tests the sincerity of faith and willingness to obey.

translation: And We called out to him, 'O Abraham!'
interpretation: This verse refers to the moment when God called out to Abraham immediately after he had proceeded to fulfill the command to sacrifice his son, demonstrating complete submission and willingness to obey. The divine call represents God's intervention at the critical moment of testing, affirming that Abraham had already fulfilled the purpose of the trial through his sincere intention and readiness to obey, even before the act itself was completed. This illustrates the principle that in matters of faith, the sincerity of submission and the state of one's heart in obedience to God's command holds profound significance, and that God's mercy intervenes to prevent unnecessary suffering once true devotion has been proven. The direct, personal address by name ('O Abraham') emphasizes the intimate relationship between God and His prophet, highlighting how God communicates directly with those who demonstrate complete trust and submission to His will.

translation: You have indeed fulfilled the vision. Thus do We reward the doers of good.
interpretation: This verse comes from the story of Prophet Ibrahim (Abraham) in Surat As-Saffat, immediately after he had prepared to sacrifice his son Ismail in obedience to a command he received in a dream. When Ibrahim proceeded to carry out this test of faith, God intervened, declaring that the vision had already been fulfilled through Ibrahim's sincere willingness and submission—the actual physical act of sacrifice was not what was required. This reveals a profound principle: God does not test the believer for the sake of causing them to suffer or to extract literal compliance that brings about tragedy, but rather to prove the sincerity, trust, and devotion of the heart. The fulfillment of the vision rests in Ibrahim's complete surrender to God's will, his willingness to give up what was most precious to him without hesitation. The declaration that God 'rewards the doers of good' in this way establishes that true excellence (ihsan) lies in wholehearted submission and trust in divine wisdom, even when the command seems incomprehensible or painful. God's mercy intervenes at the point of true test fulfillment, substituting the sacrifice with a ram, showing that His justice and compassion work together, and that sincere intention and obedience are what is ultimately valued, not the literal outcome alone.

translation: Indeed, this is the manifest trial.
interpretation: This verse appears in the narrative of Prophet Ibrahim (Abraham) in Surah As-Saffat, immediately following his vision commanding him to sacrifice his son and his son's submissive acceptance of this command. The verse serves as a divine commentary affirming that this command was indeed an extraordinarily severe test of faith—testing Ibrahim's willingness to submit entirely to God's will even at the cost of his beloved son, and testing the son's own faith and submission as well. The word 'bala' (trial/test) here is described as 'mubeen' (clear, manifest, evident), emphasizing that this was not an ambiguous or minor test but one whose difficulty and significance were utterly clear and undeniable. This moment represents the pinnacle of trials in prophetic narratives, where complete submission (islam) to God's command superseded even the deepest human attachments and instincts. The verse validates the magnitude of what was asked of Ibrahim and his son, setting up the subsequent divine intervention where God provides a ransom (the sacrificial animal) as a mercy, transforming the trial into a lasting lesson about faith, obedience, and divine providence that is commemorated annually in the Islamic tradition through Eid al-Adha.

translation: And We ransomed him with a great sacrifice.
interpretation: This verse refers to the story of Prophet Ibrahim (Abraham) and his son Ismail (Ishmael), when Ibrahim was commanded in a vision to sacrifice his son as a test of faith. As both father and son submitted to God's will, God intervened at the last moment and provided a ram to be sacrificed instead, sparing the boy's life. This divine ransom demonstrates God's mercy and His acceptance of the sincere devotion and obedience shown by Ibrahim and Ismail, rather than demanding the literal sacrifice of human life. The 'great sacrifice' (dhibhin azeem) is understood to refer to the ram sent by God, and this event is commemorated annually by Muslims during Eid al-Adha, where animals are sacrificed in remembrance of this act of faith, obedience, and divine mercy. The verse underscores the themes of trust in God, the testing of faith, and God's compassion in not requiring the ultimate sacrifice from His devoted servants.

translation: And We left for him [a lasting mention of honor] among later generations.
interpretation: This verse, occurring in Surah As-Saffat in the context of Prophet Nuh (Noah), reflects a recurring divine pattern in the Qur'an where righteous prophets are granted enduring legacies of praise and remembrance among subsequent generations. This 'leaving behind' refers to the preservation of their honorable reputation, their being invoked with blessings, and their stories being retold as models of faith and perseverance across all future nations and languages. It signifies that true honor and lasting remembrance come from God as a reward for steadfast devotion and patience in conveying His message, regardless of the hardships faced during one's lifetime. The verse also serves as a reassurance to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ and believers that sincere service to God's cause will be vindicated and honored through history, even if immediate worldly acceptance is denied.

translation: Peace be upon Abraham.
interpretation: This phrase is part of a recurring refrain in Surah As-Saffat where Allah bestows peace and blessing upon various prophets, including Noah, Abraham, Moses, and Aaron, after recounting episodes of their trials and devotion. In this specific context, it follows the account of Abraham's willingness to sacrifice his son in obedience to a divine command, and his subsequent reward of steadfastness being honored. The greeting of peace signifies divine approval, protection, and the eternal honor bestowed upon Abraham for his complete submission and trust in God even in the face of the most difficult test imaginable. It also serves as a model for believers, showing that ultimate peace and divine favor come to those who demonstrate unwavering faith and obedience to God's will, regardless of personal cost. This salutation elevates Abraham's status as a model of faith (hanif) and establishes a pattern of divine commendation that resonates through Islamic tradition, where Abraham is revered as a patriarch of monotheism and an exemplar of complete surrender to God.

translation: Thus do We reward the doers of good.
interpretation: This recurring refrain in Surah As-Saffat follows accounts of the prophets—Nuh, Ibrahim, Musa, Harun, and others—who remained steadfast in faith and obedience despite trials, opposition, and tests of their devotion. The verse establishes a divine principle: righteous conduct and excellence in faith (ihsan) are met with Allah's favor, protection, and honor, both in this world and the next. It is not merely a statement about past prophets but a universal principle meant to encourage believers in every generation—that sincere goodness and devotion to God are never wasted, and that Allah's justice ensures those who strive to do good will be recognized and rewarded, just as He rewarded His messengers before them.

translation: Indeed, he was among Our believing servants.
interpretation: This phrase is a recurring refrain in Surah As-Saffat, used to characterize various prophets (such as Nuh, Ibrahim, Musa, Harun, and others) after recounting how Allah delivered them and made their legacy endure among later generations. The statement serves as a divine seal of approval, affirming that the prophet's unwavering faith (iman) was the defining quality that earned him Allah's favor, protection, and honor. It emphasizes that true servanthood to Allah is rooted in sincere belief, and that such belief is the quality most praised and rewarded by God. The repetition of this formula across different prophetic narratives in the surah underscores a unifying theme: despite living in different times and facing different trials, all true prophets shared this essential characteristic of being believing servants of Allah, establishing a continuous chain of righteous devotion that believers are called to emulate.

translation: And We gave him good tidings of Isaac, a prophet from among the righteous.
interpretation: This verse refers to Prophet Ibrahim (Abraham) and the divine promise he received of a son, Isaac, who would himself become a prophet and a righteous man. This comes as a reward for Ibrahim's unwavering faith and his willingness to submit entirely to God's command, as demonstrated in the preceding verses concerning the trial of sacrificing his son Ismail. The good news of Isaac signifies continuity of Ibrahim's prophetic legacy and God's blessing upon him, establishing a lineage of prophethood through both of his sons. It underscores the Quranic theme that righteousness and steadfast devotion to God are rewarded with blessings that extend across generations, reinforcing the idea that true faith brings about lasting spiritual and worldly legacies sanctioned by divine will.

translation: And We blessed him and Isaac. And among their descendants is the doer of good and the one who is clearly unjust to himself.
interpretation: This verse, following the account of Ibrahim's trial and the ransom of his son, extends divine blessing to both Ibrahim and his son Isaac, affirming that prophethood and blessing would continue through their lineage. However, the verse immediately qualifies this blessing by noting that not all descendants would be righteous—some would be doers of good (muhsin), while others would be openly unjust to themselves (zalim li-nafsihi mubin). This serves as a theological corrective to any notion of guaranteed salvation through ancestry or bloodline alone. Being descended from a blessed prophet does not automatically confer righteousness or divine favor upon an individual; rather, each person is judged according to their own deeds and choices. The verse establishes that divine blessing upon a lineage creates opportunity and legacy, but moral and spiritual standing before God remains a matter of personal responsibility, not inherited status. This theme resonates throughout the Qur'an's treatment of prophetic families, where biological descent from righteous forebears is explicitly decoupled from guaranteed righteousness or salvation.

translation: And We certainly bestowed favor upon Moses and Aaron.
interpretation: This verse opens a passage in Surat As-Saffat that recounts God's grace toward Moses and Aaron, highlighting them as recipients of divine favor among the chain of prophets mentioned in this surah (including Noah, Abraham, Isaac, and others). The 'favor' (minnah) here refers to the prophethood, guidance, and deliverance granted to them—specifically their rescue of the Israelites from bondage and oppression in Egypt, and the revelation of guidance through them. The verse serves as an introduction to the subsequent verses that elaborate on specific blessings: their salvation from distress, their support against adversity, and the gift of the clear Scripture (the Torah) that guided their people. This pattern—recounting divine favor upon chosen messengers—reinforces a central theme of the surah: that God's mercy and support have historically been extended to those who uphold monotheism and strive in His cause, offering reassurance and a model of faith to the Prophet Muhammad and the early Muslim community facing their own trials.

translation: And We saved them both and their people from the great distress.
interpretation: This verse refers to Prophets Moses (Musa) and Aaron (Harun) and their people, the Children of Israel, whom Allah delivered from the oppression and tyranny of Pharaoh—a calamity so severe it is described as 'the great distress' (al-karb al-'azim). This deliverance encompassed not only physical salvation from slavery and persecution but also the miraculous crossing of the sea, which marked the end of Pharaoh's oppressive rule. The verse underscores a recurring Qur'anic theme: that Allah rescues His prophets and the righteous believers who follow them from grave hardship when they remain steadfast in faith, demonstrating divine justice in overturning the power of tyrants and vindicating those who suffer unjustly at their hands.

translation: And We helped them, so they became the victors.
interpretation: This verse refers to God's support of Moses and Aaron and the believers with them against Pharaoh, affirming that true victory and ultimate triumph come from divine aid rather than mere worldly power or numbers. It underscores a recurring Qur'anic theme: that when the righteous are tested and oppressed, God's assistance ultimately grants them success over their oppressors, serving as both a historical reminder and a reassurance to the believers of Muhammad's time that they too would prevail with God's help despite being outnumbered or persecuted.

translation: And We gave them both the clear Book.
interpretation: This verse refers to Moses and Aaron and affirms that God granted them the Torah, described as 'al-kitab al-mustabin' (the clear, self-evident, and clarifying Book). The term 'mustabin' emphasizes that this scripture was unambiguous in distinguishing truth from falsehood, right from wrong, and lawful from unlawful—serving as a definitive source of guidance, law, and clarification for the Children of Israel. By giving both brothers the Book, God established them as joint bearers of prophetic authority and revelation, equipping them with a clear criterion to guide their people, settle disputes, and establish divine law. This also underscores a broader Quranic theme: that divine revelation is not meant to be obscure or confusing but is deliberately made clear and accessible so that people have no excuse for misguidance. The pairing of Moses and Aaron in receiving this scripture highlights the collaborative nature of their prophetic mission, where Aaron supported Moses in conveying and implementing the clear guidance given to them for the liberation and moral/legal instruction of the Israelites.

translation: And We guided them both to the straight path.
interpretation: This verse refers to Prophets Musa (Moses) and Harun (Aaron), whom Allah guided to the straight path after granting them the Scripture and establishing them as a means of deliverance for their people. The 'straight path' signifies the path of true guidance, righteousness, and devotion to Allah—a path that leads to success in this life and salvation in the Hereafter. This guidance was not merely intellectual but practical, enabling them to fulfill their prophetic missions with wisdom and steadfastness amidst the trials of confronting Pharaoh and leading the Children of Israel. The verse underscores the Quranic theme that divine guidance to the straight path is a special favor bestowed upon the righteous and the prophets, distinguishing them from those who go astray, and it reaffirms that true guidance comes only from Allah, who chooses to bestow it upon those who sincerely strive in His cause.

translation: And We left for him (mentioned praise) among later generations.
interpretation: This verse, referring to Moses and Aaron (as indicated by the dual pronoun), affirms that God preserved their honorable remembrance among subsequent generations of people. It emphasizes that righteous prophets and their legacies are perpetuated throughout history, serving as enduring examples of faith and guidance for communities that come after them. This continuity of praise reflects divine reward for their steadfastness and devotion in conveying God's message, ensuring that their names remain associated with righteousness and truth for all later nations to remember and emulate.

translation: Peace be upon Moses and Aaron.
interpretation: This verse is part of a recurring refrain in Surah As-Saffat where Allah bestows peace and blessings upon His chosen prophets after recounting their stories. The greeting of peace upon Moses and Aaron signifies divine honor and commendation for their steadfastness, their shared mission in confronting Pharaoh, and their role in liberating the Children of Israel. By pairing them together, the verse emphasizes their partnership in prophethood—Moses as the primary messenger and Aaron as his supporter and spokesperson. This salutation serves as a model of how later generations should remember and invoke blessings upon the righteous, reinforcing the Quranic theme that true honor comes from steadfast faith and service to Allah's message, not worldly power or status.

translation: Indeed, thus do We reward the doers of good.
interpretation: This verse serves as a concluding affirmation following a narrative of divine favor shown to a righteous figure (often linked contextually to the story of Prophet Yusuf or other prophets who faced trials with patience and righteousness). It establishes a universal principle: that God's reward for excellence in faith and conduct (ihsan) is not arbitrary but a consistent divine law. 'Al-Muhsinin' refers to those who worship and act with sincerity, as if seeing God, or knowing that God sees them, striving for excellence beyond mere obligation. The verse reassures believers that no act of goodness, patience, or trust in God during hardship goes unrewarded, reinforcing the theme of divine justice and grace that rewards virtue proportionally and generously, often in ways that transform earlier suffering into honor and empowerment.

translation: Indeed, both of them were among Our believing servants.
interpretation: This verse refers to righteous figures (commonly understood in exegesis to be Prophet Zakariya and his wife, or in other contexts Prophet Lut's household or similar paired righteous servants) who are singled out for their sincere faith and devotion to God. The phrase emphasizes that true honor before God is not based on lineage, wealth, or worldly status, but on genuine belief ('iman') and servitude ('ibadah') to Him. By affirming that 'both of them' belonged to His believing servants, the verse highlights that righteousness is a shared quality that can unite spouses or companions in faith, and it serves as a model for believers to aspire toward the same sincerity and devotion in their relationship with God.

translation: And indeed, Elias (Ilyas) was among the messengers.
interpretation: This verse introduces the Prophet Elias as part of the long chain of messengers sent by God throughout history, affirming the continuity and unity of prophetic mission. By stating that Elias was 'among the messengers,' the Qur'an emphasizes that he, like Noah, Abraham, Moses, and others mentioned in this same chapter (Surah As-Saffat), was granted divine revelation and tasked with calling his people away from idolatry toward the worship of the one true God. This serves to reinforce the Qur'anic theme that all prophets shared the same core message of monotheism, and that Elias's story—though less detailed than some others—fits within this universal pattern of prophetic struggle against polytheism, as he specifically confronted his people's worship of the idol Ba'l, calling them back to the worship of the 'Lord of the worlds.' The verse also serves a rhetorical purpose within the surah's structure, which recounts various prophets in succession to demonstrate the consistency of divine guidance and the recurring rejection faced by messengers, while assuring believers of ultimate vindication and peace, as reflected in the verses that follow this declaration.

translation: When he said to his people, 'Will you not fear Allah (be righteous and mindful of Him)?'
interpretation: This verse refers to the Prophet Lut (Lot), peace be upon him, addressing his people as he began to call them to righteousness and warn them against their transgressions. The rhetorical question 'Will you not fear Allah?' is a common prophetic opening used throughout the Qur'an to awaken moral consciousness before delivering a specific warning or guidance. It establishes the foundation of taqwa (God-consciousness) as the basis for accepting the message that follows, implying that their current behavior stems from a lack of this fear and mindfulness of divine accountability. This introductory address sets the stage for Lut's subsequent condemnation of his people's sexual immorality and societal corruption, framing the entire confrontation within the context of a prophet's compassionate yet firm call to his community to return to righteousness before facing consequences.

translation: Do you call upon Ba'l and forsake the best of creators?
interpretation: This verse is part of the story of Prophet Elias (Elijah), peace be upon him, as he confronted his people who had turned to worshipping an idol named Ba'l instead of Allah. The rhetorical question highlights the irrationality of idolatry: Ba'l, a lifeless idol crafted by human hands, possesses no power to create, sustain, or benefit anyone, whereas Allah is described as 'the best of creators,' the one who brought all things into existence with perfect wisdom and power. The verse exposes the absurdity of abandoning the true, all-powerful Creator in favor of a powerless, man-made object, and it serves as a broader critique of any form of misplaced devotion where people prioritize worldly idols, wealth, status, or other distractions over their sincere worship and recognition of Allah. It calls on believers to reflect on where they direct their ultimate loyalty and worship, emphasizing that true wisdom lies in recognizing and submitting to the One who is truly deserving of worship.”}}

translation: Allah is your Lord and the Lord of your forefathers.
interpretation: This verse affirms the oneness and eternal nature of God's lordship across all generations, emphasizing that the same God who created and sustains the present generation also created and sustained their ancestors. It serves as a rebuttal to idolatry by pointing out that the deity worthy of worship is not a new or invented concept but the same single Creator throughout human history. This argument is typically used in the Qur'an to confront those who justify their polytheism by appealing to the traditions of their forefathers, reminding them that even their ancestors ultimately derived their existence and sustenance from the one true God, not from the idols they worshipped.

translation: But they denied him, so indeed, they will be brought [for punishment].
interpretation: This verse refers to the people of Prophet Ilyas (Elijah) who rejected his call to worship Allah alone and abandon the idol Ba'al. The verse serves as a warning that those who reject the message of the prophets will be summoned and presented before Allah on the Day of Judgment to face the consequences of their disbelief. It reflects a recurring Qur'anic theme found throughout Surah As-Saffat, where the stories of various prophets are recounted to show the pattern of rejection by disbelieving nations followed by divine consequences, while the believers who followed these prophets were saved. This serves as both a historical lesson and a warning to the Prophet Muhammad's contemporaries who were similarly denying his message.

translation: Except the sincere servants of Allah.
interpretation: This phrase appears as a recurring refrain in Surah As-Saffat, marking an exception clause that distinguishes the sincere, devoted servants of Allah from the rest of humanity who fall into misguidance, idolatry, or the schemes of Satan. The 'mukhlaseen' (sincere ones) are those whose worship and devotion to Allah are purified of hypocrisy, worldly motives, and divided loyalties—they serve Allah for His sake alone. Throughout the surah, this group is repeatedly exempted from punishment, from being led astray by Satan, and from the fate of the wrongdoers and deniers of truth mentioned in the surrounding verses. The repetition of this phrase after various warnings about those who will face divine punishment serves to emphasize that sincerity and devotion to Allah—free from pretense or ulterior motive—acts as a protective shield from both spiritual and ultimate punishment. This sincerity is portrayed as a distinguishing characteristic of the righteous throughout Islamic theology, suggesting that outward religious practice alone is insufficient; what matters is the purity of intention behind one's devotion.

translation: And We left for him [favorable mention] among later generations.
interpretation: This verse refers to Prophet Nuh (Noah) and signifies that God preserved his name, his story, and his legacy of faith as an enduring blessing for all generations that would come after him. It establishes a pattern seen throughout the Qur'an regarding righteous prophets: their honorable reputation and the remembrance of their devotion to God persists through time, serving as a lasting example for subsequent peoples. This divine preservation of memory serves both as a reward for Nuh's patience and steadfastness in the face of his disbelieving people, and as a means of transmitting moral and spiritual guidance across the ages, ensuring that the lessons of his life remain accessible to all later generations who reflect on sacred history.

translation: Peace be upon Elias (Il-Yaseen).
interpretation: This verse occurs within the Qur'an's recounting of the prophet Elias (Ilyas), whose name here is rendered in the variant form 'Il-Yaseen.' It follows the pattern seen with other prophets mentioned in Surah As-Saffat, such as Noah, Abraham, and Moses and Aaron, where after recounting their righteous struggle against idolatry and their steadfastness in calling their people to worship God alone, God bestows upon them a salutation of peace that will be remembered by later generations. This peace is a divine honor and blessing, signifying that Elias's legacy as a devoted servant and messenger who fought against the worship of Baal and called his people back to the worship of the one true God is preserved eternally and praised among all communities who came after him. It reflects the Qur'anic theme that those who strive sincerely in God's cause, enduring hardship and rejection from their own people, are granted lasting honor, remembrance, and divine commendation across all generations of believers, illustrating God's justice in rewarding steadfast faith and righteous struggle (jihad) in the face of a corrupt and idolatrous society.

translation: Indeed, thus do We reward the doers of good.
interpretation: This recurring refrain in Surah As-Saffat follows accounts of various prophets—Nuh, Ibrahim, Musa, Harun, and others—who faced trials, remained steadfast in faith, and submitted to Allah's command even in the most difficult circumstances, such as Ibrahim's willingness to sacrifice his son. The verse establishes a divine principle: righteous conduct and excellence in faith (ihsan) are met with Allah's reward and favor. It is not merely about the specific historical reward given to each prophet, but establishes a timeless law of divine justice—that those who strive for excellence in worship and conduct, who submit sincerely to Allah's will even when tested, will be honored and rewarded by Him. The repetition of this phrase after each prophetic narrative serves as a unifying thread, demonstrating that the mercy and reward shown to these righteous figures of the past is not an isolated event but a consistent pattern of divine justice that extends to all who embody ihsan—excellence and sincerity in faith and action—across all generations.

translation: Indeed, he was among Our believing servants.
interpretation: This phrase is a recurring refrain in Surah As-Saffat, used to conclude the accounts of several prophets—including Noah, Abraham, and Moses and Aaron—affirming their station as true, faithful servants of God. It serves as a divine seal of approval, emphasizing that these figures are singled out not merely for their prophethood but for their unwavering faith (iman) and sincere submission to God. The phrase functions rhetorically as a refrain that unites the stories of different prophets into a single narrative theme: that true servanthood to God is defined by faith, and that the righteous of every era are counted among His believing servants, a status that transcends time and individual circumstance, offering a model for all believers to emulate in their own relationship with God.

translation: And indeed, Lot was among the messengers.
interpretation: This verse affirms the prophethood of Lot within the Qur'an's recurring narrative pattern of recounting earlier prophets to reassure Muhammad and the early Muslim community of the continuity of divine revelation. By stating that Lot was 'among the messengers,' the verse situates him within the same prophetic lineage as Noah, Abraham, and others mentioned in the surrounding verses of Surah As-Saffat, emphasizing that all prophets faced rejection from their own people yet were ultimately vindicated by God. This serves as a consolatory and admonitory device: consolatory for Muhammad, who faced similar rejection from the Quraysh, and admonitory for the disbelievers, reminding them that the people of Lot were destroyed for their persistent immorality and rejection of the messenger sent to guide them. The verse thus functions as part of a theological argument for the unity of the prophetic message across history and the consistent pattern of divine justice toward those who reject it.

translation: [Mention] when We saved him and his family, all together,
interpretation: This verse refers to Prophet Lut (Lot) and recounts how Allah delivered him and his household from the destruction that befell his disobedient people. The salvation was complete and total ('ajma'een - all together), emphasizing Allah's mercy in rescuing the righteous believer and his family from calamity. However, this deliverance was not unconditional for every family member, as the following verses clarify that his wife was left behind among those who perished, having sided with the disbelieving townspeople rather than with the truth her husband represented. This teaches that divine salvation is tied to faith and righteous conduct rather than mere family or blood ties, and that one's ultimate fate rests on individual choice and belief rather than association alone.

translation: Except an old woman among those who remained behind.
interpretation: This verse refers to the wife of Prophet Lut (Lot), peace be upon him, within the narrative of his people's destruction for their sinful practices. When Allah commanded Lut to depart by night with his believing family to escape the impending punishment, his wife was excluded from salvation because she remained loyal to her disbelieving people rather than to her husband's message. She is described as 'among those who remained behind' (al-ghabireen), meaning she stayed with the condemned townspeople in spirit and allegiance, despite being physically part of Lut's household, and thus she perished along with them in the destruction. This serves as a powerful lesson that blood relations or marital ties do not guarantee salvation; rather, one's faith and righteous conduct determine one's fate. It illustrates that even within the household of a prophet, individual accountability before Allah supersedes family bonds, emphasizing that salvation is earned through belief and obedience to divine guidance, not through mere proximity to righteousness.

translation: Then We destroyed the others.
interpretation: This verse is part of a recurring Qur'anic narrative pattern in which a prophet is sent to a disbelieving nation, warns them, is rejected except by a few believers, and then divine punishment befalls the rejecters while the righteous are saved. The phrase emphasizes the totality and certainty of God's justice—those who persisted in disbelief and corruption despite clear warning were utterly destroyed, serving as a historical lesson and warning to later generations about the consequences of arrogance, disbelief, and moral corruption in the face of divine guidance.

translation: And indeed, you pass by them in the morning,
interpretation: This verse, addressed to the Quraysh and the people of Mecca, refers to the ruins of the people of Lot, whose cities were destroyed and overturned as punishment for their sins. The verse reminds the listeners that on their trade journeys to Syria, they physically pass by the remnants of this destroyed civilization both in the morning and, as the following verse states, at night. This serves as a tangible, visible sign and warning of divine punishment for those who reject the messengers and persist in immorality—yet despite seeing this evidence with their own eyes, most people fail to reflect or take heed, continuing in their heedlessness.

translation: And by night. Then will you not use reason?
interpretation: This verse appears as the concluding part of a passage (as in Surah As-Saffat, 37:138) referring to the people of Lot, whose ruined city the Quraysh and other travelers would pass by both during the day and at night on their trade journeys. By reminding the listeners that they physically pass by these visible ruins at all times, day and night, the verse is a rhetorical challenge: the evidence of divine punishment for disbelief and immorality is right before their eyes, repeatedly and unmistakably. The rhetorical question 'Then will you not use reason?' underscores that the truth of prophetic warnings and the reality of divine justice are not hidden or abstract but empirically observable in history and geography. It calls on the audience to engage their intellect ('aql), which in the Quranic worldview is the faculty that should lead a person from observation of the world to recognition of moral and theological truths—specifically, that heedlessness and corruption lead to ruin, and that the signs of this are left standing deliberately as lessons for those who will reflect rather than merely look without understanding.

translation: And indeed, Jonah was one of the messengers.
interpretation: This verse affirms Jonah's (Yunus) status as a genuine prophet of God, sent with a divine message to his people. It comes in the context of a broader narrative recounting the stories of earlier prophets, placing Jonah within this prophetic lineage. The affirmation serves to validate his mission despite the trials he faced, including his initial flight from his duty and his time in the belly of the whale, emphasizing that even after such a lapse, he remained among God's chosen messengers. This underscores the Quranic theme that prophethood is a divine selection that endures despite human weakness, and that God's mercy extends to His messengers who turn back to Him in repentance, as Jonah did when he called out from the darkness.

translation: When he fled to the laden ship.
interpretation: This verse refers to the Prophet Yunus (Jonah), who departed from his people in frustration without divine permission to continue his mission of calling them to faith, and boarded a heavily laden ship. The word 'abaqa' is notably used elsewhere in the Qur'an to describe a slave fleeing from his master, indicating the gravity of Yunus's departure from his prophetic duty. This episode illustrates that even prophets, who are chosen and guided by God, can act out of very human emotions like frustration and impatience when faced with a seemingly unresponsive community. The subsequent events—being cast into the sea and swallowed by the whale—serve as a divine lesson and correction, teaching perseverance in fulfilling one's duty despite hardship, and demonstrating that God's mercy extends even to His prophets when they err, provided they turn back to Him in repentance, as Yunus does in the verses that follow.

translation: Then he drew lots, and was among the losers (those who were cast out/defeated in the drawing).
interpretation: This verse refers to Prophet Yunus (Jonah) after he fled aboard a ship in disobedience to God's command. When the ship was overwhelmed by a storm, the sailors believed someone aboard must be at fault and decided to cast lots to determine who should be thrown overboard to lighten the vessel and appease the sea. Yunus participated in this casting of lots and was selected—he 'lost' the draw three times, according to traditional accounts. This moment represents a turning point in the narrative: despite his status as a prophet, Yunus was subjected to the same trial as any ordinary person, and the outcome of the lots signaled divine decree at work even through what seemed like chance. It underscores the theme that no one, not even a prophet, is exempt from accountability when they act against divine instruction, and that apparent randomness in worldly affairs can be the means through which God's will unfolds. This episode sets the stage for Yunus being cast into the sea and subsequently swallowed by the great fish, leading to his eventual repentance and deliverance.

translation: Then the fish swallowed him while he was blameworthy (deserving blame).
interpretation: This verse refers to Prophet Yunus (Jonah), who fled from his people in frustration without divine permission after they rejected his message, and boarded a ship. When the ship was overloaded, lots were cast and he was thrown overboard, whereupon a great fish swallowed him. The phrase 'while he was blameworthy' indicates that his departure from his people without God's command was a lapse for which he was held accountable, despite being a prophet. This episode illustrates that even prophets can err in moments of human frustration, and that true severity of trial can follow swiftly from such missteps. Yet the broader narrative, continuing in subsequent verses, emphasizes God's mercy: Yunus's sincere repentance and glorification of God within the darkness of the fish's belly leads to his deliverance, teaching that acknowledgment of fault and turning back to God opens the path to forgiveness and relief from distress, no matter how dire the circumstance.

translation: Had he not been of those who glorify [Allah],
interpretation: This verse refers to Prophet Yunus (Jonah) after he was swallowed by the great fish. It teaches that his constant practice of glorifying and remembering God—even before his moment of crisis—was the spiritual lifeline that saved him. The verse that follows states he would have remained in the belly of the fish until the Day of Resurrection had it not been for this. The lesson drawn by scholars is that a believer's habitual remembrance of God (dhikr) and reliance on Him in times of ease builds the spiritual capital that sustains them in times of extreme hardship. Yunus's cry of repentance, 'There is no deity except You; exalted are You. Indeed, I have been of the wrongdoers' (21:87), is seen as the culmination of this disposition to glorify God, and it was this sincere turning to God, rooted in his established practice of tasbih, that secured his deliverance from what seemed an inescapable fate.

translation: He would have remained in its belly until the Day they are resurrected.
interpretation: This verse is part of the narrative concerning Prophet Yunus (Jonah), who fled from his people and was subsequently swallowed by a great fish after being cast into the sea. The complete verse states that had he not been among those who glorify God, he would have remained inside the fish's belly until the Day of Resurrection—meaning the fish's belly would have become his permanent grave, entombing him for eternity. This underscores the gravity of his situation and the miraculous nature of his deliverance. The preceding glorification saved him, demonstrating that sincere remembrance and glorification of God, even in the depths of despair and seemingly inescapable circumstances, can lead to divine mercy and rescue. The verse serves as a profound lesson on the power of tasbih (glorification of God) as a means of seeking relief from distress, and it illustrates God's ability to save His servants from the most dire and hopeless situations when they turn to Him in sincere devotion and repentance.

translation: So We cast him onto the barren shore while he was ill.
interpretation: This verse recounts the aftermath of Prophet Yunus (Jonah) being released from the belly of the whale after his period of repentance and supplication to God. Having been swallowed as a consequence of fleeing his prophetic duty and abandoning his people without divine permission, Yunus's deliverance was not into comfort but onto a barren, desolate shore, weakened and sick from his ordeal. This illustrates a recurring Quranic theme regarding repentance and divine mercy: even when God forgives and rescues a servant from dire consequences, the process of restoration may still involve hardship and vulnerability. The barrenness of the land mirrors Yunus's depleted physical and spiritual state, emphasizing that salvation does not always mean an immediate return to ease but can be the beginning of a humbling recovery. It also underscores God's continued care for him despite his earlier shortcomings, as the following verses describe a plant being grown to shade and nourish him, symbolizing that divine providence sustains those who turn back to Him even after failure, gradually restoring them rather than abandoning them to their weakened state.

translation: And We caused a gourd vine to grow over him.
interpretation: This verse refers to the Prophet Yunus (Jonah) after he was expelled from the belly of the whale, sick and exposed upon a barren shore. God caused a gourd plant—known for its broad leaves, shade, and resistance to flies due to its bitter sap—to grow over him as a divine mercy, providing shelter, comfort, and nourishment during his recovery. This illustrates God's meticulous care even in the smallest details of restoring His servant after severe trial and near-death affliction. The choice of the gourd plant specifically, rather than any other vegetation, demonstrates that divine providence extends to practical, physical needs and that God's mercy manifests in tangible, nurturing ways even after moments of disobedience and hardship. It symbolizes renewal, healing, and the compassionate restoration that follows sincere repentance, as Yunus had cried out to God from within the whale before being delivered to this place of recovery.

translation: And We sent him to a hundred thousand [people] or more.
interpretation: This verse refers to the Prophet Yunus (Jonah), continuing the narrative from the preceding verses that describe his being swallowed by the whale and then cast onto the shore. After his ordeal and recovery, God sent him to a large population—stated as a hundred thousand or more—to deliver His message. The phrase 'or more' is understood by most commentators as emphasizing the vastness of the number rather than expressing uncertainty on God's part, since God's knowledge is complete and precise. This serves rhetorically to highlight the scale of the mission entrusted to Yunus despite his earlier moment of despair and flight from his responsibility. The verse underscores the theme of divine mercy and second chances: although Yunus initially abandoned his people in frustration, God not only forgave him but also restored him to a renewed and even larger prophetic mission. It illustrates that God's plans and mercy transcend human shortcomings, and that true repentance can lead to restored purpose and success, as evidenced by the subsequent verse describing how this entire population believed and was granted enjoyment of life for a time.

translation: So they believed, and We gave them enjoyment [of life] for a time.
interpretation: This verse refers to the people of Prophet Yunus (Jonah), who, upon witnessing the signs of impending divine punishment, sincerely repented and believed before the punishment actually descended upon them. Because of their genuine faith and repentance, Allah lifted the punishment from them and allowed them to continue living and enjoying the provisions of worldly life for an appointed term. This stands as a unique exception among the stories of punished nations in the Qur'an, illustrating that sincere repentance before witnessing the actual punishment (as opposed to repentance at the moment of death or suffering) can indeed avert divine wrath. It serves as a message of hope and mercy, showing that Allah's forgiveness is available to those who turn to Him in true faith before it is too late, while also emphasizing that the respite granted is temporary ('to a time'), reminding believers that worldly life itself is but a temporary enjoyment before the ultimate reckoning in the Hereafter.

translation: So ask them [O Muhammad]: Does your Lord have daughters while they have sons?
interpretation: This verse addresses the polytheists of Mecca who attributed daughters to Allah (claiming angels were His daughters) while favoring sons for themselves, considering male offspring more honorable. The rhetorical question exposes the inherent contradiction and injustice in their belief system: they ascribed to the Divine what they themselves considered inferior or undesirable, revealing both their disrespect toward God and their own flawed values regarding gender. This challenges them to recognize the absurdity of projecting human preferences and societal biases onto the Creator, who is beyond such limitations and whom they do not even honor with what they consider their best. It serves as a broader critique of baseless, self-serving theological claims that reflect human prejudice rather than genuine revelation or reason.

translation: Or did We create the angels as females while they were witnesses?
interpretation: This verse is one in a series of rhetorical challenges in Surah As-Saffat directed at the pagan Arabs who claimed that the angels were female and were, in some sense, 'daughters of Allah.' The Qur'an exposes the irrationality of this belief by asking whether they were present to witness the angels' creation in order to verify their gender. Since no human could have observed such a creation, the question highlights that this claim was mere speculation and baseless assertion, not grounded in any real knowledge or revelation. It serves to dismantle the theological errors of the polytheists, particularly their attribution of offspring to God, which the Qur'an consistently rejects as incompatible with the transcendence and oneness of the Divine. The verse thus functions as part of a broader argument affirming Allah's incomparability and the absurdity of ascribing human or gendered characteristics, or children, to Him.

translation: Unquestionably, it is out of their falsehood that they say,
interpretation: This verse refers to the pagans of Mecca who fabricated lies about God, particularly attributing offspring to Him (as the following verses clarify, referring to their claim that angels are 'daughters of God'). The Qur'an condemns this as pure invention (ifk), a deliberate distortion of truth stemming from their own ignorance and bias rather than any divine revelation or sound reasoning. The phrase 'alā innahum' (Unquestionably, indeed) serves as an emphatic introduction, alerting the listener that what follows is a decisive refutation of a baseless claim. This sets up the subsequent verses where the Qur'an challenges the logical inconsistency of attributing daughters to God while the pagans themselves preferred sons, exposing the hypocrisy and arbitrariness of their theological assertions that were not grounded in evidence but merely in inherited conjecture and wishful fabrication.

translation: "Allah has begotten," and indeed, they are liars.
interpretation: This verse is part of a larger passage (Qur'an 37:151-152) in which the Qur'an refutes the pre-Islamic Arab polytheists' claim that Allah had offspring—whether angels as daughters of God, or other divine progeny attributed to Him in various pagan belief systems. The verse categorically denies this claim and labels those who make it as liars, emphasizing the core Islamic theological principle of Allah's absolute transcendence and uniqueness (tawhid). The concept of God "begetting" implies a biological or generative process that would make the divine comparable to created beings, subject to time, reproduction, and multiplicity—all qualities incompatible with the Qur'anic conception of God as eternal, indivisible, and utterly unlike His creation. This verse thus serves as a direct polemic against both pagan Arabian beliefs and, by extension, any theology that attributes literal offspring to God, reinforcing the Qur'an's insistence that Allah is singular, self-sufficient, and beyond the need or capacity for progeny.

translation: Has He chosen daughters over sons?
interpretation: This rhetorical question is part of a Qur'anic rebuke of the pagan Arabs' hypocritical and illogical beliefs about Allah and the angels. The disbelievers claimed that angels were the 'daughters of Allah,' yet they themselves despised having daughters and considered female children as a source of shame, often practicing female infanticide. The verse exposes the absurdity and inconsistency of their position: they attribute to Allah something they themselves reject and find undesirable for their own lives. By posing this question, the Qur'an highlights the illogic of ascribing offspring to Allah at all—since He is transcendent and free from the need for progeny—while simultaneously condemning the deeper moral corruption of a society that devalues daughters. It is both a theological correction and a moral indictment of their skewed values.

translation: What is the matter with you? How do you judge?
interpretation: This verse is a rhetorical rebuke directed at those who make unjust or irrational judgments, particularly concerning matters of faith, morality, or the distinction between believers and disbelievers, the righteous and the wicked. The Qur'an frequently poses this question after presenting a logical argument or comparison, challenging the listener to recognize the absurdity or injustice of equating things that are fundamentally different, such as treating the obedient and the sinful alike, or failing to use reason to discern truth from falsehood. It calls on the human intellect to reflect honestly and consistently rather than following bias, desire, or flawed reasoning when reaching conclusions about moral and spiritual truths.

translation: Then will you not remember?
interpretation: This rhetorical question appears at the end of several Qur'anic passages that present evidence of God's power, signs in creation, or accounts of previous nations, serving as a direct challenge to the listener's reasoning faculties. The phrase implicitly rebukes heedlessness, suggesting that the truth being conveyed is not obscure or requiring elaborate proof, but rather something that should naturally prompt reflection (tadhakkur) in anyone who pauses to consider it. The verb 'tadhakkur' implies not learning something new but recalling an innate or already-evident truth, as if the recognition of God's oneness and signs is embedded in human nature (fitrah) and merely needs to be awakened through contemplation. By posing it as a question rather than a command, the verse invites self-examination, placing responsibility on the individual to break through heedlessness and willful forgetfulness rather than ignorance, implying that disbelief often stems from a failure to reflect rather than a lack of evidence.

translation: Or do you have a clear authority [for what you claim]?
interpretation: This verse is part of a rhetorical challenge posed to the disbelievers and polytheists who attributed daughters to Allah or claimed knowledge of unseen matters, such as asserting a kinship between Allah and the jinn or claiming angels are female. The question demands evidence for such baseless assertions—do they possess any clear proof, scripture, or divine sanction that supports their claims? The implicit answer is no; they have no such authority. This rhetorical device is used throughout this section of Surah As-Saffat to expose the irrationality and unfounded nature of pagan beliefs, emphasizing that truth claims about the divine must be grounded in revelation or clear evidence rather than mere speculation, ancestral custom, or fabrication. It underscores the Quranic emphasis on epistemological accountability—that significant theological claims cannot be made without substantiation.

translation: Then bring your book, if you should be truthful.
interpretation: This verse is a rhetorical challenge directed at those who fabricate claims against God or deny the truth of revelation—such as those who claimed angels were daughters of God, or who rejected the Qur'an and prophethood. The demand to 'bring your book' is a demand for scriptural or textual proof supporting their false assertions. Since no such book exists that validates their claims, the challenge exposes the baselessness of their position. It underscores a recurring Qur'anic argumentative strategy: inviting skeptics to substantiate their claims with concrete evidence, knowing that they cannot, thereby affirming the truth of the Qur'an's message by contrast.

translation: And they have claimed between Him and the jinn a lineage (kinship), but the jinn themselves know well that they will be brought forth (arraigned for judgment).
interpretation: This verse addresses a specific polytheistic belief held by some pagan Arabs who claimed a familial or genealogical relationship between God and the jinn—akin to the way some claimed angels were 'daughters of God.' By asserting that the jinn themselves are fully aware that they will be summoned and presented before God for judgment, the verse dismantles the very premise of their claim: the jinn are not divine kin or partners with God, but are themselves created beings, accountable servants who will stand before Him for reckoning like all other creatures. Their own awareness of their coming judgment proves their subordinate, created status, refuting any notion of kinship or equality with the Divine. This serves as a broader argument against shirk (associating partners with God), using the jinn's own epistemic position against those who elevate them to divine status.

translation: Glory be to Allah, far above what they attribute (to Him).
interpretation: This verse is a declaration of Allah's absolute transcendence (tanzih), exalting Him above the false descriptions, attributes, partners, offspring, or imperfections that disbelievers and polytheists ascribe to Him. It serves as a rebuttal to specific claims made in the surrounding verses—such as attributing children, partners, or human-like qualities to the Divine—affirming that Allah is utterly free from any limitation, resemblance to creation, or deficiency that His creatures might imagine or assert about Him. The phrase functions both as worship and as theological correction, reminding believers to maintain a pure conception of God's unique and incomparable nature.

translation: Except the sincere servants of Allah.
interpretation: This phrase is a recurring refrain in Surah As-Saffat, appearing after descriptions of the punishment and misguidance awaiting disbelievers, idolaters, and those who fabricate false claims about Allah (such as attributing offspring to Him or worshipping jinn). The exception carved out for 'the sincere servants of Allah' (al-mukhlaseen) distinguishes those whose devotion is pure and undivided from the corrupted beliefs and fates of others. These sincere servants are protected from the self-deception, arrogance, and consequent punishment that befalls those who deviate from true monotheism. The term 'mukhlaseen' implies not merely sincerity in intention but a purified devotion free from shirk (associating partners with Allah) and the whisperings of Satan, as mentioned elsewhere in the Quran where Satan himself acknowledges he has no power over Allah's sincere servants. This recurring phrase serves as a structural and theological pivot, repeatedly reminding the listener that true faith and sincere worship exempt one from the fates of arrogant deniers, false deities, and misguided ancestors narrated throughout the surah.

translation: So indeed, you and whatever you worship
interpretation: This verse is part of a continuous statement that extends into the following verse, addressed to the disbelievers and idolaters. It declares that neither they nor the false deities they worship have any power to seduce or mislead anyone away from the truth of God, except those who are already destined for the Fire due to their own choices. This affirms the powerlessness of idols and false gods, emphasizing that ultimate guidance and misguidance rest with God alone, and that human beings bear responsibility for the path they choose to follow.

translation: You [disbelievers and your idols] cannot tempt anyone away from Him.
interpretation: This verse is part of a divine response addressed to those who worship false deities, declaring that neither they nor the objects of their worship possess any real power to seduce or lead people away from God's truth. The verse affirms that misguidance is not something idols or disbelievers can impose through their own power; rather, only those whom God has decreed will end up in the Fire—due to their own choices and hardened hearts—will be affected by such temptation. It underscores the limitation of created things, whether idols or disbelieving instigators, in altering the ultimate spiritual destiny of those who are sincere believers protected by God. The verse serves as a reassurance to the faithful that external forces of deception have no true power over them unless they are already inclined toward corruption and destined for punishment.

translation: Except him who is [destined] to burn in the Hellfire.
interpretation: This verse comes within a passage addressing the disbelievers and their false deities, clarifying that neither they nor what they worship have the power to lead anyone astray from God except those who, by their own choice and disbelief, are already destined for the Fire. The verse underscores the principle of personal responsibility and divine justice in Islamic theology: misguidance is not imposed externally by idols or Satan without the individual's own inclination toward disbelief and sin. Those who end up in Hellfire are not victims of external forces beyond their control but are those whose own corrupted will and persistent rejection of truth make them susceptible to being led astray. This reflects the broader Quranic theme that while Satan and false gods may invite people to error, they have no real power over the sincere and protected believers in God—only over those who have already opened themselves to misguidance through their own choices. It is a statement about the limits of external temptation in the face of genuine faith, and the self-selecting nature of damnation.

translation: And there is not among us [angels] except that he has a known station.
interpretation: This verse is spoken by the angels, affirming their complete submission to God's order and their rejection of any claim to divinity made by polytheists who associated angels with God or worshipped them. Each angel occupies a fixed, appointed rank or position in the cosmic hierarchy ordained by God, with specific duties and no autonomy to exceed or alter that station. This declaration emphasizes the angels' humility and total servitude before God, contrasting their orderly, obedient existence with the chaos of shirk (associating partners with God). It also serves as a broader theological statement about the created order: all beings, including the loftiest of creatures like angels, exist within a structured system of hierarchy and purpose set by the Creator, with none possessing inherent divine power or equal standing with God.

translation: And indeed, we [angels] are those arranged in ranks.
interpretation: This verse is part of a declaration made by the angels (as indicated by the surrounding verses in Surat As-Saffat, 37:164-166), affirming their devoted station before God. The angels describe themselves as standing in ordered ranks, ready in perpetual worship and service to the Divine. This imagery of angels arranged in rows evokes the discipline, obedience, and humility of the angelic host, who have no will of their own except to submit completely to God's command. The verse serves as a model for human worship as well, particularly in the context of congregational prayer, where believers are instructed to stand in straight, orderly rows—mirroring the angels' perfect submission and unity. It also serves as a rebuke to the polytheists mentioned earlier in the surah, contrasting the angels' true, humble worship of God alone with the false claims some made about angels being God's daughters or partners in divinity.

translation: And indeed, we are those who glorify [Allah].
interpretation: This verse is part of a declaration made by the angels in Surah As-Saffat, where they describe their own nature and role in the cosmic order. Following verses where the angels state they each have a known station (166) and that they stand in ranks (165), this verse affirms that their essential function is the continuous glorification (tasbih) of Allah. This serves multiple theological purposes: it refutes the pagan Arab belief that angels were daughters of God or deities deserving worship themselves, instead establishing them as humble, obedient servants whose entire purpose is worship. The verse also provides a model for human worship, suggesting that just as the angels exist in a state of perpetual glorification, believers should strive to maintain remembrance and praise of Allah as a central feature of their spiritual lives. The use of the emphatic construction 'inna lanahnu' (indeed, we are) underscores the certainty and completeness of the angels' devotion, contrasting with human inconsistency in worship.

translation: And indeed, they used to say,
interpretation: This verse is a fragment from Surah As-Saffat (37:167-170), where it refers to the pagan Arabs (or earlier disbelievers) who used to boast that if they had possessed the scriptures and guidance given to earlier nations, they would have been sincere worshippers of God alone. The verse sets up this claim, which is followed in subsequent verses by their rejection of that very guidance when it actually came to them through the Qur'an and Prophet Muhammad. This illustrates a recurring Qur'anic theme: the gap between people's hypothetical claims of faithfulness and their actual response when truly tested with guidance, exposing human tendency toward empty rhetoric and self-deception when confronted with real opportunities for righteousness.

translation: If only we had a reminder from the former peoples,
interpretation: This verse is part of a statement attributed to the Meccan disbelievers, continued in the following verse where they claim, 'We would surely have been sincere servants of Allah.' This was their excuse for rejecting Muhammad's message—they claimed that had they possessed a scripture or reminder like those given to earlier nations (such as the Torah or Gospel), they would have been devoted and faithful worshippers of God alone, unlike their ancestors who fell into idolatry. The Qur'an presents this as a hypothetical justification the disbelievers used to excuse their lack of faith, suggesting they blamed their paganism on simply not having received prior guidance. However, this excuse is immediately refuted in the following verses, which point out that now they have indeed received a reminder—the Qur'an itself—yet they still disbelieve in it, exposing their claim as hollow and insincere. This rhetorical device exposes human tendency to make excuses for disbelief, only to reject the truth when it actually arrives, revealing that the real issue was never a lack of guidance but a refusal to accept it due to arrogance, stubbornness, or attachment to ancestral traditions.

translation: Except the chosen (sincere, devoted) servants of Allah.
interpretation: This verse appears in the context of Surah As-Saffat, following a description of the deviant beliefs and ultimate punishment of those who worship false deities or make blasphemous claims about Allah, such as attributing offspring to Him. The phrase serves as an exception clause, distinguishing the sincere and devoted servants of Allah from those condemned. These 'mukhlasin' are the believers who have purified their worship and devotion exclusively for Allah, free from associating partners with Him or succumbing to misguided beliefs. They are spared from the punishment and misguidance described in the preceding verses because their sincerity and exclusive devotion protect them from the errors of shirk (polytheism) and the deception of Satan, who himself acknowledges in the Qur'an that he has no power over Allah's sincere servants. This verse thus highlights the protective nature of sincere faith and devotion, suggesting that true sincerity in worship serves as a shield against spiritual corruption and the schemes of misguidance.

translation: So they disbelieved in it, but they will come to know.
interpretation: This verse serves as a stern warning to those who reject divine truth and revelation. The phrase captures a moment of willful disbelief—people turning away from clear signs or guidance that has come to them. The concluding words, 'but they will come to know,' carry an ominous weight, pointing toward an inevitable reckoning, whether in this world through the unfolding of consequences, or in the Hereafter when the reality of what they denied will become undeniably clear. This reflects a recurring Qur'anic theme: that rejection of truth does not diminish its reality, and that time itself will vindicate what was once dismissed, often when it is too late for the deniers to benefit from this realization. It underscores the moral accountability inherent in conscious disbelief, especially after truth has been made evident, distinguishing it from mere ignorance.

translation: And indeed, Our word has already preceded for Our servants, the messengers,
interpretation: This verse refers to God's prior decree and promise regarding His messengers—namely, that they and those who follow them would ultimately be granted victory and support against their opponents, while their enemies would be brought low. It affirms a divine law or precedent (sunnah) that runs throughout the history of prophethood: that truth prevails over falsehood and that God's chosen messengers are never abandoned to the ultimate triumph of their adversaries. This 'preceding word' establishes a sense of certainty and comfort, particularly for the Prophet Muhammad and the early Muslim community facing persecution, reassuring them that the outcome of their struggle has already been established by divine decree, consistent with how God supported all previous prophets against their disbelieving peoples.

translation: Indeed, they are the ones who will be helped (made victorious).
interpretation: This verse is part of a passage in Surah As-Saffat affirming God's promise to His messengers and prophets. It follows a declaration that God's 'word' (His decree) had already gone forth for His servants, the messengers, that they would surely be granted victory and support against their adversaries. The verse establishes a divine law or pattern (sunnah) running throughout sacred history: those who are sent with the truth, despite facing rejection, mockery, and persecution from their communities, are ultimately granted triumph by God, whether through worldly vindication, the eventual spread and endurance of their message, or decisive support in the confrontation between truth and falsehood. The use of the emphatic construction and the passive voice ('the ones who will be helped') underscores that this victory is not something the messengers achieve by their own strength or effort, but is a grace bestowed upon them by God as a direct consequence of their fidelity to their mission. This serves as both a consolation to the Prophet Muhammad, who faced similar opposition from his own people, and a broader theological statement about the ultimate triumph of truth over falsehood, reassuring believers that apparent setbacks or persecution in this world are not indicative of ultimate failure, since divine support is assured for those who stand for the truth.

translation: And indeed, Our host - it is they who will be the victors.
interpretation: This verse appears in a context affirming God's unwavering support for His prophets and righteous servants against their adversaries. It reflects a recurring Qur'anic theme in which divine promises of victory are made to the believers, especially the messengers, assuring them that despite apparent setbacks or the numerical and military superiority of their opponents, the ultimate triumph belongs to God's party. The term 'our host' (jundana) signifies not merely physical armies but the entire force of divine support—comprising angels, destiny, and the inevitable unfolding of God's plan—that stands behind those who follow His guidance. This serves as a source of reassurance and steadfastness for believers facing persecution or hardship, reminding them that worldly appearances of strength or weakness do not determine the final outcome; rather, it is God's will and decree that assure the eventual success and dominance of truth over falsehood.

translation: So turn away from them for a while.
interpretation: This verse is part of a recurring refrain in Surah As-Saffat addressed to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him), instructing him to temporarily withdraw from and be patient with those who reject his message and mock him. The phrase 'for a while' (hatta heen) indicates that this estrangement is not permanent but has a divinely appointed end point, after which the disbelievers will witness the truth of the warnings given to them, whether through worldly consequences or ultimately in the Hereafter. This command reflects a broader Quranic theme of counseling patience and strategic withdrawal for prophets facing persistent rejection, trusting that divine justice will unfold in its appointed time rather than requiring immediate confrontation. The verse also serves to reassure the Prophet that the disbelievers' mockery and resistance is temporary, and that he should not be disheartened by it, as they will eventually see the fulfillment of what they were warned about.

translation: And watch them, for they will [soon] see.
interpretation: This verse is part of a sequence in Surah As-Saffat in which God instructs the Prophet Muhammad to turn away from the disbelievers who mock and reject the message, and to wait and observe, for a time will come when they themselves will clearly witness the truth of what they denied—whether through worldly defeat, the unfolding of divine signs, or ultimately on the Day of Judgment. The command carries a tone of reassurance to the Prophet and believers that patience will be vindicated, while serving as a warning to the disbelievers that their current blindness to truth will be replaced by undeniable, firsthand realization of the consequences of their rejection.

translation: So is it Our punishment that they seek to hasten?
interpretation: This verse is a rhetorical rebuke directed at those who, in their disbelief and arrogance, mockingly demanded that God's promised punishment be brought upon them immediately, as if daring Him to prove its reality. The question exposes the folly and recklessness of such a demand—rather than reflecting on the warnings given to them through revelation and the examples of destroyed nations before them, they responded with impatience and defiance, seeking to hasten what should rightly be feared and avoided through repentance. The verse underscores a broader Quranic theme: divine punishment operates according to God's wisdom and timing, not human provocation, and those who wish for its hastening reveal their spiritual blindness, for when it does come, it will be far too late for them to escape its consequences.

translation: Then, when it descends into their courtyard, evil is the morning of those who were warned.
interpretation: This verse depicts the suddenness and severity of divine punishment when it finally arrives for those who persistently rejected warnings.
