Those who were belittled for their faith or poverty may, in reality, be elevated, while the mockery itself becomes a point of reflection and humility for its perpetrators when the true outcomes of belief and disbelief are revealed.

translation: Indeed, that is true - the mutual dispute of the people of the Fire.
interpretation: This verse affirms the certainty of the arguments and recriminations that will take place among the inhabitants of Hell, as described in the preceding verses where leaders and followers blame one another for their shared fate. The phrase 'that is truth' serves as a divine confirmation that this scene is not mere imagery but a real event that will occur on the Day of Judgment. The verse underscores a broader Quranic theme: that in the Hereafter, the alliances, loyalties, and justifications people relied upon in worldly life will collapse into mutual blame and hostility. Those who followed corrupt leaders will accuse them of leading them astray, while the leaders will deny responsibility, each trying to shift blame to escape punishment. This serves as a warning to believers in this world to critically examine whom they follow and what they believe, rather than blindly trusting authority figures or popular opinion, since such blind following will offer no excuse or refuge in the Hereafter.

translation: Say, [O Muhammad], 'I am only a warner, and there is no deity except Allah, the One, the Prevailing (Al-Qahhar).'
interpretation: This verse establishes the core mission and message of the Prophet Muhammad in its most distilled form. By declaring himself 'only a warner,' he disclaims any divine attributes, miraculous powers beyond revelation, or authority to compel belief—his role is limited to conveying a message and alerting people to consequences, not controlling outcomes or possessing godlike power himself. This directly counters the polytheists' demands for signs, wonders, or his claim to supernatural status, redirecting focus entirely to the message rather than the messenger. The second half pivots to the theological heart of that message: radical monotheism. The pairing of 'Al-Wahid' (the One) with 'Al-Qahhar' (the Subduer, the Dominant, the Irresistible) is deliberate—unity of divinity is asserted alongside absolute, overpowering sovereignty. This combination counters any notion of shared divine power or competing deities, since true oneness necessarily entails total dominance over all creation. The name Al-Qahhar in particular conveys that Allah's will cannot be resisted or thwarted by any force, including the false gods the disbelievers worshipped alongside Him. Thus the verse functions as both a humbling clarification of prophetic limitation and an uncompromising assertion of divine supremacy, collapsing the distance people often try to place between themselves and ultimate accountability by making clear that no intermediary power—human or idol—can shield them from the One who overwhelms all.

translation: Lord of the heavens and the earth and all that is between them, the Almighty, the Ever-Forgiving.
interpretation: This verse encapsulates two seemingly contrasting yet complementary divine attributes: absolute power (al-'Aziz) and boundless forgiveness (al-Ghaffar). The pairing is deliberate and profound—it establishes that God's dominion over all creation, the heavens, the earth, and everything between them, is not exercised through tyranny or harsh domination, but is tempered with mercy and forgiveness. This juxtaposition teaches that true power is not diminished by forgiveness; rather, the capacity to forgive while possessing absolute might is itself a sign of greater strength and majesty. The verse appears in a context addressing human arrogance and disbelief, reminding the listener that the One who controls the entire cosmos, who has no rival in power, still chooses repeatedly to forgive His creation. This serves as both a warning against defying such overwhelming power and a message of hope that repentance will be met with divine mercy, encouraging believers to turn to God without despair over their sins, since the same God who commands the universe is also the one who continually pardons those who seek Him.

translation: Say: It is momentous news.
interpretation: This verse refers to the message of the Qur'an itself, and specifically to the truth of the Resurrection and the Day of Judgment, which the disbelievers were disputing and turning away from. By instructing the Prophet to declare it 'a great news' (naba'un azeem), God emphasizes the gravity and ultimate significance of this revelation above all worldly concerns. It is 'great' not because of its magnitude in size, but because of its consequence—it concerns the fate of every soul, the reality of accountability before God, and the truth of life after death. The verse comes as a response to those who mocked or doubted the Prophet's message, affirming that what he brings is not trivial talk but a matter of supreme importance that demands serious attention and reflection, something from which people carelessly and heedlessly turn away at their own peril.

translation: You are turning away from it.
interpretation: This phrase is part of a Qur'anic address (Surah Sad, 38:67-68) where the Prophet is instructed to say that what he brings is 'momentous news' (naba' 'azim), yet his addressees—the disbelieving Meccans—turn away from it in heedlessness and arrogance. The verse captures the tragic irony of human indifference toward truth of ultimate significance: the message of revelation, resurrection, and divine reckoning. Rather than engaging with its weighty implications for their eternal fate, the disbelievers dismiss it, distracted by worldly concerns, pride, or stubborn denial. The verse serves as a rebuke highlighting willful negligence—it is not that the message lacks importance or clarity, but that the listeners choose aversion over reflection, exemplifying a recurring Qur'anic theme of humanity's self-imposed blindness to profound truths that are placed clearly before them.

translation: I had no knowledge of the Exalted Assembly when they disputed.
interpretation: This verse is spoken by the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) at God's command, referring to the heavenly assembly of angels disputing over the creation of Adam, as recounted earlier in Surah Sad. The Prophet, being unlettered and not privy to the unseen realm, had no independent knowledge of this celestial event—the angels' discourse, their questioning of why a being who would cause corruption and bloodshed was to be created, and God's response establishing Adam's superior knowledge. This lack of prior access to such hidden matters underscores that the Prophet's knowledge of this episode, and of the unseen generally, comes purely through divine revelation, not through human means such as inheritance, study, or mystical insight on his own part. It serves as evidence of the authenticity of his prophethood: how else could he know of events in the unseen celestial realm unless God informed him? This rhetorical strategy reinforces the Qur'an's claim to divine origin by pointing to information the Prophet could not have obtained through ordinary human channels, addressing skeptics who doubted his prophetic mission and challenging them to explain how he could possess such knowledge otherwise.

translation: "Nothing is revealed to me except that I am only a clear warner."
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the limited and specific nature of the Prophet Muhammad's role and knowledge. He explicitly disclaims any special knowledge beyond what has been revealed to him, and what is revealed centers on his function as a 'clear warner' (nadhir mubin). This serves multiple theological purposes: it counters accusations that he is claiming divine knowledge of the unseen (ghayb) or supernatural powers beyond prophethood; it humbles the Prophet's status before his community, affirming he is a human messenger rather than a divine figure; and it clarifies that revelation itself is purposive and bounded—its primary function is warning humanity of consequences, not satisfying curiosity about hidden matters like the exact timing of the Day of Judgment or other speculative questions the disbelievers often posed. The word 'mubin' (clear/manifest) reinforces that this warning is not cryptic or ambiguous but openly comprehensible, placing the burden of response on those who hear it. This self-limitation also reflects a broader Qur'anic theme found in multiple verses where the Prophet is instructed to deny supernatural claims attributed to him by skeptics, redirecting attention instead to the moral and spiritual message he was sent to deliver.

translation: [Mention] when your Lord said to the angels, 'Indeed, I am going to create a human being from clay.'
interpretation: This verse opens the divine narrative of Adam's creation, emphasizing God's sovereign will and foreknowledge in bringing humanity into existence from humble, inanimate matter—clay. By addressing the angels beforehand, God establishes that the creation of humankind is a deliberate, purposeful act, not incidental, and sets the stage for the angels' subsequent response and the unique status that will be granted to this new creation. The use of 'basharan' (a human being, flesh) rather than a term emphasizing spiritual nature underscores the physical, earthly origin of humans, which stands in contrast to the spiritual nature of angels and to Iblis's claim of superiority due to his fiery origin. This sets up the theological tension explored in the following verses regarding humility, obedience, and the test of pride versus submission to God's command.

translation: So when I have fashioned him and breathed into him of My spirit, fall down before him in prostration.
interpretation: This verse recounts God's address to the angels regarding the creation of Adam. It establishes the unique dignity bestowed upon humankind: the human form, once perfected in its physical creation, is ennobled by the direct infusion of a divine spirit (ruh), a spirit whose nature is known only to God. This act elevates humanity above the rest of creation, including the angels, who are commanded to prostrate—not in worship of Adam, but in acknowledgment of God's creative will and the special honor He has conferred upon this new being. The prostration signifies obedience to God's command rather than worship of a created being, and it sets the stage for the narrative of Iblis's refusal, which becomes the archetype of pride and disobedience against divine will.

translation: So the angels prostrated, all of them together,
interpretation: This verse describes the moment following God's command to the angels to prostrate before Adam, newly created from clay. The emphasis on 'all of them together' underscores the totality and unanimity of the angels' obedience, highlighting their nature as beings who do not disobey God's commands and act in complete submission to His will. This immediate and collective compliance sets the stage for the subsequent refusal of Iblis, whose exception to this universal prostration becomes the central act of defiance in the narrative. The angels' prostration is not worship of Adam himself, but an act of honoring God's creation and acknowledging the special status and knowledge granted to humankind, as well as demonstrating the angels' own humility and complete submission to the divine decree, contrasting sharply with the pride that leads to Iblis's downfall.

translation: Except Iblis; he refused and was arrogant, and he became one of the disbelievers.
interpretation: This verse recounts the moment when Allah commanded the angels to prostrate before Adam, and all complied except Iblis (Satan). His refusal stemmed from arrogance (istikbar), as he considered himself superior to Adam, reasoning that he was created from fire while Adam was created from clay. This arrogance is portrayed as the root cause of his transformation from a being who worshipped and obeyed Allah into a disbeliever (kafir). The verse establishes a foundational theological lesson: disbelief and rebellion against divine command often originate from pride and a refusal to accept one's place in the divine order. Iblis's sin was not merely disobedience but a deeper spiritual corruption—valuing his own self-perceived merit over submission to God's explicit command. This episode serves as a cautionary tale throughout the Quran about the dangers of arrogance, envy, and self-exaltation, warning believers that such traits can lead to spiritual ruin and alienation from God's mercy, just as they did for Iblis, who became the archetype of the external tempter leading humanity astray.

translation: He said, 'O Iblis, what prevented you from prostrating to that which I created with My two hands? Were you arrogant, or were you among the exalted?'
interpretation: This verse recounts God's direct questioning of Iblis (Satan) after his refusal to bow to Adam. The phrase 'created with My two hands' emphasizes the special honor and direct divine craftsmanship bestowed upon Adam, distinguishing him from other creations that came into being simply through the command 'Be.' This elevates humanity's status and underscores why refusal to honor Adam was particularly grave. God's question is rhetorical and accusatory, forcing Iblis to confront the true motive behind his disobedience: arrogance (istikbar). The second part of the question, 'or were you among the exalted,' is a sarcastic rebuke, exposing the absurdity of Iblis's self-perceived superiority. This passage illustrates a foundational theological lesson on the nature of pride as the root of the first act of disobedience in creation, establishing arrogance as a spiritual disease that blinds one to truth and leads to rebellion against divine command, even when the reasoning behind that command is not fully understood. It also sets the precedent for the eternal enmity between Iblis and humankind, rooted in this moment of refusal driven by a sense of superior origin (fire over clay) rather than true understanding of divine wisdom.

translation: He [Iblis] said: 'I am better than him; You created me from fire, while You created him from clay.'
interpretation: This verse records Iblis's response when Allah questioned why he refused to prostrate before Adam. It reveals the root of Iblis's sin: arrogance (kibr) rooted in a flawed comparison based on material origin rather than divine command or inherent worth. Iblis assumes that fire is superior to clay, and therefore he is superior to Adam, failing to recognize that true honor comes not from the substance of one's creation but from obedience to Allah's command and the special dignity Allah bestowed upon Adam by teaching him the names of all things and commanding the angels to prostrate before him. This moment illustrates the danger of logical reasoning divorced from humility and submission to divine wisdom—Iblis uses what seems like a rational argument to justify disobedience, demonstrating how intellectual pride can lead to spiritual ruin. His refusal, based on a self-serving hierarchy of creation, becomes the paradigm for human arrogance and the belief that one's own judgment supersedes divine instruction. This verse thus serves as a warning against comparing oneself to others based on superficial or material distinctions, and against allowing pride to override obedience to God's command.

translation: He said, "Then get out of it, for indeed, you are expelled (accursed/outcast)."
interpretation: This verse records God's response to Iblis after his refusal to prostrate before Adam out of arrogance and his claim of superiority due to being created from fire rather than clay. God's command to 'get out' signifies Iblis's expulsion from the elevated spiritual station and company of the angels, stripping him of his former rank. The term 'rajim' (رجيم), meaning cursed, driven away, or pelted/stoned, indicates a permanent state of disgrace and banishment from divine mercy, a status that follows him as a symbol of rejection for his pride and disobedience. This marks the foundational moment of enmity between Iblis and humanity, as his expulsion stems directly from his refusal to honor Adam, setting the stage for his subsequent vow to mislead humankind. The verse underscores the gravity of arrogance (istikbar) as a sin, illustrating that pride and refusal to submit to a divine command—even when one feels superior—leads to spiritual ruin and exile from God's grace.

translation: And indeed, upon you shall be My curse until the Day of Judgment.
interpretation: This verse is part of God's pronouncement against Iblis (Satan) after his refusal to prostrate before Adam. It establishes that Satan's rejection and banishment from divine mercy is not a temporary punishment but extends throughout the entire span of human history, lasting until the Day of Judgment when final accounts are settled. The curse represents complete spiritual expulsion and condemnation, marking Satan as the eternal adversary of humanity. This sets up the theological framework for the ongoing cosmic struggle between good and evil, where Satan becomes the tempter of humankind until the appointed end time, at which point he will face his ultimate reckoning alongside all those he has misled. The phrase 'Day of Judgment' (yawm al-din) signals that this curse has a definite endpoint tied to divine justice, after which Satan's fate and punishment will be fully realized and made manifest.

translation: He said, 'My Lord, then reprieve me until the Day they are resurrected.'
interpretation: This verse captures Iblis's (Satan's) response after being cursed and expelled from Allah's mercy for refusing to prostrate to Adam. Rather than seeking repentance or forgiveness, Iblis asks for an extended lifespan until the Day of Judgment, revealing his intent to use this time to mislead humanity rather than reform himself. This request, which Allah grants (though only until a specific appointed time, not literally until the Resurrection itself), establishes the cosmic drama of temptation and free will that defines human existence. Iblis's petition demonstrates arrogance persisting even in defeat—he does not ask for mercy or redemption, but for the opportunity to prove his argument that humans are unworthy of the honor given to them over him. This moment explains the theological origin of evil's active role in the world: it is not random but purposeful, driven by wounded pride and a desire for vindication through humanity's corruption. The granting of this request also underscores the Islamic concept that human trials and temptations serve a purpose in the divine plan, testing genuine faith and moral choice against persistent, intelligent opposition until the end of time.

translation: He [Allah] said, "Indeed, you are of those given respite."
interpretation: This verse records Allah's response to Iblis (Satan) after he refused to prostrate before Adam and was subsequently cursed and expelled. Iblis had requested a reprieve, asking to be given respite until the Day of Resurrection so that he could attempt to mislead humankind. Allah's granting of this respite demonstrates several theological principles: first, it shows that Allah's power extends even to permitting the adversary of humanity to operate within a bounded timeframe, underscoring that nothing occurs outside divine will and decree. Second, it establishes the cosmic test of human existence—Iblis's temptations become the very mechanism through which human free will, faith, and moral choice are exercised and proven. Third, the granting of respite rather than immediate destruction reveals a dimension of Allah's wisdom and mercy, allowing the drama of guidance versus misguidance to unfold across human history rather than foreclosing it. The respite is not a sign of weakness or indulgence toward evil, but rather a deliberate feature of creation's design, in which human beings are given the capacity to resist temptation and earn their ultimate reward through genuine struggle rather than through an existence devoid of trial. This moment thus sets the stage for the entire narrative of human moral responsibility, obedience, and the eternal consequences of choosing between guidance and the whisperings of Satan.

translation: Until the Day of the time well-known.
interpretation: This phrase is part of God's response to Iblis (Satan) after he refused to prostrate before Adam and was cast out, asking for respite until the Day of Resurrection. God grants him respite, but not indefinitely—only until 'the Day of the time well-known,' referring to a specific, predetermined moment known only to God, understood to be the Day of Judgment when all creation will be resurrected. This phrase emphasizes several theological points: first, that even Satan's defiance and the respite granted to him operate within the bounds of divine decree and knowledge—nothing, not even the rebellion of Iblis, escapes God's sovereign plan. Second, it underscores that the timing of the Hour is a matter of exclusive divine knowledge, hidden from all creation including Satan himself, who is given a general assurance of delay but not specific knowledge of when it will occur. Third, this serves as a reminder to humanity that the period of worldly existence and testing, during which Satan is permitted to tempt and misguide, has a definite end point fixed by God, after which accountability and judgment will commence. The 'known time' thus represents both a limit on evil's temporal power and a certainty of ultimate divine justice.

translation: He [Iblis] said: 'Then by Your might, I will surely mislead them all.'
interpretation: This verse records Satan's defiant oath after his expulsion from Allah's mercy for refusing to bow to Adam. Rather than repenting, Iblis swears by Allah's own 'izzah (might, glory) to dedicate himself to misleading all of humankind. This is significant because Iblis implicitly acknowledges Allah's supreme power even as he rebels against His command, showing that his defiance is not born of doubt about Allah's sovereignty but of arrogance and envy toward Adam. The oath 'by Your might' underscores that Iblis recognizes he can only act within the limits Allah permits him—he has no power of his own, only what is allowed for the testing of humanity. This sets up the cosmic drama of free will: humans are granted the capacity to choose between guidance and misguidance, with Satan as an avowed adversary who will use whispering, temptation, and deception as his tools. The verse also foreshadows the exception Iblis himself will later acknowledge (that he cannot mislead Allah's sincere, devoted servants), highlighting that true faith and sincerity serve as protection against his schemes.

translation: Except Your sincere servants among them.
interpretation: This phrase appears in the Qur'anic narrative concerning Iblis (Satan), who, after being cast out of Allah's mercy for refusing to prostrate before Adam, vows to mislead humanity from the straight path. He declares that he will tempt and deceive people from every direction, except for those who are truly sincere and devoted servants of Allah. This exception highlights a central theological principle: that genuine sincerity (ikhlas) in faith and devotion to Allah serves as a protective shield against satanic deception. Those who purify their intentions solely for Allah's sake, free from hypocrisy, worldly desires, or divided loyalties, are granted divine protection from Satan's influence. This verse underscores that while Satan has power to whisper and tempt, he has no real authority over those whose hearts are anchored in sincere devotion to God. It also serves as a reminder to believers of the importance of cultivating ikhlas as a means of spiritual safeguarding, and it reflects Allah's mercy in that despite Satan's declared enmity, the sincere servants remain under divine protection, beyond the reach of his schemes.

translation: He [Allah] said: 'Then the truth—and the truth I say—'
interpretation: This verse comes in the context of Surah Sad, following the account of Iblis's defiance and his vow to mislead humanity (apart from Allah's sincere servants). Here, Allah affirms His own declaration with emphatic certainty, using the repetition of 'al-haqq' (the truth) as both a solemn oath and a statement of fact. The phrase prepares for the pronouncement that follows in the next verse—that Hell will be filled with Iblis and all those who follow him. The doubling of 'the truth' underscores the absolute certainty and unchangeable nature of Allah's decree: it is not merely a prediction but a binding truth that will inevitably come to pass. This also reflects a broader Qur'anic theme where Allah's speech itself is identified with truth (haqq), affirming His sovereignty over judgment and destiny, and reinforcing that His word is self-verifying and requires no external validation.

translation: "I will surely fill Hell with you and with those who follow you among them, all together."
interpretation: This verse is part of Allah's declaration to Iblis (Satan) after his refusal to prostrate to Adam and his vow to mislead humanity. It represents Allah's response and warning, affirming that divine justice will ultimately prevail over Satan's rebellion and deception. The statement establishes a cosmic principle: those who knowingly choose to follow Satan's path of disobedience, arrogance, and misguidance—despite having been given guidance and free will—will share in the consequence of that choice alongside him. This is not a declaration of predetermined fate for all humans, but rather a statement about the natural outcome for those who deliberately align themselves with Satan's call to rebellion against God. It underscores the Qur'anic theme of personal accountability—that Hell is reserved for those who actively choose misguidance after being shown the truth, and that following Satan's whispers and temptations has real spiritual consequences. The verse also serves as a stark warning to believers throughout the text, reminding them of the enmity between humanity and Satan that was established at the very beginning of creation, and calling them to remain vigilant against his influence.

translation: Say, 'I do not ask you for any reward for it, nor am I one of the pretenders (those who affect or fabricate what is not true).'
interpretation: This verse establishes the sincerity and authenticity of the Prophet Muhammad's message by addressing two potential doubts that skeptics might raise. First, by declaring that he seeks no material compensation or reward from his audience for delivering the message, he removes any suspicion that his motives are self-interested or mercenary. This distinguishes him from false prophets or charlatans who might exploit religious claims for personal gain. Second, by stating he is not among 'al-mutakallifin'—those who affect, pretend, or burden themselves with claims beyond their true knowledge or capacity—he asserts that his message is not fabricated, exaggerated, or artificially constructed. He is not pretending to a status or knowledge he doesn't possess, nor is he forcing himself to say things beyond what has been genuinely revealed to him. This verse thus serves as a declaration of prophetic integrity, emphasizing that the Quranic message comes from divine revelation rather than human invention, and that the messenger's role is one of authentic transmission rather than self-serving innovation or performance. It also implicitly invites the listener to evaluate the message on its own merits rather than dismissing it based on assumptions about the messenger's hidden agenda.

translation: It is not but a reminder to the worlds (all mankind).
interpretation: This verse affirms the universal nature and purpose of the Qur'an. Coming at the end of a passage describing divine signs and the reliability of the message brought through the Prophet, this verse clarifies that the revelation is not confined to a particular people, time, or place, but is a 'dhikr' (reminder, remembrance, admonition) intended for all of creation—'al-'alamin' encompassing all nations, peoples, and perhaps even jinn and humankind collectively. The word 'dhikr' suggests that the Qur'an does not bring entirely new information but reawakens an innate recognition of truth already present in human nature (fitrah)—reminding people of their covenant with God, their purpose, and the moral and spiritual truths they may have forgotten or ignored. This verse also serves as a rebuttal to those who doubted the message's legitimacy, affirming that it carries universal relevance and is not merely poetry, soothsaying, or madness as detractors claimed, but a serious, meaningful guidance for all of humanity across all times.

translation: And you will surely know its news after a while.
interpretation: This verse, which closes Surah Sad, follows the Prophet's declaration that the Qur'an is nothing but a reminder to all the worlds and that he asks no reward for conveying it. The verse serves as a solemn warning to those who deny or doubt the truth of the message: the ultimate reality and significance of what has been revealed will become undeniably clear in time, whether through the unfolding of worldly events, the Day of Judgment, or both. It conveys a sense of patient certainty on the part of the Prophet and believers, affirming that truth does not depend on immediate acceptance or vindication—time itself, and ultimately the Hereafter, will confirm the authenticity of the message and the consequences of rejecting it. The phrase implies a deferred but certain reckoning, urging the listener toward reflection rather than hasty denial.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. The revelation of the Book is from Allah, the Almighty, the All-Wise.
interpretation: This opening verse establishes the divine origin and authority of the Qur'an, serving as an introduction to the surah. By emphasizing that the revelation comes from Allah described with the attributes 'Al-Aziz' (the Almighty, the Mighty) and 'Al-Hakim' (the All-Wise), the verse underscores two essential qualities: power and wisdom. This pairing reassures the listener that the Book is not merely a human composition but originates from a source of supreme authority and perfect wisdom, meaning every command, prohibition, and narrative within it is purposeful and just. The mention of these specific divine names at the outset also sets the tone for the surah's content, which often deals with themes of sincerity in worship, the consequences of rejecting truth, and the ultimate justice of Allah—all of which require both His might to enforce and His wisdom to perfectly ordain.'

translation: Indeed, We have sent down to you the Book in truth, so worship Allah, sincere to Him in religion [devotion].
interpretation: This verse establishes the divine origin and authenticity of the Quran as a revelation given to Prophet Muhammad with purpose and truth, not as mere human composition or falsehood. The subsequent command flows logically from this truth: because the revelation is genuine and from God, the appropriate response is sincere, exclusive worship of Allah alone. The term 'mukhlisan' (sincere/pure) emphasizes that worship must be free from hypocrisy, showing off, or mixing devotion with worship of others besides God. This verse establishes the foundational Islamic principle of tawhid (monotheism) in worship - that religious devotion (ad-deen) must be purified and directed solely to Allah, without partners, intermediaries, or ulterior motives. It connects the authenticity of revelation directly to the ethical and spiritual obligation of sincere monotheistic worship, suggesting that true acceptance of the Quran's truth naturally leads to unadulterated devotion to God alone.

translation: Unquestionably, to Allah belongs pure, sincere devotion (ad-din al-khalis). And those who take protectors besides Him [say], 'We only worship them that they may bring us nearer to Allah in position.' Indeed, Allah will judge between them concerning that over which they differ. Indeed, Allah does not guide he who is a persistent liar and disbeliever.
interpretation: This verse addresses the polytheists' rationalization for worshipping intermediaries—idols, saints, or other beings—alongside Allah. Their justification was not that these entities possessed independent divinity, but that they served as intercessors to draw them closer to Allah, much like courtiers might mediate access to a king. The verse categorically rejects this reasoning, establishing that true religious devotion (din) must be exclusively and purely directed to Allah alone, without intermediaries, partners, or associates. The phrase 'ad-din al-khalis' emphasizes sincerity and purity of worship—devotion uncontaminated by divided loyalties or alternative objects of reverence. The verse then shifts to eschatological judgment, affirming that Allah Himself will resolve the theological disputes between monotheists and polytheists on the Day of Judgment, when the truth of these matters will be definitively settled. The closing statement—that Allah does not guide the persistent liar and disbeliever—serves as a sobering warning: those who knowingly fabricate theological justifications for shirk (associating partners with Allah) and persist in disbelief despite recognizing truth are spiritually self-condemned, having chosen falsehood over the clear guidance available to them. This verse thus functions as both a theological corrective against intercessory polytheism and a reminder of ultimate accountability before Allah.

translation: If Allah had intended to take a son, He could have chosen whatever He willed from what He creates. Glory be to Him! He is Allah, the One, the All-Prevailing.
interpretation: This verse refutes the notion that God has offspring, a belief held by various groups the Qur'an addresses, including those who claimed Jesus or angels were God's children. The argument is logical: if God, in His omnipotence, had wished to have a son or child, He would not need to beget one through the natural process of procreation—He could simply select or create any being He chose and designate it as such. The very suggestion of begetting implies need, continuity, and a partner, all of which are incompatible with absolute divine self-sufficiency. The verse then moves to exalt God above such human-like limitations with 'Glory be to Him,' emphasizing His transcendence. It concludes with two divine attributes: al-Wahid (the One, indivisible and without partner) and al-Qahhar (the Subduer or All-Prevailing, who has absolute power over all creation). Together, these names affirm God's absolute unity and supreme sovereignty, making the concept of divine offspring both unnecessary and theologically incoherent, as it would compromise His oneness and imply a sharing of His essence or power.

translation: He created the heavens and the earth in truth. He wraps the night over the day and wraps the day over the night, and He has subjected the sun and the moon, each running [its course] for a specified term. Unquestionably, He is the Exalted in Might, the Perpetual Forgiver.
interpretation: This verse presents the orderly, purposeful creation of the cosmos as evidence of God's power and wisdom. The imagery of night and day wrapping over one another, like a turban being wound, conveys a continuous, cyclical process rather than an abrupt alternation—suggesting the seamless, precise mechanism governing the universe. The subjection of the sun and moon to fixed courses underscores that nothing in creation moves arbitrarily; all follows a determined plan set by the Creator, pointing to divine wisdom and intentionality rather than chance. The concluding pairing of God's attributes—the Exalted in Might ('al-'Aziz') and the Perpetual Forgiver ('al-Ghaffar')—is significant: it links cosmic power with mercy, implying that the same God who commands the vast, unerring order of the heavens and earth is also the one who forgives human failings. This juxtaposition invites reflection that the grandeur and precision of creation should lead humans not to despair before divine power, but to trust in His mercy, recognizing that the One capable of such magnificent order is equally capable of boundless forgiveness.

translation: He created you from a single soul, then made from it its mate, and sent down for you eight pairs of cattle. He creates you in the wombs of your mothers, in stages, one creation after another, within three veils of darkness. That is Allah, your Lord; to Him belongs all sovereignty. There is no god but Him. How then are you turned away?
interpretation: This verse draws together cosmology, biology, and theology to argue for the oneness and sovereignty of God. It begins with the singular origin of humanity, emphasizing a shared essence that undercuts claims of division or hierarchy among people. The mention of the four kinds of livestock in male-female pairs situates human life within a broader created order that is itself purposefully designed and provided for human benefit. The description of embryonic development 'in stages, one creation after another, within three veils of darkness' reflects an early articulation of the staged, hidden nature of gestation—understood traditionally as referring to the abdominal wall, the womb, and the amniotic membrane—pointing to a meticulous, ongoing act of creation happening unseen within the body. This intimate, continuous creative process is presented as evidence of God's direct involvement in the most hidden and vulnerable stages of human life, making the subsequent rhetorical question all the more pointed: if God is responsible for such intricate, unseen acts of creation and for sustaining all life through provision, then sovereignty and worship belong to Him alone. The closing question 'how then are you turned away?' is not merely rhetorical but an indictment of human inconsistency—those who acknowledge God's creative power in theory yet direct worship, loyalty, or ultimate trust toward other than Him in practice.

translation: If you disbelieve, then indeed Allah is free of need of you. And He does not approve disbelief for His servants. And if you are grateful, He approves it for you. And no bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another. Then to your Lord is your return, and He will inform you of what you used to do. Indeed, He is Knowing of that within the breasts.
interpretation: This verse establishes the absolute self-sufficiency of God, who derives no benefit from human worship and suffers no loss from human disbelief—gratitude and faith are for the believer's own spiritual good, not a favor done to the Divine. It also articulates a foundational principle of individual moral accountability: no soul can bear the sin of another, rejecting any notion of inherited guilt or vicarious atonement. Each person stands responsible solely for their own deeds. The verse closes with a reminder of the ultimate return to God, who possesses complete knowledge of the inner contents of hearts, meaning that outward actions alone do not suffice—sincerity and inner intention are fully known and will be the basis of judgment. Together, these elements emphasize humility before divine independence, personal responsibility, and the futility of hypocrisy, since nothing concealed within the heart escapes God's awareness.

translation: And when affliction touches man, he calls upon his Lord, turning to Him in repentance. Then, when He bestows upon him a favor from Himself, he forgets that for which he called upon Him before, and sets up rivals to Allah to mislead [others] from His way. Say, 'Enjoy your disbelief for a little; indeed, you are among the companions of the Fire.'
interpretation: This verse exposes a recurring pattern of human psychology: sincere turning to God only in times of desperate need, followed by ingratitude and forgetfulness once relief comes. The crisis strips away pretension, revealing an instinctive recognition of a single, true Lord to whom one appeals in genuine humility. Yet prosperity and ease breed amnesia—not just personal forgetfulness, but an active construction of substitute objects of devotion ('andad), whether wealth, status, idols, or ideologies, which then serve to lead others astray as well. The phrase 'to mislead from His way' suggests this is not merely private backsliding but becomes a social force, propagating falsehood. The divine response—'enjoy your disbelief a little'—is deeply ironic, granting the very worldly pleasure and security the person sought while stripping it of ultimate value, since it is temporary and precedes inevitable reckoning. The verse thus functions as a mirror held up to the believer, warning against conditional faith that surfaces only in hardship and vanishes in comfort, and calling instead for consistent, grateful remembrance of God regardless of circumstance.

translation: Is one who is devoutly obedient during periods of the night, prostrating and standing [in prayer], fearing the Hereafter and hoping for the mercy of his Lord, [like one who does not]? Say, 'Are those who know equal to those who do not know?' Only those of understanding will be reminded.
interpretation: This verse draws a contrast between the believer who spends the night in worship—alternating between prostration and standing prayer—out of fear of accountability in the Hereafter and hope in divine mercy, and one who lives heedlessly without such devotion. The rhetorical question about those who know versus those who do not underscores that true knowledge is not merely intellectual but is manifested in conscious, humble worship and awareness of ultimate consequences. The verse closes by affirming that only people of genuine insight and reflective hearts ('ulul-albab) are capable of recognizing this truth and acting upon it, suggesting that real wisdom is inseparable from spiritual mindfulness and moral responsibility.

translation: Say, [O Muhammad], 'O My servants who have believed, fear your Lord. For those who do good in this world is good, and the earth of Allah is spacious. Indeed, the patient will be given their reward without measure.'
interpretation: This verse addresses believers directly through the Prophet, calling them 'My servants' as a term of divine intimacy and honor. It establishes that taqwa (God-consciousness and reverent fear) is the foundational response to faith. The promise of 'good in this world' for those who do good (muhsinin) suggests that righteousness brings its own rewards even before the Hereafter—whether through inner peace, blessings, or favorable outcomes. The mention of Allah's earth being 'spacious' serves as both literal and spiritual guidance: if believers face persecution, hardship, or inability to practice their faith freely in one place, they are permitted and even encouraged to emigrate elsewhere, as geography should never be a barrier to worship and righteous living. This reflects the historical context of early Muslims facing oppression in Mecca, encouraging migration to places where they could practice faith safely, but the principle extends universally—one should seek environments conducive to righteousness rather than remaining trapped in oppressive circumstances. The verse concludes with a profound promise that those who practice sabr (patience, perseverance, steadfastness) will receive rewards 'without account' or measure—meaning without limit, calculation, or proportion to their deeds. This limitless reward for patience distinguishes it from other virtues, suggesting that patience in adversity, patience in obedience, and patience in avoiding sin represents one of the most spiritually valuable qualities, deserving of extraordinary, immeasurable divine recompense.

translation: Say: Indeed, I have been commanded to worship Allah, sincerely devoting my religion to Him alone.
interpretation: This verse establishes the core principle of tawhid (monotheism) and ikhlas (sincerity) as the foundation of worship. The Prophet is instructed to declare openly that his worship is not based on personal preference, cultural custom, or social pressure, but on divine command. The word 'mukhlisan' (sincerely devoting) emphasizes that true worship must be free from any form of association with other deities, hypocrisy, or ulterior motives such as seeking praise or worldly gain. This verse serves as a direct rebuttal to polytheism, asserting that genuine devotion requires exclusive dedication to God alone, without dividing one's loyalty or intentions between Him and anything else. It also reflects the broader Quranic theme that true faith is not merely about outward rituals but about the purity and sincerity of one's inner intention (niyyah) directed solely toward the Creator.

translation: And I have been commanded to be the first of those who submit [to Allah].
interpretation: This verse is spoken in the voice of the Prophet Muhammad, declaring his personal obligation and priority in embracing complete submission to God. Being 'first' here signifies not necessarily chronological precedence, but moral and spiritual primacy—he is to be the foremost exemplar of islam (submission) among his community, leading by example rather than merely by instruction. It underscores the principle that a messenger must embody the message he conveys: before calling others to surrender their will to God, he himself must demonstrate the most complete and sincere submission. This establishes the Prophet's role as the perfect model of faith and obedience, setting the standard that all believers are called to emulate, and reinforces the Quranic theme that true leadership in faith begins with one's own submission before guiding others.

translation: Say: 'Indeed, I fear, if I disobey my Lord, the punishment of a tremendous Day.'
interpretation: This verse instructs the Prophet Muhammad to declare openly his own accountability before God, emphasizing that even he, as the chosen Messenger, is not exempt from the consequences of disobedience. It underscores the principle that prophethood does not confer immunity from divine judgment, reinforcing the universality of accountability before God. By expressing fear of 'a tremendous Day'—a reference to the Day of Judgment—the verse highlights the gravity of that reckoning, which surpasses all worldly concerns. It also serves a rhetorical purpose in the Qur'an's broader argument against the disbelievers: if the Prophet himself, who receives divine revelation, fears the consequences of disobedience, how much more should ordinary people be mindful of their own deeds and submit to God's guidance. This verse thus models humility and taqwa (God-consciousness) as the proper disposition of a believer, regardless of one's station, and reaffirms that sincerity and obedience to God are matters of personal responsibility rather than privilege or status.

translation: Say, 'It is Allah I worship, being sincere to Him in my religion.'
interpretation: This verse establishes the core principle of tawhid (monotheism) and sincerity of worship (ikhlas) in Islam. The Prophet is instructed to declare that his worship is directed exclusively to Allah, free from any form of association of partners (shirk) or ostentation (riya). The word 'mukhlisan' (sincerely/purely) emphasizes that true worship must be devoted entirely to God alone, without mixing in worship of others or seeking worldly recognition. This sincerity of intention is considered foundational to all acts of worship in Islamic theology - the inner purity of devotion matters as much as, if not more than, the outward performance of religious duties. The verse serves as a declaration of personal commitment and a model for believers to purify their intentions in all acts of worship and submission to God.

translation: So worship what you wish besides Him. Say: Indeed, the losers are those who will lose themselves and their families on the Day of Resurrection. Unquestionably, that is the manifest loss.
interpretation: This verse comes as a stern rebuke addressed to those who reject the call to worship God alone, following the Prophet's declaration that he would never abandon his faith even if offered worldly power. The command 'worship what you wish besides Him' is not a genuine permission but a statement of condemnation and warning, conveying divine contempt for their obstinate choice—they are left to their own devices as a consequence of their persistence in disbelief. The true measure of loss is then redefined: it is not material failure but spiritual and eternal ruin. Those who squander their own souls through disbelief, and who likewise fail to secure the salvation of their families by not guiding them to faith, will discover on the Day of Judgment that they have lost everything that truly mattered—themselves and their loved ones—since no worldly gain can compensate for the loss of one's eternal soul. The verse closes with emphatic certainty ('unquestionably') to drive home that this, and nothing else, constitutes the clearest and most absolute form of loss, reorienting the audience's understanding of success and failure away from worldly standards toward eternal consequence.

translation: They shall have coverings of fire above them, and coverings [of fire] beneath them. That is what God uses to warn His servants: 'O My servants, fear Me!'
interpretation: This verse vividly depicts the terrifying fate awaiting those who reject faith and lead others astray, portraying them as utterly enveloped by punishment from every direction, with no escape or shelter. The imagery of fire above and below emphasizes total encompassment of divine retribution, leaving no gap for relief. Crucially, the verse frames this fearsome description not merely as a threat but as a pedagogical tool—God uses the fear of such a fate to instill reverence and caution in His servants. The direct address 'O My servants, fear Me' shifts from description to divine summons, personalizing the warning and calling believers to a conscious, active fear (taqwa) that should shape their moral and spiritual conduct. This fear is not meant to produce despair but righteous mindfulness, motivating obedience and steering believers away from the arrogance and misguidance that lead to such punishment.

translation: And those who avoid false gods, lest they worship them, and turn in repentance to Allah - for them are glad tidings. So give good tidings to My servants.
interpretation: This verse establishes a criterion for identifying those deserving of divine glad tidings: it is not merely refraining from worshipping idols out of indifference, but actively shunning taghut - false gods, tyrannical authorities, or anything worshipped besides Allah - combined with a sincere, continual turning toward Allah in repentance and devotion. The pairing of these two actions is significant: rejection of falsehood alone is insufficient without the positive orientation toward truth. The verse also reflects a broader Quranic theme that true faith requires both negation (la ilaha) and affirmation (illallah) - the rejection of all forms of idolatry, whether literal idols or metaphorical ones like wealth, power, or ego, alongside wholehearted devotion to Allah. The command to Muhammad to 'give good tidings to My servants' personalizes this promise, framing it as a direct address from Allah through His Messenger, emphasizing that this good news is reserved specifically for those who meet both conditions - a distinguishing mark of true servitude ('ibad) to Allah.

translation: Those who listen to the word and follow the best of it - those are the ones whom Allah has guided, and those are the possessors of understanding.
interpretation: This verse establishes a criterion for true wisdom and intelligence: the capacity to listen attentively to various ideas, arguments, and perspectives, and then discern and follow what is best among them. It is not merely about hearing, but about active, critical engagement with speech and discourse, leading to the selection of what is most true, beneficial, and virtuous. This describes an intellectual and spiritual openness combined with sound judgment - the opposite of blind conformity or rejecting ideas without consideration. Those who possess this quality of discernment are described as being divinely guided, suggesting that this very capacity for discerning the best among what is heard is itself a sign of, or a means to, Allah's guidance. The verse thus links true intellect (ulul-albab, 'possessors of understanding/the kernel of things') not with mere accumulation of knowledge, but with the wisdom to evaluate, compare, and choose the most excellent path among competing ideas and counsel.

translation: So, can he upon whom the word of punishment has become justly due [be saved]? Can you then rescue one who is [already] in the Fire?
interpretation: This verse addresses the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) directly, consoling him regarding his intense desire to guide all people to faith, including those who stubbornly persist in disbelief and wrongdoing. The rhetorical question underscores a fundamental principle: once a person's own choices have sealed their fate through persistent rejection of truth and corruption of soul, no amount of external effort—even from a prophet—can alter the outcome of divine justice. The 'word of punishment' refers to the just verdict that befalls those who, after being given ample opportunity and clear signs, knowingly choose disbelief and transgression as their permanent way of being. The 'Fire' here may be understood both literally as the eschatological Hellfire and metaphorically as the self-destructive state of spiritual blindness and moral corruption such persons inhabit even in this world. The verse teaches that guidance (hidayah) ultimately rests with God alone, and the Prophet's role is to convey the message, not to compel or guarantee salvation for every individual. This serves to relieve the Prophet of a burden of responsibility beyond his capacity, while also serving as a sobering reminder to listeners that their own choices carry eternal weight, and that willful, confirmed rejection of truth reaches a point of no return where no intercession or human effort can reverse the consequence of one's own deliberate path.

translation: But those who feared their Lord will have lofty chambers, above which are built [other] lofty chambers, beneath which rivers flow. [This is] the promise of Allah; Allah does not fail in [His] promise.
interpretation: This verse contrasts the fate of the righteous with that of the deceived disbelievers described earlier in the surah. The imagery of multi-tiered chambers with flowing rivers beneath them symbolizes the elevated and secure status of paradise, a place of permanence and tranquility in stark contrast to the darkness and confusion of hell mentioned previously. The repetition of 'Allah' emphasizes divine reliability and the certainty of fulfillment of promises—unlike worldly promises which may be broken, God's covenant with the pious is absolute and guaranteed. The verse ultimately serves to reassure believers that taqwa (God-consciousness and righteousness) is rewarded with structured, layered blessings, reflecting both physical splendor and spiritual elevation, reinforcing the theme of divine justice central to this portion of the Qur'an.

translation: Have you not seen that Allah sends down water from the sky and causes it to flow as springs [and rivers] in the earth; then He brings forth thereby crops of varying colors; then they dry up and you see them turned yellow; then He makes them [scattered] debris. Indeed in that is a reminder for those of understanding.
interpretation: This verse presents the cycle of water and vegetation as a sign pointing to deeper truths about existence and divine power. The progression—rain descending, seeping into the earth, emerging as springs, nourishing diverse crops, then those crops flourishing, aging, yellowing, and finally crumbling to dust—mirrors the broader pattern of all worldly life: a trajectory of growth, vitality, decline, and dissolution. The verse invites reflection not merely on nature's mechanics but on the transience of all created things, including human life and worldly achievements. Just as lush greenery inevitably withers and returns to dust, so too do human endeavors, wealth, and even life itself follow this same arc of emergence and return. The phrase 'for those of understanding' (li-ulil-albab) signals that this is not a simple observation but requires contemplative intelligence to grasp its fuller implication—that the one who orchestrates this precise and recurring cycle in nature has power over resurrection and the ultimate return of all things to Him. The verse functions rhetorically within the broader Quranic argument for both divine providence and the reality of the afterlife, using the empirically observable world as evidence for truths beyond immediate sensory experience.

translation: Is he whose breast Allah has expanded to [acceptance of] Islam, so that he is upon a light from his Lord, [like one whose heart is sealed]? So woe to those whose hearts are hardened against the remembrance of Allah. Those are in manifest error.
interpretation: This verse draws a stark contrast between two spiritual conditions of the human heart. The 'expansion of the breast' refers to a divine gift of receptivity, openness, and inner peace that Allah grants to those who sincerely seek guidance, allowing them to perceive truth as if illuminated by light—symbolizing clarity, certainty, and moral insight that governs their perception of reality. This is not something earned through human effort alone but is described as a grace from God, suggesting that true faith involves both human striving and divine facilitation. In contrast, the 'hardened heart' represents a state of spiritual calcification where a person becomes impervious to reminders of God, moral lessons, and signs in creation—such a heart loses its capacity for reflection, humility, and change. The rhetorical question format implies the answer is self-evident: no reasonable person would equate these two states. The 'woe' pronounced upon the hardened-hearted is not merely a curse but a description of their self-imposed condition—they have chosen, through repeated rejection and heedlessness, to close themselves off from guidance, resulting in a kind of spiritual blindness that the verse calls 'manifest error,' meaning it is not hidden or ambiguous but plainly visible to anyone who observes their state. The verse ultimately serves as both a warning and an invitation: a warning against allowing one's heart to become rigid and unreceptive through persistent sin and heedlessness, and an invitation to seek the kind of spiritual opening that allows one to live by divine light rather than mere worldly calculation.

translation: Allah has sent down the most beautiful of speech, a Book consistent, repeating [its teachings], from which the skins of those who fear their Lord shiver. Then their skins and their hearts soften at the remembrance of Allah. That is the guidance of Allah by which He guides whom He wills. And whoever Allah leaves astray - for him there is no guide.
interpretation: This verse describes the Qur'an as unparalleled in its eloquence and internal harmony, being 'mathani' in that its stories, warnings, and promises recur and reinforce one another throughout the text without contradiction. The physical and emotional response described - the shivering of skin followed by its softening along with the heart - illustrates the dual nature of faith's effect on the believer: first an awe-inspired reaction to the mention of divine power, judgment, and the consequences of disobedience, followed by a settling into tranquility and comfort upon remembering Allah's mercy. This progression from fear to peace is presented as the authentic sign of true faith, distinguishing sincere believers from those whose hearts remain hardened. The verse concludes by affirming that this receptivity to guidance is itself a divine gift, not something humans can manufacture through will alone; guidance ultimately comes from Allah, and its absence - being left astray - leaves no alternative path to truth, underscoring human dependence on divine grace for spiritual orientation.

translation: "Then is he who shields himself with his face from the worst of the punishment on the Day of Resurrection [like one who is secure]? And it will be said to the wrongdoers: 'Taste what you used to earn.'"
interpretation: This verse draws a stark contrast between the believer who is saved and the wrongdoer who, on the Day of Judgment, has no means of defense left except to try to ward off the fire with his own face—the most exposed and dignified part of the body, normally never used for such a purpose. This image conveys utter helplessness, humiliation, and the total collapse of whatever pride or arrogance the wrongdoer possessed in worldly life. The rhetorical question underscores that such a person's situation can never be equal to that of the righteous who are protected by God. The statement that follows—'taste what you used to earn'—makes clear that the suffering is not arbitrary but the direct, just consequence of the choices and deeds the person accumulated through their own free will. Ultimately, the verse serves as a warning that worldly power, denial, or self-deception will offer no shield against divine justice, and that one's own actions are what determine one's fate in the Hereafter.

translation: Those who came before them also denied [the truth], so the punishment came upon them from where they did not perceive.
interpretation: This verse serves as a warning drawn from the fate of earlier nations who rejected their prophets and messages. The key emphasis is on the phrase 'from where they did not perceive' (من حيث لا يشعرون), highlighting that divine retribution often arrives in unexpected ways, through means the disbelievers never anticipated or guarded against. Despite their confidence, planning, and sense of security, their downfall came from an entirely unforeseen direction. This underscores a recurring Qur'anic theme: human arrogance and false security are no protection against divine decree, and those who reject truth cannot anticipate or control the consequences of their denial. The verse functions as both a historical lesson and a timeless admonition, suggesting that the arrogance of rejecting truth blinds people to the very sources of their eventual downfall, which often come from directions they considered safe or had not even considered as vulnerabilities.

translation: So Allah made them taste disgrace in the life of this world, and the punishment of the Hereafter is surely greater, if only they knew.
interpretation: This verse addresses the fate of those who scheme and plot against the truth and against God's messengers, referring specifically to peoples who built elaborate structures or schemes of falsehood and arrogance, only to have them collapse upon them as divine retribution. The verse emphasizes a dual punishment: an immediate humiliation experienced in worldly life—serving as a visible sign and warning to others—and a far greater, more severe punishment awaiting in the Hereafter. The phrase 'if only they knew' underscores human shortsightedness, suggesting that if the wrongdoers truly understood the magnitude of what awaits them beyond this life, they would never have persisted in their arrogance or disbelief. The verse thus serves as both a historical reminder of divine justice enacted upon past transgressors and a timeless warning that temporal consequences, however painful, are minor compared to ultimate accountability before God.

translation: And We have certainly set forth for the people in this Qur'an every kind of parable, that they might remember.
interpretation: This verse highlights the comprehensive and purposeful nature of the Qur'an's rhetorical and pedagogical method. By employing diverse parables (amthal) covering different aspects of life, morality, and belief, the Qur'an engages multiple modes of human understanding—intellectual, emotional, and experiential—to reach people of varying dispositions and backgrounds. The use of parables is not incidental but deliberate ('We have certainly set forth'), indicating divine wisdom in communication: abstract truths about faith, the unseen, and moral accountability are made accessible through concrete, relatable imagery drawn from nature, human relationships, and historical narratives. The phrase 'that they might remember' points to the Qur'an's view of knowledge not as something entirely new to be learned, but as a reminder (dhikr) of truths already embedded in human nature (fitrah) and conscience. This reflects the broader Qur'anic theme that guidance is already available and accessible to those willing to reflect, and that forgetfulness, rather than ignorance, is often the real barrier to faith and righteous action. The verse thus serves as both a description of the Qur'an's methodology and an implicit call to engage with its teachings reflectively rather than passively.

translation: [It is] an Arabic Qur'an, without any crookedness, that they might become righteous.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the clarity and perfection of the Qur'an's revelation in the Arabic language, describing it as free from any ambiguity, contradiction, or crookedness in its guidance. The phrase 'ghayri dhi 'iwaj' (without any deviance) underscores that the message is straightforward and consistent, leaving no excuse for misunderstanding its moral and spiritual directives. The purpose stated—'la'allahum yattaqun' (that they might become righteous/God-conscious)—reveals the ultimate goal of revelation: not merely to inform but to transform human behavior toward taqwa, a state of mindful awareness of God that leads to ethical living. The choice of Arabic as the language of revelation is significant here, as it was the language of the immediate audience, ensuring the message could be fully comprehended without the distortions that might arise from translation. This verse thus serves as a declaration of the Qur'an's internal coherence and its practical purpose as a moral compass rather than merely a theological or literary text.

translation: Allah presents a parable: a man owned by quarrelsome partners, and a man belonging wholly to one man—are the two equal in comparison? Praise be to Allah! But most of them do not know.
interpretation: This parable illustrates the difference between polytheism and monotheism. A slave owned by several contentious, squabbling masters lives in confusion, torn by conflicting demands and unable to find peace, representing one who worships multiple deities with competing wills and commands. In contrast, a slave who belongs exclusively to one master lives in clarity and harmony, knowing exactly whom to serve and obey, representing one who worships Allah alone. The rhetorical question emphasizes that these two conditions are obviously not equal—unity of purpose brings peace and coherence, while division brings chaos and inner conflict. The exclamation of praise to Allah underscores that true gratitude and clarity belong to the One who is singular and undivided, the only fitting object of worship. Yet the verse concludes that most people fail to recognize this self-evident truth, remaining heedless of the spiritual and psychological benefits of monotheism over the fragmentation inherent in polytheistic belief.

translation: Indeed, you will die, and indeed, they will die.
interpretation: This verse, addressed to the Prophet Muhammad, establishes the universal reality of mortality that applies even to God's chosen messenger, countering any notion that prophets might be exempt from death or possess divine immortality. Coming in the context of Surah Az-Zumar's broader themes about the Hereafter and ultimate accountability, it serves as a theological corrective: the Prophet's mortality underscores that he is human, not divine, and that his death does not diminish his message or mission, which remains eternal even as his earthly life ends. The verse also sets up the following verses about the Day of Judgment, where all creatures—prophet and follower alike—will stand before God to dispute and be judged. By emphasizing that both the Prophet and his opponents share the same fate of death, the verse levels the ground between them in mortality while pointing to the subsequent resurrection as the true arena where distinctions in faith and deeds will matter, reinforcing the Quranic message that worldly life is transient and the real reckoning lies beyond death.

translation: Then indeed, on the Day of Resurrection, before your Lord you will dispute with one another.
interpretation: This verse concludes a passage addressing disputes among people—particularly concerning truth, guidance, and the message of revelation—by affirming that all disagreements, rivalries, and conflicting claims among humans will ultimately be brought before God for final judgment. It serves as a warning that worldly disputes, including those about faith and religious truth, will not simply dissolve or be forgotten; rather, every soul will stand accountable before the Lord, who alone possesses complete knowledge and justice to resolve all contested matters. The verse emphasizes the certainty of accountability and divine arbitration, reminding believers that ultimate resolution and justice are deferred not to human courts or power, but to God on the Day of Judgment, underscoring both the seriousness of one's conduct and beliefs in this life and the comfort that true justice will prevail in the end.

translation: So who is more unjust than one who lies about Allah and denies the truth when it comes to him? Is there not in Hell a resting place for the disbelievers?
interpretation: This verse underscores a twofold sin: fabricating falsehoods about God and rejecting divine truth once it has been clearly presented. The rhetorical question emphasizes that such a combination—actively distorting religious truth while simultaneously rejecting authentic guidance—represents the pinnacle of wrongdoing, as it involves both deception and willful denial. The closing question about Hell being a 'resting place' is deeply ironic, since Hell is the antithesis of rest and comfort; it suggests that disbelievers who commit this grave injustice will find their permanent abode in torment rather than peace, serving as a warning about the serious consequences of knowingly distorting or denying revealed truth.

translation: And the one who has brought the truth and [those who] believed in it - those are the righteous (al-muttaqun).
interpretation: This verse draws a profound connection between bringing truth and affirming it. Classical exegetes generally understand 'the one who brought the truth' as referring to Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, who delivered the message of tawhid and the Qur'an, while 'those who believed in it' refers to the believers who accepted and affirmed this message. Some scholars extend this to include all prophets who brought divine truth and all those throughout history who sincerely accepted it. The verse establishes that true taqwa (God-consciousness/righteousness) is not merely about outward religious practice, but stems from this fundamental relationship between the bearer of truth and the one who embraces it with sincere conviction. The righteous are defined here not by ritual alone, but by their active role in both conveying and accepting divine guidance. This creates a partnership between prophecy and faith - the Messenger fulfills his duty by delivering the truth, and the believer fulfills theirs by recognizing and internalizing it. The verse thus honors both the transmission and the reception of truth as essential components of righteousness, suggesting that sincerity in belief (tasdiq) is what elevates one to the station of the muttaqun.

translation: They shall have whatever they wish for with their Lord. That is the reward of the doers of good.
interpretation: This verse concludes a description of the righteous believers by affirming that their reward in Paradise is not merely fixed provisions but the fulfillment of every desire they could wish for, granted directly by God Himself. The phrase 'with their Lord' emphasizes closeness and honor, suggesting that the ultimate reward is not just material pleasure but proximity to and favor with the Divine. The closing statement, 'that is the reward of the doers of good,' establishes a moral principle: that divine generosity is the direct consequence of ihsan—excellence in faith and conduct, often understood as worshiping God as though one sees Him. This ties reward to sincerity and spiritual excellence rather than mere outward deeds, framing Paradise as the natural culmination of a life lived in conscious devotion and moral integrity.

translation: That Allah may absolve them of the worst of what they did, and reward them their due according to the best of what they used to do.
interpretation: This verse speaks to the boundless mercy and justice of God toward the righteous—those who possess sincere faith and reverence for the divine. It establishes a principle of divine grading whereby God, in His compassion, overlooks or erases the lesser sins and failings committed by a believer, while measuring that same believer's eternal reward against the finest deeds they performed. This is not a statement of moral relativism but of divine generosity: human beings are inevitably imperfect and commit both good and lesser deeds throughout their lives, yet God's reckoning on the Day of Judgment is weighted in favor of mercy rather than strict proportional justice. The verse offers profound reassurance and hope, suggesting that the believer's worst moments, provided they remain within the fold of faith and continue striving toward righteousness, will not define their final standing. Instead, it is their highest moments of devotion, charity, and obedience that will determine the nature and magnitude of their reward in the afterlife. This encapsulates a core theological theme in the Quran—that divine mercy supersedes divine wrath for those who maintain sincere belief, and that God's generosity in reckoning exceeds mere arithmetic justice, instead elevating the believer according to their best achievements rather than condemning them for their worst failures.

translation: Is not Allah sufficient for His servant? Yet they threaten you with those [they worship] besides Him. And whoever Allah leaves astray, for him there is no guide.
interpretation: This verse addresses the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) at a time when the disbelievers of Mecca were attempting to intimidate him by invoking the power of their idols and false deities, warning that these gods would harm him for rejecting them. Allah responds with a rhetorical question that carries profound reassurance: His sufficiency alone is enough for His servant, rendering any threat from false deities utterly powerless and meaningless. The verse establishes a fundamental theological principle—that true power and protection belong to Allah alone, and nothing besides Him has any real capacity to harm or benefit. The disbelievers' attempt to frighten the Prophet with lifeless idols is portrayed as inherently absurd, since these idols have no true existence of power in the first place. The verse then pivots to a broader principle about divine guidance: when Allah decrees that someone is astray due to their persistent rejection of truth and their own choices, no human effort or alternative source can guide them back, for guidance ultimately rests with Allah. This underscores both the futility of relying on anything other than Allah for protection and the seriousness of willingly turning away from truth, as such abandonment forecloses the possibility of rescue by any other means.

translation: And whoever Allah guides - for him there is no misleader. Is not Allah Exalted in Might and Owner of Retribution?
interpretation: This verse affirms that true guidance comes exclusively from Allah, and once He guides a person, no force - human or otherwise - can lead them astray, as misguidance only occurs by Allah's permission for those who reject guidance. The rhetorical question that follows serves as a powerful reminder of two complementary divine attributes: Allah's absolute power ('Aziz) and His capacity for just retribution (Dhu intiqam) against those who persist in disbelief and wrongdoing after guidance has been made clear to them. The verse thus functions as both a comfort to believers - assuring them that divine guidance, once granted, is secure - and a warning to those who reject truth, reminding them that Allah's might ensures no one can escape the consequences of their choices. The pairing of these two attributes together suggests that Allah's power is not arbitrary but is exercised with perfect justice, particularly against those who actively work against truth and misguide others.

translation: And if you ask them, 'Who created the heavens and the earth?' they will surely say, 'Allah.' Say, 'Have you then considered what you call upon besides Allah? If Allah intended harm for me, could they remove His harm? Or if He intended mercy for me, could they withhold His mercy?' Say, 'Sufficient for me is Allah; upon Him the reliant put their trust.'
interpretation: This verse exposes the logical inconsistency in the polytheists' belief system: they readily acknowledge Allah as the sole Creator of the cosmos, yet they turn to other deities or intermediaries for protection and sustenance, as though these beings possess independent power. The rhetorical questions dismantle this contradiction by forcing an admission that none of the idols or intercessors they invoke have any actual capacity to avert harm or grant mercy, since all power ultimately belongs to Allah alone. The verse thus moves from a cosmological argument (creation) to a practical, existential one (daily reliance), showing that true tawhid (monotheism) must be consistent—acknowledging Allah's sovereignty in creation logically demands acknowledging His sole sovereignty in sustenance and protection as well. The concluding declaration 'Sufficient for me is Allah' models the proper response of a believer: complete trust (tawakkul) placed only in the One who truly controls benefit and harm, rendering all other objects of worship or reliance utterly powerless and irrelevant.

translation: Say, 'O my people, work according to your position; indeed, I am working. Then you will come to know
interpretation: This verse reflects a declaration of resolute independence in matters of faith, delivered by the Prophet to those who rejected his message. It is not a statement of indifference but rather an expression of confidence rooted in divine truth. By instructing his people to 'work according to their position,' the Prophet acknowledges their free will to continue in their chosen path of disbelief or opposition, while affirming his own unwavering commitment to his mission grounded in revelation. The phrase carries an implicit warning rather than mere permission—it is a rhetorical device common in Qur'anic discourse where apparent concession masks a stern admonition.
