Some commentators connect this to the idea that the righteous were given a vision or deep spiritual knowledge of Paradise during their earthly life through faith, worship, and the Quran's descriptions, so that upon entering it, everything feels familiar rather than foreign. Others relate 'arrafahā' to the root meaning of 'fragrance' ('arf), suggesting Paradise is perfumed and made pleasant for them. The verse conveys God's generosity and care—not only will the faithful be granted entry into Paradise, but it will be a place where they feel immediately at home, each knowing their exact place, as a sign of divine honor and the fulfillment of the promise made to believers throughout their lives of struggle and devotion.

translation: O you who have believed, if you support [the cause of] Allah, He will support you and plant firmly your feet.
interpretation: This verse establishes a reciprocal relationship between divine assistance and human effort, teaching that believers must actively support the cause of Allah—through upholding His religion, defending justice, and striving in His way—in order to receive His aid. The phrase 'support Allah' does not imply that Allah needs assistance, but rather signifies supporting His religion, His messenger, and His commands. The promise that Allah will 'plant firmly your feet' refers to steadfastness in battle, firmness in faith during trials, and stability in one's convictions when facing adversity or doubt. This verse teaches that victory and inner strength are not granted passively but are earned through genuine commitment and action in service of righteous principles, establishing a divine law that those who strive for truth will be granted the strength and stability to withstand challenges.

translation: But those who disbelieve - for them is destruction, and He has made their deeds worthless.
interpretation: This verse establishes a direct contrast with the preceding description of believers who strive and are guided. Here, the fate of those who reject faith and oppose the truth is pronounced: perdition and ruin for them in this life and the next. The phrase 'adalla a'malahum' (He made their deeds go astray/worthless) indicates that despite whatever good works or efforts the disbelievers may undertake, their deeds are rendered fruitless and without value in the sight of God because they lack the foundation of true faith. This reflects a broader Quranic principle that righteous deeds require the correct intention and belief (iman) to have spiritual worth; without this foundation, even outwardly good actions do not lead to salvation or reward. The destruction mentioned is both a worldly consequence—often manifesting as defeat, humiliation, or loss of divine support—and an eternal one, as their ultimate deeds and efforts will not avail them on the Day of Judgment. This verse was revealed in the context of those who opposed the Prophet Muhammad and fought against the believers, serving as both a warning and a statement of divine justice: those who actively work against truth and righteousness will find their efforts nullified, in stark contrast to the believers whose deeds are preserved and rewarded.

translation: That is because they hated what Allah has revealed, so He rendered their deeds worthless.
interpretation: This verse explains the underlying reason for the nullification of certain people's deeds: their inner aversion to divine revelation. The verse establishes a causal relationship between internal disposition (hatred of revelation) and external consequence (the voiding of works). It teaches that good deeds are not evaluated in isolation but in connection with one's fundamental orientation toward truth. Even actions that might appear outwardly righteous or beneficial lose their spiritual value and reward when they stem from or coexist with a heart that rejects and resents divine guidance. This reflects a broader Qur'anic principle that sincerity of faith and acceptance of revelation are prerequisites for deeds to have lasting worth in the sight of Allah—mere outward compliance or isolated good actions cannot compensate for a fundamental rejection of what has been revealed. The verse serves as a warning that hypocrisy or concealed resentment toward religious truth, even while maintaining an appearance of practice, ultimately leads to spiritual bankruptcy, as Allah judges by the heart's true orientation rather than by outward performance alone.

translation: Have they not traveled through the land and seen how was the end of those before them? Allah destroyed them utterly, and for the disbelievers are similar [fates].
interpretation: This verse calls on people to reflect on history as a source of moral and spiritual lesson, urging them to observe the ruins and remnants of past civilizations that were destroyed due to their rejection of truth, arrogance, and disbelief. The exhortation to 'travel through the land' is both literal and metaphorical—encouraging empirical observation of historical evidence as well as deeper contemplation on the patterns of divine justice. The destruction mentioned is presented not as arbitrary punishment but as the natural consequence of persistent disbelief and corruption, serving as a warning that the same fate awaits those who follow similar paths of denial and transgression. The verse emphasizes the consistency of divine law across time: those who reject guidance and persist in disbelief will face consequences akin to those of earlier nations, reinforcing the Qur'anic theme that history is cyclical in its moral lessons and that human societies are accountable to a higher, unchanging standard of justice.

translation: That is because Allah is the Protector of those who believe, while the disbelievers have no protector.
interpretation: This verse establishes a fundamental principle regarding divine support and guardianship: faith in Allah brings with it His protection, guidance, and support (wilayah), encompassing both worldly success and ultimate salvation. The disbelievers, having rejected this relationship with Allah, are left without any true protector who can genuinely safeguard their interests or grant them lasting success, despite whatever temporary power or alliances they may possess. This reflects a broader Qur'anic theme that true security and triumph come only through alignment with Allah, not merely through worldly strength, numbers, or alliances. The verse often appears in contexts discussing battles or trials, reassuring believers that their ultimate victory is assured not necessarily through material superiority, but through the unwavering support of Allah, while those who deny Him are spiritually and existentially unmoored, lacking any true source of lasting aid or refuge.

translation: Indeed, Allah admits those who believe and do righteous deeds into gardens beneath which rivers flow, while those who disbelieve enjoy themselves and eat as grazing livestock eat, and the Fire will be their abode.
interpretation: This verse draws a stark contrast between two orientations toward worldly life and their ultimate destinations. The believers, whose faith is paired with righteous action, are granted eternal gardens of flowing abundance—an image of lasting fulfillment rooted in purposeful living. The disbelievers, by contrast, are depicted as consumed entirely by appetite and immediate gratification, their existence reduced to the animalistic level of eating and enjoying without higher reflection, purpose, or accountability. The comparison to grazing livestock is deliberately degrading: it suggests that a life lived without faith or moral striving, no matter how pleasurable in the moment, lacks the distinctly human capacity for spiritual elevation and meaning. Their fate—the Fire as a 'mathwa' or permanent lodging—mirrors the transience and hollowness of their worldly indulgence; just as they lived for fleeting consumption, their eternal dwelling becomes a place of consuming torment. The verse thus serves as a moral warning that a life oriented solely toward physical pleasure and self-interest, without faith and righteous deeds, ultimately leads to spiritual and existential impoverishment, despite apparent worldly enjoyment.

translation: And how many a town, which was stronger in might than your town that has driven you out, have We destroyed, and there was no helper for them.
interpretation: This verse addresses the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) following his expulsion from Mecca, offering reassurance and warning. It reminds him and the believers that many nations and communities throughout history possessed far greater strength, resources, and power than the people of Mecca who had driven him out, yet Allah destroyed them when they persisted in disbelief and rejection of the truth. The mention that 'there was no helper for them' underscores the futility of worldly power and alliances when divine judgment is decreed—no amount of military strength, wealth, or political influence could save these mighty civilizations from destruction once they had earned Allah's punishment through their arrogance and rejection of His messengers. The verse serves multiple purposes: it comforts the Prophet by placing his persecution in a larger historical context, demonstrating that his suffering is not unique but follows a pattern seen throughout history; it serves as an implicit warning to the Quraysh of Mecca that their apparent strength does not guarantee their safety from divine retribution; and it reinforces the broader Quranic theme that worldly power is ultimately subordinate to divine will, and that those who oppose the truth, no matter how formidable they appear, cannot escape the consequences of their rejection when Allah has decreed their downfall. This verse thus functions as both consolation for the persecuted believers and admonition for the persecutors.

translation: Is he who stands upon clear evidence from his Lord like one for whom the evil of his deeds has been made to seem fair, and [who] follow their own desires?
interpretation: This verse draws a decisive contrast between two fundamentally different types of people: those who base their lives on certain knowledge and insight from God, and those who have become enslaved to their own base desires, to the point that their wrongdoing appears good to them. The rhetorical question 'is he who...like one who...' is a classical Qur'anic device demonstrating that spiritual guidance and heedless self-indulgence can never be equated. The phrase 'zuyyina lahu su'u 'amalihi' (the evil of his deeds has been made to seem fair to him) describes a psychological and spiritual state in which a person's own corruption becomes normalized and even attractive to them, often as a consequence of persistently following whims rather than revealed truth. This self-deception is presented as a natural consequence of prioritizing desire ('hawa') over reason and revelation - when one habitually follows what one wants rather than what is right, the moral compass becomes inverted, and evil begins to look like good. The verse thus serves as a warning about the corrupting power of unchecked desire and the clarity that comes from grounding oneself in divine guidance ('bayyina min rabbihi') - a firm, evidentiary certainty rather than mere opinion or whim. The implicit message is that those with such clarity can see through the illusions that trap others, and the two groups cannot be considered equal in status, worth, or ultimate destiny.

translation: The likeness of the Garden promised to the righteous: in it are rivers of water unpolluted, and rivers of milk whose taste never changes, and rivers of wine delicious to those who drink, and rivers of purified honey. And therein for them are all kinds of fruits, and forgiveness from their Lord. [Are those who enjoy this] like those who abide eternally in the Fire and are given scalding water to drink that cuts their intestines to pieces?
interpretation: This verse employs vivid sensory imagery to contrast the ultimate rewards of the righteous with the torment of the damned, using the rhetorical device of comparison (mathal) that was especially resonant for its original desert-dwelling audience familiar with scarcity of clean water and the luxury of milk, wine, and honey. Each river mentioned corrects an earthly flaw—water that never stagnates or grows foul, milk that never sours, wine without the intoxicating harm or headache associated with earthly wine, and honey perfectly purified without impurities—symbolizing a paradise where natural goods exist in their perfected, uncorrupted form, free from the imperfections and decay inherent in worldly pleasures. The mention of 'all kinds of fruits' alongside these rivers emphasizes abundance and variety beyond earthly limitation. Crucially, the verse does not end with physical pleasures alone but culminates in 'forgiveness from their Lord,' indicating that divine mercy and spiritual reconciliation are the true crown of paradise, surpassing even its sensory delights. The jarring shift to the fate of those in Hell—given boiling water that destroys their very intestines—serves as a stark rhetorical antithesis, using bodily visceral horror to match the bodily visceral pleasure described moments before. This juxtaposition is not merely descriptive but argumentative: it functions as a moral syllogism asking whether the blessed state of eternal satisfaction and forgiveness can possibly be equivalent to eternal suffering and bodily destruction, compelling the listener toward ethical reflection and the pursuit of righteousness (taqwa) as the determining factor between these two radically opposed destinies.

translation: And among them are those who listen to you, until when they go out from you, they say to those who were given knowledge, 'What did he say just now?' Those are the ones upon whose hearts Allah has set a seal, and they follow their own desires.
interpretation: This verse describes a category of hypocrites or spiritually heedless people among those who outwardly attended the Prophet's gatherings. They would physically listen to his words, yet their listening was devoid of genuine attentiveness, reflection, or intention to benefit from guidance. Their question to the learned—'What did he just say?'—reveals not a thirst for understanding but indifference or mockery; they were present in body but absent in heart and mind. The verse attributes this spiritual deafness to a divine sealing of their hearts, which is not an arbitrary punishment but a consequence of their own choices: they persistently followed their desires (ahwaa) rather than submitting to truth. This illustrates a Qur'anic principle found elsewhere—that when a person repeatedly turns away from guidance in favor of whims and self-interest, Allah confirms them in that state, making it increasingly difficult for truth to penetrate their hearts. The verse also implicitly honors 'those given knowledge' as the ones capable of truly comprehending and conveying the message, contrasting them with those who, despite proximity to revelation, remain veiled by their own lack of sincerity and susceptibility to worldly concerns.

translation: And those who are [rightly] guided - He increases them in guidance and grants them their righteousness (taqwa).
interpretation: This verse articulates a theological principle of reciprocal and self-reinforcing spiritual growth: guidance is not a static, one-time event but a dynamic process that deepens for those who sincerely accept and act upon it. The verse suggests that the human response to divine guidance - acceptance and submission - is met with increase from God, creating an upward spiral of spiritual development. Furthermore, by stating that God 'gives them their taqwa,' the verse frames righteousness and piety not merely as the product of human effort or willpower alone, but ultimately as a divine gift and grace bestowed upon the sincere seeker. This underscores the Islamic theological balance between human agency (the initial choice to seek guidance) and divine grace (the increase and the gift of taqwa that follows), suggesting that the capacity to remain righteous is itself sustained by God's continuous support rather than solely by human determination.

translation: So do they await anything except that the Hour should come upon them unexpectedly? But already its portents have come. Then how will they benefit from their remembrance when it has come to them?
interpretation: This verse warns the disbelievers who persist in heedlessness despite the clear signs that the Day of Judgment is approaching—signs already manifested, including the very mission of the Prophet Muhammad himself, regarded by many commentators as one of the major portents of the Hour. The verse underscores the folly of waiting passively for a catastrophic, sudden event rather than reflecting and reforming beforehand. It emphasizes that once the Hour actually arrives, taking heed or seeking to remember and repent will be entirely futile—reminders and warnings have value only before the appointed moment, not after reality has overtaken human will and choice. Thus, the verse is a rhetorical rebuke, urging immediate reflection and moral accountability rather than complacent delay, highlighting the irrevocable and final nature of divine judgment once it manifests.

translation: So know that there is no deity except Allah, and seek forgiveness for your sin and for the believing men and believing women. And Allah knows your movement and your place of rest.
interpretation: This verse grounds the entire call to faith in the foundational declaration of tawhid—the oneness of God—positioning knowledge and certainty about this truth as the starting point for all righteous action. The command to seek forgiveness, directed even at the Prophet, establishes that no human being, however exalted, stands beyond the need for continual repentance and humility before God. By linking the Prophet's own need for forgiveness with that of the believing community, the verse creates a sense of shared spiritual struggle, dissolving any notion of a hierarchy exempt from human fallibility. The closing reference to God's knowledge of one's 'movement' and 'resting place' serves as a sobering reminder of divine omniscience that encompasses every state of human life—whether active in the world or at rest—reinforcing that sincerity in seeking forgiveness must be matched by an awareness that nothing escapes God's watchful knowledge, thus binding belief, repentance, and conscious accountability into a single coherent act of faith.

translation: And those who believe say, 'Why has a surah not been sent down [about fighting]?' But when a precise surah is revealed and fighting is mentioned therein, you see those in whose hearts is disease looking at you with a look of one who faints at death. And more appropriate for them [would be obedience and good speech].
interpretation: This verse draws a sharp contrast between sincere believers, who eagerly desire divine guidance commanding jihad as a test of faith and commitment, and the hypocrites or weak-hearted individuals among the community, whose true nature is exposed once the command to fight is actually revealed. Their outward profession of faith collapses under the weight of real sacrifice, betraying an inner sickness—doubt, cowardice, or insincerity—likened to the terror of a dying man's stare. The phrase 'so woe to them' (or 'more fitting for them') serves as both a rebuke and a warning: it would have been far better for such people to remain obedient and speak honorably rather than reveal their hypocrisy when the moment of trial arrives. The verse ultimately underscores a recurring Qur'anic theme that faith is proven not through words alone but through willingness to act upon commandments, especially the most demanding one—armed struggle—which separates genuine conviction from superficial belief.

translation: Obedience and a reasonable word. And when the matter [of fighting] is determined, then if they had been true to Allah, it would have been better for them.
interpretation: This verse addresses the gap between verbal profession of faith and actual commitment when tested. It speaks to those who outwardly express obedience and say the right things, but whose sincerity is only truly revealed when a decisive matter—such as the obligation to fight or make real sacrifice—is called for. The verse suggests that many are willing to voice agreement and loyalty in word, but when the moment demands resolute action backed by genuine conviction, their true state is exposed. The concluding statement that 'it would have been better for them' if they had been truthful with Allah underscores that sincerity and steadfastness in difficult moments—not mere verbal assent—are what bring real benefit and reward. It is a call to align one's inner conviction with outer speech, especially when commitment is tested through decisive action, as hypocrisy or half-hearted faith reveals itself precisely when matters become serious and resolved.

translation: Then would you, if you turned away, perhaps cause corruption in the land and sever your ties of kinship?
interpretation: This verse poses a rhetorical question connecting the rejection of faith and divine guidance with social breakdown. It suggests that turning away from Islam and its principles tends to result in two major harms: spreading corruption and discord throughout society, and severing the bonds of family and kinship that hold communities together. The verse implies that true faith is not merely a private matter but is integrally connected to maintaining social harmony, justice, and familial bonds. By framing this as a question, the Qur'an invites reflection on the natural consequences of abandoning righteous guidance—namely, that societies which turn away from God's commands tend toward fragmentation, conflict, and the breaking of the very relationships that sustain human civilization, particularly the sacred ties of family and blood relations that Islam places great emphasis on preserving.

translation: Those are the ones whom Allah has cursed, so He made them deaf and blinded their sight.
interpretation: This verse refers to those who turn away from Allah's guidance, sever family ties, and cause corruption in the land (as described in the preceding verses). Their spiritual deafness and blindness are not physical afflictions but a consequence of their own rejection of truth. By persistently refusing to hear and see the signs of Allah, they are described as having been cursed and rendered incapable of perceiving divine guidance altogether. This illustrates a Qur'anic theme wherein Allah seals the hearts, hearing, and sight of those who willfully reject faith as a natural consequence of their own choices, rather than as an arbitrary punishment imposed on innocent people. It serves as a warning that persistent spiritual negligence and moral corruption ultimately lead to a loss of the capacity to recognize truth and guidance.

translation: Then do they not reflect upon the Qur'an, or are there locks upon [their] hearts?
interpretation: This verse poses a rhetorical question that challenges those who fail to engage deeply with the Qur'an's message. It suggests two possibilities for why people might reject or ignore its guidance: either they simply have not made the effort to contemplate and reflect upon its meanings, or their hearts have become spiritually sealed—hardened by stubbornness, arrogance, or persistent sin to the point that truth can no longer penetrate them. The imagery of 'locks' (aqfal) implies a self-imposed or earned spiritual blockage, not an arbitrary fate, suggesting that such hardening results from repeated choices to turn away from guidance. The verse thus serves as both a call to active, thoughtful engagement with revelation and a warning about the spiritual consequences of willful heedlessness, emphasizing that true understanding of the Qur'an requires an open, receptive heart rather than superficial or resistant listening.

translation: Indeed, those who turned back on their heels [reverted to disbelief] after guidance had become clear to them - Satan enticed them, and prolonged hope [with false promises] for them.
interpretation: This verse addresses the phenomenon of apostasy among those who had once recognized the truth of divine guidance but subsequently abandoned it. The verse attributes their regression not merely to personal weakness but to the active role of Satan, who 'made fair-seeming' (sawwala) their path of disbelief and 'gave them false hope' (amla lahum) - suggesting a prolonged process of temptation involving procrastination, false reassurance, and the deferral of accountability. The phrase 'after guidance had become clear to them' emphasizes the gravity of their choice, as their turning away was not from ignorance but occurred despite full awareness of the truth. This suggests that knowledge alone does not guarantee steadfastness; it must be coupled with sincerity and resistance to psychological manipulation. The verse serves as a warning about the subtle mechanisms of spiritual regression - how doubt, procrastination, and the allure of worldly continuity can be exploited to draw believers away from conviction even after clarity has been attained, highlighting the ongoing struggle between guidance and temptation within the human heart.

translation: That is because they said to those who detest what Allah has revealed, 'We will obey you in part of the matter.' But Allah knows their secrets.
interpretation: This verse exposes the duplicity of the hypocrites (munafiqun) who outwardly professed faith but secretly colluded with those who rejected divine revelation, particularly concerning matters of warfare and communal obligation. Their pledge to 'obey in part of the matter' reveals a calculated, conditional loyalty—they were willing to align with disbelievers on certain issues while maintaining a facade of adherence to the Muslim community, likely to avoid detection or to hedge their bets depending on which side gained advantage. The verse underscores a central Qur'anic theme: that Allah's knowledge penetrates beyond outward speech and action into the hidden intentions and secret dealings of the heart. No conspiracy, however covertly arranged, escapes divine awareness. This serves as both a warning to the hypocrites that their schemes are already known and exposed, and a broader lesson to believers about the nature of true faith, which must be complete and sincere rather than partial, negotiated, or strategically compromised based on worldly alliances and self-interest.

translation: Then how [will it be] when the angels take them in death, striking their faces and their backs?
interpretation: This verse depicts the fate of those who reject faith and turn away from truth after it has become clear to them, describing the terrifying moment of death for disbelievers and hypocrites. The imagery of angels striking both the face and the back signifies total humiliation and punishment—the face representing what one presents to the world (pride, defiance, false righteousness) and the back representing retreat, cowardice, or turning away from truth. This serves as a warning within the broader context of the surah, which contrasts the fate of believers who strive in God's cause with those who oppose His messenger and revelation. The violent nature of this death scene, as opposed to the peaceful death described for righteous believers elsewhere in the Quran, underscores the consequences of willful disbelief and the rejection of divine guidance despite having received it.

translation: That is because they followed what angered Allah and were averse to His pleasure, so He rendered their deeds worthless.
interpretation: This verse explains the underlying cause behind the spiritual failure and nullification of the deeds of the hypocrites and disbelievers mentioned in the preceding verses. It establishes a causal relationship rooted in the orientation of the heart: their outward actions became void not merely because of specific sins, but because of their deliberate inclination to pursue what provokes divine displeasure while actively disliking and resisting what would please Allah. This reveals that the acceptance of deeds is contingent upon sincere intention and alignment of the heart's desires with divine will, not merely upon the performance of actions themselves. The verse underscores a broader Qur'anic principle that faith and works are inseparable from one's inner disposition—when someone's heart resents guidance and righteousness, even seemingly good deeds lose their value in Allah's sight. Thus, this serves as a warning that outward religiosity or action without genuine submission and love for what pleases God ultimately leads to spiritual bankruptcy.

translation: Or do those in whose hearts is a disease think that Allah will not bring forth their hidden malice?
interpretation: This verse addresses the hypocrites (munafiqun) who outwardly professed faith while harboring resentment, doubt, and ill-will toward the believers and the message of Islam. The 'disease in their hearts' refers to spiritual corruption—hypocrisy, envy, and weak or false faith—that festers internally even as it is concealed externally. The rhetorical question exposes their flawed assumption that their true feelings and intentions could remain hidden indefinitely. The verse serves as a warning that Allah's knowledge encompasses all that is concealed within the human heart, and that circumstances, trials, and divine revelation will inevitably expose the true nature of a person's inner state. This exposure often occurs through tests such as calls to battle, charity, or other obligations that reveal who truly believes and who merely pretends, as hypocrisy cannot be sustained indefinitely under pressure. The verse thus functions both as a caution to the hypocrites that their deception will not succeed, and as a reassurance to the believers that Allah will distinguish true faith from false pretense.

translation: And if We willed, We could show them to you, and you would know them by their mark; but you will surely know them by the tone of [their] speech. And Allah knows your deeds.
interpretation: This verse addresses the Prophet Muhammad regarding the hypocrites (munafiqun) among the believers in Medina—those who outwardly professed Islam but harbored disbelief or doubt in their hearts. God states that He could, if He wished, make these hypocrites physically identifiable through some distinguishing mark, removing all ambiguity about their true nature. However, He has chosen not to do so, leaving their identification to a more subtle sign: the manner, tone, and underlying implications of their speech. A careful listener attuned to nuance can detect inconsistencies, evasions, double meanings, or subtle slips in how hypocrites talk about faith, loyalty, and commitment—even when they attempt to disguise their true feelings. This reflects a broader principle in the Qur'an that inner states often reveal themselves through speech patterns, word choice, and the undertones of what people say, even when they try to conceal their true beliefs. The verse closes with a reminder that ultimately God's knowledge of human actions is complete and total, transcending human ability to fully discern hidden hypocrisy, reinforcing both a practical warning to be perceptive of deceptive speech and a theological assurance that divine judgment accounts for what human perception cannot fully grasp.

translation: And We will surely test you until We know those who strive among you and those who are steadfast, and We will test your affairs (reports).
interpretation: This verse addresses the believers, informing them that trials and tribulations are an inevitable and necessary part of faith. The 'knowing' attributed to God does not imply new knowledge on His part—since His knowledge is eternal and all-encompassing—but rather refers to the manifestation and actualization of what is already known to Him, making it evident in the real world through observable deeds. Testing serves to distinguish, in practice, those who genuinely strive (mujahidin) in the cause of God and remain patient (sabirin) through hardship from those whose commitment is merely claimed or superficial. The phrase 'We will test your affairs' extends this scrutiny beyond actions to intentions, reports, and reputations, meaning that one's true character, sincerity, and steadfastness are revealed and verified through the trials of life, exposing hidden truths about a person's faith and conduct that might not otherwise be apparent.

translation: Indeed, those who disbelieved and turned [others] away from the path of Allah and opposed the Messenger after guidance had become clear to them - never will they harm Allah at all, and He will render their deeds worthless.
interpretation: This verse addresses those who not only reject faith themselves but actively obstruct others from the path of truth and oppose the Prophet, doing so despite clear guidance having reached them - meaning their rejection is not from ignorance but willful defiance after knowledge. The verse emphasizes divine self-sufficiency: their opposition cannot harm Allah's sovereignty or diminish His power in any way; rather, the consequence falls entirely upon themselves. Their good deeds, which might otherwise have merit, become nullified and void because they are undermined by this fundamental act of obstruction and opposition after clarity was established. This teaches that deeds are judged not merely by their outward form but by the sincerity and submission underlying them - active hostility toward truth after recognizing it corrupts the value of one's actions in the sight of Allah.

translation: O you who have believed, obey Allah and obey the Messenger, and do not invalidate your deeds.
interpretation: This verse links faith to consistent action by warning believers that their good deeds can be nullified, not only through disbelief, but through conduct that contradicts the obedience owed to Allah and His Messenger. The juxtaposition of 'obey Allah and obey the Messenger' with the warning against invalidating one's deeds suggests that sincerity and consistency are essential to the acceptance of worship and good works. Scholars have connected this to behaviors such as showing off, raising one's voice disrespectfully above the Prophet's, disputing or arguing in ways that undermine unity, or committing major sins after performing good deeds. The verse establishes a principle that righteous action is not a one-time transaction but requires ongoing commitment to obedience; a single lapse into disobedience, hypocrisy, or disrespect toward the Messenger can erase the spiritual value of works already performed. This reflects a broader Quranic theme that faith and deeds must remain integrated and protected from corruption throughout a believer's life, as the final judgment of one's record depends on the totality and sincerity of one's conduct, not merely isolated acts of worship.

translation: Indeed, those who disbelieved and turned [others] away from the path of Allah and then died while they were disbelievers - never will Allah forgive them.
interpretation: This verse establishes a decisive theological principle regarding the finality of disbelief at the point of death. It specifically addresses those who commit a dual transgression: personal disbelief (kufr) combined with actively obstructing others from the path of God (sadd 'an sabilillah) - meaning they not only rejected faith themselves but worked to prevent others from accessing it, whether through persecution, propaganda, or creating barriers to the message's spread. The verse's structure emphasizes that the critical factor is the state of the heart at death - dying in persistent, unrepented disbelief after a life of actively opposing faith forecloses divine forgiveness. This is not a statement about God's inability to forgive, but rather about the person's own choice to seal their fate by rejecting all opportunity for repentance throughout their life and dying in that state. The verse implicitly leaves open the door of repentance during one's lifetime, no matter how late, while warning that death without such repentance, especially for those who actively worked against the truth reaching others, results in permanent exclusion from divine mercy. This serves as a severe warning against both personal rejection of truth and the more serious offense of actively preventing others from receiving guidance.

translation: So do not weaken and call for peace while you are superior; and Allah is with you, and He will never deprive you of [the reward for] your deeds.
interpretation: This verse addresses the believers during a time of conflict, urging them not to show weakness or be the first to seek a truce out of fear or fatigue, especially when they hold the position of strength. It emphasizes that true strength comes from faith and reliance on Allah, who is with the believers and supports their cause. The verse also reassures them that their efforts, sacrifices, and struggles will not go to waste—Allah will fully reward their deeds. The underlying message is one of steadfastness, courage, and trust in divine support, discouraging complacency or premature concession when one is in a position of advantage, while also reminding believers that ultimate reward lies with Allah rather than worldly outcomes alone.

translation: Verily, the life of this world is but play and amusement. But if you believe and are righteous (fear Allah), He will grant you your rewards, and He will not ask you for your wealth.
interpretation: This verse draws a contrast between the fleeting, trivial nature of worldly life—likened to play and amusement that distracts but has no lasting substance—and the enduring value of faith and piety. It reassures believers that true success lies not in material accumulation but in belief and God-consciousness, for which they will be rewarded. The closing clause emphasizes that God's call to faith is not a demand for material sacrifice or wealth; He does not seek to deprive people of their possessions. This serves to allay any fear that religious commitment entails financial exploitation, distinguishing the sincerity of divine guidance from worldly systems that often extract wealth from their followers. The verse ultimately urges a reorientation of priorities away from transient worldly pursuits toward sustained faith and righteous action, which carry eternal significance.

translation: If He were to ask you for it and press you [for it], you would withhold [out of] stinginess, and He would bring forth your malice (hidden resentments).
interpretation: This verse teaches that God's demands upon believers, particularly regarding wealth, are deliberately moderate and not excessive—He asks only for a portion (charity/zakat) rather than all of one's possessions. The verse serves as a warning about human nature: if God were to press people hard and demand everything they own, their underlying selfishness, miserliness, and spiritual weakness would be exposed. The withholding would not be a simple refusal but would reveal deeper psychological and spiritual flaws—resentment, bad faith, and hidden grudges (adghan) that lie beneath the surface of apparent piety. This illustrates a broader Quranic theme that outward compliance with religious duties can mask inner corruption, and that true faith is tested not just by what is asked, but by how one would respond if asked for more. The verse implicitly praises divine wisdom and mercy in not testing humanity beyond what it can bear, while simultaneously exposing the fragility of human generosity when pushed to its limits.

translation: Behold, you are those who are called upon to spend in the way of Allah, but among you are those who withhold. And whoever withholds, withholds only from himself. And Allah is the Self-Sufficient, while you are the needy. And if you turn away, He will replace you with another people, then they will not be like you.
interpretation: This verse addresses the human tendency toward stinginess when called to contribute wealth for communal and righteous purposes, emphasizing that such reluctance ultimately harms only the one who withholds, since Allah is wholly independent of human generosity while humanity remains dependent on Him. It serves as both a corrective rebuke and a warning: spiritual and material commitment to the divine cause is not a favor done to God but a necessity for the believer's own growth and salvation. The closing warning—that turning away would lead to replacement by a people unlike the current ones—underscores that faith communities are not irreplaceable; their continuation and favor depend on active commitment rather than passive identity, challenging believers to recognize that privilege without sacrifice can be withdrawn and given to those more willing to embody true devotion and generosity.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Indeed, We have granted you a clear, manifest victory.
interpretation: This opening verse of Surah Al-Fath was revealed following the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah, an event that appeared outwardly as a setback or compromise to the Muslims but which the Qur'an declares to be a decisive, manifest victory (fath mubin). The interpretation centers on the idea that divine judgment of success differs from human, surface-level assessment: though the treaty involved concessions that disappointed some companions, it opened the way for the unimpeded spread of Islam, peaceful interactions with the Quraysh, and eventually the bloodless conquest of Mecca. Thus the verse teaches that what seems like a limitation or difficulty, when viewed through faith and in light of its ultimate consequences, can be recognized as a clear triumph ordained by God, reassuring the Prophet and the believers that God's plan was unfolding in their favor even when immediate circumstances seemed ambiguous or unfavorable.

translation: That Allah may forgive you, [O Muhammad], your past and future sins and complete His favor upon you and guide you to a straight path.
interpretation: This verse comes directly after the proclamation of a 'manifest victory' (commonly identified with the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah) and explains the deeper spiritual purpose behind that victory for the Prophet personally. The mention of forgiveness for 'past and future sins' has been understood by many commentators not as an indication of actual wrongdoing—since the Prophet is held to be protected from major sin—but rather as an expression of his elevated station, the erasure of any minor human shortcomings, and a form of honorific address emphasizing his closeness to God. The verse reframes the political and military outcome of Hudaybiyyah as fundamentally a spiritual and moral victory: the earthly triumph is presented as a sign of God's special favor, the completion of His blessing upon the Prophet, and confirmation that he is being guided upon the straight path. In this sense, the verse links outward historical success to inward sanctification, suggesting that the hardships, sacrifices, and burdens the Prophet endured in delivering the message are being spiritually 'completed' and validated through divine endorsement.

translation: And [that] Allah may aid you with a mighty victory.
interpretation: This verse comes at the conclusion of the opening passage of Surah Al-Fath, following the announcement of a 'clear victory' (fathan mubina) granted to the Prophet Muhammad. The verse establishes a direct causal link between divine forgiveness bestowed upon the Prophet, the completion of His favor, guidance to a straight path, and ultimately, triumphant support in worldly affairs. The word 'aziz' (mighty, powerful, honorable) modifying 'victory' emphasizes that this is not merely a military success but a decisive, unassailable triumph that carries honor and dignity. The verse teaches that divine support is not arbitrary but flows from a spiritual state of righteousness and divine favor—victory is presented as a consequence and manifestation of God's grace rather than solely the result of human strategy or strength. This connects the spiritual (forgiveness, guidance) with the temporal (victory), suggesting that true, lasting success in worldly endeavors is rooted in one's relationship with the Divine. Historically, this verse is understood to reference the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah, which though appearing as a setback or compromise at the time, was reframed by the Quran as a clear victory that would lead to greater triumphs, including the eventual peaceful conquest of Mecca.

translation: He is the One who sent down tranquility into the hearts of the believers that they would increase in faith along with their faith. And to Allah belong the soldiers of the heavens and the earth, and Allah is ever Knowing and Wise.
interpretation: This verse, revealed in the context of the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah, addresses the believers who faced apparent setbacks and uncertainty regarding a truce that seemed unfavorable at the time. Allah describes how He sent sakinah—a divine calm, reassurance, and inner peace—into the hearts of the believers, which allowed their faith not merely to remain static but to actively grow and deepen even amid trial and ambiguity. This teaches that true faith is strengthened not only in moments of clear victory but especially during tests that require patience and trust in divine wisdom beyond immediate human understanding. The mention that the soldiers of the heavens and earth belong to Allah serves as a reminder that He has complete power over all means and forces; thus, the believers need not rely on worldly might alone, since ultimate security comes from divine support. The closing affirmation of Allah's knowledge and wisdom reinforces that the events unfolding, even those seeming disadvantageous, are governed by a perfect and purposeful plan, encouraging believers to trust in God's greater design over apparent circumstances.

translation: That He may admit the believing men and believing women into Gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever, and remove from them their misdeeds - and ever is that, in the sight of Allah, a great attainment.
interpretation: This verse presents the ultimate purpose and reward behind the preceding commands and guidance given to believers: eternal admission into Paradise. It emphasizes that faith, when coupled with obedience to divine guidance, leads to two intertwined blessings - entry into gardens of eternal bliss and the erasure of one's sins. The mention of both believing men and believing women explicitly affirms gender equality in spiritual reward and divine favor, countering any notion that salvation or divine recognition is restricted by gender. The phrase 'abiding therein forever' underscores the permanence of this reward, contrasting with the transient nature of worldly trials and tests of faith. The removal of sins (takfir al-sayyi'at) suggests that genuine faith and righteous action serve as expiation, not through human merit alone but through divine mercy. The closing phrase declares this outcome as 'a great attainment' (fawzan azima) in God's own estimation - not merely a human judgment of success, but the ultimate measure of achievement from the Divine perspective, reframing worldly definitions of success and placing ultimate value on the eternal over the temporal.

translation: And [so] He will punish the hypocrite men and hypocrite women, and the polytheist men and polytheist women, who assume about Allah an assumption of evil. Upon them is a misfortune of evil; and Allah has become angry with them and has cursed them and prepared for them Hell, and evil it is as a destination.
interpretation: This verse addresses those who outwardly align themselves with the believing community yet harbor doubt, suspicion, or outright rejection of Allah's power, mercy, or promises, as well as those who openly associate partners with Him. Their 'evil assumption' refers to a fundamental distrust in divine wisdom and justice—perhaps doubting that the Muslims would ever succeed, or that Allah would not support His Messenger, or questioning Allah's benevolence altogether. This inner corruption of belief, even when masked by outward conformity, is treated as a serious spiritual failing because it reflects a distorted relationship with the Divine rooted in suspicion rather than trust and submission. The 'misfortune of evil' that befalls them is often understood as a form of poetic justice: the very evil they expected or wished upon the believers turns back upon themselves. Allah's anger, curse, and the preparation of Hell underscore the severity of harboring such doubt and hostility, especially when it is coupled with hypocrisy—pretending faith while secretly undermining the community of believers. The verse ultimately serves as a warning about the spiritual and communal dangers of hidden disbelief and ill-will, emphasizing that genuine faith requires not just outward practice but sincere trust in Allah's wisdom and justice.

translation: And to Allah belong the hosts of the heavens and the earth, and Allah is ever All-Mighty, All-Wise.
interpretation: This verse affirms Allah's absolute sovereignty and command over all creation, both the visible and unseen forces of the universe—angels, celestial bodies, natural phenomena, and earthly beings and forces—all serve as instruments of His will. The mention of 'soldiers' (junud) conveys that everything in existence is marshaled under His authority, ready to act according to His command, whether to support the believers, punish the wrongdoers, or maintain the cosmic order. This serves as a reminder to the believers, particularly in the context of the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah where this verse appears, that they need not rely solely on their own limited numbers or strength, for Allah commands forces far beyond human comprehension. The pairing of 'Mighty' (Aziz) with 'Wise' (Hakim) indicates that this overwhelming power is never exercised arbitrarily but is always guided by perfect wisdom and purpose, reassuring the faithful that Allah's management of their affairs, even when outcomes seem uncertain from a human perspective, is rooted in both omnipotence and infinite wisdom.

translation: Indeed, We have sent you as a witness, a bearer of good tidings, and a warner.
interpretation: This verse addresses the Prophet Muhammad directly, outlining the threefold nature of his prophetic mission. As a 'witness' (shahid), he testifies to the truth of God's message and will bear witness over his community on the Day of Judgment regarding who believed and who rejected the message. As a 'bearer of good tidings' (mubashshir), he delivers the promise of divine mercy, paradise, and reward to those who believe and act righteously. As a 'warner' (nadhir), he cautions humanity about the consequences of disbelief and wrongdoing, namely divine punishment and loss in the afterlife. Together, these three roles encompass the complete function of prophethood: to observe and testify, to encourage through hope, and to deter through warning. This balanced approach reflects the Quran's broader methodology of combining hope and fear as motivators for faith and righteous conduct, ensuring that the message is neither one of despair nor one of complacency, but a call to responsible moral and spiritual action grounded in accountability before God.

translation: That you [people] may believe in Allah and His Messenger, and support him, and honor him, and glorify Him [Allah] morning and evening.
interpretation: This verse comes from Surah Al-Fath, following a passage describing the Prophet Muhammad's mission as witness, bearer of good tidings, and warner. It articulates the purpose behind sending the Messenger: to cultivate genuine faith among the believers. The verse employs a layered set of obligations toward both God and His Messenger. 'Support him' (tu'azziruhu) refers to aiding and defending the Prophet in his mission, while 'honor him' (tuwaqqiruhu) calls for showing him reverence and respect befitting his station. The pronoun shifts are significant to classical commentators: while belief, support, and honor are directed toward God and His Messenger together, the act of glorification (tusabbihuhu) 'morning and evening' is understood to refer back to Allah alone, since tasbih (declaring God's transcendence) is an act of worship reserved for the Divine. This grammatical distinction preserves monotheistic theology even while elevating the Prophet's status among believers. The phrase 'morning and evening' denotes constancy and regularity in remembrance of God, suggesting that devotion should punctuate the entirety of one's day as a continuous orientation of the heart rather than sporadic worship confined to formal rituals.

translation: Indeed, those who pledge allegiance to you, [O Muhammad] - they are actually pledging allegiance to Allah. The hand of Allah is over their hands. So he who breaks his word only breaks it to the detriment of himself. And he who fulfills that which he has promised Allah - He will give him a great reward.
interpretation: This verse refers to the Pledge of Ridwan, in which the Prophet's companions swore an oath of loyalty to him at Hudaybiyyah. The verse elevates this human act of allegiance to a spiritual covenant with God Himself, since the Prophet acts as God's messenger and representative. The metaphor of God's hand being above their hands signifies divine sanction, protection, and witness over the agreement, emphasizing that obedience to the Prophet is tantamount to obedience to God. The verse then establishes a principle of moral accountability: breaking a sacred vow harms only the one who breaks it, as it severs them from divine favor and community trust, while faithfulness to one's covenant - here framed as a covenant with God - earns immense spiritual reward. This teaches that oaths and commitments made in righteous causes carry weight beyond the human realm, becoming matters of personal integrity and relationship with the divine, and that steadfastness in fulfilling promises is a path to profound spiritual recompense.

translation: Those of the bedouin Arabs who stayed behind will say to you, 'Our possessions and our families kept us occupied, so ask forgiveness for us.' They say with their tongues what is not in their hearts. Say, 'Then who could have any power over Allah for you at all if He intends for you harm or intends for you benefit? Rather, ever is Allah, with what you do, Acquainted.'
interpretation: This verse addresses the hypocrisy of certain bedouin tribes who made excuses to avoid accompanying the Prophet on the expedition to Hudaybiyyah, citing concern for their property and families as a pretext for their absence. Their request for forgiveness is portrayed as insincere—a verbal formality masking inner disbelief or lack of true commitment to the faith. The verse exposes the gap between outward speech and inward conviction, a recurring theme in distinguishing genuine believers from those whose faith is merely performative. The rhetorical question that follows—asking who could possibly intervene against God's will—serves to dismantle the false logic of their excuse: if they truly believed in divine power over all outcomes, worldly attachments to wealth and family would not have justified disobedience to a Prophetic call to action, since ultimately all harm and benefit rest with God alone. The verse closes with a reminder of God's omniscience, that He knows the true intentions behind their words and actions, underscoring that no excuse or verbal plea can mask insincerity from divine knowledge. This serves as a broader lesson on the nature of true faith: it requires action and sacrifice aligned with belief, not mere verbal assertions of piety when convenient excuses arise.

translation: Nay, you thought that the Messenger and the believers would never return to their families, and that was made fair-seeming in your hearts, and you entertained evil thoughts, and you were a ruined people.
interpretation: This verse addresses the hypocrites and those Bedouins who held back from accompanying the Prophet Muhammad on the journey to Hudaybiyyah, as mentioned in the preceding verses of Surah Al-Fath. It exposes their true motive for refusing to join him: not practical excuses of family or flocks, but a deep-seated lack of faith. They had privately calculated that the small Muslim expedition into hostile Meccan territory was doomed, assuming that the Prophet and his companions would be killed or defeated and would never come back home to their families. This cynical assumption was not a passing doubt but something that became internally adorned and justified within their hearts, suggesting a psychological process whereby Satan or their own corrupted nature made treachery and bad opinion of God's promise seem reasonable and even wise to them. Their 'evil thought' (zann al-su') refers specifically to harboring a negative assumption about God's support for His Messenger and the ultimate triumph of the believers, which in Quranic theology is itself a grave moral and spiritual failing akin to distrust in divine providence. The verse concludes by branding them 'a ruined people' (qawman buran), a word connoting moral and spiritual corruption, worthlessness, and those destined for loss unless they repent. This passage thus serves as a broader commentary on the nature of hypocrisy: it is rooted not merely in outward disobedience but in an inward corruption of thought, a readiness to assume the worst about God's cause, and a self-serving rationalization that excuses cowardice and betrayal as prudence.

translation: And whoever does not believe in Allah and His Messenger - then indeed, We have prepared for the disbelievers a Blazing Fire.
interpretation: This verse establishes a direct causal link between rejecting faith in Allah and His Messenger and the consequence of eternal punishment. It appears in a context where the Qur'an is addressing matters of justice, guidance, and divine law, reinforcing that belief is not merely a private matter but carries ultimate consequences in the Hereafter. The word 'sa'ir' (blazing fire) emphasizes the intensity and justice of this requital, serving as a warning rather than an arbitrary threat - it reflects the principle that those who willfully reject clear guidance and the message brought by the Messenger have chosen a path whose natural and decreed consequence is spiritual and eternal loss. The verse also implicitly affirms the inseparability of believing in Allah and believing in His Messenger, suggesting that true faith requires acceptance of both divine unity and prophetic guidance as a unified act of submission.

translation: And to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth. He forgives whom He wills and punishes whom He wills. And Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation: This verse affirms Allah's absolute sovereignty over all creation, establishing that His authority over the heavens and the earth is total and unshared. The mention that He forgives or punishes whom He wills underscores that divine justice and mercy operate according to His perfect knowledge and wisdom, not subject to human expectation or demand—no one can dictate to Allah who deserves forgiveness or punishment. Yet this is immediately balanced by the closing affirmation that Allah is Forgiving and Merciful, indicating that His will is not arbitrary or capricious but is fundamentally inclined toward mercy and forgiveness. The juxtaposition teaches that while Allah's power to punish is real and should inspire reverence and accountability, His overriding character is one of compassion, encouraging believers to seek His forgiveness with hope rather than despair, trusting that His mercy encompasses His wrath (as other verses and hadith affirm, 'My mercy prevails over My wrath'). The verse thus combines the themes of divine omnipotence, justice, and compassionate mercy into a single statement about the nature of Allah's rule over existence.

translation: Those who stayed behind will say, when you set out to take spoils, 'Let us follow you.' They desire to change the words of Allah. Say: 'You shall not follow us; thus has Allah said beforehand.' Then they will say, 'Rather, you envy us.' Nay, but they understand not except a little.
interpretation: This verse addresses the hypocrites and those Bedouins who avoided accompanying the Prophet on a difficult expedition (traditionally understood as Hudaybiyyah), yet later sought to join when there was an easy opportunity for war spoils. Their request to 'follow' the believers to collect spoils reveals that their faith was never the true motive for companionship with the Muslims—material gain was. By wanting to 'change the words of Allah,' they sought to alter the divine decree that had already excluded them from sharing in this particular reward, as a consequence of their earlier refusal to join in hardship. The command to the Prophet to refuse them establishes a principle: participation in the rewards of faith and struggle cannot be selectively chosen only when convenient or profitable. Their shifting excuse—from indifference to accusing the believers of envy—exposes their shallow understanding of the spiritual realities at stake; they interpret matters only in terms of worldly gain and loss, unable to grasp the deeper truth that sincerity and sacrifice, not opportunism, are what qualify one for divine favor and communal honor. The verse thus underscores that hypocrisy reveals itself through selective commitment, and that divine recompense follows the sincerity of one's earlier choices, not merely the convenience of the moment to claim a share in blessings.

translation: Say to those who remained behind among the bedouins, 'You will be called against a people of great military might; you will fight them until they submit. Then if you obey, Allah will give you a good reward; but if you turn away as you turned away before, He will punish you with a painful punishment.'
interpretation: This verse addresses the bedouin Arabs who had made excuses to avoid participating in the Hudaybiyyah expedition with the Prophet, choosing to stay behind out of fear and lack of conviction. Allah informs them that this was not the end of their test—they will be given another opportunity through a future call to fight against a formidable enemy. This serves as a trial to distinguish genuine faith from hollow claims of belief. The verse establishes a direct conditional relationship between obedience and reward, disobedience and punishment, emphasizing that past failures do not permanently condemn a person if they change their behavior, but repeating the same pattern of evasion will result in severe consequences. The passage underscores a broader Quranic theme that faith must be demonstrated through action and sacrifice, particularly in moments of difficulty or danger, and that verbal profession of belief without corresponding commitment is insufficient and exposes one to divine displeasure.

translation: There is no blame upon the blind, nor any blame upon the lame, nor any blame upon the sick (for not participating in certain obligations, such as battle). And whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger, He will admit him into gardens beneath which rivers flow; but whoever turns away, He will punish him with a painful punishment.
interpretation: This verse establishes a foundational Islamic legal and ethical principle: that religious and social obligations are proportionate to one's capacity, and that genuine physical incapacity removes culpability for non-performance of duties like military service or certain communal obligations. It reflects divine mercy and justice, recognizing that Allah does not burden a soul beyond its ability. The verse then pivots to a broader theological statement about obedience and disobedience—those who sincerely obey Allah and His Messenger, within their capacity, are promised eternal reward, while willful rejection or turning away from this guidance results in severe consequence. The juxtaposition suggests that true obedience is not about uniform physical performance of duties, but about sincere submission and effort according to one's ability, while deliberate defiance of divine guidance—not incapacity—is what warrants punishment.

translation: Indeed, Allah was pleased with the believers when they pledged allegiance to you under the tree, and He knew what was in their hearts, so He sent down tranquility upon them and rewarded them with a near victory.
interpretation: This verse refers to the Pledge of Ridwan (Bay'at al-Ridwan) at Hudaybiyyah, where the Prophet's companions swore loyalty to him, even to the point of death, amid tense negotiations with the Quraysh. Allah's declaration of pleasure with them affirms the sincerity and depth of their faith, which He alone could verify by knowing the contents of their hearts—a knowledge beyond human perception. The 'tranquility' (sakinah) sent down represents divine reassurance granted to the believers during a moment of uncertainty and apparent setback, since the Hudaybiyyah treaty initially seemed unfavorable to the Muslims. The 'near victory' mentioned is understood to refer to the subsequent conquest of Khaybar, which followed shortly after, demonstrating that what appeared as a compromise was in fact a strategic and spiritual triumph. The verse underscores the themes of covenant, inner faith validated by outward action, and the way divine wisdom often reveals hidden blessings within apparent trials.

translation: And abundant spoils which they will take. And Allah is ever Exalted in Might and Wise.
interpretation: This verse comes from Surah Al-Fath, in the context of God's promises to the believers who pledged allegiance to the Prophet at Hudaybiyyah. The 'abundant spoils' refer to the material gains—understood by commentators to include the spoils of Khaybar—that would come to those faithful companions as a reward for their patience and loyalty during a time when outward victory seemed uncertain. The verse reassures believers that worldly gain here is not random fortune but a deliberate outcome ordained by God, whose closing attributes—Exalted in Might ('Aziz) and Wise (Hakim)—emphasize that His power ensures the fulfillment of His promises while His wisdom ensures that such rewards are given justly and purposefully, not merely as windfall but as recompense tied to the believers' sincerity and sacrifice.

translation: Allah has promised you many spoils of war that you will take, and He has hastened for you this [victory] and withheld the hands of men from you, that it may be a sign for the believers, and that He may guide you to a straight path.
interpretation: This verse, traditionally associated with the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah and its aftermath, addresses the believers regarding the many future gains Allah has promised them, while emphasizing that an immediate, tangible benefit—often understood as the peaceful outcome of that treaty or an early victory such as Khaybar—was granted swiftly as a foretaste of greater rewards to come. The withholding of the hands of hostile people from the believers points to divine protection during a vulnerable moment, when conflict could have erupted but was averted by Allah's intervention. This protection and the swift fulfillment of part of the promise serve as a concrete 'sign' (ayah) meant to strengthen the faith of believers, demonstrating that Allah's promises are reliable even when immediate circumstances seem uncertain or when apparent setbacks (like the terms of a treaty) mask a deeper strategic and spiritual victory. The verse closes by linking these worldly outcomes to spiritual guidance, suggesting that material events and divine signs are ultimately in service of leading the faithful along the 'straight path'—reinforcing the Qur'anic theme that worldly affairs, victories, and protections are instruments through which Allah nurtures and guides the believers' faith and conduct, rather than ends in themselves.

translation: And [He promises] another [victory] which you have not yet attained; Allah has already encompassed it. And Allah is ever, over all things, competent.
interpretation: This verse comes in the context of the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah and refers to future conquests and victories that the Muslims had not yet achieved at the time of revelation, understood by most commentators to allude to the conquest of Mecca and possibly other subsequent Islamic expansions such as the conquest of Khaybar or Persia. The phrase "Allah has already encompassed it" conveys that these future events are entirely within Allah's knowledge, power, and control, already secured and guaranteed by divine decree even though they lie beyond human present capability. This serves to reassure the believers that their apparent setback at Hudaybiyyah was not a true defeat, but rather part of a larger divine plan whose fruits would be realized in due time. The verse underscores the theme of divine omnipotence and foreknowledge, teaching that human limitations in power or foresight do not constrain God's ability to bring about outcomes already determined by Him, and that trust in divine promise should remain steadfast even when results are not immediately visible.

translation: And if those who disbelieve were to fight you, they would turn their backs [in flight]; then they would not find any protector or helper.
interpretation: This verse addresses the Muslim community, particularly in the context of the Meccan hypocrites and disbelievers who were hesitant or treacherous, reassuring believers of divine support. It emphasizes that despite the apparent strength or threats of the disbelievers, if an actual confrontation were to occur, they would lack the courage, resolve, and divine backing to stand firm, and would flee instead. The verse underscores a broader Qur'anic theme: that true strength comes from faith and reliance on God, not numbers or worldly power. Those who oppose the truth without that spiritual anchor are ultimately weak and abandoned, having no real protector (wali) or helper (nasir) when it truly matters. It serves to bolster the believers' confidence and trust in God's protection, contrasting the instability of disbelief with the steadfastness granted by faith.

translation: This is the established way (sunnah) of Allah which has already occurred before, and you will never find in the way of Allah any change.
interpretation: This verse affirms the immutability and consistency of Allah's divine laws and patterns throughout history, particularly in the context of how He grants victory and support to the believers while bringing about the downfall of those who oppose His messengers. It serves as a reassurance to the believers that the outcomes they witness—whether in triumph over adversaries or in the consequences faced by disbelievers—are not arbitrary but follow a consistent divine order that has governed all previous nations and generations. The verse underscores a theological principle central to Islamic thought: that Allah's methods of dealing with humanity, including His justice, mercy, and the natural consequences of faith versus rejection, are unchanging constants woven into the fabric of creation and history. This serves both as a warning to those who might think they can escape divine law through their own schemes, and as a comfort to believers who can trust that the same principles that brought victory and support to earlier communities of the faithful will continue to operate in their favor, reinforcing confidence in Allah's governance of worldly and spiritual affairs across time.

translation: And it is He who withheld their hands from you and your hands from them within [the valley of] Makkah after He had given you dominance over them. And Allah is ever, of what you do, Seeing.
interpretation: This verse refers to the events at Hudaybiyyah, where a confrontation between the Muslims and the Quraysh of Makkah was averted even though the Muslims had gained the upper hand militarily. The verse emphasizes that it was God's will and power, not mere circumstance, that restrained both sides from violence, allowing for a peaceful truce rather than bloodshed. This divine intervention served a greater purpose—preserving lives, including those of hidden believers in Makkah, and paving the way for the eventual peaceful conquest of the city. The verse underscores the theme that human affairs, especially matters of war and peace, are ultimately under God's control, and that He is fully aware of the intentions and actions of all parties involved, rewarding restraint and wisdom over immediate conquest.

translation: They are the ones who disbelieved and barred you from the Sacred Mosque while the sacrificial animals were prevented from reaching their place of sacrifice. And if not for believing men and believing women whom you did not know, lest you trample them and thus harm would come to you because of them without your knowledge - that Allah might admit into His mercy whom He willed. If they had been apart, We would have punished those who disbelieved among them with painful punishment.
interpretation: This verse was revealed in the context of the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah, explaining why Allah held back the Muslims from entering Mecca by force even though they had been wronged by the Quraysh's obstruction of their pilgrimage. The deeper meaning is that divine wisdom sometimes restrains believers from immediate retribution for the greater good of protecting innocent or hidden believers who live among the disbelievers and whose identities are unknown to the Muslim community. Had the believers attacked, they risked inadvertently harming fellow Muslims concealed within Meccan society, which would have brought guilt and moral stain upon them despite their good intentions. This illustrates a broader principle in divine governance: that Allah's mercy extends through intricate social bonds and hidden faith, and that strategic patience and restraint can serve higher purposes - including the eventual peaceful conversion of hearts - rather than immediate conflict. The verse also emphasizes that worldly power dynamics are secondary to Allah's plan of extending mercy to whomever He chooses, even gradually and through circumstances that seem disadvantageous to believers in the short term.

translation: [Remember] when those who disbelieved had put into their hearts zealotry - the zealotry of the time of ignorance (Jahiliyyah). But Allah sent down His tranquility upon His Messenger and upon the believers, and made binding upon them the word of righteousness (the testimony of faith), and they were more deserving of it and worthy of it. And Allah is Knowing of all things.
interpretation: This verse refers to the events surrounding the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah, when the pagan Quraysh, driven by pride and stubborn tribal arrogance reminiscent of pre-Islamic ignorance, resisted acknowledging Muhammad's prophethood by refusing to let him write 'Messenger of Allah' in the treaty document and objecting to the phrase 'In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.' Despite the humiliation this seemingly caused the Muslims, who had come intending to perform pilgrimage peacefully, Allah bestowed inner calm and steadfastness upon the Prophet and his companions, preventing them from responding with similar arrogance or rash anger. The 'word of righteousness' refers to the declaration of faith (La ilaha illallah) or the principle of patient steadfastness in truth, which the believers held firm to rather than succumbing to the tribal zealotry displayed by their opponents. The verse emphasizes that true honor and entitlement to firmness belongs to those who ground their conviction in piety and submission to God, not in worldly pride or inherited custom. It also illustrates a broader Quranic theme: that external appearances of weakness or concession can mask inner strength granted by divine tranquility (sakina), and that Allah's comprehensive knowledge encompasses the hidden intentions and future outcomes that validate the believers' patience, as the treaty would soon open the way for Islam's peaceful expansion.

translation: Certainly did Allah fulfill for His Messenger the vision in truth. You will surely enter al-Masjid al-Haram, if Allah wills, in safety, with your heads shaved and [hair] shortened, not fearing. He knew what you did not know and has arranged before that a near victory.
interpretation: This verse addresses the vision the Prophet Muhammad had of entering Mecca to perform pilgrimage, which caused confusion and disappointment among his companions when the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah initially prevented them from entering that year. The verse reassures the believers that God's promise was true and would be fulfilled, though not necessarily on the timeline or in the manner they expected. The phrase 'He knew what you did not know' emphasizes divine wisdom surpassing human understanding—the treaty, though seemingly a setback, was actually a strategic victory that would lead to greater gains, including the 'near victory' (commonly understood as the conquest of Khaybar or the eventual conquest of Mecca). This teaches that apparent delays or setbacks in the fulfillment of divine promises may contain hidden wisdom and lead to outcomes greater than immediately apparent, and that patience and trust in God's timing are essential even when circumstances seem to contradict prophetic assurances.

translation: It is He who sent His Messenger with guidance and the religion of truth to make it prevail over all religion, and sufficient is Allah as a witness.
interpretation: This verse affirms the divine origin and mission of the Prophet Muhammad's message, emphasizing that Islam was sent not merely as one faith among many but as the culmination and fulfillment of divine guidance meant to ultimately prevail in truth and influence over all other belief systems. This 'prevailing' is understood by many scholars not necessarily as political or military domination, but as a moral and spiritual ascendancy—Islam's truth being manifest and its principles enduring through history regardless of the fortunes of Muslims themselves. The closing phrase, invoking God as a sufficient witness, underscores that ultimate validation of this truth does not depend on human testimony or worldly success, but rests on divine knowledge and will, offering reassurance to believers during times when the faith's prevalence may not be outwardly apparent.

translation: Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, and those with him are firm and unyielding against the disbelievers, merciful among themselves. You see them bowing and prostrating, seeking bounty from Allah and His good pleasure. Their mark is on their faces from the trace of prostration. That is their description in the Torah. And their description in the Gospel is like a seed that sends forth its shoot, then strengthens it, so it becomes thick and stands straight upon its stalk, delighting the sowers—that He may enrage the disbelievers through them. Allah has promised those among them who believe and do righteous deeds forgiveness and a great reward.
