The Qur'an frequently begins chapters with oaths by natural phenomena to draw the listener's attention to the order, purpose, and divine wisdom embedded in creation. The scattering winds serve a vital ecological function—dispersing seeds for plant growth, moving clouds that bring rain, and maintaining atmospheric balance—all of which sustain life on earth. By swearing by this phenomenon, the verse sets a tone of reflection on the natural world as evidence of a purposeful Creator, foreshadowing the chapter's broader themes about resurrection, divine judgment, and the certainty of the Hereafter, which are affirmed by oaths that follow this one in the subsequent verses.

translation: By those [winds] that carry a heavy load (of rain-laden clouds)
interpretation: This verse is part of an oath sequence at the opening of Surah Adh-Dhariyat, in which God swears by various natural phenomena—winds that scatter, clouds that bear heavy loads of moisture, ships that glide with ease, and angels that distribute affairs by divine command. The 'carriers of a heavy load' refer to the winds or clouds that bear the weight of rain, an essential element for life and sustenance on earth. By invoking these natural forces, the verse draws attention to the intricate and purposeful workings of creation as signs of God's power and wisdom. The oath serves to authenticate and emphasize the truth that follows in the subsequent verses—namely, the certainty of the Day of Judgment and the reality of divine recompense. Just as the winds reliably carry rain to nourish the earth in a precise and ordered manner, so too is the promise of resurrection and accountability a certain and inevitable reality, woven into the very fabric of the natural order that sustains life.

translation: And by those [ships or winds] that glide with ease,
interpretation: This verse is part of a series of oaths at the beginning of Surah Adh-Dhariyat, in which God swears by natural phenomena to establish the truth of a coming reality (the Day of Judgment and the fulfillment of divine promises). 'Those that glide with ease' is commonly understood to refer to ships sailing smoothly upon the seas, though some commentators extend this to winds or celestial bodies moving effortlessly through their courses. The imagery evokes the ease and order with which God's creation moves according to His command, despite the apparent complexity and power involved—ships laden with cargo crossing vast waters, or winds and clouds traversing the sky. This smooth, purposeful movement serves as a sign (ayah) pointing to the Creator's power and wisdom, drawing a parallel to the certainty and inevitability of the resurrection and divine reckoning that follows in the subsequent verses. Just as these forces move with ease under divine command, so too will the Day of Judgment arrive with the same inevitability, regardless of human doubt or denial.

translation: And by those [angels] who distribute [divine] commands.
interpretation: This verse refers to angels who are tasked with carrying out and distributing God's decrees throughout creation—whether that be apportioning sustenance, rain, or other matters of divine ordinance. It is part of a series of oaths at the beginning of Surah Adh-Dhariyat, where God swears by various forces of nature and unseen agents (winds, clouds, ships, angels) to emphasize the certainty of the Day of Judgment and the truth of divine recompense. The angels mentioned here act as intermediaries who execute Allah's commands with precision and obedience, illustrating the orderly and purposeful nature of the universe under divine governance. This serves as a rhetorical device to draw the listener's attention to the grandeur of creation's design as evidence for the reality of resurrection and judgment, which is the central theme that follows in the subsequent verses.

translation: Indeed, that which you are promised is surely true.
interpretation: This verse affirms the certainty of the Day of Judgment and the promises of resurrection, reward, and punishment that had been foretold to humanity. Coming after oaths sworn by the winds, clouds, ships, and angels in the preceding verses, this statement serves as the conclusion to those oaths, emphasizing that the truth of the afterlife is as certain and undeniable as the natural phenomena sworn upon. The use of emphatic particles (إنما and لـ) underscores the absolute certainty of this promise, addressing the disbelievers who doubted or mocked the concept of resurrection and judgment, assuring them that despite their skepticism, what has been promised—accountability before God—will inevitably come to pass.

translation: And indeed, the Judgment (Recompense) is sure to occur.
interpretation: This verse affirms the certainty of the Day of Judgment, coming after oaths sworn by the winds, clouds, and ships (the natural forces that carry rain and sustenance) in the opening verses of Surah Adh-Dhariyat. Having sworn by these phenomena that testify to God's power and providence in sustaining life, God declares with emphatic certainty (using the particles 'inna' and 'la' for double emphasis) that the Din—the reckoning, judgment, and recompense for one's deeds—is an inevitable reality that will surely come to pass. Just as the natural order operates with unfailing regularity and purpose, so too will the moral order of divine justice be fulfilled without fail. This serves as a warning to those who doubt or deny the resurrection and accountability, reminding them that just as they witness the reliable patterns of nature, they should recognize the certainty of their ultimate return to God for judgment.

translation: By the sky full of paths (or: woven with beauty and perfection).
interpretation: This verse opens an oath formula common in the Qur'an, where Allah swears by elements of creation to draw attention to their significance as signs of His power and wisdom. The word 'hubuk' (حُبُك) refers to tracks, orbits, or a woven, well-ordered pattern—likened to the ripples on sand or the threads in woven fabric. Classical commentators have understood this as referring to the precise, intricate paths of the stars and celestial bodies, the layered structure of the heavens, or the sky's beautiful, orderly composition. The oath serves as an introduction to the verses that follow, which address the disbelievers' conflicting and inconsistent claims about the Prophet and the Qur'an. Just as the heavens exhibit perfect order, consistency, and precision in their structure, so too does truth possess coherence, while falsehood is marked by contradiction and inconsistency. The verse thus invites reflection on the cosmic order as evidence of divine wisdom and as a rhetorical contrast to human confusion and error.

translation: Indeed, you are in differing speech.
interpretation: This verse addresses the disbelievers of Mecca, highlighting the inconsistency and contradiction in their statements about the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) and the Quran. Some accused him of being a poet, others a magician, a soothsayer, or a madman, while still others claimed the Quran was ancient fables. These contradictory accusations themselves served as evidence against their credibility, since truth is singular and consistent, while falsehood multiplies into conflicting narratives. The verse serves as a rebuke, pointing out that their inability to agree on a single coherent explanation for the Prophet's message reveals their confusion and the baselessness of their rejection, in contrast to the consistent, unified truth of divine revelation.

translation: Deluded away from it (the Qur'an/Muhammad) is he who is deluded.
interpretation: This verse refers to those who reject the Prophet and the Qur'an despite clear evidence of their truth. It indicates that disbelief is not a result of a lack of proof, but rather a consequence of one's own inner corruption, misguided reasoning, or deliberate turning away from truth. The passive construction suggests that such a person has been diverted or deceived—whether by their own base desires, by Satan, or by the natural outcome of persistent denial—to the point where they can no longer perceive or accept what is self-evident to those with sound hearts and minds. It underscores the Qur'anic theme that spiritual blindness is self-inflicted through choices that corrupt one's capacity to recognize truth.

translation: Cursed (or destroyed) be the liars/conjecturers (those who speak without knowledge)!
interpretation: This verse is a divine condemnation of those who make baseless claims and guesses about matters of great importance—particularly here referring to those who denied the Resurrection and the truth of the Qur'an by speculating without knowledge or evidence. The term 'al-kharrasun' refers to people who conjecture, guess, or fabricate falsehoods, especially about unseen matters like the Day of Judgment. The curse (or statement of destruction) is a strong rhetorical device expressing God's displeasure and foretelling the ultimate failure and ruin of those who reject truth in favor of speculation, assumption, and falsehood. It serves as a warning against intellectual arrogance and baseless denial of divine truths, emphasizing that those who speak about profound realities—such as the afterlife—without true knowledge are liable to severe consequences.

translation: Those who are in [a state of] confusion and heedlessness.
interpretation: This verse describes the disbelievers who deny the Day of Judgment, portraying them as lost in a fog of ignorance and spiritual negligence. The word 'ghamrah' (confusion/overwhelming flood) conveys being engulfed or drowning in misguidance, while 'sahoon' indicates a state of careless heedlessness toward truth and ultimate accountability. Together, these terms paint a picture of people so absorbed in worldly distractions and false certainties that they fail to reflect seriously on the reality of resurrection and divine reckoning, making baseless conjectures about matters of ultimate consequence without genuine contemplation or concern.

translation: They ask, 'When is the Day of Judgment?'
interpretation: This verse reflects the skepticism and mockery of disbelievers who, upon hearing warnings about the Day of Judgment, respond not with genuine inquiry but with sarcastic challenge, demanding to know its exact timing as a way of dismissing its reality altogether. Their question is not born of sincere curiosity but of denial, implying that since they cannot know or control when it will occur, they doubt it will happen at all. This rhetorical questioning represents a common human tendency to reject matters of faith and the unseen simply because they cannot be empirically verified or scheduled according to human understanding. The Qur'an often follows such questions with affirmations of the certainty of the Day of Judgment, emphasizing that divine timing is beyond human computation and that the appropriate response to such mysteries is faith and preparation rather than dismissive questioning. The verse also serves as a rhetorical device to transition into describing the actual events and signs of that day, contrasting human impatience and doubt with divine knowledge and inevitability.

translation: The Day when they will be tried [burned] over the Fire.
interpretation: This verse refers to the Day of Judgment, describing the punishment of the disbelievers who rejected the truth and denied the reality of the Hereafter. The word 'yuftanun' (يفتنون) carries the dual meaning of being 'tried' and 'burned'—derived from the same root used for the testing of gold in fire to separate pure metal from impurity. Here it signifies that the disbelievers will be subjected to the Fire as a form of punishment and exposure, their false claims and denials now laid bare before them. This imagery connects to the broader context of the surah, which speaks of the Day when secrets are tested and revealed (as in verse 9 of the same surah, 'yu'fakuna 'anhu man ufik'), emphasizing that the trial they avoided in worldly life—the testing of faith and righteousness—will culminate in this ultimate reckoning, where the Fire itself becomes both their torment and the proof of the truth they once denied.

translation: Taste your trial (punishment); this is what you used to seek to hasten.
interpretation: This verse is addressed to the disbelievers who mockingly demanded that the punishment promised by the Prophet be brought upon them immediately, as a way of denying its reality. When the punishment finally arrives, they are told to 'taste' it—a word choice that emphasizes direct, undeniable experience rather than abstract threat. The term 'fitnatakum' (your trial/torment) suggests that the punishment itself serves as the ultimate proof and test, stripping away all possibility of further denial. The phrase 'this is what you used to seek to hasten' carries a tone of bitter irony: their impatient demand for proof, born of arrogance and disbelief, is now fulfilled in the very form they least desired. It underscores a recurring Qur'anic theme that divine recompense, though delayed, is certain, and that mocking defiance of warnings only hastens one's own reckoning rather than disproving it.

translation: Indeed, the righteous will be among gardens and springs.
interpretation: This verse describes the reward awaiting those who practice taqwa—mindful God-consciousness that leads them to obey divine commands and avoid sin. The imagery of gardens and flowing springs evokes a paradise of lushness, abundance, and tranquility, standing in deep contrast to the barren, arid landscape familiar to the verse's original audience. Beyond its literal depiction of paradise, the verse symbolizes spiritual fulfillment and peace that comes from righteous living: just as gardens require cultivation and springs provide continuous sustenance, a life of piety is portrayed as one that yields lasting spiritual nourishment and inner serenity, both in this world through closeness to God and ultimately in the hereafter through eternal reward.

translation: Taking [and enjoying] what their Lord has given them. Indeed, they were before that [in this world] doers of good.
interpretation: This verse describes the dwellers of Paradise who are depicted in the preceding verses as being among gardens and springs. It establishes a direct causal relationship between righteous conduct in earthly life and the reward of divine bounty in the hereafter. The phrase 'taking what their Lord has given them' conveys a sense of contentment, gratitude, and joyful acceptance of divine grace, rather than mere passive receipt. The verse then grounds this reward in its cause: their prior state of 'ihsan' (excellence in doing good), a Quranic concept that goes beyond mere outward compliance with religious law to encompass sincerity, spiritual excellence, and worshipping God as though one sees Him. This connects to the broader Quranic theme that paradise is not an arbitrary gift but the natural fruition of a life lived in conscious moral and spiritual excellence—their past deeds of kindness, charity, worship, and righteousness performed with sincerity and excellence now manifest as eternal reward. The verse thus serves as both a description of the believers' felicity and an implicit exhortation to the listener to emulate this quality of ihsan in their own worldly conduct.

translation: They used to sleep but little of the night.
interpretation: This verse describes one of the virtuous qualities of the righteous (al-muttaqin) mentioned in the preceding verses of Surah Adh-Dhariyat, who are promised gardens and springs in the Hereafter. Their nights were not spent in idle sleep but largely devoted to wakefulness in worship—prayer, remembrance of God, and seeking His forgiveness, as the following verse confirms ('and in the hours before dawn, they would ask forgiveness'). The sparing of sleep symbolizes their spiritual discipline and devotion, prioritizing closeness to God over bodily comfort. It reflects an ideal of self-restraint and vigilance in faith, where the night, often associated with rest and heedlessness, becomes instead a time of intimate communion with the Divine. This practice is held up as a model of piety, illustrating that true righteousness involves sustained effort and sincerity beyond outward ritual, extending into private, unseen acts of devotion performed when no one else is watching.

translation: And in the hours before dawn, they would seek forgiveness.
interpretation: This verse describes one of the virtuous qualities of the righteous believers (al-muttaqin), continuing the description begun in the preceding verses about those who spend little of the night in sleep. The pre-dawn hours (sahar) are highlighted as a especially sacred and spiritually potent time—when the world is quiet, distractions are minimal, and the heart is most receptive to sincere devotion. By choosing to rise before dawn to seek God's forgiveness (istighfar), these believers demonstrate a proactive and humble relationship with their Creator, acknowledging their own imperfections and shortcomings even while being described as righteous. This practice reflects the Islamic understanding that true piety is not about claiming moral perfection but about constant self-awareness, repentance, and turning back to God. The timing is also significant because the last third of the night is traditionally understood in Islamic theology as a time when divine mercy is especially near, making istighfar at this hour an act of both spiritual discipline and deep trust in God's responsiveness to sincere supplication.

translation: And in their wealth there was a recognized right for the one who asks and the one who is deprived.
interpretation: This verse describes a quality of the righteous, affirming that charity is not merely an act of voluntary kindness but a rightful due owed to those in need. The phrase 'a recognized right' (haqqun ma'lum) indicates that a portion of one's wealth inherently belongs to the poor and needy as a matter of justice, not simply generosity. Two categories are mentioned: 'the one who asks' (al-sa'il), referring to those who openly request help, and 'the deprived' (al-mahrum), referring to those who are in need but, out of dignity or circumstance, do not ask for assistance. This teaches believers to be proactively attentive to the needs of others, seeking out those who suffer in silence rather than waiting only for requests. The verse underscores that social responsibility and economic justice are integral to faith, and that true righteousness involves recognizing the inherent claims of the less fortunate upon the wealth of those who have been blessed with abundance.

translation: And on the earth are signs for those who are certain in faith.
interpretation: This verse points to the natural world—mountains, rivers, diverse creatures, the cycles of growth and decay, the intricate balance of ecosystems—as evidence of a wise and purposeful Creator. The phrase 'for those who are certain' (al-muqinin) is significant: it suggests that these signs are not equally perceptible or convincing to everyone. Rather, it is those who already possess a foundation of certainty and spiritual receptivity who are able to read the earth as a text full of meaning. Yaqin (certainty) here refers to a firm, experiential conviction that goes beyond mere intellectual assent—it is the kind of faith that transforms perception itself, allowing a person to see divine wisdom and purpose woven into ordinary phenomena that others might pass by without reflection. In this sense, the verse suggests a reciprocal relationship between faith and understanding: certainty opens the eyes to see signs, and contemplating these signs in turn deepens certainty. The earth becomes not just a physical dwelling but a continuous revelation, a scripture spread out in mountains and valleys, seasons and seeds, awaiting a heart prepared to read it.

translation: And [there are signs] within yourselves. Will you not then see?
interpretation: This verse directs attention inward, suggesting that the human being is itself a sign of God's creative power and wisdom, just as the heavens and earth (mentioned in the preceding verse) are signs. The intricate design of the human body, mind, and soul—the complexity of human cognition, the balance of bodily systems, and the spiritual faculties within—all point to a Creator. The rhetorical question 'will you not then see?' is a call to reflective reasoning (tabassur), urging humans to look within themselves rather than only outward, since self-knowledge and contemplation of one's own existence can lead to recognition of the divine. It implies that the truth of God's existence and power is not distant or abstract, but immediately accessible through introspection, making denial of it a failure of perception and intellectual honesty rather than a lack of evidence.

translation: And in the heaven is your provision and that which you are promised.
interpretation: This verse points to the divine origin of sustenance, indicating that rain—which is sent down from the sky—is the source of crops, water, and all that nourishes life on earth, underscoring that provision ultimately comes from God's command over the heavens rather than from human effort alone. The phrase 'and what you are promised' extends this heavenly source beyond material sustenance to encompass the promised Day of Judgment, Paradise, and all that God has pledged to the believers. By linking daily sustenance with the eschatological promise in a single breath, the verse draws a parallel between the certainty of rain descending to give life to a barren earth and the certainty of the resurrection and reward to come—both are decreed and held in the heavens, both are unseen until they arrive, and both are beyond human power to produce or prevent. It is a call to trust in God's unseen decree, recognizing that just as one relies on the sky for rain, one should place equal confidence in the fulfillment of God's promises regarding the Hereafter.

translation: So by the Lord of heaven and earth, it is indeed true, just as [surely as] you speak.
interpretation: This verse employs a powerful oath to affirm the absolute certainty of the truth being discussed—namely, the reality of sustenance, resurrection, and divine promise mentioned in the preceding verses. By swearing by the Lord of heaven and earth, God invokes the very source of creation as a witness to the truthfulness of His message. The comparison to human speech is particularly striking: just as a person cannot doubt that they themselves are speaking—it is an immediate, self-evident fact of their own experience—so too should the truths of divine revelation be regarded as equally certain and undeniable. This rhetorical device transforms an abstract theological claim into something as tangible and incontrovertible as the most basic fact of one's own existence, emphasizing that skepticism about resurrection and divine justice is as unreasonable as doubting one's own capacity for speech.

translation: Has there reached you the story of the honored guests of Abraham?
interpretation: This verse opens the account of the angelic visitors who came to Abraham in human form, later identified as bringing news of a son (Isaac) and the impending destruction of the people of Lot. The rhetorical question 'Has the story reached you?' is a Qur'anic literary device used to engage the Prophet Muhammad and the listener, creating anticipation and signaling that an important lesson follows. The guests are described as 'honored' (al-mukramin) both because Abraham treated them with great hospitality—quickly bringing a roasted calf and showing generous courtesy—and because they were honored angels sent on a divine mission. The passage sets up a broader theme in this surah about faith, divine signs, and the fate of disbelieving nations, using Abraham's hospitality as a model of righteous conduct and openness to divine guidance, while foreshadowing the contrasting story of Lot's people who rejected the same messengers.

translation: When they entered upon him and said, 'Peace,' he said, 'Peace, [you are] a people unknown.'
interpretation: This verse opens the narrative of Prophet Ibrahim (Abraham) receiving mysterious guests who were in fact angels sent by God, though he did not yet recognize them as such. The exchange of greetings reflects the deep hospitality and courtesy that was customary in Ibrahim's culture, where even unknown visitors were met with peace and respect. Ibrahim's remark that they were 'a people unknown' signals his innocent curiosity and perhaps a note of caution, as he did not recognize these strangers, yet he still responded graciously. This sets the stage for the unfolding story where the angels reveal their divine purpose—to deliver the glad tidings of a son to Ibrahim and his wife, and to warn of the impending destruction of the people of Lot. The verse emphasizes the values of hospitality, respect for guests regardless of their origin, and the idea that divine messages and tests can come through unexpected encounters with strangers.

translation: Then he turned away to his household and came back with a fat [roasted] calf.
interpretation: This verse depicts Prophet Ibrahim's (Abraham's) gracious hospitality toward his unexpected guests, who were angels in human form. Without delay or hesitation, he slipped away quietly to his family and household to prepare food, returning promptly with a fattened calf—the finest offering he could provide. This act illustrates the Quranic ideal of generous hospitality toward guests, a virtue highly esteemed in Arab and Islamic culture, where one honors visitors by offering them the best of what one has, even before knowing their true identity or purpose. Ibrahim's swift, uncomplaining action reflects his noble character and sets a model of selfless generosity, foreshadowing the revelation of his guests' divine mission to deliver news of a son and to warn of the destruction of the people of Lot.

translation: So he brought it near to them, saying, 'Will you not eat?'
interpretation: This verse refers to the story of Prophet Ibrahim (Abraham) and his encounter with the guests (angels) who visited him. Unaware that they were angels, Ibrahim, as a gracious host, prepared a roasted calf and set it before them, inviting them to eat, in accordance with the customs of hospitality deeply valued in Arab culture. When the guests did not eat, this became a sign to Ibrahim that something was unusual, since angels do not consume food, foreshadowing the revelation of their true nature and purpose—to deliver news of judgment upon the people of Lot and glad tidings of a son to Ibrahim and Sarah. This moment underscores themes of hospitality, the testing of perception, and the unfolding of divine will through seemingly ordinary human interactions.

translation: So he [Abraham] conceived fear of them. They said, 'Do not fear,' and gave him good tidings of a knowledgeable boy.
interpretation: This verse depicts the moment when Prophet Ibrahim (Abraham) hosted mysterious guests—later revealed to be angels—who did not eat the food he offered them, causing him apprehension since in his culture refusal to eat was often a sign of hostile intent. Sensing his unease, the angels immediately reassured him and revealed their true purpose: to deliver the miraculous news that he would be blessed with a son, Isaac, who would grow to possess great knowledge and wisdom. This episode illustrates several theological themes central to the Quranic narrative: the hospitality and righteousness of Ibrahim even toward strangers, the human vulnerability to fear in the face of the unknown, and God's capacity to transform anxiety into joy through divine intervention. The promise of a 'knowledgeable boy' also foreshadows the prophetic lineage that would continue through Isaac, reinforcing the theme of divine providence working through Ibrahim's family despite the seeming impossibility of the news given his and his wife's advanced age, as elaborated in subsequent verses.

translation: Then his wife came forward, crying out, and struck her face, and said: 'A barren old woman!'
interpretation: This verse depicts the astonished reaction of Prophet Ibrahim's wife, Sarah, upon overhearing the angelic messengers announce that she would bear a son despite her old age and barrenness. Her gesture of striking her face and her exclamation express natural human disbelief and astonishment at news that defies the ordinary course of nature. The episode underscores a central Qur'anic theme: God's power transcends natural limitations, and what seems impossible by human reckoning is effortless for the Divine will. Sarah's very human response—shock, incredulity, self-deprecating acknowledgment of her condition—serves to heighten the miraculous nature of the coming birth of Isaac, affirming that divine promises, however improbable they appear, are fulfilled according to God's capability rather than human expectation.

translation: They said, "Thus has your Lord said; indeed, He is the Wise, the All-Knowing."
interpretation: This verse is part of the narrative in which angelic messengers bring Abraham news of a son despite his and his wife's old age. When Abraham and Sarah express astonishment at this seemingly impossible news, the angels respond by affirming that this is the decree of God Himself, not merely their own prediction. By invoking the divine names 'the Wise' (al-Hakim) and 'the Knowing' (al-'Alim), the verse underscores that God's actions, however astonishing they may appear to human reasoning bound by natural limitations, are rooted in perfect wisdom and complete knowledge. The implicit message is that human beings should not measure divine capability by the constraints of ordinary biological or physical possibility, since God's wisdom encompasses what is hidden from human understanding and His knowledge is total and unerring. This serves as a broader theological point throughout the Qur'an: miraculous or seemingly improbable events are expressions of divine wisdom and knowledge that transcend human expectation, reinforcing trust in God's decree even when it defies ordinary expectation.

translation: He [Abraham] said, 'Then what is your business, O messengers?'
interpretation: This verse depicts Prophet Abraham's question to the angelic messengers who visited him in human form, after he had already welcomed them and offered them food. Having noticed they did not eat, and perhaps sensing their visit was not merely social, Abraham directly asks about their mission. This moment illustrates Abraham's perceptiveness and hospitality customs of the time, while also setting up the dramatic revelation that follows—that these are not ordinary guests but divine messengers sent with a dual purpose: to deliver the news of a son to Abraham and his wife, and to proceed to destroy the sinful people of Lot. The question itself reflects a broader Quranic theme of recognizing that divine messengers often appear with specific, weighty purposes that unfold through dialogue and revelation rather than immediate disclosure, emphasizing patience and the gradual unveiling of divine plans even to righteous prophets.

translation: They said, "Indeed, we have been sent to a criminal people."
interpretation: This verse is part of the narrative in which angelic messengers, after bringing glad tidings to Prophet Abraham of a son, reveal the second purpose of their mission: to bring destruction upon the people of Lot. The term 'mujrimin' (criminal/sinning people) characterizes the people of Lot as those who had transgressed moral and divine boundaries through their persistent wrongdoing, particularly their infamous sexual immorality and rejection of Lot's warnings. The angels' statement serves as a pivot in the narrative, shifting from a message of mercy and good news (the promise of a child) to one of impending divine judgment. This juxtaposition illustrates a recurring Qur'anic theme: that God's messengers and angels serve dual roles as bearers of both mercy for the righteous and retribution for the persistently sinful. The directness of the angels' speech also underscores the certainty and inevitability of divine justice once a community has crossed into irredeemable corruption, despite having been given warnings and a chance to repent through Lot's prophetic mission among them.

translation: That We may send down upon them stones of clay.
interpretation: This verse refers to the punishment sent upon the people of Lot, describing the hail of baked clay stones that were unleashed as divine retribution for their transgressions. The stones of clay symbolize a targeted, purposeful destruction, marked and prepared specifically for the wrongdoers, demonstrating that divine justice is precise and not random. This serves as a warning to all who persist in corruption and immorality, illustrating that consequences for sin can come from unexpected and seemingly natural sources, yet are ultimately directed by divine will.

translation: Marked by your Lord for the transgressors.
interpretation: This phrase comes from Surah Adh-Dhariyat (51:34), in the context of the story of the angels who visited Prophet Lot (Lut) to deliver divine punishment upon his transgressing people. The verse describes stones of baked clay that were specifically marked and designated by God for destroying those who had exceeded all bounds in sin, particularly the people of Sodom who persisted in immorality and rejected the warnings of their prophet. The term 'musrifin' (transgressors/those who exceed limits) refers to those who go beyond the bounds of decency and divine law, indicating that their punishment was not arbitrary but precisely determined and reserved for them according to divine justice. This reflects a broader Quranic theme that divine retribution is measured, intentional, and tied directly to the nature and extent of human transgression—nothing is left to chance, and each soul's fate is recorded and assigned according to its deeds.

translation: So We brought out whoever was in it among the believers.
interpretation: This verse refers to the destruction of the people of Lot (Sodom). Before unleashing the punishment upon the sinful city, God ensured the safe evacuation of the believers—Lot and his household (except his wife, who is mentioned in the following verses as having stayed behind and perished with the wrongdoers). The verse illustrates a recurring Qur'anic theme: divine justice distinguishes between the righteous and the wicked, and God never destroys a community without first delivering those who have faith. It underscores the principle that salvation is tied to belief and righteous conduct rather than mere lineage or social standing, as even within Lot's own family, his wife was not saved due to her complicity with the disbelievers. The verse also serves as a reassurance to believers of every age that steadfastness in faith, even amid a corrupt society, is rewarded with divine protection when calamity strikes.

translation: But We found not therein except one house of Muslims [those who had submitted to Allah].
interpretation: This verse is part of the narrative concerning the people of Prophet Lot (Lot). After the angels were sent to destroy the corrupt city for its sins, this verse reveals the extent of the moral devastation: when the angels searched the entire city, they found only a single household—that of Lot himself—who had submitted to God and remained righteous amid widespread corruption. This illustrates a recurring Qur'anic theme: that true faith and righteousness often exist as a small minority amidst a sinful majority, and that divine punishment, when it comes, distinguishes between the righteous and the wrongdoers, sparing only the few who maintained their submission to God. The verse also serves as a sober reminder of how thoroughly a society can become corrupted, to the point where believers become exceedingly rare.

translation: And We left therein a sign for those who fear the painful punishment.
interpretation: This verse refers to the ruins of the city of the people of Lot (Sodom), which Allah left standing as a visible, tangible warning sign for later generations. The verse specifies that this sign benefits only 'those who fear the painful punishment'—meaning that physical evidence of divine retribution is only meaningful to those whose hearts are already receptive to faith and accountability. Those lacking this fear may pass by such ruins without drawing any lesson, while believers see in them concrete proof of the consequences of disbelief and moral corruption, reinforcing the broader Quranic theme that history itself contains lessons for those willing to reflect and take heed.

translation: And in Moses [too, is a sign], when We sent him to Pharaoh with clear authority.
interpretation: This verse continues a series of examples given in Surah Adh-Dhariyat of past nations and prophets whose stories serve as signs for those who reflect. The 'clear authority' (sultan mubin) refers to the manifest proofs and miracles given to Moses, such as the staff turning into a serpent and his hand turning white without disease, which were undeniable demonstrations of divine truth sent to confront Pharaoh's tyranny and arrogance. The mention of Moses here reinforces the Quran's recurring theme that every nation was given clear signs through its messengers, yet many rejected them despite the clarity of the proof, foreshadowing Pharaoh's subsequent denial and destruction as a warning to the disbelievers of Mecca who were likewise rejecting Muhammad's message despite its clarity.

translation: But he turned away in his power and said, 'A magician or a madman.'
interpretation: This verse refers to Pharaoh's rejection of the Prophet Moses (peace be upon him) and the divine message he brought. 'His rukn' (power, might, or supporters) signifies Pharaoh's reliance on his worldly authority, army, and status rather than reflecting sincerely on the truth presented to him. Instead of engaging with the substance of Moses's message, Pharaoh dismissed it with baseless accusations—calling Moses either a sorcerer (implying deception through trickery) or a madman (implying irrationality)—both convenient labels used by those in power to avoid confronting uncomfortable truths. This illustrates a recurring pattern in the Qur'an where arrogant rulers, secure in their earthly might, reject prophets not based on reasoned argument but due to pride and the fear of losing control. The verse serves as a warning about how power and privilege can blind individuals to truth, leading them to dismiss sincere guidance through insults rather than genuine engagement.

translation: So We seized him and his soldiers, and We cast them into the sea, while he was blameworthy.
interpretation: This verse refers to the destruction of Pharaoh (Fir'awn) and his army, who were drowned in the sea as divine punishment for his tyranny, arrogance, and rejection of the message brought by Prophet Musa (Moses). The word 'مليم' (blameworthy) signifies that Pharaoh's downfall was entirely the result of his own wrongdoing—his persistent denial of truth, his oppression of the Israelites, and his claim to divinity. The verse serves as a reminder that worldly power and military might offer no protection against divine justice when one persists in arrogance and disbelief. It is part of a broader Quranic pattern of citing the fates of previous nations and tyrants (such as the people of Noah, 'Ad, Thamud, and others) as cautionary examples for the Meccan disbelievers, illustrating that those who reject God's messengers and persist in corruption will ultimately face consequences, no matter how powerful they appear in their time.

translation: And in [the story of] 'Aad [there is a sign], when We sent against them the barren wind.
interpretation: This verse refers to the destruction of the people of 'Aad, an ancient Arabian tribe known for their great strength and monumental architecture, who rejected the message of their prophet Hud. The 'barren wind' (al-rih al-'aqim) is described as barren because it brought no benefit—no rain, no pollination, no fertility—only destruction. It left nothing alive in its path, serving purely as an instrument of punishment rather than mercy. The verse is presented as one among several historical 'signs' (ayat) mentioned in this passage of Surah Adh-Dhariyat, alongside the stories of Pharaoh, Thamud, the people of Noah, and others, all illustrating a consistent divine pattern: nations that arrogantly defied their prophets and relied on their own power and civilization were ultimately destroyed by forces entirely beyond their control. The wind, an invisible and seemingly weak element of nature, becomes the means by which God humbles those who considered themselves unassailable. This serves as a reminder to the Quran's audience of the consequences of disbelief and arrogance, and of God's complete power over nature as an instrument of both sustenance and retribution.

translation: It spared nothing it came upon, but made it like decayed ruins.
interpretation: This verse describes the devastating wind sent by Allah as punishment upon the people of 'Aad, mentioned in the broader context of Surah Adh-Dhariyat where Allah recounts the fates of nations who rejected their messengers. The imagery of 'ramim' (decayed, crumbled remains, often used to describe decomposed bones or rotted matter) conveys the totality and thoroughness of the destruction—nothing was spared, and everything touched by this wind was reduced to lifeless, disintegrated debris. This serves as a stark warning and sign (ayah) for those who reflect, illustrating the consequence of persistent arrogance and disbelief despite clear warnings. The verse functions within a pattern in this surah where Allah presents historical examples of destroyed civilizations—Pharaoh, Thamud, the people of Noah—as evidence of divine power and justice, urging the listener to recognize that worldly might offers no protection against Allah's decree when a people transgress beyond the limits of forbearance granted to them.

translation: And in Thamud [was a sign], when it was said to them, 'Enjoy yourselves for a while.'
interpretation: This verse refers to the people of Thamud, to whom the Prophet Salih was sent. After they defied the warning accompanying the sign of the she-camel and hamstrung it, they were given a brief respite of three days, as mentioned elsewhere in the Qur'an, before the promised punishment befell them. The phrase 'enjoy yourselves for a while' is deeply ironic and foreboding—it is not a genuine blessing but a pronouncement of doom disguised as reprieve, emphasizing that their remaining time of worldly enjoyment was finite and would soon end in destruction. This reflects a broader Qur'anic theme found throughout the surah: nations who received clear signs and warnings from their prophets, yet persisted in arrogance and denial, were granted a temporary respite not as mercy but as a final test or countdown before divine retribution. The mention of Thamud alongside other destroyed nations (like the people of Noah, Pharaoh, and the people of Lot) in this surah serves as a cautionary sign for the Meccan disbelievers who were themselves being warned about rejecting Prophet Muhammad's message. The 'enjoyment' is thus a bitter irony—a temporary worldly pleasure that stands in stark, tragic contrast to the eternal consequence of their disbelief and arrogance.

translation: But they insolently defied the command of their Lord, so the thunderbolt seized them while they were looking on.
interpretation: This verse refers to the people of Thamud, who were given a clear sign from God—the she-camel—as proof of the truth of Prophet Salih's message. Despite this evidence and the warnings given to them, they arrogantly rebelled against their Lord's command, hamstringing the she-camel in defiance. The phrase 'while they were looking on' emphasizes that the punishment was not hidden or delayed in a way that left room for doubt; they saw the thunderbolt (a devastating blast or seismic event) approaching and could do nothing to escape it. This illustrates a broader Qur'anic theme: when a people persist in arrogance and conscious rejection of divine guidance after clear signs have been shown to them, divine punishment can come swiftly and openly, serving as a visible lesson for others. The verse underscores themes of accountability, the futility of resisting God's decree once it is set in motion, and the idea that destruction often comes at the very moment of greatest complacency or defiance.

translation: So they were unable to rise, nor could they defend themselves.
interpretation: This verse refers to the fate of the Thamud, the people of Prophet Salih, who were struck down by a devastating blast (as-sayha) as divine punishment for their defiance and for killing the she-camel that was sent to them as a sign. The verse emphasizes the totality and suddenness of their destruction—they had no time or strength to stand up, flee, or mount any resistance against the punishment that overtook them. This serves as a broader Quranic theme illustrating the futility of human power and arrogance when confronted with divine will, and stands as a warning to later generations who might witness or hear of such historical accounts of destroyed nations. The inability to rise symbolizes complete helplessness before God's decree, while the inability to be 'muntasireen' (those who are victorious or helped) underscores that no worldly power, alliance, or strength could save them from the consequences of their rejection of the prophetic message.

translation: And the people of Noah before that; indeed, they were a defiantly disobedient people.
interpretation: This verse situates the people of Noah within a chain of nations mentioned in the surah—alongside Pharaoh and other destroyed peoples—as examples of communities that rejected their prophets and persisted in moral and spiritual corruption (fisq). The term 'fasiqin' denotes those who knowingly transgress the bounds set by God, having deliberately strayed from the truth after it was made clear to them. By citing Noah's people as a precedent 'before' the others mentioned, the Qur'an establishes a pattern: divine punishment is not arbitrary but follows persistent, willful rebellion against guidance. The mention serves as a warning to the Prophet Muhammad's contemporaries, reminding them that previous nations who scorned their messengers—despite ample warning and time—met destruction, and that rejecting revelation is not a new phenomenon but a recurring human failing with consistent consequences.

translation: And the heaven We constructed with strength, and indeed, We are [its] expander.
interpretation: This verse affirms God's power and ongoing sovereignty over creation. 'Binaina-ha bi-ayd' ('We built it with power/strength') emphasizes that the heavens were constructed with divine might, not by chance or weakness. The phrase 'wa inna la-mūsi'ūn' ('and indeed We are expanders' or 'We have vast power/capacity') has been understood by many commentators, especially in light of modern cosmology, as alluding to the continual expansion of the universe—a remarkable correspondence to the scientific discovery that the universe is expanding. Classically, exegetes understood 'mūsi'ūn' to mean that God possesses vast power and capacity, able to expand and extend creation as He wills, emphasizing His limitless ability in contrast to human limitation. The verse as a whole serves as a sign (ayah) pointing to God's omnipotence, inviting reflection on the cosmos as evidence of the Creator's majesty and the deliberate, purposeful nature of the universe's structure, which is neither static nor confined but dynamic and vast, continually sustained and expanded by divine power.

translation: And the earth, We have spread it out - and how excellent are those who spread it out!
interpretation: This verse comes from a series of verses in which God points to elements of creation—the heavens, the earth, mountains, and the pairing of all things—as signs of His power and wisdom meant to prompt reflection and remembrance. By describing the earth as spread out (a vast, stable expanse suitable for habitation, agriculture, and travel), the verse highlights divine providence in making the earth hospitable for life. The phrase 'how excellent are those who spread it out' uses a grammatical form that, while referring to God alone, conveys emphasis and majesty, affirming that this act of 'spreading' was done with perfect skill and purposeful design. The underlying message is that the earth's suitability for life is not accidental but a deliberate act of divine craftsmanship, meant to inspire gratitude and recognition of the Creator's power among those who reflect on the natural world.

translation: And of all things We created pairs, that you might remember.
interpretation: This verse points to the universal principle of duality woven into the fabric of creation—male and female, day and night, heaven and earth, positive and negative forces in nature, and so on. By establishing this pervasive pattern of pairs throughout existence, the verse invites reflection on a profound theological truth: everything that exists in pairs is, by definition, dependent and incomplete without its counterpart, and therefore contingent and created. This stands in stark contrast to Allah, who is singular, self-sufficient, and without partner or equal. The 'remembrance' (tadhakkur) called for here is the recognition that the very structure of the universe—its reliance on complementary pairs for balance, reproduction, and continuity—testifies to a Creator who transcends this duality entirely. Observing the pairing in nature should lead the human mind back to the Oneness (tawhid) of God, who alone stands outside this system of paired dependency, having no partner, no equal, and no need for complement.

translation: So flee to Allah. Indeed, I am to you from Him a clear warner.
interpretation: This verse, spoken by the Prophet Muhammad (or understood as a command to all messengers to convey), calls humanity to turn away from false gods, worldly attachments, and sin, and to seek refuge and salvation solely in Allah. The command 'flee' (fa firru) conveys urgency, as though escaping from imminent danger—symbolizing the peril of disbelief and idolatry that leads to destruction. It emphasizes that true security and guidance lie only in submission to the one God, not in wealth, power, or false deities. The latter part of the verse establishes the prophetic role as a 'clear warner,' meaning that the message is unambiguous and delivered with clarity, leaving no excuse for rejection. It also underscores the mercy embedded in the warning: Allah does not leave humanity without guidance, but sends messengers to alert them to the truth before consequences unfold. Thus, the verse functions as both an urgent spiritual call to repentance and a declaration of prophetic responsibility to deliver divine truth without distortion.

translation: And do not set up with Allah another god. Indeed, I am to you from Him a clear warner.
interpretation: This verse is part of the Prophet Muhammad's declaration, instructed by Allah, affirming the core doctrine of tawhid (monotheism) and rejecting any form of shirk (associating partners with Allah). It establishes that the Prophet's role is that of a clear, unambiguous warner sent to communicate the consequences of deviating from pure monotheism, emphasizing that his message is not his own invention but a direct transmission from Allah himself. The clarity mentioned underscores that the warning leaves no excuse for misunderstanding, holding people fully accountable for heeding the call to worship Allah alone.

translation: Likewise, no messenger came to those before them except that they said, 'A sorcerer or a madman.'
interpretation: This verse consoles the Prophet Muhammad by establishing a historical pattern: the rejection and mockery he faced from his people was not unique to him but represents a recurring response that every prophet throughout history encountered from their communities. By labeling messengers as either 'sorcerer' (implying deceptive manipulation) or 'madman' (implying irrationality), disbelieving peoples sought to dismiss divine revelation without genuinely engaging with its message. This pattern reveals something about human psychology when confronted with truth that challenges established norms and power structures—rather than examining the message itself, opponents attack the messenger's character or sanity. The verse serves as both comfort and warning: comfort to the Prophet that he follows in the footsteps of all previous messengers, and a warning to his contemporaries that their rejection mirrors the failed rejections of earlier peoples who faced divine consequences for their disbelief.

translation: Have they transmitted this [response] to one another? Rather, they are a transgressing people.
interpretation: This verse follows a pattern in Surah Adh-Dhariyat where Allah notes that every nation before them—the people of Noah, Abraham's opponents, and others—accused their messengers of being sorcerers or madmen. The rhetorical question asks whether these disbelieving generations, separated by centuries, somehow coordinated or inherited this exact accusation from one another. The answer clarifies that no such transmission occurred; rather, the uniformity of their rejection stems from a shared underlying trait: transgression (tughyan) and rebellion against truth. This reveals that human arrogance and resistance to divine guidance follows recognizable patterns across history, not because of historical collusion, but because unchecked pride and defiance naturally produce the same rationalizations and denials in any era. The verse serves as a warning to the Prophet Muhammad's contemporaries that their rejection of him was nothing new, but a recurring symptom of spiritual transgression common to arrogant peoples throughout history.

translation: So turn away from them, for you are not to be blamed.
interpretation: This verse addresses the Prophet Muhammad regarding those who persistently reject the message despite clear signs and warnings, as recounted in the preceding verses about earlier peoples who disbelieved their messengers (Noah, Moses, and others) and faced destruction. God instructs the Prophet to withdraw from arguing with the obstinate deniers, reassuring him that he has fulfilled his duty of conveying the message faithfully, and that any blame for their rejection lies with them, not with him. This reflects a broader Qur'anic theme that a messenger's responsibility is limited to clear delivery of the message (al-balagh al-mubin), not forcing belief, and that the psychological burden of rejection should not weigh on the one who has sincerely conveyed divine truth. It also serves as a consolation to the Prophet during times of intense opposition, affirming that his integrity and mission remain intact regardless of others' response.

translation: And remind, for indeed the reminder benefits the believers.
interpretation: This verse is addressed to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him), instructing him to continue his mission of reminding people of the truth, even if not everyone accepts or benefits from it. The verse acknowledges that while reminders and admonitions may not sway everyone—particularly those who are heedless or disbelieving—they hold genuine value and benefit for the believers, those whose hearts are receptive to faith. This highlights a core principle in Islamic teaching: that the purpose of preaching and reminding is not necessarily universal conversion, but rather the nurturing and strengthening of faith in those already inclined toward belief. It also underscores the importance of continuous spiritual reminder (dhikr) as a means of sustaining faith, since even believers can become forgetful or heedless over time. The verse serves as a motivation for teachers, preachers, and believers in general to keep sharing beneficial knowledge and reminders of God, trusting that such efforts will bear fruit among sincere hearts, even if others remain unmoved.

translation: And I did not create the jinn and mankind except to worship Me.
interpretation: This verse establishes the fundamental purpose of creation for both jinn and humans: worship and servitude to God. The word 'worship' (ibadah) here encompasses far more than ritual acts like prayer; it signifies total submission, obedience, and acknowledgment of God's sovereignty in every aspect of life. This purpose reflects not a need on God's part—since He is self-sufficient and free of all needs—but rather a mercy and guidance to creation, pointing them toward their true fulfillment and the source of ultimate meaning. The verse implies that all other pursuits—wealth, power, pleasure—are secondary to this primary purpose, and that true success lies in recognizing and living out this relationship with the Creator. It also implicitly addresses free will: although humans and jinn are created for worship, they are not compelled to it, making their choice to worship or reject it a test of their faith and character.

translation: I do not want from them any provision, nor do I want them to feed Me.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes God's absolute self-sufficiency and independence from creation. It corrects any notion that the purpose of creating jinn and humankind to worship Him (as stated in the preceding verse) is for His benefit or need. God is not dependent on His creatures for sustenance, material support, or anything else—rather, it is creation that depends entirely on Him. This establishes the proper understanding of worship: it is not a transaction that benefits God, but an act that benefits the worshipper by aligning them with their purpose and with truth. The verse dismantles any anthropomorphic or transactional view of the divine, affirming that God, as the Creator and Sustainer of all things, stands in need of nothing, while everything stands in need of Him.

translation: Indeed, it is Allah who is the Provider, the Possessor of Power, the Steadfast (or: the Firm, the Mighty in strength).
interpretation: This verse establishes a foundational theological truth about divine self-sufficiency and sovereignty. By declaring Himself as 'ar-Razzaq' (the Provider), Allah affirms that all sustenance—physical, spiritual, and material—originates from Him alone, rendering creation utterly dependent upon Him while He depends on nothing. The pairing with 'dhul-quwwah al-matin' (Possessor of Power, the Steadfast) reinforces that this provision is not precarious or limited but backed by absolute, unshakable might. The term 'al-Matin' conveys firmness and inexhaustible strength, suggesting that Allah's capacity to provide and sustain never wanes or falters, unlike human resources which are finite and subject to depletion. This verse often appears in context addressing those who doubted or questioned divine power, serving as a corrective: it shifts the believer's reliance away from worldly means of sustenance—wealth, status, or human patrons—toward trust in God's inexhaustible capacity to provide for His creation. The rhetorical structure with 'inna' (indeed) and the emphatic 'huwa' (He, alone) underscores exclusivity, rejecting any partners or intermediaries in the act of providing. Theologically, this verse also connects to broader Qur'anic themes of tawakkul (reliance upon God) and the futility of seeking provision outside divine will, reminding believers that worldly striving must be coupled with spiritual trust in the One whose power and generosity are boundless and eternal.

translation: So indeed, for those who have done wrong is a portion [of punishment] like the portion of their companions [of old], so let them not impatiently urge Me.
interpretation: This verse addresses the disbelievers of Makkah who mocked the Prophet and demanded that punishment be hastened upon them. Allah warns that these wrongdoers will face a share of punishment similar to that which befell earlier nations who rejected their prophets—such as the peoples of Noah, 'Ad, Thamud, and others who were destroyed for their persistent disbelief and arrogance. The term 'dhanub' (share/portion) evokes the image of a bucket drawn from a well, suggesting that just as water is measured out in portions, so too is divine retribution apportioned according to a decreed measure and timing. The verse serves as both a warning and a reassurance: a warning that the same fate that befell previous deniers awaits these wrongdoers, and a reassurance to the Prophet and believers that they need not be anxious or urge Allah to hasten the punishment, for it will come at its appointed time according to divine wisdom, not according to human impatience or demand. This reflects a broader Quranic theme that divine justice operates on its own timetable, and that mockery or demands to 'hurry up' the punishment reveal a deeper spiritual blindness rather than courage, since the pattern of destruction for persistent rejection of truth is consistent throughout history.

translation: So woe to those who disbelieve, from their Day which they are promised.
interpretation: This verse is the culmination of an early Meccan surah (Adh-Dhariyat) that has been warning the deniers through reminders of past nations destroyed for their rejection of messengers—Noah's people, 'Ad, Thamud, Pharaoh. Having laid out this pattern of divine justice throughout history, the verse delivers a final pronouncement of doom upon those who persist in disbelief, specifically tying their ruin to 'their Day'—the Day of Judgment they have been warned about repeatedly yet continue to deny or mock. The phrase 'which they are promised' underscores the certainty of this appointed reckoning despite the disbelievers' scorn and impatience for it (as reflected elsewhere in the surah when they ask 'When is this Day of Judgment?'). The word 'woe' (wayl) is an Arabic expression denoting severe destruction, grief, or a specific valley in Hell according to some exegetes, intensifying the sense of impending catastrophe. The verse thus functions as both a warning and a vindication of the believers' patience, affirming that the deniers' fate is sealed and inescapable, arriving precisely as promised despite their denial of its reality.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. By the Mount,
interpretation: This opening invokes a solemn oath by Mount Sinai (al-Tur), the sacred site where Allah spoke to Prophet Musa (Moses) and where divine revelation was given. Swearing by this mountain emphasizes its sanctity as a place of divine communication and covenant. In the Qur'anic style, oaths by created things—stars, the sun, mountains, time—serve to draw attention to profound truths that follow, lending weight and solemnity to the message. The choice of Mount Sinai specifically connects this surah to the broader prophetic tradition, reminding listeners of the historical precedent of divine revelation and the seriousness of what is about to be declared: a discourse on the reality of divine judgment, the Hereafter, and the consequences of belief and disbelief. The oath sets a tone of gravity and certainty for the surah's themes concerning the Day of Judgment and Allah's power over creation.

translation: By the Book inscribed,
interpretation: This is part of an oath cluster at the opening of Surah At-Tur, where God swears by a sequence of sacred realities—Mount Sinai, a written Book, the inhabited House, the elevated canopy of heaven, and the swollen sea—to affirm the certainty of the coming punishment for the deniers of truth. 'A Book inscribed' refers most immediately to the divine scripture, understood by many commentators as either the Qur'an itself, the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz) upon which all decrees of destiny are recorded, or the scrolls of recompense in which every soul's deeds are written down. The phrase 'mastur' (inscribed, written out in orderly lines) emphasizes permanence, clarity, and deliberate record-keeping, as opposed to something vague or ephemeral. By swearing upon this written Book, God underscores that His revelation and His decree of reward and punishment are not matters of chance or forgetfulness but are fixed, documented, and binding. The oath thus prepares the listener for the forthcoming declaration that the punishment of the Lord is bound to fall, with nothing able to avert it, grounding this certainty in the image of a cosmic ledger already sealed and preserved.

translation: In parchment spread open.
interpretation: This phrase is part of a sequence of divine oaths at the opening of Surah At-Tur, where Allah swears by Mount Sinai, by a Book inscribed, and by this unrolled parchment. The 'raqq' refers to a scroll or parchment material used for writing, and 'manshur' means unrolled, unfolded, or spread out for reading. Classical exegetes have understood this as referring to the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz), the heavenly record containing divine decrees, or alternatively to scriptures revealed to humanity, including the Qur'an itself. The imagery of an unrolled scroll suggests openness and accessibility—knowledge or decree that is not hidden but laid bare for contemplation. By swearing upon such sacred and weighty things—a mountain associated with divine revelation, an inscribed book, and an open scroll—Allah emphasizes the certainty and seriousness of what follows in the surah, namely the warning about the Day of Judgment and its inevitable punishment for deniers. The oath formula itself is a rhetorical device common in Qur'anic discourse, drawing the listener's attention through solemn invocation before delivering a significant truth claim about resurrection, divine justice, and accountability.

translation: By the frequented House [al-Bayt al-Ma'mur]
interpretation: This phrase is part of an oath sequence at the opening of Surah At-Tur, where God swears by several sacred and cosmic things to emphasize the certainty of the truths that follow, particularly regarding the reality of divine punishment and judgment. 'Al-Bayt al-Ma'mur' (the frequented or constantly visited House) is traditionally understood by most commentators to refer to a celestial sanctuary directly above the Ka'bah in the heavens, perpetually visited and circumambulated by angels, just as the Ka'bah is visited by pilgrims on earth. Some scholars, drawing on hadith traditions including accounts from the Prophet's night journey (Isra and Mi'raj), describe it as a heavenly counterpart to the Ka'bah, visited daily by seventy thousand angels who never return to repeat the visit, symbolizing the inexhaustible multitude of God's creation and worship. Others have also connected it to the Ka'bah itself as a place of constant human devotion and visitation. By swearing on this frequented sanctuary, the verse underscores a cosmic order of worship that spans both heaven and earth, reinforcing the parallel between angelic devotion above and human devotion below, and establishing the sacredness and interconnectedness of creation as a witness to the truth of what God is about to declare.

translation: And by the raised canopy (roof)
interpretation: This phrase is part of a series of oaths at the beginning of Surah At-Tur, where Allah swears by various elements of creation to emphasize the certainty of the coming judgment and the truth of His message. 'The raised roof' is widely understood by commentators to refer to the sky or heaven, which serves as a canopy over the earth, held up without visible pillars. This oath draws attention to the magnificence and order of Allah's creation, inviting reflection on the One who sustains the heavens without support, as a sign of His power and a proof of His ability to resurrect the dead and fulfill His promises of reward and punishment. The grandeur of the sky, appearing as a vast ceiling above, serves as a humbling reminder of human smallness in comparison to the divine design, reinforcing the surah's themes of accountability and the reality of the Hereafter.

translation: And by the sea filled [with fire] / the swelling sea
interpretation: This verse is part of a series of solemn oaths at the beginning of Surah At-Tur, where God swears by various aspects of creation—Mount Sinai, a written scroll, the inhabited House (Ka'bah), the raised canopy (sky), and the sea—to affirm the certainty of the coming punishment for disbelievers and the truth of divine judgment. The phrase 'al-bahr al-masjoor' has been interpreted in multiple ways by classical exegetes: some understand it as the sea that will be set ablaze or turned into fire on the Day of Resurrection, drawing on the imagery in Surah At-Takwir (81:6) where 'the seas are made to boil over.' Others interpret 'masjoor' as referring to the sea being held back, restrained, or kept full and swollen, prevented by divine power from overflowing onto the land, which itself is seen as a sign of God's control over creation. Geologically and cosmologically, this oath draws attention to the sea's vastness, its mysterious depths, and its potential for transformation at the end of time, serving to remind humanity of the fragility of the natural order they take for granted and God's absolute power to alter it. The oath by the sea, like the other oaths in this passage, builds a rhetorical crescendo emphasizing that the punishment of the Lord is indeed coming and cannot be averted.

translation: Indeed, the punishment of your Lord is surely coming to pass.
interpretation: This verse, from Surah At-Tur, comes after a series of solemn oaths (by the Mount, by a Book inscribed, by the frequented House, by the raised-up roof, by the swollen sea) that serve as a dramatic preamble emphasizing the certainty of what follows. The declaration that the punishment of God is 'waqi' - literally 'falling' or 'occurring' - uses a grammatical form that conveys inevitability and imminence, as though the event is already in motion and cannot be averted. This verse functions as a divine oath-conclusion, asserting with absolute certainty that divine justice and reckoning will manifest. It serves as a warning to those who deny the Day of Judgment, affirming that despite any skepticism or delay, accountability before God is an inescapable reality woven into the fabric of existence itself, not contingent on human belief or disbelief.

translation: There is none who can avert it.
interpretation: This verse comes from Surah Al-Ma'arij, following the opening verses describing a questioner asking about an impending punishment destined for the disbelievers. This phrase emphasizes the absolute inevitability and certainty of God's decree—once a divine punishment or judgment has been ordained, no power, intercessor, or worldly force can turn it away or prevent its occurrence. It underscores God's complete sovereignty and the futility of human resistance against divine will, serving as a warning to those who doubt or mock the reality of the Day of Judgment and its consequences.

translation: On the Day when the heaven will shake and sway violently,
interpretation: This verse describes a sign of the Day of Judgment, depicting the cosmic upheaval that will mark the end of the world as we know it. The imagery of the sky 'swaying' or 'convulsing' conveys the total collapse of the natural order that humans take for granted—the heavens, normally fixed and stable, will be thrown into chaotic motion. This serves as a powerful warning to disbelievers who mock the concept of resurrection and judgment, emphasizing that the very fabric of the cosmos is subject to God's command and will be unraveled at His will. It underscores the theme found throughout this surah that the punishment awaiting deniers is certain and that the stability of the universe itself is contingent upon divine decree, not an inherent permanent feature. The verse invites reflection on human insignificance before such cosmic events and calls for recognition of God's absolute power over creation.

translation: And the mountains will move, a (severe) moving.
interpretation: This verse is part of the Quranic description of the cataclysmic events that will occur on the Day of Judgment, found in Surah At-Tur. The mountains, which are presented elsewhere in the Quran as symbols of permanence, stability, and immovability, will be set into motion and ultimately disintegrate. This serves as a powerful illustration of the complete upheaval of the natural order at the end of time, emphasizing that even the most fixed and solid elements of creation are entirely subject to God's will and will be transformed when He commands the Hour to begin. The imagery underscores the insignificance of worldly permanence compared to the absolute power of the Creator, and serves as a warning to disbelievers who doubt the reality of resurrection and judgment, reminding them that nothing in creation is truly permanent except God Himself.

translation: So woe, that Day, to the deniers!
interpretation: This verse is a recurring refrain in Surah Al-Mursalat, repeated after each description of divine signs, cosmic events, and the fate awaiting humanity on the Day of Judgment. The 'deniers' (al-mukadhdhibin) refers to those who reject the truth of revelation, the reality of resurrection, and the signs of God's power manifest in creation. The repetition serves a rhetorical and theological purpose: it functions almost like a drumbeat of warning, forcing the listener to confront, again and again, the consequences of disbelief after each proof is presented. By placing 'woe' (wayl) specifically 'that Day,' the verse emphasizes that the ultimate reckoning for denial is not immediate but deferred to the Day of Judgment, when the deniers will see the fulfillment of what they dismissed as falsehood. The verse thus serves as both a warning and a rhetorical challenge, inviting reflection on the natural and moral signs mentioned throughout the surah—such as the winds, the rain, the creation of humans, and the destruction of previous nations—as evidence that denial of God's power and justice is ultimately indefensible. It also creates a structural rhythm in the chapter, reinforcing memorization and contemplation, while underscoring the moral seriousness of rejecting faith despite clear evidence.

translation: Those who are engrossed in vain discourse, playing [heedlessly].
interpretation: This verse describes people who occupy themselves with idle talk, mockery, and frivolous argumentation concerning matters of ultimate significance—particularly the reality of the Hereafter, resurrection, and divine judgment—treating profound truths as subjects of amusement rather than serious reflection. The phrase captures a spiritual state of heedlessness (ghaflah) in which individuals deflect the weighty implications of faith through distraction, mockery, or intellectual game-playing, refusing to engage earnestly with the call to truth. It serves as a critique of those who, when confronted with warnings about accountability, respond with levity and dismissiveness rather than contemplation, highlighting the moral failure of trivializing what is of eternal consequence.

translation: The Day they will be thrust into the Fire of Hell with a violent thrust.
interpretation: This verse, from Surah At-Tur, depicts the terrifying scene of the Day of Judgment for the disbelievers and wrongdoers who denied the truth. The word 'yud'un' (are driven/thrust) conveys forceful, humiliating compulsion—unlike the believers who will be led to Paradise with honor and welcome, the deniers are violently pushed or dragged into Hellfire, stripped of any dignity or choice in the matter. This imagery underscores the total loss of control and power these individuals will experience, in stark contrast to the arrogance and free will they exercised in rejecting faith during their worldly lives. The harshness of being 'thrust' (da'an) emphasizes the inevitability and finality of divine justice, reinforcing the Quranic theme that mockery of ultimate accountability in this life leads to inescapable consequence in the next.

translation: This is the Fire which you used to deny.
interpretation: This verse depicts the moment of reckoning on the Day of Judgment when the deniers of Hellfire are confronted with the very reality they rejected during their worldly lives. The statement is delivered as a rebuke, emphasizing the irony and finality of their situation—what was once dismissed as myth, fabrication, or impossibility is now an undeniable, tangible experience. This reflects a broader Quranic theme: that disbelief in the unseen (ghayb), particularly in matters of resurrection and divine justice, does not negate their eventual reality. The verse serves as a warning to those who mock or reject eschatological truths, reminding them that denial in this life does not grant exemption from accountability in the next. It also underscores the justice of God, who allows people to witness directly the consequences of what they chose not to believe, removing all excuses on the Day of Judgment.

translation: Is this magic, or do you not see?
interpretation: This verse comes in Surah At-Tur, addressed rhetorically to the disbelievers on the Day of Judgment as they are confronted with the Hellfire they once denied. In worldly life, they had dismissed the Prophet's warnings and the Qur'an itself as mere 'sorcery' (sihr), a common accusation leveled against the Messenger by those who could not accept a supernatural origin for his message. Now, standing before the undeniable reality of divine punishment, they are mocked with their own former rhetoric: the very charge they used to deflect truth is thrown back at them. The question is double-edged—it exposes the absurdity of their past denial while affirming that what they now witness is not illusion or deception but plain, visible reality. It underscores a central Qur'anic theme: that disbelief is often not due to lack of evidence but to willful blindness, and that on the Day of Reckoning, all such rationalizations will collapse before the self-evident truth of divine justice.

translation: Burn therein; and whether you endure it patiently or do not endure it patiently, it is all the same for you. You are only being recompensed for what you used to do.
interpretation: This verse is addressed to the people of Hellfire, delivered as a decisive and final statement after judgment has been rendered. It conveys the utter finality and justice of divine recompense: unlike worldly trials where patience can sometimes mitigate suffering or lead to relief, in this context patience has no bearing on the outcome because the punishment is not a test but a consequence. The equal futility of patience or impatience underscores that the time for choice, repentance, and moral effort has passed entirely—what remains is pure consequence. The phrase 'you are only being recompensed for what you used to do' reinforces the Qur'anic principle of perfect justice: suffering here is not arbitrary or excessive, but precisely commensurate with one's own actions and choices made freely during worldly life.
