It serves as a sobering reminder that the opportunity for righteous action and patience exists only in this world, and that moral agency and its consequences are tied inseparably to the time before death and judgment.

translation: Indeed, the righteous will be amid gardens and bliss.
interpretation: This verse affirms the ultimate reward awaiting those who maintain taqwa—conscious God-fearing piety manifested through obedience, righteousness, and avoidance of sin. The 'gardens' (jannat) symbolize eternal paradise, while 'na'eem' refers to comprehensive bliss encompassing spiritual, sensory, and emotional fulfillment beyond worldly comprehension. The verse serves as both a promise and a motivation, contrasting the temporary struggles and self-restraint required of the pious in worldly life with the everlasting, unblemished joy that awaits them in the afterlife. It underscores the Quranic theme that true success is measured not by worldly gain but by one's relationship with God and adherence to righteousness, with the reward being proportionate to one's sincerity and devotion.

translation: Rejoicing in what their Lord has given them, and their Lord has protected them from the punishment of the blazing Fire.
interpretation: This verse describes the state of the righteous in Paradise, emphasizing two complementary blessings: positive enjoyment and negative protection. The word 'fakihin' (rejoicing/delighting) conveys not merely passive contentment but an active, joyful savoring of divine gifts—comparable to delighting in fine fruits, suggesting continuous pleasure without satiety or boredom. This joy is directly attributed to what their Lord 'gave them' (atahum), underscoring that paradise's pleasures are gifts of divine grace rather than earned wages in a transactional sense, even though they follow righteous deeds. The second clause shifts to divine protection from the 'adhab al-jahim' (punishment of the blazing Fire), reinforcing that true bliss in the Hereafter is twofold: the presence of everlasting pleasure and the absolute absence of fear or suffering. The repetition of 'their Lord' (rabbuhum) in both clauses emphasizes the personal, relational nature of this divine care—it is not an impersonal cosmic reward system but the direct, intimate favor of a Sustainer who both gives and shields. This juxtaposition of positive delight and negative deliverance encapsulates the completeness of salvation: it is not enough to escape punishment: felicity requires also to be given a surplus of good, just as it is not enough to possess a surplus of good; the heart cannot truly rest unless the shadow of punishment is removed entirely. The verse exemplifies Qur'anic eschatology's holistic view of recompense, where spiritual fulfillment is inseparable from psychological security.

translation: "Eat and drink in satisfaction for what you used to do."
interpretation: This verse depicts the words of welcome spoken to the righteous believers upon their entry into Paradise, often attributed to the angels or as a divine address. It represents the ultimate reward for a life of faith and good deeds, where previous struggles, sacrifices, and acts of obedience to God are now met with eternal ease, pleasure, and contentment. The phrase "bima kuntum ta'maloon" (for what you used to do) establishes a direct causal link between one's earthly actions and the heavenly reward received, emphasizing the Islamic principle of divine justice and recompense. It is not merely a reward of idle pleasure, but one earned and deserved, affirming that the enjoyment in Paradise is the fruit of righteous striving, patience, and sincerity in worship during worldly life. The invitation to "eat and drink" also evokes a sense of complete security and abundance, signifying that in the Hereafter, the believer is free from all previous hardships, anxieties about sustenance, or fear of loss—everything is now given in pure, wholesome enjoyment (hanee'an), without any negative consequence or impurity.

translation: Reclining on couches arranged in rows, and We shall marry them to fair ones (houris) with wide, beautiful eyes.
interpretation: This verse is part of the Qur'anic depiction of the rewards awaiting the righteous in Paradise. The imagery of reclining on arranged couches conveys a state of perfect ease, honor, and leisure, free from the toil, anxiety, and discomfort of worldly life. The 'couches arranged in rows' also suggests companionship and social harmony among the blessed, as they are positioned together rather than isolated. The pairing with 'hur al-'ayn' (translated as fair, wide-eyed companions) symbolizes the fulfillment of desire and the granting of pure, idealized companionship as part of the complete happiness of Paradise. Classical exegetes understand this imagery as both literal and symbolic—literal in describing actual rewards promised to believers, and symbolic in representing the totality of comfort, beauty, and relational fulfillment that contrasts with the trials and deprivations of earthly existence. The verse functions within a larger passage enumerating the delights of Paradise to motivate righteous action and patient endurance in this world, reassuring believers that ultimate justice and reward belong to God, who compensates the faithful with blessings beyond human imagination.

translation: And those who believed and whose descendants followed them in faith - We joined with them their descendants, and We did not deprive them of anything of their deeds. Every person, for what he earned, is retained (in pledge).
interpretation: This verse establishes a principle of divine mercy and justice regarding family bonds in Paradise. It teaches that when the descendants of believers follow them in faith, even if their deeds or spiritual station are lesser, God elevates them to be reunited with their righteous forebears in the hereafter, preserving family ties as a mark of grace. Importantly, this elevation does not come at the expense of the original believers' rewards - nothing is diminished from their own earned deeds to make up for this gift to their offspring. The verse thus balances two principles: the comfort of family unity in the afterlife as a divine favor, and the inviolable principle of individual accountability, where every soul remains responsible for and bound by its own actions, unable to transfer the burden or benefit of deeds to another. The pairing of these ideas suggests that while God's mercy can bridge gaps in spiritual attainment within families through faith as the connecting thread, this mercy operates as pure grace added atop justice, not as a replacement for the fundamental law that each soul is held in pledge for what it has earned.

translation: And We shall provide them with fruit and meat, whatever they desire.
interpretation: This verse is part of a passage in Surah At-Tur describing the rewards awaiting the righteous believers in Paradise. It emphasizes the generosity and abundance of divine provision, where the inhabitants of Paradise are not merely given sustenance out of necessity, but are granted whatever delicacies—fruits and meats—they desire, highlighting a state of complete satisfaction and ease. This stands in contrast to worldly life, where desires are often limited by scarcity, effort, or circumstance. The verse underscores a core Qur'anic theme: that the ultimate reward for faith and righteous deeds is a state of limitless comfort, pleasure, and fulfillment granted by God's mercy, where believers experience abundance and ease as a reflection of divine favor rather than their own labor.

translation: They will pass among themselves a cup [of wine] wherein there is no idle talk and no sin.
interpretation: This verse describes a scene of the people of Paradise enjoying each other's company while sharing drink from a cup. Unlike intoxicating drink in worldly life, which leads to foolish speech, quarrels, and sinful behavior, this heavenly drink is purified of all such negative consequences. The verse emphasizes that the pleasures of Paradise are perfected and free from the flaws that accompany similar pleasures in this world—there is no drunkenness that leads to vain talk, no cause for sin, and no regret. It reflects the Quranic theme that the rewards of the righteous in the afterlife are elevated beyond worldly limitations, offering pure companionship and joy without the moral or social harms associated with earthly indulgence.

translation: And there will circulate among them (servant) youths [especially] for them, as if they were pearls well-protected.
interpretation: This verse is part of a longer passage in Surah At-Tur describing the delights and comforts awaiting the righteous in Paradise. The imagery depicts eternal youths who serve the inhabitants of Paradise, attending to their needs with grace and beauty. The comparison to 'well-protected pearls' evokes qualities of purity, radiance, and preciousness—pearls hidden within shells are shielded from tarnish, dust, or corruption, remaining flawless and luminous. This simile suggests that these attendants possess an untouched, pristine beauty, free from any blemish or impurity, reflecting the perfected and idealized nature of everything in Paradise. The verse contributes to the broader Quranic portrayal of the afterlife as a realm where believers are surrounded by beauty, comfort, and service, free from the hardships and imperfections of worldly life, as a reward for their faith and righteous deeds.

translation: And they turned to one another, questioning each other.
interpretation: This verse depicts a scene of mutual reflection and dialogue among the people of Paradise, who turn to one another to recount and discuss their past lives, especially their experiences of faith and the trials they endured in the worldly life. This mutual questioning serves to highlight their shared gratitude for having been saved from the Fire and granted eternal bliss, and it emphasizes the communal and social nature of the reward in the Hereafter, where believers share in joy and reminisce together about Allah's mercy upon them.

translation: They will say, 'Indeed, before this, we were among our families fearful [of Allah's punishment].'
interpretation: This verse is part of a conversation among the people of Paradise, who reflect back on their worldly lives to explain the cause of their salvation. They attribute their ultimate success not to their good deeds alone, but to the inner state of piety that produced those deeds: a persistent, humble fear of Allah while they lived among their families in the world. This 'ishfaq' (apprehensive concern) was not paralyzing anxiety but a vigilant awareness of accountability that kept them from heedlessness and sin, even amid the comforts and distractions of family life. The verse highlights that true taqwa (God-consciousness) is cultivated in the private, everyday sphere of one's household—not only in public religious observance—and that this quiet, sustained reverence is what Allah rewards with eternal security and peace in the Hereafter, as contrasted with the torment of those who lived heedlessly.

translation: But Allah has favored us and protected us from the punishment of the scorching fire (As-Samum).
interpretation: This verse is part of a dialogue among the people of Paradise as they recount their earthly lives and reflect upon the mercy that delivered them from damnation. It conveys a profound sense of gratitude and humility, acknowledging that their salvation was not earned through their own merit alone but was a gift and favor bestowed by Allah. The phrase 'As-Samum' refers to the intensely scorching wind or fire of Hell, emphasizing the severity of the punishment from which they were spared. This passage underscores the Islamic theological principle that entry into Paradise is ultimately an act of divine grace, even for those who performed righteous deeds and maintained piety during their worldly lives. It also serves as a reminder to believers of the preciousness of divine protection from punishment, encouraging continual gratitude and reliance on Allah's mercy rather than complacency or self-righteousness regarding one's deeds.

translation: Indeed, we used to call upon Him before. Verily, He is the Most Kind, the Most Merciful.
interpretation: This verse comes from Surah At-Tur, where the people of Paradise recall their earthly life and testify that their prior devotion—their supplication, worship, and reliance upon God before death—was the very reason for the divine mercy and favor now bestowed upon them. It establishes a causal link between sincere faith and righteous conduct in this world and the ultimate reward in the Hereafter, affirming that God's nature as 'Al-Barr' (the Most Kind, the Source of all goodness) and 'Ar-Rahim' (the Most Merciful) is not arbitrary but responsive to the devotion of His servants. The verse underscores a theological principle central to Islamic belief: that God's mercy, while vast and freely given, is especially manifest toward those who maintain a continuous relationship of worship and supplication with Him throughout their lives, and that this relationship is itself a form of preparation for the ultimate encounter with His grace in the afterlife.

translation: So remind [O Muhammad], for you are not, by the grace of your Lord, a soothsayer or a madman.
interpretation: This verse addresses the Prophet Muhammad directly in response to accusations made against him by his opponents in Mecca, who tried to discredit his message by labeling him either a 'kahin' (a soothsayer or fortune-teller, associated with jinn-inspired pronouncements and rhymed utterances) or 'majnun' (one possessed or insane). The verse serves a dual purpose: first, it commands the Prophet to continue his mission of reminding and admonishing people despite the hostility he faces; second, it firmly refutes these slanderous labels by grounding his sanity and legitimacy in divine favor ('ni'mat Rabbika' - the grace/blessing of your Lord). The mention of 'your Lord's grace' is significant—it implies that prophethood itself is a blessing bestowed by God, and that the clarity, wisdom, and moral integrity the Prophet displayed are evidence against the charges of madness or soothsaying. Soothsayers were known for ambiguous, often deceptive utterances tied to pre-Islamic divination practices, while madness implied loss of rational faculty. By contrast, the Quran positions prophetic revelation as the opposite: clear, coherent, morally purposeful guidance. This verse thus reassures the Prophet of his legitimacy and steels him against the psychological toll of public ridicule, while also implicitly challenging the audience to reconsider their baseless accusations in light of the evident wisdom of his character and message.

translation: Or do they say, 'A poet, for whom we await a misfortune of time (i.e., death)'?
interpretation: This verse addresses the accusations made by disbelievers against the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him), who dismissed him as merely a poet while waiting for calamity or death to befall him so his message would end. The verse reflects the pattern of rejection faced by prophets, where opponents resort to labeling divine revelation as mere poetry—a common literary form they understood—rather than accepting it as genuine revelation from God. Their hope that time and death would silence him reveals their desperation and lack of substantive arguments against the truth he presented. This sets up the rhetorical response in subsequent verses, where God challenges them to produce anything comparable if they truly believe their claims, exposing their accusations as baseless and born of hostility rather than reasoned objection.

translation: Say: Wait, for indeed I am, with you, among those who wait.
interpretation: This verse reflects a posture of calm defiance and trust in divine justice that the Prophet is commanded to adopt toward those who oppose or mock his message. Rather than responding to hostility with anger or anxious argument, he is instructed to tell the disbelievers to 'wait and see'—implying that the outcome of this conflict between truth and falsehood will inevitably be revealed with time. By adding that he himself is 'among those who wait,' the Prophet signals that he shares in this patient anticipation, confident that Allah's promise of vindication for the believers and reckoning for the deniers will come to pass. It is not a threat spoken in weakness, but an assured statement rooted in certainty of God's plan, teaching believers to respond to taunts and challenges with steadfastness rather than haste, trusting that time itself will prove where truth lies.

translation: Or do their minds command them to this? Or are they a transgressing people?
interpretation: This verse is part of a rhetorical challenge directed at those who accused the Prophet Muhammad of fabricating the Qur'an or being a poet/soothsayer. God poses a series of probing questions (preceding and following this verse) to expose the irrationality of their rejection. Here, the question asks whether their own reasoning faculties (ahlam, meaning intellects or mature judgment) could possibly lead them to such baseless accusations, implying that no sound mind would arrive at such conclusions. The second half of the verse offers an alternative explanation: perhaps their rejection stems not from intellectual reasoning at all, but from being a people characterized by tughyan—transgression, arrogance, and rebellion against truth. The verse thus frames their disbelief as either a failure of reason or a moral failing of pride and obstinacy, suggesting that genuine, unbiased contemplation would lead to acceptance of the message, and that their resistance is therefore rooted in willful arrogance rather than legitimate intellectual doubt.

translation: Or do they say, 'He has invented it [the Qur'an]'? Nay, but they do not believe.
interpretation: This verse addresses the disbelievers' accusation that the Prophet Muhammad fabricated the Qur'an himself rather than receiving it through divine revelation. God refutes this claim not merely by denying the accusation, but by exposing its true motive: the real issue is not genuine doubt about the Qur'an's authorship, but a fundamental refusal to believe. The verse suggests that the charge of fabrication is merely a pretext or excuse used by the disbelievers to avoid confronting the truth of the message. Their rejection stems from stubbornness, arrogance, or unwillingness to submit to the implications of faith, rather than from any legitimate intellectual concern about the Qur'an's origin. This is reinforced by the preceding verses in the passage, which challenge the disbelievers to produce something comparable to the Qur'an if they truly believe it to be a human creation—a challenge they cannot meet, further exposing the hollowness of their claim and confirming that their disbelief is willful rather than reasoned.

translation: Then let them produce a statement like it, if they should be truthful.
interpretation: This verse is part of a rhetorical challenge posed to those who doubted the divine origin of the Qur'an, questioning whether it was merely the fabrication of Muhammad. God, through this challenge, dares the skeptics to produce something comparable to the Qur'an in its eloquence, wisdom, and spiritual depth if they truly believe it is a human creation. The inability of anyone to meet this challenge throughout history is presented by Muslims as evidence of the Qur'an's miraculous nature and divine origin. This challenge reflects a broader theme in the Qur'an of inviting critical engagement while asserting its unique inimitability (i'jaz al-Qur'an), reinforcing the claim that no human discourse can match its linguistic and spiritual power.

translation: Or were they created out of nothing, or were they themselves the creators?
interpretation: This verse poses a rhetorical argument directed at those who deny God and reject the truth of revelation. It presents a logical dilemma with only impossible alternatives: either human beings came into existence without any cause or creator whatsoever, or they created themselves. Both possibilities are absurd upon reflection, since nothing can bring itself into being from nothing, and nothing can be the cause of its own existence before it exists. By exposing the irrationality of these alternatives, the verse compels the listener to accept the only remaining and reasonable conclusion: that there must be a Creator who brought them into existence. This is part of a broader Quranic method of using reason and logical argumentation to point toward the necessity of God's existence, challenging disbelievers to examine the origins of their own being rather than dismissing the signs of creation around them. The verse serves as an invitation to contemplation on one's own existence as evidence of a deliberate, purposeful act of creation by God, rather than being products of chance or self-origination.

translation: Or did they create the heavens and the earth? Rather, they are not certain.
interpretation: This verse is part of a rhetorical sequence in Surah At-Tur challenging the disbelievers who reject the Prophet and the truth of revelation without offering any coherent alternative explanation for their own existence or the origin of the universe. The verse poses a direct logical challenge: since the deniers did not create the heavens and the earth themselves, they have no grounds to claim authority over ultimate truths or to dismiss the message of the Qur'an through mere speculation. The phrase 'rather, they are not certain' exposes the real basis of their rejection—not reasoned conviction or evidence, but doubt, whimsy, and intellectual laziness. It implies that true certainty (yaqeen) can only come from acknowledging the Creator's sovereignty over creation, and that their skepticism toward revelation stems from a deeper uncertainty about fundamental realities, including their own origins and the nature of existence itself. The verse thus turns the burden of proof back onto the skeptics, suggesting that denial without a coherent cosmological or epistemological foundation is intellectually unstable and self-contradictory.

translation: Or do they possess the treasuries of your Lord? Or are they the ones in control?
interpretation: This verse is part of a sequence of rhetorical questions in Surah At-Tur directed at the disbelievers who arrogantly reject the Prophet's message and claim authority to judge matters of revelation and sustenance without any real basis. The verse exposes the absurdity of their position by asking whether they possess the treasuries of Allah's mercy, provision, and knowledge, or whether they hold dominion and control over the affairs of creation. Since neither is true, the implicit answer is a decisive no, demonstrating that their objections and arrogant claims to authority are baseless. The treasuries of the Lord refer to His infinite power over sustenance, guidance, and decree, which belongs to Him alone. The verse thus serves to humble human pretensions to ultimate control, reminding the listener that true sovereignty and the dispensation of blessings rest solely with Allah, not with any created being who merely objects to or doubts divine revelation.

translation: Or do they have a ladder [to the heavens] by means of which they listen? Then let their listener produce a clear authority.
interpretation: This verse is a rhetorical challenge directed at the disbelievers who claimed knowledge of the unseen or who rejected revelation without basis. It mocks the idea that they could have any means of ascending to the heavens to eavesdrop on divine decrees or angelic knowledge, as was sometimes claimed by soothsayers and polytheists who asserted access to hidden truths. By asking whether they possess a 'ladder' to the heavens, the Qur'an exposes the absurdity of their claims to authority over matters of the unseen, such as denying prophethood, resurrection, or divine revelation. The demand that their 'listener' bring forth 'clear proof' underscores the Qur'anic principle that all claims—especially those made in opposition to revealed truth—must be substantiated with real evidence, not mere assertion or fabricated spiritual authority. It is part of a series of challenges in this passage that dismantle the baseless premises underlying the disbelievers' rejection of the Prophet's message, showing that their denial rests on arrogance and invention rather than genuine knowledge or legitimate authority.

translation: Or has He daughters while you have sons?
interpretation: This verse is a rhetorical question exposing the irrationality and hypocrisy of the pagan Arabs who claimed that angels were 'daughters of Allah,' while simultaneously holding daughters in low esteem in their own society—even practicing female infanticide out of shame—and preferring sons for themselves. The verse highlights the absurdity of attributing to God something they themselves considered undesirable or inferior, while reserving for themselves what they valued most. It underscores a broader Quranic argument against the illogical and self-serving nature of their theological claims, pointing out that they fashioned beliefs about the divine based on their own cultural biases rather than genuine revelation or sound reasoning. The verse serves as part of a larger passage (Surah At-Tur) that systematically dismantles the polytheistic beliefs of the Meccans by appealing to logic and consistency.

translation: Or do you [O Muhammad] ask them for payment, so they are burdened by debt?
interpretation: This verse is a rhetorical question posed to the Prophet Muhammad, used to refute any possible justification the disbelievers might have for rejecting his message. God is reassuring the Prophet and highlighting the unreasonableness of the disbelievers' rejection by pointing out that he does not ask them for any worldly compensation, wage, or payment in exchange for delivering the message of Islam. Since he seeks no financial reward that would burden them with debt, there is no legitimate worldly excuse for their refusal to accept the truth. The underlying message is that the disbelievers' rejection stems not from any reasonable grievance but from their own arrogance, stubbornness, and spiritual blindness. This verse is part of a series of rhetorical questions in this passage of Surah Al-Qalam that collectively dismantle the excuses of those who reject the Prophet's message, emphasizing that the call to faith is purely for the benefit of humanity and carries no hidden agenda of material gain for the one delivering it.

translation: Or do they have [knowledge of] the unseen, so they write it down?
interpretation: This verse is part of a series of rhetorical questions in Surah Al-Qalam directed at those who rejected the Prophet Muhammad's message and mocked him. The verse challenges the disbelievers' arrogance in rejecting divine revelation and making judgments about matters beyond human knowledge. It implies that they have no access to the unseen (al-ghayb)—no divine knowledge, no record from God, no legitimate basis—to support their claims, denials, or predictions about the Prophet's fate or the truth of his message. The rhetorical question exposes the baselessness of their position: since they cannot claim to possess hidden knowledge that they have written down as a source of authority, their opposition to the Qur'an and the Prophet is shown to be mere conjecture, arrogance, and stubbornness rather than reasoned conviction. This serves to reinforce that true knowledge of the unseen belongs to God alone, and human beings who reject revelation without legitimate knowledge are acting out of pride rather than true understanding.

translation: Or do they intend a plot? But it is those who disbelieve who are the ones ensnared [by their own plot].
interpretation: This verse addresses the disbelievers among the Quraysh who schemed against the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) and plotted to undermine his message. The rhetorical question exposes the futility of their scheming: whatever plans they devise against the truth will ultimately backfire upon themselves. God's decree and support for His Messenger cannot be overturned by human conspiracy. The verse reflects a broader Qur'anic theme that those who plot against divine truth and righteousness are, in reality, trapping themselves in a snare of their own making. Their cunning becomes the very instrument of their downfall, either in this world through exposure and defeat, or in the Hereafter through divine punishment. This serves as a reassurance to believers that no matter how elaborate the schemes of their opponents, ultimate victory belongs to truth, and those who conspire against it will find their efforts turned back upon them.

translation: Or do they have a god other than Allah? Exalted is Allah above whatever they associate with Him [in worship].
interpretation: This verse is a rhetorical challenge directed at the disbelievers who deny the Oneness of Allah and attribute partners to Him. By posing the question 'Or do they have a god other than Allah?', the verse exposes the absurdity and baselessness of polytheism, since no other deity possesses the power to create, sustain, or control the universe as Allah does. The question format is meant to silence any claim to the contrary, as there is no rational or evidential basis for believing in another god. The verse then immediately follows with a declaration of Allah's transcendence—'Exalted is Allah above what they associate with Him'—which serves both as a theological correction and an act of worship in itself (tasbih). This declaration emphasizes that Allah is utterly free from any partners, equals, or deficiencies that the polytheists falsely ascribe to Him. The juxtaposition of the rhetorical question with the affirmation of Allah's purity underscores the Qur'an's central message of tawhid (the oneness of God), reminding believers that true worship and reliance must be directed to Allah alone, who is beyond comparison or association with any created being or false deity.

translation: And if they were to see a fragment from the sky falling, they would say, 'Piled-up clouds.'
interpretation: This verse illustrates the depth of denial and stubborn disbelief among those who reject the truth. Even if confronted with an extraordinary, undeniable sign—such as a piece of the sky literally falling—the disbelievers would still seek a mundane, rationalized explanation rather than accept it as a divine sign or warning of punishment. This reflects a psychological pattern where the mind refuses to acknowledge what contradicts its preconceived worldview, no matter how compelling the evidence. The verse underscores a broader Quranic theme that disbelief is often not due to lack of evidence but due to willful rejection and self-deception, as people rationalize away even the clearest signs to maintain their denial.

translation: So leave them until they meet their Day in which they will be struck with terror (thunderstruck/swoon).
interpretation: This verse instructs the Prophet (peace be upon him) to disengage from futile argument with the disbelievers who persistently reject the truth despite clear signs. Rather than continuing to contend with them, he is told to leave them to their fate, deferring judgment to the appointed Day—understood as the Day of Resurrection or a moment of sudden calamity—when they will be overcome with terror and shock as divine reality becomes undeniable. The verse conveys a tone of divine patience coupled with certainty of eventual reckoning: human defiance and denial are temporary, and a decisive moment of truth awaits in which falsehood collapses and the deniers face the consequence of their disbelief. It serves as both a consolation to the believers, affirming that justice will ultimately prevail, and a warning to the obstinate that their current arrogance will give way to helplessness and dread when confronted with the undeniable truth of divine judgment.

translation: The Day when their scheming will not avail them at all, nor will they be helped.
interpretation: This verse refers to the Day of Judgment, describing the utter helplessness of the disbelievers who had plotted and schemed against the truth and against the believers during their worldly lives. All their cunning strategies, deceptions, and conspiracies—whatever power or cleverness they relied upon—will prove completely useless when they face divine reckoning. The verse emphasizes that on that Day, no worldly tactic, alliance, or scheme can shield a person from accountability, and no one will come to their aid or rescue them from the consequences of their disbelief and wrongdoing. This serves as a warning that ultimate power and protection belong to God alone, and human schemes against truth are futile in the face of divine justice.

translation: And indeed, for those who have wronged, there is a punishment before that, but most of them do not know.
interpretation: This verse refers to the wrongdoers—those who persisted in disbelief and injustice—and affirms that beyond whatever suffering they may experience in this worldly life, there awaits a further, more severe punishment in the Hereafter, distinct from any worldly trials or even from the preliminary torments of the grave. The phrase 'before that' (دون ذلك) indicates a punishment that precedes or is separate from the ultimate chastisement already described in the preceding verses concerning the Day of Judgment, suggesting layers of consequence for wrongdoing. The closing statement that 'most of them do not know' underscores a central Quranic theme: human heedlessness and the failure to truly grasp or believe in the unseen consequences of one's actions. This ignorance is not merely intellectual but reflects a deeper spiritual blindness—a refusal to reflect on the signs of accountability that surround them. The verse thus serves as both a warning and an indictment, highlighting that the wrongdoers' suffering is not limited to a single moment of reckoning but is multifaceted, while their lack of awareness perpetuates their heedless pursuit of injustice, making the eventual reckoning all the more severe when it finally dawns on them.

translation: And be patient for the judgment of your Lord, for indeed, you are before Our Eyes. And glorify the praise of your Lord when you arise.
interpretation: This verse addresses the Prophet Muhammad directly, offering him comfort and reassurance during a period of hardship, rejection, and mockery from his opponents in Mecca. The command to 'be patient' (isbir) is not passive resignation but an active, steadfast endurance while awaiting God's judgment and vindication against those who deny him. The phrase 'you are in Our eyes' (bi-a'yunina) is a profound expression of divine protection and intimate care—it conveys that the Prophet is under God's constant watch, guard, and support, never abandoned despite appearances of isolation or struggle. This divine surveillance implies both protection from harm and validation of his mission. The subsequent command to glorify God with praise 'when you arise' links patience with worship, suggesting that remembrance of God, particularly upon waking or standing (possibly referring to rising for prayer, including the night vigil), is the spiritual practice that sustains one through trials. The verse thus establishes a rhythm between enduring hardship and turning to worship as the means of strength, reminding believers that divine attention and support accompany those who remain patient and devoted, even when human eyes fail to see or validate their struggle.

translation: And during a part of the night, exalt Him [glorify Him in prayer], and after [or during] the setting/retreat of the stars.
interpretation: This verse instructs the Prophet (and by extension, believers) to engage in acts of worship—particularly glorification and prayer—during specific times of the night, especially in the period just before dawn when the stars begin to fade and recede from view. This 'idbar an-nujum' (retreat of the stars) is often understood to refer to the pre-dawn hours, a time traditionally associated with the Fajr prayer and with heightened spiritual receptivity, when the world is quiet and the believer's devotion is less distracted by worldly affairs. The verse emphasizes the continuous nature of worship, encouraging remembrance of God not only during the day but also through the night and into the transition toward morning, reflecting a rhythm of devotion that mirrors the natural cycles of the cosmos—the night, the stars, and the coming of dawn—as signs of God's order and a call to align one's spiritual life with this divine pattern.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. By the star when it descends (or sets/falls).
interpretation: This opening oath invokes the star at the moment of its setting or falling as a solemn witness, establishing the truthfulness and weight of what follows in the surah—namely, the defense of the Prophet's character and the authenticity of his revelation. The choice of a celestial body in its descent is significant: just as the star follows a precise, divinely ordained course and does not fall in error or randomness, so too the Prophet's words and visions (described in the following verses) are not the product of misguidance, whim, or personal desire, but are guided communications from a higher source. The imagery also evokes awe and cosmic grandeur, situating human revelation within the vast order of the universe, and suggests that just as the star's trajectory is fixed and purposeful despite appearing to 'fall,' the Prophet's experience of revelation—however it may be questioned by skeptics—follows a true and intentional path from Allah.

translation: Your companion [Muhammad] has not strayed, nor has he erred.
interpretation: This verse, from the opening of Surah An-Najm, is a divine defense of Prophet Muhammad's integrity and spiritual soundness, directly refuting the accusations of the Meccan disbelievers who claimed he was misguided, deluded, or possessed. The word 'dalla' (strayed) refers to deviation from the right path through ignorance or loss of direction, while 'ghawa' (erred) refers to deliberate deviation into falsehood or misguided desire. By negating both terms, God affirms that the Prophet's guidance is neither the result of confusion nor of succumbing to base desires—his message and conduct are firmly rooted in truth. This sets the stage for the following verses, which clarify that his speech is not from personal whim but divine revelation, establishing the authenticity and divine origin of his prophethood.

translation: Nor does he speak out of [his own] desire.
interpretation: This verse refers to Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) and affirms that his speech concerning divine revelation is not derived from personal whims, inclinations, or self-interest. It establishes the divine source and authority of his prophetic utterances, particularly the Qur'an, distinguishing them from ordinary human speech that might be influenced by desire, bias, or subjective motives. The verse serves as a foundational assertion of the authenticity and reliability of revelation, emphasizing that what the Prophet conveys as scripture or guidance originates from God rather than from his own imagination or wishes, thereby validating his role as a trustworthy conduit of divine message.

translation: It is not but a revelation revealed.
interpretation: This verse is part of a sequence in Surah An-Najm that defends the Prophet Muhammad against accusations that he was speaking from personal desire, error, or misguidance when he conveyed the Quran. The verse affirms that his speech concerning the divine message is not fabricated or self-generated but is directly communicated to him by Allah through revelation (wahy). This establishes the doctrine of prophetic infallibility in conveying scripture, distinguishing the Prophet's role as a mere conduit for divine communication rather than an originator of the message. It underscores the broader Quranic theme of the transcendence and divine origin of the text itself, countering contemporary Meccan skeptics who claimed the Prophet was either possessed, a poet, or speaking from his own imagination.

translation: He was taught by one mighty in power,
interpretation: This verse refers to the Angel Gabriel (Jibril), described as 'mighty in power,' who brought the divine revelation to Prophet Muhammad. It emphasizes that the Quran was not a product of the Prophet's own invention or poetic imagination, but was conveyed to him through a powerful, divinely appointed intermediary. The phrase underscores the majesty and strength of the angelic being entrusted with this sacred task, affirming the authenticity and divine origin of the revelation while also highlighting the awesome nature of the unseen world and its inhabitants who serve as messengers between God and humanity.

translation: One of soundness (and power), then he rose/stood in his true form.
interpretation: This verse is part of a sequence in Surah An-Najm describing the Prophet Muhammad's encounter with Angel Jibril (Gabriel) in his actual celestial form, rather than the human guise in which he usually appeared. 'Dhu mirrah' describes Jibril as possessing great strength, soundness, and majestic power—emphasizing his formidable angelic nature. 'Fastawa' indicates that he then rose up, stood firm, or settled into his true, awesome form on the horizon, filling the sky. This moment is presented as evidence countering accusations that the Prophet was deluded or that his revelations were mere fancy; rather, it affirms that he witnessed a real, overwhelming spiritual encounter with a being of immense power, underscoring the authenticity and majesty of the revelation being delivered to him.

translation: While he was in the highest horizon.
interpretation: This verse is part of the Qur'anic account in Surah An-Najm describing the Prophet Muhammad's encounter with the angel Gabriel (Jibril) in his true, majestic form. The 'highest horizon' refers to the celestial position where Gabriel appeared, emphasizing the grandeur and vastness of this heavenly being who filled the horizon with his form. This description serves to validate the authenticity of the revelation the Prophet received, countering accusations from skeptics that he was deluded or that the Qur'an was merely his own invention. By affirming that he witnessed this celestial sight with clarity, the verse establishes the divine and transcendent origin of the message being conveyed, situating the Prophet's experience within a tradition of genuine prophetic encounters with the angelic realm.

translation: Then he drew near and came closer,
interpretation: This verse is part of the Qur'anic description in Surah An-Najm of the Prophet Muhammad's (peace be upon him) encounter with the angel Gabriel in his true form, an event associated with the beginning of revelation and, according to many commentators, also connected to the night journey and ascension (Isra and Mi'raj). The phrase describes a progressive, intimate nearness—first a general approach ('dana') followed by an even closer drawing near ('tadalla')—emphasizing the extraordinary proximity achieved between the Prophet and the divine messenger. Scholars have debated whether this nearness refers to Gabriel approaching Muhammad or, in mystical interpretations, to the Prophet's spiritual closeness to God Himself during this transcendent experience. The doubling of verbs conveying approach underscores the unparalleled intimacy and sacredness of this moment of revelation, suggesting a closeness that transcends ordinary human experience and signifies the unique spiritual rank of the Prophet.

translation: So he was at a distance of two bow-lengths or even closer.
interpretation: This verse describes the extraordinary closeness achieved during the Prophet Muhammad's (peace be upon him) ascension (Mi'raj), when he drew near to the divine presence in a manner beyond ordinary human experience. The imagery of 'two bow-lengths or even closer' employs a measurement familiar to the Arabs—the distance between the archer's hand holding the bow and the hand pulling the string—to convey an extreme and intimate proximity. This expression signifies not a physical spatial distance in the literal sense, but rather the unparalleled spiritual nearness and honor granted to the Prophet, emphasizing the unique and exalted nature of this encounter that transcends ordinary human-divine interaction. Scholars have debated whether this nearness refers to the Prophet's proximity to Allah directly or to the angel Gabriel in his true form, with the majority of classical exegetes leaning toward interpretations that preserve Allah's transcendence while affirming the magnitude of this singular spiritual experience granted to the Prophet during one of the most significant events in Islamic sacred history.

translation: So He revealed to His servant what He revealed.
interpretation: This verse refers to the revelation given by Allah to Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) during his miraculous encounter with the angel Gabriel (Jibreel), as described in the opening verses of Surah An-Najm. The phrasing is deliberately indirect and mysterious—'what He revealed' is left unspecified—conveying the sacredness, intimacy, and ineffable nature of this divine communication. This rhetorical technique emphasizes that the content and experience of this revelation transcends ordinary human language and understanding, reserved for the Prophet alone in that moment. It underscores the special, elevated status of Muhammad as 'His servant' ('abdihi), a term of honor denoting humility and closeness to Allah simultaneously. The verse affirms the authenticity and divine origin of the Prophet's visionary experience, countering accusations from skeptics that his revelations were mere imagination or deception, and situates this encounter within a broader Quranic narrative asserting the reality of prophetic revelation as a direct, unmediated communication from the Divine.

translation: The heart did not lie about what it saw.
interpretation: This verse, from Surah An-Najm, refers to the Prophet Muhammad's visionary experience—traditionally understood as his encounter with the Angel Gabriel in his true form, or his vision during the Night Journey (Isra and Mi'raj). The verse serves as a divine affirmation of the authenticity and truthfulness of this spiritual experience, countering any doubts raised by skeptics among the Quraysh who questioned the Prophet's claims. By stating that his 'heart'—understood here as the seat of perception, inner vision, and spiritual consciousness—did not distort, fabricate, or misrepresent what it witnessed, the verse establishes that the Prophet's inner faculties faithfully and accurately registered a genuine supernatural experience. This is not merely about physical eyesight but about the integrity of the Prophet's entire being as a trustworthy recipient of divine revelation. The verse thus functions as a broader statement on the reliability of prophetic experience: true spiritual perception, when it comes through a purified and sincere heart, is not subject to illusion, hallucination, or deceit. It underscores the Quranic theme that the Prophet was neither insane nor lying, but was granted authentic access to realities beyond ordinary human perception, and his faculties correctly transmitted what he witnessed without corruption or exaggeration.

translation: So do you dispute with him concerning what he saw?
interpretation: This verse addresses the disbelievers of Mecca who doubted and argued with Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) about his vision, understood to refer to his sighting of the Angel Gabriel in his true, majestic form, as described in the preceding verses of Surah An-Najm. The rhetorical question serves as a rebuke to those who questioned the authenticity of the Prophet's direct spiritual experience, emphasizing that what he witnessed was not a product of imagination or deception but a genuine encounter affirmed by divine revelation. The verse underscores the theme of the Prophet's truthfulness and the reliability of his testimony regarding matters beyond ordinary human perception, chastising the skeptics for their stubborn refusal to accept firsthand prophetic witness simply because it fell outside their own experience or expectations. It reflects the broader Quranic argument that revelation and the Prophet's visionary experiences are not matters for casual dispute by those who were not present or privy to such sacred encounters.

translation: And indeed he saw him in another descent,
interpretation: This verse refers to the Prophet Muhammad witnessing the angel Gabriel in his true, majestic form for a second time, as mentioned in the context of the Night Journey and Ascension (Isra and Mi'raj) narrative in Surah An-Najm. The first encounter is mentioned earlier in the surah, and this verse confirms that this vision was not a singular or illusory event but was repeated, reinforcing the authenticity and reality of the Prophet's experience. This second sighting is traditionally understood to have occurred near Sidrat al-Muntaha (the Lote Tree of the utmost boundary), a sacred point marking the limit of created knowledge and the boundary between the heavens and the divine presence. The repetition serves to validate the Prophet's prophetic experience against any doubts raised by skeptics, affirming that what he witnessed was a genuine spiritual reality rather than a hallucination, dream, or deception, thus strengthening the credibility of the revelation he received and the mission he was tasked with.

translation: Near the Lote Tree of the utmost boundary (Sidrat al-Muntaha).
interpretation: This verse comes from Surah An-Najm, in the passage describing the Prophet Muhammad's extraordinary vision during the Mi'raj (ascension). The Sidrat al-Muntaha, or 'Lote Tree of the utmost boundary,' marks a cosmic location at the furthest extent of created knowledge and space, beyond which no creature—including angels—may pass. It symbolizes the boundary between the finite realm of creation and the infinite, unknowable divine reality. This is the point where the Prophet witnessed signs of his Lord's greatness, representing the furthest point reachable by created beings in their ascent toward the Divine. The tree serves as a marker of ultimate limits, a place where human and angelic knowledge reaches its terminus, beyond which lies only what God alone knows. It has been understood by commentators as signifying the peak of spiritual attainment and the threshold of divine mysteries that remain beyond full human comprehension, even for the greatest of prophets.

translation: Near it is the Garden of Refuge (Jannat al-Ma'wa).
interpretation: This verse occurs in Surah An-Najm as part of the description of the Prophet Muhammad's (peace be upon him) vision at Sidrat al-Muntaha (the Lote Tree of the utmost boundary) during the Night Journey and Ascension (Isra and Mi'raj). The phrase indicates that Jannat al-Ma'wa, one of the named gardens of Paradise, is located near this cosmic boundary marker, the Sidrat al-Muntaha, which represents the furthest point of creation accessible to created beings and the limit of angelic and human knowledge. This positioning signifies that Paradise exists beyond the known boundaries of the physical universe, in a realm close to the Divine Presence itself. The name 'Jannat al-Ma'wa' (Garden of Refuge or Shelter) suggests this is the final resting place and sanctuary for righteous souls, a place of ultimate security and comfort after the trials of worldly life and the Day of Judgment. The verse underscores the extraordinary nature of the Prophet's spiritual journey, as he was granted a vision of realities that mark the very edges of existence, demonstrating his unique station among creation and the authenticity of his prophetic experience.

translation: When there covered the Lote Tree that which covered it.
interpretation: This verse refers to the Prophet Muhammad's miraculous night journey and ascension (al-Mi'raj), describing the moment he reached Sidrat al-Muntaha, the Lote Tree marking the boundary of the heavens beyond which no creation may pass. The deliberate vagueness of 'that which covered it' is a rhetorical device signifying the overwhelming, ineffable nature of what enveloped the tree—understood by commentators to be divine light, angels in countless numbers, or manifestations of God's glory so magnificent and awesome that human language is incapable of describing them. This linguistic restraint conveys the limits of human comprehension when confronted with the sacred and transcendent; some realities of the divine realm exceed what words can capture, and the repetition of the verb 'covered' (yaghsha) without specifying its subject emphasizes the majesty and mystery of this encounter at the threshold between creation and the Divine presence, reinforcing the extraordinary and unique nature of the Prophet's spiritual journey witnessed directly by him alone.

translation: The eye did not waver, nor did it transgress [its limit].
interpretation: This verse describes the Prophet Muhammad's vision during the Mi'raj (his miraculous ascension), referring to his encounter with Gabriel in his true angelic form or his vision of the divine signs. The verse emphasizes the absolute truthfulness and precision of this experience: the Prophet's eye neither deviated from what it saw nor exceeded or exaggerated it. This is a testament to the reliability of his perception—he saw exactly what was shown to him, without distortion, hallucination, or embellishment. It underscores that this was a real, divinely granted vision rather than a figment of imagination, confusion, or exaggeration, establishing the credibility of the extraordinary spiritual experience being described in the surrounding verses of Surah An-Najm.

translation: He certainly saw of the greatest signs of his Lord.
interpretation: This verse refers to the Prophet Muhammad's extraordinary vision during the Night Journey and Ascension (Isra and Mi'raj), affirming that he witnessed some of the greatest signs of Allah's power and majesty. It comes in the context of the preceding verses describing his encounter with the angel Gabriel in his true form and his nearness to the Divine Presence. The verse serves to validate the authenticity of the Prophet's spiritual experience against the skepticism of his contemporaries, emphasizing that what he saw was not a product of imagination, deception, or madness, but a genuine unveiling of cosmic and divine realities beyond ordinary human perception. It underscores the unique station of prophethood, wherein chosen messengers are granted glimpses into the unseen (al-ghayb) as proof of their mission and as a means of strengthening their certainty and resolve in conveying the divine message to humanity.

translation: Have you then considered al-Lat and al-'Uzza?
interpretation: This verse opens a rhetorical challenge directed at the pagan Meccans who worshipped these two prominent idols/goddesses (along with Manat, mentioned in the following verse) as intercessors between themselves and God. By asking them to 'consider' or 'reflect upon' these deities, the Qur'an is setting up a logical argument against idolatry—inviting the listeners to actually think critically about the nature and power of these idols rather than following ancestral custom blindly. The rhetorical question implies that upon genuine reflection, one would recognize these idols as powerless, lifeless objects with no divine attributes, unable to create, sustain, benefit, or harm anyone. This sets the stage for the subsequent verses that explicitly deny these idols any legitimate claim to divinity, exposing the irrationality of associating partners with God when these so-called deities are merely names the Meccans and their forefathers invented, without any authority or evidence from God. The verse thus functions as the beginning of a broader critique of shirk (polytheism) and a call to monotheistic reasoning.

translation: And Manat, the third, the other one?
interpretation: This verse is part of a passage (Surah An-Najm, 53:19-20) in which the Qur'an names three idols worshipped by the pagan Arabs of Mecca—al-Lat, al-Uzza, and Manat. By referring to Manat as 'the third, the other one,' the verse employs a somewhat dismissive tone, emphasizing her lesser status even among the pagan deities, before the following verses go on to challenge the logic of idol worship entirely. The rhetorical question posed here and in the preceding verses sets up the Qur'an's argument against the Meccans' practice of attributing daughters (the goddesses) to God while they themselves preferred sons, exposing both the theological error of polytheism and a social inconsistency in their own values. This passage is historically significant as it is associated with the so-called 'Satanic Verses' incident, though the authentic Qur'anic text firmly rejects any legitimacy of these idols as intercessors or deities, affirming instead the absolute oneness of God (tawhid).

translation: Is the male for you and the female for Him?
interpretation: This verse is a rhetorical rebuke directed at the pagan Arabs of Mecca who claimed that the angels were the daughters of Allah, while they themselves despised having daughters and strongly preferred sons. The verse exposes the glaring inconsistency and selfishness in their belief system: they reserved for themselves what they considered preferable (sons) while ascribing to Allah what they themselves viewed as inferior (daughters). This is presented as an irrational and unjust division, highlighting the absurdity of their theological claims, which were not based on revelation or evidence but on baseless conjecture and cultural bias. The verse thus serves as part of a broader critique in this passage of idolatrous beliefs that attribute offspring to Allah, emphasizing His transcendence above such human concepts of kinship and gender preference.

translation: That, then, is an unfair/unjust division.
interpretation: This verse comes in the context of the Qur'an's rebuke of the pre-Islamic Arabs who attributed daughters to God while favoring sons for themselves, and who worshipped idols they called the 'daughters of God' (such as al-Lat, al-'Uzza, and Manat). The verse exposes the logical and moral inconsistency of their position: they disdained daughters for themselves yet ascribed them to the Divine, and they divided worship between God and lifeless idols with no rational basis. This 'division' refers both to their inequitable distribution of roles between male and female offspring in their own social practice, and more pointedly to their irrational apportionment of divinity—granting some share of godhood to beings that have no power, no creative role, and no evidence to support such status. The phrase condemns this as a 'crooked' or 'unjust' division, highlighting the arbitrary, self-serving, and illogical nature of human attempts to parcel out divine attributes according to desire rather than truth, rather than submitting to the oneness and uniqueness of God alone.

translation: They are nothing but names which you and your forefathers have named, for which Allah has sent down no authority. They follow nothing but assumption and what their souls desire, while there has already come to them guidance from their Lord.
interpretation: This verse addresses the pagan practice of venerating idols, particularly female deities like Al-Lat, Al-Uzza, and Manat, exposing them as mere human inventions lacking any divine sanction. The verse establishes a crucial epistemological principle: religious claims require revealed authority (sultan) rather than inherited custom or wishful thinking. By stating these are 'names you and your forefathers named,' the Qur'an challenges the authority of ancestral tradition itself as a basis for belief, a radical departure in a culture that prized lineage and precedent. The phrase 'they follow nothing but assumption and what their souls desire' identifies two false foundations for belief—speculative conjecture (zann) and base desire (hawa)—contrasting them with the certainty that comes from divine guidance. The verse's conclusion, noting that guidance had indeed reached them from their Lord, underscores their culpability: their error was not due to ignorance but to willful rejection of clear guidance in favor of comfortable, inherited illusions. This establishes a broader Qur'anic theme that truth must be grounded in revelation rather than cultural inertia or emotional attachment.

translation: Or is it that man shall have whatever he wishes for?
interpretation: This verse is a rhetorical question that rebukes human presumption and the illusion of entitlement. It comes in the context of Surah An-Najm's criticism of those who worship idols—particularly the pagan belief in the intercessory power of goddesses like Al-Lat, Al-Uzza, and Manat—hoping these would grant their wishes and desires without any basis in truth or divine sanction. The verse exposes the fallacy that human desire alone dictates reality or that wishing for something makes it deserved or granted. It underscores a central Quranic theme: that ultimate authority, provision, and the granting of outcomes belong to God alone, not to human whims, idols, or false intermediaries. By extension, it serves as a broader admonition against arrogance and wishful thinking disconnected from righteous action and submission to divine will—reminding humanity that true success and reward are earned through faith and deeds, not simply desired into existence.

translation: So to Allah belong the Last [life] and the First [life].
interpretation: This verse affirms Allah's absolute sovereignty over both the Hereafter (al-akhirah) and this worldly life (al-ula), and by extension over all time, creation, and existence. It comes in the context of Surah An-Najm discussing the limits of human intercession and false hopes placed in idols, emphasizing that ultimate authority, judgment, and outcomes in both realms—this world and the next—rest solely with Allah, not with any intermediary or created being. The ordering of 'the last' before 'the first' is often understood to emphasize the primacy of concern for the Hereafter, reminding believers that the ultimate reality and final reckoning belong to Allah, even as He also governs the present world from its beginning.

translation: And how many angels are there in the heavens whose intercession avails nothing except after Allah has given permission to whom He wills and approves.
interpretation: This verse addresses the mistaken belief of the polytheists that their idols or intermediaries could intercede for them before Allah, by pointing out that even the angels—beings of immense power and proximity to the divine, far superior to any idol—cannot intercede on behalf of anyone without Allah's explicit permission. This establishes a fundamental theological principle: intercession is not an independent right that any being possesses, but a privilege granted solely by Allah's will. The verse specifies two conditions for valid intercession: Allah's permission ('for whom He wills') and His approval or pleasure ('and approves'), meaning intercession will only be granted for those whose beliefs and deeds are pleasing to Him. This refutes the pagan Arabs' justification for idol worship, which rested on the claim that their deities would intercede for them with Allah. If even the noble angels have no autonomous power of intercession, then certainly lifeless idols have none. The verse thus redirects all hope of intercession away from created beings and toward Allah alone, reinforcing the doctrine of tawhid (divine oneness) and showing that salvation ultimately depends on Allah's sovereign will and His pleasure with the one seeking intercession.

translation: Indeed, those who do not believe in the Hereafter name the angels with female names.
interpretation: This verse addresses the pre-Islamic Arab practice of referring to angels as female beings, often associating them with deities or calling them 'daughters of Allah.' The Qur'an condemns this practice on two levels. First, it is presented as baseless speculation—an assertion made without any knowledge or divine revelation, but rather based on mere assumption and inherited custom, as the following verses clarify. Second, the verse links this error directly to disbelief in the Hereafter, suggesting a deeper connection: those who deny the Hereafter lack proper understanding of the unseen realm and divine matters altogether, leading them to make unfounded claims about the nature of angels. Their denial of resurrection and accountability reflects a broader deficiency in recognizing the reality of metaphysical truths, which manifests in their careless and unsubstantiated characterization of angels. The verse thus serves as a critique of attributing human categories, particularly gender, to purely spiritual beings whose true nature is known only to God, and highlights how disbelief in one unseen truth can lead to erroneous beliefs about other unseen matters.

translation: And they have no knowledge thereof. They follow nothing but conjecture, and indeed, conjecture avails nothing against the truth.
interpretation: This verse addresses those who make claims about matters of unseen reality—such as asserting that angels are female or attributing partners to God—without any genuine knowledge or evidence to support their position. The Qur'an draws a sharp distinction between 'ilm (verified knowledge, whether through revelation or sound reasoning) and dhann (conjecture, assumption, or baseless speculation). The verse establishes an epistemological principle: belief or assertion about significant matters, especially theological ones, must be grounded in knowledge rather than guesswork, inherited custom, or wishful thinking. Conjecture may feel compelling or be widely held, but it carries no weight when weighed against truth—it cannot substitute for or overturn what is actually real. This serves as a broader caution against following assumptions, unexamined traditions, or desires in place of seeking actual knowledge, particularly in matters of faith and metaphysical claims.

translation: So turn away from whoever turns away from Our remembrance and desires nothing but the life of this world.
interpretation: This verse instructs the Prophet (and by extension believers) to disengage from those who deliberately reject divine guidance and are wholly absorbed in worldly pursuits, having no interest in spiritual remembrance or the hereafter. It is not a command to abandon da'wah or compassion, but rather a directive not to force guidance upon those who have consciously chosen heedlessness and materialism as their life's purpose, since faith cannot be coerced upon hearts closed off by their own choice. It also serves as a consolation to the Prophet, reassuring him that he is not responsible for the guidance of those who willfully reject truth, shifting the burden of accountability back onto the individual's own choices rather than the messenger's efforts. Additionally, the verse delineates a criterion for distinguishing the heedless from the mindful: an exclusive, consuming focus on 'the life of this world' as the final and only object of pursuit, to the exclusion of any memory or recognition of the divine. This worldly orientation is presented as a conscious turning away, implying moral responsibility rather than mere ignorance.

translation: That is the extent of their knowledge. Indeed, your Lord is most knowing of who strays from His way, and He is most knowing of who is rightly guided.
interpretation: This verse addresses the limitations of worldly knowledge, particularly in relation to those who pursue only the apparent, material aspects of life (referring back to the preceding verses about those who desire only this worldly life). It establishes a critical boundary: human understanding, even when extensive, remains superficial and bounded compared to divine knowledge. The repetition of 'most knowing' (a'lam) emphasizes God's comprehensive and perfect awareness of the inner realities of guidance and misguidance—realities that are not always visible through external observation or human reasoning alone. This serves as a humbling reminder that ultimate judgment about who is truly guided or astray belongs to God alone, not to human assessment based on outward appearances or limited knowledge. It also implicitly warns against arrogance in claiming certainty about others' spiritual states, while affirming that God's justice is rooted in perfect knowledge of hearts and intentions, not just actions or circumstances.

translation: And to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, that He may recompense those who do evil for what they have done and recompense those who do good with the best reward.
interpretation: This verse establishes God's absolute sovereignty over all creation as the foundation for divine justice. Because everything belongs to Him, He has complete authority and knowledge to judge all beings justly. The verse presents a moral symmetry: evildoers will be recompensed according to their deeds, while those who do good will receive 'al-husna' (the best/most beautiful reward), which many commentators interpret as Paradise or a reward exceeding what their good deeds merited through God's grace. This establishes the principle that divine justice is not arbitrary but is intrinsically linked to human moral agency and choice, while also hinting that God's mercy toward the righteous exceeds strict proportional justice, as goodness is rewarded with something described as 'most beautiful' rather than merely equivalent.

translation: Those who avoid the major sins and immoralities, only [committing] slight lapses - indeed, your Lord is vast in forgiveness. He is most knowing of you when He produced you from the earth and when you were fetuses in your mothers' wombs. So do not claim yourselves to be pure; He is most knowing of who fears Him.
interpretation: This verse establishes a realistic and compassionate standard of righteousness, distinguishing between grave sins that define moral corruption and the minor, almost inevitable human failings that do not negate one's fundamental piety. By grounding this distinction in God's intimate knowledge of human origins—from dust to embryonic development—the verse emphasizes that divine judgment is rooted in a complete understanding of human nature and its inherent weaknesses, not in an unforgiving demand for flawlessness. The concluding prohibition against self-purification serves as a check against spiritual arrogance and hypocrisy, reminding believers that true taqwa (God-consciousness) is known only to God, who sees beyond outward claims of righteousness into the sincerity of the heart. This theological framework thus balances moral accountability with divine mercy, encouraging humility rather than self-righteous judgment of one's own spiritual status.

translation: Have you seen the one who turned away?
interpretation: This verse opens a passage (continuing into the following verses about one who 'gave a little then withheld') that refers to a specific individual who, after showing some initial inclination toward faith or righteousness, turned his back on it—traditionally understood by commentators to allude to a man who was persuaded to abandon support for the Prophet ﷺ after being promised that he would bear any burden of sin in return, then reneged out of stinginess once a small payment was made. More broadly, the verse serves as a rhetorical device, inviting the listener to reflect on and recognize a recognizable human type: one who possesses the capacity for truth and generosity but, swayed by greed, fear of loss, or worldly attachment, withdraws from commitment to what is right. It functions as an indictment of moral inconsistency and the human tendency to abandon higher obligations when they become costly, setting up the subsequent verses that question whether such a person has knowledge of the unseen that justifies his self-assured withholding and refusal to give in charity or support of truth.

translation: And who gave a little, then withheld?
interpretation: This verse continues the description of a particular disbeliever—identified in classical exegesis as al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah or a similar figure—who turned away from the truth after some initial inclination toward it. He gave a small token of charity or support, perhaps to ease his conscience or maintain appearances, but then stopped (akda, literally 'struck rock,' like a digger who hits bedrock and gives up). This phrase captures the broader Quranic critique of insincere, half-hearted commitment—someone who makes a token gesture of righteousness without true dedication, then abandons it entirely when it becomes inconvenient or costly. The imagery of 'striking rock' suggests a self-imposed limit, as though the person artificially halted their own generosity, unlike genuine givers who give consistently from sincere faith. It stands as a warning against performative piety and the danger of valuing worldly life over the Hereafter, as the surrounding verses emphasize that such a person 'turned away' after being reminded, caring only for immediate worldly concerns rather than ultimate accountability.

translation: Or does he have knowledge of the unseen, so that he sees [it]?
interpretation: This verse is part of a rhetorical rebuke directed at a disbeliever (traditionally identified as one who turned away from faith after giving a little charity, then withheld the rest). The question is posed sarcastically to expose the absurdity of his claims or assumptions about the afterlife, reward, or unseen matters. The implication is that no human possesses independent access to the unseen (al-ghayb)—such knowledge belongs to God alone. By asking 'does he have knowledge of the unseen so that he sees it,' the verse challenges the arrogance of a person who makes confident pronouncements or behaves as though he has certainty about matters beyond human perception, such as the outcome of his deeds or the nature of divine judgment, when in fact he has no legitimate basis for such certainty. It serves as a broader Quranic theme reminding humanity of the limits of human knowledge and the need for reliance on revelation rather than speculation or self-serving rationalization.

translation: Or has he not been informed of what is in the scriptures of Moses?
interpretation: This verse is part of a passage (Qur'an 53:36-62) rebuking those who reject the message and follow their own desires without accountability, particularly referencing a man who gave a little in charity and then withheld the rest, claiming knowledge of the unseen. The rhetorical question points to the continuity of divine revelation across prophets: the same fundamental truths—accountability for one's deeds, the reality of resurrection, and divine justice—were conveyed in the scriptures of Moses (and Abraham, mentioned in the following verse) just as they are conveyed in the Qur'an. By invoking earlier scripture, the verse establishes that the message of personal responsibility is not a novel claim but part of an established prophetic tradition, leaving the disbeliever without excuse for ignorance, since this same truth had already been communicated through previous messengers and their sacred texts.

translation: And Abraham, who fulfilled [his covenant/commitments]?
interpretation: This verse refers to Prophet Abraham's complete faithfulness to the trials and commands God placed upon him, including his willingness to sacrifice his son, his rejection of idolatry, and his steadfast devotion despite severe tests. The phrase 'who fulfilled' signifies that Abraham completed every duty and trust assigned to him by God without wavering, serving as a model of total submission and sincerity in faith. This verse is part of a broader passage in Surah An-Najm that references earlier scriptures (the scrolls of Moses and Abraham), affirming the continuity of divine revelation and the exemplary nature of Abraham's unwavering obedience as a standard for believers.

translation: That no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another.
interpretation: This verse establishes the fundamental principle of individual moral and spiritual accountability before God. It affirms that each soul is solely responsible for its own actions, sins, and choices, and that no one—regardless of relationship, status, or love—can carry the weight of another's wrongdoing on their behalf. This rejects any notion of inherited guilt or vicarious atonement where one person's sins are transferred to or absorbed by another. It underscores the justice of divine judgment, where every person stands accountable only for what they themselves have earned or committed. This principle also carries practical implications for human relationships and ethics, emphasizing personal responsibility rather than blame-shifting, and reinforcing that salvation or punishment is an individual matter between the soul and its Creator, not something that can be delegated, inherited, or borrowed from others.

translation: And that there is nothing for man except that for which he strives.
interpretation: This verse establishes a foundational principle of individual moral accountability and the justice of divine recompense: a person's ultimate reward or recompense is tied directly to their own effort, intention, and deeds, not to the actions, merits, or status of others—including ancestors, relatives, or those they associate with. It refutes notions of inherited salvation, vicarious atonement, or benefiting from someone else's good deeds without one's own striving. The verse emphasizes personal responsibility: wealth, lineage, or the piety of one's forebears cannot substitute for one's own sincere effort (sa'y) toward righteousness. This encourages active striving in faith and good works, rather than passive reliance on intercession or family merit, reinforcing the broader Qur'anic theme that salvation and divine favor are earned through one's own conscious choices and actions in this life.

translation: And that his effort will surely be seen.
interpretation: This verse is part of a sequence in Surah An-Najm affirming the principle of individual accountability, following the statement that no soul bears another's burden and that man gets nothing except what he strives for. Here it is emphasized that one's deeds and efforts are not hidden or wasted, but will be made manifest and witnessed—ultimately before God on the Day of Judgment, where every striving, whether good or evil, will be brought to light and evaluated. This underscores the Quranic ethic that human effort has real consequence and will not go unnoticed, serving as both a motivation to strive righteously and a warning against heedless or harmful action, since all deeds are recorded and will eventually be disclosed and recompensed.

translation: Then he will be recompensed for it with the fullest recompense.
