This duality mirrors the surah's own structure, which alternates between describing God's overwhelming power (creating the heavens, controlling the cosmos, promising judgment) and His tender generosity (providing fruits, rivers, gardens, and companionship in Paradise). By ending on this note, the surah suggests that true recognition of God's favors leads naturally to reverence for His name and essence, closing the loop between gratitude for blessings and acknowledgment of the One who bestows them. The verse also functions liturgically, having become a common phrase of praise recited by Muslims, reinforcing the Quranic theme that remembrance of God's names is itself an act of worship and blessing.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. When the Occurrence occurs,
interpretation: This opening verse of Surah Al-Waqi'ah announces the certainty of the Day of Judgment, referred to as 'the Occurrence' or 'the Inevitable Event.' The use of this title rather than a more common term emphasizes the absolute certainty and unavoidability of this cosmic event—it is not described as a possibility but as something that will definitively 'occur.' The grammatical structure, using the past tense for a future event, is a rhetorical device common in Qur'anic Arabic to convey the certainty of what is being described, as though it has already happened. This verse sets the tone for the chapter, which goes on to describe the dramatic transformations of the earth and sky, and the sorting of humanity into distinct categories based on their deeds, underscoring themes of divine justice and the ultimate reckoning that awaits all of creation.

translation: There is no denial of its occurrence.
interpretation: This verse refers to the inevitability and certainty of the Day of Judgment (Al-Waqi'ah, 'The Event'). It establishes that when this cataclysmic event occurs, there will be no one able to deny, falsify, or refute that it has happened—its reality will be undeniable and self-evident to all. This sets the tone for the rest of the chapter, which goes on to describe the dramatic cosmic upheavals that will accompany this event and the subsequent sorting of humanity into distinct categories based on their deeds, emphasizing that despite human skepticism or disbelief in the present life, the ultimate reckoning is an absolute certainty that cannot be argued away when it finally comes to pass.

translation: Abasing (some), exalting (others).
interpretation: This verse describes one of the fundamental effects of the Day of Judgment (al-Waqi'ah). On that day, the social order and hierarchies of this worldly life will be completely overturned. Those who were arrogant, powerful, and held high status in this world due to wealth, lineage, or worldly authority—yet who disbelieved and transgressed—will be brought low and humiliated. Conversely, those who were considered lowly, weak, oppressed, or insignificant in worldly terms, but who held true faith and righteousness, will be elevated and honored. This phrase encapsulates the ultimate justice of God, where true worth is measured not by worldly status but by faith and deeds. It serves as a powerful reminder that the values and hierarchies of this temporary world will be inverted in the eternal reckoning, humbling the proud and exalting the humble believers.

translation: When the earth is shaken with a violent shaking,
interpretation: This verse opens the description of the Day of Judgment in Surah Al-Waqi'ah, depicting the cataclysmic physical upheaval of the earth as a sign of the cosmic order collapsing. The violent shaking represents the complete undoing of the natural world as humanity knows it, signaling that the stability and permanence people took for granted in worldly life is illusory. This earthquake-like convulsion serves as the first in a sequence of apocalyptic events that strip away all false securities, forcing recognition that only the reality of the Hereafter and divine judgment remains constant. The verse sets a tone of awe and terror appropriate to the surah's purpose of dividing humanity into three categories based on their deeds, as the shaking of the earth symbolizes the shaking of all human certainties and the exposure of ultimate truth.

translation: And the mountains will be crushed to pieces,
interpretation: This verse is part of the opening sequence of Surah Al-Waqi'ah (The Inevitable Event), which describes the cataclysmic events that will occur when the Day of Judgment arrives. The imagery of mountains—typically seen as symbols of permanence, stability, and immovable strength—being utterly pulverized into fine dust or scattered particles conveys the complete dissolution of the natural order as humanity knows it. This serves as a powerful demonstration of divine omnipotence: if even the mountains, the most solid and enduring features of the earth, can be reduced to nothing, then all worldly structures, hierarchies, and illusions of permanence will likewise collapse. The verse functions rhetorically to prepare the listener for the radical transformation of reality that accompanies the Resurrection, emphasizing that on that day, the familiar physical laws governing creation will be suspended, and nothing in the material world will remain as it once was. This sets the stage for the subsequent verses describing humanity being sorted into distinct groups according to their deeds.

translation: And they [the mountains] will become scattered dust.
interpretation: This verse is part of the description of the cataclysmic events that will occur on the Day of Judgment, specifically referring to the mountains, which are among the most solid and enduring features of the earth, being utterly pulverized and reduced to fine, scattered particles of dust blown about in the air. The imagery conveys the complete dissolution of the familiar physical order of creation, emphasizing the overwhelming power of God to dismantle even what humans perceive as permanent and immovable. This serves as a stark reminder of the transience of the material world and the absolute nature of divine power, preparing the listener for the account of the Hereafter that follows, where the old order gives way entirely to a new reality determined by one's deeds in worldly life.

translation: And you will be [divided] into three classes.
interpretation: This verse introduces the tripartite division of humanity that will be revealed on the Day of Judgment, setting the stage for the subsequent verses which identify these three groups: the Companions of the Right, the Companions of the Left, and the Foremost (as-Sabiqun). This classification emphasizes that on that day, all previous worldly distinctions of wealth, lineage, and status will dissolve, replaced by a new moral and spiritual hierarchy based solely on one's faith and deeds. The foremost are those who excelled in righteousness and drew nearest to God, representing the smallest but most elevated group; the Companions of the Right are the generally righteous who will receive their record in their right hand, destined for reward; and the Companions of the Left are those condemned for their wrongdoing, destined for punishment. This tripartite structure reflects the Quranic theme that ultimate human worth is determined not by social categories but by one's relationship to divine guidance and conduct in life.”

translation: So those on the Right Hand - what are those on the Right Hand?
interpretation: This verse refers to one of the three groups into which humanity will be divided on the Day of Judgment, as described in Surah Al-Waqi'ah. The 'Companions of the Right Hand' are the blessed and righteous believers whose deeds will be recorded in their right hands, symbolizing honor, success, and divine favor. The rhetorical question 'what are those on the Right Hand?' is a stylistic device used in the Qur'an to emphasize the extraordinary and elevated status of this group, inviting the listener to ponder the immense blessings and rewards that await them, which cannot be fully captured in ordinary description. This sets up the subsequent verses that elaborate on the paradise and delights awaiting these righteous people, in contrast to the 'Companions of the Left Hand' who will face punishment, and the 'Foremost' who will be nearest to God.

translation: And the companions of the left - what are the companions of the left?
interpretation: This verse refers to those who will receive their record of deeds in their left hand on the Day of Judgment, symbolizing their status as people of misfortune and wrongdoing. The rhetorical question format, repeating 'what are the companions of the left,' emphasizes the gravity and dreadfulness of their fate, leaving the full horror to the imagination before it is elaborated upon in subsequent verses. These are the people who disbelieved and transgressed, and this classification stands in contrast to the 'companions of the right' mentioned elsewhere in the same chapter (Al-Waqi'ah), establishing a tripartite division of humanity on the Day of Resurrection based on their deeds and faith in worldly life.

translation: And the foremost, the foremost (in faith and good deeds) —
interpretation: This verse refers to those who are first and foremost in righteousness, faith, and devotion to God—those who excel in good deeds and race ahead in obedience to Him. The repetition of the word 'foremost' (as-sabiqun as-sabiqun) emphasizes and confirms their elevated status, distinguishing them as a unique category among the three groups of people mentioned in this chapter (the foremost, the companions of the right, and the companions of the left). Traditionally, this group is understood to include the prophets, the truthful, the martyrs, and the most devoted believers who were foremost in embracing faith and performing righteous deeds in this worldly life, and who will consequently be foremost in attaining nearness to God and the highest ranks of Paradise in the Hereafter. The emphatic repetition serves to underscore that their precedence in faith directly corresponds to their precedence in reward and honor before God.

translation: Those are the ones brought near [to Allah].
interpretation: This verse refers to the foremost believers—those who excelled in faith and righteous deeds in worldly life—and describes their elevated status in the Hereafter. Being 'brought near' (al-muqarrabun) signifies the highest rank of proximity to Allah, surpassing even the general reward of Paradise given to other righteous believers. This group, mentioned in the context of the three categories of people on the Day of Judgment (the foremost, the companions of the right, and the companions of the left), represents the spiritual elite who attained closeness to the Divine through their exceptional devotion, sincerity, and precedence in goodness. Their nearness is not merely physical placement in Paradise but an intimate spiritual relationship with Allah, reflecting the Islamic concept that the ultimate reward for the believer is not just bliss and comfort, but divine closeness and pleasure.

translation: In Gardens of Bliss.
interpretation: This phrase describes the ultimate reward awaiting the righteous believers in the Hereafter. 'Jannat al-Na'eem' (Gardens of Bliss/Delight) refers to a specific station of Paradise characterized by unending pleasure, comfort, and joy, free from any form of suffering, sorrow, or deficiency. The phrase appears in various contexts throughout the Quran, often following descriptions of the righteous deeds of believers—such as faith, charity, patience, and devotion to God—emphasizing the direct link between righteous conduct in this worldly life and the eternal reward in the next. The imagery of gardens evokes abundance, life, beauty, and tranquility, standing in stark contrast to the barrenness and hardship often associated with worldly trials. This serves as both a promise and a motivation for believers to strive for righteousness, reinforcing the Quranic theme that true and lasting happiness is found not in temporary worldly pleasures but in the eternal bliss granted by God to those who earn His pleasure through faith and good deeds.

translation: A multitude from among the former peoples.
interpretation: This phrase occurs in Surat al-Waqi'ah, describing the foremost in faith (al-sabiqun) who will be nearest to God in Paradise. The verse indicates that this elite group of the foremost believers will consist largely of a great multitude from earlier generations and nations, those who lived closer to the time of earlier prophets and were among the first to respond to truth with sincerity. This highlights the idea that righteousness and precedence in faith were abundant among the earlier communities of believers, while the subsequent verse contrasts this with a smaller number from later generations, suggesting that as time progresses and people move further from prophetic guidance, true sincerity and excellence in faith become rarer. It serves as both a mark of honor for earlier righteous generations and a subtle exhortation to later generations to strive to be among the foremost despite the challenges of their times.

translation: And a few from the later generations.
interpretation: This verse comes from Surah Al-Waqi'ah, describing the foremost people (al-sabiqun) who will be nearest to God in Paradise. The preceding verse states that many of them will be from earlier generations, while this verse clarifies that only a few will be from later generations. This reflects a theological point about the diminishing of righteousness and spiritual excellence over time—as humanity moves further from the earliest generations of believers (including the earliest followers of the Prophet Muhammad), fewer people attain the highest ranks of faith and closeness to God. It underscores the Islamic notion that the earliest Muslim community, particularly the Companions of the Prophet, held a unique and exalted spiritual station that becomes increasingly rare to replicate as time progresses, though it does not foreclose the possibility of a minority achieving such distinction in later times.

translation: On thrones woven [with gold and jewels]
interpretation: This verse describes the thrones of the foremost believers in Paradise, those closest to Allah. The word 'mawdunah' (woven) suggests thrones intricately interlaced with gold, pearls, and precious stones, conveying both opulence and exquisite craftsmanship. This imagery emphasizes the honor and majesty bestowed upon the righteous, portraying Paradise as a realm of unimaginable luxury and comfort that transcends worldly experience. The woven construction also symbolizes permanence and security, as interlaced materials are more durable and stable than simple construction, suggesting that the rewards of Paradise are everlasting and unshakeable, unlike the fleeting pleasures of this world.

translation: Reclining on them, facing one another.
interpretation: This verse depicts the companions of Paradise reclining upon adorned couches or thrones, positioned so that they face one another rather than with their backs turned. This detail conveys the perfected social harmony of the afterlife: unlike worldly gatherings where seating may create distance, hierarchy, or discomfort, the arrangement in Paradise ensures full intimacy, equality, and mutual engagement among companions. Facing one another symbolizes the removal of all worldly barriers—rivalry, envy, awkwardness, or social anxiety—that often mar human relationships. It suggests an eternal state of pure companionship, where believers can enjoy each other's presence directly and joyfully, reflecting the Qur'anic theme that Paradise is not only a place of physical reward but also of perfected emotional and social fulfillment, free from the imperfections of earthly interaction.

translation: There will circulate among them (immortal) youths made eternal,
interpretation: This verse describes a scene of paradise in which eternally youthful servants attend to the believers, serving them without ever aging or passing away. The imagery emphasizes the perpetual, unchanging bliss of Paradise, where even the service rendered to its inhabitants is free from the decay, fatigue, or mortality that characterizes worldly life. These 'ever-youthful' attendants symbolize the perfection and permanence of divine reward, in contrast to the transient nature of earthly existence. Classical commentators note that these youths are a distinct creation, meant solely to serve the people of Paradise, and their eternal youth reflects the timeless and incorruptible nature of the heavenly abode itself.

translation: With cups, pitchers, and a glass [of wine] from a flowing spring.
interpretation: This verse describes the rewards awaiting the righteous in Paradise, depicting vessels—cups and pitchers—filled with a pure, continuously flowing drink. Unlike earthly wine, this drink from Paradise causes no intoxication, headache, or sin, as clarified in subsequent verses. The imagery emphasizes abundance, purity, and the ease of enjoyment in the afterlife, where believers are served without effort, symbolizing the honor and comfort bestowed upon them by God as a reward for their faith and good deeds in worldly life.

translation: They will not be given headaches thereby, nor will they be intoxicated (or their minds impaired).
interpretation: This verse describes the wine of Paradise served to the righteous, emphasizing that unlike earthly wine, it carries none of its harmful effects. The imagery contrasts the imperfection of worldly pleasures with the perfected, pure pleasures of the afterlife. Earthly intoxicants bring temporary euphoria followed by pain, confusion, or loss of reason, but the drink of Paradise offers pure enjoyment without any negative consequence—no headache, no diminished mental clarity, no regret. This reflects a broader Quranic theme that Paradise is a realm where believers receive the idealized, flawless version of what they only imperfectly experienced or desired in worldly life. It suggests that true, lasting pleasure is one unmarred by suffering or loss of self-control, and that divine reward is characterized by completeness and freedom from the flaws inherent in worldly existence.

translation: And fruit from whatever they may choose.
interpretation: This verse is part of the Qur'anic depiction of the rewards awaiting the righteous in Paradise. It emphasizes the theme of unrestricted abundance and personal choice as a hallmark of divine generosity—unlike worldly life, where access to fruits and provisions is limited by season, availability, or means, the inhabitants of Paradise are granted complete freedom to select whatever fruit pleases them, without constraint or scarcity. This reflects a broader Qur'anic motif in which the delights of Paradise are described in terms that transcend earthly limitations, serving as a powerful contrast to the trials, labor, and restrictions of worldly existence. The emphasis on choice ('yatakhayyarun'—from a root meaning to select the best) also underscores the idea that Paradise is a realm of ease and satisfaction tailored to the desires of its inhabitants, a fitting reward for those who exercised patience and restraint in their earthly lives by submitting to God's will rather than following every desire.

translation: And the flesh of birds, from whatever they desire.
interpretation: This verse is part of a sequence in Surah Al-Waqi'ah describing the sensory delights awaiting the foremost believers (al-Sabiqun) in Paradise. The mention of bird flesh available according to one's desire emphasizes the limitless abundance and effortless gratification of Paradise, where sustenance is not earned through labor or constrained by scarcity, as in worldly life, but is immediately accessible simply through wishing for it. This reflects a broader Qur'anic theme that the rewards of the afterlife transcend the limitations and toil of earthly existence, offering a state of complete ease, pleasure, and fulfillment of desire as a recompense for righteous deeds and devotion performed in the temporal world. The specific choice of bird meat, considered a delicacy in Arabian culture, underscores the luxurious and refined nature of these heavenly provisions, elevating the imagery beyond mere sustenance to one of exquisite enjoyment reserved for those nearest to God.

translation: And [there are] fair ones with wide, beautiful eyes,
interpretation: This verse appears in Surah Al-Waqi'ah in the description of the rewards awaiting the righteous (As-Habul-Yameen, the Companions of the Right) in Paradise. The 'hoor 'een' refers to pure, beautiful companions granted to the believers as part of the delights of Paradise, symbolizing purity, beauty, and the fulfillment of desires in the eternal abode. Classical commentators such as Ibn Kathir describe them as maidens of Paradise, created by Allah, possessing wide and lovely eyes, untouched by any human or jinn before, representing the sublime and incomparable nature of heavenly rewards that transcend worldly experience. This imagery serves to emphasize the vast difference between the transient pleasures of this world and the eternal, perfected joys of the Hereafter, motivating believers toward righteousness and devotion through the promise of divine generosity and aesthetic perfection in the afterlife.

translation: Like unto hidden pearls.
interpretation: This verse, from Surah Al-Waqi'ah, describes the pure companions granted to the people of Paradise (specifically those foremost in faith, as mentioned in the preceding verses). The comparison to 'hidden' or 'well-guarded' pearls evokes an image of pristine, untouched beauty—pearls that have never been exposed to handling, dust, or impurity, remaining perfectly preserved within their shells. This imagery conveys purity, preciousness, and protection, suggesting beings of flawless and untainted beauty reserved exclusively for the righteous as a reward. The metaphor also implies rarity and value, as pearls are treasured for their scarcity and the care taken to protect them, reflecting the honored and cherished status of the dwellers of Paradise and the blessings bestowed upon them.

translation: A reward for what they used to do.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 32:17) speaks of the hidden delights of Paradise that no soul knows, prepared as a just recompense for the righteous deeds believers performed in worldly life. It underscores the Islamic principle of divine justice: that eternal reward is directly tied to one's faith and good actions, emphasizing that nothing is wasted and every sincere effort toward righteousness is ultimately repaid by God in a measure beyond human imagination.

translation: They will not hear therein any vain talk or sinful speech.
interpretation: This verse describes the pure social atmosphere of Paradise, contrasting it with the corrupted speech of worldly gatherings. In this life, human conversation is often marred by idle chatter, gossip, lies, boasting, and sinful talk that leads to discord. In Paradise, this verse promises that the companionship of the believers will be free from any such corruption—no vain, meaningless speech (laghw) and no speech that incites or constitutes sin (ta'theem), such as accusations, backbiting, or falsehood. This reflects the perfected moral and spiritual state of its inhabitants, where hearts have been purified of malice and tongues of harm, allowing for pure, wholesome fellowship. It also serves as an implicit exhortation to believers in this world to strive to purify their own speech and gatherings from vain and sinful talk, as a reflection of the ultimate reward awaiting them.

translation: Except the words, 'Peace, peace.'
interpretation: This verse describes the serene atmosphere of Paradise for the righteous (the Companions of the Right), who, unlike the condemned who endure vile speech and recrimination in Hell, will hear nothing idle, sinful, or quarrelsome. Instead, their only discourse—whether from each other, from the angels, or from God Himself—will be mutual greetings of 'Salam' (peace). This repetition of 'salama salama' emphasizes the totality and purity of this tranquility: an environment entirely free of conflict, falsehood, or distress, where peace is both the content and the very medium of communication, reflecting the ultimate spiritual reward of harmony and contentment.

translation: And the companions of the right hand - what are the companions of the right hand?
interpretation: This verse introduces the second of the three groups into which humanity is divided on the Day of Judgment, as described in Surah Al-Waqi'ah. The rhetorical question format - asking about the companions of the right hand after naming them - is a stylistic device used throughout the Qur'an to evoke wonder, anticipation, and emphasis on the extraordinary nature of what is being described. This group, also known as 'Ashab al-Yamin,' represents the blessed and righteous believers who will receive their book of deeds in their right hand, a traditional sign of honor and good standing in Arab culture. Unlike the foremost (as-sabiqun), who are the elite of the elite achieving the highest ranks through exceptional devotion, the companions of the right hand represent the general body of righteous believers who fulfilled their religious obligations and lived according to divine guidance, though perhaps not reaching the same extraordinary spiritual heights as the foremost. The subsequent verses go on to describe their reward in Paradise - gardens of bliss, comfort, and ease - contrasting sharply with the fate of the companions of the left hand (the damned) described later in the same chapter. This verse serves as a pause for reflection, inviting the listener to contemplate the immense honor and favor that awaits this category of believers before the specific details of their blessings are revealed.

translation: Among thornless lote trees,
interpretation: This verse is part of a sequence in Surah Al-Waqi'ah (verses 27-33) describing the sensory delights awaiting the 'Companions of the Right'—those blessed souls in Paradise. The lote tree (sidr) was known in the Arabian environment as a thorny, often unremarkable tree valued mainly for shade in harsh desert conditions. By describing it here as 'mukhdud'—stripped of thorns, or made abundant and fruitful—the verse transforms a familiar but flawed earthly object into a perfected version of itself in the afterlife. This reflects a broader Qur'anic rhetorical strategy: taking elements of the listeners' lived experience, things they valued yet which carried imperfection or difficulty, and depicting their idealized, flawless counterparts in Paradise. The removal of thorns symbolizes the removal of hardship, pain, and want altogether—conveying that the rewards of the afterlife are not entirely foreign or unimaginable, but are the beloved things of this world freed from their defects and limitations. It speaks to a theology of continuity between creation and recompense, where Paradise is both familiar and sublimely transcendent.'

translation: And [banana] trees layered with fruit,
interpretation: This verse is part of a sequence describing the physical delights awaiting the righteous companions of the right hand in Paradise. The imagery of talh (often understood as banana or plantain trees, though some early commentators relate it to a flowering tree) with fruit stacked in abundant, orderly layers conveys a sense of effortless and inexhaustible provision. Unlike the toil required for agriculture in earthly life, these trees yield their bounty in perfect, ready-to-enjoy arrangement, symbolizing the ease, abundance, and aesthetic harmony of the heavenly reward. The specific mention of this fruit, alongside other paradisiacal imagery in the surrounding verses (shade, flowing water, extended fruit), reinforces the Quran's rhetorical strategy of using sensory, tangible pleasures familiar to its original audience to evoke the ineffable nature of the afterlife reward, making the abstract concept of eternal bliss comprehensible through concrete, desirable imagery rooted in the natural world they knew.

translation: And extended shade.
interpretation: This verse is part of a sequence in Surah Al-Waqi'ah describing the rewards awaiting the people of the right hand (As-hab al-Yamin) in Paradise. The 'extended shade' symbolizes perpetual comfort and protection, free from the harshness of heat or sunlight, reflecting a state of eternal ease and tranquility. Unlike the fleeting shade of this worldly life, this shade is described as 'mamdud' (extended or outstretched), suggesting it is boundless and unceasing, never shifting or diminishing as earthly shade does with the movement of the sun. This imagery evokes a paradise characterized by permanence and lack of discomfort, reinforcing the contrast between the temporary trials of worldly existence and the everlasting peace of the hereafter. It speaks to the human yearning for rest and relief from life's burdens, assuring believers that their patience and righteousness will be rewarded with an environment of perfect serenity.

translation: And poured-out [flowing] water.
interpretation: This phrase appears in Surah Al-Waqi'ah among the description of the delights awaiting the People of the Right Hand in Paradise. The 'poured-out water' signifies continuously flowing, abundant streams—unlike the scarce and laboriously drawn water of earthly life. It symbolizes ease, purity, and endless abundance granted to the righteous, water that flows freely without the need for effort to access it, contrasting sharply with the toil required to obtain water in this worldly life. This imagery, paired with other described pleasures like shaded trees and abundant fruit, emphasizes a paradise characterized by effortless comfort and perpetual provision, reflecting divine generosity toward those who merited such reward through faith and righteous deeds.

translation: And abundant fruit,
interpretation: This phrase appears in Surah Al-Waqi'ah describing the rewards awaiting the righteous companions of the right hand in Paradise. The mention of 'abundant fruit' signifies the limitless and ever-available provisions of Paradise, contrasting with the limited and seasonal nature of fruits in worldly life. The abundance here conveys not merely quantity but also variety and continuous availability without depletion, symbolizing the generosity of divine reward and the complete satisfaction of desires without any scarcity or labor involved in obtaining them, as everything in Paradise is granted freely as a gift from God to those who earned His pleasure through faith and righteous deeds.

translation: Neither limited [in season] nor forbidden [in reach].
interpretation: This verse describes the fruits of Paradise granted to the righteous (as mentioned in the preceding verses about abundant fruit). Unlike worldly fruits, which are seasonal and often restricted by ownership, scarcity, or social barriers, the fruits of Paradise are perpetually available and freely accessible to all who dwell there, without any limitation of time or any prohibition preventing one from enjoying them. This reflects the boundless and perfect nature of divine generosity in the Hereafter, contrasting sharply with the limitations and inequalities of earthly life.

translation: And couches [of distinction] raised high.
interpretation: This verse is part of the description of the rewards awaiting the righteous (Ashab al-Yamin or the foremost believers) in Paradise, as detailed in Surah Al-Waqi'ah. The 'raised couches' symbolize honor, elevated status, and luxurious comfort bestowed upon the inhabitants of Paradise. Classical commentators have offered multiple layers of meaning: some understand 'raised' literally, referring to the physical height and splendor of the furnishings, reflecting the grandeur of Paradise compared to worldly furnishings. Others interpret the elevation as symbolic of the spiritual rank and nearness to God that believers will attain, with the physical height of the furniture mirroring the loftiness of their status in the Hereafter. Additionally, some scholars suggest that the raised couches indicate ease of access and a vantage point, allowing those seated to survey the beauties of Paradise around them without obstruction. The imagery reinforces the Qur'anic theme that Paradise, unlike earthly abodes, offers forms of pleasure and dignity far surpassing worldly experience, where even furniture becomes a sign of honor and divine favor rather than mere material comfort.

translation: Indeed, We have produced them [the women/companions of Paradise] in a [new] creation.
interpretation: This verse is part of a passage (Surah Al-Waqi'ah, 56:35-38) describing the rewards of Paradise for the righteous, particularly those described as foremost in faith. The verse refers to the companions created for the people of Paradise, indicating that these beings are brought into existence through a special, distinct act of creation—not born in the ordinary worldly manner, but specifically fashioned for the eternal abode. This emphasizes the miraculous and unique nature of Paradise, where everything, including its inhabitants and companions, is perfected and suited for everlasting joy, free from the imperfections and limitations of worldly existence. The following verses describe these companions as virgins, loving, and of equal age, symbolizing purity, devotion, and harmony in the eternal reward prepared for the faithful.

translation: And We have made them virgins,
interpretation: This verse appears in Surah Al-Waqi'ah (56:36), within a passage describing the rewards awaiting the foremost believers in Paradise (56:35-37). It refers to the companions created by God for the people of Paradise, describing them as being made into a special creation—eternally youthful and renewed in purity. Classical commentators such as Ibn Kathir explain that this refers to the righteous women of this world who, upon entering Paradise, are transformed and restored to a state of perpetual virginity and freshness, regardless of their worldly state before death. This is understood as part of the complete renewal of creation in the Hereafter, where physical and spiritual imperfections of earthly life are removed, and believers are granted forms suited to eternal, unblemished joy. The verse emphasizes the theme of divine recreation and the qualitative difference between worldly existence and the perfected, everlasting life of Paradise, where beauty, purity, and love between spouses are made complete and without the cares or circumstances of the temporal world.

translation: Companions of equal age, full of love.
interpretation: This verse describes the righteous believers' companions in Paradise, often understood to refer to the maidens (hur) created especially for the inhabitants of Paradise. The word 'urub (عربا) conveys qualities of passionate love, devotion, and amorous affection toward their husbands, while atraban (أترابا) means they are all of the same age, specifically youthful—traditionally understood as around thirty-three years old, the age of perfect maturity and beauty. This verse is part of a broader description in Surah Al-Waqi'ah of the rewards awaiting the foremost believers (as-sabiqun), emphasizing that Paradise offers companionship that is perfectly matched, loving, and eternally youthful, free from the imperfections, jealousies, and aging processes of worldly relationships. The equality in age among these companions also symbolizes the harmony and freedom from rivalry or hierarchy that characterizes relationships in Paradise, contrasting with earthly relationships that may be affected by differences in age, status, or circumstance.

translation: For the companions of the right hand.
interpretation: This phrase refers to 'Aṣḥāb al-Yamīn' (the People of the Right Hand), a term used in the Qur'an to describe the blessed believers who will receive their book of deeds in their right hand on the Day of Judgment, symbolizing their righteousness and salvation. Being 'of the right hand' is contrasted with 'Aṣḥāb al-Shimāl' (the companions of the left), who represent the sinners and disbelievers destined for punishment. The imagery draws on ancient symbolic associations where the right side represents honor, good fortune, and divine favor, while the left represents disgrace and misfortune. This phrase is used in various Qur'anic contexts to describe the rewards, gardens, and ease that await the righteous, emphasizing divine justice wherein each soul's eternal fate is tied to its deeds in worldly life. It serves as a reminder of accountability and the hope of mercy for those who live according to faith and righteousness.

translation: A multitude from the former [earlier] generations/peoples.
interpretation: This fragment comes from the depiction of the Companions of the Right and the Foremost in Surah Al-Waqi'ah, where the inhabitants of Paradise are categorized into groups. The phrase describes one such group as 'a multitude from the earlier generations' — meaning a great number of the righteous who lived in earlier times, among earlier nations and communities of belief, as opposed to a smaller number from later generations. The verse underscores that righteousness and closeness to God were abundant among the earliest peoples who received and followed divine guidance faithfully, serving as a reminder that salvation is tied not to the era one lives in but to the sincerity of one's faith and deeds. It also subtly reflects on the diminishing proportion of the foremost believers in later times, inviting reflection on the believer's own striving.

translation: And a multitude from the later generations.
interpretation: This verse appears in Surah Al-Waqi'ah as part of the description of the 'Companions of the Right' (Ashab al-Yamin), one of the three groups of people on the Day of Judgment. The verse states that this group will include a multitude (thullah) from both the earlier generations and the later generations of believers. This is significant when contrasted with the foremost group (as-Sabiqun), described earlier in the surah, where it is said there will be 'a multitude from the first generations and a few from the later generations' (56:13-14). The parallel structure but different proportions suggest that while the highest spiritual rank of the foremost becomes increasingly rare as humanity moves further from the Prophetic era, the more moderate righteous path of the Companions of the Right remains equally accessible and populated across all generations, both past and future. This offers a message of hope and inclusivity, affirming that righteousness and salvation remain attainable for people in every era, even as the pinnacle of excellence becomes scarcer with time.

translation: And the companions of the left (misfortune) - what are the companions of the left?
interpretation: This verse comes from Surah Al-Waqi'ah, which describes the three categories of people on the Day of Judgment: the foremost (as-sabiqun), the companions of the right (ashab al-yamin), and the companions of the left (ashab al-shimal). The rhetorical repetition 'what are the companions of the left?' serves as a dramatic device to emphasize the dreadful and incomprehensible nature of their fate, building suspense before the subsequent verses reveal the horrific punishments awaiting them - scorching wind, boiling water, and the shade of black smoke. The term 'left' carries symbolic weight across Semitic and Arabic linguistic traditions, associated with ill-fortune, rejection, and damnation, in contrast to the 'right' which symbolizes blessing and salvation. This verse sets up the moral division of humanity based on their deeds and belief, warning the disbelievers and the sinful of the catastrophic consequences that await them, while using the interrogative structure to provoke reflection and fear in the listener about the gravity of this fate that words alone cannot fully capture.

translation: In a scorching wind and scalding water,
interpretation: This verse comes from Surah Al-Waqi'ah, describing the torment awaiting the 'Companions of the Left'—those who disbelieved and lived heedlessly, denying the Hereafter. The 'samoom' refers to an intensely hot, piercing wind that penetrates the pores, representing an unbearable, inescapable torment that afflicts the body from within. The 'hameem' refers to boiling, scalding water, which the damned are made to drink or which scalds them, symbolizing the complete reversal of worldly comforts they once enjoyed through disbelief and arrogance. Together, these two elements—a tormenting wind and boiling water—paint a vivid sensory image of physical suffering that mirrors the spiritual corruption of those who rejected faith. The verse serves as a stark warning, contrasting sharply with the cool shade and flowing water promised to the righteous elsewhere in the same surah, emphasizing that the pleasures and comforts denied to God in this life will be inverted into their opposite forms of suffering in the next.

translation: And a shade of black smoke.
interpretation: This verse is part of the Qur'an's depiction of the fate of the 'companions of the left' (ashab al-shimal) in the Hereafter, found in Surah Al-Waqi'ah. After describing their torment in scorching wind and boiling water, the verse adds that even the shade meant to offer relief from heat will itself be a source of suffering—not cool, refreshing shade, but a canopy of thick, black, acrid smoke. This imagery subverts the natural expectation of shade as comfort, turning it into an extension of punishment. It reflects a broader Qur'anic rhetorical technique of inverting the familiar symbols of ease and mercy into instruments of torment for those who rejected faith and lived in heedless indulgence, driving home the totality and inescapability of the suffering reserved for them, in stark contrast to the gardens, cool shade, and springs promised to the righteous elsewhere in the same surah.

translation: Neither cool nor pleasant (beneficial).
interpretation: This phrase comes from Surah Al-Waqi'ah, describing the fate of the 'Companions of the Left' — those condemned to Hellfire. It follows the mention of a shadow of black smoke (ظِلٍّ مِنْ يَحْمُومٍ) that envelops them. Normally, shade offers relief from heat, and is associated with comfort and refreshment, such as the cool, pleasant shade enjoyed by the righteous in Paradise. Here, the Qur'an inverts this expectation: the shade in Hell provides no such relief. It is 'not cool' (لا بارد), offering no respite from the scorching heat, and 'not pleasant' or 'generous' (لا كريم), meaning it brings no comfort, blessing, or beneficial quality whatsoever. This phrase emphasizes the utter desolation and hopelessness of the punishment — even the one thing that might be expected to offer some comfort (shade) is itself a source of suffering, underscoring the totality and severity of the torment awaiting those who rejected faith and lived in sin. It serves as a stark contrast to the lush, cool, and generous shades described for the righteous elsewhere in the Qur'an, reinforcing the moral lesson of divine justice and the consequences of one's deeds.

translation: Indeed, before that they were indulged in luxury (given to a life of ease and excess).
interpretation: This verse refers to those destined for punishment, explaining that their downfall was rooted in their worldly privilege: they had lived in comfort, wealth, and self-indulgence before facing judgment. This 'luxury' (israf/taraf) is portrayed throughout the Qur'an not merely as material wealth but as a spiritual condition—one that bred heedlessness, arrogance, and moral complacency. Immersed in ease, they neglected gratitude to God, dismissed warnings from prophets, and prioritized pleasure over accountability. The verse thus serves as a moral diagnosis: unchecked affluence, when divorced from humility and remembrance of God, can corrupt the soul and lead to ultimate ruin, serving as a warning to any community that mistakes comfort for divine favor or immunity from consequence.

translation: And they used to persist in the great sin.
interpretation: This verse describes the habitual wrongdoers—those destined for punishment—who, during their worldly lives, deliberately and repeatedly clung to the gravest of sins, most commonly understood by commentators as shirk (associating partners with God) or outright disbelief in the resurrection and accountability. The term 'al-hinth al-'azim' (the great sin) signifies not a momentary lapse but a persistent, willful pattern of transgression against clear truth. Their obstinacy is highlighted as a key reason for their condemnation: it was not ignorance or a single mistake that doomed them, but a stubborn, continuous choice to reject guidance and indulge in corruption despite having the capacity to repent and reform. This verse serves as a warning that unrepentant persistence in major sin—especially disbelief in divine truths—leads to severe consequences in the Hereafter, contrasting with those who, even if they erred, turned back to God in sincere repentance.

translation: And they used to say, 'When we die and become dust and bones, will we indeed be resurrected?'
interpretation: This verse depicts the skepticism and disbelief of those who denied the Day of Resurrection, expressing their incredulity that after the complete decomposition of the body into dust and bones, life could be restored. Their rhetorical question reflects a worldview limited to material observation, unable to conceive of God's power to recreate what has been utterly destroyed. The Qur'an presents this attitude as emblematic of those who reject the unseen and rely solely on sensory experience, setting up the response that follows in subsequent verses affirming that both earlier and later generations will indeed be gathered and resurrected. The verse highlights a recurring theme in the Qur'an: the denial of bodily resurrection was one of the strongest objections raised by disbelievers against the Prophet's message, and their mockery is quoted to be subsequently refuted by emphasizing divine omnipotence over creation and recreation.

translation: Or our forefathers of old?
interpretation: This phrase is part of the disbelievers' rhetorical questioning about resurrection, found in Surah As-Saffat (37:17). The full context involves the skeptics mockingly asking whether they, and even their long-deceased ancestors, could possibly be resurrected after becoming dust and bones. By invoking 'our forefathers of old,' the disbelievers attempt to make the concept of resurrection seem even more absurd, reasoning that if their own resurrection seems implausible, then certainly the resurrection of ancestors who died long ago and whose remains have completely disintegrated would be even more inconceivable. This reflects a common argument used by those who denied the Day of Judgment in early Islamic discourse—using the vast span of time and multiple generations of death as evidence against the possibility of bodily resurrection. The Quran addresses this skepticism by affirming God's complete power over creation and recreation, emphasizing that the one who created life initially has full capability to restore it, regardless of how much time has passed or how many generations have perished.

translation: Say, [O Muhammad]: Indeed, the former peoples and the later peoples...
interpretation: This verse begins a response to the disbelievers who doubted the reality of resurrection and the Day of Judgment, mentioned earlier in Surah Al-Waqi'ah. The Prophet is commanded to affirm with certainty that all of humanity—both those who lived in ancient times ('the former peoples') and those who will come after ('the later peoples')—are included in God's plan for judgment. The verse emphasizes the universality and inevitability of resurrection, countering the skepticism of those who believed that death marked the absolute end of existence. It sets up the continuation of the verse, which specifies that all these generations will be gathered together at an appointed time on a 'known Day'—the Day of Judgment—underscoring that no one, regardless of era or status, escapes accountability before God. This serves as both a warning to the heedless and a reaffirmation of divine justice that transcends time.

translation: Will surely be gathered together for the appointed time of a known Day.
interpretation: This verse affirms the certainty of the Day of Judgment as a fixed, predetermined event known precisely to God, though hidden from human knowledge. The phrase emphasizes two key theological points: first, that all of humanity—every soul from every era—will be assembled together at this singular moment, erasing the boundaries of time and generation that separate people in worldly life; second, that this gathering is not random or uncertain but occurs at a specific 'appointed time' (miqat), a term also used for fixed points of pilgrimage and covenant, suggesting divine precision and inevitability. The 'known day' refers to God's perfect knowledge of when this Day will occur, even though it remains unknown to creation. This serves as a powerful reminder of accountability: no one escapes this appointment, and the gathering itself symbolizes the ultimate unity of all souls before their Creator for judgment, regardless of when they lived or died. It reinforces the Quranic theme that life's apparent finality in death is not an end, but a prelude to this inevitable reckoning.

translation: Then indeed you, O you who are astray and who deny the truth,
interpretation: This verse is part of Surah Al-Waqi'ah's description of the fate awaiting disbelievers in the Hereafter. It directly addresses those who have gone astray from the path of truth and who deny the reality of resurrection and divine judgment. The verse serves as a transition, setting up the subsequent description (in the following verses) of what awaits such people—namely, eating from the tree of Zaqqum and drinking boiling water, as punishment for their disbelief. The direct address 'O you who are astray and deny' emphasizes personal accountability and serves as a stern warning, contrasting the fate of the deniers with that of the righteous and those brought near to God mentioned earlier in the surah. It underscores the Quranic theme that misguidance (dalal) and active denial (takdhib) of truth are linked—one who strays from guidance often ends up rejecting the very signs that could have corrected their path.

translation: You will surely eat from a tree of Zaqqum
interpretation: This verse is part of a passage in Surah Al-Waqi'ah describing the fate of the people of the left hand (companions of Hell) and those who deny the Day of Judgment. The tree of Zaqqum is described elsewhere in the Qur'an as a bitter, thorny tree that grows from the bottom of Hellfire, with fruit resembling the heads of devils. It serves as a stark contrast to the delicious fruits and pleasures promised to the righteous in Paradise. The forced consumption of this bitter tree represents the torment and humiliation of the disbelievers, who, despite their hunger in the Hereafter, will only find food that increases their suffering rather than satisfies them. This imagery functions as a severe warning to those who reject faith and mock the concept of resurrection and divine justice, emphasizing that earthly denial of spiritual truths leads to eternal consequences of a horrific nature.

translation: And filling with it the bellies [stomachs].
interpretation: This verse is part of a passage describing the fate of the sinners and deniers of the Day of Judgment, who will be forced to eat from the tree of Zaqqum, a tree that grows from the bottom of Hellfire with fruit like the heads of devils. This particular verse emphasizes the torment of being compelled to fill their stomachs with this bitter, thorny food, which brings no nourishment but only pain and suffering. It symbolizes the stark contrast between worldly indulgence in forbidden pleasures and the eternal consequence of such choices, where what once seemed satisfying becomes a source of agony. The imagery serves as a warning about the irreversible nature of divine punishment for those who reject faith and mock the truth, highlighting the physical and spiritual torment awaiting them in the Hereafter.

translation: Then you will drink on top of it from scalding water.
interpretation: This verse is part of a description of the torment awaiting the condemned in Hellfire, following the preceding verses about eating from the tree of Zaqqum. Having filled their bellies with this bitter, thorny fruit, the damned are then forced to drink boiling, scalding water on top of it. This combination intensifies their suffering—rather than quenching hunger or thirst, the scalding water exacerbates their internal agony, tearing at their intestines. The imagery serves as a stark warning about the consequences of disbelief and denial of the Day of Judgment, emphasizing that the torments of Hell are not merely painful but are designed to compound misery upon misery, contrasting sharply with the delights promised to the righteous who drink from pure, pleasant springs in Paradise.

translation: Then you will drink as the drinking of thirsty camels.
interpretation: This verse describes the fate of the disbelievers and deniers in Hellfire, continuing from the preceding verses that depict them eating from the tree of Zaqqum and filling their bellies with it, then drinking scalding water. The comparison to 'al-him' (thirsty, diseased camels afflicted with an insatiable thirst that water cannot quench) conveys an image of desperate, uncontrolled, and ultimately futile consumption. Just as camels suffering from this ailment drink excessively yet never find relief from their thirst, the people of Hell will drink boiling water in a similarly desperate and endless manner, yet it will not satisfy them or ease their torment—rather it will tear apart their insides. This is a vivid and visceral illustration of the horror and hopelessness of their punishment, emphasizing that their suffering is perpetual and without remedy, standing in stark contrast to the delights, pure drinks, and ease afforded to the righteous described elsewhere in the same surah.

translation: This will be their provision on the Day of Recompense.
interpretation: This verse concludes a description of the torment awaiting the deniers and wrongdoers (those of the Left Hand) in the preceding verses of Surah Al-Waqi'ah, which describe scorching wind, boiling water, and the shade of black smoke, along with eating from the bitter tree of Zaqqum. The word 'nuzul' ironically refers to the hospitality or welcoming meal traditionally given to a guest upon arrival, here subverted to mean the torturous reception awaiting the sinners upon their arrival in the Hereafter. This rhetorical device emphasizes the stark reversal of expectations: rather than being welcomed with comfort, they are 'welcomed' with punishment, underscoring the justice of divine recompense (yawm ad-din, the Day of Judgment) where each soul receives exactly what its deeds have earned, with no mercy for those who persisted in disbelief and rejection of truth during worldly life.

translation: We created you — so why do you not affirm the truth?
interpretation: This verse is part of a series of rhetorical questions in Surah Al-Waqi'ah in which God reminds human beings of their origin and dependence upon Him—in creation, in sustenance, in life and death—as proof of His power and the truth of resurrection. By asserting 'We created you,' God points to the self-evident fact of human origination from nothing, which logically should lead to belief in His ability to recreate and resurrect. The rhetorical 'so why do you not believe' (falaw-lā tuṣaddiqūn) is a reproach directed at those who deny the resurrection despite acknowledging, even implicitly, that they did not create themselves. The verse functions as part of a broader argument from creation to resurrection: if God had the power to bring humans into existence from nothing, denying His power to raise them again after death is irrational and inconsistent. It calls on the listener to use reason and observation of their own existence as a path toward faith in the unseen realities of the afterlife.

translation: Have you then considered that which you emit [in semen]?
interpretation: This verse is part of a series of rhetorical questions in which God invites human beings to reflect on the origins of their own existence as proof of divine power and wisdom. By drawing attention to the male emission involved in human reproduction, the verse asks whether it is humanity or God who truly creates and shapes life from this humble substance. The implicit answer is that human beings have no independent role in determining the outcome of conception—it is God alone who forms the embryo, determines its characteristics, and brings it into being as a fully formed person. This serves as an argument against human arrogance and self-sufficiency, reminding people that even the most intimate and seemingly 'natural' biological process is entirely under divine control. By extension, the verse functions as a broader proof for the resurrection: if God can create human life from a mere drop of fluid, He is certainly capable of recreating life after death. The verse thus combines empirical observation of human biology with a theological argument, using a common and universally relatable human experience to point toward the recognition of God's power, wisdom, and the reality of the afterlife.

translation: Is it you who create it, or are We the Creator?
interpretation: This verse appears in Surah Al-Waqi'ah in a series of rhetorical questions posed by God to humanity, directing attention to the mystery of human reproduction and conception. The specific reference is to the sperm-drop (nutfah) that humans emit, and whether human beings themselves are responsible for transforming this substance into a living being with form, consciousness, and life. The rhetorical question demands acknowledgment that despite human involvement in the act of procreation, the actual creative power that shapes a drop of fluid into a complete human being with a soul, organs, and consciousness belongs entirely to God. This is part of a broader argumentative strategy in the surah to establish God's sovereignty through examples drawn from phenomena intimately familiar to human experience—creation, sustenance, water, fire—to counter denial of resurrection and divine power. The verse humbles human pretensions to self-sufficiency by pointing out that even the most intimate and fundamental process of human existence, one's own coming into being, is not within human control or comprehension, but is entirely the work of divine will and power. This serves as a foundation for the surah's larger argument that the God who created humans from nothing is equally capable of resurrecting them after death.

translation: We have decreed death among you, and We are not to be outstripped (prevented or outrun),
interpretation: This verse appears in a passage (Qur'an 56:57-62) where God challenges the disbelievers who doubted the resurrection by pointing to His power as manifest in the very processes of life they witness, particularly in the creation of a human being from a drop of fluid. Here, God asserts that He is the one who has fixed death as an inescapable measure apportioned among all of humanity—no one is exempt, and all is set according to a precise divine ordering, not left to chance. The second clause, 'We are not to be outstripped,' conveys that nothing in creation can overpower, outmaneuver, or impose limits on God's will: He is not subject to any force that could hinder Him from carrying out what He decrees. The verse thus serves as a logical bridge in the argument for resurrection—if God has such absolute and unchallengeable command over the taking of life, determining its exact timing and extent for every creature, then He equally possesses the power to recreate and raise the dead, and nothing can prevent Him from doing so on the Day of Judgment, just as nothing prevented Him from bringing death upon them in the first place. It underscores the futility of denying God's power simply because resurrection seems paradoxically harder to imagine than the mystery of death and original creation, which humans already witness and accept.

translation: [We have decreed death among you] so that We may replace your likenesses and create you in [forms and conditions] that you do not know.
interpretation: This verse comes in the context of Surah Al-Waqi'ah's discussion of death and resurrection, where Allah reminds humanity of His complete power over creation. The verse affirms that death is not an end but a divine decree that serves a purpose within Allah's plan—He has the power to replace the current generation with others resembling them, and to recreate human beings in forms and states entirely unknown to them. This speaks to the Islamic belief in resurrection and the afterlife, emphasizing that just as Allah created humanity initially from nothing, He possesses the same power to recreate them in the Hereafter, in forms and circumstances beyond human comprehension or experience. The verse serves as a rebuttal to those who doubt the possibility of resurrection, pointing to Allah's demonstrated ability to bring about transformation and renewal as evidence that bringing about an afterlife is well within His divine capability. It also carries a deeper philosophical message about the impermanence of worldly existence and human arrogance in assuming they fully understand the nature of creation and existence, when in reality Allah's creative power extends to realms and forms entirely outside human knowledge or imagination.

translation: And you have already known the first creation (your origin), so why do you not reflect/take heed?
interpretation: This verse comes within a passage of Surah al-Waqi'ah addressing those who doubt the resurrection and the power of God to recreate life after death. God reminds humanity that they already have direct knowledge and experience of 'the first creation'—that is, their own origination from nothing, formed from the union of a man and woman, developed in stages, and brought into existence as living beings. Since this initial act of creation was itself a wondrous and improbable act of divine power, it should logically follow that a second creation—resurrection after death—is no more difficult for God to accomplish than the first. The rhetorical question 'why do you not remember/take heed?' is a call to use reason and reflection: if one accepts the reality of their own existence as proof of God's creative power, then denying the possibility of resurrection is inconsistent and reflects heedlessness rather than genuine doubt. The verse thus uses the undeniable fact of human origin as rational evidence for the truth of the afterlife, urging people to draw the obvious conclusion from what they already know rather than willfully ignoring it.

translation: Have you seen that [seed] which you sow?
interpretation: This verse opens a rhetorical sequence in which God directs human attention to the act of farming—one of the most fundamental and seemingly self-controlled human activities—in order to dismantle the illusion of human autonomy. By asking people to 'see' or reflect upon what they plant, the verse sets up the following verses' revelation that it is not the farmer who causes the seed to grow, but God who brings forth life from the soil. The rhetorical question invites the listener to pause and genuinely consider a process they take for granted, moving from the mundane act of scattering seeds to a deeper recognition of divine causation behind growth, germination, and harvest. It is part of a broader Qur'anic strategy of using everyday phenomena—semen, water, fire, vegetation—as proofs of God's power over creation and, by extension, resurrection. The farmer's labor is acknowledged, but the verse insists that labor alone does not create life; it merely plants the conditions, while the actual transformation from seed to sprout to harvest is entirely God's doing.

translation: Is it you who sow it, or are We the sower?
interpretation: This verse is part of a series of rhetorical questions in Surah Al-Waqi'ah in which God directs human attention to the ordinary processes of life—here, agriculture—to demonstrate that ultimate causation belongs to Him alone. While human beings perform the outward act of planting a seed, they have no power over the actual process of germination, growth, and life that transforms that seed into a living plant. The verse strips away the illusion of human self-sufficiency and control, reminding people that even in the most mundane and seemingly human-controlled activities, divine power is the true operative force. By posing it as a question, the verse invites reflection rather than mere assertion, encouraging the listener to recognize their own dependence on God's continuous creative action, and to see every blade of grass as a sign of His sustaining power rather than proof of human mastery over nature.

translation: If We willed, We could surely make it [the crop] into broken debris, and you would remain in astonishment.
interpretation: This verse is part of a sequence in Surat al-Waqi'ah in which God directs human attention to the crops people cultivate, reminding them that it is God—not human effort alone—who causes seeds to grow and produce yield. The verse warns that if God willed, He could instantly turn the ripened, hoped-for harvest into dry, worthless debris, leaving the farmers stunned and lamenting their lost labor and investment. The purpose is to shatter the illusion of human self-sufficiency and control over nature, compelling reflection on total dependence upon divine providence. It also serves as a broader metaphor: all worldly achievements and efforts are contingent upon God's will and could be nullified at any moment, encouraging gratitude, humility, and recognition of God's sovereignty over sustenance and life itself.

translation: Indeed, we are burdened with loss (debt)!
interpretation: This verse is part of a passage in Surah Al-Waqi'ah (56:63-67) where Allah presents a parable about agriculture to prove His power over resurrection and sustenance. Allah asks whether it is He or the farmers who cause the seed to grow. The disbelievers, upon seeing their crops suddenly destroyed despite their labor, would cry out in despair, saying 'Indeed, we are burdened with loss/debt!' This exclamation reflects human helplessness when faced with forces beyond their control, despite their effort and investment. The verse serves as a reminder that all growth, sustenance, and life ultimately depend on Allah's will, not merely human effort, and that the same power that can destroy crops instantly can also bring about resurrection after death. It is a call to recognize divine sovereignty over natural processes that people often take for granted.

translation: Nay, we are deprived!
interpretation: This verse is part of a parable in Surah Al-Waqi'ah where Allah draws attention to the seeds people sow and cultivate. He poses the question of who truly causes the crop to grow—the farmer or Allah. The verse describes the lament of those who, had their crops been destroyed despite their labor, would cry out in despair, declaring themselves ruined and stripped of their livelihood. This exclamation captures human vulnerability and the illusion of self-sufficiency: despite effort, tilling, and investment, the outcome ultimately rests with Allah's will. The verse serves as a rhetorical device to humble people who take credit for sustenance and bounty that is, in truth, bestowed only through divine mercy. It underscores a central Qur'anic theme—that gratitude is owed to Allah alone, since He could withhold blessing at any moment, leaving even the most diligent cultivator with nothing, as a reminder against arrogance and heedlessness regarding the true source of provision.

translation: Have you considered the water that you drink?
interpretation: This verse is part of a series of rhetorical questions in Surah Al-Waqi'ah in which God directs human attention to the most basic elements sustaining life—here, water—to prompt reflection on their origin. The implicit question that follows (as the subsequent verse makes explicit) is whether it is humanity that sends this water down from the clouds or whether it is God. By highlighting something as ordinary and indispensable as drinking water, the verse invites people to recognize that even the most mundane aspects of their survival depend entirely on divine provision rather than human power or ingenuity. It serves as an argument against heedlessness and ingratitude, urging the listener to move from taking sustenance for granted to acknowledging the Creator behind the natural processes that make life possible.

translation: Is it you who sent it down from the rain clouds, or are We the senders?
interpretation: This verse is part of a series of rhetorical questions in Surah Al-Waqi'ah in which God directs human attention to the most basic elements of sustenance—here, rainwater—to demonstrate that despite human ability to observe and even seemingly 'produce' phenomena through technology or effort, the actual origination and control of natural processes belongs to God alone. The clouds (muzn) gather and release water through a complex atmospheric process entirely beyond human command; no one can compel a cloud to release rain at a chosen time or place. By posing this as a direct question, the verse invites reflection and humility, countering human arrogance or forgetfulness regarding the source of life's necessities. It reinforces the broader Qur'anic theme that the natural world, which humans depend upon utterly, operates according to divine will, and that acknowledging this dependency is the beginning of gratitude and faith rather than a presumption of self-sufficiency.

translation: If We willed, We could make it bitter (salty), so why are you not grateful?
interpretation: This verse comes in a sequence from Surah Al-Waqi'ah where Allah reminds humanity of His blessings by posing rhetorical questions about the water they drink. Having just mentioned that He sends down fresh water from clouds, Allah points out that it is entirely within His power to make that same water undrinkably bitter or salty, rendering it useless despite its abundance. The verse emphasizes human dependence on divine will for even the most basic and taken-for-granted necessities of life. Fresh water is not something humans created or can guarantee through their own efforts—its sweetness and drinkability is a continuous grace from Allah. The rhetorical question 'so why are you not grateful?' serves as a rebuke to those who consume Allah's blessings without acknowledging their source or expressing gratitude through worship and obedience. This reflects a broader Quranic theme of using natural phenomena as signs (ayat) that point to Allah's power and generosity, inviting reflection on how fragile and contingent human sustenance truly is, entirely dependent on the Creator's continuous will rather than any inherent right or entitlement.

translation: Have you then considered the fire which you kindle?
interpretation: This verse is part of a series of rhetorical questions in which God directs human attention to everyday phenomena—here, the fire that people strike or kindle for their own use—to prompt reflection on the true source of such blessings. The fire itself depends on wood, which depends on trees, which depend on water and soil, all ultimately originating from God's creative power. The underlying message is that humans merely use and benefit from what God has already provided and sustained; they do not truly create the tree from which the fire-producing wood comes, nor the natural laws that allow combustion. This serves as an argument for recognizing divine power and generosity, leading toward gratitude and the affirmation of God's role as the sole Creator and Sustainer, countering human arrogance or forgetfulness about the origin of the resources they take for granted.

translation: Is it you who bring into being the tree from which it [the fire] is kindled, or are We the Creator?
interpretation: This verse is part of a sequence in Surah Al-Waqi'ah in which God directs human attention to ordinary, everyday phenomena—here, the fire people kindle for use—to demonstrate that ultimate causation and creative power belong to Him alone. By asking rhetorically whether humans created the tree (wood) that fuels their fire, the verse exposes the illusion of human self-sufficiency: people may strike the flint or gather the wood, but they did not bring into existence the natural materials or processes that make fire possible in the first place. The rhetorical question functions as a proof of divine power and a call to humility, reminding the listener that even the most mundane acts of human life depend entirely on God's prior act of creation. It thus reinforces the broader argument of the passage that if God can create such fire from a simple tree, He is equally capable of resurrection and recreation of life after death.

translation: We have made it [the Fire] a reminder and a provision for the travelers (wayfarers).
interpretation: This verse refers to fire, mentioned in the preceding verses about the fire produced from trees (flint/wood), as a sign of God's creative power that should remind human beings of the Hellfire and of divine blessings. The fire serves two purposes: it is 'tadhkirah' (a reminder) — prompting reflection on God's power to generate fire from green, moist wood, and by extension, a reminder of the Fire of the Hereafter — and 'mata'an' (a provision or benefit) for 'al-muqwin', those who travel through desolate, empty lands (wayfarers, travelers in the wilderness) who depend on fire for warmth, light, cooking, and safety. In the harsh desert context of pre-Islamic Arabia, fire was essential for survival during journeys through barren terrain. The verse thus draws attention to an everyday phenomenon — the kindling of fire — as evidence of divine providence and power, encouraging gratitude and reflection on how something as ordinary as fire points to greater truths about God's ability to create, sustain, and also to resurrect and judge, tying this mundane blessing to the larger theological themes of the surah concerning the Hereafter and God's signs in creation.

translation: So glorify the name of your Lord, the Most Great.
interpretation: This verse comes as a concluding command following descriptions of the Hereafter and the fates of the three groups of people (those brought near, the companions of the right, and the deniers). Having established the certainty of these truths, God instructs the Prophet—and by extension all believers—to respond with tasbih (glorification), affirming God's transcendence above any imperfection, partnership, or limitation. The glorification is directed at 'the name' of the Lord, emphasizing that even invoking His name carries sanctity. The attribute 'al-'Azeem' (the Most Great) underscores that the magnitude of what has just been described—resurrection, judgment, paradise, and punishment—is itself a reflection of God's immense power and majesty, and the appropriate human response to contemplating such realities is worshipful humility and praise rather than arrogance or denial.

translation: So I swear by the positions of the stars (or: the setting places of the stars)
interpretation: This verse opens a solemn oath sequence in Surah Al-Waqi'ah, using the vastness and precision of the stars' positions in the cosmos as a witness to the truth that follows—namely, the sanctity and majesty of the Qur'an itself (affirmed in the subsequent verses). The phrase 'مواقع النجوم' points to the exact locations, settings, or orbits of the stars, suggesting the immense, calculated order of the universe. By swearing upon such a grand and mysterious phenomenon, God emphasizes the magnitude of the oath, implying that just as the precise positioning of celestial bodies is a sign of divine power and order, so too is the Qur'an a precisely ordained and noble revelation, not to be doubted or denied. Some commentators also interpret this as alluding to the gradual, piecemeal revelation of the Qur'an itself, mirrored in the dispersed yet purposeful placement of the stars across the sky.

translation: And indeed, it is an oath—if you but knew—a great [oath].
interpretation: This verse follows immediately after God's oath 'by the positions (or settings) of the stars' (56:75), and it serves to underscore the magnitude and solemnity of that oath. By declaring that the oath itself is 'great,' the verse draws attention to the cosmic and symbolic significance of the stars' positions—often understood to refer to the precise, orderly descent and arrangement of the Qur'an's revelation, mirroring the precise order of the cosmos. The phrase 'if you but knew' is a rhetorical device that challenges the listener's limited human understanding, suggesting that the true depth and importance of this oath—and by extension, the sanctity of what follows it (the Qur'an's status as a protected, noble Book, as stated in the subsequent verses)—exceeds ordinary human comprehension. It is a call to humility and reflection, inviting the listener to recognize that the scale of divine knowledge and power behind this oath is far greater than what the human intellect can fully grasp.

translation: Indeed, it is a noble Qur'an,
interpretation: This verse, from Surah Al-Waqi'ah, affirms the exalted and dignified nature of the Qur'an itself. The term 'kareem' (noble/generous) signifies that the Qur'an is a source of immense benefit, honor, and value to humanity, embodying both majesty in its origin and generosity in the guidance, mercy, and wisdom it bestows upon those who engage with it. This declaration comes in a context where the surah has been addressing the nature of revelation and the fate of souls, serving as a defense of the Qur'an's authenticity against those who doubted its divine origin. By describing it as 'kareem', the verse emphasizes that the Qur'an is not merely a book of information but a treasure that elevates and ennobles its reciters and believers, reflecting the generosity of its divine source, Allah, who is Himself described with the same attribute of being Al-Kareem (The Generous/Noble).

translation: In a Preserved Book.
interpretation: This verse refers to the Qur'an's existence in the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz), a transcendent, guarded repository beyond the reach of corruption, alteration, or the touch of impurity. It affirms the divine origin and incorruptibility of the Qur'an, emphasizing that its true source is a sacred, hidden register inaccessible to anyone except through purity, as the following verse clarifies that none can touch it except the purified. This establishes the sanctity of the Qur'an and underscores the spiritual and ritual purity required to properly engage with its truth, distinguishing its heavenly origin from any earthly text.
