Historically, this ruling was abrogated shortly after revelation when it was found that it discouraged genuine seekers, demonstrating the Quran's responsiveness to communal welfare and the flexible application of wisdom in legislation.

translation: Are you afraid to offer charity before your private consultation [with the Messenger]? Then if you do not do so, and Allah has turned to you in forgiveness, then establish prayer and give zakah and obey Allah and His Messenger. And Allah is Acquainted with what you do.
interpretation: This verse follows an earlier command requiring Muslims to give charity before holding a private consultation with the Prophet, a measure meant to discourage frivolous or excessive requests and to honor the Prophet's time while also helping the poor. When this proved burdensome and few complied, the verse acknowledges human hesitation and financial apprehension, then shows Allah's mercy in lifting the obligation. Rather than leaving believers without guidance, it redirects them to the foundational and sustainable acts of worship—prayer and zakah—and renews the call to obedience to Allah and His Messenger. The verse illustrates a broader principle in Islamic legislation: rulings can be context-specific and subject to abrogation or adjustment when they prove impractical, reflecting divine wisdom and compassion rather than rigidity. It also emphasizes that true piety is ultimately expressed through consistent, foundational obligations rather than one-time or situational acts, and closes with a reminder of Allah's complete awareness of human actions and intentions, reinforcing accountability even amid flexibility in law.

translation: Have you not seen those who took as allies a people upon whom Allah is wrathful? They are neither of you nor of them, and they swear to falsehood while they know.
interpretation: This verse addresses the hypocrites in Medina who secretly allied themselves with certain Jewish factions upon whom Allah's wrath had fallen due to their breaking of covenants and opposition to the Prophet. The verse exposes the duplicitous nature of the hypocrites, describing them as belonging to neither camp—not truly part of the believing community despite outward profession of faith, nor genuinely part of those they secretly supported. This state of belonging nowhere reflects the spiritual and social instability of hypocrisy itself. The verse further condemns them for swearing false oaths knowingly, emphasizing that their sin is compounded by deliberate deception rather than ignorance. This passage serves as a warning against divided loyalties that compromise one's integrity and a condemnation of using false oaths to conceal betrayal, highlighting that Allah is fully aware of hidden alliances and the true intentions behind outward claims of loyalty.

translation: Allah has prepared for them a severe punishment. Indeed, evil is what they used to do.
interpretation: This verse serves as a concluding warning typically found after descriptions of hypocrites, disbelievers, or those who betray trusts and conspire against the believing community. It establishes a direct causal link between actions and consequences: divine punishment is not arbitrary but is the just result of deliberate, sustained wrongdoing. The phrase 'prepared' (a'adda) indicates premeditation and certainty—this is not a spontaneous reaction but a fitting, pre-ordained consequence for those who consciously choose corruption. The closing clause, emphasizing the evil nature of 'what they used to do,' underscores habitual, repeated behavior rather than a single lapse, highlighting that it is the persistent pattern of transgression—such as treachery, deceit, or active opposition to truth—that warrants such severe consequence. The verse functions both as a warning to those described and as a moral lesson for the broader audience about the seriousness with which Allah regards betrayal and corruption.

translation: They have taken their oaths as a shield, and so they have hindered [others] from the way of Allah; for them is a humiliating punishment.
interpretation: This verse describes hypocrites who used their professed oaths of faith—sworn declarations of belief and loyalty to Islam and the Muslim community—as a protective cover to conceal their true disbelief and hostile intentions. By hiding behind these false oaths, they avoided suspicion and punishment while actively working to obstruct others from following the path of Allah, whether through spreading doubt, discouraging converts, or aiding the enemies of the believers. The verse exposes the moral corruption of using sacred speech—oaths that invoke Allah's name—as a tool of deception rather than sincerity. Because they exploited religious language for worldly protection while working against the truth, their punishment is described as humiliating (muhin), a fitting consequence that mirrors their own degrading betrayal: just as they debased the sanctity of oaths for selfish ends, they will be disgraced in a manner that strips away the false dignity they sought to maintain through their deception.

translation: Their wealth and their children will not avail them at all against Allah. Those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein forever.
interpretation: This verse addresses the disbelievers and hypocrites, emphasizing that the worldly possessions and offspring in which people place their pride, security, and hope will be utterly powerless on the Day of Judgment to ward off divine punishment. In the worldly life, wealth and children are often sources of status, protection, and leverage, but before Allah's justice, these material and relational assets hold no currency. The verse underscores a central Qur'anic theme: ultimate value lies in faith and righteous deeds, not in worldly accumulation or lineage. Those who rejected truth and relied solely on their worldly standing will find themselves among the permanent inhabitants of Hell, as their rejection of divine guidance, not their lack of resources, determines their fate. This serves as a warning against misplaced trust in material security and a call to prioritize spiritual accountability over worldly attachments.

translation: On the Day when Allah will resurrect them all together, they will swear to Him just as they swear to you [believers], thinking that they have something [to stand on]. Unquestionably, it is they who are the liars.
interpretation: This verse addresses the hypocrites who habitually swore false oaths to the believers in worldly life to conceal their true disbelief and deceit, protecting their standing among the Muslim community. The verse reveals that on the Day of Judgment, this ingrained habit of dishonesty will persist even before God Himself—they will swear false oaths to Him just as they did to people, deluding themselves into believing that such oaths might actually benefit them or provide some cover, as they did in the temporal world. This reflects the depth of their self-deception and moral corruption: lying has become so habitual that they attempt it even in the face of divine omniscience, where all deeds and intentions are fully known and oaths are utterly futile. The closing declaration—that they are truly the liars—serves as God's final, authoritative verdict, exposing their self-delusion and affirming that no falsehood can stand before divine judgment. The verse underscores the theme that hypocrisy and deceit, however successful in deceiving other humans, cannot deceive God and will be definitively unmasked in the Hereafter.

translation: Satan has gained mastery over them and made them forget the remembrance of Allah. Those are the party of Satan. Unquestionably, the party of Satan - they are the losers.
interpretation: This verse describes the spiritual condition of hypocrites who align themselves with falsehood and deception rather than truth. By allowing Satan to dominate their hearts, they become heedless of God, abandoning prayer, gratitude, and moral accountability. Their identity shifts from belonging to the community of believers to belonging to 'the party of Satan' - a designation that signifies not merely wrongdoing but a fundamental allegiance and orientation of the soul. The verse establishes a stark binary: there is the party of God, characterized by remembrance, sincerity, and truth, and there is the party of Satan, characterized by forgetfulness, deception, and alliance with falsehood. The declaration that this party will be the 'losers' is emphatic, using the particle 'ألا' (unquestionably) to remove any doubt. This loss is not necessarily worldly - the hypocrites may appear successful, wealthy, or socially secure - but it is existential and ultimate, referring to their loss of true success in the sight of God and in the Hereafter. The verse serves as a warning that forgetting God is not a neutral or passive state but an active spiritual capitulation that has Satan as its architect and eternal loss as its consequence.

translation: Indeed, those who oppose Allah and His Messenger - those will be among the most humbled.
interpretation: This verse establishes a decisive principle regarding those who set themselves in active opposition to divine guidance and the Prophet's authority, using the term 'yuhaddoona' which conveys the sense of being in a state of hostility or contention, as if drawing a boundary line against God's will. The verse promises that such opposition, however powerful or defiant it may appear in worldly terms, ultimately results in humiliation and disgrace rather than the honor or victory the opposers might seek. This reflects a broader Quranic theme that true strength and honor come only through alignment with divine truth, while resistance to it - regardless of apparent worldly power, wealth, or social standing - leads to spiritual and often worldly abasement. The verse serves as both a warning to those contemplating opposition to the Prophet's message and as reassurance to believers that steadfast enemies of truth will face ultimate humiliation, reinforcing the Quranic pattern of inverting worldly expectations of power and status based on one's relationship to divine guidance.

translation: Allah has decreed: 'I will surely prevail, I and My messengers.' Indeed, Allah is Strong and Mighty.
interpretation: This verse affirms a divine, irrevocable decree that truth and its bearers will ultimately triumph over falsehood and its adherents, regardless of apparent setbacks or the strength of opposing forces. The pairing of God with His messengers signifies the inseparable bond between divine will and prophetic mission—the victory of the messengers is, in essence, the manifestation of God's own victory, since they act as His instruments on earth. The attributes 'Strong' (qawiyy) and 'Mighty' (ʿazeez) are invoked here as the guarantee behind this promise: God's power is not contingent on worldly circumstances, numbers, or temporary adversity. This serves as a source of reassurance for believers facing persecution or discouragement, reminding them that historical struggles between truth and falsehood are temporary tests, while the final outcome is already settled by divine decree. It also carries a warning to those who oppose the messengers, framing their resistance as futile against an irresistible cosmic order established by God Himself.

translation: You will not find a people who believe in Allah and the Last Day having affection for those who oppose Allah and His Messenger, even though they were their fathers, their sons, their brothers, or their clan. Those are the ones in whose hearts He has written faith and strengthened them with a spirit from Him. And He will admit them to gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein eternally. Allah is pleased with them, and they are pleased with Him - those are the party of Allah. Unquestionably, the party of Allah - they are the successful.
interpretation: This verse establishes that true faith requires a higher loyalty that transcends even the closest bonds of kinship and family when those relationships conflict with one's commitment to God and His message. The verse suggests that genuine believers cannot maintain real love or alliance with those who actively oppose the fundamental truths of faith, regardless of blood ties - whether parents, children, siblings, or tribe. This is not a call to abandon family relationships entirely, but rather speaks to where one's ultimate allegiance and emotional/spiritual solidarity must lie when there is direct conflict between faith and kinship loyalty. The 'writing of faith in hearts' and being 'strengthened with a spirit' describes an internal transformation that creates this capacity for prioritizing principle over blood relation - it is not merely intellectual belief but a deep spiritual reinforcement. The verse concludes by defining this quality as membership in 'the party of Allah' (hizb Allah), suggesting that true community and belonging is defined by shared commitment to divine truth rather than by tribal, ethnic, or familial bonds. This creates an alternative basis for social cohesion and identity - one built on shared values and submission to God rather than blood ties - and promises that this reorientation of loyalty, though potentially costly in worldly terms, leads to ultimate success and divine pleasure, mutually reciprocated between the believer and God.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth glorifies Allah, and He is the Almighty, the All-Wise.
interpretation: This opening verse establishes the theme of divine transcendence and sovereignty that pervades the entire surah. The declaration that everything in the heavens and earth glorifies God speaks to a cosmic reality in which all of creation—whether through conscious worship, as with humans and angels, or through the very nature of their existence and the natural laws they follow, as with celestial bodies, mountains, and all created things—bears witness to and acknowledges its Creator. This glorification is not merely verbal praise but encompasses the entire mode of existence of created things, which by their order, design, and function testify to the perfection and majesty of their Maker. The pairing of 'Al-Aziz' (the Almighty, the Mighty One who cannot be overcome) with 'Al-Hakim' (the All-Wise, whose every act and decree is rooted in perfect wisdom) establishes the dual nature of divine authority: God's power is not arbitrary or capricious but is always exercised in accordance with supreme wisdom. This sets the tone for what follows in the surah, which calls believers to sincere faith, charitable spending, and steadfastness, reminding them that the One who commands such things is both supremely powerful and infinitely wise, and thus worthy of complete trust and obedience.

translation: It is He who expelled those who disbelieved among the People of the Book from their homes at the first gathering. You did not think that they would leave, and they thought that their fortresses would protect them from Allah; but Allah came upon them from where they did not expect, and He cast terror into their hearts, so that they destroyed their houses with their own hands and the hands of the believers. So take a lesson, O you who have insight.
interpretation: This verse refers to the expulsion of the Jewish tribe of Banu al-Nadir from Medina following their treachery against the Muslim community and their conspiracy with the Quraysh and other enemies of the Prophet Muhammad. Despite their strong fortifications, which gave them a false sense of security, divine intervention instilled such fear in their hearts that they dismantled their own homes rather than leave them intact for the Muslims, aided by the believers themselves in this destruction. The verse highlights several theological and moral lessons: first, that worldly defenses—whether military, economic, or social—cannot shield those who oppose divine will; second, that psychological terror, described as being 'cast into the hearts,' is portrayed as a direct act of God's power, demonstrating that unseen forces can overturn seemingly secure human plans; third, the irony that the Banu Nadir themselves participated in their own downfall by destroying their own homes, symbolizing self-inflicted ruin resulting from betrayal and arrogance. The closing call 'so take a lesson, O you who have insight' invites believers to reflect deeply on the causes and consequences of this event—namely, the folly of relying on material strength instead of righteousness and faith, and the certainty that divine justice will prevail over human treachery, regardless of how secure one's position may appear.

translation: And if not that Allah had decreed for them exile, He would have punished them in this world; and for them in the Hereafter is the punishment of the Fire.
interpretation: This verse refers to the Jewish tribe of Banu Nadir in Medina, who broke their covenant with the Muslims and were subsequently besieged and expelled from their homes. The verse explains that exile was itself a form of divine punishment, decreed by God as a consequence of their betrayal, and emphasizes that had God not ordained this particular fate for them, He would have inflicted a harsher worldly punishment upon them. It underscores the theological principle that worldly punishments, however severe they may seem, are in fact a mercy compared to the fuller measure of justice reserved for the Hereafter, where unrepented wrongdoing will meet with the punishment of Hellfire. The verse thus serves as both a historical commentary on a specific event and a broader warning about the consequences of treachery and disbelief, affirming that divine justice operates across both temporal and eternal dimensions.

translation: That is because they defied Allah and His Messenger. And whoever defies Allah - then indeed, Allah is severe in punishment.
interpretation: This verse establishes a causal link between opposition to divine authority and the consequences that follow. The term 'shaqqaqu' (defied/opposed) conveys the image of a deep rift or schism—going beyond mere disagreement to active hostility against the guidance brought by Allah and His Messenger. The verse functions as a general principle rather than being limited to a specific historical incident: it explains why certain punishments or defeats befell those who resisted the Prophet's message, while simultaneously serving as a timeless warning. The repetition of 'man yushaqiq Allah' (whoever defies Allah) universalizes the statement, making it applicable beyond the immediate context to anyone who chooses active resistance against divine will. The severity mentioned is not arbitrary cruelty but reflects the gravity of rejecting truth after it has been made clear, emphasizing that opposition to Allah's message carries real consequences, both worldly and otherworldly. This serves theologically to reinforce the idea that divine justice is proportionate and purposeful, not capricious, and that defiance against clear guidance is treated with utmost seriousness precisely because of what is at stake for both the individual and the community.

translation: Whatever palm trees you cut down or left standing on their roots, it was by Allah's permission, and so that He might disgrace the defiantly disobedient.
interpretation: This verse was revealed in the context of the Muslims' siege of Banu Nadir, when some palm trees were cut down and burned as part of the military campaign, causing controversy among the Muslims and criticism from the Jews who accused them of corruption and destruction. The verse clarifies that whether the trees were cut down or left standing, both actions occurred with divine sanction and as part of a deliberate strategy, not mere destruction or inconsistency. It establishes that wartime measures, even ones that might seem harsh like destroying property, can be legitimate when they serve a just cause and are not arbitrary. The deeper purpose stated here—to humiliate the transgressors—shows that such actions were meant to break the resolve and morale of those who broke their covenants and opposed the Muslim community, demonstrating that worldly consequences can serve as a form of divine recompense for disobedience and treachery. The verse also underscores the principle that human actions, when undertaken within the bounds of what is permitted, fall under divine will and wisdom, even when their immediate wisdom is not obvious to all observers.

translation: And whatever Allah restored to His Messenger from them - you did not spur any horse or riding camel for it, but Allah gives His messengers power over whom He wills. And Allah is over all things competent.
interpretation: This verse addresses the distribution of wealth and property acquired from the Banu Nadir, a Jewish tribe expelled from Medina, without any military engagement by the Muslims. The key theological point being established is that this gain (fay') came about through Allah's direct intervention rather than through the Muslims' own martial effort - no cavalry charges or camel-mounted raids were needed to secure it. This distinction matters because it establishes a different legal category for this wealth compared to spoils of war (ghanimah) won through combat, which explains why the subsequent verses lay out a different distribution scheme, with greater allocation to the Prophet for communal purposes rather than primarily to the fighters. The verse also makes a broader theological point about divine sovereignty: that Allah grants authority and dominion to His messengers over others according to His own will and wisdom, not merely as a reward for human effort or strategy. This serves to remind the believers that ultimate causation and power rest with Allah, and that apparent victories or acquisitions of power are manifestations of divine will working through history, reinforcing humility and gratitude rather than pride in military prowess among the believers.

translation: Whatever Allah has restored to His Messenger from the people of the towns [as spoils without battle] belongs to Allah and to the Messenger, and to [his] near relatives, orphans, the needy, and the wayfarer, so that it will not be a perpetual distribution among the rich among you. And whatever the Messenger gives you, take it; and whatever he forbids you, refrain from. And fear Allah; indeed, Allah is severe in punishment.
interpretation: This verse establishes a principle of economic justice regarding wealth acquired without conflict, ensuring it does not circulate exclusively among the wealthy but is distributed to benefit the broader community, including the vulnerable. It also affirms the authority of the Prophet's commands and prohibitions as binding guidance for believers, linking obedience to him with piety and the awareness of divine accountability. The underlying message emphasizes both social equity and the necessity of following prophetic guidance as a safeguard against the concentration of power and resources in the hands of a few.

translation: [This is] for the poor emigrants who were expelled from their homes and their properties, seeking bounty from Allah and [His] approval, and supporting Allah and His Messenger. Those are the truthful.
interpretation: This verse honors the Muhajirun (emigrants) who left Mecca for Medina, sacrificing their homes, wealth, and security for the sake of their faith. It establishes a criterion for true faith: genuine believers are those whose actions align with their words, demonstrated through real sacrifice rather than mere verbal profession. Their migration was not motivated by worldly gain but by seeking divine favor and supporting the cause of Islam. The verse also serves a broader purpose in the Qur'anic discourse on charity distribution, specifically addressing why the poor Muhajirun deserve priority consideration among those receiving support from war spoils (fay'), since they lost everything in their commitment to faith. The phrase 'those are the truthful' sets a standard of sincerity—true belief is proven through willingness to endure hardship and loss for principle, not merely claimed through speech.

translation: And those who, before them, had settled in the home [of emigration] and in faith - they love those who emigrated to them and find not any want in their breasts of what they [the emigrants] were given, but give them preference over themselves, even though they were in privation. And whoever is protected from the stinginess of his soul - it is those who will be the successful.
interpretation: This verse praises the Ansar (the Helpers of Medina) for their exemplary generosity, brotherhood, and selflessness toward the Muhajirun (the Meccan emigrants who fled persecution). It establishes a profound ethical principle: true faith manifests not merely in belief but in concrete acts of altruism, particularly in overcoming the natural human instinct toward self-preservation and material attachment. The verse identifies freedom from greed and stinginess (shuhh al-nafs) as the defining characteristic of success in the eyes of God, suggesting that the struggle against one's own acquisitive and self-interested tendencies is a central spiritual battle. By linking communal solidarity, hospitality to the displaced, and inner purification from miserliness, the verse frames economic and social generosity as inseparable from genuine faith, making the Ansar a timeless model for how a community of believers should treat those who arrive seeking refuge and support, even at personal cost.

translation: And those who came after them say, 'Our Lord, forgive us and our brothers who preceded us in faith, and do not place in our hearts any resentment toward those who believed. Our Lord, indeed You are Kind and Merciful.'
interpretation: This verse describes the prayer of later generations of believers who follow the early Muslims (the Muhajirun and Ansar). It establishes several important theological and ethical principles: first, it affirms the continuity of faith across generations, showing that the community of believers extends through time and that later believers maintain spiritual solidarity with their predecessors through prayer and seeking forgiveness on their behalf. Second, it explicitly instructs believers to guard their hearts against rancor, envy, or ill-will (ghill) toward fellow believers, particularly addressing potential tensions that could arise between different groups within the early Muslim community, such as between the earlier converts and those who came later, or between different factions that had historical grievances. This request to purify the heart of resentment is presented as something to actively pray for, acknowledging that such negative feelings are a natural human tendency that requires divine assistance to overcome. The verse thus serves as a model for communal unity and brotherhood in faith, teaching that genuine faith should be accompanied by love and goodwill toward other believers rather than jealousy or bitterness, especially regarding matters of precedence or status in religious achievement. The invocation of God's attributes as Ra'uf (Kind/Gentle) and Rahim (Merciful) at the conclusion emphasizes that achieving this purity of heart is only possible through divine grace and compassion.

translation: Have you not seen those who are hypocrites saying to their brethren among the People of the Book who disbelieved, 'If you are expelled, we will surely leave with you, and we will never obey anyone against you, and if you are fought, we will surely help you'? But Allah testifies that they are indeed liars.
interpretation: This verse exposes the hollow nature of hypocrisy by revealing the gap between words and action. The hypocrites of Madinah pledged solidarity with the disbelieving Jewish tribe facing expulsion, promising to share their exile, resist outside pressure, and fight alongside them if attacked. These were empty promises made to bolster the confidence of their allies and perhaps to maintain a secret alliance against the Muslim community. Allah Himself intervenes to certify their falsehood before events even unfold, demonstrating that hypocrisy is fundamentally a disease of insincerity where grand declarations of loyalty mask self-interest and cowardice. The verse teaches that true alliance and loyalty are tested in moments of real sacrifice, and those who speak boldly in private counsel often abandon their promises when actual risk materializes, as is confirmed in subsequent verses where the hypocrites fail to follow through on any of these pledges.

translation: If indeed they are expelled, they will not go forth with them; and if indeed they are fought, they will not aid them. And even if they should aid them, they will surely turn their backs [in flight]; then they will not be aided.
interpretation: This verse exposes the hollow nature of the hypocrites' pledges of support to their allies among the disbelievers (referring to the Banu Nadir or similar groups who were confident of backing from the hypocrites and other Jewish tribes). The verse reveals in successive conditional clauses the worthlessness of such alliances: the hypocrites will not share in exile, will not fight alongside them, and even in the unlikely event they do join the battle, they will flee rather than fight, leaving their allies utterly without aid. This serves as a broader lesson about the unreliability of alliances built on hypocrisy and self-interest rather than true faith and conviction, and reassures the believers that the schemes and promised support behind their enemies are illusory and will ultimately fail them when truly tested.

translation: You [believers] are more fearsome in their hearts than Allah. That is because they are a people who do not understand.
interpretation: This verse describes the psychological state of the hypocrites and disbelievers who, despite claiming or professing faith in God, harbor a greater practical fear of the believers than of Allah Himself. This paradox reveals the shallowness and corruption of their belief: true faith should produce fear and reverence of God above all else, yet their hearts are dominated by worldly concerns—fear of worldly power, military strength, or social consequences from the Muslim community rather than fear of divine accountability. The verse attributes this inverted sense of priorities to their lack of understanding (la yafqahun), meaning they fail to truly comprehend the nature of God, His power, and the reality of the unseen. Their fear is directed at what is visible and immediate (the believers' strength) rather than at what is ultimate and unseen (God's power and judgment). This serves as a broader lesson about the nature of genuine faith versus superficial or hypocritical religiosity—true believers are meant to fear God above all creation, and failing to do so, even while outwardly professing belief, indicates a fundamental deficiency in comprehension and spiritual insight.

translation: They will not fight against you all together except in fortified towns or from behind walls. Their might among themselves is great; you would think them united, but their hearts are divided. That is because they are a people who do not reason.
interpretation: This verse addresses the hypocrites and their allies who outwardly appear strong and unified but lack the courage and conviction to engage in direct, open confrontation with the believers. Their apparent solidarity is superficial; in reality, their loyalties are fragmented and their internal disputes are fierce, as each faction pursues its own worldly interests rather than a shared higher purpose. The Qur'an attributes this disunity and cowardice to their lack of true understanding (aql)—they fail to comprehend the deeper truths of faith, loyalty, and purpose, relying instead on fear, self-interest, and tribal or factional loyalty. The verse serves as a reminder that true strength and unity come from sincere faith and shared conviction, not from mere appearances or coalitions built on fear and self-preservation.

translation: Like the example of those shortly before them: they tasted the evil consequence of their affair, and for them is a painful punishment.
interpretation: This verse continues the depiction of the Banu al-Nadir, a Jewish tribe expelled from Medina for breaking their covenant with the Muslims and conspiring against them. The Qur'an draws a parallel between their fate and that of an earlier group who met a similar end shortly before—understood by most exegetes to be the pagan Meccans defeated at the Battle of Badr, or alternatively the Banu Qaynuqa, another Jewish tribe expelled earlier for treachery. Both groups, despite their worldly power and alliances, suffered humiliation and loss in this world as a direct consequence of their own actions—their arrogance, betrayal, and rejection of truth. The verse serves as a warning: the worldly punishment they experienced is not the end of their reckoning, for a more severe, painful punishment awaits them in the Hereafter. The repetition of 'wobal amrihim' (the evil consequence of their affair) emphasizes that calamity was not random misfortune but the direct, deserved outcome of their own choices and betrayals. This serves as a broader lesson to the believers and to all who might consider treachery or disbelief: worldly defeat is often a precursor to eternal consequence, and history repeats its patterns of justice for those who violate trust and truth.

translation: [Their example is] like that of Satan when he says to man, 'Disbelieve.' But when he disbelieves, he says, 'Indeed, I am disassociated from you. Indeed, I fear Allah, Lord of the worlds.'
interpretation: This verse draws an analogy comparing the hypocrites—who encouraged their allies to resist and fight but then abandoned them when real danger arrived—to Satan's relationship with humanity. Satan eagerly whispers temptation, urging disbelief and disobedience, exploiting human weakness to lead people astray. Yet once the person has fallen into sin or disbelief and must face the consequences, Satan disowns them entirely, revealing his true nature as a deceiver with no loyalty or genuine investment in those he misleads. His claim of 'fearing Allah' is not born of sincere faith but rather an acknowledgment of Allah's absolute power and the reality of divine judgment, from which even Satan cannot escape. The verse exposes the pattern of those who incite others toward wrongdoing—they offer false promises of support, exploit trust, and ultimately abandon their followers to bear the full weight of consequences alone. It serves as a warning against following any voice, human or otherwise, that calls toward disobedience of Allah, for such guidance is hollow and the one who gave it will vanish the moment accountability arrives, leaving the deceived to face ruin in isolation while the deceiver seeks only self-preservation.

translation: So the end of both of them was that they are in the Fire, abiding therein eternally. And that is the recompense of the wrongdoers.
interpretation: This verse concludes the parable of Satan and the one he deceives, illustrating the ultimate fate shared by both the tempter and the tempted when the latter follows misguidance of their own will. It serves as a sobering reminder that seduction into disbelief or wrongdoing, whether from an external source like Satan or from one's own base desires, leads to a shared destiny of eternal punishment. The verse underscores the Qur'anic principle of personal accountability: despite being led astray by an external force, the one who chooses to follow remains responsible for their choice, and divine justice applies equally to both the misleader and the misled. It stands as a warning against trusting deceptive promises and highlights the eternal consequences of injustice and wrongdoing (zulm) in its broadest sense—toward oneself, others, or God.

translation: O you who have believed, fear Allah. And let every soul look to what it has put forth for tomorrow - and fear Allah. Indeed, Allah is Acquainted with what you do.
interpretation: This verse calls believers to cultivate taqwa (God-consciousness) as the foundation of a righteous life, and then urges self-examination: each person should reflect on the deeds, intentions, and spiritual provisions they are sending ahead for 'tomorrow'—understood as the Day of Judgment or the afterlife. The repetition of the command to fear Allah frames this self-accounting within constant awareness of divine oversight, while the closing affirmation that Allah is fully aware of all actions reinforces accountability. The verse thus establishes a cycle of introspection and moral responsibility: true faith requires not only belief but ongoing evaluation of one's conduct in light of ultimate accountability before God.

translation: And do not be like those who forgot Allah, so He made them forget themselves. It is they who are the rebellious transgressors (al-fasiqun).
interpretation: This verse draws a direct causal link between spiritual neglect and existential self-loss. To 'forget Allah' means to live heedless of one's accountability to a higher moral order, to let worldly distraction, pride, or desire eclipse the remembrance of one's Creator. The punishment described is not external but deeply internal: as a consequence, such people 'forget themselves'—they lose authentic self-knowledge, lose sight of their own purpose, moral compass, and spiritual nature. This self-forgetting manifests as a kind of inner emptiness or alienation, where one acts without true self-awareness, chasing illusions of identity through status, wealth, or ego rather than through one's relationship with the divine. The verse suggests that remembrance of God (dhikr) is not merely a ritual duty but is actually the very foundation of authentic self-understanding—without it, the human being becomes a stranger to their own soul, adrift and purposeless, which is the essence of 'fisq' (moral transgression/deviance). The verse thus serves as both warning and invitation: neglecting the sacred leads to self-estrangement, while remembering God is the path to true self-realization and integrity.

translation: Not equal are the companions of the Fire and the companions of Paradise. The companions of Paradise - they are the attainers of success.
interpretation: This verse establishes a decisive moral and existential distinction between two ultimate destinies, rejecting any notion of moral relativism or equivalence between those who choose disbelief and corruption versus those who choose faith and righteousness. It comes as a conclusion to themes often discussing hypocrisy, the abandonment of divine remembrance, and the consequences of forgetting God - as seen in the preceding verses of Surah Al-Hashr. The statement serves as a definitive judgment that the path of righteousness and the path of transgression cannot lead to the same end, countering any worldly argument that outcomes in this life might be the only measure of success. By declaring the people of Paradise as 'al-fa'izun' (the triumphant, the successful ones), the verse redefines true success not in terms of worldly power, wealth, or status, but in terms of ultimate spiritual attainment and eternal salvation. This serves both as a warning to those who might equate worldly achievement with true success, and as a consolation and motivation for believers who may face hardship, persecution, or disadvantage in worldly terms while remaining steadfast in faith.

translation: Had We sent down this Qur'an upon a mountain, you would have seen it humbled and split asunder from fear of Allah. And these examples We present to the people that they might reflect.
interpretation: This verse employs a powerful hyperbole to convey the immense weight, majesty, and spiritual power of the Qur'an's message. Mountains are universally recognized symbols of strength, permanence, and immovability. By stating that even such a solid, mighty mountain would crumble and be humbled if it could comprehend and receive the Qur'an, the verse highlights the profound seriousness and transformative force of divine revelation. The implicit contrast being drawn is with the human heart, which, despite being far more fragile than a mountain, often remains hardened, indifferent, or heedless when confronted with the same revelation. This serves as a rebuke and a call to self-reflection: if an inanimate mountain would respond with awe and submission, why do human beings—endowed with reason and spiritual capacity—fail to be moved by the same words? The verse closes by explaining the purpose of such vivid parables: they are given so that people might engage in deep reflection (tafakkur) about the nature of existence, their relationship with the divine, and the weight of the responsibility that comes with receiving guidance. It is ultimately a call to humility, awe, and genuine contemplation rather than heedless or superficial engagement with sacred truth.

translation: He is Allah, other than whom there is no deity, Knower of the unseen and the witnessed. He is the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.
interpretation: This verse opens a sequence (in Surah Al-Hashr) that systematically establishes the absolute oneness and transcendence of God through His names and attributes. By affirming that He alone knows both the hidden (ghayb) and the visible (shahada) realms, the verse establishes His comprehensive knowledge as a foundation for His sole right to worship. The pairing of 'La ilaha illa Huwa' with knowledge of all realms of existence - seen and unseen - emphasizes that true divinity requires total awareness, something no created being possesses. The verse then grounds this transcendent, all-knowing God in mercy through the names Al-Rahman and Al-Raheem, suggesting that divine power and knowledge are inseparable from divine compassion. This sets the tone for the subsequent verses that will enumerate many more of God's names, creating a theological portrait where majesty and mercy coexist as complementary aspects of the same divine reality, rather than contradictory forces.

translation: He is Allah, besides whom there is no deity—the Sovereign, the Holy, the Source of Peace, the Granter of Security, the Overseer, the Almighty, the Compeller, the Supreme in Greatness. Glory be to Allah, far above what they associate with Him.
interpretation: This verse, from Surat al-Hashr, presents a cluster of divine names that together establish God's absolute uniqueness, authority, and transcendence. Each name builds a dimension of His majesty: as Sovereign (al-Malik), He possesses ultimate dominion over all creation; as Holy (al-Quddus), He is utterly pure and free from any imperfection or need; as the Source of Peace (al-Salam), He is the origin of all safety and wholeness, untouched by flaw; as the Granter of Security (al-Mu'min), He affirms truth and grants faith and safety to His creatures; as the Overseer (al-Muhaymin), He witnesses and safeguards all things; as the Almighty (al-'Aziz), He is invincible in power; as the Compeller (al-Jabbar), His will overrides all resistance and He restores what is broken; and as Supreme in Greatness (al-Mutakabbir), He alone deserves true greatness, beyond any creature's claim to it. The verse closes with a declaration of God's transcendence over any partners ascribed to Him, directly refuting polytheism. The rhetorical effect of stacking these names is to overwhelm the listener with the sheer scope of divine perfection, making clear that no being—human or otherwise—can share in these attributes, and that true monotheism (tawhid) requires recognizing God's singular, incomparable nature in both His essence and His actions.

translation: He is Allah, the Creator, the Originator, the Fashioner; to Him belong the most beautiful names. Whatever is in the heavens and the earth glorifies Him, and He is the Exalted in Might, the Wise.
interpretation: This verse presents a progressive description of divine creative power through three linked attributes: al-Khaliq (the Creator, who brings things into existence from nothing), al-Bari' (the Originator, who shapes and differentiates matter into distinct forms), and al-Musawwir (the Fashioner, who gives each creation its unique form and identity). This sequence mirrors the actual process of creation - conception, initiation, and detailed formation - emphasizing that God's creative act is not a single simple event but a comprehensive, purposeful process. The mention of 'the most beautiful names' (al-asma al-husna) points to the Islamic theological tradition of the 99 names of God, each reflecting a different facet of His perfection. The verse concludes by noting that all of creation - everything in the heavens and earth - naturally glorifies and testifies to God, suggesting an inherent, cosmic orientation toward the divine that exists independent of human acknowledgment. The closing pairing of 'the Exalted in Might' (al-'Aziz) with 'the Wise' (al-Hakim) balances God's absolute power with His perfect wisdom, indicating that His might is never arbitrary but always guided by wisdom and purpose.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. O you who believe! Do not take My enemy and your enemy as allies, showing affection to them, while they have disbelieved in what has come to you of the truth, expelling the Messenger and yourselves [from your homes] because you believe in Allah, your Lord. If you have come out to strive in My cause and to seek My pleasure, [do not take them as allies]. You confide to them affection, while I am most knowing of what you conceal and what you declare. And whoever does so among you has certainly strayed from the straight path.
interpretation: This verse addresses the believing community's relationship with those who are openly hostile to the faith and its adherents, warning against forming secret bonds of loyalty or affection with such enemies merely for worldly ties, convenience, or kinship. The historical occasion involved a companion who sent a letter to the Meccan polytheists warning them of the Prophet's plans, motivated by concern for family members who remained in Mecca, despite his personal faith and loyalty to Islam. The verse establishes a principle that faith and true allegiance to Allah supersede other loyalties when those other parties actively work against the faith community and have expelled believers for their belief alone. It emphasizes divine omniscience—Allah knows what is concealed in hearts as well as what is openly declared—making clear that hidden alliances or sympathies cannot escape His knowledge. The verse does not prohibit kindness or justice toward non-believers in general, as clarified in subsequent verses of the same chapter, but specifically addresses those who have demonstrated active enmity, aggression, and persecution against believers because of their faith. The concluding warning that such conduct constitutes straying from the 'straight path' underscores that secretly allying with active enemies of faith against one's own community is considered a serious deviation, as it undermines the trust, solidarity, and security necessary for the believing community to survive and practice their faith openly.

translation: If they gain dominance over you, they would be enemies to you, and extend against you their hands and their tongues with evil, and they wish that you would disbelieve.
interpretation: This verse, from Surat al-Mumtahanah, warns the believers against taking certain hostile disbelievers as allies or confidants, clarifying the true nature of such enemies despite any outward appearances of friendliness. It teaches that if these adversaries were given the opportunity or power over the believers, their underlying hostility would be revealed through both physical harm ('their hands') and verbal abuse, slander, or false accusations ('their tongues'). The deepest desire of such enemies is not merely worldly harm but the spiritual destruction of the believers—wishing for them to abandon their faith altogether. The verse serves as a caution about discernment in alliances, urging believers to recognize genuine threats to their faith and community regardless of superficial courtesies, and to understand that loyalty and trust should be reserved for those who do not harbor such enmity toward their core beliefs and well-being.

translation: Never will your relatives or your children benefit you; on the Day of Resurrection He will separate between you. And Allah is Seeing of what you do.
interpretation: This verse addresses the believers who had ties of kinship with disbelievers, emphasizing that on the Day of Judgment, worldly bonds of family and lineage will hold no weight in determining one's salvation. Each soul will be judged solely on the basis of its own deeds and faith, severing the reliance people place on familial connections or offspring to intercede or protect them from divine accountability. The mention that Allah is 'Seeing' of what they do reinforces that every action is recorded and observed, underscoring personal responsibility over inherited or relational status. This serves as a call to prioritize one's relationship with God and righteous conduct over worldly attachments, since on that Day, even the closest relationships will be rendered powerless to intervene.

translation: There has already been for you a good example in Abraham and those with him, when they said to their people, 'Indeed, we are disassociated from you and from whatever you worship besides Allah. We have denied you, and there has appeared between us and you animosity and hatred forever until you believe in Allah alone' - except for the saying of Abraham to his father, 'I will surely ask forgiveness for you, but I have not [power to do] anything for you against Allah.' [They said], 'Our Lord, upon You we have relied, and to You we have returned, and to You is the final destination.'
interpretation: This verse establishes the principle of al-wala' wal-bara' (loyalty and disavowal) as a foundational model for believers' relationships with those who reject monotheism, using Abraham as the exemplar of uncompromising devotion to Allah alone. The declaration of eternal enmity toward idolatry is not about personal hatred toward individuals but about absolute rejection of shirk (associating partners with Allah) and the false objects of worship themselves. The exception clause regarding Abraham's promise to pray for his father's forgiveness is significant—it acknowledges natural filial compassion while simultaneously setting a boundary: Abraham immediately clarifies he has no power to save his father from Allah's judgment, meaning his prayer was conditional on his father's potential guidance, not an endorsement of maintaining spiritual allegiance with disbelief. This nuance teaches that personal kindness and hope for a relative's salvation must never be confused with religious loyalty or validation of their disbelief. The verse closes with a model of tawakkul (complete reliance on Allah) and inabah (turning back to Him), showing that the harshness of disavowal from falsehood is balanced by humble submission and trust in Allah's ultimate judgment, reminding believers that human relationships and outcomes are ultimately surrendered to Allah's will, not determined by human effort alone.

translation: Our Lord, make us not a trial for those who disbelieve, and forgive us, our Lord. Indeed, You are the Exalted in Might, the Wise.
interpretation: This verse is part of the supplication of Ibrahim (Abraham) and Isma'il (Ishmael) as they built the Ka'bah. The request not to be made 'a trial' (fitnah) for the disbelievers carries a dual meaning: first, a plea that the believers not be oppressed or persecuted in a way that would cause disbelievers to feel vindicated in their rejection of faith, or that would make believers themselves fall into temptation and abandon their faith under pressure; and second, a plea that the believers not be given such worldly power or dominance over disbelievers that it becomes a means of arrogance or injustice, which could itself become a trial corrupting the believers' character. The juxtaposition with seeking forgiveness acknowledges human fallibility even among the righteous and prophets, teaching that no one, however elevated in status, should feel secure from sin or trial, but must constantly seek Allah's mercy. The closing invocation of Allah's attributes as 'the Exalted in Might' and 'the Wise' reinforces that true power and protection from trials, as well as the wisdom to grant forgiveness appropriately, belong solely to Allah, teaching believers to rely on Him rather than their own strength or righteousness when facing opposition or adversity.

translation: Indeed there is for you in them an excellent example for whoever hopes for Allah and the Last Day. And whoever turns away - then indeed, Allah is the Free of need, the Praiseworthy.
interpretation: This verse refers back to the example of Abraham and those with him, who openly disavowed their idolatrous people and declared enmity toward falsehood for the sake of God. The verse establishes that true faith requires more than private belief - it demands a visible stance, a willingness to break with one's community, kin, or tradition when they stand opposed to God's truth, just as Abraham did even toward his own father. This exemplary conduct is framed as a model specifically for 'whoever hopes for Allah and the Last Day' - meaning it is not a universal social prescription but a spiritual criterion tied to one's ultimate orientation and eschatological hope. The closing statement that God is 'Free of need, the Praiseworthy' serves as a reminder that human loyalty or disloyalty, adherence or turning away, adds nothing to God's completeness; God's praiseworthiness is intrinsic and not contingent on human recognition. This serves both as a comfort to believers who sacrifice worldly ties for faith - their sacrifice is not for God's benefit but their own spiritual gain - and as a warning to those who turn away, since their rejection diminishes nothing of God's majesty but only harms themselves.

translation: Perhaps Allah will put, between you and those among them [the disbelievers] whom you have taken as enemies, affection. And Allah is competent, and Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation: This verse, revealed in the context of the Prophet's dealings with the Meccan polytheists, particularly in relation to the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah and the restrictions on marital and social ties with hostile disbelievers, offers hope and reassurance to the believers. It teaches that enmity between peoples is not necessarily permanent and that Allah has the power to transform hostility into friendship and love. This points to a broader principle in Islamic thought: human relationships, even those marked by deep conflict, are not fixed by divine decree into perpetual hatred. Political and social circumstances can change, and former adversaries may become reconciled, even embrace the same faith, as indeed happened when many of the Quraysh who had fought against the Muslims later accepted Islam and became integrated into the Muslim community as brothers. The verse closes with a reminder of Allah's power (qadir) to bring about such change, and His attributes of forgiveness and mercy (ghafur rahim), suggesting that the resolution of enmity is tied to divine mercy extended both to believers who were once harsh toward disbelieving relatives, and to disbelievers who may eventually find guidance. The verse ultimately counsels patience and trust in Allah's wisdom regarding the future of human relationships, discouraging believers from assuming that current hostilities are eternal or beyond hope of reconciliation.

translation: Allah does not forbid you from those who have not fought you because of religion and have not driven you out of your homes - that you deal kindly and justly with them. Indeed, Allah loves those who act justly.
interpretation: This verse establishes a foundational principle of Islamic ethics regarding relations with non-Muslims, clarifying that hostility is not the default stance toward all non-believers. Rather, the prohibition on friendship and alliance applies specifically to active aggressors—those who wage war against Muslims or forcibly expel them from their homes. Peaceful non-Muslims who pose no threat are to be treated with kindness (birr) and justice (qist), two distinct but related virtues: birr implies generosity, compassion, and good treatment, while qist implies fairness and equity in dealings. The verse closes by affirming that Allah's love is specifically directed toward those who uphold justice, universalizing justice as a value that transcends religious boundaries and applies to all human relationships, including with those outside the faith community. This reflects a broader Qur'anic ethic that ties legitimate conflict to specific acts of aggression rather than to religious difference itself.

translation: Allah only forbids you from those who fought you because of religion and expelled you from your homes and supported [others] in your expulsion - [He forbids] that you make allies of them. And whoever makes allies of them, then it is those who are the wrongdoers.
interpretation: This verse clarifies the preceding command of kindness toward non-Muslims by drawing a precise legal and moral boundary: the prohibition against befriending or allying with disbelievers is not universal but specifically targeted at those who actively waged war against Muslims because of their faith, forcibly drove them from their homes, and conspired or assisted others in that expulsion. This refers historically to the Meccan polytheists who persecuted the early Muslim community, forcing the migration to Medina, and who continued hostilities afterward. The verse establishes that hostility is warranted only toward active aggressors, not toward all non-believers as a category—reinforcing that Islamic ethics distinguish between peaceful coexistence and necessary opposition to those who persecute based on religious identity. The closing warning that those who ally with such aggressors are 'wrongdoers' (zalimun) underscores the gravity of betraying the community's trust by siding with those who have proven themselves enemies through violent action, not merely through differing belief. This establishes a principle of reciprocity and justice: enmity is earned through hostile deeds, not assigned based on religious difference alone.

translation: O you who have believed, when believing women come to you as emigrants, examine them. Allah is most knowing of their faith. Then if you know them to be believers, do not return them to the disbelievers; they are not lawful [wives] for them, nor are they lawful [husbands] for them. But give the disbelievers what they have spent [on their dowries]. And there is no blame upon you if you marry them when you have given them their due compensation. And hold not to marriage bonds with disbelieving women, but ask for what you have spent and let them ask for what they have spent. That is the judgment of Allah; He judges between you. And Allah is Knowing and Wise.
interpretation: This verse was revealed in the context of the treaty of Hudaybiyyah, which stipulated that Muslims fleeing to Medina would be returned to the Meccan disbelievers, while those fleeing in the opposite direction would not be returned. The verse addresses the specific case of women who emigrated to Medina professing faith, clarifying that despite the general terms of the treaty, women could not be sent back because doing so would risk placing a believing woman under the authority or marital bond of a disbeliever, which is deemed incompatible given the dissolution of marriage ties between believers and disbelievers. The command to 'examine' them refers to verifying the sincerity of their professed faith, not forcing them to prove an inner state irrefutably, since only Allah truly knows what is in hearts. The verse establishes a practical and financially fair process: the dowry money the disbelieving husband had spent on her is to be compensated, preventing economic injustice from the separation. Similarly, if Muslim women are divorced or separated from their unbelieving spouses, any dowry a Muslim man spent should be reclaimable from the former disbelieving husbands, and vice versa, maintaining reciprocity and fairness between the two communities despite their political and religious opposition. The prohibition against holding onto marriage ties with disbelieving women underscores the broader principle that the Qur'an articulates: marriage is a bond rooted in shared faith and communal loyalty, and the rupture of religious unity necessitates the rupture of marital unity as well. This verse, therefore, is not merely a historical directive tied to a specific treaty but encodes a theological statement about the nature of the Muslim community as one bound together by faith commitments that supersede tribal, marital, or economic relations with those outside the fold, while still insisting on principles of equity and fairness even toward the disbelieving party.

translation: And if any of your wives have gone from you to the disbelievers and you subsequently gain [something in return], then give those whose wives have gone the equivalent of what they had spent. And fear Allah, in whom you are believers.
interpretation: This verse addresses the practical and financial arrangements that arose during the early Islamic period when marriages crossed the boundary between the Muslim community and the disbelievers, particularly in the context of treaties like Hudaybiyyah. When a wife left a Muslim husband to join the disbelievers, that husband lost the dower (mahr) and provisions he had invested in the marriage. The verse establishes a principle of communal compensation: if the Muslims later receive spoils, booty, or compensation from the other side as part of dealings with the disbelievers, a portion should be set aside to reimburse the husband who suffered this loss, matching what he originally spent. This reflects the Quran's broader concern with equity and mutual responsibility within the community, ensuring that individuals are not left to bear disproportionate financial burdens resulting from circumstances tied to the larger political and social conflict between believers and disbelievers. The closing exhortation to 'fear Allah, in whom you are believers' ties this financial regulation back to faith itself, reminding the believers that even in matters of property and marriage, their conduct must be grounded in taqwa (God-consciousness) and trust in divine justice, rather than purely in personal grievance or retaliation against the other party's actions.

translation: O Prophet, when believing women come to you pledging allegiance to you that they will not associate anything with Allah, nor steal, nor commit unlawful sexual intercourse, nor kill their children, nor bring forth a slander they have invented between their hands and their feet, nor disobey you in what is right - then accept their pledge and ask forgiveness for them of Allah. Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation: This verse establishes the terms of a formal covenant between women who embraced Islam and the Prophet Muhammad, outlining foundational ethical and spiritual commitments expected of believing women within the early Muslim community. The conditions listed - rejecting polytheism, avoiding theft, sexual immorality, infanticide (a reference to the pre-Islamic practice of killing unwanted children, particularly daughters), fabricating lies, and disobedience in righteous matters - reflect core moral obligations that parallel those required of men, affirming women's inclusion as full moral agents within the faith community with direct accountability to God and the Prophet. The phrase 'slander invented between their hands and their feet' is traditionally understood as a reference to falsely attributing children to husbands who are not their biological fathers, protecting lineage and family integrity. By instructing the Prophet to accept their pledge and seek forgiveness for them, the verse emphasizes that conversion and commitment to these principles granted women a formal, dignified status in the community, with access to divine mercy regardless of past transgressions, underscoring Islam's egalitarian spiritual framework at the moment of entry into the faith.

translation: O you who have believed, do not take as allies a people with whom Allah has become angry. They have despaired of the Hereafter just as the disbelievers have despaired of those in the graves.
interpretation: This verse warns believers against forming close alliances or loyalties with those who have earned divine wrath due to their persistent disbelief and rejection of truth. The description that such people 'have despaired of the Hereafter' indicates a deep spiritual state where they have abandoned any hope or belief in resurrection, judgment, and accountability. The comparison to disbelievers despairing of 'those in the graves' refers to the pagan Arabs' conviction that the dead would never be resurrected—a complete severance from any belief in an afterlife. By grouping the people who incurred Allah's anger with this hopeless disposition, the verse suggests that their rejection of faith has become so entrenched that they live only for worldly life, having no stake in eternal matters. The warning to believers is thus both spiritual and practical: aligning with such people risks adopting their despair and worldly orientation, compromising one's own faith commitments and the integrity of the believing community's values and loyalties.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth glorifies Allah, and He is the Almighty, the All-Wise.
interpretation: This opening verse establishes the theme of divine transcendence that runs throughout the surah. The declaration that all creation—animate and inanimate, in the heavens and on earth—engages in glorification of Allah points to a cosmic order in which everything, by its very nature and existence, testifies to its Creator. This is not merely verbal praise but an ontological state: all things, through their obedience to the laws governing them and their inherent design, proclaim the perfection and transcendence of Allah above any imperfection or partnership. The pairing of 'Al-Aziz' (the Almighty, the Invincible) with 'Al-Hakim' (the All-Wise) balances power with wisdom, indicating that Allah's dominion over creation is not arbitrary but infused with purpose and precision. This sets the tone for the surah's subsequent calls to believers for sincerity, unity, and striving in His cause, since the One who commands such universal glorification is both supremely powerful and supremely wise in His commands.

translation: O you who have believed, why do you say what you do not do?
interpretation: This verse is a rebuke directed at believers who make claims, promises, or declarations of commitment—particularly regarding faith, jihad, or righteous deeds—without following through with corresponding action. It establishes a core Islamic ethical principle: that integrity requires alignment between speech and deed. The verse (part of a passage that continues to condemn this behavior as greatly hated by God) serves as a call for sincerity, warning against hypocrisy and empty rhetoric. Historically, it is understood to relate to believers who pledged eagerness for battle or sacrifice in the name of faith but then hesitated or failed to act when the moment came. More broadly, it instructs all believers that true faith must be demonstrated through consistent action, not merely verbal affirmation, and that accountability before God includes being judged for the gap between one's words and one's conduct.

translation: Great is hatred in the sight of Allah that you say what you do not do.
interpretation: This verse addresses the moral failing of hypocrisy between word and deed, specifically condemning those who make claims, promises, or declarations of faith and commitment without following through with corresponding action. In its immediate context, this verse follows a call to believers to fight in Allah's cause and precedes it, chastising those who professed eagerness for righteous deeds or jihad but failed to act when the time came. More broadly, it establishes a fundamental Islamic ethical principle that speech must be matched by sincere action—that faith is not merely verbal affirmation but requires tangible commitment and consistency between one's claims and one's conduct. The verse elevates this inconsistency to the level of being deeply hateful to God, suggesting that empty words, false promises, or professed intentions that go unfulfilled constitute a serious spiritual and moral defect, undermining trust, integrity, and the authenticity of one's relationship with the divine. This teaching has been understood to apply broadly to all forms of hypocrisy, including making religious commitments, vows, or pledges that one does not intend to keep, and serves as a call for believers to ensure alignment between their professed values and their actual behavior.

translation: Indeed, Allah loves those who fight in His cause in a row (line) as if they were a solid structure.
interpretation: This verse praises believers who stand united and disciplined when striving for a righteous cause, likening their unity and steadfastness to a tightly bonded, unshakeable building. The imagery emphasizes that strength comes not merely from numbers but from cohesion, order, and mutual support—each individual acting as a firmly placed brick that reinforces the whole structure. It teaches that collective discipline, solidarity, and unwavering commitment to a just cause are qualities beloved by God, extending beyond literal warfare to any communal effort requiring unity and steadfast resolve in the face of adversity.

translation: And [mention] when Moses said to his people, 'O my people, why do you harm me while you certainly know that I am the messenger of Allah to you?' And when they deviated, Allah caused their hearts to deviate. And Allah does not guide the defiantly disobedient people.
interpretation: This verse highlights the pain and injustice Moses endured from his own people despite their knowledge of his prophethood, drawing a parallel to the Prophet Muhammad's own experience with disbelievers and hypocrites among his community. The verse establishes a spiritual principle: when people willfully turn away from truth after recognizing it, Allah does not forcibly guide them, but rather allows their hearts to continue in the deviation they themselves chose. This is not depicted as an arbitrary punishment but as a natural consequence of persistent moral and spiritual rebellion (fisq)—a sealing of the heart that results from repeated choices to reject guidance. The verse serves as both a warning against disbelief and a reminder that divine guidance is contingent upon sincere receptivity; those who are fundamentally defiant and rebellious place themselves beyond the reach of guidance through their own actions and attitudes, not through any injustice on Allah's part.

translation: And [mention] when Jesus, son of Mary, said, 'O Children of Israel, indeed I am the messenger of Allah to you confirming what came before me of the Torah and bringing good tidings of a messenger to come after me, whose name is Ahmad.' But when he came to them with clear evidences, they said, 'This is obvious magic.'
interpretation: This verse affirms the continuity of prophetic revelation, portraying Jesus as both a confirmer of the Mosaic law and a herald of a final messenger yet to come, identified by the name Ahmad, understood by Muslim scholars as referring to Muhammad. Linguistically, 'Ahmad' shares the same root as 'Muhammad,' both derived from the Arabic root for praise, suggesting a spiritual and etymological link between the prophets. The verse reflects the Islamic belief in a unified chain of monotheistic prophecy, where each messenger validates and builds upon the message of those before him, emphasizing the unbroken succession from Moses to Jesus to Muhammad. The rejection of Jesus's clear signs as 'obvious magic' underscores a recurring Qur'anic theme: that many people, despite witnessing undeniable proofs, dismiss divine truth due to disbelief, arrogance, or attachment to inherited tradition. This rejection mirrors the pattern of resistance faced by earlier prophets and foreshadows the similar rejection Muhammad would face from his own people, reinforcing the Qur'an's broader narrative of human stubbornness in the face of divine guidance and the recurring struggle between truth and denial throughout prophetic history.

translation: And who is more unjust than one who invents a lie against Allah while he is being invited to Islam? And Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people.
interpretation: This verse addresses the severe moral and spiritual culpability of someone who fabricates falsehoods about God even after being presented with the truth of Islam and invited to accept it. The rhetorical question underscores that rejecting guidance through deliberate deception, especially after having access to clear invitation and knowledge, represents one of the gravest forms of wrongdoing. The verse establishes a principle about divine guidance: it is not arbitrarily withheld, but rather those who persist in willful injustice—particularly the injustice of lying about God—effectively close themselves off from receiving guidance. This reflects a broader Qur'anic theme that guidance is connected to sincerity and openness to truth; those who knowingly distort or deny it, especially after being called to it, place themselves beyond the reach of divine direction as a consequence of their own choices and moral corruption.

translation: They want to extinguish the light of Allah with their mouths, but Allah will perfect His light, even though the disbelievers dislike it.
interpretation: This verse addresses the futile attempts of disbelievers to suppress or negate the truth and guidance that Allah has revealed, likened to the impossible task of extinguishing a great light merely by blowing breath from one's mouth. The imagery conveys the weakness and insignificance of human opposition when measured against divine truth—mere words, propaganda, or mockery cannot diminish what Allah has ordained to spread and illuminate. The verse reassures believers that no matter how fierce the opposition, the message of Islam, representing divine guidance and truth, is destined to prevail and be perfected by Allah's will. It encapsulates a broader theological theme found in the Qur'an: that human schemes against divine purpose are ultimately powerless, and history itself will vindicate the truth even if those who reject it find this outcome distasteful or resist it with all their might. The verse thus serves both as a consolation to the early Muslim community facing persecution and as a timeless assertion of the inevitability of truth's triumph over falsehood.

translation: It is He who sent His Messenger with guidance and the religion of truth to make it prevail over all religion, even though the polytheists detest it.
interpretation: This verse affirms the divine purpose behind the mission of Prophet Muhammad ﷺ: he was not sent merely to convey a personal message, but to establish a complete way of life—encompassing guidance (al-huda, meaning knowledge and proof) and the religion of truth (din al-haqq, meaning practical implementation and worship)—that would ultimately triumph over all other systems of belief and ideology. The 'prevailing' (yuzhirahu) spoken of here is understood by many scholars not as the eradication of all other religions from existence, but as establishing Islam's truth, evidence, and ultimate dominance in argument and civilizational strength, such that its superiority becomes manifest wherever it is fairly presented. The verse closes by acknowledging the inevitable resistance of the mushrikin (polytheists), who oppose this truth due to vested interests, arrogance, or attachment to inherited customs. This phrase recurs in the Qur'an as a divine promise of ultimate vindication—reassuring believers that opposition and hostility, however intense, cannot ultimately overturn the truth God has sent, and that history itself will bear witness to Islam's enduring moral and intellectual triumph.

translation: O you who have believed, shall I guide you to a transaction that will save you from a painful punishment?
interpretation: This verse introduces a call to the believers, framing faith and righteous action as a form of 'trade' or 'transaction' with God—a metaphor drawn from commerce that would have resonated deeply with the Quraysh, who were known traders. The rhetorical question creates anticipation and engages the listener's attention before revealing what follows (belief in God and His Messenger, and striving in His cause with wealth and lives, as the subsequent verses explain). The underlying message is that true profit and security from suffering—both worldly and especially in the Hereafter—are not found in ordinary material transactions but in a spiritual exchange: offering devotion, sacrifice, and struggle in God's path in return for salvation from painful punishment and the attainment of forgiveness and eternal reward. This framing elevates faith and good deeds to the level of the most vital and rewarding investment a person can make, redirecting the believers' understanding of value and profit from the temporal to the eternal.

translation: [It is that] you believe in Allah and His Messenger and strive in the cause of Allah with your wealth and your lives. That is better for you, if you only knew.
interpretation: This verse presents the path to salvation and success as consisting of two essential, interconnected components: sincere faith (iman) in Allah and His Messenger, and active struggle (jihad) in His cause using both material resources and personal effort. The pairing of 'wealth and lives' indicates that true devotion requires the willingness to sacrifice what one values most tangibly (possessions) and what one values most intimately (one's very self or life). The verse frames this not as a burden but as a transaction of supreme benefit to the believer—'that is better for you'—suggesting that the immediate worldly costs of such commitment are vastly outweighed by spiritual and ultimate rewards. The closing phrase 'if you only knew' implies a critique of short-sightedness or lack of deeper understanding among those who hesitate, suggesting that true knowledge or insight into the nature of existence and the afterlife would make this sacrifice an obvious and rational choice rather than a difficult one. This verse is often understood as emphasizing that faith is not merely a passive internal belief but must manifest through active, costly commitment and struggle in service of a transcendent purpose.
