translation: He will forgive you your sins and admit you into gardens beneath which rivers flow, and pleasant dwellings in gardens of eternity [Eden]. That is the great attainment.
interpretation: This verse presents the reward promised to those who believe in God and His Messenger and strive in His cause with their wealth and selves, as mentioned in the preceding verse. The forgiveness of sins is mentioned first, establishing that spiritual purification precedes the attainment of paradise—believers are cleansed of their past wrongdoings as a prerequisite to entering eternal bliss. The gardens with flowing rivers symbolize abundance, life, and continuous blessing, contrasting with the transient and often arid struggles of worldly existence. The mention of 'pleasant dwellings' emphasizes not just abstract spiritual reward but a holistic, sensory, and comfortable existence in the afterlife, addressing both physical and spiritual needs. 'Gardens of Eden' invokes the primordial paradise, suggesting a return to an original, uncorrupted state of being, free from the trials and tribulations of earthly life. The phrase 'that is the great attainment' underscores that this reward surpasses any worldly success, wealth, or achievement, framing the entire verse as the ultimate incentive for sacrifice and devotion. The verse thus functions rhetorically to motivate believers by presenting an eternal, tangible, and deeply satisfying reward as the culmination of faith and effort, reframing worldly sacrifice as a minor and temporary cost compared to everlasting gain.

translation: And [He will grant you] another [blessing] which you love: help from Allah and a near victory. So give good tidings to the believers.
interpretation: This verse comes directly after Allah offers believers a 'trade' that saves them from painful punishment—striving in His cause with wealth and lives. Here, as an additional incentive beyond the eternal reward of Paradise promised earlier, Allah adds a worldly, immediate blessing: divine support and a victory that is near at hand, widely understood by commentators to refer to the conquest of Mecca. This reflects a recurring Qur'anic pattern where spiritual commitment is met not only with otherworldly reward but also with tangible, worldly vindication, reinforcing the believers' trust that sincere struggle and sacrifice in faith will not go unanswered even within their own lifetimes. The command to 'give good tidings' underscores the role of the Prophet, and by extension believers themselves, as bearers of hope and encouragement to the community, strengthening resolve and morale in times of hardship by emphasizing that triumph is not distant or abstract but imminent and certain by God's decree.

translation: O you who have believed, be supporters of Allah, as when Jesus, the son of Mary, said to the disciples, 'Who are my supporters for Allah?' The disciples said, 'We are supporters of Allah.' Then a faction of the Children of Israel believed, and a faction disbelieved. So We supported those who believed against their enemy, and they became dominant.
interpretation: This verse calls on believers to emulate the steadfast loyalty and active commitment shown by the disciples of Jesus when he asked who would stand with him in the cause of God. Their unequivocal answer—'We are supporters of Allah'—represents a model of faith translated into collective action and solidarity. The subsequent division among the Children of Israel, between those who believed and those who disbelieved, illustrates how faith commitments inevitably create distinctions within a community, testing sincerity and resolve. Allah's support for the believers who remained loyal, leading to their eventual triumph over their adversaries, serves as a divine promise and encouragement to the Muslim community: true, active support for God's cause—manifested through unity, sacrifice, and moral courage—will be met with divine aid and the ascendance of truth over falsehood, even amid internal struggles and opposition.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth glorifies Allah, the Sovereign, the Most Holy, the Exalted in Might, the Wise.
interpretation: This opening verse of Surah Al-Jumu'ah establishes a cosmic framework in which all creation—animate and inanimate, visible and invisible—is engaged in constant, spontaneous glorification (tasbih) of God, affirming His transcendence above any imperfection or limitation. The four divine attributes invoked here are carefully chosen to convey a comprehensive picture of God's nature: al-Malik (the Sovereign) establishes His absolute dominion over all existence, emphasizing that nothing lies outside His authority; al-Quddus (the Most Holy/Pure) signifies that He is utterly free from any flaw, partner, or deficiency, sanctified beyond human comprehension; al-'Aziz (the Exalted in Might) speaks to His invincible power and majesty, that He cannot be overcome or opposed; and al-Hakim (the Wise) indicates that all His actions and decrees are rooted in perfect wisdom, nothing occurring without purpose. By opening the surah this way, before addressing the specific guidance given to the Prophet and the community that follows, the verse situates human worship and obedience within a much larger reality—one where the entire universe already testifies to God's perfection. This serves as a rhetorical and spiritual preparation for what follows in the surah, particularly regarding the responsibilities given to the Muslim community (including the injunctions about the Friday prayer later in the chapter), reminding believers that their worship is not an isolated act but part of the natural order of the entire cosmos, which already submits to and praises its Creator.

translation: It is He who has sent among the unlettered people a Messenger from themselves, reciting to them His verses, purifying them, and teaching them the Book and Wisdom, although they were before in clear error.
interpretation: This verse highlights the significance of Prophet Muhammad's mission to the Arabs, who were largely unlettered and without a prior scripture-based tradition. It emphasizes four key functions of his prophethood: reciting divine revelation, spiritual purification, and teaching both the literal text of scripture (the Book) and its deeper wisdom and practical application (the Hikmah). The mention that they were previously 'in clear error' underscores the transformative nature of revelation, suggesting that guidance does not depend on prior literacy or civilization but on divine selection and grace. The verse also carries a universal implication, as the Messenger's role extends beyond the immediate Arab community to all of humanity, framing the Qur'an as a means of intellectual and moral awakening for any people regardless of their starting condition.

translation: And [He sent him] to others among them who have not yet joined them. And He is the Exalted in Might, the Wise.
interpretation: This verse continues from the preceding verse, which describes God sending an unlettered Messenger among the unlettered people (the Arabs) to recite His verses, purify them, and teach them the Book and wisdom. This verse extends that mission beyond the immediate audience of the Prophet's first followers to 'others who have not yet joined them' — understood by many classical commentators to refer to all future generations of believers, including non-Arabs, who would come to embrace Islam across time and geography. It signals the universal and transtemporal nature of the Prophet's message, not confined to a single community or era. The closing affirmation that God is 'the Exalted in Might, the Wise' underscores that this expansive, unfolding spread of guidance is orchestrated by divine power and wisdom, not mere historical accident — God's might ensures the message's endurance and reach, while His wisdom ensures its perfect suitability for every people who receive it in their own time.

translation: That is the bounty of Allah which He gives to whom He wills, and Allah is the possessor of great bounty.
interpretation: This verse affirms the doctrine of divine grace and sovereignty: whatever blessing, favor, prophethood, guidance, or special gift is bestowed upon any individual or community is not earned through merit alone but is granted according to Allah's own will and wisdom. It serves as a reminder against arrogance or entitlement, encouraging humility and gratitude, since the distribution of such favor rests entirely with Allah, whose generosity is vast and limitless. The verse also implicitly counters envy or resentment toward others who receive blessings, since all bounty ultimately flows from the same divine source, which is boundless and beyond human measure.

translation: The likeness of those who were entrusted with the Torah, then did not uphold it, is as the likeness of a donkey carrying volumes [of books]. Wretched is the likeness of the people who denied the signs of Allah. And Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people.
interpretation: This verse offers a pointed critique of those who possess sacred knowledge but fail to internalize or act upon it. The image of a donkey carrying books is a vivid metaphor: the animal bears the weight of the texts without any comprehension of their content or benefit from their wisdom. Similarly, those referenced here—understood to be certain among the Children of Israel—had been given the Torah, a repository of divine guidance, yet reduced their relationship with it to mere custodianship rather than genuine understanding and practice. The verse suggests that knowledge without application or sincere engagement is hollow; the mere possession of scripture, without living by its teachings, renders one no different from a beast of burden performing a mechanical task. This serves as a broader warning to all who receive revelation—including the Muslim community receiving the Qur'an—that the value of scripture lies not in ceremonial reverence or rote memorization alone, but in internalizing its message and allowing it to transform conduct and belief. The concluding statement that Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people underscores that this failure to engage authentically with divine guidance is itself a form of injustice (zulm), and that guidance is not forced upon those who willfully turn away from truth after it has been made clear to them.

translation: Say: 'O you who are Jews, if you claim that you are the allies (friends) of Allah, to the exclusion of other people, then wish for death, if you are truthful.'
interpretation: This verse challenges a claim of exclusive religious privilege by proposing a definitive test: if the Jews of Medina truly believed themselves to be God's chosen and favored people destined for Paradise above all others, they should logically desire death, since it would lead them swiftly to that promised reward. The Qur'an points out the contradiction between their claims of special divine favor and their actual attachment to worldly life, which (as the following verses state) made them 'the people most attached to life.' The verse thus exposes a gap between professed belief and genuine conviction, suggesting that true certainty about one's spiritual standing with God would naturally produce indifference to death rather than fear of it. It serves as a broader principle about how claims of special status before God should be matched by corresponding attitudes and behavior, not merely asserted as an identity marker without existential consequence.

translation: And they will never wish for it [death], ever, because of what their hands have put forth. And Allah is Knowing of the wrongdoers.
interpretation: This verse addresses those among the Children of Israel who claimed exclusive favor with God, asserting that paradise was reserved for them alone. The Qur'an challenges them that if their claim were true, they should wish for death to hasten their reward, yet they would never do so because of their awareness of their own sins, transgressions, and the corruption of their deeds and beliefs. Their refusal to wish for death reveals an inner recognition of guilt and wrongdoing, contradicting their outward claims of righteousness and divine favoritism. The verse closes with a reminder that God's knowledge encompasses all wrongdoers, serving as both a warning and an affirmation that no hidden sin or false claim escapes divine awareness, holding people accountable for the discrepancy between their professed faith and their actual conduct.

translation: Say, 'Indeed, the death from which you flee will surely meet you. Then you will be returned to the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, and He will inform you of what you used to do.'
interpretation: This verse addresses the human instinct to avoid confronting mortality, often through distraction, denial, or the pursuit of worldly pleasures and power. The Qur'an confronts this evasion directly, declaring that death is an inescapable appointment that will find every soul regardless of efforts to flee it. The verse then shifts focus beyond death itself to what follows: a return to God, described as the Knower of both the unseen (ghayb) and the witnessed (shahadah) realms—emphasizing that nothing, whether hidden intentions or visible deeds, escapes divine knowledge. The ultimate purpose of this reminder is accountability; death is not an end but a transition to a reckoning where one's entire life of action will be disclosed and evaluated. This serves as a moral corrective, urging believers to live with consciousness of their eventual return rather than in denial of mortality, and to recognize that avoiding the thought of death does not grant immunity from its reality or from the justice that follows it.

translation: O you who have believed, when the call is made for prayer on the day of Jumu'ah [Friday], then proceed to the remembrance of Allah and leave off trade. That is better for you, if you only knew.
interpretation: This verse establishes the obligation of the Friday congregational prayer and instructs believers to prioritize the remembrance of God over worldly transactions once the call to prayer is sounded. The command to 'leave off trade' signifies that no business, however profitable, should take precedence over the duty to gather for collective worship. By framing this as 'better for you,' the verse teaches that spiritual discipline and communal devotion yield greater benefit than material gain, even if this benefit is not immediately apparent to those preoccupied with worldly pursuits. The verse also reflects the broader Islamic principle of balancing worldly responsibilities with spiritual obligations, emphasizing that dedicating specific, regular time to collective worship strengthens both individual faith and community cohesion.

translation: And when the prayer has been concluded, disperse within the land and seek from the bounty of Allah, and remember Allah often that you may succeed.
interpretation: This verse, part of the instructions concerning Friday (Jumu'ah) prayer, establishes a balanced model of life that integrates worship with worldly engagement. After the congregational prayer ends, believers are not commanded to remain in seclusion or withdraw from worldly affairs, but rather to return to their work, trade, and daily pursuits—'seeking the bounty of Allah,' which refers to lawful economic activity and sustenance. This reflects Islam's rejection of monasticism and asceticism that isolates individuals from productive life. However, the verse immediately qualifies this worldly engagement with the command to 'remember Allah often,' indicating that the pursuit of livelihood should never eclipse spiritual consciousness. The remembrance of Allah is not confined to the mosque or the moments of ritual prayer but should permeate all activities—business dealings, labor, and social interactions—so that worship and worldly life become integrated rather than separated into distinct spheres. The verse closes with 'that you may succeed,' linking true success (falah) not merely to economic prosperity but to maintaining this harmony between spiritual devotion and material responsibility. Success in the Qur'anic sense is holistic, encompassing both the health of the soul and the sustenance of the body, both the hereafter and the present world.

translation: And when they saw a trade or diversion, they rushed off to it and left you standing. Say, 'What is with Allah is better than diversion and than trade, and Allah is the best of providers.'
interpretation: This verse was revealed in response to an incident during the Prophet Muhammad's Friday sermon when a caravan arrived in Medina with trade goods, accompanied by drumming to announce its arrival. Many of the congregation left the mosque mid-sermon to attend to the commercial opportunity, leaving the Prophet speaking to a nearly empty assembly. The verse addresses this lapse in priorities, rebuking the believers for valuing immediate worldly gain and entertainment over attentiveness to the Prophet and the spiritual guidance he was delivering. The rhetorical correction—'what is with Allah is better'—establishes a principle about the proper ordering of priorities: worldly pursuits, whether commerce or amusement, however legitimate in their own right, should never take precedence over acts of worship and devotion to God, especially when one is already engaged in them. The closing affirmation that Allah is the best of providers reassures believers that sustenance and provision ultimately come from God, not from any particular transaction or opportunity, so abandoning worship for the sake of trade reflects a misplaced trust in worldly means rather than in divine providence. The verse thus serves as a broader lesson on discipline, mindfulness, and maintaining spiritual focus even when worldly distractions present themselves urgently.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. When the hypocrites come to you [O Muhammad], they say, 'We bear witness that you are indeed the Messenger of Allah.' And Allah knows that you are indeed His Messenger, and Allah bears witness that the hypocrites are indeed liars.
interpretation: This verse exposes the fundamental disconnect between outward speech and inward belief that characterizes hypocrisy (nifaq). The hypocrites utter a statement that is objectively true—that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah—yet their testimony is condemned as a lie. This is not because the content of their words is false, but because their declaration lacks sincerity and conviction; they speak words of faith without the corresponding belief in their hearts, using the profession of faith as a social or political cover rather than as genuine testimony. The verse draws a crucial distinction between Allah's own confirmation of Muhammad's prophethood—stated as an independent divine fact ('Allah knows that you are indeed His Messenger')—and the hypocrites' verbal claim of the same truth. Allah does not need or rely on their testimony to validate His Messenger; rather, He exposes the falseness of their intention behind an otherwise true statement. This illustrates a broader Quranic principle that faith is not measured merely by verbal profession but by the truthfulness of one's heart and the alignment between inner conviction and outer expression. The hypocrites' sin lies not in what they say, but in the deceptive gap between their speech and their actual disbelief, making their testimony a form of lying despite its literal truth.

translation: They have taken their oaths as a shield, and thus they have hindered [others] from the way of Allah. Indeed, evil is what they have been doing.
interpretation: This verse refers to the hypocrites who used their sworn oaths of faith as a protective cover or disguise to conceal their true disbelief and malicious intentions. By outwardly swearing allegiance to Islam while secretly working against it, they were able to infiltrate the Muslim community, sow discord, and divert people away from the path of Allah without facing immediate suspicion or consequence. The oath, meant to be a sacred bond affirming truth, was corrupted into a tool of deception. This exposes a particularly insidious form of hypocrisy: not merely private disbelief, but the active weaponization of sacred speech acts to undermine the faith community from within while appearing to belong to it. The verse condemns this behavior as deeply evil precisely because it exploits trust and sanctified language for destructive ends, making it more dangerous than open hostility since it operates under the guise of legitimacy and shared commitment.

translation: That is because they believed, then disbelieved, so a seal was set upon their hearts, so they do not understand.
interpretation: This verse addresses a pattern of spiritual inconsistency: individuals who initially embraced faith but subsequently rejected it. The 'sealing of the hearts' is presented not as an arbitrary punishment imposed without cause, but as a consequence that follows from their own choice to abandon belief after having known it. This reflects a broader Qur'anic principle that persistent rejection of truth, especially after having recognized it, leads to a hardening of spiritual perception—an inability to comprehend or internalize guidance even when it is presented. The 'seal' metaphorically represents the loss of receptivity to further revelation or admonition, not because they are incapable of understanding in a general intellectual sense, but because their hearts have become closed off to spiritual truths due to their own vacillation and disbelief. This serves as a warning about the dangers of apostasy and the spiritual consequences of turning away from faith after having experienced it, suggesting that such reversals can lead to a deeper, more entrenched state of unbelief.

translation: And when you see them, their bodies please you; and if they speak, you listen to their speech. [They are] as if they were propped-up pieces of wood. They think every shout is against them. They are the enemy, so beware of them. May Allah destroy them; how are they deluded?
interpretation: This verse describes the hypocrites (munafiqun) of Medina, exposing the gap between their outward appearance and inner reality. Their physically impressive bodies and eloquent, persuasive speech create a favorable first impression, yet these qualities are hollow and lifeless, like timber propped against a wall—seemingly substantial but devoid of inner strength, faith, or genuine conviction. Their chronic guilty conscience and cowardice are revealed through their paranoid assumption that any public announcement, alarm, or criticism must be directed at them, betraying their awareness of their own duplicity and the fragility of their concealed disbelief. The verse delivers a stark warning to the believing community: despite their claims of being part of the Muslim community, these individuals are the true internal enemy, more dangerous than external foes because they operate from within while harboring treachery. The divine curse 'qatalahum Allah' is an idiomatic expression of condemnation, and the closing rhetorical question about their being 'deluded' or 'turned away' from truth emphasizes the tragic irony that despite having access to clear guidance, they choose falsehood, highlighting how self-interest, cowardice, and spiritual corruption can lead people to abandon obvious truth.

translation: And when it is said to them, 'Come, the Messenger of Allah will ask forgiveness for you,' they turn aside their heads, and you see them turning away while they are arrogant.
interpretation: This verse describes the hypocrites (munafiqun) in Medina, exposing their inner rejection of guidance despite outward claims of faith. When invited to seek the Prophet's intercession for forgiveness—an opportunity that should be welcomed by anyone sincerely seeking spiritual benefit—they physically turn away, a gesture signifying contempt and refusal. Their arrogance (istikbar) is identified as the root cause: they consider themselves above needing to seek forgiveness through the Prophet, or they disdain submitting to his authority even in a matter meant for their own benefit. The verse illustrates a broader spiritual principle: arrogance blinds a person to opportunities for repentance and guidance, causing them to reject even what is offered out of mercy for their own good. Their physical gestures—turning their heads, turning away bodily—mirror and manifest their internal spiritual state of rejection and pride, showing how outward behavior reveals inner disbelief despite verbal professions of faith.

translation: It is the same for them whether you (O Muhammad) ask forgiveness for them or do not ask forgiveness for them; Allah will never forgive them. Indeed, Allah does not guide the defiantly disobedient people.
interpretation: This verse refers specifically to the hypocrites (munafiqun), such as Abdullah ibn Ubayy, whose outward profession of faith concealed persistent disbelief and active hostility toward the Prophet and the believers. It establishes that divine forgiveness is not a matter of ritual intercession alone but is contingent upon the sincerity of one's inner state and willingness to abandon disbelief and defiance. Even the Prophet's supplication, though powerful, cannot override the fixed principle that Allah withholds guidance and forgiveness from those who have chosen persistent rebellion (fisq) as their settled condition, having rejected truth after it was made clear to them. The verse thus underscores that guidance is a divine grant tied to one's own moral choices and sincerity, not something that can be secured merely through the intercession of others when the heart remains closed. It also serves to console the Prophet, clarifying that his efforts to reconcile the hypocrites, however well-intentioned, are not a failure on his part but a reflection of their own spiritual corruption.

translation: They are the ones who say, 'Do not spend on those who are with the Messenger of Allah until they disperse [and abandon him].' Yet to Allah belong the treasures of the heavens and the earth, but the hypocrites do not understand.
interpretation: This verse refers to the hypocrites of Medina, particularly in the context of the Banu al-Mustaliq expedition, who urged others to withhold financial support from the poor Muhajirun (emigrants) who were with the Prophet, hoping that economic pressure would cause them to abandon him and disperse. The verse exposes the shortsightedness and arrogance of this scheme, reminding that all provision and sustenance ultimately belong to Allah alone, who controls the treasures of the heavens and the earth. The hypocrites' plot is portrayed as futile because they fail to grasp this fundamental truth—that human attempts to control others through economic deprivation cannot override divine provision. Their lack of understanding ('la yafqahun') is not merely intellectual but spiritual: they cannot comprehend the nature of true power and sustenance, mistakenly believing that material control equates to real authority, when in fact ultimate authority and provision rest with Allah alone.

translation: They say, 'If we return to Madinah, the mightier [party] will surely expel the weaker therefrom.' But honor and might belong to Allah, and to His Messenger, and to the believers—but the hypocrites do not know.
interpretation: This verse refers to the sedition of Abdullah ibn Ubayy, the leader of the hypocrites in Madinah, who boasted that upon returning from a military expedition, his faction (whom he called 'the mighty') would expel the Prophet Muhammad and the Muslims (whom he disparagingly called 'the lowly') from the city. Allah refutes this arrogant and false claim by declaring that true honor, strength, and dignity (al-'izzah) belong exclusively to Him, and by extension to His Messenger and the believers who follow divine guidance, not to those who rely on worldly numbers, wealth, or tribal power. The verse exposes the hypocrites' fundamental misunderstanding of the true source of strength and honor—they measure power in worldly terms of social status and faction size, failing to comprehend that genuine honor derives from faith and submission to God rather than from worldly position. This serves as a reminder that apparent worldly power structures are ultimately subordinate to divine will, and that those who oppose the believers while appearing outwardly strong are, in the ultimate reckoning, the truly weak and diminished, regardless of their self-perception or temporal influence.

translation: O you who have believed, let not your wealth and your children divert you from the remembrance of Allah. And whoever does that - then those are the losers.
interpretation: This verse warns believers against allowing worldly attachments—wealth and children—to become sources of distraction from spiritual obligation and God-consciousness. While family and material provision are not condemned in themselves, the verse identifies a psychological and spiritual danger: that the love, anxiety, and effort invested in securing and enjoying these blessings can crowd out the remembrance of God, which is meant to anchor a believer's entire life. The remembrance of Allah (dhikr) here refers not merely to ritual acts of worship but to a pervasive awareness of divine presence and purpose that should inform how one earns, spends, and raises a family. The verse frames this neglect not as a minor lapse but as a fundamental loss (khusran), suggesting that a life absorbed entirely in worldly accumulation and attachment—even to legitimate and cherished things—while forgetting one's ultimate relationship with the Creator, results in a kind of spiritual bankruptcy. The implicit teaching is that wealth and children are trusts and tests, not ends in themselves, and that true success lies in maintaining equilibrium: engaging with the world and its responsibilities while never losing sight of the transcendent purpose that gives those engagements meaning.

translation: And spend from what We have provided you before death comes to one of you and he says, 'My Lord, if only You would delay me for a short term so I would give charity and be among the righteous.'
interpretation: This verse urges believers to act on opportunities for charity and righteousness without delay, warning against procrastination. It depicts the regret of a soul at the moment of death, pleading for more time to rectify past neglect through charitable giving and good deeds. The request for a 'short term' underscores that even a brief extension would be used for righteousness, highlighting the clarity that death brings to one's priorities—too late. The verse serves as a reminder that the time for action is now, in life, since death arrives without warning and no soul is granted a second chance once its appointed time has come. It emphasizes that spending in charity is not merely a transaction of wealth but a spiritual investment that must be made while one still has the capacity to do so, as the afterlife offers no opportunity for such deeds.

translation: And Allah will never delay a soul when its appointed time has come. And Allah is well acquainted with what you do.
interpretation: This verse establishes the fixed nature of the appointed time of death (ajal) for every soul, emphasizing that once this divinely ordained moment arrives, it cannot be postponed through any human effort, wealth, or power. This is a profound statement on the limits of human agency and the absolute sovereignty of Allah over life and death. The verse follows naturally from discussions in this portion of Surah Al-Munafiqun about wealth and children potentially distracting believers from the remembrance of Allah, and warnings about spending in charity before death arrives with regret. The certainty of death's fixed timing serves as a sobering reminder that delaying good deeds or repentance in hopes of a future opportunity is futile, since no one can predict or alter when their term will end. The concluding phrase, that Allah is fully aware of what people do, connects this metaphysical truth to moral accountability—since the timing of death is beyond human control, what truly matters is how one acts during the time granted, as all actions are observed and recorded by Allah. This creates a powerful incentive for immediate righteous action rather than procrastination, since one's deeds are the only matter within human control, while the appointed end remains entirely in Allah's hands.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth glorifies Allah; to Him belongs the dominion, and to Him belongs all praise, and He is over all things competent.
interpretation: This opening verse establishes the theological foundation for the entire sura by affirming the universality of God's sovereignty and the cosmic scope of His glorification. The declaration that 'whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth' glorifies Allah encompasses all creation—sentient and non-sentient, human and non-human—suggesting that existence itself is oriented toward praising its Creator, each thing testifying to His majesty through its very nature and mode of being, even without verbal articulation. The pairing of 'dominion' (al-mulk) with 'praise' (al-hamd) links sovereignty to worthiness of gratitude, implying that God's rule is not merely powerful but also inherently praiseworthy and just. The closing affirmation of His absolute power over all things ('qadir') serves as a rational basis for the preceding claims: because He possesses unlimited capability, both His kingship and the praise due to Him are not arbitrary assertions but necessary consequences of His nature. This verse thus sets a tone of awe and comprehensive submission, inviting the listener to recognize their own place within a universe already engaged in cosmic worship.

translation: It is He who created you, and among you is a disbeliever, and among you is a believer. And Allah is Seeing of what you do.
interpretation: This verse highlights a fundamental aspect of human existence: despite being created by the same God, humanity diverges in belief and disbelief. This divergence is not attributed to any flaw in creation itself, but rather to the exercise of free will granted to human beings, allowing them to choose their path—whether toward faith or rejection. The verse underscores the principle of divine justice and accountability, as it concludes with the assertion that Allah is fully aware and observant of all actions. This serves as both a reminder and a warning: while individuals are free to choose their beliefs and actions, they are also responsible for them, and nothing escapes God's watchful awareness. The verse thus reinforces the coexistence of human agency and divine omniscience, situating human diversity in belief within a framework of ultimate accountability before God.

translation: He created the heavens and the earth in truth, and He shaped you and perfected your shapes. And to Him is the final return.
interpretation: This verse establishes two foundational truths about God's relationship to creation. First, the heavens and earth were not created randomly or without purpose ('bil-haqq' - in truth/with purpose), implying inherent meaning and order in existence that points to divine wisdom. Second, by highlighting the creation and perfection of human form specifically, the verse draws attention to humanity's special status within creation - not merely existing, but being shaped with care and excellence ('ahsana suwarakum' - He perfected your forms). This refers both to physical form and, by extension, the inherent dignity and potential given to human beings. The verse then concludes with the reminder that despite this careful crafting and the apparent independence of worldly life, everything returns to God ('ilayhi al-masir'). This creates a theological framework where creation's order and humanity's distinguished form are not ends in themselves, but are purposeful signs meant to direct consciousness toward accountability and return to the Creator. The juxtaposition of creation's perfection with the certainty of return serves as a call to recognize that physical excellence and worldly existence are temporary stewardships, not permanent possessions.

translation: He knows what is in the heavens and the earth, and He knows what you conceal and what you reveal. And Allah is Knowing of that within the breasts.
interpretation: This verse establishes the absolute and all-encompassing nature of divine knowledge as a foundation for human accountability and moral consciousness. By affirming that God's knowledge extends not only to the vast cosmos but to the most hidden inner states—thoughts, intentions, and secrets harbored within the heart—the verse removes any illusion that one's inner life is a private sanctuary beyond scrutiny. The progression from the cosmic (heavens and earth) to the intimate (what is concealed and revealed) to the most profound interior (what is in the breasts) creates a rhetorical movement that closes off every possible space where a person might imagine themselves hidden from God. This has profound implications for taqwa (God-consciousness): it suggests that sincerity of intention matters as much as outward action, since both are equally known. The verse thus serves as both a comfort to the sincere believer, whose hidden devotion is seen and valued, and a warning to the hypocrite, whose outward piety cannot mask inner corruption. It reinforces the theological principle that human beings exist in a state of perpetual transparency before the divine, making genuine faith a matter of the heart rather than mere outward conformity.

translation: Has there not come to you the news of those who disbelieved before? They tasted the evil consequence of their affair, and for them is a painful punishment.
interpretation: This verse serves as a warning to the listeners by invoking the historical precedent of earlier disbelieving nations who rejected the messages of their prophets. The rhetorical question 'has there not come to you' implies that the knowledge of these past nations' fates is well-known and undeniable, serving as a lesson that should prompt reflection. 'Tasted the evil consequence of their affair' indicates that their worldly destruction or suffering was a direct and immediate result of their own choices and disbelief, not an arbitrary punishment imposed on them. The word 'tasted' suggests an experiential, visceral encounter with the results of their actions—something they directly felt and understood. The verse then moves beyond the worldly punishment to indicate that 'for them is a painful punishment' in the Hereafter, establishing a dual consequence: both immediate worldly suffering and eternal punishment in the afterlife. This structure reinforces the Qur'anic theme that disbelief and rejection of divine guidance carry consequences on multiple planes of existence, and that the stories of past nations are not merely historical accounts but serve as moral and spiritual lessons for present and future generations to heed the call of faith and avoid repeating the same errors.

translation: That is because their messengers used to come to them with clear proofs, but they said, 'Shall mere mortals guide us?' So they disbelieved and turned away, and Allah dispensed with them. And Allah is Self-Sufficient, Praiseworthy.
interpretation: This verse addresses the root cause of the destruction of previous nations: their arrogant rejection of human messengers. The disbelievers' objection—'Shall mere mortals guide us?'—reveals a flawed reasoning that assumed divine guidance could only come through angels or beings unlike themselves, rather than accepting that God chooses human messengers who share the human condition yet are divinely supported with revelation. Their disbelief was thus rooted in misplaced expectations about how guidance should manifest, leading them to reject clear signs (bayyinat) simply because the messenger was human. The phrase 'wa istaghna Allah' (Allah dispensed with them) emphasizes that God's self-sufficiency means He has no need for their belief or obedience; their rejection harms only themselves, not Him. This is reinforced by the closing attributes 'Ghani' (Free of need) and 'Hamid' (Praiseworthy), which together affirm that God's essence and worthiness of praise are independent of human acknowledgment—He is inherently self-sufficient and deserving of praise regardless of whether creation recognizes it. The verse thus serves as both a historical lesson and a theological statement about the nature of divine guidance and divine independence from creation.

translation: Those who disbelieve claim that they will never be resurrected. Say: 'Yes, by my Lord, you will surely be resurrected, then you will surely be informed of what you did. And that, for Allah, is easy.'
interpretation: This verse addresses the denial of resurrection held by disbelievers, countering their claim with a divine oath sworn by the Prophet upon his Lord. The emphatic structure—'Yes, by my Lord, you will surely be resurrected'—uses oath-taking to lend maximum certainty to a matter beyond empirical verification in this worldly life, appealing to faith grounded in trust in God's power rather than observable proof. The verse then links resurrection directly to accountability: being raised is not an end in itself but a prelude to being informed of one's deeds, establishing the moral logic of the afterlife as the venue where the truth of human actions is disclosed and judged. The closing phrase, that this is 'easy for Allah,' addresses the disbelievers' underlying skepticism, which often rested on the perceived impossibility of reviving decayed bodies. By asserting the ease of resurrection for God, the verse reframes the issue not as a matter of physical plausibility but of divine omnipotence—what seems impossible by human measure is trivial for the Creator who originated life in the first place. This rhetorical move shifts the burden of doubt: denial of resurrection is framed not as a reasonable skepticism but as a failure to properly conceive of God's unlimited power, reinforcing the broader Quranic theme that disbelief in the Hereafter stems from a limited understanding of divine capability rather than from sound reasoning.

translation: So believe in Allah and His Messenger and the light which We have sent down. And Allah is Aware of what you do.
interpretation: This verse calls upon humanity to embrace a threefold faith: belief in Allah as the singular divine source, belief in His Messenger as the conveyor of divine guidance, and belief in 'the light' which refers to the Qur'an itself as a source of illumination that dispels the darkness of ignorance and misguidance. The pairing of faith with the reminder that Allah is fully aware of human actions serves as both comfort and admonition—comfort for believers that their sincere deeds are recognized, and admonition for those who might feign belief or act contrary to it, since nothing escapes divine knowledge. The verse encapsulates the comprehensive nature of Islamic faith, which is not merely intellectual assent but is meant to translate into righteous action, all under the watchful awareness of God.

translation: On the Day when He will gather you for the Day of Gathering - that is the Day of Mutual Loss and Gain. And whoever believes in Allah and does righteousness - He will remove from him his misdeeds and admit him to gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever. That is the great attainment.
interpretation: This verse refers to the Day of Judgment as 'the Day of Mutual Loss and Gain' (Yawm at-Taghabun), a term that captures the reversal of fortunes that will be revealed on that day. Those who seemed successful in worldly terms - wealthy, powerful, or heedless of faith - will discover their true loss, while those who were humble, oppressed, or overlooked because of their faith will discover their true gain. It is the day when the real balance sheet of human life is disclosed, and illusions of worldly success or failure are stripped away. The verse then pivots to offer hope: belief in God coupled with righteous action leads to the erasure of past sins and eternal reward in Paradise. This structure - warning followed by promise - is characteristic of Qur'anic rhetoric, using the stark imagery of cosmic reckoning to motivate ethical and spiritual transformation in the present life. The eternality of the gardens beneath which rivers flow underscores that this is not a temporary respite but a permanent state of fulfillment, framed as 'the great attainment' (al-fawz al-'azim), suggesting that true success is measured not by temporal gain but by one's standing before God.

translation: And those who disbelieve and deny Our signs - those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein eternally, and wretched is the destination.
interpretation: This verse establishes a decisive contrast with the believers mentioned in the preceding verses, outlining the consequence for those who combine two failings: kufr (disbelief or ingratitude toward God) and takdhib (active denial or rejection) of divine signs. The pairing of these two terms is significant - it is not merely a lack of belief but a willful rejection of clear evidence presented to them, whether through revelation, natural signs, or prophetic guidance. The designation 'companions of the Fire' (ashab al-nar) mirrors the earlier designation of 'companions of Paradise,' creating a structural parallel that emphasizes the binary outcome of human choice and accountability. The eternity of this dwelling (khalidina fiha) underscores the permanence of the consequence tied to a fundamental orientation of the soul rather than isolated acts, suggesting that sustained, willful rejection of truth shapes one's ultimate destiny. The closing phrase 'wretched is the destination' serves as a divine commentary that reinforces the gravity of the outcome, inviting reflection on the weight of one's choices in this life and their eternal ramifications. The verse functions didactically within the broader Quranic discourse to motivate righteous belief and sincere acceptance of divine guidance by vividly contrasting the fates of believers and disbelievers.

translation: No calamity strikes except by the permission of Allah. And whoever believes in Allah - He will guide his heart. And Allah is Knowing of all things.
interpretation: This verse establishes a foundational theological principle regarding divine decree (qadar) and its relationship to faith. It teaches that every misfortune, trial, or calamity that befalls a person occurs within the scope of Allah's permission and knowledge, meaning nothing happens randomly or outside His sovereign will. This is not meant to absolve human responsibility for sin, but rather addresses afflictions beyond human control. The second part reveals a profound spiritual truth: true faith in Allah produces inner guidance and tranquility of heart, especially in the face of trials. When a believer truly submits to the reality that calamities occur by divine permission, their heart becomes settled, accepting, and at peace rather than filled with despair, resentment, or confusion. This guidance of the heart is itself a divine gift to those who believe - it is Allah who guides the heart to patience, acceptance, and understanding when misfortune strikes. The verse closes by affirming Allah's complete knowledge of all things, reinforcing that behind every trial lies divine wisdom and purpose, even when that purpose is not immediately apparent to the one suffering. This connects faith, trial, and psychological/spiritual stability - suggesting that the believer's resilience in hardship stems directly from their conviction in Allah's wise governance of all affairs.

translation: And obey Allah and obey the Messenger; but if you turn away, then upon Our Messenger is only [the duty of] clear conveyance [of the message].
interpretation: This verse establishes that obedience to Allah and His Messenger is a fundamental obligation for believers, yet it also clarifies the limits of the Messenger's responsibility. The Prophet's role is not to force belief or compel people's hearts, but solely to deliver the divine message clearly and faithfully. If people choose to turn away despite this clear communication, the responsibility and consequence of that rejection falls upon themselves, not upon the Messenger. This reflects a broader Quranic principle regarding free will and accountability: guidance has been made manifest and unambiguous, so human beings bear the burden of their own choices. It also serves to console and reassure the Prophet Muhammad, relieving him of the burden of controlling outcomes that are beyond his power, as his duty ends with sincere and clear transmission of revelation.

translation: Allah - there is no deity except Him. And upon Allah let the believers rely.
interpretation: This verse affirms the absolute oneness of Allah (tawhid), declaring that no other deity exists alongside Him. Following this declaration of monotheism, believers are commanded to place their complete trust (tawakkul) in Allah alone. This trust is not passive resignation but an active spiritual state that should accompany one's efforts, recognizing that ultimate outcomes rest with Allah. The connection between affirming Allah's oneness and relying solely on Him teaches that true faith requires both correct belief and the corresponding practical attitude of dependence on the Divine, rather than placing one's ultimate trust in worldly causes, other people, or one's own power and resources.

translation: O you who have believed, indeed, among your spouses and your children are enemies to you, so beware of them. But if you pardon, overlook, and forgive - then indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation: This verse warns believers that the natural love for one's spouse and children can become a source of spiritual danger when those bonds are used to distract from obedience to God, pressure one into sin, or draw one away from righteous priorities—such as emigrating for faith, spending in charity, or fulfilling religious duties. The term 'enemy' here does not imply malice in the ordinary sense, but rather highlights how deep attachment to family can become a test that competes with devotion to God, sometimes leading a person to compromise their principles for the sake of pleasing loved ones. The believer is urged to remain vigilant against this subtle temptation, recognizing that excessive indulgence or fear of displeasing family members can lead to moral or spiritual compromise. However, the verse immediately tempers this warning with a call to compassion: despite this caution, believers are encouraged to forgive, overlook faults, and show mercy toward their spouses and children rather than react with harshness or retaliation. This balance reflects the Quranic ethic of maintaining firm commitment to faith and truth while still practicing patience, clemency, and love within the family. The concluding mention of God's own forgiveness and mercy serves as a model for human behavior—just as God forgives human weakness, so too should believers extend forgiveness to those closest to them, even when their family ties test their faith.

translation: Your wealth and your children are only a trial (fitnah), and with Allah is a great reward.
interpretation: This verse teaches that worldly attachments—wealth and offspring, the two things people most naturally love and strive for—are tests of faith rather than ultimate goals in themselves. They can distract a believer from obedience to God, tempt one toward greed, favoritism, or neglect of religious duty, and create anxiety that compromises moral integrity. By framing them as 'fitnah,' the verse cautions believers not to let love for family or material possessions override their commitment to righteousness and devotion to God. At the same time, it reassures that steadfastness in this trial is not without recompense: those who manage these attachments with piety and in accordance with divine guidance will be rewarded immensely in the Hereafter, a reward far surpassing the temporary comforts of wealth and children in this life.

translation: So fear Allah as much as you are able and listen and obey and spend [in charity]; it is better for yourselves. And whoever is protected from the stinginess of his own soul - it is those who are the successful.
interpretation: This verse establishes a principle of proportionate obligation in faith: believers are not asked to achieve an impossible, absolute perfection in piety, but rather to strive to the best of their capacity. This is a merciful qualification that distinguishes sincere effort from unattainable perfectionism, acknowledging human limitation while still demanding genuine striving. The verse then links this tempered piety to three practical commands: attentive listening, obedience, and spending in charity. Charitable giving is singled out as something that benefits the giver's own soul, not merely the recipient, reframing generosity as self-interest in the deepest spiritual sense. Finally, the verse diagnoses stinginess (shuhh) not merely as withholding wealth but as a disease of the self, an inner trait that must be guarded against or purified. Success and salvation are tied directly to overcoming this inner possessiveness and miserliness, suggesting that the real battle is internal to the soul rather than purely about external acts of giving. Being 'protected' from this trait implies it requires divine aid combined with personal effort, positioning the struggle against greed as central to spiritual accomplishment.

translation: If you loan Allah a goodly loan, He will multiply it for you and forgive you. And Allah is Appreciative and Forbearing.
interpretation: This verse employs the metaphor of a loan to describe charitable giving and righteous spending in the cause of God, emphasizing that such acts are not losses but investments that yield multiplied spiritual and often material rewards. By framing generosity as something given to God Himself, the verse elevates ordinary acts of charity into a sacred transaction, removing any sense of the giver being owed by the recipient, since the true creditor is divine. The promise of multiplication reflects divine generosity exceeding human generosity many times over, while the mention of forgiveness links material sacrifice to spiritual purification, suggesting that charitable giving can expiate sins. The closing divine attributes—Shakur (Appreciative) and Halim (Forbearing)—reinforce this message: God acknowledges and rewards even small acts of goodness with gratitude disproportionate to their size, while His forbearance means He does not hasten punishment for shortcomings, encouraging believers to give generously without fear of being impoverished or judged harshly for their imperfections.

translation: Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, the Almighty, the Wise.
interpretation: This verse affirms God's complete and all-encompassing knowledge, extending beyond what is perceptible to human senses (the witnessed/shahada) to include all that is hidden, unseen, and unknowable to creation (the ghayb) - including the future, people's inner thoughts and intentions, and the unseen realms of existence. Paired with this comprehensive knowledge are two complementary divine attributes: 'Al-Aziz' (the Almighty/Mighty), signifying God's unmatched power and ability to execute His will without opposition, and 'Al-Hakim' (the Wise), indicating that this power and knowledge are always exercised with perfect wisdom and purpose. Together, these attributes assure believers that nothing escapes God's awareness, and that His governance of creation—whether in matters hidden or apparent—is never arbitrary but is rooted in infinite wisdom and sovereign authority. This combination of knowledge, power, and wisdom serves as a foundation for trust in divine justice and the unfolding of events, even when their underlying reasons are not immediately apparent to human understanding.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. O Prophet, when you [men] divorce women, divorce them for their stipulated period (iddah) and count the period accurately, and fear Allah, your Lord. Do not expel them from their houses, nor should they leave, unless they commit a clear immorality. These are the limits set by Allah, and whoever transgresses the limits of Allah has certainly wronged himself. You do not know; perhaps Allah will bring about after that a [different] matter.
interpretation: This verse establishes the proper procedure for divorce in Islamic law, emphasizing that it must be conducted with precision and accountability regarding the waiting period (iddah), which serves to confirm the woman is not pregnant and allows time for reconciliation. The instruction to count the period accurately underscores the legal and social importance of this process for determining lineage and remarriage eligibility. The prohibition against expelling women from their homes during this period, except in cases of proven serious misconduct, reflects a concern for the woman's dignity, stability, and protection during a vulnerable time, while also preserving the possibility of reconciliation since cohabitation might lead to reconsideration. The verse frames these rules as divine 'limits' (hudud), indicating they are not merely social customs but sacred boundaries whose transgression constitutes self-harm in a spiritual sense—wronging one's own soul by violating divine law. The closing statement, suggesting that Allah may bring about a new situation afterward, points to the wisdom in not rushing toward irreversible separation, as circumstances and hearts may change, leaving room for divine intervention or reconciliation even after the decision to divorce has been initiated.

translation: And when they have [nearly] reached their term, either retain them according to what is acceptable or part with them according to what is acceptable. And bring to witness two just people from among you and establish the testimony for [the sake of] Allah. That is instructed to whoever should believe in Allah and the Last Day. And whoever fears Allah - He will make for him a way out.
interpretation: This verse addresses the proper conduct at the end of a woman's waiting period (iddah) following divorce, instructing that the decision to reconcile or finalize separation must be made with fairness, kindness, and dignity rather than manipulation or harm. The requirement to have just witnesses formalizes the decision, protecting the rights of both parties and preventing later disputes, while framing the testimony as ultimately being 'for Allah' emphasizes sincerity and accountability beyond mere legal formality. The closing statement broadens the lesson beyond divorce law: righteous conduct and trust in Allah during difficult, constrained circumstances—such as the end of a marriage—become a model for how piety (taqwa) opens a way out of hardship in all aspects of life. The 'way out' is not limited to the marital context but serves as a general spiritual principle that conscientious fear of Allah and adherence to His limits brings relief and solutions even in situations that seem to offer none.

translation: And He will provide for him from where he does not expect. And whoever relies upon Allah - then He is sufficient for him. Indeed, Allah will accomplish His purpose. Allah has already set for everything a [decreed] extent.
interpretation: This verse, part of a larger passage on piety and trust in God (typically linked to the preceding verse about Allah making a way out for those who fear Him), emphasizes that divine provision often arrives through unforeseen and unexpected means, beyond human calculation or planning. It establishes tawakkul (reliance on Allah) as a core spiritual principle: when a believer places complete trust in God after making the necessary effort, Allah becomes sufficient for all their needs, alleviating anxiety about outcomes. The verse affirms Allah's absolute power to fulfill His will and purpose without obstruction - nothing can prevent what He decrees. The closing phrase about Allah setting a measure (qadar) for everything speaks to the comprehensive divine ordering of creation, where every event, provision, and circumstance occurs according to a precise, predetermined measure and timing known fully only to Allah. This encourages believers to accept divine decree with patience and confidence, understanding that apparent delays or unexpected paths to blessing are part of a wise, measured plan rather than random chance.

translation: And those of your women who have despaired of menstruation, if you are in doubt, their waiting period is three months, and [also for] those who have not yet menstruated. And for those who are pregnant, their term is until they deliver their burden. And whoever fears Allah - He will make for him ease in his matter.
interpretation: This verse addresses the legal waiting period (iddah) required of divorced or widowed women in categories not covered by the standard menstrual-cycle-based waiting period mentioned elsewhere in the Qur'an. It clarifies three specific cases: women who have reached menopause and no longer menstruate, women who have not yet begun menstruating due to young age, and pregnant women. For the first two groups, the waiting period is set at three months, providing a clear standard where the natural marker of menstrual cycles is absent. For pregnant women, the waiting period is tied to a definitive biological event—childbirth—ensuring clarity about parentage and the end of the marital bond's legal implications. The verse closes with a broader spiritual principle that transcends the specific legal ruling: those who maintain consciousness of Allah and live within the bounds of His commandments will find their affairs made easier. This closing statement serves to reassure believers that complex legal and personal matters, such as divorce and its aftermath, become more manageable when approached with piety and trust in divine guidance, emphasizing that adherence to Allah's law is not meant to create hardship but rather to provide structure that ultimately eases life's difficulties.

translation: That is the command of Allah, which He has sent down to you. And whoever fears Allah - He will remove from him his misdeeds and magnify for him a reward.
interpretation: This verse concludes a passage dealing with divorce regulations in Surah at-Talaq, emphasizing that the detailed legal rulings just given are divine ordinances, not merely social customs, underscoring their binding authority. The verse then pivots to a broader spiritual principle: taqwa (God-consciousness and mindful obedience) is the key that unlocks divine mercy and reward. The promise that Allah will expiate one's sins and amplify one's reward serves as a motivating conclusion, suggesting that compliance with difficult or seemingly burdensome legal rulings (such as those concerning divorce, waiting periods, and family obligations) is itself an act of taqwa that carries spiritual benefit beyond the immediate worldly matter. This reflects a recurring Quranic pattern where specific legal instructions are framed within a larger theological context, reminding believers that obedience to divine law, even in mundane social matters, is connected to one's ultimate spiritual standing and the purification of the soul.

translation: House them (the divorced women) where you dwell, according to your means, and do not harm them in order to straiten [the conditions] upon them. And if they are pregnant, spend on them until they deliver their burden. And if they suckle [the child] for you, then give them their payment, and consult among yourselves in a fair manner; but if you are in discord, then another woman may suckle for him [the father].
interpretation: This verse establishes the legal and ethical framework for the treatment of women during the waiting period ('iddah) following divorce, particularly emphasizing the husband's continued financial and moral responsibility. It mandates that the divorced woman be provided suitable housing commensurate with the husband's means, explicitly prohibiting any harassment or coercive tactics intended to pressure her—such as restricting her living space—into forfeiting her rights or leaving before her waiting period concludes. The verse extends special protection to pregnant women, obligating the husband to maintain full financial support until childbirth, recognizing the shared responsibility for the unborn child regardless of the marital dissolution. Furthermore, it addresses the practical matter of nursing: if the mother breastfeeds the child after divorce, she is entitled to fair compensation for this service, treating it as a distinct economic contribution rather than an assumed maternal duty. The instruction to 'consult among yourselves in a fair manner' underscores the Quranic principle that even in the dissolution of marriage, matters concerning children should be resolved through mutual consultation and goodwill rather than unilateral decision-making or conflict. Finally, the provision allowing for another wet-nurse in cases of irreconcilable disagreement demonstrates the law's pragmatic flexibility, prioritizing the child's welfare above potential discord between the parents while still ensuring the child's needs are met through alternative means. This passage reflects a broader Quranic ethic of ensuring that the breakdown of marriage does not result in the abandonment of mutual obligations, particularly toward vulnerable parties—women during 'iddah and children requiring care and sustenance.

translation: Let a man of wealth spend according to his wealth, and let him whose provision is restricted spend according to what Allah has given him. Allah does not burden any soul beyond what He has given it. Allah will bring about, after hardship, ease.
interpretation: This verse establishes a principle of proportional financial responsibility, particularly in the context of maintenance obligations such as those owed to a divorced wife or dependents, as discussed in the surrounding verses of Surah At-Talaq. It affirms that Allah's commands are always calibrated to human capacity, never demanding beyond what one is able to give—a core expression of divine justice and mercy. The wealthy are expected to give generously in proportion to their means, while those of limited means are not condemned for giving less, since their obligation is measured against what they actually possess, not against an absolute standard. The closing promise—that ease follows hardship—serves as both consolation and reassurance, teaching that straitened circumstances are temporary and that Allah's providence ensures relief will come. Together, the verse weaves practical legal guidance on spending with a broader theological message about trust in divine wisdom during times of difficulty.

translation: And how many a town rebelled against the command of its Lord and His messengers, so We called it to a severe account and punished it with a terrible punishment.
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 65:8) serves as a historical and moral warning drawn from the fates of past communities who arrogantly defied divine guidance and the messengers sent to them. The phrase 'how many' (كأين) signals that this is not an isolated incident but a recurring pattern throughout history, lending universal weight to the lesson. The pairing of 'severe account' (حساباً شديدا) with 'terrible punishment' (عذاباً نكرا) indicates a two-fold consequence: first a rigorous divine reckoning that leaves no excuse unexamined, and then a punishment whose severity matches the magnitude of the rebellion. The verse functions rhetorically within its surah to reinforce exhortations to piety and obedience by reminding the audience that divine law is not merely advisory but carries real consequences enacted in history, implicitly urging contemporaries to learn from these destroyed civilizations rather than repeat their defiance.

translation: So it tasted the evil consequence of its affair, and the end of its affair was loss.
interpretation: This verse comes at the conclusion of a passage (Qur'an 65:8-9) recounting the fate of earlier towns and communities that defied the command of their Lord and His messengers. Having rebelled against divine guidance, these communities were brought to a severe reckoning and made to suffer a harsh punishment unlike any other. The verse encapsulates the inevitable outcome of such defiance: the 'tasting' of the bitter fruit of their own rebellious conduct. The imagery of tasting suggests an experiential, inescapable confrontation with the real consequences of one's choices—not an abstract punishment imposed externally, but the natural, almost organic result of a community's collective sin and arrogance. The phrase 'the end of its affair was loss' underscores the ultimate futility and ruin that follows turning away from divine commandments, emphasizing that worldly power, resources, or civilization offer no protection against moral and spiritual failure. The verse serves as both a historical reminder and a timeless warning to any community or individual: rejection of guidance and persistence in transgression against what is right leads inevitably to spiritual and often tangible loss, reinforcing the Qur'anic theme that true success (falah) is tied to obedience and submission to God's will, while disregard for it results in loss both in this world and the hereafter.

translation: Allah has prepared for them a severe punishment. So fear Allah, O you of understanding who have believed. Allah has indeed sent down to you a message of remembrance.
interpretation: This verse comes as a warning following a description of the fate of those who transgressed against Allah's commands and His messengers, and is addressed specifically to 'those of understanding' (ulul-albab), signifying that true comprehension of divine warnings requires both intellect and faith. The pairing of reason with belief suggests that genuine taqwa (God-consciousness) is not blind obedience but arises from reflective understanding of consequences. The mention that Allah has sent down a 'dhikr' (reminder/message) to them refers to the Qur'an itself, which is being revealed in real-time as moral and legal guidance, including the surrounding verses on divorce, waiting periods, and family responsibility. The verse thus bridges a stern warning about punishment for disobedience with a reassurance that guidance has been clearly provided, leaving no excuse for heedlessness. It also elevates the believers' status by addressing them as people of insight, distinguishing them from those who ignored similar warnings in the past, and calling them to internalize the Qur'an not merely as law but as a living reminder meant to shape consciousness and conduct in every aspect of life, including the intimate details of marriage and separation discussed in this surah.

translation: A Messenger reciting to you the clear verses of Allah, that He may bring those who believe and do righteous deeds out of darkness into light. And whoever believes in Allah and does righteousness, He will admit him into gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever. Allah has indeed granted him an excellent provision.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the role of the Prophet as a conveyor of divine revelation whose clear, unambiguous verses serve as guidance for humanity. The imagery of moving 'from darkness into light' symbolizes the transformative power of faith coupled with righteous action—darkness representing ignorance, disbelief, and moral confusion, while light represents knowledge, guidance, and spiritual clarity. The verse establishes a direct causal relationship between genuine faith (iman) and righteous deeds ('amal salih), indicating that true belief must manifest in ethical conduct to achieve this transformation. The promised reward of eternal gardens with flowing rivers represents not merely a physical paradise but the ultimate fulfillment and peace that comes from a life aligned with divine purpose. The phrase 'Allah has granted him an excellent provision' suggests that this reward is both material and spiritual sustenance, perfectly suited to the needs of the soul, contrasting with the fleeting and imperfect provisions of worldly life. The eternal nature of this reward ('abadan') underscores the permanence of divine justice and mercy for those who maintain their faith through righteous action throughout their lives.

translation: It is Allah who created seven heavens and of the earth, the like thereof. The command descends between them so that you may know that Allah is over all things competent and that Allah has encompassed all things in knowledge.
interpretation: This verse affirms the vastness and precision of Allah's creation—seven heavens and a corresponding structure of the earth—as a sign of His absolute power and limitless knowledge. The 'descending of the command' refers to Allah's continuous governance of the cosmos, including the laws of nature and the revelation guiding humanity, flowing through all these created realms. The purpose stated is didactic: humans are meant to reflect on the scale and order of creation to arrive at certain knowledge of two complementary divine attributes—omnipotence (qudrah) and omniscience ('ilm). These are not abstract theological claims but are meant to inspire humility and trust: if Allah governs multiple heavens and earths with perfect knowledge and power, then nothing in human affairs, however small or hidden, escapes His control or awareness. The verse closes the surah (At-Talaq) by grounding its legal and ethical injunctions—about divorce, provision, and piety—in a cosmic framework, reminding believers that obedience to Allah's commands is rational given the totality of His knowledge and power over creation.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. O Prophet, why do you forbid [yourself] what Allah has made lawful for you, seeking to please your wives? And Allah is Forgiving, Merciful.
interpretation: This verse opens Surah At-Tahrim and addresses a specific incident in which the Prophet Muhammad, out of a desire to placate domestic tension among his wives, vowed to abstain from something permissible to him (traditionally understood to be either honey or his relationship with a servant woman, Maria the Copt). God gently rebukes him—not for sin, but for unnecessarily restricting himself regarding something lawful simply to appease his wives' feelings. The verse establishes an important principle in Islamic theology: that no one, not even the Prophet, has the authority to make forbidden what God has made permissible, since legislative authority over halal and haram belongs to God alone. By phrasing the rebuke as a question followed immediately by the assurance of God's forgiveness and mercy, the verse balances correction with compassion, showing that even the Prophet's well-intentioned personal choices in household matters can be subject to divine guidance. It also underscores the tension between prioritizing domestic harmony and upholding fixed religious principles, suggesting that emotional accommodation should not override or alter established divine rulings. The verse sets the stage for the rest of the surah, which addresses the Prophet's relationship with his wives and matters of household conduct, while reaffirming God's ultimate authority over matters of permissibility and prohibition.

translation: Allah has already ordained for you [Muslims] the dissolution of your oaths. And Allah is your protector, and He is the Knowing, the Wise.
interpretation: This verse was revealed in the context of an incident involving the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him), who had made a vow to abstain from something permissible (related to honey or one of his wives, according to various accounts) in order to please some of his wives. Allah here clarifies that making such a vow about lawful matters does not have to be permanently binding—He has established a legal mechanism (kaffarah, or expiation) by which believers can release themselves from oaths they have sworn, particularly when those oaths involve forbidding themselves something that is otherwise permissible. This reflects the broader Islamic principle that religion should not be used to create undue hardship or asceticism beyond what Allah has prescribed. The verse reassures the believers, and particularly the Prophet, that Allah as their Guardian and Protector (mawla) has provided an easy way out of such self-imposed restrictions, since He is fully aware of human nature and legislates with wisdom. It establishes that oaths taken in emotion or to please others, which involve prohibiting the permissible, can be expiated rather than permanently binding one to hardship, demonstrating the balance and mercy embedded in Islamic law.

translation: And [remember] when the Prophet confided to one of his wives a statement; and when she informed [another] of it and Allah showed it to him, he made known part of it and ignored a part. And when he informed her about it, she said, 'Who told you this?' He said, 'I was informed by the Knowing, the Acquainted.'
interpretation: This verse refers to an incident in which the Prophet Muhammad shared a private matter in confidence with one of his wives, who then disclosed it to another of his wives, breaching that trust. God informed the Prophet of this breach through revelation, and he confronted her with partial knowledge of what had happened, choosing discretion by not revealing everything he knew. When she asked how he had learned of this, he attributed his knowledge to God, the All-Knowing and All-Aware, emphasizing that divine revelation exposes hidden matters and that God supports His Messenger by informing him of what transpires even in private, domestic affairs. The verse underscores themes of trust, confidentiality within marriage, and the Prophet's reliance on divine guidance in navigating personal and household matters, while also serving as a broader lesson to his wives (and by extension all believers) about the importance of safeguarding confidences and the consequences of betraying them, especially when it concerns the Prophet himself. The passage sets the stage for the subsequent verses in which God addresses the wives directly, urging repentance and reaffirming the importance of supporting the Prophet in both private and public life.

translation: If you two (wives) turn in repentance to Allah, [it is best], for your hearts have deviated. But if you support one another against him (the Prophet), then indeed Allah is his protector, and Gabriel, and the righteous among the believers; and the angels, after that, are [also] his supporters.
