interpretation: This verse addresses a specific incident involving two of the Prophet Muhammad's wives (traditionally identified as Aisha and Hafsa) who had aligned together in a way that caused the Prophet distress, reportedly related to a matter of confidentiality or domestic disagreement. The verse serves multiple functions: it is a direct admonition urging repentance, acknowledging that their hearts had inclined toward wrongful behavior; it is a warning against collaborating against the Prophet's wellbeing; and it is a powerful reassurance of divine support. The escalating list of supporters—Allah Himself, then Gabriel, then righteous believers, then all the angels—establishes a hierarchy of backing that emphasizes the Prophet's protection is total and overwhelming, regardless of any domestic tension he might face. This teaches that even the Prophet's closest family relationships were subject to moral accountability before God, while simultaneously affirming that those who serve God's message, even amid personal difficulties, remain under comprehensive divine protection. The verse also establishes a broader principle about marital conduct and loyalty, suggesting that spouses should not unite against each other in ways that cause harm, and that personal repentance is always the path back to righteousness when one's heart has strayed from what is proper.

translation: Perhaps, if he divorced you [all], his Lord would substitute for him wives better than you - submitting [to Allah], believing, devoutly obedient, repentant, worshipping, and traveling [for His cause] - previously married and virgins.
interpretation: This verse was revealed during a period of domestic tension between the Prophet Muhammad and his wives, and it serves as a stern admonition to them. The underlying message addresses the wives collectively, warning that their status as wives of the Prophet does not grant them immunity from accountability; rather, it carries greater responsibility. The verse establishes a list of qualities that would characterize ideal replacement wives - qualities rooted in spiritual submission, faith, obedience, repentance, devotion, and piety - rather than qualities of lineage, beauty, or worldly status. This reflects a broader Qur'anic principle that nearness to a prophet or righteousness by association means nothing without genuine personal piety and submission to God. The mention of both 'previously married and virgins' indicates that marital history is irrelevant to spiritual worth. The verse functions both as a corrective rebuke to the Prophet's wives at that specific historical moment and as a timeless teaching that righteousness, not status or worldly position, is what truly matters in the sight of God.

translation: O you who have believed, protect yourselves and your families from a Fire whose fuel is people and stones, over which are [appointed] angels, harsh and severe; they do not disobey Allah in what He commands them but do what they are commanded.
interpretation: This verse establishes that faith carries a dual responsibility: safeguarding not only one's own soul but also one's household from spiritual ruin, which here is symbolized by a Fire so intense that even stones (often understood as idols once worshipped) serve as its fuel alongside wrongdoers. The mention of stern, unwavering angels who execute divine command without deviation underscores the absolute certainty and justice of this punishment—there is no possibility of bribery, negotiation, or mercy outside of Allah's own will. The verse implicitly calls believers to take an active role as guardians and teachers within their families, instructing them in righteousness, enforcing moral discipline, and modeling obedience to Allah, since failure to do so endangers not just oneself but those under one's care. It reflects the Islamic principle that faith is not merely a private matter but a communal and familial trust, where the head of a household bears accountability for the spiritual wellbeing of those he leads, mirroring the obedience of the angels themselves who perform their duties without question or defiance.

translation: O you who disbelieved, make no excuses today. You are only being recompensed for what you used to do.
interpretation: This verse depicts a scene of the Day of Judgment where disbelievers, having witnessed the truth they once denied, attempt to offer excuses or apologies for their rejection of faith. They are told that excuses are futile at this point—the time for repentance and correction has passed. The verse emphasizes the principle of divine justice: that the punishment or consequence faced is not arbitrary but a direct and proportionate result of their own choices and deeds in worldly life. It underscores the Quranic theme of accountability, teaching that true opportunity for change exists only in this life, and that on the Day of Judgment, actions speak for themselves without need for justification or defense.

translation: O you who believe! Turn to Allah in sincere repentance. It is hoped that your Lord will remove from you your misdeeds and admit you into gardens beneath which rivers flow, on the Day when Allah will not disgrace the Prophet and those who believed with him. Their light will run before them and on their right hands; they will say, 'Our Lord, perfect for us our light and forgive us; indeed, You are over all things competent.'
interpretation: This verse calls believers to a repentance (tawbah nasuha) that is sincere, complete, and lasting—one that involves genuine remorse, immediate cessation of sin, and firm resolve never to return to it. The conditional phrasing 'it is hoped' reflects both the mercy of Allah and the need for humility, reminding believers that salvation is never to be taken for granted but earnestly sought. The imagery of the Day of Judgment, when the Prophet and the faithful will not be humiliated, contrasts the fate of hypocrites and disbelievers with that of true believers, whose light—a symbol of faith, guidance, and good deeds—illuminates their path both physically and spiritually. That this light precedes them and shines at their right hand signifies the manifestation of their righteous deeds and unwavering faith, which will guide them toward salvation. Their plea for Allah to 'complete' their light suggests an awareness that human faith and virtue are always incomplete and in need of divine sustenance, especially in the trials of the Hereafter where hypocrites' light is said to be extinguished. The concluding affirmation of Allah's omnipotence closes the verse with reassurance that forgiveness and the perfection of guidance lie entirely within His power, reinforcing both fear and hope as essential components of true faith.

translation: O Prophet, strive hard against the disbelievers and the hypocrites and be harsh with them. Their abode is Hell, and wretched is the destination.
interpretation: This verse commands the Prophet Muhammad to confront two sources of threat to the Muslim community: open disbelievers who oppose Islam outwardly, and hypocrites who outwardly profess faith while secretly undermining it. The 'striving' (jihad) encompasses verbal, political, and if necessary military effort, while being 'harsh' refers to firmness in principle and resolve rather than personal cruelty—maintaining uncompromising truth in the face of opposition and deception. The warning about Hell underscores that the ultimate consequence of persistent disbelief and hypocrisy is severe, serving both as a deterrent and a reminder of divine justice. The verse reflects a broader Qur'anic theme that hypocrisy, due to its deceptive and corrosive nature, can be even more dangerous to the community's cohesion than open hostility, thus requiring decisive and unwavering response from leadership.

translation: Allah presents an example of those who disbelieve: the wife of Noah and the wife of Lot. They were under two of Our righteous servants but betrayed them, so their husbands did not avail them anything against Allah, and it was said, 'Enter the Fire with those who enter.'
interpretation: This verse establishes that spiritual kinship, not blood or marital ties, determines one's standing before Allah. Even being married to a prophet—among the most righteous of Allah's servants—offers no salvation if one harbors disbelief or betrays the truth internally. The 'betrayal' here is not necessarily moral infidelity but a betrayal of faith: these women outwardly lived with righteous men yet rejected their message and secretly worked against them, revealing hypocrisy. The verse serves as a counterpoint to the example that follows it (Pharaoh's wife), emphasizing that salvation is a matter of individual faith and righteousness, not proximity to righteous people. It warns believers, particularly women in the early Muslim community, that familial or marital connection to righteousness provides no automatic protection, just as the next verse will show that wickedness in one's household does not condemn the righteous either. This underscores the Quran's broader theme of individual moral accountability before Allah.

translation: And Allah presents an example for those who believe: the wife of Pharaoh, when she said, 'My Lord, build for me near You a house in Paradise, and save me from Pharaoh and his deeds, and save me from the wrongdoing people.'
interpretation: This verse presents the wife of Pharaoh (traditionally named Asiya) as a model of faith for believers, demonstrating that true faith is a matter of individual conscience and choice, independent of one's social or political circumstances. Despite being married to the most tyrannical and arrogant ruler mentioned in the Quran, who claimed divinity for himself, she maintained her faith in the One God. Her prayer reveals the proper priorities of a believer: she does not ask for worldly comfort, status, or even rescue in this life, but asks for a home with Allah in Paradise, placing eternal spiritual reward above temporal power and luxury. Her explicit request to be saved 'from Pharaoh and his deeds' shows her moral rejection of the oppression and tyranny associated with her husband's rule, even as she remained in his household. This verse teaches that proximity to corruption and worldly power does not preclude righteousness, and that believers—regardless of how dire or compromising their circumstances—can maintain inner purity and devotion to God, trusting in divine justice and the ultimate reward of the Hereafter over the false security of worldly status.

translation: And Mary, the daughter of Imran, who guarded her chastity, so We breathed into her [womb] through Our Spirit, and she believed in the words of her Lord and His scriptures, and was among the devoutly obedient.
interpretation: This verse presents Mary as the supreme exemplar of faith and virtue for all believers, male and female alike, placed at the conclusion of a chapter that otherwise addresses the wives of the Prophet. Her chastity is not merely physical but represents a complete guarding of the self from corruption, a purity that made her a vessel worthy of the miraculous. The 'breathing of Our Spirit' refers to the miraculous conception of Jesus, affirmed here without elaboration on the mechanics, emphasizing instead divine agency and the extraordinary nature of the event as a sign rather than a biological or theological claim about divinity. Her belief in 'the words of her Lord and His scriptures' highlights that her greatness stemmed not from the miracle alone but from her internal faith and submission—she accepted divine revelation and trusted in God's decree even when it brought social hardship and accusation. The final description, being 'among the devoutly obedient' (qanitin, a masculine plural form used inclusively), elevates her to the rank of the righteous regardless of gender, suggesting that piety and nearness to God are not bound by gender categories. The verse thus serves as a corrective and a model: true honor before God derives from faith, obedience, and moral integrity rather than status, lineage, or worldly position, directly relevant to the preceding verses about believing women rising above their circumstances through sincere devotion.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Blessed is He in whose hand is the dominion, and He is over all things competent (able to do all things).
interpretation: This opening verse of Surah Al-Mulk establishes the absolute sovereignty of Allah over all creation. The declaration that 'dominion' (al-mulk) rests entirely in His hand emphasizes that all authority, ownership, and control in the universe—whether over life, death, kingship, or fate—belongs exclusively to Him, with no partner or rival. The word 'tabaraka' (Blessed is He) conveys a sense of transcendence and abundant goodness emanating from this absolute power. Pairing this sovereignty with the statement that He is 'over all things competent' reassures the believer that this power is not abstract or distant but actively capable and exercised—nothing lies outside the scope of His ability. This verse sets the tone for the rest of the surah, which goes on to describe the signs of His power in creation and serves as a reminder to reflect on the magnitude of divine control as a source of both awe and comfort for the faithful.

translation: He who created death and life to test you as to which of you is best in deed - and He is the All-Mighty, the All-Forgiving.
interpretation: This verse establishes that life and death are not random occurrences but deliberate creations with divine purpose, reversing the common assumption that life precedes death in importance by naming death first. The purpose stated is testing (balaa), indicating that existence itself is a moral and spiritual trial rather than merely a biological or temporal process. The emphasis is on quality of deeds (ahsanu 'amalan - 'best in deed') rather than mere quantity, suggesting that sincerity, excellence, and intention matter more than sheer volume of actions or outward religiosity. The pairing of God's attributes at the end - Mighty and Forgiving - balances justice with mercy: He has the power to hold all accountable for this test, yet He is also ready to forgive those who fall short, acknowledging human fallibility within the trial. This framing suggests that life's meaning is found not in avoiding death or clinging to life, but in how one conducts oneself knowing that both are divinely ordained stages of a single continuous test of character and conduct.

translation: He who created seven heavens in layers. You do not see in the creation of the Most Merciful any inconsistency. So return your vision [to the sky]; do you see any flaw?
interpretation: This verse, from Surah Al-Mulk, calls attention to the precise and harmonious order of the cosmos as evidence of God's perfect design and power. By describing the seven heavens as created in layers without any disorder, discrepancy, or flaw, the verse invites the listener to engage in empirical reflection—to literally look up and search for imperfection. The repeated invitation to 'return the vision' twice (here and in the following verse) emphasizes that careful, repeated observation of creation will only reinforce the conclusion of flawless design rather than reveal any defect. This serves as a rational proof for God's oneness and omnipotence, suggesting that the very integrity and consistency of the natural order should lead humanity to recognize the Creator's wisdom and reject doubt or disbelief. It reflects a broader Quranic theme wherein the natural world functions as a sign (ayah) pointing toward divine truth, accessible to human reason and observation.

translation: Then look again and again—your sight will return to you, dazzled and weary.
interpretation: This verse comes after a description of the seven heavens created without any flaw or inconsistency, and it issues a challenge to the observer: look repeatedly, as many times as you wish, for any crack, defect, or disorder in the cosmic order. The repeated act of looking signifies human diligence and the natural inclination to search for imperfection, yet the result is the same each time—no fault is found. The vision itself becomes exhausted and humbled, returning 'disappointed' and 'fatigued,' which conveys both a physical and spiritual reality: the human intellect and senses are limited when confronted with the vastness and perfection of divine creation. This serves as a rhetorical proof for the oneness and power of God, inviting reflection on how the flawless design of the universe testifies to a single, all-knowing Creator, since any multiplicity of creators would have introduced inconsistency or conflict in the cosmic system. The verse ultimately humbles human arrogance by demonstrating that even persistent scrutiny cannot uncover any defect in God's creation, reinforcing the theme of divine perfection and the limits of human perception when faced with the grandeur of the heavens.

translation: And We have certainly adorned the nearest heaven with lamps [stars], and We have made them [as] missiles against the devils, and We have prepared for them the punishment of the Blaze.
interpretation: This verse highlights the dual purpose of the stars in the lowest heaven: they serve as a means of beauty and illumination for the sky, reflecting divine artistry and order in creation, while also functioning as a defense mechanism against the shayatin (devils) who might attempt to eavesdrop on the heavenly realm for forbidden knowledge. The 'missiles' symbolize divine protection of the unseen world from corruption and deception, reinforcing the idea that evil forces are kept at bay by God's design. Additionally, the mention of the punishment of the Blaze (Hellfire) for these devils underscores the moral framework of the universe, where those who seek to defy divine order face consequences. This verse, therefore, serves as a reminder of both the aesthetic and protective aspects of creation, illustrating the balance between beauty and vigilance against malevolence.

translation: And for those who disbelieve in their Lord is the punishment of Hell, and wretched is the destination.
interpretation: This verse establishes a direct relationship between rejecting one's Lord and the consequence of Hell, emphasizing that disbelief is fundamentally a matter of the heart's relationship with God rather than merely intellectual doubt. The phrase "disbelieve in their Lord" (كفروا بربهم) specifically uses the term "Rabb" (Lord/Sustainer), highlighting that disbelief is an act of ingratitude toward the One who nurtures and sustains them, making their rejection particularly severe since it denies their very source of existence and care. The verse concludes with "wretched is the destination" (وبئس المصير), which serves as a divine commentary that underscores the finality and misery of this outcome, contrasting implicitly with the favorable destination promised to believers elsewhere in the Qur'an. This serves as both a warning and a call to reflection, urging listeners to recognize the gravity of disbelief by presenting Hell not merely as punishment but as the natural and just consequence of turning away from one's Sustainer.

translation: When they are thrown therein, they will hear its roaring as it boils up.
interpretation: This verse, from Surah Al-Mulk, describes the terrifying sensory experience awaiting the disbelievers as they are cast into Hell. The imagery is deliberately visceral and auditory rather than merely visual, emphasizing the sound of the fire—a 'shahiq' which evokes the braying or groaning of a distressed animal, suggesting something monstrous and alive. The phrase 'wa hiya tafuur' (as it boils/seethes) conveys Hell as a cauldron of immense agitation, constantly churning with intense fury against those within it. This portrayal serves a rhetorical and theological purpose: it is not simply a description of physical punishment but an evocation of Hell's own 'rage' or eagerness to consume the wrongdoers, as if the fire itself possesses a form of sentient hostility toward sin. This personification intensifies the warning, making the consequence of disbelief and rejection of divine guidance viscerally real and psychologically terrifying to the listener, reinforcing the Qur'an's broader rhetorical strategy of using vivid sensory detail to compel moral reflection and repentance.

translation: It almost bursts with rage. Every time a group is thrown into it, its keepers ask them, 'Did there not come to you a warner?'
interpretation: This verse depicts Hell as having such intense fury toward the disbelievers that it is personified as nearly tearing itself apart in rage when they are cast into it. The imagery emphasizes the severity of divine punishment and the justified nature of that punishment. The question posed by the keepers of Hell to each group of sinners—'Did there not come to you a warner?'—serves as a rhetorical device establishing the principle of divine justice: no soul is condemned without first having received guidance and warning through a prophet or messenger. This underscores the Qur'anic theme that God does not punish people arbitrarily or without giving them the opportunity to heed warnings and repent. The rhetorical question also serves to condemn the disbelievers from their own admission, as the following verses show them confessing that warners did indeed come to them, but they rejected and denied the truth. Thus, this verse establishes both the terrifying reality of Hell's torment and the moral accountability of those who willfully ignore divine guidance despite having been warned.

translation: They will say: 'Yes, indeed a warner came to us, but we denied him and said: Allah has not sent down anything; you are only in great error.'
interpretation: This verse depicts the confession of the disbelievers in Hell when questioned by its keepers about whether a warner had come to them. Their admission reveals a crucial truth: condemnation is not due to a lack of guidance, but to the willful rejection of it. They acknowledge that prophets did come bearing divine revelation, yet they responded with denial and arrogance, dismissing the message as falsehood and even accusing the messengers themselves of being misguided. This reflects a common pattern of human defiance—when confronted with truth that challenges one's desires or established ways of life, there is a tendency to deny its divine origin altogether rather than engage with it honestly. The verse serves as a stark warning that on the Day of Judgment, no excuses of ignorance will be accepted from those who had access to guidance but chose arrogance and rejection instead. It underscores the principle of divine justice: Allah does not punish a people until He has sent them a clear warning, and the responsibility for disbelief lies squarely with the one who consciously chooses to reject the truth.

translation: And they will say: 'If only we had listened or reasoned, we would not have been among the companions of the Blazing Fire.'
interpretation: This verse depicts the confession of the damned in Hellfire, acknowledging too late that their doom resulted not from a lack of opportunity but from their own willful failure to use the faculties of hearing and reason that God had given them. The admission highlights a central Qur'anic theme: humans are accountable beings endowed with intellect and the capacity to receive guidance, and salvation or damnation hinges on whether they genuinely engage these faculties—listening attentively to revealed truth and reflecting upon it—rather than passively or stubbornly disregarding them. Their regret underscores that disbelief is ultimately a moral and intellectual failing rather than an unavoidable fate, reinforcing the Qur'an's insistence on human responsibility for one's beliefs and actions.

translation: So they will admit their sin. Then far removed [from mercy] are the companions of the Blaze.
interpretation: This verse depicts the moment of confession by the disbelievers condemned to Hell, as described in the preceding verses of Surah Al-Mulk. Having denied the warnings of the prophets in worldly life, they now openly acknowledge their wrongdoing and rejection of divine guidance once they witness the reality of punishment. However, this confession comes too late to benefit them, as the time for repentance and the acceptance of truth has passed. The phrase 'fasuhqan' (so far removed, or perdition) is a curse or expression of utter rejection and distance from God's mercy, emphasizing the finality and severity of their fate. The verse serves as a sobering reminder that acknowledgment of sin without prior sincere repentance and righteous action in life holds no redemptive value in the Hereafter, underscoring the Quranic theme that true faith and accountability must be exercised before death, not after one faces the consequences of denial and sin in the afterlife.

translation: Indeed, those who fear their Lord unseen will have forgiveness and a great reward.
interpretation: This verse highlights the sincerity of true faith by emphasizing the phrase 'bil-ghayb' (unseen/in secret). It praises believers who maintain God-consciousness (taqwa) and reverent fear of their Lord even when no one is watching them, when they are alone, and even though God Himself is unseen to them. This is a test of authentic devotion as opposed to performative piety done for social approval. The fear referenced here is not mere terror but a profound awe and consciousness of God's presence and judgment that shapes one's private conduct, thoughts, and moral choices even in complete solitude. Because such devotion stems from genuine internal conviction rather than external pressure or the desire to be seen by others, it is considered of the highest spiritual value. The promised reward—forgiveness of sins and a great, abundant recompense—reflects the principle that deeds rooted in sincerity (ikhlas) are those most beloved to God and most generously rewarded, as opposed to acts of outward compliance that may mask inner heedlessness.

translation: And conceal your speech or proclaim it - indeed, He is Knowing of that within the breasts.
interpretation: This verse affirms God's absolute and complete knowledge of all things, whether hidden or revealed. It teaches that there is no difference between what a person whispers secretly and what they announce publicly, because God's knowledge encompasses both the spoken word and the innermost thoughts, intentions, and secrets harbored within the heart. This serves as a reminder to believers of constant divine awareness, encouraging sincerity and righteousness in both private thoughts and public actions, since nothing can be concealed from the Creator who knows the deepest recesses of human consciousness.

translation: Does He not know, He who created? And He is the Subtle, the All-Aware.
interpretation: This verse presents a rhetorical question that affirms God's complete and intimate knowledge of all creation, including the hidden thoughts and secret deeds of human beings discussed in the preceding verses about concealing or proclaiming one's speech. The logic is self-evident: the Creator who fashioned every being and endowed it with its nature, capacities, and inner workings must necessarily possess total knowledge of what He created, down to the finest detail. The two divine names invoked—al-Latif (the Subtle, the One who perceives the most minute and imperceptible realities) and al-Khabir (the All-Aware, the One fully informed of inner realities and hidden matters)—reinforce this point by emphasizing not just general knowledge but penetrating awareness of subtlety and secrecy itself. This serves as a powerful reminder that nothing—no whispered intention, no concealed thought, no secret action—escapes divine awareness, since the very source of one's existence and faculties is the same source of all-encompassing knowledge. It calls the listener to recognize that privacy from other humans is not privacy from God, grounding accountability and mindfulness in the logical relationship between Creator and created.

translation: It is He who made the earth subservient and tractable for you, so walk through its regions and eat of His provision; and to Him is the Resurrection.
interpretation: This verse establishes a theological foundation for human engagement with the natural world. By describing the earth as 'ذلولا' (subservient, tamed, made easy to traverse—the term used for a camel broken in for riding), God indicates that the earth's order, stability, and resources are a deliberate gift, not an accident, making human life and sustenance possible. The command to 'walk in its paths' and 'eat of His provision' is an invitation to active engagement with the world—travel, labor, trade, and enjoyment of the earth's bounty—framing worldly industry and exploration as legitimate and even encouraged activities, so long as they are understood as drawing upon divine provision rather than self-sufficient human achievement. The verse closes by redirecting attention from the material and temporal toward the ultimate destiny: 'to Him is the Resurrection.' This juxtaposition ties together two seemingly disparate domains—worldly activity and eschatological accountability—suggesting that the freedom to work and benefit from the earth is not an end in itself but exists within a larger moral and spiritual framework. The earth's resources are provisional and instrumental, meant to sustain life during the test of worldly existence, while the final return to God reminds the believer that all mobility, sustenance, and achievement in this life are ultimately subordinate to divine judgment and the hereafter. Thus the verse balances practical engagement with the world and transcendent awareness, urging gratitude and responsible stewardship rather than heedless indulgence or despair.

translation: Do you feel secure that He who is in the heaven will not cause the earth to swallow you up when it shakes violently?
interpretation: This verse is a rhetorical warning directed at those who grow complacent in their disbelief or arrogance, feeling falsely secure from divine accountability simply because punishment has not yet befallen them. By referencing Allah as 'He who is in the heaven' (a phrase denoting His transcendence, power, and dominion rather than a literal spatial location), the verse emphasizes His complete authority over all creation, including the earth beneath human feet—the very ground people trust as stable and secure. The image of the earth swallowing people up or shaking violently serves as a reminder of historical punishments (such as what befell Qarun or other disobedient peoples) and underscores human vulnerability despite apparent safety. The underlying message is a call to humility and God-consciousness (taqwa): no one is beyond the reach of divine power, and the natural world itself operates entirely at His command, capable of becoming an instrument of punishment at any moment. This serves as a broader meditation on the illusion of human self-sufficiency and control over one's fate.

translation: Do you feel secure that He who is in the heaven will not send against you a storm of stones? Then you will know how was My warning.
interpretation: This verse is part of a series of rhetorical questions in Surah Al-Mulk directed at those who feel secure in their defiance of God, falsely assuming that their worldly power or the earth's stability protects them from divine retribution. The reference to God being 'in the heaven' signifies His transcendence, majesty, and absolute authority over all creation, not a literal physical location. The 'storm of stones' (hasiban) evokes the fate of previous nations destroyed by God's punishment, such as the people of Lot, serving as a historical warning. The verse challenges human complacency and arrogance, reminding the disbelievers that the same power that sustains the heavens and earth can just as easily bring about their destruction. The concluding phrase, 'then you will know how was My warning,' underscores the certainty of divine justice and the ultimate realization of truth that will come to those who dismissed the warnings of the prophets, serving as both a threat and a call to reflection on one's own vulnerability before the Creator.

translation: And indeed, those before them denied [the truth], so how terrible was My rejection/denial [of them, i.e., My punishment]!
interpretation: This verse serves as a warning to the disbelievers of Mecca by invoking the fate of earlier nations who rejected their prophets and messages. The rhetorical question 'how terrible was My denial' refers to God's severe punishment and censure of those past peoples who refused to accept divine guidance. The word 'nakeer' conveys both the sense of disapproval/condemnation and the punishment that followed it, emphasizing that when a civilization persistently rejects truth despite clear warnings, the consequence is a decisive and devastating reckoning. The verse functions as historical evidence within a broader argument: just as previous deniers faced destruction despite their power and numbers, so too will those who currently reject the Prophet Muhammad's message face similar consequences if they persist in their denial. This serves both as a warning and as a call to reflect on history as a source of moral and spiritual lessons, reinforcing the Qur'anic theme that divine justice operates consistently across all eras and nations.

translation: Have they not seen the birds above them, spreading their wings and folding them? None holds them up except the Most Merciful. Indeed, He is, of all things, Seeing.
interpretation: This verse invites reflection on a simple, everyday phenomenon—birds flying overhead, their wings extended and contracting—as a sign pointing to the sustaining power of God. The natural mechanics of flight, which humans can observe and even come to understand scientifically, do not negate the deeper truth that it is ultimately the Almighty's continuous sustaining power that keeps birds aloft against gravity. This serves as a broader argument for God's providence: if He maintains the delicate balance that allows a bird to stay in the air, how much more does He sustain and watch over all of creation, including human beings. The verse closes with a reminder of God's all-encompassing vision, suggesting that His care and awareness extend to every detail of existence, no matter how seemingly small, reinforcing His role as both creator and constant sustainer of the natural order.

translation: Or who is it that will be a host for you to help you besides the Most Merciful? The disbelievers are in nothing but delusion.
interpretation: This verse confronts the disbelievers with a rhetorical challenge, exposing the futility of relying on any power other than God for support and protection. It emphasizes that no army, ally, or worldly force can substitute for divine aid, and that those who reject faith in God are deceiving themselves by placing trust in false sources of strength. The verse underscores the Qur'anic theme of tawhid (the oneness of God) by highlighting that ultimate security and victory come only from the Most Merciful, and that any reliance on other than Him is a form of self-deception (ghurur) that leaves one spiritually and existentially vulnerable.

translation: Or who is it that could provide for you if He withheld His provision? Nay, but they persist in insolent transgression and aversion.
interpretation: This verse challenges the disbelievers' false sense of self-sufficiency by posing a rhetorical question that exposes humanity's total dependence on God for sustenance. No false deity, patron, or human power could replace divine provision if Allah chose to withhold it. The verse underscores that all wealth, food, and sustenance ultimately come from God alone, and no other being possesses the independent power to provide for creation. Rather than acknowledging this obvious truth and responding with gratitude and humility, the disbelievers stubbornly persist in 'utuww' (arrogant transgression) and 'nufoor' (aversion/flight from truth). This reveals a psychological and spiritual stance of willful rejection despite clear evidence—their rejection is not due to lack of proof but due to pride, obstinacy, and a deliberate turning away from guidance. The verse thus illustrates a recurring Quranic theme: that disbelief often stems not from ignorance but from arrogance and an unwillingness to submit to self-evident truths about one's dependence on the Creator.

translation: Is then he who walks fallen on his face more rightly guided, or he who walks upright on a straight path?
interpretation: This verse presents a powerful metaphor contrasting two modes of existence: one who stumbles blindly, face down, unable to see where he is going, versus one who walks upright with clear vision and purpose along a straight path. The image evokes the state of disbelief and misguidance—groveling, directionless, and vulnerable to every obstacle—compared to the state of faith, which grants the believer an upright posture, clarity of vision, and a defined sense of direction toward truth. The rhetorical question demands an obvious answer, emphasizing that guidance through revelation and submission to God grants dignity, stability, and purposeful orientation in life, while rejection of this guidance leaves one disoriented, degraded, and perpetually off-balance, unable to control his own path or destiny.

translation: Say: 'He it is Who brought you into being, and made for you hearing, and sight, and hearts (minds and understanding). Little thanks do you give.'
interpretation: This verse addresses human ingratitude by highlighting the fundamental faculties—hearing, sight, and intellect/heart—that God has granted as the very tools of perception, learning, and moral discernment. These are not mere biological functions but the means by which humans access knowledge, truth, and ultimately faith itself. The rhetorical structure, commanding the Prophet to 'say' this to disbelievers, serves as a direct challenge to those who deny resurrection or divine origin: the same God who created their very means of understanding is the one they fail to acknowledge. The phrase 'little thanks do you give' is not merely about verbal gratitude but points to the deeper failure to use these faculties as intended—to reflect, reason, and recognize the signs of God in creation and revelation. The verse thus implies that ingratitude here is not just emotional shortcoming but intellectual and spiritual negligence, since the very organs of thought and perception, if used properly, would lead one to faith and acknowledgment of the Creator rather than denial.

translation: Say, 'He it is who has multiplied you throughout the earth, and to Him you will be gathered.'
interpretation: This verse addresses the disbelievers who question the reality of resurrection, reminding them that the same God who originated and spread humanity across the earth—dispersing them into nations, tribes, and generations from a single origin—possesses the same power to gather them all back together on the Day of Judgment. The argument draws a logical parallel between creation's beginning and its end: the One capable of the initial act of creating and multiplying life has no difficulty in reversing that dispersal by reuniting all beings for accountability. It emphasizes divine sovereignty over the entire process of existence, from origin to return, and serves as a rational proof against those who doubt the Hereafter, since denying resurrection would be inconsistent with acknowledging God's evident power already demonstrated in the marvel of human proliferation throughout the world.

translation: And they say, "When will this promise be fulfilled, if you are truthful?"
interpretation: This verse reflects the recurring challenge posed by disbelievers to the Prophet and believers, demanding to know when the promised Day of Judgment or divine punishment would occur. Their question is rhetorical and mocking rather than a genuine inquiry, revealing their skepticism and denial of the unseen. By demanding an immediate timeline, they attempt to discredit the warnings of resurrection and accountability, treating the delay as proof of falsehood rather than recognizing it as part of divine wisdom and patience. The verse underscores a broader Quranic theme: that the timing of divine matters is known only to God, and human impatience or mockery does not alter the certainty of their fulfillment.

translation: Say: 'Knowledge [of that] is only with Allah, and I am only a clear warner.'
interpretation: This verse addresses the disbelievers' persistent demands to know the exact timing of the promised punishment or the Hour. The Prophet Muhammad is instructed to clarify the boundaries of his mission: he is not endowed with knowledge of the unseen, particularly the precise timing of divine decrees, as such knowledge belongs exclusively to Allah. His role is strictly defined as a 'clear warner' (nadhir mubin), meaning his responsibility is to deliver the message plainly and unambiguously, warning people of the consequences of disbelief, without claiming any power to predict or control when that warning will be fulfilled. This establishes a crucial theological principle distinguishing between the Creator's omniscience and the Messenger's limited, though vital, function of conveying divine guidance. It also serves to deflect attempts by skeptics to discredit prophethood by demanding signs or timelines that fall outside the scope of a messenger's duty, reinforcing humility and submission to Allah's sole authority over the unseen (al-ghayb).

translation: But when they see it [the punishment] drawing near, the faces of those who disbelieved will be distressed, and it will be said, 'This is that for which you used to call.'
interpretation: This verse depicts the moment of reckoning when disbelievers, who had mockingly demanded that the promised punishment or Day of Judgment be hastened, finally witness it approaching. Their arrogant defiance turns instantly to visible dread and despair—their faces betraying the horror they feel. The statement 'this is that for which you used to call' is a rebuke delivered by angels or as a divine declaration, highlighting the irony and folly of their former mockery: what they sarcastically demanded to see as proof of the Hereafter's falsehood is now undeniably present before them, with no escape or denial possible. The verse underscores the theme of divine justice and the ultimate exposure of truth, where human arrogance and skepticism toward spiritual warnings are shown to be self-defeating once confronted with reality.

translation: Say: 'Have you considered: whether Allah destroys me and those with me, or has mercy upon us, who will protect the disbelievers from a painful punishment?'
interpretation: This verse challenges the disbelievers' preoccupation with the fate of the Prophet and his followers, redirecting attention to their own precarious spiritual state. The rhetorical question exposes a logical flaw in the disbelievers' reasoning: whether the believers are destroyed or shown mercy by Allah has no bearing whatsoever on the disbelievers' own impending punishment. Their fixation on wishing harm upon the Prophet is ultimately irrelevant to their fate, for no outcome befalling the believers can serve as a shield or rescue for the disbelievers themselves. The verse thus shifts the focus from a worldly contest between believers and disbelievers to the ultimate reality that each soul faces its own reckoning before Allah. It underscores that salvation cannot be transferred, borrowed, or deflected from one party to another, and that no human power or alliance can intervene against divine punishment. The implicit message is one of stark accountability: the disbelievers' hope that the Prophet's misfortune might validate their position or bring them relief is a vain illusion, since their own painful fate remains fixed regardless of what happens to the believers.

translation: Say, 'He is the Most Merciful (ar-Rahman); we have believed in Him, and upon Him we have placed our trust. So you will come to know who it is that is in manifest error.'
interpretation: This verse responds to the disbelievers' rejection and mockery of the name 'ar-Rahman' (the Most Merciful), a name they found unfamiliar or objected to using for God. The Prophet is commanded to affirm his faith and complete reliance upon God despite their denial. The verse carries a decisive tone of warning: time itself will prove who is truly misguided—those who reject the Merciful God and His message, or those who believe in Him. It underscores that ultimate truth will be vindicated, and the arrogance of disbelief will eventually be exposed as manifest error, serving as both a reassurance to believers and an admonition to skeptics.

translation: Say, 'Have you considered: if your water were to sink into the earth, then who could bring you flowing [spring] water?'
interpretation: This verse closes Surah Al-Mulk with a powerful rhetorical challenge that underscores human dependence on divine providence for even the most basic necessities of life. Water, which sustains all living things and which people often take for granted, is presented here as a sign of God's continuous mercy and control over creation. The verse asks the listener to imagine a scenario where groundwater levels drop and springs run dry, a plausible natural occurrence beyond human control or remedy. By posing this as a rhetorical question, the verse forces reflection on the fact that no human technology, wealth, or power could restore such a vital resource if God were to withdraw it. The underlying message is a call to gratitude and humility, reminding believers that their existence depends entirely on forces outside their command, and that the One who provides sustenance deserves worship and recognition rather than arrogance or heedlessness. It also serves as a subtle warning against taking divine blessings for granted, suggesting that the natural order itself testifies to God's sovereignty and that human survival is contingent upon His continued favor.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Nun. By the pen and what they inscribe.
interpretation: This opening of Surah Al-Qalam begins with one of the mysterious disjointed letters (Nun) whose precise meaning is known only to Allah, followed by a solemn oath sworn by the pen and the act of writing. This oath elevates the status of knowledge, writing, and the recording of wisdom, affirming that the written word is a sacred trust through which divine revelation and human understanding are preserved. It serves as a direct rebuttal to the disbelievers who accused the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ of madness, for God swears by the very instrument of learning and civilization to emphasize that the one who brought this articulate, wise revelation could not possibly be insane. The verse establishes a profound connection between divine revelation and the tools of literacy, suggesting that the pen and what it records—including scripture, knowledge, and human affairs—are themselves testimonies to truth and order in creation.

translation: By the grace of your Lord, you are not a madman.
interpretation: This verse was revealed to console the Prophet Muhammad in response to accusations from his detractors in Mecca who claimed he was insane or possessed because of the revelations he received and his message of monotheism. The verse refutes this claim by attributing the Prophet's sanity, clarity of mind, and prophetic mission directly to the blessing and favor of God. It establishes that his character and message are a mercy from Allah, not the product of madness, thereby affirming his credibility and the divine origin of his mission in the face of slander and rejection.

translation: And indeed, for you is a reward never ending.
interpretation: This verse, from Surah Al-Qalam, is part of God's direct address and consolation to the Prophet Muhammad during a period when he was being accused by his detractors of madness. By affirming that his reward is 'ghayru mamnun' (uninterrupted, unceasing, and not diminished or begrudged), the verse serves two purposes: first, it assures the Prophet that his immense patience and steadfastness in delivering his message, despite the ridicule and hardship he faced, will be met with a continuous, everlasting recompense from God that will never be cut off or reduced. Second, the word 'mamnun' also carries the connotation of a favor given with an expectation of gratitude or as a means of making someone feel indebted. By negating this quality, the verse emphasizes that the Prophet's reward is a pure, unconditional grant from God, free from any of the burdens or obligations that accompany human-given gifts, thus affirming the sincerity and magnanimity of divine recompense for righteous conduct and suffering endured for a just cause.

translation: And indeed, you are of a great moral character (khuluq 'azeem).
interpretation: This verse is God's direct address to Prophet Muhammad, affirming that his character, conduct, and inner nature embody the highest standard of moral excellence. It serves both as a defense against the accusations of his detractors, who in the preceding verses had called him mad or possessed, and as a foundational statement establishing the Prophet as the living exemplar of the Qur'anic message. The 'great moral character' encompasses qualities such as honesty, patience, mercy, humility, forgiveness, and steadfastness in the face of adversity. By affirming his character before detailing his mission further, the verse underscores that the truth of his prophethood is evidenced not only by revelation but by the integrity and nobility of his lived example, making him a model ('uswa hasanah) for believers to emulate in all aspects of life.

translation: So you will see, and they will see.
interpretation: This verse, from Surah Al-Qalam, is addressed to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) during a time when he faced accusations of madness from his detractors in Mecca. It forms part of a rhetorical pairing with the following verse, which clarifies the subject: 'which of you is the afflicted one [with madness].' The statement serves as a divine assurance and a prophecy of vindication—God promises that time will reveal the truth to both the Prophet and his opponents. It is a declaration that the unfolding of events, the success of the Prophet's mission, and the ultimate judgment of history will make plain who was truly guided and who was in error. The verse carries a tone of patient confidence, instructing the Prophet to endure present hardship and slander because clarity and proof will come with time, exposing the falsehood of his critics and affirming his sanity and prophethood.

translation: Which of you is the one afflicted with madness.
interpretation: This phrase comes from Surah Al-Qalam, in the context where the disbelievers of Mecca accused Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) of being majnun (possessed or mad) because he called them to abandon idol worship and accept the message of pure monotheism. Allah responds to this slander by asserting that the Prophet is not mad, and that it will soon become evident—to both the Prophet and his detractors—who is truly afflicted with delusion. The rhetorical question turns the accusation back upon the disbelievers themselves, suggesting that their rejection of clear truth and their stubborn clinging to falsehood is the real madness, not the Prophet's call to guidance. This verse serves as a divine vindication of the Prophet's sanity and mission, while subtly condemning the irrationality of those who reject manifest truth out of arrogance or tribal loyalty. It also reflects a broader Quranic theme where worldly judgments of sanity and wisdom are inverted by divine truth—those who appear respectable by worldly standards may be spiritually and morally the ones truly lost.

translation: Indeed, your Lord is most knowing of who strays from His way, and He is most knowing of the [rightly] guided.
interpretation: This verse establishes that ultimate knowledge of guidance and misguidance rests with God alone, not with human judgment. It serves as a consolation and corrective to the Prophet Muhammad, who was deeply grieved by the rejection of his message by many of his people. The verse reassures him that he is not responsible for forcing belief upon others or for their choice to reject guidance; his duty is only to convey the message clearly. The deeper meaning is theological: since only God possesses complete knowledge of each person's heart, intentions, circumstances, and ultimate spiritual state, human beings—including prophets—cannot fully judge who is truly guided or misguided based on outward appearances alone. This serves as a check against arrogance or presumption in religious judgment, reminding believers that salvation and guidance are matters of divine knowledge and will, beyond full human comprehension. It also implicitly encourages trust in divine justice and wisdom in distinguishing between those who sincerely seek the truth and those who willfully turn away from it.

translation: So do not obey the deniers.
interpretation: This verse is addressed to Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him), instructing him not to compromise with or yield to those who reject the truth of his message, particularly the disbelievers of Mecca who sought to persuade him to soften his stance or make concessions in his preaching. It establishes a principle of steadfastness in conviction, warning against capitulating to pressure from those who deny faith, even when they offer worldly incentives or flattery to dilute the message. The verse underscores that truth should not be compromised for the sake of appeasing those who reject it, and it serves as a broader lesson for believers to maintain firmness in their principles against those who would seek to lead them away from righteousness through deception or temptation.

translation: They wish that you would compromise (be pliant/conciliating), so that they would compromise (in return).
interpretation: This verse addresses the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him), revealing the desire of his opponents among the disbelievers that he should soften his stance on the truth, compromise on the principles of monotheism, or show flexibility regarding idol worship and their practices, so that they, in turn, would be lenient and accommodating toward him. The verse exposes their strategy of seeking a middle ground that would dilute the message of Islam, trading firmness in faith for social or political ease. It serves as a warning against compromising core religious truths for the sake of worldly acceptance or to avoid conflict, emphasizing that steadfastness in conveying the message, even amid pressure to dilute it, is essential to prophetic integrity. The verse underscores a timeless principle: those opposed to truth often seek not outright rejection but a watering-down that renders the message harmless to their interests, and the believer is called to resist such pressures to maintain the clarity and integrity of divine guidance.

translation: And do not obey every despicable swearer of oaths.
interpretation: This verse is part of a series of descriptions (continuing in subsequent verses) characterizing a specific disbeliever who opposed the Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ), traditionally identified by commentators as al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah or a similar figure from the Meccan elite. The verse warns against being swayed by a person who habitually swears oaths to bolster false claims, using excessive oath-taking as a manipulative tactic to appear credible or trustworthy. The term 'mahin' (despicable/contemptible) suggests moral weakness and baseness of character, implying that such a person's frequent swearing is itself a red flag—an attempt to compensate for a lack of genuine integrity or truthfulness. The verse establishes a broader principle: one should be wary of individuals who rely on excessive oaths and insistent asseverations to persuade others, as this behavior often masks deception, moral corruption, or an attempt to manipulate through false piety. It instructs believers, particularly the Prophet, to exercise discernment and not be swayed by rhetorical tactics divorced from genuine righteousness, setting a standard for evaluating character based on substance rather than performative declarations of truthfulness.

translation: A slanderer, going about with malicious gossip.
interpretation: This verse is part of a series of descriptions (Surah Al-Qalam, verses 10-13) characterizing a morally corrupt individual whom the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ was warned not to obey or be swayed by, despite that person's wealth and social status. The 'hammaz' (slanderer) is one who habitually finds fault with others, often through subtle backbiting, sneering, or defamation, while 'mashsha'in binamim' (one who goes about with calumny) refers to someone who actively spreads malicious talk between people to sow discord, break relationships, and create enmity. The verse highlights a specific moral failing: the deliberate and habitual act of talebearing—carrying gossip from one group to another with the intent to harm. This behavior is condemned throughout Islamic ethics because it destroys trust, fractures communities, and reflects a corrupt character that prioritizes personal malice or gain over the wellbeing of others. The Quranic context suggests that such character traits, regardless of a person's external wealth or children (mentioned in surrounding verses), make them unworthy of being followed or given undue deference, as true worth lies in moral integrity rather than material success.

translation: A hinderer of good, a transgressor, a sinner.
interpretation: This phrase is part of a longer description (in Surah Al-Qalam) of a contemptible, morally corrupt individual whom the Prophet is warned not to obey or be swayed by, despite his wealth and social standing. 'Preventer of good' indicates someone who obstructs charity, kindness, and beneficial deeds—either by withholding his own wealth from those in need or by actively discouraging others from doing good. 'Transgressor' (mu'tad) describes one who oversteps the bounds set by God and violates the rights of others, acting with aggression and excess. 'Sinner' (athim) characterizes him as habitually steeped in wrongdoing, someone whose character is defined by persistent moral and religious violation. Together, these three traits paint a portrait of a person whose defining qualities are selfishness, hostility toward righteousness, and entrenched sinfulness—serving as a warning against being influenced by such individuals regardless of their apparent power or charisma.

translation: Harsh and cruel, and moreover, baseborn (or notorious for evil).
interpretation: This verse is part of a longer passage in Surah Al-Qalam (68:10-16) that catalogues the vile character traits of a particular disbeliever who mocked and opposed the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ—traditionally identified by commentators as Al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah, a wealthy and influential figure of Quraysh. After listing earlier faults such as habitual swearing, slander, obstruction of good, and transgression, the Qur'an adds this final, cutting description: 'utullin' (harsh, coarse, violent in temperament) and 'zanim' (a term with layered connotations—someone attached to a lineage without truly belonging to it, akin to an illegitimate offshoot, or one notorious and infamous for wickedness, like a conspicuous mark of shame). The juxtaposition is deliberate and devastating: despite his wealth, sons, and social standing (mentioned in the surrounding verses), his inner character is coarse and his reputation stained by moral corruption so apparent that it marks him as illegitimate to true nobility, akin to a graft that does not belong to the tree it is attached to. The verse exemplifies a broader Qur'anic rhetorical strategy of deflating worldly markers of status—wealth, lineage, social prominence—by exposing the moral bankruptcy underlying them. It suggests that true honor and legitimacy are rooted in righteousness and faith, not in material fortune or tribal affiliation, and that arrogant rejection of truth often stems from or produces such base character traits.

translation: [Simply] because he is a possessor of wealth and children.
interpretation: This phrase is part of a larger passage (Surah Al-Qalam, 68:10-16) describing a contemptible, arrogant disbeliever who rejects divine revelation. The verse highlights the flawed reasoning of such a person: he dismisses faith and truth not based on genuine reflection or evidence, but simply because his worldly wealth and numerous offspring have made him arrogant and self-satisfied. He mistakenly believes that his material prosperity is a sign of his own worth or even of divine favor, when in reality it is often a test, and in this context, is linked to moral corruption—lying, slandering, and obstructing good. The verse serves as a warning against equating worldly success with righteousness or truth, and criticizes those who let arrogance from material blessings blind them to spiritual guidance and prevent them from accepting truth with humility.

translation: When Our verses are recited to him, he says, 'Legends of the former peoples.'
interpretation: This verse describes the arrogant and dismissive response of disbelievers, particularly those who possessed wealth and status, when confronted with divine revelation. Rather than engaging sincerely with the message, they dismiss it as mere myths or fables passed down from ancient civilizations, equating the Quran with folklore rather than acknowledging it as genuine revelation from God. This reaction stems from pride, stubbornness, and an unwillingness to submit to truth that challenges their worldview or threatens their social position. The verse highlights a recurring pattern in human nature where those who reject faith often rationalize their rejection by trivializing sacred teachings, reducing profound spiritual guidance to the status of old stories with no real authority or relevance. This dismissal serves as a defense mechanism, allowing them to avoid the moral and spiritual accountability that acceptance of the message would demand.

translation: We shall brand him on the snout (nose).
interpretation: This verse refers to the arrogant disbeliever described in the preceding verses—one who rejected the signs of God, was obstinate, and mocked the believers while boasting of his wealth and lineage. The 'branding on the snout' is a metaphor for severe, lasting disgrace and humiliation, both in this life and especially in the Hereafter. The nose/snout, being a prominent feature of the face, represents one's honor and pride; to be marked there signifies a public and permanent mark of shame that cannot be hidden, reflecting divine retribution for arrogance and rejection of truth. This image conveys that those who exalt themselves in defiance of God will ultimately be brought low in the most visible and humiliating manner.

translation: Indeed, We have tried them as We tried the companions of the garden, when they swore that they would surely harvest it in the morning,
interpretation: This verse opens the parable of the owners of a garden, a story told to the disbelievers of Mecca as a warning. The 'trial' (balw) refers to a test of gratitude and righteousness through the blessing of provision and wealth. The garden owners, in their account, swore an oath to pick their fruit early in the morning, deliberately intending to do so secretly and swiftly so as to exclude the poor from their customary share of the harvest. Their sin was not merely the harvesting itself, but the conspiracy of selfishness and the deliberate withholding of charity, compounded by their failure to say 'if God wills' (in sha'Allah), reflecting an arrogant assumption of control over outcomes without acknowledging divine will. This sets up the subsequent narrative where God destroys their garden overnight as a direct consequence of their miserliness and lack of humility, serving as an allegory for the Meccans who denied the Prophet and withheld charity, illustrating that worldly blessings are tests, and ingratitude coupled with greed invites swift divine retribution.

translation: And they did not say, "If Allah wills."
interpretation: This phrase appears in the story of the owners of the garden (Surat al-Qalam) who resolved to harvest their fruits early in the morning, secretly, in order to deny the poor their rightful share. The verse notes that they made this plan without adding the qualifier "In sha' Allah" (if God wills), meaning they did not acknowledge their dependence on God's will or seek His permission for their intentions. This omission reflects their arrogance and self-reliance, assuming they had full control over the outcome of their plans without reference to divine decree. As a consequence, their garden was destroyed overnight, teaching that human plans are always subject to God's will, and that forgetting this truth—especially when combined with greed and the intent to deprive others—invites misfortune and loss. The verse serves as a broader moral lesson about humility, gratitude, and the necessity of recognizing God's sovereignty over all human endeavors.

translation: Then a visitation from your Lord came upon it while they were sleeping.
interpretation: This verse is part of the parable of the owners of the garden (Surah Al-Qalam) who resolved to harvest their fruits secretly at dawn, intending to withhold charity from the poor, without saying 'if Allah wills.' As divine punishment for their greed and arrogance, a calamity (often understood as a fire or destructive storm) struck their garden by night while they slept, unaware and powerless to prevent it. The verse illustrates the suddenness and totality of divine decree—that human plans and schemes, however carefully calculated, are ultimately subject to the will of Allah, who can bring ruin upon the heedless in an instant, especially when they forget to acknowledge His sovereignty and neglect their social and moral obligations toward the less fortunate.

translation: So it became like a blackened, barren wasteland [as if harvested in the night].
interpretation: This verse refers to the parable of the owners of the garden (As-hab al-Jannah) mentioned in Surah Al-Qalam. These men had inherited a fruitful garden from their father but secretly plotted to harvest it early in the morning, intending to exclude the poor from their customary share of the produce—an act of greed and ingratitude toward the blessings Allah had given them. As divine punishment for their selfishness and broken intention to withhold charity, a calamity (often understood as a fire or storm) struck the garden overnight. When they arrived expecting to reap a bountiful harvest, they found it utterly destroyed, resembling 'al-sareem'—a term describing a dark, scorched, barren land stripped of all its vegetation, as if it had been harvested and left desolate, or as black as the darkness of night. The swift transformation from a flourishing garden to a lifeless ruin serves as a powerful lesson on the consequences of miserliness, the fleeting nature of worldly wealth, and the importance of fulfilling one's obligations to the poor and needy. It illustrates that Allah's blessings can be swiftly withdrawn from those who show ingratitude and selfishness, reminding believers that true prosperity is tied to gratitude, generosity, and remembrance of God's favor rather than schemes of greed.

translation: So they called out to one another in the early morning,
interpretation: This verse is part of the parable of the owners of the garden (Qur'an 68:17-33), a story told to illustrate the consequences of greed and ingratitude toward God's blessings. The owners of a fruitful garden had secretly plotted the night before to harvest their crops early in the morning, specifically to prevent the poor from receiving their customary share of the harvest, as their father used to allow. This verse depicts the moment they rouse one another at dawn, eager and conspiratorial, to carry out their selfish plan in secrecy before anyone else could claim a portion. Their urgency and coordination in sneaking off early reveals their determination to withhold charity and their confidence in their own cleverness, not realizing that God was already aware of their intentions. The narrative serves as a moral lesson that schemes to deny others their rightful due, even when meticulously planned, cannot escape divine knowledge and justice, foreshadowing the destruction of their garden as swift retribution for their miserliness and broken covenant of generosity.

translation: [Saying], "Go early to your crop if you intend to harvest."
interpretation: This verse belongs to the narrative in Surah Al-Qalam about the owners of a garden whose father used to set aside a portion of its harvest for the poor. After his death, his sons resolved to harvest the garden early in the morning, in secrecy, so that no needy person would know and come to claim a share. This verse captures their whispered plan to slip out before dawn, driven by greed and a desire to deny charity to the poor. Their scheming becomes the prelude to divine punishment: that very night a calamity struck the garden, reducing it to ashes before they could carry out their plan. The episode serves as a moral lesson on the dangers of miserliness, broken obligations to the poor, and forgetting God's blessings, showing that worldly wealth can be swiftly taken away when one abandons generosity and gratitude.

translation: So they set off, while they were whispering to one another,
interpretation: This verse is part of the story of the owners of the garden (ashab al-jannah) in Surah Al-Qalam, a parable about a group of brothers who inherited a fruitful orchard from their father. Unlike their father, who used to set aside a portion of the harvest for the poor, these brothers conspired to harvest the fruits early in the morning secretly, intending to keep all the produce for themselves and deny the poor their customary share. The act of lowering their voices and whispering to each other as they set out reveals their guilty conscience and deliberate secrecy—they knew their intention was wrong and sought to conceal it from the needy who might overhear and come seeking charity. This moment captures human greed, selfishness, and the attempt to evade moral and social responsibility through stealth. The verse serves as a warning about the consequences of miserliness and the breaking of righteous traditions of charity, as the story continues to show how their orchard was destroyed overnight as divine punishment, leaving them devastated upon arrival. It illustrates a broader Quranic theme that wealth is a trust, and withholding it from the deserving due to greed invites divine retribution, while also demonstrating how sin often begins with quiet, calculated secrecy before being exposed to consequence.

translation: [Saying]: 'Let no needy person enter it upon you today.'
interpretation: This phrase is part of the story in Surah Al-Qalam of the owners of a garden who, inspired by greed and a desire to keep all their harvest for themselves, secretly plotted at night to harvest their crops early in the morning before the poor and needy could come to claim their customary share, as their father used to allow. They swore an oath to exclude any needy person from entering the garden that day, deliberately withholding charity. This act of selfishness and breaking the tradition of generosity became the cause of their punishment, as God destroyed their garden overnight, turning it to ruin as a lesson about the consequences of greed, the denial of charity to the poor, and the failure to say 'God willing' when making plans, reflecting arrogance and forgetfulness of divine will and accountability.

translation: And they set out early in the morning, with firm resolve, assuming they had full power [over their harvest].
interpretation: This verse belongs to the parable of the owners of the garden narrated in Surah Al-Qalam (68:17-33). Their righteous father used to leave a portion of the harvest for the poor and needy, but after his death his sons resolved to deny this charity. This verse captures the moment they set out stealthily at dawn, hearts hardened with determination to reap the entire harvest for themselves, confident and self-assured in their own capability and control over their wealth. Their 'power' here is ironic and short-lived: Allah sends a calamity in the night that destroys the garden entirely before they can carry out their plan, rendering their supposed capability utterly powerless. The verse exposes the arrogance of those who feel secure in their wealth and scheme to withhold charity, serving as a warning that true power and provision belong to Allah alone, and that miserliness and broken covenants of generosity invite divine retribution.

translation: So when they saw it, they said, 'Indeed, we are lost (astray)!'
interpretation: This verse comes from the story of the owners of the garden in Surah Al-Qalam. These men had secretly plotted to harvest their orchard early in the morning, deliberately intending to deny the poor their customary share of the produce, unlike their righteous father who had always set aside a portion for the needy. As punishment for their miserliness and secret plotting, God sent a calamity that burned and destroyed the garden overnight. When they arrived expecting to find their bountiful harvest, they instead found it reduced to ashes and ruin. Their first reaction upon seeing the devastation was disbelief and confusion so profound that they assumed they had simply taken a wrong turn and arrived at the wrong location - hence their exclamation 'we are lost/astray,' meaning lost in direction. Only in the following verse do they come to the painful realization that they are not geographically lost but rather spiritually and materially 'deprived' (محرومون) - that this is divine retribution for their greed and intention to withhold charity from the poor. The verse captures the psychological moment of shock and denial before the full weight of consequence and guilt sets in, illustrating a broader Quranic theme that selfishness and the withholding of rightful charity from the needy invites divine punishment, and that worldly possessions can be stripped away instantly as a test and a lesson.

translation: "Rather, we have been deprived [of provision]."
interpretation: This verse continues the parable in Surah Al-Waqi'ah about farmers who, upon seeing their crops ruined by God's will, first exclaim that they are burdened with debt and loss, then correct themselves to recognize a deeper truth: that their loss is not merely financial misfortune but a sign of being utterly deprived of divine favor and sustenance. The shift from "we are in debt/ruined" to "we are deprived" reflects a movement from worldly complaint to spiritual realization—acknowledging that all provision, growth, and sustenance ultimately depend on God's will, not human effort alone. It serves as a humbling reminder that human beings have no true ownership over nature's bounty; they are utterly dependent on God's mercy, and when that mercy is withheld, all human toil and expectation come to nothing. The verse underscores themes of divine omnipotence, human helplessness, and the illusion of self-sufficiency in the face of God's absolute control over sustenance and life.

translation: The most moderate (or most just/reasonable) among them said: 'Did I not say to you, why do you not glorify [Allah]?'
interpretation: This verse comes from the story of the owners of the garden (Surah Al-Qalam) who conspired to harvest their fruits secretly at dawn, intending to withhold charity from the poor. After Allah destroyed their garden as punishment for their greed and lack of gratitude, they blamed one another. Among them, one individual—described as 'the most moderate' or 'most balanced' in judgment—had earlier urged them to remember Allah and glorify Him instead of pursuing their selfish, miserly scheme. His words here, spoken in hindsight after the calamity, serve as a reminder of his earlier warning: had they turned to Allah in remembrance and gratitude (tasbih) rather than scheming to deprive the poor, they would have avoided this disaster. This highlights the Qur'anic theme that remembrance of Allah and humility before His blessings protect against the corrupting effects of greed, while neglecting gratitude invites loss and ruin. It also shows that within every group, there may be a voice of conscience or wisdom that calls others back to righteousness, even if that voice is ignored until it is too late.

translation: They said, 'Glory be to our Lord! Indeed, we were wrongdoers.'
interpretation: This verse comes from the story of the owners of the garden (Surah Al-Qalam) who conspired to harvest their produce secretly in the morning to deny the poor their rightful share, only to find their garden destroyed overnight. Upon realizing their error, they exclaim this declaration of repentance. The statement 'Glory be to our Lord' signifies an acknowledgment of God's absolute justice and power, affirming that He is above any injustice—it is they who have failed, not God who has wronged them. By declaring themselves 'wrongdoers' (zalimeen), they take full responsibility for their greed and selfishness, recognizing that their punishment was a direct consequence of their own moral failure. This verse illustrates a pattern found throughout the Qur'an: human beings, when confronted with the consequences of their transgressions, often turn to sincere acknowledgment of divine transcendence paired with humble self-accountability. It serves as a model for true repentance—one that begins with exalting God's perfection before confessing one's own faults, teaching that the path back to righteousness starts with recognizing both God's justice and one's own culpability in wrongdoing.

translation: Then they turned to one another, blaming each other.
interpretation: This verse is part of the story of the owners of the garden (as recounted in Surah Al-Qalam) who conspired to deny the poor their rightful share of the harvest and had their garden destroyed as punishment. After witnessing the devastation, they turned on one another in mutual recrimination, each blaming the other for the sinful plan. This depicts a universal human tendency: when wrongdoing leads to disaster, people often seek to shift blame rather than immediately acknowledge their own fault. The verse sets up the subsequent scene where they eventually recognize their own transgression against God and repent, illustrating the psychological and moral process of guilt, denial, mutual accusation, and ultimately sincere self-reckoning before God.

translation: They said, 'Woe to us! Indeed, we were transgressors.'
