Instead of anguish, He grants them 'nadrah' (a radiant glow of happiness visible on their faces, reflecting inner contentment and the freshness of divine favor) and 'suroor' (deep, heartfelt joy and delight). The verse illustrates the principle that true righteousness, done purely for God's sake without seeking worldly recognition, is met with both outward and inward reward in the Hereafter—a transformation from the fear of accountability to the bliss of divine acceptance and Paradise.

translation: And He has rewarded them, because they were patient, with a Garden and silk [garments].
interpretation: This verse refers to the righteous servants of God who endure hardship, hunger, and trials in this worldly life while remaining steadfast in faith and good deeds. Their reward for this patience (sabr) is twofold: spiritual—the eternal bliss of Paradise—and sensory—the comfort of fine silk garments, a luxury forbidden to men in this life but granted in the Hereafter as a symbol of honor and ease. The verse establishes a direct causal link between patient endurance of difficulty and the attainment of divine reward, illustrating the Qur'anic principle that steadfastness in the face of trials is met with compensation far exceeding the suffering endured. The pairing of 'Garden' (spiritual/eternal reward) with 'silk' (sensory/material comfort) reflects the holistic nature of Paradise, which satisfies both the soul's longing for closeness to God and the body's desire for comfort and beauty, all granted as recognition of the believers' perseverance.

translation: Reclining therein upon thrones [or couches], they will see therein neither [burning] sun nor [bitter] cold.
interpretation: This verse describes the perfected comfort of the righteous in Paradise, emphasizing the absence of extremes that cause discomfort in earthly life. The reclining posture on adorned couches signifies total relaxation, security, and honor, free from labor or need. The mention of neither scorching sun nor freezing cold symbolizes the removal of all forms of suffering and the attainment of perfect climatic and physical ease—an environment that is neither too harsh nor too severe in any direction, but perfectly temperate and pleasant. This reflects the Qur'anic theme that Paradise is a realm where the believers are liberated from the hardships and contrasts of worldly existence, enjoying instead a state of complete contentment and divine favor.

translation: And its shades will be close over them, and its clusters of fruit will hang low, within easy reach.
interpretation: This verse describes a scene of Paradise (Jannah) promised to the righteous, emphasizing complete comfort and ease without effort. The nearness of the shade protects them from any discomfort such as heat, while the fruit clusters being made to bend low means they can be reached and enjoyed whether standing, sitting, or reclining, without needing to exert any effort to pluck them. This imagery stands in stark contrast to the toil and labor required to cultivate and harvest fruit in worldly life, symbolizing that in Paradise, all forms of struggle, hardship, and barriers between desire and fulfillment are removed. It reflects divine generosity and the ultimate reward for patience and righteousness, where everything is provided in abundance and accessible effortlessly as a mark of honor and ease bestowed by God upon the inhabitants of Paradise.

translation: And vessels of silver and cups of crystal will be passed around among them,
interpretation: This verse is part of a longer passage in Surah Al-Insan describing the rewards of the righteous in Paradise. It depicts the luxurious and refined manner in which the inhabitants of Paradise will be served by attendants, emphasizing sensory delight and honor. The mention of silver vessels and crystal-clear cups merges two materials that would normally be opposites in nature—silver is opaque while crystal is transparent—yet in Paradise they are combined, suggesting that the laws and limitations of the worldly realm do not apply in the hereafter. This miraculous blending symbolizes the extraordinary, otherworldly quality of divine reward, where even mundane objects of daily life become transcendent and perfect. The imagery conveys comfort, abundance, and dignity, portraying Paradise as a place where believers are cared for with elegance and precision beyond earthly comprehension, reinforcing the Quran's broader theme of recompense for patience and righteousness in worldly life.

translation: Vessels of silver, which they have measured in due measure.
interpretation: This verse describes the refined nature of paradise, where the servants of Allah are served drinks in crystal-clear vessels made of silver—a material and craftsmanship that combines the transparency of glass with the luster of silver, something impossible in earthly experience. The phrase "measured in due measure" indicates that these vessels are filled precisely according to the desire and satisfaction of those being served, with perfect proportion—neither too much nor too little. This reflects the meticulous care and generosity of divine hospitality, where even the smallest details of reward are tailored exactly to bring complete delight and contentment to the righteous, symbolizing the perfection and justice of Allah's provision in the Hereafter.

translation: And they will be given to drink therein a cup [of wine mixed with] ginger.
interpretation: This verse describes one of the delights awaiting the righteous in Paradise, continuing the Qur'an's depiction of the rewards given to those who fulfilled their vows and fed the needy despite their own want, as described earlier in Surah Al-Insan. The 'cup' refers to a drink served to the inhabitants of Paradise, and its mixture with ginger (zanjabil) signifies a refined, aromatic, and pleasurable taste that was apparently prized among the Arabs of the time as an exotic and desirable flavoring. Unlike worldly drinks that intoxicate and harm, this drink is purely pleasurable without any negative effects, befitting the perfected and blissful nature of Paradise. The mention of a specific, named spring (as the following verse identifies it as 'Salsabil') emphasizes the particularity and perfection of divine reward, where even the smallest sensory details are tailored to delight the righteous. This imagery serves to contrast the fleeting and often corrupting pleasures of earthly life with the pure, everlasting, and perfectly suited pleasures of the afterlife, reinforcing the Qur'anic theme that true and lasting satisfaction is found only through obedience to God and reserved for the hereafter.

translation: A spring therein named Salsabil.
interpretation: This verse describes one of the flowing springs of Paradise reserved for the righteous, named Salsabil, whose name itself connotes something that flows smoothly and easily down the throat, pleasant and delicious to drink. The naming of this spring signifies the tangible, sensory reality of Paradise's rewards—it is not an abstract or symbolic paradise but one with specific, named features that the righteous will experience directly. The water's ease of flow (sal meaning smooth, sabil meaning path or way) suggests effortless pleasure without the toil or difficulty associated with earthly life, where obtaining water or sustenance often requires labor. This stands in contrast to worldly existence, where even life's necessities come with struggle. The specificity of naming this spring also reflects the Qur'an's broader technique of making the afterlife vivid and real to the listener, encouraging righteous action by painting a picture of reward that is detailed, sensory, and desirable—water that is not merely thirst-quenching but named, celebrated, and distinguished among the rivers and springs of Paradise.

translation: And there will circulate among them young boys made eternal; when you see them, you would think them scattered pearls.
interpretation: This verse describes a scene of Paradise in which youthful attendants, untouched by aging or decay, serve the righteous. Their description as 'eternal' (mukhalladun) signifies that they remain forever in their youthful, unblemished state, embodying the timelessness of Paradise itself, where nothing withers or fades. The comparison to 'scattered pearls' evokes radiant beauty, purity, and luminous perfection—pearls being scattered rather than strung suggests abundance and a dazzling, almost overwhelming visual effect, as if countless luminous forms move gracefully among the inhabitants of Paradise. The verse emphasizes the sensory and aesthetic delights promised to believers, where service is rendered by beings of unspoiled beauty, reinforcing the Qur'anic portrayal of Paradise as a realm that transcends the limitations, decay, and imperfections of worldly existence. It also reflects the generosity of divine reward, where even the attendants are made exquisite, enhancing the comfort and joy of the blessed.

translation: And when you look there, you will see bliss and a great dominion.
interpretation: This verse describes the scene of Paradise as experienced by its righteous inhabitants, who were mentioned in the preceding verses of Surah Al-Insan. The phrase 'إِذَا رَأَيْتَ' ('when you look') is addressed generally, inviting anyone—including the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ or any observer—to envision the splendor of Paradise. Wherever the eye turns in that realm, it beholds 'نَعِيمًا' (bliss, delight, comfort) and 'مُلْكًا كَبِيرًا' (a great dominion or kingdom). This 'great dominion' signifies not only the vastness and majesty of the physical surroundings—gardens, rivers, palaces—but also the honor and authority granted to the believers themselves, who are elevated to a status of nobility and sovereignty unlike anything in worldly life. It reflects the Qur'anic theme that the rewards of the Hereafter far surpass earthly kingship, both in scale and in the quality of joy, serving as a powerful incentive to those who preserve patience, faith, and good deeds despite worldly hardship.

translation: Upon them will be garments of fine green silk and rich brocade, and they will be adorned with bracelets of silver, and their Lord will give them to drink a pure drink.
interpretation: This verse is part of a vivid description of the rewards awaiting the righteous in Paradise, found in Surah Al-Insan. The imagery of green silk garments and silver bracelets conveys luxury, beauty, and honor, reflecting a state of eternal comfort and dignity granted by God. The color green, often associated with life, renewal, and tranquility in Islamic tradition, reinforces the sense of paradise as a place of lush, everlasting peace. The mention of a 'pure drink' given directly by their Lord signifies not only physical refreshment but spiritual purification—suggesting that in the afterlife, the believers are cleansed of all worldly impurities, sins, and suffering. The verse ultimately emphasizes the direct, personal relationship between God and the faithful, as it is God Himself who honors and nourishes them, underscoring that the ultimate reward for patience and righteousness in this life is both material splendor and spiritual fulfillment in the hereafter.

translation: Indeed, this is for you a reward, and your effort has been appreciated.
interpretation: This verse concludes a passage describing the magnificent rewards of Paradise granted to the righteous—gardens, silk garments, silver vessels, and flowing rivers. It serves as a divine declaration addressed to the inhabitants of Paradise, affirming that these blessings are not arbitrary gifts but a just recompense (jazaa) for their deeds in worldly life. The phrase 'your effort has been appreciated' (sa'yukum mashkoora) emphasizes that God acknowledges and values human striving—whether through worship, charity, patience, or moral steadfastness. The word 'shukr' (gratitude/appreciation) is significant here, as it reverses the usual relationship where humans are called to be grateful to God; instead, God is described as being grateful to His servants, honoring their efforts with eternal reward. This conveys a profound theological point: that no sincere effort made for the sake of God is wasted or overlooked, and that divine justice ensures a direct correspondence between one's deeds and their ultimate recompense.

translation: Indeed, it is We who have sent down the Qur'an to you [O Muhammad], a gradual revelation.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes divine ownership and intentionality behind the revelation of the Qur'an through the emphatic repetition 'Inna nahnu' (Indeed, We, We), underscoring that God Himself is the direct source of this scripture, countering any doubts about its authenticity or origin from any other source. The phrase 'tanzeelan' (a gradual sending down) highlights that the Qur'an was not revealed all at once but descended progressively over the course of the Prophet Muhammad's mission, according to the unfolding needs, circumstances, and events faced by the early Muslim community. This gradual method served pedagogical and psychological purposes: it allowed the Prophet and his followers to internalize teachings steadily, provided revelation as guidance and reassurance during times of hardship, and ensured the message was contextually responsive rather than abstractly imposed. This verse also serves as a consolation to the Prophet, reminding him that the burdens and trials he faces in conveying the message are divinely overseen and that patience is required as the revelation unfolds according to God's wisdom and timing, not according to human urgency or the demands of skeptics who might wish it revealed all at once.

translation: So be patient for the judgment of your Lord, and do not obey from among them a sinner or a disbeliever.
interpretation: This verse is addressed to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him), instructing him to remain steadfast and patient in carrying out and awaiting the fulfillment of God's decree, despite the opposition and hostility he faced from the disbelievers of Mecca. The command not to obey 'a sinner or a disbeliever' refers to the pressure he faced from influential figures among his opponents who tried to get him to compromise on matters of faith, soften his message, or abandon his mission altogether. The verse reinforces the idea that steadfastness in conviction must not be swayed by the demands or temptations of those who reject the truth, and that ultimate vindication rests with divine judgment rather than human opposition. It also serves as a broader principle for believers: patience in adversity and firm adherence to moral and spiritual principles, refusing to yield to the influence of those who are ungrateful or transgress against God's commands.

translation: And remember the name of your Lord morning and evening (or: at dawn and in the late afternoon).
interpretation: This verse enjoins the believer to maintain a constant, rhythmic remembrance (dhikr) of God that frames the entirety of daily life, marked by its two boundary points—the beginning of the day and its end. Rather than confining worship to isolated ritual moments, it calls for an enduring consciousness of the Divine that anchors a person's waking hours. The mention of 'bukratan' (morning) and 'asilan' (evening/late afternoon) evokes the natural cycle of light and darkness, suggesting that remembrance of God should be as natural and recurring as the rising and setting of the sun. This verse is often connected to the practice of regular prayer and invocation, reinforcing the idea that spiritual discipline sustained at the edges of the day cultivates an inner steadiness that carries through all human affairs, protecting the heart from heedlessness (ghaflah) and anchoring the self in gratitude and awareness of its Creator throughout trials and daily labor alike.

translation: And from the night, prostrate to Him, and glorify Him through a long portion of the night.
interpretation: This verse, addressed to the Prophet Muhammad, calls for extended nighttime worship as a means of spiritual strengthening and preparation for the heavy responsibility of prophethood. The night is emphasized throughout the Qur'an as a time particularly conducive to devotion—free from worldly distractions, quiet, and intimate—allowing for deeper concentration in prayer and remembrance of God (dhikr). The command to prostrate and glorify God for a 'long' stretch of the night underscores the importance of sustained, dedicated worship beyond the obligatory daily prayers, reflecting a practice of voluntary night prayer (qiyam al-layl or tahajjud) that became a hallmark of the Prophet's personal devotion and was later encouraged among believers as a path to drawing closer to God, purifying the soul, and gaining spiritual resilience to face the challenges of conveying the message of Islam.

translation: Indeed, these [people] love the immediate [life of this world] and leave behind them a Heavy Day.
interpretation: This verse critiques those who are consumed by worldly desires, prioritizing immediate pleasures, wealth, and gratification over spiritual preparation. The 'Heavy Day' refers to the Day of Judgment, described as burdensome due to the weight of accountability, reckoning, and consequences that await. By 'leaving it behind,' these people neglect or willfully ignore the inevitable reality of divine judgment, choosing short-term gratification over long-term spiritual responsibility. The verse serves as a warning against materialism and heedlessness, urging believers to balance worldly engagement with awareness of the Hereafter.

translation: We have created them and strengthened their joints and frame, and when We will, We can replace them with others like them, a complete replacement.
interpretation: This verse is a powerful assertion of divine sovereignty over human existence, reminding mankind of its utter dependence on God for its very creation and physical constitution. By emphasizing that God Himself fashioned the human body and gave it its strength and cohesion ('shadadna asrahum'), the verse counters any notion of human self-sufficiency or autonomy from the Creator. The second half delivers a sobering warning: the same power that brought humanity into being can just as easily remove it and replace it with another creation entirely. This serves as a corrective to arrogance and heedlessness, particularly relevant in the context of Surah Al-Insan's broader themes of gratitude, the trial of free will, and the consequences of belief versus disbelief. It underscores that no individual or generation is irreplaceable in the divine plan—existence itself is a gift that can be withdrawn, and humanity's continuation is contingent entirely upon God's will, not any inherent right or permanence of their own. This should instill humility and recognition of one's contingent status before the Eternal and Self-Sufficient Creator.

translation: Indeed, this is a reminder, so whoever wills may take to his Lord a way.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the voluntary nature of faith and spiritual guidance. The Qur'an is presented as a reminder (tadhkirah) - not a compulsion - that awakens the innate human capacity to recognize truth. The phrase 'whoever wills' underscores the principle of free will in Islam: guidance is made clear and accessible, but each individual must choose to act upon it. The 'way to one's Lord' refers to the path of righteousness, obedience, and spiritual closeness to God, suggesting that this path is available to all who sincerely seek it, but it requires personal intention and effort. This verse reflects a recurring Qur'anic theme that divine guidance is offered freely, yet human beings bear responsibility for their own choices and ultimate spiritual direction.

translation: And you do not will except that Allah wills. Indeed, Allah is ever Knowing and Wise.
interpretation: This verse affirms the doctrine of divine will as the ultimate ground of human volition: human beings possess genuine capacity to choose and act, but their choices and acts do not occur outside or independent of Allah's overarching will and decree. It establishes a balance between human free will and divine sovereignty—human beings are morally responsible for their choices (as implied by earlier parts of the surah discussing guidance and reward), yet nothing happens in creation, including the exercise of that will, except within the scope of what Allah has willed to permit or bring about. The verse closes with the attributes 'Knowing' and 'Wise,' indicating that Allah's will is not arbitrary but is exercised with complete knowledge of all circumstances, intentions, and outcomes, and with perfect wisdom in ordaining what occurs. This serves to remind believers that ultimate power and control rest with Allah alone, fostering humility, reliance upon Him (tawakkul), and recognition that even one's own capacity to intend and strive for guidance is itself a gift sustained by divine will.

translation: He admits whom He wills into His mercy, but for the wrongdoers He has prepared a painful punishment.
interpretation: This verse affirms the dual reality of divine justice and mercy as complementary, not contradictory, attributes of God. Admission into mercy is not arbitrary favoritism but reflects God's complete knowledge of hearts and deeds, extended according to His wisdom to those who are receptive to guidance. The contrast with the fate of the wrongdoers (al-zalimin) underscores that human choices carry real consequences. Those who persist in injustice—whether against themselves, others, or in rejecting truth—set themselves apart from the mercy that is otherwise described elsewhere in the Qur'an as encompassing all things. The verse closes a passage describing the rewards of the righteous in the afterlife by reminding the reader that paradise is not an automatic entitlement but the fruit of sincere faith and righteous action, while willful wrongdoing invites painful consequence. The juxtaposition serves as both comfort to believers and warning to the heedless, reinforcing the Qur'anic theme that divine mercy is vast but not divorced from moral accountability.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. By those [winds or angels] sent forth in succession,
interpretation: This opening verse of Surah Al-Mursalat begins with a divine oath, a common rhetorical device in the Qur'an used to draw attention to the weight and certainty of what follows. The term 'al-mursalat' (those sent forth) has been understood by commentators in multiple ways: some interpret it as referring to the winds that Allah sends in successive gusts, carrying rain and mercy to the earth as a sign of His power and benevolence; others understand it to refer to angels dispatched by Allah to carry out His commands, moving in sequence and order according to divine decree. The word '"urfa" conveys the sense of continuity, succession, or recognition—suggesting these forces come one after another in a discernible, purposeful pattern rather than randomly. By swearing upon these phenomena, whether natural or angelic, the verse establishes a tone of solemnity and sets the stage for the surah's broader themes concerning the Day of Judgment, divine order in creation, and the certainty of the resurrection. The invocation of forces that operate in sequence and fulfill their appointed roles without deviation serves as an implicit parallel to the inevitability of the events that will be described later in the surah—just as the winds or angels fulfill their missions precisely as ordained, so too will the Hour and its reckoning come to pass exactly as decreed.

translation: By those [winds] that blow violently,
interpretation: This verse is part of a series of oath formulas at the beginning of Surah Al-Mursalat, in which Allah swears by natural forces—winds and storms—to draw attention to their power and order as signs of His creative might. Most classical commentators (such as Ibn Kathir and al-Tabari) understand 'al-'asifat' to refer to violent, storm-force winds that Allah sends by His command, demonstrating His control over nature. Some interpreters also read this as a metaphorical reference to angels who swiftly and forcefully carry out divine commands, moving as rapidly and powerfully as storm winds. The oath serves a rhetorical purpose: by swearing upon these forceful, uncontrollable natural phenomena, the verse implicitly emphasizes the certainty and inevitability of what follows in the surah—namely, warnings about the Day of Judgment and the fulfillment of divine promises. Just as violent winds are undeniable and overwhelming in their effect, so too will be the fulfillment of what is promised regarding resurrection and judgment.

translation: By those [winds] that spread [clouds] far and wide,
interpretation: This verse is part of a series of oaths at the opening of Surah Al-Mursalat, in which God swears by various forces of nature or by angels carrying out His commands. 'An-nāshirāt' (those that spread) is commonly understood to refer to the winds that disperse and spread clouds across the sky, scattering rain-bearing clouds to various lands as part of God's natural order. Some commentators alternatively interpret this as referring to angels who spread out the scrolls of divine revelation or records of deeds. The oath serves to draw attention to the orderly, purposeful forces in creation—whether natural or angelic—as a prelude to affirming the certainty of the Day of Judgment, which is the central theme that follows in the surah. Just as the winds spread clouds in a precise and purposeful manner, so too will the events of the Hereafter unfold exactly as decreed, despite human doubt or denial.

translation: And those [winds or angels] that separate, separating distinctly,
interpretation: This verse continues a series of oaths at the beginning of Surah Al-Mursalat, in which Allah swears by various forces of nature or by angels. The phrase 'those that separate, separating distinctly' is commonly understood to refer to the verses of the Qur'an or to angels who distinguish and separate truth from falsehood, right from wrong, and lawful from unlawful with clear precision. Some commentators interpret this as referring to the winds that separate clouds or scatter them, while others see it as referring to angels who bring down divine decrees that clearly differentiate between matters. The emphasis on 'separating distinctly' underscores the clarity and decisiveness with which divine revelation distinguishes moral and spiritual truths, leaving no ambiguity between guidance and misguidance. This oath serves to authenticate the certainty of the Day of Judgment, which is affirmed later in the surah, by invoking the precision and order found in both the cosmic and moral realms as evidence of divine wisdom and purposeful design.

translation: And those [angels] who deliver a reminder,
interpretation: This verse refers to the angels, particularly Jibril (Gabriel), who are tasked with delivering divine revelation and messages of guidance to the prophets. The 'reminder' (dhikr) signifies the revealed scriptures, especially the Qur'an, which serves to remind humanity of their covenant with God, the truths of faith, and the consequences of their deeds. This is part of a series of oaths at the beginning of Surah Al-Mursalat, where Allah swears by various forces—winds, angels, and natural phenomena—to emphasize the certainty of the Day of Judgment and divine revelation. The angels who 'cast down' or 'deliver' this reminder act as intermediaries between the divine and human realms, ensuring that guidance reaches humanity so that none may claim ignorance of their moral and spiritual responsibilities.

translation: As an excuse or a warning.
interpretation: This phrase appears in Surah Al-Mursalat (77:6), within a sequence of solemn oaths sworn by God using the winds and angels sent forth in successive waves. The phrase 'عُذْرًا أَوْ نُذْرًا' (as justification or warning) describes the purpose of these forces being dispatched: they serve either to establish a clear excuse—removing any argument people might make on the Day of Judgment that they were not given fair warning—or to serve as an explicit warning of the consequences of disbelief and wrongdoing. The two words are linked by their shared root and rhyming sound, emphasizing that divine revelation and the signs sent to humanity leave no room for people to claim ignorance; they are left with no valid excuse since they have been duly cautioned. This sets up the chapter's broader theme of the certainty of the Day of Judgment and the accountability that follows, as the oaths build toward affirming that what has been promised will surely come to pass.

translation: Indeed, what you are promised [i.e., the Resurrection and Judgment] will surely occur.
interpretation: This verse is a solemn affirmation of the certainty of the Day of Judgment and all that has been promised regarding it—resurrection, reckoning, reward, and punishment. It comes amid oath-based openings in the Qur'an where Allah swears by natural phenomena to emphasize the truth of a forthcoming statement. The word 'إنما' (indeed, only) combined with the emphatic لام (لواقع) underscores absolute certainty, leaving no room for doubt or denial. 'واقع' means to fall or occur inevitably, like something that is bound to happen as a matter of established fact, not mere possibility. This serves as a direct response to the disbelievers who mocked and doubted the reality of resurrection after death, asserting that despite their skepticism, the appointed reckoning is an unshakeable truth that will certainly come to pass, no matter how distant or improbable it may seem to the human mind bound by worldly experience.

translation: And when the stars are effaced,
interpretation: This verse is part of a sequence of cosmic upheavals described in Surah Al-Mursalat that herald the arrival of the Day of Judgment. The effacing or blotting out of the stars signifies the complete dismantling of the familiar cosmic order that humanity has always relied upon for navigation, timekeeping, and a sense of stability in the universe. Stars, which have shone constantly since creation and symbolize permanence and guidance, losing their light represents the collapse of the entire created order at the end of time. This imagery is meant to impress upon the listener the magnitude and certainty of the Day of Judgment, when even the most fixed and seemingly eternal aspects of the universe will cease to exist as humans know them. It serves as a powerful rhetorical device to shake listeners out of complacency about worldly life and urge them to reflect on their accountability before God, since if even the stars—symbols of permanence—can be extinguished, then surely the resurrection and judgment that seem distant or unimaginable to skeptics are equally within divine power and certainty.

translation: And when the sky is split open/torn asunder
interpretation: This verse is part of a series of cosmic upheaval verses describing the signs of the Day of Judgment, found in Surah Al-Infitar. The splitting open of the sky represents the complete dismantling of the natural order that humans have always known, symbolizing that the heavens, which appear as a solid, permanent dome overhead, will tear apart like a fabric. This imagery conveys the magnitude of the Resurrection—it is not a minor adjustment but a total collapse of the cosmic structure, emphasizing divine omnipotence over creation. The tearing of the sky also symbolically represents the removal of barriers between the heavens and earth, allowing angels to descend and the unveiling of truths that were previously hidden from human perception, as everyone is confronted with the reality of their deeds and the certainty of divine judgment.

translation: And when the mountains are blown away.
interpretation: This verse is part of a sequence of cosmic upheavals described at the opening of Surah At-Takwir, which depicts the dramatic dismantling of the natural order on the Day of Judgment. Mountains, which in the Qur'anic worldview symbolize permanence, stability, and immovable strength, are shown here being utterly obliterated—scattered like dust or wool. This imagery serves to underscore the absolute power of God over creation and the transience of even the most seemingly eternal features of the physical world. By presenting such an unimaginable event—the destruction of mountains—the verse prepares the human mind to grasp the totality of the cosmic transformation that will accompany the Hour, stripping away any illusion that the material world offers lasting security. It calls the listener to recognize that only the Divine is truly permanent, and that all creation, however majestic, is subject to His will and command.

translation: And when the messengers are appointed a time [for their gathering].
interpretation: This verse is part of the opening sequence of Surah Al-Mursalat, where Allah swears by various forces of nature—the winds sent forth, the storms, those who spread and scatter—building toward a description of the Day of Judgment. The mention that 'the messengers are appointed a time' refers to the gathering of all the prophets and messengers on the Day of Resurrection, when they will be brought together at a specific, divinely appointed moment to testify concerning their nations—whether the people believed in them and followed their guidance or rejected them. This appointed time signifies the certainty and precision of God's plan: just as the messengers were sent at specific times during history to guide humanity, they will be summoned again at a specific time to bear witness before their Lord. It underscores the theme of accountability that runs through the surah, emphasizing that nothing in the unfolding of the Hereafter is left to chance—every event, including the convening of the messengers, occurs according to a fixed, predetermined schedule set by Allah's wisdom and justice.

translation: For what Day has it been appointed?
interpretation: This verse is part of a rhetorical sequence in Surah Al-Mursalat, following the mention that messengers' appointed times (or the witnesses summoned) have been set. The question 'For what Day has it been appointed?' functions as a dramatic pause that heightens anticipation before the answer is given in the following verse: 'For the Day of Decision' (Yawm al-Fasl). This rhetorical device is characteristic of the Qur'an's eschatological passages, where questions are posed and then answered to fix the listener's attention on the certainty and magnitude of the Day of Judgment. The repetition of such questions throughout this surah serves to impress upon the audience the inevitability of that Day, when all deferred matters—the testimonies of prophets, the fates of nations, and the deeds of every soul—will finally be settled and adjudicated by God.

translation: For the Day of Decision (Separation/Judgment).
interpretation: This phrase refers to the Day of Judgment, called 'the Day of Decision' (Yawm al-Fasl) because it is the day when Allah will definitively separate truth from falsehood, and the righteous from the wicked. It is the day when all disputes among humanity will be conclusively settled, when every soul will be judged according to their deeds, and the ambiguities and uncertainties of worldly life will be resolved with absolute clarity. This term emphasizes the finality and certainty of divine judgment, contrasting with the doubt and disagreement that characterizes human affairs in this world. The naming itself serves as a warning, reminding believers that what seems undetermined now will be decisively settled in the Hereafter.

translation: And what can make you know what is the Day of Judgment (Separation)?
interpretation: This rhetorical question emphasizes the overwhelming and incomprehensible magnitude of the Day of Judgment, referred to here as 'the Day of Separation' because it is when truth is distinguished from falsehood, believers from disbelievers, and the righteous from the wicked. The phrasing 'what can make you know' underscores that human language and imagination are insufficient to grasp the full reality of this event—it transcends ordinary comprehension. This rhetorical device, used repeatedly throughout the Qur'an for events of immense significance, serves to heighten anticipation and awe, compelling the listener to recognize that the Day of Judgment is not a matter to be taken lightly or dismissed, but a certain reality whose true nature remains beyond full human understanding until it is witnessed.

translation: Woe, that Day, to the deniers!
interpretation: This verse is a recurring refrain in Surah Al-Mursalat, repeated after descriptions of various signs of God's power—such as the natural phenomena, the stories of destroyed nations, and the events of the Day of Judgment. Its repetition serves as a rhythmic and rhetorical device that emphasizes the severity of the consequences awaiting those who deny the truth, the resurrection, and divine signs. Each time the refrain appears, it follows a specific proof or sign of God's might and justice, implying that denial in the face of such overwhelming evidence is particularly inexcusable. The 'woe' signifies deep anguish, destruction, and regret that the deniers will face on the Day of Judgment, serving as both a warning to disbelievers and a rhetorical pause that reinforces the chapter's central theme: the certainty of resurrection and divine justice despite human skepticism.

translation: Did We not destroy the former peoples?
interpretation: This verse is a rhetorical question posed by Allah, serving as a stern warning to the disbelievers of Makkah by invoking historical precedent. It reminds the audience of the fate of earlier nations—such as the peoples of Noah, 'Ad, Thamud, and others—who rejected their prophets and persisted in arrogance and disbelief, and who were consequently destroyed through divine punishment. The rhetorical form of the question implies an obvious affirmative answer, compelling the listener to acknowledge this established pattern in history. It functions within the surah's broader refrain 'Woe that Day to the deniers,' reinforcing the theme that the destruction of past nations is a sign and lesson for those who deny the Hereafter and divine retribution, suggesting that a similar fate awaits those who continue in heedlessness. The verse also sets up the following verses, which note that such destruction will likewise befall later generations who follow in the footsteps of disbelief, establishing a continuous divine law of accountability throughout human history.

translation: Then We shall cause the later ones to follow them.
interpretation: This phrase reflects a recurring Qur'anic motif found in passages recounting the destruction of past nations—such as the peoples of Noah, Lot, Thamud, and others who rejected their prophets. After describing the ruin of a particular transgressing community, the Qur'an often adds that subsequent generations who persist in similar disbelief and corruption will likewise be made to follow the same fate. The statement serves as a warning that divine justice is not limited to a single historical moment but operates as a consistent law: whoever repeats the sins of earlier corrupt nations—rejecting guidance, indulging in oppression, or denying the signs of God—will be swept into the same pattern of consequence. It underscores the Qur'an's broader theme that history is not merely a sequence of isolated events but a moral continuum in which people are held accountable according to the same standards as those who came before them.

translation: Thus do We deal with the criminals.
interpretation: This verse serves as a solemn refrain emphasizing the certainty and consistency of divine justice. It affirms that the punishment or consequence described for wrongdoers is not arbitrary but follows an established pattern—God's treatment of those who persist in sin, reject truth, and commit transgressions is consistent throughout history. The verse functions as a warning, reminding the audience that the fate of previous sinful nations or individuals serves as a precedent for how God responds to criminality and moral corruption, reinforcing the theme of accountability and the inevitability of justice in the divine order.

translation: Woe, that Day, to the deniers!
interpretation: This refrain, repeated ten times throughout Surah Al-Mursalat, serves as a solemn warning directed at those who deny the truth of divine revelation, the reality of resurrection, and the signs of God's power evident in creation. Each time the verse appears, it follows a description of a specific sign or event—whether natural phenomena like rain and growth, historical punishments of past nations, or scenes from the Day of Judgment itself. The repetition functions as a rhetorical and psychological device, hammering home the point that denial carries severe consequences and that no excuse will avail the deniers when they face the reality they once rejected. The word 'woe' (wayl) evokes both a specific valley in Hell according to some exegetes and a general expression of ruin, loss, and anguish. By addressing 'the deniers' specifically—not all of humanity—the verse distinguishes between those who have faith and remain mindful of accountability and those who arrogantly reject clear evidence of truth despite its availability. The Day referenced is the Day of Judgment, when all pretense and denial will be stripped away, and the deniers will witness firsthand the consequences of their disbelief, making this a powerful call to reflection and repentance for the listener before that reckoning arrives.

translation: Did We not create you from a despised/humble fluid?
interpretation: This verse is a rhetorical question posed to humankind, particularly addressing those who deny the resurrection and arrogantly disbelieve in God's power. By reminding people that they originated from something as lowly and insignificant as a drop of fluid, the verse serves to humble human pride and challenge claims of self-sufficiency or greatness. The implicit argument is that the One who created humans from such humble beginnings—transforming a mere fluid into a fully formed, conscious being—possesses the power to resurrect them after death. It is part of a broader Qur'anic rhetorical strategy of using humanity's own origins as evidence against their denial of an afterlife, highlighting the contrast between human arrogance and the lowliness of our biological origins, thereby pointing toward dependence on the Creator and the certainty of return to Him for judgment.

translation: Then We placed him as a sperm-drop in a firm, secure resting-place.
interpretation: This verse comes from the sequence in Surah Al-Mu'minun describing the stages of human creation. After mentioning that man was created from an extract of clay, and his progeny from a drop of fluid (nutfah), this verse describes how that drop is placed in the womb—described as 'qarar makin,' a firm and secure resting place. This highlights God's precise design of human reproduction, emphasizing the womb's protective and nurturing function, which safeguards the earliest, most vulnerable stage of human life. The verse underscores divine wisdom and care in the biological process of creation, inviting reflection on how even the most hidden and seemingly insignificant stages of existence are governed by purposeful, protective order established by the Creator.

translation: Until a known decree (a known term/measure).
interpretation: This phrase appears in Surah Al-Mursalat (77:22), within a passage reflecting on human origins and God's creative power. It follows the mention of the 'despised fluid' placed in 'a firm resting place' (the womb), stating that it remains there 'until a known decree' — meaning for a fixed, predetermined period of gestation ordained by God. This underscores the Qur'anic theme that every stage of human creation, from conception to birth, unfolds according to a precise, divinely appointed measure and timing, not by chance. It serves as evidence of God's meticulous design and foreknowledge, inviting reflection on the orderliness of creation as a sign of divine wisdom and power, and implicitly pointing toward the certainty of resurrection, since the One who ordains such precise biological timelines can equally ordain the Hereafter.

translation: So We determined [it], and excellent are the determiners.
interpretation: This verse comes within a passage describing the stages of human creation—from a drop of fluid, to a clinging clot, shaped and given form. The verse emphasizes Allah's precise power and wisdom in measuring out (qadarna) every stage of creation with perfect order, proportion, and purpose. The phrase 'fa-ni'ma al-qadirun' (excellent are the determiners/those who have power) is a self-praise affirming that Allah's capacity to ordain, measure, and bring into being is unmatched in its perfection. It underscores the theological principle of divine qadar (decree and measure)—nothing in creation, especially the intricate development of human life, happens by chance; everything is precisely calibrated by divine wisdom and power. This serves as an argument in the surah for the reality of resurrection: the One who could so precisely originate and measure human life from its beginning is certainly capable of recreating it after death.​

translation: Woe, that Day, to the deniers!
interpretation: This refrain, repeated throughout Surah Al-Mursalat, serves as a solemn warning directed at those who reject the truth of divine revelation, the reality of resurrection, and the signs of God manifest in creation. The phrase 'that Day' refers to the Day of Judgment, when the consequences of disbelief and denial will become starkly evident. By repeating this warning after describing various signs of God's power—such as natural phenomena, the fates of previous nations, and the processes of creation—the verse emphasizes that denial is not a neutral act but one that carries severe spiritual consequences. The repetition itself functions rhetorically to instill a sense of dread and to prompt reflection in the listener, inviting them to recognize the evidence of truth around them rather than dismiss it. It underscores the Quranic theme that disbelief, especially willful rejection of clear signs, leads to loss and suffering in the Hereafter, serving both as a warning and a call to faith and accountability.

translation: Have We not made the earth a container/receptacle?
interpretation: This verse, from Surah Al-Mursalat, poses a rhetorical question emphasizing God's wise design of the earth. The word 'kifāt' refers to something that gathers, holds, or contains. In context (followed by the next verse mentioning 'the living and the dead'), it signifies that the earth serves as a holding place for both the living during their lifetimes and the dead after they pass, as graves. This highlights divine providence and order in creation, where the earth is structured to sustain life above its surface and to receive bodies within it after death, serving as a temporary repository until the Day of Resurrection. The verse invites reflection on the earth's dual function as both a dwelling place and a burial ground, pointing to the comprehensive wisdom behind creation and serving as evidence of God's power to resurrect, since the one who made the earth to contain and preserve is equally capable of bringing forth life from it again.

translation: The living and the dead.
interpretation: This phrase comes from Surah Al-Mursalat (77:25-26), where Allah asks, 'Have We not made the earth a receptacle, for the living and the dead?' The verse highlights the earth as a vessel that sustains the living upon its surface while also receiving the dead within its depths. This serves as a sign of Allah's wisdom and power, demonstrating how the earth serves a dual purpose in the cycle of life and death, and pointing to His control over both states of existence as evidence of His ability to resurrect the dead on the Day of Judgment.

translation: And We have placed therein lofty, firmly-rooted mountains, and We have given you sweet water to drink.
interpretation: This verse appears in Surah Al-Mursalat as part of a series of divine signs highlighting Allah's power and favor upon humanity, following mention of the earth as a place of gathering for the living and dead. The towering mountains serve a stabilizing function, anchoring the earth and preventing it from shaking beneath its inhabitants, while also standing as monuments to divine majesty and permanence. The provision of sweet, fresh water—as opposed to the salty water of seas—represents a vital, life-sustaining blessing that is easily taken for granted yet essential for survival. Together, these two signs (mountains and fresh water) are presented as evidence of deliberate, purposeful creation rather than random occurrence, inviting reflection on the Creator's wisdom and care. The verse implicitly challenges the deniers mentioned throughout the surah (with the recurring refrain 'woe that day to the deniers') to recognize that a Creator who so meticulously provides for sustenance and stability on earth is equally capable of resurrection and judgment, and that such deliberate design demands gratitude rather than denial.

translation: Woe, that Day, to the deniers!
interpretation: This verse is a recurring refrain in Surah Al-Mursalat, appearing after a series of descriptions of the signs of God's power and the events of the Day of Judgment. Each time it is repeated, it serves as a solemn warning directed at those who deny the truth of divine revelation, the resurrection, and the consequences of their deeds. The repetition itself is rhetorically powerful, functioning almost like a drumbeat that punctuates the chapter, forcing the listener to pause and reflect after each proof or sign mentioned. The 'deniers' (al-mukadhdhibin) refers broadly to those who reject the message of the Qur'an, the reality of the Hereafter, and the justice of God. 'Woe' (wayl) is understood by commentators as a term signifying severe punishment or a valley in Hell reserved for the wicked, though it is also used idiomatically to express dire consequence and condemnation. The phrase 'that Day' ties this woe directly to the Day of Judgment, which has just been described with imagery of cosmic upheaval—stars extinguished, the sky split open, mountains blown away—underscoring that the denial of such undeniable truths will not go unanswered. Thematically, this verse reinforces the Qur'an's insistence on accountability: those who dismiss divine signs in this worldly life will face a reckoning precisely in the moment when those signs are fully and inescapably realized.

translation: Proceed to that which you used to deny.
interpretation: This verse is addressed to the deniers and disbelievers on the Day of Judgment, commanding them with scorn and rebuke to go forth toward the very punishment—Hellfire—whose existence they had rejected and mocked during their worldly lives. It represents the moment when disbelief confronts undeniable reality, as those who dismissed warnings of divine reckoning as mere myths or threats are now forced to walk toward the consequence they refused to believe in. The imperative "depart" or "proceed" carries a tone of contemptuous command, stripping away any possibility of argument, excuse, or escape—the time for denial has passed, and only the stark confrontation with truth remains. This moment encapsulates the Quranic theme of recompense, where disbelief in the unseen is answered by being made to witness and experience that same unseen reality in its fullest, undeniable form.

translation: "Proceed to a shadow [of smoke] having three columns,"
interpretation: This verse appears in Surah Al-Mursalat, in a passage describing the Day of Judgment and the fate of the deniers. The 'shadow with three branches' refers to a shadow of smoke from Hellfire that rises and billows into three distinct columns or pillars, yet provides no relief or protection. This is a bitter irony, for shadow is normally sought for shade and comfort, but this shadow offers no coolness, no protection from heat, and no shelter from the flame—it is a mockery of true shade. The three branches have been understood by commentators as representing the way smoke naturally disperses and rises in forked plumes, or symbolically as representing the totality and inescapability of the punishment surrounding the condemned from multiple directions. The verse follows immediately after descriptions of commands given to the wrongdoers to depart toward their punishment, reinforcing the theme of the chapter that repeatedly asks, 'Woe, that Day, to the deniers,' emphasizing how what they once denied—the reality of resurrection and judgment—confronts them inescapably.

translation: [It gives] no shade and does not avail against the flame.
interpretation: This verse continues the description from the preceding ayah of the shadow of smoke that will envelop the disbelievers on the Day of Judgment, splitting into three columns. Here it clarifies that despite appearing to offer shade, this smoke provides no actual coolness or protection—unlike true shade which shields from heat. It is utterly useless against the scorching flames of Hell, offering no relief or defense whatsoever. This imagery emphasizes the futility and despair of the punishment awaiting those who denied the Hereafter: even what might seem like a refuge (shade) turns out to be deceptive and powerless against the suffering they face. The verse underscores the totality of divine justice—there is no escape, no false comfort, and no partial mercy for those who rejected truth, as every apparent recourse is rendered meaningless in the face of their punishment.

translation: Indeed, it throws up sparks as [huge as] a castle.
interpretation: This verse is part of a description of Hellfire (referenced in the preceding verses of Surah Al-Mursalat) emphasizing its terrifying and overwhelming nature. The comparison of the sparks to the size of a castle or fortress serves to convey the immense scale and intensity of the fire, something beyond ordinary human experience. This imagery is meant to instill a sense of awe and fear in the listener, reinforcing the seriousness of divine warnings about the Day of Judgment and the consequences of denying the truth. The hyperbolic scale of the sparks reflects the rhetorical style of the Qur'an in depicting the afterlife, using vivid and dramatic imagery to impress upon the human mind realities that exceed normal comprehension, thereby urging reflection and righteous action in worldly life.

translation: As if they were yellow camels (or ropes).
interpretation: This verse is part of a description of the massive sparks thrown up by Hellfire, mentioned in the preceding verses as being like castles or fortresses. Here, the sparks are likened to 'jimālatun sufr'—a phrase classically understood to mean yellow or golden-hued camels, evoking the image of a herd of camels moving together, capturing both the multitude and the swift, surging movement of the sparks. Some early commentators also read it as thick ropes of ships, twisted and dark-golden in color. In either reading, the imagery conveys something of massive scale, overwhelming force, and a strange, almost majestic visual quality to something terrifying, reinforcing the Qur'an's rhetorical strategy of using familiar, tangible imagery from the Arabian environment (camels being central to Arab life) to convey the terror and magnitude of the Day of Judgment and its punishments, making the unimaginable scale of divine judgment graspable through concrete, recognizable similes.

translation: Woe, that Day, to the deniers [of truth]!
interpretation: This refrain, repeated throughout Surah Al-Mursalat, serves as a solemn warning directed at those who deny the truth of divine revelation, the reality of resurrection, and the signs of God's power evident in creation. Each time it appears, it follows a description of a specific proof or event—whether natural phenomena, the fate of past nations, or scenes of the Hereafter—emphasizing that denial is not merely intellectual disbelief but a willful rejection despite clear evidence. The repetition itself functions rhetorically, building a rhythmic and haunting refrain that impresses upon the listener the gravity and inevitability of accountability on the Day of Judgment, reinforcing that those who dismiss these signs as falsehood will face dire consequences for their heedlessness and arrogance.

translation: This is a Day on which they will not speak.
interpretation: This verse describes a terrifying moment on the Day of Judgment when the wrongdoers, overwhelmed by the horror of what they face and the undeniable evidence of their deeds, are rendered utterly speechless—unable to offer excuses, arguments, or defenses. It reflects the completeness of divine justice: all pretenses, denials, and arguments people used in worldly life become useless before the truth of their accountability. This silence marks a stage of helplessness before judgment is pronounced, contrasting with another stage later described in the Qur'an where people do speak, swear false oaths, and argue—showing the multiplicity of terrifying scenes on that Day, each highlighting a different aspect of human humiliation and loss of power when standing before God.

translation: And no permission will be given to them so they can make excuses.
interpretation: This verse describes the state of the disbelievers on the Day of Judgment, emphasizing the finality and justice of divine judgment. Unlike in worldly courts where the accused may offer excuses or explanations for their wrongdoing, on that Day, the deniers will not even be granted the opportunity to speak in their own defense. This underscores that the evidence against them will be so overwhelming and their guilt so self-evident that no excuse could possibly suffice. It reflects the complete closure of the chance for repentance or justification once the Hereafter arrives, reminding believers of the urgency of turning to God and living righteously in this life, before the time for excuses has passed forever.

translation: Woe, that Day, to the deniers!
interpretation: This refrain, repeated throughout Surah Al-Mursalat, functions as a solemn warning directed at those who reject the truth of divine revelation, the reality of the Day of Judgment, and the signs of God's power evident in creation. Each time it appears, it follows a description of a natural phenomenon or a historical account of destroyed nations, linking the denial of truth to inevitable consequence. The 'deniers' (al-mukadhdhibin) refers specifically to those who, despite having access to clear signs and warnings, choose to dismiss them as falsehood or mere poetry, prioritizing worldly skepticism over spiritual accountability. The repetition itself serves a rhetorical and didactic purpose: it rhythmically punctuates the surah, creating a sense of inescapable judgment that intensifies with each mention, forcing the listener to confront their own position—are they among those who deny, or those who believe? The word 'woe' (wayl) is not merely an expression of sorrow but is understood traditionally as a specific valley or form of punishment in Hell, making this phrase a concrete threat rather than an abstract lament. Thus, the verse encapsulates the surah's central theme: the certainty of resurrection and judgment, and the dire fate awaiting those who reject this certainty despite overwhelming evidence.

translation: This is the Day of Judgment (the Day of Separation); We have gathered you together with those who came before.
interpretation: This verse depicts the scene on the Day of Resurrection when all humanity—both the present generation being addressed and all the generations that came before them throughout history—will be assembled together before God for judgment. The term 'Day of Separation' (yawm al-fasl) emphasizes that this day will decisively distinguish between truth and falsehood, between the righteous and the wicked, and between those who believed the warnings of the prophets and those who denied them. The gathering of 'you and the former peoples' underscores the universality of this reckoning—it is not limited to one community or era but encompasses all of humanity since the beginning of creation. This serves as a powerful reminder that no soul will be judged in isolation; rather, the collective moral history of mankind will be laid bare simultaneously, making manifest the consequences of belief and disbelief across all ages, and affirming that divine justice applies equally and comprehensively to every generation.

translation: So if you have a plan, then plan against Me.
interpretation: This verse occurs in Surah Al-Mursalat, addressed to the deniers and disbelievers on the Day of Judgment, after they are told to go to the shadow that has three columns which offers no relief from the flame. It is a divine challenge and a declaration of utter powerlessness on their part. On that Day, when all worldly schemes, deceptions, and plots that the disbelievers once relied upon to resist truth or escape accountability have become meaningless, Allah mockingly invites them to employ any cunning or strategy they wish—knowing full well they have none and can have none. This rhetorical challenge underscores the absolute sovereignty of Allah and the complete helplessness of those who once schemed against the truth, revealing the futility of human plotting against divine will, especially in the moment when all pretense and power have been stripped away and only the stark reality of judgment remains.

translation: Woe, that Day, to the deniers!
interpretation: This verse is a recurring refrain in Surah Al-Mursalat, repeated after each description of signs of God's power, the realities of the Day of Judgment, and the fates of past nations. It serves as a solemn warning directed at those who deny the truth of resurrection, divine revelation, and accountability. The repetition itself is rhetorically powerful, functioning almost like a drumbeat that punctuates the surah's argument: after every proof or sign presented, the text pauses to declare the grave consequence awaiting those who reject it. The word 'woe' (ويل) connotes deep grief, destruction, or a specific valley in Hell reserved for the damned, according to some exegetes. By addressing 'that Day' specifically, the verse ties the deniers' fate directly to the Day of Judgment, when the deception and arrogance they displayed in life will be exposed and punished. The verse is not merely a threat but an invitation to reflection, urging the listener to consider the signs mentioned throughout the surah—creation, divine mercy, and justice—and to avoid the fate of those who dismiss them as falsehood.

translation: Indeed, the righteous will be amid shades and springs.
interpretation: This verse describes a scene from Paradise promised to those who were mindful of God (al-muttaqin) during their earthly lives. The imagery of shades and flowing springs evokes comfort, coolness, and abundance—qualities highly valued in the arid desert environment of pre-Islamic Arabia where the Qur'an was revealed. The shade represents protection and relief from harsh heat, while the springs symbolize purity, refreshment, and eternal sustenance. Together, these elements contrast sharply with the torment awaiting the wrongdoers described elsewhere in the same chapter (Surah Al-Mursalat), reinforcing the Qur'anic theme of recompense: those who maintained taqwa (God-consciousness, piety, and righteous restraint) will be rewarded with eternal ease and tranquility, free from the hardships and anxieties of worldly or infernal existence. This verse functions as part of a broader rhetorical structure in the surah that juxtaposes the fates of the righteous and the deniers of truth, using vivid sensory imagery to make the abstract concept of divine justice tangible and emotionally resonant for the listener.

translation: And fruits from whatever they desire.
interpretation: This verse is part of a description of the rewards awaiting the righteous in Paradise. It emphasizes the limitless abundance and personal satisfaction available to the inhabitants of Paradise, where every desire for fruit, representing pleasure and sustenance, is fully satisfied without restriction or lack. This reflects the Qur'anic theme that Paradise offers not just basic provision but the fulfillment of personal wishes and delights, contrasting with the limitations and struggles of worldly life. The mention of fruit specifically evokes sensory pleasure, freshness, and variety, symbolizing the complete and perfect nature of divine reward for those who lived righteously.

translation: Eat and drink with enjoyment for what you used to do.
interpretation: This verse depicts the divine address to the righteous believers on the Day of Judgment as they enter Paradise. It represents the ultimate reward and vindication for a life of faith and good deeds. The phrase 'eat and drink in satisfaction' conveys not merely physical nourishment but complete contentment, free from any anxiety, toil, or impurity that characterized earthly consumption. Crucially, the verse ties this blessed state directly to past actions—'for what you used to do'—establishing the Quranic principle that eternal reward is earned through one's conduct and choices in worldly life. This serves as both a comfort to believers, affirming that their patience and righteousness were not in vain, and a motivational call to the living, encouraging them to pursue righteous deeds in anticipation of such everlasting pleasure. The invitation to eat and drink without restriction or guilt also symbolizes the removal of all the limitations, prohibitions, and hardships that accompanied righteous living in this world, replaced now with pure, unearned-feeling joy that is, in fact, the direct consequence of earned merit.

translation: Indeed, thus do We reward the doers of good.
interpretation: This refrain, repeated throughout Surah As-Saffat after recounting the trials and deliverance of prophets like Noah, Abraham, and others, establishes a divine principle: righteous conduct and excellence (ihsan) are met with God's favor, protection, and reward. The verse functions as a theological conclusion drawn from narrative examples, teaching that those who maintain faith, patience, and moral excellence even amid severe tests—such as Abraham's willingness to sacrifice his son or Noah's endurance through the flood—will be recognized and rewarded by God. The word 'muhsinin' (doers of good) refers not merely to good deeds but to a state of spiritual excellence where one worships and acts as if seeing God, or knowing that God sees them. This repeated affirmation serves as both comfort to believers facing hardship and a moral exhortation, linking historical prophetic narratives to a timeless principle of divine justice and mercy that transcends any single story.

translation: Woe, that Day, to the deniers!
interpretation: This verse is a recurring refrain in Surah Al-Mursalat, repeated after each description of a sign of God's power or a scene from the Day of Judgment. It serves as a solemn warning directed specifically at those who deny the truth of revelation, the resurrection, and divine justice. The repetition functions rhetorically to hammer home the certainty and severity of the consequences awaiting deniers, creating a rhythmic and almost liturgical emphasis that contrasts the wonders of creation and the terrors of the Hereafter with the heedlessness of those who reject them. 'That Day' refers to the Day of Judgment, when the deniers will face the full weight of their disbelief, having dismissed the signs given to them in both the natural world and through prophetic revelation. The verse thus functions as both an indictment and a dire admonition, urging reflection on the fate of those who refuse to acknowledge truth despite clear evidence.

translation: Eat and enjoy yourselves a little; indeed, you are criminals.
interpretation: This verse is addressed to the deniers of truth and wrongdoers, delivered in a tone of stern rebuke and warning. It acknowledges that they may indulge in worldly pleasures, consumption, and enjoyment for a brief period—the short span of earthly life—but this indulgence is granted only temporarily and does not signify divine approval or escape from accountability. The phrase 'qalilan' (a little) emphasizes the fleeting, insignificant nature of worldly enjoyment when compared to the eternal consequences awaiting those who reject truth and commit transgressions. The declaration 'innakum mujrimun' (indeed, you are criminals) serves as a direct indictment, stripping away any illusion of security their temporary comfort might provide. The verse functions as a form of divine irony or sarcasm, permitting their indulgence precisely because their reckoning is certain and imminent, reminding the listener that worldly pleasure pursued in defiance of truth is ultimately a prelude to judgment rather than genuine success.

translation: Woe, that Day, to the deniers [of the truth].
interpretation: This verse is a refrain repeated throughout Surah Al-Mursalat, following descriptions of God's signs in creation, the inevitability of the Day of Judgment, and the fate of past nations who rejected their prophets. Each repetition functions as a solemn warning directed at those who deny the truth of revelation and resurrection despite clear evidence. The phrase 'that Day' refers to the Day of Judgment, when denial will no longer be possible and the consequences of rejecting divine guidance will become manifest. The rhetorical repetition serves to emphasize accountability: every mention of a sign, blessing, or warning is paired with this refrain to stress that disbelief and denial carry serious consequences, reinforcing the moral and theological message that truth will ultimately prevail and falsehood will be exposed, with those who persistently deny it facing severe reckoning.

translation: And when it is said to them, 'Bow down [in prayer],' they do not bow down.
interpretation: This verse describes the obstinate disbelievers who refuse to submit to God even when directly commanded to perform the simplest act of worship—bowing in prayer. Bowing (ruku') symbolizes humility and submission to the divine will. Their refusal represents not merely a physical unwillingness to perform a ritual act, but a deeper spiritual arrogance and rejection of submission to God's authority. This stubbornness is emblematic of those who, despite clear signs and calls to faith, persist in pride and denial, choosing disbelief over humble acknowledgment of their Creator.

translation: Woe, that Day, to the deniers!
interpretation: This refrain, repeated throughout Surah Al-Mursalat, serves as a solemn warning directed at those who reject the truth of divine revelation, the reality of the Hereafter, and the signs of God's power evident in creation. The phrase 'that Day' refers to the Day of Judgment, when the consequences of disbelief and denial will become starkly manifest. By repeating this warning after describing various proofs of God's power—such as the creation of humans, the sending of rain, the growth of vegetation, and the eventual destruction of the world—the verse emphasizes that denial of these clear signs is inexcusable and will result in severe consequences. The repetition itself functions rhetorically to drive home the gravity of rejecting faith, creating a rhythmic and ominous refrain that underscores accountability and the inevitability of divine justice for those who persist in disbelief despite the abundant evidence presented to them.

translation: Then in what statement after this (i.e., after the Qur'an) will they believe?
interpretation: This rhetorical question serves as a severe rebuke and warning to those who reject the clear signs and revelations of God. If the eloquent, miraculous, and truthful words of the Qur'an—filled with warnings, proofs, and accounts of previous nations' destruction—fail to move disbelievers to faith, then no other message or discourse could possibly convince them. It underscores the finality and sufficiency of divine revelation as the ultimate proof of truth, implying that rejection of it stems not from a lack of evidence but from willful obstinacy and spiritual blindness. The verse also serves as a refrain of accountability, reminding the audience that excuses for disbelief will not be accepted when the clearest guidance has already been presented.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. About what are they asking one another?
interpretation: This opening verse of Surah An-Naba (The Tiding) poses a rhetorical question referring to the intense disputes and discussions among the disbelievers of Makkah regarding the Day of Resurrection and the Prophet's message. The question format is used to draw attention to the seriousness and controversy surrounding this 'great news' (an-naba al-azeem), which the following verses identify as the reality of resurrection and judgment. The rhetorical question serves to emphasize the significance of the matter being questioned and to prepare the listener for the weighty revelation that follows, highlighting human tendency to argue about profound truths rather than simply accepting divine guidance.

translation: About the great news.
interpretation: This verse refers to the Day of Resurrection, which is described as 'the great news' (an-naba al-'azim) because of its immense significance and the certainty of its occurrence, despite the disbelievers' doubt and disagreement about it. The verse comes as a response to the opening question in Surah An-Naba, 'What are they asking one another about?' The 'great news' encompasses the reality of resurrection, judgment, and the afterlife—matters that the disbelievers of Makkah were skeptical about and frequently disputed among themselves. By calling it 'great,' the Qur'an emphasizes that this is not a trivial matter to be dismissed through argument or denial, but rather the most consequential truth that will ultimately be witnessed by all of humanity, when the righteous and the wrongdoers will see the full manifestation of divine justice.

translation: That concerning which they are in disagreement.
interpretation: This verse refers to the Day of Resurrection and the Hereafter, the great news (al-naba' al-'azeem) mentioned in the preceding verses. The disbelievers of Mecca disputed among themselves about this reality—some denied it outright, some doubted it, and others mocked those who believed in it. The Qur'an highlights that despite human disagreement and skepticism, the truth of resurrection and divine judgment remains certain and will be affirmed in due time, regardless of whether people choose to accept or deny it.

translation: No indeed! They will come to know.
interpretation: This brief, emphatic verse serves as a stern warning to those who deny the reality of the Resurrection and the Day of Judgment, as referenced in the preceding verses about the disputed matter over which people disagree. The word 'Kalla' (No indeed/Nay) forcefully rejects their denial and skepticism, while 'they will come to know' promises that the truth they currently doubt or dismiss will be made undeniably clear to them. This is understood as referring to the moment of death, the grave, or the Day of Resurrection itself, when the disbelievers and skeptics will witness firsthand the reality they rejected—too late for it to benefit them. The repetition of this phrase (appearing twice in close succession in the surah) emphasizes the certainty and inevitability of this reckoning, serving as a rhetorical device to instill both warning and conviction about the truth of divine judgment.

translation: Then, no! They are going to know.
interpretation: This verse is a solemn repetition of warning directed at those who deny or dispute the reality of the Resurrection and the Day of Judgment, as introduced earlier in Surah An-Naba. The repeated phrase 'كلا سيعلمون' (No! They are going to know) emphasizes the certainty and inevitability of the truth that the deniers reject. The doubling of the warning—first stated, then repeated with added emphasis through 'ثم' (then)—serves a rhetorical purpose: it intensifies the threat, suggesting escalating realization. The disbelievers will first come to know the truth at the moment of death, and then again, more fully and undeniably, on the Day of Judgment itself when they face the consequences of their disbelief. This structure reflects the Qur'anic style of emphasis through repetition, used to impress upon the listener the gravity and certainty of a coming reckoning that cannot be postponed or avoided, regardless of how much one might dispute or mock it in worldly life.

translation: Have We not made the earth a resting place (a cradle/bed)?
interpretation: This verse opens a series of rhetorical questions in Surah An-Naba that invite reflection on the signs of God's power and mercy in creation. By describing the earth as a 'mihad'—a cradle, bed, or resting place—the verse emphasizes the earth's suitability and hospitality for human life, much as a cradle is prepared with care for an infant. The imagery suggests stability, comfort, and provision, implying that the earth's flatness, firmness, and capacity to sustain life are not accidental but are deliberately designed by God as a nurturing habitat for humanity. The rhetorical form of the question ('Have We not...?') is meant to elicit an affirmative acknowledgment from the listener, reinforcing gratitude and recognition of divine favor, while also serving as an implicit argument for God's power to resurrect the dead, since the One who so meticulously prepared the earth for life is equally capable of restoring it after death—a theme that becomes explicit later in the surah's discussion of the Day of Judgment.

translation: And the mountains as pegs (stakes).
interpretation: This verse is part of a sequence in Surah An-Naba describing God's creative power and the design of the earth as a hospitable, stable dwelling for humanity. By likening mountains to 'awtad' (pegs or stakes used to secure a tent), the verse evokes the image of the earth as a great tent whose stability is anchored by the mountains, preventing it from shaking or drifting. This reflects an early understanding that mountains serve a stabilizing geological function, anchoring the earth's crust, while also serving as a rhetorical device to draw attention to the deliberate, purposeful order of creation. Theologically, it reinforces the broader argument of the passage: that the precise, functional design of the natural world—sky, mountains, day and night, rain and vegetation—serves as evidence of a wise Creator and as a prelude to affirming the reality of resurrection and divine judgment, since the One who established such firm and purposeful order in creation is equally capable of recreating life after death.

translation: And We created you in pairs.
