The verse instills a sense of constant moral awareness (taqwa), encouraging individuals to act righteously even in private, knowing they are never truly unobserved.

translation: Honorable, writing (recorders).
interpretation: This phrase refers to the noble angels known as Kiraman Katibin, who are assigned by Allah to accompany every human being and meticulously record their deeds, both good and bad. The verse comes in the context of Surah Al-Infitar, which discusses the Day of Judgment and accountability. The description 'honorable' (kiraman) emphasizes the dignified and trustworthy nature of these recording angels, underscoring that human actions are not left unnoticed or unaccounted for. This serves as a reminder to believers that every word and deed is being carefully documented, reinforcing the concept of divine accountability and encouraging mindfulness in one's conduct, knowing that nothing escapes this precise angelic record-keeping system that will be presented as evidence on the Day of Resurrection.

translation: They know what you do.
interpretation: This phrase refers to the noble angels (Kiraman Katibin) appointed to record every human being's deeds, as mentioned in the preceding verses of Surah Al-Infitar. It serves as a powerful reminder of constant divine surveillance through these appointed scribes, emphasizing that nothing a person does—whether good or evil, public or private—escapes notice or documentation. This awareness is meant to instill a sense of accountability and mindfulness in believers, encouraging righteous conduct since every action is being meticulously recorded for the Day of Judgment, when these records will be presented as evidence of one's deeds in life.

translation: Indeed, the righteous will be in bliss.
interpretation: This verse affirms the reward awaiting those who live righteously, contrasting with the fate of the wicked mentioned in the surrounding verses (who will be in Hellfire). The 'bliss' (na'im) refers to the eternal delight and comfort of Paradise, which is described elsewhere in the Qur'an as containing rivers, gardens, companionship, and the pleasure of being near God. The verse serves as a moral and theological assurance that moral conduct and piety in this worldly life have ultimate cosmic significance—that justice will be served in the Hereafter, where the righteous (al-abrar, those who fulfill their duties to God and to others with sincerity and excellence) will be recompensed with everlasting joy, free from the trials, sorrows, and limitations of earthly existence. It underscores the Qur'anic theme of the Day of Judgment as the moment when deeds are weighed and outcomes are determined accordingly, reinforcing the incentive for believers to strive for righteousness in their conduct.

translation: And indeed, the wicked (al-fujjar) will surely be in Hellfire (Jahim).
interpretation: This verse comes from Surah Al-Infitar, which describes the Day of Judgment and its consequences. It establishes a direct parallel with the preceding verse about the righteous dwelling in bliss, creating a dualistic framework that divides humanity into two ultimate destinies based on their earthly conduct. The term 'fujjar' specifically refers to those who habitually and defiantly transgress moral and religious boundaries, not merely occasional sinners but those characterized by persistent wickedness, corruption, and rebellion against divine guidance. The word 'Jahim' denotes a blazing, intensely hot fire, emphasizing the severity of the punishment. The verse serves as both a warning and a statement of divine justice, reinforcing the Quranic theme that moral choices in worldly life have eternal consequences. It reflects the broader Islamic theological principle of accountability, where actions are weighed and recompensed in the afterlife, reinforcing the necessity of righteous living, repentance, and adherence to divine commandments as a means of avoiding this fate.

translation: They will burn in it (the Fire) on the Day of Recompense.
interpretation: This verse refers to the wicked and sinful—those who denied the truth and transgressed—who will be cast into Hellfire on the Day of Judgment. The 'Day of Recompense' (Yawm al-Din) emphasizes that this punishment is not arbitrary but a just consequence delayed until the appointed time when all deeds are accounted for. The verse underscores the certainty of divine justice: though the wrongdoers may seem to escape consequence in worldly life, the Day of Din is when ultimate reckoning occurs, and entry into the Fire becomes their recompense for persistent denial, corruption, and transgression against God's commands. The use of 'yaslawnaha' (they will burn in it) conveys an ongoing, immersive suffering rather than a momentary punishment, highlighting the severity and inescapability of the consequence awaiting those who rejected faith and righteousness during their earthly lives.

translation: And they will not be absent therefrom.
interpretation: This verse concludes a passage in Surah Al-Infitar describing the fate of the wicked (al-fujjar) who are cast into the blazing Fire (al-Jahim) on the Day of Judgment. The statement that they will not be 'absent' from it signifies the permanence and inescapability of their punishment—unlike worldly suffering from which one might find temporary relief or distraction, the torment of Hell for the unrepentant sinners is continuous and unending. They cannot be removed from it even momentarily, nor can they be heedless or unaware of it, as both meanings are carried in the Arabic 'gha'ibeen' (absent/unaware). This serves as a stark contrast to the preceding description of the righteous who dwell in everlasting bliss, reinforcing the Qur'anic theme of ultimate and eternal consequences for one's deeds, and eliminating any false hope of eventual escape or cessation of suffering for those who denied the Day of Judgment and lived in corruption.

translation: And what can make you know what is the Day of Recompense?
interpretation: This rhetorical question emphasizes the overwhelming and incomprehensible magnitude of the Day of Judgment, suggesting that its reality is so immense that it surpasses ordinary human understanding. By posing this question to the Prophet (and by extension to all listeners), the verse underscores that no matter how much one contemplates this day—when every soul will be held accountable for its deeds—the full truth of its gravity, the justice it entails, and the consequences it brings cannot be fully grasped through human imagination alone. It serves as a rhetorical device to heighten anticipation and awe before further description of that day is given, reminding believers of the limits of human knowledge in comprehending divine matters and the ultimate reckoning that awaits all of creation.

translation: Then what will make you know what the Day of Judgment is?
interpretation: This verse employs a rhetorical device of repetition and amplification, following an earlier mention of 'the Day of Judgment,' to emphasize the incomprehensible magnitude and gravity of that Day. By posing the question twice (here and in the preceding verse), the Qur'an underscores that human understanding and imagination are fundamentally insufficient to grasp the full reality, terror, and significance of the Day when all souls will be held accountable before God. It serves to awaken the listener's awe and attention, reminding them that no earthly experience can prepare them for the ultimate reckoning, where no soul will have power to help another, and all matters will belong entirely to God.

translation: The Day when no soul will possess for another soul any power [to help], and the command, that Day, is entirely with Allah.
interpretation: This verse depicts the Day of Judgment as a moment of absolute reckoning in which all worldly bonds, alliances, and forms of intercession based on kinship, wealth, or status become utterly powerless. No person—however beloved, powerful, or closely related—will be able to intervene on behalf of another. This underscores the complete dissolution of human agency and social hierarchies that operated in worldly life, replacing them with the singular, unmediated authority of God. The phrase 'the command, that Day, is entirely with Allah' emphasizes that while in worldly life people often perceive themselves or other authorities as holding power and making decisions, on that Day it becomes unmistakably clear that ultimate sovereignty has always belonged to God alone. This serves as a sobering reminder to believers that they should not place ultimate trust or hope in human relationships or worldly power for salvation, but should recognize their utter dependence on divine mercy and justice.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Woe to those who give less [than due].
interpretation: This verse opens a surah that condemns fraud in weights and measures, specifically targeting those who demand full measure when receiving but cheat others when giving. Beyond the literal commercial context, it establishes a broader principle of justice and fairness in all dealings between people. The warning of 'woe' signals severe consequences for those who exploit others through deception, even in seemingly small matters. This reflects the Quran's emphasis that genuine faith must manifest in honest conduct in everyday transactions, and that cheating others—even in minor amounts—is a serious moral and spiritual failing that will be held accountable before God. The verse also implicitly teaches that economic justice is intertwined with spiritual integrity, as dishonesty in trade reflects a deeper corruption of character and disregard for divine accountability.

translation: Those who, when they take a measure [from] people, take in full.
interpretation: This verse describes the hypocritical and exploitative behavior of those who demand their full due when receiving from others, yet—as the following verses reveal—cheat others when it is their turn to give. It exposes a double standard rooted in selfishness: insisting on fairness and fullness for oneself while diminishing what is owed to others. This verse opens a broader condemnation of commercial fraud, particularly the practice of shortchanging buyers in weight or measure, which was common in pre-Islamic Arabian trade. Beyond the literal marketplace context, the verse carries a universal moral lesson about justice, reciprocity, and the hypocrisy of demanding rights from others while denying the same rights to them. It sets up a contrast between self-interest and the Islamic ethical principle that one should treat others as one wishes to be treated, emphasizing that genuine faith requires consistency between how one claims rights and how one fulfills obligations to others.

translation: And when they measure or weigh for others, they give less.
interpretation: This verse is part of the opening of Surah Al-Mutaffifin (The Defrauders), which condemns those who demand full measure when receiving from others but cheat when giving. It exposes a fundamental hypocrisy in commercial and social dealings: insisting on one's own rights while shortchanging others. The verse addresses a specific, concrete form of injustice—fraud in weights and measures—but its implications extend to any situation where a person applies double standards, taking full advantage for themselves while shortchanging others in their obligations. The Qur'an here establishes a principle of reciprocal fairness and warns against the moral corruption that arises when self-interest overrides justice and honesty in dealings with other people. This sin is treated with particular severity in the Qur'an, as the surah goes on to warn of severe punishment for this seemingly 'minor' economic sin, elevating it to a matter of serious theological and ethical concern because it reveals a deeper corruption of character—one who is willing to deceive and harm others for personal gain while demanding full justice for themselves is spiritually deficient, lacking true consciousness of accountability before God.

translation: Do they not think that they will be resurrected?
interpretation: This verse occurs within Surah Al-Mutaffifin, immediately following condemnation of those who cheat in weights and measures—taking full measure when receiving but giving less when measuring for others. The rhetorical question posed here serves as a probing indictment of such people's moral psychology: their fraudulent behavior stems from a failure to truly internalize belief in the Resurrection and the ultimate accountability before God. The verse suggests that genuine conviction in being raised again for judgment would naturally restrain unjust conduct in worldly transactions. By framing this as a question—'do they not think?'—the Qur'an highlights a kind of willful heedlessness or practical disbelief, where people may nominally affirm resurrection as a doctrine yet live as though no reckoning awaits them. This connects ethical conduct directly to eschatological consciousness, implying that true faith in the Hereafter should manifest in honest dealings, and that cheating others reveals a deeper spiritual deficiency rather than merely a social or economic failing.

translation: For a Great Day.
interpretation: This phrase refers to the Day of Judgment, described here with the adjective 'great' (ʿaẓīm) to emphasize its immense significance and the overwhelming nature of what will occur on it. It appears in the context of a rhetorical question posed to those who cheat in weights and measures, asking whether they do not realize that they will be resurrected for this momentous Day. The verse serves as a warning that worldly transgressions, however small they may seem, will be accounted for on a Day whose magnitude dwarfs all earthly concerns—a Day when all humanity will stand before God for judgment, when the consequences of one's deeds, both great and small, will be fully revealed and reckoned.

translation: The Day when mankind will stand before the Lord of the worlds.
interpretation: This verse refers to the Day of Judgment, emphasizing the moment when all of humanity, regardless of status, wealth, or power held in worldly life, will rise and stand in complete submission before Allah, the Lord and Sustainer of all creation. The phrase 'Rabb al-alameen' (Lord of the worlds) underscores Allah's universal sovereignty over all realms of existence—not just humanity, but all creation. This standing represents a moment of absolute accountability, where the illusions of worldly power and the deceptions practiced by the unjust (referenced in the preceding verses about those who cheat in measurements) will be stripped away. It serves as a stark reminder that every soul will ultimately face divine judgment, and that no one can evade accountability for their actions, particularly those who deal unjustly with others through fraud and deception in their worldly dealings. The verse functions as a moral deterrent, calling believers to live with consciousness of this ultimate reckoning.

translation: Nay! Indeed, the record of the wicked is in Sijjeen.
interpretation: This verse establishes that the deeds of the wicked and sinful are recorded and preserved in a place or state called Sijjeen, a term linguistically related to 'imprisonment' or being 'confined,' suggesting something low, narrow, and restrictive. This stands in stark contrast to the later description of the righteous, whose records are kept in 'Illiyyin' (the highest place). The verse serves as a warning and affirmation that nothing escapes divine accounting—every sinful act is meticulously documented in a lowly register, symbolizing the spiritual degradation and confinement that corresponds to the nature of wrongdoing itself, setting the stage for the Day of Judgment when these records will be unveiled and consequences meted out accordingly.

translation: And what will make you know what Sijjeen is?
interpretation: This rhetorical question emphasizes the incomprehensible severity and significance of Sijjeen, a term referring to a lowly, confining register or place where the records of the wicked are kept, as mentioned in the surrounding verses of Surah Al-Mutaffifin. The rhetorical device 'what will make you know' is used by the Qur'an to signal that the matter being discussed is of such magnitude or unfamiliarity that ordinary human understanding cannot fully grasp it without divine clarification, which follows in subsequent verses describing it as a 'written register.' This device heightens the sense of awe and warning, impressing upon the listener the seriousness of the fate of the wicked, whose deeds are recorded in this lowly, sealed book, symbolizing their spiritual degradation and the certainty of divine accounting.

translation: A written record, inscribed.
interpretation: This verse refers to 'Sijjeen,' the register in which the deeds of the wicked and sinners are recorded, as mentioned in the preceding verses of Surah Al-Mutaffifin. It emphasizes that the deeds of the transgressors—those who cheat in weights and measures and reject the Day of Judgment—are not forgotten or lost, but are meticulously documented in a clear, fixed, and unalterable record. This inscription signifies the certainty and permanence of accountability: nothing escapes divine knowledge, and every soul's actions are preserved for the reckoning. The imagery of a 'written' and 'inscribed' book underscores the seriousness and inevitability of divine justice, contrasting the fate of the wicked with that of the righteous, whose deeds are recorded in 'Illiyyun,' a register of honor mentioned later in the same surah.

translation: Woe, that Day, to the deniers!
interpretation: This verse is a recurring refrain in Surah Al-Mursalat, repeated ten times throughout the chapter, each time following a description of a sign of God's power—whether in creation, in the cycle of destruction of past nations, or in the events of the Day of Judgment. The repetition serves as a rhetorical and theological hammer, driving home the consequences awaiting those who deny the truth of revelation and the reality of resurrection. 'That Day' refers to the Day of Judgment, a moment when the deniers' disbelief will be exposed as catastrophically mistaken, and 'woe' (wayl) conveys both a curse and a description of the severe punishment and despair they will face. The verse functions almost like a liturgical refrain, reinforcing after each argument or sign presented that rejection of such clear truths carries grave consequences, inviting the listener to reflect and choose belief rather than denial.

translation: Who deny the Day of Judgment [Recompense].
interpretation: This verse opens a passage that identifies a particular moral type by its root spiritual failing rather than by a single bad deed. The denial of the Day of Judgment is presented as the hidden cause behind a chain of social and ethical failures that follow in the subsequent verses—harshness toward the orphan, failure to urge the feeding of the poor, heedlessness in prayer, ostentation in worship, and withholding small kindnesses. The implication is that belief in ultimate accountability is what disciplines human conscience and motivates compassion, justice, and sincerity. Without this belief, a person may still outwardly perform religious acts, but inwardly lack the ethical seriousness that true faith produces. Thus, denial here is not merely an intellectual position about an afterlife but a practical orientation that manifests in indifference to others' suffering and in treating worship as empty ritual rather than genuine devotion. The verse thereby links theology directly to ethics, suggesting that one's treatment of the vulnerable and one's sincerity in worship are the truest tests of whether one actually believes in ultimate moral accountability, regardless of what one professes verbally.

translation: And none denies it except every transgressor, sinner.
interpretation: This verse refers to the denial of the Day of Judgment mentioned in the preceding verses of Surah Al-Mutaffifin. The Qur'an here establishes a moral and psychological principle: rejection of divine accountability is not a matter of intellectual honesty but stems from a corrupted character. The two qualities mentioned—'mu'tad' (transgressor, one who exceeds limits) and 'athim' (sinner, one steeped in wrongdoing)—are presented as the root causes of disbelief in the Hereafter, not its consequence. In other words, it is not that such people have examined the evidence and rationally concluded that there is no afterlife; rather, their habitual transgression against moral and divine boundaries, combined with persistent sinning, has hardened their hearts and corrupted their spiritual perception, making them psychologically motivated to deny a reality that would otherwise hold them accountable. This suggests a Qur'anic view that denial of ultimate justice often serves as a self-serving psychological defense mechanism for those who wish to continue their transgressions without the burden of future accountability, rather than being a product of genuine skepticism or rational inquiry.

translation: When Our verses are recited to him, he says, 'Legends/tales of the ancients.'
interpretation: This verse describes the arrogant, dismissive response of a disbeliever (traditionally understood to refer to figures like al-Walid ibn al-Mughira) when confronted with divine revelation. Rather than engaging sincerely with the message, he contemptuously labels it as mere mythology or fables inherited from previous generations, a common accusation leveled against the Quran by its early opponents in Mecca. This dismissal reflects a broader pattern of rejection rooted not in reasoned refutation but in prideful denial and a refusal to seriously consider the possibility of divine truth. The phrase 'asatir al-awwalin' (tales of the ancients) appears multiple times in the Quran as a recurring charge from skeptics, suggesting it was a stock phrase used to delegitimize the revelation without substantive engagement with its content or claims.

translation: Nay! Rather, that which they used to earn has covered their hearts with rust (has sealed over their hearts).
interpretation: This verse addresses the spiritual consequence of persistent sin. The word 'rān' (رَان) describes a rust-like film or covering that forms over a mirror or metal surface when left unpolished, obscuring its reflective capacity. The verse teaches that the heart is not inherently and permanently corrupted by a single act, but becomes progressively sealed through the accumulation of sinful deeds ('mā kānū yaksibūn' - what they used to earn/acquire). Each wrongdoing leaves a mark, and repeated transgressions without repentance build up a layer that eventually blocks the heart's capacity to perceive truth, feel remorse, or receive guidance. This connects to a broader Qur'anic and Prophetic teaching that sins create black spots on the heart, and that this covering is not an external curse imposed arbitrarily by God, but a natural consequence earned through one's own choices and actions. The verse thus emphasizes human responsibility: spiritual blindness and hardness of heart are self-inflicted outcomes of accumulated moral failure, serving as a warning that one's deeds directly shape one's capacity for faith and moral perception, and implicitly calling for continuous self-purification and repentance before the heart becomes irrevocably sealed.

translation: Nay! Indeed, on that Day they will be veiled from their Lord.
interpretation: This verse, from Surat al-Mutaffifin, refers to the wrongdoers and deniers of the Day of Judgment who are described earlier in the surah as sinners whose hearts have become rusted and covered by their misdeeds. The 'veiling' from the Lord is understood by most classical exegetes to mean a deprivation of the honor of seeing or being near to Allah—an exclusion from His mercy, grace, and the spiritual closeness granted to the righteous. Since the righteous are later described as looking upon their Lord with vision and favor, the veiling of the wicked stands in deliberate contrast: it signifies their spiritual banishment and humiliation on the Day of Judgment as a consequence of their disbelief and corruption, denying them the ultimate reward of divine proximity that the faithful will enjoy.

translation: Then indeed, they will [enter to] burn in Hellfire.
interpretation: This verse comes in the context of Surah As-Saffat's discussion of the misguided ones who follow their forefathers blindly and worship false deities, rejecting the truth brought by the prophets. The verse serves as a stark warning of the ultimate consequence awaiting those who persist in disbelief and deviation despite having received divine guidance. The word 'then' (thumma) indicates a sequence - after their worldly life of misguidance, denial, and following falsehood, their final destination is the Hellfire. The phrase 'لصالو' (to burn/roast in) conveys an intense, direct immersion in the fire, not merely proximity to it - emphasizing the severity and inescapability of this punishment. This verse functions as a theological principle about divine justice: those who choose to follow corrupt traditions over revealed truth, and who prioritize blind imitation of ancestors over rational reflection and accepting prophetic guidance, will face the natural and just consequence of their choices in the Hereafter. It underscores the Quranic theme that true accountability exists beyond this worldly life, and that the comfort of following the crowd or ancestral customs offers no protection against divine judgment when those customs contradict truth.

translation: Then it will be said, 'This is that which you used to deny.'
interpretation: This verse depicts a moment on the Day of Judgment when disbelievers, having denied the reality of resurrection, divine punishment, or the Hereafter during their worldly lives, are confronted directly with the very reality they rejected. The statement is delivered to them as they face the Fire or the consequences of their disbelief, serving as a moment of undeniable confirmation and reckoning. The rhetorical power of this verse lies in its stark simplicity—there is no elaborate argument or debate, only a simple declarative statement that exposes the futility of their former denial. This reflects a broader Qur'anic theme that truth, once obscured by arrogance or heedlessness in this life, becomes starkly and inescapably clear in the next, leaving no room for excuse, argument, or further disbelief. The moment represents the ultimate humiliation of those who mocked or dismissed warnings about accountability before God, as they are made to witness firsthand what they spent their lives denying.

translation: Nay! Indeed, the record of the righteous is in 'Illiyyin (the highest register/place).
interpretation: This verse establishes a cosmic ledger system that mirrors and contrasts with the fate of the wicked (whose record is in Sijjin, mentioned earlier in the surah). 'Illiyyin signifies the loftiest, most exalted stratum of existence—linguistically derived from 'uluw (height/elevation)—symbolizing both a physical register of deeds and a spiritual station of honor near the Divine. The verse affirms that the good deeds and faith of the righteous are not merely recorded for judgment but are elevated, cherished, and preserved in a place of dignity, reflecting God's recognition and honoring of their moral striving. This stands as a counterpoint to materialist denial (addressed by the opening 'Nay!' which refutes the deniers' doubts about resurrection and accountability), affirming that human moral choices have lasting cosmic significance and that the righteous are rewarded with nearness to the sacred, their worth inscribed in the highest order of creation.

translation: And what can make you know what 'Illiyyun is?
interpretation: This rhetorical question emphasizes the immense and ineffable nature of 'Illiyyun, the exalted register or station in which the deeds and souls of the righteous are recorded, as mentioned in the preceding verses of Surah Al-Mutaffifin. By posing this question, the Qur'an signals that 'Illiyyun transcends ordinary human comprehension—it is a lofty, sublime realm or record so elevated that no earthly description can fully capture its reality. This rhetorical device, common in the Qur'an, is used to draw the listener's attention to profound realities of the unseen (al-ghayb), creating a sense of awe and anticipation before further description is given. It underscores the vast difference between the ultimate destinies of the righteous, whose deeds ascend to this exalted station, and the wicked, whose record is described in contrast as 'Sijjeen', a lowly and confined place. The naming itself, derived from 'uluw' (height/elevation), reflects the honor, nearness to Allah, and spiritual elevation granted to the sincere and righteous believers.

translation: A written record, inscribed.
interpretation: This phrase appears in Surah Al-Mutaffifin, describing the nature of the heavenly ledgers—either Sijjeen, the record of the wicked, or Illiyyeen, the record of the righteous, depending on context. It emphasizes that human deeds are not forgotten or left to chance but are meticulously documented in a fixed, permanent register. The word 'marqum' (inscribed/marked) conveys the idea of something clearly written and sealed, beyond alteration or erasure, underscoring divine justice: every soul's actions are accounted for in a precise, unchangeable ledger that will be presented on the Day of Judgment. This serves as both a warning to the sinful and a reassurance to the righteous that their deeds are preserved and will be justly rewarded.

translation: Witnessed by those brought near [to Allah].
interpretation: This verse refers to 'Illiyyin, the lofty register in which the deeds of the righteous are recorded, as mentioned in the preceding verses of Surah Al-Mutaffifin. The verse states that this exalted record is witnessed by al-muqarrabun, the angels or souls brought near to Allah's presence—those of the highest spiritual rank. This witnessing signifies the honor and authenticity given to the deeds of the righteous, as they are attested to by the most elevated beings in creation. It also implies a hierarchy of nearness to the Divine, where only those already close to Allah have the privilege of witnessing this sacred record, underscoring the immense honor awaiting the righteous whose deeds are inscribed therein and affirmed by the most noble witnesses.

translation: Indeed, the righteous will be in [a state of] bliss.
interpretation: This verse affirms the ultimate reward awaiting those who lived righteously, establishing a direct contrast with the fate of the wicked mentioned in the surrounding verses who will be in Hellfire. The word 'na'eem' (bliss/delight) conveys not merely the absence of suffering but an active state of pleasure, comfort, and joy in Paradise. The use of 'inna' (indeed) at the start emphasizes certainty, removing any doubt about this outcome. This verse functions within a broader Quranic theme of moral accountability, where the believers' patience in righteousness during worldly life—often accompanied by hardship, restraint from sin, and devotion to God—is repaid with eternal comfort. The abrar (righteous) are typically understood as those who excel in faith, charity, and piety, going beyond minimal obligations. The brevity and directness of the verse reflects the certainty and simplicity of divine justice: good deeds lead to good outcomes, just as the preceding verses establish that the wicked face punishment. It serves as both a comfort to believers facing difficulty in this life and a motivational reminder of the eternal stakes of moral choice.

translation: Upon [lofty] couches, they will gaze.
interpretation: This verse describes the righteous believers (al-abrar) in Paradise, reclining upon elevated, adorned couches or thrones as a sign of honor, ease, and sovereignty. The act of "gazing" carries a dual meaning in the exegetical tradition: on one hand, it refers to their contemplation of the splendors of Paradise—the gardens, rivers, and divine bounties bestowed upon them as a reward for their faith and patience in worldly life. On the other hand, several commentators connect this verse to the preceding passages in Surah Al-Mutaffifin, which describe how the wrongdoers used to mock and scorn the believers in the world. Thus, this gazing is understood as a reversal of fortune: those who were ridiculed are now elevated in honor and comfort, looking down—literally and figuratively—upon the humiliation and punishment of those who once wronged them. This juxtaposition serves as a powerful reminder of divine justice, where the arrogance of the oppressors in this life is met with their disgrace in the Hereafter, while the patience of the believers is rewarded with everlasting ease and vindication.

translation: You will recognize in their faces the radiance of bliss.
interpretation: This verse describes the righteous (al-abrar) as they are rewarded in Paradise, following earlier verses that speak of their reclining on couches and gazing upon the delights granted to them. The 'radiance of bliss' (nadrat an-na'im) refers to a visible glow or brightness that appears on their faces—an outward sign of the inward joy, contentment, and spiritual fulfillment they experience. This imagery conveys the idea that true happiness in the Hereafter is not hidden but manifest, transforming one's very countenance. It also serves as a contrast to the fate of the wicked described elsewhere in the same surah, whose faces or records of deeds reflect disgrace and suffering. The verse emphasizes that genuine reward for righteousness yields a visible, radiant transformation, suggesting that inner spiritual states have outward physical manifestations, and that divine recognition of good deeds brings about complete, undisguised joy on the Day of Judgment.

translation: They will be given to drink of pure wine, sealed.
interpretation: This verse describes a reward of the righteous in Paradise: a pure, untainted drink that is 'sealed' (makhtūm), signifying its exclusivity, preciousness, and purity—untouched and unspoiled until opened for those who have earned it. The seal symbolizes that this drink is reserved specifically for the inhabitants of Paradise, uncorrupted by any impurity, unlike worldly wine which intoxicates and causes harm. Classical commentators note that the seal itself is often described as musk (as in the following verse), emphasizing the exquisite and incorruptible nature of this heavenly reward, a divine token of honor bestowed upon the faithful who maintained righteousness and justice in their worldly dealings, in contrast to the fraudulent dealers (al-mutaffifin) condemned earlier in the surah.

translation: Its seal is musk - so for this let those who compete, compete.
interpretation: This verse concludes the description of the sealed, pure wine given to the righteous in Paradise, whose seal or final taste is musk - a scent universally prized for its purity and lasting fragrance, unlike earthly wine which ends in bitterness or intoxication's unpleasant aftermath. The verse then issues a profound call to redirect human competitive instinct: whereas people typically compete fiercely for wealth, status, power, and worldly pleasures, the Qur'an redirects this natural drive toward its proper object - the eternal rewards of Paradise. The phrase 'let the competitors compete' acknowledges competition as an inherent part of human nature, but reframes its worthy object. Rather than condemning ambition or striving, it channels it toward righteousness, good deeds, and nearness to God. This represents a spiritual recalibration of values: true success and status lie not in accumulating transient worldly gains but in earning the eternal, incorruptible rewards described in this passage - a vision meant to inspire believers to race toward moral excellence and devotion with the same intensity others reserve for worldly ambition.

translation: And its mixture is of Tasnim,
interpretation: This verse continues the description of the delights of Paradise reserved for the righteous (al-abrar), specifically referring to a sealed, pure wine (rahiq makhtum) mentioned in the preceding verses. Tasnim is described as the loftiest and most exquisite spring or fountain in Paradise, its very name suggesting elevation or that which flows downward from on high, as if poured from the heights. The verse indicates that the exclusive drink of the righteous is blended or mixed with this supreme spring, elevating their reward above the ordinary. What is remarkable theologically is that Tasnim itself, in the verse that follows, is described as a spring from which only those brought near to God (al-muqarrabun) drink directly and purely, while for the righteous it serves merely as an admixture. This establishes a hierarchy of spiritual rank in the afterlife, where the nearest to God enjoy the purest and most direct experience of divine favor, while others experience it in a diluted, though still blissful, form. The imagery evokes not just physical pleasure but spiritual proximity to the Divine as the ultimate currency of reward, with the quality and purity of one's heavenly drink symbolizing one's spiritual station and closeness to God's presence.

translation: A spring from which those brought near [to Allah] drink.
interpretation: This verse describes 'Tasneem,' identified in the preceding verse as the purest and most exalted drink of Paradise, reserved specifically for al-Muqarrabun—those brought nearest to Allah in rank and spiritual closeness. Unlike other described rewards that are mixed with Tasneem for the righteous (al-Abrar), the muqarrabun drink from this spring directly and undiluted, signifying their elevated station above ordinary believers. This reflects a hierarchy of reward in the afterlife corresponding to one's nearness to God through faith, righteousness, and devotion in worldly life. The imagery emphasizes that spiritual proximity to the Divine in this life translates into experiential intimacy with divine blessings in the next, where the purest source of delight is reserved for those whose entire being was oriented toward closeness to their Lord.

translation: Indeed, those who committed crimes used to laugh at those who believed.
interpretation: This verse describes the mockery and ridicule that disbelievers directed at believers in worldly life, highlighting the arrogance of those who committed sins and crimes against the faithful. The context, within Surah Al-Mutaffifin, sets up a dramatic reversal that unfolds in subsequent verses, where on the Day of Judgment, the roles are inverted—believers will be the ones looking on with satisfaction at the plight of their former mockers. This reflects a broader Quranic theme of divine justice, where temporary worldly power and social status (including the ability to scorn and belittle others) hold no bearing on ultimate outcomes in the afterlife. The verse serves as both a consolation to believers who face persecution or ridicule for their faith and a warning to those who derive pleasure from mocking others' sincere devotion, reminding readers that true judgment and vindication belong to God alone, not to worldly hierarchies of mockery and power.

translation: And when they passed by them, they used to wink at one another (in mockery).
interpretation: This verse depicts the arrogant disdain of the disbelievers toward the believers in worldly life. The 'winking' (تغامز) signifies silent, mocking gestures exchanged among the wrongdoers as a sign of ridicule and contempt whenever they encountered the faithful. It illustrates how the arrogant elite, confident in their worldly status and wealth, would belittle and scorn those who held true faith, viewing them as insignificant or foolish. This verse is part of a broader passage warning of the reversal of fortunes on the Day of Judgment, where those who were mocked will instead be the ones laughing at the arrogant, who will then face the consequences of their disdain and disbelief. It serves as a reminder that worldly mockery of the righteous is temporary, and ultimate vindication belongs to those who remained patient and faithful despite being scorned.

translation: And when they returned to their own people, they would return jesting.
interpretation: This verse describes the arrogant disbelievers who mocked the believers, and then would return to their own families or circles delighting and joking about the believers they had just ridiculed. It portrays their callousness and self-satisfaction in sin—finding entertainment and amusement in belittling the faithful, oblivious to the serious consequences awaiting them. This behavior exemplifies a moral blindness where mockery of truth and righteousness becomes a source of light-hearted pleasure, setting the stage for the stark reversal described in the following verses, where on the Day of Judgment the believers will instead be the ones laughing at the disbelievers' plight.

translation: And when they saw them, they would say, 'Indeed, these are truly astray.'
interpretation: This verse describes the arrogance and scorn of the disbelieving criminals toward the believers during worldly life, as detailed in the surrounding verses of Surah Al-Mutaffifin. The wrongdoers, who were themselves astray from truth and steeped in sin, looked upon the faithful—who had humbled themselves before God and devoted their lives to righteousness—and mockingly declared them to be the misguided ones. This reflects a profound inversion of values: those who rejected faith considered sincere devotion and moral restraint to be foolishness or error, while they viewed their own indulgence in worldly pleasures and disregard for divine accountability as the correct path. The verse exposes the blindness and self-deception of the disbelievers, who judged true guidance as deviance because it contradicted their own desires and arrogance. This sets the stage for the striking reversal described later in the surah, where on the Day of Judgment, the mockers themselves will be ridiculed by the believers, as the truth of who was truly astray is made manifest. The verse serves as a reminder that worldly judgments of righteousness are often inverted, and that ultimate truth will be revealed in the Hereafter, vindicating the faithful and condemning those who mocked them.

translation: But they had not been sent as guardians over them.
interpretation: This verse addresses the arrogant disbelievers who used to mock and ridicule the believers in worldly life, as described in the preceding verses of Surah Al-Mutaffifin. It clarifies that these scoffers had no legitimate authority, mandate, or divine appointment to monitor, judge, or scorn the faithful. Their derision was presumptuous and unwarranted, as they were never charged with overseeing the believers' conduct or faith. This sets up the contrast delivered in the following verses, where on the Day of Judgment the roles are reversed: those who mocked will themselves be mocked, and the believers will look on with amusement at the fate of their former tormentors. The verse underscores a broader Quranic theme of accountability—that no human has the right to assume a position of spiritual superiority or guardianship over others that belongs only to God, and that arrogance in this life will be met with humiliation in the Hereafter.

translation: So today the believers are laughing at the disbelievers.
interpretation: This verse refers to the Day of Judgment and describes a reversal of fortunes between believers and disbelievers. In the preceding verses of this surah (Al-Mutaffifin), it is described how the wicked disbelievers used to mock and ridicule the believers in worldly life, winking at one another and deriding their faith. Here, the situation is inverted: on the Day of Resurrection, it is now the believers who look upon the disbelievers—who are suffering the consequences of their arrogance and rejection of truth—and laugh at them, not out of cruelty, but as a vindication of their faith and patience. This reflects a broader Quranic theme of divine justice, where those who were oppressed, scorned, or belittled for their faith in this world will witness the ultimate triumph of truth and justice in the Hereafter, finding relief and satisfaction in seeing that the mockery they endured was answered by a far greater and eternal consequence for those who disbelieved.

translation: Upon thrones (or couches), they will gaze.
interpretation: This verse describes the people of Paradise reclining upon adorned couches or thrones, a posture signifying honor, ease, repose, and sovereignty after the trials of worldly life. The act of 'gazing' or 'looking' indicates their state of contentment and leisurely observation of the delights, blessings, and scenes of Paradise around them, including the beauty of their surroundings and perhaps the recompense given to others. It reflects the ultimate state of security and tranquility, where believers are free from worry, exertion, or any need to strive, simply enjoying and witnessing the eternal rewards granted to them by God, a stark contrast to the toil and uncertainty of earthly existence.

translation: Have the disbelievers been [fully] rewarded for what they used to do?
interpretation: This verse comes at the conclusion of Surah Al-Mutaffifin, following a description of the believers in Paradise gazing upon and perhaps laughing at the disbelievers who once mocked them in worldly life. The rhetorical question posed here serves as a powerful affirmation rather than genuine inquiry—it asserts that the disbelievers have indeed received the full and just recompense for their mockery, arrogance, and rejection of truth. The verse encapsulates the Qur'anic theme of divine justice being perfectly realized in the Hereafter: those who scorned the faithful and dismissed the Day of Judgment as fantasy will find themselves recompensed precisely according to their deeds, with no injustice done to them. The rhetorical structure invites the listener to reflect and conclude affirmatively on their own, reinforcing the certainty of ultimate justice and the reversal of worldly fortunes—where the oppressed and mocked believers become the ones who witness the humiliation of their former oppressors.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. When the sky is split open,
interpretation: This verse opens Surah Al-Inshiqaq and sets the scene for the Day of Judgment, describing the cosmic upheaval that will mark the end of the world as we know it. The 'splitting' of the sky signifies the complete breakdown of the natural order that humans take for granted—the heavens, long regarded as a stable and unreachable dome, will tear apart in total submission to Allah's command. This image establishes the theme of the surah: that all creation, including the very fabric of the universe, is entirely subject to divine will and will ultimately testify to and obey Allah's decree. It serves as a dramatic prelude to the surah's broader message about human accountability, the revelation of hidden deeds, and the ultimate return of every soul to its Creator, reminding listeners that the illusion of worldly permanence will give way to the undeniable reality of resurrection and judgment.

translation: And it has listened to its Lord and was obligated [to do so].
interpretation: This verse refers to the earth (or sky, depending on context) on the Day of Judgment, when it submits and responds obediently to the command of its Lord, as it is right and proper for it to do. The earth, like all of creation, is inherently submissive to Allah's will, and on that momentous day, it will fulfill its duty by yielding completely to His command—whether by splitting open, casting out what is within it, or flattening out. This submission is not reluctant but is what is rightfully due from creation to its Creator, emphasizing that all things in existence, even inanimate ones, are ultimately obedient to Allah's decree. It serves as a powerful reminder to humanity that if even the earth submits so completely and rightfully to Allah, how much more should human beings—who possess intellect and free will—submit to their Lord's commands and prepare for the accountability that awaits them.

translation: And when the earth is stretched forth,
interpretation: This verse is part of a sequence in Surah Al-Inshiqaq describing the cosmic upheavals that will occur on the Day of Judgment. The 'spreading' or 'flattening' of the earth refers to the complete transformation of the earth's current form—its mountains leveled, its features erased—so that it becomes a flat, open expanse. This imagery conveys the totality of the earth's transformation at the end of time, stripping away all that once gave it shape and familiarity, to prepare it as a bare stage upon which humanity will be gathered for reckoning. The verse underscores the theme that nothing in the material world, however fixed and permanent it seems, is immune to God's power to alter and dissolve on the appointed Day.

translation: And it casts out what is within it and empties itself.
interpretation: This verse is part of a sequence describing cosmic signs of the Day of Judgment in Surah Al-Inshiqaq. Here, 'it' refers to the earth, which on that day will split open, cast forth everything contained within it—the bodies of the dead, buried treasures, and hidden secrets—and become completely emptied and barren. The imagery conveys total transformation and exposure: nothing remains concealed, and the earth relinquishes all it once held, symbolizing the dissolution of the worldly order and the revelation of all that was hidden in preparation for divine judgment and reckoning.

translation: And it listens and obeys its Lord, and it is rightfully bound to do so.
interpretation: This verse, from Surah Al-Inshiqaq, refers to the earth on the Day of Judgment. It describes the moment when the earth, like the heavens mentioned in the preceding verses, submits completely and obediently to the command of its Creator. The phrase 'wa huqqat' (and it is duty-bound/rightfully so) emphasizes that this total submission is not optional or forced in an unnatural sense, but is the very purpose for which the earth was created—it is fulfilling its rightful duty. This illustrates the theme running through the surah that all of creation, including the earth itself, inherently recognizes and submits to divine authority, standing in contrast to humanity's choice in whether to submit willingly or face reckoning for refusal.

translation: O mankind, indeed you are laboring toward your Lord with [great] exertion and will meet it [the result of that labor].
interpretation: This verse addresses every human being directly, emphasizing the inherent struggle and toil that characterizes human life. The word 'kadh' conveys a sense of strenuous effort, striving, and hardship that is unavoidable in the human condition. The verse establishes that this labor is purposeful—it is directed 'toward your Lord,' meaning that all human striving, whether recognized or not, ultimately moves toward an encounter with God. The phrase 'fa-mulaqihi' (and you will meet it/Him) signifies the certainty of this encounter, pointing to the Day of Judgment when every soul will face the consequences and reality of its earthly efforts. This verse serves as a profound reminder of life's purpose: human existence is not aimless but is a journey of continuous effort culminating in accountability before the Creator. It calls for conscious awareness that every struggle, every endeavor, and every moment of toil in this worldly life is ultimately oriented toward a divine reckoning, urging believers to direct their efforts toward righteousness since the meeting with their Lord is inevitable.

translation: Then as for he who is given his record (book of deeds) in his right hand,
interpretation: This verse begins the description of the Day of Judgment's outcome for the righteous. Receiving one's record in the right hand is a symbol of success, honor, and divine favor, as the right side is traditionally associated with blessing and good fortune in Islamic tradition. This person, having lived a life of faith and good deeds, is granted this sign that distinguishes them from the wrongdoers, who will receive their record in their left hand or behind their back. The verse sets up a joyous proclamation that follows, where the righteous person celebrates their good fortune, inviting others to read their record, reflecting their confidence and relief after the trial of judgment. This moment represents the culmination of a life of accountability, where one's earthly deeds are finally and fully revealed, and those who followed the path of righteousness are rewarded with the ultimate vindication of their choices.

translation: Then he will be called to account with an easy reckoning,
interpretation: This verse refers to the believer who, as described in the preceding verses, is given their Book of Deeds in their right hand—a sign of righteousness and salvation. The 'easy reckoning' mentioned here signifies a merciful review of one's deeds on the Day of Judgment, free from harsh interrogation. Scholars interpret this ease as God's grace extended to those who lived with faith and sincerity, where their good deeds are acknowledged and their shortcomings are overlooked or forgiven, in contrast to those who will face a rigorous and painful accounting for their disbelief and wrongdoing, as described in the verses that follow.

translation: And he will return to his people in happiness.
interpretation: This verse describes the joyful state of a believer who, on the Day of Judgment, is given their record of deeds in their right hand—a sign of salvation and divine favor. Having been reassured through an easy reckoning, they return to their family and loved ones (whether in the gathering place of the Hereafter or symbolically to their eternal abode) filled with happiness and relief. This joy stems from the certainty of having attained Allah's mercy and the removal of all fear and anxiety about their fate. The verse contrasts with the fate of those who receive their book behind their backs, emphasizing the stark difference between the outcomes of righteous and sinful lives, and serves as both a comfort to believers and a motivation to live righteously in anticipation of this joyous reunion.

translation: But as for he who is given his record [of deeds] behind his back,
interpretation: This verse refers to the Day of Judgment, when each person will receive the record of their deeds. Those who receive it behind their back—rather than in their right hand—are the disbelievers and sinners who rejected faith and righteous conduct. The image of receiving the record behind the back symbolizes utter disgrace, rejection, and the inability to face one's own deeds directly; it reflects a person who turned away from truth and accountability in worldly life, and so is made to turn away even in the manner of receiving the proof of their deeds. This positioning also conveys helplessness and humiliation, as the natural posture for receiving something behind one's back implies the arm being twisted or contorted, foreshadowing the physical and spiritual anguish that will follow, including the despair described in the subsequent verses where such a person wishes for destruction rather than facing the consequences of their unbelief and wrongdoing.

translation: Then he will call for destruction.
interpretation: This verse refers to the wrongdoer who, on the Day of Judgment, receives the record of their deeds behind their back—a sign of their disbelief and rejection of accountability in worldly life. Overwhelmed by despair upon seeing the totality of their sins laid bare, such a person will cry out for "thuboor" (utter destruction or annihilation), wishing for their own complete nonexistence rather than facing the consequences of their deeds. This calling out for destruction symbolizes the depth of regret and hopelessness experienced by those who denied the Hereafter, only to find themselves facing an inescapable reckoning. The verse serves as a stark warning: the human cry for self-annihilation will be futile, for death will not be granted as an escape—instead, they must face the blazing Fire that awaits them, as stated in the verses that follow. This passage emphasizes the finality of divine judgment and the absence of any refuge for those who lived in heedless denial of their accountability to God.

translation: And he will be made to burn in a Blazing Fire.
interpretation: This verse continues the description from Surah Al-Inshiqaq of the fate awaiting those who receive their Book of Deeds behind their backs on the Day of Judgment—symbolizing their rejection of truth and disbelief during worldly life. Having despaired and called for destruction (as mentioned in the preceding verses), such a person is now consigned to the blazing Fire of Hell. This outcome is presented as a direct consequence of their choices: they lived heedlessly, never believing they would be held accountable, and thus face the ultimate recompense for their arrogance and denial of resurrection. The imagery of burning in sa'ir (a specific term for a raging, blazing fire) emphasizes both the intensity and justice of divine punishment reserved for those who turned away from faith and righteous conduct.

translation: Indeed, he used to be among his people, rejoicing.
interpretation: This verse refers to the state of the believer, destined for Paradise, prior to his resurrection and judgment—describing his life in the world. He lived among his family and kin in a state of joy and contentment, though this happiness was not merely frivolous worldly pleasure, but rather a reflection of his faith and righteous heart. His joy was untroubled by deep anxiety over his ultimate fate, because he lived in accordance with God's guidance, trusting in His mercy. This contrasts sharply with the fate of the wicked described in the verses that follow, who lived carelessly, assuming they would never be held accountable. The verse thus serves as a reminder that true, lasting joy is rooted in righteousness and faith, and that such joy in this life can be a precursor to the eternal joy of the Hereafter, as a reward for having lived with gratitude and mindfulness of God among one's family and community.

translation: Indeed, he thought that he would never return [to Allah].
interpretation: This verse refers to the disbelieving person described in the preceding verses of Surah Al-Inshiqaq, who lived heedlessly, believing that death marked the absolute end of existence and that he would never be resurrected or held accountable before his Lord. This false assumption—that there would be no return, no judgment, and no consequence—is presented as the root cause of his arrogance, ingratitude, and sinful behavior. The verse serves as a warning that such denial of the afterlife is precisely what leads people into moral corruption, since the absence of belief in accountability removes the restraint that would otherwise guide righteous conduct. By exposing this false certainty, the Qur'an emphasizes that every soul will indeed return to its Creator to be judged according to its deeds, contradicting the disbeliever's presumption and affirming the reality of resurrection and divine reckoning.

translation: Yes! Indeed, his Lord was ever, of him, Seeing.
interpretation: This verse responds to the preceding description of a disbeliever who assumed he would never be resurrected or held accountable, living heedlessly as though free from divine observation. The emphatic 'Yes!' (bala) refutes his false assumption, affirming that resurrection and accountability are certain. The verse then grounds this certainty in God's eternal, comprehensive awareness of every human being—nothing a person does, intends, or conceals escapes His sight. The phrase 'kana bihi baseeran' (was ever, of him, Seeing) uses a form emphasizing continuity and permanence, indicating that God's watchfulness over this individual was not a reaction to his deeds but an ever-present reality throughout his life. This serves as a sobering reminder that human denial or heedlessness does not alter divine reality: one may forget or deny accountability, but one is never outside the scope of God's knowledge and observation. The verse thus functions as both a correction of human arrogance and a foundation for the certainty of judgment that follows in the subsequent verses, where oaths are sworn affirming that humanity will indeed progress through stages toward an inevitable reckoning.

translation: So I swear by the twilight glow,
interpretation: This verse opens an oath sequence in which God swears by the twilight (the reddish glow after sunset), and in subsequent verses by the night and the moon, leading to an oath about the stages of human life and transformation. The twilight marks a transitional moment between day and night, light and darkness, symbolizing change and transition. This sets up the surah's central theme: just as the twilight gives way to night and the moon waxes toward fullness, human beings likewise pass through successive stages and conditions in life, and ultimately will be raised up and called to account before God. The oath by this natural phenomenon underscores the certainty and seriousness of the truths that follow, as oaths in the Qur'an typically draw attention to the significance of what is being affirmed, in this case, the inevitability of resurrection and divine judgment.

translation: By the night and what it envelops (or gathers together).
interpretation: This is an oath taken by Allah, swearing by the night and the darkness it brings, which gathers and covers all things, concealing them from sight just as the day had revealed them. The imagery of the night 'enveloping' or 'gathering' suggests the way darkness collects and brings together all creatures and creation under its cover, a time of rest and concealment. This oath, part of a series of oaths at the opening of Surah Al-Inshiqaq (The Splitting Open), serves to draw attention to the certainty of what follows—specifically the affirmation that humanity will progress through stages of existence, ultimately facing accountability before their Lord. The natural phenomena invoked (twilight, night, the moon) represent cycles of transition and change, mirroring the spiritual transitions and the ultimate transformation that awaits every soul.

translation: And by the moon when it becomes full.
interpretation: This verse is part of a series of oaths at the opening of Surah Al-Inshiqaq, in which God swears by celestial phenomena—here the moon reaching its fullness—to draw attention to the orderly, cyclical patterns of creation as evidence of divine power and design. Just as the moon moves through stages of waxing and waning until it reaches completion, this imagery serves as a metaphor for the stages of human life and the inevitability of change and transformation, pointing toward the certainty of resurrection and the Day of Judgment, which the surah goes on to describe. The oath by the moon's fullness underscores that nothing in creation remains static; everything moves toward its appointed culmination, just as humanity will move through stages toward meeting its Lord.

translation: You shall surely pass through stage after stage (state after state).
interpretation: This verse addresses humankind, affirming that every person will inevitably pass through a succession of states and conditions—from the stages of creation (a drop of fluid, then a clinging form, then birth), through childhood, youth, old age, death, and ultimately resurrection and the stages of the Hereafter. The oath 'la-tarkabunna' (you shall surely ride/traverse) emphasizes the certainty of this progression, serving as a reminder that just as one cannot halt the stages of worldly life, one cannot escape the reality of resurrection and divine judgment. This verse follows the description of cosmic upheavals at the end of the world, reinforcing that human transformation and accountability are as certain and inevitable as the transformation of the heavens and earth on the Last Day.

translation: So what is [the matter] with them that they do not believe?
interpretation: This verse is a rhetorical question posed by God expressing astonishment and rebuke at the persistent disbelief of those who reject faith despite clear signs. Coming in the context of Surah Al-Inshiqaq, after descriptions of the splitting of the sky, the reckoning of deeds, and the fate of the righteous and the wicked, this question highlights the irrationality of disbelief when confronted with such overwhelming evidence of divine power and the certainty of resurrection. It is not merely seeking information but serves as a challenge, implying that there is no valid excuse for their refusal to believe—neither intellectual nor moral. The rhetorical nature underscores human accountability: disbelief is not due to lack of evidence but to arrogance, heedlessness, or willful denial of truths that are self-evident to anyone who reflects sincerely on creation, revelation, and their own mortality.

translation: And when the Qur'an is recited to them, they do not prostrate [in submission].
interpretation: This verse, from Surat al-Inshiqaq, rebukes the disbelievers among the Meccans for their arrogant refusal to respond to the recitation of the Qur'an with humility and submission to God. Prostration here symbolizes the natural and appropriate response of a believing heart upon hearing divine revelation—an act of acknowledging God's majesty and truth. The disbelievers' failure to prostrate reflects a deeper spiritual blindness and stubborn denial despite having witnessed the signs of God in the universe and having heard clear revelation. This verse is traditionally associated with a recommended prostration (sujud at-tilawah) for reciters and listeners, so that believers, in performing the very act the disbelievers refused, demonstrate their contrasting humility and faith. The verse thus draws a sharp line between those who yield to truth in reverence and those who, out of pride, reject it outright, setting up the warning of painful punishment that follows for the deniers.

translation: Nay! Those who disbelieve persist in denial.
interpretation: This verse comes in the context of Surah Al-Inshiqaq's discussion of the resurrection and the splitting of the heavens, where Allah affirms that despite clear signs—the Qur'an being recited to them, and the natural world bearing witness to divine power—the disbelievers' rejection is not due to a lack of evidence or reasoning, but stems from willful stubbornness and arrogance. The word 'bal' (nay/rather) serves as a corrective, dismissing any excuse they might have, and shifting the blame from the message itself to the deliberate choice of the disbelievers to reject truth. It underscores that disbelief here is an active, persistent behavior ('yukadhdhibun' is in the present/continuous tense), suggesting an ongoing pattern of denial rather than a single moment of doubt. This highlights the Qur'anic theme that guidance is available to all, but some hearts choose arrogance and denial over submission, making them responsible for their own spiritual blindness rather than victims of insufficient proof.

translation: And Allah is most knowing of what they keep within themselves (conceal in their hearts).
interpretation: This verse addresses the inner disbelief, doubt, and rejection that the deniers harbor within their hearts regarding the Quran and the Day of Judgment, even if they do not always express it openly. It serves as a warning that Allah's knowledge encompasses not only outward actions and words but also the hidden thoughts, intentions, and resistance that people conceal within themselves. The verse emphasizes divine omniscience as a form of accountability—no inner rejection or secret disbelief escapes Allah's awareness, reinforcing the certainty that all will ultimately be held responsible for both their outward deeds and their innermost convictions.

translation: So give them tidings of a painful punishment.
interpretation: This verse employs the rhetorical device of irony, using the word 'bashshir' (give glad tidings) — normally reserved for good news — to introduce the opposite: a severe, painful punishment. This ironic usage intensifies the warning, underscoring the certainty and gravity of the consequence awaiting those who persist in disbelief, hypocrisy, or sin despite having been given clear guidance. It reflects a broader Qur'anic rhetorical pattern where such phrasing is used to convey the inevitability and justice of divine retribution, often following a description of the wrongdoing that warrants it. The painful punishment typically refers to the torment of the Hereafter, serving as a stern admonition meant to provoke reflection and repentance in this worldly life.

translation: Except those who believe and do righteous deeds - for them is a reward uninterrupted (never ending).
interpretation: This verse comes as an exception following a description of humanity's general state of loss or decline (as in Surah Al-'Asr). It establishes a divine exemption clause: while mankind in general is described as being in a state of loss, those who combine two essential elements - genuine faith (iman) and righteous deeds ('amal salih) - are excluded from this loss. The verse emphasizes that faith alone is insufficient without corresponding righteous action, and action alone without proper faith/intention is likewise incomplete; both must work together. The reward promised is described as 'ghayru mamnun' - uninterrupted, unceasing, or without end - signifying that unlike worldly rewards which are temporary and diminish over time, the reward for believers who do good deeds is eternal and without any form of diminishment, cutting off, or even the psychological burden of being reminded of a favor (as 'mann' can also mean to remind someone of a favor done, implying the reward comes without any sense of grudging or obligation attached, but purely as divine grace).

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. By the sky containing great stars (constellations).
interpretation: This opening oath, found at the beginning of Surah Al-Buruj, invokes the vast, star-studded sky as a witness to the truth of what follows in the surah. The 'buruj' (constellations or great stars) represent the majestic order, precision, and grandeur of Allah's creation, pointing to His power and the deliberate design of the universe. Classical commentators note that swearing by such a magnificent sign serves to draw the listener's attention to the certainty and seriousness of the message that follows—namely, the account of the believers who were persecuted and burned in a trench (the People of the Ditch), and the assurance that divine justice ultimately prevails. The heavens, with their fixed and orderly stations, symbolize permanence and justice, contrasting with the transient cruelty of tyrants on earth, and foreshadowing that Allah's power, as vast as the cosmos itself, ensures that oppression will not go unanswered.

translation: And by the promised Day,
interpretation: This verse is part of a series of oath-formulas at the beginning of Surah Al-Buruj, in which God swears by the sky with its constellations, by the promised Day, and by witnesses and the witnessed. 'The promised Day' refers to the Day of Judgment, the Day that has been foretold throughout revelation to every prophet and nation. By invoking this Day as an oath, the verse emphasizes its absolute certainty—just as the oath itself testifies to truth, so too does the coming of this Day stand as an undeniable reality. This sets the tone for the surah's broader message about the ultimate triumph of truth and justice over falsehood and oppression, as illustrated in the subsequent narrative of the believers who were persecuted and burned in trenches (the people of the ditch), yet whose faith remained steadfast. The mention of this Day assures the oppressed that divine justice will prevail, even if it is delayed beyond worldly life, reinforcing themes of patience, faith, and the certainty of accountability before God.

translation: And by the witness and the witnessed.
interpretation: This verse is part of a series of oaths at the beginning of Surah Al-Buruj, following oaths by the sky with constellations, the promised Day, and now the witness and the witnessed. Classical exegetes have offered various interpretations of these two terms: the witness has been understood as referring to Friday (the day of congregation and testimony), to the angels who record deeds, to the Prophet Muhammad who bears witness over his nation, or to Allah Himself as the ultimate witness over all creation. The witnessed has been interpreted as the Day of Judgment (when all deeds are presented and witnessed), as humanity who will be gathered and witnessed on that day, or as the day of Arafah during Hajj. The oath structure itself serves a rhetorical purpose in Qur'anic discourse, drawing attention to the solemnity and certainty of what follows—in this case, a warning about the fate of those who persecute believers, exemplified by the story of the People of the Ditch (Ashab al-Ukhdud) that follows in subsequent verses. By invoking both the one who observes and that which is observed, the verse establishes a cosmic framework of accountability: nothing escapes witness, whether through divine knowledge, angelic recording, or the eventual gathering of all creation for judgment, reinforcing the theme of ultimate justice for the oppressed and consequence for the oppressors.

translation: Cursed (destroyed) were the companions of the ditch (al-Ukhdūd).
interpretation: This opening verse of Surah al-Burūj refers to an incident in which believers who held fast to their faith in God were persecuted by a tyrannical ruler and his people, who dug trenches filled with fire and cast the believers into them for refusing to renounce their faith. The verse pronounces condemnation and doom upon the perpetrators of this atrocity, affirming that those who inflict cruelty upon the faithful for their belief will face divine retribution. It serves as a historical reminder and moral lesson that oppressors who persecute believers because of their devotion to God will ultimately be held accountable, while the steadfastness of the believers, even unto death, is honored and vindicated by God. The passage underscores the broader Qur'anic theme that worldly power and cruelty cannot triumph over truth and faith, and that God witnesses and will judge all such injustices.

translation: The fire full of fuel,
interpretation: This verse is part of the account of the 'People of the Ditch' (Ashab al-Ukhdud) in Surah Al-Buruj, which recalls a historical atrocity in which tyrannical rulers dug trenches of fire to persecute and burn believers who refused to renounce their faith in God. The description of the fire as 'full of fuel' emphasizes its intensity and the deliberate cruelty of those who kindled it, sustaining it to inflict maximum suffering. Beyond the historical reference, the verse serves as a broader moral lesson: it illustrates the lengths to which oppressors will go to crush faith and the steadfastness of believers who, even facing death by fire, maintained their conviction. It also sets up a contrast developed later in the surah between the transient, man-made fire of persecution and the eternal fire of divine punishment awaiting the oppressors, as well as the gardens of Paradise awaiting the steadfast believers.

translation: When they sat by it [the fire].
interpretation: This verse continues the narrative of the People of the Ditch (Ashab al-Ukhdud) mentioned earlier in Surah Al-Buruj. It describes the persecutors who dug a trench, filled it with fire, and then sat around it as spectators, watching the suffering they inflicted upon the believers who refused to renounce their faith. The image of them 'sitting' emphasizes their callousness and deliberate cruelty—this was not a hasty or impulsive act of violence but a calculated, prolonged spectacle of torture that they observed with apparent satisfaction or indifference. This verse serves to highlight the depth of moral corruption of those who oppose the believers, setting up the contrast with the steadfastness of the faithful who maintained their conviction even unto death, and foreshadowing the divine judgment that awaits such oppressors.

translation: And they were witnesses to what they were doing to the believers.
interpretation: This verse comes from Surah al-Buruj, in the account of the People of the Ditch (Ashab al-Ukhdud), who persecuted and burned believers for their faith. The verse emphasizes that the persecutors were fully conscious, willing witnesses to their own cruelty—they watched deliberately as the believers were tortured and killed, taking a sadistic satisfaction in the spectacle rather than acting out of ignorance or distance. This underscores the depth of their moral culpability: their crime was not committed in secrecy or denial but was consciously observed and endorsed by them as it unfolded, making their persecution a fully intentional and witnessed act of oppression against people whose only 'crime' was belief in God. The verse serves as a condemnation of active, knowing cruelty and sets up the subsequent verses' warning of divine justice and the ultimate fate of oppressors versus the steadfast faithful.

translation: And they resented them not except because they believed in Allah, the Almighty, the Praiseworthy.
interpretation: This verse refers to the People of the Ditch (Ashab al-Ukhdud), believers who were persecuted and burned alive by a tyrannical ruler simply for their faith in God. The verse emphasizes the injustice and irrationality of persecution based solely on belief, highlighting that the only 'crime' of the victims was their devotion to Allah, described here through two of His attributes: al-Aziz (the Almighty, the Mighty) and al-Hamid (the Praiseworthy, worthy of all praise). This pairing is significant—it reassures believers that even though the oppressors held worldly power and inflicted real suffering, true power and ultimate praise belong to God alone, who will vindicate the faithful. The verse serves as a timeless commentary on religious persecution, affirming that steadfast faith, even unto death, is honored by God, and that the apparent triumph of oppressors is temporary, while divine justice and praise are eternal. It also implicitly condemns any tyranny that punishes belief itself as a crime, framing such persecution as a profound moral inversion—where faith, which should be celebrated, becomes the pretext for brutality.

translation: He to Whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth. And Allah is, over all things, a Witness.
interpretation: This verse affirms Allah's absolute sovereignty over all creation, emphasizing that nothing exists outside His dominion and control.
