It follows the account of the believers who were persecuted and burned in trenches for their faith, serving as a reassurance that despite the apparent triumph of tyrants and the suffering of the righteous in this worldly life, ultimate authority belongs to Allah alone. The declaration that Allah is a 'Witness' over all things underscores that no injustice goes unseen or unrecorded—every act of oppression and every instance of steadfast faith is known to Him. This serves as both a warning to oppressors that they will be held accountable, and a comfort to the oppressed that their suffering is witnessed by the One who holds true power over the heavens and the earth, and that justice will ultimately be served in the Hereafter if not in this world.

translation: Indeed, those who persecuted the believing men and believing women and then did not repent - for them is the punishment of Hell, and for them is the punishment of the Burning Fire.
interpretation: This verse refers to the People of the Ditch (Ashab al-Ukhdud), those who persecuted and burned believers for their faith, as recounted earlier in Surah Al-Buruj. It establishes a severe warning that persecuting others for their religious belief is among the gravest of sins, deserving double emphasis on punishment - both the general punishment of Hell and the specific punishment of burning, which mirrors the method of their crime. The verse underscores a principle of justice where the nature of punishment corresponds to the nature of the transgression. It also emphasizes that the door to repentance remains open even after such grave sins, but willful persistence without repentance seals one's fate. This teaches that religious persecution and the denial of others' freedom to believe is not merely a worldly crime but carries profound spiritual consequences, affirming the sanctity of faith and conscience in Islamic theology.

translation: Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds will have gardens beneath which rivers flow. That is the great triumph.
interpretation: This verse establishes a direct and unbreakable link between faith and righteous action as the twin conditions for ultimate success. Faith alone, as an internal conviction, is presented as insufficient without its manifestation in righteous deeds; likewise, good deeds devoid of sincere faith lack their true spiritual foundation. The imagery of gardens with flowing rivers evokes a paradise of abundance, life, and refreshment, standing in stark contrast to the barren, arid landscapes familiar to the original audience, thereby making the reward vivid and deeply appealing. By calling this outcome 'the great triumph,' the verse reframes the entire purpose of worldly existence: true success is not measured by material wealth, power, or worldly achievement, but by one's standing in the eternal life to come. This serves as both a promise of hope for believers who strive sincerely and a subtle call to action, urging the listener to pair belief with consistent virtuous conduct.

translation: Indeed, the Seizure (grip) of your Lord is severe.
interpretation: This verse serves as a solemn warning emphasizing the overwhelming power and severity of God's punishment when He chooses to seize or punish those who persist in wrongdoing, arrogance, or rejection of divine guidance. It comes in a context (typically linked to the stories of past nations like the people of Pharaoh, 'Ad, and Thamud) reminding the listener that no earthly power can withstand or escape divine retribution. The statement functions both as a deterrent against transgression and as a reassurance to believers that injustice will not go unanswered, since the same Lord who shows mercy and patience also possesses absolute authority to enforce justice decisively when the time comes.

translation: Indeed, it is He who originates [creation] and repeats it.
interpretation: This verse affirms God's absolute power over creation by emphasizing that He alone initiates existence from nothing and has the ability to bring it back after its cessation, as in resurrection after death. It underscores a central theme in Islamic theology: that the same divine power responsible for the first creation is fully capable of recreating life, serving as a rational proof for the resurrection. Just as He originated the universe and human beings without any prior model, He will restore them again on the Day of Judgment. This serves both as a reassurance to believers of the certainty of the afterlife and as a rebuttal to those who doubt resurrection by appealing to the logic of the first creation—if He could create once from nothing, repeating the process is, if anything, even easier for His limitless power.

translation: And He is the Oft-Forgiving, the Most Loving.
interpretation: This verse pairs two divine attributes that together reveal the character of God's relationship with creation: forgiveness and love. The pairing is significant—God's forgiveness is not cold or merely legalistic, but flows from genuine love and affection for His creation. 'Al-Wadud' (the Most Loving/Affectionate) is a rare and intimate divine name, suggesting warmth, tenderness, and a deep bond of care. By linking forgiveness with love, the verse teaches that when God forgives, it is an expression of His loving nature, not a reluctant concession. This offers believers reassurance that repentance is met not just with pardon but with genuine divine affection, encouraging a relationship with God based on hope and intimacy rather than fear alone. It also models for believers the ideal of combining justice (forgiving wrongs) with love (maintaining warmth and care) in their own relationships with others.

translation: Possessor of the Throne, the Glorious.
interpretation: This verse describes Allah as the sovereign master of the Throne, which symbolizes His absolute dominion over all creation, and as 'Al-Majeed' (the Glorious/Most Honorable), signifying His supreme majesty, honor, and greatness. This description comes in the context of Surah Al-Buruj, following accounts of the persecution of believers (such as the People of the Ditch), serving to reassure the faithful that despite worldly oppression and suffering, ultimate power and glory belong to Allah alone. It establishes that no earthly tyrant or throne can compare to the eternal, glorious sovereignty of Allah, offering comfort that justice and majesty rest with Him regardless of temporal injustices witnessed on earth.

translation: [He is] Perfect Doer of whatever He intends.
interpretation: This phrase affirms the absolute and unrestricted power of Allah, emphasizing that His will is never thwarted and His actions require no permission, assistance, or constraint from any created being. Unlike human doers, whose intentions are often frustrated by limitations of ability, time, or circumstance, Allah's will and His action are one and the same—whatever He intends to do is immediately and perfectly accomplished. This verse typically appears in contexts affirming divine sovereignty and often follows descriptions of Allah's power to punish tyrants or protect the believers, reminding the reader that no earthly power, however mighty it may seem, can stand against the decree of God. It instills both awe and comfort: awe at the limitless nature of divine power, and comfort for the believers that their ultimate protector and judge faces no obstacles in executing justice or bestowing mercy.

translation: Has there come to you the story of the hosts?
interpretation: This verse, which opens a passage in Surah Al-Buruj, serves as a rhetorical introduction drawing the Prophet Muhammad's (and the listener's) attention to a forthcoming historical account of powerful armies or forces who opposed God's messengers and believers. The rhetorical question format is a common Quranic device meant to pique curiosity and prepare the listener for a lesson about the fate of tyrannical powers who persecuted the faithful, specifically foreshadowing the stories of Pharaoh and Thamud mentioned in the subsequent verses. It emphasizes that despite the apparent might of oppressive forces, they ultimately fail against divine will, offering reassurance to believers facing persecution that history testifies to the downfall of tyranny and the preservation of faith.

translation: And Pharaoh, and Thamud
interpretation: This phrase evokes two of the most notorious examples of tyranny and rejection of divine guidance mentioned throughout the Qur'an. Pharaoh represents the archetype of arrogant political power who claimed divinity and oppressed the Israelites, while Thamud represents a once-mighty civilization that defied their prophet Salih and rejected the miraculous she-camel sent as a sign. Both were destroyed despite their apparent strength and achievements—Pharaoh with his armies and monuments, Thamud with their skill in carving dwellings from rock. Their pairing serves as a warning that worldly power, technological prowess, and material success offer no protection against divine justice when a people persist in arrogance, oppression, and rejection of truth. This serves as a rhetorical device reminding listeners that history provides ample precedent for the consequences of transgression, urging reflection on human accountability before God.

translation: But those who disbelieve persist in denial.
interpretation: This verse comes in the context of Surah Al-Inshiqaq, following discussion of the Day of Judgment, the splitting of the sky, and the recitation of the Quran. After describing how believers should respond with humility and submission when the truth is presented to them (as indicated in the preceding verses about prostrating when the Quran is recited), this verse contrasts that proper response with the attitude of disbelievers. Rather than reflecting on the signs of Allah, the coming of judgment, and the truth of revelation, the disbelievers' default state is one of persistent rejection and denial. The verse highlights a psychological and spiritual condition rather than a single act of disbelief - it describes an ongoing, entrenched pattern of denying truth even when evidence and signs are presented clearly before them. This sets up the warning in the following verses about Allah's full knowledge of what they conceal in their hearts and the painful punishment awaiting them, contrasted with the reward for those who believe and do righteous deeds. The verse serves as a pivot point, transitioning from general description of the Day of Judgment to specific address of the disbelievers' stubborn rejection as a willful choice rather than an innocent misunderstanding.

translation: And Allah encompasses them from all around (from behind them).
interpretation: This verse affirms God's total, inescapable knowledge and power over the disbelievers mentioned earlier in the surah—those who persecuted the believers. The imagery of being surrounded 'from behind' conveys that no matter how powerful or secure the wrongdoers feel, they cannot outmaneuver or escape divine control; God holds them encompassed from every side, including from directions they cannot perceive or guard against. It serves as a reassurance to the believers that their oppressors' apparent dominance is illusory, since ultimate authority and encompassing power belong to God alone, who will hold all accountable for their deeds.

translation: Nay, it is a glorious Qur'an,
interpretation: This verse comes at the conclusion of Surah Al-Buruj, which recounts the story of the persecuted believers (the People of the Ditch) and affirms God's power and justice. After describing the fate of tyrants and the reward awaiting the faithful, this verse serves as a decisive rebuttal to the disbelievers' accusations against the Qur'an—that it was mere poetry, sorcery, or fabrication. The word 'majeed' (glorious/noble) emphasizes the Qur'an's exalted status, its divine origin, and its permanence as a source of guidance. It is 'glorious' because it contains truth, wisdom, and the accounts of previous nations as lessons, and because it is preserved from corruption, as the following verse about the 'Preserved Tablet' (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz) affirms. This declaration reassures believers that despite worldly persecution and the mockery of skeptics, the Qur'an's majesty and truth remain uncontested and eternal, standing as a testament to God's unassailable message.

translation: In a Preserved Tablet.
interpretation: This phrase concludes a passage in Surah Al-Buruj describing the Qur'an as 'qur'anun majeed' (a Glorious Qur'an) that exists 'fi lawhin mahfooz' (in a Preserved Tablet). This refers to al-Lawh al-Mahfuz, the Preserved Tablet, understood in Islamic tradition as the primordial, heavenly record wherein all divine decrees, destinies, and revealed scripture—including the complete and eternal form of the Qur'an—are inscribed before their manifestation in the created world. The phrase affirms the transcendent origin and incorruptibility of the Qur'an: it is not merely a human text subject to alteration, but a reflection of a changeless, safeguarded original that exists beyond time and space in the knowledge and decree of God. This serves as a reassurance to believers of the Qur'an's authenticity and permanence, protected from distortion or loss, and underscores the theme of divine sovereignty over all affairs, including the trials of the believers mentioned earlier in the surah—showing that worldly oppression and persecution cannot alter the preserved truth and ultimate justice already established with God.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. By the sky and the night-comer (At-Tariq).
interpretation: This opening oath introduces Surah At-Tariq by invoking the heavens and a mysterious nocturnal phenomenon—traditionally understood as a bright, piercing star—to draw the listener's attention to profound truths that will follow. In Qur'anic rhetoric, God often swears by elements of His creation to emphasize their significance as signs (ayat) pointing to greater realities, particularly His power and the certainty of resurrection and judgment. The 'night-comer' that pierces through darkness symbolizes something that arrives unexpectedly and penetrates what is hidden, foreshadowing the sura's theme of divine awareness of all things, including what lies within every soul. The vastness and order of the sky paired with this piercing celestial body sets a tone of awe and contemplation, preparing the reader for the deeper message about human origins, accountability, and the Day of Judgment that unfolds in subsequent verses.

translation: And what can make you know what is the night-comer (at-Tariq)?
interpretation: This rhetorical question follows the opening oath 'By the sky and the night-comer' and serves to heighten the listener's sense of awe and curiosity before the answer is given in the next verse, identifying the Tariq as 'the piercing star.' This rhetorical device—posing a question about something and then answering it—is a common Qur'anic technique used to draw attention to phenomena of cosmic significance, signaling that what follows carries profound meaning beyond ordinary human comprehension. The 'night-comer' refers to that which appears or strikes in the darkness, traditionally understood as a brilliant, piercing star that shines through the night sky. By emphasizing that even the Prophet himself (and by extension, all believers) cannot fully grasp the nature of this phenomenon without divine clarification, the verse underscores the vastness of God's creation and the limits of human knowledge, preparing the reader for the surah's larger message about divine watchfulness—since every soul has a guardian watching over it, just as this piercing star watches over and illuminates the night.

translation: The piercing star.
interpretation: This phrase describes the star referenced in the preceding verse as a brilliant, piercing light that cuts through the darkness of the night sky. The imagery evokes a star of intense luminosity—possibly a reference to a specific bright star or to stars in general whose light penetrates the vast darkness of space to reach the earth. This serves as a sign of Allah's power and precision in creation, and is often connected to the verses that follow about every soul having a guardian watching over it, drawing a parallel between the piercing light that reveals what is hidden in darkness and the all-seeing vigilance of the Creator over human affairs. The piercing quality of the star's light also symbolizes how divine truth and revelation cut through falsehood and ignorance.

translation: Indeed, there is no soul but has over it a guardian (watcher).
interpretation: This verse affirms that every human soul is under constant divine surveillance through appointed angels who record its deeds, both good and evil, as mentioned elsewhere in the Qur'an (such as the 'Kiraman Katibin' - the Noble Writers). It comes in the context of Surah At-Tariq's oath about the piercing star, emphasizing that nothing a person does escapes notice. This serves as a moral reminder that human beings are never truly alone or unobserved; their actions have consequences that are being meticulously tracked for the Day of Judgment. The verse underscores the themes of accountability and divine omniscience, encouraging believers to live righteously knowing that every soul is watched over, and that ultimately all deeds will be brought to account before God.

translation: So let man consider from what he was created.
interpretation: This verse calls upon human beings to reflect deeply on their own origin as a means of fostering humility before God. The following verses clarify that man is created from a fluid that gushes forth, emerging from between the backbone and the ribs—an image emphasizing the humble, unremarkable biological origin of human life. The rhetorical purpose of this reflection is to counter human arrogance and self-sufficiency: if a person pauses to truly consider the modest and fragile circumstances of his own creation, he should recognize his utter dependence on his Creator. This connects to the broader theme of the surah, which moves from contemplating human origins to affirming that the same God who initiated life has the power to resurrect and judge it, as indicated in the subsequent verses about God's ability to bring man back to life. Thus, the verse functions as an invitation to self-examination that leads logically to acknowledging divine power over both creation and resurrection, and ultimately to moral accountability in light of that power.

translation: He is created from a gushing fluid.
interpretation: This verse, from Surah At-Tariq, refers to the creation of the human being from a spurting or ejaculated fluid, pointing to the origin of human life in the reproductive process. It serves as evidence within the surah's broader argument for bodily resurrection: the God who originated human life from such a humble and seemingly insignificant fluid, and organized it into a fully formed being, possesses the power to resurrect that being after death. The verse invites reflection on human origins as a means of instilling humility, countering arrogance, and affirming belief in the Creator's power over life, death, and the Hereafter.

translation: Issuing from between the backbone and the ribs.
interpretation: This verse, from Surah At-Tariq, describes the creation of man from a fluid that emerges from between the backbone (spine) and the ribs (chest), referring to the male and female reproductive contributions. It serves as evidence in the surah for the power of God to resurrect the dead, arguing that the One who could create man from such an origin is certainly able to bring him back to life after death. It invites reflection on the origins of human creation as a sign of divine power and purpose.

translation: Indeed, He is able to bring him back.
interpretation: This verse refers to God's power to resurrect the human being after death, bringing him back to life just as He originally created him. It comes in the context of Surah At-Tariq, which begins by describing the creation of man from a fluid emerging from between the backbone and ribs, emphasizing God's creative power over human origins. The verse serves as a logical argument: the same God who demonstrated power in the initial creation of man from a seemingly insignificant substance certainly retains the power to recreate or resurrect him after death. This is part of the Qur'an's broader argument for the resurrection, using the evidence of the original creation as proof that a second creation (resurrection) is not only possible but inevitable. The verse also carries an implicit warning, reminding humans of their accountability before the One who has power over both their creation and their return to life for judgment.

translation: On the Day when all secrets will be tested and disclosed.
interpretation: This verse refers to the Day of Judgment, when every hidden thought, intention, and deed concealed within the human heart will be brought to light and scrutinized. The Arabic word 'sara'ir' refers to secrets—not merely actions hidden from others, but the innermost convictions, faith, hypocrisy, sincerity, or doubt that a person harbored in their heart during worldly life. 'Tubla' conveys the sense of testing, trial, and exposure—implying that on that Day, there will be no distinction between what was public and what was private; all will be laid bare before God for judgment. This serves as a powerful reminder that outward piety or deception cannot mask inner reality indefinitely, and that true accountability extends beyond visible actions to the hidden state of one's soul, faith, and intentions. It underscores the Islamic theological emphasis on sincerity (ikhlas) and the futility of hypocrisy, since ultimate judgment rests on what is concealed within, not merely what is performed outwardly for show in this transient world.

translation: Then he will have no power, nor any helper.
interpretation: This verse comes at the culmination of a passage in Surah At-Tariq describing the Day of Judgment, when inner secrets will be tested and exposed. It emphasizes human helplessness before God on that Day—all the strength, wealth, status, allies, and protectors a person relied upon in worldly life will prove utterly powerless. The verse underscores the Qur'anic theme of ultimate accountability: no worldly power or social support network can shield anyone from divine judgment. It serves as a sobering reminder that true security lies not in human power structures or alliances but in one's deeds and relationship with God, since on that Day every soul stands stripped of all the false supports it once trusted in.

translation: By the sky which returns (i.e., which cycles, bringing rain again and again)
interpretation: This verse is an oath sworn by God, invoking the sky's property of 'raj'' (return/cycling) as a sign of His power. The 'returning' quality of the sky refers to its continuous cycle of producing rain, which falls to earth, evaporates back up, and returns again—a perpetual cycle that sustains life. This oath, paired with the following verse about the earth splitting open (for vegetation to sprout), serves as evidence for the resurrection: just as God demonstrates His power through these natural, observable cycles of return and renewal in creation, He is equally capable of returning the dead to life. The imagery connects the physical world's patterns of repetition and renewal to the theological argument for an afterlife, suggesting that the same divine power that orchestrates rainfall's return and vegetation's emergence can likewise resurrect human beings after death.

translation: By the earth which cracks open (with sprouting plants and springs).
interpretation: This verse is part of a solemn oath in Surah At-Tariq, paired with the preceding oath by the sky with its recurring rain. The 'earth that cracks open' refers to how soil splits apart to allow vegetation to sprout forth and water to spring up, demonstrating the earth's capacity for renewal and growth. Together with the sky that cycles rain, these two oaths from nature serve as evidence for the central claim that follows—that the Qur'an itself is a decisive discourse (qawlun fasl), not a frivolous jest. Just as the earth splits to bring forth life from what seems barren and inert, and the sky brings forth rain in recurring cycles, so too does divine revelation bring forth truth and guidance from what might seem like ordinary speech. The imagery also subtly points to resurrection: just as the earth splits open to bring forth new life from buried seeds, so will it split open again to bring forth the dead on the Day of Judgment, reinforcing the verse's implicit argument for the reality of resurrection and divine justice.

translation: Indeed, it is a decisive word (statement).
interpretation: This verse refers to the Qur'an itself, affirming that it is 'fasl' - a decisive, conclusive discourse that clearly distinguishes truth from falsehood, right from wrong, and separates genuine guidance from misguidance. The term 'fasl' carries the connotation of a final judgment or verdict that settles matters definitively, leaving no ambiguity. In context, following verses that swear oaths by the sky and the earth's phenomena (the rain-bearing sky and the vegetation-producing earth as signs of God's power to resurrect), this declaration establishes that the Qur'an's message - particularly regarding resurrection, divine justice, and moral accountability - is not frivolous speech or jest ('wa ma huwa bil-hazl' in the following verse), but serious, authoritative truth. It asserts the Qur'an's self-authenticating nature as a criterion (furqan) that definitively separates believers from disbelievers, truth from error, and that will ultimately be vindicated through the reality it describes, particularly the Day of Judgment when all matters will be conclusively resolved.

translation: And it is not a jest.
interpretation: This phrase refers to the Qur'an itself, affirming that its words, warnings, and teachings are not frivolous or trivial speech, but are serious, weighty, and decisive truth. It comes in context after an oath affirming that the Qur'an is a decisive word (qawlun fasl) that separates truth from falsehood. The verse underscores the gravity of divine revelation, cautioning against treating its message—particularly its warnings about resurrection and judgment—as mere jest or something to be taken lightly. It calls on the listener to recognize the seriousness of the message and respond with reflection rather than dismissal or mockery.

translation: Indeed, they are plotting a plan (scheming a scheme).
interpretation: This verse refers to the disbelievers who reject the Qur'an and the Prophet Muhammad, describing their persistent efforts to plot and scheme against the truth—whether through denial, deception, or conspiracy to undermine the message of Islam. It highlights their calculated and determined opposition, framing their resistance not as passive disbelief but as active, strategic plotting. The verse sets up a contrast with what follows, where God declares that He too has His own plan (kayd) in response, emphasizing divine power and control over human schemes. This serves as reassurance to the believers that no matter how cunning or persistent the opposition's plotting may be, it is ultimately futile against God's will and timing.

translation: "But I am devising a plan."
interpretation: This phrase is part of a sequence of verses (Surah At-Tariq, 86:15-17) in which Allah responds to the plotting and scheming of the disbelievers against the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ and the message of Islam. The preceding verse states that the disbelievers are devising their own schemes (كيدا) to undermine the truth, reject the Qur'an, and oppose the believers. In response, Allah declares that He too has a plan—one that is infinitely more powerful, wise, and certain to prevail. This is not a plan in the human sense of scheming, but rather a divine assurance that Allah's will and justice will ultimately triumph over any human conspiracy or opposition. The verse conveys a sense of divine confidence and control over the outcome of worldly affairs, reassuring the believers that no matter how elaborate or determined the plots of their enemies may be, Allah's plan—rooted in perfect knowledge, power, and justice—cannot be thwarted. It is followed by an instruction to the Prophet to be patient and allow the disbelievers a little respite, implying that their downfall or the fulfillment of divine justice will come in due time, according to Allah's perfect timing, not through hasty human intervention.

translation: So give the disbelievers respite, grant them a gentle, brief respite.
interpretation: This verse, found in Surah Al-Tariq, addresses the Prophet Muhammad amid the rejection and hostility of disbelievers, instructing patience rather than haste in seeking their punishment. The word 'ruwaydan' conveys gentleness and a measured, limited span of time, suggesting that God's delay in punishing the disbelievers is not indefinite neglect but a calculated grace period. This respite is not a sign of weakness or indifference on God's part, but rather an expression of divine wisdom and mercy, allowing people the opportunity to reflect and potentially turn toward faith before the appointed reckoning. It also serves as a reassurance to the Prophet and believers that the apparent delay in divine justice is temporary and purposeful, reinforcing trust in God's ultimate plan and timing over human impatience for immediate retribution.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High.
interpretation: This opening verse of Surah Al-A'la establishes the fundamental act of worship: the glorification (tasbih) of God's name, emphasizing His transcendence through the attribute 'Al-A'la' (the Most High). The command to glorify 'the name' rather than simply 'your Lord' suggests that God's essence is so exalted that even His name carries sanctity beyond full human comprehension. This verse sets the tone for the entire chapter, which goes on to describe God's creative power and providence, reminding the believer that true worship begins with recognizing divine transcendence above all creation, all comparisons, and all limitations that the human mind might attempt to impose. It calls for a constant spiritual orientation of praise and acknowledgment of God's supreme and incomparable status in all affairs of existence.

translation: Who created and proportioned [all things],
interpretation: This verse glorifies God as the Creator who not only brings things into existence but also gives them perfect proportion, balance, and order. 'Khalaqa' (created) refers to the act of bringing something into being from nothing, while 'fa-sawwa' (and proportioned) indicates the refinement and perfection of that creation—giving each thing its proper form, function, and harmony suited to its purpose. This encompasses the entire cosmos, including the intricate design of the human body, the natural world, and the celestial order. The verse invites reflection on the precision evident in creation as a sign of divine wisdom and power, countering any notion of randomness or chaos in existence. It is part of a sequence of verses praising God's attributes before turning to themes of guidance, mercy, and the eventual judgment of human deeds.

translation: And He who determines [the nature of things], and thereby guides [all creation to their purposes].
interpretation: This verse speaks to the comprehensive nature of divine providence, linking creation (taqdeer, meaning measuring out or determining) with guidance (hidayah). It suggests that God did not simply create things and leave them without direction, but rather built guidance into the very fabric of existence. Every creature, from the smallest insect to the largest celestial body, has been given an innate capacity to fulfill its purpose - instinct in animals, the laws of physics in matter, and moral/spiritual capacity in humans. This reflects a worldview where creation and guidance are inseparable acts of divine wisdom: nothing is made in vain or left without the means to reach its intended end. For humanity specifically, this encompasses not only physical and biological guidance (how to nurse, how to survive) but also the deeper spiritual guidance through revelation and innate moral conscience (fitrah), enabling humans to distinguish right from wrong and find their way back to their Creator.

translation: And He who brought forth the pasture
interpretation: This verse is part of a sequence in Surah Al-A'la glorifying Allah through His acts of creation and sustenance. By bringing forth pasture—vegetation and grazing land for livestock—Allah demonstrates His power to generate life and sustenance from the earth, providing for both animals and, by extension, humans who depend on livestock for food, clothing, and other needs. This verse highlights the orderly and purposeful nature of creation, where every element, including plant life, serves a function within a divinely established ecosystem. It also serves as a precursor to the following verse, which describes how Allah then causes this same pasture to wither, illustrating the transient nature of worldly provisions and the cyclical pattern of growth and decay that Allah governs. Together, these verses invite reflection on divine power and wisdom, encouraging gratitude and trust in Allah's sustenance, while also serving as a metaphor for the temporary nature of worldly life compared to the eternal life of the Hereafter.

translation: And He makes it dark, decayed stubble.
interpretation: This verse continues the depiction of God's power over creation and nature, following the mention of bringing forth green pasture. Here, the vegetation that once flourished is transformed into dry, blackened debris, illustrating the transient nature of worldly life. Just as lush pasture inevitably withers and turns to dark refuse, so too do all things in this world eventually fade and perish. This serves as a metaphor for the impermanence of worldly existence, reminding believers that despite the beauty and vitality of life, all things are subject to decay and return to dust, underscoring the eternal power and sovereignty of the Creator who both gives life and brings about its end.

translation: We shall make you recite, so you will not forget,
interpretation: This verse is addressed to Prophet Muhammad, offering reassurance during the period of Quranic revelation. God promises that He Himself will ensure the Prophet retains and recites the revealed words accurately, alleviating any anxiety the Prophet may have had about forgetting portions of the revelation before they could be recorded or memorized by his community. This divine guarantee underscores that the preservation of the Quran is not dependent on human memory alone but is assured through God's direct intervention. It also establishes the miraculous nature of the Quran's transmission, affirming that the unlettered Prophet could receive and retain lengthy, complex revelations only through divine assistance, a sign of the text's supernatural origin and the reliability of its transmission across generations.

translation: Except what Allah wills. Indeed, He knows what is declared and what is hidden.
interpretation: This verse qualifies the preceding divine promise that the Prophet would not forget the revelation, reminding that even this assurance remains subject to God's absolute will—nothing is guaranteed independent of His decree. The exception clause underscores that God's knowledge and power are not bound by the normal processes He has set in motion; He could cause forgetting if He willed, yet He has chosen not to. This is followed by the affirmation that God knows both what is spoken openly and what is concealed in the heart, extending the theme beyond mere memory of scripture to encompass all human thought and intention. Together, the verse establishes a foundation of divine omniscience and sovereignty: God's will governs all outcomes, including the very faculties of memory and expression, and nothing—whether uttered aloud or hidden within the soul—escapes His awareness. This serves as a reminder of human dependence on God's grace even in matters that seem assured, and of the comprehensive nature of divine knowledge that encompasses both the visible actions and the secret inclinations of every being.

translation: And We will ease you toward ease (the way of facility/comfort).
interpretation: This verse, addressed to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him), is a divine promise that God will facilitate for him the path of righteousness, making acts of worship, the delivery of the message, and adherence to good conduct easy and accessible for him. 'Al-yusra' (ease) is often understood to refer to the Sharia of Islam itself, which God describes elsewhere as a religion of ease rather than hardship, and to the facilitation of good deeds for those who have taqwa (God-consciousness) and act with sincerity, as mentioned in the surrounding verses. The broader context of Surah Al-A'la reassures the Prophet that he need not strain himself anxiously over the outcome of his mission, for God Himself will smooth the way for him, both in receiving and conveying revelation, and in his personal character and worship, so that goodness becomes natural and unburdensome rather than forced.

translation: So remind, [O Prophet], if the reminder should benefit.
interpretation: This verse instructs the Prophet Muhammad (and by extension all who convey guidance) to continue the mission of reminding people of truth, even though not everyone will respond positively. The conditional phrase 'if the reminder benefits' does not mean the Prophet should calculate in advance who deserves to hear the message and withhold it from others; rather, it acknowledges a general truth about human receptivity—that admonition only takes root in hearts that are willing to listen and reflect, as clarified in the following verses which distinguish between those who fear God and the wretched who turn away. The verse establishes a principle of divine wisdom: guidance must be offered freely and consistently, since the giver of the reminder cannot always know beforehand whose heart will be softened by it. It places the responsibility of conveying truth on the messenger, while the outcome—whether the reminder is accepted—rests with the free will of the listener and the mercy of God. This reflects the broader Quranic theme that prophetic duty is to deliver the message, not to compel belief or determine results.

translation: He who fears [Allah] will be reminded.
interpretation: This verse comes from Surah Al-A'la and speaks to the nature of receiving divine admonition. It indicates that the reminder and guidance contained in the revelation will benefit those whose hearts are receptive—specifically those who possess taqwa, or God-consciousness, and a reverential awe of their Creator. The verse establishes a principle about spiritual receptivity: it is not merely the hearing of guidance that matters, but the disposition of the heart that receives it. Those who fear Allah are humble, attentive, and willing to change their behavior in light of truth, so the reminder takes root in them and produces positive effect. This sets up a contrast with the following verse, which describes the wretched one who turns away, showing that the same message can either guide or be ignored depending on the state of the listener's heart. It underscores that divine guidance is universally offered, but its benefit is conditional upon one's humility and fear of God.

translation: But the most wretched will avoid it (the reminder).
interpretation: This verse continues the theme from the preceding verses of Surah Al-A'la, which speak of the Qur'anic reminder and admonition. While the one who fears Allah will be reminded and benefit from the message, this verse describes the opposite type of person—the 'most wretched' (al-ashqa)—who turns away from and avoids the truth. This wretchedness is not merely worldly misfortune but a spiritual state resulting from one's own choices: a hardened heart that rejects guidance despite its clarity. The avoidance is deliberate, stemming from arrogance, attachment to worldly life, and unwillingness to submit to truth. This sets up a contrast that continues in the following verses, where the fate of this wretched one is described as entering the great Fire, where he neither dies nor lives, as the ultimate consequence of turning away from divine guidance when it was made accessible and clear.

translation: Who will [enter to] burn in the greatest Fire.
interpretation: This verse describes the fate of the wretched one who denies the truth and turns away, as referenced in the surrounding verses of Surah Al-A'la. The 'greatest Fire' (an-nar al-kubra) refers to the Hellfire of the Hereafter, distinguished from any worldly fire or suffering by its eternal and supreme intensity. The use of the superlative 'greatest' implies a contrast with lesser fires or trials experienced in worldly life, emphasizing that no earthly punishment or hardship compares to the ultimate consequence awaiting those who reject guidance and persist in wretchedness and disbelief. This serves as a stern warning about the ultimate consequence of choosing the fleeting life over the eternal truth, reinforcing the theme of accountability that runs through the surah.

translation: Then he will neither die therein nor live.
interpretation: This verse describes the state of the wretched soul in Hell who, unlike those who die and find release, is condemned to a perpetual state between death and life—suffering is so intense that death would be a mercy, yet death does not come, and life, in any meaningful sense, is denied as well. This conveys the idea of eternal torment without the possibility of annihilation or relief, emphasizing the severity and permanence of punishment for those who reject faith and persist in wrongdoing, as a stark warning against disbelief and sin.

translation: He has certainly succeeded who purifies himself.
interpretation: This verse establishes that true success and prosperity in both this life and the Hereafter are tied not to wealth, status, or worldly achievement, but to spiritual self-purification. The Arabic term 'tazakka' implies an active, ongoing process of cleansing the soul from vice, arrogance, and heedlessness, while cultivating sincerity, humility, and devotion to God. The verse appears in a passage that follows instructions to glorify God's name and precedes warnings against being seduced by worldly life over the eternal Hereafter. Thus, it serves as a pivotal statement that reframes the entire human endeavor: genuine felicity comes from inner transformation—submitting one's will to divine guidance, remembering God, and acting righteously—rather than from external accumulation. It suggests that salvation is earned through personal effort toward moral and spiritual refinement, making self-purification the key criterion by which success is ultimately measured in the sight of God.

translation: And mentions the name of his Lord and prays.
interpretation: This verse, from Surah Al-A'la, describes the one who truly succeeds and attains purification—the believer who remembers God through constant remembrance (dhikr) of His name and expresses this remembrance through formal prayer (salah). The sequence here is significant: inner remembrance precedes and gives meaning to outward ritual worship. The mention of God's name signifies a heart oriented toward the Divine in gratitude, humility, and awareness, and this internal state naturally culminates in the act of prayer, which serves as the physical and spiritual manifestation of that remembrance. The verse teaches that genuine prayer is not merely mechanical performance but flows from a consciousness of God that permeates one's being before and during the act of worship itself.

translation: But you prefer the life of this world,
interpretation: This verse highlights a fundamental human tendency to prioritize immediate, worldly pleasures and gains over the eternal rewards of the Hereafter. It appears in a context contrasting the fleeting nature of worldly life with the lasting value of the afterlife, serving as a critique of misplaced priorities. The verse calls attention to the human weakness of being drawn to what is tangible and immediate—wealth, comfort, status—rather than investing in spiritual growth and preparation for eternal life. It serves as a reminder and a gentle rebuke, urging believers to reconsider their priorities and recognize that true success lies in balancing worldly responsibilities with spiritual and eternal considerations, rather than being consumed entirely by transient desires.

translation: And the Hereafter is better and more lasting.
interpretation: This verse, found in Surah Al-A'la, serves as a corrective to human priorities, contrasting the fleeting nature of worldly life with the permanence of the afterlife. The preceding verses criticize those who prefer the life of this world despite the Hereafter being superior in both quality ('khayr' - better) and duration ('abqa' - more lasting/eternal). The implicit argument is one of rational priority: if given a choice between something temporary and something eternal, and the eternal option is also qualitatively superior, rational beings should orient their actions and values toward that eternal reality rather than being consumed by transient worldly pursuits. This verse functions as a theological corrective to materialism and short-term thinking, reminding believers that true success is measured by eternal consequence rather than immediate worldly gain. It also serves as motivation for moral and spiritual discipline, suggesting that sacrifices made in this world for righteousness are investments in a superior, everlasting reward.

translation: Indeed, this is in the former scriptures.
interpretation: This verse concludes a passage in Surah Al-A'la affirming that the core teachings just mentioned—exhorting purification of the soul, remembrance of God, and prioritizing the eternal life over the fleeting world—are not novel inventions but timeless truths that have been consistently revealed throughout human history. The following verse specifies that these truths were present in the scriptures of Abraham and Moses, establishing continuity among the prophetic messages. This serves to validate the Qur'an's message by linking it to the unbroken chain of divine revelation, emphasizing that the fundamental moral and spiritual principles it conveys are universal and have always been part of God's guidance to humanity, rather than being specific to one time, people, or prophet.

translation: [Mentioned in] the scriptures of Abraham and Moses.
interpretation: This verse concludes Surah Al-A'la, affirming that the core teachings of this surah—the call to purification, remembrance of God, and the recognition that the Hereafter is superior to worldly life—are not novel teachings but timeless truths that have been consistent throughout prophetic history. By invoking the scriptures of Abraham and Moses, the verse establishes continuity between the message of the Quran and the earlier revelations given to these two major prophetic figures, who are foundational to the Abrahamic tradition. This serves multiple rhetorical purposes: it validates the Quran's message by showing it aligns with previously revealed wisdom, it challenges the Meccan polytheists who claimed ancestral traditions while ignoring the actual teachings of their forefather Abraham, and it emphasizes that essential spiritual truths—the primacy of the eternal over the temporal, the need for self-purification, and the importance of remembering God—represent a unified divine message transcending any single time period or community. The reference also subtly critiques those who possess scriptures yet fail to internalize their fundamental message, suggesting that despite textual differences across revelations, the ultimate truths about human purpose and priority remain unchanged.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Has there come to you the narration of the Overwhelming [Event]?
interpretation: This opening verse of Surah Al-Ghashiyah introduces the Day of Judgment through the term 'Al-Ghashiyah' (the Overwhelming/Enveloping Event), a name that evokes the terror of that day as it will overwhelm and engulf all creation with its intensity. The rhetorical question 'Has there come to you...' is a common Qur'anic device meant to capture the listener's attention and create anticipation, signaling that profound and weighty news is about to be conveyed. This serves as a dramatic introduction, preparing the audience for the vivid and contrasting descriptions that follow in the surah—describing the fate of the disbelievers who will face humiliation and torment, and the believers who will enjoy bliss and honor in Paradise. The verse establishes the theme of ultimate accountability and the reality of the afterlife as central to the surah's message, urging reflection on one's actions in this worldly life in light of the inevitable reckoning to come.

translation: Some faces, that Day, will be humbled (downcast).
interpretation: This verse opens a description of the Day of Resurrection by contrasting the states of different faces, reflecting the inner states of their owners. The 'humbled' or 'downcast' faces belong to those who rejected faith, disobeyed God, or lived in arrogance during their worldly life. On that Day, all the pride, defiance, and self-assurance they once displayed will be stripped away, leaving them in visible humiliation and disgrace before their Lord. This downcast appearance is not merely physical exhaustion but represents the shame, fear, and despair of souls confronted with the truth they denied and the consequences they ignored. The verse serves as a stark warning, reminding believers that outward arrogance and heedlessness in this life will be answered with abasement in the Hereafter, while setting up a contrast (made explicit in the following verses) with other faces that will be joyful and at ease due to their righteous deeds and sincere devotion.

translation: Laboring, exhausted.
interpretation: This phrase comes from Surah Al-Ghashiyah (88:3), describing the faces of certain people on the Day of Judgment. It refers to those who toiled and labored throughout their worldly lives, exhausting themselves in works and deeds, yet their efforts were misdirected—spent in disbelief or in deeds devoid of true faith and sincerity toward God. Despite their exhaustion and hard work, their labor avails them nothing in the Hereafter because it was not grounded in righteous faith. This serves as a warning that mere effort or toil in life, without proper faith and intention directed to God, does not guarantee salvation or reward; the quality and direction of one's deeds matter as much as the effort itself. It contrasts worldly striving without spiritual purpose against the ultimate accountability before God, where only deeds rooted in true belief and sincerity are of lasting value.

translation: It will burn in a scorching fire.
interpretation: This verse continues the description from the preceding verse of the faces of the wretched on the Day of Judgment—those who were arrogant and toiled in vain in worldly life. It describes their fate: exposure to an intensely hot, blazing fire as punishment for their disbelief and rejection of truth. The word 'حَامِيَة' (scorching/intensely hot) emphasizes the extreme severity of this fire, far beyond any worldly flame, serving as a stark warning about the consequences of arrogance, heedlessness, and rejecting divine guidance. This imagery is meant to instill fear and prompt reflection on one's deeds and beliefs before the Day of Reckoning arrives.

translation: They will be given to drink from a boiling spring.
interpretation: This verse is part of a vivid sequence in Surah Al-Ghashiya describing the fate of the wretched on the Day of Resurrection. Having just been described as burning in a scorching Fire, their torment is intensified by being denied even the relief of refreshing drink—instead, they are given water from a spring that has reached a scalding, boiling temperature. This detail functions rhetorically as a deliberate inversion of Paradise's imagery, where the righteous drink from pure, flowing springs (as described later in the same surah). The contrast heightens the horror: what should be a source of relief and sustenance becomes another instrument of suffering. The scorching spring symbolizes the complete reversal of comfort in Hell, where every natural source of relief is transformed into torment, underscoring the totality and inescapability of the punishment for those who rejected faith and lived heedlessly.

translation: They will have no food except from a bitter thorn plant (dari').
interpretation: This verse describes the fate of the disbelievers in Hell, depicting the utter deprivation and torment they will endure. The 'dari'' referenced here is understood to be a thorny, bitter desert plant—so vile and poisonous that even animals refuse to eat it. By stating that this is the only 'food' available to the people of Hell, the verse emphasizes the complete absence of nourishment, comfort, or relief in their punishment. It is not sustenance in any real sense, as the following verses clarify that this food neither satisfies hunger nor provides any benefit, but only adds to their suffering. This imagery serves as a stark contrast to the delicious fruits and pleasures promised to the righteous in Paradise, reinforcing the Qur'anic theme of recompense—where the nature of one's sustenance in the afterlife directly mirrors the spiritual choices made in worldly life. The verse functions as both a warning and a vivid illustration of divine justice, highlighting the vast difference between the rewards of the faithful and the torment awaiting those who reject guidance.

translation: It neither nourishes nor avails against hunger.
interpretation: This phrase is part of a description in Surah Al-Ghashiya of the torment awaiting the people of Hell, who will be fed only from a bitter, thorny plant called Dari'. The verse emphasizes the utter futility and hopelessness of their suffering: unlike ordinary food, which sustains the body and alleviates hunger, this infernal food provides no benefit whatsoever. It conveys a profound message about the nature of divine punishment—it is not merely painful but also purposeless in providing any relief or sustenance, symbolizing the eternal, unrelieved suffering of those who rejected faith and lived in heedless indulgence in worldly life. The imagery serves as a stark contrast to the descriptions of Paradise's delicious and satisfying provisions, reinforcing the moral lesson that actions in this life have real and lasting consequences in the Hereafter.

translation: Some faces, that Day, will be radiant (with joy and bliss)
interpretation: This verse describes the state of the believers on the Day of Judgment, whose faces will glow with happiness, contentment, and ease as a reflection of the inner peace and reward granted to them for their faith and good deeds. The radiance mentioned is not merely physical but symbolizes the deep spiritual satisfaction and relief that comes from receiving Allah's mercy and the good news of eternal reward in Paradise. This verse typically follows or precedes descriptions of those whose faces are humiliated or downcast, creating a stark contrast between the fates of the righteous and the wrongdoers on that momentous Day, emphasizing the justice of divine recompense.

translation: Pleased with its endeavor.
interpretation: This verse continues the description from the preceding verse of the blessed faces on the Day of Judgment, which are described as radiant and joyful. Here, the reason for their contentment is specified: they are satisfied with the deeds and efforts they put forth during their earthly lives. This refers to the believers who strove sincerely in righteousness, worship, and good works, and who now witness the fruits of their labor in the form of eternal reward in Paradise. Their pleasure is not merely with the reward itself, but with their own striving—they can look back upon their life's efforts with satisfaction, knowing that their sacrifices, patience, and devotion were not in vain. This stands in contrast to those who will have toiled in disbelief or sin, whose efforts (mentioned in surrounding verses) lead only to exhaustion and punishment. The verse emphasizes the Islamic principle that true success is measured not by worldly outcomes but by the sincerity and righteousness of one's efforts in the sight of God, and that ultimate contentment comes from having lived a life aligned with faith and virtue.

translation: In a lofty garden,
interpretation: This verse comes from Surah Al-Ghashiyah, describing the state of the blessed faces on the Day of Judgment who are described as joyful, content with their striving, residing in an elevated, exalted garden. The 'height' of the garden signifies not merely physical elevation but spiritual and existential exaltation—a station of honor, nearness to God, and ultimate reward for righteous deeds. This contrasts sharply with the preceding description of other faces that are humiliated, toiling, and weary, who will be in a blazing fire and made to drink from a boiling spring. The loftiness of the garden symbolizes the dignity, peace, and elevated status granted to the believers who worked righteousness in this world, now free from toil, fear, or hardship, enjoying the heights of paradise both literally and metaphorically as a place beyond the reach of any affliction or lowliness.

translation: Therein they will hear no vain talk.
interpretation: This verse describes one of the spiritual and experiential qualities of Paradise as promised to the righteous. Unlike earthly gatherings, which are often filled with idle chatter, gossip, falsehood, or hurtful speech, the dwellers of Paradise are shielded from any form of vain, meaningless, or sinful talk. This reflects the purity and perfection of the heavenly abode, where every interaction is elevated and free from the flaws that mar human communication in worldly life. It emphasizes that Paradise is not only a place of physical comfort but also of spiritual and social tranquility, where believers are free from the irritations, conflicts, and emptiness that vain speech often brings in this world. The absence of lagha (idle or vain talk) signifies a higher state of existence where truth, peace, and meaningful communion prevail, reinforcing the contrast between the imperfections of worldly life and the completeness of the eternal reward.

translation: Therein is a flowing spring.
interpretation: This verse is part of a description of the rewards of Paradise awaiting the righteous, contrasting with the earlier depiction of the torment of the disbelievers. The mention of a 'flowing spring' (ayn jariyah) evokes an image of abundant, perpetually running water—a powerful symbol of life, purity, and ease in a desert culture where water was precious and often scarce. Unlike stagnant or finite sources, a flowing spring never depletes, suggesting the eternal and inexhaustible nature of Paradise's blessings. This imagery also contrasts with the boiling water and bitter food mentioned for the people of Hell in the preceding verses, reinforcing the stark duality between the two destinies. The flowing spring represents not just physical refreshment but spiritual tranquility, continuous divine favor, and the removal of all hardship and scarcity that characterized earthly existence.

translation: Therein are couches [thrones] raised high.
interpretation: This verse is part of a description of the rewards awaiting the righteous in Paradise, found in Surah Al-Ghashiyah. The 'raised thrones' symbolize honor, elevated status, and majestic comfort granted to the believers. The elevation signifies not merely physical height but spiritual and social exaltation—those who lived in humility and faith on earth are lifted to positions of dignity and nobility in the Hereafter. This imagery of elevated seating also evokes royal or sovereign status, suggesting that the faithful are treated as honored guests or even kings in the gardens of Paradise, free from the burdens and lowliness of worldly life, reflecting divine generosity and the reversal of earthly hierarchies where true honor is bestowed according to piety rather than worldly power.

translation: And goblets set in place.
interpretation: This verse is part of a sequence in Surah Al-Ghashiyah (The Overwhelming) describing the sensory delights awaiting the righteous in Paradise. The 'goblets set in place' evokes an image of readiness and ease—vessels for drink are not merely available but already arranged, positioned, and waiting, requiring no effort or anticipation from those who will use them. This reflects a broader Qur'anic theme of Paradise as a realm where desires are anticipated and fulfilled without labor or delay, contrasting with the toil and uncertainty of worldly life. The passive construction ('set in place') suggests divine provision and hospitality, as though an unseen host has prepared everything in advance for the arrival of the blessed, reinforcing the idea that Paradise is a place of effortless comfort, honor, and generous service bestowed by God upon the faithful.

translation: And cushions lined up in rows.
interpretation: This verse appears in Surah Al-Ghashiyah as part of a vivid description of the comforts awaiting the righteous in Paradise. The image of cushions arranged in neat rows evokes a sense of order, luxury, and hospitality, reminiscent of a grand gathering or banquet prepared for honored guests. It reflects the Quranic style of using tangible, familiar imagery—furnishings, raised couches, flowing cups—to convey the ultimate reward of eternal comfort and dignity that transcends earthly experience, inviting believers to reflect on the ease and honor that await them in the Hereafter as a contrast to the toils and trials of worldly life.

translation: And carpets spread out.
interpretation: This verse is part of a series of descriptions in Surah Al-Ghashiyah depicting the luxurious comforts awaiting the righteous in Paradise. The 'spread out carpets' (zaraabiyy mabthoothah) evoke an image of opulence, ease, and abundance—rich carpets scattered generously throughout the gardens of Paradise, available wherever one wishes to sit or rest. This imagery, following mentions of raised couches, flowing cups, and cushions arranged in rows, serves to contrast the believer's eternal reward with the suffering described for disbelievers earlier in the surah. The spreading out of carpets suggests not scarcity but overwhelming plenty, a space of rest and dignity where every need is anticipated and fulfilled without the toil associated with worldly luxury. It reflects the Quranic style of using tangible, sensory imagery familiar to its original Arab audience—fine carpets being a sign of wealth and comfort—to make the abstract concept of divine reward vivid and desirable, encouraging reflection on the eternal versus the temporal and motivating righteous conduct through the promise of lasting ease and honor in the Hereafter.

translation: Do they not look at the camels, how they are created?
interpretation: This verse invites reflection on the camel as a sign of God's creative power and wisdom, urging the disbelievers of Mecca—who were intimately familiar with camels as essential to their desert life—to contemplate this familiar creature with fresh eyes. The camel's remarkable design, its ability to endure harsh desert conditions, go without water for extended periods, carry heavy loads, and thrive in an environment hostile to most life, serves as evidence of deliberate and purposeful creation rather than random chance. By pointing to something so ordinary and close at hand, the verse demonstrates that profound signs of divine wisdom are not distant or hidden but are present in everyday life, accessible to anyone willing to observe thoughtfully. This rhetorical device—starting with the near and tangible before moving to the sky, mountains, and earth in subsequent verses—follows a pedagogical pattern in the Quran of building from the familiar to the cosmic, inviting a progression of contemplation that moves the heart toward acknowledging a Creator behind the intricate order of the natural world.

translation: And at the sky - how it is raised?
interpretation: This verse is part of a series in Surah Al-Ghashiyah (88:17-20) that invites human beings to reflect upon the natural world as evidence of God's power and wisdom. By asking how the sky was raised without visible pillars or support, the Qur'an calls attention to the vastness, order, and apparent suspension of the heavens above the earth as a sign of divine creation and design. This rhetorical questioning is meant to provoke contemplation (tafakkur) in the observer, encouraging them to move from observing the physical phenomenon to recognizing the Creator behind it. The verse employs the method of drawing attention to everyday, overlooked wonders—the sky above every person at all times—as a direct and accessible proof of God's existence and omnipotence, requiring no specialized knowledge, only sincere reflection. It also implicitly challenges the disbelievers mentioned earlier in the surah who deny resurrection and divine accounting, by pointing to the grandeur of creation as evidence that the One who raised the heavens is equally capable of recreating and resurrecting humanity.

translation: And at the mountains, how they are raised (firmly set up)?
interpretation: This verse is part of a series of rhetorical questions in Surah Al-Ghashiyah inviting human beings to reflect on the natural world as evidence of God's creative power and wisdom. By pointing to the mountains and their firm, upright establishment, the verse calls attention to their function as stabilizers of the earth and symbols of permanence and strength. The implicit argument is that such a majestic and purposeful feature of creation could not have come into being by mere chance, but points to a deliberate, all-powerful Creator. This reflection is meant to move the disbelieving listener from heedless denial to contemplation, humility, and ultimately faith, recognizing that the One who can erect mountains with such stability is fully capable of resurrection and recompense, the central themes of the surah.

translation: And at the earth - how it is spread out?
interpretation: This verse is part of a series of rhetorical questions in Surah Al-Ghashiyah inviting human beings to reflect on the natural world as evidence of divine creative power and wisdom. By pointing to the camel, the sky, the mountains, and finally the earth, the Qur'an directs attention to everyday, familiar phenomena that people often take for granted. The specific mention of the earth being 'spread out' (sutihat) evokes its vast, level expanse that makes it habitable and suitable for life, agriculture, travel, and settlement—despite being, in reality, a sphere. This apparent flatness from the human vantage point is presented as a sign (ayah) of deliberate design rather than random occurrence. The verse calls on the disbelievers, particularly the stubborn among the Quraysh who denied resurrection and divine creation, to use their God-given reason and observation to recognize that such order and functionality could not arise without a wise and powerful Creator. It is an invitation to move from empirical observation of the physical world to spiritual and theological conclusions about God's existence, power, and the truth of revelation.

translation: So remind, [O Muhammad]; you are only a reminder.
interpretation: This verse addresses the Prophet Muhammad directly, clarifying the nature and limits of his mission. The term 'dhakkir' (remind) emphasizes that his role is one of admonition and recollection—bringing people back to truths already embedded in their innate nature (fitrah)—rather than coercion or control over their hearts. The phrase 'innama anta mudhakkir' (you are only a reminder) uses the restrictive particle 'innama' to delimit his function precisely: he is not a compeller, judge, or guardian over people's ultimate choices, but a conveyor of guidance. This verse comes in the context of surah Al-Ghashiyah, following descriptions of the Hereafter, paradise, and hell, and it serves to console and instruct the Prophet that his duty is fulfilled through sincere conveyance of the message, not through forcing belief. It also distributes moral responsibility properly: accountability rests with each individual who receives the reminder, not with the one who delivers it. This has broader theological implications about free will, the purpose of prophethood, and the relationship between divine guidance and human choice—affirming that faith must be a matter of conviction rather than compulsion, while also affirming the real, though limited, purpose of prophetic mission as one of moral and spiritual illumination.

translation: You are not a controller over them.
interpretation: This verse addresses Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him), clarifying the nature and limits of his mission. It comes immediately after the command to 'remind' (fadhakkir innama anta mudhakkir - 'so remind, for you are only a reminder'), establishing that his role is one of conveying the message, admonishing, and guiding—not one of coercion or forcing belief upon people. The word 'musaytir' implies a dominator, controller, or one who has power to compel others' will. This verse teaches a fundamental principle in Islamic theology regarding free will and the nature of faith: belief must be a matter of genuine conviction and choice, not imposition. The Prophet's responsibility was to deliver the message clearly and sincerely, to warn and to guide, but ultimate acceptance or rejection rests with each individual, and judgment belongs to God alone (as the following verses clarify, mentioning that it is to God that they will return and He will hold them accountable). This verse also serves as a source of comfort and clarification for the Prophet, alleviating any undue burden he might feel about people's refusal to believe—his duty was fulfilled through sincere conveyance of the message, not through guaranteeing results. It establishes a broader principle about the nature of religious authority in Islam: no human being, including the Prophet himself, possesses the right to compel others into faith, as genuine faith must emerge from inner conviction rather than external force.

translation: Except he who turns away and disbelieves.
interpretation: This verse comes in the context of discussions about ultimate accountability before God, often following mention of those who will be saved or spared punishment due to their faith and righteous deeds. The exception clause here identifies a specific category of people who are excluded from God's mercy or exempted from salvation: those who deliberately turn away from guidance and truth, and who then disbelieve. The phrase 'تولى' (turned away) suggests a conscious act of rejection after having been presented with the truth—implying willful avoidance rather than mere ignorance. 'كفر' (disbelieved) reinforces this by denoting an active denial of faith. Together, these two verbs describe a person who has had the opportunity to accept guidance but chooses instead to reject it and persist in disbelief. The verse serves as a warning that while God's mercy is vast and encompasses many, it does not extend to those who knowingly and stubbornly reject His signs and messengers. This highlights the Qur'anic theme that accountability is tied to one's response to having received clear guidance, and that willful denial, as opposed to innocent unawareness, carries serious spiritual consequences.

translation: Then Allah will punish him with the greatest punishment.
interpretation: This verse refers to the fate of those who turn away from faith, reject the truth, and persist in disbelief despite having been warned. The 'greatest punishment' is understood to refer to the eternal torment of the Hellfire in the Hereafter, as distinguished from any lesser punishments or trials that may befall a person in worldly life. This contrast between a lesser, temporary suffering and the 'greatest' ultimate punishment serves as a warning that worldly consequences pale in comparison to the eternal reckoning awaiting those who willfully reject guidance. The verse emphasizes divine justice and accountability, reinforcing the Quranic theme that actions and beliefs in this life have consequences of ultimate significance in the next.

translation: Indeed, to Us is their return.
interpretation: This verse affirms the doctrine of ultimate return to God, emphasizing that all human beings, regardless of their deeds or status in worldly life, will inevitably return to their Creator. It comes in the context of Surah Al-Ghashiyah, which discusses the Day of Judgment and the contrasting fates of those who disbelieved and those who believed and did good. The verse serves as a reminder that life in this world is temporary and that accountability before God is certain. It underscores divine sovereignty and justice, assuring that no one escapes the final reckoning. This statement also offers comfort to believers, as it implies that worldly injustices will be rectified in the hereafter, and it serves as a warning to those who deny the resurrection, affirming that their return to God is an inescapable truth regardless of their disbelief.

translation: Then, indeed, upon Us is their reckoning.
interpretation: This verse affirms that ultimate accountability for all human deeds rests solely with God. It follows verses describing how people will return to God, emphasizing that no one else—no intermediary, authority, or worldly power—has the right or ability to judge or reckon with creation except Allah Himself. This serves as both a warning to the wrongdoers that they cannot escape divine justice, and a reassurance to the believers that true justice will ultimately prevail, since it is in the hands of the All-Knowing and All-Just. It also reflects a core theological principle in Islam: that the final judgment of every soul's actions belongs exclusively to God, reinforcing human responsibility while affirming divine mercy and justice over human affairs.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. By the dawn.
interpretation: This verse opens Surah Al-Fajr with a solemn oath sworn by Allah upon the dawn, invoking a moment of profound natural transition from darkness to light. The dawn symbolizes renewal, hope, and the emergence of clarity after a period of concealment—a fitting introduction to a surah that goes on to discuss the fates of past nations destroyed for their arrogance and oppression, and that calls the human soul to self-reflection and accountability. By swearing by the dawn, Allah draws attention to the recurring, miraculous rhythm of creation as a sign of His power and wisdom, inviting the listener to recognize that just as light reliably follows darkness, moral and spiritual truths will likewise be illuminated despite apparent obscurity, and that ultimate justice and reckoning are certain to break forth like the dawn after the night of worldly trial.

translation: And by the ten nights
interpretation: This verse is part of a series of oaths with which Surah Al-Fajr opens, in which God swears by the dawn, by ten nights, by the even and the odd, and by the night as it passes. The 'ten nights' are widely understood by commentators to refer to the first ten nights (or days) of the month of Dhul-Hijjah, a period considered among the most sacred in the Islamic calendar, during which the rites of Hajj are performed and the Day of Arafah occurs. These nights are associated with intensified worship, repentance, and good deeds. By swearing an oath upon them, God draws attention to their sanctity and spiritual significance, signaling to the listener that what follows carries weighty truth. The oath also serves a rhetorical function common in Qur'anic discourse: invoking natural or temporal phenomena whose value is self-evident to the audience, thereby lending solemnity and certainty to the message that follows—ultimately a warning about the fate of past arrogant nations and a reminder of human accountability before God.

translation: By the even and the odd,
interpretation: This verse is part of a series of oaths at the beginning of Surah Al-Fajr, where God swears by various aspects of creation to draw attention to profound truths. 'The even and the odd' refers to the fundamental mathematical and metaphysical duality found throughout creation—all numbers, all things, can be categorized as either paired (shaf') or singular (watr). Many commentators interpret this as alluding to the nature of existence itself: everything in creation comes in pairs (male and female, day and night, heaven and earth, body and soul) except for God, who is absolutely One and Odd in the sense of being without partner or peer. This oath thus subtly points to the doctrine of Tawhid (divine Oneness) by contrasting the paired nature of all created things with the singular, unparalleled nature of the Creator. Other interpretations connect the 'even and odd' to specific sacred numbers, such as the ten nights of Dhul-Hijjah (even) and the Day of Arafah (odd), or to the five daily prayers (some odd like Maghrib with three rak'ahs, others even). The oath serves to emphasize the comprehensiveness of God's dominion over all categories of existence, whether paired or singular, as a prelude to the warnings and promises that follow in the surah regarding the fate of past nations and the certainty of divine judgment.

translation: By the night when it departs (passes/journeys on).
interpretation: This is one of a series of solemn oaths at the opening of Surah Al-Fajr, in which God swears by various phenomena of time—dawn, ten nights, the even and the odd, and the night as it passes—to draw attention to the rhythmic, divinely ordained order of time and creation. The night 'journeying on' evokes its steady, purposeful movement toward dawn, symbolizing how periods of darkness, hardship, or trial in human life are never static but are always moving toward resolution and light. By swearing on this natural progression, God underscores the certainty of His promises—particularly the warnings and reminders that follow in the surah about the fate of past arrogant nations (like 'Ad and Thamud) and the ultimate accountability awaiting humanity. It suggests that just as the night inevitably gives way to day, worldly power, oppression, and heedlessness will inevitably give way to divine justice and reckoning.

translation: Is there in that an oath (sufficient) for one who possesses reason/intellect?
