interpretation: This verse opens Surah Al-Falaq and establishes the proper posture of a believer before the unseen dangers of the world: seeking refuge not in talismans, charms, or one's own strength, but directly in Allah, described here as 'Lord of the daybreak.' The daybreak symbolizes the emergence of light out of darkness, representing Allah's power to bring relief, clarity, and safety out of fear, ignorance, and harm. By commanding the Prophet (and by extension every believer) to say this phrase, the verse teaches that true protection comes from acknowledging God's sovereignty over all creation, including the hidden forces of evil—whether from jealous souls, malevolent magic, or the darkness of night. It sets the spiritual tone for the specific evils enumerated in the following verses, reminding the reader that reliance on God is the ultimate safeguard against all forms of harm, seen and unseen.

translation: From the evil of that which He created.
interpretation: This verse is part of Surah Al-Falaq, a chapter of seeking refuge with Allah from various forms of harm. This particular phrase establishes a comprehensive principle: that evil and harm can emanate from anything within the vast scope of creation—whether from animals, natural phenomena, human beings, jinn, or any other created thing. By saying 'from the evil of what He created' rather than naming specific threats, the verse teaches believers to seek protection from the unknown and unseen dangers that permeate existence, acknowledging that harm can come from any source in the created world. This phrase sets up the more specific mentions that follow in the chapter (the darkness, those who practice witchcraft, the envier) as particular manifestations of this general category of evil. It also carries a theological nuance: it attributes evil to specific created things that may cause harm, rather than to the Creator Himself, maintaining that Allah creates all things but the harm comes from how certain created beings or phenomena act or are used, placing the believer's trust and refuge solely in the Creator who has power over all His creation.

translation: And from the evil of the darkness [night] when it settles (or: when it overspreads).
interpretation: This verse refers to seeking refuge from the evils associated with the night, particularly when darkness falls and envelops everything. Classical commentators note that 'ghasiq' refers to the night, and 'idha waqab' describes its onset or deepening—when darkness spreads and conceals. Nighttime is highlighted because it is traditionally when harmful creatures emerge, when wrongdoers feel emboldened to commit misdeeds under cover of darkness, when fears and anxieties tend to intensify due to the unknown, and when human vigilance naturally decreases during sleep, leaving one more vulnerable. Some scholars also connect this to the setting of the moon or stars, symbolizing times of spiritual darkness or trial. The verse teaches that one should turn to God for protection during these vulnerable periods, recognizing that both physical darkness and metaphorical darkness (ignorance, evil, despair) are under divine control, and seeking refuge in God is the means to safety from the unseen dangers these times may bring.

translation: And from the evil of the blowers (women) in knots.
interpretation: This verse refers to the practice of sorcery or black magic, specifically a form of witchcraft that was practiced by blowing or spitting on knots tied in string or rope while reciting incantations, intended to cast spells and cause harm to others. The verse is part of a series of supplications in Surah Al-Falaq seeking Allah's protection from various forms of evil, including the hidden and insidious evil of those who practice magic to harm others through deceptive, covert means. This highlights the Islamic teaching that magic and sorcery are real forms of harm that one should seek divine protection from, emphasizing reliance on Allah against unseen malevolent forces and human treachery that operates through secrecy and manipulation.

translation: And from the evil of an envier when he envies.
interpretation: This phrase, part of Surah Al-Falaq, teaches the believer to seek refuge in Allah from the harm caused by envy (hasad). Envy is highlighted as a destructive spiritual and psychological force because the envier wishes for the removal of blessings from another person, and may act—through words, schemes, or even supernatural means like the evil eye—to bring that harm about. By specifying 'when he envies,' the verse acknowledges that envy itself may exist silently in the heart without necessarily causing harm until it is acted upon or manifested through intention and ill will. This teaches that while envious feelings may arise naturally in people, the real danger lies in acting upon them or allowing them to manifest into harmful action. Seeking refuge in Allah from this evil underscores human vulnerability to the malice of others and the need for divine protection against forces that cannot always be seen or controlled, reinforcing reliance on Allah as the ultimate protector against both seen and unseen harms.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Say: 'I seek refuge in the Lord of mankind.'
interpretation: This verse opens Surah An-Nas, the final chapter of the Qur'an, and establishes the foundation for the entire surah's protective supplication. By commanding the Prophet (and by extension every believer) to explicitly declare seeking refuge, Allah teaches that true protection from harm—especially spiritual and psychological harm—must be sought through conscious, verbal affirmation of dependence on God. The specific designation 'Lord of mankind' (Rabb an-Nas) is significant: rather than invoking a general divine name, it emphasizes Allah's particular sovereignty, nurturing, and sustaining relationship with humanity specifically. This sets up the logical framework for the rest of the surah, which will identify Allah also as 'King of mankind' and 'God of mankind' before naming the specific threat (the whisperings of the retreating whisperer, Satan). The threefold invocation of lordship, kingship, and divinity over humanity before mentioning the enemy establishes a hierarchy of power—reminding the supplicant that no matter how insidious or persistent the whispered temptation or evil suggestion, it operates only within the dominion of One who is simultaneously the nurturer, sovereign ruler, and deity of all people. The verse thus teaches that refuge is not sought in amulets, rituals, or human protection, but in direct, personal address to God through humble, repeated verbal acknowledgment of one's vulnerability and God's absolute authority over the human condition.

translation: The King of mankind.
interpretation: This phrase, from Surah An-Nas, identifies Allah as the sovereign Ruler and absolute Authority over all of humanity. It is the second of three attributes mentioned in succession (King, God, and the One sought for refuge) that together establish the totality of Allah's dominion—His kingship signifies ownership and governance over human affairs, distinguishing His rule from any earthly king whose authority is limited and temporary. This sets the foundation for seeking refuge in Him from whispered evil, as the One who possesses complete sovereignty is uniquely capable of granting true protection.

translation: The God of mankind.
interpretation: This phrase is the concluding verse of Surah An-Nas, the final chapter of the Qur'an. It forms part of a progressive series of three descriptions of God introduced in this surah—Lord of mankind, King of mankind, and God of mankind—each emphasizing a different aspect of divine sovereignty. 'Ilah' (God) signifies the only true object of worship, affirming that God alone deserves worship and devotion, in contrast to any false deities people might turn to. This verse, together with the preceding two, builds a comprehensive picture of God's relationship to humanity: He is their Sustainer and Nurturer (Lord), their ultimate Sovereign and Authority (King), and the sole rightful object of worship and reliance (God). The placement of this declaration at the end of the Qur'an, in a surah dealing with seeking refuge from whisperings of evil, underscores that true protection from spiritual harm comes from recognizing and submitting to God as the only one worthy of worship, whose authority and care encompass all of mankind without exception.

translation: From the evil of the whisperer who withdraws (slinks back and hides),
interpretation: This phrase is part of Surah An-Nas, the final chapter of the Qur'an, which is a seeking of refuge from the evil whisperings of Satan. The term 'al-waswas al-khannas' describes Satan's characteristic method of temptation: he whispers evil suggestions and doubts into the hearts of people, but he is described as 'khannas,' meaning one who withdraws, slinks away, or hides—particularly when a person remembers God. This suggests that Satan's influence is not overpowering but insidious and furtive, retreating whenever the heart turns to divine remembrance (dhikr), yet returning to whisper again when one is heedless. The verse teaches that the believer's defense against this constant, hidden psychological and spiritual assault lies in seeking refuge in God, acknowledging that only divine protection can ward off these subtle, recurring temptations that target the human heart and mind from within.

translation: Who whispers into the breasts (hearts) of mankind.
interpretation: This verse describes the method by which Satan (and by extension, the jinn and evil human tempters referenced in the surah) operates: not through overt force or visible coercion, but through subtle, insidious suggestion implanted directly into the human heart and mind. The 'whispering' (waswasah) represents the fleeting, seductive thoughts that tempt a person toward doubt, sin, despair, or wrongdoing, often so quietly that one may not even recognize their source. This verse underscores the internal nature of spiritual struggle—evil does not always come from external threats but can arise as intrusive thoughts within one's own consciousness. By identifying this whisperer explicitly, the surah equips the believer with the awareness needed to recognize such promptings for what they are, rather than internalizing them as one's own authentic will or identity. This recognition is itself the first step toward seeking refuge in God, as commanded in the earlier verses of this surah, since naming and identifying the source of temptation diminishes its power and encourages conscious resistance through remembrance and reliance on divine protection.

translation: From among the jinn and mankind.
interpretation: This is the concluding phrase of Surah An-Nas, the final chapter of the Qur'an. It completes the description of 'the whisperer who withdraws' (al-waswas al-khannas) mentioned earlier in the surah, clarifying that this source of evil whispering and temptation can come from two origins: jinn (unseen spiritual beings, including Satan) and humans themselves. This teaches that evil influence is not limited to supernatural temptation alone, but can also come from other people who whisper doubt, malice, or corruption into one's heart through gossip, manipulation, or bad counsel. The verse thus broadens the scope of spiritual vigilance required, reminding believers to seek refuge in God not only from unseen demonic suggestion but also from the harmful influence of other human beings who may act as agents of temptation and discord in one's life.
